</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.180.3" class="koboSpan">He
holds a PhD in economics, an MA in Development Economics and a BA in
economics.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">Professor Wayne K. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">Talley</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">Wayne K.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.182.2" class="koboSpan">Talley
is Professor of Economics at Old Dominion University, Norfolk, Virginia,
where he is the Executive Director of the Maritime Institute and holds
the designations of Eminent Scholar and the Frederick W.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.182.3" class="koboSpan">Beazley
Professor of Economics. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.182.4"
class="koboSpan">He is an internationally recognised transportation
economist, having held visiting international academic positions at the
University of Oxford (England), University of Sydney (Australia), City
University London (United Kingdom), University of Antwerp (Belgium) and
University of Wollongong (Australia) and visiting US positions at the
Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (Woods Hole, Massachusetts),
Transportation Systems Center, US Department of Transportation
(Cambridge MA), Interstate Commerce Commission (Washington DC) and the
National Aeronautics and Space Administration (Langley, Virginia).
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.182.5" class="koboSpan">He is
the Editor-in-Chief of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and
Transportation
Review</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan"> and deputy Editor-in-Chief of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan">Asian Journal of Shipping and
Logistics</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.186.2"
class="koboSpan">His 2009 book,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan">Port
Economics</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan">, is the first textbook in this area.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">Professor Michael Tamvakis</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">Michael
Tamvakis trained as an economist at the Athens University of Economics
and Business in Greece. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.190.2"
class="koboSpan">He then joined the International Centre for Shipping,
Trade and Finance at the (then) City University Business School; first
as a student on its MSc programme, and then as a member of its academic
staff. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.190.3"
class="koboSpan">He received his PhD from City and is currently
Professor of Commodity Economics and Finance at Cass Business School,
City University London. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.190.4"
class="koboSpan">He lectures in international commodity trade, commodity
risk management and shipping economics.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.190.5" class="koboSpan">His
research interests are in the areas of commodity economics, energy
derivatives and shipping economics.</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_page_xxvii"></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">He has published in academic journals such as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan">Energy Economics, Energy Policy, Journal of Alternative
Investments, Journal of Derivatives, Logistics and Transportation
Review</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime Policy and
Management</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.196.1" class="koboSpan">Professor Ulla Tapaninen</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">Ulla Tapaninen
PhD is a professor of Maritime Logistics at the Centre for Maritime
Studies (CMS), University of Turku.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.197.2" class="koboSpan">She
received her PhD in 1997 in logistics modelling.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.197.3" class="koboSpan">She has
worked for 10 years as a development manager and environmental manager
in a large Finnish RoRo-shipping company.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.197.4" class="koboSpan">Since
2006 she has been in charge of maritime logistics research at the CMS.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.197.5" class="koboSpan">Since
1992, she has worked as a researcher, project director and board member
in dozens of projects in the areas of maritime and cross-border
transportation, logistics information handling and maritime safety and
environment.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">Associate Professor Helen Thanopoulou</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">Helen A.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.2"
class="koboSpan">Thanopoulou studied at the University of Athens and
University of Paris (Panthéon-Sorbonne).
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.3" class="koboSpan">She
holds a Doctorate in Maritime Studies from the University of Piraeus
where she taught briefly.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.4" class="koboSpan">She
spent eight years in Wales, as Lecturer and later Senior Lecturer at
Cardiff University serving, after 1999, as a Director of
shipping-related postgraduate courses.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.5" class="koboSpan">She
returned to Greece in 2004 taking an Assistant Professor’s post at the
University of the Aegean, in the Department of Shipping, Trade and
Transport on Chios island.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.6" class="koboSpan">She has
published on shipping-related subjects including crises,
competitiveness, investment patterns, liner alliances and ports and
maritime innovation. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.7"
class="koboSpan">In 2008, in Dalian, she was elected Council member of
the International Association of Maritime Economists (IAME).
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.8" class="koboSpan">She is
serving her second term as Council member of the Hellenic Association of
Maritime Economists (ENOE).
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.199.9" class="koboSpan">She has
been a Guest Editor and member of Editorial Boards, currently of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan">Journal of Shipping, Trade and
Transport</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.201.2"
class="koboSpan">She is a regular guest lecturer at academic
institutions in Greece and abroad.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">Dr Ioannis Theotokas</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">Ioannis
Theotokas is Associate Professor at the Department of Shipping, Trade
and Transport of the University of the Aegean.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.203.2" class="koboSpan">He has
a background of economics specialising in Shipping Management.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.203.3" class="koboSpan">He
received his PhD from the University of Piraeus (1997).
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.203.4" class="koboSpan">His
research interests include topics in Management, Human Resource
Management and Strategic Management applied to shipping business.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.203.5" class="koboSpan">He has
participated as principal researcher in research projects and
consultancy studies. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.203.6"
class="koboSpan">He is the co-author (with G.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.203.7"
class="koboSpan">Harlaftis) of the book
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan">Leadership in World Shipping.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">Greek
Family Firms in International
Business</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2009).
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.205.2" class="koboSpan">He has
published 23 papers in academic journals and books and has presented
over 25 peer-reviewed papers at international scientific
conferences.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">Professor Eddy van Devoorde</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">Eddy Van de
Voorde is Full Professor at the University of Antwerp, Faculty of
Applied Economics. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.207.2"
class="koboSpan">His activities are situated in Maritime Economics, Port
Economics, Air Transport and Logistics.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.207.3" class="koboSpan">He is
in charge of many new research projects, financed by various Belgian and
international governments and private organisations.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.207.4" class="koboSpan">Much of
his research, particularly in the field of modelling freight transport,
results in a long list of
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_page_xxviii"></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan">publications in important journals.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.208.2"
class="koboSpan">Recently, he was co-author of various standard-works in
the field of transport economics and models.</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">He is also a
professor at the University of Ghent and at the Technical University of
Delft, and he is visiting professor at different foreign universities,
such as Lisbon, Bari, London and MIT (Cambridge, Boston).
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.209.2" class="koboSpan">In the
past years he fulfilled different functions in international scientific
associations, such as being the vice-chair of the International
Association of Maritime Economists (IAME), vice-chair of the scientific
committee of the World Conference on Transport Research Society (WCTRS)
and vice-chair of the Benelux Interuniversity Association of Transport
Economists (BIVEC). </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.209.3"
class="koboSpan">He is also a member of a scientific editorial staff of
seven international journals, such as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime Policy and
Management</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan">Transport
Policy</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan">Transportation
Research-E</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan">, and the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan">International Journal of Transport
Economics</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.218.1" class="koboSpan">In 2005, he
was awarded in Genoa a prestigious international prize, the Premio
Internationale delle Communicazioni “Cristoforo Colombo”, for his
scientific research in the field of Maritime Economics.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">Dr Andreas Vergottis</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">Andreas
Vergottis was awarded his MSc Econometrics from the London School of
Economics in 1984 and his PhD in Business Administration from City
University Business School in 1988.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.220.2" class="koboSpan">In 1989
he joined Tufton Oceanic Ltd as shipping analyst, responsible for
screening various projects involving debt, mezzanine and equity
financing of shipping transactions.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.220.3" class="koboSpan">In 1996
he was recruited by Warburg (subsequently acquired by UBS) as sector
coordinator for global shipping analysis.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.220.4" class="koboSpan">In
addition to regular research coverage on 30 listed shipping companies,
he participated in several IPO and M&A transactions within the shipping
industry. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.220.5"
class="koboSpan">In 2002 he rejoined Tufton Oceanic Ltd as Head of
Research. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.220.6"
class="koboSpan">He assisted in launching the Oceanic Hedge Fund with
\$5m starting capital which currently has grown to \$1.8bn assets under
management. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.220.7"
class="koboSpan">He is presently based in Hong Kong, where Tufton
Oceanic Ltd have recently opened a new representative office.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.220.8" class="koboSpan">He is a
visiting professor at Cass Business School, City University
London.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">Mr Kurt J. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.221.2" class="koboSpan">Vermeulen</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">Kurt Vermeulen
is a Visiting Lecturer on Shipping Strategy at Cass Business School,
City University London. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.2"
class="koboSpan">He provides consultancy services in this area.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.3"
class="koboSpan">Assignments focus on multidisciplinary approaches
involving issues pertaining to strategy, business intelligence,
competitive intelligence and corporate finance.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.4" class="koboSpan">Prior
to this, Kurt was a Vice President in Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A) at a
predecessor bank of JP Morgan Chase.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.5" class="koboSpan">His
transactional experience focused on the transport, chemicals and
financial services industries.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.6" class="koboSpan">He was
a Guest Lecturer on M&A to MSc Shipping, Trade & Finance students at
Cass Business School. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.7"
class="koboSpan">Previous to that, Kurt worked as a solicitor on
corporate and commercial law matters.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.8" class="koboSpan">He has
a Lic. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.9"
class="koboSpan">Iuris. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.222.10"
class="koboSpan">(LLM)</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan"> cum
laude</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan"> in commercial and financial law from the University of
Gent (Belgium) and also studied German and EU competition law
(Wettbewerbsrecht, Kartellrecht) and law and economics at the Law
Faculties of the University Hamburg (Germany) and the University
Osnabrück (Germany). </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.224.2"
class="koboSpan">He subsequently obtained, whilst employed, a Spec.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.224.3" class="koboSpan">Lic.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.224.4" class="koboSpan">(MSc)
Port & Marine Sciences
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan">magna cum
laude</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan"> from the University of Gent, a MA in Eastern European
Studies
</span><span class="italic"><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan">cum
laude</span></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan"> from the University of Gent and a MSc in Shipping,
Trade and Finance from Cass Business School.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.228.2" class="koboSpan">He is a
member of the Society of Competitive Intelligence Professionals
(SCIP).</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_page_xxix"></span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">Dr Michalis Voutsinas</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">Michalis
Voutsinas works as an independent researcher with particular interests
in shipping financial history and risk management of shipping companies.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.230.2" class="koboSpan">He was
awarded with an MSc in Shipping, Trade and Finance from Cass Business
School, City University London, an MSc in Applied Economics and Finance
from Athens University of Economics and Business and a BSc in Economics
from the same institution.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.230.3"
class="koboSpan">Michalis was honoured with a prize, from Athens
University of Economics and Business and a scholarship from Greek
Shipowners’ Association.</span>

## <span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">Professor Manered Zachcial</span>

<span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">Manfred
Zachcial belongs to the Board of Directors of the Institute of Shipping
Economics and Logistics (ISL), Bremen, and has a chair of economics and
statistics at Bremen University.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.232.2" class="koboSpan">Manfred
Zachcial has been working on economics, land and maritime transport
projects since 1972. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.232.3"
class="koboSpan">He is a leading authority on shipping economics,
statistics, transport planning, logistics and maritime information
systems. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.232.4"
class="koboSpan">In addition to his academic responsibilities, Professor
Zachcial advises governments and international agencies on
transportation strategies, port and shipping, and on the feasibility of
various transport infrastructure developments.
</span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.232.5" class="koboSpan">His
research activities have resulted in numerous published works on
modelling in both land and maritime transport, including transhipments
at European sea ports. </span><span id="frontmatter3.xhtml_kobo.232.6"
class="koboSpan">One of his major research activities is the analysis
and forecast of world container shipping along the whole transport
chains including hinterland transports and their determinants.</span>

</div>

</div>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Maritime Business During the Twentieth Century: Continuity and Change</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0058)

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Gelina</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Harlaftis</span></span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0001" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0001"><span

class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">and
</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Ioannis</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">Theotokas</span></span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0002" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0002"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a>

## <span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">The historical process
is dynamic, and the changes that occurred during the course of world
shipping in the past century, embedded some of the structures of the
nineteenth century. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.11.2"
class="koboSpan">The methodological tools of a historian and an
economist will be used in this chapter, tracing continuity and change in
the twentieth century shipping by examining maritime business at a
macro-and micro level. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.11.3"
class="koboSpan">At the core of the analysis lies the shipping firm, the
micro-level, which helps us understand the changes in world shipping,
the macro-level.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">The shipping firm
functions in a specific market, and the shipping market can only be
understood as an international market, in a multiethnic environment.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">The first part
of this chapter follows the developments in world shipping, analysing
briefly the main fleets, the routes and cargoes carried, the ships and
the main technological innovations.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">The second part
provides an insight on the main structural changes in the shipping
markets by focusing on the division of liner and tramp shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.12.4" class="koboSpan">The third part
reveals from inside the shipowning structure and its changes in time in
the main twentieth century fleets: the British, the Norwegians, the
Greeks and the Japanese; it is remarkable how similar their organisation
and structure proves to
be.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0003" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0003"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan"> Maritime business has always been an internationalised
business. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">In the
last five centuries of capitalist development, European colonial
expansion was only made possible with the sea and ships; the sea being
but a route of communication and strength rather than of isolation and
weakness. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.14.3" class="koboSpan">Wasn’t
it Sir Walter Raleigh in the late sixteenth century, one of Elizabeth’s
main consultants who had set some of the first rules for the British
expansion? </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.14.4" class="koboSpan">“He
who commands the sea commands the trade routes of the world.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.14.5" class="koboSpan">He who commands
the trade routes, commands the trade.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.14.6" class="koboSpan">He who commands
the trade, commands the riches of the world, and hence the world
itself.” </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.14.7" class="koboSpan">The
real truths are tested in history and time.</span>

## <span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_4"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Developments in World Shipping</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">There were two main
developments in the nineteenth century that pre-determined the path of
the world economies: an incredible industrialisation of the West and its
dominance in the rest of the world.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">During that
period the world witnessed an unprecedented boom in world exchange of
goods and services, an unprecedented boom of international sea-trade.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">The basis of the
world trade system of the twentieth century was consolidated in the
nineteenth century: it was the flow of industrial goods from Europe to
the rest of the world and the flow of raw materials to Europe from the
rest of the world. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.16.4"
class="koboSpan">In this way, deep-sea going trade became increasingly
dominated by a small number of bulk commodities in all the world’s
oceans and seas; in the last third of the nineteenth century, grain,
cotton and coal were the main bulk cargoes that filled the holds of the
world fleet. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.16.5" class="koboSpan">At
the same time, the transition from sail to steam, apart from increasing
the availability of cargo space at sea, caused a revolutionary decline
in freight rates, contributing further to the increase of international
sea-borne trade. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.16.6"
class="koboSpan">Europe, however, remained at the core of the world
sea-trade system: until the eve of the World War I, three quarters of
world exports in value and almost two thirds of world imports concerned
the old
continent.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0004" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0004"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">It does not come as a
surprise then, that European countries owned the largest part of the
ocean-going world fleet during this period.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">Due to
technological innovations, the international merchant fleet was able to
carry an increasing volume of cargoes between continents with greater
speed and lower cost. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.18.3"
class="koboSpan">By the turn of the twentieth century Great Britain was
still the undisputable world maritime power owning 45% of the world
fleet, followed by the United States, Germany, Norway, France and Japan,
(see
</span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fig0002" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0002"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.20.2"
class="koboSpan">Over 95% of the world fleet belonged to 15 countries
that formed the so-called “Atlantic economy”; what is today called the
“developed” nations of the OECD countries.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.20.3" class="koboSpan">Meanwhile, at
the rival Pacific Ocean, Japan was preparing to be the rising star of
world shipping in the twentieth century.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">Pax
Brittanica</span></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the incredible increase of world economic
prosperity of more than one hundred years closed abruptly with the
beginning of World War I. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.22.2"
class="koboSpan">The main cause was the conflict of the big industrial
European nations for the expansion of their economic and political
influence in the non-European world.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.22.3" class="koboSpan">It was the
result of the competition of western European nations for new markets
and raw materials that determined the nineteenth century and peaked in
the beginning of the twentieth century as the influence of the
industrialisation of western European nations became more distinct.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.22.4" class="koboSpan">At the beginning
of the twentieth century almost all of Asia and Africa were in one way
or another under European colonial control.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">The factors that
created the international economy of the nineteenth century proved
detrimental during the two destructive world wars of the twentieth
century by multiplying their effects.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">Firstly, the
formation of gigantic national enterprises in Europe and the United
States and their concentration in vast industrial complexes with
continuous amalgamations of small and medium companies resulted in an
exponential increase of world production.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.23.3" class="koboSpan">Second, the
search for markets beyond Europe that would absorb the excessive
industrial production, resulted in the fierce competition of British,
German, French and American capital in international capital investments
worldwide. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.23.4" class="koboSpan">The
result was the creation of multinational companies and banks that led to
the development of monopolies on a national and international level.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.23.5" class="koboSpan">Within this
framework, the great expansion of the United States and German fleets
took place, along with the multiple</span>

<div id="Ch01.xhtml_fig0002" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_5"></span>[](#Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0002)

[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00002.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0002)

</div>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">mergers and
acquisitions in the northern European liner shipping business and the
gradual destruction of small tramp shipping companies, particularly in
Great Britain.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">The interwar economy
never recovered from the shock of World War I that influenced the whole
structure of the international economy resulting in the worst economic
crisis that the industrial world had seen in 1929.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.26.2" class="koboSpan">During the
interwar period world shipping faced severe problems stemming from a
contracting world sea-trade, decreasing world immigration and increasing
protectionism. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.26.3"
class="koboSpan">The economic crisis did not affect the main national
fleets in the same way. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.26.4"
class="koboSpan">The impact was particularly felt in Britain.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.26.5" class="koboSpan">This is the
period of the economic downhill of mighty old Albion.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.26.6" class="koboSpan">It was World War
I that weakened Britain and allowed competitors to challenge its
maritime hegemony. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.26.7"
class="koboSpan">The withdrawal of British ships from trades not
directly related to the Allied Cause opened the Pacific trades to the
Japanese. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.26.8"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, both Norway and Greece were neutrals,
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_6"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan">which meant that their fleets were able to profit from
high wartime freight rates (Greece entered the war in 1917).
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">Norwegian and
Greek ships were able to trade at market rates for three years while
most of the British fleet was requisitioned and forced to work for low,
fixed remunerations. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.27.3"
class="koboSpan">Freight rates in the free market remained high until
1920, after which they plummeted; while there was a brief recovery in
the mid-1920s, the nadir was reached in the early 1930s.</span>

[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_fig0002)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan"> records the development of the world fleets of the
main maritime nations from 1914 to 1937.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.29.2" class="koboSpan">During this
period the world fleet increased at one third of its prewar size.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.29.3" class="koboSpan">The British
fleet remained at the same level with a slight decrease of its
registered tonnage, but its percentage of the ownership of the world
fleet decreased from 43% to 31% due to the increase of the fleets of
other nations. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.29.4"
class="koboSpan">The interwar period was characterised by the
unsuccessful attempt of the United States to keep a large national fleet
with large and costly subsidies to shipping entrepreneurs.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.29.5" class="koboSpan">Most of the
increase of the world fleet in the interwar period apart from the US was
due to the Japanese, the Norwegians and the Greeks, who proved to be the
owners of the most dynamic fleets of the century.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.29.6" class="koboSpan">Their growth was
interconnected with the carriage of energy sources.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.29.7" class="koboSpan">The most
important change in the world trade of the interwar period was the
gradual decrease of the coal trade and the growing importance of
oil.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">The main coal producer
(and exporter) in 1900 was the UK, with 225 million metric tons or 51%
of Europe’s production. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.30.2"
class="koboSpan">By 1937 Britain was still Europe’s main producing
country with 42% of European output.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.30.3" class="koboSpan">In 1870 the
production of oil was less than 1 million tons and in 1900 oil was still
an insignificant source of energy; world production of 20 million tons
met only 2.5% of world energy consumption.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.30.4" class="koboSpan">Because
production was so limited there was little need for specialised vessels;
tankers, mostly owned by Europeans, accounted for a tiny 1.5% of world
merchant tonnage. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.30.5"
class="koboSpan">But all this changed in the interwar period: by 1938
oil production had increased more than 15 times; it was 273 million tons
and accounted for 26% of world energy
consumption.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0005" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0005"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> The tanker fleet, had grown to 16% of world tonnage,
and although it was mostly state-owned, independent tanker owners
started to appear in the 1920s. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.32.2"
class="koboSpan">The largest independent owners of the interwar period
were the
Norwegians.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0006" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0006"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">Technological
innovations continued in the twentieth century; the choices and
exploitation of technological advances by shipping entrepreneurs
determined the path of world shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.2" class="koboSpan">The first half
of the twentieth century was characterised on the one hand by the use of
diesel engines and the replacement of steam engines and on the other, by
the massive standard shipbuilding projects during the two world wars.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.3" class="koboSpan">Diesel engines
that appeared in 1890 were only used in a more massive scale on motor
ships during the interwar period particularly in Germany and the
Scandinavian countries; the cost of fuel being 30% to 50% lower than
that of the steam engines. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.4"
class="koboSpan">Standardisation of ship types and shipbuilding
programmes were introduced in World War I when Germans sunk the allied
fleets in an unprecedented submarine war.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.5" class="koboSpan">The world had
not yet realised what industrialisation and massive production of
weapons for destruction could do. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.6"
class="koboSpan">The convoy system had been abandoned and naval
battleships with their complex weapons were ready to confront the enemy.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.7" class="koboSpan">But it was the
allied merchant steamships that were the artery of the war, transporting
war supplies. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.8"
class="koboSpan">And this armless merchant fleet became an easy target
to the new menace of the seas: the German submarines.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.34.9" class="koboSpan">From 1914 to
1918, 5,861 ships or 50% of the allied fleet was sunk.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">Replacement of the
sunken fleet took place between 1918 to 1921 in US and British
shipyards. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">It
was the first time that standard types of cargo ships, the “standards”
as
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_7"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">they came to be called, were built on a large scale.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.36.2" class="koboSpan">The “standard”
ships became the main type of cargo ship during the interwar period;
they were steamships of 5,500 grt.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.36.3" class="koboSpan">It was these
“standard” ships that Greeks, Japanese and Norwegian tramp operators
purchased </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">en masse</span></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan"> from the British second hand market and expanded their
fleets amongst the world economic crises.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.38.2" class="koboSpan">For similar
reasons during World War II the United States and Canada launched the
most massive shipbuilding programmes the world had known, using new and
far quicker methods of building ships: welding.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.38.3" class="koboSpan">During four
years they managed to build 3,000 ships, the well-known Liberty ships,
that formed the standard dry-bulk cargo vessel for the next 25
years.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0007" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0007"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan"> Greek, Norwegian, British and Japanese tramp operators
all came to own Liberty ships, in one way or another up to the late
1960s.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">The second half of the
twentieth century was characterised by an incredible increase of world
trade that towards the end of the century was described as the
globalisation of the world economy.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.2" class="koboSpan">The period of
acceleration was up to 1970s; world trade from about 500 million metric
tons in the 1940s climbed up to more than three billion metric tons in
the mid-1970s. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.3"
class="koboSpan">If the history of world maritime transport in the first
half of the twentieth century was written by coal and tramp ships, in
the second half the main players were oil and tankers.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.4" class="koboSpan">During this
period, sea-trade was divided into two categories: liquid and dry cargo.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.5" class="koboSpan">Almost 60% of
the exponential growth of world sea trade was due to the incredible
growth of the carriage of liquid cargo at sea, oil and oil products.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.6" class="koboSpan">There was also
impressive growth in the five main bulk cargoes: ore, bauxite, coal,
phosphates and grain. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.7"
class="koboSpan">To carry the enormous volumes required to feed the
industries of the West and East Asia, the size of ships carrying liquid
and dry cargoes had to be increased.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.8" class="koboSpan">The second half
of the twentieth century was characterised by the gigantic sizes of
ships and their specialisation according to the type of cargoes.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.9" class="koboSpan">The last third
of the century was marked by the introduction of container ships.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.41.10" class="koboSpan">The new “ugly”
ships revolutionised the transport system for industrial goods.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Up to the 1960s the
main carriers of the world fleet remained the same with the US and
Britain continuing to hold their decreasing shares in world shipping,
followed by the continually rising Greece, Japan and Norway
(</span>[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_fig0002)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.44.2"
class="koboSpan">Flags of convenience were used informally by all
maritime nations but in the immediate post-war years more extensively by
Greek and American shipowners. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.44.3"
class="koboSpan">Flags of convenience that were later to be called open
registries became a key manifestation of the American maritime policy
and a determining feature of post war shipping that guaranteed
economical bulk
shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0008" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0008"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan"> By using flags of convenience, shipowners of
traditional maritime countries were able to maintain control of their
fleets benefiting from low cost labour.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.46.2" class="koboSpan">Sletmo relates
the third wave of shipping with the transnationalisation of shipping
through flagging out and dependence upon manpower from low-cost
countries.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0009" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0009"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan"> After the repetitive freight rates crises of the 1980s
flag of convenience were extensively used by all western and eastern
maritime nations.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">The 1970s marked a new
era: this period was characterised by the final loss of the
pre-dominance of European maritime nations, with the exception of the
Greeks that continue to keep their first position to the present day,
and of the Norwegians that despite the great slump of the 1980s, kept
their share of the market in the 1990s.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">During the last
third of the twentieth century the increase of the size of the world
fleet shipping continued but slowed down.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.49.3" class="koboSpan">The United
States has kept, mostly under flags of convenience, a much lower
percentage, while Japan remains steadily in the second position
(</span>[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_fig0002)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.51.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.51.2"
class="koboSpan">The rise of new maritime nations from Asia was evident;
by 1992
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_8"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan">China owned more tonnage than Great Britain, while
South Korea was close. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.52.2"
class="koboSpan">The world division of labour in world shipping had
changed
dramatically.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0010" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0010"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan"> The booming markets of the period 2004–2008
contributed to the sharp increase in the world fleet, and to the slight
change in the hierarchy of world maritime powers.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">Great Britain
and Norway decreased their fleet and share in the world shipping, while
Greece and Japan followed the opposite direction and increased both
their tonnage and share. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.54.3"
class="koboSpan">Germany made a very impressive comeback rapidly
increasing its tonnage, especially of containerships.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.54.4" class="koboSpan">A remarkable
change was that of China. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.54.5"
class="koboSpan">Being the driving force of the world economy, China is
continually developing its fleet. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.54.6"
class="koboSpan">The conditions that prevail in the world shipping and
shipbuilding markets after the collapse of the freight markets in 2008,
make safe the forecast that sooner or later, China will become the
driving force in world shipping.</span>

## <span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping Markets</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">Following world
shipping developments, the shipping markets had taken its twentieth
century form since the last third of the nineteenth century.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">Before the 1870s
the shipping market was unified. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.56.3"
class="koboSpan">By the last third of the nineteenth century the
distinction of the shipping market into two categories, liner and tramp
shipping started gradually to adapt.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.56.4" class="koboSpan">Liner ships
carried general cargoes (finished or semi-finished manufactured goods)
and tramp shipping carried bulk cargoes (like coal, ore, grain,
fertilisers, etc.) For the next 100 years, until the 1970s, liner and
tramp shipping markets continued more or less on the same lines.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.56.5" class="koboSpan">This one century
of shipping operations can be distinguished into two sub-periods
(</span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_cap_lbl0001" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0001"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">During the first
period, from the 1870s to the 1940s, the cargoes carried by liner and
tramp shipping were not always clearly defined: liner ships could carry
tramp cargoes and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan">vice-versa</span></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.61.2"
class="koboSpan">Although there was a substitution between the two
distinct markets, the main structures of each one were diametrically
different: oligopoly and protectionism for the liner market with the
formation of the shipping cartels from the 1880s, the conferences, and
almost perfect competition for tramp ships.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">The unprecedented
increase of world production and trade in the first post-World War II
era brought more distinct changes in the structure of the markets that
led to a gradual decrease of substitution between the
markets.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0011" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0011"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan"> In tramp/bulk shipping, the introduction of new liquid
bulk cargoes on a massive scale, like oil, and of the main dry bulk
cargoes as mentioned above (coal, ore, fertilisers and grain) led to the
creation of specialised bulk markets and to the building of ships to
carry specific cargoes (</span>[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_cap_lbl0001)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.66.2"
class="koboSpan">The liner market continued along the same lines of
oligopoly but witnessed increased competition into their protected
markets from competitors from developing and socialist countries.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">The 1970s were the
landmark decade for the liner industry; unitisation of the cargoes,
called also containerisation, had been introduced during the 1960s but
became widespread during the 1970s, brought a revolution in the
transport of liner cargoes
(</span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_cap_lbl0002" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0002"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan">).While in 1970 the world container fleet was of
500,000 TEU by 1980 this had increased by more than six times to reach
3,150,000
TEU.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0012" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0012"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan"> The new organisation of liner shipping that demanded
excessive investments in infrastructure (terminals, cargo handling
facilities, ships, equipment and agencies), led to an increase in ship
and port productivity, an increase in ship
size,</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0013" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0013"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan"> and economies of scale and decrease of transport
cost.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0014" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0014"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>

<div id="Ch01.xhtml_fig0003" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00003.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Shipping markets, 1870s–1970s" /></span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_9"></span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0001" id="Ch01.xhtml_cap_lbl0001"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">
Shipping markets, 1870s–1970s</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch01.xhtml_fig0004" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00004.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Shipping markets, 1970s–2000s" /></span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_10"></span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0002" id="Ch01.xhtml_cap_lbl0002"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">
Shipping markets, 1970s–2000s</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_11"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">Containerisation included radically new designs for
vessels and cargo-handling facilities, global door-to-door traffic,
early use of information technology, and structural change of the
industry through the formation of consortia, alliances and international
mega-margers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0015" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0015"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan"> The above led to a total transformation of the liner
shipping companies that became the archetype of a globalised
multinational shipping company. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">The high capital investments required to operate a
unitized general cargo transport system led to consolidation in liner
shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0016" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0016"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan"> This transformation was further provoked by the
continuous trend to globalisation.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.85.2" class="koboSpan">Liner companies
ought to serve the transport needs of their customer on a global basis.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.85.3" class="koboSpan">Although
consolidation in liner shipping was increasing from the 1970s, during
the 1990s it progressed faster. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.85.4"
class="koboSpan">Liner companies were enforced to establish global
networks in order to meet their customers’ needs.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.85.5" class="koboSpan">The enlargement
of the companies’ size through mergers and acquisitions and the
formation of global alliances were the necessary steps toward this.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.85.6" class="koboSpan">Strategic
alliances between competitors have become the dominant form of
cooperation in liner
shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0017" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0017"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan"> Alliances allow competing liner operators to exploit
economies of scope and to offer to shippers global geographical
coverage.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0018" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0018"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan"> It has been stated that increased complexity and
intra-alliance competition among partners undermine the stability of
strategic
alliances.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0019" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0019"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
class="koboSpan"> Indeed, many changes have been noted over the years.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">For example, the
Grand Alliance in 1995 had as members the Hapag Lloyd, NYK, NOL, and
P&O. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.91.3" class="koboSpan">A few years
later MISC entered the alliance while NOL left to follow the New World
Alliance. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.91.4"
class="koboSpan">Recently MISC withdraw and today the alliance includes
the Hapag-Lloyd, the NYK and the OOCL, the seventh, ninth and twelfth
biggest liner
companies.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0020" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0020"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">In parallel, strategies
of internal development, merger and acquisitions have led to an increase
in the concentration of the supply of liner services.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">The combined
market share of the top four liner companies increased by 7% in a period
of three years, i.e. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.93.3"
class="koboSpan">from 31% in 2004 to 38.4% in 2007, while the
Herfindahl—Hirschmann Index of the top four players (HHI–4) increased by
182%, from 268 in 2004 to 449 in
2007.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0021" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0021"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">For example, the
biggest liner shipping company in the world, the Danish Maersk, which
has a market share of 15%, operates more than 500 containerships ((two
millions TEU) of which 211 are owned by the company) and more than 50
terminals worldwide, while its network includes more than 150 local
offices worldwide. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.95.2"
class="koboSpan">In 1999 Maersk acquired Sealand, the biggest American
liner shipping company, the first company in the world to introduce
innovative container technology, while in 2005 it acquired P&O Nedlloyd,
then the third biggest liner company.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.95.3" class="koboSpan">It is thus
evident that such a multinational company is a global network by itself
and offers global services to its clients.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.95.4" class="koboSpan">This kind of
development resulted in a total re-structuring in the port systems of
the various regions and created the need for minor shipping lines to
serve regional transport needs or offer feeder services for global liner
companies. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.95.5" class="koboSpan">The
major liner companies approach main international ports, from which
minor shipping lines distribute the products to regional ports through
the so-called feedering
services.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0022" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0022"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan"> These two groups of companies, the big and minor
container companies are not in competition with each other, rather they
complement each other.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">On the contrary, the
development of tramp shipping did not involve such innovative
technological developments and no dramatic changes took place in the
organisation and structure of markets.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">The general
pattern has not changed over the last 140 years.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.98.3" class="koboSpan">However, since
the 1970s we are not talking of tramp shipping, but of bulk shipping
since the type of ship does not characterise the market anymore, but
instead the cargoes that are transported.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.98.4" class="koboSpan">Four main
categories of bulk cargo are
distinguished:</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0023" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0023"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan"> the liquid
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_12"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan">bulk (crude oil, oil products and liquid chemicals),
the five major bulk (iron ore, grain, coal, phosphates and bauxite),
minor bulk (steel products, cement, sugar forest products etc) and
specialist bulk cargoes with specific handling or storage requirements
(motor vehicles, refrigerated cargo, special cargoes).
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.101.2" class="koboSpan">Gradually need
adapted to demand, and the “tramp” ship was replaced by specialised
ships that were built according to the bulk cargoes and the specialised
bulk shipping markets; reefer ships for the refrigerated cargo, chemical
tankers for chemical gases, lpg and lng for liquefied petroleum and
natural gas, heavy lift vessels for specific cargoes etc.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">Globalised bulk
shipping, even to the present day, is an industry based on trust.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">Companies form
networks of collaborating competitors on the basis of common national
cultures of traditional maritime nations such as Britain, Greece, Norway
and Japan (</span>[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_cap_lbl0002)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.104.2"
class="koboSpan">Even members of the same network compete with each
other and competitiveness is based on cost.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.104.3" class="koboSpan">During the
twentieth century size did not play an important role in the
competitiveness of the
company.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0024" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0024"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"> Bulk shipping consists of companies of various sizes –
these vary from large companies of more than 50 large ships to
single-ship companies that directly compete with each other.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">For example in
1970, the Greek-owned shipping company of Stavros Niarchos and the
Norwegian shipping company of Wilhem Wilhelmsen which operated more than
60 ships co-existed and competed with the British Turnballs that
operated five ships and the various Bergen-based and Piraeus-based small
companies that operated ships of similar characteristics.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">Tramp shipping
was mainly formed by groups of family enterprises which retained many
characteristics of a multinational
enterprise.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0025" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0025"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan"> No matter what the size of these enterprises, their
organisation, structure and strategies had a lot in
common.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0026" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0026"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping Companies</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">Overall analysis of
the main trends in world shipping fleets and their markets throughout
the twentieth century does not provide us with an understanding of the
structure of the maritime industry.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.111.2" class="koboSpan">The core of the
economy is the firm; the core of the maritime industry is the shipping
company. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.111.3" class="koboSpan">In
this section we will briefly review the actual players, the shipping
companies of the four main twentieth century nations: the British, the
Norwegians, the Greeks and the Japanese.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.111.4" class="koboSpan">In the first
three European nations, we can distinguish similar patterns of
organisation and structure in the shipping companies worldwide that
concerned both liner and tramp shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.111.5" class="koboSpan">First an
important aspect of shipping companies was their connection with a
specific home port; second was the ownership and management of the
company by distinct families for multiple generations; third was the use
of a regional network for drawing investment funds, and fourth was the
existence of an international network of overseas agencies that
collaborated closely with trading houses on a particular oceanic region,
or on a particular commodity
trade.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0027" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0027"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 The British</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">British commercial and
shipping business in the nineteenth century developed along the lines of
its colonial empire, and the inter-Empire and British external trade
that was operated by close-knit global business networks.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.114.2" class="koboSpan">At the
beginning of the twentieth century British shipping was world’s largest
fleet owning 40% of the world’s tonnage, followed by Germany which owned
one-fourth of its size. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.114.3"
class="koboSpan">In 1918 a government
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_13"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan">committee reported that “at the outbreak of war, the
British Mercantile Marine was the largest, the most up-to-date and the
most efficient of all the merchant navies of the
world”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0028" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0028"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan"> The fleet was particularly hit during the interwar
period, where it saw some of its leading shipping companies like the
Royal Mail disintegrate and some of its main tramp-shipping owners leave
the stage. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">It
has been argued that British performance has been affected by the
“unfair competition” of countries that subsidised their liner fleets
like France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, or the
low-cost tramp operators like the Greeks that took large portions of its
share in the Atlantic trade, and by the reluctance of British shipowners
to invest in the new technology of diesel engines and tankers during the
interwar
period.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0029" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0029"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">World War II did not
really affect the British share in world shipping which by 1948 had
reached its pre-war level. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.119.2"
class="koboSpan">Until 1967, Britain despite its decreasing share,
remained world’s maritime leader and UK fleet continued to grow until
1975. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.119.3" class="koboSpan">Part of
its 1975 tonnage, however, the year when the British fleet reached its
peak, was foreign-owned and this “masked the extent to which British
interest in merchant shipping had already declined before the downward
plunge after
1975”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0030" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0030"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan"> From 1975 to the beginning of the twenty-first century
there was a continuous decrease in the UK register due to the
“flagging-out” of the British-owned fleet.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.121.2" class="koboSpan">By 2007 British
shipping under all flags was in tenth position with only 2.35% of world
tonnage.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0031" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0031"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">The regional dimension
in maritime Britain has played an important role in the organisation of
both tramp and liner business. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.123.2"
class="koboSpan">The main poles of liner shipping have traditionally
been Liverpool and London followed by Glasgow and Hull.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.123.3" class="koboSpan">The newly
emerging liner shipping companies from the mid-nineteenth century
onwards were very strongly connected with a big home port, like London,
Liverpool, Glasgow and Hull, where strong shipping elites were
formed.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0032" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0032"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan"> For example, the Peninsular and Oriental (P&O), based
in London, was established by Wilcox and Anderson in 1837 and
specialised in trade with India and Australia; the Cunard Company,
established by Samuel Cunard, Burns and the MacIvers in 1839 specialised
in the north Atlantic; the British India (BI) shipping company, based in
Glasgow, was established in 1856 by the MacKinnon shipping group and
specialised in the Indian ocean; the Ocean Steam Ship Company known as
the Blue Funnel Line, based in Liverpool, was established by the Holt
family in 1865 and specialised in trade with southeastern Asia.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">The
Union-Castle Line, was established in the 1850s and run by Donald
Currie, specialised in South Africa by the 1870s, the Elder-Dempster
based in Liverpool, was formed by Alexander Elder and John Dempster in
1868 and specialised in African trade; Lleyland, Moss, McIver and
Papayanni, all based in Liverpool, were established in the 1840s and
1850s and were involved in the Mediterranean.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.125.3" class="koboSpan">Hull was the
home port of the Wilson Line, established by the Wilson family –
“Wilson’s are Hull and Hull is Wilson’s” –, that traded in all oceans
and
seas.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0033" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0033"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan"> In 1910 there were 65 liner companies that owned 45%
of the British fleet. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.127.2"
class="koboSpan">And all, during the previous 30 years, had organised
themselves in closed cartels of the sea, the conferences, according to
the oceanic region they traded, securing their share in the world
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0034" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0034"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">The five largest liner
companies in 1910 were British India, White Star Line, Blue Funnel Line,
P&O and Elder Dempster (see
</span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fig0005" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0005"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.131.2"
class="koboSpan">Low freight rates and a widespread depression in the
late 1910s led to intense competition and a wave of mergers that
produced giant lines in the five years before World War I.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.131.3" class="koboSpan">The most
notorious example is the Royal Mail Steam Packet Co that from 1903 to
1931 was led by Owen Philipps (later Lord Kylsant).
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.131.4" class="koboSpan">Within 30 years
Royal Mail reached its peak, owning 11% of British fleet, and its nadir
in 1931 when it was liquidified, producing a major crisis</span>

<div id="Ch01.xhtml_fig0005" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_14"></span>[](#Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0005)

[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00005.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0005)

</div>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_15"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan">in British shipping business circles.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">In a remarkable
series of acquisitions Royal Mail acquired Elder Dempster in 1910,
Pacific Steam in 1910, Glen Line and Lamport Holt in 1911 and
Union-Castle in
1912.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0035" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0035"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan"> Another giant emerged just before the war, when
Peninsular and Oriental apart from the Blue Anchor Line, acquired
British India Steam Navigation and its extensive shipping and trading
interests in India. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.135.2"
class="koboSpan">P&O continued its acquisitions and mergers throughout
the interwar period and in contrast to Royal Mail, remained the largest
British shipping concern throughout the twentieth century.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">Mergers and
amalgamations of lines into groups under common ownership continued in
the interwar period and changed the structure of British liner
shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0036" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0036"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan"> The economic crisis of the 1930s hit British shipping
hard. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.138.2" class="koboSpan">The
contraction of the tramp shipping sector (which was lost to Norwegians
and Greeks) and the concentration to fewer liner companies was evident:
in 1939 there were 43 British liner companies which owned 61% of the
fleet. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.138.3" class="koboSpan">The
demolition of Royal Mail, and the intervention of the British banking
system to save Britain’s largest liner concerns, brought a restructure
of liner ownership in the 1930s that defined its path in the second half
of the twentieth century.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">As
</span>[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_fig0005)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicates, in 1939 P&O, the Ellerman group of
companies, Cunard, Blue Funnel and Furness Lines appeared in the top
five positions. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.2"
class="koboSpan">P&O through consecutive mergers and amalgamations
became the indisputable queen of the Indian Ocean and Pacific routes;
apart from British India Steam Navigation in 1914.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">In 1917 and
1919 it acquired another seven lines that serviced those routes.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.4" class="koboSpan">In the 1960s
and 1970s P&O remained the largest shipping group of the world; after
the 1970s it adjusted to the container revolution, adopted a globalised
ownership, expanded to the port terminal business and diversified into
the bulk, ferries and cruise sectors.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.5" class="koboSpan">In 1996 P&O
Container Limited, the liner branch of the group, merged with Nedlloyd
to form P&O Nedlloyd and the new company became the third biggest liner
company, before its acquisition by Maersk Line.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.6" class="koboSpan">Ellerman
acquired a number of smaller Liverpool lines that traded in the
Mediterranean before World War I and its biggest acquisition was in 1916
when it amalgamated with Wilson Line; its importance contracted in the
post-World War II period. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.7"
class="koboSpan">Cunard, another giant of the “big five” of British
shipping traditionally engaged in the Atlantic passenger services since
1840s, had acquired three or four lines during the second and third
decade of the twentieth century. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.8"
class="koboSpan">It profited largely from the demolition of Royal Mail
when it acquired White Star Line in 1934.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.141.9" class="koboSpan">Persisting in
passenger shipping, however, it eventually lost its importance in the
post-war period.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">The Blue Funnel (Ocean
Steam Ship Company) group of companies owned by the Holt family
exemplified family capitalism in liner shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.142.2" class="koboSpan">Based in
Liverpool and specialising in far eastern trade, it also profited from
the demolition of Royal Mail and amalgamated with Elder Dempster which
held the African trades. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.142.3"
class="koboSpan">It continued to trade strongly well into the second
half of the twentieth century. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.142.4"
class="koboSpan">The Cayzer family from Glasgow formed the Clan Line in
1890, established the British and Commonwealth group in 1956 by
amalgamating with the Union-Castle Line, another line that had belonged
to the disintegrated Royal Mail group; it continued its business
throughout the twentieth century.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.142.5" class="koboSpan">Until the
beginning of the twentieth century the Furness group was one of the main
British tramp shipping operators, who later diversified into liner
shipping. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.142.6" class="koboSpan">By
taking part in the acquisitions and amalgamations and exploiting the
demolition of Royal Mail of which it acquired a fair share, it proved,
along with P&O, to be one of the most important shipping groups of the
twentieth century; it has also been among the first British liner groups
to continue operating in tramp/bulk shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_16"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">Liner shipping companies are associated with the most
glorious part of British shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.143.2" class="koboSpan">Liner companies
owned the most famous, luxurious steamships of the latest technology.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.143.3" class="koboSpan">British liner
steamships carried millions of passengers, and became widely known as
the proud manifestation of power of the mighty British Empire which
ruled the waves. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.143.4"
class="koboSpan">Most of the owners of British liner companies, among
Britain’s most powerful capitalists, were commoners who became Lords or
were knighted: Lord Kylsant of Royal Mail, Lord Inchcape of British
India, Sir Alfred Jones of Elder Dempster, to mention only a few.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.143.5" class="koboSpan">British
historians have told the stories of the main British liner
business.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0037" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0037"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan"> But liner shipping throughout the nineteenth and
twentieth centuries formed less than half of the large British
fleet.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">In fact, it was the
less glorious ships of less technological achievement that formed more
than half of the British fleet which fed the industries of the Empire.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.146.2" class="koboSpan">Tramp shipping
formed the largest part of the British mercantile marine up to the Great
War with 462 companies owning 55% of the fleet.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.146.3" class="koboSpan">The Industrial
Revolution determined the areas in which British tramp operators
developed in close connection with deep-sea export coal trade: The
Northeast ports and Wales became the main hubs of British
tramp-operators in combination with those of the Clyde in Scotland who
were traditionally connected with the trading worldwide networks of the
Scottish merchants.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">In 1910 the shipping
companies of the Northeast ports, namely Newcastle, Sunderland,
Hartlepool, Middlesbrough, Whitby, Scarborough and Hull handled almost
one third of British tramp shipping
tonnage.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0038" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0038"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan"> Some of the most powerful British shipping families
came from this area: the Furnesses, Turnballs, Ropners and Runcimans.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.149.2" class="koboSpan">The next most
dynamic group in tramp shipping were Scottish tramp operators who
handled 18% of British tramp shipping in 1910.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.149.3" class="koboSpan">Some of the
best known Scottish tramp shipowning families were the Burrells and the
Hoggarths. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.149.4"
class="koboSpan">Wales also emerged as a generator of tramp companies.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.149.5" class="koboSpan">Wales drew
human capital from the West Country as well and shipping companies
established in Wales operated 9% of the British tramp fleet in 1910.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.149.6" class="koboSpan">With Cardiff as
the central port, tramp shipping thrived in the Welsh ports from Chester
to
Llanelli.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0039" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0039"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan"> The best known Cardiff tramp operators were the Hains,
Morells, Tatems and Corys. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.151.2"
class="koboSpan">London and Liverpool drew branch offices from almost
all these tramp operators and both cities handled 42% of the British
tramp fleet in 1910.</span>

[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_fig0005)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicates the evident importance of tankers and the
non-existence of independent tanker owners; one of the great failures of
British tramp owners was that they did not enter the tanker business.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.153.2" class="koboSpan">The main big
tanker owners remain the petroleum companies like the Anglo-American Oil
Co in 1910, British Tanker Co and Anglo-Saxon Petroleum in 1939 and
British Petroleum in the post-World War II period.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.153.3" class="koboSpan">The new
structure in the organisation of tramp/bulk shipping, were the
management companies under which one finds some of the traditional
British tramp owners. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.153.4"
class="koboSpan">Denholm Management is a good example of a management
company. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.153.5" class="koboSpan">In
1970 it managed 38 ships for 17 shipping companies including Turnbull
Scott
Shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0040" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0040"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">Contrary to the
beliefs that want family capitalism to belong only to the Mediterranean,
family prevailed in both the British liner and tramp maritime business.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">Big liner
companies might have been joint-stock companies, but ownership was
usually spread among a select circle of family and friends; families
like the Cayzers, Ellermans, Brocklebanks, Holts, Furnesses and Swires
retained their command over major British
lines.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0041" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0041"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan"> The case was stronger in British tramp companies, that
were family-owned companies that kept ownership and management of the
companies and used intermarriages to expand
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_17"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">and keep the business within closed circles.
