</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.158.2" class="koboSpan">From the most
prominent ones like the Runcimans, the Turnbulls, the Ropners, to the
medium and smaller ones, kept business in the family for several
generations. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.158.3"
class="koboSpan">One of the great handicaps of British shipping,
however, has been the loss of the importance of the regional dimension
of maritime Britain; regions and ports that reproduced shipping
entrepreneurship.</span>

### <span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 The Norwegians</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">Norway is considered
as a leading maritime nation not only due to the high percentage of
owned tonnage since the nineteenth century, but also due to the shipping
sector’s position in the
economy.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0042" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0042"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan"> In Norway, “shipping is indeed an industry of its
own”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0043" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0043"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan"> Norwegians have traditionally carried bulk cargoes,
lumber, grain and fish along the Northern European and Atlantic
routes.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0044" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0044"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan"> Shipowing has been an important business in all ports
of Norway’s extensive coastline. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.166.2"
class="koboSpan">The regions of Oslo and Oslofjord, the South Coast, the
Western and Northern Norway included almost 60 ports active in shipping
and shipowning activities, most of whom were engaged in tramp shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.166.3" class="koboSpan">More
importantly, shipping absorbed a large portion of investment and labour
of the country. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.166.4"
class="koboSpan">The success of the Norwegian shipping industry during
the nineteenth century is related to the “collective mobilisation of
resources” at the local level, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.166.5" class="koboSpan">the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">partsrederi</span></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan"> system, according to which, members of the local
community provided resources for the construction and operation of a
ship, becoming shareholders of the shipowning company and receiving the
resulting
profits.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0045" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0045"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">With a developed
expertise in wooden and later metallic sailing ships that continued well
into the twentieth century some areas, closely connected to the
traditional shipbuilding industry failed to make the transition from
sail to steam. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.170.2"
class="koboSpan">The region of Adger in the South Coast of Norway for
example, during the years prior to World War II, owned between 55% and
58% of the Norwegian iron and steel sailing ship tonnage, but failed to
invest successfully into steam
shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0046" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0046"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">The structural
transformations of Norwegian shipping differentiated the relative
importance of each port to its development, without changing the
regional pattern. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.172.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies continued to be located in specific
ports throughout the twentieth century.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.172.3" class="koboSpan">While the
majority of shipping companies are now established in Oslo, ports like
Bergen, Grimstad, Stavanger, Arendal and Kristiansand still remain
important maritime centres. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.172.4"
class="koboSpan">It is argued however that the transition of the
Norwegian shipping from sail to steam meant the emergence of a new
“industry (mostly) outside the old one”.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.172.5" class="koboSpan">According to
Wicken: “The shipping companies were established in urban areas, mostly
around Oslo and Bergen. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.172.6"
class="koboSpan">Many companies were not closely incorporated into local
communities, but emerged from interaction between individual Norwegian
entrepreneurs and large international
corporations.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0047" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0047"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">As Norway’s external
trade could not support the development of a competitive shipping
industry, Norwegian shipowners, like the Greeks, based their expansion
on their ability to produce cost-effective shipping services and to
serve the needs of international trade.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.174.2" class="koboSpan">Equally, they
exploited their competence in managing ships and the abundance of low
cost and high quality Norwegian seamen and became the main cross trader
fleet of the world in the last third of the nineteenth century and the
first half of the twentieth century.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.174.3" class="koboSpan">Their
involvement in liner shipping was limited and with the exception of the
interwar period, when a percentage between 25% and 30% was engaged in
liner trades, the corresponding figures for the whole of twentieth
century has not surpassed 15%
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_18"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">of the
fleet.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0048" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0048"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan"> Norwegians invested heavily in bulk shipping and
especially in tankers and have been major players in this sector since
the 1920s. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.177.2" class="koboSpan">The
high share of tankers in Norwegian fleet, along with the high share of
motorships and the low average age of the vessels, are considered as the
main features of Norwegian shipping’s rapid expansion during the
interwar
period.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0049" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0049"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">47</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan"> The business strategy of expanding the market share in
tanker shipping proved to be a source of strength as well as of
weakness. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.179.2"
class="koboSpan">Norway prospered during the expansion of the tanker
market until the 1970s when it was hit hard during the crisis of
1973.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0050" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0050"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">48</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan"> Its massive orders for supertankers along with their
low ratio of liquid to fixed asset made them highly
vulnerable.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0051" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0051"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">49</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan"> Despite its diversification to offshore activities and
its exploitation of the know-how in managing ships to enter the market
of third party ship management, it remains a major power in the bulk
shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.183.2"
class="koboSpan">However, its leading position in the world fleet is
very much down to the innovative strategies of the many shipping
companies which from the 1960s onwards entered specialised bulk shipping
markers like those of gas, and chemicals.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.183.3" class="koboSpan">They are now
considered to be the leading
group</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0052" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0052"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">50</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan"> of these markets or that of open-hatch bulk
carriers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0053" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0053"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">51</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">Norwegian shipping is
characterised by rivalry and cooperation and a strong emphasis on
competence and
networking.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0054" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0054"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">52</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan"> A large percentage of shipping companies can be
considered as network firms whose relationships with partners rely on
trust.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0055" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0055"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">53</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan"> In this context, the role of families in the
establishment and development of shipping companies was crucial.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.191.2" class="koboSpan">Companies are
family owned enterprises of family owned
conglomerates.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0056" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0056"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">54</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan"> Various families, tied to particular ports,
established their companies during the end of the nineteenth century or
the first decades of the twentieth century, and most of them continue to
be active to the present day. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.193.2"
class="koboSpan">Bergesen, Olsen, Knutsen, Naess, Reksten, Odfjell,
Rasmussen, Wilhelmsen, Stolt Nielsen, Fredriksen, Westfal-Larsen, Hoegh
and Uglands are only a few of the families that ran the leading
companies of the Norwegian shipping during the twentieth century.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.193.3" class="koboSpan">Representative
cases of family businesses with a long tradition in shipping are Wilh.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.193.4" class="koboSpan">Wilhemsen and
Odfjell, as both remained at the forefront of world shipping for the
whole of their history.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">The company of Wilhelm
Wilhemsen was founded in 1861 in Tonsberg by Morten Wilhelm Wilhelmsen
who was also a successful shipbroker.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.194.2" class="koboSpan">As early as
1870 he started to invest in steamships acquiring shares in various
ships and in 1887 he made his first steamship
purchase.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0057" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0057"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">55</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan"> By 1910, when the founder of the company died, the
fleet consisted of 31 steamships.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.196.2" class="koboSpan">In 1911, the
company, after several years of scepticism, finally entered the liner
trades in cooperation with Fearnley and Eger operating the Norwegian
Africa and the Australia Line. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.196.3"
class="koboSpan">At approximately the same time Wilhelmsen entered the
tanker market. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.196.4"
class="koboSpan">In 1912 the first two tankers were ordered and a fleet
of this type of ships was created.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.196.5" class="koboSpan">In the
forthcoming years Wilhelmsen’s involvement in liner trades became
stronger while the tanker operation was abandoned.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.196.6" class="koboSpan">After World War
II, Wilhelmsen focused again on tanker business and in expanding in the
liner trades. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.196.7"
class="koboSpan">Although during 2000 it was still active in the bulk
sector, its core activity was in liners and it was considered as the
leader of Ro-Ro and Car Carriers
sector.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0058" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0058"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">56</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan"> In 1999 the Wilhelmsen Lines merged with the Swedish
Wallenius Lines creating a worldwide network, which was further expanded
with the acquisition of the car carrier division of Hyundai Merchant
Marine in 2002. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.198.2"
class="koboSpan">Today, the Wilhelmsen group is involved in many sectors
of international shipping. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.198.3"
class="koboSpan">Operating a fleet of 166 car cariers and Ro-Ro through
three different operating companies (Wallenius-Wilhelmsen Logistics,
EUKOR Car Carriers and American Roll-on-Roll off Carrier) controls 27%
of the global car carrier
fleet.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0059" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0059"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">57</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Group is also active in the third-party management
sector
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_19"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan">as well as in maritime services and logistics.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.201.2" class="koboSpan">After more than
140 years, Wilhelmsen is still a dynamic globalised shipping group,
which remains family controlled.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">Odfjell was
established in 1916 in Bergen by Abraham and Frederik Odfjell, both
captains. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.202.2"
class="koboSpan">During its early years the company was active in tramp
shipping, operating dry cargo ships, while during the late 1930s it
expanded to specialised tankers which carried different liquid cargoes.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.202.3" class="koboSpan">During the late
1950s the Odfjell family decided to increase involvement in the
specialised market for chemical cargoes.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.202.4" class="koboSpan">The company
gradually reduced its involvement in bulk markets focusing on
chemicals.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0060" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0060"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">58</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan"> During the late 1960s Odfjell entered the tank storage
business. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">This
shift to specialisation included certain innovative strategic decisions
that gave Odfjell a clear head in the chemical market and made the
company the leading Norwegian chemical tanker operator.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.204.3" class="koboSpan">Cooperation
with other companies, (for example the Westfal-Larsen & Co and Christian
Haaland of Haugesund), technological innovation and vertical integration
contributed to Odfjell’s dominance in the chemical
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0061" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0061"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">59</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">In 1986 the company
was listed on Oslo Stock Exchange but the control remained with the
Odfjell family. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.206.2"
class="koboSpan">In 1990s Odfjell implemented a strategy of expansion
with sophisticated new ships as well as with second-hand
purchases.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0062" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0062"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">60</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan"> In 2000 following the consolidation trends in the
chemical market it merged with the chemical branch of Greek-owned
company Ceres which owned a fleet of 17 chemical tankers operating in
the Seachem pool. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.208.2"
class="koboSpan">After the merger the Odfjell family owns 28% of the
shares and the Livanos family 18.5%.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.208.3" class="koboSpan">This merger
brought together two traditional families and created synergies not only
on the tangibles, but even more importantly on the intangibles.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">Odfjell cooperates
mainly on a 50–50% basis with companies that are active in regional
trades. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.209.2" class="koboSpan">Its
fleet consists of 93 parcel tankers (March 2009).
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.209.3" class="koboSpan">It owns and
operates tank terminals in Europe, America and Asia, while it is also
active in the tank container business.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.209.4" class="koboSpan">Odfjell
considers itself as a “leading logistics service provider of specialty
bulk liquids” on a worldwide
basis,</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0063" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0063"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">61</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan"> which continues to operate its businesses from
Bergen.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">Norwegian shipping
also consists of leading entrepreneurs like E.D.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.2" class="koboSpan">Naess and H.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.3" class="koboSpan">Reksten, whose
lives were constantly compared with the Greeks Onassis and Niarchos.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.4" class="koboSpan">The Norwegian
US citizen Erling Dekke Naess became active in shipping after having
studied and worked in the UK. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.5"
class="koboSpan">Having invested extensively in whaling in the 1920s, he
entered the tanker business in the 1930s.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.6" class="koboSpan">With the
outbreak of World War II Naess moved to New York and there he became
head of Nortraship, the governmental organisation that administered
Norway’s requisitioned merchant fleet to the Allies.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.7" class="koboSpan">Naess became
one of the major shipping players in the newly emerging America’s
economic capital New York. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.8"
class="koboSpan">His relations with American oil companies and his
involvement in the tanker business and flags of convenience made him
among world’s largest cosmopolitan shipowners.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.9" class="koboSpan">Involved both
in dry and liquid bulk shipping, like his Greek counterparts, in the
1950s he turned to the cheap and efficient Japanese shipyards to order
his bulk carriers and tankers. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.10"
class="koboSpan">Using Bermuda as his official base, he really
administered his fleet from London with his Anglo-American Shipping
company. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.212.11" class="koboSpan">This
eventually became Anglo-Norness and collaborated closely with the
British P&O.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">But it was his
decision to sell his fleet for \$208 million a few months before the
first oil boom and the great depression in the tanker freight markets
that made him known as the shipowner who predicted the oncoming crisis.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.213.2" class="koboSpan">Naess
attributed this decision to his study of the business
cycles.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0064" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0064"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">62</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is very probable, however, that at that point in
time Naess was not the owner of “his” fleet which belonged to the
company Zapata Norness, but was only “an honorary chairman of the board”
as it was reported that he
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_20"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan">had already sold his fleet for a much lower price in
the
1960s.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0065" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0065"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.217.1" class="koboSpan">63</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan"> Whatever the truth, his exodus remained glamorous, and
he never stopped his interests in shipowning.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.218.2" class="koboSpan">In
collaboration with the Greek tanker owners he established the Intertanko
in the mid-1970s of which he became President, while he returned to
business again in the early 1980s.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.218.3" class="koboSpan">His use of
various nationalities to shelter his companies, of various flags on his
ships, and of crews of various nationalities mean that most Norwegian
analysts not regard him as a Norwegian shipowner, and not to include his
ships in the Norwegian fleet. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.218.4"
class="koboSpan">A nation that prided itself on its maritime
infrastructure only accepted the term Norwegian-owned after the 1980s
crisis and the formation of NIS.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">Hilmar Reksten
followed a path similar to that of Naess – his ending however was
different, as he was hardly hit by the depressed freight rates of the
1970s. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.219.2" class="koboSpan">In his
case, the strong involvement in tanker business functioned both as
strength and weakness in the different phases of the downfalls and
upheavals in the shipping business.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.219.3" class="koboSpan">Reksten ordered
his first tanker in 1938 and expanded into the tanker sector after World
War II. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.219.4" class="koboSpan">He was
convinced about the high profits to be made from tankers, so he focused
on the market for oil transport, created a fleet of large tankers and
operated them in the spot
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0066" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0066"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">64</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan"> This strategy proved extremely successful in the
period before 1973, when the freight rates were continuously rising.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.221.2" class="koboSpan">Reksten became
one of the biggest tanker owners worldwide, but this strategy proved
unsuccessful in the depressed freight markets after 1974 and finally led
to bankruptcy in the late 1970s. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.221.3"
class="koboSpan">His chartering strategy made him the shipowner who “had
more tonnage available for assignments in the red-hot spot market” than
any other, but a few years later made him the one who “had more tonnage
laid up than any other”. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.221.4"
class="koboSpan">Thus, his “spectacular rise was overshadowed by his
even more spectacular
downfall”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0067" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0067"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">65</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">But Norway is a
maritime nation, and apart from the above mentioned well-known
shipowning families, the backbone of the fleet still rests in the
hundreds of small shipping companies active in shipping for shorter or
longer periods, which although not as innovative and dynamic as the
larger companies, have contributed to making Norway among the top
maritime nations worldwide. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.223.2"
class="koboSpan">The shipping companies are at the core of the Norwegian
Maritime Cluster which consists of various internationally competitive
sectors (shipping, ship brokers, ship consultants, yards, equipment,
other shipping services, shipbuilding, shipbrokering, classification
etc) located along the Norwegian
coast.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0068" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0068"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">66</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 The Greeks</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.226.1" class="koboSpan">If at the northest tip
of Europe lies one of the most dynamic European nations, at the
southeast tip of Europe lies another dynamic maritime nation that became
the world leader in the maritime business over the last 30 years.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.226.2" class="koboSpan">Greek-owned
shipping developed since the nineteenth century as an international
cross trader almost exclusively involved into tramp shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.226.3" class="koboSpan">It carried bulk
cargoes, particularly grain, from the Black Sea and coal from north
western Europe, along the routes of Mediterranean waters.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.226.4" class="koboSpan">Greek-owned
shipping eventually evolved into a worldwide tramp shipping fleet in the
twentieth century. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.226.5"
class="koboSpan">Its main strength was the development of a tight
maritime business network in Europe in the nineteenth century and
globally in the
twentieth.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0069" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0069"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">67</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">In 1850, just 20 years
after the formation of Greece, the small backward state owned a fleet
almost equivalent to that of Holland and Norway.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.228.2" class="koboSpan">Although by
1880 the Greek fleet could not compare to those of Britain, Norway,
Italy, France or Germany, it was in the same league as Russia, Sweden
and Spain and was larger than those of Denmark, the Netherlands,
Austria-Hungary or Portugal. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.228.3"
class="koboSpan">In 1910 Greece had the ninth largest
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_21"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan">fleet in Europe, which consisted almost exclusively of
ocean-going vessels for the transport of bulk cargoes and tramp ships
engaged in the international cross trades.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.229.2" class="koboSpan">By comparison,
the fleets of Russia, Austria-Hungary, Italy, France and Spain consisted
mostly of liners operating on regular routes and owned by large, often
subsidised, shipping companies which essentially carried passengers and
industrial or package
products.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0070" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0070"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">68</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">During the interwar
period world shipping faced severe problems stemming from a contraction
of seaborne trade, decreased world migration and increasing
protectionism. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.231.2"
class="koboSpan">World War I weakened Britain and allowed competitors to
challenge its maritime hegemony. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.231.3"
class="koboSpan">The Greeks took advantage of the disposal of tonnage at
extremely low prices and were able to expand during the worst period of
the crisis. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.231.4" class="koboSpan">The
fleet, which suffered severe losses during World War II not only
reconstructed itself after the War, but also grew at an unprecedented
rate. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.231.5" class="koboSpan">Until the
1960s the main maritime nations remained the same, with Britain and the
US clinging to their decreasing share of world shipping, followed by
Greece, Japan and Norway. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.231.6"
class="koboSpan">Although flags of convenience were widely used, in the
immediate postwar years they were resorted to more extensively by Greek
owners. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.231.7" class="koboSpan">The
1970s marked the start of a new era; this was characterised by the final
loss of the pre-dominance of European maritime nations, with the
exception of the Greeks who have maintained their leadership to the
present day.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">Timely adjustments to
changes of world trade and to technological shifts kept Greek shipowners
in the forefront of world shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.232.2" class="koboSpan">The spectacular
growth of Black Sea grain exports in which the Greek sailing ship fleet
was involved, provided the capital for the subsequent transition from
sail to steam by Greek shipowners that was completed at the turn of the
twentieth century. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.232.3"
class="koboSpan">After World War I the lost steamships were replaced by
the “standard” type of cargo ships that were built during the war while
after World War II, the lost ships were replaced by the war-built
“Liberty ships” which became the standard dry-bulk cargo vessels for the
next 25 years.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">Part of the Greeks’
success during the postwar period was due to their entry into the tanker
market in the late 1940s and the 1950s.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.233.2" class="koboSpan">The first
shipowners to do so were Aristotle Onassis and Stavros Niarchos, both of
whom benefited from the Norwegian experience in tankers at this
propitious international conjuncture.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.233.3" class="koboSpan">Niarchos’ and
Onassis’ expansion strategy was quickly followed by many of the
successful “traditional" shipowners, primarily those who had settled in
New York during the World War II.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.233.4" class="koboSpan">The
trailblazers’ success also created access to the American financial
market for other Greek shipowners.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.233.5" class="koboSpan">By 1974 the
Greek-owned tanker fleet had become the largest in the world, comprising
17% of the global fleet. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.233.6"
class="koboSpan">Starting from scratch in 1945, this fleet reached 8.2
million grt in 1965; 14.7 million grt in 1970; and 21.8 million grt in
1974. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.233.7" class="koboSpan">Tankers
represented between 40 and 48% of the overall capacity of the
Greek-owned fleet in the years 1958–1975.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.234.1" class="koboSpan">Family capitalism that
prevailed in the structure of Greek-owned maritime business was also
pivotal in the success of the fleet.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.234.2" class="koboSpan">At the
beginning of the twentieth century there were about 200 families, all
specialised now in shipping, running 250 shipping firms.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.234.3" class="koboSpan">By the end of
the twentieth century about 700 families were running more than 1,000
shipping firms. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.234.4"
class="koboSpan">After a short interval in New York, in the 1940s and
1950s, by the last third of the twentieth century the Greek-owned fleet
had the same operational centres (Piraeus and London) as at its
beginning, but its entrepreneurial network was not now confined to
European waters but extended to all oceans of the world.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">The management, and
all the branch offices of Greek shipping companies throughout the
twentieth century continued to be in the hands of members of the same
family</span>

<div id="Ch01.xhtml_fig0006" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_22"></span>[](#Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0006)

[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00006.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0006)

</div>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_23"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan">or co-islanders.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.237.2" class="koboSpan">In this way
kinship, island and ethnic ties ensured the cohesion of the
international Greek maritime network.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.237.3" class="koboSpan">The unofficial
but exclusive international “club” was extremely important for their
economic survival. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.237.4"
class="koboSpan">It provided access to all the expertise of shipping:
market information, chartering, sales and purchase, shipbuilding,
repairing, scrapping, financing, insurance and P & I clubs.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.237.5" class="koboSpan">It also
provided consultancy from older and wiser members and information about
the activities of the most successful members of the group.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.237.6" class="koboSpan">Imitation
proved an extremely useful “rule-of-thumb".
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.237.7" class="koboSpan">The main
strength of the Greeks then, has been the formation of an exclusive
“Greek” transnational network of family enterprises that interacted with
local, national and international shipping networks and organisations,
local, national and international financial institutions and
organisations.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">The regional dimension
has also proved extremely important in Greek-owned shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.238.2" class="koboSpan">During the
first two thirds of the twentieth century the so-called traditional
shipping families, all involved for multiple generations in shipping
activities, predominate and came from the islands of the Ionian and the
Aegean. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.238.3" class="koboSpan">On the
eve of World War I the biggest shipowning groups came almost exclusively
from the islands of the Ionian sea, as a continuity of the
entrepreneurial networks of the nineteenth century.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.238.4" class="koboSpan">Apart from the
Embiricos family that originated from the Aegean island of Andros, and
formed the most powerful shipowning group of the first third of the
century, the rest, Dracoulis Bros, Svoronos, Lykiardopoulos, Yannoulatos
and Vaglianos came from the Ionian islands of Cephalonia and Ithaca (see
</span><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fig0006" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fig0006"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.240.2"
class="koboSpan">The importance of shipowners from Chios did not begin
but later; in 1914 only the shipowning groups of Scaramanga and
Michalinos stemmed from Chios.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">If the Ionian Sea
dominates in the first third of the century, in the last two thirds the
Aegean took over. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.241.2"
class="koboSpan">It is in the interwar period that the family groups of
the maritime islands of the Ionian were replaced by the family groups of
the Aegean islands. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.241.3"
class="koboSpan">In this way, the five brothers of Ioannis Goulandris
from Andros, the five sons of Elias G.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.241.4" class="koboSpan">Kulukundis from
Kasos, the sons of the Embiricos from Andros, the four sons of George
Livanos, the two sons of the Ioannis Chandris and those of the large
family of Laimos, all from Chios, served as officers on their fathers’
steamships and eventually became directors in the offices in Piraeus and
London and shipowners themselves.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.241.5" class="koboSpan">For more than
60 years, as </span>[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
3</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_fig0006)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicates, the same names of the above mentioned
families figure in the top ten positions of Greek shipping.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.243.2" class="koboSpan">The only “
foreigners” that broke into the tightly knit shipowning circle were
Aristotle Onassis and Stavros Niarchos, both of whom, however, followed
the rules. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.243.3" class="koboSpan">They
married within the traditional shipowning circle – the daughters of
Stavros Livanos. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.243.4"
class="koboSpan">The importance of the old traditional families, most of
them active for at least three generations, eventually started to fade
and give way to new shipowners; the new blood in Greek-owned shipping
came from masters, first engineers and employees of shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.243.5" class="koboSpan">In the list of
the top shipowners of 2008 as it appears in
</span>[<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">Table
3</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_fig0006)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan">, none of them came from traditional families.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.245.2" class="koboSpan">They were new,
post-war shipowners: Angelicoussis, Economou, Tsakos, Prokopiou,
Diamantidis, Restis, Georgiopoulos, Haji-ioannou, Martinos and
Panayiotides. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.245.3"
class="koboSpan">The strength of Greek-owned shipping was that it
managed to reproduce itself and provide new and dynamic entrepreneurs
that enlarged the fleet to unprecedented size at the beginning of the
twenty first century. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.245.4"
class="koboSpan">And as in the Norwegian case, apart from those found in
the top, it is the hundreds of medium- and small-scale shipowning
companies who form the backbone and the seedbed for the expansion of
Greek-owned shipping.</span>

### <span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_24"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 The Japanese</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">Japan’s unique
seclusion from the world trade for more than two centuries, makes its
maritime history of the last 100 years quite extraordinary.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">The Japanese
could not escape integration into the world economic system; the United
States needed bases for their merchant fleets and were able to persuade
Japan to open up to the “barbarians" in 1853.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.247.3" class="koboSpan">The demand for
modernisation brought the end of the old feudal system and the shogun.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.247.4" class="koboSpan">Japanese
business, its dominance in the world economy of the twentieth century
has attracted the attention of a number of economists and historians;
the incredible “otherness” however, combined with the language barriers,
still means that its maritime business history remains, for many, a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan">terra
incognita.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0071" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0071"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">69</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan"> For the purposes of this chapter we will limit
ourselves to a short analysis of the continuity and change of the
Japanese maritime business, which remains highly comparable to that of
its European counterparts.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.251.1" class="koboSpan">It was really by
following the Meiji (the enlightened power) Restoration in 1868 and the
nation’s industrialisation that Japan’s shipping showed a remarkable
expansion: in the mid-nineteenth century Japan did not own a single
ocean going vessel – 60 years later it was third in the world maritime
powers. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.251.2" class="koboSpan">The
rapid development of Japanese shipping was the product of a combination
of government initiative and active entrepreneurship.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.251.3" class="koboSpan">Japanese
shipping developed, like the British, by serving the country’s external
trade and has been equally divided between liner and tramp.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.251.4" class="koboSpan">The
competitiveness of Japanese shipping firms however, was to a great
extend the result of a strategy of creating cooperating links with
foreign companies in global webs that connect networks of different
countries.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0072" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0072"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">70</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan"> The first period of Meiji Restoration was marked by
the government support to the private line Mitsubishi Shokai.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.253.2" class="koboSpan">In the early
1880s the Government provided half of the capital for the establishment
of a new firm, the Kyobo Unyu Kaisha.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.253.3" class="koboSpan">The intense
competition between the two companies led the Government to pursue their
amalgamation, thus, a new state aid firm, the Nippon Yusen Kaisha (NYK,
Japan Mail Steamship Company Ltd) was established.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.253.4" class="koboSpan">The company
operated with this status, providing specified services up to 1892, when
it became a private
enterprise.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0073" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0073"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan">71</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan"> It expanded into transoceanic business in 1890s by
opening lines to India, the USA, Australia and
Europe.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0074" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0074"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">72</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan"> NYK remained the largest Japanese shipping company for
most of the time after its founding.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.257.2" class="koboSpan">Based in Tokyo,
it was meant as a liner company from the beginning.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.257.3" class="koboSpan">The other
company emerged from Japan’s private businessmen and in that contrasted
the formation of NYK. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.257.4"
class="koboSpan">Based in Osaka, Osaka Shosen Kaisha (OSK, Osaka
Mercantile Steamship Co) emerged in 1884 from the combined forces of
Osaka’s leading 55 shipowners and merchants.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.257.5" class="koboSpan">OSK was
subsidised and in return provided regular services.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.257.6" class="koboSpan">Both NYK and
OSG operated in a way similar to that of British firms, purchased their
ships from Britain and employed western deck officers and
engineers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0075" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0075"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">73</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan"> Unlike its competitor NYK, the OSK operated its fleet
mainly within East Asia up to the early stage of the interwar
years.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0076" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0076"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">74</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.261.1" class="koboSpan">Japanese shipping
companies were of two types. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.261.2"
class="koboSpan">The first type was called shasen and included those
companies that owned most of their ships, operated regular lines and
were receiving government subsidies.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.261.3" class="koboSpan">The second type
was called shagaisen and included firms that, usually, operated
irregular lines and did not receive subsidies.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.261.4" class="koboSpan">This second
type included firms that were owners of their ships, others that were
operators and others that combined both
functions.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0077" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0077"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">75</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan"> Since these two large shipping companies were
distinguished from all others in terms of their size, type of operation
and
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_25"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">government subsidy, their ships were called
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">shasen </span></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">(company ships), while all the others were called
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan">shagaishen
</span></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">(non-company
ships)</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan"> These terms roughly indicated the difference between
liner and tramp shipping. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.270.2"
class="koboSpan">Numerous shagaishen firms stemmed from the traditional
shipowners or operators that traded in the coastal trade and Japanese
seas. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.270.3" class="koboSpan">They were
mainly tramp operators who, particularly during and after World War I,
extended their activities in overseas trade to Korean and Chinese
coasts.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">Being able to operate
more freely and flexibly during World War I Japanese shipping was one of
the primary beneficiaries of the war, in terms of
profitability.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0078" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0078"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.272.1" class="koboSpan">76</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan"> The limited loss of Japanese fleet during World War I
(7% of its tonnage) meant that in the interwar period, Japanese shipping
expanded and its network of routes was extended to all regions of
Southeast Asian, to India, Africa and South America.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.273.2" class="koboSpan">NYK and OSK
were able to become part of the British system of conferences and opened
their path to the City of London and the Baltic Exchange.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.273.3" class="koboSpan">During the
shipping boom of World War I a large number of capitalists invested in
ships and the tonnage of shaigasen companies increased impressively.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.273.4" class="koboSpan">Most of the
shaigasen shipowners were not operators themselves but chartered their
ships to foreign and Japanese trading companies as well as to the NYK
and OSK. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.273.5" class="koboSpan">In the
1930s five large-scale shaigasen operators, Yamashita, Mitsui, Kawasaki,
Kokusai and Daido came to dominate Japanese shipping along with the NYK
and OSK. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.273.6"
class="koboSpan">Yamashita, based in Kobe, specialised in long-distance
ocean-going shipping, while Kawasaki profited from its connection with
its production in its shipyards. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.273.7"
class="koboSpan">All shaigasen Japanese companies had access in the
London maritime market and were involved in the British second-hand
sales and purchase market.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">The third forerunner
of Japan’s steam shipping, and different from the above started from the
Mitsui family, who had prospered in Japan as merchants and financiers
since the late seventeenth century, and who were the prime financiers of
the new Meiji government. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.274.2"
class="koboSpan">They established in 1876 the Mitsui Bussan Kaisha (MBK,
Mitsui Trading Co) that with branch offices in Shanghai, Hong Kong,
Paris, New York, London and Singapore was oriented in foreign trade,
dealing with both bulk trade (coal, rice, cotton) and general
manufactured
goods.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0079" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0079"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.275.1" class="koboSpan">77</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan"> Mitsui, that was part of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan">sogoshosha</span></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan"> (general trading company) system, operated a large
fleet to cover its transport needs.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.278.2" class="koboSpan">This company
proved to be the pioneer in the eventual expansion of Japanese firms on
a global basis. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.278.3"
class="koboSpan">It was the first Japanese firm to penetrate global
commercial networks, as it opened its London branch in
1879.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0080" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0080"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">78</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.280.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the post-war era, the company expanded and
eventually became the main competitor of NYK by merging with OSK – what
came to be called MOL (Mitsui-OSK
Lines).</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0081" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0081"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">79</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan"> The merger was the result of the consolidation process
of Japanese shipping, which, apart from it, resulted also to the merge
of Nitto Shoshen and Daido Kaiun to form the Japan Line and the
Yamashita Kisen and Shinnihon Kisen to form the Yamashita Shinnihon
Steamship Co.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan">If the first half of
the twentieth century formed the base for the development of Japanese
shipping, the second half created the conditions for its proliferation.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.283.2" class="koboSpan">The ships lost
during the World War II were quickly replaced by new, technologically
advanced ships. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.283.3"
class="koboSpan">Demand conditions and the existence of related and
supporting industries are considered to be among the features that can
define the prospects of a national industry to compete in the world
markets.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0082" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0082"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">80</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan"> During its modern history, but especially in the
second half of the twentieth century, Japanese shipping developed to
respond on the needs of a high volume internal demand.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.285.2" class="koboSpan">In 2001 the
import dependency of Japan in major resources accounted 97.9% for coal,
99.7% for crude oil, 96.9% for natural gas, 100% for iron ore, wool and
raw cotton, 94.7% for soy beans, 88.8% for wheat and
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_26"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan">84.6% for
salt.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0083" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0083"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">81</span></a></sup><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.288.1"
class="koboSpan"> Japan’s dependency on seaborne trade led the shipping
industry in search of technological and managerial innovations that, on
the one hand would increase the effectiveness of shipping companies,
while on the other would decrease the transport cost of both the raw
materials and the final products of the industries.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.288.2" class="koboSpan">These
innovations have allowed, for example, the Japanese steel firms to be
competitive in world markets, although they have to import very much of
their needed raw
materials.</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0084" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0084"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">82</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.290.1" class="koboSpan">The internationally
competitive shipbuilding industry of Japan played a crucial role in this
effort and continues to do so. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.290.2"
class="koboSpan">Its development however, was not depended on the
development of shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.290.3" class="koboSpan">Of course, it
offered the demand conditions that defined the prospects of shipbuilding
industry to become competitive and penetrate the export market and to
attract orders by shipowners of new dynamic fleets, like the Greeks, who
became the main customers of the Japanese shipbuilders from 1960s
onwards. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.290.4" class="koboSpan">This
self-contained path of shipbuilding industry explains why its market
share achieved the 50% (the late 1960s) while the respective of the
shipping industry did not exceed the 15.5% (in
2008).</span><sup><a href="#Ch01.xhtml_fn0085" id="Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0085"><span
id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.291.1" class="koboSpan">83</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.292.1" class="koboSpan">Japanese shipping
continues to be dominated by a few number of giant shipping groups, who
manage a great number of owned ships, as well as an even greater number
of chartered ships, many of them owned by other Japanese companies.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.292.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
Mitsui OSK Lines operates a diversified fleet of more than 800 ships,
the NYK a fleet of almost 800 ships and the K-Line a fleet of almost 500
ships. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.292.3" class="koboSpan">In
parallel, a great number of medium sized operators, active mainly in
bulk shipping add to the dynamism of Japanese shipping industry.</span>

## <span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.293.2" class="koboSpan">Continuity and Change</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.294.1" class="koboSpan">The analysis of the
shipping industry and of the main markets has revealed the structural
transformations and changes that occurred during the twentieth century.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.294.2" class="koboSpan">The hierarchy
of maritime powers changed, as new maritime nations emerged and most
traditional maritime countries lost their competitiveness and decreased
their market share. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.294.3"
class="koboSpan">The changing patterns of development in the
international trade along with the technological advances determined the
path of the industry. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.294.4"
class="koboSpan">Shipping markets have followed the path to
globalisation and specialisation has become the drive for their
development.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">In this context,
shipping companies have moved towards the necessary organisational
adaptations. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.295.2"
class="koboSpan">Liner shipping companies expanded to the newly
developed markets and served almost any destination worldwide.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.295.3" class="koboSpan">The need for
efficiency and effectiveness led them to adapt to unitisation investing
in containerships and terminals and gradually turned to become transport
providers that cover the needs of their customers in a global basis.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.295.4" class="koboSpan">The main drive
for the achievement of both the critical size and the global coverage
are new forms of cooperation that is, the consortia and the strategic
alliances. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.295.5"
class="koboSpan">Either through cooperation, internal development or
mergers and acquisitions, liner operators strive to become the global
players of a global market. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.295.6"
class="koboSpan">In a rather playful game of fate, the beginning and the
end of the twentieth century were marked by the same trends.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">Bulk shipping
continues to be a sum of markets that are organised along the needs of
the cargoes they transport. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.296.2"
class="koboSpan">Contrary to the liner sector, bulk shipping continues
to be characterised by volatility, which increased the risk for the
companies. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.296.3"
class="koboSpan">Decisions regarding the choice of the type of ship, the
timing of the investment and chartering
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_page_27"></span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">determine the long-term survival of the companies.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.297.2" class="koboSpan">Information
remains one of the most critical factors for success.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.297.3" class="koboSpan">Dry, liquid and
specialised markets like gas and chemicals create a mosaic that
incorporates many distinct organisational forms.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.297.4" class="koboSpan">For the more
recently created specialised markets, concentration of tonnage and
consolidation of companies were the means for companies who seek to
cover the transport needs of global customers.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.297.5" class="koboSpan">For the dry and
liquid markets on the other hand, the tramp character continued to exist
throughout the past century, although certain transformations have
diminished its presence.</span>

<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">Structural changes on
the demand side have provoked the introduction and disparity of
cooperation of the commercial side of their operation, mainly through
the formation of pools. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.298.2"
class="koboSpan">Trust continues to be at the core of the business: for
the main players it is the factor that allows the formation of networks
of collaborating competitors. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.298.3"
class="koboSpan">Bulk shipping has traditionally been a sector that
rewarded the entrepreneurial spirit, adaptation and flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.298.4" class="koboSpan">The business
environment for bulk shipping companies during the past century became
more regulated and shipping operation more formalised.
</span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.298.5" class="koboSpan">To a certain
extent however, these changes diminished the entrepreneurial character
and created the need to balance between the necessity to conform to the
business’s environment requirements and the necessity to adapt for
competitiveness. </span><span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.298.6"
class="koboSpan">Still, the beginning and the end of the past century
saw the largest part of world’s main tramp operators work more or less
on similar lines.</span>

class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_bck_fn0001)<span id="Ch01.xhtml_kobo.300.1"

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_34"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_35"></span>[<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 2</span>\
<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Globalisation — the Maritime Nexus</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0069)
============================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Jan</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Hoffmann</span></span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_fn0086" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_fn0086"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">and
</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Shashi</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">Kumar</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_fn0087" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_fn0087"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction: Globalised Business in a Globalised Economy</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">“Globalisation” means
different things to different people.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">For some, it is
the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan">raison
detre</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan"> for
poverty and global financial crisis; for others, it is a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">sine qua
non</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan"> for
economic development and a rise in standard of living.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Even “When did
globalisation begin?” </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.15.3"
class="koboSpan">(O’Rourke and Williamson, 2000) is a disputed topic.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.15.4" class="koboSpan">For us, in this
chapter about maritime economics, it is simply a concept that describes
a </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan">trend </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan">in international trade.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">It means (a)
that trade is growing faster than the world’s GDP; and (b) that this
trade is not only in finished goods and services, but also increasingly
in components and services that are used within globalised production
processes. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.17.3"
class="koboSpan">Maritime transport is growing because it is required to
move traded goods and components, and trade in maritime services is
itself taking place on an ever more global scale.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">Transport is one of the
four cornerstones of globalisation.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">Together with
telecommunications, trade liberalisation and international
standardisation, the increased efficiency of port and shipping services
has made it even easier to buy and sell merchandise goods, raw materials
and components almost anywhere in the world.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.18.3" class="koboSpan">International
standards and homogenous products foster global competition.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.18.4" class="koboSpan">Trade
liberalisation allows the efficient international allocation of
resources. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.18.5"
class="koboSpan">Finally, telecommunication and transportation are the
necessary tools to transfer information and goods.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.18.6" class="koboSpan">“Despite all the
headlines and political bluster surrounding the World Trade
Organisation, NAFTA and other trade pacts, the real driving force behind
globalisation is something far less visible: the declining costs of
international transport”
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">The Journal of
Commerce</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">,
15 April 1997).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_36"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">At the same time, maritime business itself is probably
the most globalised industry. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.21.2"
class="koboSpan">Most maritime transport is provided between two or more
countries, and the service providers no longer need to be nationals of
the same countries whose cargo they move.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.21.3" class="koboSpan">In fact, a
simple commercial transaction may easily involve people and property
from a dozen different countries: A Greek-owned vessel, built in Korea,
may be chartered to a Danish operator, who employs Philippine seafarers
via a Cypriot crewing agent, is registered in Panama, insured in the UK,
and transports German made cargo in the name of a Swiss freight
forwarder from a Dutch port to Argentina, through terminals that are
concessioned to port operators from Hong Kong and Dubai.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.21.4" class="koboSpan">International
standardisation, an important component of globalisation in general,
also affects shipping: without standardised containers globalised
shipping and intermodal networks would not be possible.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.21.5" class="koboSpan">Equivalently,
international operators are now in a position to take a concession of a
container terminal located in any port in the world, suppliers of port
and ship equipment produce and sell globally, and ISO and IMO standards
concerning quality, safety and training apply equally on all
international waters.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">The remainder of this
chapter will look at the mutual relationship between maritime business
and globalisation. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.22.2"
class="koboSpan">Section 2 discusses how trends in international
maritime transport affect globalisation, and section 3 looks at the same
relationship, but from the opposite direction, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.22.3" class="koboSpan">how the maritime
business is affected by globalisation.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.22.4" class="koboSpan">Section 4
provides summary and conclusions.</span>

## <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">Maritime Transport and its Relevance for Globalisation</span>

### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Global trade, and how it is being moved</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">2.1.1 The share of the maritime mode of transport</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping continues to
be the dominant mode of transport for international trade.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.26.2" class="koboSpan">World seaborne
trade has grown almost continuously since World War II, with tonne-miles
increasing more than three-fold since 1970 (UNCTAD, 2009).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">Seaborne trade accounts
for 89.6% of global trade in terms of volume (tonnes) and 70.1% in terms
of value. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.27.2"
class="koboSpan">Airborne cargo has a share of just 0.27% of trade
volume and 14.1% of trade value, whilst overland and other modes
(including pipelines) account for the remaining 10.2% of volume and
15.8% of trade value (See
</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0003" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0003"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">Figures 1</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0004" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0004"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.31.2"
class="koboSpan">In 2008, total world seaborne trade, including
intra-European Union trade, is estimated to amount to about 8.17 billion
tons (UNCTAD, 2009).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">The shares of the
different modes tend to remain stable in terms of volume, but fluctuate
much more when analysing the trade value.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">During the seven
years 2000–2006, the share of seaborne trade volume has fluctuated only
between 89.04 and 89.82% (a range of 0.78 percentage points), while its
share in trade value fluctuated seven times more – between 64.48 and
70.07% (a range of 5.59 percentage points).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.32.3" class="koboSpan">The main reason
for those differences lies in the fact that the share in trade value is
strongly influenced by the price of the traded commodities.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.32.4" class="koboSpan">In particular,
the rising price of oil, but also that of other commodities, has
contributed to the rise in the share of sea-borne trade – albeit only
its </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan">value</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan"> and not its
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">volume</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.36.2"
class="koboSpan">Another trend that leads to an increase in the share of
maritime trade
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">value</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the changing composition of global maritime trade,
which includes increasingly manufactured and intermediate goods.</span>

<div id="Ch02.xhtml_fig0007" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00007.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Modal split of international trade in goods, $ billion and %, 2000–2006" /></span>

class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan">Modal split of international trade in goods, \$ billion
and %, 2000–2006</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch02.xhtml_fig0008" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00008.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Modal split of international trade in goods, million metric tonnes and %, 2000–2006" /></span>

<a href="#Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0004" id="Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0004"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">Modal split of international trade in goods, million
metric tonnes and %, 2000–2006</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan"> Global Insight, not inlcuding intra-European Union
trade</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_38"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">As regards the unit values by transport mode, in 2006,
the average value per tonne of cargo of seaborne trade was \$943, versus
\$63,184 per tonne of airborne trade and \$1,878 per tonne of trade
transported overland or by other modes, such as pipelines
(</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_fig0009" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_fig0009"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.51.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.51.2"
class="koboSpan">In other words, a tonne of airborne cargo was on
average 67 times more valuable than a tonne of seaborne cargo.</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">2.1.2 The geography of seaborne trade</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">The major loading areas
for seaborne trade today are developing regions (60.6%), followed by
developed economies (33.6%) and countries with transition economies
(5.9%). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">Asia’s
share of seaborne exports is 40%, followed in descending order by the
Americas, Europe, Africa and Oceania (UNCTAD, 2009).</span>

<a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0005" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0005"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan"> reflects the evolving participation of developing
countries in global imports and exports.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">In 1970,
developing countries still imported mostly high-value/low-volume
manufactured goods and exported above all low-value raw materials; as a
result, they exported almost four times as many tonnes of seaborne cargo
than they imported. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.55.3"
class="koboSpan">Today, developing countries participate much more in
globalised production processes. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.55.4"
class="koboSpan">Especially China, India and other Asian countries have
become important importers of commodities such as iron ore, bauxite and
grains, while at the same time increasing their share in manufactured
exports. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.55.5" class="koboSpan">This is
an interesting trend, as it illustrates that the classical distribution
of trade between developed and developing countries is no longer
valid.</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">2.1.3 The composition of seaborne trade</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">Approximately two
thirds of seaborne trade are dry cargoes and one third liquid bulk
(</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0006" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0006"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.59.2"
class="koboSpan">Dry cargoes are increasingly being carried in
containers. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.59.3" class="koboSpan">The
majority of containerised cargo is made up of manufactured goods and
high-value bulk commodities, such as time- and temperature-sensitive
agricultural products. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.59.4"
class="koboSpan">Since 1990, containerised trade has increased by a
factor of five – an average annual growth rate of almost 10%.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.59.5" class="koboSpan">In 2008, global
container trade was estimated at 137 million TEUs (UNCTAD, 2009).</span>

<div id="Ch02.xhtml_fig0009" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00009.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch02.xhtml_bck_fig0009)

</div>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_39"></span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0005" id="Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0005"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
