Transport 2009, Geneva, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_40"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">Although maritime transport has historically been
associated with the carriage of high-volume low-value goods (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">iron ore and
coal), the share of low-volume, high-value containerised trade has been
growing continuously since the container was invented half a century
ago. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.73.3" class="koboSpan">Today,
manufactured goods account for over 70% of world merchandise trade by
value. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.73.4" class="koboSpan">They
include consumption goods as well as intermediate goods, parts and
semi-finished products that have expanded in tandem with intra-company
trade, international outsourcing and globalisation.</span>

### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Trade and transport in economic theory</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">2.2.1 International trade and economic growth</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">Allowing and
facilitating trade has obvious positive impacts on economic growth.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.76.2" class="koboSpan">If Chile can
produce bananas only under glass, and Ecuador can grow grapes only on an
inaccessible highland, then both countries’ populations can eat more
bananas and grapes (i.e. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">achieve measurable economic growth) if they specialise
and trade – as long as the shipping services are less expensive than the
savings in production costs.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">Going a step further,
even if one country could produce both commodities with less land or
manpower than the other country, according to David Ricardo’s (1817)
theory of the comparative advantage, it still makes sense for both
countries to specialise and trade.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">Ricardo’s
example uses the production of cloth and wine, where Portugal has an
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan">absolute </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan">advantage concerning both: It needs 80 man-months to
produce X litres of wine and 90 man-months to produce Y metres of cloth,
whereas England needs 120 and 100 man-months respectively.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.79.2" class="koboSpan">England has a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">comparative
</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">advantage
concerning cloth, and a rational decision of Portugal and England will
imply that the first specialises in growing wine and the latter in
producing cloth, consequently leading to English exports of cloth to
Portugal and Portuguese exports of wine to England.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.81.2" class="koboSpan">This type of
specialisation, and thus also the resulting trade, can partly be
explained by the “Factor Proportions Model”, which was developed by Eli
Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin in the 1920s (Ohlin, 1933).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.81.3" class="koboSpan">This model
expands Ricardo’s basic version by including differences in the
endowment of resources. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.81.4"
class="koboSpan">Linking both models thus allows to explain trade flows
by differences in available technology, capital, manpower and natural
resources.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">Today, the academic
discussion on why and how much countries trade with each other is far
developed. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">The
impetus for new trade theories came from the limitations of the
classical models because of their relatively simplistic assumptions and
also their empirical weaknesses. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.82.3"
class="koboSpan">This was illustrated by the Leontief Paradox (1953)
when the Factor Proportions Model, discussed earlier, was applied to the
US. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.82.4" class="koboSpan">The
empirical analysis did not support the theory’s prediction that a
nation’s abundance in a particular factor of production would dominate
its exports. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.82.5" class="koboSpan">New
contributions in the post-World War II era include Vernon’s product
life-cycle theory of the mid-1960s, the new trade theory of the 1980s
(Krugman, 1981; Lancaster, 1980) and Porter’s (1990) national
competitive advantage trade theory.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.82.6" class="koboSpan">The product life
cycle theory explained the international trade patterns of the 1960s
when the US dominated the global economy and most new products
originated in that country (Vernon and Wells, 1986).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.82.7" class="koboSpan">As demand for
the product increased gradually in other developed nations, it was
initially met through US exports until the production itself moved to
those countries because of higher US labour costs.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.82.8" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
once the product became standardised, US production was
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_41"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan">typically replaced with exports from other developed
nations first and, in the long-run, exports from developing countries.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
limitations of this theory are far too many in the contemporary global
economy where production is dispersed to different parts of the world
simultaneously and no one particular nation is in a position to claim
hegemony in international trade.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">The new trade theory is
based on the increasing returns to specialisation that arise in an
industry when it is characterised by high economies of scale.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.84.2" class="koboSpan">The presence of
such economies of scale in production would lead to the existence of
only a limited number of global players in the market.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.84.3" class="koboSpan">Those firms that
are </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">first-movers
</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">may
benefit from their early entry and establish themselves, erecting entry
barriers for others. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.86.2"
class="koboSpan">It has been argued that to be successful in such an
environment, in addition to the firm being lucky, entrepreneurial, and
innovative, the nation itself must have a strategic, pro-active trade
policy that facilitates first-mover advantage in key and newly emerging
industries (Hill, 2000). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.86.3"
class="koboSpan">Porter’s national competitive advantage theory
postulates the existence of a diamond that consists of factor
endowments, demand conditions, related and supporting industries, and
firm strategy, structure and rivalry.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.86.4" class="koboSpan">The diamond will
be favourable when the four components are in place along with an
element of luck and favourable government policies as was the case for
the Japanese automobile industry in the 1980s (Porter, 1990).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">In practice, the
different theories of international trade obviously complement each
other and make their own contributions.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">They apply as
much to trade in goods as to trade in services – including maritime
transport services: Flag registries, for example, surely benefit from
economies of scale, shipyards require an endowment of capital and
labour, and London was a “first mover” concerning insurance and finance.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.87.3" class="koboSpan">Later on, we
will look in more detail at this specialisation in different maritime
sectors.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">And what does trade
mean for economic growth and well-being?
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.88.2" class="koboSpan">Under almost any
model, it is “potentially possible to find a free trade consumption
point and an appropriate lump-sum compensation scheme such that everyone
is at least as well-off with trade as they had been in autarky”
(Suranovic, 2002). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.88.3"
class="koboSpan">And, accordingly, “international economic integration
yields large potential welfare effects” (Anderson and Wincoop, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.88.4" class="koboSpan">The posterior
distribution of these benefits within society is a different matter,
beyond the scope of this chapter.</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">2.2.2 Mainstream economics and its consideration of transport</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">How does transport fit
into this analysis of trade and economic development?
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">Standard
Economics text books, if they include it at all, do so by considering it
as part of the overall transaction or arbitrage costs.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.90.3" class="koboSpan">Trade will take
place if price differences between two countries are higher than the
total transaction costs.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">Until the early 1970s,
transport and transport-related infrastructure played an important role
in location theories and development economics, including the lending
policies of the World Bank and bilateral technical cooperation.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">It was assumed
that by simply providing for infrastructure such as ports, roads and
bridges, developing countries would soon become more competitive and
catch up with the industrialised nations.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.91.3" class="koboSpan">This changed for
two main reasons: first, as transport costs declined and connectivity
and efficiency improved, it was assumed that further improvements in
transport were no longer relevant for trade and development.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.91.4" class="koboSpan">Secondly, the
relationship between transport and economic growth is quite complex, and
impacts of changes
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_42"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan">were – and still are – difficult to measure.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">Some of the
measurable results of infrastructure investments were actually
disappointing or even contrary to the expected and desired impact.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.92.3" class="koboSpan">For example, if
imports suddenly became more competitive, port investments actually led
to a closure of local industries (Pedersen, 2001; Hilling, 1996; Simon,
1996).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">(Only) once a Nobel
Memorial Prize in Economics has so far been given to authors who worked
– partly – on transport-related topics; that was in 1993, when the prize
was won by Robert Fogel and Douglass North.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">Fogel’s main
contributions included research on the role of the railways for the
development of the national economy in the United States.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.93.3" class="koboSpan">Douglass North
worked, </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">inter alia</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan">, on the economic development in Europe and the United
States before and in connection with the industrial revolution,
including the roles of sea transport and changes in the pattern of
regional specialisation and interregional trade.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Nowadays, most trade
models include transport costs or some related variables, such as
distance and common borders, to explain the geographical distribution of
international trade flows. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
class="koboSpan">In empirical research, measurable reductions in
transport costs are taken as a given exogenous trend, driven by
technological advances, that obviously promotes trade.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.96.3" class="koboSpan">O’Rourke and
Williamson (1999), for example, analyse how in different historical
periods trade grew as a result of reductions in freight rates.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">Yet still, “there isn’t
nearly as much trade as standard trade models suggest that there should
be. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.97.2" class="koboSpan">Formal trade
barriers such as tariffs and quotas are far too low to account for much
of the missing trade while changes in tariffs and quotas in the last 50
years explain too little of the growth in trade.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.97.3" class="koboSpan">Transport costs
help explain the missing trade, but distance and other location
variables are far too important in their trade suppressing effects to be
accounted for by the effect of distance and measurable transport costs.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.97.4" class="koboSpan">Fall in measured
transport costs do not fully explain the growth in trade.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.97.5" class="koboSpan">These anomalies
have until recently been ignored by the profession” (Anderson,
1999).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">Whether transport costs
have fallen or not is surely debatable, and we shall briefly discuss
this question later on. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.98.2"
class="koboSpan">What is true, however, is that by considering only
transport costs and not the other aspects (such as connectivity, safety,
security, reliability, speed, or port facilitation), many trade analysts
have not been too impressed with the advances in the field of transport
and their impact on trade growth. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.98.3"
class="koboSpan">And what has long been ignored altogether is how
increased trade influences transport costs.</span>

### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">2.3 Trade and its transport: A mutual relationship</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">2.3.1 Rediscovering transport as a determinant of trade</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">Any answer to the
question of “why do nations trade (so little)” (Anderson, 1999) needs to
look at transport costs and shipping connectivity.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.101.2" class="koboSpan">Since the late
1990s, in the context of globalisation and the analysis of its causes
and impacts, transport has moved back to the mainstream of economics and
related sciences. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.101.3"
class="koboSpan">Thompson (2000), from the World Bank, writes he is
“delighted to see the general economics profession rediscovering the
importance of transportation costs and geography in international trade
considerations”, and Pedersen (2001) explains that “during the 1990s
transport and communication appear slowly to be on their way into the
mainstream again, but now transformed into a much broader concept of
logistics, which has become an increasingly important element in the
organisation and restructuring of the globalising economy.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.101.4" class="koboSpan">From being
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_43"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">an external factor, transport has become an integrated
part of the production and distribution system”.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">Initial empirical
research which incorporates transport into trade and economic policy
analysis includes Limao and Venables (1999), who conclude that “halving
transport costs increases the volume of trade by a factor of five”.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.103.2" class="koboSpan">In a related
paper (Venables and Limao, 1999), the same authors highlight that a
“theory of trade that ignores transport costs will yield systematically
incorrect predictions about trade patterns, industrial structure, and
factor incomes”.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">To redeem such
shortcomings, several authors have in recent years incorporated measures
of transport costs into trade models.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">An overview is
provided by Korinek and Sourdin (2009), who specifically analyse
maritime transport costs as determinants of international trade and
conclude that a 10% increase in maritime transport costs is associated
with a 6 to 8% decrease in trade, other things being equal.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.104.3" class="koboSpan">Wilmsmeier and
Sanchez (2009) look specifically at food prices and conclude that any
debate on food policy “requires a good understanding of the functioning
of transport markets and their role in food transport chains”, while
Disdier and Head (2008) find a “puzzling persistence of the distance
effect on bilateral trade”.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Several international
organisations are now paying increased attention to this issue, IADB
(2009), for example, concludes that “transport costs have assumed an
unprecedented strategic importance” for Latin America and the Caribbean.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.105.2" class="koboSpan">OECD (2008)
sets out an ambitious research agenda (a) to examine the impact of
transport costs on trade; and (b) to examine the impact of different
components of transport. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.105.3"
class="koboSpan">World Bank (2009) analyses transport costs in Africa
because “(it) is well known that weak infrastructure can account for low
trade performance”. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.105.4"
class="koboSpan">UNCTAD (2004) concludes that “Improved transport
services for developing countries are key determinants of the new
international trade geography, including South–South trade and increased
merchandise exports of developing countries.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.105.5" class="koboSpan">However, not
all developing countries are so far benefiting from this new trade
geography and further efforts are required to improve transport services
and infrastructure especially for least developed and also landlocked
countries. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.105.6" class="koboSpan">The
challenge for policy makers is to initiate a virtuous cycle where better
transport services lead to more trade, and more trade in turn helps to
encourage improved transport services.”</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">2.3.2 What are the determinants of maritime transport costs?</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">Limao and Venables
(1999) and also Radelet and Sachs (1998) not only use transport cost
data to explain trade, but also undertake regressions to explain
transport costs. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.107.2"
class="koboSpan">The explanatory variables used in their analysis are
basically related to distance and connectivity, such as if countries are
land locked, or if trading partners are neighbours, and to country
characteristics such as GDP per capita.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.107.3" class="koboSpan">García Menéndez
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.109.2"
class="koboSpan">(2002) investigate the determinants of maritime
transport costs and the role they play in allocating trade across
countries for the case of the ceramic sector (tiles).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.109.3" class="koboSpan">They include a
discussion on the sensitivity of trade flows and transportation costs to
the existence of back hauling, and suggest that higher distance and poor
partner infrastructure increases transport costs notably.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.109.4" class="koboSpan">Inclusion of
infrastructure measures improves the fit of the regression,
corroborating the importance of infrastructure in determining transport
costs. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.109.5" class="koboSpan">Higher
transport costs significantly deter trade, and distance does not appear
to be a good proxy for transport costs, at least not in the ceramic
sector. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.109.6" class="koboSpan">For
Latin America, continuing
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_44"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan">work by Micco and Pérez (2001), Sanchez
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.112.2"
class="koboSpan">(2002) analyse the impact of port reform on transport
costs, and also possible determinants of the port reforms themselves.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.112.3" class="koboSpan">Hummels (1999a,
1999b, and 2000) discusses if “international transport costs have
declined”, and he introduces “time as a trade barrier”.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.112.4" class="koboSpan">One of his
conclusions is that that “each day saved in shipping time is worth 0.5
percent ad valorem, approximately 30 times greater than costs associated
with pure inventory holding” (Hummels, 2000).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.112.5" class="koboSpan">Fink
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2001) analyse how liberalisation in trade in
transport services leads to further reductions in transport costs, which
in turn lead to a further promotion of trade in goods.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.114.2" class="koboSpan">Although
criticised in its methodology and specific conclusions concerning liner
shipping’s anti-trust immunity (World Shipping Council, 2001), there is
no doubt that the liberalisation and globalisation of the maritime
business (see section 3 of this chapter), have led to a reduction of
transport costs, which is contributing to the globalisation of trade and
global production.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">What was still missing
in the earlier literature was a more thorough consideration of the
mutual relationship between trade volumes, transport costs, and the
quality of transport services. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.115.2"
class="koboSpan">For example, higher quality of service implies higher
transport costs, yet also promotes trade.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.115.3" class="koboSpan">Economies of
scale from high trade volumes have a strong negative (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.115.4" class="koboSpan">decreasing)
impact on transport costs. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.115.5"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, it appears that the strong relation between
trade and transport costs detected by Limao and Venables (1999) quoted
above does not only reflect the elasticity of trade towards transport
costs, but also almost certainly reflects the economies of scale through
which higher volumes lead to lower costs of transport.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Research on the
determinants of maritime transport costs has advanced significantly
during the current decade. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.116.2"
class="koboSpan">The basic findings of the regressions we first
presented in the earlier version of this chapter (Kumar and Hoffmann,
2002) are confirmed by numerous subsequent studies.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.116.3" class="koboSpan">Based on
results from Sanchez
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan">(2003), Wilmsmeier
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2006), and Wilmsmeier and Hoffmann (2008) as well as
the literature review provided by OECD (2008), six key determinants of
freight costs, i.e. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.120.2"
class="koboSpan">the price charged to the shipper, for maritime
transport can be summarised as follows.</span>

1.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
    class="koboSpan">Distance:</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Surely distance plays some role as a longer
    journey requires more fuel and other operating expenses.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">This impact
    is stronger for bulk shipping than for containerised liner shipping.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.122.3" class="koboSpan">For the
    latter it is found that doubling the distance increases freight
    rates by only 15 to 25%, and distance on its own will usually
    statistically explain just one fifth of the variance of container
    freight rates.</span>
2.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
    class="koboSpan">Economies of
    scale</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
    class="koboSpan">: Larger trade volumes and bigger individual
    shipments reduce unit transport costs.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">The largest
    13,000 TEU container ships cost half as much to build per TEU than
    vessels of 2,500 TEU, and employ the same number of crew.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.124.3" class="koboSpan">Larger
    trade volumes and shipments are also correlated with other
    determinants of transport costs, such as port infrastructure and
    competition between services providers.</span>
3.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
    class="koboSpan">Trade
    balances:</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
    class="koboSpan"> On many trade routes, volumes moving in one
    direction are higher than those moving in the opposite direction.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.126.2" class="koboSpan">As carriers
    then have empty ships and containers available for the return trip,
    freight rates for the return trip may be just half of the rate of
    the outbound trip. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.126.3"
    class="koboSpan">Even if individual
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_45"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
    class="koboSpan">countries have a more or less balanced trade (e.g.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.127.2" class="koboSpan">Chile and
    Korea), the freight rate from Korea to Chile may still be far higher
    than the rate from Chile to Korea, because the overall trade balance
    on the route is determined by the Chinese surplus with the United
    States.</span>
4.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
    class="koboSpan">Type and value of traded
    goods:</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Obviously transport costs vary depending on the
    type of commodity traded, i.e.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">dry bulk,
    oil, containerised cargo, or break bulk.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">If
    insurance costs are included in the overall transport costs a higher
    value per tonne of the commodity will also increase freight charges.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.129.4"
    class="koboSpan">Interestingly, it is found that for containerised
    trade, even if insurance costs are excluded, freight charges per TEU
    are still higher for higher value goods than for less costly
    commodities. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.129.5"
    class="koboSpan">Carriers used to say that the freight rate is “what
    the market can bear” – and the market for transporting toys can bear
    a higher freight rate per TEU than the market for waste paper.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.129.6" class="koboSpan">Put
    differently: The demand for transporting low-value waste paper has a
    higher price elasticity and, hence, waste paper will only be put
    into a container if freight rates are low.</span>
5.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
    class="koboSpan">Competition and transport
    connectivity:</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Competition among carriers and competition between
    different transport modes reduces transport costs, i.e.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.131.2" class="koboSpan">the freight
    rates charged to the shipper.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.131.3" class="koboSpan">If
    countries are neighbours and can trade by road, rail or pipeline,
    freight rates for sea-borne trade are lower.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.131.4" class="koboSpan">If
    countries are not connected to each other through direct liner
    shipping services, but instead containerised trade between them
    requires as least one transhipment port, freight rates also tend to
    be higher. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.131.5"
    class="koboSpan">Interestingly, it is found that once there are more
    than four carriers providing direct services, freight rates decrease
    even further – a possible interpretation is that if there are only
    up to four providers we are confronted with an oligopoly.</span>
6.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
    class="koboSpan">Port characteristics and trade
    facilitation:</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Better port infrastructure, private sector
    investment, perceived port efficiency and shorter waiting times at
    Customs have all been found to lead to lower freight rates.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">Although
    better infrastructure may actually lead to higher port costs charged
    to the carrier, the latter will still reduce his freight rate
    charged to the importer or exporter, because the gained time and
    reliability more than offsets the possible payments to the port.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">As regards
    trade facilitation as measured for example by shorter Customs
    clearance times, these tend to be correlated with lower maritime
    freight rates for imports. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.133.4"
    class="koboSpan">The efficiency of a port is closely correlated with
    a country’s per capita GDP and it is found that richer countries
    also tend to benefit from lower freight rates for their exports.
    </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.133.5" class="koboSpan">A country’s
    “maritime nexus” to globalised trade through its seaports is thus
    two-fold: better ports help countries to connect and develop – and
    at the same time more developed countries are better positioned to
    invest and reform their ports.</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">2.3.3 A note on transport and regional integration</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">If it is true that
international transport (unit-) costs are declining, and distance has a
decreasing impact on these transport costs, why then apparently regional
trade is growing (even) faster than inter-regional trade?
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">Intra-Asian
container traffic is growing
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_46"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan">faster than global container traffic.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.136.2" class="koboSpan">Intra-European
or intra-MERCOSUR trade has been increasing at a higher rate than trade
between these two regional blocks.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">Some of the
intra-regional trade growth certainly has less to do with transport but
rather with language barriers, historical trends, trade facilitation at
common borders, and lower intra-regional tariffs.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.137.2" class="koboSpan">But some of the
reasons do have a relation with transport costs and options: as shown
above, due to larger traded volumes, unit transport costs decline
(economies of scale) and frequencies and even possibly speed increases.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.137.3" class="koboSpan">Also, on a
regional level, more options (road, rail) are available.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.137.4" class="koboSpan">This in turn
reduces delivery times, allows for more just-in-time delivery, and thus
increases the demand for goods and components.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.137.5" class="koboSpan">In other words,
more trade leads to better and less expensive transport services, which
in turn again lead to more intra-regional trade.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">The impact of better
and less expensive transport on trade is equivalent to the impact of
lower tariffs, and the relatively faster growth of intra-regional trade
does not contradict the previous statement that goods and components are
increasingly purchased globally. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.138.2"
class="koboSpan">A large part of the growth of intra-regional trade
replaces previous national “trade”, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.138.3" class="koboSpan">between
counties or regions of the same country, and is not a diversion of
imports or exports that would otherwise be bought from or sold to
countries outside the region. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.138.4"
class="koboSpan">Just as “most analyses of Free Trade Agreements,
including most importantly by far the European Union, conclude that
trade creation has dominated trade diversion” (Bergsten, 1997), improved
transport costs and services on a regional level are to be seen as a
result and a component of the entire process of globalisation.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">Just as in the
relation between globalisation and international transport, the relation
between regional integration and regional transport is also two-fold:
Less expensive and better intra-regional transport services lead to
further regional integration, and at the same time regional integration
also affects the markets for transport services.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.139.2" class="koboSpan">Within the
European Union, maritime cabotage services are liberalised for European
registered vessels, trucks from all Member States are at liberty to move
national cargo in all other countries, and common standards help to
create not only a common market for goods, but also a common market for
transport services.</span>

### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">2.4 Outlook</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">Trade, and its
transport, will continue to shape the world’s economic development.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">Historically,
when transport costs were prohibitive for most products, each country,
or even town, would produce its own goods.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">Most countries
made their own toys, furniture, watches and even cars.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.141.4" class="koboSpan">Then came the
international economy; as transport costs went down and delivery times
and reliability improved, many national industries died out and
production became concentrated in a few, specialised places, from where
world markets were being served. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.141.5"
class="koboSpan">Cars and car parts were made in Detroit; watches, and
batteries, in Switzerland; furniture, and the required wood, were made
in Sweden.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">At present, we are
observing how the international economy gives rise to globalisation.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.142.2" class="koboSpan">As transport
costs decrease even further, and delivery times and reliability continue
to improve, production is again becoming less concentrated, albeit in a
different manner: cars may still be designed in Detroit, yet car parts
may be made in Mexico and assembly takes place in Malaysia; watches may
still be marketed as “Swiss”, yet most components are likely to be
imported; and a Swedish producer of furniture will franchise his name
and design, to produce local furniture with imported materials and
components from wherever these are provided at the best price and
quality.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_47"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">The same applies to shipping.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.143.2" class="koboSpan">A ship may be
registered in Antigua and Barbuda, but its owner can be German, and the
“components” of the shipping service, such as insurance, equipment, the
work of seafarers, or certificates of classification societies, are very
likely to have been purchased in many different countries.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.143.3" class="koboSpan">“The claim that
‘trade follows the flag’, often used in the past to justify support for
national fleets, has become primarily an argument of special interest
groups seeking support for maritime sector enterprises.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.143.4" class="koboSpan">It is agreed
that access to efficient maritime transport is a key variable in
economic development. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.143.5"
class="koboSpan">This does not necessarily imply fleet ownership or
government control” (Audigé, 1995).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.143.6" class="koboSpan">The next
section will look in more detail at how globalisation affects maritime
business.</span>

## <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.144.2" class="koboSpan">Globalisation and its Relevance for Maritime Business</span>

### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 The global supply chain</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">3.1.1 Global supply chain management</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">Although globalisation
is sometimes referred to as being Janus-faced for its inequitable
distribution of benefits among nations of the world, the perceptible
impact that it has had on international production and marketing are
beyond cynicism. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.147.2"
class="koboSpan">Porter (1985) thinks of the firm as a value chain
composed of a series of value creation activities, some of them (such as
production and marketing) being primary activities and the others (such
as logistics services that include shipping movements) being support
activities. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.147.3" class="koboSpan">As
firms tend to focus more on their core competencies and maintain their
competitive advantage in the global marketplace, the orientation towards
procuring raw materials and sub-assemblies from sources all over the
world, based on optimal purchasing arrangements, becomes even more
crucial. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.147.4" class="koboSpan">This,
along with the reduction in numerous trade barriers (because of the role
of the World Trade Organisation) and the apparent diminution of
ideological conflicts between leading nations of the world have led to
greater levels of outsourcing and thus, the diffusion of the value chain
across the oceans, and hence, the evolution of global supply
chains.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">Mentzer
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2001) argue that firms must have a supply chain
orientation to effectively manage the supply chain that could result in
lower costs, increased customer value and satisfaction, and competitive
advantage. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.150.2"
class="koboSpan">Leading edge logistics firms have recognised that it is
the supply chain of a firm that is in competition with that of its
competitors rather than the firms themselves (Christopher, 1992).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.150.3" class="koboSpan">The
establishment of such a supply chain requires the formation of strategic
alliances with channel members that include transportation service
providers, shipping companies being one among those.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.150.4" class="koboSpan">Integration of
transport activities is essential for the success of a supply chain and
a well-integrated transportation system’s contributions to the supply
chain could include time compression, reliability, standardisation,
just-in-time delivery, information systems support, flexibility and
customisation (Morash and Clinton, 1997).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.150.5" class="koboSpan">Although the
emphasis on building supply chain partnerships is a relatively new trend
in corporate strategy, it is not a novel concept in the maritime
business, two early examples being the evolution of the open registry
concept and that of the ship management industry.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_48"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">The objective of outsourcing non-core activities in
search of efficiency and adding value to the end customer is potentially
advantageous and adds to societal welfare – as long as the functions are
being performed at acceptable levels of quality which in today’s lexicon
for product standards is one of “zero defects”.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.151.2" class="koboSpan">The ship
owner’s effort to create a “least cost system” in the maritime business
is tantamount to designing a global supply chain based only on least
cost channel members.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">Whereas this may lead
to a loss of market share and corporate profits for the channel members
of a supply chain, deficiencies of the least cost maritime system could
have more drastic consequences, ranging from loss of life to global
climate change and environmental degradation that impacts society at
large besides the more traditional commercial losses of the business
enterprise. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.152.2"
class="koboSpan">Hence, while the temptations of using the cheapest crew
and registering the ship in a lax ship registry might be appealing to
the business acumen, the likely catastrophic magnitude of a mishap would
make the ship owner think hard before making such choices.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.152.3" class="koboSpan">Globalisation
and its underlying market forces appear to provide some guidance in this
regard as there are perceptible specialised markets for virtually any
aspect of the maritime business today that parallel the developments in
specialisation in a broader context.</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">3.1.2 Specialisation in maritime business</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">Readily observable
examples of specialisation exist in ship construction, technical
management of ships, ship repairs and dry-docking, ship registration,
crewing, shipping finance, ship chartering and brokering, and marine
insurance. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.154.2"
class="koboSpan">Analogous to the economic philosophy driving the new
trade theory in international business, some areas of specialisation in
shipping are an outcome of pro-active trade policies in combination with
luck, entrepreneurship and innovation that created a new breed of
first-movers in areas like open registries and ship construction and
repairs. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.154.3"
class="koboSpan">However, the socioeconomic conditions of the leading
nations (in specific areas of maritime specialisation) have also
contributed toward their evolution as global leaders.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">Examples of this
include small service economies that have specialised in open registries
(such as Panama, Cyprus, the Bahamas, or Bermuda), and large populous
Asian nations that provide seafarers (such as the Philippines, India,
and Indonesia). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.155.2"
class="koboSpan">Norway, combining tradition and financing from its oil
exports, is strong in shipping finance.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.155.3" class="koboSpan">London is a
leading supplier of insurance and brokering services in general,
including shipping. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.155.4"
class="koboSpan">Korea and Japan are highly industrialised countries
that build most of the world’s shipping tonnage.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.155.5" class="koboSpan">And then there
is China, not only the backbone of global commerce today but also the
primary stimulus for the unprecedented shipping boom that we witnessed
prior to the worldwide economic meltdown in 2008.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.155.6" class="koboSpan">China’s unique
style of unbridled capitalism combined with centralised planning has
elevated the nation to a position of extraordinary relevance and
abundance in shipping milieu. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.155.7"
class="koboSpan">Overall, there appears to exist a close relation
between a country’s endowment of resources and general specialisation in
services or industrial production and its specialisation in specific
maritime sectors, whereas the relation between the different maritime
sectors themselves appears to be increasingly weak.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">The other side of that
same coin is of course “concentration”; as countries specialise, the
market share of the major players is increasing (Hoffmann, 1998).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.156.2" class="koboSpan">Between January
2001 and 2008, Panama’s share of the world fleet (Gross Tons, GT) has
further grown
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_49"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">from 21 to about 23%.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Maersk now
controls 15% of the world’s container carrying capacity, up from around
6% in 1997. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.157.3" class="koboSpan">One
out of every three seafarer in 2008 was an Asian national and one out of
every two, either an Asian or an Eastern European.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.157.4" class="koboSpan">One out of
every two ships is registered in one of the top five registries (UNCTAD,
2009).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">If the world were
still divided into “maritime nations” and others, non-maritime nations
that do not participate in the maritime business, then the same
countries where carriers are based would also build and register the
ships and provide the seafarers. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.158.2"
class="koboSpan">A cross-country comparison based on indicators for
these maritime activities would produce very high correlation
coefficients. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.158.3"
class="koboSpan">The reality under globalisation, however, is quite
different.</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">3.1.3 Specialisation and clustering: The participation of Asian countries in globalised maritime business</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">Many Asian countries
have become important players in different maritime businesses.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.160.2" class="koboSpan">Bangladesh and
Pakistan have their highest market shares in ship scrapping; Indonesia
and the Philippines in the provision of ratings (seafarers other than
officers); Republic of Korea in container ship building; and Hong Kong
(China) and Singapore in international port operations through
Hutchison’s and PSA’s operations domestically and also abroad.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.160.3" class="koboSpan">Overall, Asian
countries have a greater participation in many maritime sectors than
Asia’s GDP or international trade would suggest
(</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0007" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0007"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00012.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"

<a href="#Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0007" id="Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0007"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
5</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">Asian maritime profile – Asia’s participation as
percentage of world total</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan"> Authors, based on data from different sources.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">Data is
estimated for 2004</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_50"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan">Different maritime businesses are not necessarily
located in the same countries.
</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_fig0014" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_fig0014"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan"> provides the correlation coefficients for different
industry sectors. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.171.2"
class="koboSpan">Note that a high and positive correlation should not be
confused with a direct causality.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.171.3" class="koboSpan">The data base
includes many small and landlocked countries that have zero
participation in most sectors.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">As could be expected,
port throughput and operation is closely correlated with foreign trade.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.172.2" class="koboSpan">Ship operation,
ownership and registration are also relatively strongly correlated, as
are the participation in P&I Clubs and Classification.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.172.3" class="koboSpan">Seafarers,
especially ratings, tend to come from countries with a long coastline,
which may be due to a seafaring tradition, which cannot be found in
landlocked regions or countries. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.172.4"
class="koboSpan">Ship scrapping takes place in countries that have
relatively little participation in other maritime sectors, and thus the
correlation coefficients get close to zero or even negative.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">What maritime sectors
are located in what (type of) countries?
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.173.2" class="koboSpan">As a first
preliminary exercise, we have computed the weighted average GDP per
capita of the countries that are host to different maritime sectors
(</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0008" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0008"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">Almost all sectors are
more commonly found in countries with a GDP per capita above the Asian
average and also above the world average.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.176.2" class="koboSpan">Only ship
scrapping and seafarers (especially ratings) are supplied by countries
with a relatively low GDP per capita.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.176.3" class="koboSpan">Officers are
more likely to come from countries with a higher GDP per capita than
ratings. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.176.4" class="koboSpan">The
service sectors of classification and insurance are those located in the
Asian countries with the highest GDP per capita.</span>

<div id="Ch02.xhtml_fig0013" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

alt="Figure 6: The GDP per capita in relation to different maritime sectors in Asia" /></span>

class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">The GDP per capita in relation to different maritime
sectors in Asia</span>

</div>

class="koboSpan">Note: </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">The 0% line indicates the average GDP per capita for 51
Asian countries, which is strongly influenced by the GDP per capita of

</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.182.2" class="koboSpan">The global
average GDP per capita is 131% above the Asian average.</span>

<div id="Ch02.xhtml_fig0014" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00014.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch02.xhtml_bck_fig0014)

</div>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_52"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">Most port and ship-related business activities are
based in countries whose weighted average GDP per capita is five to nine
times above the Asian average. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.184.2"
class="koboSpan">There probably exist mutual causalities.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.184.3" class="koboSpan">A country needs
a certain level of income and development to be able to become a strong
player in certain industries. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.184.4"
class="koboSpan">At the same time, being able to maintain a high market
share in different shipping sectors also contributes to a higher GDP per
capita.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">Understandably, most
countries’ policy makers would wish their country’s “maritime” market
shares to grow. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.185.2"
class="koboSpan">At the same time, the trend of concentration and
specialisation in the maritime industry leads to new challenges and
opportunities. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.185.3"
class="koboSpan">As the world can no longer be divided into maritime and
non-maritime nations, policy makers (and interested researchers and
international organisations) should attempt to find out which countries
are more likely to specialise in which maritime sectors, and why.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">As globalisation in
maritime business has led to increasing levels of specialisation in the
industry, this has had varying impacts on nations.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.186.2" class="koboSpan">Along with the
traditional maritime nations, a number of new maritime players have
evolved, some of which have very little maritime history or even a
coastline. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.186.3" class="koboSpan">A
good example is Switzerland, a land-locked nation, which is home to the
world’s largest freight forwarder and to Mediterranean Shipping Company,
one of the top five liner shipping companies in the world.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.186.4" class="koboSpan">According to
UNCTAD (2008), there are 258 Swiss ships – 29 flying the national flag
and the rest open-registry – that constitute 1.3% of the world fleet.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.186.5" class="koboSpan">The meteoric
growth of the Chinese maritime enterprise in the new millennium was
discussed earlier. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.186.6"
class="koboSpan">The following sub-section discusses salient policy
developments in traditional maritime nations as well as newcomers that
have shaped the course of maritime business.</span>

### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Policy issues</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">3.2.1 The decline of traditional maritime nations</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">The globalised economy
and the relatively invisible role played by the maritime sector in
facilitating it have led to predictable outcomes for the sector in
general. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.189.2" class="koboSpan">No one
attaches the same prominence to shipping today as Sir Walter Raleigh did
in the early 1600s when he linked the command of the sea to the
possession of the riches of the new world.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.189.3" class="koboSpan">The irony is
that the relative decline of the maritime political power is partly
because of the sophistication of contemporary shipping operations
wherein a cargo movement from Argentina to Zimbabwe or Mumbai to
Marseilles is as predictable as a commute to the suburbs.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.189.4" class="koboSpan">Thus, shipping
operations have become literally invisible in the global chain of
commerce, albeit still important and unavoidable.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.189.5" class="koboSpan">Accordingly,
the declining importance given to maritime issues is
understandable.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">Lovett (1996) provides
an excellent discussion of the rise and fall of various maritime
empires, from the Greeks and Phoenicians (480 BC) to the British, West
European and the US merchant fleet as of the early 1990s, and makes a
strong argument for a resurgence of maritime policy-making in the United
States. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.190.2"
class="koboSpan">Maritime economists have offered remedial measures to
stem the flow of maritime business interests of developed nations like
the US (e.g. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.190.3"
class="koboSpan">Kumar, 1994). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.190.4"
class="koboSpan">However, two powerful forces, in combination, have
solidified the ongoing decline of traditional maritime nations.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.190.5" class="koboSpan">One is the
power of the market forces driving the global economy and specialisation
in general, discussed earlier, and the other, the political reality at
the bargaining table.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_53"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">The political reality in the developed economies today
is such that shipping-related issues are subservient to the trade needs
of those nations. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.191.2"
class="koboSpan">The balance of power has swung visibly in favour of the
cargo owners from that of the transportation service providers (Kumar,
1987) as illustrated by the declining relevance of revered shipping
practices like the liner conference system.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.191.3" class="koboSpan">This has
impacted current transport policy-making, in the maritime sector as well
as in other modes. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.191.4"
class="koboSpan">Sletmo (2001) captures the contemporary maritime
policy-making trend by emphatically placing the supremacy of global
trade perspectives over maritime issues.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.191.5" class="koboSpan">Accordingly,
mode-specific transportation policy has become a doctrine of the past in
developed market economies, most of who were the major maritime nations
of the past. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.191.6"
class="koboSpan">Although one could argue that air movements are still
an exception because of the extensive use of bilateral negotiations
involved in air transportation, major developed nations today advocate
an integrated transport policy that favours seamless multimodal freight
movements in general.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">These nations have
thus assumed a more holistic approach in national transportation
policy-making that is conducive to the facilitation of a seamless
movement of its commerce. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.192.2"
class="koboSpan">Accordingly, the emphasis today in many developed
nations is not in the size of their fleet or their tonnage, but on
eradicating barriers to the through movement of cargoes.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.192.3" class="koboSpan">An excellent
example of this is the United States, the world’s largest trading nation
and the home of many former prestigious shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.192.4" class="koboSpan">Today, it is
left with relatively very little presence in the deep-sea fleet, in
spite of the Jones Act and other measures that oblige carriers to use US
flagged, built and manned vessels for cabotage services.</span>

<a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0009" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0009"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the maritime engagement of traditional maritime
nations as of end 2008. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.194.2"
class="koboSpan">It is to be noted that all the traditional maritime
nations with the exception of Germany and Japan have a greater share of
world trade in value than their percentage share of world fleet in
deadweight.
</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0010" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0010"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 8</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan"> (maritime engagement of newly emerging maritime
nations) however shows quite the contrary for the newly emerging
maritime nations most of who possess higher percentage of owned fleet
than their value share in international commerce.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.196.2" class="koboSpan">For Hong Kong
and Singapore, the percentage flag-share exceeds both the value
share</span>

class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
8</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime engagement of emerging new maritime nations,
