class="koboSpan"> UNCTAD, Review of Maritime Transport, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">and world fleet share
in dwt.
</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0011" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0011"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 9</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows a precipitous decline in the shipping fleet
registered in developed market economy nations, most of who also fall
under the traditional maritime countries category.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.211.2" class="koboSpan">The decline in
the fleet of these nations during the past 30 years is in direct
contrast to the gains made by fleets registered in open registry nations
and developing countries. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.211.3"
class="koboSpan">Presently, four out of every five merchant ships are
registered either under an open registry flag or in a developing
country, and owners from developed countries are more likely to choose a
foreign flag than those from countries with a lower GDP per capita
(Hoffmann </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.,</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan"> 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">Many countries’ trade
profiles in some way match their fleet profiles.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.214.2" class="koboSpan">Among the
countries with the largest shares of oil exports are Kuwait (93% of its
exports are fuels and mining products), Saudi Arabia (90%) Islamic
Republic of Iran (88%), Russia (68%), United Arab Emirates (53%) and
Indonesia (38%), and all of them also have the highest share of their
nationally controlled fleets in oil tankers.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.214.3" class="koboSpan">Among the
countries with the highest shares of agricultural exports are Brazil
(29% of its exports are agricultural products), Vietnam (21%), Indonesia
(18%), Thailand (16%), India (12%) and Turkey (10%).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.214.4" class="koboSpan">Among those
countries, Thailand, Turkey and Vietnam also have</span>

<div id="Ch02.xhtml_fig0017" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00017.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 9: Ship registration trends" /></span>

<a href="#Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0011" id="Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0011"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
9</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan">Ship registration trends</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan"> UNCTAD, Review of Maritime Transport, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_55"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">the highest shares of dry bulk carriers, and the other
three countries also have important dry bulk fleets.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.221.2" class="koboSpan">In China, Hong
Kong (China), Republic of Korea and Taiwan (Province of China) the dry
bulk fleet has the highest share, reflecting the large import demand of
iron ore, grains and other dry bulk products (UNCTAD 2008b, pp.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.221.3" class="koboSpan">41ff).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">A different picture
emerges if we look at manufactured goods, which are mostly traded in
containerised liner shipping services.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.222.2" class="koboSpan">These services
call in numerous countries’ ports, unlike oil tankers and bulk carriers,
which are usually employed on direct port-to-port voyages.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.222.3" class="koboSpan">Many container
ships are operated by companies different from the vessel owner (the
latter charters the ship to the company that provides the actual liner
shipping service). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.222.4"
class="koboSpan">All these aspects may explain why there does not appear
to exist a correlation between a country’s trade in manufactured goods
and its nationally controlled container ship fleet.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.222.5" class="koboSpan">Even China,
which accounts for about 25% of world containerised exports, has only a
very small share of containerships among its nationally controlled
fleet.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">The largest nationally
controlled fleets that also fly the national flag include oil tankers
from Brazil, India, Kuwait and Thailand; dry bulk carriers from Hong
Kong, India, Republic of Korea and Thailand as well as general cargo
ships from Indonesia, Russia, Thailand and Vietnam.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.223.2" class="koboSpan">In several
cases, these nationally flagged and nationally controlled ships are
employed in cabotage trades that often mandate the use of the national
flag, or they are nationally flagged as a consequence of some public
involvement in the vessel owning companies.</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">3.2.2 The rise of a new order in maritime business</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">While the traditional
maritime nations in general are losing their supremacy in the business,
a new group of nations have proactively enacted maritime policies that
favour their shipping base. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.225.2"
class="koboSpan">A 1996 attempt to classify nations based on their
attitude towards shipping in general listed these new centres of
maritime business as shipping-friendly whereas the policies of many of
the traditional maritime nations were listed under the shipping-hostile
category (Lovett, 1996). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.225.3"
class="koboSpan">Examples of the shipping-friendly category include
nations such as South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, all of which appear
prominently in </span>[<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
8</span>](#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0010)<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.227.2"
class="koboSpan">The ascendancy of these nations is usually focused on
specific aspects of the shipping business, such as ship operation and
construction in South Korea, or ship registration in smaller service
economies. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.227.3"
class="koboSpan">Some, such as Singapore, Brazil and China, do
apparently pursue all-out efforts to build the entire shipping milieu.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.227.4" class="koboSpan">It is entirely
conceivable in the near future that China will not only have the world’s
largest shipping companies but also the largest shipyards, busiest
ports, biggest maritime universities and the most envied maritime
infrastructure.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">It is noteworthy that
despite the efforts by shipping and seafarer organisations from some
traditional maritime nations, the open registry fleet has continued its
spectacular growth during the last two decades
(</span>[<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
9</span>](#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0011)<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.230.2"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the open registry nations have also
encountered increasing competition from some traditional maritime
nations like Norway and Denmark that have established international ship
registers to stem the outflow of their domestic tonnage to foreign
registries if not attract some of the previously lost tonnage back to
the national fleet.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">Governmental
interference in shipping has a long history (Farthing, 1993).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.231.2" class="koboSpan">Ever since the
British enacted their restrictive Navigation Acts in the mid-1600s the
global maritime business has never operated in so liberal a commercial
environment
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_56"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan">as it exists today.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.232.2" class="koboSpan">A rational
justification for this new wave of liberalism is the impact of
globalisation. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.232.3"
class="koboSpan">As maritime policies have become subservient to the
overall trade policies of major trading nations, the crux of the issue
is not the flag of registration but the overall
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">fit</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan"> of shipping services in the global supply chain.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.234.2" class="koboSpan">Under such
circumstances, the specialisation referred to earlier has led to a new
breed of maritime players where nationality is once again irrelevant.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.234.3" class="koboSpan">As an example,
the concept of giving away one’s flag to a ship owned by a foreign
entity (although not
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">pro bono</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">) and staffed by foreign crew is an illustration of
high shipping liberalism.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">A cursory examination
of the current breed of ship owners will show relatively few of the
historic shipping families but more so of investment firms, pension
funds and business conglomerates, none of which have any significant
shipping heritage. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.237.2"
class="koboSpan">Thus, it is ironical that globalisation has led to a
certain loss of identity and respectability for the industry.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.237.3" class="koboSpan">A perfect
example of this irony is the high public attention that the industry
receives when there is a shipping accident, but the total lack of
coverage that it receives from the media when it performs normally.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.237.4" class="koboSpan">The average
citizen today is more aware of the mistakes made by the maritime
industry rather than its contribution to the global commerce and our
standard of living. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.237.5"
class="koboSpan">The following subsection examines issues related to
safety at sea and employment conditions.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.237.6" class="koboSpan">It suggests
that the neo-liberalism in shipping policies has not meant a decline in
operating standards but on the contrary, a general improvement in the
safety of ships and the environment.</span>

### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Safety and employment: the victims of globalisation?</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.1 Safety at sea</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">The increasing
environmental awareness of the global community is vividly marked in all
aspects of life today including maritime business.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.240.2" class="koboSpan">Given the
inherent operating environment of merchant ships and their propensity to
be a major environmental polluter, the increasing safety and
environmental regulations imposed on the industry are only to be
expected. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.240.3" class="koboSpan">Major
shipping accidents in sensitive locations and the subsequent
investigations, such as the ones that followed
the</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan"> Erica</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan"> incidents have also tightened the maritime operational
environment.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">The International
Maritime Organization (IMO), established under the auspices of the
United Nations to promote safety standards in shipping and cleaner seas,
has a number of provisions aimed toward these objectives.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.245.2" class="koboSpan">Although some
of these conventions date back to the 1960s and 1970s, they have been
amended extensively to enhance the overall safety standards in a
globalised operating environment.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.245.3" class="koboSpan">Two recent
developments are particularly noteworthy, those being the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan">ISM (International Safety Management) Code Amendment to
the Safety of Life at Sea
Convention</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan">Amendments to the STCW (Standardization of Training,
Certification and Watchkeeping)
Convention</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan">.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan">The ISM Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and
Pollution Prevention</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"> extends the scrutiny of shipping operations and
management to the shore office and the decision makers therein.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.251.2" class="koboSpan">This is a
drastic change from prior efforts and aims to establish an
all-encompassing safety management system in compliance with legislative
and company requirements. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.251.3"
class="koboSpan">The amended
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan">STCW
Convention</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan"> introduced globally accepted minimum standards for
maritime training, evaluation criteria and assessment mechanisms.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.253.2" class="koboSpan">Given the
diversity in national origin
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_57"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan">of seafarers today and their varying levels of skill
and proficiency, the amendments have been propitious and timely.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">There is a concerted
multilateral effort now for ongoing scrutiny of the hardware and
software of the maritime business.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.255.2" class="koboSpan">Some
multilateral efforts originated as a unilateral initiative to enhance
safety and prevent pollution (such as the US Oil Pollution Act of 1990
that made double-hulls mandatory for oil tankers and certain other ships
calling at US ports and was subsequently matched by the IMO through
amendments to the multilateral
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan">MARPOL </span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan">Convention). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.257.2"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan"> incident off the Spanish coast and the pressure from
the EU led to rapid amendments to the MARPOL Convention in 2003.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.259.2" class="koboSpan">Accordingly,
single hull tankers that were to be phased out gradually by 2015 would
face an accelerated phase-out scheme by 2010.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.259.3" class="koboSpan">This does not
preclude a flag-state from extending the deadline up to 2015 for tankers
25 years and younger on a case-by-case basis.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.259.4" class="koboSpan">However, other
nations will have the right to ban such ships from entering their ports.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.259.5" class="koboSpan">The amendments
also include new double hull requirement for the transportation of heavy
grade oil such as heavy crude oil, fuel oil, bitumen, tar, and their
emulsions that came into effect from 5 April 2005.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.259.6" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
the Condition Assessment Scheme–enacted subsequent to the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan"> disaster off the Brittany coast of France in 1999
whereby flag-state administration would review and confirm the results
of a survey on a single hull tanker conducted by a classification
society to assess the condition of the ship concerned–has been expanded.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.261.2" class="koboSpan">The new CAS
requirement would apply to single hull tankers (5,000 dwt and above)
when they are 15 years old, in contrast to the previously established
25-year age threshold.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">Aside from these,
individual nations have signed agreements to enforce safety standards by
inspecting the ships that call their ports.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.262.2" class="koboSpan">Such Port State
Control agreements cover all major ship operating areas today and the
respective national enforcement authorities arrest ships that do not
meet the accepted minimum safety standards.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.262.3" class="koboSpan">As a further
embarrassment (and incentive to scrap unsafe ships), some national
authorities (e.g. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.262.4"
class="koboSpan">the UK) publish a list of “rogue” ships in the trade
media. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.262.5" class="koboSpan">Equasis
(</span>[<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan">www.equasis.org</span>](http://www.equasis.org)<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">) publishes inspection results from many P&I Clubs,
classification societies, and port state control organisations on a
global level.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">Along with the
governmental agencies, a number of non-governmental agencies such as
labour organisations (e.g. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.265.2"
class="koboSpan">the International Transport Workers’ Federation), ship
owners’ association, ship charterers, classification societies, marine
insurance firms and others have also raised the barriers and discourage
the operation of substandard ships.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.265.3" class="koboSpan">The overall
effect of these multi-pronged initiatives is visible in the following
charts that show the trend in maritime casualties, both ships lost as
well as oil spilled by ships (see
</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0012" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0012"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.266.1" class="koboSpan">Figures 10</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch02.xhtml_cap_lbl0013" id="Ch02.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0013"><span
id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.268.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.269.2"
class="koboSpan">Despite the increase in global shipping tonnage and
maritime activities in general, and despite the diffusion of ship
registration (in the neo-liberal maritime environment) to open registry
and developing nations, the safety record of the industry is laudable.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.269.3" class="koboSpan">Even one life
lost at sea is one too many, and the authors are not arguing that the
current level of safety at sea is beyond improvement, but quite the
contrary. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.269.4"
class="koboSpan">However, all numbers strongly suggest that maritime
safety is optimistic especially in light of the growing volumes of
trade. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.269.5" class="koboSpan">Another
important point to note is that the time lag between the incidence of a
shipping catastrophe in a sensitive region with political clout (such as
the EU) and the enactment of a new legislation aimed at preventing such
a catastrophe is becoming increasingly short.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.269.6" class="koboSpan">If such
regulatory steps are adopted as expeditiously (as in the</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00018.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 10: Number of ships lost" /></span>

class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
10</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.272.1"

class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan"> case) regardless of where the next shipping disaster
occurs, it would be truly spectacular progress toward safer sailing and
cleaner oceans.</span>

#### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.2 The seafarer dilemma</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.285.1" class="koboSpan">Any discussion of the
impact of globalisation on maritime business will be incomplete if the
human element is not included. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.285.2"
class="koboSpan">Various technological advances have helped reduce the
number of crew required on board a ship compared to the period before
the 1980s. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.285.3" class="koboSpan">This
has by no means diminished the role of seafarers in the maritime
business; on the contrary, crewing costs still constitute a major
component of the operating cost of a ship (Moore Stephens, 2008), and
crew-related issues remain relatively complex (IMO –
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan">Globalisation and the Role of the Seafarer
2001</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.287.2" class="koboSpan">The impacts of
globalisation on seafaring serve as excellent illustrations of the pros
and cons of globalisation in general.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_59"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.1"
class="koboSpan">Seafaring is a glorious profession and has no room for
error or negligence. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.2"
class="koboSpan">Indeed the education of a young sailor is incomplete if
it does not include indoctrination for facing calamities at sea or in
port. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.3"
class="koboSpan">Successful seafarers are unique individuals.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.4" class="koboSpan">The uniqueness
comes not from the possession of any extraordinary intellectual capacity
but from the possession of simple commonsense (euphemistically referred
at sea as behaving in a “seaman-like manner”) and from the willingness
to subject oneself to the rigors of self-discipline of the highest order
and separation from near and dear ones for prolonged periods of sailing.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.5" class="koboSpan">It also comes
from the individual’s mental and physical aptitude to face the unknown,
be that hurricane force winds, pirates, or militant stevedores pilfering
cargo in port. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.6"
class="koboSpan">The sea is certainly no place for incompetence,
negligence or complacency for it can be tranquil one day, and ruthless
another. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.7" class="koboSpan">The
only way a seafarer can gain respect from fellow shipmates is by knowing
his/her job and carrying it out in the most professional manner.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.8" class="koboSpan">These skills
are by no means restricted to any particular nationality, race, religion
or creed. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.9" class="koboSpan">On
the contrary, well-trained seafarers from a poor country can do the same
job as effectively as their well trained, colleagues from a developed
nation at drastically reduced cost to the ship owner.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.10" class="koboSpan">Herein lies
the dilemma – globalisation has opened up avenues of opportunity for
seafarers from developing countries at the expense of those from
traditional maritime countries such as the North European nations, the
United States and Japan. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.288.11"
class="koboSpan">An example of this is the recent
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan">Maersk</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan"> decision to replace 170 Danish deck officers with
“foreign competent officers at a much lower price”
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan">Journal of
Commerce</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1 October 2009).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">Today’s labour market
for seafarers is perhaps the most globalised; standards and minimum
wages are agreed globally. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.293.2"
class="koboSpan">These trends have created a schism and ruptured the
historic common bondage among seafarers of the world, built over the
years based on their professional pride and their wider view of the
world that their land-based colleagues often did not fathom.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.293.3" class="koboSpan">We live in an
era today where seafarer organisations in developed nations look upon
those from poorer nations as a potential threat to their livelihood, and
as a result, lobby for protectionist policies that restrict the mobility
of foreign crew members within their national borders.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.294.1" class="koboSpan">During the last few
decades, we have witnessed a tarnishing of the image of some seafarers,
in particular those from less developed countries who crew a majority of
the open registry and international registry vessels
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan">Ships of Shame
1992</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">).
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.296.2" class="koboSpan">However, it is
important to differentiate between the cause and the symptom.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.296.3" class="koboSpan">How many
seafarers truly want to go to sea and work on board an unsafe ship
without the expectation of coming back to their near and dear ones?
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.296.4" class="koboSpan">So, the fault
does not lie with the seafarers who crew substandard vessels, but with
those responsible for putting them on such ships without adequate
training and proper quality control in the first place.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.296.5" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
the argument that seafarers from developing countries are responsible
for all maritime disasters does not appear to be true as a number of
maritime casualties in the recent past involved ships that were crewed
by seafarers from developed nations (an example being the grounding of
the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">Exxon
Valdez</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">
off Alaska in the US).</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">Another dilemma facing
the global seafarer, especially those working on board open registry
vessels, can be attributed to the declining number of traditional ship
owners discussed earlier. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.299.2"
class="koboSpan">As ship ownership and operation shift from traditional
ship owners to pension funds and conglomerates that seek instant gain
from the sale and purchase market (for ships) or from certain tax
exemption loopholes, the seafarers’ roles and functions have been
marginalised and their loyalty made meaningless.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.299.3" class="koboSpan">With the
increasing number of open registry vessels and the outsourcing of ship
and crew management
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_60"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan">(discussed earlier), the relationship between the
management entity and the ships’ crew may sometimes not exceed the
length of a contract today unlike the life-long relationship of the
bygone pre-globalisation era. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.300.2"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, ship managers providing the crew for open
registry vessels as well as other fleets often find themselves in a
highly competitive market where there is little room for the ongoing
training of seafarers, especially given the tendency of some of their
principals to switch their management companies frequently.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.300.3" class="koboSpan">This is truly
ironic as the challenges of seafaring have never been more than what
they are now, despite all the technological advances made by
humankind.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.301.1" class="koboSpan">Currently there are
close to 1.5 million seafarers worldwide of which 44% come from Asian
countries. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.301.2" class="koboSpan">It
is estimated that there is a worldwide shortage of 33,000 officers
presently and that it will worsen in future years.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.301.3" class="koboSpan">Recruiting
seafarers has become a huge challenge even in traditional seafarer
export nations like India where changing macroeconomic conditions have
taken away the charm of a career at sea.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.301.4" class="koboSpan">Adding fuel to
the fire is the tendency to criminalise mariners irrationally.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.301.5" class="koboSpan">The collision
involving </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">Hebei
Spirit</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.303.1" class="koboSpan">,
a VLCC off the coast of South Korea that was hit by an errant heavy-lift
crane barge in 2007, is a good illustration of the seemingly
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">reverse burden of proof
</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.305.1" class="koboSpan">standard
imposed on innocent seafarers. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.305.2"
class="koboSpan">Although the actions of the ship’s Captain and Chief
Officer were endorsed as extraordinarily prudent and seamanlike by
virtually every professional association of seafarers, they were given
tough jail sentences and released only after prolonged worldwide
protest. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.305.3" class="koboSpan">The
Captain of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan">, the infamous 1999 tanker casualty off the Brittany
coast, was incarcerated immediately without trial.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.307.2" class="koboSpan">Nine years
later in 2008, he was found innocent and released.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.307.3" class="koboSpan">Such callous
treatment of seafarers does not support initiatives to recruit the
younger generation such as through IMO’s
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan">Go to Sea</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan"> campaign that began in late 2008 or its observing 2010
as the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan">year of the
seafarer</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Outlook</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">The conflicting nature
of public arguments regarding the impact of globalisation in general was
mentioned earlier. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.313.2"
class="koboSpan">There is a strong sentiment in the media that
multinationals and their home nations (typically, developed countries)
would benefit more than the developing countries who are likely to
suffer from the abuses of globalisation ranging from exploitation to
cultural degradation. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.313.3"
class="koboSpan">It is remarkable that the arguments are quite the
contrary when one looks at the impact of globalisation on maritime
business. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.313.4" class="koboSpan">The
traditional maritime nations appear to be on the losing end in terms of
national tonnage and loss of shipping-related jobs, and perceive the new
centres of shipping business (and specialisation) as potential threats
to their maritime interests. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.313.5"
class="koboSpan">Developing and newly industrialised nations, on the
contrary, appear to be the winners with increasing number of ships under
their control and better career opportunities for their seafarers.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.313.6" class="koboSpan">This trend will
continue in the neo-liberal era of maritime policies and business
environment.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">The most encouraging
outlook from our perspective is the increasing level of safety at sea
which we hope will continue to improve.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.314.2" class="koboSpan">This means
that, so far, the improvements in the quality, frequencies, reliability
and costs of maritime transport have not implied an increase in negative
externalities. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.314.3"
class="koboSpan">The challenge for policy makers will be to observe and
monitor potential future monopolistic abuses in a concentrating
industry, and to
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_61"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan">assure adequate standards of training, working
conditions and pay levels for seafarers, the pioneers on the world’s
most globalised labour market.</span>

## <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.316.2" class="koboSpan">Summary and Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">As trade in
merchandise and unfinished goods increases, so does the demand for
maritime transport services. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.317.2"
class="koboSpan">These services form part of the global logistics chain
that determines a good’s competitiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">At the same time, the
maritime business is itself strongly affected by globalisation.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.318.2" class="koboSpan">Trade in
maritime services is one of the most liberalised industries, and its
“components" such as vessels, flag registration, class inspections,
insurance and the work of seafarers are purchased globally.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">The results of these
two trends are manifold, and some may even appear to be
contradictory:</span>

- <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.320.1" class="koboSpan">The market for
  maritime transport services is growing.
  </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.320.2" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless
  the specialisation of countries in certain maritime areas has implied
  that today there are fewer remaining players in individual maritime
  sectors.</span>
- <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.321.1" class="koboSpan">A country's national
  shipping business has ever less to do with its national external
  trade. </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.321.2"
  class="koboSpan">Whereas in the past, for historic reasons and due to
  protectionist cargo reservation regimes, foreign trade was mainly
  moved by vessels registered and owned by companies of the trading
  partners themselves, who employed national seafarers and nationally
  constructed vessels, today most carriers earn their income
  transporting other countries' trade, and the trade of most countries
  is largely moved by foreign shipping companies.</span>
- <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">We observe increased
  concentration in the maritime industry, yet at the same time the
  intensity of competition has not declined.
  </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.322.2" class="koboSpan">This does not
  mean that fewer suppliers are
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
  class="koboSpan">per se</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
  class="koboSpan"> good for competition, but the impact of
  globalisation leads to both - fewer suppliers and more
  competition.</span>
- <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.325.1" class="koboSpan">Transport unit costs
  decline, and yet the incidence of maritime transport costs in the
  final value of a good increases.
  </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.325.2" class="koboSpan">The value of
  the final good not only includes its transport costs from origin to
  destination, but also the transport costs of all the components that
  have been purchased internationally.</span>
- <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.326.1" class="koboSpan">Lower transport
  costs are closely related to more trade.
  </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.326.2" class="koboSpan">This is
  partly because lower prices (freight rates) obviously encourage
  demand, and also because economies of scale lead to lower unit
  transport costs.</span>
- <span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.327.1" class="koboSpan">Ever more cargo is
  being moved across the oceans, benefiting from better maritime
  transport services and lower costs.
  </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.327.2" class="koboSpan">This has
  generally not been at the cost of safety at sea, but, on the contrary,
  the globalisation of standards by the IMO and ILO help to reduce the
  negative externalities of shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">“Transport undoubtedly
belongs to the most complicated, and therewith fascinating economic
sectors” (Verhoef
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.,</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan"> 1997). </span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.330.2"
class="koboSpan">As mainstream economists attempt to tackle the causes
and impacts of globalisation, international transport is re-entering the
debate on trade models and development theories.
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.330.3" class="koboSpan">As maritime
transport is the true
</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_page_62"></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
class="koboSpan">nexus between all trading nations, the role for
maritime economists (and IAME) in this ongoing debate is clear and
beyond doubt.</span>

</span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.529.3" class="koboSpan">(1986):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.530.1"
class="koboSpan">The Economic Environment of International
Business</span></span><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.531.1" class="koboSpan">
(4th edn.), (Prentice Hall).</span>

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch02.xhtml_kobo.533.1"

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_66"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_67"></span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 3</span>\
<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Patterns of International Ocean Trade</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0099)
============================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Douglas</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">K.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Fleming</span></span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0088" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0088"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">In 2007, before the
impacts of a global economic recession had been fully realised, nearly
7.5 billion metric tonnes of goods were shipped in commercial oceanborne
trade. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">The ocean
transport task for this movement translated to more than 31 trillion
tonne-miles.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0089" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0089"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan"> Roughly 59% of the total cargo volume moved in bulk.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">These impressive
dimensions of world seaborne trade leave unrecorded a huge amount of
empty space and deadweight lifting capacity of merchant ships steaming
in ballast towards their next loading range or leaving their loading
range only partly full of revenue cargo.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.10.3" class="koboSpan">Empty cargo
space, like empty seats on passenger airplanes, reflects something lost
forever, while vessel operating costs continue inexorably.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.10.4" class="koboSpan">This lost
potential, to an extent inevitable because of basic global patterns and
geographic separation of commodity production and commodity consumption,
will be a recurring theme in this chapter.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">The opening section of
this study contains a few reflections on centuries-old trading patterns
for ships under sail. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.11.2"
class="koboSpan">Today’s bulk commodity trades, which generate many
millions of miles of ballast steaming, each year will then be examined.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.11.3" class="koboSpan">Possibilities
for combining different bulk trades in some sort of logical geographic
sequence will be considered. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.11.4"
class="koboSpan">The general cargo trades, with particular focus on
container line service, will be investigated.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.11.5" class="koboSpan">The directional
imbalances of cargo flow on the main liner routes will be noted and
possible network adjustments and service scenarios to cope with the
empty space problem will be presented for consideration.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.11.6" class="koboSpan">Finally,
prospects for the twenty-first century will be briefly outlined.</span>

## <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">Early Patterns Under Sail</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">Thirty years ago A.D.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.13.2" class="koboSpan">Couper’s
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">The Geography of Sea
Transport</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan">” appeared on the bookshelves of students interested in
ocean trade and transport (Couper, 1972).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Professor
Couper, master mariner, geographer and head of the Department of
Maritime Studies at the University of Wales Institute of Science and
Technology (UWIST), was an expert on ocean trade patterns.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.15.3" class="koboSpan">In his book
there is a thought-provoking map entitled “World Wind
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_68"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan">Systems (January) and ocean routes of European sailing
vessels”. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">It is
drawn to a cylindrical projection, stretching apart meridians of
longitude, as does Mercator’s projection.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">It covers a
“world and a quarter” so that the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans
can be seen in uninterrupted form.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.16.4" class="koboSpan">On it are
depicted, with sweeping arrows, the major wind systems encountered at
sea in January, and five historic trade routes in the sailing ship era –
the Guinea trade triangle, the Dutch East India Co route between
Amsterdam and the East Indies, the clipper ship route between Europe and
Australia, the transatlantic Anglo-American colonial route and the
transpacific Acapulco-Manila Spanish galleon
route.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0090" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0090"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">The correlation between
the favouring winds and the chosen tracks for the trading vessels stands
out clearly on Couper’s map. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.18.2"
class="koboSpan">One knows that the chosen tracks shift seasonally as
the prevailing winds shift. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.18.3"
class="koboSpan">By summertime, for example, southwest monsoons replace
northeast monsoons in the Indian Ocean.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Basically this is a
pre-industrialisation, pre-liner service picture.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">To it one might
add many other Portuguese, Spanish, French, Dutch and British “imperial
routes” connecting mother countries with their colonies.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.19.3" class="koboSpan">And many of the
routes were controlled by state-franchised trading companies.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.19.4" class="koboSpan">To be sure, most
of these old transoceanic paths of commerce have been displayed in
historical
atlases,</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0091" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0091"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan"> usually in the form of simple lines curving around
continents and across oceans, joining points of origin and points of
destination with no attention to precise tracks, much less to seasonal
variations in ocean tracks. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.21.2"
class="koboSpan">Couper’s map suggests much more.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.21.3" class="koboSpan">Removing his
Guinea trade triangle and simplifying his winds to include only the
voyage-speeding westerlies and the trades, we have the graphic image
reflected in
</span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0014" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0014"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.23.2"
class="koboSpan">One might add to this image the patterns of favouring
ocean currents which all mariners seek.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">These old trading
patterns were “round voyages”, with outbound and homeward legs of the
voyage quite often following very different paths, not only because of
prevailing winds, ocean currents and weather but also, in the case of
the Anglo-American colonial route, to pick up and deposit cargo en
route, e.g. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">in
the Caribbean and heading north along the American east coast.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.24.3" class="koboSpan">Generally,
two-way cargo flows were available on the Spanish-controlled
Acapulco-Manila route, the Dutch-controlled East Indies route and, later
on, the British-controlled Australian route.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.24.4" class="koboSpan">However, in
cargo volume terms, there could be large directional imbalances and
seasonal variations. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.24.5"
class="koboSpan">The ships engaged in these trades were, by modern
standards, very small and often the cargoes were valuable goods –
silver, gold, silks, spices, for instance – that took up little cargo
space but generated high freight revenues when rates were
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">ad valorem</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan">-based. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.26.2"
class="koboSpan">And the “organised” nature of the trade routes
mentioned above, since they were controlled by the imperial state or by
a powerful state-franchised trading company, meant that the ships
serving the trades had fair assurance of onward or homeward cargoes.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.26.3" class="koboSpan">Empty space on
long ballast voyages was not the important consideration it was to
become in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.26.4" class="koboSpan">It should be
noted that these were, by modern definition, at least, tramp trades,
however well organised, served by relatively small, multi-purpose
sailing vessels adaptable to various cargo types, not excluding human
cargoes, slaves or emigrants.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately the
mercantilist philosophy that was fashionable in Europe in the
seventeenth, eighteenth and part of the nineteenth centuries led to
highly protected trades in which mother countries paired off with their
own colonies, enacted navigation laws which favoured ships of their own
flag and often used high tariffs against imports from rival empires.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">Merchant fleets
were really armed merchant navies, commanded to serve the state.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.27.3" class="koboSpan">When one views
these mercantilist systems in global perspective, it is clear that they
led to geographically inefficient networks in the form of many
shuttle</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0020" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00020.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: World wind systems (January) and ocean routes of European sailing vessels" /></span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_69"></span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0014" id="Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0014"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">:</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan"> World wind systems (January) and ocean routes of
European sailing vessels</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_70"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan">services within imperial frames and relatively little
“cross-trading” that could have reduced the amount of empty cargo space
sailing unproductively across the oceans.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">Ironically these
shuttle service patterns between imperial home ports and distant
overseas colonies were somewhat analogous to the much more recent UNCTAD
40–40–20 scheme for splitting cargo allotments and ocean transport
privileges 40–40 between trade partners (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.32.3" class="koboSpan">a developed and
a developing nation) and leaving only 20% for “cross-traders”.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.32.4" class="koboSpan">Of course the
political, social and general economic motivations for the two sets of
shuttle service patterns were vastly different.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.32.5" class="koboSpan">Yet the fact
remains that the general back-and-forth route configurations were quite
alike and there was a consequent accentuation of the empty cargo space
problem when there were striking differences in the volumes of cargo
flowing in either direction, as there almost always were.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0014)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan"> reveals the remarkable clipper ship route in the
Australian trade in the 1850s, outbound from Britain via Cape of Good
Hope and homeward via Cape Horn. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.34.2"
class="koboSpan">From a point in the South Atlantic, usually closer to
South America than Africa, these very fast, fine-lined sailing ships
swooped south of Cape of Good Hope into the “roaring forties” zone of
westerlies and along a looping approximation of the great circle route
to the southern coast of Australia.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.34.3" class="koboSpan">Homeward bound
in an easterly direction, the ships again dipped far into the Southern
Ocean, again with following westerly winds, and again approximating a
great circle track past Cape Horn.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.34.4" class="koboSpan">These were
ships, both American and British-owned, at the dawn of the free trade
era in the 1850s, that took maximum advantage of the winds, currents,
navigational aids of the time, and the cargo potentials, to turn profits
for their owners.</span>

## <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">British Impact on Ocean Trading Networks</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">As the world’s
front-runner in massive industrialisation, Britain by the mid-nineteenth
century seemed to have the world of commerce by its tail.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.36.2" class="koboSpan">Having abandoned
the mercantilist doctrines of the past for the principles and practices
of free trade, Britain was a leader in seaborne trade, building what
became the world’s largest steam-powered merchant fleet and the world’s
most highly developed banking, chartering, insuring, shipping and other
trade related services concentrated in the old City of London.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">The curious thing about
Britain’s spectacular and, to some extent, unilateral movement toward
freer trade was that it took place in the imperial frame, in an empire
that spread over the globe. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.37.2"
class="koboSpan">Perhaps it made practical sense to be a free-trading
imperialist when you led the world in the production of goods and
services. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.37.3" class="koboSpan">Not to
say that Britain traded only within the imperial frame, but the latter
certainly had an impact on the networks of ocean trade that were handed
down from the sailing ship era, reinforcing the radial patterns
emanating from home base. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.37.4"
class="koboSpan">If one added the radial patterns of the French and
other European powers to the British hub and spoke pattern and put the
whole in global perspective it gave a pronounced Eurocentric impression
of world commerce in the latter part of the nineteenth century.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.37.5" class="koboSpan">And it was not
really a false impression. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.37.6"
class="koboSpan">Western Europe
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan">was</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan"> the hub of world commerce.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">However, this
set of Europe-based radial networks did not necessarily reflect the most
efficient transportation system. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.39.3"
class="koboSpan">Network analysts in the modern era have noted that pure
hub and spoke networks have minimal connectivity.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.39.4" class="koboSpan">There is only
one path from any one spoke end to any other and that is via the
hub.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">A.J.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.40.2" class="koboSpan">Sargent, British
commercial geographer, recognised this network connectivity problem long
ago in his unusually perceptive study,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan">Seaways of the
Empire</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.42.2" class="koboSpan">From
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_71"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">early twentieth century data he traced movements of
British shipping in South African, Indian, Australian and other
commonwealth trades, finding that ships “disappeared” from one trade and
“reappeared” in another. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.43.2"
class="koboSpan">In between was a “hidden” ballast-voyage or half-empty
intermediate voyages moving ships to other trade routes.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.43.3" class="koboSpan">Of course this
is common tramp shipping behaviour and not infrequent liner behaviour,
and it shows that British steamship lines before World War I had ways of
coping with the radial networks and directional imbalances of trade
volumes on specific routes. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.43.4"
class="koboSpan">It reminds us, too, that, for British shipowners then,
and most shipowners today, “ocean lines are not worked for purposes of
philanthropy but to pay dividends” (Sargent, 1930, p.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.43.5" class="koboSpan">15).</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">Although we may have
heard more about their spectacular passenger liners, the British
merchant fleet in the two decades prior to World War I contained a large
number of multi-purpose freighters in the 7,000 to 8,000 deadweight
tonnage range. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.44.2"
class="koboSpan">These could be used either in tramp or liner service.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.44.3" class="koboSpan">Quite often
there would be outbound cargoes of coal from Britain to coaling stations
around the globe and return cargoes of the various products of the
colonies or other overseas areas the British lines were willing to and
allowed to serve. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.44.4"
class="koboSpan">The versatility of most of these vessels was an
important attribute, enabling the steamship lines to adjust to
directional imbalances on trade routes, ballast to other trades, if
necessary, and, in general, minimise the empty cargo space problem by
reducing the amount of non-paying ballast steaming.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">The British
coal-burners were the forerunners of the thousands of oil-burning
“10,000 tonners”, the American Liberty, Victory, and C2 types built
during World War II. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.45.2"
class="koboSpan">These vessels had the built-in flexibility and
adaptability for the carriage of various bulk and break-bulk cargoes in
various trades. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.45.3"
class="koboSpan">The prototype of the slow but amazingly serviceable
American Liberty ship was, by the way, British-designed.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.45.4" class="koboSpan">Sixty of them
were contracted to be built in American yards for the British early in
World War II (Gibson and Donovan, 2000, p.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.45.5" class="koboSpan">166).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.45.6" class="koboSpan">The thousands of
Liberty-size vessels built between 1942 and 1945 became an essential
component in Allied wartime convoys and supply chains.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">In retrospect, the
British, controlling a large portion of the world’s pre-World War I
merchant fleet, had a remarkable impact on the patterns of nineteenth
and early twentieth century ocean shipping.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.46.2" class="koboSpan">Americans must
concede, also, that it was the British who selected New York as the main
distribution point for goods that had accumulated during the War of 1812
awaiting entry into the American market.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.46.3" class="koboSpan">This gave New
York’s port its great leap forward (Albion, 1939,
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">chap.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.47.2"
class="koboSpan">1</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_ht0058)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.48.2"
class="koboSpan">It was a small group of expatriate British textile
merchants, originally from Yorkshire, who formed Black Ball Line to
provide the very first transatlantic liner service between New York and
Liverpool. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.48.3" class="koboSpan">Black
Ball booked baled cotton diverted to New York from southern US ports for
their eastbound transatlantic voyages and then lined up Yorkshire and
Lancashire textile goods for their westbound voyages (Albion, 1939, pp.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.48.4" class="koboSpan">99–100).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.48.5" class="koboSpan">It was the
British, again, who propelled world shipping into the use of
iron-hulled, propeller-driven steamships.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.48.6" class="koboSpan">And it was
Britain that gave the world the theories and, especially from 1850 to
1875, the practices of free international trade (Ellsworth, 1958,
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">chap.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.49.2"
class="koboSpan">4</span>](#Ch04.xhtml_ht0119)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

## <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">Bulk Commodity Trades: 2007</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">A.J.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.52.2" class="koboSpan">Sargent
remarked, long ago: “The ultimate determining element in the employment
of shipping lies in the sum of the geographical conditions of each
region in relation to those of other regions of the world, though the
effect of such conditions
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_72"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan">may be modified greatly by economic or political policy
on the part of individuals or Governments.”
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">(Sargent, 1931,
p. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.53.3" class="koboSpan">25).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.53.4" class="koboSpan">Sargent’s
comment pertained to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan">any</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan"> seaborne commodity trade.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">It certainly
would apply to bulk commodity shipping today, perhaps with the insertion
of “or corporations” between “individuals” and “Governments”.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">The tonnage imbalances
between exports and imports for regions of the world and for individual
ports are most striking in the bulk commodity trades.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">Very seldom are
there two way cargo flows between regions for the bulk movement of oil,
coal, iron ore or grain, even though these four broad commodity
categories contain different sub-types and grades.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.56.3" class="koboSpan">However, there
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan">are</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"> two-way movements of the ships that carry these
materials. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.58.2" class="koboSpan">One
way they are laden with cargo. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.58.3"
class="koboSpan">The other way they are ballasting, very often returning
to the original loading range, signifying that half the voyage steaming
is in ballast, a regrettable but seemingly inevitable waste of cargo
space. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.58.4" class="koboSpan">This, of
course, reflects the basic commercial geographic reality that raw
material supply sources and the markets for these materials are often
separated by large transoceanic mileages.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.58.5" class="koboSpan">It also suggests
that both shippers and carriers have been somewhat resigned to shuttle
service itineraries.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">Over the past half
century the rise of proprietary carrier fleets – oil companies owning,
or controlling by long-term charters, fleets of tankers; steel making
companies controlling dry bulk carrier fleets for the movement of their
inputs of coking coal, iron ores, etc.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">– seems to
accentuate the long ballast voyage problem.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.3" class="koboSpan">The ships
engaged in these proprietary carrier trades are often very large and
specially built for the carriage of one commodity type.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.4" class="koboSpan">There is a
built-in inflexibility when such vessels are employed.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.5" class="koboSpan">Their operations
may be confined to a back-and-forth shuttle service.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.6" class="koboSpan">The primary
purpose of the fleet is to serve the transport needs of the corporation;
therefore the emphasis has been on transport timing, cost, and
reliability, in other words on the production function.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.7" class="koboSpan">The focus,
understandably, is not on revenues from shipping since shipping is
viewed by the firm as an “in house” and “at cost” service.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.8" class="koboSpan">Unless the
normal intra-firm movements of materials are in some way disrupted, the
proprietary carrier fleet is not inclined to move from one trade route
to another. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.59.9" class="koboSpan">It
stays in the trade for which it was designed and built, or for which it
was chartered.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">The independent tramp
operator of the past and a dwindling number of owners of multi-purpose
or combined carrier fleets, today, might be inclined to move from one
trade route to another, seeking efficient geographic patterns that
maximise their rate of utilisation on paying cargo and minimise ballast
steaming.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0092" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0092"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan"> Whether this results in profit, assuming profits are
desirable, depends also, of course, on the revenue side of the
equation.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Market locations</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">In the last half of the
twentieth century many scholars in a variety of social sciences became
enamoured with concepts of “cores and peripheries”.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.64.2" class="koboSpan">Geographers
struggled to define, in precise and mappable terms, the core industrial
regions of the world. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.64.3"
class="koboSpan">The unevenness of industrial development in the spatial
sense makes this difficult. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.64.4"
class="koboSpan">Very often the available statistical data pertained to
the nation, not to the regions within it.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.64.5" class="koboSpan">And, as one
famous historian observed,
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">All</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan"> advanced economies have their ‘black holes’”, their
local pockets of backwardness (Braudel, 1984, p.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">42).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">Economists
identified the processes and stages of economic growth, the leading
sectors in specific countries, the industrial concentrations and
industrial linkages. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.66.4"
class="koboSpan">They even assigned time frames to the stages of growth
(Rostow, 1962, </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">chap.13</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_ht0313)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan">) but they were not particularly concerned with the
precise geographic dimensions. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.68.2"
class="koboSpan">However, scholars in the field of
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_73"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan">regional science (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">August Losch,
Edgar Hoover, Walter Isard) have recognised some of the intra-national
changes in industrial location which continually re-shape cores and
peripheries.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">It is well supported
statistically that the world’s most massive industrial developments over
the past two-and-a-half centuries took place in Western Europe, eastern
North America and eastern Asia, setting a pattern that profoundly shaped
ocean trade flows. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.70.2"
class="koboSpan">The early industrial cores experienced rapid growth of
the manufacturing sector, originally fuelled by coal and given great
economic momentum by ferrous metallurgy and metalusing industries.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.70.3" class="koboSpan">These regions
still contain very large markets for seaborne shipments of oil, iron
ore, coal and grain. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.70.4"
class="koboSpan">They are densely populated, too.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.70.5" class="koboSpan">To conform to
today’s realities, however, one could expand those three economically
advanced and populous regions to include all of Europe, all of North
America, and an Asia that extends from Vladivostok to Singapore to the
Indian subcontinent, parts of the Middle East and includes the islands
and archipelagoes of eastern and southeastern Asia.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.70.6" class="koboSpan">This, of course,
amounts to a gross, mostly northern hemispheric, geographic
generalisation, but it does identify three continental
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">loci</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan"> for industrial concentrations and economic growth that
generate a huge portion of world trade today.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.72.2" class="koboSpan">To be sure there
are “black holes”, rust belts, regions of economic decline.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.72.3" class="koboSpan">There are also
new industries, new technologies, new communications, new linkages and
new industrial and service locations.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.72.4" class="koboSpan">Modern
industrial globalisation and corporate outsourcing strategies complicate
the patterns of industry and commerce.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.72.5" class="koboSpan">Networks have
become more extensive and intricate.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.72.6" class="koboSpan">The southern
hemisphere and emerging economies are definitely part of the present and
future commercial picture.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">It is noteworthy that
the world’s largest markets for seaborne bulk shipments of oil, iron
ore, coal and grain are still in the northern hemisphere.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">It should be
noted, too, that a relatively small number of very large oil companies
and mining and steel-making enterprises have a great deal to do with
three of the four major bulk commodity trades.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Crude oil</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">Crude oil seaborne
shipments exceed those of any other bulk cargo movements, constituting
nearly 24% of total world seaborne trade in
2007.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0093" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0093"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan"> This tanker-borne crude oil trade totaled 1,775
million metric tonnes.
</span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0015" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0015"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan"> depicts origins and destinations and directions of
movement of 75% of the total seaborne volume of crude oil shipments in
2007.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">The major destinations
for these crude oil shipments were the oil refineries of eastern Asia,
western and Mediterranean Europe, and the east, west and Gulf coasts of
North America. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.80.2"
class="koboSpan">The largest crude oil importers were the United States,
Japan and China. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.80.3"
class="koboSpan">It is worth noting that the Europe that contains the
enlarged 27-member European Union which, if considered a bloc, is a very
important crude oil
importer.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0094" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0094"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Middle East is the primary source of supply for
these crude oil shipments but the Caribbean (Venezuela and Mexico,
especially) and both West African and North African supply sources are
important too. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.82.2"
class="koboSpan">Compared to these major sources, southeast Asian
oilfields, the North Sea offshore fields, oil piped to Near East
terminals on the Mediterranean coast for tanker shipment onward, and
Russian oil piped to Black Sea terminals generate minor, but regionally
significant, tanker trades. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.82.3"
class="koboSpan">Russia was the world’s largest crude oil producer in
2007 but domestic consumption and pipeline deliveries to points west in
Europe cut back seaborne exports.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">Both the United States
and China have been important crude oil producers as well as consumers.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">Once
self-sufficient, they now find themselves alarmingly dependent on</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0021" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00021.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Major crude oil trade routes, 2007" /></span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_74"></span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0015" id="Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0015"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan">:</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan"> Major crude oil trade routes, 2007</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_75"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan">oil imports. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.88.2"
class="koboSpan">Industrial development and a recently surging economy
plus, so far, negligible domestic oil production have placed India in
the same boat as the US, China and Japan as significant importers of
tanker-borne oil.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">Tanker itineraries
depend in part on the size and loaded draft of the vessels.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.89.2" class="koboSpan">Very large crude
carriers cannot transit the Suez Canal or the Malacca and Singapore
Straits, fully loaded, and must round the Cape of Good Hope on their
laden voyages to Europe, and the Lombok and Makassar Straits on their
laden voyages to East Asian destinations.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">Not depicted on
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0015)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the sizeable crude oil flow from Valdez, Alaska by
tanker to western US termini and refineries.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">This has been an
US domestic, “protected” trade. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.92.3"
class="koboSpan">Also not depicted are the refined products shipped in
smaller tankers, usually on shorter voyages, for instance from Caribbean
refineries to US Gulf coast and US east coast markets; and from
Southeast Asian refineries to East Asian markets.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.92.4" class="koboSpan">The total
tonnage of the oceanborne refined oil products trade amounted to 553
million metric tonnes in 2007, an impressive volume of seaborne trade,
almost a third as much as the volume of the crude oil trade.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.92.5" class="koboSpan">Also omitted
from the picture in </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0015)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the quite significant movement of liquefied natural
gas which requires specialised and expensive vessels and terminal
facilities.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Iron ore</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Iron ore in crude,
sintered or pelletised form is shipped by sea transport from sources on
all the world’s inhabited continents to metallurgical regions which have
been located predominately in the northern hemisphere.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">The arrowed lines of
</span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0016" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0016"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
class="koboSpan"> depict origins, destinations and directions of
movement of the main oceanborne flows of bulk iron ore in 2007,
representing major high volume routes and 83% of total volume of
seaborne iron ore shipments in that year.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">Total sea-borne
iron ore shipments in 2007 measured nearly 800 million tonnes,
generating more than 4.5 trillion tonne-miles in ocean transport.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.3" class="koboSpan">East Asia and
Europe were the big recipients. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.4"
class="koboSpan">In recent years, the two countries exporting the
highest volumes of iron ore have been Australia and Brazil.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.5" class="koboSpan">Australia has
been a big supplier for Japanese steelworks but China has emerged in
recent years as the world’s largest importer of Australian iron ore.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.6" class="koboSpan">Brazil ships
large tonnages on notably large bulk carriers to European, Chinese,
Japanese and other East Asian (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.7" class="koboSpan">South Korean,
Taiwanese) market destinations. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.8"
class="koboSpan">Again, China is the leading importer.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.9" class="koboSpan">South Asian
(especially Indian) exports of iron ore have climbed steadily.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.10" class="koboSpan">Once again the
Chinese market beckons. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.11"
class="koboSpan">There are numerous iron ore sources in Africa but, in
total, they generate comparatively small volumes for export mainly to
Europe and East Asia. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.99.12"
class="koboSpan">Canadian and Swedish mines produce quite impressive
volumes of iron ore for export usually in rather short-distance seaborne
trades to near neighbours such as the US, Germany, UK, etc.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">The size of the dry
bulk vessels carrying the ore affects the exact itineraries and limits
the ports that can be used in the ore trades, although not quite as
remarkably as in the crude oil trades.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">It should be
noted that long-distance ore trades, as on the Brazil–Far East route,
generate large annual tonne-mile totals.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">Very large ore
carriers, some of more than 300,000 deadweight tonnes, have performed
well on an itinerary that swings south of the Cape of Good Hope and
through the Indonesian archipelago via the Lombok and Makassar
Straits.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">Metallurgical
enterprises in the heavily industrialised regions of the northern
hemisphere have drawn for a long time on their own iron ore deposits as
well as on imported</span>
