<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0022" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00022.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Major iron ore trade routes, 2007" /></span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_76"></span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0016" id="Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0016"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan">:</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan"> Major iron ore trade routes, 2007</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_77"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">ores. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.106.2"
class="koboSpan">Four of the world’s five largest steel producers –
China, Russia, the US, India – have been large iron ore producers in the
past but China has emerged as the world’s largest iron ore importer.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">This relates to
her needs as the world’s largest steel producer.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.106.4" class="koboSpan">Japan, Germany
and South Korea now rely mostly on seaborne ore imports.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.106.5" class="koboSpan">The anticipated
twenty-first century scale of steel production will require
supplementing the old and, in some cases, depleted or uneconomically low
grade, northern hemispheric sources of iron ore supply.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.106.6" class="koboSpan">The southern
hemisphere possesses the richer and more abundant supply sources.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 Coal</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">“Hard coal” includes
steam coal, an important industrial and thermal power plant fuel and the
somewhat higher grade coking coal, heavily used in its beneficiated form
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">coke) as
blast furnace fuel in iron and steel works.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.108.3" class="koboSpan">These were the
primary energy resources of the Industrial Revolution.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.108.4" class="koboSpan">There were
abundant coal deposits in the European and North American industrial
regions, fueling their rapid nineteenth and twentieth century growth.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.108.5" class="koboSpan">In more recent
times north Chinese coal mining spurred massive Chinese development of
heavy industry. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.108.6"
class="koboSpan">Today China is both the world’s largest producer and
the largest consumer of hard coal.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">Total seaborne
movements of hard coal in 2007 measured slightly over 800 million
tonnes, generating almost 3.8 trillion tonne-miles of ocean transport.
</span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0017" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0017"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan"> depicts the major routes accounting for 65% of the
total seaborne movement of hard coal in 2007.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.111.2" class="koboSpan">Close to three
quarters of the total seaborne coal shipments are steam coal; therefore
only one quarter, the coking coal, is directly dependent on the state of
the iron and steel
industry.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0095" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0095"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">Australia has recently
outstripped all other coal exporters and the Japanese market has been
particularly important to them. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.113.2"
class="koboSpan">Chinese and Indonesian steam coal exports have recently
cut into Australia’s East Asian markets, however.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.113.3" class="koboSpan">South African
steam coal exports to Europe and Asia constituted quite steady volumes
over the last decade. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.113.4"
class="koboSpan">Quite a few years ago an interesting shipping pattern
was developed, combining US coal exports from Hampton Roads with South
African exports to the East Asian market.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.113.5" class="koboSpan">The coal was
loaded to the maximum allowable vessel draft on large bulk carriers at
Hampton Roads and the carriers “topped off” with coal in South Africa
proceeding on to Japanese or other Asian destinations.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.113.6" class="koboSpan">Other notable
sources for coal exports include Colombia which favours the European
market for steam coal shipments and western Canada which has directed
coking coal shipments towards East Asia.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.113.7" class="koboSpan">Poland mainly
serves European markets on short-distance shipping routes to
northwestern and Mediterranean Europe.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">US coking coal
exports, which were so prominent in early post-World War II times and
vital to the rebuilding of European and Japanese industrial economies,
have dropped off noticeably in the last decade.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.114.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
US, Russia and China remain huge coal producers and consumers, and still
have net surpluses for export.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">4.5 Grain</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Grain shipments
including wheat, barley, rye, oats, maize, sorghum and soybeans make up
the most inconstant patterns of the four major bulk commodity
trades.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0096" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0096"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan"> There have been large seasonal and year-to-year
fluctuations in the volumes and directions of the oceanborne grain
trade. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">Weather,
politics and transport costs can be notoriously</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0023" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00023.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: Major coal trade routes, 2007" /></span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_78"></span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0017" id="Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0017"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
4</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan">:</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan"> Major coal trade routes, 2007</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_79"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan">variable factors.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.123.2" class="koboSpan">Even so, grain
shipments have been a significant component of world seaborne commerce
since ancient times. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.123.3"
class="koboSpan">The grain trade typically attracts tramp shipping which
can adjust to the inherent variability.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.123.4" class="koboSpan">A few very
large grain companies such as Cargill, Continental Grain, Bunge, and
Dreyfus have had a large influence on the patterns of grain trade, too
(Morgan, 1979).</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">In 2007 seaborne trade
of the grain types mentioned above totaled 341 million tonnes,
generating over 1.9 trillion tonne-miles in ocean transport.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">Despite the
year-to-year fluctuations of the volumes and directions of the ocean
trading routes there have been source countries that, year after year,
have been net exporters. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.124.3"
class="koboSpan">These include the US, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and
Australia. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.124.4" class="koboSpan">The
North American continent has provided the largest volume of oceanborne
grain exports.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">South America,
especially Brazil, has become a prominent grain exporter with soybeans
and soybean meal exports rising in importance.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">In recent years
some of the regions producing the grains in Australia have suffered from
persistent drought conditions and grain exports were at a low point in
2007.</span>

<a href="#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0018" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0018"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the major grain trade routes on which 73% of the
world’s seaborne grain shipments moved in year 2007.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.127.2"
class="koboSpan">Intercontinental flows of grain are complex and, as
mentioned, vary from year-to-year.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.127.3" class="koboSpan">Parts of
Europe, e.g. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.127.4"
class="koboSpan">France, are net exporters; other parts, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.127.5" class="koboSpan">several East
European countries, have often been net importers.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.127.6" class="koboSpan">The northern
countries of South America are net importers whereas Brazil, Uruguay and
Argentina are exporters.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">The markets are
different in different countries for different types of grains, some of
which are domestically produced; others of which are not.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">East Asia, notably
including Japan, South Korea, China and Taiwan, with their large
populations and, in some cases, relatively limited available arable
land, exerts the strongest market demand for imported grains.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">To a certain
extent, the “green revolution” has rescued parts of South Asia,
especially India, from what had become an overdependence on grain
imports. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">Other
parts of the developing world have not been as fortunate.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.129.4" class="koboSpan">Africa, for
example, has some alarming agricultural problems ranging from
desertification and drought in the Sahel, to the dreadful impacts of
civil wars on farming, to ruinously low, artificially-set crop prices,
to the chaotic land-holding “reforms” in Zimbabwe, once a land of great
grain-producing potential. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.129.5"
class="koboSpan">Africa, with these problems and its fast-growing
population, has been forced to become a rather large grain importer.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.129.6" class="koboSpan">The grain
shipments are often, of necessity, enabled by foreign aid and relief
programs.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">Despite variations
from year to year in the grain production of each of the major supply
sources, and variations also in market procurement programmes, the total
annual volume of the seaborne grain trade took no wild fluctuations in
the last two decades, rising at a fairly steady pace to a high point in
2007.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0097" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0097"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan"> Actually the percentage of world grain production that
enters ocean shipping channels is comparatively small.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">Most of the
world’s largest grain producers, for instance Russia, China, India and
the United States, consume domestically a large proportion of their
annual grain production.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">4.6 A composite picture</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">Visualising the four
major bulk commodity ocean trades in geographical perspective, as rather
crudely sketched in
</span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0019"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan">, a composite picture, one recognises immediately that
a large portion of the cargo flow has been aimed at what should be
carefully</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0024" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00024.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 5: Major grain trade routes, 2007" /></span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_80"></span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0018" id="Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0018"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
5</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">:</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan"> Major grain trade routes, 2007</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0025" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00025.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Major bulk trades, composite picture, 2007" /></span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_81"></span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0019" id="Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">:</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan"> Major bulk trades, composite picture, 2007</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_82"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">branded as industrialised core regions
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">within</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan"> East Asia, Europe and North America.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.147.2" class="koboSpan">Europe and East
Asia have been the two greatest bulk commodity importers.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.147.3" class="koboSpan">North America,
while a net exporter of coal and grain, is, however, the recipient of
huge quantities of crude oil from the Caribbean (esp.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.147.4" class="koboSpan">Venezuela),
Africa, the Middle East and lesser sources.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.147.5" class="koboSpan">A sizeable
portion of the coal and grain trades has been
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan">between </span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">North America and Europe and between North America and
East Asia, trades entirely within the northern hemisphere.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">The world’s greatest
oil producing region, the Middle East, is also in the northern
hemisphere and practically athwart the main ocean shipping corridor from
East Asia across the Indian Ocean, through the Red Sea and Suez Canal,
to the Mediterranean and Western Europe.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.150.2" class="koboSpan">The largest
tankers, however, must dip into the southern hemisphere rounding the
southern edge of Africa to perform their transport task of carrying oil
to Europe or to the US. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.150.3"
class="koboSpan">(</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan"> takes graphic liberties by assuming that the main
volumes of bulk commodity ocean trade are not shipped via either the
Suez or Panama Canals.) The southern hemisphere is not “neglected” by
bulk carriers because South American, African, Indonesian and Australian
supply sources are a very significant factor in bulk commodity ocean
trade.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">When one considers
Venezuelan oil, Brazilian iron ore, Colombian coal, and Brazilian and
Argentine grain, not to mention other somewhat smaller supply sources,
South America has been an important contemporary exporter of all four
major bulk commodities entering ocean trade.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.153.2" class="koboSpan">Australia, with
its abundant mineral reserves and its grain fields, has been a
significant supplier of three of the four main bulk commodities – all
except oil. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.153.3" class="koboSpan">The
commercial ties between Australia and Japan, enabling the shipments,
especially of iron ore, were consolidated by long term contracts on
purchases and shipments and Japanese participation in infrastructure
developments to facilitate these trades (Manners, 1971, p.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.153.4" class="koboSpan">317).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.153.5" class="koboSpan">China has more
recently entered the Australian picture to become the most important
iron ore procurer of all.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan"> depicts origins, destinations and directions of
seaborne bulk commodity movements which constituted 75% of the total
volume of the crude oil, iron ore, coal and grain bulk trades and an
even greater percentage of the tonne-miles in ocean transport.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">The voyage
lengths in the oil and ore trades are apparent simply by noting the
number of routes rounding the Cape of Good Hope on
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan"> and understanding the limitations created by the
mammoth size of some of the largest tankers and ore carriers.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Of course,
there are counterbalancing scale economies in transport which have made
the mega-ships appealing to vessel operators.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.157.3" class="koboSpan">There is no
visual expression in </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan"> of the comparative tonnages of cargo flow on the
various routes, nor is there a precise picture of ocean tracks taken by
the carriers. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.159.2"
class="koboSpan">Most of the Suez and Panama transits have been “assumed
away”, whereas, in fact, these canals have been on the itineraries of
many smaller-size bulk carriers and have figured importantly on ballast
voyages.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">The composite picture
is essentially a “laden voyage” picture.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.160.2" class="koboSpan">That is to say,
ballast voyage segments are not shown and, of course, ships in ballast
have contributed almost as much to the congestion of traffic lanes and
to the incidence of accidents at sea as fully laden ships, although the
latter are more of an environmental hazard if accidents do take place.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.160.3" class="koboSpan">One can deduce
from available traffic data, much of which has been used above in
composing the picture, that the main approaches to western Europe, Japan
and the eastern coast of the US have been very heavily trafficked by
ships, full or empty, serving the industrial core regions of the
northern hemisphere that generate so much of the world’s oceanborne bulk
trade. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.160.4" class="koboSpan">One can
deduce, also, that there are
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_83"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan">traffic convergences at straits such as Malacca,
Lombok, Hormuz, Gibraltar and Dover.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.161.2" class="koboSpan">One can imagine
that there are convergences of full and empty ships rounding Cape of
Good Hope and other promontories where the dangers of “hugging the
coast” to shorten voyages can never be completely removed by traffic
separation schemes.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">The rough tracings of
global bulk commodity trades reinforce the impression that the northern
core industrial regions have been the main focus of market demand.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.162.2" class="koboSpan">And this might
also reinforce the impressions conveyed by dependency theorists a few
decades ago and voiced by the UNCTAD Committee on Shipping in the 1970s
and 1980s, suggesting that not only the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan">control </span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan">of world merchant fleets, under whatever flag, but also
the relevant supply and demand elasticities for the products exported
favor the developed nations in the industrial core regions.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.164.2" class="koboSpan">As Alexander
Yeats wrote almost 30 years ago: “The incidence (that is, the question
of who pays transport costs in a trading transaction) of freight rates
depends on the relative elasticities of supply and demand for the goods
transported. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.164.3"
class="koboSpan">Theoretical analyses show that the relevant
elasticities are such that developing countries have borne a major
portion of increased transport costs for both exports and imports”
(Yeats, 1981, p. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.164.4"
class="koboSpan">2).</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">The patterns
graphically presented in </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures
2</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0015)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">, </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan">3</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0016)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan">, </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">4</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0017)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">, </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">5</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0018)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan"> suggest that there has been a great deal of empty
space on ships steaming about the oceans, fully manned, consuming fuel,
as they ballast to their next loading range.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.175.2" class="koboSpan">There may be no
way to eradicate this problem, but the next section of the chapter
explores possible strategies by independent ship operators to ameliorate
it.</span>

## <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.176.2" class="koboSpan">Feasibility of Combining Bulk Trades</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">In the late 1970s,
when the world energy crisis was acute, Deeds (1978) and Fleming (1978)
both addressed the issue of reducing ballast steaming as a percentage of
total voyage steaming. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.2"
class="koboSpan">Both considered patterns in the bulk commodity trades.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.3" class="koboSpan">The use of
combination carriers (e.g. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.4"
class="koboSpan">OBOs) offered a flexibility that allowed the
accommodation of any of the four main oceanborne bulk commodities.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.5" class="koboSpan">The ballast
leg, in Deeds’ words, “ties together many of the world’s shipping routes
in a world where complete reciprocal specific complementarity does not
exist” (Deeds, 1978, p. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.6"
class="koboSpan">87). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.7"
class="koboSpan">In other words there are almost always regional
imbalances and ballasting becomes a necessity.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.8" class="koboSpan">Careful
routeing can reduce the percentage of ballast steaming if an OBO, for
instance, can move from one commodity trade to another.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.177.9" class="koboSpan">Deeds examined
the regional imbalances in some detail and experimented with different
combinations, alternatives and scenarios, arriving at a routeing model,
using OBOs, that would reduce ballast steaming, vastly reduce annual
fuel oil consumption for the fleet, increase the rates of vessel
utilisation and annual work capacity of each vessel, thereby reducing
the necessary size of the bulk carrier fleet.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">Deeds constructed his
final model using recorded bulk commodity trade data at a high level of
geographical generalisation. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.178.2"
class="koboSpan">Fleming’s model that combined four different bulk
commodity trades in logical geographic sequence was even more abstract.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.178.3" class="koboSpan">A comparison of
the four trades using specialised bulk carriers in back-and-forth
shuttle service on each route with an OBO fleet moving progressively
from one bulk trade to the next showed the theoretical cost and
efficiency benefits of combining the trades.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.178.4" class="koboSpan">Both
researchers were impressed by the potential of the modern-day combined
carrier but both were skeptical that the actual geographic
configurations of global bulk commodity shipments would ever match their
idealised models.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_84"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan">What has prevented the combined carrier from catching
on? </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.179.2" class="koboSpan">More than
two decades of decline in the size of the combined carrier fleet in
numbers of ships and total deadweight capacity left only 99 ships
totaling 9.3 million deadweight capacity in 2007
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">Fearnleys Review
2008</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">, p.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">64).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.181.3" class="koboSpan">One might begin
by asking who controls the oil, ore, coal and grain trades.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.181.4" class="koboSpan">Obviously the
big oil, steel, and grain trading companies have huge shipping influence
and often have had large proprietary fleets of vessels under their
ownership or firm control. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.181.5"
class="koboSpan">Understandably, these companies have been primarily
interested in the transport of their own basic raw materials or energy
resources. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.181.6"
class="koboSpan">Tying together diverse commodity trades has not been
their first priority, although the flexibility inherent in the combined
carrier may have had some appeal when their own trade was in the
doldrums. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.181.7" class="koboSpan">In
normal times, however, the industrial carrier, controlling and securing
the transport requirements for the firm, serves the production and
marketing divisions of the larger corporation and tries to provide an
efficient, reliable, timely, transportation service.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.181.8" class="koboSpan">Routeing
efficiency and low fuel consumption are not likely to be ruling
considerations, although annual work capacity of the fleet is a
significant long-term concern.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">Proprietary carriers,
especially in the oil trades, have been wooed by the dramatic economies
of scale derived from mega-ship transport despite the inflexibility in
routeing that large size adds to the inherent inflexibility of
specialised single-purpose vessels.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.182.2" class="koboSpan">Extremely low
costs per tonne-mile seem to magnify the advantages of the supertanker,
for example, and assuage the disadvantages of longer-distance voyages.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.182.3" class="koboSpan">(One sometimes
forgets that the cost per tonne of carrying a bulk commodity in a ship
of given size and specifications
is</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan"> always </span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">going to be higher on a long voyage than on a short
voyage). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.184.2" class="koboSpan">The
costs per deadweight tonne of capacity of building a combined carrier
are, to be sure, considerably higher – some estimate 25% higher – than
the costs of building a single purpose vessel of the same cargo carrying
capacity. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.184.3"
class="koboSpan">Admittedly, also, scheduling ships on back-and-forth
shuttle service between the company’s own terminal facilities, as is the
case on many of the oil company trade routes, is less complicated than
arranging more elaborate and time-consuming itineraries that combine
different trades and different commodities.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.184.4" class="koboSpan">Moreover, there
are “time economies” that come from ballasting straight home for the
next outbound voyage.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">When governments or
government agencies develop industrial or shipping policies that allow
them to intrude in the development of shipping networks and merchant
fleets, the complexion of the issues, objectives and priorities, with
respect to the transport function, may change.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.185.2" class="koboSpan">The careful
bulk commodity-routeing strategies of BISCORE when British Steel was a
nationalised venture, and in the 1960s the use of combined carriers by
SIDERMAR, the shipping wing of Finsider, the Italian state-owned steel
combine, are cases in point. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.185.3"
class="koboSpan">Perhaps there was less attention to the immediate
“bottom line” of the bulk commodity shipping operation, but more
attention to longer-term planning of voyages and voyage combinations,
usually resulting in a more efficient and productive use of the fleet.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.185.4" class="koboSpan">SIDERMAR, for a
while, combined coking coal cargoes eastbound from the US to Italian
steelworks with iron ore cargoes westbound from West Africa to the US,
the westbound shipments for the account of an
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">American </span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan">steel company (Fleming, 1968, p.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.187.2" class="koboSpan">31).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.187.3" class="koboSpan">Of course, this
sort of tramp-like service was easier in those days when
multiple-purpose “10,000 tonners” were still being used.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.187.4" class="koboSpan">The government
agencies in such cases had a proprietary interest in the transport
function. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.187.5" class="koboSpan">One
supposes that, beyond their transportation service to the national steel
company, certain general principles of fuel conservation, environmental
safety and even the implementation of national political objectives
could have come into play.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_85"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan">There is another major component in bulk commodity
ocean trading and that is the independent shipowner, or the modern
version of the tramp shipping operator.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.188.2" class="koboSpan">Some of these
shipowners, whose names have become legendary in shipping circles, built
enormous fleets of tankers or dry bulk carriers.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.188.3" class="koboSpan">Also, many of
the owners were serious students of the patterns and trends of the bulk
commodity trades. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.188.4"
class="koboSpan">Most of their vessels were “ships for hire”.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.188.5" class="koboSpan">Their fleets
were fixed on charters of various durations, from spot voyage charters
to long-term bareboat charters. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.188.6"
class="koboSpan">Quite often the long term charterers were “big oil” or
“big steel” or “big mining” concerns and, for all intents and purposes,
the ships became part of the proprietary carrier fleet.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">One of the most
successful steamship operators of the twentieth century was Erling
Naess, a Norwegian who pioneered the financing, building and operating,
under charter contracts, of fleets of OBOs and other versatile bulk
carriers. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.189.2" class="koboSpan">In
Naess’ own words: “For owners of large bulk carriers the secret of
operating a profitable shipping business is to a large extent one of
arranging trading patterns in such a way that the time at sea in loaded
condition exceeds the time at sea in ballast condition.”
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.189.3" class="koboSpan">Later, “I spent
much of my time dreaming up ‘combination trades’ in which the individual
market rates might appear uneconomic but in combination with return
trades a satisfactory return might be secured.”
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.189.4" class="koboSpan">And, still
later, “I was strongly in favour of ‘combination carriers’, later known
as OBOs, which could carry liquid or alternatively dry cargo.”
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.189.5" class="koboSpan">(Naess, 1973,
p. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.189.6" class="koboSpan">191).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.189.7" class="koboSpan">By clever
choices of trading patterns Naess was able to reduce ballast steaming
dramatically. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.189.8"
class="koboSpan">On an 89-day voyage, for instance, loading coal at
Norfolk for Japan via the Panama Canal, ballasting to the Persian Gulf,
loading crude oil for Portland, Maine and ballasting back to Norfolk he
calculated only 19 days in ballast or 25% of the total steaming days
(Naess, 1977,
p.150).</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0098" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0098"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">One concludes that it
is not necessary to have official government collaboration in the
shipping programs or even official agreements between the different
commodity trades to make combination trades work.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.191.2" class="koboSpan">The independent
steamship operator with a fleet of combined carriers should be able to
discover the efficient geographic patterns, latch on to them for as long
as the commodity flows last and the transport service is providing
mutual benefit to carrier and shipper, and retain the flexibility to
move all or part of the fleet elsewhere when contracts expire.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan">Theoretically</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan">, it’s appealing.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">To be realistic,
contemporary evidence suggests that neither combined carriers nor
combined bulk commodity trades have caught on with the big shippers or
with proprietary carrier fleets. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.194.2"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, there are many independent ship operators
today who combine bulk and break-bulk cargoes on smaller, versatile,
multipurpose vessels that still make combinations work, serving parts of
the world that may not yet generate huge cargo volumes and often do not
yet have harbours and port facilities that can handle mega-ships.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">There are a
multitude of smaller bulk trades and trade routes that do not appear on
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">Figures
2</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0015)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan"> through </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.198.2"
class="koboSpan">There are many possible combinations and there are many
tramp operations of modest size that involve much more than one bulk
commodity trade on one trade route.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.198.3" class="koboSpan">It is not
unrealistic to suppose that combinations of trades do more than
accommodate “demand for spot transit of bulk commodities” and go beyond
the “derived and marginal character of the demand for tramp shipping
services”, therefore beyond some of the usual theoretical explanations
of the rationale for these services (Metaxas, 1971, pp.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.198.4" class="koboSpan">4, 41,
230).</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">One could hardly
expect the tramp operator to adopt highly idealistic policies of ballast
reduction to help the world in an energy crisis, or of combining trades
for the sake of international good will.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.199.2" class="koboSpan">However, more
efficient patterns of movement can be more
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_86"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan">profitable patterns of movement and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan">that </span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan">should appeal to most tramp operators and independent
shipowners.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">The trade-offs between
ship size and ship versatility have been a constant concern for
commercial shipping lines whether in tramp or liner service and whether
they carry bulk or break-bulk commodities, containers, roll on/roll off
items, reefer cargoes, or passengers.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.203.2" class="koboSpan">There are
physical geographic limitations for mega-ships – shallow waters,
harbours without sufficient maneuvering room, restrictive canal
dimensions, etc. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.203.3"
class="koboSpan">And there are market limitations – insufficient or
irregular cargo flows, etc. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.203.4"
class="koboSpan">One remembers the disastrously low passenger complement
on the first eastbound transatlantic voyage of the Great Eastern, a
“ship before its time”; and one recalls the bankrupting experience of an
American container line unable to achieve break-even load factors in
their round-the-world service in the 1980s.</span>

## <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">General Cargo Trades: 2007</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">The seaborne cargo
flows in the bulk commodity trade are obviously unidirectional, from
supply sources en route to market locations, as depicted graphically in
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">Figures
2</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0015)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan">, </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan">3</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0016)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan">, </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan">4</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0017)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan">, </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan">5</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0018)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.215.2"
class="koboSpan">This creates a ballasting necessity, either to return
to the original loading range or to move “onward” to a different trade
route and, if combined carriers are used, a different commodity to
carry. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.215.3" class="koboSpan">General
cargo trades, those served by container lines, for example, nearly
always have bidirectional cargo movements.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.215.4" class="koboSpan">The need for
ballast legs without
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan">any</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan"> paying cargo aboard is not as important a concern for
liner shipping on the major general cargo routes as it has been for
tramp shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.218.1" class="koboSpan">Yet there remains a
problem that cannot be eliminated.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.218.2" class="koboSpan">Seldom are the
liner trades directionally in balance in size of cargo flows.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.218.3" class="koboSpan">This means that
a container ship very often has a high achieved load factor, in
percentage of slots filled with revenue-paying containers, in one
direction and a low load factor in the opposite direction, with many
slots filled with empty containers being “positioned” for the heavier
flow direction. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.218.4"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the directional imbalances can vary for
many different reasons, economic and political.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.218.5" class="koboSpan">One of the big
challenges for the liner operator is to cope with these imbalances that
create unused revenue cargo space if the vessels are used in simple
bidirectional shuttle service.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">6.1 Network strategies</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">As in the bulk trades,
one of the ways to cope with empty space involves routeing strategies
that discover the most appropriate itineraries, port sequences,
transhipment junctions and methods of tying one liner route to another
so that vessels can avoid the weak cargo flow direction of one liner
route by slipping into an adjoining liner route with stronger cargo
prospects. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.220.2" class="koboSpan">In
attempts to handle the directional imbalance problem and elevate the
achieved load factors (i.e. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.220.3"
class="koboSpan">capacity utilisation percentage) for the extended
voyage, some of the major container lines, Evergreen, for instance,
constructed elaborate globe – encircling network systems, choosing
strategically located hubs for transhipment purposes as they coordinated
schedules of main line and feeder services.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.220.4" class="koboSpan">Naturally they
tried to select ports of call with the most powerful cargo-generating
local and regional hinterlands. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.220.5"
class="koboSpan">Unfortunately round-the-world service with its
itinerary, network, and timing complexities, has proved difficult to
operate and difficult to market.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_87"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">There always seemed to be weak links in the
globe-encircling chain. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.221.2"
class="koboSpan">Several container lines, instead, developed pendulum
systems which allowed them to serve all three of the major industrial
core regions leaving out
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan">one</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan"> ocean: Atlantic or Pacific or Indian, and using
coordinated intermodal connections, overland, to penetrate or sometimes
cross large landmasses like North America.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.223.2" class="koboSpan">The pendulum
networks and itineraries needed to be flexible enough, and the size of
the container line fleet needed to be adjustable enough to adapt to
changing market conditions in a competitive environment.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">Doctoring a liner
network for maximum operating efficiency needs to be a constant
consideration, but doctoring it for maximum freight revenue generation
is very important too. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.224.2"
class="koboSpan">And the two types of doctoring may conflict with one
another. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.224.3" class="koboSpan">In
recent years the container lines, having rushed headlong into the
acquisition of mega-ships, scheduled these vessels on long voyages on
the heavy-volume
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan">inter-core
</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.226.1" class="koboSpan">routes
calling at relatively few ports, transhipping frequently to extend their
market reach. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.226.2"
class="koboSpan">Some gravitated towards hub-and-spoke systems.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.226.3" class="koboSpan">The latter
offer strong market-penetrating potential but one should remember that
pure hub-and-spoke networks have, in graph theoretical terms, minimal
connectivity. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.226.4"
class="koboSpan">This means that there is only one path, and no
alternatives, between any two points in the system, and that path is
either to or through the hub. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.226.5"
class="koboSpan">This translates, in fact, to lower rates of vessel
utilisation and lower annual work capacities for the fleet if both main
line and feeder services are under the same corporate roof.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.226.6" class="koboSpan">It could also
amplify the directional imbalance problem by shifting it to the feeder
services. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.226.7"
class="koboSpan">However, both the network connectivity problem and the
directional imbalance problem are not without solutions when the large
container line shifts focus from main line to feeder line and does the
necessary
network-doctoring.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0099" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0099"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">The arguments for
hub-and-spoke networks are much stronger on the revenue side of the
voyage proforma than on the cost side.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.228.2" class="koboSpan">Andrew Goetz,
in an article on the US airline industry, commented, “The widespread
adoption of hub-and-spoke networks conferred tremendous economies of
scope to airlines, as the costs of adding each additional spoke to a hub
are generally quite small in comparison to the benefits of increased
traffic feed.” </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.228.3"
class="koboSpan">(Goetz, 2002 p. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.228.4"
class="koboSpan">3). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.228.5"
class="koboSpan">Are there parallels to this in the container trades?
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.228.6" class="koboSpan">Generally
speaking, yes. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.228.7"
class="koboSpan">The carriers are willing to incur the cost
inefficiencies inherent in hub-and-spoke operations if the “traffic
feed” to and from their main line service is sufficiently enhanced and
the freight revenues sufficiently compensatory.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.228.8" class="koboSpan">Remember,
however, that hub-and-spoke operations entail transhipments, and
potential cargo can be lost to competitors who offer direct port calls
rather than transhipment service.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">6.2 Northern latitudes</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">The impact of the East
Asian, European and North American industrial core regions on general
cargo trades and, more specifically, on container trades is even more
spectacular than their impact, largely as a market destination, on bulk
commodity seaborne shipping. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.230.2"
class="koboSpan">More than 70% of global seaborne container trade is
“inter-core”</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0100" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0100"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan"> (see
</span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0020" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0020"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></a><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.234.2"
class="koboSpan">Periphery-core ocean shipping connections (see
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0019)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">) have had more significance in the bulk trades;
however there have been notable increases in break-bulk cargoes on
smaller multiple purpose as well as special purpose (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.236.2" class="koboSpan">heavy lift)
vessels. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.236.3" class="koboSpan">South
American and African container line trade with the industrialised
regions of the northern hemisphere has trended upward but is still
impeded by inadequate infrastructure for container logistics.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.236.4" class="koboSpan">In some parts
of the south it has been recently estimated that less than half of the
containerisable commodities are yet containerised.</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0026" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00026.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7: Global inter-core container trade" /></span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_88"></span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0020" id="Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0020"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
7</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan">:</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan"> Global inter-core container trade</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_89"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">Container lines have not abandoned the rest of the
world but there is no doubt that they have found most of their freight
in northern latitudes. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.241.2"
class="koboSpan">In the developed nations of the north and neighbouring
rapidly developing economies it is estimated that roughly 80% of the
containerisable general cargo is now being containerised although an
estimate of 65% for India was recently
noted.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0101" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0101"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan"> The world’s largest container lines with the world’s
largest container ships have gravitated to the heavy volume east–west
inter-core routes. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.243.2"
class="koboSpan">They offer transatlantic, transpacific and Asia–Europe
via Indian Ocean services, all north of the equator.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.243.3" class="koboSpan">These are heavy
volume routes that, together, ring the globe with cargo flows in both
directions, east–west and west–east.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.243.4" class="koboSpan">The traditional
all-water routes via the Panama Canal and Suez Canal have been
supplemented by continental overland bridge routes (sketched in
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
7</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0020)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan">), notably in and across North America.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.245.2" class="koboSpan">There are now
three options for container flows from Asia to eastern North America:
(1) transpacific, then transloading to the overland bridge; (2)
all-water transpacific eastbound via Panama Canal (with present ship
size limitations); and (3) all-water westbound, using the Suez Canal,
then transMediterranean and transatlantic.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.245.3" class="koboSpan">All these
options are used by container lines today.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.245.4" class="koboSpan">In recent
years, there has been a remarkable rise in intra-Asian seaborne
container trade on Route 2 and beyond.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">The three major
transoceanic routes and the intra-Asian as well as intra-European
seaborne container trades have attracted feeder traffic from the
southern hemisphere at strategically located points such as Singapore,
Colombo, Dubai, Algeciras, Freeport (Bahamas) and at transhipment
terminals at either end of the Panama Canal.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.246.2" class="koboSpan">At these points
the container transfer is often between medium-sized container ships on
medium-volume trade routes and the 8,000 TEU mega-ships that have been
seen more and more frequently on the ring of main-line routes.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.246.3" class="koboSpan">Recent
deliveries of Maersk’s 12,500 TEU vessels and the dampening effects of
economic recession, not to mention the escalation of bunker prices,
certainly accentuate the vessel assignment and vessel routeing problem.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.246.4" class="koboSpan">The economies
of scale measured by (low) slot costs of the megaships need to be
accompanied by economies of scope increasing traffic feed, thereby
increasing the percentage of slots filled with revenue-paying
containers.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">Large container lines
operating large container ships need to have a carefully designed global
intermodal strategy. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.247.2"
class="koboSpan">There are certain clearly defined physical geographic
constraints. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.247.3"
class="koboSpan">Vessels with sufficient beam to load more than 13
containers abreast have been too wide for the Panama Canal locks and
this generally means vessels of more than about 4,800 TEU capacity
cannot (yet) get through. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.247.4"
class="koboSpan">The widening and deepening of the Panama Canal is a
project expected to be completed by 2014.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.247.5" class="koboSpan">This should
allow transit for all but the very largest fully laden container ships
and should enhance assignments of vessels to route 1a, one of the East
Asia-eastern North America connections mentioned above (see
</span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
7</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0020)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.249.2"
class="koboSpan">Important connections between southeast Asia, India,
Pakistan, Middle East and eastern North America via the Suez Canal can
be served by large container vessels but there are still many ports
without adequate water depth to accommodate fully-laden container ships
in the 5,000–8,000 TEU capacity range; and these large ships require
terminal cranes with enough reach to handle containers lined up on the
ship 16 or 17 abreast.</span>

### <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">6.3 Directional imbalances</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.251.1" class="koboSpan">Another area of
concern is the directional imbalance of cargo flow on virtually all
container routes. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.251.2"
class="koboSpan">The large container lines, with large ships in their
fleets, need to be
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_90"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan">especially sensitive to “weak directions” and “weak
segments” in their extensive networks.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.252.2" class="koboSpan">Sometimes these
are created by extraneous factors of global geopolitics or global
economic trends like economic recession, or major currency exchange
fluctuations. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.252.3"
class="koboSpan">Periodic adjustments need to be made to respond to
changes in market demand – e.g. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.252.4"
class="koboSpan">adjustments of network configuration, itineraries,
schedules, alliances, fleet capacity, vessel sizes, not to mention
freight rate adjustments. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.252.5"
class="koboSpan">This is part of a global strategy that each line
constructs and modifies.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">From
</span><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fig0027" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fig0027"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan"> one can construct three general scenarios for
container line service:</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan">Scenario 1: Shuttle services</span></span>

- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">Container lines
  offer back-and-forth shuttle services on Routes 1.2 and 3.</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">There are no special
  physical geographic constraints except on Route 1 where only Pacific
  Coast North American ports can be used for mega-ships until the Panama
  Canal project is completed (est.
  </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.258.2" class="koboSpan">2014 or
  later).</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">The least empty
  space and the best directional balance in year 2007 occurred on Route
  3 (transatlantic) where the westbound to eastbound cargo volume ratio
  was 4.5m TEUs to 2.7m. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.259.2"
  class="koboSpan">The west/east ratio on route 1 (transpacific) was
  4.2m. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.259.3" class="koboSpan">to
  14.5m. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.259.4" class="koboSpan">The
  west-east ratio on Route 2 (Far East-Europe) was 14.7m.
  </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.259.5" class="koboSpan">to
  5.1m.</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">The highest total
  TEU traffic occurred on Route 2 which also has the best en route cargo
  prospects to/from South Asia and Middle East plus cargo transshipped
  from the southern hemisphere and ongoing traffic transatlantic along
  Route 3 to/from eastern North America.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan">Scenario 2: Round-the-world (RTW)
services</span></span>

- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">RTW services offered
  in both directions.</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">Complete all-water
  service limits vessel size to about 4,800 TEU capacity enabling Panama
  Canal transit.</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0027" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00027.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fig0027)

</div>

- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_91"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
  class="koboSpan">Using the data from
  </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.266.1" class="koboSpan">Table
  1</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_fig0027)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
  class="koboSpan">, an eastbound globe encirclement starting in Europe
  progressing from Route 2 to 1 to 3 would have accumulated 22.3m TEUs
  (intra-Asian, South Asia and Middle Eastern traffic omitted) whereas a
  circumnavigation starting in Europe, progressing westbound from Route
  3 to 1 to 2 would have accumulated 23.4m TEUs.
  </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.267.2" class="koboSpan">The balance
  between eastbound and westbound cargo volumes in 2007 was quite close.
  </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.267.3" class="koboSpan">However,
  there would have been a great deal of empty space circling the globe
  on containerships unless the operators were astute in their choice of
  transhipment ports, feeder service arrangements, etc.
  </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.267.4" class="koboSpan">and unless
  they made the most of Route 2 by tapping into the rapid growth of
  intra-Asian and South Asian cargoes which have not been included in
  the above statistical calculations.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">Scenario 3: Pendulum services</span></span>

- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">Container lines can
  construct three types of pendulum service, one centered on Europe, one
  centered on East Asia and one on North America.</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.270.1" class="koboSpan">The diagrams below
  indicate 2007 TEU volumes in millions; e = eastbound, w =
  westbound.</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0028" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00028.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.272.1" class="koboSpan">no special
  constraint on vessel size; mega-ships use east coast North America
  ports;</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.273.1" class="koboSpan">the least empty
  space of the pendulum services;</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">lowest total traffic
  potential.</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0029" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00029.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">no special
  constraint on vessel size;</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">the most acute
  directional imbalances of the three scenarios;</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">heaviest total
  traffic potential, especially if Indian and Middle Eastern traffic
  feeding in to or out of Route 2 is counted;</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">presence on the two
  heaviest volume routes: transpacific eastbound and East Asia-Europe
  westbound.</span>

<div id="Ch03.xhtml_fig0030" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_92"></span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.280.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00030.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">all water service
  via Panama Canal limits size of vessels to about 4800 TEU
  capacity;</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">presence on heavy
  cargo volume transpacific eastbound route;</span>
- <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan">most comprehensive
  access to North American intermodal system.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">These scenarios
suggest some of the general geographical factors of network structure,
traffic densities and favoured directions of movement that enter into
the container line’s thinking as global strategies are constructed.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.284.2" class="koboSpan">It should be
emphasised that there are many other factors in the decision equation,
for instance the revenue yields per filled slot which vary from one
route to another, the break-even load factors for ships of different
sizes on different routes, the degree of competition on the various
routes, the amount of traffic feed that might be expected at well-chosen
transhipment hubs. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.284.3"
class="koboSpan">And, for each container line, there are always the
possibilities of finding “special niches” to enhance market
share.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.285.1" class="koboSpan">There is no fail-safe
scenario. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.285.2" class="koboSpan">Each
requires reevaluation as market conditions change, for better or for
worse. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.285.3" class="koboSpan">The
empty space problem engendered by “weak directions” and weak route
segments can sometimes be softened by moving from one scenario, or form
of service, to another. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.285.4"
class="koboSpan">Every one of the big container lines has used shuttle
services and pendulum services in the past.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.285.5" class="koboSpan">A few of the
largest lines have tried RTW services, some like US Lines in the 1980s
very unsuccessfully (Lim, 1996). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.285.6"
class="koboSpan">Evergreen, the huge Taiwanese carrier, whose
competition really precipitated US Lines demise, announced, not much
later, the cessation of their RTW services, replacing them with pendulum
services, one centred on North America using 4,200 TEU vessels and
Panama Canal transit, and the other centred on East Asia using new 5,600
TEU
vessels.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0102" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0102"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan"> The need to accommodate mega-ships, recently of 8,000
TEU capacity or more has become a vital consideration in network
decisions. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.287.2"
class="koboSpan">Apparently the promise of low slot costs outweighs the
fears of overcapacity, leading to cut throat competition, low yields per
slot, and the inherent inflexibility in the operation of these huge
vessels.</span>

## <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.288.2" class="koboSpan">Summary and Prospects</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">Analysing the
empty-space phenomenon, whether from bulk carriers in ballast or from
container ships with low achieved load factors, one can certainly find
flaws in some of the network efficiencies.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.289.2" class="koboSpan">However, much
of the empty space problem for the world merchant fleets, in aggregate,
stems from unavoidable commercial geographic realities, namely the
spatial separation – by oceans – of regions of production and regions of
consumption and the directional imbalances of cargo flows on each trade
route. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.289.3"
class="koboSpan">“Overbuilding” in the 1990s and 2000s has added to the
problem. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.289.4" class="koboSpan">There
is very little prospect of correcting the
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_93"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">flaws in global network efficiencies by any sort of
comprehensive governmental “edict”.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.290.2" class="koboSpan">There is every
reason to hope, however, that individual steamship operators in both
bulk and liner trades will use their own ingenuity to fashion networks
and patterns of operation that will enhance their capacity utilisation,
annual fleet work capacity, and, on the revenue side, annual fleet
yields. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.290.3" class="koboSpan">There
is no general prescription for success; however, each carrier, serving a
geographical domain that is somewhat unique in its specifics, with a
fleet that is somewhat unique in vessel sizes and specifications, should
be able to differentiate itself from its competitors in some
“attractive” way. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.290.4"
class="koboSpan">Yet there have been many recent indications of
“copy-cat behavior” in the liner trades – not a good sign, perhaps, if
it leads to indiscriminately competitive efforts, overbuilding,
overcapacity, bankruptcies, emergency mergers, and the like.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.291.1" class="koboSpan">The trend towards
using mega-ships in both bulk and liner trades complicates network
strategies and, unless market demand is really robust, compounds the
empty space problem. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.291.2"
class="koboSpan">There is, as mentioned, an inherent inflexibility from
large size although, of course, the ship operators count on this being
outweighed by scale economies, measured in unit costs of
transport.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.292.1" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately the
combined carrier for bulk trades, while conceptually appealing, has not
lived up to its former promise or, in Erling Naess’ case, its former
success. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.292.2"
class="koboSpan">(Naess, 1977, </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan">chap. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.293.2"
class="koboSpan">21</span>](#Ch021.xhtml_ht0457)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.294.2"
class="koboSpan">Many operators have complained that dry and liquid bulk
commodity trades just do not mix, not only because of expensive vessel
design, cleaning costs when shifting trades, etc., but also because of
difficulties coordinating trades between two or more “masters,” each
absorbed with own-company needs. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.294.3"
class="koboSpan">Many of the remaining combined carriers still in
operation have reverted to the carriage of one commodity type, liquid or
dry. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.294.4" class="koboSpan">So much
for flexibility!</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">There is little doubt
that the twenty-first century will bring more development of southern
hemispheric trade routes, especially for container lines.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.295.2" class="koboSpan">It has been
estimated that only 50% of the containerisable commodities in the
developing economies are, in fact, containerised for ocean transport
whereas the percentage in the developed economies approaches 90.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.295.3" class="koboSpan">It is
predictable that as (or if) trade itself grows, and as the
infrastructure for container handling and intermodalism continues to
develop, the volumes of containerized cargo in all parts of the world
will increase. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.295.4"
class="koboSpan">Clearly they
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan">have </span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">increased for China, India, Brazil, Mexico, Malaysia
and others.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">China and India are
special cases, both with enormous growth potential in the container
trades. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.298.2" class="koboSpan">Well
over half the containerised cargo imported by North America and an
estimated third of global seaborne container exports involve China and
these fractions may well increase in size, despite the recent
recessionary slump in trade, as more and larger vessels offer direct
calls in China. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.298.3"
class="koboSpan">Both China and India are on the main pathway from Japan
and Korea to Europe, so their burgeoning ocean transport needs will
accentuate the east–west northern hemispheric ring of inter-core trade
routes. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.298.4" class="koboSpan">The
data that appears in </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_fig0027)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan"> for year 2007 traffic on the East Asia–Europe route,
as mentioned, do not include the sizeable “intermediate” movements, for
instance South Asia and Middle Eastern containers westbound to Europe
(2.5m TEUs) and European containers eastbound to the Middle East and
South Asia (5m TEUs ). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.300.2"
class="koboSpan">South Asia and the Middle East exported 1.2m.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.300.3" class="koboSpan">TEUs to East
Asia and imported an astounding 6.5m.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.300.4" class="koboSpan">TEUs from East
Asia in 2007. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.300.5"
class="koboSpan">Add to this a heavy volume of short-haul intra-Asia
cargo (e.g. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.300.6"
class="koboSpan">China–Japan, Japan–South Korea, China–South Korea).
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.300.7" class="koboSpan">And, part of
the heavy use of Route 2 of </span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
7</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_cap_lbl0020)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan"> is by ships serving the North America–South Asia and
Middle East connection and North America–Southeast Asia connection.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.302.2" class="koboSpan">This en route
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_94"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan">traffic potential provides rationale for the use of
mega-ships on the East Asia–Europe inter-core route and for the
development of en route transhipment
terminals.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0103" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0103"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.304.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.305.1" class="koboSpan">There is much reason
to expect the filling out of networks to and in the southern hemisphere,
especially if the South American and African economies rise to their
true potential. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.305.2"
class="koboSpan">However, it is unlikely that the dominant inter-core
pattern in northern latitudes will disappear.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.305.3" class="koboSpan">It is too
firmly etched on the mercantile maps of the globe.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.306.1" class="koboSpan">A final prediction
relates specifically to the container trades of the future.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.306.2" class="koboSpan">There has been
much talk of intermodality, total logistics chains, seamless movement of
containers, electronic data interchange, and so forth.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.306.3" class="koboSpan">These are good
ideas but not ideas that have yet been fully and perfectly implemented.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.306.4" class="koboSpan">There always
seem to be weak, often time-consuming, links in the chain.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.306.5" class="koboSpan">One trend,
however, that has been notably strong and growing stronger in recent
years has been the service contracting between carriers and shippers
based on time-volume freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.306.6" class="koboSpan">On American
container trade routes, the North America–East Asia route, for instance,
a large proportion of the total trade falls under these service
contracts. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.306.7" class="koboSpan">The
latter seem to reflect a true partnership between shipper and carrier,
unlike the more confrontational shipping arrangements of the past.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.306.8" class="koboSpan">It is hoped
that the partnership philosophy based on perceived mutual benefit will
prevail in the twenty first century.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.307.1" class="koboSpan">Container line
operations have grown spectacularly in the last half century as Levinson
describes vividly in his recent account of “how the shipping container
made the world smaller and the world economy bigger” (Levinson, 2006,
front cover). </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.307.2"
class="koboSpan">There is still, however, a large volume of baled,
crated, bagged, palletised, wheeled, lashed down, loose and “other”
general cargo on ships of various size in both tramp and liner service
on all our seas and oceans. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.307.3"
class="koboSpan">They have many of the same empty space, ballast
requirements, directional imbalances in cargo movements that have been
mentioned above and it seems certain that there are commodities that
will never fit into a container. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.307.4"
class="koboSpan">In a real sense this makes the maritime scene more
interesting.</span>

## <span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">8. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.308.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.309.1" class="koboSpan">As mentioned at the
beginning of this chapter, an important focus was to be on empty cargo
space steaming across the oceans.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.309.2" class="koboSpan">In the bulk
commodity trades very often there are shuttle services with half the
steaming time for the round voyage in ballast.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.309.3" class="koboSpan">This can be
perceived as lost cargo lifting potential but there are, of course,
extenuating circumstances such as the unavailability of return cargoes,
and, on a more positive note, the time economies of a ballast run
compared to time expended on a slow voyage in a nearby trade at a low
freight
rate.</span><sup><a href="#Ch03.xhtml_fn0104" id="Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0104"><span
id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">Tramp operators
undoubtedly search the globe for efficient and profitable patterns of
operation and there are ways that they can improve on engaging in
shuttle services if they have a fleet of versatile multi-purpose bulk
carriers. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.311.2" class="koboSpan">As
mentioned, however, the combined carriers have not been an unqualified
success in an age when vessel size and single purpose specialization
offer the cost benefits most appreciated by the proprietary
carriers.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">In the container
trades we have noted the most important trade routes and the directional
imbalances of cargo flow on those routes.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.312.2" class="koboSpan">A few
strategies were mentioned, including moving back and forth from shuttle
services to pendulum services to round-the-world services, or vice
versa, to tailor the supply of vessel space more evenly to the demand
for it when market conditions change.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.312.3" class="koboSpan">Of course, this
requires a certain amount
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_95"></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.313.1"
class="koboSpan">of operational flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.313.2" class="koboSpan">And the
carrier’s flexibility needs to be weighed against the shippers’ usual
need for reliable and uninterrupted service.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">All told,
“flexibility” enters the picture of both tramp and liner shipping in
many different shades and colours.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.314.2" class="koboSpan">It can be a
general characteristic and expectation of tramp-shipping operations.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.314.3" class="koboSpan">It is a
built-in quality of a steamship line’s network that interlocks various
trade routes and services. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.314.4"
class="koboSpan">Its opposite, inflexibility, can be inherent in the
operations of single purpose mega-ships.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">Flexibility can relate
also to a philosophy or grand strategy of company operations which
favours a thoughtful adaptability to market conditions and customer
needs.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.316.1"
class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0088)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.317.1"
class="koboSpan">University of Washington, Seattle, USA.

</span><span class="italic">[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.318.1"
class="koboSpan">dkf@u.washington.edu</span>](mailto:dkf@u.washington.edu)</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan">1.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0089)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
