</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
class="koboSpan">Fearnleys Review
2008</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.323.1" class="koboSpan">,
tables on world seaborne trade, p.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.323.2" class="koboSpan">48.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
class="koboSpan">2.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0090)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan"> Actually, there is a span of almost three centuries
between the first Spanish galleon transpacific round trip, Acapulco to

plying the Australia-Britain route.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan">3.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0091)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan"> See, for instance, the three “flow maps” depicting
colonial trades, circa 1775, on pp.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.327.2" class="koboSpan">198–199 of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.328.1"
class="koboSpan">The Times Atlas of World
History</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan">4.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0092)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
class="koboSpan"> Despite the potential for shifting from one trade to
another and despite the fact that the OBO was designed for that very
purpose, the combined carriers, today, tend to stick exclusively to one
type of bulk commodity trade and the fleet has dwindled in
number.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.332.1"
class="koboSpan">5.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0093)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.333.1"
class="koboSpan"> As calculated from
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.334.1"
class="koboSpan">Fearnleys Review
2008</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.335.2" class="koboSpan">Most of the
statistics that are the basis for the analysis of the bulk trades in
this chapter come from
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan">Fearnleys Review 2008
</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">and from
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan">SS&Y Monthly Shipping
Review</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">,
January, 2009.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.340.1"
class="koboSpan">6.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0094)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan"> On paper today it is an institutional bloc, however,
there are still quite a few unintegrated parts.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan">7.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0095)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.343.1"

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.344.1"
class="koboSpan">SS&Y Monthly Shipping
Review</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">,
January 2009, p. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.345.2"
class="koboSpan">5, which differentiates between coking and thermal coal
in the seaborne coal trade data.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.346.1"
class="koboSpan">8.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0096)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan"> Rice is not included in the data on which this
analysis of the grain trade is based.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.347.2" class="koboSpan">Soybeans,
technically not a grain, are included, however, in the calculations by
Fearnresearch.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.348.1"

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan">Fearnleys Review
2008</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.351.1" class="koboSpan">, p.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.351.2" class="koboSpan">48.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan">10.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0098)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan"> Of course, the Panamax-size, or smaller OBO vessels
used in these earlier days (mid-1960s) were easier to route; shifting
trades was easier, too.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan">11.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0099)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.355.1"
class="koboSpan"> In fact, some of the feeder line carriers move
progressively from one “spoke-end” port to another, adding connectivity
to the network. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.355.2"
class="koboSpan">Some of the ports in these “loops” are favoured with
faster cargo-transit times than others.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan">12.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0100)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.357.1"
class="koboSpan"> 70% is not, of course, a full indication of the
traffic on this route. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.357.2"
class="koboSpan">There are container ships, large and small, serving
only segments of the route. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.357.3"
class="koboSpan">Calculations of the 2007 inter-core container volumes
are drawn from the trade statistics section (numbers provided by MDS
Transmodal) of the September, October and November issues of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan">Containerisation
International</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2008).</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan">13.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0101)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan"> Evergreen, Maersk, and other container lines have
taken delivery of even larger ships recently, creating for the time
being an excess capacity for which there is no short-term, pleasant (in
cost terms) panacea in sight for the carrier, and unease for the shipper
who needs steady, reliable, reasonably priced service.</span>

<span id="Ch03.xhtml_page_96"></span>[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan">14.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0102)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan"> See
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan">Containerisation

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan">15.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0103)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan"> See
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan">Containerisation
International</span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.369.1"
class="koboSpan">, September, October and November, 2008, Trade
Statistics sections. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.369.2"
class="koboSpan">Heavy intra-Asia traffic and containers moving in and
out of </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.370.1"
class="koboSpan">segments </span></span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.371.1"
class="koboSpan">of the end-to-end Far East–Europe route (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.371.2" class="koboSpan">bidirectional
container flows on the Europe–South Asia and Middle East, and North
America–South Asia and Middle East routes) add to the Far East–Europe
end-end-to-end traffic and make Route 2 (see Figure 7) the most
significant connection of all.</span>

[<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.372.1"
class="koboSpan">16.</span>](#Ch03.xhtml_bck_fn0104)<span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.373.1"
class="koboSpan"> Assume that a combined carrier is fixed on a dry bulk
30-day voyage, laden outward and ballast return, promising a net profit
of \$150,000 or \$5,000 daily. </span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.373.2"
class="koboSpan">That might appeal more to the operator than combining
the dry bulk trade with a ballast-reducing oil trade back to the
original loading range if the combination of the two trades results in a
50-day voyage with a net profit of \$200,000 or \$4,000 daily.
</span><span id="Ch03.xhtml_kobo.373.3" class="koboSpan">The daily
profit is, in a sense, a “running bottom line”.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_98"></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_99"></span>[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 4</span>\
<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">International Trade in Manufactured Goods</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0119)
============================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Mary</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">R.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Brooks</span></span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0105" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0105"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping, on the scale
we see today, would not exist were it not for globalisation, and the
evolution and restructuring of the world’s economies after World War II.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">The increasing
specialisation of the world’s economies, and the desire for goods or
food made or grown elsewhere, along with increasing urbanisation, has
altered the demand for transport. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.8.3"
class="koboSpan">In this chapter, the focus will be on global trade in
manufactured goods and the role that shipping plays in this
market.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">Cargo transported by
ship falls into two broad categories – bulk and unitised.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.9.2" class="koboSpan">The former
usually travels via tramp vessels and includes both liquid bulk – mostly
crude oil and oil products – and dry bulk, the largest of these being
iron ore, grain and coal. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.9.3"
class="koboSpan">As the ocean transport of unitised cargo is the subject
of this chapter, bulk cargoes will only be discussed where it is
necessary to supply context.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">In the bulk sector, the
world of shipping has followed a traditional growth pattern.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">Based on
tonne-miles, crude oil, oil products and dry bulk commodities are the
most important trades in ocean shipping
(</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0021" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0021"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.12.2"
class="koboSpan">Unitised cargo (predominantly containers, and included
in other in </span>[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0021)<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">) is not dominant in terms of tonne-miles demanded; it
accounted for 25 to 28% of tonne-mile demand in the 1990s, up from 19.9%
in 1970, and it continued to grow in importance until
2007.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0106" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0106"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">However, shipping
demand in tonne-miles is only one measure of importance.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">In value terms,
trade in manufactured goods drives world prosperity, as manufactured
goods account for about 70% of world trade in value terms.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">This chapter
provides an overview of world trade in manufactured goods, the primary
user of containerised liner shipping.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.16.4" class="koboSpan">It begins by
identifying the key manufactured goods traded globally, the leading
trading nations and the accompanying trade flows.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.16.5" class="koboSpan">As air cargo is
the principal competitor of maritime transport for inter-regional trade
in manufactured goods, the role of air cargo is examined briefly.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.16.6" class="koboSpan">To complete the
picture, the trader’s view of shipping as a mode choice is discussed and
conclusions drawn about what the future may hold for the transport of
manufactured goods.</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

alt="Figure 1: World seaborne trade 1985–2007" /></span>

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan">Review of Maritime Transport

</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fig0038" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0038"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">, p. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.25.2"
class="koboSpan">15 and equivalent tables from prior years’
editions.</span>

## <span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.26.2" class="koboSpan">The Key Manufactured Goods Traded Globally</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">The world in the early
days of general cargo shipping looked nothing like the world of trade
today. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">The
heyday of trade in tea and silk financed by opium sales to China is long
gone. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.27.3" class="koboSpan">By 1900,
China’s imports had become more diversified, with cotton goods and yarn
replacing opium. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.27.4"
class="koboSpan">While tea and silk may have been China’s key exports to
Europe in 1870, by 1890 they too had diversified, giving way to
shipments of seeds, oil, beans, hides and “all other items” on the
westbound leg from
Asia.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0107" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0107"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Product development
departments 40 years ago were only beginning to contemplate many of the
manufactured goods critical to business today, such as personal
computers, mobile phones and wireless devices.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.29.2" class="koboSpan">However,
post-war consumerism was well-established by the late 1950s when Malcolm
McLean, in an effort to address inefficiencies in goods transport,
conceived the seminal idea of what has now become containerisation.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.29.3" class="koboSpan">In 1956, he
shipped the first “boxes” (really truck chassis) on the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">Ideal-X</span></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan"> from New Jersey to Houston, irrevocably changed the
way most manufactured goods are
transported</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0108" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0108"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan"> and laid the foundation for the next wave of
globalisation. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.33.2"
class="koboSpan">Mattel’s “all-American” Barbie, to use one of
Levinson’s insightful illustrations, was anything but all-American; her
plastic body, clothes and hair all came from
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_101"></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">various factories in Japan, Taiwan and
China.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0109" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0109"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan"> Barbie was conceived in 1959 and this inexpensive
item, relatively speaking, could withstand the cost of transport, be
made half-way around the globe and still be affordable for a generation
of female baby boomers. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.36.2"
class="koboSpan">Transport costs had been dropping steadily since the
end of World War II, and no longer offset the cost advantages of Asian
labour. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.36.3" class="koboSpan">Asia
continued to compete on wages and became the heart of the manufactured
goods sector over the balance of the century.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.36.4" class="koboSpan">From 1985 to
1990, the average annual growth in containerisable trade on North
America/Far East and Far East/Europe trade legs exhibited double-digit
growth rates and, after a brief slowdown in the early 1990s, growth in
trade production in many Asian nations resumed its former pace.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.36.5" class="koboSpan">Since then, the
rate of growth in merchandise trade has consistently outstripped the
rate of growth in world GDP and commodity output.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">According to the World
Trade Organisation (WTO), trade in manufactured goods accounted for
74.9% of all merchandise exports by value in 2000, significantly higher
than the 70.5% recorded in
1990.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0110" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0110"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan"> It included iron and steel, and chemicals, both of
which may be carried as bulk commodities, although the chemicals make up
a significant component of containerised trade.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">If these two
categories of manufactured goods are discounted, the remaining
manufactured goods still made up 63.3% of merchandise exports by value
in 2000. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.39.3" class="koboSpan">Then,
by far the largest category of internationally traded manufactured
products in 2000 was machinery and transportation equipment, even after
the highly visible automotive category was extracted.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.39.4" class="koboSpan">The WTO reported
that growth in 2000 was 6% in manufactured goods, 14.5% in manufacturing
exports and only 4% in world
GDP.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0111" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0111"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan"> Much of the 1990s’ growth had been driven by enhanced
labour productivity. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.41.2"
class="koboSpan">However, growth in global sales for office equipment
and production machinery was expected to slow, if not stagnate, as the
technology revolution completed its restructuring of both the office
environment and the shop floor. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.41.3"
class="koboSpan">The growth for the 2000–2007 period was 7.5% in
manufactured goods and the forecast for the office and telecom equipment
sub-sector had been realised as it was the slowest growing of all export
sectors
reported.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0112" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0112"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">In 2006, the WTO
discontinued reporting machinery and transportation equipment exports
separately so
</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0022" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0022"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">, which reports the latest available 2007 data,
includes this traded good in the Others (semi and manufactures)
category. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">The
decline seen for office and telecom equipment was also reflected in
other manufactures, although not to the same extent, as the exceptional
rise in energy and commodity prices (and hence the fuels and mining
products sector) over the seven years took a significant bite out of the
share held by most manufactured
goods.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0113" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0113"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan"> The share of manufactured goods in world merchandise
exports has declined a full 5% since 2000.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">As the 2008 data have
not yet been released by the WTO, the impact of the economic downturn on
the mix of trade is not yet known but is anticipated to be much worse as
US and European consumers slowed their spending on consumer goods and
energy prices hit a 30-year high in the summer of 2008.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">Looking ahead, the
world continues to move towards a service economy and, in general,
service production activities do not use sea transport.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">Job growth is in
economies and industries that do not contribute to shipping tonne-miles
– software, pharmaceuticals, education services, bio-technology,
eco-tourism and leisure recreation, and business services.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.49.3" class="koboSpan">The conversion
of world trade from predominantly goods-led to service-led growth is
mostly complete.</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

## <span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.62.2" class="koboSpan">Who are the Leading Traders?</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">As already noted,
export growth in the 1990s was phenomenal in Asia and this continued
throughout the economic recovery in the post-2001 period.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.63.2" class="koboSpan">North American
trade was disappointing, as it did not grow at a rate approaching that
of Western Europe, let alone Japan and the developing countries of Asia.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">By 2007, the top
10 world traders are all, with the exception of China, members of the
Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
(</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0023" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0023"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0114" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0114"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan"> Belgium and its neighbour the Netherlands are key
gateways for Europe’s trade in manufactured goods, supporting Germany’s
role as the world’s second largest consumer and the leading goods
producer.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Since the late 1990s,
the four BRIC countries – Brazil, Russia, India and China – have
captured the imaginations of trade observers and warrant closer
attention. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">While
the exports of Brazil have grown at an annual average rate of 17% since
2000, the country ranked twenty-fourth in exports still only accounts
for just over 1% of global trade and has not yet recovered its 2% share
of world merchandise exports recorded in 1948.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.68.3" class="koboSpan">More important,
Russia’s growth 2007 over 2006 was similarly dramatic; Russian
exports</span>

<div id="Ch04.xhtml_fig0033" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00033.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Leading goods traders in 2007" /></span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_103"></span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0023" id="Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0023"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">
Leading goods traders in 2007</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan"> Created from data provided by World Trade Organisation
(2008), </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">International Trade Statistics
2008</span></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">,
Table 1.8, p. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">12
of World Trade Developments section.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">grew at 17% over the
previous year, moving it to twelfth place among exporters while imports
grew 36% over the previous year, to confer the rank of sixteenth.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.76.2" class="koboSpan">However, both
countries continue to play significant global roles in supplying energy,
raw materials and food, with manufactured goods being of less
importance. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">India, like Brazil, accounts for just over 1% of global
trade and it too has not recovered its post–World War II prominence; it
is currently ranked twenty-sixth in merchandise exports, playing a
substantial role in IT, office and telecom products.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.76.4" class="koboSpan">China has been
outstripping these three. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.76.5"
class="koboSpan">Since 2001, China’s export trade has grown by four
times. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.76.6" class="koboSpan">Its
growth has been sufficiently fast to wedge it into the top 10 traders,
firmly in third place after the United States and Germany by the end of
2007 in terms of total trade, and in second place from an export
perspective.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0115" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0115"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan"> In 2008, Paul Bingham presented Global Insight’s
conclusions that the top four countries with the capacity to buy global
products (measured in terms of GDP rank in real dollars) by 2050 will be
China, the US, India and Japan, in that
order.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0116" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0116"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan"> Brazil and Russia will be in the Top 10.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.80.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore these
countries, and others in close proximity, may well benefit from the
transportation demands such growing wealth and resultant spending on
consumer goods will encourage.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">Before drawing any
conclusions about geographic interests in the trade in manufactured
goods, and what that might mean for those with an interest in shipping,
it is important to examine the major trade flows of manufactured goods
and how much of</span>

<div id="Ch04.xhtml_fig0034" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_104"></span>[](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0034)

[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00034.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0034)

</div>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">that trade is
intra-regional. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">Throughout the last two decades, trade liberalisation
and the development of the World Trade Organisation as a multilateral
forum to encourage such liberalization, when coupled with the global
restructuring of supply chains, encouraged intercontinental trade
growth. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.83.3" class="koboSpan">However,
the 1980s and 1990s also bore witness to an explosion of regional trade
agreements – the European Single Market and the subsequent broadening of
the European Union; the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">Canada–US Trade Agreement
</span></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">and later
the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan">North American Free Trade
Agreement</span></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan">; Mercosur in South America–encouraging continental
trading patterns. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.87.2"
class="koboSpan">By the end of the 1990s, approximately half of world
trade was intra-regional.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">The seven regional
trade flows in manufactured goods presented in
</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fig0034" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0034"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan"> account for a significant share of world trade.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">As shipping best
supports intercontinental and inter-regional trade, rising
intra-regional trade has a dampening effect on growth in shipping
demand. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.90.3" class="koboSpan">The
intra-regional flows of the three largest trade blocs (Europe, Asia and
North America) are particularly significant, and account for about half
of all trade in manufactured goods.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.90.4" class="koboSpan">The most
integrated market is Europe, with 73.5% of its trade classified as
intra-regional.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">“\[T\]rade flows within
regions account for a higher share of world trade than flows between
regions. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">Since
2000, this share has fluctuated from between \[sic\] 55 to 58 per cent.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.91.3" class="koboSpan">Relatively large
differences have occurred in the growth of trade within regions: North
America and Asia show a relative \[sic\] balanced growth between inter-
and intra-regional trade; Europe’s intra-trade is growing much faster
than its external trade due to the deepening of its economic integration
while South and Central America, Africa, the Middle East and the CIS
have recorded higher growth in inter-regional exports than in
intra-regional.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0117" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0117"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">Should the trend of
trade integration continue along its current path, a prospect not
unlikely given US preoccupation with homeland security and its focus on
tighter border controls (resulting in a greater administrative burden),
how much trade growth will</span>

<div id="Ch04.xhtml_fig0035" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_105"></span>[](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0035)

[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00035.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0035)

</div>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">be available for ocean
transport? </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">The
likely answer is a smaller share than is now available.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.95.3" class="koboSpan">In other words,
any rise in protectionism will dampen the demand for shipping more so
than already seen from the economic downturn.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">This then raises the
question of how focused countries are on supporting their future trade
to take advantage of global trading opportunities.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.96.2" class="koboSpan">The World
Economic Forum has undertaken to assemble a new report on this issue.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.96.3" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">Global Enabling Trade Report
</span></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">assesses
factors, other than tariffs and quotas, that become barriers to trade,
such as border administration, infrastructure, logistics and the
business environment traders must contend with in the foreign market.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">Four indices are
created
(</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fig0035" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0035"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan">) based on nine “pillars” that encourage the
development of
trade,</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0118" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0118"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"> of which two reflect strong transportation
competitiveness inputs
(</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fig0036" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0036"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">If the top 10 trading
nations by value in </span>[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0023)<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan"> are compared with the top 10 in transport and
communications infrastructure from
</span>[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch04.xhtml_fig0035)<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan">, there is only an overlap of four countries – Germany,
the Netherlands, France and the United States.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">However, it
should be remembered that</span>[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan"> Figure
3</span>](#Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0023)<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan"> represents a “size of economy” construct that
</span>[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch04.xhtml_fig0035)<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan"> does not. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.113.2"
class="koboSpan">The remaining six are all smaller economies without the
significant home markets that allow them the luxury of trade-destroying
protectionism. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.113.3"
class="koboSpan">Even more noticeable is the openness of Europe, which
has fostered growth in container trade with Asia (noted previously) as
well as rising intra-regional trade.</span>

<div id="Ch04.xhtml_fig0036" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_106"></span>[](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0036)

[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00036.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0036)

</div>

## <span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.115.2" class="koboSpan">How are Manufactured Goods Carried?</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">In some measure, the
choice of transport mode for manufactured goods is dictated by shipment
characteristics – the value to weight ratio, the value to volume ratio
and the size of the shipment. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.116.2"
class="koboSpan">However, it is not quite this simple.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">From its inception to
the late 1980s, much of the growth in container shipments could be
attributed to conversion of breakbulk and general cargoes to a container
“format” (penetration). </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.117.2"
class="koboSpan">By the late 1990s, that process was mostly complete.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.117.3" class="koboSpan">While some
commodities like scrap and specialty grains made the switch to
containers from breakbulk or dry bulk vessels, the value to density
ratio of most general cargoes not yet containerised means there will
always be some general cargoes carried conventionally.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.117.4" class="koboSpan">An excellent
example of this is project cargo.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.117.5" class="koboSpan">Often bulky,
high-value but high density, this cargo is seldom aligned dimensionally
to make the container a suitable option.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.117.6" class="koboSpan">This means of
acquiring traffic growth for liner companies has mostly run its
course.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">In finished goods
trade, a very small percentage of the delivered value of the goods is
attributed to transport. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.118.2"
class="koboSpan">A dated Canadian study notes that, in 1986, transport
costs</span>

<div id="Ch04.xhtml_fig0037" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_107"></span>[](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0037)

[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00037.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0037)

</div>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">consumed only 2–3% of
the export sales value of furniture and fixtures, and motor vehicles,
but accounted for 45% of the export sales value of
coal.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0119" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0119"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan"> A 1983 US study put the transport cost component at 4%
for electronic machinery and instruments, 8% for transportation
equipment, 12% for furniture and fixtures, but 24% for petroleum
products.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0120" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0120"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan"> A UK study of manufacturing and services industries
reported transport costs at 3–6% of production
costs.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0121" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0121"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the 20-plus years since these studies were
undertaken, the sheer size of vessels and improvements in speed of cargo
handling technologies has dramatically reduced transport costs to nearly
negligible in the total price paid by the end consumer.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.126.2" class="koboSpan">To quote a 2006
International Chamber of Shipping video, “shipping a can of beer costs
about one
cent”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0122" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0122"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore, as the
value of the goods rises, the importance of transport cost as a function
of delivered price diminishes and the value of transport time rises
(inventory carrying costs are a function of time and interest rates).
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.128.2" class="koboSpan">Because of
this, high-value goods of low density and small shipment volumes become
targets for air cargo providers. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.128.3"
class="koboSpan">Hummels attributes the rise in air freight share of
global trade to 2000 to technological advances in jet engines and the
resultant reduction in air cargo costs; he also attributes the loss of
share for air freight after 2000 to rising input costs, particularly
fuel.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0123" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0123"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">It is difficult to
allocate various commodities to the type of transport they will demand.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">The trade
statistics, while indicating the relative value of flows between
countries, provide very little indication of what moves by what mode of
transport. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.130.3" class="koboSpan">In
the world of increasingly proprietary data, only a superficial
assessment is possible.</span>

<a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fig0037" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0037"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan">, for example, indicates that modal split is not common
across export markets, but that a significant share of Canada’s
international modal split by value can be</span>

<div id="Ch04.xhtml_fig0038" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_108"></span>[](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0038)

[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00038.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0038)

</div>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">attributed to air,
particularly for Western and Eastern Europe and Oceania.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.134.2" class="koboSpan">The
representation of modal split is quite accurate; the remainder of
traffic moves by surface transport (road, rail or pipeline), and is
generally intra-regional in nature.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.134.3" class="koboSpan">In the case of
North America, the dominance of surface modes is therefore clear.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.134.4" class="koboSpan">Even so, data
errors in “mode of transport” are quite common.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.134.5" class="koboSpan">Many exporters
only know the origin of the goods, not how they were transported to
their destination; this may be because the price they charge is based on
FCA or EXW terms of sale or because they have outsourced transport
decisions to a third party logistics service supplier.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.134.6" class="koboSpan">Given the sheer
volume of transport services outsourced, it is not surprising that a
significant number of manufacturers do not know the mode of transport
used for the international leg of the journey; they may only know that a
truck picked it up.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">It has already been
noted that significant trade in manufactured goods is intra-regional in
nature, and therefore there is a potential target market for ship
operators – the short sea market.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">However,
encouraging cargo interests to switch from land transport options to
regional shipping is not easy. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.135.3"
class="koboSpan">Where there are very good land-based transport systems
in place, particularly Western Europe and North America, short sea
development has been a struggle, whereas where regional seas exist
(Eastern Europe/Baltic States/Scandanavia and the Mediterranean) that
has been less the case.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">The case for short sea
is particularly market-specific. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.136.2"
class="koboSpan">For example, a Spanish study investigated a road versus
short sea discrete mode choice, drawing conclusions about buyer
requirements, including cost considerations; it found that shippers’
choice of short sea transport is more sensitive to changes in road
transport prices than to changes in sea transport costs, and concluded
that modal switching to short sea could be induced by imposing an
‘ecotax’ on road
transport.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0124" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0124"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_109"></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan">Although severe congestion in road transport is a
widespread problem, short sea or tug/barge transport options are not
viewed as positive solutions by many
shippers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0125" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0125"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan"> While it has an image problem in both Europe and the
US, in Canada this is not the issue; lack of adoption by Canadian cargo
interests has been traced to its failure to meet specific shipper
requirements in the current operating cost environment.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.140.2" class="koboSpan">In particular,
short sea shipping has difficulty responding to shippers’ need for
specific delivery windows required of just-in-time systems, and the
usual evaluative criteria of transit times, departure frequencies and
costs continue to drive the choices made in favour of more flexible land
routings.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0126" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0126"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan"> While short sea shipping adoption languishes in North
America, it has reached a traffic volume in Europe similar to that
carried by trucks.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">In conclusion, modal
splits between truck and sea in manufactured goods are more likely based
on the product characteristics and seller/consignee preferences for fast
transit time and time-definite delivery.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.143.2" class="koboSpan">The financial
crisis may have changed the value proposition of each of these modes and
the modal splits of the future are more likely to reflect the value
proposition of the mode more closely attended by the cargo
interest.</span>

## <span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.144.2" class="koboSpan">Competition from Air Freight</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">In the early 1980s,
interest rates and the cost of capital increased the likelihood of
traders evaluating the carrying costs associated with in-transit
inventory in assessing their transport options; efforts to address these
costs contributed to tremendous growth in the air cargo industry.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.145.2" class="koboSpan">Air’s share of
total trade in 1985 was 13.7% and was forecast by Sclar and Blond to
grow to 18.2% by the year
2000;</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0127" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0127"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan"> much of the growth was expected to come at the expense
of ocean transport, and it did. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.147.2"
class="koboSpan">Air cargo growth in the 1990s was attributable to the
growth in product sectors like pharmaceuticals, electronics (office and
telecom products in particular) and automotive parts.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.147.3" class="koboSpan">Because these
products have a high value to weight ratio and tend to be
time-sensitive, shippers favour air as a mode of transport.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.147.4" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
the just-in-time nature of time-managed manufacturing and the slimming
of retail inventories to the barest necessary enhanced the shift to air
cargo in general; the consumer’s desire for mass-customised products
required the speed and agility that ocean transport is often incapable
of delivering. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.147.5"
class="koboSpan">Until the 2008 financial crisis, shippers of
high-value, low-density manufactured goods were willing to incur higher
transport costs to reduce risk in making and holding inventory.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.147.6" class="koboSpan">Time-based
competition became a new logistics necessity in the 2003–2007 period,
and air cargo thrived in these circumstances.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">In 2001, the air cargo
sector was severely tested by the collapse of the technology sector in
early
2001.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0128" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0128"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan"> With 20–25% of air cargo being high- or
information-technology products, there was a significant decline in the
volume of air cargo by the summer of 2001.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.150.2" class="koboSpan">The World Trade
Center tragedy in September had a further chilling effect on consumer
spending that also had to be absorbed by the industry.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.150.3" class="koboSpan">Air freight
volumes were low in 2002 but from 2003 to 2007 growth in air freight
volumes recovered, with growth exceeding 15% in early 2004.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.150.4" class="koboSpan">Volumes
deteriorated severely in 2008 in advance of the financial crisis of the
fall of 2008. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.150.5"
class="koboSpan">The industry projects recovery in
2011.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0129" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0129"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">As
</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0024" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0024"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan"> reveals, the largest international air cargo providers
are well-established airlines, some with passenger services, but all
with substantial cargo-handling capability.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.154.2" class="koboSpan">With the
quality of service provided by air cargo operators to trading interests,
the use of air cargo resumed its very high growth rate throughout the
2000s as higher value</span>

<div id="Ch04.xhtml_fig0039" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00039.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: Top 10 International scheduled air cargo carriers 2008" /></span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_110"></span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0024" id="Ch04.xhtml_cap_lbl0024"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
4:</span></span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">
Top 10 International scheduled air cargo carriers 2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">Note: </span></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan">FTK = scheduled freight tonne-kilometre flown</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan"> Created from data provided by IATA, World Air
Transport Statistics, downloaded from
</span>[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan">www.iata.org/whatwedo/economics/index</span>](http://www.iata.org/whatwedo/economics/index)<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.163.2"
class="koboSpan">Accessed 15 July 2009.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">perishables
established even stronger global supply chains, and those
decision-makers worried about cargo damage, just-in-time delivery and
cargo security switched to air where the economics made sense.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.164.2" class="koboSpan">According to
Mike Tretheway of InterVISTAS, new planes, engines and technologies
enabled the air cargo industry over the past decade to attract
lower-value-per-kilogram cargos, moving these air carriers into
competition for the premium end of the marine container
business.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0130" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0130"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan"> Air cargo, for example, had always dominated the
high-fashion clothing industry, but in the last five years has
established a stronger presence in the seafood market.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">The US market provides
a good illustration of the air cargo versus liner shipping relationship,
and obvious evidence of air cargo’s dominance in the transport of
high-value but light-density products.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">In dollar
terms, the ratio of US exports using ocean to those using air was 58.8%
to 41.2% in 2000 and 55.8% to 44.2% in 2001.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.167.3" class="koboSpan">On the import
side, water transport fares better, with a ratio in 2000 of 63.7% to
air’s 36.3%. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.167.4" class="koboSpan">In
2001, air cargo lost some traffic to marine, dropping to 34.0% of the
two-mode
total.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0131" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0131"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan"> On the other hand, in weight terms, air cargo has a
two-mode share of less than 1% (</span>[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
5</span>](#Ch04.xhtml_fig0038)<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">Over the past few
years, as the air freight industry has continued to innovate and reach
ever further into the premium end of the marine container cargo market,
air cargo carriers have come to see ocean carriers as key competitors
for the manufactured goods market.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.172.2" class="koboSpan">Updates on
ocean rates and competition from marine cargo options are now featured
in IATA economic briefings and market research documents.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.172.3" class="koboSpan">Particularly
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_111"></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan">noticed in the second quarter 2009 briefing was that
marine container cargo demand had fallen by 15%, less than the market
loss experienced by air freight
carriers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0132" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0132"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">Of particular interest
is the relationship between air freight and marine cargo over the
economic cycle and the recent economic downturn.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.175.2" class="koboSpan">According to
the International Air Transport Association, air freight volumes drop
four to five months before economic softening, as shippers switch to
cheaper but slower forms of transportation, like the marine mode.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.175.3" class="koboSpan">The drop in
volume is faster than the drop in world trade, but the air freight
recovery mode also features a faster rebound as manufacturers restock
source components in anticipation of the
recovery.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0133" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0133"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">While shipping will
never compete with air cargo in the perishables or emergency goods
markets because the consequential loss caused by any delay, these are
not products targeted by shipping in the first place.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.177.2" class="koboSpan">The problem for
shipping is that many high-value, low-density manufactured goods are the
high-yield business of shipping lines and quite easily switched to air
cargo. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.177.3" class="koboSpan">This is
particularly true if just-in-time systems have reduced the shipment size
to that manageable by the air carrier.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.177.4" class="koboSpan">The existence
of the air cargo option has the ability to keep transport prices for
high-value goods depressed; without sufficient cross-subsidisation
potential, lower-value, high-density product volumes will be of less
interest to the shipping lines and the total volume traded will be
less.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">The recent financial
crisis, however, has hit air cargo volumes hard, and sea has attracted
some of that business back. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.178.2"
class="koboSpan">New cooling technologies that enable the shipment of
live lobster and premium seafoods by sea (lobster formerly only had a
24-hour life span in transport) hold promise for wider application and
restoration of some lost traffic for the marine mode.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.178.3" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, it
is likely that full costing of the environmental impacts of air freight
will enhance the attraction to ocean shipping activity once the economic
downturn has passed.</span>

## <span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.179.2" class="koboSpan">The Trader's View</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">Today’s trading
perspective can be traced to the post-war rise in consumer demand.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.180.2" class="koboSpan">By the 1960s,
trade in manufactured goods had reached new heights.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.180.3" class="koboSpan">The dramatic
increase in oil prices in the 1970s, however, brought unacceptable rises
in interest rates. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.180.4"
class="koboSpan">As a result, traders turned their attention to
extracting inventory carrying costs from the system.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.180.5" class="koboSpan">Those selling
the goods sought new ways to ship that improved transit time and allowed
them to restructure their operations to diminish time-to-purchase at
retail. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.180.6" class="koboSpan">They
also began to reconsider where they produced goods, expanding their
horizons to include servicing more than just domestic markets.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.180.7" class="koboSpan">The seeds of
globalisation of production and distribution were planted.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">By now, it should be
evident that the future transport of manufactured goods by sea is
dependent on a pro-marine modal split decision by traders.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">Clearly, for
some high-value, low-density products, the choice will continue to be
air cargo. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.181.3" class="koboSpan">At
the other end of the continuum, for awkward, bulky and unconventional
machinery there will also be no choice but non-unitised ocean transport.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.181.4" class="koboSpan">In the middle
lies the largest share of manufactured goods.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.181.5" class="koboSpan">For these,
renewed focus on regional trade may encourage defection to surface
modes. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.181.6" class="koboSpan">At the
moment, it appears that the air mode is not cost-competitive with sea
and surface modes in the China–Western Europe corridor (See
</span><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fig0040" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0040"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.183.2"
class="koboSpan">While road does provide a faster alternative to sea
(about one week), the cost is three to four</span>

<div id="Ch04.xhtml_fig0040" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_112"></span>[](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0040)

[<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00040.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fig0040)

</div>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">times the ocean
container rate and security concerns about the route are ever-present.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.185.2" class="koboSpan">For most
inter-continental markets, the two primary competitors are air and ocean
container. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.185.3" class="koboSpan">The
choice of mode depends on which meets the customer’s needs better and
provides the superior value proposition when carrying costs and product
characteristics are considered.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">Research has shown
that traders’ transport decisions are multi-criteria ones.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.186.2" class="koboSpan">They take into
account product and customer requirements and specific attributes deemed
desirable in making route- and product-specific decisions.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.186.3" class="koboSpan">Over a period
of 20 years, the author has examined this decision-making process for
the liner industry, identifying a number of key purchase determinants
for a liner company’s services, and illustrated that different criteria
can be identified for different customer segments, but that these
criteria are dynamic over
time.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0134" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0134"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan"> As the industry evolved, emphasis on price diminished
and other factors like transit time grew in importance.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.188.2" class="koboSpan">The last paper
in the series concluded that shippers, consignees and freight forwarders
all have significantly different decision criteria when it comes to
choosing a carrier; these factors are also distinct
geographically.</span><sup><a href="#Ch04.xhtml_fn0135" id="Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0135"><span
id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan"> Furthermore, some customers clearly buy a package of
attributes for the rate paid while others evaluate individual attributes
separately. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.190.2" class="koboSpan">The
research also confirmed the move away from transaction-specific carrier
decisions towards relationship-building through agreements with carriers
and logistical service suppliers.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.190.3" class="koboSpan">The heavy use
of professional logistics firms and the outsourcing of these functions
are two directions traders took in the 1990s, both serving to
concentrate decision-making power over shipments in fewer hands.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">The 2001 “peak”
shipping season serves as a useful illustration of the ramifications of
traders’ decision-making on ocean carriers.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.191.2" class="koboSpan">The growth in
trade in manufactured goods is partly driven by consumer demand for
holiday gifts, particularly in North America and Europe.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.191.3" class="koboSpan">As large
retailers tie up shipping capacity in the period of August to November
each year on the Asia/North America eastbound and Asia/Europe westbound
routes, the full impact on all manufactured goods trade capacity is
felt. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.191.4" class="koboSpan">The 2001
peak season was particularly interesting to watch.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.191.5" class="koboSpan">A slowdown in
the US economy through the early summer months meant many US retailers
delayed placing orders for Christmas merchandise for as long as
possible. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.191.6" class="koboSpan">This,
coupled with increasing supply from vessel deliveries over the year,
resulted in severe difficulties for carriers with capacity well in
excess of demand. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.191.7"
class="koboSpan">Add the tragedy of 11 September 2001 to the mix, and
consumer demand plummeted. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.191.8"
class="koboSpan">The impact on available ocean capacity and transport
prices was immediate, devastating and exacerbated further by those who
took
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_113"></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan">advantage of excess air cargo capacity to cover any
shortfall. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.192.2" class="koboSpan">The
economic slowdown could have been predicted, although not far enough in
advance to address the additional vessel capacity being delivered, but
the tragedy could not.</span>

## <span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.193.2" class="koboSpan">Looking Forward</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">Over the past two
decades, the nature of transport of manufactured goods has changed as
many consumer products sectors have globalised.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.194.2" class="koboSpan">Manufacturers
can buy components in many places, distribute somewhere else for
assembly and the final products end up in a third location to be sold.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">Sometimes some
component parts have been moved seven or eight times in the process of
getting on the retail shelf or to the automotive showroom.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.194.4" class="koboSpan">Declining real
transport costs, increasing value of goods transported, a declining
weight to volume ratio, along with diminishing costs of
telecommunications and computing all encouraged a concentration of
specialised production.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">However, recently
companies producing products requiring customisation have moved the
customisation location as close as possible to the end market.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.195.2" class="koboSpan">All this means,
in an era of supply chain management, that these multiple moves are
dependent on continuous improvement activities, regular and frequent
performance monitoring and re-evaluation of the network of manufacturing
and distribution partners. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.195.3"
class="koboSpan">With a global perspective, the conclusion for container
shipping is one where large volume routes will continue to dominate but,
at the level of the trader, the product mix and route will be less
predictable. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.195.4"
class="koboSpan">Direct delivery, via air cargo, is now the norm for
many high value-to-weight segments, such as personal computers,
particularly those where products are customised to order.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.196.1" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, with the
trend to mega-retailers in North America and Europe, and the use of
fewer and fewer distribution points, the network for warehousing and
distribution has become very dynamic.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.196.2" class="koboSpan">Companies now
have the capacity for creating just-in-time systems of distribution and
that has been accompanied by an intense focus on performance monitoring.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.196.3" class="koboSpan">Constant
re-evaluation of the entire supply chain has meant frequent changes to
the network as continuous performance improvements are sought.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.196.4" class="koboSpan">If system
performance does not measure up, not only can manufacturers choose to
re-route the traffic, but they may also decide to relocate their
production or assembly facilities, thus shifting trade flows.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.196.5" class="koboSpan">The mergers and
acquisitions trend of the 1990s led to industry consolidation in many
sectors; the result is fewer, larger production facilities and those
“relocation” decisions are now in the hands of fewer and fewer “global”
shippers.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">Will world trade in
manufactured goods continue to grow in future?
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.197.2" class="koboSpan">There will be
some growth attributed to rising population, and significant growth due
to the expanding middle class in many of the world’s more populated
countries. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.197.3" class="koboSpan">As
already noted, growth in container transport demand arising from the
penetration of containerisation is less probable, as containerisation
will soon reach maximum penetration except on low-volume routes.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.197.4" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
continued incursion of air cargo into traditional ocean shipment markets
is possible as manufacturers continue to squeeze buffer time out of the
transport chain and to favour time-definite transport over the vagaries
of weather-influenced shipping. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.197.5"
class="koboSpan">Most important is the issue of whether or not the
growth of the past decade resulting from manufacturing supply chain
management and national economic specialisation has run its course.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.197.6" class="koboSpan">Most industrial
sectors have undergone a decade of consolidation; the accompanying
strategic merger and acquisition activities were intended to prepare
surviving companies for global reach in defined niches or
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_page_114"></span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">global domination.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.198.2" class="koboSpan">Any economic or
financial crisis brings with it the opportunity for corporate
restructuring; how international merger and acquisition activity will
affect both traders and transport suppliers remains to be seen.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.198.3" class="koboSpan">We can only
speculate on what the market will look like in two years.</span>

<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the future
demand for sea transport of containerised goods is unlikely to reflect
the demand patterns of the past for three critical reasons.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.199.2" class="koboSpan">First, in
serviceled economies, growth in demand comes largely from the rise in
wealth and greater consumer spending, in addition to greater demand from
rising population; here, the likelihood is that demand for consumer
products will continue to drive growth where new wealth is being
generated for an expanding middle class.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.199.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore, it
is likely that increased demand will come from BRIC and Eastern European
markets, as the rising middle class seeks to enjoy consumer products now
taken for granted by developed-country consumers.
</span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.199.4" class="koboSpan">Secondly, it is
not clear how the financial crisis will play out in terms of which key
manufacturers of these products and which providers of marine container
services will survive the economic downturn and emerge as healthy
businesses. </span><span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.199.5"
class="koboSpan">Finally, it is also not clear how the United Nations
Framework Convention on Climate Change will affect the economic value
proposition offered by transport companies to their customers; carbon
taxes or cap and trade approaches to incorporating environmental costs
into the supply chain will influence traders’ mode choices in
future.</span>

class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch04.xhtml_bck_fn0105)<span id="Ch04.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
