<div id="Ch05.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_117"></span>[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 5</span>\
<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Energy Economics and Trade</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0128)
==============================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Michael</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Tamvakis</span></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0136" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0136"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.5.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">It is a well known fact
that the international maritime industry is driven by the movement of
goods and people. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.7.2"
class="koboSpan">Maritime economists have long established that the
demand for shipping services is derived from the demand for
international trade and awareness of what drives the latter is the aim
of this chapter.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">Within the space and
scope of the next few pages, it is impossible to cover all trades and
factors that affect demand for maritime services.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">We will focus,
instead, on the economics and major trade patterns of the most important
commodity group, energy, which encompasses three very important
commodities: crude oil and products, gas and coal.</span>

## <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.9.2" class="koboSpan">Energy</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Demand for energy</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">Energy is what drives
modern economic development and for the last couple of centuries at
least, human societies have relied on hydrocarbons for the supply of
that energy. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.11.2"
class="koboSpan">Despite continuous research and initiatives into the
development of renewable, sustainable and ecologically friendly energy
resources, we very much rely on three major forms of hydrocarbons – oil,
coal and gas – for effectively 90% of the world’s primary energy
consumption (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0025" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0025"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">With the widespread use
of hydrocarbons in all aspects of economic activity, consumption of
energy commodities has been closely linked with a nation’s development
and its transition from a traditional, agriculture-based economy, to a
developed, industrialised one. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.14.2"
class="koboSpan">A recent poignant example is that of China, which from
the 1990s onwards has transformed itself into the world’s industrial
powerhouse. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.14.3" class="koboSpan">On
an aggregate basis, it is reasonable to assume that energy consumption
is directly related to the level of gross domestic product (GDP).
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0026" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0026"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows a proxy of this relationship by</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0041" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00041.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: World primary energy production" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_118"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0025" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0025"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">
World primary energy production</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">looking at the
development of industrial production and primary energy consumption in
OECD countries since 1973. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.22.2"
class="koboSpan">Notice the fundamental change in the relationship
between the two indices after 1980.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.22.3" class="koboSpan">For comparison,
the price of oil is also plotted on the same chart, and highlights the
effect it has had on energy consumption.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">The notion of a
straightforward relationship between energy consumption and GDP is quite
appealing, but rather simplistic. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.23.2"
class="koboSpan">One has to look at the disaggregated picture of energy
consumption to get a more accurate idea of the underlying demand
parameters. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.23.3"
class="koboSpan">Primary energy consumption is usually classified into
four broad categories: industrial; transport; other (incl.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.23.4" class="koboSpan">residential and
agriculture); and a fourth residual category encompassing all non-energy
uses.
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0027" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0027"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the OECD estimate of energy usage in the world,
by fuel, in 2007.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">2.1.1 Residential consumption</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">Like for any other
good, demand for energy depends on the price of the commodity and the
total disposable income of households.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">Any change in
the price of the commodity will affect the quantity purchased by
consumers. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.27.3" class="koboSpan">For
example, if the price of oil falls, its consumption is expected to
increase </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan">ceteris
paribus</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.29.2" class="koboSpan">The total change
in consumption is usually split between the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">income</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan">substitution</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan"> effects. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.33.2"
class="koboSpan">The first is attributed to the fact that with the new,
lower price the same amount of income will buy more units of the
commodity; the second effect is due to the switch from other, more
expensive substitutes to the lower-priced commodity.</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0042" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00042.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Industrial production and energy consumption in OECD" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_119"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0026" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0026"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">
Industrial production and energy consumption in OECD</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan"> OECD Key Economic Indicators, BP Statistical Review of
World Energy; Datastream</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">When analysing the
demand for specific energy commodities, it is always useful to know
their responsiveness to changes in their own price, changes in
disposable income and changes in the price of substitutes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">This
responsiveness is measured by the own price – or demand – elasticity,
the income elasticity, and the cross-price elasticity.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.39.3" class="koboSpan">The usefulness
of these three parameters was eminently demonstrated during the two oil
price shocks in 1973 and 1979. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.39.4"
class="koboSpan">While the first shock put pressure on household
incomes, which had to accommodate a larger expenditure for energy, it
did not tamper demand for oil substantially.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.39.5" class="koboSpan">This was not the
case with the second oil price shock, however, when income and price
elasticities of oil experienced a structural change and led to a
dramatically reduced demand for oil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.39.6" class="koboSpan">In yet another
demonstration of the change in these fundamental relationships, demand
for energy in recent years seems to grow unabated despite the persistent
ascent of oil prices.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">2.1.2 Industrial consumption</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">The production cost of
an industrial process depends – in the short to medium term – on the
cost of its inputs and a set of fixed costs; in the long term, of
course, all costs are variable. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.41.2"
class="koboSpan">The production cost function can be formally written as
C = ƒ(X</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">... </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.43.2"
class="koboSpan">X</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">, E, FC), where
X</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan">...X</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan"> are production inputs, E is energy and FC is fixed
cost. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">This
function</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0043" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00043.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: World energy consumption by fuel and sector, 2007" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_120"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0027" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0027"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">
World energy consumption by fuel and sector, 2007</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan">IEA Key World Energy Statistics, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">represents a slight
deviation from the usual norm of depicting production costs as a
function of capital and labour, and is more suitable for our
purposes.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">The total demand for
industrial energy can be viewed as an aggregation of all production cost
functions like the one given above.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">The effects of
price changes on energy demand will depend on the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan">rate of technical
substitution</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan">, which represents the rate at which one input of
production can be replaced by another, in order to achieve the same
cost.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">In practical terms the
rate of technical substitution shows how easily energy can be replaced
by other input factors, and how easily different sources of energy can
substitute one another in the same production process.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">Once again, a
suitable example can be taken from the two oil price crises.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.59.3" class="koboSpan">The first price
shock took industry by surprise, as no cost-effective alternatives to
oil were available. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.59.4"
class="koboSpan">The second shock, however, came after considerable
restructuring in energy usage and efficiency had been implemented, with
the result that total energy requirements were reduced and alternative
sources of energy – predominantly coal, but also natural gas and nuclear
power – replaced oil.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">2.1.3 Transport consumption</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">Energy consumption in
transport is dominated by oil, which displaced coal earlier or later in
the history of different transport means.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">In the car
industry, for example, gasoline was used since the very beginning, as it
was the most appropriate fuel for the internal combustion engine.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.61.3" class="koboSpan">At sea, coal was
dominant until after the end of the World War I, but was rapidly
replaced by oil afterwards. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.61.4"
class="koboSpan">On land, coal persisted slightly more</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0044" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00044.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: US car efficiency development" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_121"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0028" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0028"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
4:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan"> US
car efficiency development</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan"> Energy Information Administration, US Department of
Energy, 2006</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">as a source of energy
for locomotives, but eventually had to give in to oil’s undisputed
superiority.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Today, oil is used in
transport almost exclusively; perhaps the only notable exception is that
of Brazil, which has promoted the extensive use of sugar-derived biofuel
in the 1970s and, again, in current times.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">Setting aside
the past and possible future use of biofuels, very few other oil
substitutes have been used in transport; notably natural gas and liquid
petroleum gas (propane).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">Because oil has
virtually no – commercially viable – substitutes in transport, demand
for it depends very much on income and efficiency of use.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">The latter is
probably more important, as is shown in
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0028" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0028"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">, which graphs the development of car efficiency in the
United States. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.71.2"
class="koboSpan">Two indicators are used: the rate of fuel consumption
expressed in miles per gallon; and the car usage expressed in average
miles per car. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.71.3"
class="koboSpan">Two types of vehicle are also shown: passenger cars and
vans and SUVs (sports utility vehicles).
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.71.4" class="koboSpan">As one can see,
mileage was not affected substantially, despite the oil price hikes in
1973 and 1979. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.71.5"
class="koboSpan">The rapid increase in car fuel efficiency, assisted by
the mass introduction of Japanese cars in the American market, helped
sustain the great love affair of US consumers with the automotive
industry and provide endless material for ‘road movies’ to Hollywood
scriptwriters.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">Transportation is not
of course limited to road only. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.72.2"
class="koboSpan">The other two major consumers are air and seaborne
transportation. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.72.3"
class="koboSpan">The former has risen to prominence, due to the general
increase in passenger and cargo air-miles travelled and due to the fact
that
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_122"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">the fuel used (aviation turbine fuel or jet kerosene)
is one of the most valuable refined petroleum products.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
importance of shipping fuel consumption (in the form of either heavy
fuel oil of marine diesel) cannot be underestimated, given that an
estimated 75% of the world merchandise trade is seaborne.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">2.1.4 Other consumption</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">This category
encompasses all the remaining sectors of the economy, primarily energy
consumption for agricultural use and commercial buildings.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">Parameters
affecting this segment of consumption include fuel efficiency and the
degree of mechanisation of agriculture.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Supply of energy</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">Energy can be generated
by both exhaustible and renewable resources.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">The latter have
amassed considerable scientific attention and certainly have ample
potential, but their share of primary energy consumption remains very
modest and is dwarfed by the dominant position of exhaustible
hydrocarbons. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.77.3" class="koboSpan">In
this chapter we will focus only on these very hydrocarbons: oil, gas and
coal.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">Like other minerals,
energy commodities fall in the category of exhaustible resources.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">Available
reserves, rates of extraction and economic rents are some of the
parameters governing the usage of exhaustible resources.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.78.3" class="koboSpan">The theory
behind this was explored as early as 1929 by Hotelling who built a basic
economic framework for the exploitation of non-renewable natural
resources.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">Basic economic theory
anticipates that each additional unit (the “marginal” unit) of a natural
resource will be extracted as long as the economic cost of extraction –
which includes
marginal</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0137" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0137"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan"> cost and
user</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0138" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0138"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan"> cost – is lower or equal to the
price</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0139" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0139"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan"> paid for the resource plus the marginal utility of
present
consumption.</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0140" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0140"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan"> Like in most production processes, extractive firms
benefit initially from increasing returns to scale, then their average
total cost curve stays flat for some time after reaching the minimum
efficient scale, and if they decide to increase output further they are
usually faced with decreasing returns to scale.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">In the long-run,
production tends to stabilise along the bottom of their long-run average
total cost curve (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0029" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0029"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">The theory, as it
stands, implies that high-cost producers – which usually also have
limited reserves – should be the first to be squeezed out of the market
when energy prices fall and operating costs are not covered.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">It also implies
that large low-cost producers should be relatively immune to price
downswings, and continue to produce under all – but the most extreme –
market conditions.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">Alas, real life is not
as clear-cut as this model suggests.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">To take yet
another example from the oil industry; although Arab OPEC countries are
indisputably the lowest-cost producers, it is high-cost producers that
seem to be operating at full capacity, while low-cost competitors seem
to play the role of “swing’
producer”</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0141" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0141"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan"> balancing demand and supply.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">The picture becomes
even more complicated when government economic policies are taken into
account. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">Energy
supplies are of strategic importance to every government worldwide.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.94.3" class="koboSpan">If they are in
abundance, they will be used to cover domestic needs and the balance
will probably be exported; if they are in short supply, the government
will resort to imports and a certain amount of stockpiling for security
reasons.</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0045" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00045.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 5: Long-run average total cost curve" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_123"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0029" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0029"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
5:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">
Long-run average total cost curve</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">If security of supplies
is a major issue on the energy agenda, demand will tend to be biased
towards certain (perhaps low-cost) producers, and “secure” (perhaps
high-cost) suppliers will realise this and step up their production.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">Finally, if
financial flows from exports and/or export taxes are considered as well,
national fiscal and monetary policies may distort the picture even
further.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">In any project for the
extraction of mineral resources there are three main stages:
exploration, development, and production.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">Exploration may
last a few years, until proper geological surveys point with high
probability to the existence of reserves.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.99.3" class="koboSpan">Several
exploratory wells/shafts may have to be drilled in order to assess the
quality and extent of the deposits.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.99.4" class="koboSpan">Costs at this
stage can be substantial and are sunk.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.99.5" class="koboSpan">The development
stage involves extensive drilling in the case of oil and gas, and
construction of an open pit or underground mine in the case of coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.99.6" class="koboSpan">Again, costs at
this stage are sunk, and further costs might have to be incurred at
later stages of a project, in order to improve and/or extend
capacity.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">At the production
stage, most of the costs are operating costs, which tend to increase as
reserves are being depleted and more effort is required to extract them.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">This is
particularly true for coal, especially when underground mining is the
method of production.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">Energy projects use
capital quite intensively and embody a substantial amount of risk.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.101.2" class="koboSpan">Even when
adequate reserves are found, the high rate of discount applied to such
projects makes the extraction of the commodity more desirable sooner
rather than later. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.101.3"
class="koboSpan">This argument is often used to explain the intensive
exploitation of high-cost oil</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0046" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_124"></span>[](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0046)

[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00046.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0046)

</div>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">reserves like the ones
in Alaska or the North Sea, in order to maximise oil recovery as quickly
as possible.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">Another important
characteristic of the energy sector – and the mineral sector in general
– is the large extent of heterogeneity in production costs.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">Depending on
the geomorphy of the field and local climatic conditions costs can vary
considerably from one region to the next.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.104.3" class="koboSpan">In the oil
sector, for instance, capital expenditure for field development may
range from “low-cost” to “frontier areas”, as it is shown in
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fig0046" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0046"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">A similar situation is
evident in the coal industry, with Venezuela, Indonesia and South Africa
in the low to medium-cost producers, while countries like USA, Germany,
UK and France are at the other end.</span>

## <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">Oil</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">With a share of 35% in
world primary energy consumption, oil remains the leading energy
commodity, and has been so for at least the past four decades.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">Oil reserves
currently amount to just over one and a quarter trillion barrels, over
half of which are located in the Middle East.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.109.3" class="koboSpan">Latin America
is the second largest reserve holder, with deposits mainly in Mexico,
Venezuela and, more recently, Brazil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.109.4" class="koboSpan">The other
dominant reserve holder is the former Soviet Union, particularly Russia
and Kazakhstan.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">What is remarkable
about the oil sector is its imbalance in terms of reserves.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">It has to be
noted, however, that production by different countries has never been
proportional
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_125"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">to their reserves, as technology, investment capital,
and finance are not freely available to all producers, and political
conditions have often distorted economic principles of
production.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Geology and extraction</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">Oil is one of a number
of hydrocarbon compounds that can be found in the earth’s crust.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.113.2" class="koboSpan">In fact
four-fifths of the world’s sedimentary basins provide suitable
geological conditions for the formation of crude oil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.113.3" class="koboSpan">On several
occasions, parts of the earth’s crust move against each other to form an
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan">anticline</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan">, which creates a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan">reservoir</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan"> of impervious rock, where organic material is trapped
and broken down by enzymes over a period of several million years.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">A reservoir
usually contains several oil
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan">fields</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan">, some of them grouped together in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan">provinces</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.121.2"
class="koboSpan">The organic material contained in the fields is a
mixture of oil, water and gas. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.121.3"
class="koboSpan">Oil floats on top of the water, while gas provides
pressure in the field, which is invaluable for the extraction of the
precious fuel.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">Oil exploration is the
part of the oil industry that has always caught the imagination of the
masses, as it contained a huge element of risk, but offering the
possibility of extremely good returns.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">Modern oil
exploration does not rely that much on luck any more.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.122.3" class="koboSpan">A number of
scientific methods are used for the location of possible oil reservoirs
and the estimation of their reserves.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.122.4" class="koboSpan">These are
usually grouped in three main categories: geophysical analyses;
geophysical surveys; and drilling and well logging.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">Geological analysis
includes a number of alternative – and often complementary – methods,
ranging from traditional field geology (examining surface rocks), to the
use of orbiting satellites. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.123.2"
class="koboSpan">Geochemical analysis is also used, in order to
establish the presence of suitable material for the formation of oil
deposits. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.123.3" class="koboSpan">The
aim of all the above techniques, is to understand the geological
structure and history of an area, and decide whether it is worthwhile to
spend more money on exploring it.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">The main geophysical
technique used nowadays is the seismic survey, although gravimetric and
magnetic surveys can also be used to identify underlying structures that
are possibly oil-bearing. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.124.2"
class="koboSpan">Seismic surveys involve the artificial generation of
shock waves, using a variety of techniques, like controlled explosions,
dropping of weights and vibration generators (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0030" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0030"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.126.2"
class="koboSpan">The aim is to record the reflections of those waves by
the various geological strata. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.126.3"
class="koboSpan">The data are recorded by geophones, which are similar
to seismographs, and then transmitted and recorded.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">recording</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan"> stage is followed by the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">processing</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan"> of the data collected, which involves their
enhancement by computers. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.131.2"
class="koboSpan">Finally, the results are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan">interpreted</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan"> by experts, who build an image of the underground
formations and the likely location of deposits.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">All three
stages (recording, processing and interpretation) have been immensely
improved by the use of enhanced computer technology.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">The latter has
allowed the advance from 2D to 3D seismic surveys, which use a lot more
signal recorders and provide a far more accurate picture of underground
formations. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.133.4" class="koboSpan">A
traditional 2D seismic survey, until a few years ago, was shot along
individual lines, at varying distances, producing ‘pictures’ of vertical
sections of the underground formations.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.133.5" class="koboSpan">A 3D seismic
survey, on the other hand, is shot in a closely spaced grid pattern and
gives a complete, more accurate, picture of the subsurface.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">The next stage in oil
exploration is well drilling. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.134.2"
class="koboSpan">To collect more accurate survey data,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">boreholes</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan"> are drilled on top of the area suspected to contain
oil reserves. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.136.2"
class="koboSpan">Many of these
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">wildcat</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan"> drills end up as dry holes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.138.2" class="koboSpan">The purpose of
the boreholes is not only to extract the</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0047" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00047.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Seismic vibrators in the desert" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_126"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0030" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0030"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
6:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">
Seismic vibrators in the desert</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan"> Satellite Imaging Corp.,
</span>[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">www.satelliteimagingcorp.com</span>](http://www.satelliteimagingcorp.com)

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">oil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.145.2" class="koboSpan">For the
purposes of </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">well
logging</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">,
rock cuttings, core samples and geophysical data are extracted from
boreholes, giving scientists an idea of the local geological structure
and, if any oil does exist, the history, nature and extent of the
reservoir.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">The boreholes that are
successful eventually become oil
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">wells</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.150.2"
class="koboSpan">Neighbouring wells are normally grouped together to
define an oil
field</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan">To date, there are over 30,000 known oil wells.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.152.2" class="koboSpan">Of these, 330
produce just over 50% of the world’s oil output, while just 17 of them
produce over 30% of the same. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.152.3"
class="koboSpan">Some of the wells are classified as giants – each
holding over 0.5 billion barrels of reserves – while the biggest of
wells and/or fields are also known as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">elephants</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.154.2"
class="koboSpan">The largest of all oil fields, Ghawar, is located in
Saudi Arabia, and is estimated to hold approximately 70 billion barrels
of oil reserves. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.154.3"
class="koboSpan">To put this in perspective, the Ghawar field accounts
for more than a quarter of Saudi reserves (estimated at 260 billion
barrels in 2006).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">The discovery of oil
deposits and the drilling of oil producing wells is not, of course, the
end of the story. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.155.2"
class="koboSpan">The entire production process has to be organised
properly. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.155.3" class="koboSpan">This
involves a detailed reservoir management plan; the well layout and
design; design of production and evacuation facilities; and an
implementation schedule covering the drilling of wells and construction
and installation of facilities.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">The next step is to
ensure that oil can be extracted in the most efficient way.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.156.2" class="koboSpan">The reservoir’s
own pressure is usually sufficient, at least initially, to drive the oil
or gas to the surface. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.156.3"
class="koboSpan">When recovery levels are low, however, secondary
recovery enhancements can be used, whereby the reservoir’s natural drive
is supplemented with the injection
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_127"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">of water or gas.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Finally, where
both natural drive and secondary recovery are not producing the desired
production levels, enhanced oil recovery (EOR) methods can be used.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.157.3" class="koboSpan">These
techniques are considerably more expensive and must be justified by oil
market conditions. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.157.4"
class="koboSpan">EOR methods include: the heating of oil by injecting
hot water and/or steam, in order to increase its viscosity and flow;
mixture of oil with a suitable gas or liquid solvent to reduce or
eliminate residual oil trapped in the displacement process; and use of
chemical additives, which modify the properties of the water that
displaces the oil and which change the way water and oil flow through
the reservoir rock.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">Oil is not the only
fuel produced by oil wells. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.158.2"
class="koboSpan">Natural gas liquids (NGLs) are byproducts of oil
extraction. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.158.3"
class="koboSpan">NGLs include: a type of light oil called
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan">natural</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">gasoline</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan">; a mixture of petroleum – or ‘wet’ – gases, like
butane, propane and ethane; and sometimes natural – or ‘dry’ – gas,
which is methane.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">There are also
“non-conventional” sources of oil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.162.2" class="koboSpan">These include:
kerogen, which consists of hydrocarbons not yet developed into oil; tar
sands, which are impregnated with oil; and synthetic petroleum, which
can be produced – rather expensively – from coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.162.3"
class="koboSpan">Non-conventional hydrocarbons have remained largely
unexploited due to the large costs involved in their processing.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.162.4" class="koboSpan">However, in
recent years (since the early 2000s), the industry has shown renewed
interest in developing them, especially tar sands, as their production
becomes more economically viable in the light of oil prices fluctuating
between \$60–70 per barrel.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Physical characteristics</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">Oil has three physical
characteristics which have significant economic importance.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.164.2" class="koboSpan">The first one
is specific gravity. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.164.3"
class="koboSpan">Crude oils are classified as: light, or paraffinic;
medium, or mixed-base; and heavy, or asphaltic.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.164.4" class="koboSpan">Light crudes
have lower specific gravity and are easier to refine.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.164.5" class="koboSpan">Specific
gravity is measured in “degrees API”, which were introduced by the
American Petroleum Institute. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.164.6"
class="koboSpan">The lighter the oil, the more degrees API attributed to
it. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.164.7" class="koboSpan">The
baseline is the specific gravity of water, which is 10° API.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.164.8" class="koboSpan">Crudes below
22° API are considered heavy, while those above 40° API are considered
light.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">The second
characteristic is viscosity, which is sometimes measured in centistokes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">The more
centistokes, the more viscous (thick) the crude, and the harder it is to
burn. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.165.3" class="koboSpan">Two
common grades of crude oil, typically used for vessel bunkers, have
viscosities of 180 CST (intermediate fuel oil – IFO) and 380 CST (heavy
fuel oil – HFO). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.165.4"
class="koboSpan">One more detail: the centistoke value of a crude oil
changes with temperature. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.165.5"
class="koboSpan">Hence, a typical assay will contain viscosity
measurements at several different temperatures.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, a crude’s
quality also depends on its content in sulphur.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.166.2" class="koboSpan">Crudes with
high sulphur content are known as “sour” crudes, while the rest are
known as “sweet”.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Reserves</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">As with any
non-renewable natural resource, it is important to be able to establish
the stock of reserves available for future extraction.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">The total
reserves worldwide are known as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan">ultimate</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan"> reserves, but their estimation is of little practical
use. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.170.2" class="koboSpan">It is more
interesting to estimate the amount of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">oil-in-place</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">, which is an indication of recoverable reserves.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.172.2" class="koboSpan">Reserves, for
which there is conservatively reasonable certainty of production under
existing economic and operational conditions, are called
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan">proved</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan"> reserves (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0031" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0031"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0048" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00048.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7: Proven oil reserves" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_128"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0031" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0031"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
7:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">
Proven oil reserves</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">In contrast,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">probable</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan"> reserves are those whose production would be
achievable as a result of further exploration and development, or
changed economic and operating conditions.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">Frequently, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">reserves:production
ratio</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan"> is
used as an indicator of the future life of existing reserves.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.187.2" class="koboSpan">The ratio shows
the number of years that reserves will last, if production (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0032" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0032"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 8</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan">) continues at the current rate.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.189.2" class="koboSpan">The R:P ratio,
however, only offers a view of the future, extrapolated from the
present, and assuming that technology and prices remain
unchanged.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Trade in crude oil</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">From a total of
approx. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.191.2" class="koboSpan">3,900
million tons (or nearly 82 million bpd) of oil produced in 2008, some
2,700 million tons (54.6 million bpd) were traded internationally.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.191.3" class="koboSpan">Of these, over
75% was carried by sea. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.191.4"
class="koboSpan">Throughout oil’s turbulent history, international trade
has played an important role. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.191.5"
class="koboSpan">In fact, one of the biggest integrated oil companies –
Royal Dutch Shell – started life as a trade and transport
company.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">Despite the political
uncertainty associated with the region, the Middle East remains the
world’s top oil exporter, supplying approximately 37% (in 2008) of the
world’s crude oil exports
(see</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0033" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0033"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan"> Figure 9</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.194.2"
class="koboSpan">The vast majority of flows are directed towards three
man areas: North America, Northwest Europe and Asia Pacific.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">These flows
coincide</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0049" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00049.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 8: Crude oil production" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_129"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0032" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0032"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.196.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
8:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">
Crude oil production</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan">BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">very much with the
main trade routes for VLCCs and some of the larger-size tanker tonnage.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.200.2" class="koboSpan">Following
Middle East, Africa and FSU come a distant equal second.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.200.3" class="koboSpan">Western (mainly
Nigeria and more recently Angola) and North (mainly Libya and Algeria)
Africa are very important suppliers to the European Union and Nigerian
crude is also very comp etitive in transatlantic trades to the
USA.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">FSU exports are
dominated by Russia, the world’s second largest exporter after Saudi
Arabia, and Kazakhstan. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.201.2"
class="koboSpan">The importance of Russian exports to the European Union
cannot be overestimated and the supply routes start from West Siberia
through the Baltic Sea (Primorsk), and from the Caspian Sea through the
Black Sea (Novorossiysk). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.201.3"
class="koboSpan">Smaller suppliers, like Azerbaijan, generate less
exports, but they strive to disengage from their dependence on the
Russia oil pipeline system and gain direct access to the export markets
through alternative routes.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">Latin America (mainly
Venezuela and Mexico) are the most important short-haul supplier to the
USA (after Canada which largely exports to the USA via pipelines) and
are the first recourse for short term demand upsurges (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.202.2" class="koboSpan">due to cold
weather). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.202.3" class="koboSpan">The
rest of the demand generated by the world’s largest consumer of oil is
satisfied either by medium-haul (West Africa and North Sea), long-haul
(Arabian Gulf) or domestic (Alaska) supplies.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.202.4" class="koboSpan">Pacific Rim
countries are still largely dependent on the Middle East for their
imports, although some of their demand is satisfied by regionally
produced crudes in Indonesia, Australia and Vietnam.</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00050.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 9: Oil exports (crude and products), 2008" /></span>

class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
9:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">
Oil exports (crude and products), 2008</span>

</div>

class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

## <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">Oil Products</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">Much of the discussion
up to now has dealt primarily with crude oil, although trade figures
referred to both crude and products.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.209.2" class="koboSpan">In this
section, I will begin with a brief description of the refining process,
continue with the main categories of refined products and, finally,
discuss production, consumption and trade patterns for major regions,
like the United States, Western Europe and South East Asia.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Refining process</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">Although much of the
economics of the oil industry revolves around crude oil, it is the final
products that are used by the end-consumers.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.211.2" class="koboSpan">Crude oil is
rarely usable and has to be refined and broken down into products
adequate for final consumption.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">The fundamental
principle on which oil refining is based has not changed since the
nineteenth century: crude oil is heated until it is vaporised and then
the vapours are condensed separately, according to the boiling points of
their constituent molecules; the procedure is called distillation.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.212.2" class="koboSpan">Crude oil is
stored into large tanks and from there it is pumped continuously through
a series of steel tubes into a furnace.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.212.3" class="koboSpan">From there it
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_131"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">is pumped to the bottom of a tall cylindrical tower,
usually 8–24 feet in diameter and 100–150 feet in height.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.213.2" class="koboSpan">This is called
a “fractioning” tower, as it is divided into “floors”, with perforated
trays, which allow vapours to pass from lower to higher floors.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.213.3" class="koboSpan">The hydrocarbon
vapours with highest boiling points condense first, on the bottom
floors, and those with the lowest boiling points condense last, higher
up the tower. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.213.4"
class="koboSpan">The most volatile product – petrol – comes off at the
top of the tower and is then condensed separately.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">This simple
distillation procedure yields about 20% light distillates from an
average crude, and usually falls short of the commercial needs for
petrol. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.214.2" class="koboSpan">At the
same time, the process yields heavier products in quantities that exceed
consumption requirements. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.214.3"
class="koboSpan">To redress this imbalance, some of the heavier oil
distillates are further processed, using methods such as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan">thermal
cracking</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">
and </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">catalytic
cracking</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.218.2"
class="koboSpan">Both these procedures allow enhanced recovery yields of
petrol from crude: the first procedure used high temperature and
pressure to “crack” the large hydrocarbon molecules of heavier products
into smaller molecules of petrol and petroleum gas; the second process
uses catalysts to facilitate cracking under milder and more easily
controlled conditions. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.218.3"
class="koboSpan">Reverse procedures are also available, which reform
lighter gas molecules into heavier products, such as petrol.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.218.4" class="koboSpan">Finally,
several of the gases are used as feedstocks for the petrochemicals
industry.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">The outputs of the
refining process are classified into three broad categories:
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan">light</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan">middle</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">, and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan">heavy</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan"> distillates. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.225.2"
class="koboSpan">Light distillates – also known as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">white</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan">top</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan">-</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan">end</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan"> cuts – include ethane, propane, butane, naphtha (all
used as feedstock for petrochemicals), aviation turbine fuel (ATF),
kerosene, petrol and other industrial spirits.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">Middle distillate (or
middle cuts) include gas oil, diesel, marine diesel, and medium and high
grade fuels. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.232.2"
class="koboSpan">Finally, heavy distillates – also known as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">black</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">bottom</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">-</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan">end</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan"> cuts – include heavy fuels, paraffins, lubricating
waxes and greases.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.1 Refining: capacities and throughputs</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">The supply of oil
products is very much dependent on the available refining capacity
around the world. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.240.2"
class="koboSpan">In fact, refining capacity sets the upper limit to the
supply of distillates. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.240.3"
class="koboSpan">What is more interesting in terms of production,
however, is the refinery
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">throughput,
</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan"> i.e.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.242.2" class="koboSpan">the quantity of
oil being processed by refineries per annum.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.242.3" class="koboSpan">This also
allows the calculation of refinery utilisation rates, a figure most
important for the profitability of a refiner.
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0034" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0034"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.243.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 10</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the development of refining capacity through the
mid-1970s, 1980s and 1990s and in the late 2000s.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.244.2" class="koboSpan">Taking a closer
look, one can see that North America – and this is mainly the United
States – was head and shoulders above the other two important refining
regions: Western Europe (which excludes Russia, labelled ‘Eurasia’ in
</span>[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
10</span>](#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0034)<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan">), and Asia Pacific.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.246.2" class="koboSpan">However, Asia
Pacific caught up fast and is now on par with the whole of Europe and
Eurasia and above North America. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.246.3"
class="koboSpan">These three regions are top in the league of refinery
throughputs as well. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.246.4"
class="koboSpan">In 2008, United States alone produced almost 14.6 Mbpd
of oil products, with Europe and Eurasia (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.246.5" class="koboSpan">Russia)
standing at 20.6 Mbpd, and Asia Pacific at 21.5 Mbpd.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.246.6" class="koboSpan">Within the
latter region, the largest refiner used to be Japan (3.9 Mbpd in 2008),
but has now been overtaken by China (6.8 Mbpd in 2008), with Singapore
accounting for most of the remaining throughput in the region as it is a
huge transhipment and refining centre.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">Refinery throughputs
and consumption of oil products give a broad framework for the study of
patterns in international trade in oil products.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">As we are going
to see later, however, trade flows are much more complicated, and there
is often exchange of similar</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0051" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00051.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 10: World refining capacity by region" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_132"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0034" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0034"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
10:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">
World refining capacity by region</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">products between
countries which produce all distillates, but in varying proportions.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.253.2" class="koboSpan">This is, in
fact, a classic case of intra-industry trade.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.253.3" class="koboSpan">It is,
therefore, essential to look at the composition of the typical barrel of
oil – known as crude oil
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan">yields</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan"> – when studying trade patterns.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">Oil yields depend on
the distillation technology available to the refinery, the grade and
quality of the input crude, and also seasonal and consumption parameters
of the region in question.</span>

<a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fig0052" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0052"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan"> lists representative crude yields in a sophisticated
and a typical refinery in the US Gulf, during the winter and summer
periods. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.258.2" class="koboSpan">Notice
how, in both cases, yields for unleaded gasoline increase during the
summer, the season when most Americans travel around the country by car.
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0035" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0035"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 11</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the products yielded by three representative
types of crude in refineries in the US Gulf and Northwest Europe.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.261.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Consumption patterns</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">It is consumption
patterns, of course, that influence both the short and the long-term
balance of the market. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.262.2"
class="koboSpan">Different regions have different tastes for oil
products, depending on their economic activities, climatic conditions
and other consumption habits. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.262.3"
class="koboSpan">Although refinery yields can change to match demand,
imbalances do arise, and trade flows are generated in order to cover
them.</span>

<a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0036" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0036"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 12</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows consumption patterns in 2008.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.264.2" class="koboSpan">The United
States is a heavy consumer, with the emphasis on gasolines.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.264.3" class="koboSpan">Western Europe
is the second largest consumption area, with the emphasis on middle
distillates, while Japan shows a slightly more balanced picture.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Trade in products</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">Trade in oil products
is older than trade in crude, but with increasing scale economies in the
transportation of crude oil, products trade has shrank to about a third
of total trade in oil.</span>

<a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0037" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0037"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 13</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.279.1"
class="koboSpan"> depicts the development of crude and products trade
since 1975. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.279.2" class="koboSpan">As
one can see, products have fluctuated a lot less than crude oil trade,
and in recent years they have increased as a proportion of crude trade,
to about 36%.</span>

<a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0038" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0038"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 14</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.281.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the importing and exporting activity of major
regions worldwide, and their relative deficit or surplus positions.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.281.2" class="koboSpan">In terms of
regional patterns, United States, Western Europe, and Singapore are the
most active exporters and importers of oil distillates.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.281.3" class="koboSpan">The Pacific Rim
as a whole is a very important product trading region, with China, Japan
and now India being also very important players.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.281.4" class="koboSpan">From the rest
of the world, Russia and the Middle East are large net exporters of
products.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">The combination of
factors that were discussed earlier, makes the international trade in
oil products fairly complicated, and its study long enough to be the
subject of a separate treatise. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.282.2"
class="koboSpan">Partly due to this complexity, there is a very active
market in oil products, both on the floor of major commodities’
exchanges, and over the counter.</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
