## <span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_136"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.293.2" class="koboSpan">Brent Crude and Oil Pricing</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.294.1" class="koboSpan">There is a large
variety of crude oils and oil products available in the open market,
many of which are priced on a purely competitive basis.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.294.2" class="koboSpan">One such market
which developed and matured in the 1980s is the market for Brent crude,
which is extracted in the UK sector of North Sea.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.294.3" class="koboSpan">The presence of
Brent crude prices in the pricing formulae of several crudes around the
world, emphasises its international character and importance.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">Brent is named after
one of several fields, whose output is used to create a standard blend.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.295.2" class="koboSpan">In fact, there
are two distinct pipeline systems – Brent and Ninian – which contribute
towards the production. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.295.3"
class="koboSpan">In 1976 the first consignments of Brent crude were
loaded at Brent Spar, and in 1979 the terminal at Sullom Voe became
operational. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.295.4" class="koboSpan">In
the early 1990s, the production of Brent blend amounted to about 850,000
bpd. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.295.5" class="koboSpan">In the
early 2000s this figure has down by more than half, and was deemed so
low that the industry decided to launch a parallel crude oil index
reflecting four different North Sea crude oils: Brent Blend and Forties
(from the UK sector) and Oseberg and Ekofisk (from the Norwegian
sector).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">Brent blend is
denominated as a light, sweet crude, with a specific gravity of 38° API.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.296.2" class="koboSpan">Its constituent
crudes, however, have a specific gravity in the range of 30°–40° API,
and a sulphur content of 0.2–1%. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.296.3"
class="koboSpan">Standard quality is of course important, since market
participants expect at least some security in terms of the blend’s
properties.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.297.1" class="koboSpan">Brent is very much an
international crude, with about three quarters of it being exported.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.297.2" class="koboSpan">It is mainly,
though, an Atlantic basin crude, with most of the exports to the United
States, Canada and Germany. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.297.3"
class="koboSpan">Flows to the US are primarily received in Gulf ports,
where Brent’s main competitor is Nigerian crude, which has similar
physical characteristics, and other domestic sweet, light crudes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.297.4" class="koboSpan">In the UK the
main users are Shell’s refineries at Stanlow and Shellhaven, Texaco’s at
Pembroke, and Total’s at Milford Haven.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">In addition to being
an important pricing benchmark for a number of internationally traded
crude oils, Brent really drives a multi-layer market, consisting of a
number of derivative instruments, traded both on exchange floors,
electronically and over the counter.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Price reporting</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.300.1" class="koboSpan">With the collapse of
OPEC prices in the mid-1980s, there was a move towards market related
pricing. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.300.2" class="koboSpan">This
trend was already evident due to the introduction of Brent crude in the
world markets, and was accentuated with the resort of some OPEC
countries to netback pricing, which made the availability of reliable
and up to date spot prices crucial.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.300.3" class="koboSpan">As the market
for financial oil derivatives also took off, the need for reliable and
transparent price setting and reporting became crucial.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.301.1" class="koboSpan">Today there are
several oil price reporting agencies, which are used worldwide for
pricing spot and derivatives deals.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.301.2" class="koboSpan">One of the most
well known is probably Platt’s. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.301.3"
class="koboSpan">The agency was founded very early, in 1924, and
originally concentrated on products.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.301.4" class="koboSpan">It started
reporting crude prices in 1983 and is currently owned by McGraw-Hill.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.301.5" class="koboSpan">Petroleum Argus
is another well known reporting agency, which was the first to start
quoting crude oil prices in 1979.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.301.6" class="koboSpan">ICIS-LOR
started in 1978 as London Oil Reports, publishing a weekly newsletter
with price assessments. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.301.7"
class="koboSpan">In 1985 it merged with Independent Chemical Information
Services which provided price quotations for
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_137"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">chemicals and petrochemicals.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.302.2" class="koboSpan">There is also a
number of screen services, which provide up-to-date prices, such as
Reuters and Bloomberg.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.303.1" class="koboSpan">Prices are quoted on a
minute-by-minute basis for Brent and most other crudes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.303.2" class="koboSpan">Sometimes
agencies report high/low price assessments, but they mostly tend to
quote bid/ask ranges, which show the difference between the highest
offer to buy (bid) and the lowest offer to sell (ask).
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fig0057" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0057"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.304.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan"> reproduces an excerpt from ‘Platt’s Crude Oil
Marketwire’, with some of the most commonly quoted crudes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.305.2" class="koboSpan">Price
quotations are also
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan">time
stamped</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.307.1" class="koboSpan">,
especially when they are near the opening and closing times of the
markets. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.307.2"
class="koboSpan">Naturally, the most interesting price quotation is at
the closing of a market, since closing prices are often used for
settlement of contracts.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">Although individual
crudes have their own quotations, it is not uncommon that these prices
are calculated as differentials from a few
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan">benchmark</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan"> crudes. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.310.2"
class="koboSpan">Brent and WTI are such
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan">marker</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan"> crudes and are used extensively around the
world.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">As far as Brent and
WTI are concerned, the most liquid forward month is usually assessed
first; then quotations for other forward months and from dated deals are
also used to compile the daily settlement price.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.313.2" class="koboSpan">Once this
process is completed, other crudes are priced on a differential basis
and so are inter-crude spreads and inter-month spreads for other crudes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.313.3" class="koboSpan">Differentials
themselves are not
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan">ad hoc</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan"> stable; in fact, they do fluctuate, but markedly less
than absolute prices.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">5.2 Other crude markets</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">Up to now I have
focused on the Brent market and instruments.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.317.2" class="koboSpan">Despite the
market liquidity and importance for pricing of crudes around the world,
one should also bear in mind that Brent is only a small fraction of the
world crude oil production and exports.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.317.3" class="koboSpan">The bulk of oil
exports comes from countries which have their own pricing formulas, but
look to the Brent market in order to assess the true supply and demand
situation. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.317.4" class="koboSpan">This
section will discuss briefly some of the other available crudes and
their main characteristics.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">5.2.1 North Sea</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">Brent is one of a
number of crude oils produced in the North Sea.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.319.2" class="koboSpan">In the UK
sector blends from the Forties and Flotta sectors are also competing for
export shares, although they are priced as Brent spreads.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.319.3" class="koboSpan">Of the two,
Forties seems more likely to take Brent’s place as an international
crude, when the latter is exhausted.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.319.4" class="koboSpan">This is
reflected in the inclusion of Forties in the BFO composite index.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.320.1" class="koboSpan">In the Norwegian
sector, the most prominent fields are Ekofisk, Oseberg, Statfjord and
Gullfaks. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.320.2" class="koboSpan">All
of them enter the international market, as most of the Norwegian
production is exported. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.320.3"
class="koboSpan">Most of these crudes are priced against Brent, although
there is a small proportion priced against WTI.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.321.1" class="koboSpan">5.2.2 United States</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">The most prominent
crude in the United States is West Texas Intermediate.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.322.2" class="koboSpan">Like Brent, it
is a blend of several crudes with specific gravities between 34°–45° API
and sulphur content below 0.5%. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.322.3"
class="koboSpan">The par grade is 40° API and has 0.4% sulphur content,
which</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0057" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_138"></span>[](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0057)

[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00057.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0057)

</div>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_139"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
class="koboSpan">is slightly lighter and can be slightly sweeter than
Brent. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.324.2" class="koboSpan">The
physical base consists of crude deliveries at the end of the pipeline at
Cushing, Oklahoma. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.324.3"
class="koboSpan">Shipments are usually 50,000 or 100,000 bbls.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.1" class="koboSpan">Like Brent, WTI has an
active forward market. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.2"
class="koboSpan">However, the futures market is even more active and
forward looking, with months open until nine years ahead.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.3" class="koboSpan">More
specifically, consecutive months are listed for the current year and the
next five years; in addition, the June and December contract months are
listed beyond the sixth year. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.4"
class="koboSpan">WTI contracts are also more flexible than Brent
contracts, in that they allow a considerable number of alternative
crudes to be delivered. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.5"
class="koboSpan">Specific domestic crudes with 0.42% sulfur by weight or
less, not less than 37° API gravity nor more than 42° API gravity.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.6" class="koboSpan">The following
domestic crude streams are deliverable: West Texas Intermediate, Low
Sweet Mix, New Mexican Sweet, North Texas Sweet, Oklahoma Sweet, South
Texas Sweet. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.7"
class="koboSpan">Also, specific foreign crudes of not less than 34° API
nor more than 42° API are deliverable.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.8" class="koboSpan">The following
foreign streams are deliverable: U.K.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.325.9" class="koboSpan">Brent, for
which the seller shall receive a 30¢-per-barrel discount below the final
settlement price; Norwegian Oseberg Blend is delivered at a
55¢-per-barrel discount; Nigerian Bonny Light, Qua Iboe, and Colombian
Cusiana are delivered at 15¢ premiums.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.326.1" class="koboSpan">Another important US
crude is that produced in Alaska.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.326.2" class="koboSpan">Alaskan North
Slope (ANS) is extracted from the fields at Prudhoe Bay and then carried
by the Trans-Alaskan pipeline to Valdez.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.326.3" class="koboSpan">From there, it
is shipped by tankers to US West Coast and US Gulf.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.326.4" class="koboSpan">There is also a
forward market on ANS, but it is primarily priced as a spread on
WTI.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.327.1" class="koboSpan">Other US crudes
include: West Texas Sour and Light Louisiana Sweet, both of which are
priced as differentials of WTI.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">5.2.3 West Africa</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.329.1" class="koboSpan">A substantial amount
of international oil trade is generated from the west cost of Africa,
where the producer countries are Nigera, Angola, Gabon, Congo, and
Cameroon. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.329.2" class="koboSpan">Their
target markets are primarily transatlantic, notably the US.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.329.3" class="koboSpan">There are
several types of crude, but three are the most commonly known: Bonny
light; Forcados; and BBQ, a blend of Brass River, Bonny light and Qua
Iboe. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.329.4" class="koboSpan">All of
the above crudes use mainly Brent as a marker crude, but pricing on WTI
is not uncommon.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.330.1" class="koboSpan">5.2.4 Middle East and Mediterranean</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.331.1" class="koboSpan">Middle East is the
biggest exporter of crude in the world and plays, therefore, a key role
in regulating the supply side of oil trade.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.331.2" class="koboSpan">The role of the
Middle East was extensively discussed in the previous chapter and was
recently reaffirmed during the Gulf Crisis.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.332.1" class="koboSpan">One of the commonly
quoted crudes for many years was Arab light, and it is still used as a
benchmark for Middle East OPEC members.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.332.2" class="koboSpan">A relatively
newer entrant in the market is Dubai Fateh.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.332.3" class="koboSpan">This is a
medium crude of 31° API and containing up to 2% sulphur.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.332.4" class="koboSpan">It is often
considered as the equivalent of Brent in the Middle East and seems to
dominate the spot market. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.332.5"
class="koboSpan">Oman and UAE are two very active participants in the
spot crude market as well, but their grades are relatively sour.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.332.6" class="koboSpan">Pricing
formulas in the region are quite complicated, often involving
retroactive pricing. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.332.7"
class="koboSpan">Some of the often quoted prices are OSP, and MPM or
PDO,</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0142" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0142"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.334.1"
class="koboSpan"> the latter, however, seems to be priced as a spread of
Dubai.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_140"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.335.1"
class="koboSpan">In the Mediterranean the main producers participating
in the spot market have traditionally been are Libya, Egypt, Syria, and
Algeria. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.335.2" class="koboSpan">Iran
and Russia are also very active and important despite not having a
Mediterranean coast; the former from Sidi Kerir and the later from the
Black Sea. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.335.3" class="koboSpan">For
a long time Libya was disadvantaged by the US embargo, but continued to
have considerable transactions with other Mediterranean countries, Italy
in particular. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.335.4"
class="koboSpan">Spot prices are quoted for most of these crudes, and a
sample of these prices is given in
</span>[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.336.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch05.xhtml_fig0052)<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.337.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.337.2"
class="koboSpan">Brent and Dubai prices are often involved, directly or
indirectly, in the pricing formulas of Mediterranean crudes.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.338.1" class="koboSpan">Russian crude has
gained particular significance in the last eight to ten years, with the
rise of the country to the top of oil exporting nations.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.338.2" class="koboSpan">The bulk of
Russian crude from the Caspian Sea is transferred via pipeline to
Novorossyisk and from there it is shipped in tankers through Bosporus
and on to its final destination. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.338.3"
class="koboSpan">In addition to Russia (Urals), Kazakhstan (CPC blend)
and Azerbaijan (Azeri light) also ship through the same route, although
alternative pipeline routes became operational in the early 2000s which
bypass both Russia and the congested Bosporus channel.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.338.4" class="koboSpan">The most
important of these pipelines is the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline
which delivers its cargo to the port of Ceyhan in Southeast Turkey,
where it is lifted by tankers for delivery to international
clients.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">5.2.5 Far East</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.340.1" class="koboSpan">The situation in the
Far East is far from clear-cut. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.340.2"
class="koboSpan">There are several crude grades available, coming
primarily from Indonesia and Malaysia, but also from Australia, China
and Vietnam. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.340.3"
class="koboSpan">There are, however, essentially only two prices: APPI
and
ICP.</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0143" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0143"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.341.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan"> The first is assessed weekly by a panel of traders,
producers and refiners. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.342.2"
class="koboSpan">The second is assessed monthly and is based on a basket
of crudes, including Oman, Dubai Fateh, Gippsland (Australia), Minas
(Indonesia), and Tapis (Malaysia).
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.342.3" class="koboSpan">Both pricing
system have been criticised as too slow in responding to changing
circumstances; APPI is produced twice weekly and ICP monthly.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">5.2.6 Products</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.344.1" class="koboSpan">Up to now we have
concentrated exclusively on crude oil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.344.2" class="koboSpan">The fact is,
however, that there are active spot markets for products as well, which
have been in existence well before the spot market for crude.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.344.3" class="koboSpan">The products
market tends to concentrate around several main areas.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.344.4" class="koboSpan">Four of them,
Rotterdam, Houston, New York Harbor and Singapore, have considerable
refining, storage and shipment facilities, and usually offer the most
competitively priced products. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.344.5"
class="koboSpan">Other areas include the Mediterranean, Caribbean,
Arabian Gulf, New York Harbor and Japan.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">Prices are quoted for
a wide array of products, including gasoil, heating oil, marine bunkers,
jet fuel (kerosene), diesel, unleaded gasoline, RBOB (reformulated
gasoline blend stock for oxygenated blending) gasoline and naphtha,
among others. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.345.2"
class="koboSpan">Products in the
A-R-A</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0144" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0144"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan"> range are commonly quoted as “barges f.o.b.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.347.2" class="koboSpan">Rotterdam” and
are usually quoted on an f.o.b. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.347.3"
class="koboSpan">export basis. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.347.4"
class="koboSpan">Contracts are typically traded in parcels of 1–5,000
mt. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.347.5" class="koboSpan">For
shipment purposes, cargoes are normally bundled in consignments of
10–30,000 mt.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">Some fundamental
products also have an active futures market operating alongside the spot
market. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.348.2" class="koboSpan">The
products contracts traded on NYMEX, ICE and TOCOM (Tokyo</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0058" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_141"></span>[](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0058)

[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.349.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00058.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0058)

</div>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.350.1" class="koboSpan">Commodity Exchange)
are shown in
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fig0058" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0058"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.351.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan">, together with their sizes and minimum price
fluctuation per contract (tick). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.352.2"
class="koboSpan">Heating oil has been trading on NYMEX since 1979, and
is the second most active energy contract after crude oil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.352.3" class="koboSpan">Gasoline
contracts are more recent and are continuously changing to reflect the
new environmental legislation in each country.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.352.4" class="koboSpan">So in the USA,
for example, the phase-out of MTBE (methyl tertiary-butyl ether) as a
gasoline additive, meant that NYMEX introduced the trading of RBOB
gasoline, which conforms to the most recent US government environmental
regulations.</span>

## <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.353.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.353.2" class="koboSpan">Natural Gas</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.354.1" class="koboSpan">Natural gas is the
newest of hydrocarbons and, many people believe, the future of energy,
at least its medium-term future. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.354.2"
class="koboSpan">In the last 20 or so years, natural gas has experienced
an impressive growth in terms of reserve discovery, field development
and production. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.354.3"
class="koboSpan">On the demand side, gas consumption has rapidly
expanded to contest coal’s second place as a source of primary energy.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.354.4" class="koboSpan">Although not a
serious threat to oil yet, it certainly is a weighty contender, and the
most promising source of energy due to its excellent burning
properties.</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0059" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.355.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00059.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 15: Development of proven natural gas reserves" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_142"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0039" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0039"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.356.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
15:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">
Development of proven natural gas reserves</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.360.1" class="koboSpan">Gas formation is
similar to that of oil. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.360.2"
class="koboSpan">Organic matter which has been compressed and heated for
a very long period of time is the source of hydrocarbons, especially oil
and gas. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.360.3" class="koboSpan">At
greater depths both higher pressure and higher temperatures favour the
production of gas over oil. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.360.4"
class="koboSpan">This is why gas is normally associated with deep oil
deposits and the depth increases so does the probability of finding
fields which contain almost pure methane.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.360.5" class="koboSpan">Most gas comes
from ‘conventional’ fields, which allow the extraction of the commodity
using existing cost-efficient technology.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.360.6" class="koboSpan">There are,
however, additional “non-conventional” gas reserves, which are currently
either uneconomical or technically difficult to exploit.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.361.1" class="koboSpan">Although often a
by-product of oil production, most of the world’s natural gas production
comes from dedicated gas fields. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.361.2"
class="koboSpan">In its “dry” form, natural gas consists primarily of
methane (often up to 90%), small amounts of other hydrocarbons such as
ethane, propane and butane, and even smaller amounts of carbon dioxide,
oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen sulphide and rare gases.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.361.3" class="koboSpan">Gas exploration
is similar to, and associated with, oil exploration.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.361.4" class="koboSpan">Once found and
extracted, it is normally refined to remove impurities and separate
methane form other gases, which can then be further processed and
marketed separately. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.361.5"
class="koboSpan">What remains is then channelled into the distribution
network, which normally consists of pipelines, but often involves a
liquefaction plant and the use of specialised LNG carriers to carry the
liquid gas to the export markets.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_143"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.362.1" class="koboSpan">6.1 Supply determinants</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.363.1" class="koboSpan">Like oil, a
substantial amount of gas reserves are held by those who don’t consume
them heavily. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.363.2"
class="koboSpan">The picture is similar, but not identical, to that of
oil. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.363.3" class="koboSpan">Reserves
are concentrated in a few regions and are controlled by relatively few
governments. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.363.4" class="koboSpan">In
2008, there were just over 185 trillion cubic metres (tcm) of gas
reserves in the world (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0039" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0039"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.364.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 15</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.365.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.365.2"
class="koboSpan">Of these, 43 tcm (23%) were located in the Russian
Federation, and 76 tcm (41%) in the Middle East.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.365.3" class="koboSpan">Within the
latter region, two countries hold the majority of reserves: Iran and
Qatar. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.365.4" class="koboSpan">In fact,
combining the reserves of these two countries with those of Russia, they
amount to over half (53%) of the world’s total.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.365.5" class="koboSpan">It is no wonder
then that when these three, together with several more medium-size and
smaller producers decided to found the Gas Exporting Countries Forum
(GEFC) in 2001, they sent jitters to all major gas consumers, especially
Europeans. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.365.6"
class="koboSpan">Although just a “forum” for the time being, it will be
interesting to observe whether it could ultimately turn into a
“gas-OPEC”.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.366.1" class="koboSpan">Relatively smaller
reserves are located throughout the world (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0040" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0040"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.367.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 16</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan">), but the regions who use it most – North America,
Western Europe and Asia Pacific – control a mere 20% of the world’s
reserves. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.368.2" class="koboSpan">There
is always, of course, the exciting prospect of non-conventional gas
reserves, but there may be quite a few years before these can be
developed in an economical way.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.369.1" class="koboSpan">When it comes to
production figures, however, the picture is somewhat changed.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.369.2" class="koboSpan">The world’s two
largest producers of gas, by far, are Russia and the USA, followed by
Canada, Iran, Norway, Algeria, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and China (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0041" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0041"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.370.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 17</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.371.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.371.2"
class="koboSpan">The presence of the USA is of course justified as the
world’s largest consumption market,</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0060" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.372.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00060.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 16: Distribution of world gas reserves" /></span>

<a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0040" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0040"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.373.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
16:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.374.1" class="koboSpan">
Distribution of world gas reserves</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.375.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.376.1"
class="koboSpan">BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_144"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.377.1"
class="koboSpan">which is also ahead of the game in terms of
competitiveness and deregulation.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.377.2" class="koboSpan">The salient
feature of production, however, is once again the dominance of Russia,
which produced nearly one-fifth of the world’s output in 2008.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.377.3" class="koboSpan">Of the
remaining producers, Canada directs large quantities of its gas to the
US market, while all other important producers, perhaps with the
exception of Iran, market their production internationally.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.378.1" class="koboSpan">Once gas is produced
at the wellhead, it goes through a purification process which removes
NGLs (“wet” gases), water vapours, carbon dioxide, sulphur and oil (if
the gas is associated with an oil well).
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.378.2" class="koboSpan">This is
required for the “dry” gas to be of suitable quality for pipeline
transportation and further distribution.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.378.3" class="koboSpan">A sophisticated
network of
pipelines</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0145" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0145"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.379.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.380.1"
class="koboSpan"> is used to collect the gas from the wellhead, channel
it through the processing plant for purification and distribute it to
its final destination; or channel it to a port facility for cryogenic
liquefaction, load it on a specialised LNG carriers, unload it at a
regasification facility at the other end and deliver it again by
pipeline to its final destination.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.381.1" class="koboSpan">As it is evident from
the short description, the existence of a technically competent, cost
effective and low-risk transportation network is vital for the commodity
to flow in either domestic or international markets.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.381.2" class="koboSpan">This is much
easier said than done, however.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.382.1" class="koboSpan">Pipelines are
expensive and time-consuming to lay.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.382.2" class="koboSpan">The decision to
invest requires a host of factors to be taken into consideration:
technical (e.g. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.382.3"
class="koboSpan">pipeline diameter, route, sourcing of materials, safety
aspects, sourcing of skilled staff); political (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.382.4" class="koboSpan">obtaining
licences and approvals, adhering to national and international
regulations, crossing or</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0061" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00061.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 17: Gas production" /></span>

<a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0041" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0041"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.384.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
17:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.385.1" class="koboSpan">
Gas production</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.386.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.387.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0062" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00062.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 18: Gas pipelines in Europe" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_145"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0042" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0042"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.389.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
18:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.390.1" class="koboSpan">
Gas pipelines in Europe</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.391.1" class="koboSpan">by-passing country
borders); and economic (e.g. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.391.2"
class="koboSpan">supply flow from reserves and their duration, existence
of adequate demand at the receiving end) are but a few of the obstacles
(or “opportunities”) created by a pipeline project.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.391.3" class="koboSpan">The decision to
build a pipeline of use seaborne transportation is itself complex.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.391.4" class="koboSpan">Broadly
speaking pipelines are more suitable when the distance is below 5,000
km. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.391.5" class="koboSpan">LNG
transportation, on the other hand is more efficient in bringing
‘stranded’ gas reserves to distant markets.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.392.1" class="koboSpan">Probably the most
interesting aspect of the supply side of gas, as indeed of oil, are the
geopolitics and the resultant effects on security of supplies.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.392.2" class="koboSpan">We have already
seen how gas reserves are concentrated in Russia and the Middle East.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.392.3" class="koboSpan">To complicate
matters even more, the supply corridors from producers to consumers are
often ridden with problems. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.392.4"
class="koboSpan">Pipelines are the most effective means to move gas from
A to B, but they typically have to cross one or more countries, which
can often be a headache for all parties involved.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.392.5" class="koboSpan">A textbook case
is that of Russia, most of whose gas production is channelled to the EU
via other countries, including Ukraine and Belarus (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0042" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0042"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.393.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 18</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.394.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.394.2"
class="koboSpan">The stand-offs between Ukraine and Russia in late 2005
and again in 2008, whose Druzhba (Friendship) pipeline crosses through
the former, are well documented and exemplify the type of political
tensions created. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.394.3"
class="koboSpan">And this is not counting extremist groups who want to
blow up the pipeline installations!</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.395.1" class="koboSpan">Another example, in
the same vein, is Russia’s decision to lay its new major pipeline to
West Europe on the seabed of the Baltic, rather than through the
territories of old foes. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.395.2"
class="koboSpan">This refers of course to the Nord Stream pipeline
project (jointly owned by Russia’s Gazprom and Germany’s Wintershall and
E.On Ruhrgas), which is scheduled to start construction in 2010.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.395.3" class="koboSpan">The project
will directly link Vyborg in Russia to Greifswald in Germany using a
twin pipeline, 1,280 km-long, 48-inch wide, with a total capacity of 55
bcm per annum.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_146"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.396.1" class="koboSpan">6.1.1 Storage</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.1" class="koboSpan">Just like oil, gas
also has storage requirements. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.2"
class="koboSpan">There are various regulatory and economic reasons for
doing so. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.3"
class="koboSpan">Demand fluctuations has traditionally been one such
reason. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.4"
class="koboSpan">Increasingly, gas is being used for power generation;
uninterrupted power supply requires a steady supply of gas and stored
gas helps avoiding disruptions. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.5"
class="koboSpan">Typically, two types of storage are required: base-load
and peak-load. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.6"
class="koboSpan">Base-load storage is designed to address long term
demand patterns through the consumption year; for example, higher demand
in winter months, which implies that gas is injected in the storage
during the summer months and retrieved at slow and predictable rates
during the winter. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.7"
class="koboSpan">Larger depleted reservoirs tend to be used for this
storage, which are slower in responding to sudden demand surges.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.8" class="koboSpan">Peak-load
storage, on the other hand, are designed for exactly this purpose:
sudden demand surges, which they can cover with quick delivery or
relatively smaller amounts of gas.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.397.9" class="koboSpan">Salt caverns
tend to be used for this type of storage, as well as storage in LNG
form.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.398.1" class="koboSpan">6.2 Demand determinants</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.399.1" class="koboSpan">Natural gas
consumption has experienced remarkable growth; since 1980, its
consumption has doubled, from just under 1,500 bcm to just over 3,000
bcm (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0043" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0043"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.400.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 19</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.401.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.401.2"
class="koboSpan">The average growth rate during these years was a
seemingly modest 2.5% per annum, but still far better when compared to
the 1% recorded by oil. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.401.3"
class="koboSpan">A host of factors have contributed to this development.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.401.4" class="koboSpan">The rapid
increase in reserves, noted above, certainly provided a springboard for
this. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.401.5" class="koboSpan">The
clean-burning properties of natural gas, in the face of increasingly
urgent environmental concerns was another factor.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.401.6" class="koboSpan">Practically all
new power gene ration projects these days rely on CCGT (combined cycle
gas turbine) technology. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.401.7"
class="koboSpan">Increased affluence (at least in developed and rapidly
developing economies) combined with an environmental conscience make gas
an ideal choice for the modern consumer.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.402.1" class="koboSpan">Gas was first marketed
in the United States, in the late nineteenth century.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.402.2" class="koboSpan">It was not
until the 1930s, however, when technological improvements made possible
the laying of high pressure pipes over long distances, that it was
extensively marketed throughout the country.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.402.3" class="koboSpan">This started
the very long history of gas in the country which makes it the world’s
largest consumer of the commodity; 657 bcm of gas were consumed in the
USA in 2008, a staggering 22% of the world’s total (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0044" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0044"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.403.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 20</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.405.1" class="koboSpan">In Europe gas was
discovered in small quantities at Lacq (France) and the Po Valley
(Italy) in the 1950s. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.405.2"
class="koboSpan">The first substantial discovery came about in 1959 at
Groningen in the Netherlands, while Britain made the first commercially
exploitable discoveries in its sector of the North Sea in 1965.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.405.3" class="koboSpan">Since then gas
has had a predominant position in domestic consumption.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.405.4" class="koboSpan">In the EU, UK
still remains the largest consumer of gas with 94 bcm consumed in 2008.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.405.5" class="koboSpan">It is followed
closely by Germany and then Italy, France and the Netherlands.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.405.6" class="koboSpan">The EU(27) as a
group consumes a total of just over 486 bcm, more than Russia, but still
well behind US consumption. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.405.7"
class="koboSpan">In Russia, gas overtook oil as the main source of
primary energy consumption in the early 1980s.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.405.8" class="koboSpan">Since then it
has remained firmly at the top and Russia is today the second largest
gas consumer in the world, behind USA.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.406.1" class="koboSpan">In the Middle East the
most prominent consumer is Iran with 118 bcm in 2008, practically
absorbing all its indigenous production.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.406.2" class="koboSpan">It is a
surprise that one of the biggest reserve holders is not a prime
exporter, but Iran has been struggling for years to</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0063" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.407.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00063.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 19: Gas consumption development" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_147"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0043" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0043"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.408.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
19:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.409.1" class="koboSpan">
Gas consumption development</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.411.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.412.1" class="koboSpan">put the investment in
place necessary to become an influential exporter.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.412.2" class="koboSpan">In Asia
Pacific, Japan and China are the two largest consumers, with China being
the most rapidly increasing as its economy, especially manufacturing,
continues its rapid growth.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.413.1" class="koboSpan">Having seen the
leading consumers in absolute terms, it is also worth observing the
degree of penetration natural gas has achieved in primary energy
consumption.
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0045" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0045"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.414.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 21</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.415.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the relative shares of the main fuels in broad
regions around the world. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.415.2"
class="koboSpan">The picture presents us with some obvious contrasts,
but there are a few hidden ones as well.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.415.3" class="koboSpan">In North
America (which includes Mexico), South & Central America and Europe gas
accounts for a quarter of consumption.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.415.4" class="koboSpan">Africa is a bit
lower at around one-fifth, although what is not shown here is the very
low level of consumption compared to, say, North America or
Europe.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.416.1" class="koboSpan">The contrast is
between Russia and Asia Pacific: in the former gas has assumed an even
more commanding position, accounting for 55% of total consumption; in
the latter gas has a very modest share, with coal still having a
stronghold, especially in China and India.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.416.2" class="koboSpan">Given that this
is the key growth region currently and in the foreseeable future, it
will be interesting to observe how gas consumption will develop, given
that the region as a whole is in deficit, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.416.3" class="koboSpan">has to rely on
gas imports, particularly from the Middle East.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.416.4" class="koboSpan">The region is
already showing a voracious appetite for any type energy, but as
environmental concerns assume urgency, gas becomes a more palatable
choice. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.416.5" class="koboSpan">The
development of the Sakhalin II project (LNG) on Russia’s Pacific coast
shows how well aware the Russian government and IOCs (international oil
companies) are of the huge growth potential of Asia Pacific in gas
consumption. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.416.6"
class="koboSpan">And returning to our earlier</span>
