<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.432.1" class="koboSpan">geopolitical theme,
Russia’s expansion to the lucrative Asian markets shows how
diversification of consumer markets has become a strategic priority for
the country.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.433.1" class="koboSpan">Another important
aspect of gas consumption is its end use.
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0046" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0046"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.434.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 22</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.435.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows how gas is used in OECD countries, as a total
and also in various OECD country groupings.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.435.2" class="koboSpan">A third of the
gas used is for generating electricity and heat in combined cycle
plants. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.435.3" class="koboSpan">This
figure changes dramatically when one looks at OECD Pacific, however.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.435.4" class="koboSpan">What the graph
does not show is that this figure is dominated by Japan, which uses
substantial amounts of imported LNG for power generation.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.435.5" class="koboSpan">The remaining
two-thirds find their way to “final consumption”, an aggregation of
gas’s use by households (for heating and cooking), industry (for power
generation and as feedstock to other industrial processes) and
transportation. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.435.6"
class="koboSpan">For the moment, gas absorption by power plants is set
to grow, with more CCGT plants being developed.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.435.7" class="koboSpan">It will be
interesting to observe how growth in other sectors, especially the
rather negligible transportation, will change the map of how gas is
utilised by final consumers.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.436.1" class="koboSpan">6.3 Marketing and pricing</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.437.1" class="koboSpan">Natural gas is not as
extensively traded as oil and coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.437.2" class="koboSpan">Its physical
characteristics make it more difficult to handle and its high
flammability makes precision and care imperative.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.437.3" class="koboSpan">In 2008, just
over one quarter (26%) of the world production entered international
trade; the remaining (74%) was consumed domestically.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.437.4" class="koboSpan">Of the 26%
which was exported, nearly 19% was by pipeline and the remaining 7% in
liquefied form</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0067" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.438.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00067.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 23: Top gas exporters (pipeline and LNG)" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_150"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0047" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0047"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.439.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
23:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.440.1" class="koboSpan">
Top gas exporters (pipeline and LNG)</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.441.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.442.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.443.1" class="koboSpan">(see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0047" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0047"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.444.1" class="koboSpan">Figures 23</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.445.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0048" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0048"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.446.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.447.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.447.2"
class="koboSpan">Pipeline exports are predominant between Canada and the
United States (100 bcm), and between Russia and the rest of Europe (150
bcm, of which 60 bcm were exported to Germany and Italy alone).
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.447.3" class="koboSpan">Pipeline gas
also flows in large quantities from Norway (85 bcm), Netherlands (48
bcm) and Algeria (37 bcm) to Europe.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.447.4" class="koboSpan">The other
growing force in pipeline exports is Turkmenistan, This former Soviet
republic exports to Russia and Ukraine.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.447.5" class="koboSpan">However, this
is set to increase, as the country has recently (April 2007) signed a
30-year contract to supply gas to China, starting in 2009.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.448.1" class="koboSpan">LNG trade accounted
only for just over 7% of world natural gas production (and 28% of total
gas trade) and is rather small compared to trade flows of other energy
commodities; but because of the complexity of its transport logistics,
LNG flows have been meticulously documented on a voyage to voyage basis,
since the very beginning in the 1960s.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.448.2" class="koboSpan">The carriage of
the liquid itself is only one of several steps of a carefully planned
procedure, which includes carriage of gas from the point of production
to the port liquefaction facility; loading; regasification at the port
of destination; and transport to the point of consumption.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.448.3" class="koboSpan">LNG contracts
have been extensively documented and are being regularly quoted in
special publications by Cedigaz and BP.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.448.4" class="koboSpan">Examples of
existing contracts are given in the following table, which records long
term contracts by exporting country.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.449.1" class="koboSpan">As mentioned earlier,
natural gas entered international trade in a very modest way in the
1960s. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.449.2" class="koboSpan">The
first experimental voyages with LNG carriers were carried out in
the</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0068" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.450.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00068.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 24: Top gas importers (pipeline and LNG)" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_151"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0048" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0048"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.451.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
24:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.452.1" class="koboSpan">
Top gas importers (pipeline and LNG)</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.453.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.454.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.455.1" class="koboSpan">1950s, but the first
commercial trip was in 1964, between Algeria and the UK.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.455.2" class="koboSpan">A year later
LNG cargoes began flowing from Algeria to France, while in 1969, trade
between Alaska and Japan was initiated.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.456.1" class="koboSpan">In the 1970s gas
entering world trade increased to 13% of total production and new
countries appeared in the scene, like the Netherlands, Norway, Soviet
Union, Iran and Mexico. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.456.2"
class="koboSpan">The 1980s saw the opening of the submarine pipeline
between Tunisia and Italy, the beginning of trade between Malaysia and
Japan and the expansion of Soviet gas exports.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.456.3" class="koboSpan">The most
challenging issue for the economics of the industry in that decade was
the relation of gas and oil prices (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0049" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0049"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.457.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 25</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.458.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.458.2"
class="koboSpan">Traditionally, gas prices were determined on the basis
of its calorific equivalence to oil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.458.3" class="koboSpan">The 1986 oil
price collapse increased pressure for a reassessment of gas pricing
formulae, and many countries resorted to hybrid pricing mechanisms,
often incorporating one or more petroleum products, like gas oil or
gasoline. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.458.4" class="koboSpan">This
trend is still being followed, with gas prices tracking oil prices quite
closely, although gas prices do follow the prices set in the two main
energy exchanges which list gas contracts: NYMEX and ICE.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.459.1" class="koboSpan">With the emergence of
China as the world’s powerhouse of manufacturing, the much-talked-about
depletion of oil reserves and environmental concerns on the ascent,
interest in gas trade was also boosted; even more so for LNG, whose
growth has been unstoppable since the beginning of the new
millennium.</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0069" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_152"></span>[](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0069)

[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.460.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00069.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0069)

</div>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.461.1" class="koboSpan">6.3.1 LNG projects</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.462.1" class="koboSpan">An interesting
characteristic of the LNG market is the fact that the transport element
is only the last in a long chain of planning decisions that have to be
made for any individual project.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.463.1" class="koboSpan">LNG ships are probably
among the most sophisticated and technology-intensive in the world, with
prices in the region of \$220 million for a ship with a typical capacity
of 147,000 cu.m., built in the Far East.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.464.1" class="koboSpan">LNG projects are
extremely capital intensive, usually requiring billions of funds, of
which a substantial part has to be provided by equity holders.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.464.2" class="koboSpan">Projects are
usually set up as joint ventures between developed and developing
countries and involve long lead times, usually between seven to ten
years. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.464.3" class="koboSpan">Some of
the factors that need to be in place for a project to be successful
are:</span>

- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.465.1" class="koboSpan">a big enough reserve
  of gas which is unlikely to be consumed domestically for the next 20
  years at least;</span>
- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.466.1" class="koboSpan">one or more buyers
  willing to enter long-term purchase contracts;</span>
- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.467.1" class="koboSpan">a host government
  willing to be flexible on fiscal issues;</span>
- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.468.1" class="koboSpan">expertise in
  technical and safety areas; and</span>
- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.469.1" class="koboSpan">willingness of all
  parties to view the projects on a long-term, cooperative basis.</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0070" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.470.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00070.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 25: Indicative gas prices" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_153"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0049" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0049"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.471.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
25:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.472.1" class="koboSpan">
Indicative gas prices</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.473.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.474.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.475.1" class="koboSpan">With a lot more buyer
interest and more governments willing to export their production, LNG
projects took off since 2000. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.475.2"
class="koboSpan">Japan stands out as the country with most import
projects (25) in operation; USA as the one with the most import projects
under construction (6) or planned/proposed (9); Algeria as the one with
the most export projects in operation (4); and Qatar as the one
equalling Algeria’s operational exports projects and with the most
planned/proposed export projects (6).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.476.1" class="koboSpan">As mentioned just
above, an LNG project consists of several distinctive stages, namely
production, liquefaction and storage, transport and trading, storage and
regasification, and end-market distribution and sales.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.476.2" class="koboSpan">Until 2006,
technological advances and and economies of scale had kept the
construction costs of liquefaction plants in check, usually below
\$200/t/y (per ton per year) capacity.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.476.3" class="koboSpan">Reports in
2007, however, estimated a sharp increase in these costs, rising to over
\$500/t/y, sometimes reaching as much as \$1000/t/y capacity.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.476.4" class="koboSpan">To put this in
perspective, Russia’s Sakhalin II project, estimated at \$9.6 billion
originally is now facing construction costs of \$20 billion.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.476.5" class="koboSpan">Statoil’s
Snøhvyt project has experienced 50% cost inflation, to \$9.5
billion.</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0146" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0146"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.477.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.478.1" class="koboSpan">To spread the scale of
costs and the overall project risk, there is usually a divide in
ownership between the first three phases, which relate to sales, and the
final two, where buyers take over.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.478.2" class="koboSpan">In some cases –
in projects related to the Japanese market – trading houses provide the
bridge between buyers and sellers.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.479.1" class="koboSpan">The transport element
of the project comes at a later stage, usually a couple of years before
launching a new project. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.479.2"
class="koboSpan">Depending on the project, sales might be on a
c.i.f./f.o.b. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.479.3"
class="koboSpan">basis in which case the seller/buyer is responsible for
transport costs.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_154"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.480.1"
class="koboSpan">Once the project, including the transport element, is
in place the buyer and seller face the risk of operating a successful
and profitable venture. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.480.2"
class="koboSpan">Notwithstanding any technical or operational issues,
the key risk is profitability. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.480.3"
class="koboSpan">The buyer requires a long-term, steady stream of
income; the seller requires a competitively priced, highly marketable,
easily transferable commodity. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.480.4"
class="koboSpan">Long-term contracts (LTCs) have, therefore, been the
obvious choice for LNG partners (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fig0069" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0069"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.481.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.482.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.482.2"
class="koboSpan">This is not a novelty; iron ore and other mineral
commodities have been traded for decades on the back of LTCs.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.482.3" class="koboSpan">In this
contractual arrangement, the buyer normally takes the price risk and the
seller assumes the volume risk. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.482.4"
class="koboSpan">LTCs normally have take-or-pay (TOP) clauses, whereby a
buyer is obliged to pay for a certain amount of cargo, even if he does
not lift it. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.482.5"
class="koboSpan">Often there are destination clauses: the cargo can only
be destined to certain markets, it cannot be sold further on, to more
lucrative markets.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.483.1" class="koboSpan">On the other hand,
pricing is equally challenging. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.483.2"
class="koboSpan">With rapidly and constantly changing markets in
substitutes like oil and coal, gas prices need to be flexible, in order
to be representative of true market conditions, and hence competitive.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.483.3" class="koboSpan">It is not
surprising, therefore, that
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.484.1"
class="koboSpan">indexing</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.485.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.486.1"
class="koboSpan">formula</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.487.1"
class="koboSpan"> pricing is used in most, if not all, cases.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.487.2" class="koboSpan">Oil products,
more than crude oil, are used as benchmarks.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.487.3" class="koboSpan">Most North
European, North African and Caribbean LNG projects price their gas on a
combination of different refined products, such as gas oil, low-sulphur
fuel oil (LSFO), high-sulphur fuel oil (HFSO), as well as crude oil
benchmarks, such as WTI and Brent/BFO.</span>

## <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.488.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.488.2" class="koboSpan">Coal</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.489.1" class="koboSpan">Coal is a solid
mineral, composed primarily of carbon; other components of coal are
volatile hydrocarbons, sulphur and nitrogen, and the minerals that
remain as ash when the coal is burned.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.490.1" class="koboSpan">Most of the coal in
the earth’s crust was formed during the Carboniferous period – between
280 to 345 million years ago. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.490.2"
class="koboSpan">At that time much of the world was covered with
luxuriant vegetation growing in swamps.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.490.3" class="koboSpan">Many of these
plants were types of ferns, some as large as trees.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.490.4" class="koboSpan">This vegetation
died and became submerged under water, where it gradually decomposed.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.490.5" class="koboSpan">As
decomposition took place, the vegetable matter lost oxygen and hydrogen
atoms, leaving a deposit with a high percentage of carbon.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.490.6" class="koboSpan">As time passed,
layers of sand and mud settled from the water over some of the
carboniferous deposits. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.490.7"
class="koboSpan">The pressure of these overlying layers, as well as
movements of the earth’s crust and sometimes volcanic heat, acted to
compress and harden the deposits, thus producing coal.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.491.1" class="koboSpan">Coal is classified in
several sub-types, primarily according to its carbon content.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.491.2" class="koboSpan">Peat, the first
stage in the formation of coal, has a low fixed carbon content and a
high moisture content, but it does not have the same uses as commercial
coal.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.492.1" class="koboSpan">Commercial coal is
usually classified in two broad categories – brown and hard.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.492.2" class="koboSpan">The first
category includes lignite – the lowest rank of coal – and sub-bituminous
coal. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.492.3" class="koboSpan">Both of
these types are invariably used for power generation and, because of
their low quality, they are consumed in domestic markets.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.492.4" class="koboSpan">Lignite is
usually brownish-black in colour and often shows a distinct fibrous or
woody structure. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.492.5"
class="koboSpan">Lignite is inferior in calorific value to ordinary coal
because of its high (43.4%) water content and low (37.8%) carbon
content; the high (18.8%) content of volatile matter causes the lignite
to disintegrate rapidly upon exposure to air.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_155"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.493.1"
class="koboSpan">The term “hard coal” comprises all the remaining
high-quality types of coal, from bituminous coal to graphite.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.493.2" class="koboSpan">Bituminous coal
has more carbon than lignite and a correspondingly higher heating value.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.493.3" class="koboSpan">It is primarily
used for generating power, although coals closer to anthracite are
suitable for further processing into coke for steel production.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.494.1" class="koboSpan">Anthracite is a hard
coal with the highest fixed-carbon content and the lowest amount of
volatile material of all types of coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.494.2" class="koboSpan">It contains
approximately 87.1% carbon, 9.3% ash, and 3.6% volatile matter.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.494.3" class="koboSpan">Anthracite is
glossy black, with a crystal structure; although harder to ignite than
other coals, anthracite releases a great deal of energy when burned and
gives off little smoke and soot. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.494.4"
class="koboSpan">Anthracite is ideal for reduction into coke, which is
then used to fire iron ore in order to produce molten iron.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.495.1" class="koboSpan">Coke is a vital input
in the steelmaking process. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.495.2"
class="koboSpan">Coke is the name given to the hard, porous residue left
after the destructive distillation of coal; it is blackish-grey, has a
metallic lustre and is composed largely of carbon – usually about 92%.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.495.3" class="koboSpan">It has
excellent burning properties, with a heating value of 13,800 Btu/lb,
which makes it appropriate for use as a reducing agent in the smelting
of pig iron.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.496.1" class="koboSpan">Coke was first
produced as a by-product in the manufacture of illuminating gas.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.496.2" class="koboSpan">The growth of
the steel industry, however, produced a rising demand for metallurgical
coke, making it inevitable that coke should be manufactured as a chief
product rather than as a by-product.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.497.1" class="koboSpan">The earliest method of
coking coal was simply to pile it in large heaps out-of-doors, leaving a
number of horizontal and vertical flues through the piles.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.497.2" class="koboSpan">These flues
were filled with wood, which was lighted and which, in turn, ignited the
coal. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.497.3" class="koboSpan">When most
of the volatile elements in the coal were driven off, the flames would
die down; the fire would then be partly smothered with coal dust, and
the heap sprinkled with water.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.498.1" class="koboSpan">A later development
was the coking of coal in the beehive oven, so named because of its
shape. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.498.2" class="koboSpan">As in
open-air coking, no attempt was made to recover the valuable gas and tar
that were by-products of the process.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.498.3" class="koboSpan">Beehive ovens
have now been almost entirely supplanted by the modern by-product coke
ovens. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.498.4" class="koboSpan">These
ovens, usually arranged in batteries of about 60, are narrow vertical
chambers with silica-brick walls, heated by burning gas between
adjoining ovens. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.498.5"
class="koboSpan">Each oven is charged through an opening in the top with
anywhere from 10 to 22 tons of coal, which is heated to temperatures as
high as 1,482°C for about 17 hours.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.498.6" class="koboSpan">During this
period the gases from the oven are collected through another opening in
the top. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.498.7" class="koboSpan">At the
end of the coking period the red-hot coke is forced by a ram, out of the
oven, directly into a car that carries it to the quenching hood, where
it is sprinkled with water. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.498.8"
class="koboSpan">The emptying process takes only about three minutes, so
that the oven is ready for recharging with little loss of heat.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.499.1" class="koboSpan">Although we are mainly
concerned with coal for power generation and steelmaking, it is worth
taking note of another form of coal – graphite; and a coal by-product –
coal tar; both of which have a variety of industrial uses.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.500.1" class="koboSpan">Graphite is one of the
three allotropic forms of carbon; the other forms are diamond and
amorphous carbon. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.500.2"
class="koboSpan">It occurs in nature as a mineral invariably containing
impurities. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.500.3" class="koboSpan">It
is widely distributed over the world; important deposits are found in
Siberia, England, Madagascar, Mexico, Sri Lanka, Canada, and numerous
localities in the United States. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.500.4"
class="koboSpan">Graphite is made artificially by baking a mixture of
petroleum coke and coal tar pitch at 950°C for 11 to 13 weeks, then
transferring the baked product to electric graphitising furnaces and
heating it to about 2,800°C for four or five weeks.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.501.1" class="koboSpan">Although graphite is
chemically the same as diamond, it differs greatly from that mineral in
most of its physical properties. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.501.2"
class="koboSpan">Graphite is black, opaque, metallic in lustre,
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_156"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.502.1"
class="koboSpan">and has a specific gravity of 2.09 to 2.2.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.502.2" class="koboSpan">Graphite is
extremely soft, it smudges anything with which it comes into contact,
and it feels greasy or slippery to the touch.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.502.3" class="koboSpan">It is the only
non-metal that is a good conductor of electricity; unlike other
conductors of electricity, it is a poor conductor of heat.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.503.1" class="koboSpan">The cores of “lead”
pencils contain no lead but are made of graphite mixed with clay.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.503.2" class="koboSpan">Graphite is
used as electrodes in electrochemical industries where corrosive gases
are given off, and for electric arc furnaces that reach extremely high
temperatures. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.503.3"
class="koboSpan">It is used as a lubricant either by itself or mixed
with grease, oil, or water. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.503.4"
class="koboSpan">It is also used in crucibles that must withstand
extremely high temperatures, and in certain paints.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.1" class="koboSpan">Coal tar is a viscous
black liquid produced in the destructive distillation of coal to make
coke and gas. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.2"
class="koboSpan">Coal tar is a complex mixture of organic compounds,
mostly hydrocarbons. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.3"
class="koboSpan">Its composition varies with the coal, the temperature
at which it is formed, and the equipment used.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.4" class="koboSpan">Coke is usually
produced at about 1,000°C, and coal tar formed in that temperature range
consists mostly of aromatic hydrocarbons, plus phenols and some
compounds containing nitrogen, sulphur, and oxygen.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.5" class="koboSpan">The variation
in composition means that most of the compounds in coal tar are formed
during the coking process and are not present, as such, in the original
coal. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.6" class="koboSpan">Some 300
distinct compounds have been identified in coal tar, of which about 50
are separated and used commercially.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.7" class="koboSpan">Separation is
achieved through distillation, which produces benzene, toluene,
naphthalene, xylene, anthracene, phenanthrene, and other valuable
products. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.8" class="koboSpan">The
processing may be varied to give different proportions.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.504.9" class="koboSpan">Left, after
distillation, are residues of pitch used in making roads, in roofing
mixtures, and in electrodes for the production of aluminium.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.505.1" class="koboSpan">Coal tar was once
regarded as a useless nuisance. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.505.2"
class="koboSpan">Since then, however, it has led to a whole new field of
chemistry and its compounds are indispensable to a vast number of
products, including dyes, drugs, explosives, food flavourings, perfumes,
artificial sweeteners, paints, preservatives, stains, insecticides, and
resins. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.505.3" class="koboSpan">Coal
tar is also the chief source of creosols, a group of chemicals used in
antiseptics, creosote oil, paint removers, and plastics.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.506.1" class="koboSpan">As noted earlier, coal
normally contains a number of other compounds, mainly sulphur and
metallic elements, which form the ash.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.506.2" class="koboSpan">When burnt,
coal generates a number of undesirable by-products, which have largely
contributed to the image of coal as a “dirty” source of energy.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.506.3" class="koboSpan">Carbon reacts
with oxygen to produce carbon monoxide (CO) and dioxide
(CO</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.507.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.508.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.508.2"
class="koboSpan">Increased emissions of these two gases are have
contributed to the greenhouse effect on the earth’s atmosphere, with
detrimental long-term consequences for global climate.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.508.3" class="koboSpan">When burnt, the
sulphur contained in coal reacts with oxygen to form sulphur dioxide
(SO</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.509.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.510.1"
class="koboSpan">), a gas which has several useful industrial
applications. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.510.2"
class="koboSpan">If the gas is released in the atmosphere, however, it
mixes with water (H</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.511.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.512.1"
class="koboSpan">O) in a lethal combination - sulphuric acid
(H</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.513.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.514.1"
class="koboSpan">SO</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.515.1"
class="koboSpan">4</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.516.1"
class="koboSpan">) – which returns to earth as acid rain.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.516.2" class="koboSpan">Finally, coal
burning also produces a number of nitrogen oxides
(NO</span><sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.517.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.518.1"
class="koboSpan">), which also have detrimental effects on earth’s
atmosphere.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.519.1" class="koboSpan">As the coal industry
is trying to improve the image of the commodity, several attempts have
been made to improve its combustion, with the aim to reduce emission of
impurities, such as sulphur and nitrogen oxides, and increase the
efficiency of energy production. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.519.2"
class="koboSpan">Clean coal technologies (CCTs) are a relatively new,
but now more established, generation of advanced coal utilisation
processes, some of which may be increasingly commercially viable in the
21st century. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.519.3"
class="koboSpan">In general, these technologies are cleaner, more
efficient, and less costly than conventional coal-using processes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.519.4" class="koboSpan">A wide variety
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_157"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.520.1"
class="koboSpan">of CCTs exist, but all of them alter the basic
structure of coal before, during, or after combustion.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.520.2" class="koboSpan">CCTs include:
improved methods of cleaning coal; fluidised bed combustion; integrated
gasification combined cycle; furnace sorbent injection; and advanced
flue-gas desulphurisation.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.521.1" class="koboSpan">7.1 Supply characteristics</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.522.1" class="koboSpan">The supply
determinants of coal have essentially been discussed earlier in this
chapter, under the section on oil.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.522.2" class="koboSpan">One definite
advantage of coal over all other fossil fuels is its sheer abundance.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.522.3" class="koboSpan">World coal
reserves were estimated at 826 billion tonnes at the end of 2008, with
an R/P ratio of 122 years. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.522.4"
class="koboSpan">With R/P ratios of 60 years for natural gas, and 42
years for oil, coal maintains the advantage of supply security.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.522.5" class="koboSpan">Another very
interesting statistic is that while just between 6–8% of oil and natural
gas reserves are located in OECD countries, over 40% of coal reserves
are located in the OECD area, which makes coal a “politically safe”
source of energy (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0050" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0050"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.523.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 26</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.524.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.525.1" class="koboSpan">With such obvious
advantages then, why is coal not the most popular source of energy in
most countries around the world? </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.525.2"
class="koboSpan">The answer lies very much in the economics of coal
mining and the challenge to coal by the ‘new’ fuels – oil and natural
gas.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.526.1" class="koboSpan">As in any project for
the extraction of mineral resources there are three main stages in coal
recovery: exploration, development, and production.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.526.2" class="koboSpan">Exploration may
last a few years, until proper geological surveys point with high
probability to the existence of reserves.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.526.3" class="koboSpan">Several
exploratory shafts may have to be constructed in order to assess the
quality and extent of the deposits.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.526.4" class="koboSpan">Costs at this
stage can be substantial and are sunk.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.526.5" class="koboSpan">The development
stage involves the construction of an open pit (if the developer is
lucky enough to find coal near the ground surface) or the digging of an
underground mine. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.526.6"
class="koboSpan">Again, costs at this stage are sunk, and further costs
might have to be incurred at later stages of a project in order to
improve and/or extend capacity.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.527.1" class="koboSpan">At the production
stage, most of the costs are operating costs, which tend to increase as
reserves are being depleted and more effort is required to extract them.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.527.2" class="koboSpan">This is
particularly true when underground mining is the method of production.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.527.3" class="koboSpan">Another
important difference of coal mining from oil and gas extraction is that
coal has to be moved at every stage, whereas oil and gas flow naturally;
coal requires a lot more effort to break and extract, while oil simply
requires a steady pressure which will keep it flowing out of the well,
naturally.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.528.1" class="koboSpan">Another important
characteristic of the coal industry, which is also evident throughout
the mineral sector, is the large extent of heterogeneity in production
costs. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.528.2"
class="koboSpan">Depending on the geomorphy of the field and local
climatic conditions, costs can vary considerably from one region to the
next. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.528.3"
class="koboSpan">Indonesia, South Africa and Colombia, for example, are
low to medium-cost producers, while countries like Germany, UK and
France produce coal at such high costs that it is often cheaper to
import the commodity from distant, low-cost exporters.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.529.1" class="koboSpan">Apart from regional
differences, one should also expect different production costs between
surface and underground coal mines.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.529.2" class="koboSpan">Intuitively,
one would anticipate lower production costs for open pit mines; this,
however, is not always so. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.529.3"
class="koboSpan">Underground mining does suffer from increased costs for
tunnelling, roof and wall supports, adequate ventilation, and a
transport system to move coal to the surface.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.529.4" class="koboSpan">However,
because of the extent of these costs, many high-cost producers –
particularly European mines – have developed increasingly mechanised,
and more cost-efficient, ways of extracting</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0071" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.530.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00071.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 26: Proved coal reserves" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_158"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0050" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0050"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.531.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
26:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.532.1" class="koboSpan">
Proved coal reserves</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.533.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.534.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.535.1" class="koboSpan">coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.535.2" class="koboSpan">These
technologies have been largely adopted by medium-cost producers – like
US mines, for instance – resulting in lower costs for underground mines
and increased competitiveness with surface mines.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.536.1" class="koboSpan">On the other hand,
surface mines can do little to improve their earth-moving equipment,
except perhaps by using a continuous transport system, like a conveyor
belt. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.536.2" class="koboSpan">No matter
how efficient the movement of coal is, however, it cannot compensate for
the fact that there is a lot of waste material that has to be moved as
well. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.536.3" class="koboSpan">The
overall effect is, of course, that the cost per tonne of coal increases,
often making surface mines more expensive than underground mines.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.537.1" class="koboSpan">Although capital and
land are the most important contributors to extraction costs, one should
not underestimate the role of labour in coal production.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.537.2" class="koboSpan">Taking into
account the fact that coal is largely produced in OECD countries, labour
costs become quite sizeable, and labour relations are central to the
uninterrupted running of a coal mine; one has only to recall the huge
disruption caused, in the UK economy, by the long strike of coal miners
at the beginning of the 1980s.</span>

#### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.538.1" class="koboSpan">7.1.1 Reserves and production</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.539.1" class="koboSpan">Coal is found in
nearly every region of the world, but deposits of present commercial
importance are confined to Europe, Asia, Australia, and North America
(see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0051" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0051"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.540.1" class="koboSpan">Figures 27</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.541.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0055" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0055"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.542.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.543.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.543.2"
class="koboSpan">Great Britain, which led the world in coal production
until the twentieth century, has deposits in southern Scotland, England,
and Wales.</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0072" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.544.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00072.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 27: Development of coal production by region" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_159"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0051" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0051"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.545.1" class="koboSpan">Figure

Development of coal production by region</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.547.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.548.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.549.1" class="koboSpan">In western Europe,
coalfields are found throughout the Alsace region of France, in Belgium,
and in the Saar and Ruhr valleys in Germany.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.549.2" class="koboSpan">The French and
Belgian production is rather small, with the latter disappearing
altogether, after 1993. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.549.3"
class="koboSpan">Germany is still the most important Western European
producer, but its production has been falling steadily for the last 10
years. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.549.4" class="koboSpan">Most of
Germany’s deposits contain brown and sub-bituminous coal, which are of
lower calorific value and, hence, decrease total German production in
oil equivalent terms.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.550.1" class="koboSpan">Eastern European
deposits include those of Poland, the Czech Republic, Romania, Bulgaria,
and Hungary. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.550.2"
class="koboSpan">The most extensive and valuable coalfield in the former
Soviet Union is that of the Donets Basin between the Dnepr and Don
Rivers; large deposits have also recently been exploited in the Kuznetsk
Coal Basin in Western Siberia. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.550.3"
class="koboSpan">The Russian Federation holds the world’s second largest
reserves of coal, with some 157 billion tonnes in 2008, which was behind
US deposits of 238 billion tonnes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.550.4" class="koboSpan">Apart from
Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan are the other two former Soviet republics
to hold substantial reserves. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.550.5"
class="koboSpan">As in Western Europe, coal production in Eastern Europe
experienced a declining trend through the 1990s.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.550.6" class="koboSpan">This trend,
however, started a reversal in the late 1990s, with coal production
showing an increase as we have moved into the twenty-first century.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.550.7" class="koboSpan">Unlike Germany,
the former Soviet republics – especially Ukraine and Kazakhstan –
produce primarily hard coal.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.551.1" class="koboSpan">The coal reserves of
the United States are divided into six major regions.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.551.2" class="koboSpan">Only three of
these regions, however, are mined extensively.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.551.3" class="koboSpan">The most
productive region is the Appalachian field, which includes parts of
Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky,</span>

alt="Figure 28: Development of coal production by major type" /></span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0074" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.557.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00074.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 29: Top hard (steam &amp; coking) coal producers" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0053"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.558.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
29:</span></span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.559.1"
class="koboSpan"> Top hard (steam & coking) coal producers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.560.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.561.1"
class="koboSpan">IEA Coal Information, 2009</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0075" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.562.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00075.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 30: Top brown coal producers" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_161"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0054"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.563.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
30:</span></span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.564.1"
class="koboSpan"> Top brown coal producers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.565.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.566.1"
class="koboSpan">IEA Coal Information, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.1" class="koboSpan">Tennessee, Ohio, and
Alabama. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.2" class="koboSpan">In the
Midwest one large field covers most of Illinois and sections of Indiana
and Kentucky. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.3" class="koboSpan">A
thick field extends from Iowa through Missouri, Kansas, and Oklahoma.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.4" class="koboSpan">These three
regions produce the majority of the coal mined in the United States.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.5" class="koboSpan">There are large
deposits of lignite and sub-bituminous coal in North Dakota, South
Dakota, and Montana. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.6"
class="koboSpan">Sub-bituminous and bituminous coal deposits are
scattered throughout Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.7" class="koboSpan">The Pacific
Coast and Alaska have small reserves of bituminous coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.8" class="koboSpan">Almost all the
anthracite in the United States is in a small area around Scranton and
Wilkes-Barre, in Pennsylvania. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.567.9"
class="koboSpan">The best bituminous coal, for coking purposes, comes
from the Middle Atlantic states.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.568.1" class="koboSpan">Canada does not have
the massive coal reserves of the United States, but it produces very
good quality anthracite, large quantities of which it exports to Japan,
as well as Western Europe. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.568.2"
class="koboSpan">Most of Australia’s coal reserves are located in
Western Australia, close to the large iron ore reserves.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.568.3" class="koboSpan">Australia is a
substantial producer, and a very important exporter, of coal,
particularly to the Pacific Rim.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.569.1" class="koboSpan">The coalfields of
north-western China, among the largest in the world, were little
developed until the twentieth century.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.569.2" class="koboSpan">Today, however,
China is the world’s largest coal producer, although its reserves are
only about half those located in the United States; the Chinese economy
is a very intensive user of the commodity.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.570.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, the most
important producer in Africa and the Middle East is South Africa, with
reserves of over 30 billion tonnes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.570.2" class="koboSpan">The country is
essentially the only significant producer of coal in the African
continent, with a production of 250 Mtoe in 2008, all of which was hard
coal.</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0076" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.571.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00076.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 31: Development of coal consumption by region" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_162"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0055" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0055"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.572.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
31:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.573.1" class="koboSpan">
Development of coal consumption by region</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.574.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.575.1"
class="koboSpan"> BP Statistical Review of World Energy, 2009</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.576.1" class="koboSpan">7.2 Demand characteristics</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.577.1" class="koboSpan">All types of coal have
some value; as an old saying in the coal industry goes “anything pale
brown will burn”. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.577.2"
class="koboSpan">This, of course, does not necessarily mean that it will
burn efficiently. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.577.3"
class="koboSpan">Although peat is frequently used as a fuel in rural
communities and, more recently, peat and lignite have been made into
briquettes for burning in furnaces, it is brown and hard coals that are
consumed extensively; and, of these two, only hard coal is traded
internationally.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.578.1" class="koboSpan">If one were to point
at a single factor that has tremendously affected the fortunes of the
coal industry, this would be its cross-substitutability with oil and
natural gas. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.578.2" class="koboSpan">We
saw earlier that energy is needed for residential, industrial,
transport, and “other”, consumption.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.578.3" class="koboSpan">Although oil
fits very well into all types of consumption, this is no longer the case
for coal. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.578.4" class="koboSpan">Coal
has been substituted by oil and natural gas in domestic consumption; in
transport, coal burns inefficiently and is quite bulky to carry around;
in industry, however, it is still used extensively.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.579.1" class="koboSpan">Coal has two main uses
– power generation, and as a fuel in the production of other industrial
materials (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0056" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0056"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.580.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 32</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.581.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.581.2"
class="koboSpan">Coal is used extensively in power plants with
coal-fired electricity generators, as well as in other industrial
processes that use coal-fired generators.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.581.3" class="koboSpan">In industry,
coal is used in the production of steel and cement.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.581.4" class="koboSpan">For the latter,
coal is mixed with limestone and other materials, and fired to produced
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.582.1"
class="koboSpan">clinker</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.583.1"
class="koboSpan"> – the raw material which is pulverised to become
cement. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.583.2" class="koboSpan">In
steelmaking, the procedure is not that simple; coal has to be carbonised
– i.e. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.583.3" class="koboSpan">purified
– in special furnaces, in order</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0077" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.584.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00077.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 32: Consumption of steam coal by end use" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_163"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0056" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0056"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.585.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
32:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.586.1" class="koboSpan">
Consumption of steam coal by end use</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.587.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.588.1"
class="koboSpan"> IEA Coal Information, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.589.1" class="koboSpan">to produce coke, a
coal of a quality very close to that of graphite.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.589.2" class="koboSpan">Coke is then
mixed with iron ore and a flux, and fired in a blast furnace, to yield
pig iron, as we will describe in
</span>[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.590.1" class="koboSpan">chapter
6</span>](#Ch06.xhtml_ht0169)<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.591.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.592.1" class="koboSpan">Only anthracite and
high-quality bituminous coal can be used for coking; coal with such
attributes is known as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.593.1"
class="koboSpan">coking </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.594.1"
class="koboSpan">coal. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.594.2"
class="koboSpan">All other coal is used for power generation, and is
known as </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.595.1"
class="koboSpan">steam </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.596.1"
class="koboSpan">coal. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.596.2"
class="koboSpan">These two new groupings of coal should not be confused
with brown and hard coal. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.596.3"
class="koboSpan">By definition, all lignite and sub-bituminous coal is
steam coal, and so is the lower-quality bituminous coal; anything of
higher quality is suitable for coking.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.597.1" class="koboSpan">Steam coal is a very
important input in power generation, accounting for about 80% of the
variable cost of producing coal-fired electricity.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.597.2" class="koboSpan">Demand for
steam coal depends on the price of the commodity itself, the price of
other substitutes – like oil and natural gas – and the ease with which a
power plant can switch between different fuels.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.597.3" class="koboSpan">After the first
oil price shock, although coal became affordable, it was rather
difficult for coal to capture a large market share, because most power
generators were geared to use oil as fuel.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.597.4" class="koboSpan">During the
1970s, it became evident that oil was getting too expensive and too
unsafe to be relied upon; the result was increased popularity for coal,
which was readily available from politically safe areas.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.597.5" class="koboSpan">With
electricity companies and other industries changing their generators to
accommodate coal, it was little surprise to see a massive boost in coal
consumption and trade, after the second oil price shock.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.598.1" class="koboSpan">While steam coal is by
far the most important cost contributor in electricity generation, this
is not the case with coking – or metallurgical – coal, which is
estimated to</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0078" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.599.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00078.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 33: International hard coal trade" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_164"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0057" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0057"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.600.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
33:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.601.1" class="koboSpan">
International hard coal trade</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.602.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.603.1"
class="koboSpan"> IEA Coal Information, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.604.1" class="koboSpan">account about 10% of
the finished cost of steel. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.604.2"
class="koboSpan">There is no substitute for coal in blastfurnace steel
production; instead, the whole steelmaking process has to be replaced
with an electric arc furnace. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.604.3"
class="koboSpan">The increased popularity of EAFs has curtailed the
share of blast furnaces in crude steel production and has, therefore,
undermined the demand for coking coal, as well.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.604.4" class="koboSpan">While this is
true, however, new smelting reduction techniques for making steel
utilise
coal</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0147" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0147"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.605.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.606.1"
class="koboSpan"> once again and, thus, increase the demand of
coal.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.607.1" class="koboSpan">Power generation
steelmaking and cement production, are not the only uses of coal,
however. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.607.2" class="koboSpan">Coal
was also used, from the early nineteenth century to the World War II
era, for the production of fuel gas, just as coal liquefaction
techniques were used to produce liquid oil products.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.607.3" class="koboSpan">In the 1980s,
several industrialised nations showed interest in developing CCTs, but
the popularity of the environmentally-friendlier natural gas and the
availability of cheaper oil after the mid-1980s has hampered the rapid
development of such technologies.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.607.4" class="koboSpan">With the rapid
increase in crude oil prices since late 2005, however, CCTs experience a
newly found popularity once again.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.607.5" class="koboSpan">Finally, coal
has a number of additional minor uses.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.607.6" class="koboSpan">For example, it
is used as a raw material for the manufacturing of carbon electrodes;
also in pulverised form it is directly injected in blast furnaces for
steel production.</span>

### <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.608.1" class="koboSpan">7.3 Marketing and trade</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.609.1" class="koboSpan">Not all coal that is
produced, is marketed internationally.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.609.2" class="koboSpan">Brown coal has
a high humidity content, which makes it susceptible to spontaneous
combustion and, therefore, difficult to transport.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.609.3" class="koboSpan">Moreover, its
low carbon content makes brown coal uneconomical to export (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0057" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0057"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.610.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 33</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.611.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0079" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.612.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00079.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 34: Major hard coal exporters" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_165"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0058" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0058"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.613.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
34:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.614.1" class="koboSpan">
Major hard coal exporters</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.615.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.616.1"
class="koboSpan"> IEA Coal Information, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.617.1" class="koboSpan">Hard coal, however, is
quite actively traded, and a total of over 950 million metric tonnes of
coal were traded in 2008. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.617.2"
class="koboSpan">Hard coal traded is made up of steam coal (Bituminous
and sub-bituminous) and coking coal (plus anthracite).
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.617.3" class="koboSpan">Steam coal
trade is the larger of the two, but coking coal is actually the most
actively
traded.</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0148" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0148"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.618.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.619.1" class="koboSpan">The list of top
exporters of coal differs somewhat from that of top producers (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0058" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0058"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.620.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 34</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.621.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.621.2"
class="koboSpan">Some of the most important producers of coal use it
domestically; the case of China is an extreme example, whereby only a
tiny portion of the country’s production (ca.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.621.3" class="koboSpan">3%) is
exported. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.621.4" class="koboSpan">At
the other extreme, Australia channels over 75% of its production in the
export market, while the United States presents a mixed picture, with
substantial quantities of coal disappearing through domestic
demand.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.622.1" class="koboSpan">Overall, the most
prominent exporter of coal is Australia, controlling just under 20% of
steam coal exports, and over 45% of exports of coking coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.622.2" class="koboSpan">Other important
exporters of coal include the Indonesia, Russia, South Africa, China,
Colombia, United States, Canada, Poland, and India.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.623.1" class="koboSpan">Focusing on steam coal
trade now, Indonesia and Australia are the largest exporters, followed
by South Africa, and then by Russia, South Africa, Colombia and China.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.623.2" class="koboSpan">The direction
of most steam coal trade flows is Asia (especially Japan, S.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.623.3" class="koboSpan">Korea and
Taiwan), which receives over 50% of world imports.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.623.4" class="koboSpan">Japan is the
single most important importer of steam coal, absorbing 18% of world
trade. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.623.5" class="koboSpan">The
second largest importing</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0080" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.624.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00080.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 35: Major hard coal importers" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_166"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0059" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0059"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.625.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
35:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.626.1" class="koboSpan">
Major hard coal importers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.627.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.628.1"
class="koboSpan"> IEA Coal Information, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.629.1" class="koboSpan">region is Western
Europe, with Germany, UK, Italy and France the top four European
importers (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0059" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0059"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.630.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 35</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.631.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.632.1" class="koboSpan">The situation in
metallurgical coal is quite different.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.632.2" class="koboSpan">Both exports
and imports are dominated by a few large players.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.632.3" class="koboSpan">Coking coal is
not abundant, and there are only a few countries that have adequate
reserves. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.632.4"
class="koboSpan">Australia, the United States, Indonesia and Canada, are
the four most important exporters of coking coal, accounting for nearly
80% of total trade. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.632.5"
class="koboSpan">Other exporters include Vietnam, Russia and
China.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.633.1" class="koboSpan">Coking coal imports
are directed primarily to Asia and Western Europe.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.633.2" class="koboSpan">Once again,
Japan is the largest single importer of coking coal, absorbing nearly a
quarter of world exports and sourcing most of its needs from Australia.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.633.3" class="koboSpan">Because of this
interdependence, it is no surprise that both Japanese steel mills (JSMs)
and Australian coal producers enter negotiations every year, in order to
determine quantities and prices for coking coal exports.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.633.4" class="koboSpan">These
negotiations parallel those for iron ore, and they usually involve the
same companies. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.633.5"
class="koboSpan">Following Japan at a distance are China, India and S.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.633.6" class="koboSpan">Korea, each one
importing 27–29 million tonnes in 2008.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.634.1" class="koboSpan">The steam coal market
is not as concentrated as the market for coking coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.634.2" class="koboSpan">There are
several suppliers of coal in each of the large producers: in Australia
the key players are BHP Billiton, Xstrata, Rio Tinto and Anglo American.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.634.3" class="koboSpan">In South Africa
most of the production and exports are generated by Ingwe, Anglocoal,
XCSA</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0149" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0149"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.635.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.636.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the local companies
Sasol</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0150" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0150"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.637.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.638.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Exxaro.</span><sup><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fn0151" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fn0151"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.639.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0081" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_167"></span>[](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0081)

[<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.640.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00081.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0081)

</div>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.641.1" class="koboSpan">In the United States
there are many producers with producing capacities from as low as 2–4
million (short) tons per annum to as high a few hundred million tons per
annum, making the US one of the most competitive markets in the world.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.641.2" class="koboSpan">This said,
however, its top ten producers control more than half of the country’s
total production (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_fig0081" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_fig0081"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.642.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.643.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.644.1" class="koboSpan">Like steel producers,
power plants need reliable supplies of adequate quality of coal that
will make electricity generation as efficient as possible.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.644.2" class="koboSpan">Power plants
usually enter their own negotiations with coal mines and/or traders, and
any respectable procurement manager of a power plant concentrates on
four main aspects of the negotiations:</span>

- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.645.1" class="koboSpan">physical
  characteristics of the coal;</span>
- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.646.1" class="koboSpan">the reliability of
  the supplier;</span>
- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.647.1" class="koboSpan">contract
  specification; and</span>
- <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.648.1" class="koboSpan">pricing.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.649.1" class="koboSpan">Coal quality is
determined by a number of parameters, like its calorific value (measured
in kcal/kg), percent content of volatile matter, moisture, ash, and
sulphur; hargrove; and initial deformation point.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.649.2" class="koboSpan">Coal quality is
important, because low-quality coal results in: energy losses; excessive
waste material that has to be disposed of; increased corrosion and,
hence, increased maintenance costs; and increased expenses for
desulphurisation.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.650.1" class="koboSpan">As far as the supplier
is concerned, a power plant needs a counterpart with adequate
infrastructure, in an area of relative political stability, with a
healthy financial position, a long-term attitude to doing business, and
commitment to quality development, and</span>

<div id="Ch05.xhtml_fig0082" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.651.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00082.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 36: Coal import prices" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_168"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0060" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0060"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.652.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
36:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.653.1" class="koboSpan">
Coal import prices</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.654.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.655.1"
class="koboSpan">IEA Coal Information, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.656.1" class="koboSpan">cost control.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.656.2" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the
supplier should preferably have prior export experience, which will help
overcome any difficulties that may arise.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.657.1" class="koboSpan">The contract is, of
course, the most important part of the agreement, and should be fair and
equitable, which will keep both partners happy throughout its duration.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.657.2" class="koboSpan">After all, the
contract provides security of supplies for the buyer, while income
security is the main benefit for the coal producer, together with the
ability to use the contract as a loan collateral.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.657.3" class="koboSpan">Although
contracts usually include long lists of clauses for every eventuality,
it is always preferable to keep them simple, since arbitration is
expensive and time consuming. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.657.4"
class="koboSpan">Finally, contracts also make proper arrangement for the
transportation of coal from source to destination.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.657.5" class="koboSpan">Approximately
80% of the world trade in coal is carried by sea – just under 800
million tonnes in 2007. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.657.6"
class="koboSpan">Coal is in fact – with iron ore – the largest seaborne
dry bulk commodity, providing employment for all sizes of dry bulk
carriers, but particularly for Capesize and Panamax vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.658.1" class="koboSpan">Pricing is the last
stage of the agreement between buyer and seller.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.658.2" class="koboSpan">Prices are
usually set every year, in a process that is called
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.659.1"
class="koboSpan">annual price
nomination</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.660.1"
class="koboSpan">, and are usually based on the average cost of
operations plus a profit component.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.660.2" class="koboSpan">This method is
called </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.661.1"
class="koboSpan">cost-plus</span></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.662.1"
class="koboSpan"> and is the most popular – but not unique.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.662.2" class="koboSpan">Another, very
similar method uses a base price, which is estimated from the cost-plus
price, and an escalation term is attached to it.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.662.3" class="koboSpan">Finally, market
prices can also be used although, due to the large heterogeneity of the
commodity, such prices are quite difficult to determine.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.662.4" class="koboSpan">Coal prices
reflect, of course, the conditions in the energy and steel markets.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.662.5" class="koboSpan">An increase in
the price of oil (like the</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.663.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00083.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 37: Coal export prices" /></span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_169"></span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0061" id="Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0061"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.664.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
37:</span></span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.665.1" class="koboSpan">

class="koboSpan"> IEA Coal Information, 2009</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.668.1" class="koboSpan">ones in 1973 and 1979)
will increase demand for oil substitutes – like coal – and will, thus,
push prices upwards (see
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0060" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0060"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.669.1" class="koboSpan">Figures 36</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.670.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch05.xhtml_cap_lbl0061" id="Ch05.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0061"><span
id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.671.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.672.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

## <span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.673.1" class="koboSpan">8. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.673.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.674.1" class="koboSpan">Concluding the
discussion on energy commodities, we focused first on the history and
current markets for crude oil, refined products and natural gas.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.674.2" class="koboSpan">After the oil
price collapse of the mid-1980s, the world witnessed a notable switch to
open market pricing. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.674.3"
class="koboSpan">This led to the emergence of some crudes, like Brent
and WTI (and more recently Dubai), as marker crudes.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.674.4" class="koboSpan">Although not
commanding an important part of world production or trade, the markets
(spot, forward, futures and other traded or over-the-counter
derivatives) of these crude grades provide competitiveness and
transparency and are used for two very important activities in commodity
trading: price discovery and hedging.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.674.5" class="koboSpan">Few could have
predicted the roller-coaster ride of these prices in the early 2000s.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.674.6" class="koboSpan">Strong economic
growth, an apparently insatiable appetite for energy my new
industrialising economies and continued political turmoil in the Middle
East pushed oil prices a historic record high of \$147/barrel, followed
by a sharp decline down to nearly \$40 and then a continuous fluctuation
between \$60–70 up to now (autumn 2009).</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.675.1" class="koboSpan">Natural gas remains a
dynamic contender in the energy sector.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.675.2" class="koboSpan">After
experiencing a rapid growth of reserves and production, it has
stabilised its share in global primary
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_page_170"></span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.676.1"
class="koboSpan">energy consumption.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.676.2" class="koboSpan">The most
notable development in this market, especially in the new millennium, is
the increasing complexity of the trade flows.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.676.3" class="koboSpan">With new LNG
projects becoming operational, the possibility of a deeper and more
competitive spot market for LNG cargoes and new gas pipelines being
constructed or planned, this industry continues to offer exciting
opportunities for growth.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.677.1" class="koboSpan">We also discussed the
supply and demand economics of coal.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.677.2" class="koboSpan">Not long ago,
not many people believed that coal could withstand the onslaught of
natural gas on its market share. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.677.3"
class="koboSpan">Yet, this commodity never ceases to surprise.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.677.4" class="koboSpan">Coal production
and trade continued to increase through the 2000s and still enjoys a
commanding position in global primary energy consumption, particularly
so in heat and power generation. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.677.5"
class="koboSpan">With the strong growth in steel production, driven by
China, coal remained the world’s largest bulk commodity, together with
iron ore.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.678.1" class="koboSpan">Coal is still
considered a politically safe commodity.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.678.2" class="koboSpan">It is also the
heaviest contributor to carbon emissions.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.678.3" class="koboSpan">Although coal
has managed to overcome this shortfall by being quite cost effective for
power generation, the fact remains the coal industry is facing an urgent
and major overhaul. </span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.678.4"
class="koboSpan">Clean coal technologies, such as carbon capture and
sequestration, offer possibilities for the industry to clean up and
reduce the burden on greenhouse gas emissions.
</span><span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.678.5" class="koboSpan">However, these
technologies are still an experimental stage and require time, money and
perhaps the right legislative force to implement them on a large
scale.</span>

<span id="Ch05.xhtml_kobo.679.1" class="koboSpan">For the foreseeable
future and until one or more commercially viable clean and renewable
energy substitutes come to the mainstream, hydrocarbons will continue to
dominate the world energy industry and will continue to generate the
trade flows which provide the livelihood to a substantial part of the
world’s merchant fleet.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Modal Split Functions for Simulating Decisions on Shifting Cargo from Road to Sea</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0169)
