<span class="italic"><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Manfred</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Zachcial</span></span><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_fn0152" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_fn0152"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter deals with
modal split models and compares the classical binary mode choice
approaches with practical decision situations of shifting cargo from
road to sea and tries to quantify the qualitative factors influencing
the split between modes in addition to pure financial determinants.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">In a first
section the classical modal split models are briefly reviewed, to be
followed by two different examples for the application of modal split
models on European freight transport problems.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">For a long time, the
system-immanent disadvantages of inter modal transport including
maritime or rail transport compared to direct trucking have not been
quantified in monetary terms. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.8.2"
class="koboSpan">There have been only certain tentative estimates
available assuming advantages of transport cost of 15–30% in favour of
sea transport to be necessary to shift a certain amount of cargo from
road to sea or to avoid shifts from sea to road.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.8.3" class="koboSpan">Among others
scientists, the author has dealt with this problem since
years.</span><sup><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_fn0153" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_fn0153"><span
id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">Binary Mode Choice Models</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">The basis of the
empirical modal split functions tested in the following is the classical
interchange modal split model. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.11.2"
class="koboSpan">This modelling approach was dominated by
post-distribution models. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.11.3"
class="koboSpan">The advantage of this procedure is the principle
inclusion of the characteristics of the trip and the modes performing
it. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.11.4" class="koboSpan">The first
models included only one or two characteristics of the trip, almost
vehicle operation cost and travel time.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.11.5" class="koboSpan">As found by
several researchers, a S-shaped curve seemed to represent this kind of
behaviour adequately. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.11.6"
class="koboSpan">This hypothesis is shown in the following
</span><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_cap_lbl0062" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0062"><span
id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<div id="Ch06.xhtml_fig0084" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00084.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: The classical modal split function" /></span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_page_174"></span><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0062" id="Ch06.xhtml_cap_lbl0062"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">
The classical modal split function</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">Empirical tests have
shown that the forecasting ability is doubtful due to missing
explanatory parameters. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.17.2"
class="koboSpan">Among others such as qualitative factors they ignore a
number of policy-sensitive variables.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.17.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore it
seems to be necessary to modify this type of
model.</span><sup><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_fn0154" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_fn0154"><span
id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">Modelling Approach and Empirical Tests</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">Since some of the
determinants of mode choice are not possible to be quantified and
expressed in monetary terms, it seems to be necessary to apply a modal
split model which estimates system-immanent disadvantages of inter modal
transport compared to pure road haulage.</span>

<div id="Ch06.xhtml_fig0085" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00085.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">The ratio of the
proportions or transport shares of both modes is equivalent with the
probability to choose the one or the other mode.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">The components
of the formula are defined as follows:</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">P</span><sub><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">= market shares of O/D pairs</span>\
<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">λ = dispersion
parameter</span>\
<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">δ = modal disadvantage
(penalty)</span>

<div id="Ch06.xhtml_fig0086" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00086.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Linearised regression line of mode choice assuming 0.90€/km for trucking cost" /></span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_page_175"></span><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0063" id="Ch06.xhtml_cap_lbl0063"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">
Linearised regression line of mode choice assuming 0.90€/km for trucking
cost</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">Linearisation by using
logarithms results in the following formula was used for linear
regression:</span>

<div id="Ch06.xhtml_fig0087" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00087.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">The values of λ and δ
as the regression‘s unknown parameters have been calibrated by
regression analysis with (C</span><sub><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">− C</span><sub><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">) as the independent one.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.37.2" class="koboSpan">The term λδ
equals the regression's constant and λ the slope of the function.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">The theoretical modal
split function implies that both modes will have 50% market share if the
difference between total costs of both modes including all relevant
qualitative factors is zero.</span>

### <span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Test of split functions for trade data between Portugal and Germany</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">In a first example for
the application of a modified type of modal split models, the freight
traffic situation of land and sea transport between Portugal and a
number of German metropolitan areas was analysed (for example Hamburg,
Bremen, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt, Munich, Stuttgart, Cologne etc.).
</span><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_cap_lbl0063" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0063"><span
id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that the market shares between land and sea
related to each of the origin/destination pairs follow the theoretical
modal split
function.</span><sup><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_fn0155" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_fn0155"><span
id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">However, the y-axis
(indicating the cost difference of zero) is not crossed at the 50:50
distribution between sea and land, but at about the 40:60 distribution.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.44.2" class="koboSpan">This means that
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_page_176"></span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">there are determinants of demand in the market which
influence the split in addition to pure transport cost.</span>

<div id="Ch06.xhtml_fig0088" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00088.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">The function is
satisfactory from the statistical point of view with a rate of
determination of R</span><sub><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan"> = 81% and high values for the t-statistics (number in
brack ets below the regression coefficients).
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">This holds for
the fact that the regression has been calculated based upon cross
section data which per se show lower values compared to time
series.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">The numerical result
can be interpreted as follows: the regression line crosses the x-axis at
about €134. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.50.2" class="koboSpan">This
means that with regard to this transport relation (Lisbon-Germany
cities) sea transport achieves 50% of the market if the pure transport
price (including port handling charges) is by €134 cheaper than trucking
(on average). </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">If
the price differential is zero or even negative, the share of inter
modal land/sea transport is zero or close to it.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">This means also that
the market share of inter modal transport could be increased if on a
certain route the price difference could be extended (for example by
lower handling cost or lower freight rates by using economies of scale)
and/or if the qualitative disadvantage of shipping including time cost,
capital binding cost and others would be reduced.</span>

### <span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Land/sea trade flows between Germany and Poland</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">In contrast to the
modelling case presented in 3.1 where possibilities for shifting cargo
from road to sea have been analysed with respect to trade flows between
Portugal and Germany, now a different planning case is presented with
respect to estimates of cargo shifts from sea to road within and along
the Baltic Sea between Germany and Russia/ Finland.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">This topic
became relevant because of the full EU membership of Poland and the
Baltic Republics and the opening of the borders, especially of that
between Germany and Poland.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">The new situation of
free trade flows had several impacts, especially the absence of the
former long waiting times at the German/Polish border of up to 16 hours.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">This shortened
the total transit time between Germany and Russia (St Petersburg)
substantially and gave the land connection respective benefits compared
to Ro-Ro traffic between the German Baltic sea ports of Kiel, Lübeck and
Rostock. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.54.3" class="koboSpan">In
addition, there have been some other aspects in favour of road compared
to sea, especially the possibility to use large quantities of cheap
fuel, partly stored in special tanks below the truck body of up to 1,300
litres for running across Germany further in transit to other European
countries. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.54.4"
class="koboSpan">Another aspect favouring road instead of mixed land/sea
traffic across the Baltic Sea was the problem of partly missing controls
of the travelling time of truck drivers.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">These factors caused a
substantial shift of former Ro-Ro cargo to the land corridor along the
Baltic Sea with negative financial impacts on the ferry and Ro-Ro
operators. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">They
claimed for stronger regulations of land transport and financial
assistance by the German Government and the EU-Commission.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.55.3" class="koboSpan">In the meantime
most of the market biases have been resolved.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.55.4" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
this former change in competition seems to be an interesting case for
testing this type of modal split models.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.55.5" class="koboSpan">In order to help
to</span>

<div id="Ch06.xhtml_fig0089" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00089.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Empirical modal split function with and without changes of transport and time cost in Baltic Sea Trades 2003/2005" /></span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_page_177"></span><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0064" id="Ch06.xhtml_cap_lbl0064"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">
Empirical modal split function with and without changes of transport and
time cost in Baltic Sea Trades 2003/2005</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">clarify the
interactions between the changed road transport conditions and the lost
of freight on the ferries, the Institute of Shipping Economics and
Logistics, Bremen, tried to simulate the impacts by financial
terms.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">The function applied is
the same as used before, where in addition to the qualitative
improvement of land transport and lower freight rates also some effects
of disturbed competition due to timely illegal behaviour in trucking are
used as inputs to the model.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">The following
</span><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_cap_lbl0064" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0064"><span
id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the split function for the market shares of
Ro-Ro shipping across the Baltic Sea including hinterland traffic and
pure land transport by truck. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.63.2"
class="koboSpan">The dots are staying for origin/destination flows, for
example between St Petersburg and Moscow in Russia on one and Lübeck as
Baltic Sea port location and Hamburg, Berlin, Düsseldorf and Munich as
locations in the German hinterland.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">The traffic
flows from/to the latter metropolitan areas imply hinterland trucking
to/from a German Baltic port and then Ro-Ro shipments compared to
exclusive land transport by truck.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">The straight line
indicates the modal split situation "Ro-Ro shipping to road haulage" for
the base year 2003, i.e. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.64.2"
class="koboSpan">before the opening of the Polish land border, and the
broken curve the situation after the opening and free cross-bordering
traffic. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.64.3" class="koboSpan">In
principle, the market share of Ro-Ro transport is the higher, the
shorter the distances between the origins and/or destinations and the
ports are. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.64.4"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, the Ro-Ro shares are very low for the
flows between Munich and Moscow as well as Berlin and Moscow (about 5%),
while the these shares are very high for the flows between Hamburg and
especially Lübeck and St Petersburg (close to 100%).</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">For the year 2005,
there was a significant downward shift of the split function towards
lower market shares expected due to the improved traffic situation in
the land corridor along the Baltic Sea.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">This was
simulated earlier to the opening of the border being indicated by the
lower curve. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">In
the changed conditions, the Ro-Ro market share was anticipated to reach
only 40% on average, given equal transport cost for both transport
means. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.65.4" class="koboSpan">This is
especially true for all German origins and destinations not being
located
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_page_178"></span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan">close to the coast.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">For Lübeck and
also Hamburg this effect is not relevant.
</span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">After 2005, the
introduction of adequate regulations concerning fuel transport and
social rules led to a certain shift back to Ro-Ro
traffic.</span><sup><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_fn0156" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_fn0156"><span
id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">Summary and Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">A short description of
a classical modal split approach and two modifications has been
presented. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">It
could be shown that such models are suitable for deriving a better
insight into the inter-modal markets and to simulate necessary cost
reductions and/or quality improvements to realise a certain market share
for coastal shipping compared to land transport and especially road
haulage.</span>

<span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">The precondition for an
adequate assessment of effective measure is a clear knowledge of market
shares and cost structures. </span><span id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.70.2"
class="koboSpan">The modification of the classical modal split model has
been applied not only in the two planning cases presented here, but also
in transport planning studies dealing with the competition between road
and rail and between rail and
shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch06.xhtml_fn0157" id="Ch06.xhtml_bck_fn0157"><span
id="Ch06.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_180"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_181"></span>[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 7</span>\
<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">The Economics of Shipping Freight Markets</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0178)
==============================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Patrick</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">M.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Alderton</span></span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0158" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0158"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan"> and</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">Merv</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan">Rowlinson</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0159" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0159"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">The purpose of this
chapter is to provide analysis of the many economic changes that have
occurred in freight markets in recent decades.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">Whereas great
technological leaps in container, bulker, tanker and Ro-Ro shipping were
already well in train by the 1970s the three decades since have
witnessed less evident, but equally forcible changes in the shape and
composition of freight market supply and demand.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">The intention
here is to build on the solid theoretical foundations of freight markets
that the blossoming discipline of maritime economics had already
provided by the 1970s. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.12.4"
class="koboSpan">From this position, the critical changes that occurred
in freight markets will be discussed and their impact on freight markets
analysed. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.12.5"
class="koboSpan">Additionally, the intention is to focus on the new
trends already taking place in the freight market, including the
increasing impact of environmental issues on the market.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">The freight market can
be defined as the place where the buyers and sellers of shipping
services come together to strike a deal.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.13.2" class="koboSpan">Categorisation
may be made in a number of ways. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.13.3"
class="koboSpan">The charter market can be divided up into the following
four main sectors: First, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">Voyage Charter Market;
</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">under
this type of contract the charterer hires the ship to carry his cargo
for usually an agreed rate per ton.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Most of the
problems are for the shipowners with the major points of negotiation
being the freight rate and the laytime (the time the charterer wants for
cargo handling). </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.15.3"
class="koboSpan">For obvious economic reasons charterers will opt for
this market when freight rates are high and when the expectations are
that they will fall and when the demand of the commodity markets seems
unstable. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.15.4"
class="koboSpan">Second,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan">The Contract of Affreightment Market (COA);
</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">this is a
variation of consecutive voyage chartering or in other words a contract
between owner and charterer to move so much cargo on a regular basis.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">No ship is
named, which is an advantage to owners with large fleets or to owners
who are members of a “pool”. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.17.3"
class="koboSpan">Third,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.18.1"
class="koboSpan">Time Charter Market;
</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">this
market can be split into short, medium and long period of times.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">Prior to 1970
many
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_182"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan">tramp owners would have a good percentage of their
fleet under long-term (say 15-year) charters.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">This gave
stability to their business as they could estimate their income for long
periods of time. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.20.3"
class="koboSpan">However when many accepted long-term charters in the
boom year of 1970 they suffered financially in the period of inflation
that followed in 1973. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.20.4"
class="koboSpan">Since then the majority of the market has been in
short- and medium-term charters. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.20.5"
class="koboSpan">In this type of contract the charterer becomes the
disponent owner and has to accept many of the problems that might arise,
so the negotiations will usually be more complex.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.20.6" class="koboSpan">Finally,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">Bareboat Charter
Market</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">;
under this contract the shipowner will lease the bare ship to the
charterer who for practical purposes will operate the vessel as his own.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">However, in this
market often standard contract forms are seldom used so the actual
conditions will vary, though the contract can be for a long period of
time, often for the life of the ship.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.22.3" class="koboSpan">It can be used
as a way of financing a ship, particularly in a period when shipowning
enjoys certain tax advantages, as in such situations financiers can
enjoy the benefits of shipowning without the problems of having to
operate the vessel. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.22.4"
class="koboSpan">In addition the charter market manufacturers and
traders with significant annual volumes to move may express a preference
for directly owned, vertically integrated tonnage.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">The plan of work
provided here outlines the nature and composition of shipping freight
markets in the 1970s and the theoretical framework constructed by the
new school of maritime economists in this era.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">The dramatic
technological and operational changes to freight markets in the 1970s
were well in train. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.23.3"
class="koboSpan">Oil markets were becoming a dominant force in global
shipping as the seemingly insatiable oil demand by developed industrial
nations was accelerated by unin terrupted world growth (up until the
late 1970s), post-World War II. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.23.4"
class="koboSpan">The increased demand, coupled with increasing
tonne-mile factors brought about by growth in long-haul oil trades,
proved conducive to radical developments in vessel size.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.23.5" class="koboSpan">Economies of
scale were the economic
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan">zeitgeist </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">of this period as tanker and bulker sizes soared
upwards. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.25.2" class="koboSpan">Equally
dramatic changes were occurr ing in the cargo liner sector, with capital
intensive fully cellular and Ro-Ro ves sels replacing the traditional
labour intensive cargo liner. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.25.3"
class="koboSpan">During this period the dominance of North America and
Europe in world trades was being supple mented by the dynamic industrial
growth of Japan, with Korean industry begin ning to register as a world
force.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">Building on the
theoretical framework which was well established in the 1960s by the
burgeoning school of maritime economists, this chapter considers new
developments in freight markets. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.26.2"
class="koboSpan">Whereas great technological leaps in design –
containerisation, massively increased sizes in the tanker and dry-bulk
and tanker sectors, Ro-Ro shipping - accompanied by a revolution in
operational practice, occurred in the decade post-1960, later decades
have been much less dramatic. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.26.3"
class="koboSpan">However a number of areas in the freight market have
under gone significant change. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.26.4"
class="koboSpan">The intention is to explain the change process by
analys ing the shifts in the demand and supply of shipping within the
context of freight market changes.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.26.5" class="koboSpan">Though it is
perhaps too early to determine what the effects of the EU banning the
liner conference system will have on the liner and general cargo
shipping market.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">This is followed by a
statistically based analysis of the principal changes to aggregate
freight markets in the past four decades.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">The fundamentals
of derived is revisited within the context of these changes.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.27.3" class="koboSpan">Whilst it is not
proposed to challenge the main precepts of demand, it is important to
recognise that important new developments have affected specific freight
markets. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.27.4" class="koboSpan">Trends
of industrialisation and de-industrialisation have wrought changes to
the pattern of demand. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.27.5"
class="koboSpan">Additionally unforeseen events shaping the global
political economy have impacted on the freight market.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_183"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan">Finally, the concept of “green shipping” is discussed
within the context of eased environmental concern during the last few
decades. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.28.2"
class="koboSpan">Empirical evidence drawn from the operations (and
accidents) of contemporary shipping will be analysed within the context
of the fast evolving green agenda, as well as the economic pressures of
the post-credit crunch market. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.28.3"
class="koboSpan">The intention is to explain the change process via the
utilisation of a broad-based range of economic and organisational
theory. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.28.4" class="koboSpan">This
should not only contribute to the understanding of change but also
endorse the value of theory which will deepen analysis of the dynamics
of restructuring and strategy in the industrial transi tion
process.</span>

## <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.29.2" class="koboSpan">The Theoretical Framework</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">The key determinants of
demand for sea transport were clearly defined by
Chrzanowski.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0160" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0160"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> These are:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">the volume and
    quantity of cargoes to be transported;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">the distance of
    transport.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">The basic tools for
meeting this demand were met by a mixture of charter market and directly
owned tonnage. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.35.2"
class="koboSpan">The essential question this raises is what type of
allocative process was best suited to meeting these demands.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.35.3" class="koboSpan">The market
mechanism was clearly favoured by leading maritime economists.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.35.4" class="koboSpan">By the 1970s the
economic principles determining freight markets had been rigorously
defined by the new wave of maritime economists.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.35.5" class="koboSpan">From this period
a strong tradition of neo-classical economic analysis has been
maintained in maritime economics. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.35.6"
class="koboSpan">With the emphasis on cost competitiveness in open
freight markets, maritime economists have argued for the efficacy of
market forces. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.35.7"
class="koboSpan">Svendsen’s 1958
work</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0161" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0161"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"> provided a seminal analysis of the neo-classical micro
economics of freight markets, stressing the essential comparative costs
of shipping and their importance in attaining competitiveness in the
global market. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.37.2"
class="koboSpan">Thorburn</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0162" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0162"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan"> effectively employed supply and demand analysis to
develop a detailed model of shipping freight markets, identifying some
36 supply and 24 demand conditions to be found in the working
marketplace. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.39.2"
class="koboSpan">Goss</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0163" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0163"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan"> reflected the emerging macro factors which were
beginning to affect shipping markets by the late 1960s.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.41.2" class="koboSpan">The changes in
the world political order during this period led to the market model of
open freight markets being challenged.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.41.3" class="koboSpan">The once
colonial nations were beginning to pressurise for more economic
independence which included the ownership and management of merchant
shipping. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.41.4"
class="koboSpan">Additionally, open registry tonnage was becoming a
major force in the world fleet. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.41.5"
class="koboSpan">Both trends were to prove difficult for traditional
owners in the USA and in Northern Europe.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.41.6" class="koboSpan">Protectionism in
the freight market was seen as an effective response to these difficult
conditions. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.41.7" class="koboSpan">Goss
was to question the efficacy of resorting to protectionism, particularly
where it negated the benefits of the competitive
markets.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0164" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0164"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan"> Goss’ position on the open market has been a
consistent feature of the maritime literature.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.43.2" class="koboSpan">In 1993, he was
to counter calls for interv ention in the freight market:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">“International shipping
services are commonly bought and sold in competitive markets which lead
to the survival of those with the lowest private costs...
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.44.2" class="koboSpan">the relevant
principle is that of comparative
advantage.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0165" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0165"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_184"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">Gilman</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0166" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0166"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan"> heralds the great leap in technology and innovation
“that facilitated the container revolution.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.48.2" class="koboSpan">Focusing on such
major liner routes as the North Atlantic and Transpacific, Gilman
credits the great economic gains of con tainerisation on the competitive
process which ensured that leading lines would strive for
ever-increasing efficiency. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.48.3"
class="koboSpan">Jansson and Schneerson identified the benefits of a
rigorously competitive shipping liner industry, one optimises the most
economic use of the global supplies of capital and labour:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">“The best division of
labour in international sea transport is obtained when the most
efficient operators become price
leaders.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0167" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0167"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">Changes in Freight Markets</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 World trade from 1840–2000</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">World trade in the form
we know it today started in the middle of the nineteenth century as
global communications developed. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.53.2"
class="koboSpan">Before that what the ship brought back from her voyage
depended on the commercial ability of the master or the discretion of
the owner’s agent. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.53.3"
class="koboSpan">As London became the communication centre of the world
it became the trading centre of the world.</span>

<a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0065" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0065"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that although world trade has faltered from time
to time it has continued to grow. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.55.2"
class="koboSpan">Note also how after World War II from the mid-1950s
growth in demand dramatically increases and the modern trend of maritime
transport can be considered to have started.</span>

[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0065)<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan"> also shows the general increase in world trade since
World War II apart from a plateau in the 1980s caused by a slight
decline in the oil trades in that period.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.57.2" class="koboSpan">Since then the
growth has followed the same buoyant trend established in the
1960s.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_185"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Main specific markets post-1970s</span>

<a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0066" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0066"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the growth in the world container traffic from
1970–2005 and illustrates that although the global growth has been
consistently increasing (until mid-2008), the growth has varied in the
three main trading regions. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.63.2"
class="koboSpan">In 2000 World Container Ports handling increased by
8.7% but in South-East Asia and South America growth would be nearer
25%. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">Note that
some 20% of container traffic is empty containers.</span>

<a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0067" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0067"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicates the percentage of general cargo that is
containerised in the global situation.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">At many of the
major ports in the developed countries that percentage may be well into
the 90s.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 The dry bulk trades</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">In 1937 total seaborne
trade of all mineral ores was 25m tonnes.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Demand due to post-war
reconstruction caused trade to boom during the 1950s helped by
re-armament, the (Korean war) and increased consumer demand, in
particular by the motor car industry.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">During the 1960s
the bulk carrier fleet increased from seven to 70m dwt.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.68.3" class="koboSpan">During the last
few years iron ore, coal and grain have accounted for some 65% of
seaborne dry bulk cargo movements.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.68.4" class="koboSpan">Other important
bulk cargoes include bauxite, sugar, wood, wood pulp, wood chips,
fertilisers and cars (full cargoes such as cars and packaged lumber are
sometimes referred to as neo-hulk cargoes).
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.68.5" class="koboSpan">See
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0093" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0093"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">3.5 Derived demand revisited</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">The intention now is to
consider some of the specific demand factors that have altered the
freight market in recent decades. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.98.2"
class="koboSpan">The concept of derived demand serves to define and
predict the nature and pattern of demand for shipping.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.98.3" class="koboSpan">Key determinants
of</span>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0096" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_188"></span>[](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0096)

[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00096.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0096)

</div>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0097" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00097.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0097)

</div>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">demand have been
clearly identified by maritime economists.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.101.2" class="koboSpan">These include:
the level and location of economic activity, distance factors,
population levels and trend factors.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.101.3" class="koboSpan">In the last
three decades derived demand has been affected by the pattern of
deindustrialisation in the mature economies.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.101.4" class="koboSpan">This has been
reflected by changes in such staple trades as coal, iron ore and steel.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.101.5" class="koboSpan">The run down of
the coal mining industry in Northern Europe has created a heavy demand
for the deep-sea carriage of steam coal.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.101.6" class="koboSpan">Australian,
Chinese, Columbian, South African and North American coal exports have
benefited by the new international division of labour.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.101.7" class="koboSpan">The economics
of such long haul trades are facilitated by the comparative costs of sea
transport. </span>[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
4</span>](#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0070)<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0071" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0071"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates the cost competitiveness of sea transport
over long distances. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.105.2"
class="koboSpan">The assumptions made here are based on representative
cost between the three transport modes:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">Imported South
    African Coal: Voyage Chartered Capesize Vessel, 180,000 dwt Richards
    Bay-Clyde, \>6,000 nautical miles.</span>
2.  <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">UK Mined Coal:
    Rail Central Scotland-Central England Merry-go-round train.
    </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.107.2" class="koboSpan">15 trucks,
    200 miles approx. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.107.3"
    class="koboSpan">Payload 45 tonnes per truck.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">Developments in the
inland German Port of Duisburg clearly reflect the deindustrialisation
process. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">The
run down of the giant Krupp steel complex not only reduced demand for
regionally produced coal but also the import of iron ore via the ports
of Rotterdam and Antwerp. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.130.3"
class="koboSpan">The transformation of Duisburg into a centre of
logistics now emphasises the growth of container flows through the
port.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">The switch of heavy
industry to the Far East has also had a similar impact on the demand for
coking coal. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.131.2"
class="koboSpan">See
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0096" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0096"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">Tables 2</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0097" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0097"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">3.6 The impact of changes in the political economy</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">Freight markets have
also been affected by unforeseen changes in the political economy.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.137.2" class="koboSpan">The impact of
the ending of the Cold War, the welcoming of South Africa back into the
world trade network and the inexplicable decline of the industrial
giants of Japan and Korea.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">In the 1970s the
growth of the Soviet bloc fleet posed some concern for Western Defence
strategists. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.138.2"
class="koboSpan">Fearful that the low cost of the socialist ships would
enable them to penetrate crucial freight markets, it was argued that the
socialist ship-managers did not have to pay insurance charges and
benefited from low cost East European labour and fuel supplies.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.138.3" class="koboSpan">On some key
liner routes socialist ships were charging rates up to 65% lower than
con ference
rates.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0168" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0168"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan"> The rapid collapse of Communism following the periods
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_190"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan">of Glasnost and Perestroika in the late 1980s has led
to a drastic reduction of consumer power as the ex-command economy
struggled to achieve a market mechanism.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">An obvious
casualty has been the market for North American grain imports.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">The normal
shortfalls in the Soviet wheat harvest provided a sizeable market for
American and Canadian grain. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.141.4"
class="koboSpan">The impoverishment of the economy means that there is
little consumer purchasing power and that the state lacks the hard
currency to make large scale bulk purchases, regardless of the poor
state of the nation’s diet.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">Another unanticipated
outcome of the collapse of the ex-Soviet economy has been the
relinquishment of large volumes of merchant shipping into world trade
routes. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.142.2"
class="koboSpan">Additionally, the collapse of the Soviet bloc economies
in the late 1980s saw large amounts of ageing tonnage and low cost crews
entering into the open market. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.142.3"
class="koboSpan">Particularly noticeable has been the incursions of’ the
Russian Volga barges into the trades.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.142.4" class="koboSpan">These vessels
usually named Lagoda were originally intended for the calmer waters of
the Volga these vessels can now be seen in the less clement waters of
the North Sea, the Irish Sea and the Bay of Biscay.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.142.5" class="koboSpan">Whilst the
Eastern bloc seamen had hitherto enjoyed a sound world wide reputation
for professionalism, the substandard conditions and ships they now find
themselves has diluted their craft status.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.142.6" class="koboSpan">Typical of the
plight of these seamen is the example of the 20 crew of the 740 TEU
vessel, </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">Hannes C.
</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">Composed
of a mix of Russian, Romanian, Ukrainian and Filipino, the feeder
vessel’s crew found themselves dependent upon the Antwerp Port Chaplains
and their Seafarer Centre. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.144.2"
class="koboSpan">The lay-up of their vessel, following the financial
collapse of the vessel’s owners, stranded the crew without pay, food and
fuel, resulting in extreme conditions on board.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.144.3" class="koboSpan">Emergency
supplies of clothing, blankets, food, water and fuel were supplied to
the vessel by the Antwerp Seafarers’
Centre.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0169" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0169"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan"> This is just one example of numerous incidents
occurring in ports around the world involving the impoverishment and
marginalisation of seafarers in the global market.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">The impact of changes
in the international political economy is currently being felt in the
Far East, particularly the impact of China’s trade liberalisation and
the transfer of Hong Kong to the Peoples’ Republic of China as a Special
Economic Region.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">3.7 Supply</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">The supply of shipping
is made up of the carrying capacity of ships to move cargo.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.149.2" class="koboSpan">This is made up
of three main factors.</span>

<span class="bold"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">Ships </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">Ships have consistently grown bigger over the last
century. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.151.2" class="koboSpan">The
growth was slow from 1880 to 1955 but from 1955 to 1975 it was
spectacular, as owners realised the possibilities of new technologies
and trade routes. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.151.3"
class="koboSpan">In 1975, the last of the ships ordered before the oil
crisis ended the boom of the early 1970s, were being constructed.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.151.4" class="koboSpan">Since then the
situation has stabilised – tankers, for instance, have not grown any
bigger, but ferries have. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.151.5"
class="koboSpan">The number of ships: over the last century the num ber
of ships which carry things has declined but the total tonnage of ships
has greatly increased. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.151.6"
class="koboSpan">The reason for this is
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan">their size.
</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">See
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0072" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0072"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">Figures 7</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0074" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0074"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0073" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0073"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 8</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicates that the depth of water was not a major
issue until the 1960s. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.159.2"
class="koboSpan">Even in 1950 Rotterdam still had only ten metres.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.159.3" class="koboSpan">In 1970 there
were only eight ports in Europe which could accept the new class of VLCC
tankers and there were no ports with sufficient depth of water on the
east coast of North America. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.159.4"
class="koboSpan">By 1975, following a period of energetic dredging there
were 22 ports in north-west Europe which could accept such ships.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.159.5" class="koboSpan">Dredging is a
very expensive activity and the question facing port</span>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0099" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00099.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7: Growth of the world fleet" /></span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_191"></span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0072" id="Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0072"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
7:</span></span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">
Growth of the world fleet</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">managers is: “Will
ships continue to get bigger?” </span>[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
8</span>](#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0073)<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">, showing average ship size since 1850, does indicate a
levelling off in average ship size after 1980.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">If the average
of the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">five </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">largest tankers are considered for each year it can be
seen tanker size peaked around 1975.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">If the same
exercise is considered for dry bulk carriers their size seems to have
peaked around 1985–1989. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.167.3"
class="koboSpan">If so, should one dredge the old channel or develop a
new terminal in an area which enjoys deeper water?</span>

<span class="bold"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan">Port time</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan"> The less time ships spend in port the more cargo they
can carry in a year – hence reducing port time increases the supply of
ships.</span>

<span class="bold"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">Speed</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan"> Increasing speed obviously increases the supply of
ships and vice versa. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.171.2"
class="koboSpan">This is the only way supply can be adjusted in the
short term apart from laying ships up and reactivating them.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.171.3" class="koboSpan">Few marine
engines allow wide variations of speeds, but reducing speed two or three
knots can show significant economies, so “slow steaming” can be a valid
strategy in the attempt to balance supply and demand or to reduce
propulsion costs in periods of high hunker costs, as seen in the late
1970s and early 1980s.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">Perhaps a more useful
analysis is to consider the supply from the different types of
vessels.</span>

alt="Figure 9: Cruise vessels" /></span>

class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
9:</span></span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">
Cruise vessels</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0102" class="fig"

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00102.jpg"

</div>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">Originally cruise
ships tended to be relatively small catering for say less than 500
passengers as they needed to be able to manoeuvre in and out of the
smaller historical and romantic ports on the “traditional” cruise
itinerary.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">3.8 General cargo and container ships</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s
List</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">,
January 2001 uses the term ULCS (Ultra Large Container Ships) of ships
of 9,000–10,000 TEU capacity. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.183.2"
class="koboSpan">Also proposed terms–Suezmax container ship 12,000 TEU,
Malaccamax 18,000 TEU.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">In 2006 the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan">Estelle
Maersk</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">
had 170,794 gt, 158,000 dwt and could carry 12,500 TEU.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">However in 2007 a
spokes person for the Port of LA said that LA would prefer two 6,000 box
ships a week rather than an 8,000+ vessel, due to the strain the latter
put on the inland distribution services.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">In 1998 there were
only some 36 container ships with drafts greater than14 metres.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.188.2" class="koboSpan">From the
3,000-box ship of 1972, container ship size did not increase any further
until 1982 when the 4,000 box ship was introduced.</span>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0103" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_193"></span>[](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0103)

[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00103.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0103)

</div>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0104" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00104.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0104)

</div>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">From there another
size plateau was sustained until the early 1990s when the 6,500-box ship
appeared. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.191.2" class="koboSpan">As
ships’ beams increase, cranes must also increase in size.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.191.3" class="koboSpan">This involves
an increase in weight and there comes a point when the terminal cannot
take the extra load without considerable civil engineering expense.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.191.4" class="koboSpan">As ships’
drafts increase, depth of water in ports becomes a problem.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.191.5" class="koboSpan">Virtually all
major ports have 10 metres, but few can offer over 15 metres.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">For large ships to
maintain the same schedules as their smaller brethren cargo-handling
speeds will have to be increased.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.192.2" class="koboSpan">From this it
follows that the terminal area wiIl need to be increased and the inland
distribution facilities improved.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.192.3" class="koboSpan">Increasing the
size of ships may well also increase the peaking factor which can be a
serious cost problem for a centre hub port.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">The term “Ro-Ro” can
cover a variety of ships such as car ferries, specialist vehicle
carriers, of which over 50% are owned by the Japanese, and general cargo
ships which are described as having Ro-Ro capability.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.193.2" class="koboSpan">These Ro-Ro
ships are expensive: a 15,000 dwt size would be about twice the price of
a conventional ship of this size and the “wasted space” can be
considerable but their productivity is very high and their extreme
flexibility – virtually anything can be rolled on, containers, heavy
loads, large objects, etc. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.193.3"
class="koboSpan">– makes them attractive to operate.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.193.4" class="koboSpan">These ships
have also been referred to as STO/ROs in cases where the cargo is rolled
on board by forklift trucks which stow and handle the cargo as in a
warehouse. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.193.5"
class="koboSpan">Ro-Ros have also proved very useful in areas where
congestion has occurred.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_194"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan">It was originally considered that Ro-Ro was only
suitable for short distances many such ships have been operating for
years between Europe and Australia and across the Pacific – there are
also ships which are part cellular containership and part Ro-Ro.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.194.2" class="koboSpan">See
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0102" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0102"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">Tables 5</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0103" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0103"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0104" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0104"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">3.9 The dry bulk carrier</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">A bulk carrier is a
large single deck ship, say \> 10,000 dwt which carries unpackaged
cargo. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.202.2"
class="koboSpan">Statistics concerning bulk carriers may not be always
consistent as different authors and different times will arbitrarily
determine at what a single decked vessel will classed as a bulk carrier.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.202.3" class="koboSpan">The term bulk
cargo is however simply unpackaged cargo that can be poured, tipped or
pumped into the holds or tanks of the ship.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">Although there have
been colliers for centuries carrying bulk coal and grain and various
ores have also a long history of bulk carriage, the modern concept of a
variety of bulk cargoes being loaded and discharged quickly into single
deck “open hatch” dry cargo ships from modern terminals equipped for
handling </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan">bulk</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> cargoes, dates only from the mid-1950s.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping textbooks
written in the 1940s and early 1950s refer to bulkers but these seemed
to have been on the Great Lakes or part of a vertically integrated
operation. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">Like
container ships they were born of economic necessity.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.206.3" class="koboSpan">Tramp freight
rates were very depressed though demand was increasing after the Korean
war, so a cheaper means of carrying bulk cargoes had to be found.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.206.4" class="koboSpan">Also
technically it was not possible to build open hatch ships much before
this date. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.206.5" class="koboSpan">In
1962 there were only 21 bulk carriers over 40,000 dwt and the world
total of bulk carriers was only 611.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">The particular design
features of a bulk carrier are the single deck, a large hatchway and
wing tanks. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.207.2" class="koboSpan">The
upper wing tanks are shaped to give a conical transverse section to the
hatch, so that when bulk cargo is being poured in the amount of
“trimming" is reduced as the cargo is being loaded.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.207.3" class="koboSpan">When loading
bulk cargoes the danger has always been that the upper corners of the
hold would be left empty with the consequent danger of the cargo
shifting in bad weather.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">The large bulk
carriers usually trade between special terminals and therefore seldom
have any derricks or lifting gear.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">Smaller bulk
carriers have to be pre pared to discharge anywhere so will usually have
their own gear. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.208.3"
class="koboSpan">Technology to improve the handling of bulk cargoes had
been around since the end of the nineteenth century.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.208.4" class="koboSpan">For instance in
1888 grabs were mentioned for discharging grain in London as an
alternative to grain elevators and by 1935 there was an ore-discharging
plant in Rotterdam.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">The popular sizes
are:</span>

- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">10,000-25,000 dwt -
  these are some times referred to as "handysize" as they can trade to
  most ports in the world though 20,000 dwt is about the largest size
  that can use the St Lawrence Seaway.
  </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.210.2" class="koboSpan">There were
  some 77.4 million dwt in this class in 2000.</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">Handymax are
  35,000-50,000 dwt vessels. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.211.2"
  class="koboSpan">There were some 45.5 million dwt in this class in
  2000.</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">Panamax class, the
  largest size that can use the Panama Canal.
  </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.212.2" class="koboSpan">This is about
  65,000 dwt as the limiting lock width is just over 105 feet (32
  metres) and with</span>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0105" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_195"></span>[](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0105)

[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00105.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0105)

</div>

- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">a maximum LOA of 950
  feet (289.5 metres). </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.214.2"
  class="koboSpan">This class is important as much of the ore trade is
  through the Panama Canal. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.214.3"
  class="koboSpan">There were some 70.5 million dwt in this class
  in 2000. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.214.4" class="koboSpan">Note
  it is anticipated that the Panama Authorities will in the next decade
  or so increase the size of locks so the Panamax vessel will increase
  in size.</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">Capesize bulkers,
  which are 100,000-180,000 dwt and are used mainly for ore and coal on
  specific routes between well-equipped terminals.
  </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.215.2" class="koboSpan">There were
  some 86.6 million dwt in this class in 2000.</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">VLBC, bulkers
  greater than 180,000 dwt, of which most are trading between Australia
  & Japan. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.216.2" class="koboSpan">See
  </span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0105" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0105"><span
  id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.217.1" class="koboSpan">Tables 8</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
  class="koboSpan"> and
  </span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0107" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0107"><span
  id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
  class="koboSpan"> and
  </span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0075" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0075"><span
  id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 10</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
  class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">3.10 The oil tanker market</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">As can be seen from
</span>[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
5</span>](#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0069)<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan"> there has been a considerable correlation between
tanker supply and demand, though after the oil price rise in 1973 there
was, in the short term, a reduction in demand which left, for that
period, an excess of supply.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">Until around 1950 much
of the oil produced was refined at source and the refined products
transported to the consumer. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.232.2"
class="koboSpan">However, the shift in the political control of many oil
sources, such as in 1951 when the oil refineries of the Anglo-Iranian
Oil Co were nationalised, led to many countries, for strategic reasons,
refining the oil at destination instead.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.232.3" class="koboSpan">(Some argue
that the main reason for the change in the position for refining was the
rapid development of the chemical industry at this time.) Whatever the
reason, the early 1950s saw significant changes.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.232.4" class="koboSpan">For instance
between 1938–1956 oil consumption increased almost four times in western
Europe whereas refinery capacity increased almost nine times.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.232.5" class="koboSpan">One obvious
effect was a large increase in tanker cargoes
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_197"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">in the 1950s and 1960s, as the oil was now carried
twice, first as crude oil from source to refinery and then to distribute
the refined oil. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.233.2"
class="koboSpan">This development saw an increase in tanker size in
general, which led to the specific dedication of a class of tankers as
Crude Oil Carriers. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.233.3"
class="koboSpan">At the end of World War II, 16,000 dwt was considered a
large tanker, whereas by the end of the 1950s there were 100,000 dwt
tankers (the largest that could traverse the Suez Canal loaded).
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.233.4" class="koboSpan">By the end of
the 1960s when the Suez Canal was closed, the VLCC of 250,000 dwt became
a standard size and in 1972 the first of 500,000 dwt was
launched.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.234.1" class="koboSpan">At the same time there
was an increase in the number of tanker owners independent from the
major oil companies. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.234.2"
class="koboSpan">Before World War II the oil companies owned 70% of the
tanker fleet and the independents 30%.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">In the late 1970s
Saudi Arabia built two 25 million-ton oil refineries which started to
reverse the trend of the 1950s. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.235.2"
class="koboSpan">By the mid-1970s, the situation had reversed with the
oil companies owning only 30% of the tonnage, and since then this
percentage has been steadily decreasing.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.235.3" class="koboSpan">By 1998 the
independents owned 72%, oil companies 10% and governments 15%, with the
final small percentage being owned by traders.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.235.4" class="koboSpan">This growth of
independents has naturally meant a growth in tanker chartering.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.1" class="koboSpan">The above graph shows
considerable correlation between tanker supply and demand, though after
the oil price rise in 1973 there was in the short term a reduction in
demand, which left an excess of supply for that period.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.2" class="koboSpan">The steep rise
in oil prices in 1973 meant an increase in the power of OPEC
(Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries), with a consequent
reduction in the power of the large oil companies’ tanker fleets in
oil-trading and the growth of oil traders speculating in the market.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.3" class="koboSpan">These oil
traders then formed a large proportion of tanker charterers and so
affected tanker chartering in several ways.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.4" class="koboSpan">The traders
would buy a shipload of crude oil and try to sell the oil at a profit
during the voyage. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.5"
class="koboSpan">Thus much tanker chartering is “open-ended” i.e.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.6" class="koboSpan">the precise
destination is not stated when the fixture is made.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.7" class="koboSpan">This is one of
the advantages of using scale rates.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.8" class="koboSpan">In tanker
chartering, instead of quoting the freight in actual cash terms it is
quoted in scale values, which reflect the profitability in freight per
tonne-miles of the charter. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.9"
class="koboSpan">The Tanker Freight Scale was introduced by the British
and American authorities in World War II.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.10" class="koboSpan">As the scales
became popular the system was privatised and in 1962 the International
Tanker Nominal Freight Scale Association Ltd published INTASCALE.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.11" class="koboSpan">In 1969 the
Association revised the scale and called it Worldscale, again updated in
1989 as New World Scale. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.236.12"
class="koboSpan">See
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0108" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0108"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">Table 10</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">3.11 Type variations and the developments of tankers</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">Experiments had been
made in the 1920s to build combos – that is dry & wet bulkers but it was
not until the 1950s that the combination types were built in any numbers
and Universal Bulk Carriers (UBCs) were developed.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.240.2" class="koboSpan">However this
type had largely disappeared by the 1980s and were superseded by O/Os
(early 1950s) and OBOs (1965).</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">3.12 Beyond the market view?</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">So far, the freight
market has been outlined in terms of supply and demand.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.242.2" class="koboSpan">The traditional
view of the shipping market has focused upon these economic tenets.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.242.3" class="koboSpan">Shipping was a
slightly mystical business that took place in great waters!
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.242.4" class="koboSpan">Maritime
historian,
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_198"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan">Simon Daniels has summed up the pre-occupation with the
competitive freight market as a result of its development from the
Victorian era onwards when:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">“… Modest-sized cargo
ships plied the seas on shoestring budgets, scraping profits on any
cargoes they could secure, they developed principles of shipping upon
which so much the economics of shipping are
based.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0170" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0170"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">In one sense, the
shipping industry has been successful in meeting the market demands of
world trade. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.246.2" class="koboSpan">In
2008, the International Chamber of Shipping released statistics on the
quadrupling in the growth of global seaborne trade in the four decades
up to
2006.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0171" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0171"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>
<a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0076" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0076"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 11</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates the triumph of the industry in meeting the
demands of booming seaborne trade.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.249.2" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the
environmental performance measured by oil spillages from ships has shown
a marked improvement. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.249.3"
class="koboSpan">Innovations in tank cleaning, ballast water filtering
and segregation, fuel consumption and exhaust emissions have all been
achieved. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.249.4" class="koboSpan">The
amount of oil spilled from tankers has also shown a marked decline.
</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0077" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0077"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 12</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates how the tanker industry has cleaned up its
act with estimated spills falling from 172,000 tonnes in 1992 to 16,000
tonnes in 2007. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.251.2"
class="koboSpan">The problem is, however, that the environmental debate
is moving its targets at a faster rate than the shipping industry can
deliver; the reality is that the green integrity of shipping is only
guaranteed up to the next oil spill!
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.251.3" class="koboSpan">From this
position the need to achieve environmentally friendly shipping is
synonymous with the case for safe shipping.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.251.4" class="koboSpan">In addition to
oil tankers, accidents occurring to virtually any type of shipping are
likely to lead to pollution from either/and cargo and fuel oil bunkers.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.251.5" class="koboSpan">Making the
headlines in 2007 the collision of the container ship,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan">Cosco
Busan</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">
with the San Francisco Bay Bridge led to a spillage of 225,000 litres of
fuel and the resulting loss of an estimated 2,000
seabirds</span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0172" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0172"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Philippines worst ever oil spill disaster was
brought about by the grounding of the small coastal tanker,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan">Solar 1</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan"> (998 gt) in
2006.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0173" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0173"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan"> Environmentally sensitive mangrove swamps and
extensive fishing grounds over a 62km spread were seriously damaged by
spill of the vessel’s bunker
fuel.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0174" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0174"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.261.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is now proposed to consider how the green safety
issues are shaping an extra dimension to the market.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.262.2" class="koboSpan">The emphasis
will be upon the</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

class="koboSpan">ITOF</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">empirical analysis of
the industry’s safety-green performance within the context of an
intensifying environmental scrutiny.</span>
