### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.272.1" class="koboSpan">3.13 The greening of the market?</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.273.1" class="koboSpan">It is now impossible
to extricate the normal economic transactions of the freight market from
environmental standards. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.273.2"
class="koboSpan">The lessons of the Brent Spar oil rig disposal in the
mid-1990s demonstrated not only the sensitivity of marine environmental
issues, but also negative consumer reaction towards perceived abusers of
the
environment.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0175" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0175"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan"> In addition, the media view of shipping is
increasingly focusing on its environmental performance.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">Whilst it is evident
that improvements in green safety performance, have been achieved, it is
timely at this juncture to at least raise questions over the continued
commitment to attention to the environmental imperative, given the
global economic crisis post-2008 and its predictable impact on increased
cost conscious competition. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.276.2"
class="koboSpan">In 2008 shipping markets fell from their all-time peak
to a full-blown recession point by November.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.276.3" class="koboSpan">The eleven-fold
collapse of the Baltic Exchange Dry Index (BDI) from its 11,973 points
high to 891 points in this six month period was bound to raise questions
over the impact on shipping operations
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan">vis-à-vis
</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">the
environmental
imperative.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0176" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0176"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">3.14 From full speed ahead to lay-up!</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">The boom years in the
decade up to 2008 brought about an interesting paradox for many ship
operators. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.281.2" class="koboSpan">The
shortage of tonnage saw not only unprecedented increases in freight
rates but also the postponement of the scrapping of older tonnage.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.281.3" class="koboSpan">In October
2007, </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s
List</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan"> was
reporting: “No takers despite record scrap
offers.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0177" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0177"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan"> The reluctance of owners to scrap vessels when freight
rates and sale and purchase rates were at an all-time high had the
effect of retaining ageing tonnage in the world fleet.
</span>[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
12</span>](#Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0077)<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates the sudden surge in scrapping activity in
2008 as the market veered from boom to bust!</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">Up until 2008 the
industry was under pressure to deliver.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.288.2" class="koboSpan">Speed and haste
can be seen as symptoms of a booming market when ships are hard pressed
to meet tight</span>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0111" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00111.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 13: Demolition statistics 2007–2008" /></span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_200"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_cap_lbl0078"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
13:</span></span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan"> Demolition statistics 2007–2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan">Derived from Allied Shipbroking Reports in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s List</span></span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">schedules.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.295.2" class="koboSpan">The non-fatal
but potentially serious collision between two containers ships in the
Taiwan Straits in 2005 illustrated the pressures of deadlines.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.295.3" class="koboSpan">Neither the
34,617gt </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan">Washington
Senator</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.297.1" class="koboSpan">
or the 23,540gt
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan">Lykes Senator
</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">reduced
speed in the congested straits which at the time were experiencing
restricted visibility. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.299.2"
class="koboSpan">Both vessels maintained their passage speed of 17 and
18.5 knots, respectively, which was required in order to meet their
container terminal ETA’s in Hong Kong and
Vancouver.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0178" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0178"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.300.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.301.1" class="koboSpan">The epic salvage
exercise following the foundering of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">MSC
Napoli</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.303.1" class="koboSpan">
brings into question a number of operational and political/environmental
factors. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.303.2" class="koboSpan">On the
one hand an ageing container vessel being driven fairly
hard</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0179" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0179"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.304.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan"> in stormy weather conditions points to an industry in
a hurry (the vessel was reported to have departed Antwerp six days
late). </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.305.2" class="koboSpan">This was
during a period when freight rates were at a premium and tonnage
shortages pronounced. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.305.3"
class="koboSpan">Opinion in the insurance underwriting industry was to
conclude:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.306.1" class="koboSpan">“that commercial
pressures led it to sail in the way it did in these conditions, rather
than slowing down and taking appropriate
action.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0180" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0180"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.307.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">On the other hand, the
incident was met by a firm state response in terms of salvage tug
operations, beaching the vessel, securing fuel oil bunkers, and
ultimately securing the cargo and disposing of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.308.2" class="koboSpan">Maritime
opinion has averred that the mechanisms put in place in the UK following
the Donaldson Report were enacted most effectively in dealing with the
incident.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0181" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0181"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.309.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan"> Demonstrating political will and commitment to
affirmative action by responding both proactively and reactively in
maritime safety. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.310.2"
class="koboSpan">The resulting Anglo-French Coastguard shared provision
of Emergency Towing Vessels (ETVs) and the appointment of the Secretary
of State’s Representative for Maritime Salvage and Intervention (SOSREP)
were successfully engaged in averting a possible maritime catastrophe,
which would have been caused by the loss of the 2,500 containers and
over 1,000 tonnes of fuel oil, as well as jeopardising the lives of the
26 crew, who were all rescued safely by Royal Navy
helicopters.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0182" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0182"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">The whole incident
demonstrates the not only the commercial pressures on shipping
operations but also the renewed state resolve to minimalise
environmental disaster.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_201"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.313.1"
class="koboSpan">Given the extent of the market turbulence brought about
by the credit crunch, from mid-2008 onwards, it is evident that this
resolve will be tested in the future by operators seeking to survive at
the expense of the environment. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.313.2"
class="koboSpan">The following section discusses the balance between the
economics of market survival and the environmental interest.</span>

## <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.314.2" class="koboSpan">Costs, Competition and the Marine Environment</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">The juxtaposed
pressures of cost and quality, of economy and environment are all to be
found at work shaping the modern freight market.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.315.2" class="koboSpan">In a
competitive market costs will always be a key concern of operators.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.315.3" class="koboSpan">The
cost-quality dichotomy is obviously called into question given the state
of the shipping industry post-2008 market crash.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.315.4" class="koboSpan">The threat of
declining quality as a result of tough market conditions was highlighted
by Lord Donaldson, in his
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.316.1"
class="koboSpan">Safer Ships Cleaner
Seas</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">
report. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.317.2" class="koboSpan">Writing
in the early 1990s, Donaldson’s perspective was one of over capacity and
its impact on standards of safety and environmental probity in the
market. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.317.3" class="koboSpan">The
extent of sub-standard ships and their operators can be seen as a
function of over capacity, particularly in the low value dry cargo
trades. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.317.4" class="koboSpan">The
question now asked is whether these conditions could re-emerge in the
latest market crisis?</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">Three critical areas
of shipping safety are considered here: bulk carriers, the ageing tanker
problem as highlighted by the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.319.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
class="koboSpan"> disasters and short sea drybulk shipping.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.322.2" class="koboSpan">The dichotomy
between cost competition and the quality of operational standards is a
feature of modern freight markets.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.322.3" class="koboSpan">This is evident
in low value bulk markets such as scrap, aggregates and animal feeds.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.322.4" class="koboSpan">In such highly
competitive freight markets, costs are trimmed to the narrowest of
margins. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.322.5" class="koboSpan">The
enduring concerns over bulk carrier safety have been a feature of the
last three decades. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.322.6"
class="koboSpan">The 1980
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan">Derbyshire
</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.324.1" class="koboSpan">disaster
prompted concerns over bulk carrier safety.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.324.2" class="koboSpan">Foy’s study of
bulker losses in the 18-month period up until June 1987 revealed 11
founderings in the steel/scrap/iron ore
sectors.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0183" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0183"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.325.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan"> The loss of the capesize bulk carrier,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan">Alexandros
T</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan"> in
2006, indicates the continuing concern.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.328.2" class="koboSpan">The vessel
itself demonstrates the extensiveness of the global market.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.328.3" class="koboSpan">The Romanian
built, Greek managed, St. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.328.4"
class="koboSpan">Vincent & Grenadines flagged vessel, was engaged on a
charter for the carriage of 155,000 tonnes of iron ore between Brazil
and China. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.328.5"
class="koboSpan">Multinationalism was also reflected by the composition
of the 33 men crew (only five survived) – four Greek, 24 Filipino, four
Romanian, one
Ukrainian.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0184" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0184"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.329.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan"> Given that the vessel suffered a catastrophic hull
structure failure, following wave damage, it is pertinent to note that
Port State Control (PSC) inspectors had detained the vessel in 2003 with
fracture deficiencies noted in six of the vessel’s nine
holds.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0185" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0185"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.331.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.332.1"
class="koboSpan"> Although no major pollution was reported following the
break-up of the bulker 285 nm off Port Elizabeth, the potential for
bunker oil spillage is latent in any incident.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.332.2" class="koboSpan">Capesize
bulkers, for example, can carry in excess of 3,500 tones of heavy fuel
oil and 400 tonnes of marine diesel.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">By coincidence, the
Nautical Institute campaign on bulk carrier safety was released on the
day that news of the loss of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.334.1"
class="koboSpan">Alexandros
T</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan"> was
announced.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0186" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0186"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.336.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.337.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Nautical Institute highlighted the dilemmas facing
masters who find themselves facing unacceptable commercial pressures
when vessel hulls are subject to un-safe loading rates at certain
terminals. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.337.2" class="koboSpan">The
loading rate of 16,000 tonnes per hour places considerable stress on the
vessel hulls, but the faster the loading, the lower the cost of hire; so
it was apparent that some “heavy handed” charterers were influencing
their market power to obtain a rapid port
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_202"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan">turn-round time.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.338.2" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
masters faced charterers questioning over professional decision making
on the ship’s passage. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.338.3"
class="koboSpan">Charterers were more interested in expediting a fast
passage rather than allowing the master to exercise discretion in safe
passage planning and management. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.338.4"
class="koboSpan">Bulk carrier expert, Captain Cooper of the Nautical
Institute, has expressed his concern: “… that these attitudes and this
behaviour should still prevail in this supposedly enlightened and
heavily regulated world we operate
in.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0187" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0187"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.340.1" class="koboSpan">By the new millennium
attention has increasingly focused upon tankers.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.340.2" class="koboSpan">The shock of
the 1999 </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan"> break up and sinking had implications for the industry
stretching into the new decade. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.342.2"
class="koboSpan">Ostensibly, the tanker on passage between Dunkerque and
Livorno with 25,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil was a tangible example of
the coastal highway at work, a green alternative to road haulage – the
25,000 tonnes of fuel oil represents the equivalent more than 800 road
tanker journeys across the Alps. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.342.3"
class="koboSpan">However, the combination of gale force weather
conditions and an ageing, metal corroded, vessel was to prove an
environmental disaster for the French coastline and its ecology.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.342.4" class="koboSpan">It has been
estimated that compensation payments will be in the region of
€300m.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0188" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0188"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.344.1"
class="koboSpan"> For the chartering oil major, Total-Elf, the result
was not only heavy financial penalties but also the loss of corporate
reputation. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.344.2"
class="koboSpan">However, the immediate aftermath of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.345.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.346.1"
class="koboSpan"> and similar tanker disasters has led to more stringent
state intervention in the market.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.346.2" class="koboSpan">It was deemed
by French court that Total had not carried out sufficient vetting of the
ageing vessel in order to ensure its suitability.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.346.3" class="koboSpan">In June 2008,
Total was ordered to pay \$298.62m in
compensation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0189" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0189"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.347.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">Closely following the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.349.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan"> oil pollution disaster (1999), the (2002) break-up of
the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.351.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan"> off the coast of Galicia raised many questions over
the cost-quality dichotomy in tanker
chartering.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0190" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0190"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.353.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan"> The age and single-hull status of both tankers became
a factor in the post-disaster analysis.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.354.2" class="koboSpan">Evidence from
the market shows that the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.355.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan"> was a very clear exposition of globalisation at the
lower end of the
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0191" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0191"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan"> A mixture of Greek owners, Liberian (nameplate)
managers, Bahamas flag, London-Greek shipbrokers and Russian-Swiss oil
traders all were traced to the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.358.2" class="koboSpan">Underpinning
the economics of this global network of connections is the reality that
the vessels was chartered at some \$5,000 per day below the normal rate
attainable for that particular moment in time.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.358.3" class="koboSpan">It was to
become evident that the charterers were intent on seeking out ageing,
single-hull tonnage in order to undercut the market rate.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.358.4" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan"> was fixed at \$13,000 per day when it was estimated by
Clarkson’s that \$18,000 would have been asked for a more modern
tanker.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0192" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0192"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.361.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.362.1" class="koboSpan">The political outcome
of the disaster was marked by the EU in March 2009 with the Third Safety
Package (“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan"> 3
Package”),</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0193" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0193"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan"> the key elements of which are a strengthening of
regulation in:</span>

- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.367.1" class="koboSpan">Flag state
  responsibilities;</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.368.1" class="koboSpan">Auditing
  classification societies;</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.369.1" class="koboSpan">Port state
  control;</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.370.1" class="koboSpan">Vessel traffic
  monitoring;</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.371.1" class="koboSpan">Accident
  investigation;</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.372.1" class="koboSpan">Liability and
  compensation of passengers; and</span>
- <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.373.1" class="koboSpan">Insurance of
  shipowners for maritime claims.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.374.1" class="koboSpan">The North European
short sea dry-bulk trades are another example of where operational
standards are questionable. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.374.2"
class="koboSpan">Many vessels in these trades are operated under flags
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_203"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.375.1"
class="koboSpan">of convenience, having minimal crews and are driven
hard in order to remain profitable.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.375.2" class="koboSpan">Short sea
freight rates are forced down by three powerful factors:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.376.1" class="koboSpan">the extent of the
    competition from many small operators of chartered tonnage;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.377.1" class="koboSpan">the alternatives
    of road and rail haulage to coastal/short sea shipping;</span>
3.  <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.378.1" class="koboSpan">the buying
    (oligopsony) power of the large cargo generators in grain, steel,
    aggregates and also (in the feeder trades) containers.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.379.1" class="koboSpan">The problem was
recently highlighted by the grounding of the 2,446 gt vessel,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.380.1"
class="koboSpan">Antari </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.381.1"
class="koboSpan">(Larne,
2008).</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0194" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0194"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.382.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan"> This was one of a series of fatigue-related incidents
that have beset the short sea dry-cargo sector in British waters.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.383.2" class="koboSpan">These include
constructive total losses of the container feeder ship,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.384.1"
class="koboSpan">Cita</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.385.1"
class="koboSpan"> (Scilly Isles,
1997),</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0195" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0195"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.386.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.387.1"
class="koboSpan"> the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan">RMS
Mulheim</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.389.1" class="koboSpan">
(Lands End,
2003)</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0196" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0196"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.390.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the groundings of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.392.1"
class="koboSpan">Coastal
Bay</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.393.1" class="koboSpan">
(Isle of Anglesey,
2000),</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0197" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0197"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.394.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.395.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.396.1"
class="koboSpan">Jackie
Moon</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.397.1" class="koboSpan">
(Firth of Clyde,
2004).</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0198" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0198"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.398.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.399.1"
class="koboSpan"> In these instances the fatigue factor can be seen as
tangible, causal, factors in vessel grounding incidents.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.400.1" class="koboSpan">The Marine Accident
Investigation Branch (MAIB)
report</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0199" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0199"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.401.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.402.1"
class="koboSpan"> into the grounding of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan">Antari</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan"> revealed the gruelling schedule that such coastal
vessels are required to adhere to.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.404.2" class="koboSpan">The report
found that the vessel had called at 21 ports in the eight weeks prior to
the grounding. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.404.3"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore it was found that the mixture of fatigue,
absence of a lookout (in darkness) and a solitary watchkeeper was
prominent in some 23 similar incidents, observed between, 1994 and 2003.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.404.4" class="koboSpan">A sample of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.405.1"
class="koboSpan">Antari’s</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.406.1"
class="koboSpan"> port calls is included
in</span><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0112" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0112"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.407.1" class="koboSpan"> Table 11</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.408.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.409.1" class="koboSpan">The MAIB has
established that the intensive watchkeeping demands on board the seven
man crewed </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan">Antari</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.411.1"
class="koboSpan"> necessitated by the availability of just two certified
officers was a major causal factor in the grounding:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.412.1" class="koboSpan">“This intensive
pattern, typical of the short sea shipping trade, is likely to
contribute to the cumulative fatigue levels of individuals working 6
hours on/6 hours off, the</span>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0112" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.413.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00112.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0112)

</div>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_204"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.414.1"
class="koboSpan">longer they spend on board, and in this case probably
prevented the Chief Officer from obtaining adequate
rest.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0200" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0200"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.415.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.1" class="koboSpan">One way of reducing
operational costs, introduced in the early 1990s, was the One Man Bridge
Operation (OMBO). </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.2"
class="koboSpan">International Regulations stipulate that in the hours
of darkness and also poor daytime visibility, two watchkeepers will
carry out bridge duties. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.3"
class="koboSpan">Primarily, this is to limit the risk of watchkeepers
falling asleep and to provide extra lookout capabilities – a
particularly welcome support in confined and congested waters.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.4" class="koboSpan">The OMBO system
was devised as a labour saving device in that it facilitated one
watchkeeper operation. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.5"
class="koboSpan">Integral to the system is the anti-sleep alarm which
ensures that the watchkeeper does not fall asleep.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.6" class="koboSpan">The need to
respond to the alarm at frequent intervals, however, may be seen as an
irksome task by the irritated officer.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.7" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately
this has led to irresponsible behaviour with officers switching off the
system. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.8"
class="koboSpan">Invariably this results in sleeping watchkeepers and
ensuing near misses, collisions and groundings.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.416.9" class="koboSpan">The fate of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.417.1"
class="koboSpan">Cita </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.418.1"
class="koboSpan">was sealed when the Chief Officer switched off the
system on a voyage between Southampton and Belfast.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.418.2" class="koboSpan">The inevitable
happened, the Chief Officer fell asleep, and the vessel grounded on St
Mary’s Isle (Scilly Isles) at full
speed.</span><sup>[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.419.1"
class="koboSpan">24</span>](#Ch07.xhtml_fn0183)</sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.420.1"
class="koboSpan"> An identical case to the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.421.1"
class="koboSpan">Cita</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.422.1"
class="koboSpan"> was that of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.423.1"
class="koboSpan">Coastal
Bay</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.424.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.424.2" class="koboSpan">It was
established that the vessel was operated by just two watchkeeping
officers, with the Master and the Chief Officer working a fatiguing
rotating watch-on, watch-off, system.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.425.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s
List’s</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.426.1" class="koboSpan">
editorial comment, “No mystery of the sea,” argued that here was an
accident waiting to
happen!</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0201" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0201"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.427.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.428.1" class="koboSpan">These cases not only
demonstrate the economic pressures placed upon operators and their crews
but also the growing determination of the authorities to rectify the
imbalance between cost and quality operations.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.429.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Maritime safety and public concern</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.430.1" class="koboSpan">Major environmental
advances have occurred in the international maritime regime in recent
decades. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.430.2" class="koboSpan">These
include, the prevention of waste dumping waste dumping into the sea, the
outlawing of oil tank slops dumping, double hull regulations for oil
tankers, segregated ballast water systems and toxic anti-fouling hull
protection chemicals. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.430.3"
class="koboSpan">Such factors have become an essential part of the
freight market as charterers, owners and operators struggle to come to
terms with the new environmental imperative.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.430.4" class="koboSpan">The imposition
of global standards via the IMO undoubtedly leads to an increase in the
private costs of shipping. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.430.5"
class="koboSpan">This is at odds with the traditional and enduring
concept of “The Freedom of the Seas”, which has been held as an
essential component of the free market in
shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0202" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0202"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.431.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.432.1" class="koboSpan">The resilience of this
concept is clearly demonstrated by the battles to regulate the safe
passage of shipping in one of the world’s busiest seaways, the Dover
Straits. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.432.2" class="koboSpan">From
the 1880s onwards calls for increased regulation have been resisted by
shipowners and their principals on the grounds that there was a need to
retain a free
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0203" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0203"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.433.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.434.1"
class="koboSpan"> The market failure – loss of life, pollution, vessel
damage, trade disruption – resulting from shipping’s failure to manage
its own safety in such critical conditions was to prove untenable.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.434.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
public concern over the threat to coastlines has increasingly been in
evidence.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.435.1" class="koboSpan">The upsurge in vessel
traffic, in conjunction with increases in vessel size, began to manifest
as causes of rising trends in serious English Channel collisions and
groundings in the 1960s and 1970s.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.435.2" class="koboSpan">Things came
very much to a head in 1971 with a series of collisions and the
explosion of the tanker,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.436.1"
class="koboSpan">Texaco
Caribbean.</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.437.1"
class="koboSpan"> In total 51 lives were lost
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_205"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.438.1"
class="koboSpan">and chronic oil pollution was experienced on the
Channel’s
shoreline.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0204" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0204"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.439.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.440.1"
class="koboSpan"> The resulting Vessel Traffic Management Scheme (VTS)
demonstrated state traffic management in a hitherto free-for-all Channel
passage.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.441.1" class="koboSpan">Increasingly, coastal
management has intensified around the world and some surprising outcomes
have been experienced. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.441.2"
class="koboSpan">The circumstances leading to the loss of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.442.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.443.1"
class="koboSpan"> in 2002 reveal a defensive mood by the Spanish
authorities to a stricken vessel.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.443.2" class="koboSpan">Despite the
efforts of the salvors to tow the stricken tanker to a safe-haven, the
Spanish authorities ordered the tug and tow to head away from the coast.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.443.3" class="koboSpan">Much to the
chagrin of the salvors, the prospects of gaining a sheltered safe-haven,
where emergency repairs could be undertaken, were effectively
denied.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0205" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0205"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.444.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.445.1" class="koboSpan">As a sequel to the
resulting loss of the vessel and its 77,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil,
the master of the tanker found himself detained in a Spanish prison.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.445.2" class="koboSpan">As with a
number of oil pollution cases around the world since, including the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.446.1"
class="koboSpan">Tasman
Spirit</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.447.1" class="koboSpan">
(2003), and the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.448.1"
class="koboSpan">Hebei
Spirit</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.449.1" class="koboSpan">
(2007) shipcrews have found themselves to be subject to criminal
proceedings following
accidents.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0206" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0206"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.450.1" class="koboSpan">47</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.451.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 The media and the market</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.452.1" class="koboSpan">Partly the increased
attention to environment is a result of the media exposure that shipping
now finds itself exposed to, particularly when marine disaster is
located in the high profile waters of developed countries.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.452.2" class="koboSpan">Oil spills from
such unfortunate tankers as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.453.1"
class="koboSpan">Exxon Valdez, Aegean Empress, Braer, Sea Empress,
Erika, and Prestige </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.454.1"
class="koboSpan">have made dramatic headlines in the media creating an
impression of a reckless “rust bucket” shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.454.2" class="koboSpan">The
environmental disaster following the sinking of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.455.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.456.1"
class="koboSpan"> along the French coastline was reported by the
headline: “300,000 Seabirds dead.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.456.2" class="koboSpan">Only now can
Europe count the cost of Sea of
Filth.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0207" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0207"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.457.1" class="koboSpan">48</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.458.1"
class="koboSpan"> The break up of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.459.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.460.1"
class="koboSpan"> off the Spanish coast focused attention on the state
of the world’s ageing tanker fleet and its off-shore management.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.461.1"
class="koboSpan">The</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.462.1"
class="koboSpan">Independent</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.463.1"
class="koboSpan"> article, “A saga of single hulls, double standards and
too many flags of
convenience”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0208" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0208"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.464.1" class="koboSpan">49</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.465.1"
class="koboSpan"> directed criticism at a globally fragmented,
substandard industry that was more interested in cost cutting than
maintaining safe and environmentally acceptable standards of
operation.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.466.1" class="koboSpan">The loss of the
automobile carrier,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.467.1"
class="koboSpan">Tricolor,</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.468.1"
class="koboSpan"> in 2002 illustrates attention to maritime safety in
terms of financial value. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.468.2"
class="koboSpan">Abandoning the rapidly sinking vessel placed great
demands on the seamanship of the crew who managing to evacuate the
doomed vessel in 45 minutes. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.468.3"
class="koboSpan">Considering that this occurred at 02:45hrs on a cold
December morning on the approaches to the Dover Straits, it was to
become apparent that a feat of great skill and courage was achieved –
all 23 crew members were accounted for safely.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.468.4" class="koboSpan">The media,
however, demonstrated a differing view of the events, with the BBC
headline reporting that, “£30m cargo lost as ship
sinks”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0209" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0209"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.469.1" class="koboSpan">50</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.470.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrating the portrayal of maritime disaster in
monetary rather than humanistic terms.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.471.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 The management of safety</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.472.1" class="koboSpan">The question over
shipping’s environmental performance is inextricably linked with
quality. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.472.2"
class="koboSpan">Traditionally, the prevailing “blame culture” in
shipping deflected criticism towards captains and their crews.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.472.3" class="koboSpan">Three leading
accident cases, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.473.1"
class="koboSpan">Lady
Gwendolen</span></span><span class="bold"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.474.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span></span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.475.1"
class="koboSpan"> the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.476.1"
class="koboSpan">Herald of Free
Enterprise</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.477.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.478.1"
class="koboSpan">Exxon
Valdez</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.479.1" class="koboSpan">
have identified corporate shortcomings.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.479.2" class="koboSpan">The evolving
principle has become that the manner in which the vessel is maintained
and operated is a prime function of management.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_206"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.480.1"
class="koboSpan">This principle was established in a leading Admiralty
case involving the management of coastal shipping operations.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.480.2" class="koboSpan">Case law was
provided by the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.481.1"
class="koboSpan">Lady
Gwendolen</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.482.1"
class="koboSpan"> in
1965.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0210" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0210"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.483.1" class="koboSpan">51</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.484.1"
class="koboSpan"> The vessel was directly owned by the Dublin brewer,
Arthur Guinness, and was engaged on the important Dublin-Manchester
stout beer trade. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.484.2"
class="koboSpan">In order to keep to the schedule the master, Captain
Meredith, adopted the practice of navigating at full speed, relying on
radar observation, even in the frequently foggy conditions of the Irish
Sea and River Mersey. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.484.3"
class="koboSpan">Despite Guinness’ petition to limit their liability, as
(they claimed) the collision was the fault of Captain
Meredith</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0211" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0211"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.485.1" class="koboSpan">52</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.486.1"
class="koboSpan"> the brewers were deemed negligent in not adequately
monitoring the way the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.487.1"
class="koboSpan">Lady
Gwendolen</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.488.1"
class="koboSpan"> was operated. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.488.2"
class="koboSpan">Lord Justice Sellers summarised:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.489.1" class="koboSpan">“A primary concern of
a shipowner must be the safety of life at sea.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.489.2" class="koboSpan">That involves a
seaworthy ship, properly manned but also requires safe navigation.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.489.3" class="koboSpan">Excessive speed
in fog is a grave breach of duty, and shipowners should use all their
influence to prevent
it.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0212" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0212"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.490.1" class="koboSpan">53</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.491.1" class="koboSpan">Although there was no
evidence to suggest that the master was under pressure from the owners
to maintain schedules in poor weather conditions, the case does
illustrate the balance between shipping efficiency and operational
safety.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.492.1" class="koboSpan">A more serious
accident which did bring condemnation of the shoreside management was
that of the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.493.1"
class="koboSpan">Herald of Free
Enterprise</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.494.1"
class="koboSpan"> disaster in 1987, which resulted in the loss of the
ro-pax ferry in Zeebrugge Harbour with 189 passengers and crew.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.494.2" class="koboSpan">Following the
lengthy investigation into the disaster, management systems failures
were identified as a principal cause.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.494.3" class="koboSpan">The vessel
attempted to leave Zeebrugge without securing her bow doors.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.494.4" class="koboSpan">The resulting
water ingress (from the bow wave) as the vessel picked up speed quickly
led to the vessel entering into an irretrievable list
situation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0213" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0213"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.495.1" class="koboSpan">54</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.496.1"
class="koboSpan"> Such cases emphasise the duties of the shipowner, the
ship manager and the charterer. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.496.2"
class="koboSpan">The UK Department of Transport investigation into the
tragedy was to charge that “from top to bottom the body corporate was
infected with the disease of
sloppiness”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0214" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0214"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.497.1" class="koboSpan">55</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.498.1"
class="koboSpan"> Increasingly this responsibility is becoming a feature
of the freight market. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.498.2"
class="koboSpan">The aftermath of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.499.1"
class="koboSpan">Exxon
Valdez</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.500.1" class="koboSpan">
oil pollution disaster in 1989 and the resulting US Oil Pollution Act
(OPA 90) intensified the trend towards corporate
liability.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0215" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0215"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.501.1" class="koboSpan">56</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.502.1"
class="koboSpan"> The massive public outcry over the disaster has been
identified by the Ethical Corporation as marking the birth pangs of
corporate responsibility.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.503.1" class="koboSpan">Increasingly the
vicarious liability for maritime accidents is encompassing the charterer
as well as the operator. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.503.2"
class="koboSpan">Following the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.504.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.505.1"
class="koboSpan"> disaster, it has now become evident that chartering
companies, particularly the oil majors, will be targeted as a deterrent
to sub-standard operations. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.505.2"
class="koboSpan">In Europe the environmental sensitivity of large
stretches of coastline has focused attention on qualitative factors
including the charterers vetting of ships.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.505.3" class="koboSpan">Safety
standards such as ISO 9000 and the International Safety Management (ISM)
Code have placed emphasis on the management systems of not only the
operators but also the charterers.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.506.1" class="koboSpan">The reality of
shipping supply and demand is that in many markets, many shipowners
compete for the business of much fewer buyers of shipping services, the
shippers. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.506.2" class="koboSpan">The
role of the charterer is crucial to improving standards of ships in this
oligopsonistic market which bestows market power on the buyer of
shipping services. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.506.3"
class="koboSpan">Leading UK short sea operator, Michael Everard, has
argued that “Charterers should take responsibility for the ships they
charter”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0216" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0216"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.507.1" class="koboSpan">57</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_207"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.508.1"
class="koboSpan">Tanker design and operation has been held up to a great
deal of scrutiny following well publicised disasters In addition to the
potential for devastating large volume spills of crude and black oils,
there is also the problem the release of volatile organic compounds into
the atmosphere during loading operations.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.508.2" class="koboSpan">Partly this can
be seen as a result of the relocation of the oil extraction regions from
the Persian Gulf to the environmentally (thus politically) sensitive US
(Alaska) and Europe (North Sea) fields.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.508.3" class="koboSpan">This
sensitivity places a high premium on safety standards in the oil market,
as shuttle tankers replace long-haul VLCC and ULCC operations.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.509.1" class="koboSpan">The evidence on double
hull shuttle tankers in the Russian/North Sea oil trades points to a big
risk reduction compared to single hull tankers.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.509.2" class="koboSpan">A 1998
study</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0217" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0217"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.510.1" class="koboSpan">58</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.511.1"
class="koboSpan"> by US oil offshore oil specialist, Amerada Hess, in
conjunction with Lloyd’s Register, has concluded shuttle tanker were
more at risk than deepsea trading tankers because of their frequent port
calls and passages through confined waters, including the loading
location zones.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.512.1" class="koboSpan">At the turn of the
millennium much concern was expressed by Baltic and North Sea states
over the potential for an oil spill disaster given the emergence of
Russian oil flows. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.512.2"
class="koboSpan">Clearly an
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.513.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span class="bold"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.514.1"
class="koboSpan">”</span></span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.515.1"
class="koboSpan"> or a
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.516.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span class="bold"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.517.1"
class="koboSpan">”</span></span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.518.1"
class="koboSpan"> in the Baltic Danish Belt area would have horrendous
environmental implications. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.518.2"
class="koboSpan">The paradox of Russia gaining a competitive foothold in
global oil trades was that of securing low-cost sea transport whilst
guaranteeing high standards of environmental probity.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.518.3" class="koboSpan">The question
was which end of the cost–quality pendulum would the trade
target?</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.519.1" class="koboSpan">By the mid millennium,
perhaps as a positive response to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.520.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.521.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.522.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span class="bold"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.523.1"
class="koboSpan">, </span></span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.524.1"
class="koboSpan">there was tangible evidence that quality would prevail.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.524.2" class="koboSpan">Tanker safety
in the Russian oil trades was boosted in 2006 when the Swedish operator,
Stena Bulk, commissioned the 117,000dwt,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.525.1"
class="koboSpan">Stena
Arctica</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.526.1" class="koboSpan">
under the high cost Swedish flag.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.526.2" class="koboSpan">Attention to
high standards, including ice-strengthened vessels, is seen as an
imperative by
Stena.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0218" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0218"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.527.1" class="koboSpan">59</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.528.1"
class="koboSpan"> With at least an extra 10% of steel being required for
ice strengthening and a main engine system that develops 85% more power
than the average AFRAMAX
tanker,</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0219" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0219"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.529.1" class="koboSpan">60</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.530.1"
class="koboSpan"> these vessels do not belong in the lower quadrants of
the cost curve!</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.531.1" class="koboSpan">The commitment of the
vessel to the Baltic-UK/Continent oil supply chain marks as the first in
a series of 10–15 ice strengthened tankers, resulting from a
Russian-Swedish alliance. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.531.2"
class="koboSpan">The partnership with provides a synergy between Stena
Bulk’s tanker expertise with two Russian businesses, tanker operators,
Sovcomflot and oil logistics specialist,
Progetra.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0220" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0220"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.532.1" class="koboSpan">61</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.533.1"
class="koboSpan"> Such evidence points to adherence to quality in a
demanding, high risk market.</span>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.534.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 The green performance of shipping?</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.535.1" class="koboSpan">However, the world’s
growing concern over environmental factors has emphasised the quality of
shipping performance in such terms as sea and air pollution.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.535.2" class="koboSpan">The issues of
engine exhaust emission and waste treatment are two key tests of the
commitment of shipping operators to the green imperative.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.535.3" class="koboSpan">This concern
can be noted in the regulatory regime.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.535.4" class="koboSpan">For example,
regulations initiating from MARPOL on ballast water contamination can be
seen as a result of concern over the potentially damaging impact of
contaminated water in environmentally sensitive areas.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.535.5" class="koboSpan">The increased
forces towards quality shipping have become manifest in the new
millennium; however these forces will increasingly challenged by the
need to survive economically.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.536.1" class="koboSpan">An increasing area of
contemporary media focus has been on the extent of shipping‘s
contribution to greenhouse gas emissions.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.536.2" class="koboSpan">Whilst is
evident that in terms of tonne-miles
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_208"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.537.1"
class="koboSpan">shipping is by far the lowest contributor, given the
reality that shipping is the prime mover of world trade tonnages it is
tautological that its total emissions will outstrip other modes.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.537.2" class="koboSpan">It is evident
that shipping is increasingly coming under environmental scrutiny and is
becoming seen along with road haulage and air freight as a major
contributor to global warming gas emissions.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.537.3" class="koboSpan">In 2007, this
was made evident in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.538.1"
class="koboSpan">The
Guardian</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.539.1" class="koboSpan">
headline, “And you thought air travel was bad for the
climate.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0221" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0221"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.540.1" class="koboSpan">62</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.541.1"
class="koboSpan"> The tone of
newspaper’</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.542.1"
class="koboSpan">s </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.543.1"
class="koboSpan">article (plus similar criticisms) has led to a
defensive stance by the shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.543.2" class="koboSpan">The response of
the UK Chamber of Shipping (was to remind the public that shipping not
only carries 90% of world trade and, moreover, generated, “… less
greenhouse gases per tonne mile than any other form of transportation
…”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0222" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0222"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.544.1" class="koboSpan">63</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.545.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is becoming obvious that emissions scrutiny will
continue to intensify into the first decade of the millennium.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.545.2" class="koboSpan">The polemical
discussions surrounding exhaust emissions can be welcomed in that it can
only serve to sharpen the resolve of the shipping industry to
consistently improve its green performance.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.545.3" class="koboSpan">The article
maintains that global shipping is responsible for some 4.5% of total
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.546.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.547.1"
class="koboSpan"> emissions, as opposed to aviation’s 2%.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.547.2" class="koboSpan">UK Green Party
MEP, Caroline Lucas, has added to the criticism that shipping has failed
to improve its environmental performance and, “… has got away with doing
nothing and maintained a clean image which it does not
deserve”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0223" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0223"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.548.1" class="koboSpan">64</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.549.1"
class="koboSpan"> The reverberations of the article were felt across
Europe. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.549.2" class="koboSpan">In
Italy, national truck owner’s representative, Maurizio Longo, called for
a re-assessment of the environmental status of haulage
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.550.1"
class="koboSpan">vis-à-vis</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.551.1"
class="koboSpan"> shipping on the basis of an almost emissions parity
between the road and water mode:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.552.1" class="koboSpan">“Heavy goods vehicles
in Italy, for instance, produce 162,000 tonnes of nitrogen oxide a year,
while maritime traffic produces 113,000 tonnes
…”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0224" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0224"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.553.1" class="koboSpan">65</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.554.1" class="koboSpan">European Commission
(EC) concerns have focused on the impact of air pollution from ship
exhausts, in particular where heavy concentrations of shipping occurs.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.554.2" class="koboSpan">Local
communities in port areas and coastal residential spread are at the
highest levels of threat. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.554.3"
class="koboSpan">The Norwegian Marine Technology Research Institute A/S
has found evidence of high concentrates of air pollution on major
traffic flows – the Baltic, North Sea, English Channel, and Black
Sea.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0225" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0225"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.555.1" class="koboSpan">66</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.556.1"
class="koboSpan"> The global convention on marine pollution, Marpol
Annex VI, places a sulphur cap of 1.5% for ships passing through
selected Sulphur Emission Control Areas (SECA), such as the English
Channel, North Sea and Baltic territorial waters and, moreover, a cap of
0.2% (reducing to 0.1% in 2010) in EU port areas.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.556.2" class="koboSpan">From May 2006
it was incumbent on vessels \>400gt to carry an International Air
Pollution Prevention Certificate (IAPP) accompanied by an Engine
International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate
(EIAPP).</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0226" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0226"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.557.1" class="koboSpan">67</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.558.1" class="koboSpan">The English
Channel-North Sea SECA actually stretches from the Western Approaches to
Mongstad in Norway and came into force in Autumn 2007.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.558.2" class="koboSpan">The Baltic Sea
SECA came into force in May 2006.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.558.3" class="koboSpan">It is seen as
protective measure given the heavy volumes of maritime traffic in the
region; particularly as the Scandinavian nations have been particularly
vulnerable to acid rain pollution.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.558.4" class="koboSpan">The
cross-industry Shipping Emission Abatement & Trading (SEAT) committee
has identified the extent of the problem in Europe.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.558.5" class="koboSpan">At the May 2006
International Bunker Conference in Gothenburg, SEAT Secretary General
Cor Nobel outlined the challenge facing shipping given that 14% of
global NO</span><sub><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.559.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.560.1"
class="koboSpan"> and 6.5% of
SO</span><sub><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.561.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.562.1"
class="koboSpan"> came from marine-related
activities.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0227" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0227"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.563.1" class="koboSpan">68</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.564.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Conference heard that emissions pollution from
ships travelled between 400 and 1,200km inland.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.564.2" class="koboSpan">The
implications for Europe were made clear when it was added that some 70%
of
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_209"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.565.1"
class="koboSpan">shipping activity took place within 400km of land!
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.565.2" class="koboSpan">European
Commission (EC) concerns have focused on the impact of air pollution
from ships’ exhausts, in particular where heavy concentrations of
shipping affected local communities in port city and areas of coastal
residential spread.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.566.1" class="koboSpan">The impact of
emissions regulation on the market is one of rising costs.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.566.2" class="koboSpan">The
International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) has expressed concern
over the impact on voyage costs. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.566.3"
class="koboSpan">In 2002, the IBIA outlined the example of a voyage from
Gothenburg to Belfast which under proposed EC rules would require a
continuous use of 0.2 sulphur fuel as it consisted of a 100% EC voyage.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.566.4" class="koboSpan">The IBIA
estimated that vessels bunkering in European waters could face an
additional \$20 per tonne
premium.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0228" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0228"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.567.1" class="koboSpan">69</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.568.1"
class="koboSpan"> The question facing shipowners and operators is
whether such increased cost can be passed onto the shipper, ultimately
the consumer. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.568.2"
class="koboSpan">With IMO targets reducing sulphur content globally down
to 0.5% by 2020 it follows that the era of low cost fuel is drawing to a
close. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.568.3" class="koboSpan">Such
lower sulphur content fuel has the purity and, ergo, cost profile of
diesel, leading up to a doubling of
costs.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0229" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0229"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.569.1" class="koboSpan">70</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.570.1"
class="koboSpan"> Given the correlation between purer fuel oil and
higher fuel prices it follows that freight rates will need to be higher
in these areas. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.570.2"
class="koboSpan">Again it can be seen how environmental factors are
increasingly impacting on freight markets.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.571.1" class="koboSpan">The emphasis upon
green performance places stringent responsibilities on ship operators.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.571.2" class="koboSpan">The list of
waste disposal prohibited from the ship includes oil and sludge from
both bilges and cargo, garbage and extends to exhaust emissions and
ballast
water.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0230" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0230"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.572.1" class="koboSpan">71</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.573.1" class="koboSpan">Cultural change in the
disposal of waste has occurred in recent decades.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.573.2" class="koboSpan">The clean seas
strategy of the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has led to an
enhanced ethical attitude towards waste.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.573.3" class="koboSpan">The Nautical
Institute Secretary in 2000, Julian Parker, succinctly summarised the
previous “over the wall” culture: “… all the main trade routes could be
identified by from beer cans on the bottom of the
ocean”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0231" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0231"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.574.1" class="koboSpan">72</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.575.1"
class="koboSpan"> In European waters the problem of tank washing and its
over-side disposal was evident from coastline pollution.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.575.2" class="koboSpan">Main tanker
routes generated oil trails with a disastrous impact on the coastline
environment. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.575.3"
class="koboSpan">Partly the change in behaviour has been as a result of
the encouragement of such proactive strategies such as the “Green
Award”. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.575.4" class="koboSpan">Tanker
terminals such as Sullom Voe and Rotterdam make the award to vessels
which attain high environmental standards and entitles the owners to
rebates on port dues.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.576.1" class="koboSpan">Up until the impact of
environmental concern and sensitivity of the late twentieth century much
of the vessel’s waste went “over the wall” (into the sea).
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.576.2" class="koboSpan">This would
include oily rags, empty oil drums, beer and food cans and food waste.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.576.3" class="koboSpan">Concerns over
the amount of carbon soaked and plastic based wastes finding their way
into the ocean from ships led to a 1995 amendment of the International
Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (Marpol 73/78).
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.576.4" class="koboSpan">This stipulates
that all vessels over 400gt are required to have a garbage management
plan and record book. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.576.5"
class="koboSpan">A 2000 study into the efficiency of waste disposal at
sea by Captain Patraiko of the Nautical Institute has found that a
contrasting pattern of how the plans were
initiated.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0232" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0232"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.577.1" class="koboSpan">73</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.578.1"
class="koboSpan"> Clearly, the evidence of the study found that advances
were being made in the education of crews and the development of a waste
management culture. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.578.2"
class="koboSpan">Examples of waste segregation was found in 70% vessels
surveyed. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.578.3" class="koboSpan">Also,
the practice of incinerating wastes such as plastic and oil was well
advanced.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.579.1" class="koboSpan">A problem area
identified was that poor waste reception facilities in some ports.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.579.2" class="koboSpan">Examples of
positive crew attitudes to waste recycling being undermined by
inadequate port reception systems.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.579.3" class="koboSpan">These include
simply amassing the carefully segregated waste into one single
container. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.579.4"
class="koboSpan">Likewise, the efforts of the crew to achieve efficient
waste
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_210"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.580.1"
class="koboSpan">disposal standards were undermined by poor information
on port facilities and in some cases bureaucratic non-user friendly
procedures.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0233" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0233"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.581.1" class="koboSpan">74</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.582.1" class="koboSpan">Overall, the evidence
is of a positive change in waste disposal behaviour with ship’s crews
and port management increasingly adopting an environmentally friendly
response. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.582.2"
class="koboSpan">Having made this point, it remains to add that whilst
the problem of waste dumping may be diminishing, cases of infringements
are by no means rare. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.582.3"
class="koboSpan">The case of the reefer,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.583.1"
class="koboSpan">Magellan
Phoenix</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.584.1" class="koboSpan">
in 2006 points to the desperate measures that operators will take in
order to avoid the expense of implementing the correct methods of waste
disposal. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.584.2"
class="koboSpan">Following a USCG inspection in the Port of Gloucester
City, New Jersey, it was established that the vessel’s oil log was
regularly falsified in order to conceal the illegal dumping of
engine-room waste
oil.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0234" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0234"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.585.1" class="koboSpan">75</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.586.1"
class="koboSpan"> The illegal dumping of waste can be seen as a
by-product of a cost conscious market.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.586.2" class="koboSpan">Additionally
ships in a hurry, anxious to achieve a fast port turnaround time may
attempt to minimise delays by dumping oily waste at sea.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.586.3" class="koboSpan">Canadian Coast
Guards noticed one vessel 20 nm off-shore heading for the St Lawrence
Seaway at the head of an oil slick.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.586.4" class="koboSpan">This resulted
in the owners of the panamax bulk carrier,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.587.1"
class="koboSpan">Nobel
Fortuna,</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.588.1" class="koboSpan">
being fined Can
\$45,000.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0235" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0235"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.589.1" class="koboSpan">76</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.590.1"
class="koboSpan"> Arriving in a port with full waste slop tanks could
lead to examining PSC Inspectors asking probing question as to the means
of disposal! </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.590.2" class="koboSpan">A
mysterious culture of “magic pipes” (pipes which provide illicit egress
from waste tanks) and falsified waste disposal records still persists.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.590.3" class="koboSpan">However, ship
managers cannot distance themselves from the actions of their crews –
the principle of vicarious liability now prevails.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.590.4" class="koboSpan">This culture
was habitually practiced as a cost saving measure by some crews employed
by major US tanker operator, Overseas Shipholding Group (OSG).
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.590.5" class="koboSpan">Violations were
discovered in 12 of the compnies tankers, leading to a \$37m fine in US
Federal
Court.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0236" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0236"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.591.1" class="koboSpan">77</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.592.1"
class="koboSpan"> To their credit, 12 OSG crew members became
“whistleblowers” in reporting the malpractice.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.592.2" class="koboSpan">OSG
mananagement, in its defence, expressed surprise that the culture of
illegal waste disposal was still in existence in the company’s ships.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.592.3" class="koboSpan">This was seen
as a result of the endemic culture of cost cutting being in the
industry:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.593.1" class="koboSpan">“This was because the
industry, historically speaking, has seldom been profitable.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.593.2" class="koboSpan">Now we are
seeing modernisation, professionalism and even some profits, but there
are some people in the industry who still believe in cutting corners and
saving
money.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0237" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0237"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.594.1" class="koboSpan">78</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.595.1" class="koboSpan">4.5 Marketing the green image</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.596.1" class="koboSpan">An increasing area of
environmental attention lies in the need for shipping operators and
their charterers to exude a green image to the public.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.596.2" class="koboSpan">Attention to
such environmental agenda factors as low fuel consumption, to reduced
exhaust emissions of greenhouse gases and minimised oil spills are
examples where shipping lines have claimed green credibility.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.596.3" class="koboSpan">This is then
utilised as a marketing ploy. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.596.4"
class="koboSpan">The impact of environmental pressures and political
scrutiny engender a new look at how the market is structured.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.596.5" class="koboSpan">Like most other
industries that find themselves under public scrutiny, shipping has
moved towards a more pro-active marketing stance.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.596.6" class="koboSpan">From this
perspective, movements towards the green “higher ground” are a marketing
opportunity. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.596.7"
class="koboSpan">Examples of shipping lines championing such green goals
as reduced fuel consumption at sea, minimised exhaust emissions, clean
ballast water systems are now commonplace when new vessels are
commissioned. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.596.8"
class="koboSpan">Illustrating this point, the delivery of the 11,400 TEU
boxship,
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_211"></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.597.1"
class="koboSpan">CMA CGM
Andromena</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.598.1"
class="koboSpan"> in April 2009 was noteworthy not only as an addition
to the global leadership in vessel size, but also as significant move
towards the environmentally friendly ship.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.598.2" class="koboSpan">In addition to
engine and hull design improvements which provided for a 6% reduction in
fuel consumption, waste compactor systems, fast oil recovery systems
(which allow for improved removal access to bunker fuel, following a
grounding or sinking and “cold ironing” connections, which allow for a
total power shut down in port (shoreside power supplies are used as a
substitute for the ship’s diesel
generator).</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0238" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0238"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.599.1" class="koboSpan">79</span></a></sup><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.600.1"
class="koboSpan"> Joining the shipping lines in promoting the green
imperative, ports are increasingly to heralding the green case.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.600.2" class="koboSpan">A leading
exponent of cold ironing has been the Port of Los Angeles, which in
September 2007 demonstrated with the 8,500 TEU box ship,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.601.1"
class="koboSpan">Xin Ya
Zhou</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.602.1" class="koboSpan">,
the savings on greenhouse gases. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.602.2"
class="koboSpan">By shutting down the vessel’s auxiliary engines and
switching to shoreside electricity, more than a tonne of nitrogen oxides
(NO</span><sub><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.603.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.604.1"
class="koboSpan">) and particulate matter (PM) were eliminated per 24
hours port
visit.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0239" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0239"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.605.1" class="koboSpan">80</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.606.1" class="koboSpan">Grimaldi Line can
claim a considerable contribution to the sustainable transport concept
with their Euro-Med Motorway of the Sea service.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.606.2" class="koboSpan">With its 19
port itinerary spanning Southern and Northern Europe, Grimaldi Line have
been able to champion their status as a green alternative to road
haulage:</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.607.1" class="koboSpan">“The whole Euro-Med
Network is a powerful tool for modal re-balance.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.607.2" class="koboSpan">Last year the
Euro-Med lines have transported over 45 million freight tons, equivalent
to an annual total of over 90 billion tons/kilometres, 7.5 times as much
as the target set by the European Commission for the first phase of the
Marco Polo, most of which would congest and pollute the European
motorways
otherwise.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0240" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0240"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.608.1" class="koboSpan">81</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.609.1" class="koboSpan">An interesting
development in the question of hands-on quality operations was noted
with the shift in BP’s strategy in the post-2000 period.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.609.2" class="koboSpan">Bucking the
generic trend to outsource shipping operations, BP – one of the world’s
largest fleet controllers – actually set about restoring in-house
operations. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.609.3" class="koboSpan">BP
had traditionally been a major player in the tanker fleet but following
the dislocations in the post-1975 oil markets had chosen to rationalise
its directly owned fleet. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.609.4"
class="koboSpan">Between 1975 and 1990 the BP fleet shrank from over 5m
dwt to 0.2 m
dwt.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0241" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0241"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.610.1" class="koboSpan">82</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.611.1" class="koboSpan">The spotlight on oil
tanker practice following the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.612.1"
class="koboSpan">Exxon
Valdez</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.613.1" class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.614.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.615.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.616.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige </span></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.617.1"
class="koboSpan">coastal pollution disasters can be recognised as a
factor in the changing business behaviour of global oil major, BP.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.617.2" class="koboSpan">The return of
BP to large scale shipping operations has considerable implications for
the emphasis on quality. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.617.3"
class="koboSpan">Expansion programmes have projected BP into pole
