position as the UK’s most dynamic ship operator, an amazing “sea change”
in strategic behaviour from the tanker fleet rationalisations of the
1980–1990s.</span>

<a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fig0113" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0113"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.618.1" class="koboSpan">Table 12</span></a><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.619.1"
class="koboSpan"> contains details of BP’s order book in 2004, forming
part of a \$3 billion new build programme, 2001–2006.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.619.2" class="koboSpan">In 2004 the oil
major’s fleet totalled more than 40 vessels, including double-hulled
crude carriers, product carriers and liquefied natural gas carriers
(LNG), as well as some single-hulled coastal tankers.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.619.3" class="koboSpan">By 2007, this
total had doubled to 80 vessels. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.619.4"
class="koboSpan">The scale of BP’s commitment to the newbuilding market
in the early years of the New Millennium has restored BP as a major
world shipping operator. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.619.5"
class="koboSpan">The extensive building programme saw the group take
delivery of 15 ships in 2003, with a further 43 vessels delivered in the
2000–2007 period, including four high cost US builds for the Alaskan
Trades. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.619.6" class="koboSpan">It was
reported in 2004 that at any one time BP has 500 cargoes “on the water”,
300 of which are deep sea traffic.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.619.7" class="koboSpan">This includes
vessels in its own fleet, chartered tonnage and cargoes purchased on a
cost insurance</span>

<div id="Ch07.xhtml_fig0113" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_212"></span>[](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0113)

[<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.620.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00113.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch07.xhtml_bck_fig0113)

</div>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.621.1" class="koboSpan">freight basis.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.621.2" class="koboSpan">By bringing
back in-house tanker operations, BP now finds itself in prime position
to measure their efforts to improve safety by playing a more active role
in ship operations. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.621.3"
class="koboSpan">In April 2004, BP Shipping were able to claim that its
directly operated fleet had “achieved a new level of industry leading
performance”, with no reportable personal injuries or environmental
pollution incidents in a 20-months period.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.621.4" class="koboSpan">During this
time, the officers and crew accumulated 10m hours on board, with more
than 1,400 voyages safely completed, 2.7m.nm travelled and about 38mt of
cargo
carried.</span><sup><a href="#Ch07.xhtml_fn0242" id="Ch07.xhtml_bck_fn0242"><span
id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.622.1" class="koboSpan">83</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.623.1" class="koboSpan">4.6 Towards a sustainable fleet?</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.624.1" class="koboSpan">The selected evidence
discussed here places focus upon the impact of the green imperative on
the market. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.624.2" class="koboSpan">It
has been argued that green issues are bringing an extra dimension to the
definition of the shipping market.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.624.3" class="koboSpan">The context of
a dramatic-boom-to-bust scenario has been noted; the question over
shipping’s ability to follow an uncompromising course in improving
environmental performance during an economic down turn has been raised.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.624.4" class="koboSpan">Evidence from
cost-driven sectors has proved to be a salutary warning of the dangers
of market conditions inducing substandard operations.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.624.5" class="koboSpan">The impact of
public concern and the media focus on pollution incidents has been
identified as an intensifying, at times irrational, scrutiny of
shipping’s performance. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.624.6"
class="koboSpan">Increasingly, the responsibilities of management have
been made more onerous and extended to charterers as well as operators.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.624.7" class="koboSpan">Two areas where
shipping faces a strengthening in rigorous scrutiny – exhaust emissions,
waste treatment/disposal – were identified.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.624.8" class="koboSpan">Finally, the
prize of shipping marketing its improved green performance was appraised
as a positive incentive.</span>

## <span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.625.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.625.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.626.1" class="koboSpan">Throughout this
chapter we have tried to trace the changes in technology, changes in
economic pressures, changes in commercial practice, changes in global
pressures regarding the environment, changes in cultural expectations
and changes in political attempts to regulate and control the maritime
industry and hope the basic conclusions are implied in the text.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.626.2" class="koboSpan">One general
observation however is clear – that although the changes since
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_page_213"></span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.627.1"
class="koboSpan">the early 1970s has been greater than the previous
century the speed of change has not been uniform in all sectors, with
the most pressing problems facing the industries’ decision makers having
fluctuated wildly. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.627.2"
class="koboSpan">Even in 1970 few maritime economists wrote about the
environment. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.627.3"
class="koboSpan">The qualitative evidence on the way the shipping
industry delivers has highlighted the indivisibility of green issues
from the workings of the market.</span>

<span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.628.1" class="koboSpan">Maritime economics is
a relatively new area of academic study.
</span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.628.2" class="koboSpan">If one looks at
most areas of academic theory it seems that theory often lacks behind
practice. </span><span id="Ch07.xhtml_kobo.628.3" class="koboSpan">Let
us hope that the new generation of maritime economists can keep pace
with this fast-changing industry.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_217"></span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 8</span>\
<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Economics of the Markets for Ships</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0205)
======================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Siri</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Pettersen</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Strandenes</span></span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0243" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0243"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">Vessels are sold and
purchased in several markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.8.2"
class="koboSpan">New vessels are contracted and sold in the new building
market, whereas the scrapping market balances scrapping volumes and
prices. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.8.3" class="koboSpan">In the
second-hand markets vessels are sold and purchased for further trading.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.8.4" class="koboSpan">Activities in the
newbuilding and scrapping markets set the total transport capacities
available to sea borne trade and passenger transport worldwide.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.8.5" class="koboSpan">In this they
resemble other markets for capital equipment for use in production of
goods or services. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.8.6"
class="koboSpan">Transactions in the second-hand market on the other
hand, do not change the available transport capacity world-wide, but
only shift ownership of the existing transport capacity between the
different shipowners or shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.8.7" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
second-hand markets are kinds of auxiliary markets.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.8.8" class="koboSpan">(See Eriksen and
Norman</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0244" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0244"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Wijnolst and
Wergeland</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0245" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0245"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan">.)</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">In this chapter we will
discuss the elements and the functioning of the markets for ships.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.13.2" class="koboSpan">In the next
section we describe characteristics and differences of the markets in
more detail. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.13.3"
class="koboSpan">Thereafter we comment on the structure of the markets
for ships before we discuss pricing and ship values in the last section.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.13.4" class="koboSpan">The points put
forward are illustrated several places by graphs from the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">Platou
Report</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0246" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0246"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan"> published by R. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.16.2"
class="koboSpan">S. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.16.3"
class="koboSpan">Platou Shipbrokers a.s.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.16.4" class="koboSpan">on the web.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.16.5" class="koboSpan">We are thankful
to Platou for making their report available on the Internet.</span>

## <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">Main Characteristics of the Markets for Ships</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">The markets for ships
fulfill, several of the requirements needed for well functioning
markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.18.2"
class="koboSpan">Generally there are few limits to entry into these
markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.18.3" class="koboSpan">It also
is fairly easy for ship owners to stay informed on the activities and
developments in the markets compared to the situation in most other
worldwide markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.18.4"
class="koboSpan">The cost of exiting from these markets varies somewhat,
but they tend to be fairly low, as we shall point out</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_218"></span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0079" id="Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0079"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">
Real and auxiliary markets for vessels</span>

<div id="Ch08.xhtml_tbl0003" class="table"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

|  | <span class="bold"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">Real markets</span></span> | <span class="bold"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">Auxiliary markets</span></span> |
|:---|:--:|:--:|
| <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">Freight markets</span> | <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Spot freight market</span> | <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">Time charter freight market Forward freight agreements</span> |
| <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">Markets for ships</span> | <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">Newbuilding market Demolition market</span> | <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">Second-hand market</span> |
|  | <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Determination of transport capacity</span> | <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">Trading risk</span> |

<div class="table-foot">

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> Eriksen and
Norman</span><sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sup>

</div>

</div>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">below.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.34.2" class="koboSpan">Shipbrokers
operate in markets for ships and they collect relevant information and
allocate it to the decision makers in the shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.34.3" class="koboSpan">All these
characteristics indicate that well functioning markets for ships
exist.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">Demand for ships is
derived from demand for transport services.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">This has
implications for the markets for ships as it links the development in
these markets directly to the conditions in the world economy and in
international trade. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.35.3"
class="koboSpan">Since trade flows fluctuate, so do the activities in
the markets for ships. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.35.4"
class="koboSpan">Deliveries and deletions of bulk carriers in the last
10 years may illustrate the degree of fluctuations.
</span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0080" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0080"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows a wide variation in deliveries and strong shifts
in deletions over the last 10 years.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.37.2" class="koboSpan">Such variations
make timing crucially important for profits, but also more challenging
to the decision makers in shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">In addition to these
general characteristics of entry and exit and the availability of
information, the markets for ships feature some specific
characteristics. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.38.2"
class="koboSpan">They function as the market place both for ship owners
seeking ships to fulfil transport assignments and for asset players who
focus on the potential rise in ship values, when they decide whether to
enter the market. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.38.3"
class="koboSpan">Hence, variations in prices and activities in the
markets for ships attract investors that enter mainly to exploit such
price variations. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.38.4"
class="koboSpan">These players’ activities are positive in that they
increase the liquidity of the markets for ships and thus ensure better
allocation of vessels among ship owners servicing international trade.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.38.5" class="koboSpan">As long as the
asset players make rational decisions, their activity also contribute by
dampening price fluctuations and thus reduce the risk for ship owners
who enter mainly to secure transport capacity for seaborne trade.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">Similar to deep-sea
shipping freight markets, the ships are traded in worldwide markets
where agents from all over the world meet to trade.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">Ships thus, are
traded among owners in geographically separate parts of the world.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.39.3" class="koboSpan">Shipowners do
contract and scrap vessels abroad and far away from their home country.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.39.4" class="koboSpan">The bulk of
scrapping activity, for example, takes place in Asia.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.39.5" class="koboSpan">Asian countries
also dominate shipbuilding for large groups of vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">Irrespective of the
worldwide character of these markets, the activities are not evenly
spread around the world. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.40.2"
class="koboSpan">The industry has experienced a geographic shift as more
and more of the newbuilding capacity moved eastward, first to Japan and
later to South Korea. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.40.3"
class="koboSpan">Now there is also strong competition within Asia, as
China has become a major supplier in the market for new vessels together
with South Korea and Japan. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.40.4"
class="koboSpan">This move eastwards left Europe and USA with excess
shipbuilding capacity. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.40.5"
class="koboSpan">Now Asian shipyards also face excess capacity following
the high expansion in yard capacity during</span>

<div id="Ch08.xhtml_fig0114" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00114.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Deletions and deliveries of bulk carriers, 1999–2008" /></span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_219"></span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0080" id="Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0080"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">
Deletions and deliveries of bulk carriers, 1999–2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">The Platou Report
2009</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">, p.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.46.2" class="koboSpan">17</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">the recent shipping
boom. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">Building
capacity in the west partly was closed down and partly converted to
other uses, for example to producing offshore equipment.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.47.3" class="koboSpan">Some yards
switched toward building specialised ships.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.47.4" class="koboSpan">By specialised
ships we mean research ships, naval ships and vessels tailor made for a
specific trade or route. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.47.5"
class="koboSpan">In this process, subsidies was used to try to halt the
downsizing of newbuilding capacities in traditional shipbuilding nations
in the west.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">There is a long
tradition for securing quality in the newbuilding markets stemming back
to the introduction of ship classification in the nineteenth century.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.48.2" class="koboSpan">Classification
societies have inspectors on the site to oversee the construction of the
new vessels they are going to class.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.48.3" class="koboSpan">Quality
assessment and quality requirements are challenges also to the
functioning of and the activity in the other markets for ships, the
second-hand and the scrapping market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.48.4" class="koboSpan">The uncertainty
about the quality of vessels being traded poses a problem affecting the
decision makers’ information and therefore influences both pricing and
the number of vessels traded. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.48.5"
class="koboSpan">Quality is currently assessed mainly by numerous
inspections of vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.48.6"
class="koboSpan">In addition to inspections performed by class
societies, cargo owners, ports and creditors require inspections to
assess the vessel. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.48.7"
class="koboSpan">This is both costly and time consuming as commented for
example in
Fairplay.</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0247" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0247"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan"> Bijwaard and
Knapp</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0248" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0248"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan"> find that there is a possible over-inspection of
vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.52.2"
class="koboSpan">Introducing incentive contracts and signalling to
induce operators to focus on quality may reduce the number of
inspections. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.52.3" class="koboSpan">A
preliminary discussion of the possibility for such schemes in the
freight markets is found in
Strandenes.</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0249" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0249"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan"> Problems of assessing quality of vessels represent
important imperfections in the second-hand market and influence the
functioning of that market.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">Quality assessments
have other effects for the conditions in the scrapping market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">When quality
requirements increase, there will typically be a rise in the activity
level
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_220"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">in the scrapping market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
whenever policy decisions to phase out low quality vessels materialize,
this will increase the volume of tonnage sold for scrapping.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Characteristics specific to the newbuilding market</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">Here we concentrate on
how the other markets influence activities in the new building market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.58.2" class="koboSpan">By the other
markets we mean both the two other markets for ships and the freight or
passenger markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.58.3"
class="koboSpan">For more thorough discussions of the supply side in the
newbuilding market and the shipbuilding industry, see Wijnolst and
Wergeland.</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0250" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0250"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">Ideally demand for new
vessels reflects the need for transport capacity in the different vessel
categories or types. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.60.2"
class="koboSpan">It takes time, usually one to one-and-a-half years, but
sometimes up to four years, from ordering a vessel until the vessel is
delivered and starts operating in the market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.60.3" class="koboSpan">Since freight
markets are volatile this implies that vessels often are delivered into
markets with freight rate levels that differ much from the market
conditions prevailing when the vessels were ordered.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.60.4" class="koboSpan">A decision to
order a vessel should, reflect the expected future freight rates or
correspondingly the future income level over the economic life of the
new vessel. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.60.5"
class="koboSpan">Hence, a short-term dip in the freight rates upon
delivery is of limited significance to the return from the investment.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.60.6" class="koboSpan">During the time
it takes to build the vessels the long-term prospects for the freight
markets may also change and especially so if the time for delivery is
long. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.60.7" class="koboSpan">This means
that ship owners sometimes may prefer to cancel an order or to convert
the vessel into another size or kind of ship to adjust to the change in
expected future demand for transport services.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">The large variation in
the volume of new vessels ordered is one effect of such uncertainty
about the future income for the vessels and the fluctuations in the
freight markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.61.2"
class="koboSpan">See, for example,
</span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0081" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0081"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan"> on orders for new vessels as a percentage of the
fleet</span>

<div id="Ch08.xhtml_fig0115" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00115.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Order book in percentage of existing tonnage of the main vessel types" /></span>

<a href="#Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0081" id="Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0081"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">
Order book in percentage of existing tonnage of the main vessel
types</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan"> Based on
</span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0079" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0079"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan"> and 4 in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">The Platou Report
2009</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">, p.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.72.2" class="koboSpan">40.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_221"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">over the last ten-year period.
</span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0081)<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan"> also illustrates the variations that exist among the
different vessel types when it comes to fluctuation in deliveries.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">In the years
1990–2001 the order book on the other hand varied from 2 to 13% of the
existing fleet, compared to the 15–55% in later years.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Characteristics specific to the scrapping market</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">One might expect a
synchronisation of the activity levels in the new building and scrapping
market. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">This
would be the case if the economic and technical lives of vessels were
constant and similar across vessel types and contracting was made to
replacement of old tonnage. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.77.3"
class="koboSpan">We know that this is not the case and
</span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0080)<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan"> above nicely illustrates that the variations in the
volume of new transport capacity delivered are not linked directly to
the volume scrapped.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">The activity level in
the scrapping markets fluctuates, as do the freight level and conditions
in the freight markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.80.2"
class="koboSpan">Even though reactions are lagged this indicate that the
economic life of a vessel is linked to the freight level and the income
expected over the rest of the vessel’s technical life.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">Scrapping volumes
furthermore reflect political decisions on phasing out of vessels that
do not fulfil the stricter requirements on environmental and safety
standards being introduced. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.81.2"
class="koboSpan">This means that the phasing out plan for single hull
tankers set by International Maritime Organisation (IMO) is reflected in
the scrapping volumes. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.81.3"
class="koboSpan">Some single hull tankers are converted to floating oil
producing vessels instead of being scrapped.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.81.4" class="koboSpan">This also
reduces the oil carrying capacity of the tanker fleet.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">Fluctuations indicate
that the capacity level in the scrapping industry should be flexible.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">As stated above
entry into the market has hitherto been fairly easy.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.82.3" class="koboSpan">To set up a new
scrapping site one needs a beach and labour.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.82.4" class="koboSpan">This has been
available mainly in the Asian countries with China, Bangladesh, Pakistan
and India as the important locations.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.82.5" class="koboSpan">Environmental
concerns have set focus on scrapping activity both following from the
potential spills into the waters surrounding the scrapping site and the
health problems faced by workers in the scrapping industry.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.82.6" class="koboSpan">A change in
requirements will influence the costs of entry and exit in the scrapping
industry and thus the flexibility in capacity.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.82.7" class="koboSpan">In the future we
may therefore experience higher fluctuations in scrapping prices than
those we see currently. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.82.8"
class="koboSpan">The effects on pricing will be discussed in more detail
below.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">2.3 Characteristics specific to the second-hand markets</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">As pointed out in the
introduction to this chapter the second-hand markets differ from new
building and scrapping markets by being auxiliary markets in the sense
that they do not change the number of vessels or the transport capacity
offered in the markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.84.2"
class="koboSpan">This contrasts with the other markets for ships, which
have expansion or contraction of transport capacity as their main
function. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.84.3" class="koboSpan">The
purpose of a second-hand market is to reallocate vessels among operators
and thereby to increase the efficiency in markets for transport
services. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.84.4" class="koboSpan">By
doing so, second-hand markets support efficient use of capital equipment
in the shipping industry and contribute to reducing transport costs in
world trade.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">Transactions performed
in the second-hand markets also contribute to the efficiency in seaborne
transport in another way. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.85.2"
class="koboSpan">When ship owners can sell the bulk of their real
capital in a liquid second-hand market, their exit costs are pushed
down. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.85.3" class="koboSpan">Similarly
the</span>

<div id="Ch08.xhtml_fig0116" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00116.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Second-hand values for tankers (5 years old), 1999–2008" /></span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_222"></span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0082" id="Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0082"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">
Second-hand values for tankers (5 years old), 1999–2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">The Platou Report
2009,</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan"> p.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">16.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">existence of
second-hand markets facilitates entry into shipping, since potential
suppliers may buy an existing vessel and enter the transport market on
short notice. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.92.2"
class="koboSpan">Both aspects affect competition in the freight markets
in a positive way. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.92.3"
class="koboSpan">In addition shipowners may also use the flexibility to
switch markets or restructure their fleet in line with changes in
demand.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">Viable second-hand
markets do not eliminate the exit costs, however.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">Ship values
fluctuate with freight market conditions as is illustrated by
</span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0082" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0082"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.95.2"
class="koboSpan">Hence, the value of the vessel may be low when the
owner wishes to sell and exit. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.95.3"
class="koboSpan">Therefore second-hand markets reduce, but do not
eliminate, costs of exit compared to an alternative setting were ship
owners had to scrap their capital equipment to exit.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Not only ship owners
who operate vessels, but also investors who purchase and sell vessels
for asset play, enter the second-hand market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.96.2" class="koboSpan">Their activities
increase the liquidity of the second-hand market and contribute to a
better functioning market and thus to a more efficient allocation of
capital equipment in the freight market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.96.3" class="koboSpan">In a study of
the dry bulk market Alizadeh and
Nomikos</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0251" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0251"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan"> thus find that there is a negative relationship
between the volume of transactions in the second-hand market and price
volatily.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">2.4 Characteristics of markets for different vessel types</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">In the above comments
on the different markets for ships we have indicated that the situation
differs somewhat among vessel types.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">In the
newbuilding market some suppliers specialise in building a restricted
number of vessel types. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.100.3"
class="koboSpan">There are for example, yards that specialise in cruise
vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.100.4" class="koboSpan">Most
European shipbuilders concentrate on specialised vessels either cruise
vessels, ferries, fast vessels or supply or research
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_223"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan">vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.101.2"
class="koboSpan">Producing these vessels is more profitable when labour
costs are high labour than producing standardised tanker or dry bulk
carriers under similar cost conditions.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.101.3" class="koboSpan">Thus, a main
difference in supply of the different ship types in the new building
market is the location of the yards and thereby the cost level for
labour employed. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.101.4"
class="koboSpan">There is, however, an eastward move also for
specialised vessels, similar to the one experienced earlier by
contractors of standard wet and dry bulk vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">In the scrapping
market there is little differentiation on vessel type.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">The
environmental concern is also similar irrespective of type of vessel,
since all vessels contain materials that are potentially harmful to the
local environment.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">The second-hand
markets feature the clearest difference in market conditions for
different ships. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.2"
class="koboSpan">The differences reflect whether the vessel is suitable
for more than one trade or transport service.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.3" class="koboSpan">Standard
vessels such as most tankers and bulk carriers are suitable for
operating in several trades. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.4"
class="koboSpan">Hence, they can operate for a number of shipping firms
and fulfil these firms diverse transport obligations.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.5" class="koboSpan">Container
vessels may be somewhat less flexible across trades, but the
standardised types may still be used in several markets.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.6" class="koboSpan">In addition to
the effect of higher flexibility and transferability among trades
enjoyed by standardised vessels, the number of vessels that compete in
the tanker and dry bulk markets is high.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.7" class="koboSpan">This implies
more frequent transactions in the secondhand market involving these
vessel types. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.8"
class="koboSpan">As a result the second-hand market is more liquid for
these vessels than for specialised vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.103.9" class="koboSpan">At the same
time we know that the liquidity in the second-hand market is important
for efficient allocation of vessels to their best use.</span>

## <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">Alternatives to Investing in Vessels: Renting and Leasing</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Operators may choose
not to invest in vessels and instead concentrate on the commercial
operations in the markets for transport services.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.105.2" class="koboSpan">There are
several options open to operators.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.105.3" class="koboSpan">They may rent
vessels for a shorter or longer duration.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.105.4" class="koboSpan">An operator,
either an intermediator in international trade or a cargo owner, may
rent vessels for specific trips in the spot charter markets or for
longer duration in the time charter markets.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.105.5" class="koboSpan">Time charters
may be available for periods of some months and up to most of the
economic lifetime of the vessel.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">The possibility to
rent instead of investing in vessels increases the flexibility in
seaborne transport further and rises the efficiency of the markets.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">There are,
however, interdependencies between the time charter rates and ship
values. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">The
similarities in developments in market values and time charter rates are
indicated by
</span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fig0117" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fig0117"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan">, Panels A and B.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">The possibility
to avoid high prices by postponing the investment and instead hiring a
vessel in the time charter markets is therefore limited.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.108.3" class="koboSpan">Even so hiring
poses an advantage since the operator may use this to postpone the
investment in a vessel and may thus avoid tying capital into a vessel
until he has acquired further information on the conditions in the
shipping markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.108.4"
class="koboSpan">Decisions on whether to hire now and purchase later or
correspondingly to let your vessel now in order to sell it later, are
similar to buying a real option to purchase or sell a vessel.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.108.5" class="koboSpan">Real option
analysis and ship pricing is discussed in
</span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter
24</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_ht0516)<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan"> by Bendall.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">Leasing offers another
opportunity for acquiring transport capacity.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.111.2" class="koboSpan">Leasing has
little effect on the capacity offered or the operations in the transport
markets, but has</span>

<div id="Ch08.xhtml_fig0117" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_224"></span>[](#Ch08.xhtml_bck_fig0117)

[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00117.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch08.xhtml_bck_fig0117)

</div>

<div id="Ch08.xhtml_fig0118" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00118.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: Market values and freight rates for bulk carriers 1999–2008" /></span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0083"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
4:</span></span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan"> Market values and freight rates for bulk carriers
1999–2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan">The Platou Report
2009</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">,
pp. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">20 and
21</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">bearing for the way
ship owners acquire capital to invest in transport capacity.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.119.2" class="koboSpan">By leasing
vessels the ship owner engages in off-balance operations and may secure
more favourable financing than ordinary debt or equity financing.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.119.3" class="koboSpan">Leasing may
also have bearings on the tax position of the shipowning firm and
thereby reduce or postpone tax payments.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_225"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan">Leasing may influence demand in markets for ships and
the corresponding price level or ship values, if it increases the
investment opportunities open to shipowners.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.120.2" class="koboSpan">It may increase
the efficiency of the markets for vessels by lifting a potential
restriction on demand stemming from lack of capital at acceptable costs.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.120.3" class="koboSpan">Leasing of
vessels is discussed in more detail in
</span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">Part
9</span>](#part9.xhtml_ht0491)<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan"> of this volume.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">Here we only
want to point out that by facilitating demand, the option to lease also
influences the activity level and the liquidity in the market for ships
in a positive way.</span>

## <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.123.2" class="koboSpan">Market Structure and Competition</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">Above we have made
some comments on the effects on market efficiency of the characteristics
in the different markets for ships.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">In this section
we will discuss market structure and its implications in more
detail.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">We found that in
general markets for ships fulfil important requirements for efficient
markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">These
requirements are: low cost of entry and exit; access to relevant
information on market conditions and transactions; and high liquidity in
the market resulting from a fairly high number of agents demanding or
offering ships for sale. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.125.3"
class="koboSpan">Even though markets for ships in general are
competitive and efficient markets posting prices that reflect expected
future income to the owner, there are several particulars that differ
among the markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.125.4"
class="koboSpan">In this section we will point at and discuss such
special elements of the market structure for the newbuilding, scrapping
and second-hand markets for the main types of vessels.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Market structure in the newbuilding market</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">The market structure
in the newbuilding market carries several characteristics of a
competitive market. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.127.2"
class="koboSpan">There are a number of yards in different parts of the
world and several independent ship owners looking for attractive offers
to build vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.127.3"
class="koboSpan">New sites are constructed and others are converted from
constructing vessels to building other capital equipment, for example
for offshore oil production. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.127.4"
class="koboSpan">Thus, entry into and exit out of the newbuilding
markets takes place.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">The existing order
book split by yards and types of ships offers information to the agents
in this market. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.128.2"
class="koboSpan">This means that ship owners have information that may
induce them to postpone ordering new vessels from yards with high demand
or consider switching to types of vessels in lower demand at the time.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.128.3" class="koboSpan">By doing this
ship owners induce a more efficient use of the total shipbuilding
capacity with more similar time for delivery and backlog of orders
across yards and vessel types. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.128.4"
class="koboSpan">This levelling out of differences is not perfect,
however, because the different vessel types are not perfectly
interchangeable whether in operation nor in building
requirements.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">Since transport
markets fluctuate and the information on the order book is frequently
updated, ship owners may get information that makes them decide to
cancel contracts or to convert an order from one type of vessel to
another, if for example, they find that there will be delivered too many
vessels of a specific type. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.129.2"
class="koboSpan">Cancellation or conversion is prevalent in periods with
big changes in expectations. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.129.3"
class="koboSpan">Cancellations represent a cost for the ship owner and
the yard, but may result in a lower cost than the expected cost of going
on with the investment after conditions have changed.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.129.4" class="koboSpan">Hence, it opens
up for correcting earlier decisions, when conditions in the transport
market changes. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.129.5"
class="koboSpan">This also contributes to a higher efficiency in the
markets for ships by dampening potential
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_226"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">distortion effects of the fluctuations in demand for
seaborne trade on the market for new vessels, compared to what would be
the situation if cancellations or conversions were not accepted.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">Traditionally labour
unions have been strong in shipbuilding.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.2" class="koboSpan">This has led to
lower flexibility in the labour market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.3" class="koboSpan">Such
imperfections in a factor market affect newbuilding.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.4" class="koboSpan">The result has
been a setting where nations compete to keep their shipbuilding industry
to avoid layoffs. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.5"
class="koboSpan">This competition has been visible and often more
influential than competition between individual shipbuilding firms.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.6" class="koboSpan">Changes in
relative labour costs induced a movement eastward for shipbuilding
capacity, especially for standard vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.7" class="koboSpan">For such
vessels costs competition is more important than special designs or
qualities that otherwise may make the ship owner willing and capable to
pay higher prices. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.8"
class="koboSpan">When demand faced by traditional shipbuilders in
Western Europe and USA contracted, the authorities in both areas
answered by offering economic support to the shipbuilding industry in
order to reduce the need for restructuring.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.9" class="koboSpan">Later, when the
industry in the upcoming shipbuilding nations in Asia matured, they also
faced rising labour costs and competition from other Asian countries
that experienced industrial growth later.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.10" class="koboSpan">Thus, Japan
met strong competition from South Korea and more recently they both face
intense and growing competition from Chinese shipbuilders.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.11" class="koboSpan">Governmental
policies support the shipbuilding industry also in the Asian countries.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.12" class="koboSpan">The result is
a worldwide subsidy competition that presses prices.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.13" class="koboSpan">This price
effect may increase demand for new vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.14" class="koboSpan">In order to
limit the politically induced subsidisation policy OECD at one stage
regulated the maximum subsidisation allowed in the industry.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.15" class="koboSpan">For several
years subsidisation was limited to yard credits for a maximum of 80% of
the new building costs at 8% yearly interest for 8.5 years.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.16" class="koboSpan">There was a
movement to curb subsidies by 1996.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.131.17" class="koboSpan">This failed
and the negotiations were paused in 2005
(OECD</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0252" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0252"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.133.2"
class="koboSpan">The general trend of falling interest rates in
financial markets worldwide reduced the subsidisation element in such
yard credits, however. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.133.3"
class="koboSpan">For a further discussion on the subsidisation in the
new building industry see </span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan">Chapter
19</span>](#Ch019.xhtml_ht0415)<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan"> in this volume.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">What is of interest
here is the effect of such policies on ship values and the functioning
of the new building market. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.2"
class="koboSpan">By offering vessels at subsidised prices demand for new
vessels increases other things being equal and so do transport
capacities when these vessels eventually are delivered.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.3" class="koboSpan">Subsidisation
implies that new vessels are sold at a lower than optimal price, that is
at a lower price than the value of the resources going into building the
vessel. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.4" class="koboSpan">This
favours investments in new relative to buying an operating vessel in the
second-hand market and thus results in a higher supply of transport
capacity. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.5" class="koboSpan">The
result may be a pressure downward on the freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.6" class="koboSpan">A rising level
of subsidisation thus may reduce the return on investment for existing
vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.7" class="koboSpan">This
introduces a distortion into the markets for ships.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.8" class="koboSpan">Limiting
subsidisation in the new building market therefore contributes to a more
proper functioning of the markets and the relative values of new versus
existing vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.136.9"
class="koboSpan">Dikos</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0253" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0253"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan"> analysing the price formation under uncertainty and
irreversibility, argue that sub-optimal new building prices may result
also without subsidisation given the characteristics of the shipbuilding
industry marginal cost curve.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">If subsidisation
presses ship values strongly, there will also tend to be higher
scrapping activity with vessels being scrapped at younger ages than
would be the case without such subsidisation.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.139.2" class="koboSpan">The value of
all vessels will fall following the pressure on freight rates and
depending on scrapping prices, the reduction in value may push the
market value of the oldest or less valuable vessels below their
scrapping value. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.139.3"
class="koboSpan">If this link
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_227"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan">between higher delivery of new vessels and
correspondingly higher scrapping is strong, we may still end with a
close to optimal capacity of transport services.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.140.2" class="koboSpan">Subsidisation
in this case mainly results in a shortening of the economic life of the
vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.140.3" class="koboSpan">This
implies a premature destruction of capital invested in shipping, but do
not increase the total volume of transport capacity above the level
needed in international seaborne trade.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.140.4" class="koboSpan">There is little
reason to believe, however, that the effects of subsidisation are
totally absorbed in this way. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.140.5"
class="koboSpan">If not, subsidisation also induces a cost in the market
for transport services. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.140.6"
class="koboSpan">We may conclude that the newbuilding market has been
characterised by competition between shipbuilding nations and not only
by competition among shipbuilding firms.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.140.7" class="koboSpan">The resulting
subsidisation has influenced markets for ships and ship values.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Market structure in scrapping market</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">Above we saw that also
the scrapping market carries several characteristics of competitive
markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.142.2" class="koboSpan">First
and foremost it is fairly easy to enter into the scrapping market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.142.3" class="koboSpan">‘Green field’
scrapping capacity can be installed at a low cost and at short notice.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.142.4" class="koboSpan">The labour
requirement is high, but no special qualifications are asked for.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.142.5" class="koboSpan">There are also
few differences in the work or methods needed for scrapping vessels of
different type. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.142.6"
class="koboSpan">This flexibility in expanding scrapping capacity is
especially important since demand for scrapping varies greatly and in
correspondence with the wide variations in freight rates for operating
vessels (see </span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
4</span>](#Ch08.xhtml_fig0117)<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.144.2"
class="koboSpan">Above we also argued that more intense subsidisation of
new vessels may induce a shift in the volume scrapped.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.144.3" class="koboSpan">This increase
is not sudden, however, and poses fewer problems for capacity
utilisation.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">As long as demand for
scrap steel is high there will also be economic reasons for the
scrapping industry to increase capacities.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.145.2" class="koboSpan">Demand for
scrap steel varies with economic activities, but scrap steel from
vessels does not represent the marginal supply in the scrap steel
market. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.145.3" class="koboSpan">Hence,
variations in demand are smaller for scrap steel from ships than for
scrap from other sources. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.145.4"
class="koboSpan">All the same changes in the conditions in the shipping
markets of course induce changes to the scrapping industry.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.145.5" class="koboSpan">See
</span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0084" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0084"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan"> on variations in scrapping volumes.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">Similarly the phasing
out of vessels caused by changes in regulations by the IMO agreement on
single hull
tankers,</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0254" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0254"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan"> pose fewer problems to the scrapping markets as long
as the capacity adjustment is flexible.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.150.2" class="koboSpan">Scrapping
prices may be depressed for some time since the owners of those vessels
do not have further trading as an alternative.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.150.3" class="koboSpan">If the markets
for second-hand vessels are well functioning, this should be anticipated
in the values for single hull tankers, at least when the agreement was
reached by IMO and thus represent a sunk cost to the owners of these
vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.150.4"
class="koboSpan">Converting single hull tankers into floating production
units for the oil industry may relax the demand for scrapping capacity.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.150.5" class="koboSpan">This requires
yard capacity for the conversion, however.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">Under normal
conditions the ship owner can choose between scrapping and selling the
vessel for further trading. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.2"
class="koboSpan">The decision should reflect the relative costs of the
two alternatives. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.3"
class="koboSpan">This links the scrapping and second-hand market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.4" class="koboSpan">The option to
alternatively sell the vessel for further trading may vary with the type
of vessel, however. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.5"
class="koboSpan">For standard tankers and dry bulk carries and standard
container vessels sale for further trading may be a viable alternative.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.6" class="koboSpan">Specialised
vessels on the other hand, may have low value in other uses.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.7" class="koboSpan">If so,
scrapping is the main alternative open to the ship owner.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.8" class="koboSpan">Since there are
several firms offering scrapping services, the shipowner still is not
captive to that market. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.151.9"
class="koboSpan">No scrapping firm can operate as monopsonist and
dictate the scrapping value.</span>

<div id="Ch08.xhtml_fig0119" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00119.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 5: Tankers and bulk carriers sold for scrapping 1999–2008" /></span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_228"></span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0084" id="Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0084"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
5:</span></span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">
Tankers and bulk carriers sold for scrapping 1999–2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan">Source</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan">: Based on Tables 11 and 17 in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">The Platou Report
2009,</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">
pp. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.158.2" class="koboSpan">42 and
44.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">Conditions and market
structure in the scrapping market may change in the future, however.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.159.2" class="koboSpan">The relative
ease of setting up a new scrapping site is an important element in
securing well functioning and fairly competitive scrapping markets.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.159.3" class="koboSpan">Environmental
concerns may limit this by requiring more secure and costly disposal of
environmentally dangerous materials from scrapping.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.159.4" class="koboSpan">This will
increase the cost of scrapping and reduce scrapping values.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.159.5" class="koboSpan">Even more
important, these requirements will reduce the flexibility in scrapping
capacity and may increase the market power of approved scrapping firms.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.159.6" class="koboSpan">It is of less
importance whether the ship owner or the scrapping firm are made liable
for environmental protection against dangerous materials.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.159.7" class="koboSpan">There will be
effects on the functioning of the scrapping market irrespective of who
gets to be ultimately responsible.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">We may conclude that
the scrapping market is fairly competitive and has remained so for a
long time. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.160.2"
class="koboSpan">There may be changes ahead, however, since
environmental concerns may increase the requirements for entering into
this market.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Market structure in the second-hand market</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">Above we argued that
the second-hand markets for standard vessels have the characteristics of
well functioning markets. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.162.2"
class="koboSpan">The shipbroker’s network handles information and
financing is catered for by a series of international shipping banks or
shipping departments of the larger international banks, in leasing
markets and by equity financing.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">The main function of
the second-hand market is to secure efficient exploitation of the
existing capital equipment i.e. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.163.2"
class="koboSpan">the vessels serving seaborne trade.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.163.3" class="koboSpan">Being what we
called an auxiliary market since it does not alter the transport
capacity supplied, one important function of the second-hand market is
to open up for trade in risk exposure linked to investing in shipping.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.163.4" class="koboSpan">By opening up
for sale of existing vessels for further trade, these markets reduced
the risk of lock in to the investor.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.163.5" class="koboSpan">It does not
eliminate all risks, however, since the ship values vary in accordance
with the expected future return
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_229"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan">from investing in the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.164.2" class="koboSpan">Hence, a
general reduction in the market expectations has to be borne by the
current owner even though he has the option to leave the market by
selling his vessel as a sale is only possible at a depressed price when
expectations indicate a fall. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.164.3"
class="koboSpan">He may curb future losses by selling, but will also
forego any upside that might result from being in the market when
conditions improve. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.164.4"
class="koboSpan">Thus, the secondhand market reduces, but does not
eliminate the risk from investing in standard or tradable
vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">The ship owner’s
alternatives to selling a vessel for further trading are to let the
vessel on a time charter or to scrap it.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">Even if he does
not see satisfactory income opportunities from operating the vessel in
the transport market himself, he may let the vessel to another operator
for shorter or longer duration against a fixed time charter rate.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.165.3" class="koboSpan">By doing this
he may postpone or avoid selling the vessel, if he expects to gain by
operating the vessel in the future.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.165.4" class="koboSpan">This link
between the second-hand and the time and bareboat charter market
implies, however, that a reduction in the second-hand values follow a
fall in time charter freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.165.5" class="koboSpan">Again the
opportunity to let the vessel in the time charter market reduces the
risk from investing, but does not eliminate the risk for a reduced
return on the investment.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">As discussed above
investments in specialised vessels are relatively illiquid compared to
the situation when investing in standard vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.166.2" class="koboSpan">The second-hand
market may be illiquid or even non-existent for specialised vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.166.3" class="koboSpan">If the vessel
can operate in standard trades, this may represent a sales opportunity
at a lower price that do not reflect the costs of the special equipment
carried by the vessel. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.166.4"
class="koboSpan">Similarly, the opportunity to let the vessel in the
time charter market will be limited by the fact that each vessel is best
suited for operations in one or a few trades only.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">We may conclude that
the market structure and competitive situation in the secondhand markets
varies with vessel type from competitive for standard vessels to fairly
illiquid and close to monopsony for specialised ones.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">These
differences have bearings on the efficiency of the second-hand market in
reducing the risk from investing in vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.167.3" class="koboSpan">The allocative
function of the second-hand markets that secure that vessels are engaged
in their best employment, is less hurt, however, since specialised
vessels by definition have fewer alternative uses than standard
vessels.</span>

## <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">Pricing and Ship Values</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">The expected future
return from operating the vessel is the basis for ship values and thus
for pricing in the markets for ships.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.169.2" class="koboSpan">In other words
pricing in markets for ships is similar to pricing in other markets for
real capital. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.169.3"
class="koboSpan">The existence of viable secondhand markets is fairly
common for transport equipment like aircraft, cars or ships.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.169.4" class="koboSpan">This said, it
should be pointed out that the existence of viable second-hand markets
implies that ship values are quoted on a regular basis only for the kind
of vessel often traded in the market.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.169.5" class="koboSpan">Hence, for
standard vessels the markets valuation is reported daily.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.169.6" class="koboSpan">The main
difference between ships regularly quoted in second-hand markets and
more specialised vessels with few alternative uses, is that owners of
the first type of ships get regularly updated information on the market
assessment of the ships’ value. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.169.7"
class="koboSpan">Specialised vessels with no or few alternative uses to
the trade they have been built for, will not be quoted in a second-hand
market and therefore the information on the current market value will
not always be available.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_230"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">The basis for the market prices in efficient
second-hand markets thus is the expected future return from purchasing
and operating the vessel. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.170.2"
class="koboSpan">The challenge to ship owners and insurance or finance
institutions thus is to assess the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">expectations on future income
</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">for the
vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.172.2" class="koboSpan">For
older vessels the assessment must also include an evaluation of its
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan">remaining economic
life</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.174.2" class="koboSpan">This reflects
the quality and maintenance of the vessel in addition to whether new
technologies are expected that will reduce the value of existing vessels
with old technologies.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Expectations on future income</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">Extrapolative,
rational and semi-rational expectations have been used, when analysing
expected return in shipping. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.176.2"
class="koboSpan">Norman</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0255" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0255"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Beenstock and
Vergottis</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0256" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0256"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan"> are examples of studies using rational expectations,
whereas
Strandenes</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0257" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0257"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0258" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0258"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan"> assumes semi-rational expectations.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.184.2" class="koboSpan">Under
extrapolative expectations assumptions on future prices are based on the
historical development of prices and values for the individual vessel
type. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.184.3" class="koboSpan">One
example of extrapolative expectations is when future price is assumed to
be a linear function of the current prices.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.184.4" class="koboSpan">Assuming
rational expectations on future price formation on the other hand
implies that shipowners and other market agents have an economic
assessment of the future developments.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.184.5" class="koboSpan">In this case we
assume that a dynamic model of the development in the market finds the
expected future price or ship value.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.184.6" class="koboSpan">In other words
agents then are expected to have an opinion both on the long-term
equilibrium price level and the time path to be followed by the current
prices to reach that equilibrium.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.184.7" class="koboSpan">When using
semi-rational expectations, we assume that shipowners can assess the
future equilibrium conditions in the markets, but that they have no
theoretical basis for evaluating what time path prices will follow
towards long-term equilibrium.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">The common assumption
of the term structure theory is that agents expect freight rates to fall
when current short-term rates are high.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.185.2" class="koboSpan">Conversely they
expect the short-term freight rates or spot rates, to rise in the future
in periods when the current spot rates are low.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.185.3" class="koboSpan">When the spot
freight rates are close to the long-term equilibrium level the curve
depicting the expected development in freight rates is flat.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.185.4" class="koboSpan">No large
adjustment is needed for the freight rates to reach long-term
equilibrium. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.185.5"
class="koboSpan">The term structure theory is an example of a theory
that may handle semi-rational expectations.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.185.6" class="koboSpan">Originally the
term structure theory was applied to the structure of interest rates for
assets with different maturities.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.185.7" class="koboSpan">In the first
versions rational expectations were assumed.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">Prices or ship values
for vessels of different age, that is vessels with different remaining
economic life may be ‘read’ from the curves signifying the paths towards
equilibrium. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.186.2"
class="koboSpan">Older vessels resemble short-term investments, whereas
newer vessels are investments that are to be recouped over several
years. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.186.3"
class="koboSpan">Accordingly when the spot market is expected to rise in
the future, newer vessels have a higher market value than older vessels
both since they will earn an income for more years and from changing
market conditions if these are expected to improve in the future.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.186.4" class="koboSpan">Currently new
vessels will still operate in the future markets, whereas the current
older vessels then have been scrapped.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.186.5" class="koboSpan">If the market
expects the values to fall in some year’s time and to remain low for a
longer period, the value of the older vessels may be relatively high
compared to values for newer vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.186.6" class="koboSpan">They will enjoy
a better return on the capital invested for the rest of their economic
life, compared to newer vessels that may face several years in a
depressed market before their economic life expires.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.186.7" class="koboSpan">If the current
freight rates are very high, and the markets furthermore are expected to
fall to a low level even before newly</span>

<div id="Ch08.xhtml_fig0120" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00120.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Second-hand prices in percent of new building prices for five-year-old tankers" /></span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_231"></span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0085" id="Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0085"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
6:</span></span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">
Second-hand prices in percent of new building prices for five-year-old
tankers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan">Source</span></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">: R.S. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.191.2"
class="koboSpan">Platou Monthly 8 2009.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">contracted vessels can
be delivered; the values of existing vessels may lie above the price of
a new vessels.
</span><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0085" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0085"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrate this for five-year-old tanker value
relative to new building prices for similar vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.194.2" class="koboSpan">The market then
assumes that the freight rates have fallen when the newly contracted
vessels are delivered and start operating.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">Thus, they lose
out on the income opportunities in the high markets because they are
delivered only after the market conditions have normalised.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan">Strandenes</span><sup>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">14</span>](#Ch08.xhtml_fn0257)</sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan"> analysed term structure in ship values for tankers and
bulk carriers in the 1970s. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.197.2"
class="koboSpan">The analysis of the components of ship values indicated
that for panamax bulk carriers and for medium-sized tankers the
long-term equilibrium freight level was more important to the values
than the current spot freight rate.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.197.3" class="koboSpan">For large
tankers the results indicated, however, that the current spot freight
rates were of great importance for the values of these ships.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.197.4" class="koboSpan">Newer studies
of the term structure in shipping markets indicate that the results must
be corrected for ship owners’ differences in assessing the risk.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.197.5" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos’ and
Alizadeh’s</span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0259" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0259"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan"> results on the term structure for time charter rates
indicate that ship owners have time varying risk perceptions.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.199.2" class="koboSpan">This distorts
the term structure of freight rates of different durations found by the
older studies, where risk assessment was assumed to be stable over time.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.199.3" class="koboSpan">Adland
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch08.xhtml_fn0260" id="Ch08.xhtml_bck_fn0260"><span
id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan"> introduce and estimate the effect of time-varying
delivery lag in the analysis. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.202.2"
class="koboSpan">Using Capsize dry bulk carriers as an empirical example
they find that the second-hand values reflect the market fundamentals,
i.e. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.202.3" class="koboSpan">the
term-structure of freight rates, new building price and delivery lag.
