</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.202.4" class="koboSpan">Hence, the
expectations on future income and also the evaluation of ship values
have several components, risk assessment and expected income in the
freight markets for the rest of the economic life of the vessel being
the main elements. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.202.5"
class="koboSpan">The prevailing
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_232"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan">expectations are difficult to model and assess.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.203.2" class="koboSpan">Real option
analysis may increase the understanding of assessment of ship prices.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.203.3" class="koboSpan">For a
discussion of real option analysis see
</span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter
24</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_ht0516)<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> by Bendall.</span>

### <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">5.2 Economic life of a vessel</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">The relevance of term
structure theory to ship values follows from difference in the remaining
economic life of the vessel. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.207.2"
class="koboSpan">It is important to assess the length of the remaining
active life of the vessel. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.207.3"
class="koboSpan">This includes assessing both the chance of
technological obsoleteness, potential political decisions that may
render the vessel obsolete, and gaining knowledge on what influences
decisions on when to scrap the vessel as it approaches the end of its
economic life.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">The situation in the
newbuilding market will influence the decision to scrap a vessel.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">In high markets
the existence of limited shipbuilding capacity and thus extended time
for delivery, may induce ship owners to postpone the demolition of old
vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.208.3" class="koboSpan">In
extreme periods such as in the early 1970s when the time for delivery
reached four years, existing vessels obtained higher values than new
contracts since they were able to take advantage of the very high spot
freight levels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.208.4"
class="koboSpan">We have seen a similar price structure in the booming
later years as </span>[<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch08.xhtml_cap_lbl0085)<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan"> also shows. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.210.2"
class="koboSpan">The market did not expect these freight levels to
remain until the new vessels were delivered and correspondingly these
vessels would not be in for the extraordinary profits offered in that
period. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.210.3" class="koboSpan">For
that particular period these expectations turned out to be right and
several shipowners lost large amounts on their new orders.</span>

## <span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.211.2" class="koboSpan">Concluding Comments</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">In this chapter we
have focused on the markets for ships and discussed characteristics of
each type of market and pointed at the differences among them.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.212.2" class="koboSpan">We explained
that there are both real and auxiliary markets for ships.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.212.3" class="koboSpan">Transactions in
the real markets, the newbuilding and scrapping markets, change the
number and types of ships available and thus the transport capacity.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.212.4" class="koboSpan">The auxiliary
markets or the second-hand markets, do not change the total transport
capacity. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.212.5"
class="koboSpan">Transactions in these markets re-allocate ships among
ship owners and contribute thereby to a more efficient use of the
available capacity.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">There are several
agents in the markets for ships and no individual shipping company, yard
or scrapping firm can dominate the markets.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.213.2" class="koboSpan">Entry and exit
are possible. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.213.3"
class="koboSpan">Information on the activities in these market is
readily available, especially so because shipbrokers function as
intermediaries and collectors of market information.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">There are differences
among the markets, however. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.214.2"
class="koboSpan">In the newbuilding markets governments have engaged to
halt restructuring that induced shifts in the geographic localisation of
the shipbuilding industry. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.214.3"
class="koboSpan">Subsidisation influences price setting and thus
contracting. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.214.4"
class="koboSpan">The scrapping markets have functioned fairly
efficiently. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.214.5" class="koboSpan">In
the future they may be controlled more strongly by governments, who are
becoming concerned by spill of dangerous materials at the scrapping
sites. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.214.6" class="koboSpan">This may
reduce the flexibility that we have observed for available scrapping
capacity and may result in stronger fluctuations in scrapping prices in
the future. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.214.7" class="koboSpan">We
argued that the second-hand markets are efficient
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_page_233"></span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan">for standard vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.215.2" class="koboSpan">For these ships
the markets are liquid and prices are quoted regularly.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.215.3" class="koboSpan">The second-hand
markets are not equally liquid for specialised vessels.
</span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.215.4" class="koboSpan">Thus, owners of
such specialised vessels may face larger exit costs.</span>

<span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">Ship values ideally
reflect the expected future profit gained from operating the vessel for
the rest of its economic life. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.216.2"
class="koboSpan">We pointed out that the term structure theory may help
in assessing ship values and differences in values for new and existing
vessels from differences in the remaining economic life of the
individual vessels. </span><span id="Ch08.xhtml_kobo.216.3"
class="koboSpan">Newer studies have revealed, however that shipowner’s
time dependent risk assessments complicate the analyses of ship
values.</span>

## <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping cycles create
endless problems for shipping investors and analysts alike.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">The shipping
industry, like Sisyphus, the mythological character condemned to pushing
a stone up a hill, only for it to roll down again, seems to be caught in
an endless sequence of cycles over which it has no real control.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.7.3" class="koboSpan">So why bother to
issue
warnings?</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0262" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0262"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan"> How would Sisyphus have felt if each time he was half
way up the hill some smart economist was standing there to warn him that
the stone would soon be on its way down again?
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.9.2" class="koboSpan">Shipowners feel
the same way about the killjoy analysts intent on spoiling their bit of
fun during the all-too-brief freight booms.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">It is not just modern
shipping executives who feel this sense of frustration.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">A century ago in
his 1894 annual report, a London shipbroker spoke for all of us when he
wrote:</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">“The philanthropy of
this great body of traders, the shipowners, is evidently inexhaustible,
for after five years of unprofitable work, their energy is as unflagging
as ever, and the amount of tonnage under construction and on order
guarantees a long continuance of present low freight rates, and an
effectual check against increased cost of overseas
carriage.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0263" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0263"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">This masterpiece of
understatement precisely captures the sense of dedication, purpose and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">deja vu</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan"> that characterises shipping cycles today, as it
obviously did a century ago. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.15.2"
class="koboSpan">It also leaves shipping economists with a legitimate
question about what they can really contribute to the commercial
shipping industry as it beats its way through these cycles.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.15.3" class="koboSpan">Warnings aside,
what have we to say?</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">In this chapter we
study these cycles, or waves, in the shipping
market</span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.18.1"
class="koboSpan"> There are three main aims.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">First to look at
some of the general characteristics of shipping cycles and discuss how
they fit into the economics of the shipping market.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.18.3" class="koboSpan">Secondly we will
study the historical pattern of cycles (if we decide they are cycles),
so that we get an idea of the many different economic forces which
contribute to their progress. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.18.4"
class="koboSpan">We might call this “cyclical recognition”.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.18.5" class="koboSpan">Thirdly we will
discuss the causes of cycles and focus more closely on the economic
mechanisms which control them.</span>

## <span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_236"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">The Role of Cycles in Shipping Economics</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">Market cycles are the
driving force behind shipping investment and chartering.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">They are the
heartbeat of the shipping market, pumping cash in and out of the
business. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.20.3" class="koboSpan">By
forcing companies to compete with each other for a share of this wealth,
the market lures them in the direction needed to give the most efficient
use of resources. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.20.4"
class="koboSpan">In fact the “cycles” are so much a part of the culture
of the industry, that it seems hardly necessary to define them.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.20.5" class="koboSpan">However it is
worth spending a little time discussing what the industry generally
means by a cycle, and what impact the cycles have.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.20.6" class="koboSpan">This will help
to give some perspective.</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 The characteristics of shipping cycles</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">Strictly speaking a
cycle is “an interval of time during which one sequence of a regularly
recurring sequence of events is
completed”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0264" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0264"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan"> The cycle
in</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0086" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0086"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan"> Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan"> is defined by its amplitude (A), which is the distance
from peak to trough, and its frequency (F), which is the distance
between peaks (or troughs) in the cycle.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.26.2" class="koboSpan">Viewed in this
way a shape of a regular cycle C can be defined in terms of the values
of A and F.</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0121" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00121.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">Of course nobody
expects shipping cycles to be this regular.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">There is a
widely held “rule of thumb” that they last seven years, but even a
cursory examination of the tanker and bulk carrier market cycles in
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0087" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0087"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan"> confirms that in the real world the periods of feast
and famine bear little relationship to the stylised cycles
in</span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan"> Figure
1</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0086)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">The fact that the
cycles are not regular makes it even more important to understand them,
at least from the viewpoint of the shipping analyst.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">The practical
importance of cycles cannot be understated.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.33.3" class="koboSpan">In July 2008 a
280,000 dwt tanker was earning \$170,000 a day, but just 12 months later
in 2009 it was earning only \$11,000 a day.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.33.4" class="koboSpan">This volatility
in earnings has a tremendous impact on the way everyone involved in the
commercial operation of shipping views the business.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.33.5" class="koboSpan">For shipowners
it offers an incentive to “play the cycle”, earning premium revenue when
the market is high and, in an ideal world, fixing the ships on time
charter or selling out just before the market moves in to a
trough.</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0122" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00122.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: A generic “cycle” showing frequency and amplitude" /></span>

<a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0086" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0086"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan"> A
generic “cycle” showing frequency and amplitude</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0123" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00123.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: A comparison of tanker and dry bulk cycles 1970–2009" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_237"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0087" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0087"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan"> A
comparison of tanker and dry bulk cycles 1970–2009</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan"> Fearnleys, Clarkson Research Services Ltd</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Another feature of the
shipping cycle, illustrated by </span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0087)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">, is the correlation between cycles in different
segments of the market. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.2"
class="koboSpan">The spot market rates in the tanker and bulk carrier
markets are compared over the 39-year period 1970–2009.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.3" class="koboSpan">The timing of
cycles in the two markets is broadly similar, but the correlation is far
from perfect and in some cases the two market segments behave quite
differently. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.4" class="koboSpan">In
1971 and 1973 the tanker market surged way ahead of the dry bulk market
in a super-boom which the bulkers were not really included in.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.5" class="koboSpan">Note that the
market remained firm through 1974 for almost a year after the 1973 oil
crisis which happened in October 1973.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.6" class="koboSpan">But in 1980 the
bulk carrier peak was longer and stronger than the rather feeble tanker
upswing. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.7" class="koboSpan">Then in
the late 1980s both markets moved up to a new peak, but this time the
tanker market was much stronger than dry bulk.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.8" class="koboSpan">Bulkers peaked
in 1995 when tankers had a tough year, but in 1997 the tanker market
enjoyed a peak, during a rather bleak year for the bulk carrier market.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.9" class="koboSpan">But then it was
the bulk carrier market’s turn, with a spectacular boom in 2007–2008
which the tanker market could not match.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.10" class="koboSpan">If nothing else
this demonstrates that we cannot generalise about cycles by assuming
that even closely related markets have the same peaks and troughs.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.44.11" class="koboSpan">On the contrary
it suggests that different shipping segments are, to some extent at
least, isolated from each other.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">Even more prominent is
the opportunity for “asset play”, a term often used to describe
speculating on the sale and purchase of ships.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">Every shipping
investor’s ambition is to buy in at the bottom of the cycle and sell at
the peak. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.45.3"
class="koboSpan">Historically this has always been an important part of
shipowners’ revenues, especially during periods of inflation.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.45.4" class="koboSpan">The 1980s
provided one of the most spectacular opportunities ever.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.45.5" class="koboSpan">A VLCC could be
purchased in the mid-1980s for about \$3 million, but by 1989 its price
had gone up to almost \$30 million, a tenfold increase in just five
years. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.45.6" class="koboSpan">A
Capesize bulk carrier bought for \$25 million in 2002 could have been
sold for \$160 million in 2008. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.45.7"
class="koboSpan">Of course the fact that the cycles are so irregular
makes this a tricky game to play, but with so much at stake financially,
who would expect it to be simple?</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0124" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00124.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: A comparison of second-hand price and one-year TC rate for Aframax Tanker" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_238"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0088" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0088"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan"> A
comparison of second-hand price and one-year TC rate for Aframax
Tanker</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">author</span>

<a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0088" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0088"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates the link between cycles is earnings and
asset values by comparing the one-year Time Charter rate for a
five-year-old Aframax Tanker (left axis) with its market value (right
axis). </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.52.2" class="koboSpan">The
correlation coefficient of 0.87 is very close, with peaks and troughs
following the same cyclical pattern, confirming the common sense
expectation that the asset’s price will be correlated with its earning
capacity. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.52.3" class="koboSpan">With
such high volatility it is no wonder that shipowners spend so much time
considering how to take advantage of this volatility by buying low and
selling high.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">In fact the causal
mechanism underlying the cycles is simple enough.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">They are
generated by changes in the delicate balance of supply and demand for
ships. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.53.3" class="koboSpan">When
demand increases faster than supply, freight rates and second-hand
prices move up. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.53.4"
class="koboSpan">Conversely when supply exceeds demand, freight rates
are driven down by competition, and in many cases fall to the operating
cost of the ship. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.53.5"
class="koboSpan">But like many “simple” economic mechanisms, in practice
it can develop in a host of different ways.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.53.6" class="koboSpan">In the next
section of this chapter we will study the way cycles have behaved over
120 years of modern shipping. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.53.7"
class="koboSpan">This provides some practical insights into the many
different permutations of factors which can drive the supply and demand
sides of the market. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.53.8"
class="koboSpan">We will then look more closely at the cyclical
mechanism and in particular the dynamics of the market cycle, in an
effort to understand the economic framework itself.</span>

## <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">A Brief History of Shipping Cycles, 1869–2002</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">A dry freight index
covering the 140-year period from 1869–2009 is shown
in</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0089" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0089"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan"> Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.57.2"
class="koboSpan">Identifying the start and finish of each cycle is not
always easy. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.57.3"
class="koboSpan">Some cycles are clearly defined, but others leave room
for doubt. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.57.4" class="koboSpan">Does
a minor improvement in a single year,</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0125" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00125.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: Shipping cycles 1869–2009, divided into five periods" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_239"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0089" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0089"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
4:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">
Shipping cycles 1869–2009, divided into five periods</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan"> Stopford (2009):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">
(Routledge), Annex C</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">as happened in 1877,
1894 or 1986, count as a cycle? </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.65.2"
class="koboSpan">There are several of these "minicycles" where the
freight rates moved slightly above trend.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">However careful
examination of the statistics and other information suggests that taking
1869 as the starting
point</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0265" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0265"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.67.2"
class="koboSpan">I there were 15 dry cargo freight cycles during the
140-year period covered by the graph.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.67.3" class="koboSpan">For the purposes
of discussion in this chapter we will divide this sequence of 15 cycles
into five periods, which are marked in
</span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
4</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0089)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.69.2"
class="koboSpan">The first of these, period 1, covers one of the most
exciting periods of modern shipping history, when much of the basic
technology used by the industry today was developed.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.69.3" class="koboSpan">Period 2 covers
a much more difficult phase between the World War I and the World War
II, and of course it includes the Great Depression of the 1930s.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.69.4" class="koboSpan">Period 3
encompasses the second era of expansion between the end of the World War
II and the first oil crisis in 1973.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.69.5" class="koboSpan">In a very
different way this was another period when the shipping industry was
adopting new technology in response to rapid trade growth.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.69.6" class="koboSpan">Period 4 covers
the quarter-century from the first oil crisis through to the end of the
twentieth century, including the second great shipping depression in the
1980s. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.69.7" class="koboSpan">Finally
period 5 covers one of the most profitable periods in the shipping
industry’s history, incorporating a single lengthy cycle which surged to
a peak in 2008.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">In the following
sections we will review each of these periods, with two main aims.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.70.2" class="koboSpan">The first is to
establish the general economic conditions which existed on the supply
and demand sides of the shipping market during each period, to give us
an idea of the overall tone of the market.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.70.3" class="koboSpan">Secondly we will
look at the course the cycles took and try to get some sense of how the
industry saw them at the time. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.70.4"
class="koboSpan">In this way we can identify the turning points, marking
the beginning and end of each cycle and the length of each trough.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.70.5" class="koboSpan">Finally we will
examine the impact the cycles have had on shipping over the last
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_240"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">century. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.71.2"
class="koboSpan">Statistics give no sense of the real events underlying
these cycles. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.71.3"
class="koboSpan">For example the brief dips in the index during the
1930s and 1980s give no sense of the desperation and financial hardship
which shipowners suffered during these periods.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.71.4" class="koboSpan">So if we are to
obtain a better insight into the nature cycles, and their causes, we
must focus more closely at what was going on in each period.</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Period 1: Shipping cycles 1869–1914</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">The 45 years before
1914 provides an example of the tight interplay between short-term
cycles and long-term supply/demand fundamentals.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">The freight
index in
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0090" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0090"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows a long-term downward trend from 100 in 1869 to
45 in 1908. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">To
put this into cash terms, we can take the example of the freight rate
for coal from South Wales to Singapore.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.75.3" class="koboSpan">In 1869 the
freight was 27 shillings/ton, but by 1908 it had fallen to a low of 10
shillings</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0266" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0266"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.77.2"
class="koboSpan">Onto this long term trend was superimposed the series
of four shorter cycles of about ten years in length.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">This was a period of
great activity on both the demand and supply sides of the shipping
market. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">Driven
by industrialisation and the expansion of the European empires, trade
grew rapidly. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.78.3"
class="koboSpan">Continuous advances in technology on the supply side of
the shipping market helped the whole process, not least by reducing
transport costs. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.78.4"
class="koboSpan">Ships were becoming bigger and more efficient.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.78.5" class="koboSpan">In 1871 the
largest transatlantic liner was the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan">Oceanic</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">, a 3,800 gt vessel with a 3,000 horsepower engine
capable of 14.75 knots. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.80.2"
class="koboSpan">It completed the transatlantic voyage in 9½ days.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.80.3" class="koboSpan">By 1913 the
largest vessel was the 47,000 gt
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">Aquatania</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.82.2"
class="koboSpan">Its 60,000 horsepower engines drove it at 23 knots.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.82.3" class="koboSpan">The
transatlantic voyage time had fallen to under five days.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.82.4" class="koboSpan">These vessels
were</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0126" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00126.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 5: Four cycles 1869–1914" /></span>

<a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0090" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0090"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
5:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">
Four cycles 1869–1914</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan"> Stopford (2009):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">
(Routledge), Annex C</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_241"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">comparable in length with a 280,000 dwt tanker and
vastly more complex in terms of mechanical and outfitting
structure.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">Perhaps the most
important technical improvement was in the efficiency of steam engines.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">With the
introduction of the triple expansion system and higher pressure boilers
the cargo payload of steamships increased rapidly.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.3" class="koboSpan">The early steam
engines had worked at 6lbs/in pressure and consumed 10lbs of
coal/horsepower per hour. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.4"
class="koboSpan">They could carry little but bunker coal.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.5" class="koboSpan">By 1914,
pressures had increased to 165lbs/in and coal consumption had fallen to
1½lbs/horsepower per hour, giving the steamer a decisive economic
advantage, despite its high capital costs.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.6" class="koboSpan">The economic
advantage of steam ships was compounded by economies of scale.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.7" class="koboSpan">As a result, the
world fleet doubled from 16.7 million grt in 1870 to 34.6 million grt in
1910 and the continuous running battle between the new and old
technologies dominated market economics as each generation of more
efficient steamers pushed out the previous generation of obsolete
vessels. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.8" class="koboSpan">The
first to come under pressure were the sailing ships, which were replaced
by steamers. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.91.9" class="koboSpan">In
1870 steamers accounted for only 15% of the tonnage but by 1910 they
accounted for 75% of the world merchant
fleet</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0267" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0267"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.93.2"
class="koboSpan">The growth in demand was matched by equally rapid
growth in supply. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.93.3"
class="koboSpan">As shipyards gained confidence in steel shipbuilding,
production grew rapidly. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.93.4"
class="koboSpan">Between 1868 and 1912 the shipbuilding output of the
shipyards on the Wear, trebled from 100,000 grt to 320,000 grt.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.93.5" class="koboSpan">Change is never
easy and the market used a series of cycles to alternately draw in new
ships and drive out old ones. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.93.6"
class="koboSpan">The cycles can be clearly seen in
</span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
4</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0089)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan"> which shows peaks in 1871, 1881, 1889 and 1900.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 1</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan"> started in 1871, and lasted 10 years until 1881.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.97.2" class="koboSpan">During this
period rates fell steadily, as a new generation of steamers competed
with the sailing ships which continued to offer low-cost freight
carriage. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.97.3" class="koboSpan">There
was a slight recovery of rates in the second half of 1873, the year when
Mr Plimsoll published “Our Seamen”, and started his campaign which led
to the introduction of the Plimsoll line on ships.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.97.4" class="koboSpan">From there it
was downhill all the way, with rates hitting a trough in 1879, driven by
the “excessive and ever increasing supply of tonnage”.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.97.5" class="koboSpan">However in 1880
the market started to pick up and 1881, the peak of a business cycle in
the United Kingdom, saw “in almost every trade a fair amount of
business”. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.97.6" class="koboSpan">This
good start lead to a second excellent year in 1882, described by brokers
as being “exceedingly satisfactory”.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.97.7" class="koboSpan">A sure sign that
a great deal of money was made.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 2</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
class="koboSpan"> started almost immediately and rates fell through 1883
to a new trough in 1884. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.99.2"
class="koboSpan">Brokers reported that rates were unprofitable for
steamers, and even in the better months insufficient to provide for
depreciation. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.99.3"
class="koboSpan">The next three years from 1885 through to 1887 were
still dull and highly competitive, with relatively low rates.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.99.4" class="koboSpan">By this time the
newly founded liner business was working hard to establish conferences
that would protect them. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.99.5"
class="koboSpan">However things improved in 1887 and by 1888 brokers
were reporting the year as “a remarkable one in the history of shipping.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.99.6" class="koboSpan">A transformation
of the whole trade from abject depression to revival and prosperity”.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.99.7" class="koboSpan">Again we find
that this coincided with a peak in the world trade cycle.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.99.8" class="koboSpan">The good times
continued through 1889.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 3</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan"> commenced in earnest in 1890 when freight rates
slumped, driven down by heavy deliveries which greatly exceeded the
previous peak in the early 1880s.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.101.2" class="koboSpan">By 1892 the
market was in severe depression and rates remained very depressed
through 1894, and 1895. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.101.3"
class="koboSpan">By 1896 the balance seems to have been partly restored
and brokers report fluctuating rates which gave way to a much firmer
market in 1898. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.101.4"
class="koboSpan">This upward trend continued and the market moved to a
peak in 1900 which was reported to be a memorable one for the shipping
industry. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.101.5"
class="koboSpan">Brokers reported “vast trade done and large profits
safely housed”. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.101.6"
class="koboSpan">This concluded the third cycle, which had lasted the
greater part of the decade and was the worst so far.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_242"></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 4</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan"> turned out to be another long recession.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.103.2" class="koboSpan">In 1901 the
market crashed, leading to a series of very depressed years.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.103.3" class="koboSpan">This did not
let up until 1909 when the market started to believe that the worst was
over. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.103.4" class="koboSpan">For once
they were right and 1910 was an excellent year.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.103.5" class="koboSpan">Once again the
explanation of the long recession, at least as reported by the
contemporary brokers, was a recession in trade which followed the great
boom of 1900 and over production of ships.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">So what was driving
these “short” cycles? </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.104.2"
class="koboSpan">On the demand side, rapidly growing trade was dominated
by the world business cycle, whose cyclical peaks in 1872, 1883, 1892
and 1903 roughly correspond to the peaks in the shipping
cycles</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0268" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0268"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.106.2"
class="koboSpan">On the supply side shipbuilding production amplified
the demand instability by overshooting during the booms.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">This
combination laid the foundations for a sequence of cycles which got
steadily longer, with the last one stretching out for the best part of a
decade.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">Looking back over the
period, one lesson is that trade growth and technical development do not
necessarily lead to easy profits.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.107.2" class="koboSpan">Many fortunes
were made during this period, but across the market competition was
cutthroat. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.107.3"
class="koboSpan">Shipbrokers’ reports painted a dismal picture of long
recessions during which marginal tonnage struggled for survival against
a continuous stream of more cost-effective new vessels.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.107.4" class="koboSpan">There were only
a handful of years that did not warrant a complaint about the state of
the market. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.107.5" class="koboSpan">As
time progresses the complaints about over-building intensified.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.107.6" class="koboSpan">A comment on
1884 is typical “This state of things was brought about by the large
over-production of tonnage of tonnage during the three previous years,
fostered by reckless credit given by the banks and builders and
over-speculation by the irresponsible and inexperienced
owners”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0269" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0269"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan"> Fleets were growing, but there were no easy
profits.</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Period 2: Shipping cycles, 1919–1938</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">The period between the
World War I and World War II was another very difficult period for
shipowners, featuring three cycles, numbers 5, 6 and 7 shown in
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0091" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0091"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">By 1920 the sailing
ships had been driven from the seas, the rate of technical innovation
had slowed and the tone was set for a period dominated by a general
misalignment of fundamentals. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.114.2"
class="koboSpan">Jones (1957) comments “For most of the period between
the wars it appears from the statistics of laid up tonnage that the
world was over-stocked with shipping”.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.114.3" class="koboSpan">To begin with
in the 1920s trade grew rapidly at about 5% per annum.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.114.4" class="koboSpan">The problem was
on the supply side where there was acute overcapacity in the
shipbuilding industry, due to the massive expansion during the war and
new entrants to the market. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.114.5"
class="koboSpan">This ensured a weak market.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.114.6" class="koboSpan">The result was
a gradual erosion of freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.114.7" class="koboSpan">The freight
chart shown in </span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0091)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows freight peaks in 1921 and 1926.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.116.2" class="koboSpan">From there the
trend was downwards towards the recession of the 1930s.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 5</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan"> started with a peak of freight rates in 1921.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">This was one of
the highest levels of earnings experienced for many years, and was the
result of an acute shortage of merchant shipping tonnage following the
World War I which ended in 1918. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.118.3"
class="koboSpan">During the closing years of this war German U-boat
activity had greatly depleted the merchant fleet, and the shipyards had
worked flat out to fill the gap. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.118.4"
class="koboSpan">The extent of the shortage ships can be judged from the
fact that according to Fairplay the second-hand price of a steamer
increased from £71,000 in 1915 to £258,000 in 1920.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.118.5" class="koboSpan">The rapid
expansion of shipyard capacity coincided with a peak in the world
business cycle in 1920, producing the peak in freight rates shown in the
chart.</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0127" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00127.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Three inter-war cycles 1921–1936" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_243"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0091" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0091"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
6:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">
Three inter-war cycles 1921–1936</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan"> Stopford (2009):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan"> (Routledge), Annex C</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 6</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan"> commenced with the downturn in the world economy in
1922 and freight rates fell sharply to a trough in 1925, by which time
the second-hand price of a steamer had collapsed to £60,000, one quarter
of the price paid five years earlier.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.127.2" class="koboSpan">There was a
brief recovery in freight rates during 1926.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 7</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan"> was short and not severe.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">Trade grew
rapidly between 1928 and 1930, but heavy production of new ships
continued to depress the market and rates fell slightly in 1927.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">By 1929 the
shipping industry was anticipating a full recovery next year, but this
expectation was not fulfilled.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 7</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan"> started in 1931 as the shipping industry moved into
the Great Depression of the 1930s.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.131.2" class="koboSpan">The Freight
Index slumped from 115 in 1929 to a trough of 85 in 1933, the lowest
ever recorded. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.131.3"
class="koboSpan">This recession was driven by an unprecedented collapse
in the volume of seaborne trade which fell by 25% between 1931 and 1934.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.131.4" class="koboSpan">The freight
index fell by 30% to operating costs and stayed there for five years
from 1930–1935. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.131.5"
class="koboSpan">However the best indicator of the severity of the
recession is second-hand prices. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.131.6"
class="koboSpan">Between 1933–1935 good quality second-hand ships were
sold at distress prices 80–90% below their previous peak, singling this
out as a depression rather than a recession.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.131.7" class="koboSpan">However
shipyard production responded very quickly, and by 1936 the market was
moving back towards recovery.</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Period 3: Shipping cycles, 1945–1975</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">The first 25 years
after World War II saw an extraordinary growth in sea trade, which
increased from 500 million tons in 1950 to 3.2 billion tons in 1973.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">Once again this
was a period of great technical change in the shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">This time the
change</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0128" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00128.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7: Cycles in the golden era 1947–1975" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_244"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0092" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0092"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
7:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">
Cycles in the golden era 1947–1975</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan"> Stopford (2009):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan"> (Routledge), Annex C</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">was not in the
technology of shipbuilding, but in the way the industry was organised.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">This was the
era when the liner and bulk shipping industries applied the principles
of mechanisation which were being adopted so effectively in
manufacturing production on land.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">Major shippers
in the energy and raw materials took the initiative in developing
integrated transport operations designed to reduce their transport
costs. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.141.4" class="koboSpan">The
trend towards specialisation and economies of scale was continuous and
pervasive.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">Against a background
of rapidly expanding demand, it was the shipbuilding industry which set
the commercial tone for the period.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.142.2" class="koboSpan">For the first
decade from 1945–1956 there was a shortage of shipbuilding capacity, due
to the destruction of the Japanese and German yards during the war.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.142.3" class="koboSpan">The result was
a decade of prosperity (see freight chart in
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0092" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0092"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.144.2"
class="koboSpan">Cycles 8 and 9 which occurred between 1945 and 1956
illustrate the cyclical mechanism at its most favourable.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.144.3" class="koboSpan">There were two
cyclical peaks, the first in 1952 which coincided with the Korean War
and the second in 1956 which was amplified by the closure of the Suez
Canal, greatly increasing the voyage time to the East from Europe.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.144.4" class="koboSpan">Unusually both
peaks lasted longer than the preceding trough, making this a golden age
for shipping, at least compared with the depression of the 1930s and the
four deep cycles before 1914. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.144.5"
class="koboSpan">Once the shipyards in Japan and Europe got going in the
late 1950s this changed and the cycles became longer and less
profitable.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 10</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">, which lasted from 1957 to
1966</span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan"> probably ranks third in severity behind the 1980s
recession and the 1930s recession.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.148.2" class="koboSpan">It was
triggered by an extreme combination of supply and demand developments.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.148.3" class="koboSpan">On the demand
side, the world economy had a severe downturn in 1957 (see
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0096" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0096"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 11</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">), and this resulted in a reduction in the volume of
seaborne trade, just as the world shipyards were expanding to meet the
massive investment demand placed during the 1956 Suez boom.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.150.2" class="koboSpan">The recession
was very severe in the late 1950s, and only started to show sign of
recovery in the early 1960s. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.150.3"
class="koboSpan">Freight</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0129" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00129.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 8: Three dry cargo cycles 1975–1995" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_245"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0093" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0093"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
8:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">
Three dry cargo cycles 1975–1995</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan"> Stopford (2009):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan"> (Routledge), Annex C</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">rates slumped to a low
level and stayed there for almost a decade.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.158.2" class="koboSpan">However this
low level of earnings is not a reliable guide to the cashflow of the
shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.158.3"
class="koboSpan">During the 1960s shippers placed many long-term time
charters for bulk carriers and tankers.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.158.4" class="koboSpan">These were
generally negotiated at levels which gave an adequate return on capital,
so the majority of shipowners had a firm cashflow, and only marginal
vessels were traded on the spot market, receiving the low rates reported
here. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.158.5" class="koboSpan">It was
really an extended period of weak rates.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 11</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan"> was short and not very deep.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.160.2" class="koboSpan">The market
finally peaked moderately in 1970 (the tanker market had a much stronger
peak). </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.160.3" class="koboSpan">Cycle 12
was even shorter. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.160.4"
class="koboSpan">The market slumped in 1971, and with a very large
orderbook analysts were predicting that the market would not recover
until 1976, proving once again how wrong forecasts can be.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.160.5" class="koboSpan">In 1973 the
market moved into one of the best peaks in its history.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">By the end of this
period shipbuilding output was geared to high growth, making the market
very sensitive to any small downturn.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.161.2" class="koboSpan">There were
profits to be made by those who judged the cycles correctly, but this
was a very competitive period.</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Period 4: Shipping cycles, 1975–1995</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">In the mid-1970s,
following the 1973 oil crisis, the shipping environment changed again.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.163.2" class="koboSpan">The fourth
section of our review brings a sequence of three cycles shown in
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0093" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0093"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 8</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">, each of which had a very different character.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">After two
decades of continuous growth there was a fall in sea trade in the
mid-1970s, followed by a major dip in the early 1980s.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.165.3" class="koboSpan">The scale of
this downturn in trade rivalled the 1930s in its severity.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.165.4" class="koboSpan">In the tanker
market the sprint for size lost momentum and the fleet, which had
previously been young and dynamic, grew old and sluggish.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.165.5" class="koboSpan">Shippers became
less confident about their future
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_246"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">transport requirements, and the role of tanker owners
as subcontractors gave way to an enlarged role as risk takers trading on
the “spot” market.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 12</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan"> started in the spring of 1975 when the dry cargo
market collapsed after the remarkable boom of 1974.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">The bigger
sizes of vessels had already started to move into recession during the
second half of 1974, but in 1975 even the small bulk carriers were
affected. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.3" class="koboSpan">This
downturn was triggered by a deep recession in the world economy, which
followed the 1973 oil crisis. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.4"
class="koboSpan">The steel industry was very depressed, with 20 to 30%
over capacity, and the chronic over tonnage in the tanker market forced
combined carriers into dry cargo, increasing the oversupply.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.5" class="koboSpan">In 1976 the
market remained depressed, though the trade volume was busy, and many
owners were beginning to face liquidity problems.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.6" class="koboSpan">About 5 million
deadweight of dry cargo ships and 6 million deadweight combos were in
lay-up. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.7" class="koboSpan">By 1977
the market had started to edge upwards, with an improvement in the steel
industry and the thermal coal trade which was benefitting from a high
oil prices. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.8"
class="koboSpan">However the real recovery came in 1979, driven by a 7%
growth in the major bulks and supply growth of only 2.5%, due to the
run-down of the order book. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.9"
class="koboSpan">Finally the boom reached a peak in 1980, driven by a
strong steel industry and heavy congestion in continental ore
discharging ports and the coal ports in the United States.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.168.10" class="koboSpan">This strong
bull market with one year time charter rates lasted until March 1981
when it started to collapse.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 13</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan"> certainly turned out to be unlucky for the dry bulk
shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.170.2"
class="koboSpan">Rates fell steadily during 1982 and the deep recession
in the world economy had a major impact on the movement of dry cargo.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.170.3" class="koboSpan">By 1983 the
one-year Time Charter rate for a Panamax bulk carrier was down to
\$4,700 a day, less than the operating cost of a 65,000 dwt ship
operating under the German flag. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.170.4"
class="koboSpan">However investors remained liquid from the high profits
earned during the previous three years and this triggered heavy
counter-cyclical investment in the “cheap” new bulk carriers being
offered by the shipyards. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.170.5"
class="koboSpan">The surge of deliveries which followed completely
swamped the recovery in the world economy which happened in 1985–86.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.170.6" class="koboSpan">Defaults on
time charters, and a long period when freight rates left owners with
little cash beyond the level required to pay operating expenses created
a serious liquidity crisis in the industry.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.170.7" class="koboSpan">As one broker’s
report put it “the equity was drained out of the industry”.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">By the summer of 1986
the financial distress was so great that a Panamax bulk carrier which
had recently been delivered for a price in excess of \$25 million could
be purchased for \$8 million. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.171.2"
class="koboSpan">Bankers found that their customers could not even meet
interest payments, and the collateral value of the ships had shrunk to a
fraction of their market value when the finance had been put in place.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.171.3" class="koboSpan">Some bankers
withdrew from the industry, foreclosing on loans and taking heavy
write-offs. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.171.4"
class="koboSpan">However like all shipping recessions, eventually supply
and demand adjusted, and by 1989 rates were back to the level of
1980.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 14</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan"> started off with a boom very much like the one
experienced in 1979 and 1980. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.173.2"
class="koboSpan">However the following years were quite different.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.173.3" class="koboSpan">Although there
was a recession in the world economy, bulk carrier investors had by now
become so conservative in their ordering activity that deliveries fell
to a very low level in the early 1990s.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.173.4" class="koboSpan">This meant that
Cycle 14 was unusually shallow, as is clearly apparent in
</span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
8</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0093)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.175.2"
class="koboSpan">Rates fell briefly to \$10,000 a day in 1992, after
which they recovered, reaching a new peak in 1995 (some might regard
this as a long plateau rather than a cycle).
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.175.3" class="koboSpan">The cycle ended
with an exceptionally firm market, with an acute shortage of handy bulk
carriers in the Pacific during the summer of that year.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.175.4" class="koboSpan">In April 1995
Panamax bulk carriers were earning \$17,000 per day and Capesize bulk
carriers \$25,000 per day, the highest ever recorded.</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0130" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00130.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 9: The great shipping cycle 1995–2008" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_247"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0094" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0094"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
9:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">
The great shipping cycle 1995–2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan"> Stopford (2009):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan"> (Routledge), Annex C</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">3.5 Period 5: Shipping Cycle 1995–2008</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">The next period got
off to a bad start. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.184.2"
class="koboSpan">As the market improved in the mid-1990s, the
conservative investment policy followed by the dry bulk market in the
early 1990s evaporated, and bulk carrier deliveries, which had fallen to
4.7 m dwt pa in 1992, increased to 18.7 million deadweight in 1998, just
as the Asia Crisis started to bite, driving the market down to a severe
trough.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan">Cycle 15</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">: The cycle bottomed out in 1998 and then, as
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0094" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0094"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 9</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows, the dry cargo market started a long upward
journey leading finally to a peak a decade later in the summer of 2008.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.188.2" class="koboSpan">This proved to
be the most extreme cycle in the history of shipping.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.188.3" class="koboSpan">During the boom
markets of 1995 (Cycle 14) Capesize bulk carriers had set a new record
of \$25,000 a day earnings, but in the summer of 2008 the peak fixture
for a Capesize bulk carrier was \$304,000 a day, and average earnings
for July 2008 were \$150,000 a day.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.188.4" class="koboSpan">At this point a
five-year-old second-hand Capesize bulk carrier, which could have been
purchased six years earlier for \$24 million, was worth \$160 million.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.188.5" class="koboSpan">The market
peaked in July, and then in September as the credit crisis deepened,
experienced one of the most extreme falls ever seen in the shipping
market. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.188.6" class="koboSpan">By
November 2008 Capesize bulk carriers were earning only \$2,500 a day.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.188.7" class="koboSpan">So Cycle 15 was
in every way as extreme as the 1980s, but this time in a generally
positive way.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">The explanation of
this cycle seems to have been a fortunate combination of events in the
shipping market. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.189.2"
class="koboSpan">On the demand side, following the two short recessions
of 1998 and 2001, the world economy embarked on five years of positive
growth with GNP for 2003–2008 averaging over 4% per annum growth, the
longest boom since the 1960s. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.189.3"
class="koboSpan">This prosperity was enhanced fir shipping Chinese
economic growth. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.189.4"
class="koboSpan">Starting in the late 1990s, Chinese industry grew very
rapidly, with surging exports of containerised goods and a major
infrastructure and real estate development programme which
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_248"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan">boosted Chinese steel production from 126 Mt in 2000 to
501 Mt in the year to June 2009. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.190.2"
class="koboSpan">This vastly exceeded expectations and shipping
investors had not ordered vessels in anticipation of the growing iron
ore imports. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.190.3"
class="koboSpan">The shortage of ships which developed was reinforced by
congestion as the iron ore and coal terminals could not cope with the
rapidly growing demand. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.190.4"
class="koboSpan">Just to complete the positive picture, the ships built
during the 1970s shipyard bubble were reaching 30 years of age and the
result was heavy scrapping. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.190.5"
class="koboSpan">Taken together this created five years of sustained and
exceptionally profitable earnings by dry bulk vessels.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.190.6" class="koboSpan">The fall in
late also 2008 followed a familiar pattern with an economic crisis
coinciding with increasing deliveries due to heavy investment during the
preceding boom.</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0131" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00131.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch09.xhtml_bck_fig0131)

</div>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_249"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">3.6 The length of cycles and volatility</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">If we look at the
statistics of the cycles we discussed in the previous section, we find
that between 1872 and 2008, the average shipping cycle had a frequency
of 7.7 years from peak to peak
(</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fig0131" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fig0131"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.195.2"
class="koboSpan">The average cycle length of 7.8 years over the period
1947–2008 was similar to the 7.6 years average between 1872 and 1936.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.195.3" class="koboSpan">This certainly
gives credibility to the shipping folk law that shipping cycles last
seven years.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.196.1" class="koboSpan">However only one of
the cycles actually lasted seven years.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.196.2" class="koboSpan">The longest was
13 years (from 1895–2008), one lasted ten years, three lasted nine
years, two five years and one lasted six years.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.196.3" class="koboSpan">So some cycles
were eight or nine years longer than others.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.196.4" class="koboSpan">A very big
difference to a business struggling to survive, so as a predictive
device this analysis is not much help!</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">Another aspect of the
cycle which it is useful to analyse is the variation in the frequency of
cycles. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.197.2" class="koboSpan">This
can be estimated by using the standard deviation of the cycle length,
measured from peak to peak. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.197.3"
class="koboSpan">This statistic is shown at the bottom of
</span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_fig0131)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan">, for three periods.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.199.2" class="koboSpan">Firstly the
average for the whole period 1872–2008; second the average for the first
period 1872–1937; and finally the average for the second period
1947–2008. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.199.3" class="koboSpan">Over
the whole period the standard deviation is 2.6 years.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.199.4" class="koboSpan">However cycles
in the earlier period had at standard deviation of 2.5 years, whilst the
later period had a standard deviation of 2.8 years.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">This is an interesting
result. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.200.2" class="koboSpan">We know
that provided the underlying data distribution is normal, the length of
a cycle is 95% certain to fall within a range plus or minus two standard
deviations of the mean. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.200.3"
class="koboSpan">On the basis of the last 50 years, we would expect
cycles to last between 2.1 years and 10.3 years.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.200.4" class="koboSpan">This confirms
the volatility of the shipping market and offers a warning to anyone
interested in the future of the shipping market.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.200.5" class="koboSpan">It is
comforting to predict that the market will improve next year (the famous
“hockey stick” forecasting model), but this analysis demonstrates that
rapid recoveries are not typical, though they do happen.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.200.6" class="koboSpan">This makes it
all the more important to study each cycle as a unique event, examine
the fundamentals and determine what factors will drive the next
cycle.</span>

## <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.201.2" class="koboSpan">Cyclical Mechanisms and the Causes of Cycles</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 The supply/demand model</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">So, having established
that the shipping market is cyclical, albeit in an irregular way, we now
need to explain what causes them.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.203.2" class="koboSpan">If we can do
that it offers the hope that we can use analysis to narrow down the
statistical uncertainty about the length of cycles discussed in the
previous section.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">The usual way to
analyse this process is the supply/demand model.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">Most economists
accept that the shipping market is driven by a competitive process in
which supply and demand interact to determine freight rates (see
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0095" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0095"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 10</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.206.2"
class="koboSpan">A change in the relative demand and supply of ships
leads to a shortage or surplus of tonnage, which in turn triggers an
increase or a reduction in freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.206.3" class="koboSpan">When demand
exceeds supply it drives freight rates up and the market responds by
investing in more new ships, which have now become very profitable.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.206.4" class="koboSpan">Conversely when
supply outstrips demand, competition drives freight rates down and
owners start to scrap uneconomic ships.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.206.5" class="koboSpan">Shipping cycles
can usually be explained by this supply; demand model, and indeed we saw
plenty of evidence</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0132" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00132.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 10" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_250"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0095" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0095"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
10</span></span></a>

</div>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">of this mechanism at
work in the preceding discussion of the freight cycles.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.209.2" class="koboSpan">It is useful to
distinguish exogenous and endogenous factors.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.209.3" class="koboSpan">An
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan">endogenous</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan"> factor is an event or mechanism within the shipping
market which triggers or accentuates a cycle, whilst an
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan">exogenous
</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">factor
is some external event such as a business cycle in the world economy
which triggers a cyclical pattern.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.213.2" class="koboSpan">Both are
important.</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Demand factors contributing to the shipping cycle</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">Starting with the
demand side of the model, by far the most important cause of shipping
cycles is the business cycle in the world economy.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.215.2" class="koboSpan">This injects a
cyclical pattern into the demand for ships which works through into sea
trade. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.215.3"
class="koboSpan">Historically there has been a close relationship
between cycles in world industrial production and cycles in seaborne
trade. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.215.4" class="koboSpan">This is
illustrated in </span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
11</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0096)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan"> which compares the percentage change in seaborne trade
with the percentage change in industrial production from 1951–2009.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.2" class="koboSpan">Although the
correlation is far from perfect, it certainly exists, especially during
extreme fluctuations in the world economy.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.3" class="koboSpan">During the
major economic crisis of 1957, 1973 (first oil crisis), 1981 (second oil
crisis), 1997 (Asia crisis), 2009 (credit Crisis) the correlation was
particularly clear. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.4"
class="koboSpan">In other years it was less marked, but still visible.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.5" class="koboSpan">Common sense
tells us that this is precisely what we should expect.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.6" class="koboSpan">When world
industry goes into recession the steel mills use less raw materials,
energy consumption drops, power stations import less coal and motorists
drive less, so the oil trade reduces.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.7" class="koboSpan">Cumulatively
this drags down the demand for sea transport.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.8" class="koboSpan">When the world
economy recovers the whole process reverses and the demand for seaborne
imports escalates. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.217.9"
class="koboSpan">In fact the majority of freight “booms” shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.218.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0087)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan"> coincided with peaks in the economic cycle.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">Why does the world
economy have cycles? </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.220.2"
class="koboSpan">There has been much academic study of these short
cycles in the world economy, which were identified by J Kitchin
(1923).</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0270" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0270"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan"> He suggested that these cycles were due to businesses
over-estimating inventory requirements during cyclical upswings, and
then cutting back too much during recessions.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.222.2" class="koboSpan">This injected
volatility into their purchasing activity, which tended to accentuate
the</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0133" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00133.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 11: Comparison of cycles in world GDP and seaborne trade" /></span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_251"></span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0096" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0096"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
11:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">
Comparison of cycles in world GDP and seaborne trade</span>
