<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan"> Compiled by Martin Stopford from United Nations,
Fearnleys, various</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">downswing of the cycle
and emphasise the upswing. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.228.2"
class="koboSpan">Whilst this explanation does not demonstrate the
original cause of the fluctuations, it suggests that once the economy
starts to “vibrate” this endogenous mechanism will tend to emphasise the
“vibrations” making them more clearly identifiable as cycles.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">Another mechanism
which contributes to the business cycle is the multiplier and
accelerator. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.229.2"
class="koboSpan">This mechanism leads to cycles because when the economy
picks up and an increase in investment occurs, it raises income by a
larger amount (the investment multiplier), which in turn may produce an
increase in demand for the product (the income accelerator) generating
demand for more investment goods, so that the economic system expands
rapidly. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.229.3"
class="koboSpan">Eventually labour and capital become fully utilised and
the expansion is sharply halted, throwing the whole process into
reverse. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.229.4" class="koboSpan">This
creates a basic instability in the economic ‘machine’.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">Investigation of this
type of cycle in the nineteenth century was carried out by
Juglar</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0271" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0271"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan"> who studied cycles in France, the United States and
England, and from this concluded that there is a longer cycle of about
seven to 12 years driven by investment.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.232.2" class="koboSpan">The basic
mechanism is similar to the Kitchin cycle in that it is built around
systematic under correction and over correction, but in this case the
variable at work is investment. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.232.3"
class="koboSpan">During the upswing there is a tendency to invest
heavily in plant and machinery, but once the peak is reached and
capacity is more than sufficient to meet demand, investment activity
slows sharply and less works back into the economy through a multiplier
effect to generate a sharp downswing.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">Another major factor
influencing the demand for ships are economic shocks which suddenly
change the demand for sea transport.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.233.2" class="koboSpan">Shock factors
from recent years include the oil crises of 1973 and 1979, the Asia
Crisis in 1997 and the Gulf war in 1990–1991.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.233.3" class="koboSpan">By their nature
these events are unpredictable, but that does not reduce their
importance.</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_252"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.234.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Supply factors contributing to shipping cycles</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">The main cyclical
force on the supply side of the shipping market is the investment cycle
and in particular the time lag between ordering a new ship and taking
delivery. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.235.2"
class="koboSpan">Depending on the state of the shipyard orderbook and
the type of ship being ordered, this can be anything from 18 months to
three years, and during this period ship demand may have changed.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.235.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
shipowners often place large numbers of orders during the peak of the
market cycle when freight rates are high and second-hand ships look
expensive compared with new buildings.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.235.4" class="koboSpan">If the freight
market peak is driven by a world business cycle, by the time the ships
are delivered it is quite likely that the world economy will have
plunged into recession, dragging down freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.235.5" class="koboSpan">As a result,
the new ships arrive in the market just at the time when they are least
needed, driving down freight rates even further.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.235.6" class="koboSpan">Naturally this
discourages shipowners from ordering new ships, and the whole process is
thrown into reverse. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.235.7"
class="koboSpan">Few orders are placed, so when the world economy
recovers a few years later, few new ships are being ordered and this
reinforces the upward trend in freight rates.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.236.1" class="koboSpan">The historical review
of freight cycles in section 3 provided plenty of evidence that this
time lag mechanism has been a great part of the shipping cycle for at
least the last 140 years. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.236.2"
class="koboSpan">Surely shipowners should by now have learnt their
lesson and developed a strategy of counter-cyclical ordering?
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.236.3" class="koboSpan">In fact there
are numerous examples of precisely this happening.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.236.4" class="koboSpan">For example in
the early 1980s shipowners ordered many small bulk carriers at the
trough of the recession, and the same thing happened in 1999 after the
Asia crisis. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.236.5"
class="koboSpan">They argued that the ships were cheap and they would
take delivery in the upswing. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.236.6"
class="koboSpan">Unfortunately it is difficult to beat the market.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.236.7" class="koboSpan">On both
occasions when the world economy recovered, heavy deliveries of new
ships kept freight rates down. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.236.8"
class="koboSpan">Counter-cyclical ordering just meant that the shipping
market missed out on its “boom”, demonstrating that shipowners need to
be quite clever to “beat the cycle”.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">One of the most
important factors driving at the shipping cycle is market sentiment.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.237.2" class="koboSpan">The delays
between economic decisions and their implementation can make cyclical
fluctuations more extreme. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.237.3"
class="koboSpan">Many years ago Professor Pigou put forward the theory
of “non-compensated
errors”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fn0272" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0272"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan"> If people act independently, their errors cancel out,
but if they act in an imitative manner a particular trend will build up
to a level where they can affect the whole economic system.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.239.2" class="koboSpan">Thus periods of
optimism or pessimism become self-fulfilling through the medium of stock
exchanges, financial booms and the behaviour of investors.</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 Secular trends and structural factors impacting on cycles</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">Finally there are
long-term structural factors to consider.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.241.2" class="koboSpan">It was clear
from the review of cycles in section 3 that during some periods the
shipping industry faced very different characteristics from others.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.241.3" class="koboSpan">For example
1870–1914, 1950–1973 and 1995–2008 were periods of brisk demand growth.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.241.4" class="koboSpan">The shipping
cycles were clearly influenced by these currents in the economic
fundamentals of supply and demand, and contributed significantly to the
“market tone” over extended periods.
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_fig0134" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_fig0134"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows my assessment of these factors during the period
under review, ranked by the relative prosperity of</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0134" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_253"></span>[](#Ch09.xhtml_bck_fig0134)

[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00134.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch09.xhtml_bck_fig0134)

</div>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">the shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.245.2" class="koboSpan">We can briefly
summarise the impact which the alignment of the fundamentals had on
market conditions in the following terms:</span>

1.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
    class="koboSpan">Prosperity</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
    class="koboSpan">: Top of the list was the prosperous 1950s when
    rapidly growing demand coincided with a shortage of shipbuilding
    capacity.</span>
2.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
    class="koboSpan">Competitive</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
    class="koboSpan">: There were three periods of intensely competitive
    activity characterised by growing trade and shipbuilding capacity
    that expanded fast enough to keep up with demand.</span>
3.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
    class="koboSpan">Weak:</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
    class="koboSpan"> There was a weak market in the 1920s when growing
    demand was damped by over-capacity in the shipbuilding market</span>
4.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
    class="koboSpan">Depression</span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
    class="koboSpan">: There were two depressions, in the 1930s and the
    1980s when falling trade coincided with shipbuilding
    over-capacity</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan">Analysis of these
long-term cycles in supply and demand is an area where maritime
economists do have something to say.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.254.2" class="koboSpan">The challenge
is to help the shipping industry remember the past and anticipate the
future. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.254.3" class="koboSpan">To do
this models can be used to improve the clarity of the analysis message
with better information, improved analysis, clearer presentation and
greater relevance to the decisions made in the commercial shipping
market.</span>

## <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.255.2" class="koboSpan">The Dynamics of Shipping Cycles</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">So far in this chapter
we have concentrated on the dynamics of the shipping supply/demand
model. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.256.2" class="koboSpan">The
freight market analysis suggests that there is a cyclical component in
the shipping market generated by business cycles in the world economy
and reinforced by the time-lag taken to adjust supply to demand and the
frequent miscalculation by shipowners of the future level of demand.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.256.3" class="koboSpan">We now need to
ask two questions: first, “How do business cycles feed through into the
key variables in which the shipowner is interested – freight rates and
prices?” </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.256.4" class="koboSpan">and,
secondly, “Are the cycles predictable?”</span>

### <span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_254"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Do business cycles affect freight rates?</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">The simplest way to
deal with the first question is statistical analysis comparing the
historic pattern of cycles in the world economy, seaborne trade and
freight rates. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.258.2"
class="koboSpan">To make such an analysis it is necessary to analyse
these variables into a form in which they are directly comparable.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.258.3" class="koboSpan">The technique
used is to take a five-year moving average for the basic statistical
series and compute the deviation of the actual observation from the
five-year trend. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.258.4"
class="koboSpan">When the variable moves above zero this indicates a
cyclical upswing or “boom” and when the variable swings below zero it
indicates a depression. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.258.5"
class="koboSpan">The analysis for the dry cargo trade in
</span>[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
11</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0096)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicates the remarkable degree to which the world
business cycle has influenced dry cargo trade since 1970.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.260.2" class="koboSpan">There has been
a series of alternating peaks and troughs, with particularly severe
troughs which followed the 1973 and 1979 oil crises and the 1999 Asia
crisis. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.260.3" class="koboSpan">It is
worth making the point that the use of OECD industrial production to
represent world economic activity is a statistical convenience that
becomes less valid as the Third World takes a larger share of world
economic activity. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.260.4"
class="koboSpan">The problem in carrying out an analysis of this type is
the difficulty of obtaining a long, but up-to-date, time series for
world industrial output.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.261.1" class="koboSpan">Turning to the
financial variables,
</span><a href="#Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0097" id="Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0097"><span
id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 12</span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the relationship between dry cargo cycles and
cycles in the dry cargo freight rate.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.263.2" class="koboSpan">The correlation
is close, with freight market booms coinciding with trade booms in 1974,
1980, 1989, 1995 and 2008. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.263.3"
class="koboSpan">This indicates that in the dry cargo market the growth
rate of dry cargo trade has, in the past been an good indicator of
freight rate movements, though not a precise one.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.263.4" class="koboSpan">It is, however,
necessary to be cautious in extrapolating this relationship into the
future,</span>

<div id="Ch09.xhtml_fig0135" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00135.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 12: Cycles in dry cargo trade and one year TC" /></span>

<a href="#Ch09.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0097" id="Ch09.xhtml_cap_lbl0097"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
12:</span></span></a><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.266.1" class="koboSpan">
Cycles in dry cargo trade and one year TC</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">author</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_255"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan">since determination of freight rates depends upon
supply as well as demand. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.269.2"
class="koboSpan">During the period covered by this analysis the supply
of dry cargo vessels was broadly in line with the demand on a trend
basis. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.269.3" class="koboSpan">As a
result, peaks in trade caused a shortage of shipping capacity, so that
freight rates rose, whilst recession in sea trade caused a surplus of
shipping capacity and freight rates fell.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.269.4" class="koboSpan">This pattern
will not occur if there is a permanent mis-alignment between supply and
demand, as happened in the tanker market.</span>

## <span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.270.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.270.2" class="koboSpan">Are Business Cycles Predictable?</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">Our analysis of the
shipping market has raised several warning flags about the dangers of
relying on simple “rules of thumb” about the cyclical nature of the
shipping market, but it has also shown the importance of the industrial
business cycle in determining the underlying performance of seaborne
trade and freight rates. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.271.2"
class="koboSpan">Inevitably this raises the question of whether business
cycles are predictable.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.272.1" class="koboSpan">The statistical
analysis discussed earlier in the chapter offered convincing evidence
that the concept of a regular seven-year cycle has little merit as a way
of predicting the future of market.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.272.2" class="koboSpan">In reality the
cycles may be three years or 10 years in length.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.272.3" class="koboSpan">From a
practical business perspective that is much too wide a range to be
acceptable, so we must look elsewhere.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.273.1" class="koboSpan">Our analysis of supply
demand models suggested that this might be a fruitful avenue.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.273.2" class="koboSpan">Although there
are far too many variables at work to hope to predict cycles accurately,
at least analysis of world economy and the shipping investment cycle can
help to narrow down the possibilities which lie ahead, and give decision
makers some idea of the risks which they are of taking.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.273.3" class="koboSpan">Indeed one of
the most useful applications of the supply demand model is to examine
the impact of the shipping investment cycle.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.273.4" class="koboSpan">One lesson
which is all too apparent from the historical analysis of shipping
cycles is the extent to which the market is driven by supply-side
factors, and in particular the ordering activity of shipowners.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.273.5" class="koboSpan">Analysts often
deplore the fact that shipowners order at the top of a cycle, but when
they try “counter-cyclical” ordering at the bottom of the cycle, the
result can be equally disastrous.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">On the demand side of
the market, business cycles are clearly a dominant force, though one
which can be very difficult to predict.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.274.2" class="koboSpan">However the
historical analysis suggests that it is vital to be aware of the
possibility of serious recessions in demand.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.274.3" class="koboSpan">The two really
serious depressions in the shipping industry both coincided with a major
depression in the world economy (in 1931 and 1983), so provided we can
obtain some forewarning of these factors that can be very helpful.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.274.4" class="koboSpan">Statisticians
have, over the years, developed leading indicators that give an advance
indication of turning points in the economy.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.274.5" class="koboSpan">For example,
the OECD publishes a leading indicators index, which is based on orders,
stocks, the amount of overtime worked, the number of workers laid off,
in addition to financial statistics such as money supply, company
profits and stock market prices. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.274.6"
class="koboSpan">It is suggested that the turning point in the lead
index will anticipate a similar turning point in the industrial
production index by about six months.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.274.7" class="koboSpan">To the analyst
of short-term market trends such information is helpful.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.275.1" class="koboSpan">In conclusion, whilst
we can usefully employ the concept of a “cycle” to discuss fluctuations
in seaborne trade, cyclical peaks and troughs do not follow in an
orderly progression. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.275.2"
class="koboSpan">As the graphs show, seaborne trade generally recovers
from each trough, but it is difficult to say in which year this will
occur or how strong the recovery will be.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.275.3" class="koboSpan">We must take
many other factors into account before drawing such a conclusion.</span>

## <span id="Ch09.xhtml_page_256"></span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.276.2" class="koboSpan">Summary</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">In this chapter we
started by observing that the shipping market can change very quickly
and that decisions by shipowners about the sale, purchase and chartering
of vessels depend crucially upon timing.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.277.2" class="koboSpan">In the space of
a few months the market value of a vessel may change by millions of
dollars. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.277.3" class="koboSpan">The
cycles are certainly not regular, appearing as fluctuations in revenue
of variable length. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.277.4"
class="koboSpan">Different market segments, especially tankers and bulk
carriers have exhibited similar cyclical patterns during some periods,
but in others they have diverged significantly, suggesting that each
segment of the shipping market must be treated separately.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.277.5" class="koboSpan">We also noted
that cycles in shipping revenue work through into cycles in the price of
second-hand assets.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">A cycle is defined as
an interval of time during which one sequence of a regularly recurring
sequence of events is completed. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.278.2"
class="koboSpan">In section 3 we set about reviewing the sequence of
fluctuations in freight rates which have occurred during the period
1869–2008. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.278.3" class="koboSpan">A
total of 15 cycles were identified, with an average length of 7.7 years
and a standard deviation of 2.6 years.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.278.4" class="koboSpan">Although this
confirms the “rule-of-thumb” that shipping cycles last seven years, the
standard deviation suggests that this specific outcome is not
particularly likely. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.278.5"
class="koboSpan">At a 95% confidence level we can expect shipping cycles
to last between 2.1 years and 10.3 years.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">In the absence of
regularity, the best approach to analysing cycles is to understand their
causes, and this was discussed in Section 4.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.279.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping cycles
are a manifestation of fluctuations in supply and demand and freight
rates are highly sensitive to quite small movements in either of these
variables. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.279.3" class="koboSpan">On
the demand side of the market the main driving force is the world
business cycle, and reference was made to the short business cycles
identified by Kitchin and the longer investment cycles identified by
Juglar. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.279.4" class="koboSpan">These
introduce volatility into the demand side of the market, though random
economic shocks occur such as the 1973 oil crisis or the closure of the
Suez Canal in 1956.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">On the supply side of
the market the outstanding influence is the investment cycle, as
shipowners struggle to match investment to the essentially unpredictable
demand cycles. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.280.2"
class="koboSpan">The genuine uncertainty which triggers these
supply-side fluctuations is reinforced by a market sentiment which
Professor Pigou first identified as “non-compensatory errors”.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">Finally we noted the
long-term secular trends which set the tone for the shipping market over
periods of the 20 or 30 years. </span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.281.2"
class="koboSpan">These trends are characterised by differences in the
underlying growth rate of seaborne trade, due to economic developments
in the world economy, and the level of shipbuilding capacity.</span>

<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">In view of their lack
of regularity, the best hope of predicting business cycles is to analyse
the underlying causes and project them forward.
</span><span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.282.2" class="koboSpan">Many analysts
use computer models for this purpose, and although the forecasts may not
always be accurate, they help to narrow down uncertainty and give
decision-makers a better feel for the way things might develop.</span>

[<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch09.xhtml_bck_fn0261)<span id="Ch09.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan">Clarkson Research Studies, London, UK.

class="koboSpan">martin.stopford@clarksons.com</span>](mailto:martin.stopford@clarksons.com)</span>

<div class="footnote" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Recreating the Profit and Loss Account of Voyages of the Distant Past</span>](#Preface1.xhtml_bck_ht0244)

## <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">The study of
historical freight rate fluctuations over the previous two centuries has
attracted the attention of several economists both maritime and
non-shipping specialists. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">The nature of these studies varies and could be
sub-divided in descending order of profusion into:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">long term shipping
    productivity gains and associated secular fall in across the board
    ocean freight rates;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">single route
    specific studies;</span>
3.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">the nature and
    periodicity of cyclical fluctuations;</span>
4.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">construction of
    freight rate indices;</span>
5.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">the contribution
    of falling freight rates to the reduction in barriers to
    trade;</span>
6.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">returns on capital
    to shipping investors; and</span>
7.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">port productivity
    trend developments</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">The literature is
growing at exponential rate yet in certain respects the accumulation of
knowledge at times resembles more a "Copernican" lens approach.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">It sorely lacks
a "Newtonian" methodical tidying up system.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.27.3" class="koboSpan">The appendix
contains a non-exhaustive list of such studies.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.27.4" class="koboSpan">However, in
spirit the closest pro-genitor of the present one, is Lewis (1941),
which to our knowledge has never been referenced in the subsequent
shipping literature.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">Empirical
investigations have been constrained by the nature of available data
with the lowest hanging fruit collected first.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">In general data
on freight rates proliferate. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.28.3"
class="koboSpan">This has encouraged several studies of type (a), (b),
(c), (d) and (e) above.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Contrary to this, data
on shipping profits is scant hence type (f) studies are rare.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.29.2" class="koboSpan">In theory one
could recreate the profit and loss account of a benchmark ship by using
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_260"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">a bottom up approach.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">Here the
economic historian starts with the easily available freight rate data.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.3" class="koboSpan">He then makes
certain deductions for costs and divides by the length of the voyage in
days to arrive at a measure of unit profit.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.4" class="koboSpan">However, the
input requirements of sufficient accuracy through the various steps are
very stringent. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.5"
class="koboSpan">Thus, to our knowledge, only Davis (1957), Evans (1964)
and Vergottis (2005) have attempted such a task for the periods
1670–1730, 1850–1860 and 1950–1974 respectively.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.6" class="koboSpan">An alternative
approach is to unearth historic actual voyage accounts.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.7" class="koboSpan">Here Kaukiainen
(1990) is the prime example but a rather solitary one.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.8" class="koboSpan">The third
alternative, is a detailed analysis of the market performed by an
industry expert of the bygone era who had full command of the facts.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.9" class="koboSpan">This is in
contrast to the economic historian of today who tries to recreate the
puzzle from fragments of surviving information.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.30.10" class="koboSpan">Such a jewel
of expert witness analysis, is equally rare but Allen (1855), provides a
thorough and exhaustive evaluation of the Tyne/London collier route and
the comparative advantage of steam versus sail in that market.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
historical analysis of port productivity trend developments of type (g),
are also extremely rare and sketchy.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.31.2" class="koboSpan">This is despite
certain valiant efforts notably by North (1968).
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.31.3" class="koboSpan">Where they do
exist they tend to be of descriptive rather than quantitative nature, as
the required time series data is hard to assemble.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">Archaeologists can
infer the existence of cities, their economic activities, trading links,
wars etc from little more than pottery shreds.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">In our case the
existence of freight rate data, which generally is very good, represent
the pottery fragments. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.32.3"
class="koboSpan">These can be used to "unearth" the complete picture of
the centuries old tramp ship operator economics and their time charter
equivalent profits ("TCE"), relating to voyages of the distant past.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.32.4" class="koboSpan">Accordingly
this article presents a hitherto unutilised fourth alternative to shed
light on the darkest areas of shipping literature, dealing with
profitability of ships and port productivity developments of the distant
past. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.32.5" class="koboSpan">This
alternative is a cliometric model which utilizes a multi-route network
top down approach. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.32.6"
class="koboSpan">Here the inter-relationship of freights over the cycle
is analysed in tandem, across several route arteries of the chosen
network. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.32.7" class="koboSpan">The
network cliometric top down approach makes use of the cardinal rule of
tramp shipping. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.32.8"
class="koboSpan">According to this rule, arbitrage forces quickly equate
the daily time charter equivalent earnings of all routes for ships of
the same type, engaged in them simultaneously.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">In the case of a
stable network of routes where, as first approximation, vessel speed is
treated as given over the cycle, the tramp arbitrage law results in a
cliometric system of linear equations of disarming simplicity.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">All that is
required is:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">minimum of two
    export outlets combined with two import destinations;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">synchronous
    freight rate observations across the 2×2 network at two distinct
    points in the cycle, say "cycle low" and "cycle high".</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">These eight freight
rate data points can mathematically reveal the hidden profit and loss of
the tramp arbitrageur in all its essential details route by route
including the following hitherto unknowns:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">port turnaround
    time;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">vessel and cargo
    related port charges as per "custom of the trade";</span>
3.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">time charter
    equivalent profit.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_261"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan">This is done with the minimum of knowledge regarding
the commercial characteristics of the representative tramper, such as
cargo capacity, speed, fuel consumption and bunker prices.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.40.2" class="koboSpan">Freight rate
and bunker price data are generally readily available.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.40.3" class="koboSpan">The skeleton
commercial specification of the typical tramper of various eras is also
generally known.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the implied
system of linear equations is recursive and can be solved first for port
turnaround time, then for port charges and then for time charter
equivalent profit. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.41.2"
class="koboSpan">This holds the promise that the most obscure subsets of
shipping literature may be illuminated by taking a methodical top down
cliometric tramp arbitrage approach.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.41.3" class="koboSpan">It also
suggests the potential for new insights across the whole spectrum of
maritime economic history. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.41.4"
class="koboSpan">It helps to tidy up and systematize several strands of
shipping research.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Armstrong (1993),
highlights the risks of using inferred data as substitute for the raw
original. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.2"
class="koboSpan">Parallel to cliometric approaches such as the one
suggested in this article, the more stringent and time consuming process
of searching for lost original data should be pursued.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.3" class="koboSpan">Modern IT
technology holds the promise that one day such data on port turnaround
performance may be "unearthed", collated and analysed.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.4" class="koboSpan">However even
then there would be certain risks in linking recorded freight rate time
series to observed vessel port turnaround performance measurements.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.5" class="koboSpan">On the one
hand, in tramp shipping, the recorded freight rate time series reflects
what was agreed in the loading and discharge clauses of a charter party.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.6" class="koboSpan">It does not
necessarily reflect what was actually achieved by ships at the ports.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.7" class="koboSpan">Thus one needs
to unearth old charter parties rather than port arrival and departure
records. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.8" class="koboSpan">On the
other hand, during sail ship days and early steamship era, such clauses
often amounted to no more than the phrase “as per custom of the port”.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.9" class="koboSpan">To make matters
worse, the sharing of terminal costs between shipowner and charterer
varies and can be ad hoc from contract to contract.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.10" class="koboSpan">Once again
this necessitates the tracing and analysis of the detailed wording of
several clauses of very old and most likely untraceable charter party
contracts. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.42.11" class="koboSpan">The
cliometric top down approach presented here overcomes all these issues
though the cautionary note of Armstrong is recognised.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">In our view, the ideal
approach should combine "easy to develop" cliometric calculations with
"needle in haystack" efforts to retrieve original data.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.43.2" class="koboSpan">These can act
as a reality check on each other and provide a framework for
interpretation and analysis. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.43.3"
class="koboSpan">In this spirit, at the end of this article, we go one
step further and explore a bottom up analysis of tramp route
profitability using all types of information and methodologies available
to the economic historian.</span>

### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">1.1 The cliometric top down framework</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">Without loss of
generality and in order to simplify exposition consider first the
sailing ship era where cost of fuel was zero.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">The time
charter equivalent earnings on any route are given by the following
formula:</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0136" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00136.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">E time charter
equivalent earnings ("TCE")</span>\
<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">F freight rate per
unit of cargo</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_262"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">C cargo size</span>\
<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">T terminal charges at
all ports involved</span>\
<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">S total time in
sailing/transit between all ports involved</span>\
<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">P total time spent for
queuing, loading, discharge at all ports involved</span>\
<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">V defined as S + P:
complete voyage duration</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">The cliometric
investigation starts by noting that equation (1) can be reformulated
as:</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0137" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00137.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0138" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00138.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">Thus the freight rate
of each route is made of two components.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">The first
component α, is route specific and varies with the idiosyncratic port
charges. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.59.3" class="koboSpan">The
second component β\*Ε, implies that all freight rates move up and down
in tandem with the common time charter equivalent market rate.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.59.4" class="koboSpan">However, the
β-sensitivity of each route to the broader market time charter earnings,
is also idiosyncratic and reflects the voyage duration.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.59.5" class="koboSpan">In turn the
voyage duration β, can be subdivided into a steaming time component and
a port turnaround time element.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">Our rudimentary
cliometric model treats F, C and S as known inputs and then solves for
the unkowns P, T, E and V. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.60.2"
class="koboSpan">More sophisticated versions can be developed whereby
the latter list of unknowns grows "at the expense" of the former list of
known inputs.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">In passing it is noted
that equation (2) suggests that a freight rate index can be constructed
by simply taking the arithmetic average of rates across several routes.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">The index then
represents the theoretical freight rate for the network "average route".
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.61.3" class="koboSpan">The α of the
index is the mean α of all the routes in the network, and thus captures
the average port charges across all routes.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.61.4" class="koboSpan">Similarly, the
index will capture the mean β of all the routes, representing average
voyage duration.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">1.1.1 Network stability</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">The notion of "regime
change" and its opposite "network structure stability" is introduced
here, before proceeding with the rest of the analysis.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.63.2" class="koboSpan">We define
"network structure stability" as a situation where the parameters α and
β in equation (2) remain stable over a certain period of time for a
certain network of routes for each of its arteries of complete round
voyages. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">In the
case of the constant α, this will tend to hold true by the fact that
port charges are tariff based and can remain unchanged for decades.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.63.4" class="koboSpan">In case of the
slope co-efficient β, this will tend to trend lower with productivity
changes in either or both the sailing speed of ships and/or their port
turnaround times. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.63.5"
class="koboSpan">Also the change of trade flows, the inversion between
fronthaul and backhaul routes and the triangulation of previous singular
routes imply "regime change".</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">Both α and β have been
reducing over the span of decades.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.64.2" class="koboSpan">However over a
typical full cycle of say five years’ duration, may be considered as
approximately constant. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.64.3"
class="koboSpan">One should not naively make such an assumption.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.64.4" class="koboSpan">Fortunately
"network structure stability" can be tested.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.64.5" class="koboSpan">This can be
done either visually by plotting several freight rates on the same chart
or in scatter plots. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.64.6"
class="koboSpan">It can also be tested via econometric means.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.64.7" class="koboSpan">Regarding the
latter, we note that equation (2) implies all freight rates in different
arteries of the
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_263"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">same stable network will be linearly related to each
other. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">Hence a
scatter plot of two freight rate time series should closely resemble a
straight line in case of network stability.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">The
cross-correlation matrix of the freight rates of all arterial routes
should be populated with one not just on the diagonal but on all
off-diagonal entries, in the absence of "regime change".
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.65.4" class="koboSpan">Off course in
working with stochastic versions of the above equations one should
tolerate certain deviation from the limiting pure ideal of 100%
correlation and pure straight line scatter plot patterns.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">"Regime change" is not
necessarily bad for the econometric investigation.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">Normally it can
be identified (e.g., the point when a fronthaul route reverts to
backhaul status can be easily detected) and thus controlled for.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">It produces a
richer set of equations recombining the same parameters.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.66.4" class="koboSpan">This can be
exploited in order to calculate the unknown parameters with better
statistical accuracy.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">1.1.2 The cliometric mathematical system of equations</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Given a minimum of two
export outlets ("X" and "Y") and two import destinations ("M" and "N"),
the tramp arbitrage rule results in the following system of
equations:</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0139" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00139.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">F</span><sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">xm </span></sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">reight rate on route linking export port X to import
destination M</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span><sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan">xm</span></sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan"> = T</span><sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan"> + T</span><sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">; terminal charges at each end from export port X to
import destination M</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">S</span><sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">xm</span></sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan"> sailing transit time from export port X to import
destination M (round voyage basis)</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">P</span><sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">xm</span></sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan"> = P</span><sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan"> + P</span><sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></sub><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">; port turnaround time at export port X and import
destination M</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">and similarly for
other permutations of the subscripts.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">The
superscripts L and H represent "cycle low" and "cycle high"
observations.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">At this stage we treat
cargo size C as fixed across routes and through the cycle for the
benchmark tramp ship just to simplify exposition.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">In the
econometric application presented below this restriction is
relaxed.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">The recursive nature
of the system can be exploited by taking the difference between "cycle
high" and "cycle low" observations, which allows the unknown terminal
charges to drop out of the picture.</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0140" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00140.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_264"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan">This results in three equations and four unknowns, the
latter being the port turnaround times for the round voyages.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">To close the
system equation (12) is added:</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0141" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00141.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">Equations (9)–(12) can
be solved for the unknown round voyage port turnaround times.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">The next step involves
taking either equations (3)–(5) or (6)–(8) and adding the following
equation (13) to close the system and solve for terminal charges:</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0142" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00142.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Finally time charter
equivalent earnings E can be calculated for any stage of the cycle, as
all the formerly unknowns that enter a round voyage TCE calculation have
been solved for.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">In case where there
are more export and import points than the simple 2×2 network described
above, the resulting system of linear equations is over-determined.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.101.2" class="koboSpan">A subset of
equations suffices to solve for the unknowns.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.101.3" class="koboSpan">In econometric
analysis using stochastic versions of the equations, it offers the
advantage of using additional information to derive results and stress
test them for accuracy and robustness through statistical means.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">Moving on the
steamship era, the cost of bunkers has to be factored into equation (1).
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">The
engineering technology of representative trampers is well recorded.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.3" class="koboSpan">Harley (1970)
provides a succinct summary. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.4"
class="koboSpan">Consumption of bunkers for a given speed of the
benchmark tramp ship is documented and considered as known input number
in our cliometric model. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.5"
class="koboSpan">Price of bunkers is also readily available.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.6" class="koboSpan">Hence the
bunker cost per tonne of cargo carried can be calculated.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.7" class="koboSpan">For ease of
computation, the imputed bunker cost per tonne is deducted from the
recorded freight rate per tonne.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.8" class="koboSpan">Thus "net of
bunkers freight rates" are derived.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.9" class="koboSpan">The rest of
the analysis can then proceed precisely as has been presented above for
the sail ship era. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.102.10"
class="koboSpan">Once again more sophisticated cliometric models can be
developed which solve for bunker consumption and speed rather than treat
these as assumed known inputs.</span>

### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">1.2 Case study: the Northern European coastal coal freight market 1848–1936</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">The Northern European
coastal coal freight market represents a neat compact network of routes
to apply the various methodologies described above.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">The two main
export outlets are Tyne (Newcastle, Blyth, Wear) and Wales (Cardiff,
Swansea). </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.104.3" class="koboSpan">The
main import destinations are London, Hamburg, Havre, Rouen, Caen, St
Malo, Dieppe, Honfleur and Brest.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.104.4" class="koboSpan">It is well
known that shipping coal out of the main export UK outlets to nearby
UK/North European ports was predominantly a one way market.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.104.5" class="koboSpan">Tramp coasters
departed from Tyne or Wales loaded with coal, discharged their cargo in
nearby destinations and ballasted back to the load ports empty.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Some routes are more
liquid than others and offer more regular and complete freight rate time
series. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.105.2" class="koboSpan">Weekly
freight rate data with certain gaps have been assembled for the period
1848 to 1936. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.105.3"
class="koboSpan">For the purpose of this study and subsequent
investigations
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_265"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">around 42,000 freight rate data points were collected
spanning almost a century of cyclical swings and trend developments.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">The process of
data collection is ongoing.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">1.2.1 Historic backdrop 1848–1936</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">At the beginning of
our overall study the 300 tonne collier sail ship reigned supreme.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">In summer 1852
the first 650 dwt tonne steamer was introduced in the Tyne/London route.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.108.3" class="koboSpan">After minor
teething problems, the concept quickly proved successful.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.108.4" class="koboSpan">Thus by 1870
steamers had practically displaced the sailing collier in many of the
Northern European coastal routes.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.108.5" class="koboSpan">The size of
coastal steamers increased progressively with about 1,000 dwt tonnes
being the representative tramper during the period 1880–1900.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.108.6" class="koboSpan">The average
size of coastal collier increased rapidly after the turn of the
nineteenth century with 1,450 dwt vessel becoming the benchmark coastal
tramper by 1910. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.108.7"
class="koboSpan">By 1936, a combination of economic, industrial and
political factors resulted in severe shrinkage of the North European
near-sea coal freight market. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.108.8"
class="koboSpan">This delineates the end of our investigation
period.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">1.2.2 Preliminary tests of network stability</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">The simple tramp
arbitrage model suggests that freight rate observations on a basket of
routes that are part of stable network should be 100% correlated with
each other. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.110.2"
class="koboSpan">Starting with the sail ship era,
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_cap_lbl0098"
id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0098"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the freight rate patterns for three of the major
routes during the period summer 1848 to winter 1859.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.112.2" class="koboSpan">If there is a
flaw in the conceptual model, a simple chart would normally reveal it
easier than "black box" computations.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">The figure highlights
the close correlation between the various routes during the sail ship
era. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.113.2" class="koboSpan">It also
shows that the London short haul route has a low beta as one would
expect given that the slope coefficient, against the unobservable common
time charter equivalent, is proportional to voyage duration.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">Numeric correlations
are provided in
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0144" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0144"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan"> below. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.116.2"
class="koboSpan">The tramp arbitrage model suggests that not only the
diagonal but also the non-diagonal entries should not differ materially
from 1.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">It is recommended
that correlations should be computed over periods that include at least
one full cycle. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.117.2"
class="koboSpan">Correlations computed around a period where the market
is constantly at a flat low would fail to shed light on the underlying
stability, or lack thereof, of the network.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.117.3" class="koboSpan">Typically
during cycle lows, freight rates and the unobservable TCE remain totally
flat, with TCE "stuck" at around operating cost level.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.117.4" class="koboSpan">Thus the whole
of the recorded variance taken during a protracted cycle low would be
"noise".</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">Moving to the
steamship era, we tend to observe a boom at the turn of each decade.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">All these
booms look very much alike with each other in terms of their main
features. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.118.3" class="koboSpan">We
show the detailed figures for the full cycle Jan 1888 to Dec 1893
period, being very representative of the patterns observed in all other
steamship full cycle periods around the turn of each decade.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">We have grouped the
various freight rate plots under different permutation schemes.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.119.2" class="koboSpan">For practical
purposes the first thing to identify before plotting the charts is the
most liquid route, in the sense that it has the fewest observation gaps
in the series. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.119.3"
class="koboSpan">This we</span>

class="koboSpan">call the benchmark route.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">For the
outbound routes from Tyne the destination to Havre is our chosen
benchmark route. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.125.3"
class="koboSpan">For the outbound routes from Wales the same destination
Havre is chosen as the benchmark route.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">Perusal of the data
should be done in the context of the various distances involved.
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0164" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0164"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan"> contains a distance matrix.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.221.2" class="koboSpan">Everything
else equal, freight rates on longer distance routes should tend to be
higher than those on shorter haul routes.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">The chart patterns
conform to the arbitrage tramp framework.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.222.2" class="koboSpan">The longer
hauls command higher freight rates per tonne.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.222.3" class="koboSpan">All routes
tend to oscillate in synchronous correlated patterns.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.222.4" class="koboSpan">The
correlation matrices presented below provide a numerical measure of
this. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.222.5" class="koboSpan">The
correlation data is split into three different tables.
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0165" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0165"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the correlation of all routes out of Tyne.
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0166" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0166"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the correlation of all routes out of Wales.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.226.2" class="koboSpan">Finally
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0167" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0167"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the correlation of the Tyne routes with the
Welsh routes.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">The remainder of this
article is divided in two parts which jointly span the period 1848 to
1936. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.229.2" class="koboSpan">The
first part of the study is the cliometric top down exercise which
due</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0164" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00164.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0164)

</div>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0165" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_278"></span>[](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0165)

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00165.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0165)

</div>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0166" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00166.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0166)

</div>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0167" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00167.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0167)

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_279"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">to data limitations is restricted to the period 1885 to
1936. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.234.2" class="koboSpan">The
second part of the study is a bottom up approach spanning the period
1848 to 1914.</span>

### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">1.3 Coastal colliers: the cliometric top down approach 1885–1936</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.236.1" class="koboSpan">The rudimentary
cliometric model requires overlapping data from two export outlets.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.236.2" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately,
overlapping data from both Tyne and Wales are hard to find, at least so
far, prior to 1885. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.236.3"
class="koboSpan">Thus the cliometric sub-part of our broader historic
investigation, can only be applied to the period 1885–1936.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">From 1885 up to World
War I there had been a freight market boom at around the turn of each
decade. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.237.2" class="koboSpan">A
couple of more full cycles followed after World War I up to the end of
our investigation period. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.237.3"
class="koboSpan">We take each of these boom time "cycle high" freight
records and couple them with the adjacent years "cycle low" rate
observations to implement the cliometric analysis separately for each
full cycle.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">1.3.1 Statistical methodology</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">The coastal market
provides freight rates for more routes that our simple 2×2 illustrative
model network. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.239.2"
class="koboSpan">Thus statistical methods of best fit are
suitable.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">We expect a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">priori</span></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan"> that port turnaround time has to be a positive number.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.242.2" class="koboSpan">This can be
imposed as a constraint to the econometric routine.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.242.3" class="koboSpan">The same
applies for port charges.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.243.1" class="koboSpan">We also expect from
experience and the persistent recurrence of layups during downturns,
that at cycle low, TCE should be about equal to cash running cost.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.243.2" class="koboSpan">That can be
added as a further constraint to the best fit optimisation method.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.243.3" class="koboSpan">We do not make
such an assumption arbitrarily. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.243.4"
class="koboSpan">Fortunately, our data sources, in several cases, come
along with commentary which highlight the incidence of widespread lay
ups as and when they occurred. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.243.5"
class="koboSpan">More precisely, the commentary characterises certain
freight rate levels as being "lay-up related".</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">We have run several
versions of cliometric calculations as follows:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">fully
    unconstrained;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">partly
    constrained so that cycle low TCE equals externally and
    independently calculated cash running costs;</span>
3.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">partly
    constrained so that port time and port charges are positive
    numbers;</span>
4.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">fully constrained
    so that port time and port charges are positive numbers, while cycle
    low TCE is also constrained to equal to the independently and
    externally estimated cash running costs.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">The fully
unconstrained computations did not satisfy all the above a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan">priori</span></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"> expectations. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.251.2"
class="koboSpan">We have decided to present below the results of the
partly constrained method (b) where cycle low TCE is assumed to be equal
to cash running costs. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.251.3"
class="koboSpan">Given the discrepancies of the fully unconstrained
computations, our results so far have to be seen as tentative and work
in progress.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">1.3.2 Results</span>

<a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0168" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0168"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the rapid improvement in port turnaround time,
estimated cliometrically post-1885, with the introduction of steam
technology for both vessel and terminals.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.254.2" class="koboSpan">We have
co-mingled in </span>[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
6</span>](#Ch010.xhtml_fig0168)<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan"> the post-1885 top down cliometric findings, with the
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_280"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan">1850–1914 bottom up results to be presented in the
second part of this study. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.257.2"
class="koboSpan">This is in order to bring out in summary form the full
story of the steamship revolution from its very beginning up to and
beyond the total elimination of sailers.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">The cliometric top
down figures shown in the last column are generally larger than the
bottom up estimates. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.258.2"
class="koboSpan">This may be because the cliometric study picks up
waiting time between two consecutive voyages while the bottom up
approach does not. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.258.3"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, the magnitude of the decline in port
turnaround time from the sail ship era to the steamship days is clearly
demonstrated.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">We turn our attention
now to the cliometrically estimated profitability performance by
sub-period groupings in post-1885 era.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.259.2" class="koboSpan">For this
purpose we have calculated the daily TCE across all routes.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.259.3" class="koboSpan">It is a small
step to move from TCE to return on capital employed.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.259.4" class="koboSpan">As in
Vergottis (2005), we prefer to present our results in terms of return on
capital employed. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.259.5"
class="koboSpan">This is because over time the size and nature of ships
changes as is obvious from </span>[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
6.</span>](#Ch010.xhtml_fig0168)<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan"> Thus their TCE’s are not easily comparable to the
point of</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0168" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00168.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0168)

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_281"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan">quickly becoming meaningless as a comparison of the
charter revenues between say a 300 tonne sailer and a 1775 tonne steamer
would suggest. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.263.2"
class="koboSpan">In contrast, return on capital is comparable over time
and across different asset classes no matter how apart in time or nature
they are. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.263.3" class="koboSpan">For
cyclical analysis it has the advantage that it tends to mean-revert.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.263.4" class="koboSpan">This reflects
the fact that in competitive markets super-profits or super-losses tend
to be eventually eliminated. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.263.5"
class="koboSpan">This is because the long run supply curve tends to
become elastic around the fully build-up cost level.</span>

<a href="#Ch010.xhtml_cap_lbl0118"
id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0118"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 21</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_cap_lbl0121"
id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0121"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">24</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan"> show the full cycle returns for the dominant benchmark
collier steamer at the turn of each decade where market rose from cycle
low to cycle high and reverted back to cycle low.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.268.1" class="koboSpan">The intervening years
which are not shown in the charts, are cycle low years where TCE just
about covered cash operating costs.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.268.2" class="koboSpan">This implies
negative returns on capital, post depreciation charges in the order of
–5% annualised. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.268.3"
class="koboSpan">The results for the World War I period have not been
computed despite the availability of freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.268.4" class="koboSpan">It is well
known that returns were extremely high during the war but distorted by
abnormal conditions. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.268.5"
class="koboSpan">We have not computed the war time returns because that
would require a more in depth analysis of risk and insurance aspects
which go beyond the scope of this study.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">It can be seen that,
once steamship became the dominant technology, the market got saturated
and commoditised. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.269.2"
class="koboSpan">This is borne out by the fact that returns on capital
were commensurate with cost of capital if not sub-par over a full cycle.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.269.3" class="koboSpan">Decade-wide
returns were even lower as the intervening years not charted were cycle
low periods, with the notable exception of World War I.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.269.4" class="koboSpan">This seems to
indicate that by 1885, the entry of steamers into the coastal market had
reached mature saturation levels.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.269.5" class="koboSpan">The
mechanisation of short haul coal routes out of UK was in that sense near
complete.</span>
