### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">1.4 Bottom up approach 1848–1914</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">In this section, we
utilise a bottom up approach to analyse the steamship revolution in the
Northern European coastal coal freight market and its trend development
over time. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.287.2" class="koboSpan">For
each era we compute the fully build up freight rate breakeven point.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.287.3" class="koboSpan">This
calculation is based on a fixed target return on capital employed for
new replacement capacity. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.287.4"
class="koboSpan">This should provide a measure of "mid-cycle" freight
rates given the tendency of freely competitive markets, such as tramp
shipping, to mean-revert towards cost of capital related remuneration.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.287.5" class="koboSpan">We also
compute a lay-up rate level equal to cash cost.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.287.6" class="koboSpan">This should
provide a measure of "floor" rates over the low phase of the
cycle.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">The starting point
for our analysis is the tail end of the collier sailing ship era.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.288.2" class="koboSpan">This is
presented in
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0173" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0173"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.291.1" class="koboSpan">The exclusive source
for the computations here is the exhaustive study of Allen (1855).
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.291.2" class="koboSpan">It was
presented to a professional audience of shipbuilders and shipowners of
both sailers and steamers. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.291.3"
class="koboSpan">It comes complete with a question and answer session
between the author and the professional audience.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.291.4" class="koboSpan">It merits
broad recognition as it targets the most critical juncture of steamship
revolution. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.291.5"
class="koboSpan">This is the stage where mechanisation of ships
proceeded beyond the narrowly specialised liner passenger, and
government subsidised mail operations.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.291.6" class="koboSpan">It heralds the
introduction of steamship technology to the voluminous raw material bulk
markets.</span>

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.292.1" class="koboSpan">Table
7</span>](#Ch010.xhtml_fig0173)<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan"> suggests that prior to the introduction of steamships,
a rate of 8.14 shillings per tonne was required in order to provide a
10% return on capital on a new sailer.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.293.2" class="koboSpan">The cash costs
of the operation of a sailer were 5.88 shillings per tonne and this
provides a floor measure for market lows prior to the introduction of
steamships.</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0173" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_284"></span>[](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0173)

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00173.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0173)

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">The first steamship
introduced in the Tyne/London market was the John Bowes which carried
its first cargo of coal in July 1852.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.295.2" class="koboSpan">Its instant
success was followed by a wave of new steamship orders targeting this
short haul market.
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0174" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0174"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">Table 8</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates the economics for the steamship mode on
the main east coast coal route. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.297.2"
class="koboSpan">Once again we rely entirely on Allen (1855) for our
computations.</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0174" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_285"></span>[](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0174)

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00174.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0174)

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_286"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan">The steamship innovation involved a number of tradeoffs
in comparison with the competing sailing mode.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.2" class="koboSpan">Steamships
suffered from substantially higher construction, voyage related, and
running costs. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.3"
class="koboSpan">However, they compensated through much higher
productivity in both sailing and port turnaround time.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.4" class="koboSpan">The sailing
time gains related to the higher average speed of seven knots or above,
which was largely independent of the weather.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.5" class="koboSpan">The port
turnaround gains partly relate to the application of steam power in
loading and unloading devices. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.6"
class="koboSpan">Such gains also reflect the ability of steamships to
maintain a fixed schedule largely independent of weather.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.7" class="koboSpan">This enabled
the shore-side port operations to be co-ordinated, fine tuned, and
speeded up around the predictable arrivals of tonnage and cargoes.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.8" class="koboSpan">Indeed it
seems that a queuing convention was almost instantly established.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.9" class="koboSpan">Accordingly
cheap to rent sailers would be removed from berth to allow expensive
steamships to load and discharge cargo with quick dispatch.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.299.10" class="koboSpan">Mechanisation
of ports proceeded in parallel with the mechanisation of ships in a self
reinforcing virtuous circle.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.300.1" class="koboSpan">The steamship
economics compare favorably to that of the sailer in the Tyne/London
route, as comparison between </span>[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan">Tables
7</span>](#Ch010.xhtml_fig0173)<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span>[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan">8</span>](#Ch010.xhtml_fig0174)<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.304.2"
class="koboSpan">The steamer required a rate of 6.90 shillings per tonne
in order to generate 10% return on new construction.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.304.3" class="koboSpan">Thus at the
outset, the capital breakeven point for a steamer is 15% lower than that
of a sailer. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.304.4"
class="koboSpan">Looking at it from a slightly different angle, the
standard steamship would enjoy a return on capital of over 20% at the
previously mentioned rate of 8.14 shillings per tonne required by a
sailer in order for the latter to breakeven.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.304.5" class="koboSpan">At the
beginning, investment in cargo steamships did entail certain risks of
"venture capital" type. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.304.6"
class="koboSpan">However the productivity gains of steamships in short
haul markets were of sufficient magnitude to attract risk capital.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.304.7" class="koboSpan">This explains
the new ordering wave for short haul steamer colliers that ensued.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.304.8" class="koboSpan">The lay-up
rate for steamships was also a reduced 5.09 shillings per tonne,
representing a 14% decline in relation to the cash breakeven levels for
sailers.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.305.1" class="koboSpan">Our next market
snapshot is around year 1865, by which time further significant
productivity gains had been squeezed out of steamship operations.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.305.2" class="koboSpan">This expanded
the number of annual trips performed by steamships on the Tyne/London
route from around 30 per annum in 1855, to 40 and above per annum by
1865. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.305.3" class="koboSpan">Allen
(1855), p. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.305.4"
class="koboSpan">319, foresees this development clearly.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.305.5" class="koboSpan">Whereas, at
the time of writing, 30 voyages per annum had been calculated as being
the fair average productivity "…there can be little doubt, that an
average of 36 voyages may be attained, after more experience has been
gained in working the vessels, and proper arrangements made for rapidly
discharging the cargoes, and speedily repairing any damage to machinery,
etc, from collision, or otherwise".
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.305.6" class="koboSpan">It is apparent
that the forthcoming productivity gains visible to Allen (1855), do not
rely on increased speed and reduced transit time.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.305.7" class="koboSpan">Instead they
lie in faster port turnaround times and reduced technical off-hire per
annum.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.306.1" class="koboSpan">Accordingly in
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0175" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0175"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.307.1" class="koboSpan">Table 9</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan">, we have sketched such developments accumulated over
the first decade or so of steamship operations experience.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.308.2" class="koboSpan">Our main
source here is the accounts of s/s Londonderry which plied the
Tyne/London route regularly. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.308.3"
class="koboSpan">These accounts provide a broad enough sample of over
170 representative voyages performed sequentially over the years
1865–1868. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.308.4" class="koboSpan">The
foresight of Allen (1855), allows us to connect the dots with higher
degree of confidence. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.308.5"
class="koboSpan">The unit freight rates achieved by SS Londonderry are
nearly identical to the benchmark Tyne/London collier rates of our
database. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.308.6" class="koboSpan">This
reinforces the view that these 170 voyages are representative of the
broader market and the cross comparability of our several strands of
analysis.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.309.1" class="koboSpan">We have allowed for a
marginal increase in speed and corresponding reduction in transit time
over the first decade of steamship experience.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.309.2" class="koboSpan">We estimate
that roundtrip</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0175" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_287"></span>[](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0175)

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00175.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0175)

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">time for steamships
on the benchmark east coast coal route, was reduced from 10.7 days in
1855 to 8.5 days in 1865. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.311.2"
class="koboSpan">Out of the total decline of 50 hours in round trip
time, 48 hours related to faster port turnaround improvement and only a
mere two hours from reduced transit time.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.311.3" class="koboSpan">Despite a
modest increase in unit bunker cost, the fully built
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_288"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan">up cost breakeven freight rate is reduced from 6.90
shillings per tonne for a steamship plying the route in 1855 to 6.35
shillings per tonne for similar ship in 1865; a percentage decline of
8%. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.312.2" class="koboSpan">The lay up
rate drops by a smaller 5% amount down to 4.82 shillings per tonne over
the same period.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">In
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0176" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0176"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">Table 10</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan">, we move forward to year 1880 and repeat our breakeven
rate calculations after a further accumulation of additional 15 years of
steamship experience. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.315.2"
class="koboSpan">One parameter worth highlighting is the significant
increase in average steamship cargo sizes in the short sea collier
routes. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.315.3" class="koboSpan">By
1880, the benchmark coal cargo on the east coast short haul route had
risen close to 1,000 tonnes compared with the early days of steamers
when parcels of 600 tonnes were the standard.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.315.4" class="koboSpan">This
translates to significant additional economies of scale gained across
almost all lines of the voyage profit and loss account.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.315.5" class="koboSpan">Specifically,
we identify economies of scale achieved in construction costs, running
expenses, and voyage steaming costs.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.315.6" class="koboSpan">Accordingly,
we estimate that by 1880, the fully built up breakeven level had dropped
down to 4.23 shillings per tonne.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.315.7" class="koboSpan">This
represents a whopping 34% decline in comparison to the 1865 level.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.315.8" class="koboSpan">Lay-up rates
also dropped to 3.42 shilling per tonne, a substantial 29% decline over
the 15-year period.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">Finally in
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0177" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0177"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">Table 11</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.318.1"
class="koboSpan">, we perform breakeven calculations for year 1910,
representing an additional 30 years of steamship innovation.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.318.2" class="koboSpan">Once again we
note an increase in average cargo size to about 1,450 tonnes.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.318.3" class="koboSpan">This also
implies further economies of scale in construction costs, running
expenses and voyage steaming costs.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.318.4" class="koboSpan">Accordingly
the fully built up breakeven level is slashed by a further 26% down to
3.12 shillings per tonne. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.318.5"
class="koboSpan">The lay up rate reduces by 22% in comparison to 1880,
down to 2.66 shillings per tonne.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">1.4.1 Tyne/London coal freight market — productivity gains and long-term development in rates</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.320.1" class="koboSpan">The long-term decline
in freight rates on the key Tyne to London coastal market may now be
reviewed in pictorial format.</span>

<a href="#Ch010.xhtml_cap_lbl0122"
id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0122"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 25</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
class="koboSpan"> depicts the development in freight rates on the east
coast key coal route over the period 1848 to 1911.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.322.2" class="koboSpan">In addition to
the fluctuating market rates, the chart includes two smoother lines.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.322.3" class="koboSpan">The upper line
represents the full cost breakeven point inclusive of capital costs.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.322.4" class="koboSpan">As already
mentioned, this should tend to represent the midcycle point of the
market. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.322.5" class="koboSpan">The
lower smooth line represents the development in cash breakeven point.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.322.6" class="koboSpan">This should
represent a floor resistance level during the cycle low phase of the
market.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.323.1" class="koboSpan">The breakeven lines
show a step down change in summer 1852 when the reference replacement
ship is switched from a sailer to the more efficient steamer.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.323.2" class="koboSpan">This step
change fully mirrors the modal economics analysed in
</span>[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.324.1" class="koboSpan">Tables
7</span>](#Ch010.xhtml_fig0173)<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span>[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan">8</span>](#Ch010.xhtml_fig0174)<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">After this step
decline, breakeven rates trend smoothly downwards with the occasional
upward interruption. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.328.2"
class="koboSpan">The later reflects the cyclical rise in bunker prices
that takes place when the economy booms.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.328.3" class="koboSpan">The long-term
trend decline is driven primarily by a combination of two factors.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.328.4" class="koboSpan">First, the
economies of scale implied by a relentless increase in the average size
of colliers. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.328.5"
class="koboSpan">Secondly, productivity gains implied by ever faster
port turnarounds.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.329.1" class="koboSpan">The relative returns
on replacement cost achieved by steamer and sailer are shown in
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_cap_lbl0123"
id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0123"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 26</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
class="koboSpan"> over the first two decades of mutual competition.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.331.2" class="koboSpan">The healthy
returns enjoyed by steamers stand in contrast to the poor returns on
sailers. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.331.3" class="koboSpan">This
explains the eventual dominance of the former and the rapid extinction
of the later.</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0176" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_289"></span>[](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0176)

</div>

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00177.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0177)

</div>

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00178.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 25: Long term decline in Tyne/London coal freight rates" /></span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_291"></span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0122"

id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 25</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.337.1"
class="koboSpan">Long term decline in Tyne/London coal freight
rates</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0179" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00179.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 26: Return on capital employed for steamer and sail ship summer 1848 to summer 1870" /></span>

<a href="#Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0123"
id="Ch010.xhtml_cap_lbl0123"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 26</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.340.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan">Return on capital employed for steamer and sail ship
summer 1848 to summer 1870</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_295"></span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_296"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">1.4.2 Route network portfolio analysis</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.347.1" class="koboSpan">The London/Tyne route
is well documented. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.347.2"
class="koboSpan">This has allowed us to sketch its detailed developments
over several decades. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.347.3"
class="koboSpan">For other routes there is only scant information which
does not allow for similar approach.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.347.4" class="koboSpan">However, we
can make use of the insights offered by the tramp arbitrage framework.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.347.5" class="koboSpan">This allows us
to evaluate developments across the broader collier coastal
network.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">Time charter
equivalent earnings E have been estimated for the Tyne/London route.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.348.2" class="koboSpan">Because of
arbitrage, similar earnings are imputed to all other routes of the
network. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.348.3"
class="koboSpan">Freight rates are readily available for other network
routes. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.348.4"
class="koboSpan">Reference is now made to equation (2).
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.348.5" class="koboSpan">A simple
regression can provide estimates for parameters α and β of any route
against the E common to all routes.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.348.6" class="koboSpan">Reference is
also made to the definitions of α and β.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.348.7" class="koboSpan">It can be seen
that once α and β have been estimated for any route, its port charges
and voyage duration structure is fully revealed.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.349.1" class="koboSpan">As regards the
technicalities of the regression a few comments are in order.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.349.2" class="koboSpan">We have broken
up β in a steaming and port turnaround component.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.349.3" class="koboSpan">The former is
known and thus has been taken to the left hand side of the equation to
create a modified independent variable for the regression, namely
freight rates net of bunkers and net of steaming time rental.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.349.4" class="koboSpan">Thus our β
estimate in our modified regression can be interpreted straightforwardly
as port turnaround days. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.349.5"
class="koboSpan">We have also included a time trend for port turnaround
to reflect the relentless productivity improvements through the periods
under review. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.349.6"
class="koboSpan">We apply the regressions separately for each decade.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.349.7" class="koboSpan">Effectively we
are assuming that the route network remains largely stable during each
decade apart from trend port turnaround development.</span>

<a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0180" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0180"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.350.1" class="koboSpan">Table 12</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.1"
class="koboSpan"> summarises the results of these regressions.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.2" class="koboSpan">Some
interesting comments can be made around these results.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.3" class="koboSpan">First,
R-squared is very high in all cases.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.4" class="koboSpan">Second, the
time-path development of the β estimates over the decades is
significant. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.5"
class="koboSpan">It indicates progress in port turnaround time in
quantitative terms. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.6"
class="koboSpan">Network average port turnaround time, sum-total at both
ends, during the late stages of the sail ship era is estimated at 24.8
days. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.7" class="koboSpan">The
following decade shows substantial progress with steamship port
turnaround time, sum-total at both ends, slashed to 6.6 days.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.8" class="koboSpan">Ten years
later, in 1870, this figure drops to 5.5 days.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.9" class="koboSpan">By 1880, there
is a set-back in estimated port turnaround times, rising to 7.4 days.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.10" class="koboSpan">One possible
explanation for this set-back is the development of larger deep sea
trampers. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.11"
class="koboSpan">This necessitated the removal from berth of cheaper
small steamship coastal vessels in order to accelerate dispatch of the
bigger more expensive ships. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.12"
class="koboSpan">By 1890, coastal collier network average port
turnaround improves once again to 3.2 days.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.13" class="koboSpan">In 1900 we
notice another deterioration, with turnaround time rising to 4.2 days
before falling again to 2.9 days by 1910.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.14" class="koboSpan">It should be
noted that these are inferred numbers from stochastic equations and an
element of noise is always inherent in such figures.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.351.15" class="koboSpan">However, the
broad trends over the decades is believed to be correctly reflected in
these numbers.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.352.1" class="koboSpan">Thirdly, we turn to
the regression estimates of the constant term α.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.352.2" class="koboSpan">Multiplying α
with vessel size gives the estimated total port charges, sum-total at
both ends, per ship per roundtrip.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.352.3" class="koboSpan">In the early
years, French ports were notoriously expensive, with Rouen being the
worst culprit. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.352.4"
class="koboSpan">Towards 1870, France reduced its port charges but Rouen
always remained the most expensive port within our sample.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.352.5" class="koboSpan">That is
reflected in the regression estimates consistently throughout the
period.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.353.1" class="koboSpan">Fourthly, as we move
across the decades, it is obvious that for certain routes stochastic
noise may shift the α estimate in certain direction, and then the
regression compensates</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0184" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_297"></span>[](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0184)

[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00184.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0184)

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.355.1" class="koboSpan">by shifting the β
estimate in the opposite direction.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.355.2" class="koboSpan">This is
required to generate the best fit to the target time charter earnings
figure.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.356.1" class="koboSpan">1.4.3 Port charges</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">In
</span>[<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.358.1" class="koboSpan">Table
6</span>](#Ch010.xhtml_fig0168)<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan"> the port turnaround times estimated through the top
down cliometric approach, and the bottom up method were presented and
compared.
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0184" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0184"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.360.1" class="koboSpan">Table 13</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan"> does the same for port charges.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.362.1" class="koboSpan">It is obvious that
the two methods have resulted in offsetting compensating adjustments.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.362.2" class="koboSpan">The cliometric
approach tends to inflate port turnaround time and deflate port charges.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.362.3" class="koboSpan">In contract,
the bottom up approach results in lower port turnaround time but higher
port charges. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.362.4"
class="koboSpan">When it comes to estimating bottom line time charter
results, both methods result in similar figures.
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_cap_lbl0124"
id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0124"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 27</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates this with the figures for the 1890 cycle
being representative of the relative patterns for all other
cycles.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">Both methods give
near identical results for the cycle low periods.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.365.2" class="koboSpan">At cycle low
the computed time charter results are practically equal to cash
operating costs. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.365.3"
class="koboSpan">It is only in the case of the cliometric top down
method that this equality between cycle low earnings and cash costs has
been imposed by design.</span>

<div id="Ch010.xhtml_fig0185" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00185.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 27: Comparison of computed daily time charter earnings (E)" /></span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_298"></span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0124"
id="Ch010.xhtml_cap_lbl0124"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.367.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 27</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.369.1"
class="koboSpan">Comparison of computed daily time charter earnings
(E)</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.370.1" class="koboSpan">During boom periods,
the bottom up method simulates higher time charter earnings than the top
down cliometric approach. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.370.2"
class="koboSpan">This is because of the lower port turnaround times
estimated by the former method.</span>

#### <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.371.1" class="koboSpan">1.4.4 Alternative bottom up approach</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.372.1" class="koboSpan">We turn now to
original sources for port charges.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.372.2" class="koboSpan">These have
been retrieved from various editions of Dock & Port Charges of the
United Kingdom, and Dues and Charges on Shipping in Foreign Ports.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.372.3" class="koboSpan">These
directories show port tariff structures worldwide.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.372.4" class="koboSpan">The
directories also provide actual detailed accounts of port charges
incurred by specific ships calling at the various ports.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.372.5" class="koboSpan">For the ports
mentioned in this article, many of these detailed accounts represent
coastal collier ship calls. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.372.6"
class="koboSpan">We utilise this information to run an alternative
bottom up approach. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.372.7"
class="koboSpan">This alternative bottom up approach rests on the
following assumptions:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.373.1" class="koboSpan">port charges as
    per the above-mentioned directories;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.374.1" class="koboSpan">at cycle low,
    time charter earnings equal cash operating costs;</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.375.1" class="koboSpan">Using the above
assumptions, we look at each route separately and solve for the implied
port turnaround time. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.375.2"
class="koboSpan">The results are shown in
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0186" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0186"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.376.1" class="koboSpan">Tables 14</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.377.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0190" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0190"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.378.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.379.1"
class="koboSpan"> for year 1875.
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0193" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0193"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.380.1" class="koboSpan">Tables 16</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.381.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch010.xhtml_fig0196" id="Ch010.xhtml_bck_fig0196"><span
id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.382.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan"> repeat the exercise for year 1910.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.384.1" class="koboSpan">The alternative
bottom up approach seem to resemble the results arrived through our
initial bottom up approach. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.384.2"
class="koboSpan">This suggests that the cliometric top down approach
overestimates true port turnaround times and underestimates port
charges.</span>

## <span id="Ch010.xhtml_page_312"></span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.398.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.398.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.399.1" class="koboSpan">In this article we
have suggested new methods for analysing historic developments in
freight rates. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.399.2"
class="koboSpan">We have applied these methods to the coal coastal
collier markets. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.399.3"
class="koboSpan">The cliometric top down approach has been presented.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.399.4" class="koboSpan">Its attraction
lies in:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.400.1" class="koboSpan">the appeal and
    relevance of the arbitrage principle to the tramp shipping
    markets;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.401.1" class="koboSpan">the simplicity of
    the resulting mathematical structure;</span>
3.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.402.1" class="koboSpan">the ease of
    implementation;</span>
4.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.403.1" class="koboSpan">the ability to
    tidy up several strands of shipping research; and</span>
5.  <span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.404.1" class="koboSpan">the nature of the
    new queries that arise when results do not conform to expectations
    or other evidence.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.405.1" class="koboSpan">However, when applied
to the coastal collier market, certain inconsistencies arose.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.405.2" class="koboSpan">We believe,
that the cliometric top down approach requires quality raw data and deep
understanding of the structure of the network and its potential
instability. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.405.3"
class="koboSpan">Network instability can be an advantage for the
econometric investigation but needs to be monitored, and any changes
properly detected and modeled. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.405.4"
class="koboSpan">This is not difficult to implement but the scope of
this first attempt has not reached that far.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.406.1" class="koboSpan">However, we do not
think that the inconsistencies of the cliometric approach reflect
network instability. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.406.2"
class="koboSpan">Instead we highlight that small changes in the
assumptions of the commercial features of the representative tramper,
produce rather large shifts in end results.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.406.3" class="koboSpan">This suggests
that future research requires a sharpening of the pencil at this
front.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.407.1" class="koboSpan">The bottom up
approach was also applied to the coast collier market.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.407.2" class="koboSpan">This gave
results which seem to be more consistent with evidence and expectations.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.407.3" class="koboSpan">The fact that
two alternative variations of the bottom up approach gave very similar
results, reinforce the appeal of these methods.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.407.4" class="koboSpan">They also
reinforce the faith in the validity of the end results.</span>

<span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.408.1" class="koboSpan">Looking ahead, the
inter-relationship of freights that Lewis (1941) highlights, seem to be
an extremely fruitful approach for tidying up several strands of
research and for gaining insights and knowledge into some of the
hitherto darkest areas of maritime economic history.
</span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.408.2" class="koboSpan">The network
route portfolio approach is the way forward for historic freight rate
analysis. </span><span id="Ch010.xhtml_kobo.408.3" class="koboSpan">A
combination of top down and bottom up approaches, sheds more light and
triggers more interesting questions for further research, when pursued
in combination rather than isolation.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_318"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_319"></span>[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 11</span>\
<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">An Overview of the Dry Bulk Shipping Industry</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0264)
==================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Amir</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">H.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Alizadeh</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan"> and</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Nikos</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">K.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan">Nomikos</span></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0277" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0277"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">Dry bulk shipping was
developed as a result of the need to reduce transportation costs when
shipment size of commodities increased enough for the commodity to be
carried in shiploads and economies of scale could be utilised.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">This goes back
to the nineteenth century when small wooden ships, fully laden with
coal, were employed to meet the increasing demand for coal
transportation between North England and London.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">Nowadays, the
number of commodities carried on a “one ship, one cargo” basis has
increased, thanks to world economic growth, increased demand for raw
materials and energy commodities, liberalisation in international trade,
trans-nationalisation of industrial processes as well as technological
advances in shipbuilding and design.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.12.4" class="koboSpan">The growth in
international trade led to a corresponding expansion of the bulk
shipping fleet to match the requirements of seaborne bulk trade.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">The total seaborne
trade in commodities reached an estimated 8,128 million metric tonnes
(mmt) in 2008. </span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0125"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0125"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates the evolution of seaborne trade in major
dry and liquid bulk commodities between 1965 and 2008.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">It can be seen
that the volume of international seaborne trade has increased from 1,750
million to more than 8,226 million tonnes over the same period,
representing an average annual growth rate of 3.5%.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.15.3" class="koboSpan">The largest
proportion of the seaborne trade was in dry bulk commodities with an
estimated quantity of 3,065 mmt, followed by liquid bulk commodities,
2,950 mmt and other dry cargo and manufactured goods, 2,114
mmt.</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0278" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0278"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan"> More specifically, the dry bulk shipping fleet
transported 843 mmt iron ore, 795 mmt coking and steam coal, 322 mmt
grains, 107 mmt of bauxite, alumina and phosphate rock and 1,105 mmt of
minor dry bulk commodities such as cement, sugar, fertilisers, etc.,
which makes the dry bulk shipping market by far the largest sector of
the world shipping industry in terms of volume and weight.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">In fact, at the
end of 2009, the cargo carrying capacity of the world dry bulk fleet of
418 million tonnes was 34.7% of the total world shipping fleet and the
number of dry bulk ships exceeded 7,300 (see endnote 1).Therefore, it is
not surprising that a large number of studies have been devoted to
analysing the formation and behaviour of</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0199" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.18.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00199.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Pattern of international seaborne trade in major commodities" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_320"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0125"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0125"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan"> Pattern of international seaborne trade in major
commodities</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">Note</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan">: Container and natural gas seaborne trade data are
available from 1986.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan">Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">dry bulk freight
(charter) rates, chartering decisions and policies, transportation
strategies and fleet deployments and operations of the dry bulk shipping
industry.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">Additionally,
technological developments led to more sophisticated and larger ship
designs, aiming not only to realise the economies of scale, but also to
match specific cargo and trading route requirements.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.26.2" class="koboSpan">The latter
depend very much on commodity trade patterns and industrial production
processes in the world economy.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">The purpose of this
chapter is to provide an overview of the dry bulk shipping market and
discuss current issues and developments in this area.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">In particular,
we discuss the segmentation of the dry bulk shipping market into
different sub-sectors due to different physical and economic factors
such as commodity parcel size, the underlying shipping routes, the
physical characteristics of the loading and discharge ports as well as
the vessel’s design features. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.27.3"
class="koboSpan">We also present the structure of the shipping markets
as well as the theory for the determination of freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.27.4" class="koboSpan">Additionally,
we present empirical evidence on issues relating to the properties of
the dry bulk shipping freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.27.5" class="koboSpan">These issues
include the seasonal behaviour of the freight market; testing the
dynamic interrelationships between freight rate levels and volatilities
for different size vessels in the spot and period markets; testing the
expectations hypothesis of the term structure and modelling time-varying
risk premia in the formation of long-term rates and finally,
investigating the existence of time-varying risk premia in the market
for newbuilding and second-hand vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">The structure of this
chapter is as follows. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.28.2"
class="koboSpan">The next section describes the structure of the dry
bulk market and its contribution to the international transport by
connecting the sources of supply and demand for raw materials.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">Section 3
reviews the formation of spot and time-charter freight rates and
discusses important issues regarding the behaviour of these rates such
as seasonality, volatility and market efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.28.4" class="koboSpan">The
relationship between freight rates for contracts with different duration
as well as interrelationship
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_321"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan">and spill over effect between freight rate levels and
volatilities across segments of the dry bulk market are also discussed
in section 3. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.29.2"
class="koboSpan">Section 4, first presents the determination of dry bulk
ship prices and then reviews the behaviour of prices in newbuilding,
second-hand and scrap prices for dry bulk ships.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.29.3" class="koboSpan">The issue of
efficiency of the market for dry bulk ships is also considered and
findings of some recent studies are discussed.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.29.4" class="koboSpan">Finally,
section 5 concludes this chapter.</span>

## <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">Market Segmentation Within the Dry Bulk Shipping Industry</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">The significant growth
in international seaborne commodity trade along with developments in the
shipbuilding industry in the past 50 years or so is a manifestation of
the liberalisation in international trade and the inherent economies of
scale existent in seaborne commodity transportation.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.31.2" class="koboSpan">This has
encouraged the construction of specialised ships of various sizes, which
can be employed in the transportation of certain types of commodities
over certain trading routes. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.31.3"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, within the dry bulk sector, different
sub-markets with distinctive characteristics in terms of supply and
demand features, operational characteristics, risk and profitability,
have been developed. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.31.4"
class="koboSpan">Generally speaking, the decision to hire a certain type
of vessel for ocean transportation of a certain commodity depends on
three main factors; first, the type of the commodity to be transported;
secondly, the parcel size and thirdly, the trade route and the physical
characteristics and infrastructure at the loading and discharge
ports.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">For the purposes of
shipping operations, market analysis and research, commodities are
generally distinguished into the following categories: liquid bulk, dry
bulk, general cargo and unitised (containers).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">There are also
specialised cargoes such as natural gas, refrigerated cargoes,
automobiles, forest products and live-stocks, which require special
types of ships for transportation.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.32.3" class="koboSpan">Since it is the
type of commodity that determines which type of ship the charterer
(cargo owner or shipper) requires for the transportation of his/her
cargo, any change in the trade pattern for that commodity is reflected
in the demand and freight rates for different types of vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.32.4" class="koboSpan">For example, in
the past two decades industrial developments in the Far East, especially
South Korea and China have increased the demand for capesize vessels in
that region. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.32.5" class="koboSpan">As
another example, the demand for capesize vessels in the Atlantic has
been reduced due to an increase in the European Union’s (EU) grain
production and a corresponding decline in EU’s grain imports from the
United States after the 1980s.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">The second factor that
a charterer should bear in mind before taking any decision to hire a
vessel is the conventional shipment size of each commodity, generally
known as the “commodity parcel size”.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">This is defined
as the amount of cargo, in tonnes, that can be carried by sea
considering the economies of scale and associated transportation and
storage costs for that commodity.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.33.3" class="koboSpan">The commodity
parcel size also depends on the economics of the industrial process or
consumption of such commodities as raw materials for industrial goods
and other finished products. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.33.4"
class="koboSpan">For certain commodities such as iron ore, crude oil and
coal, the economies of scale in sea transportation have reduced the
transportation costs to such an extent that it is most economical to
hire large vessels for carriage of these commodities by sea.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.33.5" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
parcel sizes for those commodities are quite large (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.33.6" class="koboSpan">for iron ore
80,000 to 300,000 tonnes). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.33.7"
class="koboSpan">However, agricultural commodities are carried in
smaller shipments, e.g. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.33.8"
class="koboSpan">from 12,000 to 60,000 tonnes, again
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_322"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">depending on the type of cargo transported.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.34.2" class="koboSpan">This is mainly
because of the perishable nature of those commodities and the fact that
they need specialised storage facilities (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.34.3" class="koboSpan">special storage
silos). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.34.4"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, traders prefer smaller shipments as it
enables them to store and market these products in time.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.34.5" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the higher storage and inventory costs of agricultural commodities and
oil products, compared to lower value goods such as iron ore and coal,
suggest that it is more economical to transport these commodities in
smaller consignments.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, when the
shipper is deciding which size vessel to hire, he must consider factors
such as the trading route, the physical characteristics of ports of
loading and discharge, such as berth size and draught, as well as the
existence of cargo handling facilities at the ports.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">The draught
factor is important because large ships with deep draughts cannot
approach ports with shallow harbours and the costs of lightening them at
the anchorage should be compared against the capacity loss when using
smaller vessels. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.35.3"
class="koboSpan">In ports where cargo-handling facilities are lacking,
small and geared vessels are needed.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.35.4" class="koboSpan">In general,
shippers try to minimise the associated transportation costs by hiring
an optimal size vessel after considering all the above named factors,
which led to segmentation of the dry bulk shipping into five different
sectors according to the cargo carrying capacity of the vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.35.5" class="koboSpan">These are
Handysize (25,000–35,000 dwt), Handymax (35,000–45,000 dwt), Supramax
(45,000–55,000), Panamax (55,000–75,000 dwt) and Capesize (80,000 dwt
and over, mainly 120,000, 150,000 and 175,000 dwt) markets.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.35.6" class="koboSpan">Historical
growth and the composition of the dry bulk fleet in terms of vessel
size, is presented in </span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0126"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0126"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.37.2"
class="koboSpan">At the end of 2009, the world dry bulk fleet consisted
of 2,861 Handysize vessels with total capacity of 76.43 mdwt; 1,856
Handymax vessels with a total capacity of 91.4 mdwt; 1,627 Panamax
vessels with a total capacity of 120.76 mdwt; and 939 Capesize vessels
with a total capacity of 166.93 mdwt.</span>

<a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fig0201" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fig0201"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan"> summarises the associated cargo types and major
trading routes that dry bulk vessels serve.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
Handysize and Handymax vessels are mainly engaged in the transportation
of grain commodities from North and South America and Australia</span>

category</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_323"></span>[](#Ch011.xhtml_bck_fig0201)

[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00201.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch011.xhtml_bck_fig0201)

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_324"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">to Europe and Asia and minor dry bulk commodities such
as bauxite and alumina, fertilisers, rice, sugar, steel and scrap around
the world. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.46.2" class="koboSpan">Due
to their small size, shallow draught and cargo handling gears, these
vessels are quite flexible in terms of the trading routes and ports that
they can serve. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.46.3"
class="koboSpan">Panamax and Supramax vessels are used primarily in
coal, grain and to some extent in iron ore transportation, from North
America and Australia to Japan and Western Europe.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.46.4" class="koboSpan">These vessels
are not equipped with cargo handling gears and have deeper draught;
therefore, they are engaged in transportation of fewer commodities than
Handysize bulk carriers, as they are not as flexible.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.46.5" class="koboSpan">The majority of
the Capesize fleet is engaged in the transportation of iron ore from
South America and Australia to Japan, Western Europe and North America
and also in coal transportation from Australia and North America to
Japan and Western Europe. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.46.6"
class="koboSpan">Due to their deep draught and limited number of
commodities that they transport, the operation of these vessels in terms
of trading routes and ports they can approach is restricted.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">It has also been
argued in the literature that the risk/return characteristics of dry
bulk carriers vary across vessel sizes.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">In particular,
Kavussanos,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0279" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0279"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0280" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0280"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.51.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Alizadeh and
Nomikos</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0281" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0281"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan"> show that freight rate volatilities and second-hand
ship price volatilities are higher for larger vessels compared to
smaller ones and relate such differences to operational flexibility and
trading restrictions of larger vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">This strong
contrast in risk/ return and operational profitability among different
size of dry bulk carriers stems from differences in their supply,
demand, freight rate and price determination factors which reflect their
trading and operational flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.53.3" class="koboSpan">This in turn
implies a high degree of disaggregation in this shipping sector.</span>

## <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">The Dry Bulk Freight Market</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">A freight contract is
an agreement under which the shipowner agrees to provide a sea
transportation service to the charterer or shipper for a specified
amount of money per day for ship hire, or per tonne of cargo transported
between two ports, known as the freight rate.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">This service is
provided under certain contractual agreements and documentation, known
as the charter party. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.3"
class="koboSpan">Depending on the type and duration of the service
required by charterers, different types of charter contracts have been
developed and used in international shipping.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.4" class="koboSpan">These can be
classified into five main types: Voyage Charter Contract; Contract of
Affreightment (CoA); Trip Charter Contract; Time-Charter Contract; and
Bareboat or Demise Charter Contract.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.5" class="koboSpan">Under each type
of contract, duration of the service is specified, type and the amount
of cargo to be carried is agreed, methods of payment are standardised
and costs and expenses are allocated to the agents involved.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.6" class="koboSpan">Charter
contracts are normally negotiated between shipowners and charterers
through brokers and, once the terms are agreed, the charter party is
drafted and signed by the two parties.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.7" class="koboSpan">Single-voyage,
trip-charter and time-characters are the most common types of contracts
used in the dry bulk market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.8"
class="koboSpan">Single-voyage and trip-charter contracts, although
different in their method of payment and cost allocations, can be
classified as short-term or spot charter shipping contracts since they
both cover only a single voyage or trip.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.9" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, time-charter contracts are long-term (period) contracts and cover
more than one voyage. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.55.10"
class="koboSpan">In the following sections we discuss the formation of
freight rates under voyage and time-charter contracts and present
results of recent studies on the behaviour and interrelationship of dry
bulk shipping freight rates.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_325"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Spot freight rate formation</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">As in any other
market, the shipping freight market is also characterised by supply and
demand schedules (functions), each of which depends on several factors
that interact constantly for the equilibrium freight rate to be
determined. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.57.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, to see how shipping freight rates are
determined one has to study the supply and demand for freight services,
their shapes and the way they behave and interact.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">Starting with the
demand for shipping services, it has been well documented that this is a
derived demand which depends on several factors such as, world economic
activity, international seaborne trade, seasonal and cyclical changes
for different commodities transported by sea, the distance between
sources of production and consumption of commodities (see
Stopford</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0282" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0282"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.60.2"
class="koboSpan">The supply of shipping services is the amount (tonne
miles) of transportation service offered by shipowners based on the
optimisation of their fleet revenue.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.60.3" class="koboSpan">The supply of
shipping services at any point in time depends on the stock of fleet
available for trading, shipbuilding production, scrapping rate and
losses, fleet productivity and the level of freight rates in the market.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.60.4" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
freight rates at any point in time, reflect the balance between supply
and demand for shipping services which, in turn, depend on factors such
as world economic activity, the stock of fleet, political events,
international commodity trade, etc.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.60.5" class="koboSpan">(Stopford (see
endnote 5)).</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">It has also been shown
in the shipping economics literature that, while demand for ocean
shipping is inelastic, the supply of shipping services is convex in
shape due to the limitation of supply at any given point in time.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">This convexity
in the shape of the supply curve implies that the supply for shipping
services is highly elastic at low freight rate levels (points A to B in
</span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0127"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0127"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">) and becomes inelastic when freight rates are at very
high levels (points B to C in </span>[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0127)<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.65.2"
class="koboSpan">The reason for such bimodality of the elasticity of the
shipping supply curve is the availability of excess capacity during
periods when the market is in recession; that is, when vessels cannot
find employment, are laid up, slow steam or even carry part cargo and
freight rates are at very low levels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">Under such
market conditions, any changes in demand due to external factors such as
seasonal changes in trade or random shocks (events) can be absorbed by
the extra available capacity and, therefore, the impact on freight rates
would be relatively small. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.65.4"
class="koboSpan">For instance, in
</span>[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0127)<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">, assuming the demand curve is
D</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"> and given the supply function, the equilibrium freight
rate is at FR</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.71.2"
class="koboSpan">An increase in demand would shift the demand curve to,
say, D</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan"> and, assuming that in the short term the supply curve
for shipping services does not move, the new equilibrium freight rate
will be determined through the new intersection between the demand and
supply curves. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.73.2"
class="koboSpan">This means that the freight rate will increase to a new
level, FR</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan">, which represents a relatively small increase compared
to the increase in demand.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">As market conditions
improve, vessels are employed until the point where the stock of fleet
is fully utilised and any increase in supply is only possible by
increasing productivity through increasing speed and shortening port
stays and ballast legs. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.76.2"
class="koboSpan">Under such conditions, the supply curve becomes almost
vertical and inelastic. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, any changes in demand due to external
factors such as seasonal change in trade, random events, etc.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.76.4" class="koboSpan">would result in
a relatively large change in freight rate levels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.76.5" class="koboSpan">For instance,
in </span>[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0127)<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan">, when freight rate is at
FR</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan">3</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">, supply and demand schedules are very tight and the
fleet is fully utilised. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.80.2"
class="koboSpan">In this case if, due to some external factors, demand
for shipping services increases and the demand curve shifts from
D</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">3</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan"> to D</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan">4</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">, then assuming supply in the short term is constant,
the new equilibrium freight rate shoots up from</span>

class="koboSpan"> Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan">FR</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">3</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan"> to FR</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
class="koboSpan">4</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">, which is a relatively large increase.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.97.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore, it
can be argued that market conditions, availability of fleet and level of
freight rates are important factors influencing the magnitude of price
changes and volatility in the market.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.97.3" class="koboSpan">Alizadeh and
Nomikos (see endnote 20) provide a detailed examination of the
relationship between market conditions and volatility of freight
rates.</span>

<a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0128"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0128"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents historical movements of voyage or spot
freight rates, in US \$/mt, for Capesize vessels in four major routes:
namely, iron ore from Tubarao to Japan and</span>

id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"> Historical spot freight rates for four major Panamax
