class="koboSpan">Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Rotterdam and coal
from Queensland to Japan and Rotterdam.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.105.2" class="koboSpan">It can be seen
that, while there are co-movements between the series in the long run,
short-run movements are quite different across these voyage charter rate
series. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.105.3" class="koboSpan">The
existence of co-movements between the series in the long run can be
explained by the fact that these rates are driven by the same common
factor; that is, the aggregate demand for international commodity
transport and general supply conditions for Capesize vessels and their
services. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.105.4"
class="koboSpan">Differences between the behaviour of voyage freight
rates for Capesize ships in the short term are due to some distinct
factors related to trade in a specific route, port conditions and the
availability of tonnage over a short period in that specific route.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.105.5" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
</span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0129"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0129"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents the historical movement of voyage charter
rates for four Panamax routes, namely: grain from US Gulf to Rotterdam
and Japan and coal from Hampton Roads to Rotterdam and US Gulf to
Rotterdam. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.107.2" class="koboSpan">The
reporting of grain routes has been discontinued since 2008 as the bulk
of trade in those routes has shifted towards trip-charter
contracts.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Time-charter rate formation</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">While voyage or spot
freight rates are determined through the interaction between current
supply and demand schedules and conditions for shipping services,
time-charter or period rates are believed to be determined through the
market agents’ expectations about future spot rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">The theory
which relates the spot rates to time-charter rates is known as the
expectations hypothesis and the term structure relationship.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.109.3" class="koboSpan">This theory is
developed in the bond and interest rate markets and first adapted and
used to explain the relationship between spot and period charter rate in
shipping, by
Zannetos</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0283" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0283"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan"> and later on by Glen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0284" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0284"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan"> Hale and
Vanags</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0285" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0285"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Kavussanos and
Alizadeh,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0286" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0286"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"> among others.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan">The Term
Structure</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan"> relationship is based on the no arbitrage argument
which states that the agents (shipowner or charterers) should be
indifferent in entering into a long-term
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_328"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan">charter contract or a series of spot/voyage contracts
over the life of the long-term contract.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">In other
words, it is assumed that the freight market is efficient and agents
should not be able to make excess profit by choosing to operate under
either type of contract consistently.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">To illustrate the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">Term
Structure</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan"> relationship in the shipping freight market and the
formation of time-charter rates, consider the following example.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">At any point
of time, a shipowner has the option to operate under a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan"> period
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span><sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></sup></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan"> contract or a series of spot contracts each with a
duration of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan"> period
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan">\<</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan">=</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan">/</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan">) and a rate of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">FR</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.144.2"
class="koboSpan">Obviously, the shipowner may know what is the freight
rate for the first voyage, but has to adapt some form of expectations
about the future evolution of spot rates over the life of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span><sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></sup></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan"> contract. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.147.2"
class="koboSpan">Let us assume these are
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00205.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">, where
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">E</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the expectation operator at time
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan"> and also that the shipowner has to pay
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00206.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan"> as voyage cost for the first voyage and expected
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00207.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan"> for subsequent voyages.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.158.2" class="koboSpan">Then the
shipowner should be able to compare the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan"> earnings given the expected earnings from the spot
market operation. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.160.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, assuming that shipping freight markets are
efficient, there should not be any difference between the discounted
present value of earnings from an
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan"> period
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span><sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></sup></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan"> contract and the discounted present value of a series
of spot voyage, each with a duration of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan"> periods. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.167.2"
class="koboSpan">This can be written mathematically as:</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0205" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00208.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">where,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">r</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the discount rate,
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00209.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the expected spot charter rate at time
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan"> of a contract which lasts over
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan"> periods from
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan">t+im</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan"> to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">t+</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan">(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">i+1</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">)</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">m a</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan">nd
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan">=</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan">n/m</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan"> is a positive integer indicating the number of spot
charter contracts in the life of a time-charter contract.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00210.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the expected voyage costs.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.191.2" class="koboSpan">The difference
between expected spot rates, </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00211.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan"> and expected voyage costs,
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00212.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan"> reflects the expected earnings in the spot operation
on a daily basis, or the expected time-charter equivalent of spot rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.195.2" class="koboSpan">Equation (1)
can be used to derive the n period
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan"> rate at time
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan">, in terms of expected spot or voyage charter rates,
expected voyage costs and discount rate as:</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0206" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00213.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">However, one
important difference between the spot and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan"> operations is the security of the period contract
compared to the spot operation, because under a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> contract the shipowner is guaranteed to receive
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan">TC </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan">rates whatever happens to the market over the life of
the period
contract.</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0287" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0287"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan"> In contrast, under the spot operations the earnings of
the shipowner may vary depending on the future condition of the spot
market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.209.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, there is a risk element which should be
considered in the spot and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan"> rates relationship.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.211.2" class="koboSpan">The risk
element can be interpreted as the price that the shipowner is willing to
pay to pass the uncertainty of the spot market to the charterer.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.211.3" class="koboSpan">This is also
known as the risk premium, ø, which is in fact a discount in the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan"> rate, which the shipowner is prepared to forego in the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan"> market compared to the spot market earnings, to obtain
a secure long term
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan"> contract. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.217.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, we can write:</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0207" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00214.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_329"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan">A number of arguments have been put forward in the
literature as to why the risk premium term enters into the relationship.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.219.2" class="koboSpan">First,
shipowners operating in the spot market are generally exposed to higher
price risk in comparison to those operating in the time-charter market
because spot rates show higher fluctuations compared to time-charter
rates. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.219.3"
class="koboSpan">Secondly, for a shipowner operating in the spot market,
there is the possibility of unemployment risk, when the owner may not be
able to fix a voyage contract for a period of time.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.219.4" class="koboSpan">Thirdly, there
are cases when the owner has to relocate the vessel from one port to the
other for a new spot charter contract which involves substantial time
and costs. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.219.5"
class="koboSpan">Finally, if voyage spot rates (rather than trip-charter
spot rates) are compared to time-charter rates, shipowners are also
exposed to voyage (mainly bunker) cost fluctuations.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.219.6" class="koboSpan">Thus,
shipowners operating in the time-charter market are prepared to offer a
discount to cover the risk, to which they are exposed, when operating in
the spot market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.219.7"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, the charterer will take the risk of
operating in the spot market during the life of the time-charter
contract subject to a discount over the spot rates.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the
sentiment of the banks and lenders in shipping finance is another
important factor in the shipowner’s decision to operate in the spot or
the time-charter market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.220.2"
class="koboSpan">Financiers view differently, clients (shipowners) who
are committed to long term shipping contracts, when financing a ship
purchase or newbuilding, since this ensures a relatively more secure
stream of income for the shipowner and reduces the probability of loan
default. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.220.3" class="koboSpan">Thus,
shipowners may be prepared to forego a certain amount of earnings when
fixing their vessel on a long-term contract, as opposed to short-term
ones, in order to fulfil the lender’s requirements for the loan.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.220.4" class="koboSpan">This argument
can be quite important during periods of market uncertainty, suggesting
that the premium might be time-varying (see Kavussanos and Alizadeh (see
endnote 9)).</span>

<a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0130"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0130"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 6</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan"> to </span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0132"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0132"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">8</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan"> plot six-month, one-year and three-year time-charter
rates for Capesize, Panamax and Handysize dry bulk carriers over the
period 1992 to 2010, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.224.2" class="koboSpan">In general,
time-charter rates seem to show less short-term fluctuations compared to
spot rates. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.224.3"
class="koboSpan">This is expected as long-term charter contracts have
been argued to be a weighted average of expected spot rates over the
life span of the long term contract (see, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.224.4" class="koboSpan">Zannetos (see
endnote 6) and Glen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 7)).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.226.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
fluctuations in period rates are expected to be smoothened through the
aggregation of expected spot rates, which is thought to be the
underlying assumption in the formation of period rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.226.3" class="koboSpan">Moreover,
period time-charter contracts are normally used by industrial and
trading firms for the transportation of industrial commodities, such as
iron ore and minerals, which more or less follow regular trading
patterns over the year. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.226.4"
class="koboSpan">In contrast to time-charter contracts, voyage charter
contracts are generally used for transportation of commodities with
irregular and cyclical patterns such as grain (see Stopford (see endnote
5)). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.226.5" class="koboSpan">It is
also well known that industrial charterers use time-charter contracts to
meet most of their long-term transportation requirements and use spot
contracts for their extra needs, which might be seasonal or cyclical.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.226.6" class="koboSpan">This type of
chartering behaviour is reflected in the patterns observed in contracts
of different duration. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.226.7"
class="koboSpan">It seems that the longer the duration of the contract,
the smoother the rates.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the plot
of time-charter rates of dry bulk carriers indicates a large increase in
the levels and volatility of these rates over the past few years.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.227.2" class="koboSpan">More
precisely, while until mid-2003 time-charter rates for Capesize vessels
fluctuated roughly between 10,000 \$/day to 25,000 \$/day and for
Panamax vessels between 6,000 \$/day and 18,000 \$/day, after mid-2003,
fluctuations in time-charter rates for these ships have increased and
rates have reached levels of 140,000 \$/day for Capesize and 75,000
\$/day for Panamax</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0208" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00215.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Historical six-month, one-year and three-year time-charter rates for Capesize dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_330"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0130"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0130"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan"> Historical six-month, one-year and three-year
time-charter rates for Capesize dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan"> Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0209" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00216.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7: Historical values of six-month, one-year and three-year time-charter rates for Panamax dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0131"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
7:</span></span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan"> Historical values of six-month, one-year and
three-year time-charter rates for Panamax dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan"> Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">ships.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.238.2" class="koboSpan">The main
reason time-charter rates for dry bulk carriers were pushed to such
unprecedented levels was the increase in demand and shortage of supply
in recent years.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Seasonal behaviour of dry bulk freight rates</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">In the shipping
industry fluctuations in ship prices and freight rates are considerable
compared to rates and prices in other sectors of the world economy.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.240.2" class="koboSpan">Unexpected
changes</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0210" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00217.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 8: Historical values of six-month, one-year and three-year time-charter rates for Handysize dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_331"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0132"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0132"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 8:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan"> Historical values of six-month, one-year and
three-year time-charter rates for Handysize dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan">Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">and sharp movements
in freight rates, over short periods of time, hinder the decision-making
process whilst, at the same time, provide the opportunity for
substantial gains or losses for those involved.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.246.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
comprehending and analysing these movements in the market is an
essential first step for any decision maker in the shipping
industry.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping freight
rates reflect the supply-demand balance for freight services.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">The demand for
shipping services is a derived demand, which depends on the following
factors. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.247.3"
class="koboSpan">First, the economics of the commodities transported by
sea; that is, the level of production and consumption for the commodity
to be transported. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.247.4"
class="koboSpan">Secondly, the global economic conditions, world
economic activity and finally macroeconomic variables of major
economies, which translate to international trade in commodities.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.247.5" class="koboSpan">These
macroeconomic variables are shown elsewhere to have random variations as
well as deterministic seasonal components in most cases (Beaulieu and
Miron,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0288" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0288"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan">
Dickey</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0289" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0289"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Canova and
Hansen</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0290" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0290"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.253.2"
class="koboSpan">Trade figures in several commodities are also shown to
be seasonal; for instance, there are seasonal variations in the grain
trade. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.253.3"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, it is possible that those seasonalities are
transmitted to shipping freight rates and prices; see for instance,
Denning </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0291" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0291"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan"> on seasonality of the Baltic Freight Index, BFI
(see</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0292" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0292"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">Investigating the
seasonal behaviour of shipping freight rates is important and has both
economic and econometric implications.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.259.2" class="koboSpan">From the
economic point of view, revealing the nature and true behaviour of
seasonal fluctuations in freight rates can be of interest to shipowners
and charterers in their chartering strategies, tactical operations and
budgeting. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.259.3"
class="koboSpan">From the econometric point of view, it is important to
investigate the existence of seasonal behaviour in the freight rates for
the purposes of modelling and forecasting these series.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.259.4" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and
Alizadeh</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0293" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0293"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan"> examine the seasonal behaviour of dry bulk freight
rates and compare them (a) across different size vessels; (b) across
freight contracts with different maturities; and (c) under different
market condition. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.261.2"
class="koboSpan">The results of their study on seasonality of freight
rates for three different size dry bulk carriers are summarised in
graphical form in </span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0133"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0133"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 9</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan"> to </span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0135"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0135"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">11</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.265.2"
class="koboSpan">Each bar indicates the</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0211" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00218.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 9: Comparison of seasonal changes in freight rates for Capesize dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_332"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0133"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0133"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 9:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan"> Comparison of seasonal changes in freight rates for
Capesize dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan"> Capesize, Capesize 1 and Capesize 3, represent the
spot, one-year and three-year TC rates, respectively</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0212" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00219.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 10: Comparison of seasonal changes in freight rates for Panamax dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0134"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
10:</span></span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan"> Comparison of seasonal changes in freight rates for
Panamax dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.274.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan">Panamax, Panamax 1 and Panamax 3, represent the spot,
1-year and 3-year TC rates, respectively</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">average percentage
increase or decrease in the freight rate over that particular season.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.276.2" class="koboSpan">There are
several points which can be observed here.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">First, freight rates
for all dry bulk carriers increase significantly in the first quarter
and decrease significantly in summer months.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.277.2" class="koboSpan">This may be
due to two reasons; the reduction in the level of industrial production
and trade in midsummer, or switch of spot operators to time-charter
operation after the end of the Japanese and harvest-led spring upsurge,
which causes an over-supply in the time-charter market.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.277.3" class="koboSpan">Also, since
time-charter rates are linked to the current and expected spot rates, a
drop in the</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0213" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00220.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 11: Comparison of seasonal changes in freight rates for Handysize dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_333"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0135"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0135"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
11:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">
Comparison of seasonal changes in freight rates for Handysize dry bulk
carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.281.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan"> Handysize, Handysize 1 and Handysize 3, represent the
spot, one-year and three-year TC rates, respectively</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan">spot market is
transmitted to the time-charter market accordingly.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.283.2" class="koboSpan">There is no
seasonal change in the third and the fourth quarter of the year.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.283.3" class="koboSpan">The only
exception is an increase in Panamax spot rates in the autumn.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">Secondly, for all
vessel types, the seasonal spring increase and summer drop in freight
rates decline as duration of contracts increases.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.284.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
the impact of seasonal fluctuations is more pronounced for the spot
rates and declines as we move to the one-year and three-year
time-charters, across all types of vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.284.3" class="koboSpan">This is
because one-year time-charter rates, say, are formed as the expected
future spot rates over the year (see Section 3.2).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.284.4" class="koboSpan">Therefore, one
would expect that one-year time-charter rates would have already
incorporated expected future seasonal variations and are smoother than
spot rates. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.284.5"
class="koboSpan">However, spot rates reflect the current market
conditions and any seasonal change in demand for shipping has a direct
impact on spot or short-term rates.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.285.1" class="koboSpan">Thirdly, the
magnitude of seasonal change is related to the size; that is, freight
rates for larger vessels show relatively greater seasonal change
compared to smaller ones. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.285.2"
class="koboSpan">The weaker seasonal increase or decline in average
freight rates for smaller size vessels may be attributed to their
flexibility, which enables them to switch between trades and routes more
easily compared to the larger ships.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, seasonal
changes in freight rates for all dry bulk carriers are more pronounced
during a freight market expansion and less distinct when the market is
in recession. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.286.2"
class="koboSpan">This is in line with the shape of the supply and demand
curve for freight services in freight rate determination as shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0127)<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.288.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.288.2"
class="koboSpan">More precisely, when the market is in the expansion
phase, supply is inelastic and any seasonal change in demand can result
in a sharp change in freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.288.3" class="koboSpan">Whereas, when
the market is in recession, there is spare capacity and tonnage, the
supply function for freight services is elastic and any seasonal change
in demand for freight services can be absorbed by excess supply, which
may result in a moderate change in freight rates.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, another
point worth noting is that the degree of seasonal fluctuation of
shipping freight rates varies across vessel sizes and duration of
contract. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.289.2" class="koboSpan">For
instance, the
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_334"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">impact of seasonal fluctuations is more pronounced for
the spot rates and declines as we move to the one-year and three-year
time-charters, across all types of vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.290.2" class="koboSpan">This is
because one-year time-charter rates, say, are formed as the expected
future spot rates over the year (see e.g.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.290.3" class="koboSpan">Beenstock and
Vergottis</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0294" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0294"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.291.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.292.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, one would expect that one-year time-charter
rates would have already incorporated expected future seasonal
variations and are smoother than spot rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.292.3" class="koboSpan">In addition,
spot rate seasonalities are expected to be higher than time-charter rate
ones to incorporate possible periods of unemployment (see endnote 9).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.292.4" class="koboSpan">As a
consequence differences in freight rate seasonalities between sectors
are eliminated since they depend less on the idiosyncratic factors
influencing rates in sub-markets and more on the duration (type) of the
contract involved. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.292.5"
class="koboSpan">These arguments extend to longer duration, three-year
time-charter contracts.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">The higher seasonal
fluctuations of spot rates compared to time charter rates may be further
explained as the result of the chartering strategy of industrial
charterers (e.g. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.293.2"
class="koboSpan">power stations and steel mills).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.293.3" class="koboSpan">This type of
charterers use long-term charter contracts not only to fulfil their long
term requirements in terms of supply of raw materials, but also to
secure and maintain their transportation cost at a relatively fixed
level over a long period. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.293.4"
class="koboSpan">They use the spot market then in order to meet their
seasonal or cyclical requirements.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.293.5" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
they may enter the spot market at certain seasons, which leads to an
increase in demand in the spot market and consequently the freight rates
at those periods.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.294.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Volatility of dry bulk shipping freight rates</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">From the academic
point of view, several studies are devoted to assessing, modelling and
forecasting the volatility of shipping freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.295.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
Kavussanos (see endnote 2), examines time-varying volatilities of the
dry bulk freight rates across vessel sizes as well as their aggregate
spot and time-charter rates using time-varying volatility models such as
Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (ARCH) and Generalised
Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH) models (see
Alizadeh and
Nomikos</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0295" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0295"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan"> for more details on modelling volatility of shipping
freight rates). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.297.2"
class="koboSpan">He reports that the pattern and magnitude of
time-varying volatilities in the dry bulk freight markets are different
across vessel sizes. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.297.3"
class="koboSpan">In particular, freight rates for larger vessels tend to
be more volatile than smaller ones.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.297.4" class="koboSpan">In another
study on time-varying volatilities of ship prices, Kavussanos (see
endnote 2) examines the dynamics of volatilities of second-hand prices
for different size dry bulk carriers.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.297.5" class="koboSpan">He concluded
that, in general, price volatilities in the dry bulk sector respond
together and symmetrically to external shocks; however, there are
differences, which are due to market segmentation and the fact that
these vessels are employed in different routes and trades.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.297.6" class="koboSpan">Also, he noted
that price volatilities are positively related to the size of vessel;
that is, prices for larger vessels show higher volatilities compared to
those of smaller ones. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.297.7"
class="koboSpan">This is attributed to the fact that larger vessels are
less flexible than smaller ones in terms of trading routes and
commodities that they carry. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.297.8"
class="koboSpan">As a result, responses of profitability and prices for
larger vessels to any unexpected changes in the market are more drastic
compared to smaller vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">To illustrate how the
volatility of dry bulk shipping freight rates evolves over time, we plot
the estimated time-varying volatility of spot, six-month and one-year
time-charter rates for capesize and Panamax vessel, using GARCH.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.298.2" class="koboSpan">The estimated
volatilities are presented in </span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0136"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0136"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 12</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0137"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0137"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan">13</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan"> for Capsize and Panamax vessel, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.302.2" class="koboSpan">It can be seen
that volatility of all types of freight contracts tend to move over time
as the market condition changes.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.302.3" class="koboSpan">In particular,
it can be noted that there are periods of relatively low</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0214" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00221.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 12: Time-varying volatility of spot, six-month, one-year and three-year time-charter rates for Capesize dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_335"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0136"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0136"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.304.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
12:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.305.1" class="koboSpan">
Time-varying volatility of spot, six-month, one-year and three-year
time-charter rates for Capesize dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0215" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00222.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 13: Time-varying volatility of spot, six-month, one-year and three-year time-charter rates for Panamax dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0137"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0137"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.307.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
13:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">
Time-varying volatility of spot, six-month, one-year and three-year
time-charter rates for Panamax dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.309.1" class="koboSpan">volatility followed
by periods of extremely high volatility across all freight contracts, a
phenomenon known as volatility clustering in financial economics.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.309.2" class="koboSpan">The highest
volatility observed in the market was over the second half of 2008, when
the shipping market collapsed as a result of the downturn in the world
economy. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.309.3"
class="koboSpan">During that period, estimated annualised volatilities
of capesize and panamax freight rates were 300% and 180%, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.309.4" class="koboSpan">This can be
compared to the historical spot freight rate volatilities of 95% and 60%
in the Capesize and Panamax shipping sectors, respectively.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_336"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan">Alizadeh</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0296" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0296"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan"> utilises multivariate GARCH models to investigate
freight rate volatility transmissions between different dry bulk size
vessels, both in the spot and time-charter markets.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.312.2" class="koboSpan">Results of
volatility models reveal that there are unidirectional volatility
spillover effects from larger to smaller size vessels in the spot and
period markets. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.312.3"
class="koboSpan">It is argued that volatility transmissions could be due
to substitution effects amongst different size of ships in the dry bulk
market as well as the higher sensitivity of freight rate for larger
vessels to unexpected news compared to small ones which may force
operators of larger vessels to switch to and from the market for smaller
vessels and subsequently disturb the supply and demand balance in those
markets.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">In a recent study,
Alizadeh and
Nomikos</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0297" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0297"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan"> use an augmented exponential GARCH model (EGARCH-X) to
examine the relationship between the shape of the term structure and the
volatility of dry bulk freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.315.2" class="koboSpan">Using a
freight dataset covering the period from January 1992 to September 2007,
they find evidence which supports the argument that volatility of
freight rates is related to the shape of the term structure of freight
rates. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.315.3" class="koboSpan">More
precisely, they argue that there is a non-linear relationship between
volatility of freight earnings and the slope of forward curve in the
form of a cubic function implying that the rate of increase in
volatility increases (decreases) as the degree of forward curve market
backwardation (contango) increases.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">3.5 The efficiency of dry bulk freight markets</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">The relationship
between spot and period (time-charter) rates has always been a pivotal
issue in modelling shipping freight markets.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.317.2" class="koboSpan">Several
studies in the literature are devoted to examining this relationship
utilising different theories, methodologies and various data sets.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.317.3" class="koboSpan">The studies on
the relationship between long- and short-term rates can be classified
into two categories. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.317.4"
class="koboSpan">On the one hand there are attempts to model long-term
rates assuming that some form of expectations mechanism relates
long-term to short-term freight rates and the efficient market
hypothesis holds (e.g. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.317.5"
class="koboSpan">Zannetos (see endnote 6), Beenstock and Vergottis (see
endnote
17)</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0298" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0298"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.319.1"
class="koboSpan">, Glen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 7) and
Strandenes</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0299" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0299"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.323.2"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, a number of studies test the
efficient market hypothesis and investigate the validity of the
expectations hypothesis in the relationship between short and long term
rates (e.g. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.323.3"
class="koboSpan">Hale and Vanags (see endnote 8) and
Veenstra</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0300" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0300"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.324.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.326.1" class="koboSpan">The notable work of
Zannetos (see endnote 6) was the first attempt to study the relationship
between long- and short-term tanker rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.326.2" class="koboSpan">He provides
comprehensive theoretical arguments and analyses to establish the
theoretical relationship between long and short term tanker freight
rates during the 1950s. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.326.3"
class="koboSpan">Zannetos points out the similarities between money
markets and freight markets and argues that period rates should
represent a weighted average of future spot rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.326.4" class="koboSpan">He also
proposes the “elastic expectations” theory in the formation of long-term
rates, but fails to provide supporting evidence.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.327.1" class="koboSpan">Glen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.328.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 7) propose a present value model for the
relationship between spot and time-charter rates in the tanker market
and transform the relationship to estimate an autoregressive distributed
lag model which relates period rates to lagged spot rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.329.2" class="koboSpan">They find a
different lag structure to that proposed by Zannetos and conclude that
the expectations in the formation of period rates may not be elastic.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.329.3" class="koboSpan">Strandenes
(see endnote 22) argues that period rates are formed through agents’
“semi-rational expectations”. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.329.4"
class="koboSpan">She finds that current spot and long-run equilibrium
rates are both important determinants of time-charter rates for Panamax
dry bulk carriers, medium and large tankers.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.329.5" class="koboSpan">However, her
estimation results show that current spot and long-run
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_337"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan">equilibrium rates have different impacts on the
formation of long-term rates across different types of vessels; i.e.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.330.2" class="koboSpan">results are
not consistent across sizes.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.331.1" class="koboSpan">Beenstock and
Vergottis (see endnote 17, 21) assume that Rational Expectations (RE)
and the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) in the formation of
time-charter rates are valid and base their integrated shipping industry
model on these assumptions. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.331.2"
class="koboSpan">They find that current and expected spot rates are
significant determinants of time-charter rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.331.3" class="koboSpan">However, they
do not attempt to investigate the validity of EMH and rational
expectations in the formation of period rates.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.332.1" class="koboSpan">Hale and Vanags (see
endnote 8) test the EMH and RE in the formation of freight rates using
disaggregated dry bulk market series and find no support for the theory.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.332.2" class="koboSpan">Veenstra (see
endnote 23) reports further results on the expectations hypothesis and
the term structure relationship of dry bulk voyage and time-charter
rates. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.332.3"
class="koboSpan">Although his study suffers from methodological issues
(see Kavussanos and Alizadeh (see endnote 9)), he concludes that the
results support the expectations hypothesis of the term structure for
three size dry bulk carriers. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.332.4"
class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and Alizadeh (see endnote 9), use the
present value relationship between long-term and short-term rates and
modify a series of tests, proposed initially by Campbell and
Shiller</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0301" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0301"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.334.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0302" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0302"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan"> for the bond market, to investigate the relationship
between short and long term freight rates in the dry bulk shipping
sector and test for the validity of the Expectations Hypothesis of the
Term Structure (EHTS) in the formation of long-term rates for three
different size dry bulk carriers.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.336.2" class="koboSpan">Tests employed
include; the perfect foresight spread test, restrictions on the Vector
Autoregressive (VAR) model, variance ratio and cointegration tests.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.336.3" class="koboSpan">These tests
are more robust than those that had been employed previously in studies
of shipping freight rates, as they directly take into account the
stochastic properties of freight rate series, an important fact which is
strongly recommended in the literature in order to avoid several
statistical
problems.</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0303" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0303"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.338.1" class="koboSpan">More specifically,
the EHTS is tested (see endnote 9) using the following present value
relationship between the spot and period time-chartr rates:</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0216" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.339.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00223.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.340.1" class="koboSpan">where
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00224.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.343.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00225.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.344.1"
class="koboSpan"> are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.345.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.346.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.348.1"
class="koboSpan"> period spot and time charter contracts, respectively,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.349.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan"> is an integer,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.351.1"
class="koboSpan">r</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the discount rate and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan">E</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.355.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the expectations operator.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.355.2" class="koboSpan">The EMH in the
formation of long-term rates (or the relationship between long-term
rates and expected spot rates) implies that the above equation should be
empirically valid. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.355.3"
class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and Alizadeh9 use different transformations
of the above model for one-year and three-year time-charter rates for
three different size dry bulk carriers.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.355.4" class="koboSpan">Based on a
series of tests, they find that the EMH is rejected.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.356.1" class="koboSpan">They then propose a
model which relates spot and long-term time-charter rates and takes into
account the risks associated with the spot market.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.356.2" class="koboSpan">This model
uses an Exponential Generalised Autoregressive Heteroskedasticity in the
Mean, (EGARCH-M)
(Nelson</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0304" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0304"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan">)
framework.</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0305" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0305"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.359.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan"> They find that the coefficient of time-varying risk
premium, which relates long term and short term freight contracts, is
negative. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.360.2" class="koboSpan">In
other words, shipowners are prepared to offer a discount, which varies
over time, to fix charter contracts with longer terms to maturity
(time-charters) compared to when they operate in the spot market.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_338"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan">The argument that they put forward for the existence of
such negative risk premia is based on the fact that shipowners operating
in the spot markets are generally exposed to four types of risk, in
comparison to those operating in time-charter markets.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.361.2" class="koboSpan">First, spot
rates show higher fluctuations compared to time-charter rates;
risk-averse shipowners may thus respond to this by fixing their vessels
in the period market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.361.3"
class="koboSpan">Secondly, for a shipowner operating in spot markets
there is always a chance that the owner may not be able to fix a
contract for a period of time (unemployment risk) even when operation
and chartering is well planned. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.361.4"
class="koboSpan">Thirdly, there are cases when the owner has to relocate
a vessel from one port to another for a new spot charter contract;
depending on the occasion this may take some time and involve
substantial costs. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.361.5"
class="koboSpan">Finally, if voyage spot rates (rather than trip-charter
spot rates) are compared to time-charter rates, shipowners are also
exposed to voyage (mainly bunker) cost fluctuations (see endnote 18).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.361.6" class="koboSpan">Thus,
shipowners operating in the time-charter market are prepared to offer a
discount to cover the risk, which they are exposed to when operating in
the spot market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.361.7"
class="koboSpan">It seems that the magnitude of this discount is time
dependent and reflects the degree of uncertainty in the market.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.362.1" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the
sentiment of the banks and lenders in shipping finance might be another
important factor influencing shipowners’ decision to operate in the spot
or the time-charter market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.362.2"
class="koboSpan">Financiers view differently clients (shipowners) who
are committed to long-term shipping contracts when financing a ship
purchase or newbuilding, since this ensures a relatively more secure
stream of income for the shipowner and reduces the probability of loan
default. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.362.3" class="koboSpan">Thus,
shipowners may be prepared to offer a discount when fixing their vessel
on a long-term contract, as opposed to short-term ones, to fulfil the
lender’s requirements for the loan.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.362.4" class="koboSpan">This argument
can be quite important during periods of market uncertainty, supporting
further the existence of time-varying risk premia in shipping freight
markets.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.363.1" class="koboSpan">The fact that time
charter rates can deviate from their theoretical values for considerable
time periods has an important implication as risk neutral or risk prone
operators can make excess profits by hiring vessels in the time-charter
market, when time-charter rates are under priced and operating them in
the spot market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.363.2"
class="koboSpan">Agents involved in freight trading can utilise the
difference between actual and theoretical time-charter rates as an
indicator of which contract to choose at any point in time.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.363.3" class="koboSpan">Thus, risk
neutral shipowners may choose to operate in the spot market when actual
time-charter rates are below their theoretical values and switch to the
time-charter market when actual time-charter rates are greater than
their theoretical values.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.364.1" class="koboSpan">3.6 Interrelationships and spillover effects across dry bulk freight markets</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">It has been argued
earlier, as well as in the literature (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.365.2" class="koboSpan">Stopford (see
endnote 5), Kavussanos (see endnotes 2, 3)), that the dry bulk market is
disaggregated by size and each size vessel is involved in the
transportation of certain commodities with a low degree of substitution
between vessels of different sizes.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.365.3" class="koboSpan">This implies a
degree of segregation in the behaviour of freight rate levels and
volatilities. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.365.4"
class="koboSpan">However, sometimes vessels of adjacent size categories
are used as substitutes; for instance, Panamax instead of Handysize,
Capesize instead of Panamax and vice versa.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.365.5" class="koboSpan">Such
substitutions become more significant when the demand in one market is
relatively higher than in the other market and is enough to attract,
say, larger vessels to accept part cargoes and make a profit.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.365.6" class="koboSpan">There
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_339"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan">might be occasions when charterers prefer to hire
smaller vessels for the transportation of commodities, which are
conventionally carried by larger vessels; for example by splitting the
large consignment into two or three shipments.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.366.2" class="koboSpan">This is
usually the case when importers prefer or switch to “just in time”
inventory management techniques, or try to top up their seasonal
requirements, which might be less than a large shipment.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.367.1" class="koboSpan">The above argument
suggests that although different size dry bulk carriers are not perfect
substitutes, they may overlap in their cargo transportation capabilities
or even be linked through intermediate size vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.367.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore, one
would expect that shocks to any sub-sector might be transmitted to other
sub-sectors. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.367.3"
class="koboSpan">For instance, if there is an increase in demand and
subsequently freight rates for Handysize vessels, other size categories
such as Panamax vessels may react by participating in the Handysize
market by accepting part cargoes, if this is found to be more
profitable. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.367.4"
class="koboSpan">This shift from one market to the other will cause an
over supply in the Handysize market and a shortage of supply in the
Panamax market and, as a result, Handysize rates will drop and Panamax
rates will rise. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.367.5"
class="koboSpan">This process will continue until both markets
stabilise; that is, until supply equals demand in each market and there
is no opportunity to make extra profit by switching between
markets.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.368.1" class="koboSpan">By investigating the
form of interrelationships among these sub-markets in shipping can shed
light to important issues such as the degree of substitutability between
different dry bulk sub-sectors and the speed of stabilisation of freight
rates in each market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.368.2"
class="koboSpan">Beenstock and
Vergottis</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0306" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0306"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.369.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.370.1"
class="koboSpan"> investigated the spillover effects between tanker and
dry bulk markets. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.370.2"
class="koboSpan">They trace the spillover effects between the markets
through the market for combined carriers, shipbuilding and scrapping
markets using dynamic econometric models and simulation techniques.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.370.3" class="koboSpan">Alizadeh (see
endnote 19), extends the findings of this study, by investigating the
spillover effects between different segments within the dry bulk sector
of the shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.370.4"
class="koboSpan">He employs cointegration, vector error correction
models (VECM) and impulse response analysis instead of dynamic
structural models. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.370.5"
class="koboSpan">Charter contracts with different terms to maturity
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.370.6" class="koboSpan">spot,
one-year and three-year time-charter rates, are analysed and comparisons
are made to highlight differences in spillover effects within the spot
markets in comparison to those of time-charter markets).</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.371.1" class="koboSpan">Additionally, the
same study also investigates the existence of volatility spillovers from
one sub-sector to other sub-sectors within the spot and time-charter
markets. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.371.2" class="koboSpan">This
is done by using a multivariate VECM in the mean with a multivariate
generalised autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH)
specification, in what is termed a VECM-GARCH model.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.371.3" class="koboSpan">These types of
models have been used in the financial economics literature to assess
the integration as well as the transmission of information between the
capital, interest rates or commodity markets worldwide (see for
instance, Koutmos and
Booth,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0307" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0307"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.372.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.373.1"
class="koboSpan"> Koutmos and
Tucker</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0308" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0308"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.374.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.375.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Kavussanos and
Nomikos</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0309" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0309"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.376.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.377.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.378.1" class="koboSpan">In total, three
different systems (for spot, one-year and three-year time-charter rates)
of VECM and VECM-GARCH models for freight rates for three size vessels
have been estimated over the period January 1980 to August 1997 for the
purposes of this analysis. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.378.2"
class="koboSpan">Impulse response analyses on the estimated models
reveal that the interaction between freight rates for different size
vessels are higher in the spot market than one-year and three-year
time-charter markets. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.378.3"
class="koboSpan">This might be due to the difference between the
charterers’ decision making process on hiring vessels in the spot market
and time-charter markets. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.378.4"
class="koboSpan">Decisions on hiring vessels in the spot market are
thought to be more instantaneous, based on short terms and sometimes
urgent transportation
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_340"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.379.1"
class="koboSpan">requirements. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.379.2"
class="koboSpan">In contrast to the spot market, decisions made by
charterers to hire vessels in the period market are in general based on
detailed analysis of costs and transportation needs.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.379.3" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
there might be situations where owners operating in the spot market find
that even a part cargo is better than waiting for a full load.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.379.4" class="koboSpan">They may even
accept a part cargo on a back haul voyage rather than returning to the
loading area in ballast. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.379.5"
class="koboSpan">Such decisions by owners in the spot market increase
the competition between vessels of different sizes for cargo and
consequently increase the interaction between their freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.379.6" class="koboSpan">As a result,
shocks to freight rates for any size vessel in the spot market are
transmitted across to freight rates for other size categories faster
than shocks in the period charter markets.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.380.1" class="koboSpan">Analysis of spillover
effects between volatilities of freight rates for different size vessels
in the spot and period markets reveal that volatilities of freight rates
for Capesize vessels affect volatilities of freight rates for smaller
vessels across the contract maturity spectrum.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.380.2" class="koboSpan">More
specifically, shocks to the Capesize market are transmitted to the
market for smaller vessels without any feedback effects.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.380.3" class="koboSpan">The
unidirectional volatility spillovers from Capesize market to the market
for smaller vessels can be explained by the fact that the market for
larger vessels is more sensitive to news than the market for smaller
size vessels. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.380.4"
class="koboSpan">This is because small vessels are more flexible than
Capesize vessels in terms of operational flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.380.5" class="koboSpan">As a result,
shocks to freight rates for smaller vessels, due to changes in the
demand for transportation of certain types of commodities over a
particular route, may be absorbed by employment of those vessels in
other trading routes. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.380.6"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, the number of routes and trades at
which large vessels operate is limited.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.380.7" class="koboSpan">As a result,
unexpected changes in the market for those vessels may have a greater
impact on the whole dry bulk market compared to the effect of unexpected
events the market for smaller vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.381.1" class="koboSpan">In addition, the
carrying capacity of larger vessels compared to smaller ones and the
agents’ expectations about movements of vessels between markets might be
an important factor in causing volatility spillovers.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.381.2" class="koboSpan">Given that the
carrying capacity of a Capesize vessel is two times that of a Panamax
vessel (three times that of a Handysize vessel), move of one Capesize
vessel to the Panamax market, during the downturn in the Capesize market
or a relatively good Panamax market, may satisfy the demand for two
Panamax vessels. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.381.3"
class="koboSpan">In an opposite situation, two Panamax vessels are
required to satisfy the demand for one Capesize vessel.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.381.4" class="koboSpan">This suggests
that crossovers of larger vessels to markets for smaller vessels may
have greater impact on the supply and demand balance in markets for
smaller vessels compared to the impact on supply and demand balance in
the market for larger vessels caused by the move of smaller vessels to
the market for large vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.382.1" class="koboSpan">Another interesting
finding of this study is that levels of time-varying volatilities of
freight rates in each of the spot and period (one-year and three-year)
markets are directly related to vessel size; that is, the level of
time-varying volatility is higher for larger vessels compared to smaller
ones. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.382.2" class="koboSpan">Results
also indicate that the level of time-varying volatilities for each size
vessel are also related to the duration of contract; that is, the longer
the duration of contract, the lower the level of time-varying
volatility. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.382.3"
class="koboSpan">This is because time-charter rates reflect weighted
average of expected future spot rates and therefore sharp changes in
spot rates are smoothened when time-charter rates are formed.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.382.4" class="koboSpan">Also, spot
rates are more influenced from current market conditions and news,
whereas period rates depend on agents’ expectations about the future
market conditions over a period of time.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_341"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.383.1" class="koboSpan">3.7 Implied forward time-charter rates</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.384.1" class="koboSpan">The existence of
freight contracts with different maturities (durations) in the shipping
industry offers both shipowners and charterers flexibility in their
decisions regarding chartering and operational activities.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.384.2" class="koboSpan">As discussed
above, short-term or spot charter rates are determined through the
interaction between current supply and demand for shipping services,
whereas long-term period rates are believed to be determined through
agents’ expectations about future short-term rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.384.3" class="koboSpan">Several
studies have investigated the relationship between spot and long-term
charter contracts (see e.g. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.384.4"
class="koboSpan">Hale and Vanags (see endnote 8), Veenstra (see endnote
23), and Kavussanos and Alizadeh (see endnote 9), among others).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.384.5" class="koboSpan">The general
focus of these studies is how time-charter rates are formed through
expected spot rates and whether such a relationship is in line with the
notion of the efficient market hypothesis (EMH).</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.385.1" class="koboSpan">The most important
implication of EMH in relation to the shipping freight market is that
charter contracts, with different maturities, should be related in such
a way that charterers/shipowners be indifferent to operating under a
period contract or a series of consecutive short term contracts over the
life of the long term contract. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.385.2"
class="koboSpan">Otherwise, there will be instances where the difference
between the two chartering strategies can be exploited by agents to make
excess profit without taking additional risk.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.385.3" class="koboSpan">The
relationship between short-term and long-term contracts, known as the
term structure relationship, is embedded in theories such as the
expectations hypothesis of the term structure (EHTS).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.385.4" class="koboSpan">According to
the EHTS long term time-charter rates, say for one year, should reflect
the weighted average of expected monthly (spot) freight contracts over
the next 12 months. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.385.5"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, any deviation from such a relationship is
explained through the existence of time-varying risk premia.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.386.1" class="koboSpan">Let
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.387.1"

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan"> denote the time-charter rate at a given time
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.389.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.390.1"
class="koboSpan"> with maturity
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.392.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.392.2"
class="koboSpan">If we observe two time-charter rates with different
maturities, say
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.394.1"
class="koboSpan"> and

class="koboSpan">2 </span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan">and assume that the EMH holds, the implied forward
time-charter rate for period

class="koboSpan">can be calculated.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.407.2" class="koboSpan">This is due to
the fact that if EMH holds, agents should be indifferent in chartering a

class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.418.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, using the present value model and assuming a
constant discount rate,

class="koboSpan">r</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.420.1"
class="koboSpan">, we can wrie:</span>

</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.431.2" class="koboSpan">Rearranging

</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.448.1"

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.449.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the implied forward six-month time-charter rate at
time </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.450.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.451.1"
class="koboSpan"> for
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.452.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.453.1"
