class="koboSpan">6.</span></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.455.1" class="koboSpan">In a recent study,
Alizadeh </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.456.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0310" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0310"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.457.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.458.1"
class="koboSpan"> investigated the predictive power of the implied
forward </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.459.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.460.1"
class="koboSpan"> rates as a forecast of future
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.461.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.462.1"
class="koboSpan"> rates in comparison with other statistical models in
the dry bulk market such as Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average
(ARIMA), Vector Autoregressive (VAR) and Vector Error Correction model
(VECM). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.462.2" class="koboSpan">Using
historical 12- and six-month time-charter rates for capesize, Panamax
and Handymax dry bulk carriers and variety of forecast performance
measures, they report that implied
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.463.1"
class="koboSpan">TC </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.464.1"
class="koboSpan">rates significantly outperform all statistical models
in all three dry bulk sub-markets.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.464.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
they find that these implied forward time-charter rates are unbiased
predictors of time-charter rates observed in the future; that is, the
average forecast error of implied
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.465.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.466.1"
class="koboSpan"> rates is zero and there is no systematic pattern in
their behaviour. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.466.2"
class="koboSpan">This finding is important because it can be regarded as
additional evidence on the reliability of the forecasts produced by
implied forward
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.467.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.468.1"
class="koboSpan"> rates in the dry bulk marker.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.469.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, Alizadeh
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.470.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.471.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 33) also investigated whether agents can
make excess profit by simple chartering strategies based on technical
trading rules. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.471.2"
class="koboSpan">This is interesting because if the notion of EMH is
valid, then there should not be any possibility for making excess profit
through chartering strategies. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.471.3"
class="koboSpan">They examined whether hiring in vessels for long period
charters (12 months) and re-letting them over shorter periods (two
consecutive six-month periods), is profitable.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.471.4" class="koboSpan">The trading
strategy is based on application of technical analysis on the
differential between short-term and long-term charter rates (the
spread). </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.471.5" class="koboSpan">For
instance, they use simple moving average (MA) chartering strategy
defined as follows: “charter in a vessel on a 12-month
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.472.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.473.1"
class="koboSpan"> and simultaneously re-let the vessel on a six-month
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.474.1"
class="koboSpan">TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.475.1"
class="koboSpan"> if the current spread between the
two</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.476.1"
class="koboSpan"> TC</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.477.1"
class="koboSpan"> rates exceeds the average of the spread over the last
Y weeks”. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.477.2" class="koboSpan">The
study also reports that the simple MA trading rules generate substantial
profit when they are implemented in an out-of-sample evaluation period
and that technical trading models perform better on the basis of a
rolling or continuously expanding estimation
sample.</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0311" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0311"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.478.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.479.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.479.2" class="koboSpan">The Market for Ships</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.480.1" class="koboSpan">The market for ships
consists of three different sub-markets, namely: the newbuilding market;
the second-hand market; and the scrap market.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.480.2" class="koboSpan">Within each
submarket, the interaction between supply and demand for the asset
determines the vessel price. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.480.3"
class="koboSpan">Almost all ship sales and purchases (S&P) are carried
out through specialist S&P brokers, with the exception of newbuildings,
which may be ordered by investors to shipyards directly.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.480.4" class="koboSpan">The sale and
purchase of ships is a lengthy process, which can take anything between
a few weeks and several months to complete.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.480.5" class="koboSpan">This process
involves different stages of placing the ship in the market, the
negotiation of price and conditions of contract, preparing the
memorandum of agreement, inspections and final closing of the deal,
after which the ship is delivered to the buyer.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_343"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.481.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Factors determining ship prices</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.482.1" class="koboSpan">The factors affecting
the price of a vessel can be classified into vessel specific and market
specific. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.482.2"
class="koboSpan">Vessel-specific factors are those related to the
particulars and condition of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.482.3" class="koboSpan">These are
size, type, age and the general condition of the vessel, as well as
quality of design, build, equipment and engine.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.482.4" class="koboSpan">In general, we
expect larger vessel to be more expensive than smaller ones, older
vessels to be less expensive than newer vessels and certain types of
specialist vessels (e.g. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.482.5"
class="koboSpan">LNG carriers, Ro-Ro vessels, cruise liners) to be more
expensive than conventional box shaped bulk carriers.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.482.6" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the general condition and state of the vessel is important because well
maintained vessels tend to be more employable compared to those that are
not maintained properly. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.482.7"
class="koboSpan">The age of vessel is another important factor in
determination of the second hand price of vessels, since generally older
ships are less expensive than modern ones.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.482.8" class="koboSpan">This is
because not only ships are subject to depreciation and, as time passes,
lose part of their
value,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0312" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0312"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.483.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.484.1"
class="koboSpan"> but also because advances in shipbuilding technology
over time mean that more modern ships are built with better
specifications in terms of fuel consumption and efficiency as well as
operating
efficiency.</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0313" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0313"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.485.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.486.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.487.1" class="koboSpan">Market conditions are
also an important factor in the determination of and changes in, vessel
price. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.487.2" class="koboSpan">It is
generally believed and documented in the shipping economics literature
that ships are capital assets which generate income and they are priced
after their expected profitability (see
</span>[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.488.1" class="koboSpan">chapter
13</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_ht0313)<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.489.1"
class="koboSpan"> of Alizadeh and Nomikos (see endnote 18) for details)
using an asset pricing model. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.489.2"
class="koboSpan">The most important factor in the determination of ship
prices are the current and expected earnings or operational revenue of
the vessel over her life. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.489.3"
class="koboSpan">What determines current and expected earnings for a
ship is the general state of the freight market.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.489.4" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
current and expected freight rate levels and market conditions are
amongst the most important factors in ship price formation.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.490.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 The newbuilding market</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.491.1" class="koboSpan">As the name suggests,
the newbuilding market is the market for newly built ships or ships
which are ordered by shipping companies, shipowners and investors to be
delivered after the construction period, which takes between several
months and a few years. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.491.2"
class="koboSpan">The perfect market condition also holds for this market
as not only international shipowners take several quotations from
various shipyards before placing orders, but also there are no barriers
for shipyards to market their products internationally and to compete
with other shipyards. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.491.3"
class="koboSpan">Newbuilding prices are also determined through supply
and demand factors for new ships and are generally negotiated and
settled between investors and shipyards.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.491.4" class="koboSpan">In general,
Newbuilding prices depend on the market condition and other determinants
such as steel prices, the level of freight rates, the backlog of the
shipyard (or the shipbuilding industry in general), terms of contract,
etc. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.491.5" class="koboSpan">For
example, in a good market, when freight rates are high and shipyards’
orderbooks are full, newbuilding prices may rise considerably, whereas
when the freight market is depressed and shipbuilding activity is low,
newbuilding prices may fall rapidly.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.491.6" class="koboSpan">This is
because shipyards are willing to accept orders at very low prices to
survive and avoid down sizing.</span>

<a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0138"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0138"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.492.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 14</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.493.1"
class="koboSpan"> plots monthly newbuilding prices for three sizes of
dry bulk carriers over the period January 1976 to April 2008, except
Capesize prices, which are available from April 1979.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.493.2" class="koboSpan">It can be seen
that newbuilding prices vary by vessel size but show</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0220" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.494.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00237.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 14: Newbuilding prices for different size dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_344"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0138"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0138"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.495.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
14:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.496.1" class="koboSpan">
Newbuilding prices for different size dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.497.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.498.1"
class="koboSpan">Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.499.1" class="koboSpan">similar behaviour
over time. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.499.2" class="koboSpan">In
fact, it can be argued that these series follow similar patterns and
move together in the long run, that is, price levels follow a similar
cyclical pattern. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.499.3"
class="koboSpan">For example, price levels for all size vessels show
peaks between 1980 to 1982 and 1989 to 1992, whilst there are troughs in
price levels between 1976 to 1979, 1983 to 1988 and 1992 to 1997.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.499.4" class="koboSpan">The cyclical
behaviour of newbuilding prices is believed to be the combined result of
fluctuations in world economic activity (international seaborne trade)
and the investment (ordering) behaviour of shipowners (see, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.499.5"
class="koboSpan">Tinbergen,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0314" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0314"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.500.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.501.1"
class="koboSpan">
Vergottis,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0315" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0315"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.502.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.503.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Stopford (see endnote 5)).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.503.2" class="koboSpan">More
precisely, when investors expect the freight market to rise, they place
new orders to take advantage of the positive market prospects.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.503.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
there is excess demand for new vessels, orderbooks grow and prices will
rise. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.503.4" class="koboSpan">By the
time, the new vessels are delivered: (1) there might be an excess
tonnage in the market due to excessive orders; (2) the freight market
may collapse due to excess supply, both from reduction in scrapping of
old vessels as well as the arrival of new deliveries; (3) or, even the
demand for shipping services may collapse due to the drop in the world
economic activity. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.503.5"
class="koboSpan">This effect is then transmitted back to the
shipbuilding market through investment decisions of agents, reducing the
demand for newbuildings and prices for new ships.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.503.6" class="koboSpan">Shipbuilding
cycles, which are caused by the mismatch between investors’ expectations
and the world’s economic activity, have been repeatedly observed in the
shipping industry.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.504.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 The second-hand market</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.505.1" class="koboSpan">The second-hand
market, better known as the sale and purchase market, is the market for
vessels, which are ready for trade and aged anything between one year
and 20 years or more. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.505.2"
class="koboSpan">In terms of liquidity, about 1,000 vessels are bought
and sold in the sale and purchase market every year, out of which about
30% are dry bulk carriers and 30% tanker ships, that is, at least one of
each vessel every day. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.505.3"
class="koboSpan">The sale and purchase market is known as one of the
most competitive markets in the world as it is an open market and buyers
and sellers are under no obligation to follow any sort of price
restrictions.</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0221" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.506.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00238.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 15: Historical five-year second-hand prices for different size dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_345"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0139"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0139"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.507.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
15:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.508.1" class="koboSpan">
Historical five-year second-hand prices for different size dry bulk
carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.509.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.510.1"
class="koboSpan"> Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.511.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore, prices are
determined through supply and demand conditions in the market which, in
turn, depend on the current and expected world economic activity, the
current and expected freight market conditions, the current and expected
bunker prices and the current and expected ship prices.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.511.2" class="koboSpan">In other
words, second-hand prices directly depend on the profitability of the
market (see for example
Beenstock,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0316" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0316"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.512.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.513.1"
class="koboSpan"> Beenstock and Vergottis (see endnote 17) and
Strandenes (see endnote 22)).</span>

<a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0139"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0139"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.514.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 15</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.515.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents monthly prices for five-year old second-hand
prices for three different sizes of dry bulk carriers over the period
January 1976 to April 2008. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.515.2"
class="koboSpan">A visual inspection reveals that second-hand prices for
different size bulk carriers move together in the long run.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.515.3" class="koboSpan">This is the
case as the price series are thought to be linked through a common a
stochastic trend, i.e. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.515.4"
class="koboSpan">the world economic activity and the volume of
international seaborne trade (see Glen (see endnote 43)).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.515.5" class="koboSpan">However, short
run dynamics of second-hand prices do not seem to be identical.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.515.6" class="koboSpan">These
differences are due to variations in the demand for different size
vessels and the profitability of the freight market for each size
because current and expected freight rate levels are argued to be the
major determinants of second-hand prices.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.516.1" class="koboSpan">Another interesting
point which can be observed from the evolution of the price series is
that when the market is in recession (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.516.2" class="koboSpan">prices are at
lowest levels), the three-price series converge and the difference
between prices reduces compared to when the market is good.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.516.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
during the 1982 to 1986 recession, prices for Handysize, Panamax and
Capesize vessels seem to converge.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.516.4" class="koboSpan">The price
difference between a second-hand Capesize and second-hand Handysize
during this period is less than \$8m.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.516.5" class="koboSpan">When the
market is in expansion phase, second-hand prices diverge as larger
vessels become relatively more expensive than smaller ones.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.516.6" class="koboSpan">For example,
between 1988 and 1994, the difference between second-hand prices for
Capesize and Handysize vessels is between of \$15m and \$20m.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.516.7" class="koboSpan">Since it is
the operational profitability that determines second-hand prices, the
divergence and convergence of prices can be explained by the relative
profitability of these vessels under different market conditions.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.516.8" class="koboSpan">For
example,</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0222" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.517.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00239.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 16: Historical scrap prices for different size dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_346"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0140"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0140"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.518.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
16:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.519.1" class="koboSpan">
Historical scrap prices for different size dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.520.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.521.1"
class="koboSpan"> Clarkson’s SIN</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.522.1" class="koboSpan">larger vessels
generate more revenue and operating profit during expansion periods as
they can be used for carrying larger amount of cargo; however, they bear
the higher risk of unemployment during recessions due to their
operational inflexibility. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.522.2"
class="koboSpan">In contrast to larger vessels, smaller bulk carriers
are not as profitable during periods of market expansion, but they are
more flexible and can switch between trades during recessions.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.522.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
smaller vessels are more likely to be employed in tight markets in
comparison to larger vessels and generate reasonable profit even in bad
times.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.523.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 The scrap or demolition market</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.524.1" class="koboSpan">The third market for
ships is where those ships, which are not economical to operate, are
sold for demolition or scrapping.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.524.2" class="koboSpan">Ship-breakers
buy scrap vessels from shipowners for their scrap metal on a \$/ldt
(light displacement
tonnes</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0317" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0317"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.525.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.526.1"
class="koboSpan">) basis and dismantle them to reuse the steel and other
parts and equipment on board the vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.526.2" class="koboSpan">The age at
which ships are sold for scrap varies over time and largely depends on
the condition of the freight market as well as the second-hand, the
newbuilding and the scrap markets.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.526.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
when freight rates are low and the expectations for future market
improvements are not so positive, owners of relatively inefficient
vessels, which may have been laid up due to unemployment, may be forced
to sell their vessels for scrap to avoid further losses.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.526.4" class="koboSpan">Consequently
the increase in supply of scrap vessels causes the scrap price to fall.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.526.5" class="koboSpan">When freight
rates are relatively high and there is a shortage in the supply of
shipping services, even older, less efficient vessels could be
profitable; therefore, there may not be any pressure to scrap old and
inefficient vessels. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.526.6"
class="koboSpan">As a result, there will be a shortage of supply in the
scrap market, which causes the scrap price to rise.</span>

<a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0140"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0140"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.527.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 16</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.528.1"
class="koboSpan"> plots the monthly scrap prices, in million US\$, for
different sizes of dry bulk over the period January 1976 to February
2008, respectively. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.528.2"
class="koboSpan">In general, scrap prices tend to follow the trend in
shipping freight markets. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.528.3"
class="koboSpan">Scrap values of larger vessels are higher than those of
smaller vessels in both sectors because of their greater steel</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0223" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.529.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00240.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 17: Historical newbuilding, five year old second-hand and scrap prices for Panamax dry bulk carriers" /></span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_347"></span><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0141"
id="Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0141"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.530.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
17:</span></span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.531.1" class="koboSpan">
Historical newbuilding, five year old second-hand and scrap prices for
Panamax dry bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.532.1" class="koboSpan">content and light
displacement weight. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.532.2"
class="koboSpan">In addition, scrap prices for all types of ships seem
to have reached record highs in 2008, due to the bullish freight market
conditions, increase in world scrap steel prices and the limited number
of vessels available for scrapping.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.532.3" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
it seems that scrap prices for larger vessels show relatively greater
variation compared to those of smaller ships.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.532.4" class="koboSpan">This is
evident from the range within which scrap prices fluctuate.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.532.5" class="koboSpan">For instance,
while historical scrap values of Capesize vessels vary between \$1.5m
and \$12m, historical scrap prices for Handysize dry bulk carrier vary
between \$0.3m and \$5m.</span>

<a href="#Ch011.xhtml_cap_lbl0141"
id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0141"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.533.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 17</span></a><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.534.1"
class="koboSpan"> plots the historical newbuilding, second-hand and
scrap prices for Panamax dry bulk carriers.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.534.2" class="koboSpan">It can be seen
that newbuilding and scrap prices set an upper and a lower barrier for
second-hand Panamax prices, respectively and second-hand prices for
five-year-old Panamax fluctuate within this band over time.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.534.3" class="koboSpan">However, an
interesting point is that when the shipping market is in recession (1982
to 1986), second-hand prices are closer to scrap prices and when the
market is at its peak (1988 to 1990 and 2003 to 2008) second-hand prices
are close to newbuilding prices.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.534.4" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
when the dry bulk market is exceptionally profitable and the orderbooks
for newbuildings are relatively full, the second-hand price can exceed
the newbuilding price, as was the case for the period 2006 to 2008.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.534.5" class="koboSpan">This is mainly
because investors are prepared to pay a premium for immediate delivery
in the second-hand market to avoid waiting for a relatively long time
for newbuilding delivery. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.534.6"
class="koboSpan">In recent years, given the record levels of orderbook
and delivery time of four to five years (up to 2011 and 2012 for orders
placed in 2007), having a second-hand ship was preferred to placing a
newbuilding order. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.534.7"
class="koboSpan">This is because, given the freight rate levels,
investors can benefit from high freight revenue and recoup part of their
investment rather than waiting for newbuilding delivery, which may take
a few years.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.535.1" class="koboSpan">The higher
sensitivity of second-hand prices to market conditions implies that
secondhand prices are more volatile than newbuilding and scrap price.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.535.2" class="koboSpan">However, scrap
or demolition prices for ships generally depend on world scrap steel
prices and ship-breaking
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_348"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.536.1"
class="koboSpan">activities. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.536.2"
class="koboSpan">This means that the volatility of scrap prices for
ships is linked to the volatility and changes in the market for scrap
steel, rather than the changes in freight market.</span>

### <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.537.1" class="koboSpan">4.5 Efficiency of the market for dry bulk carriers</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.538.1" class="koboSpan">One of the most
important and interesting areas in the shipping economics literature is
the determination of ship prices.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.538.2" class="koboSpan">Many studies
have been devoted to modelling, evaluating and forecasting ship prices
and their volatilities in the past, among these are: Strandenes (see
endnote 22), Beenstock (see endnote 39), Beenstock and Vergottis (see
endnotes 17, 21), Charmeza and
Gronicki,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0318" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0318"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.539.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.540.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Kavussanos (see endnotes 2, 3).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.540.2" class="koboSpan">Studies on the
determination of ship prices, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.540.3" class="koboSpan">Strandenes
(see endnote 22) and Beenstock and Vergottis (see endnotes 17, 21),
consider ships as capital assets and share the same theoretical
framework. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.540.4"
class="koboSpan">Present value models, which posit that the price of an
asset should reflect the discounted present value of expected income
that the asset may generate over its life, are used extensively in
modelling ship prices. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.540.5"
class="koboSpan">The major difference among the studies on ship price
determination is the way they deal with the expectations about the
future income generated by ships.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.540.6" class="koboSpan">More
precisely, they assume that the EMH is valid and utilise different forms
of expectations hypothesis in their pricing models.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.540.7" class="koboSpan">For example,
Strandenes (see endnote 22) assumes that expectations are semi-rational,
while Beenstock (see endnote 39) and Beenstock and Vergottis (see
endnotes 17, 21) assume rational expectations in price formation.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.541.1" class="koboSpan">Hale and
Vanags</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0319" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0319"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.542.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.543.1"
class="koboSpan"> dispute the assumption of rational expectations and
the EMH in models for ship prices and argue that such assumptions should
be investigated and their validity must be verified prior to any
modelling and forecasting. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.543.2"
class="koboSpan">This is because rejection of these hypotheses may have
serious consequences on the ensuing empirical results.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.543.3" class="koboSpan">They argue
that for the EMH to be valid, prices for different size vessels should
incorporate all the available information; that is, given past prices,
no other information should improve the predictability of prices.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.543.4" class="koboSpan">They propose a
test based on the cointegration approach and Granger- causality between
prices for the three sizes of bulk carriers.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.543.5" class="koboSpan">They find that
not only there are cointegrating relationships between the price series,
but also prices Granger-cause each other.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.543.6" class="koboSpan">They conclude
that their results cast doubt on the validity of the EMH and RE in price
formation in the dry bulk sector.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.543.7"
class="koboSpan">Glen</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0320" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0320"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.544.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.545.1"
class="koboSpan"> re-examines the informational efficiency in dry bulk
carriers price determination using Johansen’s multivariate cointegration
test,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0321" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0321"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.546.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.547.1"
class="koboSpan"> which is more powerful compared to the test employed
in Hale and Vanags (see endnote 42), although his finding are similar.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.547.2" class="koboSpan">However, he
attributes the link between prices for different size vessels to the
existence of common stochastic trends rather than the failure of the
EMH.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.548.1"
class="koboSpan">Wright</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0322" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0322"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.549.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.550.1"
class="koboSpan"> attempts to examine different forms of expectations in
the formation of second hand prices for small dry bulk carriers for the
period 1980 to 1990 using quarterly data.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.550.2" class="koboSpan">He tests three
different hypotheses, namely, rational, static and adaptive expectations
hypotheses. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.550.3"
class="koboSpan">Apart from statistical issues, such as the direct use
of non-stationary variables, his tests also suffer from theoretical
shortcomings, so not much reliance can be placed on these results.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.550.4" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
for the sake of completeness, we report here that he finds mixed results
and concludes that ship prices are formed under a mixture of
expectations depending on market conditions.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.551.1"
class="koboSpan">Alizadeh,</span><sup><a href="#Ch011.xhtml_fn0323" id="Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0323"><span
id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.552.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.553.1"
class="koboSpan"> employs cointegration and non-linear tests on the VAR
model proposed by Campbell and Shiller (see endnote 24) to examine the
present value model and the EMH in the determination of newbuilding and
second-hand prices in the dry bulk sector.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.553.2" class="koboSpan">One advantage
of the VAR approach is that stochastic properties of variables
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_349"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.554.1"
class="koboSpan">are explicitly considered.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.554.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the bivariate model of Campbell and Shiller is extended to a trivariate
model, which incorporates the residual (scrap) values as the third
variable in the model. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.554.3"
class="koboSpan">He employs the following present value model, which
relates the price of a ship (either newbuilding or second-hand) to the
discounted present value of expected profits, generated through
chartering operations plus the discounted present value of her expected
residual alue:</span>

<div id="Ch011.xhtml_fig0224" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.555.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00241.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.556.1" class="koboSpan">Where
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.557.1"
class="koboSpan">P</span></span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.558.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.559.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the price of the vessel,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.560.1"
class="koboSpan">E</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.561.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.562.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the expectations operator (expectations formed at
time </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.563.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.564.1"
class="koboSpan">),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.565.1"
class="koboSpan">E</span></span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.566.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.567.1"
class="koboSpan">Π</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.568.1"
class="koboSpan">t+i</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.569.1"
class="koboSpan"> represents expected profit in period
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.570.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.571.1"
class="koboSpan">+i,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.572.1"
class="koboSpan">E</span></span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.573.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.574.1"
class="koboSpan">R</span><sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.575.1"
class="koboSpan">t+j</span></sub><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.576.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the expected discount rate and
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.577.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00242.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.578.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the expected terminal value of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.578.2" class="koboSpan">Variables in
(8) are found to be non-stationary, a fact which would invalidate direct
tests for EMH. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.578.3"
class="koboSpan">As a result, the Campbell and Shiller transformation is
used to re-parameterise (8) and hence, obtain a model with stationary
variables.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.579.1" class="koboSpan">Two distinct cases
are considered for testing the price efficiency of newbuilding vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.579.2" class="koboSpan">In the first
case, it is assumed that the vessel operates for five years and her
value after five years reflects the price of a five-year old second-hand
vessel; the second-hand price is then used as her terminal value.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.579.3" class="koboSpan">In the second
case, it is assumed that the new-building will be used for her entire
economic life and, as a result, the residual value is her scrap price.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.579.4" class="koboSpan">A limited
economic life of 20 years is assumed for a newbuilding and 15 years for
a five year-old second-hand vessel.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.580.1" class="koboSpan">Alizadeh (see endnote
19) also investigates another implication of the EMH, which requires
unpredictability of excess (or abnormal) one period returns, that is
returns on shipping investments over the market return.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.580.2" class="koboSpan">The EMH
implies that one period excess returns should be independent of
information available at time
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.581.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.582.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.582.2"
class="koboSpan">In other words, in an efficient market abnormal returns
should be unpredictable; otherwise, excess profit making opportunities
may be identified and exploited by a group of investors.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.583.1" class="koboSpan">Empirical results
from the tests, based on equation (4), reject the EMH in the market for
newbuilding and second-hand dry-bulk vessels.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.583.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
it is found that excess returns on shipping investments (second-hand
vessels) over LIBOR are highly predictable, which is again against the
notion of informational efficiency in the market for second-hand
dry-bulk ships. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.583.3"
class="koboSpan">These findings can be explained by the fact that
investors in the shipping industry are characterised by heterogeneous
behaviour and different investment objectives and horizons and hence may
use different pricing models, discount factors or weights depending on
their investment objectives and horizons.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.583.4" class="koboSpan">This seems to
be a very important point since the EMH requires homogeneous investment
behaviour and pricing formulas across all the investors.</span>

## <span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.584.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.584.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.585.1" class="koboSpan">The aim of this
chapter was to provide a description of the dry-bulk shipping markets
and discuss current issues and developments in this area.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.585.2" class="koboSpan">In particular
the segmentation of the dry bulk markets in different sub-sectors, which
is due to the different physical and economic factors which determine
supply and demand conditions in these sectors, is discussed and the
factors which contribute to this segmentation are identified and
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_page_350"></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.586.1"
class="koboSpan">analysed. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.586.2"
class="koboSpan">These factors include, among others, the commodity
parcel size, the nature of the underlying shipping routes, the physical
characteristics of the loading and discharge ports as well as the
vessel’s design features. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.586.3"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the conditions under which the dry bulk
market can be categorised as a perfect market are highlighted and
discussed.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.587.1" class="koboSpan">Additionally, this
chapter also presents recent empirical evidence on issues relating to
the properties of the dry bulk shipping freight rates, such as the
seasonal behaviour of freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.587.2" class="koboSpan">The magnitude
and pattern of seasonal fluctuations is measured and compared across
freight rates for different size vessels as well as contract durations.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.587.3" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the
seasonal behaviour of freight rates is examined and compared under
different market conditions.</span>

<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.588.1" class="koboSpan">Empirical evidence on
the term structure relationship between long and short term rates for
different sizes of dry bulk carriers is also presented.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.588.2" class="koboSpan">Recent studies
in the literature have employed a variety of testing methods to test the
validity of the expectations hypothesis.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.588.3" class="koboSpan">Their results
indicate rejection of the expectations hypothesis of the term structure
which may be due to the time-varying perception of the risk of the
agents involved in the market. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.588.4"
class="koboSpan">The interrelationships between freight rate levels and
spillover effects between freight rate volatilities for different size
dry bulk carriers within the spot, one-year and three-year time-charter
markets are also analysed. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.588.5"
class="koboSpan">Finally, results from recent studies on the existence
of time-varying risk premia in the market for newbuilding and
second-hand vessels, are also presented.</span>

[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.720.1"
class="koboSpan">34.</span>](#Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0311)<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.721.1"
class="koboSpan"> It must be pointed out that, from a practical point of
view, it may not be possible for a ship-operator to take the opposite
position (i.e. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.721.2"
class="koboSpan">charter a vessel in on two consecutive 6-month charters
and re-let the same vessel on a 12-month charter) but one can use
six-month time-charter contract with an option to extend for a further
six-months. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.721.3"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, this strategy would also be feasible for an
owner (i.e. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.721.4"
class="koboSpan">charter in vessels on two consecutive 6-months
time-charter contracts and charter out an
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.722.1"
class="koboSpan">owned</span></span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.723.1"
class="koboSpan"> vessel on a 12-month charter).
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.723.2" class="koboSpan">However, in
their simulations they take the view of a ship operator and impose the
restriction that vessels can only be chartered in on a 12-month TC basis
and then re-let. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.723.3"
class="koboSpan">This is likely to underestimate the profitability of
the technical chartering strategies and is similar to a short-sale
restriction in financial markets.</span>

[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.724.1"
class="koboSpan">35.</span>](#Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0312)<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.725.1"
class="koboSpan"> Ships are considered to be capital assets with limited
life of normally 20 to 40 years depending on the type, size and quality
of built. </span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.725.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, they are depreciated at a relatively high
rate.</span>

[<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.726.1"
class="koboSpan">36.</span>](#Ch011.xhtml_bck_fn0313)<span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.727.1"
class="koboSpan"> Modern efficient ships not only consume less fuel for
propulsion in comparison to older ships, they are designed to operate
with smaller crew which also reduces operating costs.
</span><span id="Ch011.xhtml_kobo.727.2" class="koboSpan">Generally,
modern ships benefit from better design and material quality which
requires less maintenance and is also supposed to elongate their
economic life.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">David</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Glen</span></span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0324" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0324"><span
