class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">and
</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Steve</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">Christy</span></span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0325" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0325"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">What is a tanker?
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">A tanker is
defined as a vessel that is designed specifically to carry liquid
cargoes. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.11.3"
class="koboSpan">Refined oil products and crude oil are the most common
types of cargo carried in such vessels, but tankers also transport
chemicals, wine, vegetable and other food oils.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.11.4" class="koboSpan">The market for
crude oil tankers is by far the largest.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.11.5" class="koboSpan">The markets for
crude oil and refined products are often referred to as the tanker
trades. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.11.6" class="koboSpan">This
chapter reviews the world tanker market as it stands at the start of
2009. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.11.7" class="koboSpan">It has
two objectives:</span>

- <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">to provide the
  reader with an outline of events that have shaped the present tanker
  market;</span>
- <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">to review economic
  theories of tanker market dynamics.</span>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">The Shaping of the Present Tanker Market</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">On the 1 January 2009,
the world tanker fleet, (measured in terms of carrying capacity, the
deadweight tonne) stood at 379.1mn
dwt.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0326" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0326"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan"> The world fleet consists of around 3,605 vessels of
25,000 dwt or more, all engaged in activities related to the extraction,
storage, and distribution of both crude oil and its refined
products.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0327" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0327"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan"> One might assume that this level of activity has been
reached by a steady, continuous expansion of the industry, but this is
far from the case. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">In fact, the 1990s was a decade of “recovery” for the
industry from shocks that affected it in the early 1970s, and which led
to record deadweight tonnage capacity by the early 1980s.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.19.3" class="koboSpan">The period
since 1999 has seen the first tanker market boom that has been driven by
commercial factors rather than by war and political events.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_356"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, the story does not start in the tanker market
at all. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">Its
behaviour can only be understood by knowing something of the economic
development of the oil industry itself.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.20.3" class="koboSpan">The reason for
this is simple. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.20.4"
class="koboSpan">The great bulk of oil is transported from its
production areas to the main consumption areas by sea.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.20.5" class="koboSpan">Some is
transported by pipeline, and road and rail transport are used as well
for intra-country movements; but approximately 95% of the inter-area oil
movements are seaborne. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.20.6"
class="koboSpan">In 2008, approximately 2.7 billion tonnes of crude and
products was exported, from a total production level of 3.9 billion
tonnes.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0328" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0328"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan"> Thus 67% of the world’s total oil production was moved
across the world, predominantly by sea, generating the source of demand
for oil transportation services, and creating the demand for oil tanker
services.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0329" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0329"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">The major oil
consumption regions happen to be net importers of oil, so their demand
creates a need to move oil safely and efficiently from its various
sources. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">The
oil tanker, which emerged as a specialised vessel during the 1940s and
1950s, was developed to meet that need.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">Oil transportation can
be viewed as a productive input, a part of the process that turns crude
oil extracted from the ground or from under the sea, into a variety of
refined products, from petrol for cars, heating oil, marine diesel fuel,
feedstock for the chemical and plastics industry.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.25.2" class="koboSpan">The capital
investment required to develop the industry was very large, with
significant expenditure required to develop oilfields, construct
refineries, and develop distribution systems for the products in the
rapidly growing markets of the United States and Western Europe.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.25.3" class="koboSpan">The industry
evolved as a ‘vertically integrated’ structure, with several very large
multi-national companies dominating all aspects of exploration,
extraction, storage, distribution and refining of the product.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.25.4" class="koboSpan">Investment in
tankers is on-going, with approximately 5% of the fleet delivered
annually by the world’s shipyards.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.25.5" class="koboSpan">In addition,
there is an active market in the buying and selling of existing tankers
for continued trading. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.25.6"
class="koboSpan">Whilst this does not represent new capacity, it does
indicate that there are relatively few barriers for new entrants wishing
to join the industry.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">This economic
arrangement, whilst efficient, meant that the principal owners of oil
tankers, and of course, their principal users, were the oil majors.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.26.2" class="koboSpan">By the late
1960s, the seven oil majors that dominated the global industry became
known as the “Seven Sisters”. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.26.3"
class="koboSpan">The industry was highly integrated and very
concentrated. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.26.4"
class="koboSpan">The dominant players at the time included Esso, BP,
Shell, Mobil, Texaco, and Gulf. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.26.5"
class="koboSpan">In addition, many European countries had one
state-owned oil company “champion”; Italy had ENI, France had Elf and
Total. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.26.6" class="koboSpan">In other
parts of the world, state-owned companies were significant local
players; for example, Petrobras in Brazil.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.26.7" class="koboSpan">The very
largest companies had large departments whose function was to manage
each of the segments of the oil production process.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.26.8" class="koboSpan">Oil
transportation was one of those segments.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">The domination of the
“Seven Sisters” of the retail side of the oil industry has declined from
its peak of the late 1960s. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.27.2"
class="koboSpan">One reason for this was the emergence of a spot market
for lots of refined petrol from Rotterdam, the result of refinery
overcapacity. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.27.3"
class="koboSpan">New companies entered the retail market, and put
competitive pressure on the incumbents.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.27.4" class="koboSpan">The world of a
regulated market was finally destroyed by the Arab–Israeli war of
October 1973, and the resulting embargo of oil exports to certain
European countries including the Netherlands, along with a dramatic rise
in the oil price, from \$1.80 per barrel to nearly \$40 during
1973–80.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0330" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0330"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">The dramatic rise in
the world crude oil price, coupled with the nationalisation of American
and European oil interests in the Middle East and Libya, led to a
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_357"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">transformation of world economic growth prospects and a
shift in the balance of economic power towards OPEC (Organisation of
Petroleum Exporting
Countries).</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0331" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0331"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> A major, and long-lived slowdown in world economic
growth occurred, and a new era for the oil industry began.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">In the period
since 2000, oil demand continued to grow, boosted by the emergence of
India and China as significant consumers of energy as they grew at
sustained high rates.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">Much of the present
structure of the tanker market has been created by these events.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">Indeed, the
past two decades could be argued to be the first period in which the
tanker market was primarily driven by economic and environmental issues,
rather than politics. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.33.3"
class="koboSpan">Political events of course, are always of potential
consequence – they are woven into the history of both the industry and
the tanker market.</span>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.34.2" class="koboSpan">Oil Consumption</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">The world’s demand for
oil is large, and grew at around 1.3% per annum between 2000 and 2008.
</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0142"
id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0142"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the trend in world oil consumption over the past
35 years. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.37.2"
class="koboSpan">Demand declined after 1973, recovered, peaked in
1979–80, and then fell until 1985.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.37.3" class="koboSpan">In fact, world
oil consumption peaked at around 3,100mn tonnes in 1979, and declined by
approximately 10%, to 2,801mn tonnes in 1985.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.37.4" class="koboSpan">The 1979 peak
was not surpassed until 1990; and even in 1995 it had only reached
3,200mn tonnes, rising to 3,500mn tonnes in 2000.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.37.5" class="koboSpan">Between 2000
and 2008 consumption continued to grow, reaching an all time record of
3,937mn tonnes in 2007, then declining to 3,928mn tonnes in
2008.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0332" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0332"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup>

<a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fig0226" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0226"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that the trend growth in oil consumption over
the past ten years was 1.3% per annum, consistent with the 2002
International Energy Agency (IEA) forecast (1.4%), which was conditional
on assumptions about the behaviour of the price of crude oil.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.40.2" class="koboSpan">Its 2008
projection predicts growth at around 1% per annum until 2030.</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0225" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00243.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: World oil consumption 1965–2008" /></span>

<a href="#Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0142"
id="Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0142"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">World oil consumption 1965–2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">Source</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">: Derived from data from BP Review of World Energy,
2009</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0226" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_358"></span>[](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0226)

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00244.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0226)

</div>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">This is slower than
recent experience, but still positive, despite developing environmental
concerns over greenhouse gas emissions, and policy initiatives designed
to lower the world’s consumption of fossil fuels.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.48.2" class="koboSpan">In June 2009
the IEA revised its medium-term growth projection (to 2014) to 0.6% per
annum, from the 1.1% projected in
2008.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0333" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0333"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is possible that such revisions may be reversed in
a year or two, when the word economy has recovered from the 2008–9
downturn.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">The composition of oil
consumption has also altered over the period, and will continue to alter
in the future. </span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0142)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the oil consumption of the OECD countries for
1965–2008. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">It
is clear from visual inspection that the share of non-OECD members has
increased over the past two decades.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.3" class="koboSpan">Despite its
declining share (74% in 1965; 62% in 2000; 56% in 2008), the economic
performance of the OECD countries is still important for the growth in
demand for oil. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.4"
class="koboSpan">By far the most significant player in this sector is
the USA. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.5" class="koboSpan">In
2008 it alone accounted for nearly 1,100mn tonnes of oil (down from a
2005 peak of 1,140mn tonnes), or just under 23% of the world’s
consumption. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.6"
class="koboSpan">The whole of Europe and Eurasia accounts for 955mn
tonnes, whilst Asia accounts for around 1,180mn tonnes.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.7" class="koboSpan">Japan, Asia’s
wealthiest economy, (which has not exhibited its former growth pattern
and that of the other countries in the South East/Pacific Asian
economies), consumed 222mn tonnes, in 2008, approximately the same as it
consumed in 1973. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.8"
class="koboSpan">The major new contributors to growth since 2000 have
been China, whose consumption has risen from 224mn tonnes to 376mn
tonnes, and India, 106mn tonnes to 135mn tonnes in 2008.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.53.9" class="koboSpan">As
</span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0142)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows, the emerging market economies now account for
40% of world oil consumption. </span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0142)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that the OECD’s share has fallen sharply in the
last decade. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.57.2"
class="koboSpan">The present pattern of regional consumption is shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_fig0226)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_359"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan">A number of points are worthy of note.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">Firstly, it is
clear that the annual growth of world oil consumption rose significantly
between 1990–2000 and 2000–2008, from 0.01% per annum to 1.26%.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.3" class="koboSpan">The Middle
East’s own consumption has risen, reflecting its own economies’
diversification and development. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.4"
class="koboSpan">South and Central America and the Asia pacific regions
have also grown above the world average.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.5" class="koboSpan">Second, the
previous decline in consumption in the economies that constitute the
former Soviet Union has been reversed.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.6" class="koboSpan">This reflects,
at least in part, the well-known problems affecting these economies in
the period 1989–1998. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.7"
class="koboSpan">Oil consumption in this region remains lower than that
in the Middle East, although its growth rate has increased to 1.1% a
year. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.8" class="koboSpan">Third,
the changing balance of importance, tilting economic impacts more
towards the emerging market economies and away from the traditional
major oil consumers, continues apace.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.9" class="koboSpan">North America’s
share of oil consumption has declined to 27.4%, Asia Pacific’s rising to
30.1%. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.10" class="koboSpan">This
trend is set to continue. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.60.11"
class="koboSpan">The 2008 World Energy outlook projects all of increase
in oil demand to 2030 to be derived from non-OECD countries, with 80%
plus from China, India and the Middle East
region.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0334" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0334"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.62.2" class="koboSpan">Economic Drivers of Oil Consumption</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">Having briefly
outlined the present profile of oil consumption and its regional
pattern, attention is now turned to addressing the question as the
principal factors driving oil consumption.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.63.2" class="koboSpan">The standard
set of economic factors are: Incomes (the price of crude oil and its
refined products; the price of substitute products; the price of
complementary products) Tastes; Political factors, and Expectations.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">The exposition
is necessarily short. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.63.4"
class="koboSpan">The relationship between Incomes or Gross Domestic
Product (GDP) and oil consumption or its constituent components has been
extensively studied. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.63.5"
class="koboSpan">Professor Dahl has published a survey of 100
econometric studies of the relationship between gdp and petrol
demand.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0335" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0335"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan"> She concluded that the income elasticity of demand was
greater than unity, which implies that gasoline consumption will grow
faster than the economy under examination.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">The survey
reports estimates of between 0.80 and 1.38 for the long-run
response.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0336" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0336"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan"> The short-run response was much lower however, between
0.4 and 0.5.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">The second key element
in the behaviour of oil consumption is the reaction of consumers to
changes in the real price. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.68.2"
class="koboSpan">Dahl reports estimated values of –0.22 to –0.31 for
short-run values, and –0.58 to –1.02 for long-run values derived from
the 100 studies surveyed. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.68.3"
class="koboSpan">These figures are indeed inelastic (the proportionate
fall in demand is significantly less than the proportionate rise in the
price), but they relate to just gasoline demand, which constitutes
around 30% of world oil
consumption.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0337" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0337"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>

<a href="#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0143"
id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0143"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the time path of real (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">adjusted to
reflect the changing purchasing power of the dollar over time) and
nominal price (dollar price in the relevant year) of Arabian Light oil
from 1972 – 2008, in annual average form.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">The data shows
tremendous variations, from \$1.90 per barrel in 1972, to \$10.41 in
1974, peaking at \$35.69 in 1980, declining to \$12.95 in 1986, before
peaking again at \$20.50 in 1990, declining to a low of around \$8.00 in
the late 1990s, before rising in the boom of 2000, following the
introduction of production quotas by OPEC members in the second quarter
of 1999. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.71.4" class="koboSpan">The
price of Brent Oil, which is highly correlated with Arabian Light, had
reached \$30 per barrel in 2002. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.71.5"
class="koboSpan">From 2002–2008 the annual average price has risen to
historically high levels, reaching \$97 per barrel for 2008.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.71.6" class="koboSpan">This increase
masks the</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0227" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00245.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Real and nominal prices of crude oil, 1970–2008" /></span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_360"></span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0143"
id="Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0143"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan">Real and nominal prices of crude oil, 1970–2008</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan">Source</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">: BP Statistical Review of World Energy 2009</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">considerable
volatility that exists within the year itself, but even on an annualised
basis, the changes have been dramatic.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">It should be
noted that Arabian Light is not traded as such, but is subject to
“netback pricing” – a notional crude price based on the value of
constituent products from a barrel of oil on the Rotterdam market, after
deducting refining and sea transportation costs.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0143)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan"> clearly shows that many of the peaks in the oil price
are associated with Middle-East wars or other globally significant
economic events. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.80.2"
class="koboSpan">It should be noted that the Iraq war of 2002 made
little impact, the main drivers being oil demand and capacity issues.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.80.3" class="koboSpan">The only item
that might need further explanation is the apparent change in direction
in the nominal price before and after 1979–1980.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.80.4" class="koboSpan">The primary
causes were the world recession of 1979–1982, and the accelerating
substitution of oil by coal for power generation, along with initiatives
to reduce energy consumption in the principal consuming areas.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.80.5" class="koboSpan">It has been
argued that the eventual abrupt relinquishment of the high price oil
strategy in April 1986 was the result of joint undertakings between the
world’s largest consuming nation and the OPEC’s largest producer.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">The second reason
relates to the changing pricing policy of OPEC members themselves.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.81.2" class="koboSpan">By the
mid-1980s, after five years of oil prices between \$25 and \$20, oil
production from the North Sea, and Alaska provided competition from
non-OPEC suppliers; and OPEC, watching the decline in oil demand,
dramatically altered its policy on oil pricing.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.81.3" class="koboSpan">Prior to the
change, OPEC would try to maintain the real value of its earnings in
nominal dollar terms. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.81.4"
class="koboSpan">Whenever the dollar fell in value, (as it did in the
1970s), the nominal price of oil was raised to offset the fall.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.81.5" class="koboSpan">In the
mid-1980s, OPEC members changed their policy, switching to “netback
pricing”. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.81.6" class="koboSpan">This
change, in response to declining market share as Mexican and North Sea
production became more important, meant that the real price of crude oil
was no longer being maintained. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.81.7"
class="koboSpan">OPEC was under the impression that the marginal cost of
non-OPEC crude was \$21/barrel, and tacitly applied an \$18 “benchmark”
price for the basket of OPEC crudes.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.81.8" class="koboSpan">In fact, the
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_361"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">real price of crude oil fell to its lowest value since
the early 1970s, following the 1986 watershed.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">The history of
oil pricing since 1990 has been one of high volatility and subject to
prolonged stock-building as more non-OPEC oil came on stream.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.82.3" class="koboSpan">In addition,
there has been periodic weakness in demand, before its recovery in the
late 1990s.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">When the “real price”
series is examined in </span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0143)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">, the changes in oil price over the past 30 years are
even more exaggerated. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.85.2"
class="koboSpan">It is clear that only in 2007 did oil prices exceed the
levels last seen in 1979–1981. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.85.3"
class="koboSpan">Prices have eased off since, but the high real oil
price in recent years reflected two elements – a resurgence of demand
growth, as noted above, and a tightening of refinery capacity margins,
which itself was in part due to the low oil prices observed in the
1990s, which mitigated against significant investment in refineries
during the period.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">A noteworthy element
of the surveys by
Dahl</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0338" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0338"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">absence</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">, in many of the econometric studies, of cross-price
effects. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">There
may be two reasons for this. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.3"
class="koboSpan">First, the investigations ignored the effects by
failing to include any cross-price elements in their model.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.4" class="koboSpan">For example, it
could be argued that the demand for petrol will be negatively influenced
by downward changes in the price of public transport, where it is
available. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.5" class="koboSpan">Thus
cross-price effects may influence oil consumption.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.6" class="koboSpan">Secondly, the
investigators may have tried such factors, and discarded them, when they
prove to be statistically unimportant.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.7" class="koboSpan">Indeed, given
the low own-price elasticities of demand, it would not be surprising if
cross-price elasticities were negligible.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.8" class="koboSpan">Economic theory
implies that the smaller the degree of substitutability between goods or
services, the lower the level of cross-price elasticity.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.90.9" class="koboSpan">For many uses,
oil products have few, if any substitutes.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">Oil demand can be
affected by changes in the price of complementary products.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">For gasoline
consumption a vehicle is required.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.91.3" class="koboSpan">For fuel oil, a
power station. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.91.4"
class="koboSpan">In many cases the price of the oil product is extremely
small as a proportion of the overall costs of deriving the service that
it generates. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.91.5"
class="koboSpan">It is true, however, that two of the key drivers of the
growth in oil consumption in the past 50 years were the rise of the
motor vehicle, and the switch to oil as a source for power generation,
away from coal. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.91.6"
class="koboSpan">The former is an example of complementarity; the latter
an example of price substitution.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">Shifts in tastes can
influence demand. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.92.2"
class="koboSpan">The rise of the motor car has been a major event in the
western economies, and appears to be happening in the developing
economies too. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.92.3"
class="koboSpan">Until the 1970s, little or no regard was being paid to
the negative effects of this expansion; namely the rise in carbon
dioxide emissions, the growing evidence of the damage that lead
additives to petrol caused, and the rising levels of environmental
damage caused by the exploitation of the word’s resources.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.92.4" class="koboSpan">Environmental
awareness has been raised significantly over the past 25 years, and this
has had an impact on the oil industry.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.92.5" class="koboSpan">Energy
conservation has become a key issue, although the more cynical observer
is more likely to point to the oil price increase of 1973 as being the
event that forced many governments to develop such policies.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.92.6" class="koboSpan">In addition, a
number of significant oil pollution incidents led to successively
tighter regulatory frameworks governing the production, distribution and
transportation of
oil.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0339" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0339"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">Since the end of World
War II, oil has been a strategic resource.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">The fact that
significant shares of the world’s oil resources are located in the
Middle East and the Soviet Union meant that Western Europe was
particularly vulnerable to disruption of oil supplies.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.94.3" class="koboSpan">The USA
switched from being self-sufficient in oil to becoming increasingly
dependent on oil, in particular from North Africa, the Middle East,
Venezuela and West Africa. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.94.4"
class="koboSpan">Major political crises punctuate the history of the oil
industry, and have identifiable effects on the tanker market.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.94.5" class="koboSpan">The UK and
French attempt to occupy
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_362"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan">the Suez Canal, following its nationalisation by Egypt,
and the nationalisation of US oil interests in Libya, created tensions
in the Near- and Middle East, which focused on the conflict between
Israel and the Palestinians. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.95.2"
class="koboSpan">The Egypt–Israeli war of 1967 caused the closure of the
Suez Canal for eight years, and led to another clash in 1973.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.95.3" class="koboSpan">This was the
event that precipitated a major shift in the economic balance of oil, as
OPEC exercised its economic power, and raised the price of crude oil by
400% in the space of a few months.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.95.4" class="koboSpan">Political
instability remains a theme at the present time.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.95.5" class="koboSpan">The 1981–1989
Iran-Iraq war, the 1990 invasion of Kuwait by Iraq, the 2001 Iraqi
invasion of Kuwait and the consequent invasion of Iraq by the USA and
her allies, the continuing tensions between Israel and the Palestinians,
all show that oil is still a strategic product.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.95.6" class="koboSpan">However, a very
significant change has occurred which makes it likely that embargoes
will be less likely – there has been a significant shift in OPEC’s
pricing strategy.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">The demand for oil is
also affected by players’
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">expectations</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan"> of future events.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">Oil prices are
volatile; nowadays some of the risk volatility can be hedged against by
taking out forwards or futures contracts on the International Petroleum
Exchange. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.98.3"
class="koboSpan">Whether or not all of the risk can be hedged depends on
the efficiency of the markets and the nature of the contracts available.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.98.4" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
the presence of these markets allows oil companies to hedge some of the
risk of current price volatility by “taking a position” on the paper
markets to offset some of the risk.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">The existence of such
markets can also generate forward prices, which can be viewed as the
market’s guess as to the future path of present (spot) prices.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">In some recent
economic theories, current prices for a commodity or financial asset are
viewed as being entirely determined by the expected price.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.99.3" class="koboSpan">In other words,
today’s price is determined by the today’s expectation of tomorrow’s
price. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.99.4" class="koboSpan">When
political uncertainty increases, market expectations are for a shortage
of oil in the future, and this leads to a sharp increase in the present
price of oil. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.99.5"
class="koboSpan">Thus expectations may play a key role in understanding
market dynamics. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.99.6"
class="koboSpan">It might be noted that the very high prices achieved by
crude oil in 2007 have been blamed on “speculative” activity, with
forward prices driving spot prices.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.99.7" class="koboSpan">This conjecture
is very hard to verify.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">It has been shown
that the demand is very insensitive to own price, but quite sensitive to
economic growth. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">The sharp change in conditions in 1973 led to lower
growth trends for oil demand, and a significant incentive to lower the
intensity of oil use. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.100.3"
class="koboSpan">Both of these effects led to decline in oil consumption
until 1985–1986, with 1975 levels reappearing only in the late 1990s.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.100.4" class="koboSpan">The continuing
future growth of demand is sensitive to economic growth, switches to
alternative energy sources, and increasing improvements in the
efficiency in which oil is used, for example, in the fuel efficiencies
of motor car
engines.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0340" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0340"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">World Oil Production Trends</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">Not surprisingly,
world oil production tends to track demand very well.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.103.2" class="koboSpan">There is an
important element that “gets in the way” of this relationship however –
oil is produced in regions were there is little demand, and traded.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.103.3" class="koboSpan">The time taken
to move the oil to its region of consumption means that there is
inventory, either in the form of oil on ships or in storage tanks at
oilfields, oil terminals and refineries.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.103.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,
since 1973 many countries have instituted strategic reserves of oil, in
the event of any oil export embargo repeating itself.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.103.5" class="koboSpan">One estimate
of the OECD countries’ crude and product
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_363"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan">inventory puts it at 2.7bn barrels, or 355mn tonnes,
roughly 57 day’s supply at 2009 consumption
levels.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0341" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0341"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">Production can
therefore be divorced from consumption to a certain extent, and there
will be periods when demand exceeds current production and vice versa.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">But over the
longer period, it is consumption that drives production.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">Comparison of
the average annual growth rate over the period 2000–2008 for world oil
consumption and production yields figures of 1.26% and 1.1%
respectively.</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Regional production patterns</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">Examination of
regional patterns yields a different story
(</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fig0228" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0228"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.110.2"
class="koboSpan">In the period 1990–2000, North American production
declined slightly, and there were significant falls in production in the
economies of the former Soviet Union (FSU).
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.110.3" class="koboSpan">Elsewhere
Europe and South America experienced the largest growth in production.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.110.4" class="koboSpan">In the period
2000–2008, the Russian Federation recovered lost ground, growing at 6.1%
per annum, whilst output from African countries grew strongly.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.110.5" class="koboSpan">However, it is
the Middle East that still dominates world production, with a 32% share
in 2008, unchanged from 2000. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.110.6"
class="koboSpan">Whilst this is lower than at some points in the past,
it is also higher than at other times, particularly in the early
1980s.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">Putting the two
tables of production and consumption together leads to the generation of
a crude estimate of the need to move oil between one region and others;
this generates a “derived demand” for oil tanker services.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.111.2" class="koboSpan">BP’s estimates
of inter-area oil movements are shown in
</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fig0229" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0229"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">These figures will
not correspond to the volumes of oil traded by sea, because the data
includes other modes of transport, but they give a general indication of
the major directions that oil is traded.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.114.2" class="koboSpan">In fact, many
of the movements shown in the Table will be</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0228" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00246.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0228)

</div>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0229" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_364"></span>[](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0229)

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00247.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0229)

</div>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">entirely by sea; for
example, exports from West Africa to the USA and Europe, exports from
the Middle East to Japan. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.117.2"
class="koboSpan">The trade data emphasises the importance of Middle East
exports in the oil trade; In 2000, nearly 50% of the world’s oil was
exported from that region. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.117.3"
class="koboSpan">By 2008, this had fallen to 37% as some countries
diversified their oil supplies. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.117.4"
class="koboSpan">Note that the Asia-Pacific region, containing some of
the most dynamic economies, obtained 61% of its oil from this
region.</span>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">Tanker Demand</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">It is clear from
inspection of </span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
3</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_fig0229)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan">, that the need to service consumption from the major
oil production centres leads to a demand for the transportation of oil,
either in its crude (unrefined) form, or in the form of refined
products.</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">6.1 Derived Demand</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">Maritime economists
define this demand for this service as a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">derived</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan"> demand. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.125.2"
class="koboSpan">That is, the need to move oil is not demanded for its
own sake, as there is no intrinsic value or utility in so doing.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.125.3" class="koboSpan">The movement
is made to “add-value” to the commodity, by selling it in a market where
the marginal utility to the consumer is much higher than it is at the
point of production. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.125.4"
class="koboSpan">The process of moving the cargo is not directly
determined by the consumer, as it is a part of the “supply-chain”
process, and is best viewed as part of the production process.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.125.5" class="koboSpan">This means
that the act of transporting oil is in effect, a factor input, and the
laws that apply to factor demand apply to oil.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.125.6" class="koboSpan">There are four
“Marshallian
rules”</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0342" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0342"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan"> of factor demand.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_365"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">These rules are useful in indicating, from first
principles, the likely demand responsiveness for oil movements to
changes in freight rates. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.128.2"
class="koboSpan">The rules are as follows:–</span>

1.  <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">The elasticity of
    demand for the factor input (oil transportation) will be higher
    (lower), the higher (lower) the elasticity of demand for the final
    product (petrol, fuel oil, feedstock, heating oil, etc).</span>
2.  <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">The elasticity of
    demand for the factor input will be higher (lower), the higher
    (lower) the degree of substitutability between the factor and other
    factor inputs in the production process.</span>
3.  <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">The elasticity of
    demand for the factor input will be higher (lower) the higher
    (lower) the share that the input takes of the overall costs the
    consumer of the final product.</span>
4.  <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">The elasticity of
    demand for the factor input will be higher, the higher the
    elasticity of supply of the factor input.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">Having already
discussed some of the evidence of the income and price elasticities of
demand for the final product, it is easy to realise that the above rules
imply that the elasticity of demand for oil transportation with respect
to changes in the cost of transporting it (the freight rate, in the case
of shipping) is very likely to be extremely small, if not zero.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">The reason for
this is to be found in rules 1 to 3.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">Rule 1 implies
that the freight rate elasticity of demand will be proportional to the
own price elasticities of demand for the final good, which has been, at
the most optimistic, been estimated at –1, with most studies in the
short run yielding –0.4. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.133.4"
class="koboSpan">Rule 2 implies that this elasticity will be lower, the
lower the degree of substitutability.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.133.5" class="koboSpan">Whilst oil
pipeline transportation can and does, have a significant role in certain
parts of the world, the fact remains that the overwhelming majority of
oil has to be moved by sea, or not at all.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.133.6" class="koboSpan">Rule 3 implies
that the smaller the share of the input cost as a proportion of the
final landed price to the consumer, the lower the freight rate
elasticity. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.133.7" class="koboSpan">In
the UK, it is estimated that the freight cost component in the retail
price of petrol is around 1p on a current price of around £1.00 a litre;
large variations in the freight rate will have almost no noticeable
effect on the retail price in the UK.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">The conclusion from
the combination of empirical evidence and economic theory is that oil
transportation demand will be highly price inelastic in most situations,
but elastic with respect to changes in economic activity.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.134.2" class="koboSpan">Where
substitute transportation forms exist however, such as major oil
pipelines, or alternative fuels for vehicles, such as in Brazil, cross
price elasticities may be considerable.</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">6.2 Demand measurement</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">It has been
demonstrated that large volumes of oil are annually transported from
region to region. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.136.2"
class="koboSpan">This provides
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">one</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicator of the derived demand for oil movements.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.138.2" class="koboSpan">Transportation
is a non-storable
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">service</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan">; it requires the movement of the oil cargo between two
geographical points for that service to be performed.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.140.2" class="koboSpan">Oil demand has
to be measured in two ways. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.140.3"
class="koboSpan">First, in terms of the tonnes of oil being moved per
time period; and second, in terms of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan">tonne
miles</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">
being demanded per time period. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.142.2"
class="koboSpan">Transportation service demand is a flow demand, and it
is the product of cargo volume and distance travelled per time period
that generates overall
demand.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0343" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0343"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan"> Average voyage length is thus a proxy for route
structure, since changes in that structure, say a</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0230" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_366"></span>[](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0230)

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00248.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0230)

</div>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">significant shift to
short haul trades, will reduce tonne mile demand even if oil volume
demand is unchanged. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.146.2"
class="koboSpan">A shift towards long haul routes does the
opposite.</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">6.3 Tanker demand trends</span>

<a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fig0230" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0230"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan"> gives some information on the trends in tanker demand,
in terms of tonnes of cargo carried and tonne miles performed per year,
for the period 1990–2008. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.149.2"
class="koboSpan">It is worth noting that the average haul of crude and
products movements is around 5,000 miles over this period.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.149.3" class="koboSpan">Whilst this
appears to be relatively constant, it has not always been thus.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.149.4" class="koboSpan">In 1967 the
average haul was 4,775 miles; in 1977, 6,651 miles.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.149.5" class="koboSpan">The closure of
the Suez Canal between 1967 and 1975 clearly divorced tonne miles demand
from tonnes demand. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.149.6"
class="koboSpan">Over the period 1968–1973 tonne mile demand grew at an
annual average of 21.4% per annum, whereas tonnage demand grew at 13.6%
per annum; for the period 1978–1983 tonnage demand fell by 5.6% per
annum, whilst tonne mile demand declined by 9.0% per
annum.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0344" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0344"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan"> For the tanker markets, the main reasons for
discrepancies between tonne mile demand and tonne demand are the closure
of strategic routes, such as the Suez Canal, and the changing structure
of oil demand patterns, towards or away from long haul trades.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.151.2" class="koboSpan">The early
1970s also saw the rise of the 200,000 tonne-plus tanker, or Very Large
Crude Carrier (VLCC), which became dominant on long haul crude oil
movements, essentially from the Middle East, to Europe and the Far East,
since modified by a growing trade from West Africa to the Far East.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.151.3" class="koboSpan">The size and
draft of these vessels made laden transit of the Suez Canal impossible,
but the new technology provided sufficient scale economies to make the
“distance” considerations irrelevant.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">Table
4</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_fig0230)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows clearly that the volume of oil transported has
grown over the past ten years. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.153.2"
class="koboSpan">The oil trade movement map published by
BP,</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0345" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0345"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that there is a wide variation in the volume of
cargoes being moved on the principal oil trade routes, whose structure
has remained relatively stable, but which can change in response to new
oil-field; developments, interruptions of existing supplies, and
changing patterns of oil consumption.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">There are new
major oil flows from West Africa to the Far East, and Singapore has
become a major focal point for oil movements, reflecting the dynamism of
the region in the past decade.</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0231" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00249.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Real tanker prices 1970–2005" /></span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_367"></span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0144"
id="Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0144"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan">Real tanker prices 1970–2005</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">Source</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan">: Authors</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">6.4 Cyclical features</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">The data so far
presented might suggest to the reader that demand trends are rather long
term and gentle. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.163.2"
class="koboSpan">In fact, there are very marked cycles of economic
activity in the shipping markets, and the tanker industry is no
different. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.163.3" class="koboSpan">It
was argued that the most recent tanker boom, which peaked in 2001, is
the first for many years that has not been triggered by an external
shock, such as a Middle-East war.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.163.4" class="koboSpan">The marked
cyclical nature of the industry can be seen in
</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0144"
id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0144"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">, which shows the behaviour of real tanker prices for
three size classes over the period 1970–2005.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">The positive
deviation from the trend shows the boom periods, the negative deviation,
“recession”. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.165.3"
class="koboSpan">Asset values are a good measure of the expectations
held by agents of future earnings and profitability.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.165.4" class="koboSpan">The most
recent cycle upturn occurred in 2003 and came to an end in 2009.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.165.5" class="koboSpan">In the early
part of the present cycle, some commentators claimed that the cycle had
disappeared. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.165.6"
class="koboSpan">Obviously they were ill-informed.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">An alternative view
of the market is to examine tanker charter rates, the “hire price” (in
dollars per day) set for running a tanker for one’s own use, but not
owning it. </span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0145"
id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0145"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the historical development of one year rates
from 1990 to May 2009.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">The peaks in hire
rates, in 1997–1998 and in 2001, are marked, especially in 2008.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.169.2" class="koboSpan">The recent
“boom” from 2004–2008 is also apparent.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.169.3" class="koboSpan">These periods
do not correspond to external events, and are a sign that the tanker
market escaped the legacy of the 1970s and
1980s.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0346" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0346"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">Whilst every player
in the tanker industry is aware that their business is cyclical, no-one
has been able to develop a successful method of consistently forecasting
the points at which the cycle switches from one phase to another.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.171.2" class="koboSpan">The cyclical
behaviour of rates reflect the cyclical growth in demand, and supply,
neither of which change at a constant rate.</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00250.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: Alframax one-year TC rates 1990–2009" /></span>

id="Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0145"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">Alframax one-year TC rates 1990–2009</span>

</div>
