## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.180.2" class="koboSpan">Tanker Supply</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">7.1 The structure and composition of tanker supply</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">The tanker supply
situation has become increasingly fragmented over the past 30 years.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.182.2" class="koboSpan">Analysts and
industry observers now segment the supply side into a number of
different categories. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.182.3"
class="koboSpan">Whilst overall macroeconomic conditions will drive all
segments, each component of the market has its own characteristics.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.182.4" class="koboSpan">After
reviewing fleet developments in broad terms, these segments will be
examined in more detail.</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">7.2 Tanker fleet development</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">The world tanker
fleet is defined as all those vessels that are classified as being
dedicated to the movement of crude oil or refined products.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.184.2" class="koboSpan">It constitutes
approximately 33% of the world’s cargo fleet.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.184.3" class="koboSpan">Conventional
analysis defines the smallest as 25,000 dwt, a convention adopted here.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.184.4" class="koboSpan">In addition, a
number of vessels were designed and built to operate in both the oil and
dry bulk cargo trades. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.184.5"
class="koboSpan">These are called combination carriers, and can be used
to carry either iron ore, or bulk, or crude oil.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.184.6" class="koboSpan">In 1999 there
were 159 such vessels, or 16.0mn dwt.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.184.7" class="koboSpan">This contrasts
with the 3,307 tankers, or 287.4mn dwt.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.184.8" class="koboSpan">The potential
oil carrying fleet includes both of these types.
</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fig0233" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0233"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan"> provides some summary statistics for the tanker fleet
itself.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">The falling average
age of the fleet reflects the industry’s phasing out of single hull
tankers with double hull vessels, as required under the IMO “phase out”,
and the improved profitability of tanker ownership from 2000 on.</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0233" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_369"></span>[](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0233)

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00251.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0233)

</div>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">7.3 Structure of tanker supply</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">The world’s tanker
fleet is segmented into various submarkets.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.190.2" class="koboSpan">The
segmentation is by size and by product type.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.190.3" class="koboSpan">Analysts
distinguish between the markets for products tankers and crude oil
tankers, and between a number of important size ranges of both of these
segments.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">The distinction
between crude and products is an important one.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.2" class="koboSpan">The small
products tankers have segmented (parcel tanks).
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.3" class="koboSpan">The current
fleet of products carriers includes vessels over 120,000 dwt, all of
which have tank coatings and more complex cargo pipe work and pumping
arrangements to protect the vessel against its highly corrosive and
volatile cargo, whilst also maintaining and protecting the cargoes
specification. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.4"
class="koboSpan">Generally, product carriers are significantly smaller
in size than crude tankers. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.5"
class="koboSpan">Both construction and operating costs are higher for
product vessels. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.6"
class="koboSpan">The increasing concerns over product contamination have
led to these ship types limiting their trading to clean or white
petroleum products. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.7"
class="koboSpan">Whilst it is possible to carry “dirty cargoes” in these
vessels, the consequent contamination risk to future cargoes means that
switching back would be difficult, and owners incur cleaning costs for
the removal of residues, before their vessel becomes acceptable to
potential charterers for the carriage of clean products again.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.8" class="koboSpan">No crude
vessel is used to carry products, so there is a significant degree of
segmentation between these market components.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.9" class="koboSpan">The “clean”
sector is also very different in terms of industrial concentration.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.191.10" class="koboSpan">This is a
market that academic maritime economists have largely
ignored.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0347" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0347"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">More problematic is
the segmentation of the crude oil market by ship size.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.193.2" class="koboSpan">The main
workhorses of the tanker industry are now the Very Large and Ultra Large
Crude Carriers, (VLCC/ULCC), defined broadly as vessels of 200,000 dwt
or above; vessels of 120\<200,000 dwt, which can transit the Suez Canal
(Suezmax</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0348" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0348"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan">), the Aframax Tanker, of around 80,000–120,000 dwt,
and the Panamax tanker, 55–80,000 dwt.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.195.2" class="koboSpan">Products
tankers tend to be smaller (25–50,000 dwt), although there are some
quite large vessels (100,000 dwt) in this category.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.195.3" class="koboSpan">Essentially,
the wide variation in draft/beam specification in vessels means that
there is considerable potential overlap between
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_370"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">these segments, but it is the case that the different
ship sizes are generally found on different routes, reflecting the
underlying economic drivers.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">The VLCC/ULCC market
is the one that has suffered the most in the past.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.197.2" class="koboSpan">Vessels of
200,000 dwt or more did not become significant in numbers until the
mid-1970s, at the time of economic slowdown.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.197.3" class="koboSpan">For some years
in the early 1980s, no-one placed any orders at all for this size of
vessel. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.197.4" class="koboSpan">Thus
from a rapidly increasing, young fleet, the VLCC sector became a story
of weak trading conditions and an ageing fleet.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">The Oil Pollution
Act, OPA90, which followed from the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan">Exxon V
aldez</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">
oil pollution incident in 1989, and the accelerated phase out of single
hull vessels agreed after the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2002) and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1999) disasters under IMO MarPol Regulation 13G, have
had a great impact on the structure of the fleet.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">Good trading
conditions, particularly after 2003, have also had an influence.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.204.3" class="koboSpan">Seventy-five
per cent of the 147mn dwt that constitute the 200,000 dwt + sector are
aged 15 years or less, and 60% are aged 10 years or
less.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0349" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0349"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan"> The phase out of single hull tankers, and recent
record high rates, have created a modern, young VLCC sector.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">ULCC’s have
largely disappeared.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">The primary routes
for these vessels are long haul, mainly from the Middle East, to Japan
and the Far East, but increasingly, West Africa to the Far East.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.207.2" class="koboSpan">Trading into
the North American east coast is restricted by port and draft
limitations, although vessels can call at
LOOP.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0350" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0350"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan"> Significant increases in VLCC activity can thus raise
tonne mile output significantly, because of the combination of ship size
and voyage distance. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.209.2"
class="koboSpan">Trading to Europe is the other primary route.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.209.3" class="koboSpan">At 1 January
2009, there were 506 vessels of 147mn dwt, and an orderbook for a
further 67 more to be delivered
2010–2011.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0351" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0351"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">The Suezmax tanker
trades on more specific routes. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.211.2"
class="koboSpan">In the mid-2000s, half of the Suezmax fleet was
deployed on the trade from Nigeria and other West African loading
terminals to the USA and
Europe</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0352" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0352"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">, with trading being generally restricted to the
Atlantic basin. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.213.2"
class="koboSpan">The fleet has an age profile which is even younger than
the VLCC’s, with 66% being less than 15 years old, and a staggering 81%
being younger than 10 years, of a fleet of 364 vessels of 55.3mn dwt.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.213.3" class="koboSpan">There were 260
vessels, or 38mn dwt, in this sector in 2002, indicating a buoyant
segment in the past few years.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">The age profile of
the Aframax fleet is now not noticeably different from the larger
tankers.. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.214.2"
class="koboSpan">There were 467 vessels of 45mn dwt as at February 2002,
growing to 792 vessels and 82mn dwt at end 2008.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.214.3" class="koboSpan">The Panamax
sector is a smaller segment of the market, with 390 vessels totalling
27mn dwt. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.214.4" class="koboSpan">The
Panamax fleet expanded as crude oil exports from the west coast of South
America increased and found their way to the US Gulf refineries.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.214.5" class="koboSpan">At the same
time, the increasing number of products carrier movements from the US
Gulf and Venezuela to the US west coast will necessitate more coated
tankers to transit the Panama Canal, and therefore be subject to the
canal’s present 32.3 metre beam restriction.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">Products tankers’
load factors are much higher than for crude vessels and long balancing
ballast voyages usually only apply to the large products carriers, and
they tend to operate on shorter haul routes.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.215.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
cubic capacity tends to be the main limiting factor for products
carriers. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.215.3" class="koboSpan">The
clean products tend to be lighter, having lower specific gravities, than
those for dirty products and crude oil.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.215.4" class="koboSpan">In fact,
vessels carrying full cargoes of clean products do not attain their
maximum deadweight draft. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.215.5"
class="koboSpan">An important trade is moving refined products from the
Caribbean refineries to the US east coast.</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_371"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">7.4 Tanker ownership structures</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.217.1" class="koboSpan">The tanker market has
undergone a significant change in the composition of ownership over the
past 35 years. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.217.2"
class="koboSpan">Three key elements can be identified in this process.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.217.3" class="koboSpan">Firstly, the
emergence of significant refinery overcapacity in Europe.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.217.4" class="koboSpan">In the period
1965–1971, capacity increased by
50%.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0353" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0353"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.218.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan"> This process created a “spot market” for oil and oil
products in Rotterdam, and helped to alter the structure of the UK’s
market for petrol. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.219.2"
class="koboSpan">Second, the collapse in tanker demand in the 1970s led
to many oil companies changing their tanker strategy.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.219.3" class="koboSpan">Analysis of
data provided by Gibsons shows significant changes in the proportions of
the tanker fleet that were employed by the oil majors in terms of owned
vessels, the proportion hired on long term (5–10 years) time charters,
or employed on a “spot” basis. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.219.4"
class="koboSpan">The transformation from a highly controlled structure,
where oil companies relied on spot market transactions for only 10% of
their needs, to a situation where they take approximately 90% of tanker
capacity from the spot market, was greatly accelerated by the drop in
demand in the 1970s, which was accompanied by a severe oversupply of
tonnage, especially in the VLCC segment.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">The third element
that helped to transform the structure of ownership has been the
significant shift in attitudes to environmental pollution, mentioned
earlier. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.220.2" class="koboSpan">In
1989, the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">Exxon
Valdez</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">
struck a submerged reef whilst sailing in the Prince William Sound,
Alaska, laden with crude oil. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.222.2"
class="koboSpan">The vessel struck rocks, and lost 37,000 tons of crude
oil through her single hull into the sea.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.222.3" class="koboSpan">Whilst not a
large spill by historic
standards,</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0354" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0354"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan"> the political reaction in the USA had ramifications
that are still felt today. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.224.2"
class="koboSpan">The ratification of the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 led
to many major oil corporations deliberately reducing their direct
ownership of oil tonnage, in an attempt to reduce their exposure to
liability in the event of future
incidents.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0355" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0355"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan"> The decline in the apparent role of the major oil
companies, and the rise of the so-called “independent” tanker owners,
means that in economic terms, the market has become more competitive
than it was. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.226.2"
class="koboSpan">In 2009, only a few of the original “Seven Sisters”
have a significant direct ownership of tankers, for example, BP.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">The standard method
of examining the degree of dominance of specific companies in an
industry is to measure its degree of industrial concentration.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.227.2" class="koboSpan">The simplest
way is to measure the share of the industry total accounted for by the
five largest or 10 largest companies.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.227.3" class="koboSpan">Whilst this
method has weaknesses, it is simple and easy to understand.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.227.4" class="koboSpan">In 2002, the
largest oil company fleet was Vela, of Saudi Arabia, which owned 5.9 mn
dwt. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.227.5" class="koboSpan">They were
followed by Petrobras (Brazil) and NITC (Iran) with 3.7 mn dwt each.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.227.6" class="koboSpan">ExxonMobil was
fifth largest with 2.3mn dwt, and the total for the five largest oil
companies was 27mn dwt. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.227.7"
class="koboSpan">The five largest independents owned 70.8 mn dwt, and
the smallest of these, Astro tankers, would rank fourth, irrespective of
organisation type.
</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fig0234" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0234"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan"> provides data on the tanker fleets
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan">owned</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan"> by the top 20 tanker owners in 2009.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.231.2" class="koboSpan">The industry
has been transformed by the emergence of publicly quoted tanker
companies. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.231.3"
class="koboSpan">Traditionally independent companies were essentially
private companies, not subject to the rules required for a publicly
quoted entity. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.231.4"
class="koboSpan">But many of the larger independents have “floated” on
stock markets as a means of raising finance.
</span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">Table
6</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_fig0234)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the largest companies in each sector.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.234.1" class="koboSpan">The five largest
companies accounted for 15% of the world’s tanker fleet in 2002, whilst
the 10 largest companies would account for 25%.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.234.2" class="koboSpan">In 2009,
irrespective of sector, the corresponding figures are 15% and 24% in
terms of deadweight. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.234.3"
class="koboSpan">Looking at tanker numbers, the 2009 figures are 9% and
16% respectively. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.234.4"
class="koboSpan">These figures are very low</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0234" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_372"></span>[](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0234)

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00252.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0234)

</div>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.236.1" class="koboSpan">compared to many
industrial market structures. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.236.2"
class="koboSpan">They imply that acting singly the very largest tanker
owners have no potential to influence market behaviour.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.236.3" class="koboSpan">Even if the
five largest companies got together to try to influence rates, they
would not have sufficient market power to do so.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">The tanker market has
become more fragmented than it was in the past.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.237.2" class="koboSpan">In the 1960s,
the oil companies owned significantly more tonnage, and contracted a
very large share of independent owner’s vessels as well.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.237.3" class="koboSpan">With 90% of
oil company needs being met from the spot market, it is clear that they
do not have the potential to influence rates.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.237.4" class="koboSpan">Whether this
composition remains the same for the next decade is difficult to
surmise. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.237.5" class="koboSpan">One
major oil company has reversed strategy and become a significant tanker
owner,
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_373"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">but others, such as ExxonMobil and Chevron-Texaco, no
longer figure in the top 30 tanker owners.</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">7.5 Impact of external regulation on tanker supply: The environmental dimension</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">The present structure
and future transformation of the tanker industry has been directly
affected by regulatory changes brought in by the US Government and the
IMO. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.240.2" class="koboSpan">Both of
these changes were triggered by oil pollution caused by the grounding or
loss of oil tankers at sea. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.240.3"
class="koboSpan">The first incident,
the</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan"> Exxon
Valdez</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">
incident in 1989, has already been referred to.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.2" class="koboSpan">The passing of
the Oil Pollution Act in 1990 by the US Congress had two effects on the
world’s tanker markets. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.3"
class="koboSpan">First, it led to the decision, by the IMO, to introduce
double-hull tanker technology embodied in regulation 13F, which came
into effect in 1992. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.4"
class="koboSpan">This required all new tankers over 20,000 dwt to be
double hulled. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.5"
class="koboSpan">Tankers of specific size and vintage had to comply with
OPA requirements which phased in the double hull specification over
time. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.6" class="koboSpan">Vessels
not complying with the rules would not be permitted to trade in US
waters. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.7" class="koboSpan">The
IMO was also spurred into the adoption of a phase-out programme for
existing single-hulled tankers, regulation 13G, which was based on the
OPA90 legislation. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.8"
class="koboSpan">OPA90 also required that all owners trading into the US
should have a certificate of financial responsibility, in effect a
providing a guarantee that they would be able to pay for the costs of
any accident shown to be their responsibility.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.242.9" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
if the owners were shown to be grossly negligent, their liability to
damages is unlimited.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.243.1" class="koboSpan">The choice of
double-hull technology to improve the safety of crude oil transportation
has not been unchallenged. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.243.2"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, its worthiness on the basis of economic costs
and benefits has also been
questioned.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0356" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0356"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan"> At the time of its introduction, other forms of
increasing safety were being discussed, including the use of hydrostatic
balancing. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.245.2"
class="koboSpan">Under this alternative, single hull vessels would not
have their cargo tanks fully loaded.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.245.3" class="koboSpan">Instead, they
would be loaded until the point sea pressure from the outside of the
tank wall would be greater than the pressure of the oil.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.245.4" class="koboSpan">This meant
that any rupture would mean that sea water would ingress rather than oil
escape. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.245.5" class="koboSpan">There
would be a loss of cargo carrying potential of around 15%.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.245.6" class="koboSpan">Whilst this is
a feasible solution in
principle,</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0357" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0357"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan"> the market rejected it.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">The major oil
charterers refused to accept single-hulled vessels certificated for this
process, and, in consequence, double-hull has become the
standard.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">An important effect
of the OPA law should be noted. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.248.2"
class="koboSpan">The legal liability under the OPA regulation was laid
squarely at the feet of the owner of the vessel, not the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan">charterer.
</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">Oil
companies noted this, and Exxon, who owned the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan">Exxon
Valdez</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">,
and who thus were liable for the claims resulting, began to reduce its
fleet of owned tankers. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.252.2"
class="koboSpan">It was a deliberate strategy, because any future oil
pollution incident would appear to be focussed upon the owner, rather
than the charterer. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.252.3"
class="koboSpan">The fewer the ships that they directly owned, the
smaller the risk exposure. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.252.4"
class="koboSpan">This trend has continued, as the earlier discussion on
ownership in 2009 pointed to the absence of the traditional oil
majors.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">Other events which
have affected the market were the losses of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan">and</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan">
Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.257.2"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan">Erika</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan"> was a 24-year-old single-hulled 37,000 dwt tanker
which literally split in two and sank in the Bay of Biscay, carrying
30,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil Dunkerque to Livorno in
Italy.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0358" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0358"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan"> Both sections sank on 13 December 1999.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.261.2" class="koboSpan">During her
life the vessel had changed names seven times and been classed by four
different classification
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_374"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan">societies. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.262.2"
class="koboSpan">She was owned by a Maltese registered company, The
vessel had apparently passed its recent classification survey, and had
been chartered from an Italian shipowner.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.262.3" class="koboSpan">The oil washed
up on the Brittany coast at a crucial time for tourism, causing
significant loss of business to French fishing and tourism industries,
as well as significant clean-up costs.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.262.4" class="koboSpan">The French
authorities reacted by arresting the Total-Fina managers responsible for
chartering the vessel, as well as those directly responsible for the
ship’s operation. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.262.5"
class="koboSpan">The implication of this action is that not only is the
shipowner liable in the event of an oil pollution incident, the
charterer themselves may also be liable when the judicial process is
completed.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">Charterers for oil
tankers re-appraised their policies as a consequence of this action.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.263.2" class="koboSpan">Tanker brokers
reported the first signs of significant price premiums for new tonnage,
as owners of old tonnage suddenly found that the charterers had begun to
discriminate by
age.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0359" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0359"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.264.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan"> As a direct consequence of this incident, the EU
proposed that the phase-out of single-hulled tankers, agreed at the IMO
after the US unilateral action in OPA90, should be
accelerated.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0360" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0360"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.266.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan"> The accelerated phase-out was adopted by the IMO in
2001.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.268.1" class="koboSpan">In November 2002, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige
</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan">developed cracks in her hull off the North-Wet coats of
Spain. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.270.2" class="koboSpan">Her
request to move into more sheltered waters was refused by the Spanish
authorities and she split and sank, spilling crude oil that polluted
French and Spanish beaches. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.270.3"
class="koboSpan">As a consequence, the planned phase out of single hull
tankers was accelerated yet again.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">It is unsurprising,
but perhaps disappointing, to note that the two major legislative
changes affecting the operation of the tanker industry per se in the
past decade have both been a result of a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan">reaction</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan"> by governments and international organisations to the
political pressures created as a result of a well-publicised
environmental
accident.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0361" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0361"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan"> The South Korean government introduced a 2010 phase
out on single hull tankers after the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan">Hebei Spirit
</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan">incident in November 2007.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.277.2" class="koboSpan">Indeed,
Gibsons has formed the view that it is unlikely that many single hull
tanker owners will opt to continue trading after 2010.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.277.3" class="koboSpan">It was thought
that some would continue to trade, primarily in the Far East, up until
2015, providing that the vessel was less than 25 years old and flag
registry permission from both loading and disembarking countries had
been obtained. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.277.4"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan">Hebei Spirit
</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">and
other incidents in the Far East have changed that
perception.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0362" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0362"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">There is a widespread
perception in the industry that the tanker market has significantly
improved its performance in terms of oil spills and tanker accidents,
post-</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan">Prestige</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.283.2"
class="koboSpan">There is now some evidence to support this view.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.283.3" class="koboSpan">Homer and
Steiner</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0363" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0363"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan"> used probit or binomial models to determine the key
drivers of the time series of US Coastguard data on oil spills.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.285.2" class="koboSpan">They found
that both the introduction of tighter monitoring under OPA’90 and the
shift to double hull tankers were statistically significant explanatory
factors in oil spill incidents. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.285.3"
class="koboSpan">Glen,</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0364" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0364"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan"> using a similar approach, showed that the introduction
of double hull technology had reduced the expected number of oil spills
over the period from an expected 72 per year in the absence of double
hulls, to 21 per year, given seaborne trade levels.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.287.2" class="koboSpan">However,
attempts to detect impacts from OPA’90 and the introduction of the ISM
code in 1998 were unsuccessful. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.287.3"
class="koboSpan">The key change appears to be double hull
technology.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">The IMO has also
moved to reduce the amount of airborne pollution generated by shipping,
namely reducing NO</span><sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">x and S</span><sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">O outputs from marine engines, especially in sulphur
oxide emission control areas (SECAs).
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.292.2" class="koboSpan">These changes,
and those related to the drive to reduce
C</span><sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan">O emissions from shipping, are not specific to tankers
so are not developed here.</span>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_375"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">8. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.295.2" class="koboSpan">The Economics of Tanker Markets</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">8.1 Freight rate and ship price behaviour</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.1" class="koboSpan">Tanker freight rates
and asset prices display marked features.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.2" class="koboSpan">Freight rates
are expressed in either \$/tonne, a dollar lump sum amount, or in
WorldScale. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.3"
class="koboSpan">The WorldScale system is well established, replacing
its predecessor, IntaScale. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.4"
class="koboSpan">It in turn originated in World War II, when the UK’s
ministry of transport set up a set of common scales to be used to
reimburse tanker owners for the use of their requisitioned assets.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.5" class="koboSpan">Expressing
rates in dollars per tonne of cargo delivered was felt to be
uninformative when trying to make comparisons of the relative revenues
being charged for across different routes.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.6" class="koboSpan">This is
because the voyage fixture cost will be affected by fuel prices in the
region, the voyage distance, the port dues being charged, and of course
the vessel size. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.7"
class="koboSpan">The WorldScale system in effect tries to provide a
“standard”, a reference marker, to allow some comparison to be made
across routes. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.8"
class="koboSpan">It is based on setting up a Reference rate, “WorldScale
Flat”, which is to be charged for the carriage of one tonne of cargo
between any two ports. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.9"
class="koboSpan">The absolute value of the Flat rate depends on an
assumed bunker price, and is based on a 75,000 dwt tanker with specific
fuel consumption and speed. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.10"
class="koboSpan">Port and cargo discharge dues are surveyed annually at
every port, and the fuel costs for the voyage are estimated.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.11" class="koboSpan">In addition,
a fixed notional daily hire charge is included.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.12" class="koboSpan">WorldScale
Flat is then arrived at. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.13"
class="koboSpan">The WorldScale Association calculates these flat rates
for thousands of voyage possibilities.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.14" class="koboSpan">The rate is
based on a round voyage and allows a standard 48 hours for both loading
and discharging. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.15"
class="koboSpan">WorldScale flat rates are updated annually; from the
mid-1970s they were updated twice a year, because of high inflation
rates. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.297.16" class="koboSpan">In
1989, WorldScale reverted to an annual review and update of the Flat
Rate, as inflation rates stabilised.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">Any spot voyage
fixture that takes place on the market is then translated from the
\$/tonne cargo into a WorldScale equivalent.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.298.2" class="koboSpan">Given the cost
structure of ships, even if a 250,000 dwt vessel were to earn the same
net revenue as the reference 75,000 dwt vessel, its rate would be well
below WS100, the reference value.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.298.3"
class="koboSpan">Norman</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0365" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0365"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan"> states that the advantages of a scale system are; the
simplification of communication, the simplification of charter parties
for option fixtures by the replacement of alternative freight rates by
one scale reference, the simplification of charter parties for
consecutive voyage agreements, and the simplification of the
comparability of earning opportunity, because differences due to voyage
length and port cost s have been embodied in the flat rate itself.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.300.2" class="koboSpan">Norman
demonstrated that the ability to make comparisons across routes was more
to do with the high correlation and limited variation of bunker fuel
prices around the world than the reference system itself.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.300.3" class="koboSpan">The existence
of WorldScale does cause a second problem.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.300.4" class="koboSpan">Whilst freight
rates are often quoted in WorldScale (strictly, nominal WorldScale),
time charter rates are quoted in \$ per day, and the prices of ships,
both new and second-hand, are also quoted in \$.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.300.5" class="koboSpan">To match spot
earnings to time charter hire rates therefore requires a transformation
– and time charter rates are sometimes quoted as WorldScale Equivalent.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.300.6" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
owners convert their prospective revenues, less commission, and the
particular voyage related costs, to produce a time charter equivalent
daily rate. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.300.7"
class="koboSpan">This is the first stage in the voyage budgeting and
accounting process.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.301.1" class="koboSpan">The pattern of tanker
freight rates has not changed in any significant way in the past 20
years. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.301.2" class="koboSpan">Spot
rates are quoted for the various size segments discussed briefly above.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.301.3" class="koboSpan">The behaviour
of tanker spot rates over the past is illustrated in
</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fig0235" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fig0235"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.302.1" class="koboSpan">Figures 5(a)</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0146"
id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0146"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">5(d)</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0235" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00253.jpg"

</div>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00255.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

alt="Figure 5: (a) Spot rates current VLCC 2000–2009; (b) Spot rates Suexmax 2000–2009; (c) Spot rates Aframax 2000–2009; (d) Spot rates Handy Size Clean 2000–2009" /></span>
