id="Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0146"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan">(a) Spot rates current VLCC 2000–2009; (b) Spot rates
Suexmax 2000–2009; (c) Spot rates Aframax 2000–2009; (d) Spot rates
Handy Size Clean 2000–2009</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.313.1"
class="koboSpan">Source</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan">: Gibsons</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">The charts illustrate
two basic points. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.315.2"
class="koboSpan">One is the great volatility of rates; on the Middle
East to Japan route, spot rates reached WS168 at the end of 2000; but
six months later, they had fallen to WS39.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.315.3" class="koboSpan">In December
2007 the monthly average was WS207, July 2008, WS30.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.315.4" class="koboSpan">By May 2009,
the rate was WS29! </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.315.5"
class="koboSpan">More formally, the coefficient of variation (the ratio
of the standard deviation to the mean), which allows comparison of
volatility across series with different mean values, is found to be 0.54
for the VLCC, 0.39 for Suezmax, 0.31 for Aframax, and 0.28 for the Handy
Clean series. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.315.6"
class="koboSpan">This means that the volatility of the series increases
with ship size, with the clean trades being notably less volatile.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.315.7" class="koboSpan">The peaks can
be observed across all the routes and oil cargoes shown, which
illustrates the second feature, the very high correlation of rates
across all routes. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.315.8"
class="koboSpan">Similar patterns exist for all sizes.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">The behaviour of both
the new and second-hand price of ships is also of interest.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.316.2" class="koboSpan">It is well
known that both of these prices fluctuate over time, reflecting changing
conditions in the freight market.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.316.3" class="koboSpan">The behaviour
of the real price of new buildings was noted earlier.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.316.4" class="koboSpan">The
relationship between the relative prices of different tanker sizes is
not constant over time; nor is the relationship between the second hand
price of a vessel and the newbuild and scrap prices of a similar
type.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">The relationship
between the asset price and freight earnings has been the central focus
of recent econometric studies of the tanker market, as will be discerned
in the following sections.</span>

### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">8.2 The demand and supply approach</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">The standard approach
to analysing the tanker market has been to use the static competitive
model. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.319.2" class="koboSpan">This
approach can be split into two interrelated segments – the modelling of
demand and supply for oil tanker services, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.319.3" class="koboSpan">transport
demand and supply; and the modelling of the change in the stock of
tankers that provide the services, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.319.4" class="koboSpan">the
newbuilding, second-hand tankers, and scrapping markets.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_378"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan">It has already been established that the industry
structure is very fragmented. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.320.2"
class="koboSpan">It has also been shown that the derived demand for
tanker services is extremely inelastic with respect to the freight rate.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.320.3" class="koboSpan">How does
tanker supply respond?</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.321.1" class="koboSpan">The conventional
answer to this question is to employ the argument that the tanker supply
side is determined by competitive conditions.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.321.2" class="koboSpan">The standard
economic model of perfect competition requires four principal
assumptions to be made before it can be applied.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.321.3" class="koboSpan">They
are:</span>

1.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
    class="koboSpan"> The presence of a large number of
    buyers</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.323.2"
    class="koboSpan">In the tanker market, the buyer is the charterer of
    the tanker service. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.323.3"
    class="koboSpan">There are indeed, hundreds, if not thousands, of
    individual companies who hire tankers.</span>
2.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
    class="koboSpan"> The presence of a large number of
    sellers</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.325.2"
    class="koboSpan">It has already been established that the largest
    owners of oil tankers control only a very small percentage of the
    tanker fleet, and this percentage has, if anything, declined in the
    last 30 years. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.325.3"
    class="koboSpan">There are hundreds of tanker owners.</span>
3.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Free entry and
    exit</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.327.2"
    class="koboSpan">An important feature of a competitive market is the
    ability for new entrants to win business without being impeded by
    existing companies, or suffering from a significant cost
    disadvantage when they enter.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.327.3" class="koboSpan">If this
    condition.</span>
4.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.328.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Homogeneous
    product</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.329.2"
    class="koboSpan">In order to ensure that buyers view each supplier’s
    service as identical, the product offered must be very similar.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.329.3" class="koboSpan">The
    ‘product’ in this case is the safe and reliable transportation of
    the cargo, as specified by the contract.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.329.4" class="koboSpan">Providing
    that tanker owners ensure that their vessels’ can comply with this
    condition, the only criteria for choosing between competing
    suppliers is the freight
    rate.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0366" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0366"><span
    id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.330.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup>
5.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Full
    information</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.2"
    class="koboSpan">The market is extremely well served by the
    specialised shipbroking companies who keep in constant contact with
    both owners and charterers on a 24-hour basis all round the world.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.3" class="koboSpan">These
    companies have offices in strategic points all round the world to
    offer this service. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.4"
    class="koboSpan">The role of London is crucial, because it is
    located in a timezone that allows trade with the Far East and New
    York in the same trading day.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.5" class="koboSpan">This
    unique position makes London the ideal base for such companies.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.6" class="koboSpan">In
    addition, there are many specialist companies offering consultancy
    services to companies. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.7"
    class="koboSpan">All this activity means that charterers and owners
    are continuously informed of recent events and prices.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.8" class="koboSpan">Many
    shipping fixtures are publicly reported, with all salient details
    available. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.332.9"
    class="koboSpan">This makes the provision of market information
    relatively cheap and very efficient.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">Overall then it would
appear that all of the fundamental assumptions of perfect competition
are fulfilled when one examines the tanker market, particularly the
crude sector. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.333.2"
class="koboSpan">This means that modelling its behaviour using demand
and supply analysis can thus be justified.</span>

#### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.334.1" class="koboSpan">8.2.1 Explaining the freight rate</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">The nature of supply
differs between the short-run period, defined as the period in which the
tanker fleet is unchanged in size, and the long run, in which the tanker
fleet is allowed to contract or expand.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.335.2" class="koboSpan">Contraction
occurs if the rate of scrapping of tankers
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_379"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan">exceeds the rate of newbuilding deliveries; expansion
when newbuilding deliveries exceed
scrapping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0367" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0367"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.338.1" class="koboSpan">The short run supply
schedule for the market as a whole is assumed to have a “reverse L”
shape, which is very elastic (flat) when there is a low demand for
tanker services relative to the existing fleet size, but which becomes
very inelastic (vertical) as demand approaches full capacity of the
existing fleet (</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0147"
id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0147"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.339.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.340.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.340.2"
class="koboSpan">The “flat” range of the supply curve is created by the
ability to “mothball” tanker tonnage by placing the vessel in layup when
trading conditions are poor, and freight earnings are low.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.340.3" class="koboSpan">As demand
approaches the potential maximum productive capacity of the present
fleet, all lay ups are brought into use, and the ability to further
expand supply becomes very limited.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.340.4" class="koboSpan">This explains
the vertical section of the short run supply
curve.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0368" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0368"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.341.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan"> The position of the short run cost curve is also
indicative of the overall level of marginal cost.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.342.2" class="koboSpan">One very
important determinant of this is the assumed value of factor input
prices. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.342.3" class="koboSpan">In the
case of ships, the most significant of these in the short run is the
price of bunker fuel, since most of the short run variable costs are
related to voyage activity. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.342.4"
class="koboSpan">The position of the short run costs curve will shift
upwards if bunker price rise significantly, and shift downwards if they
fall.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">The 80:20 split is
based on the analysis by
Platou</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0369" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0369"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.344.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.345.1"
class="koboSpan"> of tanker rate volatility– they argue that practically
all of the variations that are observed in the tanker market are
observed when the utilisation of the fleet was in the last 20%– this is
consistent with the shape of the supply curve above – elastic over the
80% range, but becoming less and less elastic until full capacity
utilisation was achieved.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">It is important to
remember that this is a model for the short run supply of shipping.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.346.2" class="koboSpan">The assumption
is being made that the stock of tankers is unchanged; variations in
tonne miles produced are generated by variations in lay-ups, storage,
and speed.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.347.1" class="koboSpan">In a perfectly
competitive market, the short run “floor” for prices is given by the
short run marginal cost of producing output above the minimum short run
average variable cost floor. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.347.2"
class="koboSpan">Adland and
Strandenes</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0370" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0370"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.349.1"
class="koboSpan"> have shown how close this is to empirical reality for
the VLCC market, in a groundbreaking study.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.349.2" class="koboSpan">They show that
for most periods between 1988 and 2005, the spot rate for VLCC’s rarely,
if ever, fell below the</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0239" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00257.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Short run supply curve for tanker services" /></span>

<a href="#Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0147"
id="Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0147"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.351.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan">Short run supply curve for tanker services</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0240" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00258.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7: VLCC spot freight rates vs short-run marginal cost" /></span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_380"></span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0148"
id="Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0148"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.355.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.357.1"
class="koboSpan">VLCC spot freight rates vs short-run marginal
cost</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan">Source</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan">: Adland, R. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.359.2"
class="koboSpan">and Strandenes, S.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.359.3" class="koboSpan">(2007)
</span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.360.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0143)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan">, p. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.361.2"
class="koboSpan">198. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.361.3"
class="koboSpan">Reproduced by permission of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan">Journal of Transport Economics and
Policy</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.364.1" class="koboSpan">estimated short-run
marginal cost, and in many periods was well above that “floor”.
</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0148"
id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0148"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.365.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan"> is reproduced from their article.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.367.1" class="koboSpan">How “realistic” is
the “reverse L” model? </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.367.2"
class="koboSpan">Adland and
Strandenes</span><sup>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan">45</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_fn0370)</sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.369.1"
class="koboSpan"> have generated such a supply curve for the actual VLCC
tanker fleet. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.369.2"
class="koboSpan">Their supply curve looks remarkably like the
theoretical one shown in </span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.370.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0147)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.371.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.371.2"
class="koboSpan">As they point out, the modernisation of the tanker
fleet has led to less variation in fuel consumption between the vessels
as the age distribution is reduced, leading to a near horizontal supply
curve over a large range of tonnage.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.372.1" class="koboSpan">Putting the very
inelastic demand schedule together with the varying elasticity supply
schedule generates a model of the equilibrium spot freight rate for
tanker services. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.372.2"
class="koboSpan">as shown below, in
</span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0149"
id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0149"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.373.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 8</span></a><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.374.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.374.2"
class="koboSpan">The important feature to note about this figure is the
asymmetric response of the freight rate to shifts in the position of the
demand curve. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.374.3"
class="koboSpan">When demand increases from D0 to D1, a large
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.375.1"
class="koboSpan">shift</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.376.1"
class="koboSpan"> in demand, there is little effect on the market
freight rate, because of the presence of unemployed or underemployed
vessels. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.376.2" class="koboSpan">The
equilibrium freight rate moves from P1 to P2, whilst tonne miles
increase from Q1 to Q2. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.376.3"
class="koboSpan">When demand shifts again, from D1 to D2, which is a
smaller </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.377.1"
class="koboSpan">shift</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.378.1"
class="koboSpan"> in demand, spare capacity is less readily available,
so the result is larger increase in rate.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.378.2" class="koboSpan">The freight
rate rises from P2 to P3, and tonne miles increase from Q2 to Q3.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.378.3" class="koboSpan">Finally, when
demand shifts from D2 to D3, tanker supply is perfectly inelastic, and
small shifts in demand generate large increases in rates.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.378.4" class="koboSpan">In this case,
the freight rate rises rapidly from P3 to P4 but tonne miles performed
rise only slightly from Q3 to Q4.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.379.1" class="koboSpan">The long run supply
of tanker services is found by allowing the short run supply schedule to
shift its position over time. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.379.2"
class="koboSpan">As the total fleet expands, the curve will shift down
(slightly) and to the right, reflecting two elements.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.379.3" class="koboSpan">Firstly, new
tankers tend to be more efficient than old ones.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.379.4" class="koboSpan">The long
economic life means that technical change</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0241" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.380.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00259.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 8: Modelling tanker demand and supply in the short run" /></span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_381"></span><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0149"
id="Ch012.xhtml_cap_lbl0149"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.381.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 8</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.382.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan">Modelling tanker demand and supply in the short
run</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.1" class="koboSpan">will be embodied in
the new vessels, particularly in terms of the fuel consumption of new
engines, levels of automation, and days off-hire for servicing and
repair will be lower. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.2"
class="koboSpan">So a similar size vessel, when replaced with its modern
equivalent, will have a lower short run marginal cost per tonne mile.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.3" class="koboSpan">This change is
gradual, but its cumulative effect is important.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.4" class="koboSpan">Second, owners
do not necessarily replace same sized vessels with their modern
equivalent. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.5" class="koboSpan">As
trade volumes change, the optimal vessel size for a specific trade route
will alter. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.6"
class="koboSpan">When demand grows in volume, average tanker sizes will
increase. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.7"
class="koboSpan">Because of the scale economies inherent in ship size,
irrespective of type, larger vessels will tend to mean lower short-run
marginal costs. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.8"
class="koboSpan">It is important to note however if the fleet is doubled
in size, the same basic short run supply relationship will still exist.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.9" class="koboSpan">There will
always be a finite productive capacity whatever the size of the fleet,
and hence, with sufficient demand volume, a limit on short-run output.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.10" class="koboSpan">But this is
not true of long-run supply. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.11"
class="koboSpan">In principle, the long run supply will expand in line
with demand. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.12"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, the efficient allocation of resources requires
that the capital embodied in the tanker companies should be sufficient
to meet long term demand needs, but no more.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.384.13" class="koboSpan">It is
expected then, that over time, the growth in the tanker fleet should be
in proportion to the growth in the level of tonne mile demand.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.385.1" class="koboSpan">The application of
this model helps to explain the short-run fluctuations in freight rates
observed in the market, which are viewed as the result of the
interaction of the short run supply schedule with the shifting demand
schedule. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.385.2" class="koboSpan">The
long-term trend will appear as demand trends assert themselves, and
supply adjusts through the expansion or contraction of the fleet.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.385.3" class="koboSpan">It is thus
possible to explain both short-run volatility of freight rates and
profits, and at the same time, explain the long-term trend decline in
the real costs of transporting oil, brought about by the use of larger
and more technically efficient ships.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.385.4" class="koboSpan">Given that
demand responds primarily to the balance between economic activity and
the prevailing level of tanker supply (the fleet), whilst costs are
directly affected by the behaviour of bunker prices, it is not
surprising to find that these three variables are regularly employed as
explanatory factors in the econometric modelling of the tanker freight
rate.</span>

#### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_382"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.386.1" class="koboSpan">8.2.2 Freight rates and profitability by tanker size</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.387.1" class="koboSpan">The above analysis
has taken for granted that the market for all tankers is the same: the
market for 50,000 dwt crude is identical to the market for 350,000 dwt
crude vessels. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.387.2"
class="koboSpan">But one or two authors have suggested that the changes
that occurred in the 1970s have made that assumption incorrect.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.387.3" class="koboSpan">The different
size classifications of tankers have already been outlined.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.387.4" class="koboSpan">The key
question is: do these different segments behave differently, in economic
terms, or are they all so highly correlated that it is still valid to
analyse the market as if it were a single entity?
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.387.5" class="koboSpan">Earlier
research suggested that there are indeed sufficient differences to
warrant separate analysis, which has been confirmed more recently by
others. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.387.6"
class="koboSpan">Svendsen showed that different tanker sizes had
different own-price and cross-price elasticities of demand with respect
to freight rates. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.387.7"
class="koboSpan">This implies some degree of differentiation in the
market. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.387.8"
class="koboSpan">Glen,</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0371" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0371"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.388.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.389.1"
class="koboSpan"> in a study of tanker profitability in the 1970s,
showed that the gross profit margins varied widely between sizes, and
that large tankers had significantly greater variability in those
margins. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.389.2" class="koboSpan">If
the tankers were all in the same market, the variability should have
been the same. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.389.3"
class="koboSpan">More recently, Kavussanos showed that there are
significant differences in the volatility of tanker freight rates by
size, and therefore, significant differences in the level of risk
associated with owning different sizes of tankers.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.389.4" class="koboSpan">This implies
that, viewed as a financial asset, they are distinct.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.389.5" class="koboSpan">This result
has been confirmed by Glen and
Martin.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0372" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0372"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.390.1" class="koboSpan">47</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.391.1" class="koboSpan">The question arises,
does this mean that the segments of the tanker market can be viewed as
independent of each other? </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.391.2"
class="koboSpan">The answer to this is a resounding no, because although
the segments within the tanker market may have become more distinct,
allowing them to behave differently in the short run, it does not follow
that they are unrelated in the long run.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.391.3" class="koboSpan">This is
because shipowners have the choice of investing in all of these segments
– none is closed to them. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.391.4"
class="koboSpan">Thus free entry and exit exists in all parts, so that
market imbalances may exist for a few years, but will be self-corrected
by different rates of entry and exit in the sectors.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.391.5" class="koboSpan">Thus, if the
market for VLCC’s is badly hit, this sector will have very high lay-ups,
higher than average scrapping rates, and few new orders – owners will be
concentrating on the sectors that are relatively more profitable – until
the excess supply problem is resolved.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.391.6" class="koboSpan">In the long
run then, one would expect to see the same common factors driving each
of these sectors, and common trends appearing.</span>

#### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.392.1" class="koboSpan">8.2.3 Term structure relations</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.393.1" class="koboSpan">The simple demand
supply explains the determination of the spot rate, but does not
directly help analyse the behaviour of time charter rates.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.393.2" class="koboSpan">One way of
exploring the relationship between these two is to note the similarity
between the term structure of interest rates, whereby long-term rates on
interest are explained in terms of short-term rates, and the tanker
market, in which the period rate which is return to the owner, is
expected to be equivalent to the sum of the expected discounted returns
earned by the owner if they operated their tanker on the spot market
over the same time horizon as the relevant period charter, In an
efficient market, the only difference between these two should be a
liquidity premium, normally assumed to be negative, because by hiring
the vessel for a longer period, the owner has transferred some of the
risk of ownership to the charterer.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.393.3" class="koboSpan">The
hypothesised relationship can be written as:</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0242" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.394.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00260.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_383"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.395.1"
class="koboSpan">which states that a time charter equivalent of n period
duration will be equal to the present value of the expected returns
obtained from trading in the spot market (V).
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.395.2" class="koboSpan">The last term
in the expression can be positive or negative as it reflects the
liquidity cost or benefit from being in the spot market, which depends
on present market conditions. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.395.3"
class="koboSpan">In rising markets the owner would prefer to be trading
in the voyage market, but if the market is declining, fixing a period
charter is preferable, and the “liquidity premium” is
reversed.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0373" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0373"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.396.1" class="koboSpan">48</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.397.1"
class="koboSpan"> This relationship can be transformed, in terms of the
‘spread’ or the difference between the time charter rate of a given
period and the appropriate spot rate.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.397.2" class="koboSpan">It can be
shown that the spread is a function of the expected future changes in
the corresponding spot rate. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.397.3"
class="koboSpan">Veenstra, using modern econometric methods, has tested
this model, and argues that it is a valid representation of the
relationship between spot and time charter rates, with the exception of
that for the VLCC
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0374" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0374"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.398.1" class="koboSpan">49</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.399.1" class="koboSpan">This so-called
“present value” relationship is very important, as it also appears when
the determinants of the price of ships are examined.</span>

#### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.400.1" class="koboSpan">8.2.4 The price of ships</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.401.1" class="koboSpan">The price of
second-hand ships correlates very well with movements of spot and
timecharter rates. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.401.2"
class="koboSpan">When market conditions are very good, second-hand
prices are high, and in some extreme cases have risen close to, and even
above, the newbuilding price of an equivalent sized tanker.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.401.3" class="koboSpan">When market
conditions are poor, the second hand price may be closer to the value
implied if the vessel were to scrapped; its value determined by the
prevailing price of scrap. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.401.4"
class="koboSpan">Both of these situations have been observed in the
past. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.401.5" class="koboSpan">In the
poor market conditions of the early 1980s, second-hand prices were at
the scrap price “floor”. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.401.6"
class="koboSpan">In 2001 and 2007, some second-hand tankers were being
sold at newbuild prices.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.402.1" class="koboSpan">The key to
understanding this lies in the present value relation introduced in the
previous section. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.402.2"
class="koboSpan">This time, the relationship is between the ship price,
(the asset), and the stream of earnings it is expected to generated to
the owner whilst they trade it. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.402.3"
class="koboSpan">This is best defined in present value terms.</span>

<div id="Ch012.xhtml_fig0243" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00261.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.404.1" class="koboSpan">where the second-hand
price, P</span><sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.405.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.406.1"
class="koboSpan"> is determined by the expected future profits earned by
trading the vessel, plus any income, discounted back to the present,
obtained when it is disposed of
D</span><sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.407.1"
class="koboSpan">t+n</span></sub><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.408.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.408.2"
class="koboSpan">This last term represents either the price received
from another shipowner if the vessel is sold on for further trading, or
the scrap value. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.408.3"
class="koboSpan">The former is determined by the expected future second
hand price of the vessel, the latter, the expected price of scrap.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.408.4" class="koboSpan">Since the
expected future price of a second-hand ship depends on earnings, the
relationship implies very high levels of correlation between freight
rates, bunker costs, scrap prices and the second-hand price.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.409.1" class="koboSpan">Putting these
elements together provides a model of tanker market behaviour.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.409.2" class="koboSpan">Freight rates
are determined by the joint interaction of the supply of, and demand for
tanker services. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.409.3"
class="koboSpan">The latter is very insensitive to the freight rate
itself; it has been shown to be highly price inelastic.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.409.4" class="koboSpan">But demand is
sensitive to changes in expectations about the future, and to political
and other external events that can impact on it.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.409.5" class="koboSpan">The reaction
of the freight rate to shifts in demand will depend in part, on the
level of utilisation of the existing fleet.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.409.6" class="koboSpan">At high levels
of employment, shifts in demand will create large
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_384"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan">movements in the freight rate; but when there are
significant numbers of vessels laid up, supply is more elastic and
freight rates will tend to be less volatile.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.1" class="koboSpan">Because of the fact
that second-hand tanker prices are driven by expected future earnings,
high levels of freight rates will lead to greater expected profits and
an immediate rise in second-hand prices.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.2" class="koboSpan">The variation
in the price of tankers is thus highly correlated with events in the
spot market. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.3"
class="koboSpan">High profits mean increasing orders, and an increased
level of tanker deliveries in the near future.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.4" class="koboSpan">If demand
growth declines, or fails to grow as anticipated, the increased level of
deliveries will lead to a lowering of spot rates in the future as the
newbuildings are delivered. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.5"
class="koboSpan">In addition, at high levels of demand, older vessels,
which might have been scrapped, are traded for longer.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.6" class="koboSpan">This reduces
the supply of tankers for scrap and raises the scrap price.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.7" class="koboSpan">At the same
time, the pressure of owners on yards increases, and newbuilding prices
will tend to rise. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.8"
class="koboSpan">Thus freight rates, second hand prices, scrap prices
and newbuild prices will tend to move together in a cyclical fashion.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.411.9" class="koboSpan">This process
is driven by the interaction of many owners, charterers, shipbuilders
and shipbrokers, none of whom have any significant control over their
environment.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.412.1" class="koboSpan">Although this model
of dynamic behaviour appears to be very plausible, some of the
econometric studies carried out in the past few years have cast a shadow
over its veracity. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.412.2"
class="koboSpan">In particular, work stemming from Kavussanos and
Alizadeh</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0375" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0375"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.413.1" class="koboSpan">50</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.414.1"
class="koboSpan"> has been very important in highlighting the empirical
failure of the joint term structure – rational expectations hypotheses
that underpin this approach. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.414.2"
class="koboSpan">Although their studies focused on the dry bulk sector,
their findings are important enough to be mentioned here, as there is no
reason to expect that dry bulk and tanker markets will be different in
terms of expectations formation.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.414.3" class="koboSpan">Their findings
suggest that the link between spot and time charter rates, and between
ship prices and time charter rates, is not of the form required to
satisfy the hypothesis of constant market expectations on the part of
market players. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.414.4"
class="koboSpan">Either expectations must be heterogeneous, or they vary
over time or both of the above must be true.</span>

#### <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.415.1" class="koboSpan">8.2.5 Tanker long-run cost structures</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.416.1" class="koboSpan">One area of the
tanker market that has been neglected by maritime economists of late is
the structure of long run costs.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.416.2" class="koboSpan">Tanker average
size has stabilised, with the largest vessels being smaller than they
were 15 years ago. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.416.3"
class="koboSpan">Most of the ULCC fleet has disappeared, with only a
handful of 400,000 dwt plus vessels still existing.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.416.4" class="koboSpan">The question
arises: Have economies of scale changed in this industry?</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.417.1" class="koboSpan">In a recent study
Glen and
Reid</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0376" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0376"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.418.1" class="koboSpan">51</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.419.1"
class="koboSpan"> revisited the traditional modelling of ship costs,
using data provided by Gibsons. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.419.2"
class="koboSpan">A simple method of estimating scale economies is to
construct cost elasticity estimates for the various elements of ship
costs, namely, capital, operating, and voyage.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.419.3" class="koboSpan">The authors
found, somewhat to their surprise, that the estimated elasticity
coefficients for these components were more or less identical to those
reported in the literature, often 30 years ago.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.419.4" class="koboSpan">Using the
resulting elasticity estimates, the cost structure by route length and
ship size were calculated. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.419.5"
class="koboSpan">These showed that optimal tanker size increased with
round voyage length, as one would expect.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.419.6" class="koboSpan">What was more
interesting is the fact that the unit costs for a fully laden vessel
continued to decline on most voyage lengths, up to and beyond the
400,000 dwt size. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.419.7"
class="koboSpan">This suggests that the “optimal tanker size” for a
given route is not determined solely by costs, but is driven by the
present lot size requirements of oil refineries, and the ideal lot sizes
used
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_385"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.420.1"
class="koboSpan">by charterers and oil traders.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.420.2" class="koboSpan">In other
words, demand characteristics appear to drive ship size rather than pure
cost considerations.</span>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.421.1" class="koboSpan">9. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.421.2" class="koboSpan">Alternative Views</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.422.1" class="koboSpan">The above discussion
has concentrated on the “traditional view” of the dynamics of the tanker
market. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.422.2" class="koboSpan">But
not all maritime economists are “convinced” by this story.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.422.3" class="koboSpan">In the past
decade, a number of significant contributions have tried to develop
alternative ways of explaining the observed dynamics of freight rate
behaviour over time.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.423.1" class="koboSpan">One approach is has
been to argue that rates follow a time path determined by stohastic
differential equations. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.423.2"
class="koboSpan">These equations have two elements.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.423.3" class="koboSpan">The first
component models or predicts the behaviour of the “mean” or average rate
value. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.423.4" class="koboSpan">But to
that is added a second component, which adds a forecast of the likely
expected variance that will occur, the most likely “deviation” from the
mean. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.423.5" class="koboSpan">Putting
these two elements together gives a dynamic path for rates to follow.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.423.6" class="koboSpan">Such an
approach avoids worrying about the niceties of order and scrapping
levels, and despite its mathematical sophistication, is “mechanical” in
the sense that it require no insight into the market being studied.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.423.7" class="koboSpan">These models
have been put to use in valuing ships, given this requires forecasting
the future time path of ships. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.423.8"
class="koboSpan">For example,
Tvedt</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0377" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0377"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.424.1" class="koboSpan">52</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.425.1"
class="koboSpan"> models the dynamic path of freight rates over time and
obtains valuations for a VLCC for a number of different conditions, such
as the ‘options’ to scrap or to lay up.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.425.2" class="koboSpan">He shows that
the scrap option adds little to the value of a VLCC at the start of its
life, but is more valuable if the vessel has only 10 years to “live”.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.425.3" class="koboSpan">This is a
reassuring result, in the sense that it fits with one’s own
intuition!</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.426.1" class="koboSpan">Adland and Strandenes
(2007)</span><sup><a href="#Ch012.xhtml_fn0378" id="Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0378"><span
id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.427.1" class="koboSpan">53</span></a></sup><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.428.1"
class="koboSpan"> have tried to combine elements of this approach with
elements of understanding the market dynamics.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.428.2" class="koboSpan">They argue
that the conventional model, discussed above, is flawed because it has
no explanation for the upper bound of spot rates if tanker movement
demand is truly freight rate inelastic.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.428.3" class="koboSpan">This is not
hard to see, because the floor is the short run marginal price, and the
ceiling would be the maximum price that the shipper is prepared to pay
to move the cargo. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.428.4"
class="koboSpan">If demand is price inelastic, this is infinite in
theory, but in practice, the company would be bankrupt before infinity
was reached! </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.428.5"
class="koboSpan">Their model is an attempt to address this problem by
estimating an implied demand relation and modelling scrapping and
deliveries to determine supply over time.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.428.6" class="koboSpan">The result is
a dynamic model that has elements of stochastic processes, yet also
models the demand limitation side.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.429.1" class="koboSpan">This brings the third
possibility, one not explored to any real extent at present.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.429.2" class="koboSpan">That is,
instead of viewing the market as a perfectly competitive entity with
lots of identical elements, suppose each element was regarded as unique.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.429.3" class="koboSpan">After all,
every tanker is slightly different in some way from every other tanker.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.429.4" class="koboSpan">In this
situation, the rate obtained for each vessel is unique, and to be
determined almost by “auction”. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.429.5"
class="koboSpan">Modelling the bidding and contracting process between
shipowners and charterers (or their agents) may be a fruitful way of
analysing the dynamics of the tanker market in the future.</span>

## <span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.430.1" class="koboSpan">10. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.430.2" class="koboSpan">Summary and Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.431.1" class="koboSpan">The tanker market is
a fascinating sector of the shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.431.2" class="koboSpan">It has played
a pivotal role in the transportation of oil from the major production
centres to the major
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_386"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.432.1"
class="koboSpan">consuming ones.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.432.2" class="koboSpan">The industry
is dynamic, and very sensitive to political and environmental
issues.</span>

<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.433.1" class="koboSpan">The tanker market has
proved to be a fruitful sector for applied economic research, ranging
from modelling of rate and price behaviour, to measuring the economic
impact of oil pollution on the environment.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.433.2" class="koboSpan">Whilst the
composition of the individual players has changed considerably over the
past 30 years, it is still a very good example of a competitive
industry. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.433.3" class="koboSpan">It
exhibits many of the behavioural traits that are associated with fierce
competition, and will no doubt continue to do so in the future.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.433.4" class="koboSpan">This chapter
has:</span>

1.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.434.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Outlined developments in the oil
    industry</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.435.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.435.2"
    class="koboSpan">The market for tanker services is derived from the
    movement of oil, and an understanding of the tanker market is not
    possible without an understanding of the structure of the oil
    industry. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.435.3"
    class="koboSpan">It was shown that some 60% of the world’s oil is
    traded across regional boundaries.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.435.4" class="koboSpan">The oil
    tanker market directly serves this trade.</span>
2.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.436.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Examined the demand for
    tankers</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.437.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.437.2"
    class="koboSpan">It was shown that demand is derived, and this
    characteristic means that the demand for tankers is essentially
    perfectly inelastic with respect to the cost of transporting
    it.</span>
3.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.438.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Explored the supply of tanker
    services</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.439.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.439.2"
    class="koboSpan">The low degree of industrial concentration was
    discussed, and the structure of tanker supply was explained.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.439.3" class="koboSpan">The impact
    of oil pollution on future tanker supply was discussed.</span>
4.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.440.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Reviewed the economics of the tanker
    market</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.441.1"
    class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.441.2"
    class="koboSpan">Section 8 discussed the determination of freight
    rates, and the interaction between the freight market and the market
    for new and second-hand tankers.
    </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.441.3" class="koboSpan">These
    relationships have formed the focus of research efforts in this area
    in the past decade.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.483.1"
class="koboSpan">10.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0335)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.484.1"

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.511.1"
class="koboSpan">15.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0340)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.512.1"
class="koboSpan"> It should be noted that the prevailing oil demand
forecasts of the early 1970s were totally unsustainable in terms of the
rationale underlying the demand projection; the notion that supply, or
oil discoveries and production, could continue to expand exponentially,
and of course without political and environmental resistance.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.512.2" class="koboSpan">Could output
actually have reached the projected 200 million barrels a day by year
2000? </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.512.3" class="koboSpan">(Actual
consumption was almost 75m b/d.)</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.513.1"
class="koboSpan">16.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0341)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.514.1"

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.515.1"
class="koboSpan">17.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0342)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.516.1"
class="koboSpan"> Named after the economist, Alfred Marshall, who first
developed them.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.517.1"
class="koboSpan">18.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0343)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.518.1"
class="koboSpan"> The distinction may not make a lot of difference in a
market with a constant route structure, because average voyage length
may remain constant over time. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.518.2"
class="koboSpan">If there is a dramatic change in voyage length, the
demand for shipping services can be significantly affected even if
tonnage movements are constant. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.518.3"
class="koboSpan">For example, the average voyage length for oil rose
dramatically in 1967 with the closure of the Suez Canal, from 4,775 to
6,540 miles in 1974. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.518.4"
class="koboSpan">Demand for tanker services, measured in tonne miles,
rose in proportion to this, assuming that oil volume demand remained
constant.</span>

class="koboSpan">, various issues, OECD Paris.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.527.1"
class="koboSpan">21.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0346)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.528.1"
class="koboSpan"> The time charter rate is the daily rate, in thousands
of dollars, that is paid to hire a vessel by a charterer from its owner
or present operator. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.528.2"
class="koboSpan">The rate is a charge for the use of the vessel,
complete with crew, insurance and other costs, except for those related
to voyages, i.e. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.528.3"
class="koboSpan">fuel, food, port and cargo dues.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.528.4" class="koboSpan">The most
extreme form of charter, and bare-boat charter, for 25 years, would give
the charterer the use of the vessel for that lifetime.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.528.5" class="koboSpan">The charterer
would then pay the entire costs of operating the vessel, including
manning and insurance. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.528.6"
class="koboSpan">A bare-boat charter is in effect, a rent to the owner
for the use of the capital tied up in the vessel.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.529.1"
class="koboSpan">22.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0347)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.530.1"
class="koboSpan"> The products and chemical tanker segments are much
more concentrated than the crude sector.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.530.2" class="koboSpan">The European
Commission has closed (May 2008) an ongoing enquiry into rate making in
the chemical parcel tanker sector, with no action being taken.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_page_388"></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.531.1"
class="koboSpan">See </span>[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.532.1"
class="koboSpan">www.jotankers.com/AboutJoTankers/Media/tabid/102/newsid525/2/The-EuropeanCommission-closes-the-chemical-tanker-case/Default.aspx</span>](http://www.jotankers.com/AboutJoTankers/Media/tabid/102/newsid525/2/The-EuropeanCommission-closes-the-chemical-tanker-case/Default.aspx)

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.533.1"
class="koboSpan">23.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0348)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.534.1"
class="koboSpan"> These vessels are sometimes called “one million
barrel” tankers. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.534.2"
class="koboSpan">There are approximately seven barrels to one tonne of
crude oil, so this translates into 130,000 tonnes.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.534.3" class="koboSpan">The measure is
a convenient parcel size for transporting, storing, and trading.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.603.1"
class="koboSpan">41.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0366)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.604.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is possible, under certain local conditions, for
owners to be able to charge a premium; if for example, only one vessel
is open for cargoes at a particular terminal at a particular time.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.604.2" class="koboSpan">This will not
last long however; the mobility of tankers ensures that such premia
rapidly disappear.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.605.1"
class="koboSpan">42.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0367)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.606.1"
class="koboSpan"> This corresponds to the notion that capital, at least
that tied up in the tanker, is the fixed factor of production.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.606.2" class="koboSpan">In economics,
the short run is defined as the time period in which the firm cannot
vary the employment of at least one factor of production.</span>

[<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.607.1"
class="koboSpan">43.</span>](#Ch012.xhtml_bck_fn0368)<span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.608.1"
class="koboSpan"> For a discussion of a model constructed for tankers on
this basis, see Wijnolst, N. </span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.608.2"
class="koboSpan">and Wergeland, T.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.608.3" class="koboSpan">(1996):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.609.1"
class="koboSpan">Shipping</span></span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.610.1"
class="koboSpan"> (Delft, Delft University Press).
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.610.2" class="koboSpan">The principle
is to estimate the short-run marginal costs of tankers, and then rank in
increasing order of cost, until all vessels are included.
</span><span id="Ch012.xhtml_kobo.610.3" class="koboSpan">The result is
the short-run supply curve, and it looks similar to the one used in the
text.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Economics of Short Sea Shipping</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0313)
====================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Enrico</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Musso</span></span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0379" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0379"><span

class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Ana Cristina</span></span>
