class="koboSpan">Paixão</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan">Casaca</span></span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0380" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0380"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan"> and</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan">Ana</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">Rita</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">Lynce</span></span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0381" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0381"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">‡</span></a>

## <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">1.1 Purpose</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">The idea of promoting
short sea shipping (SSS) aims at achieving a more sustainable transport
network, where least damaging transport modes have a role to play.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">SSS statistics
concerning safety are relatively good when compared with other means of
transport.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0382" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0382"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is claimed that the development of SSS is crucial
to enhance land-sea intermodality, thus pursuing (i) environmental
benefits since it reduces pollution levels and road transport accidents
and (ii) economic benefits; within this context SSS reduces transport
networks congestion levels, reduces investments in transport
infrastructure and increases port hinterlands' competitiveness the
international
markets.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0383" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0383"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">SSS has been growing
significantly over the past 40 years mainly due to the growth of
intra-regional trade and the boost of hub-and-spoke maritime transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">Its importance
is high in the South-East Asia and Europe but other regions of the world
are also considering it. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.22.3"
class="koboSpan">The American continent, particularly North America, and
Australia are looking carefully at the European experience as a learning
process so that they can also implement SSS or coastal shipping as it is
called in some regions of the globe.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.22.4" class="koboSpan">Yet, there
seems to be a gap between present growth rate and the goals of policy
makers, namely in the European Union (EU).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.22.5" class="koboSpan">So far, growth
seems limited to captive markets, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.22.6" class="koboSpan">connections of
mainland with islands and deep-sea shipping (DSS) feeder services.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.22.7" class="koboSpan">SSS does not
appear to be a real alternative to land transport, namely road haulage,
when intra European trade is being considered.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.22.8" class="koboSpan">The logistics
needs of shippers and just-in-time production philosophies have fostered
the road transport usage due to its inherent advantages in detriment of
waterborne transport services.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_392"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">In the light of the above paragraphs, this chapter aims
at looking at the European SSS arena not only for the experience gained
over the years (i.e. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.23.2"
class="koboSpan">other regions of the world can look at the benefits it
offers and what needs to be done towards its implementation), but also
because the lack of adequate statistical data from a regional
perspective prevents a deeper insight into other SSS geographical areas.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.23.3" class="koboSpan">To achieve this
objective, the present work is structured in five sections.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.23.4" class="koboSpan">Section 1
presents the purpose of the work, addresses the concept of SSS and shows
the lack of consistency in what definitions are concerned.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.23.5" class="koboSpan">Section 2
concerns SSS market information; it considers modal split, the demand
and the supply sides of SSS markets and in doing this it looks at the
average size of short sea vessels.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.23.6" class="koboSpan">Section 3
considers SSS in a multimodal context; it investigates the geographic
and economic conditions for integrating SSS in a multimodal transport
chain so that a shift of cargo from road to sea takes place, looks at
the factors influencing SSS competitiveness, investigates SSS obstacles
and challenges and presents a list of possible policies for SSS in a
multimodal context. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.23.7"
class="koboSpan">Section 4 investigates the European SSS policies and
general policies that support its development and Section 5 concerns
conclusions and further comments.</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">1.2 A definition of short sea shipping</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">Despite many efforts,
the literature still lacks an unambiguous definition of SSS as pointed
out by Van de Voorde and Viegas (1995) and Marlow
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.27.2"
class="koboSpan">(1997).</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0384" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0384"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0385" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0385"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan"> Some authors consider it to be the same as cabotage,
i.e. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.31.2" class="koboSpan">all
seaborne traffic between ports of the same country, sometimes including
frontier ports of adjacent
countries</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0386" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0386"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan"> while others envisage it as an alternative mode to
land
transport.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0387" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0387"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan"> Marlow
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.37.2"
class="koboSpan">(1997) presented a tailored definition suitable for
specific situations. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.37.3"
class="koboSpan">The authors defined SSS as seaborne flows of all kinds
of freight performed by vessels of any flag, from EU Member States to
whichever destination within the territory embracing Europe, the
Mediterranean and Black Sea non-European countries (see endnote 4).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.37.4" class="koboSpan">In this regard,
Peeters </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.39.2"
class="koboSpan">(1995) acknowledged the existence of many
regional-based (often European-based)
definitions.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0388" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0388"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">Against this
framework, the literature also proposes very pragmatic definitions.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.41.2" class="koboSpan">Stopford (1997)
states that SSS is normally a maritime transport within a region,
essentially serving port-to-port feeder traffic which can be in
competition with land
transport,</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0389" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0389"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan"> while Bjornland (1993) considers SSS as waterborne
movement of goods that does not cross the
ocean.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0390" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0390"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan"> Sometimes this pragmatism turns to tautology since
some authors consider that SSS includes any services which are not
considered to be DSS, or which are related to relatively short
distances.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0391" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0391"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0392" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0392"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan"> Within this perspective, Papadimitriou (2001)
considered SSS a maritime transport service that excludes deep sea
crossing; instead, the author acknowledged that SSS embraced pure
national cabotage services, maritime connections between mainland and
the islands, international cabotage services as well as sea-river
transport performed by coastal vessels leaving aside the pure inland
waterway
navigation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0393" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0393"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">From a technological
viewpoint, some authors focus on ships’ characteristics.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">Against this
perspective Van de Voorde and Viegas (1995) suggested that it would be
better to define SSS in terms of trading patterns rather than ships
characteristics, since it is not practical from an operational viewpoint
the 100% exclusive use of ships in SSS or DSS (see endnote 3).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.51.3" class="koboSpan">The authors
followed Linde’s viewpoint that from a broad perspective considers SSS
as a global phenomenon, but from a narrow viewpoint relates the
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_393"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan">concept to the European SSS which is operated within a
large European area and managed by European shipping
companies.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0394" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0394"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0398" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0398"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">The concept of coastal
shipping is also addressed by Bagchups and Kuipers (1993) who defined
coastal shipping as all forms of maritime transport within Europe and
between Europe and adjacent regions, irrespective of whether it involves
small oceangoing vessels, large ocean-going vessels or
coasters.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0399" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0399"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"> Paixão and Marlow (2002), in an attempt to present a
holistic definition, defined SSS as a complex maritime transport
service, performed by five classes of ships capable of carrying unitised
and non-unitised cargo, offered by different channel intermediaries
within well-defined European geographical boundaries (see endnote
16).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">At a European policy
level, the concept of SSS was addressed in the 1992 communication on the
European common transport policy.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">The European
Commission (hereinafter the Commission) envisaged SSS as a means to
shift goods from road to sea making use of underused capacity and the
document in question does not present a definition of the
concept.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0400" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0400"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan"> Despite this, in 1992, the Commission defined maritime
cabotage as a maritime service that embraced (i) the carriage of
passengers and goods by sea between ports situated on the mainland of
one Member State without call at islands (mainland cabotage); (ii)
offshore supply services; and (iii) services between ports of one
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan">Member
State</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">
where one or more ports are situated on islands (island
cabotage).</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0401" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0401"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan"> The above definition shows that SSS clearly has a
broader meaning than maritime cabotage, which seems to have a merely
juridical meaning (based on state borders), instead of an economic one
(potential competition between sea and land transport).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">The European
SSS definition was first presented in its 1995 communication on
SSS.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0402" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0402"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan"> In an attempt to harmonise the concept, the European
Conference of Ministers of Transport, the United Nations Economic
Commission for Europe, and the Commission got together in 2001 and
defined SSS as the movement of freight between intra-European ports and
between European ports and other ports as long as the latter were
located along a coastline bordering Europe as is the case of North
Africa.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0403" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0403"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"> An insight into the definition provided by the
Commission in 1995 (see endnote 21) clearly shows that both definitions
are similar but the recently motorways of the sea (MoS) concept
presented by the Commission as the
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">crème de la
crème</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">”
of European SSS
services</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0404" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0404"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan"> contributed to increase further the lack of consensus
regarding a SSS definition and how these services can be decoupled from
MoS services. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.73.2"
class="koboSpan">Following the Commission’s view of the MoS concept as a
floating infrastructure, Baird (2007) presented the seaway concept as
the ships’ decks where cargo is moved, which can be measured in lane
meters and compared with road and rail infrastructure, and raises the
issue about public investment in surface transport, given that with a
few exceptions the shipbuilding industry cannot be
subsidised.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0405" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0405"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">Consequently, it can
be said that so far there is no generally accepted SSS definition, since
different criteria are used for defining it, namely (i) geographical
criteria (based on the length of maritime leg); (ii) supply criteria
(based on type/size of vessels, or on being part of a longer journey);
(iii) demand or commercial criteria (competition with land transport;
distinction between feeder or intra-regional traffic; nature of cargo);
(iv) juridical criteria (ports belonging to the same state).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">Moreover, some
definitions are tailored for a certain geographical space, or for a
certain time and correspondent level of technical
progress.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0406" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0406"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan"> Unfortunately, the numerous and ambiguous definitions
imply the non-homogeneity of the (few) available data and statistics,
leading to some confusion in the scientific and technical debate.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">As Wijnolst
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.79.2"
class="koboSpan">(1993) point out, statistics are often neither reliable
nor consistent, since flows vary considerably according to the
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_394"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">definition considered; definitions of import and export
may also vary and differences exist also in goods classification
criteria.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0407" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0407"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">The solution to
overcome this vagueness can be linked with the possibility to choose an
existing definition or proposing an additional one.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">The best
approach should, nevertheless, outline two important keypoints
underlying all the definition efforts presented in the literature.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.82.3" class="koboSpan">One is
certainly whether land transport is possible or sea transport has no
alternatives (one or both ports being located in an island without
tunnels or bridges connecting them).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.82.4" class="koboSpan">In this case
there is a captive market with no or very little competition from other
modes (air transport for passengers or some high value-added goods;
pipelines for liquid bulks). </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.82.5"
class="koboSpan">If a land alternative does exist, this sets a
structural difference compared to DSS as for market organisation and
competition between substitute issues.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.82.6" class="koboSpan">The framework
proposed in Section 3 addresses this situation.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.82.7" class="koboSpan">The case for
SSS competing with land transport is thus the most interesting from a
theoretical viewpoint and for policies and future development.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">The second key
question is whether SSS is the main leg of a regional intermodal
traffic, or a feeder service belonging to a hub-and-spoke cycle based on
DSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">While at
an intra-regional transport level SSS introduces an intermodal option
competing with land transport, at a feeder traffic level it is normally
the opposite: the maritime hub-and-spoke cycle is a unimodal solution
where SSS competes with land transport feeders (rail or road) which
would set an intermodal transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.83.3" class="koboSpan">Most remarks
proposed in this chapter apply to both cases.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.83.4" class="koboSpan">Yet the current
debate and policy issues mainly refer to the opportunities of enhancing
intermodality based on a SSS leg, while less interest is shown for SSS
as feeder traffic to DSS, unless this traffic can be alternatively
supplied by SSS or by land transport.</span>

## <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.84.2" class="koboSpan">Short Sea Shipping Market Information</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">Over the last four
decades, the importance of SSS has been increasing all over the world
especially due to the growth of feeder traffic (as a result of growing
DSS transport) and the reduction of port calls in the DSS market because
of increasing vessel size. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.85.2"
class="koboSpan">With a coastline of about 89,000 kilometres (km),
having 60/70% of the industries located within a 150–200 km range from a
port, the EU has definitely one of the most suited geographical areas
for the development of SSS (see endnote 21).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.85.3" class="koboSpan">In addition, a
transport network made up of 97,600 km of conventional and high speed
railway lines, 70,200 km of road infrastructure, 25,000 km of inland
waterways (IWW) of which 12,000 km are included in the combined
transport network, 439 ports of which 319 are seaports (remaining ones
are IWW ports) has made EU one of the most relevant SSS markets in the
world, along with Asia. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.85.4"
class="koboSpan">Feeder trade will obviously follow the developments in
transhipment hubs, which are rapidly occurring in the Caribbean, Middle
East and South America. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.85.5"
class="koboSpan">The next paragraphs provide information about the
European SSS market modal split, demand and supply.</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 The European Union modal split</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">Since 1970, freight
transport in Europe has grown significantly (see
</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fig0244" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0244"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">) as a result of the European economic growth and
commercial exchanges taking place at a European and international
levels. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.89.2" class="koboSpan">This
trend has been witnessed at a worldwide</span>

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0244" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_395"></span>[](#Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0244)

[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00262.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0244)

</div>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">level as shown in the
UNCTAD Review of Maritime Transport and Fearnleys market reports.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">In conformity
with </span>[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_fig0244)<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan">, the movement of freight transport tripled from 1970
until 2006. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.93.2"
class="koboSpan">Over this period the movement of freight by air is very
small and has stabilised relatively to the total cargo being moved and
according to the data provided in
</span>[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_fig0244)<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan">, it is expected that its share will remain more or
less the same.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Freight movement by
pipeline has increased in terms of billion tonne-km (tb-km), but from a
market perspective it has lost 1.5% between 1970 and 2007.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.96.2" class="koboSpan">This can be
attributed to the use of alternative energies which are more
environmentally friendly, in detriment of the fossil oils as well as, to
the fact that liquefied natural gas (LNG) is also being transported by
waterborne transport, which implies that the pre- and on-carriage legs
of the LNG supply chain will make use of pipelines to reach the final
consumer. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.96.3"
class="koboSpan">Although the demand for IWW transport has increased
over the years, in terms of market share, it has been unable to follow
the trends of sea and road transport
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_396"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">markets. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.97.2"
class="koboSpan">Data from </span>[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_fig0244)<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that its market share was reduced almost by
half. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">Freight
moved by rail has also been subject to a negative trend, even though
freight being moved by rail increased from 282.0 tb-km (1970) up to
452.0 tb-km (2007).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">As a result, two
modes have been responsible for moving freight and for accommodating the
growth that has taken place. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">In 1970, road transport was responsible for moving 487
tb-km, about the same as sea transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">Between 1970
and 1990 freight being moved by road doubled relatively to 1970 (the
base year), and the same trend occurred between 1990 and 2007, but
within a shorter period of time (16 years).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.100.4" class="koboSpan">The reason for
such a shorter cycle is explained by the 2004 and 2007 enlargements of
the EU and because data from 1995 onwards concerns the EU-27 rather than
the EU-15. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.100.5"
class="koboSpan">From a market share perspective this growth results
from the ability of road transport in absorbing the market share
decreases that occurred in rail and IWW, from the SSS inability to meet
customers’ needs and from cargo derived from growing market economies.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.100.6" class="koboSpan">According to
2007 data provided by the EUROSTAT, road transport is responsible for
45.6% of the freight being moved in Europe.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">In what concerns sea
transport, this mode has not been able to increase its market share
despite the effort made by the Commission at a policy level since 1992
in the quest of sustainable alternatives to road transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.101.2" class="koboSpan">Freight being
moved by sea also suffered an increase from 472.0 tb-km up to 2007,
reaching 1575.0 tb-km. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.101.3"
class="koboSpan">However, the growth cycle appears to be longer.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.101.4" class="koboSpan">Cargo being
moved by sea doubled between 1970 and 1991 (one year more when compared
to road), and because of its weaknesses it has increased only 64.7%
between 1991 and 2007. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.101.5"
class="koboSpan">The annual average growth since 1995 until 2007 is 2.8%
against 3.8% in road transport which explains its market share decrease.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.101.6" class="koboSpan">After reaching
a market share of 40.1% in 1991, SSS share of goods being moved has been
decreasing relatively to road transport and in 2007 accounted for a
37.3% of the market. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.101.7"
class="koboSpan">The data also provides no evidence that a reverse of
the present trend will materialise in the near future, unless the road
is subject to further strict rules and regulations as it does happen in
the maritime sector and the small medium sized short sea operators adopt
more collaborative strategies among them (see endnote 16).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.101.8" class="koboSpan">The present
economic and financial crisis also does not contribute to change the
above mentioned behaviour, and the question raised is how SSS is able to
grasp the 14% of freight being moved by long-distance haulage.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">From another
perspective SSS accounts for 69% of all international traffic taken
place within the EU against 18% performed by road.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">SSS average
journeys are longer (1,385 km) than road (100 km) (see endnote 13).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.102.3" class="koboSpan">The opposite
situation takes place when domestic traffic is considered; here SSS is
responsible for carrying 6% of the total tonnes being moved against road
transport which carries over 80% of freight.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.102.4" class="koboSpan">Data provided
in </span>[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_fig0244)<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_cap_lbl0150"
id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0150"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"> also suggest that sea and road market shares should
always be under constant monitoring and an analysis between the two of
them makes sense in the European arena where more and more focus is
given to environmental issues.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">SSS competition with
land transport, particularly with road, is high due to geographical
reasons and due to comparatively highly developed land transport
infrastructure. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.107.2"
class="koboSpan">To these factors, others can be added which have very
much resulted from economic growth and crisis or policy changes.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.107.3" class="koboSpan">Examples are
the opening of the European internal market in 1992, the restructure of
companies’ production and distribution systems, the enlargement of the
EU and inventory management strategies like just-in-time, have given to
road transport a real boost in its development thanks to its superior
flexibility and relatively low
prices.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0408" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0408"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0410" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0410"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan"> Indeed, sea transport needs to be accommodated</span>

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0245" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00263.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Modal split in %*" /></span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_397"></span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0150"
id="Ch013.xhtml_cap_lbl0150"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan"> Modal split in %\*</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan"> EUROSTAT (various)</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">\* Data from 1970
concerns the EU-15 rather than the EU-27</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">at specialised
infrastructures (i.e. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.118.2"
class="koboSpan">ports/terminals), breaking the overall logistics chain
more often than road transportation and preventing, sometimes the
information to flow smoothly among the different actors.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.118.3" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
one must bear in mind than road infrastructure has been financed by
public funds, to a great extent.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.118.4" class="koboSpan">The
considerable difference between the averaged distances performed by SSS
and road leads to say they are partially separated up to the distance of
300 km, since it is difficult to find an alternative to road transport
inherent flexibility. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.118.5"
class="koboSpan">The railway sector lacks investment, which explains why
the potential for SSS for such short distances is not so high, unless
the threshold for competitiveness with road transport is considerably
shortened. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.118.6"
class="koboSpan">This point is one of the critical issues of the recent
EU transport policy as pointed out in the 2001 White
Paper.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0411" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0411"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">The present modal
split, where road and sea are responsible for about 82.9% of all freight
being moved in 2007 (SSS has been able to keep up with road transport
growth) can also be explained by the lack of investment in transport
infrastructure since 1975, resulting in numerous bottlenecks and a daily
congestion of 7,500 km, even though the Commission has embarked on the
development of a comprehensive trans-European transport network to
promote the modal shift to underused capacity (rail, SSS and IWW) and of
a policy that resulted in the liberalisation of freight rail freight
services in January 2007. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.120.2"
class="koboSpan">As for competition with land transport the choice of
lift-on-lift-off (Lo-Lo) or roll-on-roll-off (Ro-Ro) operations will
depend upon the distances to be covered and port costs incurred (see
endnote 16).</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 The demand side of the European short sea shipping market</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">For the purpose of
the present study, only data related to cargo/freight will be
considered, which implies that the movement of passengers is left out of
the analysis. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.122.2"
class="koboSpan">In the European Union 70% of its external trade and 30%
of its internal trade goes by sea.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.122.3" class="koboSpan">Of this 30%,
according to Drewry (1993), two-thirds concerns intra-North European
traffic, 30% relates to trade between North and South Europe, leaving
just a 3.3% of the total short sea trade as pure intra-South European
movements.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0412" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0412"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan"> This division of the SSS market can be explained by
the higher concentration of cargo in the ports located in the Le
Havre-Hamburg range, about 70% of the European industry is located
mainly in the six original founder EU Member States, and because the
North and Baltic Seas very much promote the use of SSS.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">In what
concerns the movement of cargo towards
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_398"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan">the South of Europe competition with land transport is
stronger both for feeder and intra-regional traffic.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">Channel ports
are facing overcapacity due to competition from the Channel Tunnel,
while the opening of road haulage to Eastern European firms has provided
low cost alternatives to both shipping and railways.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.125.3" class="koboSpan">This has
contributed to a fall in the freight rates squeezing the SSS industry
profitability which has been fostered by the pressure that DSS operators
exert over short sea operators when negotiating standard shipping
services to the final destination.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">The problem related
with the analysis of the SSS demand side concerns the lack of available
data at European level; only recently has this issue been addressed
subject to Council Directive 95/64/EC of 8.12.1995.
</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fig0246" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0246"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the quantity of cargo being moved by SSS
annually between 2000 and 2006. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.128.2"
class="koboSpan">Data concerning EU-15 is available since 2000 and its
annual average growth is about 30% and supports the idea that SSS has
not been able to grasp cargo from road transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.128.3" class="koboSpan">From an EU-27
perspective little conclusions can be taken since data is only available
from 2004 when the former Central and Eastern European countries
(CEECs), Malta and Cyprus became EU
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan">Member
State</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">s.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">The only
conclusion possible to be drawn at the present moment is that its annual
average growth is about 2.6% which can be explained by these countries
geographical location, since the former CEECs rely on road and rail
modes rather than on SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.130.3"
class="koboSpan">In 2006, the total goods transported by the EU-27 SSS
accounted for more than 1.9 billion tonnes, corresponding to 62% of the
maritime trade. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.130.4"
class="koboSpan">Both the North and Mediterranean Seas played a major
role in the movement of goods inside the EU, reporting 599 million
tonnes (28.1%) and 560 million tonnes (26.3%),
respectively.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0413" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0413"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">From a country
perspective, Ireland, Spain and Finland have witnessed the biggest
annual average growths between 2000 and 2006, 6.6%, 7.5% and 4.3%
respectively (see endnote 32). </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.132.2"
class="koboSpan">The Spanish annual growth is explained by the trade
performed between the mainland and the islands and because some new
ports have been added to the statistics.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.132.3" class="koboSpan">This situation
highlights that the data gathered at an EU level must fill in some gaps,
even though it provides a good indication of the cargo being moved.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.132.4" class="koboSpan">The cargo
moved falls within five different categories: liquid bulk, dry bulk,
containers, RO-RO units and the cargo which refers to all unknown cargo.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.132.5" class="koboSpan">The analysis
that follows has been carried out from an EU-27 perspective.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">According to 2006
data, the bulk market represents 69.2% of the cargo being moved by SSS,
and seen from an individual perspective, the liquid bulk and the dry
bulk short sea markets account for 49.5% and 19.7%, respectively, of the
whole cargo being moved by sea (see endnote 32).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">These figures
are in line with the 2007 statistical data provided by Drewry, where the
liquid bulk and dry bulk short sea markets accounted for 50% and 20% of
the overall cargo being moved on that
year.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0414" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0414"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan"> The main active countries in the liquid bulk market
are France, Italy, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom (UK).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">Together they
handled 624.3 million tonnes equivalent to 66.2% of</span>

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0246" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00264.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0246)

</div>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_399"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">the liquid bulk short sea market.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.137.2" class="koboSpan">As far as the
dry bulk short sea market is concerned, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands
and the UK dominate, and most dry bulk cargo is transported in cargo
sizes of 1,000 and 2,000 tonnes subject to long term and spot voyage
contracts.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0415" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0415"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan"> Likewise, they handled 200.7 million tonnes (53.3% of
the dry bulk short sea market).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">Ro-Ro units follow
the dry bulk short sea market (12.8%).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.140.2" class="koboSpan">This can be
explained by the high concentration of ferry vessels’ operations in the
North and Baltic Seas. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.140.3"
class="koboSpan">Germany, Italy, Sweden and the UK are responsible for
the biggest share of units being handled.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.140.4" class="koboSpan">Together, they
handled 206.0 million tonnes equivalent to 84.2% of the Ro-Ro short sea
market. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.140.5"
class="koboSpan">Interesting to see that the data for EU-15 and EU-27
are very close to one another which suggests that the new countries had
a very low impact on the cargo being moved in this market segment.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.140.6" class="koboSpan">Most of the
countries cases are self explanatory but in the case of the UK, it
should be highlighted that the country is a gateway for cargo originated
from/destined to Ireland which makes use of a sea-road transport system
to/from mainland Europe.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">Container short sea
market ranks in the fourth place and has presented a 10.5% market share
for both 2006 and 2007 (see endnotes 32, 33).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">Germany,
Italy, the Netherlands and Spain dominate the container short sea
market, and this is highly explained by the geographical location.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">In the case of
Italy, the country is strategically located in the Mediterranean to the
extent that divides it into two navigational areas the Eastern Med and
the Western Med, and this can very much be attributed to the position of
Gioia Tauro container terminal that serves about 55 different
Mediterranean ports. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.141.4"
class="koboSpan">Germany is a gateway to the Baltic and to the CEECs.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.141.5" class="koboSpan">The four
countries handle 152.2 million tonnes which represents 76.2% of the
market. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.141.6"
class="koboSpan">Despite being in fourth place, the market for the EU-15
has witnessed an 8% annual average growth rate (see endnote 32).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.141.7" class="koboSpan">This explains
why the container short sea market is reported to be one of the most
dynamic markets of the shipping industry, both in feeder traffic and
intra-regional trade.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">The number of
containers being moved on an annual basis can be seen in
</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fig0247" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0247"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.144.2"
class="koboSpan">The annual average growth rate is not provided by
Amerini (2008) but the data provided shows that the number of containers
did not increased considerably after the enlargement, which suggests
that well strategically located ports in the EU-15 geographical area
were already responsible for handling cargo particularly destined to the
Central Eastern European Countries.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.144.3" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the
number of TEUs reported empty provides empirical evidence to sustain the
presence of unbalanced trades as shown in other studies caused by
density of population, separation of production and consumption markets,
type of goods and alternative
infrastructure.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0416" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0416"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0417" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0417"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan"> Germany, Spain, the Netherlands and the UK greatly
contribute to this situation due to their hub-and-feeder status, and
which contributes to increase the freight rates charged to the final end
user.</span>

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0247" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00265.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0247)

</div>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_400"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">Finally, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands and the UK are
responsible for the biggest share of other cargo, totalising 72.8
million tonnes or 50.9% of the market.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">Absolute trade
volumes continue to rise in Europe.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.151.2" class="koboSpan">Growth of
trade patterns will create additional demand for SSS movements and
additional demand for feeder vessels.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.151.3" class="koboSpan">The expanding
economies of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries
present further opportunities for the European SSS sector, which can
only be fostered through the implementation of strict environmental
controls to reduce the amount of emissions into the atmosphere.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.151.4" class="koboSpan">Ro-Ro and the
container market offer potential for modal shift as together they
account for 23.3% of the goods being moved by sea, and because the
market is far from having reached a mature state.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.151.5" class="koboSpan">In the case of
containerised cargo, the market shows a service gap since shippers have
not been offered the desirable service frequency they claim since the
volumes being moved are insufficient and that explains why so many
containers are being moved by road.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">From a port
perspective, Rotterdam accounts for the biggest share of cargo handled
through ports (7.4%) to be followed by Antwerp, Marseilles, Hamburg and
Le Havre, most of them located in the Le Havre–Hamburg geographical
range. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.152.2" class="koboSpan">What is
interesting to see in this overall picture is that Rotterdam handled
more SSS cargo (184.4 million tonnes) than deep sea cargo (168.4 million
tonnes) (see endnote 32), which shows how important Rotterdam is to the
overall European SSS market.</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">2.3 The supply side of the European short sea shipping market</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">The high number of
journeys (of normally less than four days, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.154.2" class="koboSpan">the ferries
that ply the Baltic Sea and the English Channel) makes management and
organisation costs of SSS comparatively high, although the cost
structure is very different for feeder and intra-regional markets.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.154.3" class="koboSpan">In the first
case, costs are mainly vessel related: capital (or charter), operating
and voyage costs. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.154.4"
class="koboSpan">Overhead and administration costs are relatively small.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.154.5" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
feeder carriers rely mostly upon chartered vessels (with the exception
of a few Asian
carriers).</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0418" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0418"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the second case, the carrier involved in
intra-regional intermodal SSS will bear high costs for handling cargo
and providing land transport. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.156.2"
class="koboSpan">Administrative overhead costs will also be higher.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.156.3" class="koboSpan">Despite these
technicalities, the definition of what is a short sea vessel is a
subject of much debate since different authors present different
definitions.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">Hoogerbeets and
Melissen (1993), state that the European SSS can be divided into three
main ships’ categories: the traditional single-deck bulk carriers, the
container-feeder vessels and the
ferries.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0419" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0419"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan"> Crilley and Dean (1993) report that vessels operating
in the SSS market have frequently been defined as sea-going
cargo-carrying ships that transported both freight and passengers with a
gross tonnage (GT) less than 5,000, and that ships with a GT less than
100, non-propelled vessels, and harbour or IWW vessels were not part of
the
definition.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0420" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0420"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan"> Peeters
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.163.2"
class="koboSpan">(1995) created a splitting line between short sea and
deep sea vessels. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.163.3"
class="koboSpan">The authors considered that the former comprehend all
ships whose deadweight capacity is less than or equal to 10,000
deadweight tonnes (dwt) which is equivalent to an average ship of about
of about 8,000 GT (see endnote 7).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">Marlow
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.166.2"
class="koboSpan">(1997) pointed out that the SSS fleet is normally
identifiable as a number of carriers with similar characteristics (SSS
is usually performed by vessels up to a certain size and conversely
vessels up to a certain size are usually deployed in SSS).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.166.3" class="koboSpan">Even if these
parameters are likely to change significantly over time, they estimate
that SSS include tankers and bulk carriers up to 13,000 GT and/or 20,000
dwt; general
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_401"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">cargo and break bulk carriers up to 10,000 GT and/or
10,000 dwt; and combined passenger/cargo ships and Ro-Ro vessels between
1,000 GT and/or 500 dwt and 30,000 GT and/or 15,000 dwt (see endnote 4).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">Stopford in
1997 considered SSS vessels to be within the 400 to 6,000 dwt range
against some authors that talk about 10000+ dwt (see endnote 8).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">Paixão and Marlow
(2002) identified five types of SSS vessel categories (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">the
traditional single-deck bulk carriers, the ferries, container feeder
vessels, a fleet of bulk carriers and tankers and sea-river ships often
with retractable wheelhouses), provided and individual description of
each of the vessels and investigated the differences between Lo-Lo and
Ro-Ro operations (see endnote 16).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.168.3" class="koboSpan">This
classification which partly agrees with the one provided by Hoogerbeets
and Melissen (1993), is similar to the one provided by Verlaat (2008)
(see endnote
38).</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0421" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0421"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan"> The difference between Verlaat and Paixão and Marlow
is that the former considered the fleet of tankers, dry bulk carriers
and traditional single-deck bulk carriers often used in the carriage of
neo bulk within the same category of conventional ships.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">Besides the
traditional ships mentioned in the above paragraphs, the short sea
market has been witnessing a trend towards the introduction of faster
ships such as wave pierce catamarans, air cushion vehicles, hydrofoil,
surface effect ships, and the small waterplane area twin hull (SWATH).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.171.2" class="koboSpan">Their main
problem concerns their consumption levels to perform their designed
service speed; any increase in their speed means an increase in the cost
of bunkers, a decrease in their cargo carrying capacity meaning a
revenue reduction. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.171.3"
class="koboSpan">The question to be raised at this point is to ask
shippers about their interest in having their cargoes being moved by
this type of vessels. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.171.4"
class="koboSpan">Despite being able to shorten cargo transit times and
provide high service levels, how far they are willing to pay higher
freight rates when Becker
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.173.2"
class="koboSpan">(2004) recognised that the high speed vessel market
offers potential to compete with certain road transport market
segments.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0422" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0422"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">Overall, short sea
ships are normally much smaller than deep sea ones although there is a
trend towards an increased vessel size.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.175.2" class="koboSpan">Several
reasons explain why such vessels are small: (i) demand is normally weak
for SSS routes; and (ii) the high number of short journeys requires
smaller ships in order not to spend too much time in port calls.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.175.3" class="koboSpan">The lack of an
unambiguous definition, towards the size and types of ships that work in
the SSS market, causes additional problems when authors try to
characterise the fleet operating in this market which may be a reason
why most studies on fleet analysis set the dividing line between SSS and
DSS at 10,000 dwt or 6,000 GT.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">According to a
Lloyd’s Register survey quoted in Peeters
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.178.2"
class="koboSpan">(1995), by the end of 1992, the world SSS fleet
amounted to 68.5% of the existing fleet corresponding to 9.6% in terms
of GT, 8.9% in terms of the total dwt carrying capacity with an average
size equal to 1,319 GT. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.178.3"
class="koboSpan">From a European perspective, the same survey estimated
that the European SSS fleet amounted to 57.3% of the existing European
fleet corresponding to 7.9% in terms of GT, 6.7% in terms of the total
dwt carrying capacity with an average size equal to 1654 GT.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.178.4" class="koboSpan">The figures
reported on ships which are supposed to be employed in SSS show that on
a worldwide basis there seems to be a quite constant share of ships
employed in SSS, as well as in terms of GT and dwt.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.178.5" class="koboSpan">The same
survey showed that general cargo and liquid bulk carriers prevail in the
EU SSS fleet. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.178.6"
class="koboSpan">Peeters
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.180.2"
class="koboSpan">went on saying that the average age of the world SSS
fleet was 18 years, two years younger than the European one that
amounted to 20 years (see endnote 7).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">The Colton Company
(1997) estimated that the European SSS fleet was made up of 5,650 units
embracing 5,000 sea-river ships often with a retractable wheel house,
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_402"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">400 containerships ranging between 100 and 700 TEUs and
250 Ro-Ro ships. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.182.2"
class="koboSpan">Most popular container ships moved 200 TEUs and the
most popular sizes of sea-river ships presented deadweight capacities
between 1,500 and 2,200
tonnes.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0423" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0423"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan"> However, the data provided presents two main problems
since the short sea dry and liquid bulk carrier fleet was left out of
the calculations and there is no reference to the year that the data
relates to. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.184.2"
class="koboSpan">The Commission in its report on the implementation of
Council Regulation 3577/92, presented data relatively to the 1996 and
1998 SSS fleet (see
</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fig0248" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0248"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">), and considered for this purpose ships of less than
10,000
dwt.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0424" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0424"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">The data supplied by
the Commission does not discriminate the type of ships being considered
which prevents from having a real perception of the composition of the
actual fleet. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.188.2"
class="koboSpan">What type of ships predominate in each group of Member
States is unknown and even if the ratio of dwt to GT were to be used to
identify if the fleet is mainly formed by passenger/cargo ferry and
Ro-Ro (ratio of dwt to GT below 1) or by tankers and dry cargo vessels
(ratio of dwt to GT above 1), its outcome would be far from being a
reliable one. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.188.3"
class="koboSpan">The data supplied by the Commission also shows no
evidence that sea-river ships have been included in the calculations and
so, the number of ships calculated for 1998 are well below those
estimated by the Colton Company in 1997.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">The only possible
conclusion is that the SSS fleet has increased in numbers and in
dimension but very slightly. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.189.2"
class="koboSpan">The average SSS vessel size in terms of GT and dwt for
1996 were 4,267 and 4,909, respectively and that the figures for 1997
amount to 4,288 and 5,149, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.189.3" class="koboSpan">Various
studies on the SSS have observed a gradual increase in the average size
of the SSS vessel. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.189.4"
class="koboSpan">According to Dynamar quoted in Peeters
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.191.2"
class="koboSpan">the SSS vessel average size increased from 1,400 dwt in
1970 up to 2,000 dwt in 1980, and up to 2,400 dwt in 1990 (see endnote
7).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">According to Lloyd’s
Marine Intelligence Unit (LMIU) quoted in Wijnolst (2005) the 2003
European SSS fleet from Baltic Sea to the Black Sea comprehended 10,000
ships between 500 and 10,000 GT of which 3,825 and 2,110 ships were
older than 25 and 30 years, respectively and that a total of 3,460
shipowners operated in the European short sea
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0425" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0425"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan"> Part of the 2004 world short sea fleet can be seen in
</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fig0249" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0249"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan"> since vessels operating on the SSS were aggregated in
eight different categories, rather than in ten as shown
in</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fig0250" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0250"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan"> Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.198.2"
class="koboSpan">Smits left out the general cargo and ropax fleets which
according to the 2007 data represent about 47% of the world short sea
fleet and all vessels below 1000 dwt which are about 10,000
vessels,</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0426" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0426"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan"> and such a situation</span>

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0248" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
