</div>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_404"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan">creates a distortion relatively to the 2003 data.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
if the percentage split provided by Peeters
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.206.2"
class="koboSpan">(1995) is applied, (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.206.3" class="koboSpan">the EU-27
short sea fleet amounts to 31.5% of the world short sea fleet) what can
be said is that the European short sea fleet embraces about 9166 vessels
including those with a deadweight below 1,000 tonnes.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.206.4" class="koboSpan">Shipowners
based in Germany, the Netherlands Greece and Italy dominate the market
and control 62% of this short sea
fleet.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0427" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0427"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup>

[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">Table
5</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_fig0249)<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan"> also provides the average deadweight for the eight
vessel segments, and what can be said is that short sea vessels’ sizes
have increased for the past years, which meet the findings reached by
Marlow </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.211.2"
class="koboSpan">in 1997 (see endnote 4).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.211.3" class="koboSpan">The added
value of </span>[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
5</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_fig0249)<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan"> rests on its ability to provide more detailed
information for the different types of cargo being moved by sea rather
than the statistics provided by the EUROSTAT, but prevents possible
comparisons with the data gathered by other consultancy houses and/ or
eventually EUROSTAT.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">The Lloyd’s Fairplay
data of the worldwide short sea fleet quoted in Lindstad (2008), shows
that at the end of 2007, the world short sea fleet includes 10 vessel
categories and is much more accurate than the 2004
data.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0428" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0428"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">47</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan"> With the assumption that the EU-27 short sea fleet
represents 31.5% of the world short sea fleet, it can be estimated that
the EU-27 short sea fleet has about 13,050 units, which means an average
yearly growth of 7.6% relatively to 2003 where data quoted in Wijnolst
(2005) was provided by LMIU. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.216.2"
class="koboSpan">The average size of short sea vessels goes on
increasing and against the findings of Corres and Psaraftis who
estimated the average size of short sea vessels to be around 11,000 dwt
by
2007–2008,</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0429" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0429"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.217.1" class="koboSpan">48</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan"> the average size appears to be within the range of
above 30,000+ dwt, much at the expense of the tanker fleet size employed
in the SSS market.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">The biggest problem
of the European short sea fleet is still its age and the main concern of
an ageing short sea fleet is its pollutant emissions which in 2000
accounted for 36% of the total nitrogen oxide
(NO</span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">) and 6% of total greenhouse emissions.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.221.2" class="koboSpan">The problem of
an ageing short sea fleet is not new, since it has already been
mentioned by Øvrebø in 1969 (see endnote 25) and more recently by Lowry
in 2008 who identified that the dry bulk short sea fleet had an average
age of 31 years (see endnote 34).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.221.3" class="koboSpan">This suggests
that a renewal scheme is desirable for SSS to be competitive with road
transport and to be integrated into multimodal/intermodal transport
chains. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.221.4" class="koboSpan">The
absence of legislative measures enforcing the renewal of the fleet has
been a negative influence since until recently the dwt of most short sea
vessels was under 5,000. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.221.5"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, short sea operators do not possess sufficient
funds to embark on a short sea fleet renewal programme, the costs of
building a small ship are four-and-a-half times more per dwt, and bank
credit is very expensive (see endnote 48).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">The resultant reduced
profitability is therefore a serious strategic concern in capital
intensive companies planning for growth and the renewals that have taken
place result more often than not from the existing rivalry between
shipowners operating in this market, from port state control inspections
and the enforcement of important legislation to protect the environment.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.222.2" class="koboSpan">Most focus has
been giving to the development of efficient vessels ranging from 30,000
up to 300,000 dwt while the SSS fleet has been more or less neglected.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.222.3" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
this trend has started to reverse due to the numerous research and
development projects being funded by the European Commission in last
years in the quest for more efficient ships such as the CREATE3S new
generation of short sea
vessels,</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0430" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0430"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">49</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan"> the ENISYS ship
concept</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0431" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0431"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">50</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan"> or generic short sea vessels based on a common
platform and built in series as it happened in the past (see endnote
48).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_405"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan">In 1994, Wijnolst
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.229.2"
class="koboSpan">had already acknowledged that SSS technology and
operations needed to be changed before any significant modal split
materialised.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0432" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0432"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">51</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">The point is that new
ships are needed to compete with road transport on cost, speed,
flexibility, reliability without jeopardising safety and the
environment, attractive sailing times, maintained transit times, and
guarantee of delivery. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.231.2"
class="koboSpan">Two key aspects that these ships must target are the
reduction of the turnaround time in port and the ability to develop
intermodal solutions that meet the needs of the entire logistics chains.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.231.3" class="koboSpan">If significant
reductions of 20–25% are achieved in terms of cost and lead time a modal
shift is expected to occur (see endnote 50), an improvement relatively
to the 35% reduction required to shift cargo from road to sea as
suggested by APAS in
1996.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0433" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0433"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">52</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan"> Under the present environment and taking into account
the modal split presented in </span>[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_cap_lbl0150)<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">, an analysis of SSS in a multimodal supply chain
context makes sense in the European arena, as competition with land
transport is higher due to geographical reasons and to the comparatively
highly developed land transport infrastructure.</span>

## <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.236.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.236.2" class="koboSpan">Short Sea Shipping in a Multimodal Supply Chain Context</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Geographic and economic conditions for developing short sea shipping: a theoretical framework</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">Maritime transport is
normally part of a transport cycle involving other transport modes.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.238.2" class="koboSpan">The maritime
leg can be a complex cycle, when organised from a hub-and-spoke
perspective, involving ships of different size to attain economies of
scale/density on some routes. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.238.3"
class="koboSpan">Since the goal is to attain the cheapest, fastest and
most reliable transport conditions (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.238.4" class="koboSpan">to minimise
the generalised cost), the demand for sea transport is related to the
generalised cost of the whole transport cycle.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.238.5" class="koboSpan">From a
microeconomic approach, the use of generalised costs explain the user’s
choice (i.e. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.238.6"
class="koboSpan">providing transport solutions for producers), but the
use of total costs (including infrastructure and external costs) from a
macroeconomic approach explain general utility enabling a shift of
volumes from congestioned land infrastructure to sea.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">The proposed
framework considers jointly geographic and economic conditions involved
in the mode choice, and identifies the critical thresholds in land/sea
distances and land/sea generalised costs which determine SSS potential
competitiveness. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.239.2"
class="koboSpan">It applies either to the case of a SSS intermodal chain
competing with land transportation, or to feeder traffic for DSS.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.239.3" class="koboSpan">The boost of
intermodality over the last 30 years is due both to increasing benefits
and decreasing transhipment costs, as: (i) the growth of world trade
allowed economies of scale not conceivable before, also because
production functions are more capital intensive and involve relevant
fixed costs; and (ii) new handling techniques reduced costs, times and
risks of transhipment. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.239.4"
class="koboSpan">If SSS replaces a part of a journey otherwise performed
by a single vehicle, the additional modal change implies higher
generalised costs. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.239.5"
class="koboSpan">Total time increases, while reliability, punctuality
and safety are jeopardised by bottlenecks, congestion, mistakes,
damages, among others. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.239.6"
class="koboSpan">These costs are compensated by savings that the
different modes/vehicles allow in the different part of the journey,
because of changing cargo volumes and economies of scale/density.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.239.7" class="koboSpan">SSS is chosen
when the optimisation of modes/vehicles on the different
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_406"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan">legs generates benefits higher than the additional
transhipment costs. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.240.2"
class="koboSpan">In both key areas (feeder traffic and intermodal
traffic competing with land transport) a simple cycle is replaced by a
complex one. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.240.3"
class="koboSpan">Unlike SSS captive markets, where there is no user’s
choice and the goal is to minimise generalised costs of modal change,
SSS is chosen only if it allows generalised benefits higher than the
generalised costs of additional transhipments.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
problem under study fits within the approach
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">à la</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan">
Hoover</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0434" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0434"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">53</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan"> as it accounts for different terminal and haulage
costs of the different modes, which cause different costs per mile,
which explains why different modes have a different competitiveness for
different distances, and therefore different markets and why at a
European level, the different modes are competitive in different
distances.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0435" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0435"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">54</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan"> While road transport has low terminal costs but
relatively high line haul costs, sea transport has high (generalised)
terminal costs but comparatively lower transport costs and rail has
intermediate levels for both terminal and transport costs.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">Since terminal
costs do not vary with distance, road transport will be cheaper on
shorter journeys and sea transport on the longer ones.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.247.3" class="koboSpan">Such a
framework points out the conditions for SSS competitiveness.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.247.4" class="koboSpan">The paragraph
that follows considers the case of SSS as a main leg of an
intra-regional transport chain, competing with land transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.247.5" class="koboSpan">The approach
is similar if a feeder traffic case was being considered.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">In
</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_cap_lbl0151"
id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0151"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan">, a journey
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan">OD</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan"> is considered, where in the central leg
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan">AB</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan"> both road and sea transport are available, while only
road transport is available in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan">OA</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan">BD</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.258.2"
class="koboSpan">The function a shows total transport cost if only road
haulage is chosen. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.258.3"
class="koboSpan">The function
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan">b </span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan">shows the cost of transport using SSS in the central
leg. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.260.2" class="koboSpan">While
modal change costs are added in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan">A</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan"> and in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan">B</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">, a lower cost is paid on the leg AB.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.264.2" class="koboSpan">SSS is then
advantageous when
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">AB</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan"> is long enough to compensate higher terminal
costs.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">Unless
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">O</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan"> A</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan">B</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.274.1"
class="koboSpan">D</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan"> are aligned,</span>[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan"> Figure
2</span>](#Ch013.xhtml_cap_lbl0151)<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan"> only accounts for economic conditions and not for
geographic conditions when competition is being considered.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.277.2" class="koboSpan">To find out
the combination of economic (transport and terminal costs) and
geographic variables (land and intermodal distances) which jointly
account for SSS competitiveness, a land transport
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan">OD</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.279.1"
class="koboSpan"> by mode
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.280.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.281.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan"> (e.g. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.282.2"
class="koboSpan">road haulage) and an alternative
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan">OABD</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan"> based on mode
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan"> for
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.288.1"
class="koboSpan">OA</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">BD</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan"> and on SSS indicated as mode
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan"> for
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan">AB</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan"> must be compared.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.296.2" class="koboSpan">Ports
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">A</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan">B</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan"> are not aligned with
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan">OD</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.303.1" class="koboSpan">If
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the maritime distance between ports
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan">A</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan">B</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan">; T the transhipment generalised cost in ports;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan">tm</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.313.1"
class="koboSpan">tm</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan"> transport rates per mile of a given cargo unit; and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.316.1"

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
class="koboSpan">D</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan">; then total transport costs are:</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.329.1" class="koboSpan">for intermodal

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0253" class="fig"

</div>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.334.1" class="koboSpan">If
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.335.1"
class="koboSpan">y</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the difference between road distance
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.337.1"

class="koboSpan"> and feeder road legs
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.339.1"

class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan">BD</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan"> of SSS transport, the (3) can be written as:</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.344.1" class="koboSpan">setting the
combination of geographic and economic conditions for competitiveness of
SSS, as in </span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_cap_lbl0152"
id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0152"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.345.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.346.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.346.2"
class="koboSpan">Each journey
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan">OD</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.348.1"
class="koboSpan"> identifies a set of
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.349.1"
class="koboSpan">x, y</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan">) satisfying or not the condition (4), according to
transhipment costs, and rates per mile of modes
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.351.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.355.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.356.2"
class="koboSpan">Obviously the competitiveness increases by reducing
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.357.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan">tm</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan">, or by increasing
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan">tm</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">A key point is that
if </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan"> allows more relevant economies of scale than
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.369.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.370.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.371.1"
class="koboSpan">, as is normally the case for short sea compared to
road transport, the increase in traffic flows reduces the slope of the
(4), thus increasing competitiveness of the former.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.371.2" class="koboSpan">This is just a
joint representation of geographic and economic conditions which make
viable a SSS-based alternative to land transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.371.3" class="koboSpan">The approach
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.372.1"
class="koboSpan">à la</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.373.1"
class="koboSpan"> Hoover allows finding out each transport mode economic
distance since (i) terminal and transport costs weight</span>

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0256" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.374.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00274.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Geographic and economic conditions for competitiveness of SSS" /></span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_408"></span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0152"
id="Ch013.xhtml_cap_lbl0152"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.375.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.376.1"
class="koboSpan"> Geographic and economic conditions for competitiveness
of SSS</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.377.1" class="koboSpan">differently in
different modes; (ii) costs in different modes are a function of cargoes
and cargo units characteristics; (iii) reducing terminal costs in ports
lowers the threshold distance for SSS, as it moves downwards the (4);
and (iv) higher returns to scale in SSS cause a growth in traffic to
reduce SSS threshold distance, by a rotation of (4).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.378.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, SSS economic
competitiveness relies upon the contemporaneous occurrence of five
conditions which are: (1) cargo volumes involved cause pure transport
costs for sea transport lower than for road transport; (2) different
origins and/or destinations do not allow to employ the sole maritime
transport (since cargo volumes do not fulfil the condition (1)); (3)
distances involved are longer than the threshold distances for sea
transport; (4) location of origins/destinations of single shipments
allow the unification of parcels on some legs in order to satisfy
condition (1); and (5) lower generalised costs of using the best
transport mode on each leg are higher than additional generalised costs
deriving from transhipment. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.378.2"
class="koboSpan">According to Baird (1997) for a coastal service in the
UK to be successful, it would need to guarantee that the costs were
competitive, goods delivery times were maintained, and the service was
reliable relatively road transport alone (see endnote 35).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.379.1" class="koboSpan">When referred to SSS
as feeder traffic, different returns to scale account for the
hub-and-spoke organisation. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.379.2"
class="koboSpan">Limits to economies of scale are now on the demand
side, and increasing returns to scale can be pursued only by grouping
cargoes on the main leg. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.379.3"
class="koboSpan">Volumes and costs per mile being equal, the longest is
the main leg AB, the most competitive is the hub-and-spoke solution
using SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.379.4"
class="koboSpan">Conditions (1), (2) and (5) will be here referred to
thresholds for ships of different sizes.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.379.5" class="koboSpan">Condition (5)
will refer to transhipment from SSS to DSS.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.380.1" class="koboSpan">As for competition
between SSS and road transport for the feeder service, since a haulage
feeder service is normally needed for the final part of the journey, the
comparison is between savings allowed by maritime feeder and costs of an
additional transhipment (from the feeder to the deep-sea ship), that
is:</span>

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0257" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.381.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00275.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_409"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.382.1"
class="koboSpan">The same conditions apply, since there are combined
effects of economic distance, size of shipments and location of
origins/destinations.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.383.1" class="koboSpan">This approach
outlines the conditions that make SSS competitive, even when not forced
by geographical (or, in the short run, infrastructural) constraints.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.383.2" class="koboSpan">The same
framework applies to both main current strategic areas of SSS: an
intermodal transport competing with land transport, or a feeder traffic
competing with road/rail feeders.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.383.3" class="koboSpan">As already
noted, this framework allows both a microeconomic and a macroeconomic
approach, with different implications.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.383.4" class="koboSpan">In the former,
short term generalised cost (given the infrastructure) account for
behaviour of transport operators and consequent modal split.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.383.5" class="koboSpan">In the latter,
total direct and external long run costs (including infrastructure and
energy) account for a macroeconomic comparison, resulting in a
cost-benefit assessment which pursues a higher welfare.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.384.1" class="koboSpan">In its microeconomic
approach, the proposed framework refers to generalised, not to
out-of-pocket costs. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.384.2"
class="koboSpan">Generalised costs correspond to production costs only
in perfect competition. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.384.3"
class="koboSpan">In freight transport, shippers happen not to decide
transport mode neither select the route, and multimodal transport
operators (MTOs) are likely to choose modes/routes according to their
convenience. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.384.4"
class="koboSpan">Monopoly, or collusion between providers (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.384.5" class="koboSpan">due to
horizontal and vertical integration of the supply chain) can cause a
substitution between time and cost, reducing costs and increasing times
without (or with little) reduction of prices for shippers.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.384.6" class="koboSpan">The case for
passenger transport is different, since users directly choose the mix of
modes by comparing the generalised cost of each solution, and their
preference will thus account for their choice.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.384.7" class="koboSpan">It is probably
no accident that intermodality is barely chosen unless forced by
geographical constraints or by huge savings in monetary costs, or unless
other options are totally congested or restricted.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.385.1" class="koboSpan">In other words,
intermodality allows increasing productivity, but may cause a decreasing
quality (for the cargo, not necessarily for the vehicle) with higher
time and lower reliability, punctuality and safety.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.385.2" class="koboSpan">If there is
not a high level of competition this trade off may encompass a transfer
of costs from the producer to the consumer.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.385.3" class="koboSpan">The market
organisation is then crucial for the benefits to spread on the demand
side, allowing higher accessibility of regional markets, specialisation
of production, and cumulative growth of regions involved.</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.386.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Factors influencing the competitiveness of SSS</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.387.1" class="koboSpan">According to
Sub-section 3.1, the more SSS will be competitive, the more substantial
reduction in generalised port costs is attained; the longer is the
maritime leg with respect to the total length of the journey; the higher
is the ratio of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan">y</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.389.1"
class="koboSpan"> to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.390.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan"> in (4); the bigger are cargo volumes; the higher is
the ratio of land transport generalised costs to sea trans port
ones.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.392.1" class="koboSpan">Besides these key
issues, some additional remarks are worthwhile.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.392.2" class="koboSpan">First, the
growing importance of ports and their performance/efficiency involves
not only efficient modal change and handling, but logistic and
distribution functions. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.392.3"
class="koboSpan">Choices concerning number and location of ports and
logistic platforms on which the SSS network will hinge are strategic,
since they pursue the optimal trade off between economies of density,
pushing for concentration of flows which reduce the ratio
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan">tm</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.394.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.395.1"
class="koboSpan">/</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.396.1"
class="koboSpan">tm</span></span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.397.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.398.1"
class="koboSpan"> in (4); and minimisation of road feeders, pushing for
dispersion of flows which cause higher values of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.399.1"
class="koboSpan">y</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.400.1"
class="koboSpan"> and positively affects (4).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.400.2" class="koboSpan">Case-by-case
search for optimal equilibrium is a major operational
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_410"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.401.1"
class="koboSpan">research issue, and a key issue for SSS development
strategies. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.401.2" class="koboSpan">It
is notable that virtually all issues highlighted – threshold distances,
demand volumes and their origin/destinations, returns to scale in
competing modes, number and location of intermodal nodes, etc.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.401.3" class="koboSpan">– have been
addressed so far in a largely empirical way, frustrating most of the
potential of SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.401.4"
class="koboSpan">There has been no strategy at all, and SSS nodes have
followed, more often than not, strategies of big transport
operators.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.402.1" class="koboSpan">Another point
implicit in (4) is that implementing SSS should not result in
fragmentation and complications of relations between shippers and
transport operators, difficulties in organising and controlling the
logistic chain, problems arising from liabilities, damages or losses,
among other issues. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.402.2"
class="koboSpan">This means that implementing SSS requires the
integrated management of the entire SSS-based logistic chain.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.402.3" class="koboSpan">On one side
the risk is that economies of scale/scope related to the management of
the whole logistic cycle can set relevant barriers to entry, issue of
alliances and co-operation strategies.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.402.4" class="koboSpan">On the other
side, if the control of the chain is taken up outside the maritime link,
this may squeeze profitability and limit operational control of SSS
operator, who faces, in a door-to-door cycle, relevant fixed costs, and
does not enjoy any spatial protection of its market, thus coupling high
competition and low profitability.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.402.5" class="koboSpan">Moreover, by
operating on one link of the chain, there is no influence/control over
the quality of the door-to-door service, and no control on key factors
influencing the demand; comparison between SSS and competing modes
requires that the whole cycles are compared.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.403.1" class="koboSpan">The above mentioned
factors, although not explicitly modelled in the proposed approach, are
likely to influence deeply the cost elements of (4), which can vary with
high levels of uncertainty, not proportionally to distance, and change
rapidly over time. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.403.2"
class="koboSpan">In this context, Paixão Casaca and Marlow (2005)
investigated the service attributes required by shippers when making use
of multimodal transport chains comprising a sea leg.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.403.3" class="koboSpan">The authors
found out eight dimensions which differed from the ones advocated in the
several policy documents of the Commission and which comprised by
decreasing order of importance (i) carrier’s logistic network design and
speed; (ii) cost of door-to-door service, its reliability/quality; (iii)
the carrier’s behaviour during sales and after-sales; (iv) carrier’s
involvement in the forwarding industry; (v) service guarantee; (vi)
carriers’ corporate image; (vii) carriers’ commercial/operational
policies and their relationship with shippers and finally (viii)
investment
policy.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0436" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0436"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.404.1" class="koboSpan">55</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.405.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Putting short sea shipping in operation: obstacles and challenges</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.406.1" class="koboSpan">Any further SSS
development will necessarily rely upon its possible microeconomic
competitiveness (in terms of generalised costs), more than upon its
macroeconomic desirability. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.406.2"
class="koboSpan">Yet, since most researcher and policy makers agree on
the need of enhancing SSS, it is useful to resume a checklist of main
benefits and costs from the macroeconomic and political viewpoint.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.406.3" class="koboSpan">Paixão and
Marlow (2002) have listed SSS strengths and weaknesses (see endnote 16)
and a summary of the benefits offered by SSS can be summarised as
follows:</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.407.1" class="koboSpan">low environmental
  costs: it generates much less emissions per tonne-km (tkm) caused by
  the average transport (average goods, average road and rail gradient,
  average energy split) in Europe than road and rail transport, as shown
  in
  </span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fig0258" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0258"><span
  id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.408.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.409.1"
  class="koboSpan">.</span>

<div id="Ch013.xhtml_fig0258" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_411"></span>[](#Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0258)

[<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00276.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch013.xhtml_bck_fig0258)

</div>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.411.1" class="koboSpan">fewer accidents,
  namely for human life safety: in 2007, 42,448 fatalities occurred in
  road accidents within the EU-27 corresponding to 99.8%, and 76 losses
  of lives were registered in rail transport (excluding suicides); air
  transport was responsible for four losses, but this figure increased
  up to 181 in
  2008.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0438" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0438"><span
  id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.412.1" class="koboSpan">57</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.413.1"
  class="koboSpan"> Data provided by EUROSTAT does not include sea
  losses, however according to Lloyd's Register Fairplay data provided
  by the International Chamber of Shipping and the International
  Shipping Federation Website sea transport was responsible for about
  260 losses of life worldwide, which shows how safe this mode of
  transport
  is.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0439" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0439"><span
  id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.414.1" class="koboSpan">58</span></a></sup>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.415.1" class="koboSpan">lowering congestion
  of land transport networks: presently 7,500 km of roads are
  congestioned on a daily basis;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.416.1" class="koboSpan">low energy
  consumption;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.417.1" class="koboSpan">larger economies of
  scale;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.418.1" class="koboSpan">higher flexibility
  of transport costs to shifts in demand, and low need for new
  infrastructure;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.419.1" class="koboSpan">more competitive
  environment than for (rather monopolistic) land transport
  networks;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.420.1" class="koboSpan">advantages for
  maritime economy and namely for shipyards;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.421.1" class="koboSpan">development of
  peripherals and isolated regions (of difficult or impossible access
  with other transport modes), and enhanced competitiveness of
  hinterlands economies facing international markets.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_412"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.422.1"
class="koboSpan">On the other side, the development of SSS also brings
about some disadvantages, such as:</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.423.1" class="koboSpan">partial increase of
  pollution: unlike other emissions, sulphur dioxide
  (SO</span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.424.1"
  class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.425.1"
  class="koboSpan">) emissions are much higher than in other modes (see
  above);</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.426.1" class="koboSpan">partial increase of
  accidents, namely with major environmental damages;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.427.1" class="koboSpan">congestion in port
  nodes;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.428.1" class="koboSpan">negative impact on
  other transport sectors, as well as on the industry of infrastructure
  construction and related sectors;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.429.1" class="koboSpan">low flexibility in
  service times, due to larger unit capacity and consequent lower
  frequency of service for any origin/destination (O/D) link;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.430.1" class="koboSpan">lower reliability
  of scheduled departure and arrival times (mainly due to weather
  conditions);</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.431.1" class="koboSpan">higher risk of
  damages and loss.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.432.1" class="koboSpan">It is not sure a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.433.1"
class="koboSpan">priori</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.434.1"
class="koboSpan"> that the comparison between costs and benefits is
always positive, even if most policy makers consider costs largely
exceeded by benefits since to absorb road traffic a minimum distance of
1,500 km is
required.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0440" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0440"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.435.1" class="koboSpan">59</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.436.1"
class="koboSpan"> Nevertheless, some points should be
highlighted:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.437.1" class="koboSpan">As for
    environmental effects, the balance is likely to be positive, since
    SO</span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.438.1" class="koboSpan">2
    </span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.439.1"
    class="koboSpan">higher emissions can be reduced (see below).
    </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.439.2"
    class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, nobody can extrapolate this statement
    on a long term, as no forecasts on future levels of polluting
    emissions are highly reliable, namely for land transport, where a
    major research effort is being done to attain propulsion systems
    environmentally friendly.</span>
2.  <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.440.1" class="koboSpan">As for congestion
    of transport infrastructure, the congestion of land transport
    network is clearly more damaging and less remediable, for the
    economy as a whole, than the congestion of existing port
    nodes.</span>
3.  <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.441.1" class="koboSpan">Under the
    viewpoint of economic effects, namely in total production costs of
    transport, clearly the lower flexibility of land transport costs is
    replaced by a lower flexibility in transit times and a lower
    punctuality; there is a trade off between quality and cost, and the
    effects on demand are likely to be different for different segments
    of the market (as for types of cargoes and cargo units), due to
    different values of price-elasticity and time-elasticity.</span>
4.  <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.442.1" class="koboSpan">As for
    macroeconomic Keynesian impact, the replacement of a demand in land
    transport and infrastructure construction with a demand in maritime
    transport, shipyards and port infrastructure construction, needs to
    be carefully investigated and quantified; yet it does not appear a
    reason to stop a possible change if otherwise desirable.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.443.1" class="koboSpan">Even if case-by-case
assessments and surveys can lead to results sometimes different, it
seems acceptable that in a macroeconomic vision SSS should develop
further, and that policies aiming at implementing it are consequently
well founded.</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.444.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Possible policies for short sea shipping in a multimodal context</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.445.1" class="koboSpan">If previous
paragraphs showed that some conditions influencing SSS are given (on the
geographical side, land and sea distances; as for demand, the nature of
cargoes, and, to some extent, their volumes), most other elements
influencing competitiveness of SSS
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_413"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.446.1"
class="koboSpan">can be changed through suitable policies.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.446.2" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
it must be clear that what jeopardises the competitiveness of SSS is the
unfair competition played by land transport, namely road haulage, in
terms of much higher environmental costs, and much higher public
financing of infrastructure. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.446.3"
class="koboSpan">Strictly speaking, equalising environmental and fiscal
externalities of all transport modes should be the ultimate goal of any
policy aiming at a fair modal split (and not simply at the growth of
SSS, which might well be not desirable).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.446.4" class="koboSpan">As a
consequence, first best policies for SSS do not concern necessarily SSS,
but should focus on internalising major external costs of land
transport.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.447.1" class="koboSpan">In the light of the
above paragraphs, and taking into account the framework outlined above,
a number of actions which apply to different areas can be identified.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.447.2" class="koboSpan">Firstly, ports
are key nodes for the effectiveness of SSS, since ships’ times in port
are high and amount to more than 60% of ships’ total voyage time and
represents 70 to 80% of waterborne transport services total cost or more
than half of maritime freight (see endnote
21).</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0441" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0441"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.448.1" class="koboSpan">60</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.449.1"
class="koboSpan"> A well-defined port strategy can greatly influence a
modal shift towards the use of SSS.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.449.2" class="koboSpan">Instead of
focusing only on inter-port competition, ports should determine their
SSS hinterland, look at shippers’ requirements in order to facilitate
short sea operators. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.449.3"
class="koboSpan">The actions listed below to promote modal shift should
increase fluidity of transit in ports, reliability and on time delivery,
by minimising quality components of generalised cost.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.450.1" class="koboSpan">Second, comparisons
between transport rates highlight two areas where positive actions can
be deployed: internalising all costs following the user pays principle,
or at least equalise the level of external costs.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.450.2" class="koboSpan">These actions,
involve infrastructure, turn to land use/planning policies, developed
either for optimising transport performance, or for reinforcing the
cohesion and economic proximity of different regional economies.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.450.3" class="koboSpan">Finally,
policies can involve the transport industry and providers of transport
services, by inducing changes both into the market and
technical/industrial organisation, and on cargoes and shippers’
organisation. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.450.4"
class="koboSpan">Policies and actions appear to fall into seven main
strategic areas namely infrastructure policies, law and regulations,
commercial actions, organisational actions and policies, pricing
policies, technological actions and logistics strategies.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.450.5" class="koboSpan">The paragraphs
that follow describe each of these policies.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.451.1"
class="koboSpan">Infrastructure
policies</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.452.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.452.2"
class="koboSpan">Infrastructure policies address both
planning/construction and location of infrastructure that influence SSS
competitiveness. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.452.3"
class="koboSpan">Main actions include:</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.453.1" class="koboSpan">improvement of
  ports to the needs of SSS, namely widening space for SSS traffic (most
  present terminals would be inadequate if SSS attracted relevant
  traffic flows), modification of ports' layout and creation of
  dedicated terminals/areas;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.454.1" class="koboSpan">improvement of
  handling plants in ports, namely through a further diffusion of
  containerisation in SSS;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.455.1" class="koboSpan">enhancement of port
  accessibility and connections between ports and land networks (road
  and rail); since competition between road and rail has been estimated
  around 170-250
  km,</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0442" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0442"><span
  id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.456.1" class="koboSpan">61</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.457.1"
  class="koboSpan"> connections with rail networks are crucial for
  expanding ports' market areas;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.458.1" class="koboSpan">IWW development and
  promotion of a better balanced modal split between land transport and
  IWW, whose integration with SSS is easier and more efficient than for
  land transport;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.459.1" class="koboSpan">redesign port
  procedures to eliminate activities that create costs;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.460.1" class="koboSpan">make use ofVTMIS to
  continuously monitor vessel arrival in port and as such introduce
  just-in-time procedures to improve port capacity management.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_414"></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.461.1"
class="koboSpan">Law and
regulations.</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.462.1"
class="koboSpan"> These aim at enhancing competition to increase the
efficiency and attract further investment and at eliminating distortions
caused by excess of regulations for SSS, and lack of environmental
regulations (or of their enforcement) on road transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.462.2" class="koboSpan">Main actions
should include measures targeting at:</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.463.1" class="koboSpan">liberalising access
  to market, namely abolishing flag reservations on domestic traffic,
  including the concept of public service;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.464.1" class="koboSpan">integrating
  bureaucratic (customs/administrative) procedures in order to
  simplify/reduce difficulties and times (the MarNIS EU research project
  output can be a means to achieve this end);</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.465.1" class="koboSpan">equalising external
  costs;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.466.1" class="koboSpan">integrating
  different contracts and liabilities;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.467.1" class="koboSpan">regulating port
  services and their inputs, thus allowing a higher efficiency of port
  operations.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.468.1"
class="koboSpan">Commercial actions.
</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.469.1" class="koboSpan">They
seek to overcome the perception of SSS as an obsolete, not transparent,
and not suitable mode of transport for the present needs of production
and logistics, with low flexibility, reliability, frequency and speed.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.469.2" class="koboSpan">Measures
needed include:</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.470.1" class="koboSpan">restoring the image
  of SSS from that of an old-fashioned, slow and complex transport mode
  to a modern element in the logistic chain, characterised by high
  speed, reliability, flexibility, regularity, frequency, and cargo
  safety;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.471.1" class="koboSpan">clearly show the
  difference between SSS and other modes of transport, in particularly
  road;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.472.1" class="koboSpan">information aimed
  at restoring trust; logistic operators and shipowners should fight for
  market transparency and to promote information on conditions of
  supply;</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0443" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0443"><span
  id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.473.1" class="koboSpan">62</span></a></sup>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.474.1" class="koboSpan">specific
  information on safety (see above) helping to promote a positive
  image;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.475.1" class="koboSpan">define and
  publicise key performance indicators.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.476.1"
class="koboSpan">Organisational actions and
policies.</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.477.1"
class="koboSpan"> These actions involve either the industrial or the
technical organisation with the purpose of reorganising SSS-related
operators. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.477.2"
class="koboSpan">Such actions should:</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.478.1" class="koboSpan">reorganise and
  allow a better modal integration to fulfil just-in-time requirements
  and compensate the additional breaks of bulk; frequency and
  reliability of scheduled times are the key issues, which implies the
  existence of 24/7 port services, and a better organisation of
  storage/distribution areas;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.479.1" class="koboSpan">stimulate
  co-operation and collaboration of SSS operators as suggested by Corres
  and Psaraftis (see endnote 48), stimulate co-operation of SSS
  operators with shippers and forwarders to offer comprehensive networks
  and door-to-door services at competitive prices, thus integrating the
  strengths of different modes into seamless customer-oriented services.
  </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.479.2" class="koboSpan">Either SSS
  operators need partners to carry out the land legs of intermodal
  chain, or land operators must be ready to use SSS for a relevant part
  of their journeys at the expense of short sea operators losing control
  over the market. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.479.3"
  class="koboSpan">A good example is the Turkish company UN Ro-Ro that
  operates several trade routes between Turkey and Italy;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_415"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.480.1"
  class="koboSpan">concentrate SSS flows on a limited number of ports,
  in order to achieve higher economies of density and provide more
  frequent services; possibly locate them close to major metropolitan
  areas in order to be more competitive in delivery times; the MoS
  concept is an opportunity to achieve this objective so that a
  guaranteed service quality and frequency is obtained;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.481.1" class="koboSpan">promote
  specialisation of terminals and alliances between port
  operators;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.482.1" class="koboSpan">promote
  concentration in the road haulage industry, to incentive road-SSS
  intermodal journeys which are more competitive for non-accompanied
  trailers;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.483.1" class="koboSpan">promote
  standardisation of cargo units (e.g.
  </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.483.2"
  class="koboSpan">"europallets" do not allow a standard ISOl maritime
  container to be filled with two rows of pallets) in order to reduce
  costs of modal change in those trades where these standardised cargo
  units are possible;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.484.1" class="koboSpan">locate value-added
  services (VAS) in SSS ports to better integrate port functions with
  logistical services provided by forwarders and MTOs.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.485.1"
class="koboSpan">Pricing
policies.</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.486.1"
class="koboSpan"> Since the quality component of generalised cost is
comparatively high, SSS must be cheaper in monetary
costs.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0444" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0444"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.487.1" class="koboSpan">63</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.488.1"
class="koboSpan"> Some possible price-based actions are:</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.489.1" class="koboSpan">compensating lower
  quality (higher times for ships and cargoes) by lower prices;
  Pettersen Strandenes and Marlow (2000) suggest a two-parts port
  tariffs partly related to port stay and waiting time: prices inversely
  related to quality should enhance competitiveness of SSS and incentive
  port operators to improve
  quality</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0445" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0445"><span
  id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.490.1" class="koboSpan">64</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.491.1"
  class="koboSpan">;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.492.1" class="koboSpan">pricing policies
  promoting fair competition between transport modes by: charging for
  the cost of building infrastructure in all modes (the user pays
  principle); harmonising financing and pricing policies in different
  ports; internalising external costs,, particularly in road
  haulage;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.493.1" class="koboSpan">lowering port taxes
  (which, unlike pricing for using infrastructure, does not correspond
  to a real recovery of production cost) indirectly to attain the same
  results.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.494.1"
class="koboSpan">Technological
actions.</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.495.1"
class="koboSpan"> The age and the low specialisation of SSS ships are
consequences, rather than causes, of low profitability.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.495.2" class="koboSpan">Higher
investments in new ships and R&D, and generally in technological
advance, are needed. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.495.3"
class="koboSpan">Some useful action can be:</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.496.1" class="koboSpan">development of high
  speed ships, to reduce the gap with road in terms of time; even if
  competition between faster and more expensive road haulage and a
  slower and cheaper SSS rely solely on the value of time for the
  user;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.497.1" class="koboSpan">new vessels and
  advanced flexible ship designs to better integrate SSS (namely with
  high speed ships) within logistic chains;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.498.1" class="koboSpan">harmonisation of
  standards for information and communication technologies (ICT) and
  development of "community systems" to reduce costs of information
  input;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.499.1" class="koboSpan">harmonisation of
  standards concerning cargo units (see above), to achieve higher
  occupancy rates and highly or fully automated handling
  techniques;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.500.1" class="koboSpan">research reducing
  polluting emissions of ships, like
  SO</span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.501.1"
  class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.502.1"
  class="koboSpan">, namely by lowering the sulphur content in bunker
  fuel oils or equipping the ships with exhaust gas cleaning systems
  (see endnote 21).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_416"></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.503.1"
class="koboSpan">Logistics strategies.
</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.504.1" class="koboSpan">The
following logistics strategies can be considered to implement SSS in a
multimodal context and which meet the findings of Paixão Casaca and
Marlow (2005):</span>

- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.505.1" class="koboSpan">adoption of a total
  quality-management philosophy;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.506.1" class="koboSpan">consider the
  transport chain from an integrative perspective;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.507.1" class="koboSpan">consider
  freight-forwarding a core competency;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.508.1" class="koboSpan">develop
  partnerships and alliances to provide door-to-door transport;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.509.1" class="koboSpan">think about the
  importance of inland clearance depots and terminals in order to create
  networks;</span>
- <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.510.1" class="koboSpan">make use of
  outsourcing and adopt a time-management strategies to comply with
  shippers'
  requirements.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0446" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0446"><span
  id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.511.1" class="koboSpan">65</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.512.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.512.2" class="koboSpan">The European Short Sea Shipping Policy</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.513.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 European Union short sea shipping policies</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.514.1" class="koboSpan">Road increased modal
share and its continued growth in freight (see Section 2) is leading
European road transport systems into serious problems with regard to
congestion and safety, and as a consequence environmental impact of road
transport is causing public concern.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.514.2" class="koboSpan">Under the
given conditions, the EU has been developing and supporting a more
sustainable transport policy from economic, social and environmental
viewpoints.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0447" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0447"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.515.1" class="koboSpan">66</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.516.1" class="koboSpan">Although the
Commission addressed the issue of SSS in 1985 when proposing freedom in
providing maritime transport services for cabotage and intra-EU trades,
the matter was left behind until 1992.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.516.2" class="koboSpan">The 1992 White
Paper released by the Commission considered that transport should adopt
a holistic approach rather than one based on the individual
characteristics of the modes especially when road freight transport is
expected to grow by 60% until 2013.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.516.3" class="koboSpan">What was being
asked was the development of collaborative attitudes between the
different transport modes so that each one complemented the other in
such a way that the efficient running of transport services was being
promoted. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.516.4"
class="koboSpan">Through this action, the Commission was trying to
promote the development of multimodal transport services over the long
distances in opposition to unimodal transport, namely road transport.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.516.5" class="koboSpan">However, if
these actions are not truthfully supported by all actors, and in the
absence of new policy measures, growth will be concentrated on road
transport for both goods and passengers.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.516.6" class="koboSpan">Road is the
only mode capable of offering the tailored logistics needs of transport
users, and because stricter environmental rules regarding road transport
are being implemented up to 2014 (the Euro V and Euro VI) to reduce the
impact of road transport on the environment.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.517.1" class="koboSpan">The shift of goods
from road to underused transport capacity, in particular rail, SSS and
IWW, became one the objectives of the European Common Transport Policy
(see endnote 19). </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.517.2"
class="koboSpan">The Commission outlined future priorities based on the
need to reconcile the demand for mobility with the requirements of the
environment, in line with the principle of sustainable mobility.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.517.3" class="koboSpan">This
Communication examines SSS potential contribution to the achievement of
sustainable mobility. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.517.4"
class="koboSpan">It includes a series of recommendations addressed to
Member States, their regional and local authorities as well as the
maritime industries themselves. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.517.5"
class="koboSpan">It also includes ideas for actions which can most
appropriately be undertaken at Union level.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.517.6" class="koboSpan">It is intended
to seek the political support
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_417"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.518.1"
class="koboSpan">of the Council for these recommendations.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.518.2" class="koboSpan">In what
concerns the revitalisation of SSS, the Commission embarked on a
promotion programme.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.519.1" class="koboSpan">In 1995, the first
communication on SSS was presented by the Commission and it targets at
bringing SSS to an equal footing with other modes of transport by
focusing on three important areas: (i) improving the quality and
efficiency of SSS services; (ii) improving port infrastructure and port
efficiency; and (iii) preparing SSS for a wider Europe.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.519.2" class="koboSpan">The
Communication presented an action programme embracing a comprehensive
list of measures to be undertaken by the Commission, Member States
government, local/regional authorities, port authorities and maritime
industries players (see endnote 21).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.519.3" class="koboSpan">The reasons
for enhancing SSS in the EU are (i) promoting the general sustainability
and safety of transport, by providing an alternative to congested road
transport, also in order to reach
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.520.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.521.1"
class="koboSpan"> target under the Kyoto Protocol; (ii) strengthening
the cohesion of the community, facilitating connections between Member
States and European regions, and revitalising peripherals regions; and
(iii) increasing the efficiency of transport in order to meet current
and future demand arising from economic growth.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.522.1" class="koboSpan">A progress report
from the Commission was presented in 1997 following a Council resolution
on SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.522.2" class="koboSpan">This
report showed that improvements to SSS roundtables should be organised
at a national level with the participation of all interested
stakeholders so that the peculiar problems that affect SSS could be
sorted
out.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0448" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0448"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.523.1" class="koboSpan">67</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.524.1"
class="koboSpan"> The 1999 Communication on SSS examined its potential
in the framework of sustainable and safe mobility, its integration in
European logistic transport chains, its image and existing barriers to
the development of SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.524.2"
class="koboSpan">It recommends further action and identified three main
reasons why SSS should be promoted at a Community level: (i) to promote
the general sustainability of transport; (ii) to strengthen the cohesion
of the community; and (iii) to increase the efficiency of transport in
order to meet current and future demands arising from economic growth.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.524.3" class="koboSpan">In this
regard, the Commission published a list of further actions (see endnote
13).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.525.1" class="koboSpan">As an environmentally
friendlier alternative to road transport, SSS must be integrated into
the logistics chain, its links with other modes must be improved, and
the quality of service must be closer to the customer’s needs.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.525.2" class="koboSpan">Port
installations should be organised in such a way so that they can match
better the requirements of SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.525.3"
class="koboSpan">According to the Commission, firms should integrate SSS
into door-to-door services; intermodal logistic chains should be created
to attract cargo in the long term.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.525.4" class="koboSpan">The success of
SSS relies on the cooperation and coordination of all stakeholders (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.525.5" class="koboSpan">public
authorities, shipping operators, ports, forwarders, freight
consolidators and logistics companies).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.525.6" class="koboSpan">Actions
towards standardisation/simplification in administrative procedures of
Member States are needed, and ports are encouraged to promote SSS within
their commercial strategies.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.526.1" class="koboSpan">In June 1999 the
Commission acknowledged that SSS needed to become a truly intermodal
door-to-door concept; an essential element in its development was its
integration in the European logistic supply chains to fulfil its users’
requirements and be perceived with a new dynamic image (see endnote 13).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.526.2" class="koboSpan">This second
two-yearly progress report underlines that turnaround delays,
infrastructure constraints and non-transparent charges are a relevant
problem for SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.526.3"
class="koboSpan">It also suggests that (i) ports should consider to set
up dedicated short sea terminals in larger ports and providing other
specialised services to SSS; (ii) the obligations in some ports to use
separate pilots could be re-examined where the ship’s master is
certified to carry out the pilotage on his own;
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_418"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.527.1"
class="koboSpan">(iii) administrative procedures should be standardised
and simplified, since documentation required in SSS is more than for
road transport; improvements are possible namely in a uniform acceptance
of IMO FAL forms, delegation of tasks to one authority or to a third
part, permission to start unloading ships before reporting procedures
have been finalised, increased use of electronic data interchange; and
(iv) incentives to research aiming at reducing polluting emissions of
ships are recommended.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.528.1" class="koboSpan">The 2001 White Paper
on European transport policy for 2010 highlights the role that SSS can
play in curbing the growth of heavy goods vehicle traffic, rebalancing
the modal split and bypassing land bottlenecks and its development can
also help to reduce the growth of road transport, restore the balance
between modes of transport, bypass bottlenecks and contribute to
sustainable development and
safety.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0449" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0449"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.529.1" class="koboSpan">68</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.530.1"
class="koboSpan"> The entire the strategy underlying the 2001 White
Paper is based on the need to shift the balance between modes since road
transport growth caused high congestion and environmental costs (see
endnote 68). </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.530.2" class="koboSpan">A
specific chapter is dedicated to the development of MoS, where it is
stressed once more that SSS is a real alternative to land transport, and
that (i) certain shipping links, providing a way around major
bottlenecks in land transport networks, should be made part of the
TEN-T; (ii) regulated competition in ports must be implemented, through
clearer rules for access to the port service
market;</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0450" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0450"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.531.1" class="koboSpan">69</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.532.1"
class="koboSpan"> (iii) rules governing operation of ports must be
simplified; (iv) one-stop-shops should be created to bring together all
links in the logistics chain (consignors, shipowners, shipping, road,
rail and IWW operators); and (v) advanced telematic services in ports
should be developed in order to improve operational reliability and
safety. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.532.2"
class="koboSpan">Fortunately work has been done in this direction;
electronic port clearance for vessels and goods is now possible at some
ports and there is also an SSS guide to customs procedures.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.532.3" class="koboSpan">If the outcome
of the MarNIS EU research project is implemented, much of the
informational constraints that take place will disappear and most
important it will be a valuable tool to implement just-in-time
strategies in a port environmental level since ports will be able to
manage much better the flow of ships arriving in port, and consequently,
their capacity.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.533.1" class="koboSpan">In response to the
2001 White Paper on the European Transport Policy and to the June 2002
informal meeting of the EU Transport Ministers held in Gijón (dedicated
to SSS), the European Commission presented in 2003 an action programme
for the promotion of SSS and to remove obstacles to its development.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.533.2" class="koboSpan">SSS has a high
priority in the European agenda and therefore, barriers have been
clearly identified, requiring different levels of actions at community,
regional and national level. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.533.3"
class="koboSpan">The action programme as presented by the European
Commission in April 2003 consisted of 14 individual actions grouped into
three broad categories, namely legislative, technical and operational
categories.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0451" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0451"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.534.1" class="koboSpan">70</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.535.1" class="koboSpan">To monitor the
progress achieved since 1999 in the light of the 2003 Programme for the
Promotion of SSS, the Commission presented in 2004 a new Communication.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.535.2" class="koboSpan">While
highlighting the obstacles it presented the achievements reached so far
in the light of the 2003 action
programme.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0452" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0452"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.536.1" class="koboSpan">71</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.537.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is the view of the Commission that SSS has proven
its ability to reach competitiveness levels normally attributed to road
alone and pressure is being exerted on SSS to expand its full
contribution towards alleviating current and future transport problems
in Europe. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.537.2"
class="koboSpan">While listing the most significant SSS developments at
Community and national levels, it also lists the obstacles that still
hinder SSS development faster. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.537.3"
class="koboSpan">Like the 2003 communication, this one also refers to
the MoS concept.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_419"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.538.1"
class="koboSpan">On 13 July 2006, the Commission adopted a mid-term
review of the programme for the promotion of SSS.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.538.2" class="koboSpan">The review
evaluates the results of the 14 actions introduced in 2003 to enhance
the efficiency of SSS in Europe and mentions that SSS is still growing,
that numerous obstacles still hinder SSS and that some of the original
measures should be retargeted to put the MoS concept in operation by
2010. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.538.3" class="koboSpan">It
examines the possibility of extending the scope of SSS promotion through
its integration in multimodal logistics supply chains in order to
maintain the modern image that SSS has already
acquired.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0453" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0453"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.539.1" class="koboSpan">72</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.540.1" class="koboSpan">The Blue Book on
maritime transport released in October 2007, states that the Marco Polo
and the TEN-T programmes will go on supporting the creation of MoS/ SSS
networks.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0454" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0454"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.541.1" class="koboSpan">73</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.542.1"
class="koboSpan"> The MoS/SSS differs from DSS, given the competition it
suffers from land transport despite having lower externalities than land
transport, having a high potential for maintaining European
technological know-how in maritime transport and being a source of job
creation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0455" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0455"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.543.1" class="koboSpan">74</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.544.1"
class="koboSpan"> In January 2009, the Commission updated its strategic
goals and recommendations relatively its maritime transport strategy up
to 2018 and once more reinforced its importance at a European
level.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0456" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0456"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.545.1" class="koboSpan">75</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.546.1"
class="koboSpan"> Reference is made to the adoption of positive measures
that support SSS to increase sea exchanges in all the European maritime
façades. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.546.2" class="koboSpan">These
measures will include the creation of a European maritime transport
space without barriers the full deployment of the MoS but also the
implementation of measures for port investment and performance.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.547.1" class="koboSpan">In this regard and in
sequence of the 2006 mid-term review the Commission presented a
Communication and an action plan to establish a European maritime
