transport space without barriers, whose objective is to eliminate or
simplify administrative procedures in the intra-EU maritime transport,
given the role that short sea shipping can play in the intermodal
freight logistics
chain</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0457" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0457"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.548.1" class="koboSpan">76</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.549.1"
class="koboSpan"> and a proposal for a Directive on reporting
formalities for ships arriving in and/or departing from ports of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.550.1"
class="koboSpan">Member
State</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.551.1" class="koboSpan">s,
thereby repealing Directive 2002/6/EC which met the changes of Community
legislation and the FAL
Convention.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0458" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0458"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.552.1" class="koboSpan">77</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.553.1"
class="koboSpan"> More recently, in March 2009, the Commission reviewed
the 14 actions presented in the 2003 Programme for the Promotion of SSS
and its main conclusion is that SSS is far from being fully integrated
in the door-to-door supply chain.</span>

### <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.554.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 European Union general transport policies</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.555.1" class="koboSpan">Besides the dedicated
SSS policy released by the Commission, the EU has been releasing some
general transport policies that influence SSS.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.555.2" class="koboSpan">The
liberalisation of domestic transport markets which allows free access to
EU operators in cabotage transport of all Member States is certainly the
most relevant concrete action that caused higher competition at lower
prices. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.555.3" class="koboSpan">With
the relevant exception of the Greek Islands, the internal market has
been liberalised since 1 January 1999 under Regulations 4055/1986 and
3577/1992.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0459" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0459"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.556.1" class="koboSpan">78</span></a><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.557.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0460" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0460"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.558.1" class="koboSpan">79</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.559.1"
class="koboSpan"> Other guidelines that have been developed are
potentially relevant to SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.559.2"
class="koboSpan">The trans-European transport network (TEN-T) approved
in
1996,</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0461" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0461"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.560.1" class="koboSpan">80</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.561.1"
class="koboSpan"> concerning infrastructure planning is a tool to
enhance the domestic market and the perspectives of the EU enlargement:
ports, originally not included in the TEN-T framework, have been
subsequently
integrated</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0462" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0462"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.562.1" class="koboSpan">81</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.563.1"
class="koboSpan"> and today, the TEN-T framework is ruled by Decision
884/2004/EC.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0463" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0463"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.564.1" class="koboSpan">82</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.565.1"
class="koboSpan"> The regulations on infrastructure financing and
pricing should limit distortions favouring road transport and push for a
fair competition between transport
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_420"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.566.1"
class="koboSpan">modes. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.566.2"
class="koboSpan">The liberalisation of the IWW market is expected to
help SSS to become a link of the intermodal chain.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.566.3" class="koboSpan">The
implementation of equitable behaviours in the field of environment and
safety are expected to create a level playing field.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.566.4" class="koboSpan">The
harmonisation/ liberalisation processes should increase the efficiency
in all transport modes, proportionally more for those less liberalised
so far (such as rail and sea transport), compared to road
haulage.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.567.1" class="koboSpan">The 2007 Commission’s
Communication on a European ports
policy</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0464" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0464"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.568.1" class="koboSpan">83</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.569.1"
class="koboSpan"> within the broad European strategy of keeping freight
moving aims at a creating a port system capable of coping with the
future challenges of European transport needs.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.569.2" class="koboSpan">The 1997 Green
Paper on ports and maritime infrastructure had already urged some
measures, </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.570.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia</span></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.571.1" class="koboSpan">,
links between ports and TEN-T, enhancement of ports’ role in the
intermodal chain, transparency of prices, and the adoption of a strategy
based on the user pays principle, which are relevant to the development
of
SSS.</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0465" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0465"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.572.1" class="koboSpan">84</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.573.1"
class="koboSpan"> From another viewpoint, other political and
environmental options, such as the goal of reducing road congestion and
external costs of road haulage, are clearly able to positively influence
the market for SSS. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.573.2"
class="koboSpan">Also Psaraftis quoted in Papadimitriou (2001)
acknowledges that SSS is regarded as a key factor of European economic
cohesion and proximity between regions, namely between West and East
Europe and highlights the importance of setting rules for a fair
competition between transport modes, through infrastructure pricing and
financing, and internalisation of external costs (see endnote 12).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.573.3" class="koboSpan">Papadimitriou
also underlines the well-known and already mentioned problems in
developing SSS (costs and times of ports nodes, inadequate intermodal
integration, complexity of procedures, costs of the additional breaks of
bulks, lack of transparency, inadequacy to requirements of just-in-time)
(see endnote 12).</span>

## <span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.574.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.574.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion and Further Comments</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.575.1" class="koboSpan">Even though the
worldwide coastal shipping is very important and plays a key role in the
distribution of goods, the European SSS has reached a high development
stage in the world, and other geographical areas such as the United
States, Canada, and Australia countries are looking at what is being
done at the European level. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.575.2"
class="koboSpan">A significant share of the European SSS traffic is
concentrated in the Baltic and North Sea, but it is in the Mediterranean
that the best examples of SSS can be found.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.575.3" class="koboSpan">Despite this,
there are still opportunities for further development in the Ro-Ro and
container market segments. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.575.4"
class="koboSpan">SSS growth is mainly related to captive markets caused
by geographic/infrastructure constraints, by feeder traffic for
hub-and-spoke deep-sea transport, by smaller ports’ hinterland and in
this regard it can hardly compete with surface transport, namely road
haulage, when both land and sea links are available between origin and
destination. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.575.5"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, this business area is the most important
one for policy makers facing the problems of growing congestion and high
environmental and infrastructure costs of land transport.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.576.1" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, the
European SSS fleet has a big problem concerning its high average age,
which the absence of legislative measures enforcing the renewal of the
fleet has contributed to it. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.576.2"
class="koboSpan">Short sea operators do not possess sufficient funds to
embark on a short sea fleet renewal programme, – the costs of building a
small ship are high, and bank credit is very expensive.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.576.3" class="koboSpan">The resultant
reduced profitability is a serious strategic concern in capital
intensive companies planning for growth and the renewals that have taken
place result more often than not from the existing rivalry between
shipowners
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_421"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.577.1"
class="koboSpan">operating in this market, from port state control
inspections and the enforcement of important legislation to protect the
environment. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.577.2"
class="koboSpan">The point is that new ships are needed to compete with
road transport on cost, speed, flexibility, reliability without
jeopardising safety and the environment, attractive sailing times,
maintained transit times, and guarantee of delivery.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.578.1" class="koboSpan">There is wide
interest about critical factors in competition between SSS and land
transport. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.578.2" class="koboSpan">As
shown in Sections 2 and 3, low competitiveness is sometimes due to
geographic characteristics (too-short distances between origin and
destination, a bad ratio of maritime distance to land transport
distance) or to demand characteristics (types of goods, volumes, etc.).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.578.3" class="koboSpan">Yet, low
competitiveness is often due to supply factors concerning either SSS or
competing modes where it is both possible and desirable to intervene,
since they do not come from a fair competition between modes, but from
imbalances in the costs of different modes, namely external costs;
infrastructure costs, pricing and subsidisation; and transaction costs
due to conditions outside the market (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.578.4"
class="koboSpan">administrative/custom regulations, etc.).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.579.1" class="koboSpan">Actions are being
planned by a few Member States, where the domestic market is more
relevant and where the sector is important from a national policy
perspective, and by the EU, to the extent that efforts are being
undertaken by experts and policy makers to remove distortions that
prevent fair competition between modes, or at least to attain a more
balanced modal split. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.579.2"
class="koboSpan">The proposed measures include those outlined in Section
3 (including infrastructural, organisational, pricing, commercial,
regulatory technological and logistics measures) which aim at ensuring a
smooth transit of goods in ports; integrate SSS in intermodal logistic
chains; draw generalised costs as near as possible to the real cost of
transport (including external costs, energy and infrastructure),
equalising the level of cost externalisation in the different modes,
through both internalisation of environmental costs and the financing of
infrastructure. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.579.3"
class="koboSpan">However, so far, researchers and policy makers have
just agreed, with few exceptions, that developing SSS is desirable and
the first effective actions are now being implemented.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.579.4" class="koboSpan">The remarks
that follow about changing scenarios might be useful to assess the
potential effectiveness of future policies.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.580.1" class="koboSpan">The huge outsourcing
of logistic functions shows that logistics, while remaining highly
strategic for firms, become more and more specialised.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.580.2" class="koboSpan">Its complexity
in the era of globalisation requires higher quality and efficiency in
transport activities. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.580.3"
class="koboSpan">The need for distribution networks and the consequent,
relevant scale/networks economies should be favourable to SSS only if it
is able to fulfil higher and higher requirements in terms of quality
standards (speed, punctuality, reliability).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.580.4" class="koboSpan">Otherwise, the
need for speedy door-to-door, just-in-time services will be better
matched by road haulage, despite higher transport costs per unit.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.580.5" class="koboSpan">Transport
monetary costs are just a (small) part of the overall logistic cost,
what makes it difficult to attract traffic flows on a low price basis
(see endnote
3).</span><sup><a href="#Ch013.xhtml_fn0466" id="Ch013.xhtml_bck_fn0466"><span
id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.581.1" class="koboSpan">85</span></a></sup><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.582.1"
class="koboSpan"> The strategic role of logistics implies that the
quality elasticity of the demand (for logistic/transport services) is
much higher than price elasticity.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.582.2" class="koboSpan">The
outsourcing of logistic functions can be for SSS either an opportunity
or a threat.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.583.1" class="koboSpan">In the global market,
control of logistic flows has become a crucial competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.583.2" class="koboSpan">Transport is
part of a set of services that must match the logistic needs of the
shippers. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.583.3"
class="koboSpan">Network economies influence the geographic organisation
of logistic operators. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.583.4"
class="koboSpan">This means that potential for SSS is also related to
the ability of ports to act not only as transhipment sites but as nodes
of value-added services and logistic functions.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.583.5" class="koboSpan">The
integration of a port within a (infrastructure and service) network
becomes more
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_422"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.584.1"
class="koboSpan">important than the traditional concept of port
hinterland. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.584.2" class="koboSpan">A
proactive role of ports in integrating different links of logistic
chains clearly becomes a key issue for SSS.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.1" class="koboSpan">With fair competition
between modes, there would be opportunities for a further growth of SSS,
since its overall costs are comparatively low.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.2" class="koboSpan">The goal must
be internalising both environmental and infrastructure costs in the
prices paid by the users (user pays principle).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.3" class="koboSpan">Higher regard
for the environment may lead to policies on road transport which will
make the ratio of costs for users more favourable to maritime transport,
so that relevant flows would shift from road to sea, starting with
dangerous goods. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.4"
class="koboSpan">The ongoing research is producing significant results
in reducing pollution and noise and increasing the safety of road
transport. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.5"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, it is not sure that road transport will
still be so little sustainable as it has been so far.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.6" class="koboSpan">Dire problems
in the public finances of most developed countries (which normally have
both a developed infrastructure network, and high levels of public
expenditure for social/welfare issues) should result in lower public
aids to infrastructure financing.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.7" class="koboSpan">Besides,
improving land networks becomes more and more difficult because of
territorial and environmental problems.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.8" class="koboSpan">The growing
rigidity and cost of transport infrastructure is thus a major
opportunity for developing SSS (apart for the need to increase port
capacity). </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.585.9"
class="koboSpan">Regulations on infrastructure public financing and
pricing should reduce present inequalities.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.586.1" class="koboSpan">Too much attention
may have been paid on SSS competitiveness relatively to road haulage.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.586.2" class="koboSpan">In the future
not only SSS-based intermodality will compete with road transport, but
also rail-based intermodality, namely with the development of high-speed
railways. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.586.3" class="koboSpan">SSS
and rail can be direct competitors, unlike today where low
competitiveness of rail is due to technologic and managerial
backwardness. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.586.4"
class="koboSpan">Also, international integration, namely in the EU
context, could promote easier procedures and techniques in land
transport (harmonisation of railways technologies and standards,
development of rail freeways). </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.586.5"
class="koboSpan">It may be meaningful that among new intermodal
technologies which are being developed in order to reduce costs and
times of transit in intermodal nodes, most are tailored on road-rail
intermodality (swapbodies, piggyback, bimodalism) and only a few can
help SSS-based intermodality (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.586.6" class="koboSpan">palletwide
containers).</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.587.1" class="koboSpan">It has been shown
that SSS market contestability is crucial.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.587.2" class="koboSpan">Strictly
speaking, the market appears to be contestable since there are no
barriers to entry or to exit, and incursions are possible from new
entrants operating on other SSS routes (although slightly less from DSS
because of differing ships’ size).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.587.3" class="koboSpan">Thus,
liberalisation should be desirable.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.587.4" class="koboSpan">Yet within
logistic networks contestability can be jeopardised by operators with
dominant position on the whole chain (see endnote 3).
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.587.5" class="koboSpan">Big maritime
carriers influence more and more intermodal networks, ports and logistic
platforms at the regional/continental level.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.587.6" class="koboSpan">Vertical
integration may give, namely in the feeder traffic, a low level of
competition, which could spread on the infra-regional SSS market,
because of probable economies of scope.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.587.7" class="koboSpan">Also, vertical
integration of supply chains will require alliances/mergers between SSS
operators and other carrier or terminal operators, particularly if the
MoS concept is put in operation by 2010 as desired by the
Commission.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.588.1" class="koboSpan">It is presently
highly uncertain if the elasticity of transport demand to gross domestic
product (GDP) will still be so high in the near future.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.588.2" class="koboSpan">The potential
for a revival of regional development/trade patterns is presently being
investigated, namely after that (i) some excesses of globalisation bring
about relevant externalities and inequalities; (ii) diffusion of
economic growth makes it more and more difficult to exploit cheap
inputs, and firms’ requirements are shifting from cheap inputs to
efficient infrastructure and public utilities, technological skills,
legal and political reliability, etc.; and
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_page_423"></span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.589.1"
class="koboSpan">(iii) the present financial and economic crisis is
showing the social problems that a globalised economy can cause.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.589.2" class="koboSpan">A possible
revival of intra-regional growth and trade patterns would be an
opportunity for SSS.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.590.1" class="koboSpan">It is very difficult
to forecast whether SSS opportunities will overcome the threats, and if
policy guidelines will be effective and helpful.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.590.2" class="koboSpan">The potential
for SSS will depend both on the growth of transport and on the possible
modal shift from land transport, which is in turn a function of a number
of elements which are restraining its uninterrupted growth, like
congestion and long-run capacity limits.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.590.3" class="koboSpan">Once developed
beyond some relevant thresholds, the growth of SSS is likely to develop
cumulative effects since average costs should decrease more than in land
transport. </span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.590.4" class="koboSpan">As
described in Section 4, the key issue in ensuring a fair level of SSS
development is to neutralise the effect on modal shift of different
levels of market failures, namely in the fields of external costs,
public expenditure on a natural monopoly such as infrastructure
networks, and oligopoly/monopoly within the maritime transport
industry.</span>

<span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.591.1" class="koboSpan">Consequently, a
paramount role of economic policy has to be developed by states, unions
of states and international organisations, not only in ensuring fair
competition and free access to the market of SSS, but also in order to
equalise the level of cost externalisation in different modes.
</span><span id="Ch013.xhtml_kobo.591.2" class="koboSpan">Thus, there
should be three major guidelines on the agenda of policy makers to fair
competition within sea transport, through liberalising access to the
market and harmonising regulations; between transport modes, through the
harmonisation of regulations concerning public aids to transport (namely
in financing infrastructure); and between transport modes, through the
internalisation of external costs of transport.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_432"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_433"></span>[<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 14</span>\
<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Competition and Cooperation in Liner Shipping</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0332)
==================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">William</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Sjostrom</span></span><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0467" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0467"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">Liner shipping is the
business of offering common carrier ocean shipping services in
international trade. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.7.2"
class="koboSpan">Since it became an important industry in the 1870s, it
has been characterised by various agreements between firms.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.7.3" class="koboSpan">Historically,
since the formation in 1875 of the Calcutta Conference, the conference
system was the primary form of agreement in liner shipping.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.7.4" class="koboSpan">Variously called
liner conferences, shipping conferences, and ocean shipping conferences,
they are formal agreements between liner shipping lines on a route,
always setting (possibly discriminatory) prices, and sometimes pooling
profits or revenues, managing capacity, allocating routes, and offering
loyalty discounts. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.7.5"
class="koboSpan">Conferences agreements were quite successful and in
many cases have lasted for years. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.7.6"
class="koboSpan">In the last two decades, conferences have begun to be
supplanted by alliances (particularly in the American and European
trades, where legislative changes have been unfavourable to them), which
are less complete (they do not, for example, set prices) but encompass
more broadly defined trade routes.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">Section 1 will review
cooperative agreements in the liner industry, including conferences and
alliances, as well as the historical origins of that cooperation.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">Section 2
reviews the primary models that have been used to explain the conference
system, including models of monopolizing cartels, contestability,
destructive competition, and the empty core.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.8.3" class="koboSpan">Section 3
reviews a variety of practices and alleged practices in liner shipping,
including predatory pricing, loyalty contracts, price discrimination,
and price and output fixing. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.8.4"
class="koboSpan">Finally, section 4 offers a brief conclusion.</span>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1.1 Cooperation</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">International liner
shipping has long been dominated by collusive agreements, originally
conferences and more recently alliances.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">Conferences
have been used since at least the 1870s, when the industry was being
established. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.10.3" class="koboSpan">In
recent years, these agreements have been supplemented and replaced by
other kinds of agreements such as
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_434"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan">consortia and alliances.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">The focus of
this chapter is on explaining the economic models of competition used to
analyse cooperation in liner shipping for purposes of competition
policy.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">Conferences are
organisations of shipping lines operating on a particular route.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">At different
times, subject to various regulations, they have set tariffs, employing
policing agencies to check on adherence to the tariff.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">Members have
been fined out of the membership bonds they
post.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0468" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0468"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan"> They may also allocate output among their members, by
either cargo quotas or more commonly sailing quotas.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">If ships always
sailed at the same capacity, which they do not, cargo and sailing quotas
would be identical. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.14.3"
class="koboSpan">Sailing quotas are, however, probably easier to
enforce. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.14.4" class="koboSpan">They
may also pool revenues and allocate particular ports on a given
route.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0469" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0469"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan"> All of these practices have been used by conferences
throughout their history. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.16.2"
class="koboSpan">For example, in the late nineteenth century and into
the beginning of the twentieth century, as part of the Calcutta
Conference, the P&O, the BI, and the Hansa line had an agreement about
the number of sailings each would make out of
Hamburg.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0470" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0470"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">In the 1970s, liner
consortia were formed by conference members as a supplementary means of
conference
enforcement.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0471" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0471"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan"> They are essentially a system of common agency.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">More
significant has been the rise of the strategic alliance.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.20.3" class="koboSpan">They were first
used in the
1990s,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0472" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0472"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan"> and there is some evidence that conferences are being
displaced by alliances, perhaps because of the declining antitrust
immunity of conferences. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.22.2"
class="koboSpan">Alliances engage in cross route rationalisation, and
there is some evidence that the rationalisation reduces costs by taking
advantage of economies of
density.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0473" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0473"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan"> Unlike conferences, they do not issue a common tariff,
but they cover much broader trade routes.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">Only recently
have economists begun to examine them.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.24.3" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately,
the state of research is limited to a lot of speculation about their
functions and effects, and a few facts, without substantial testing of
models of alliances.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">Speculation on the
reasons for alliances has focused on risk reduction and scale economies.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.25.2" class="koboSpan">The claims
about risk reduction focus on two issues.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.25.3" class="koboSpan">First,
alliances give liners companies access to other routes without investing
in ships, thereby reducing the risk of new
investment.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0474" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0474"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan"> Second, by reserving slots on ships from other members
of the alliance working other routes, liner companies reduce risk by
diversifying into multiple
routes.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0475" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0475"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Although no evidence
has been produced in support of the expansion explanation of risk, there
is cross-industry evidence that firms use strategic alliances for this
reason.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0476" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0476"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan"> Explanations that focus on diversifying through
multiple routes face the problem that investors can already diversify
their portfolios by investing in multiple lines on different routes.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.31.2" class="koboSpan">If there is
evidence for this explanation, it will likely have to come from focusing
on managerial risk. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.31.3"
class="koboSpan">There is cross-industry evidence that managers with
specialised skills diversify to protect themselves against bankruptcy
and job
loss.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0477" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0477"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">The claims about scale
economies</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0478" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0478"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan"> focus on economies in marketing and allocating ships
to ports to reduce shipping time.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">The evidence
available supports these explanations, with evidence that alliances
reduce
costs</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0479" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0479"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"> and raise capacity
utilisation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0480" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0480"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan"> How well these explanations work will, however, have
to address the evidence that alliances are in decline over the last
decade.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0481" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0481"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">1.2 Historical origins</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Because sailing ships
are subject to the vagaries of the wind, liner shipping offering regular
scheduled service had to wait for the arrival of the steam
vessel,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0482" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0482"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan"> although the thirteenth century Venetians operated
what can be interpreted as a liner service to the
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_435"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">eastern Mediterranean using a combination of oar and
sail.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0483" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0483"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan"> Steam did not begin to be a competitor to the sailing
ship until the development of the compound engine in the late 1860s and
the triple expansion engine in the early
1880s.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0484" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0484"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan"> These developments substantially improved fuel economy
and increased speed to about 10–12 knots.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">The compound
engine cut fuel consumption by over half compared to a single cylinder
steam engine. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.49.3"
class="koboSpan">Essentially, it involved adding additional cylinders to
the steam engine, each additional cylinder reusing steam before it
cooled. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.49.4" class="koboSpan">The
increase in fuel economy also expanded the space available for cargo.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.49.5" class="koboSpan">Steam vessels
began to offer regular, scheduled service, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.49.6" class="koboSpan">liner service.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.49.7" class="koboSpan">It is in liner
shipping that conferences have thrived.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">Curiously, sailing
vessels belonged to conferences operating on the UK–Australia route and
the Germany–South America
route,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0485" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0485"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan"> and there were early British coastal conferences
involving sailing vessels as
well.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0486" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0486"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan"> By and large, however, these were exceptions.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">The UK–Calcutta
conference is usually described as the first conference, and it is
certainly the first modern conference.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">It started in
1875, consisting of five carriers: the P&O (Peninsular and Oriental
Steam Navigation Co), the BI (British India), and the City, Clan, and
Anchor Lines. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.55.3"
class="koboSpan">Within a decade or so, the conference extended its
coverage of ports of origin from only the UK to the rest of northern
Europe.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">It was followed
quickly by the development of other conferences.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">In the 30 years
following the formation of the UK–Calcutta conference, conferences were
formed on most of the major trade routes out of the UK and northern
Europe. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.56.3" class="koboSpan">The
Australia conference was started in 1884, the South African conference
in 1886, the West African and northern Brazil conferences in 1895, the
River Plate conference in 1896, the west coast of South America
conference in 1904, and a conference covering the North Atlantic trade
around
1900.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0487" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0487"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"> Most of these conferences covered the outbound trade
from Europe, leaving the inbound trades of mostly bulk commodities to
tramp
vessels.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0488" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0488"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">There were precursors,
however. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">A
conference from 1850 to 1856 on the North Atlantic involved the British
and North American Steam Packet Company (the Cunard Line) and the New
York and Liverpool United States Mail Steamship Company (the Collins
Line).</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0489" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0489"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan"> Glasgow ship owners may have fixed rates with a
conference system in the
1860s.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0490" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0490"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan"> In addition, the Transatlantic Shipping Conference was
formed in 1868. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.64.2"
class="koboSpan">It was concerned, however, with issues such as uniform
bills of lading and improving methods for inspecting cargo, and did not
become involved in rate setting until
1902.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0491" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0491"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan"> Although conferences are generally associated with
international shipping, there were precursors in British coastal
shipping as early as the
1830s.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0492" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0492"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Conferences were
limited to the liner trades, without any success in the bulk
trades.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0493" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0493"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan"> There were also conferences in the passenger shipping
trade.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0494" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0494"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">It is commonly assumed
by historians of shipping conferences that they were formed in response
to excess capacity, typically based on documents produced by
participants in the
trade.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0495" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0495"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan"> A common version of this argument is that the opening
of the Suez Canal, by shortening the distance between Europe and Asia,
created excess capacity, but this version is not supported by the
evidence.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0496" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0496"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan"> Sailing vessels could not use the Canal.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.76.2" class="koboSpan">Existing
steamships had been built for short routes through the Mediterranean Sea
or the Red Sea, and most of them were scrapped after the opening of the
Canal. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, after the opening of the Canal, there were
increases in net steamship production, which increased later in the
1870s with the introduction of the double expansion engine.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.76.4" class="koboSpan">The continued
steamship production is inconsistent with excess capacity.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">One alternative to
cooperation would be merger. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.77.2"
class="koboSpan">Merger is generally a substitute for collusion, but it
is not a perfect substitute because merger increases agency
costs.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0497" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0497"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan"> The
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_436"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">only known attempt to explicitly replace a conference
with a merger was the largely unsuccessful International Mercantile
Marine
Company.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0498" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0498"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">The Ocean Shipping
Reform Act of 1998 changed the treatment of conferences under American
antitrust law, effectively eliminating the ability of conferences to
control their members by mandating secret and independent action.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">EC regulation
4056/86, which gave conferences an exemption from EC competition law,
was repealed effective October 2008.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.82.3" class="koboSpan">Given that
agreements and mergers are substitutes, we should expect an increase in
industry concentration. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.82.4"
class="koboSpan">Sys</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0499" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0499"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that mergers have increased worldwide industry
concentration, using a wide variety of measures, including the Gini
coefficient and the Herfindahl index.</span>

## <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.85.2" class="koboSpan">Alternative Models of Agreements</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">Most work on shipping
conferences has involved four kinds of models: monopolistic cartels;
contestable markets; destructive competitive; and empty
cores.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0500" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0500"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan"> The argument that conferences are monopolistic cartels
is at least as old as Alfred
Marshall,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0501" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0501"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan"> who argued that conferences could act as monopolists
because there were substantial scale economies in the industry that led
to a small number of firms. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.90.2"
class="koboSpan">Lenin and the Marxist historian J.A.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.90.3" class="koboSpan">Hobson
described shipping conferences as vivid examples of the tendency toward
the concentration of
capital.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0502" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0502"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan"> The other explanations arose largely as responses to
the cartel model. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.92.2"
class="koboSpan">Destructive competition and its modern variant, the
empty core, are alternative explanations of why conferences exist.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.92.3" class="koboSpan">Contestable
markets have been used to criticise the proposition that conferences can
usefully be described as monopolistic cartels.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.92.4" class="koboSpan">This matters
for competition policy, because if conferences are not monopolising
cartels, then competition policy need not address them.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">Models of competition
are important for making sense of the role agreements play in liner
shipping, and seeing whether those insights can be generalised to other
industries. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.93.2"
class="koboSpan">They are also important for competition policy.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.93.3" class="koboSpan">Assuming that
competition authorities are attempting to increase
competition,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0503" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0503"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan"> it is important to establish whether a particular
practice reduces competition rather than having an alternative purpose.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">If it can be
established that a practice does not reduce competition, it needs no
further analysis for purposes of competition policy.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">The term “competition”
is routinely used vaguely, with differing and sometimes inconsistent
meanings. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
class="koboSpan">Sometimes it used simply to mean the number of sellers
(both as a measure of concentration and as a measure of how far to the
right the supply curve lies). </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.96.3"
class="koboSpan">Sometimes it is used to mean low measured
profitability,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0504" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0504"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan"> which is taken to mean the absence of monopoly and
monopoly profit. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.98.2"
class="koboSpan">Sometimes it is used to mean that buyers have good
substitutes; sometimes it is used simply to mean that the seller faces a
downward sloping, rather than perfectly inelastic demand curve.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">Rather than getting
absorbed in a semantic debate, it is simpler and more useful to think
about competition by the outcome: the mark-up of price over marginal
cost.</span>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Non-cooperative game-theoretic models of collusion: cartel enforcement</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">It is easy to get
involved in pointless and unproductive discussions about what it
“really” means to be a cartel. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.101.2"
class="koboSpan">It is simpler to simply define a cartel, following the
conventional
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_437"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">practice of economists, as an agreement that attempts
to get its members to act jointly as a monopolist.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">Agreements
that serve other purposes, such as preventing destructive competition,
reducing risk, or trade promotion, should simply be referred to as
such.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">In perfect
competition, output allocation is simple and automatic.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.103.2" class="koboSpan">Each seller
produces an output such that its marginal cost is equal to the market
price. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.103.3" class="koboSpan">In a
cartel, prices are increased, but output must be reduced.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.103.4" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
each firm’s output must be centrally directed.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.103.5" class="koboSpan">Each firm
produces an output such that marginal cost is less than the price,
giving each firm an incentive to raise output and upset the cartel
arrangement. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.103.6"
class="koboSpan">The primary problem for any monopolising cartel is
therefore enforcement. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.103.7"
class="koboSpan">Enforcement means that output increases must be
punished,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0505" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0505"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan"> but first they must be
detected.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0506" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0506"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">One argument
disputing the cartel explanation should be dispensed with quickly.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.107.2" class="koboSpan">A seller with
market power will raise price until its rivals’ products are good
substitutes. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.107.3"
class="koboSpan">(It will raise price until marginal cost equals
marginal revenue. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.107.4"
class="koboSpan">Positive marginal cost implies positive marginal
revenue, and positive marginal revenue implies an elastic demand.) The
frequent assertion that conferences cannot be monopolies or monopolistic
cartels because they face too many good
substitutes</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0507" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0507"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan"> may be the opposite: they face good substitutes
because they act monopolistically.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">A number of attempts
have been made to test whether shipping conferences can be explained by
cartel models. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.110.2"
class="koboSpan">Fox measured the effect of the number of firms in a
conference and a conference’s market share on freight
rates.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0508" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0508"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan"> She finds that freight rates fall when the conference
market share falls. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.112.2"
class="koboSpan">She also finds that as the number of conference members
rises, freight rates also fall, which is consistent with Stigler’s
theory of
oligopoly,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0509" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0509"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan"> specifically that increased numbers in a cartel
increase the cost of coordination and therefore lower price.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">In a separate paper,
Fox looked at the provision in the US Shipping Act of 1984 that allows
conference members to deviate from conference rates on ten days,
notice.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0510" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0510"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan"> A cartel model would predict that allowing independent
action, even though it is public rather than secret price cutting,
should undercut conferences because it makes enforcing the conference
tariff more difficult. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.117.2"
class="koboSpan">She fails, however, to find evidence that the Act made
any difference at all to conferences.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">Paul Clyde and James
Reitzes, in an ingenious study, distinguished between increased freight
rates because of increased conference market share and because of
increased market
concentration.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0511" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0511"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan"> They find statistically significant but economically
insignificant effects of increased market concentration on freight
rates, but, contrary to the results in Fox, no effect of increased
conference market shares on freight rates.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">It is worth
emphasising that focusing on price can be misleading.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.121.2" class="koboSpan">Conferences
can raise price because they restrict output (making shippers worse off)
or because they add value, thereby raising demand and raising output.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.121.3" class="koboSpan">A better test
would be to focus on the effect of conferences on output.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.121.4" class="koboSpan">Some insight
can be gained from a study of trans-Atlantic passenger shipping cartels
in the first decade of the twentieth
century.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0512" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0512"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan"> The authors estimated that westward migration fell by
20–25% because of the passenger cartels operating that decade.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">Deltas, Serfes, and
Sicotte took a historical approach, using a sample of 47 pre-World War I
conferences.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0513" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0513"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan"> They looked for reasons why a cartel might be easier
to negotiate and enforce, arguing that a cartel can then successfully
impose stricter, less flexible terms on its members.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.126.2" class="koboSpan">Enforcement is
easier if there is multi-market contact.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.126.3" class="koboSpan">The basic
intuition is that punishment for deviations from a cartel agreement in
one market can be carried out in several markets.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.126.4" class="koboSpan">It also argues
that enforcement is also
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_438"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan">easier if one or more of the firms has a large global
market share. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.127.2"
class="koboSpan">In that case, it is easier for the large firm to
transfer ships to a market to carry out punishment.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.127.3" class="koboSpan">Agreements are
easier to negotiate if there are a small number of firms and if there is
heterogeneity in size, allowing a large firm to dominate the agreement.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.127.4" class="koboSpan">A strict,
inflexible agreement is also more sustainable if entry is less
likely.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">This argument should
not be confused with the idea that a firm operating in multiple markets
can cross-subsidise predatory pricing to prevent destabilising entry.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.128.2" class="koboSpan">Gordon
Boyce</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0514" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0514"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">47</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan"> argues that because the International Mercantile
Marine (a combination of five transatlantic lines sponsored by J.P.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">Morgan formed
in the period 1900–1902) ran diversified lines from the UK to Canada,
the US, and Australasia, it could use cross-subsidization to harm
smaller, single route firms. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.130.3"
class="koboSpan">Boyce’s argument requires highly inefficient capital
markets, because both the predator and its victim are borrowing for a
price war. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.130.4" class="koboSpan">The
predator is merely borrowing from its own income
stream.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0515" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0515"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">48</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">A different approach
is to use developments in what has been called the New Empirical
Industrial Organization. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.132.2"
class="koboSpan">The approach can be seen in
</span><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0153"
id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0153"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 1</span></a><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0154"
id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0154"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></a><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.136.2"
class="koboSpan">In models of monopoly and of perfect competition, an
increase in demand raises price and output, and a decrease in demand
lowers both, as shown in </span>[<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0153)<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.138.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, the consequences of a rise or fall in demand
cannot separate the two models. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.138.3"
class="koboSpan">Suppose instead that</span>

<div id="Ch014.xhtml_fig0259" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00277.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1" /></span>

<a href="#Ch014.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0153"
id="Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0153"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></span></a>

</div>

<div id="Ch014.xhtml_fig0260" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00278.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2" /></span>

<a href="#Ch014.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0154"
id="Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0154"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></span></a>

</div>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_439"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">the demand rotates (becoming steeper or flatter).
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.143.2" class="koboSpan">In a model of
perfect competition, this does not raise or lower price or output.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.143.3" class="koboSpan">In a model of
monopoly, however, flattening the demand curve raises marginal revenue
relative to demand, thereby lowering price and raising output.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.143.4" class="koboSpan">Making demand
steeper lowers marginal revenue relative to demand, thereby raising
price and lowering output. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.143.5"
class="koboSpan">This can be seen in
</span>[<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0154)<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">Start by writing the
market demand curve as P(Q), so that price depends on quantity sold.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.146.2" class="koboSpan">The slope of
the demand curve is ΔP/ΔQ. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.146.3"
class="koboSpan">Marginal revenue is P + (ΔP/ΔQ)Q.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.146.4" class="koboSpan">The second
term is the difference between marginal revenue and price.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.146.5" class="koboSpan">Static
oligopoly models predict how much of that difference is
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">perceived</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan"> by sellers. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.148.2"
class="koboSpan">Let λ be the fraction of that difference that is
perceived by sellers. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.148.3"
class="koboSpan">The marginal revenue as perceived by sellers is P +
λ(ΔP/ΔQ)Q.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">Different oligopoly
models imply different values of λ.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.149.2" class="koboSpan">In monopoly,
the whole marginal revenue is perceived, so λ = 1.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.149.3" class="koboSpan">In perfect
competition (or Bertrand Nash equilibrium), none of the marginal revenue
is perceived (marginal revenue is simply market price), so λ = 0.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.149.4" class="koboSpan">In Cournot
Nash, the economist’s standard model of noncooperative equilibrium, λ is
the Hirshman-Herfindahl index (the sum of the squared market
shares).</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0516" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0516"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">49</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">The value of λ is
found by equating perceived marginal revenue to marginal cost.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.151.2" class="koboSpan">As a simple
example, suppose the demand curve is:</span>

<div id="Ch014.xhtml_fig0261" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00279.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">where P is price, Q
is output, and Z is a demand shifter.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.153.2" class="koboSpan">Note that the
slope of the demand curve is
β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan"> + β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">Z, so that Z can also rotate the demand curve, as in
</span>[<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0154)<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan"> above.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">Given the demand
equation, marginal revenue can be written as P +
(β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan"> + β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan">Z)Q, and therefore perceived marginal revenue can be
written as P + λ(β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan"> + β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan">Z)Q. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.168.2"
class="koboSpan">Write industry marginal cost as:</span>

<div id="Ch014.xhtml_fig0262" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00280.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">where W measures some
input
price.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0517" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0517"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">50</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan"> (If δ</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan"> = 0, then marginal cost is constant.) Profit is
maximised when perceived marginal revenue equals marginal cost, that is,
when:</span>

<div id="Ch014.xhtml_fig0263" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00281.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">Equation 1 (the
demand function) and equation 2 (the profit maximisation condition), can
be estimated jointly, and λ can be estimated from the ratio of the
coefficient of ZQ in equation 2 (–
λβ</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan">) to its coefficient in equation 1
(β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0518" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0518"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">51</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">One important
drawback to this approach is that the value of λ is not clearly
specified in a cartel model, and that poses a problem for measuring
whether agreements in liner shipping are cartel arrangements.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.182.2" class="koboSpan">A costlessly
enforced cartel would have λ = 1, that is, it would behave like a
monopolist. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.182.3" class="koboSpan">It
would equate industry marginal revenue to industry marginal cost.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.182.4" class="koboSpan">Note that
equating marginal revenue to marginal cost is the same as setting
marginal revenue minus marginal cost (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.182.5" class="koboSpan">marginal
profit) equal to zero. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.182.6"
class="koboSpan">At the industry profit maximum, a small increase in
output costs roughly zero
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_440"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">in profits. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.183.2"
class="koboSpan">Cartel enforcement is not costless, however, because
setting price above marginal cost gives cartel members an incentive to
cheat. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.183.3" class="koboSpan">At the
industry profit maximum, a small increase in output does not lower
profits, but preventing it incurs positive enforcement costs.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.183.4" class="koboSpan">It follows
that the cartel equilibrium involves higher output and lower price than
the monopoly
equilibrium.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0519" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0519"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">52</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan"> The economic theory of cartels tells us λ will be less
than one and greater than its non-cooperative equilibrium value, but
little beyond that. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.185.2"
class="koboSpan">Where it lies in between those two values depends on
the costs of cartel enforcement.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">These techniques
allow both a measure of the extent of competition in the market and a
way to test alternative theories of markets.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.186.2" class="koboSpan">Even though
cartel models do not make a specific prediction about the value of λ,
the models are good for estimating how, for example, various legislative
changes alter the value of λ. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.186.3"
class="koboSpan">Using these techniques, Wilson and
Casavant</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0520" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0520"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">53</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan"> offered evidence that the US Shipping Act of 1984
raised the value of λ (in other words, raised prices), except where the
Act explicitly allowed conference members to independently deviate from
conference rates, in which case it lowered λ (in other words, lowered
prices). </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.188.2"
class="koboSpan">Unfortunately, although this approach could tell us a
lot about the effect of regulation in the industry, Wilson and Casavant
are the only authors I am aware of who apply these techniques to liner
shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">Now that these
techniques are laid out in detail, there is scope for more formal
testing of a variety of questions about competition, including the
assumption that bulk shipping is best explained by models of perfect
competition.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0521" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0521"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">54</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Non-cooperative game-theoretic models of collusion: contestable markets</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">The theory of
contestable markets focuses heavily on sunk costs.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.192.2" class="koboSpan">It draws on
the insight that potential competitors are a constraint on pricing
behaviour as much as actual competitors.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.192.3" class="koboSpan">Suppose in a
market there are no sunk costs and incumbent firms do not respond to
entry by lowering prices. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.192.4"
class="koboSpan">Then entry is costless in the sense that all costs of
entry can be recovered on exit. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.192.5"
class="koboSpan">Entry is therefore riskless.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.192.6" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the
entrant can make its entry decision without regard to strategic
decisions by the incumbent.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">Suppose a market had
only one seller. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.193.2"
class="koboSpan">The seller could not act as a monopolist because an
entrant would undercut it. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.193.3"
class="koboSpan">If entry is costless, schemes to exclude entry do not
work because the entrant cannot be threatened with losses on entry.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.193.4" class="koboSpan">Should the
entrant face the prospect of losses, it can always costlessly depart
until the problem goes away.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">John Davies has
focused attention on the degree to which liner firms face sunk costs,
and the risks of retaliatory
price-cutting.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0522" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0522"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">55</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan"> He has provided evidence that sunk costs are low, and
that retaliation is slow. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.196.2"
class="koboSpan">That is, he has shown that the assumptions of
contestability are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan">roughly</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan"> satisfied by the liner market.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.198.2" class="koboSpan">If the liner
market is contestable, then conferences may have difficulty acting like
monopolising cartels. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.198.3"
class="koboSpan">Whatever service they provide, they must do so at
(economic) cost, lest they are uncut by
entry.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0523" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0523"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">56</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">An important,
unresolved difficulty is how sensitive contestable markets to deviations
from the assumptions of zero fixed costs and no retaliatory pricing.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.200.2" class="koboSpan">There are
theoretical grounds for believing that very small deviations from these
assumptions can have large consequences for
contestability,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0524" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0524"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">57</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan"> but little effort has been made to empirically
quantify the problem.</span>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_441"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">2.3 Destructive competition</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">Destructive
competition arguments come in two forms.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">The usual form
among maritime economists focuses on high sunk costs, inelastic demand,
and the risks to carriers of “overtonnaging” or excess capacity.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.204.3" class="koboSpan">(The next
section discusses another version, the theory of the core.) Daniel Marx
is the primary early
exponent,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0525" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0525"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">58</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the argument has been made by industry
practitioners.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0526" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0526"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">59</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan"> Maritime historians have tended to favour this
argument as
well.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0527" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0527"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">60</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan"> In this argument, because a large proportion of costs
is sunk, it follows that price would have to fall substantially before
sellers would leave the market. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.210.2"
class="koboSpan">Brooks argues:</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">“The high barriers to
exit give shipowners reasons to delay capacity reduction; unless prices
are good for scrap or the second-hand market is buoyant, there is a
tendency to hope that a redeployment opportunity will materialise or be
created. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.211.2" class="koboSpan">This
results in an industry with an almost perpetual state of capacity
oversupply.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0528" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0528"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">61</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">The assertion of high
exit barriers implies inelastic short run market supply.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.213.2" class="koboSpan">It is
frequently asserted that the demand for liner shipping services is
highly inelastic. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.213.3"
class="koboSpan">A combination of inelastic supply and demand leads to a
highly unstable price. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.213.4"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, carriers are exposed to increased risk of
losses, and shippers face substantial uncertainty about freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.213.5" class="koboSpan">On this
explanation, conferences offer reduced risk to both carriers and
shippers.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">This explanation
suffers from two serious
flaws.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0529" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0529"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">62</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan"> First, if fluctuating prices lead to periods of
losses, then they must also lead to periods of offsetting gains.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.216.2" class="koboSpan">Carriers will
not enter unless the risk-adjusted present value of profits is positive.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.216.3" class="koboSpan">If long run
changes in the market occur such that the present value of profits is
negative, firms will (efficiently) leave the market, and the losses are
their signal to do
so.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0530" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0530"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.217.1" class="koboSpan">63</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan"> Second, if shippers valued rate stability, they could
write forward contracts.</span>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">2.4 Cooperative game-theoretic models of collusion: the empty core</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">A more recent and
theoretically coherent revival of the idea of destructive competition is
the theory of the
core,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0531" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0531"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">64</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan"> which has been applied several times to
conferences</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0532" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0532"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">65</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
alliances.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0533" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0533"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">66</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.1" class="koboSpan">The theory of the
core focuses on avoidable fixed costs and the integer problem (the
number of firms in an industry must be an integer).
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.2" class="koboSpan">With avoidable
fixed costs and rising marginal cost, the relevant average cost curve is
U-shaped. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.3" class="koboSpan">No
output will be produced at any price below minimum average cost.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.4" class="koboSpan">When price
rises to a firm’s minimum average cost (p\*), that firm will enter at
the output q\* where average cost is minimised.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.5" class="koboSpan">The firm will
produce q ≥ q\* if p ≥ p\*. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.6"
class="koboSpan">Under perfect competition, the firm’s output will
therefore be either 0 or q ≥ q\*.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.7" class="koboSpan">Suppose firms
are identical. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.8"
class="koboSpan">Then at p\*, industry output must be an integer
multiple of q\* (the integer problem).
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.9" class="koboSpan">It would be
only by chance that demand at p\* would be an integer multiple of q\*.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.10" class="koboSpan">It is
therefore possible that demand and supply would not intersect.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.226.11" class="koboSpan">The problem
would go away if a firm were willing to produce a fraction of q\*, but
avoidable fixed costs mean that no firm could profitably do so.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_442"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan">If inventories were inexpensive, a firm could produce
only part of the time and provide a fraction of q\* with inventories.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.227.2" class="koboSpan">In
transportation industries especially, however, output is cargo or
passenger space. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.227.3"
class="koboSpan">Once the ship or airplane leaves, empty space is gone,
so inventories are
impossible.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0534" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0534"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">67</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan"> The only way to create inventories is to have excess
