capacity, which can lead to an empty core.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">The integer problem
does not necessarily lead to an empty core, but is likely to under some
circumstances. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.230.2"
class="koboSpan">Consider an example attributable to George
Bittlingmayer.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0535" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0535"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">68</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan"> Suppose taxis can carry at most two passengers, and
that the cost of a taxi trip is independent of whether there are zero,
one, or two passengers. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.232.2"
class="koboSpan">Admittedly, these assumptions are likely to be
factually inaccurate. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.232.3"
class="koboSpan">Most taxis can squeeze in an extra passenger in a
pinch, and extra passengers reduce mileage.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.232.4" class="koboSpan">These
assumptions, however, capture the same points that a more realistic but
also more complex model would. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.232.5"
class="koboSpan">First, there are some scale economies: once a taxi
carries one passenger, the marginal cost of a second is less than the
average cost. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.232.6"
class="koboSpan">Second, there are capacity constraints: marginal cost
exceeds average cost beyond some output.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">Assume each taxi’s
cost of a trip to the airport is £5, and that there are no sunk costs,
so the competitive supply of taxi trips is constant at £5 per trip.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.233.2" class="koboSpan">Assume as
well, for simplicity, that each possible passenger is willing to pay £10
for a taxi trip, so a taxi trip is efficient (relative to no trip) even
if there is only one passenger. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.233.3"
class="koboSpan">Suppose four people want to make a trip to the airport.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.233.4" class="koboSpan">They will take
two cabs, each with two passengers, and each pair of passengers will pay
£5. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.233.5" class="koboSpan">How they
divide the £5 cost between them is irrelevant to the problem.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.234.1" class="koboSpan">Suppose instead that
only three people, imaginatively named A, B, and C, want to make the
trip. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.234.2" class="koboSpan">The
efficient solution is for the three to take two taxis, generating a
surplus of 3 × £10 – 2 × £5 = £20.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.234.3" class="koboSpan">In this case,
however, the problem of dividing the £10 cost of the two taxis
eliminates the possibility of a competitive equilibrium.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.234.4" class="koboSpan">One
possibility is that A and B travel together, pay £2.50 each, and let C
travel alone and pay £5. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.234.5"
class="koboSpan">C, however, could offer to let A travel with him if A
pays £1. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.234.6" class="koboSpan">C is
better off, paying only £4 instead of £5, and A is better off, paying
only £1 instead of £2.50. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.234.7"
class="koboSpan">B is left, however, paying £5 instead of £2.50, leaving
B in the same position as C was originally to upset the
allocation.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">An equilibrium
allocation has to ensure that no coalition (A, B, or C alone, pairs of A
and B, A and C, or B and C, or the grand coalition of A, B, and C) can
do better by upsetting the existing allocation.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.235.2" class="koboSpan">If
X</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the surplus to customer i, i=A,B,C, then an
equilibrium allocation has to satisfy the following constraints:</span>

<div id="Ch014.xhtml_fig0264" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00282.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">The first constraint
states that any two passengers travelling together can get a combined
surplus of £15. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.239.2"
class="koboSpan">The second constraint states that the best all three
passengers can get is the surplus from the efficient solution of
travelling in two taxis. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.239.3"
class="koboSpan">Summing all three terms in the first constraint implies
that ΣX</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan"> ≥ £22.50, which is inconsistent with the second
constraint. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.241.2"
class="koboSpan">There is no equilibrium allocation.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.241.3" class="koboSpan">In this
example, q\*=2, and if demand is not a multiple of two, there is no
equilibrium.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">The absence of
equilibrium in market exchange poses a problem for the participants in
the market, both buyers and sellers, because it necessarily raises the
costs of contracting. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.242.2"
class="koboSpan">Sellers will try to protect themselves from the
consequences of the integer problem
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_443"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan">by selecting technology with lower capacity and higher
costs.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0536" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0536"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">69</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is therefore in the mutual interests of buyers and
sellers to find a way to achieve an allocation through non-market means.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.245.2" class="koboSpan">It remains
true that an individual buyer or seller has an incentive to disrupt the
allocation, just as in a cartel model.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.245.3" class="koboSpan">Unlike a
cartel model, however, buyers as a group do not have an incentive to
assist the deviating party.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">The example suggests
two of the more interesting implications of the model of the empty core.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.246.2" class="koboSpan">First, it is
worth noting that there are ways of resolving the problem.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.246.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
if the three passengers were friends, they might simply split the cost
three ways because an attempt by two of them to exclude the third would
result in the loss of a valuable friendship.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.246.4" class="koboSpan">Alternatively,
there might be a social custom, the violation of which would result in
being ostracised, dictating that in such cases there be some fair
division of the cost. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.246.5"
class="koboSpan">It is important, however, to recognise that these
methods of resolving the problem are not market solutions.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.246.6" class="koboSpan">This implies
that collusion may be a means of resolving the problem of an empty core,
although merger and vertical integration may be alternatives.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.246.7" class="koboSpan">Archibald,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0537" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0537"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">70</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan"> provide laboratory evidence that with high avoidable
costs, players formed cartels, and that those cartels produced more
efficient results than competition.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">Second, suppose there
were sunk entry costs. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.250.2"
class="koboSpan">Then the necessity of earning a return on the initial
sunk investment, aggravated by the prospect of facing the costs of an
empty core, would limit entry. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.250.3"
class="koboSpan">In the example, suppose there are only three taxis.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.250.4" class="koboSpan">Then there is
an empty core if demand is three or five, but not otherwise.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.250.5" class="koboSpan">If demand were
seven or greater, because capacity is only six, competition would drive
the price up to the reservation price of £10, and only six passengers
would travel. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.250.6"
class="koboSpan">The empty core would only occur when demand was low,
for example if the industry were in decline or if demand were a low draw
from a high variance distribution.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.251.1" class="koboSpan">Two systematic tests
of the empty core model have been made.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.251.2"
class="koboSpan">Sjostrom</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0538" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0538"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">71</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan"> focused primarily on demand conditions.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.253.2" class="koboSpan">Two important
results are that increased conference market share raises output and
that conferences are more dominant when demand is more variable, both
consistent with an empty core and contrary to a monopoly model.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.253.3" class="koboSpan">Sjostrom does
not specify the precise mechanism whereby increased share increases
output. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.253.4" class="koboSpan">Given
the results in the study by Clyde and
Reitzes</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0539" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0539"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan">72</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan"> that increased market share has trivially positive
effect on freight rates, the increased output presumably comes from less
costly contracting and more efficient production.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan">Pirrong</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0540" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0540"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">73</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan"> focuses on measuring the assumptions of the model,
providing evidence of rising marginal cost and U-shaped average cost
curves (implying fixed costs). </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.258.2"
class="koboSpan">With cost data from the routes to Europe from the North
and South Atlantic ports of the US, he estimates alternative cost
functions. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.258.3" class="koboSpan">Of
particular interest is his successful use of the semi-logarithmic cost
function, with the form (simplifying from Pirrong) lnC =
β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan">0</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan"> + β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan">Q, where C is total cost and Q is output.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.262.2" class="koboSpan">With
β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan"> \> 0, the marginal cost function is rising
(∂</span><sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">C/∂Q</span><sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan"> = β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub> <sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan">C \> 0) and the average cost function is U-shaped
\[∂(C/Q)/∂Q = (C/Q)(β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan">Q-1), which is negative if Q \<
1/β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.274.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan"> and positive if Q \<
1/β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan">\]. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.277.2"
class="koboSpan">Pirrong’s empirical results imply falling average cost
over a substantial range of output, which in turn implies that the
integer problem is significant. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.277.3"
class="koboSpan">He also discusses why the model implies the absence of
conferences in tramp shipping, which is consistent with only two
attempts, both unsuccessful, to form conferences in tramp
shipping.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0541" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0541"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">74</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">Empty core models
have been successfully applied to other industries as well, from
airlines,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0542" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0542"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">75</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.281.1"
class="koboSpan"> to cast iron
pipe,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0543" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0543"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">76</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan"> to the Australian tomato
industry.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0544" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0544"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">77</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan"> It has also been successfully applied more generally
to the problems of merger and
trusts,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0545" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0545"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">78</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan"> although there has been some empirical
dissent.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0546" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0546"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">79</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_444"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.289.2" class="koboSpan">Liner Shipping Practices</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.290.1" class="koboSpan">Three liner practices
have generated some controversy.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.290.2" class="koboSpan">Predatory
pricing and loyalty contracts are ways in which liners may have
attempted to preclude entry. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.290.3"
class="koboSpan">The effect of price discrimination on cartel stability
is more problematic. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.290.4"
class="koboSpan">In a cartel model, it is destabilising because it
attracts entry. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.290.5"
class="koboSpan">In an empty core model, it is a way of increasing
output when there are falling average costs.</span>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.291.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Predatory pricing</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.292.1" class="koboSpan">The most common
allegations of predatory pricing, especially in the early years of
conferences, revolved around the use of “fighting ships”.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.292.2" class="koboSpan">The conference
would, in response to an entrant, allegedly lower the rates on one of
its vessels to compete with the entrant until the entrant lost money and
left the market. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.292.3"
class="koboSpan">John McGee casts doubt on the use of fighting
ships,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0547" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0547"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">80</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan"> describing them as instances of normal competition,
but Basil
Yamey</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0548" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0548"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">81</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan"> cites the opinion in the 1891 decision by the law
lords in the House of Lords in the case of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">Mogul Steamship Co.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.297.2" class="koboSpan">v McGregor,
Gow & Co. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.297.3" class="koboSpan">et
al</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0549" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0549"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">82</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan"> for an example of the use of fighting
ships.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0550" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0550"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.301.1" class="koboSpan">83</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is not clear, however, from Yamey’s discussion
whether predatory pricing was successful in this instance.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.302.2" class="koboSpan">When, in 1885,
Mogul sent two ships to Hankow, an inland port on the Yang-tse River
(another non-conference firm sent a ship as well), the China conference
responded by sending ships to Hankow, inducing a fall in rates, which
the Court in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan">Mogul</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan"> described as unprofitable.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.304.2" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, the two Mogul ships and the third independent ship sailed
sufficiently full that they did not have to carry ballast (effectively
garbage carried to stabilise the ship when there is too little cargo),
whereas some of the conference ships sailed empty.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.304.3" class="koboSpan">Although Mogul
was not admitted to the China conference, it was given some landing
rights on the Yang-tse.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.305.1" class="koboSpan">wwo more recent
contributions have improved our understanding of the ways in which
conferences may have used predatory pricing to control entry.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.305.2" class="koboSpan">Fiona Scott
Morton, studying pre-World War I conferences, finds evidence supporting
the “long purse” theory of predation, whereby firms can profitably
engage in predation if their financial resources are large relative to
the
prey.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0551" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0551"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.306.1" class="koboSpan">84</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan"> A long purse theory requires that capital markets are
sufficiently costly that the prey cannot gain access to capital to
survive the price war, whereas the predator can, most likely because the
predator already owns larger liquid assets before the war
starts.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0552" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0552"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">85</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.309.1" class="koboSpan">In a later study with
the sociologist Joel
Podolny,</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0553" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0553"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">86</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan"> Scott Morton extended her earlier results primarily by
finding that entrants with high social status were less likely to be
preyed upon. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.311.2"
class="koboSpan">The social status of an entrant is used as a measure of
the extent to which an entrant could be relied upon to cooperate with
the conference. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.311.3"
class="koboSpan">They also show that the effect of social status
declined with the age of the entering firm.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.311.4" class="koboSpan">This is
consistent with the idea that information about a firm becomes more
public over time and therefore the conference had less need to rely on
social status as a proxy.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">These results are
consistent with Gordon Boyce’s
discussion</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0554" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0554"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">87</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan"> of the International Mercantile Marine (IMM), a
combination of five transatlantic lines sponsored by J.P.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.314.2" class="koboSpan">Morgan and
formed in the period 1900–1902. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.314.3"
class="koboSpan">The IMM had alliances with two German lines,
Norddeutscher Lloyd (NDL) and the Hamburg Amerika Line (HAPAG), with
whom it had a ten-year route allocation agreement.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.314.4" class="koboSpan">Boyce argued
that IMM’s connection to Morgan gave it access to “abundant
capital”.</span>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_445"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Loyalty contracts</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">Conferences used two
kinds of loyalty contracts: the deferred rebate and the dual rate
contract (sometimes called contract rates).
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.316.2" class="koboSpan">Under a dual
rate system, the shipper signs an agreement to deal exclusively with the
conference, and in turn receives a discount on the freight rate.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.316.3" class="koboSpan">If the shipper
uses a non-conference carrier, the conference imposes a fine.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.316.4" class="koboSpan">Under a
deferred rebate system, if the shipper deals exclusively with the
conference for, say, six months (the typically length of time), and then
deals exclusively with the conference for next six months, the shipper
receives a rebate of an agreed proportion of his freight bill from the
first six months. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.316.5"
class="koboSpan">The deferred rebate was a novel contract first
introduced successfully by the UK–Calcutta Conference in
1877</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0555" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0555"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">88</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.318.1"
class="koboSpan"> after being proposed in 1873 on the Yang-tse River
trade.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0556" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0556"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">89</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan"> The deferred rebate system was prohibited in US trades
by the 1916 Shipping Act.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.321.1" class="koboSpan">There are two
important distinctions between the two systems.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.321.2" class="koboSpan">First, under
the deferred rebate system, the shipper loses interest on the price cut.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.321.3" class="koboSpan">Second, the
conference incurs lower enforcement costs with the deferred rebate
because it does not have to enforce the fine by going to
court.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0557" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0557"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">90</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan"> Perhaps because of these differences, discounts under
deferred rebates tended to be larger than under dual rate contracts,
typically double the
size.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0558" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0558"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.324.1" class="koboSpan">91</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan"> Under both systems, the conference must incur the
costs of determining whether the contract has been broken, giving rise
to estimates of violations of the loyalty agreements of 5–15% of
shippers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0559" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0559"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.326.1" class="koboSpan">92</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan"> In a recent study, however, Pedro Marín and Richard
Sicotte used the event study technique to show that loyalty agreements
made significant contributions to
profitability.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0560" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0560"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">93</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.329.1" class="koboSpan">Whichever system a
conference used, deferred rebate and dual rate systems usually applied
to only certain commodities. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.329.2"
class="koboSpan">For example, the Far East Conference introduced the
deferred rebate when it was formed in 1879, but certain bulk commodities
such as rice and silk were excluded from the loyalty
arrangement.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0561" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0561"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.330.1" class="koboSpan">94</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
class="koboSpan"> Moreover, the loyalty requirement was typically waived
if the conference were unable to provide sufficient capacity within a
reasonable
time.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0562" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0562"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.332.1" class="koboSpan">95</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">Loyalty contracts are
designed to encourage customers to use a particular seller exclusively.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.333.2" class="koboSpan">The shipper is
charged a lower price in exchange for dealing exclusively with the
conference. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.333.3"
class="koboSpan">One question is whether they serve to exclude new
entry, or whether they serve to reduce costs by gaining economies of
regularity, such as easier planning.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.333.4" class="koboSpan">A second
question is, assuming they serve to exclude entry, whether such
exclusion is efficient.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.334.1" class="koboSpan">Under constant
marginal costs, loyalty contracts are an unprofitable method of
deterring entry. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.334.2"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, the customers who are most deterred from
dealing with the entrant are those the conference least wants to deter,
i.e. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.334.3" class="koboSpan">those
owed the largest
rebate.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0563" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0563"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">96</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan"> Nevertheless, they can exclude an entrant constrained
in its ability to offer a service of sufficiently high frequency to
satisfy shipper
demand.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0564" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0564"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">97</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan"> Loyalty contracts reduce uncertainty for conference
members by ensuring them a less variable flow of cargo, which is
particularly valuable given the cost structure that makes full ships
particularly
attractive.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0565" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0565"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">98</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.340.1"
class="koboSpan"> Because reduced uncertainty lowers costs and prices,
these arguments are consistent with evidence that shippers were
favourable to dual rate
contracts.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0566" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0566"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.341.1" class="koboSpan">99</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan"> The pre-World War I West Africa Conference used a
deferred rebate system, which small shippers favoured but large
shippers, who had better options to charter an entire ship,
opposed.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0567" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0567"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">100</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_446"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.344.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Price discrimination</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">Conference freight
tariffs for a long time were detailed and lengthy, with different
freight rates for each commodity shipped.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.345.2" class="koboSpan">An important
issue of contention is the extent to which those differing rates are the
consequence of cost differences or price discrimination.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.345.3" class="koboSpan">Differences in
cost could arise from,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.346.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.347.1" class="koboSpan">,
differences in density (called the stowage factor), difficulties in
handling the cargo, insurance, and the need for refrigeration.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.347.2" class="koboSpan">Differences in
transport demand elasticities could arise from differences in the costs
of waiting: more valuable and more readily perishable goods would bear a
higher freight rate for quick service.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.347.3" class="koboSpan">Even after the
widespread use of containers, which have made cargoes more homogeneous,
these tariffs have remained in effect.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">Allegations that
conferences price discriminate by charging higher freight rates to
higher valued commodities are of long standing.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.348.2" class="koboSpan">One claim is
that they are simply attempts to extract additional profits from a
monopoly
position.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0568" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0568"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.349.1" class="koboSpan">101</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan"> The alternative view is that conferences price
discriminate because the large element of fixed common costs requires
price discrimination to cover
costs.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0569" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0569"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.351.1" class="koboSpan">102</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.352.1" class="koboSpan">On the monopoly
interpretation, price discrimination is destabilising for the
conference. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.352.2"
class="koboSpan">Price discrimination makes entry more attractive
because entrants are encouraged to focus on the high priced end of the
market. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.352.3" class="koboSpan">The
conference sacrifices stability and durability in exchange for higher
profits now.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.353.1" class="koboSpan">On the common cost
interpretation, price discrimination increases the stability and
durability of the conference because it allows the conference to expand
output and therefore is in the joint interests of the conference and
shippers as a form of Ramsey
pricing.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0570" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0570"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.354.1" class="koboSpan">103</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.355.1" class="koboSpan">An important
difficulty is that Ramsey pricing is necessary only if marginal cost
prices do not cover costs, which means that firms are operating under
falling average costs. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.355.2"
class="koboSpan">This seems inconsistent with several firms in a
conference. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.355.3"
class="koboSpan">Having several firms all operating in the region of
falling average costs may be consistent with efficiency, although not
with perfect competition. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.355.4"
class="koboSpan">With U-shaped average cost curves, it is usually
efficient to bring in an additional producer at a level of demand lower
than that level necessary to bring the additional producer into the
market under
competition.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0571" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0571"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.356.1" class="koboSpan">104</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.357.1"
class="koboSpan"> U-shaped average cost curves capture the technology
problem, because they imply a range of output over which marginal cost
is less than average cost, so that marginal cost prices do not cover
total costs.</span>

<a href="#Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0155"
id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0155"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0572" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0572"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.359.1" class="koboSpan">105</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the easiest way to see this result.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.360.2" class="koboSpan">Demand is BB’.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.360.3"
class="koboSpan">MC</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan"> is industry marginal cost with one producer, and
MC</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan"> is industry marginal cost with two identical cal
producers (which assumes a cost minimising division of output between
the two producers). </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.364.2"
class="koboSpan">Average cost is U-shaped and reaches a minimum at
average cost AA’ and output L. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.364.3"
class="koboSpan">With one producer, efficient output is K.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.364.4" class="koboSpan">At that
output, total value (the area under the demand curve) is OBCK.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.364.5" class="koboSpan">The cost of
output L is OADL, and the cost of the extra output K-L is LDCK.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.364.6" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
total surplus is ABCD.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">With two producers,
efficient output is J, where demand intersects
MC</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.367.2"
class="koboSpan">Perfect competition cannot sustain that outcome because
with two producers, price would be below A, and price would not cover
average cost. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.367.3"
class="koboSpan">To see whether it is efficient to have two producers
rather than just one, first calculate total cost if output is J.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.367.4" class="koboSpan">With output H
(equal to 2L, because average cost is minimised for one producer at L
and for two producers at 2L = H), cost is OAGH (average cost times
output). </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.367.5" class="koboSpan">If
output is reduced from H to J, costs fall by JFGH (the area under the
marginal curve between</span>

<div id="Ch014.xhtml_fig0265" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00283.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3" /></span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_447"></span><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0155"
id="Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0155"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.369.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></span></a>

</div>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.370.1" class="koboSpan">J and H).
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.370.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
cost of output J is OAGFJ. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.370.3"
class="koboSpan">Total value is OBFJ (the area under the demand curve),
so net surplus is ABE – EFG. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.370.4"
class="koboSpan">The net gain in surplus from switching from one to two
producers is therefore CDE – EFG.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.370.5" class="koboSpan">It is
efficient to add a second producer if CDE \> EFG.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.370.6" class="koboSpan">To sustain a
second producer under perfect competition, demand must intersect
MC</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.371.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.372.1"
class="koboSpan"> at point G, and the area EFG equals zero.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.372.2" class="koboSpan">It follows
that it is efficient to bring in an additional producer at a lower level
of demand than would be supported by perfect competition.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.1" class="koboSpan">A number of attempts
have been made to find out whether conferences practice price
discrimination. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.2"
class="koboSpan">A number of attempts have been made to measure price
discrimination by regressing the freight rate for different commodities
against the price of the commodity and a group of variables intended to
capture differences in transport costs.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.3" class="koboSpan">The
fundamental difficulty is identifying variables that capture differences
in demand elasticities without also identifying differences in costs.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.4" class="koboSpan">A
statistically significant regression coefficient on commodity price is
usually asserted to be evidence of price discrimination.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.5" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately,
higher priced goods usually carry higher insurance costs and frequently
require more delicate handling. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.6"
class="koboSpan">To identify price discrimination, we would have to know
the (unknown) coefficient implied by these higher costs and look for
evidence of a higher coefficient.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.7" class="koboSpan">The cost
variables, moreover, might include price discrimination elements.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.8" class="koboSpan">For example,
refrigerated goods usually carry a higher freight rate.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.9" class="koboSpan">The higher
rate may the result of the extra costs of refrigeration, or the result
of the less elastic demand implied by the perishability of the goods.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.10" class="koboSpan">To complicate
matters, it could easily include both elements, so the model cannot
identify the separate effects. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.373.11"
class="koboSpan">A long series of
papers</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0573" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0573"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.374.1" class="koboSpan">106</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.375.1"
class="koboSpan"> have failed to answer this question because they
failed to tackle the identification problem.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.375.2" class="koboSpan">Two papers
have made attempts to solve this identification problem.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.376.1" class="koboSpan">Clyde and
Reitzes</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0574" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0574"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.377.1" class="koboSpan">107</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.378.1"
class="koboSpan"> have made an innovative attempt to separate the
effects of market power from cost differences by using panel data
(different commodities on
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_448"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.379.1"
class="koboSpan">fourteen routes over four years) in a fixed effects
model. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.379.2" class="koboSpan">By
using dummy variables for each commodity, they try to control for cost
differences. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.379.3"
class="koboSpan">The relevant part of their regression is
r</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.380.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.381.1"
class="koboSpan"> = β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.382.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan">s</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.384.1"
class="koboSpan">j</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.385.1"
class="koboSpan"> + β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.386.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.387.1"
class="koboSpan">s</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan">j</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.389.1"
class="koboSpan">p</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.390.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan">, where r</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.392.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the freight rate for commodity i on route j,
s</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.394.1" class="koboSpan">j
</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.395.1" class="koboSpan">is the
conference market share on route j, and
p</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.396.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.397.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the price of commodity i on route j.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.397.2" class="koboSpan">It follows
that ∂r</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.398.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.399.1"
class="koboSpan">/∂s</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.400.1"
class="koboSpan">j</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.401.1"
class="koboSpan"> = β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.402.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan"> + β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.405.1"
class="koboSpan">p</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.406.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.407.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.407.2"
class="koboSpan">If conferences are price discriminating, then a drop in
competition from independent carriers (an increase in
s</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.408.1"
class="koboSpan">j</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.409.1"
class="koboSpan">) will not only raise freight rates
(β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.411.1"
class="koboSpan"> \> 0), but will raise them more for higher valued
commodities (β</span><sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.412.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.413.1"
class="koboSpan"> \> 0). </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.413.2"
class="koboSpan">Clyde and Reitzes find no evidence for discriminatory
pricing.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.414.1" class="koboSpan">A recent paper by
Hummels, Lugovskyy, and
Skiba</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0575" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0575"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.415.1" class="koboSpan">108</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.416.1"
class="koboSpan"> tries to solve the problem by looking at changes in
import duties. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.416.2"
class="koboSpan">As product price rises, a given increase in the freight
rate produces a smaller proportional change in product price, so a
higher product price implies a less elastic transport demand.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.416.3" class="koboSpan">Changes in
import duties change the elasticity of transport demand without changing
transport costs, so they become a way to identify price discrimination.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.416.4" class="koboSpan">They find
substantial price discrimination, with a 1% increase in an import duty
raising freight rates 1–2%, and consequent substantial effects on
developing country trade.</span>

### <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.417.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Price and output fixing</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.418.1" class="koboSpan">Conferences not only
fix prices, they set both minimum and maximum outputs.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.418.2" class="koboSpan">It is much
easier to make sense of the role of maximum output rules.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.418.3" class="koboSpan">In a cartel
model, maximum output rules prevent price from falling to competitive
levels. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.418.4" class="koboSpan">In an
empty core model, a maximum output rule allows for efficient use of
capacity.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0576" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0576"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.419.1" class="koboSpan">109</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.420.1" class="koboSpan">Why though a minimum
output rule? </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.420.2"
class="koboSpan">One explanation consistent with both cartel and empty
core models is entry deterrence.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.420.3" class="koboSpan">Entry
deterrence is important in both cartel and monopoly models.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.420.4" class="koboSpan">In cartel
models, entry lowers price; in empty core models, entry destroys
equilibrium. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.420.5"
class="koboSpan">Fusillo</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0577" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0577"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.421.1" class="koboSpan">110</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.422.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Wu</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0578" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0578"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.423.1" class="koboSpan">111</span></a></sup><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.424.1"
class="koboSpan"> offer evidence that conference liners create excess
capacity for strategic entry deterrence.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.424.2" class="koboSpan">In an open
conference system, if conferences are successful in imposing entry
barriers to non-conference lines, the entrant may attempt to by-pass
those barriers by joining the conference.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.424.3" class="koboSpan">If the minimum
output is set high enough, the entrant may end up expanding capacity on
the route to unprofitable levels.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.424.4" class="koboSpan">This
limit-pricing strategy requires the conference to commit to the minimum
output rules by guaranteeing its sailing schedules.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.424.5" class="koboSpan">As with any
irreversible commitment, however, this would expose the conference to
the risks of a mistake. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.424.6"
class="koboSpan">An entrant might overestimate demand and therefore
mistakenly enter, leaving the conference with excess
capacity.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0579" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0579"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.425.1" class="koboSpan">112</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.426.1" class="koboSpan">Minimum output rules
are also consistent with the efficiency argument, raised in
</span>[<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.427.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch014.xhtml_cap_lbl0153)<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.428.1"
class="koboSpan"> in the previous section, that with large fixed costs,
it may be efficient to operate where marginal cost is below average
cost.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.429.1" class="koboSpan">Alternatively,
consistent with a cartel model, the minimum output rule may be a way of
excluding small, high cost sellers from the conference.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.429.2" class="koboSpan">The
willingness to adhere to a minimum output may be a way of signaling low
costs. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.429.3" class="koboSpan">Every
agreement has to ensure it is not eroded by attracting high cost
entrants.</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.430.1" class="koboSpan">Albert Ballin, the
managing director of the Hamburg-America Line (Hapag) wrote in
1914:</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.431.1" class="koboSpan">“Especially a very
strong and powerful party must continuously bear in mind the question,
whether the advantages of relying on the free interplay of market forces
would not
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_page_449"></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.432.1"
class="koboSpan">be far greater than the benefits from inhibiting
influence of a conference, which after all flow more to its weaker than
its stronger members.”</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.433.1" class="koboSpan">Hapag was at the time
the world’s largest shipping line.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.433.2" class="koboSpan">Although
Ballin was implying that Hapag was among the stronger, there is some
evidence that it was by no means the most profitable, which is
counter-evidence to the idea that minimum output quotas were about
excluding high cost
entrants.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0580" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0580"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.434.1" class="koboSpan">113</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.435.1" class="koboSpan">Revenue pooling can
be a method of sustaining price discrimination and preventing internal
cheating in a cartel. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.435.2"
class="koboSpan">It can also be a means of ensuring low cost production
by separating the decision about efficient output allocation from
individual firm
profitability.</span><sup><a href="#Ch014.xhtml_fn0581" id="Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0581"><span
id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.436.1" class="koboSpan">114</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.437.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.437.2" class="koboSpan">Concluding Remarks</span>

<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.438.1" class="koboSpan">Although our
understanding of cooperation in liner shipping has improved in recent
years, there is still much that remains a mystery.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.438.2" class="koboSpan">In particular,
research on strategic alliances remains largely descriptive and has not
expanded to the careful testing applied to other industries.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.438.3" class="koboSpan">Maritime
economists have much to keep them busy.</span>

[<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.439.1"
class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0467)<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.440.1"
class="koboSpan">Senior Lecturer in Economics, Centre for Policy
Studies, National University of Ireland, Cork.

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.958.1"
class="koboSpan">Journal of Law and
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.959.1"
class="koboSpan">, 23, 289–330.</span>

[<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.960.1"
class="koboSpan">113.</span>](#Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0580)<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.961.1"
class="koboSpan"> Broeze, F. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.961.2"
class="koboSpan">(1993): “Shipping policy and social-darwinism: Albert
Ballin and the weltpolitik of the Hamburg-America Line 1886–1914”,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.962.1"
class="koboSpan">The Mariner’s
Mirror</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.963.1" class="koboSpan">,
79, 419–436.</span>

[<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.964.1"
class="koboSpan">114.</span>](#Ch014.xhtml_bck_fn0581)<span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.965.1"
class="koboSpan"> Letwin, W. </span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.965.2"
class="koboSpan">(1965):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.966.1"
class="koboSpan">Law and Economic Policy in America: The Evolution of
the Sherman Antitrust Act</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.967.1"
class="koboSpan"> (Chicago: University of Chicago Press); Wilson, T.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.967.2" class="koboSpan">(1962):
“Restrictive Practices” in Miller, J.P.
</span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.967.3" class="koboSpan">(ed.),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.968.1"
class="koboSpan">Competition, Cartels and their Regulation
</span></span><span id="Ch014.xhtml_kobo.969.1"
class="koboSpan">(Amsterdam, North Holland).</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_457"></span>[<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 15</span>\
<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">The Response of Liner Shipping Companies to the Evolution of Global Supply Chain Management</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0348)
================================================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Trevor</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">D.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Heaver</span></span>
<a href="#Ch015.xhtml_fn0582" id="Ch015.xhtml_bck_fn0582"><span
id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">The purpose of this
chapter is to review developments in liner shipping in the light of the
evolution of concepts and practices associated with supply chain and
logistics management. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.8.2"
class="koboSpan">The long-term developments have featured the shift in
management philosophy away from managing functions individually to
managing them as linked components of supply chain business processes
(Lambert, 2001). </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.8.3"
class="koboSpan">This has had important implications for the
expectations of shippers and the service decisions of shipping
companies. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.8.4"
class="koboSpan">Recently, shippers have shifted their strategies and
priorities as a result of challenges in international logistics
associated first with the congested conditions in container trades,
especially in 2004–2005, and then with the recession of 2008 and
2009.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">For many years,
shipping lines were encouraged by their cost structure and the service
interests of shippers to extend their services through horizontal and
vertical corporate integration. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.9.2"
class="koboSpan">The horizontal integration was pursued through internal
growth, mergers and acquisitions and the on-going evolution of
alliances. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.9.3" class="koboSpan">The
vertical integration was achieved through shipping companies or the
corporations of which they are a part extending their services through
internal growth and acquisitions in three main areas.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.9.4" class="koboSpan">They are the
management of container terminals, the provision of intermodal services
and the provision of logistics services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.9.5" class="koboSpan">The relationship
of each of these services with the shipping activities deserves
individual attention.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">The extent and forms
of integration have varied over the years as the challenges and
opportunities for service suppliers have changed in the light of
economic conditions and the interests of shippers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
the trade boom and congested conditions of 2004–2005 brought to light
discontinuities in logistics management practices and
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_458"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan">in transportation capabilities associated, in
particular, with port hinterland connections.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">As a result,
attention has focused more than previously on the effective coordination
among operations in and related to ports irrespective of ownership.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.11.3" class="koboSpan">This makes it
appropriate to distinguish between the use of ‘integration’ referring to
corporate and related organisational relationships and “coordination”
referring to communication and operating relationships.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.11.4" class="koboSpan">This is to
avoid the use of “integration” for both common ownership and the
coordination of services and to give greater recognition to the
challenges of achieving effective coordination along logistics
chains.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">In this chapter the
evolving conditions in supply chain management and logistics are
reviewed. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">This
sets the stage to describe the responses of lines.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">Both the
horizontal and vertical restructuring of lines are covered but the
emphasis is on the latter. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.12.4"
class="koboSpan">This part of the chapter draws, in particular, on
Evangelista </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.14.2"
class="koboSpan">(2001) and Heaver (2002).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.14.3" class="koboSpan">Interpretation
of the patterns of relationships draws on the literature dealing with
supply chain management, out-sourcing and transaction cost economics.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.14.4" class="koboSpan">The evolving
organisational relationship between the shipping and logistics services
of lines is explored in the concluding part of the chapter.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.14.5" class="koboSpan">The interests
and conduct of shippers in the allocation of traffic among lines and in
the negotiation of liner rates and services appear vital to the
relationships of shipping with logistics services.</span>

## <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Evolving Conditions in Supply Chain Management and Logistics</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">Liner shipping is but
one of the myriads of service and product activities that are necessary
for the delivery of the goods and services required by consumers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">The
opportunities and challenges faced by the lines are affected by the
network environment in which they operate.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">As the
environment changes under technological, economic and political
conditions, so the lines have opportunities to follow strategies that
give them an advantage in serving customers needs.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.16.4" class="koboSpan">These
strategies have implications for the organisational structure of the
liner industry. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.16.5"
class="koboSpan">This section of the chapter starts by defining the
concepts of supply chain and logistics management and then proceeds to
examine the implications of customer needs and the associated challenges
and opportunities for shipping. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.16.6"
class="koboSpan">It concludes by describing some of the changes in the
logistics industry that affect the position of liner shipping
companies.</span>

### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 The definition of supply chain management and logistics management</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">The advance of more
integrated approaches to the management of intra-corporate and
inter-corporate relationships is well documented (Hall and Braithwaite,
2001). </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">Even
though Hall and Braithwaite suggest “there is little point in seeking to
document a perfect definition for supply chain management”, a definition
is useful as it captures the importance of coordination.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.18.3" class="koboSpan">Mentzer
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.20.2"
class="koboSpan">(2001) define supply chain management as: “the
systematic, strategic coordination of the traditional business functions
and the tactics across these business functions within a particular
company and across businesses within the supply chain, for the purposes
of improving the long-term performance of the individual companies and
the supply chain as a
whole.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch015.xhtml_fn0583" id="Ch015.xhtml_bck_fn0583"><span
id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan"> That the “chains” referred to are more likely
“networks” of private and public goods and services
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_459"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">providers distributed globally is one of the possible
shifts in the terminology that, fortunately, is generally treated as too
esoteric to worry about.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Supply chain
management is the wide framework within which logistics functions.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">The definition
of logistics by the US Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals,
formerly the Council of Logistics Management, reflects this.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.24.3" class="koboSpan">The definition
is: “Logistics is that part of the supply chain process that plans,
implements, and controls the efficient, effective forward and reverse
flow and storage of goods, services, and related information between the
point of origin and the point-of-consumption in order to meet customers’
requirements.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch015.xhtml_fn0584" id="Ch015.xhtml_bck_fn0584"><span
id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan"> It recognises that logistics management is only a part
of the supply chain.</span>

### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Customer needs and the challenges and opportunities for liner shipping</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">Global improvements in
logistics performance have contributed to and been required by increased
competition in product markets. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.28.2"
class="koboSpan">The reduction of tariff and other trade barriers,
improvements in the efficiency of transport services and the increased
value and reduced weight of many products have all contributed to the
ability of products from distant locations to compete locally.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">Multi-national
firms that used to be organised with regional marketing and production
divisions switched to product-based supply chains that source and market
globally. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.28.4"
class="koboSpan">Spatial competition (the competition in common markets
for products from far away) is more important now than ever
before.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Increased competition
heightens pressures for the redesign of supply chains and logistics
systems. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.29.2" class="koboSpan">The
competition drives the need to reduce costs while, at the same time,
maintaining or improving service levels.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.29.3" class="koboSpan">While the
actions taken to reduce costs and to improve services work concurrently
and dynamically, it is convenient to describe them individually.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.29.4" class="koboSpan">Such actions
are considered next, prior to considering their implications for
shipping lines.</span>

#### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">2.2.1 Developments in logistics</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">Four strategies
provide examples of the central role for logistics in improving supply
chain performance. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.31.2"
class="koboSpan">They are: sourcing in low-cost locations; just-in-time
delivery; postponement; and improving supply chain visibility.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan">Sourcing in low-cost locations:
</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan">Industries have always made trade-offs among alternate
locations based on the benefits of locating close to low cost resource
inputs compared with the benefits of proximity to markets.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">Typically,
industries in which labour costs are high gravitate to low wage-cost
locations. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.33.3" class="koboSpan">The
ability of firms to do this is dependent on efficient logistics services
to get products to where they are needed.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.33.4" class="koboSpan">Examples of the
pull of low cost production are the shift of manufacturing textile,
footwear, automobile, electronic and toy products to Asia, particularly
China. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.33.5" class="koboSpan">However,
the attractiveness of shifting to low-cost production locations has
decreased recently if logistics conditions for those locations have not
been compatible with the operation of manufacturing and retailing with
low inventories. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.33.6"
class="koboSpan">For example, the changing pattern of activities in the
hard disk drive industry in Asia has been affected by various aspects of
time responsiveness, including transit and order cycle times (McKendrick
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">., 2000). </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.35.2"
class="koboSpan">Similarly, the location and role of facilities of the
Taiwanese computer manufacturer
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_460"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">Acer reflects the trade off between costs of
manufacture and assembly in Asia and the time of delivering product to
consumers (Nemoto and Kawashima, 2000).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.36.2" class="koboSpan">The congestion
experienced in ports in 2005 and the need for quicker responsiveness in
supply chains made evident during the 2008–2009 recession have increased
the value placed on shorter and more diversified supply chains.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.36.3" class="koboSpan">Shippers remain
attracted to low cost locations but have become more alert to the
logistics disadvantages that they may imply for their supply
chains.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">Just-in-time delivery:
</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">The
concept of just-in-time delivery (JIT) has been a major reason for the
redesign of logistics systems. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.38.2"
class="koboSpan">The successful use of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">kanban</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan"> system in the Japanese automobile industry had a major
influence on all industries around the world as they have shifted to new
delivery systems. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.40.2"
class="koboSpan">JIT is just one approach to reducing inventories in
supply chains through frequent, small quantity and highly reliable
deliveries. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.40.3"
class="koboSpan">These deliveries are timed to respond to immediate user
needs; the products are pulled through the supply chain by demand.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.40.4" class="koboSpan">This is a major
difference to the time when goods were produced in long, low-cost runs
based on forecasts well ahead of demand.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.40.5" class="koboSpan">When
manufacturers are the immediate recipients of goods, terms such as lean
manufacturing are used to describe the new environment.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.40.6" class="koboSpan">When the
recipients are retailers, the term lean retailing may be used.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">For these systems to
work effectively transportation services must be reliable; delivery is
required at precise times. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.41.2"
class="koboSpan">Many systems are also built on short lead times,
thereby placing requirements for premium transportation or geographical
proximity of the supplier to the user.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.41.3" class="koboSpan">However, the
benefits of reliability as an attribute of transportation which reduces
inventory costs are fundamental in logistics.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.41.4" class="koboSpan">The
consequences of relatively low reliability and the long transit times
generally associated with liner shipping have received heightened
attention as a result of the congestion of 2004–2005 and then the need
for agile responses to the recession of 2008–2009.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan">Postponement:
</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">The
strategy of postponement involves the delay of processes.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.43.2" class="koboSpan">Manufacture of
products may be delayed until a customer places an order; this is most
likely when product manufacture or assembly can be done quickly.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.43.3" class="koboSpan">More
frequently, undifferentiated products are held in a centralised
inventory, thereby reducing the total inventory held and the costs built
into it. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.43.4" class="koboSpan">When
more information is obtained about demand, differentiating processes can
be performed whether the final manufacture of a product, the labelling
to national market requirements or simply shipping to one market rather
than another.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">For products with
highly uncertain demand, the ability to defer production until as much
as possible is known about demand is especially advantageous.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.44.2" class="koboSpan">Thus, the
geographical shifts of manufacturing in the textile industry reflect the
predictability of demand for particular product groups.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.44.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
increased manufacture of fashion textiles has taken place in the
Caribbean and Central America at the expense of Asia as time to North
American customer has assumed greater importance (Abernathy
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">., 2001). </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.46.2"
class="koboSpan">Similarly, the efforts of the automobile industry to
provide individual car buyers with the style, colour and options they
desire within ever-shorter times and at reasonable cost requires a
responsive supply chain. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.46.3"
class="koboSpan">The nature of trade-offs can be illustrated with an
example.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">Car seats are usually
assembled close to the auto assembly plants, for the obvious reason that
their bulk makes them expensive to transport.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
manufacture of components of seats may be more widely distributed, for
example in the manufacture of leather seat covers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.47.3" class="koboSpan">This
manufacturing is labour intensive.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.47.4" class="koboSpan">As a result,
production
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_461"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">is found in Asia often using imported materials.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.2" class="koboSpan">The finished
covers may be shipped back by sea container.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.3" class="koboSpan">Products of
good quality have been produced in systems that have had long though
precise round-trip cycles. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.4"
class="koboSpan">However, the pressures to give car buyers choice and
fast delivery, at reasonable cost, is difficult for such a supply chain.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.5" class="koboSpan">To achieve the
responsiveness to meet variable demands without excessive inventory
close to auto markets requires a much more flexible logistics system.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.6" class="koboSpan">In the absence
of forecasts of demand long enough in advance, some seat covers, at
least, may have to be sent by airfreight.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.7" class="koboSpan">The difference
in costs between sea and airfreight is such that the viability of
exports from Asia is threatened. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.8"
class="koboSpan">The challenge increases the competitiveness of
alternate locations with low labour costs closer to the major markets,
for example, Eastern Europe for Western Europe and Mexico or the
Caribbean for North America. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.48.9"
class="koboSpan">A general consequence for consumers if effective supply
solutions are not found is that the range of options available in short
times becomes limited.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">Supply chain visibility:
</span></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">Reductions in the order cycle and delivery lead times
have been achieved through many changes in the design and operation of
supply chains and logistics systems.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.50.2" class="koboSpan">Vital
contributions to the changes have been made by the developments in
information and communications technologies (ICT).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">Notable has
been the transfer of data and other information resulting in reduced
order cycle times. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.50.4"
class="koboSpan">However, another vital benefit of ICT systems is
enhanced supply chain visibility.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Firms are striving to
achieve better visibility, forwards and backwards, along their supply
chains. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">Forward
information reveals point of sale information from bar code scanning,
shared real time or frequently through automatic electronic
transmission. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.51.3"
class="koboSpan">This allows members of supply chains to make quick and
consistent decisions (with different levels of sophistication among
supply chains) about replenishment based on common information.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.51.4" class="koboSpan">It enables the
use of cost-effective methods such as Manufacturing Resource Planning or
Continuous Replenishment Planning and avoids the violent fluctuations of
inventories associated with sequential and delayed information provided
along disjointed supply chains (Forrester, 1958).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.51.5" class="koboSpan">Visibility
backward along supply chains enables receivers to be fully aware of the
status of orders so that early actions can be taken to minimise costs
associated with delays in supplies or with changes in requirements.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.51.6" class="koboSpan">The visibility
of the status of purchase orders from the time they are placed until
goods are delivered is one of the competitive services offered by major
logistics service companies. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.51.7"
class="koboSpan">Visibility is a key benefit at the heart of
increasingly sophisticated supply chain software.</span>

#### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">2.2.2 Challenges and opportunities for liner shipping</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">Each of the strategies
described above is associated with a range of changes in the
characteristics of supply chains and logistics systems.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">These create
challenges and opportunities for shipping lines.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Relationships among
supply chain participants tend to be closer.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">To achieve
this, buyers seek to use fewer suppliers of particular goods and
services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.54.3" class="koboSpan">For
shipping lines and other carriers, this means that shares of shippers’
business are larger but go to fewer firms.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.54.4" class="koboSpan">One of the
attributes desired by shippers as they develop closer relationships with
fewer lines is that those lines have an extensive service network able,
therefore, to serve them in various trade lanes.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.54.5" class="koboSpan">The pressure on
lines is to develop more extensive service networks.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">The reduction of time
is becoming a more important logistics strategy to reduce costs and to
improve customer service. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.55.2"
class="koboSpan">Hummels estimates that for manufactured goods imported
into the US each day of travel is worth an average of 0.8% of the value
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_462"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">of the good and that each day in transit reduces the
probability of a country as a source by 1.5% (Hummels, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">The related
feature is the greater attention to reliability of products and
processes. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.3" class="koboSpan">The
costs of “disruptions,” whether associated with variations in demand,
logistics or supplier performance warrant close attention (Levy, 1995).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.4" class="koboSpan">The effects of
disruptions are particularly great when lead times are long, even with
good information systems, hence the importance of the unanticipated
congestion in 2005. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.5"
class="koboSpan">Greater recognition of the costs of disruptions
discourages strategies of reliance on low-cost long supply chains and
encourages the use of a variety of sources and the use of, at least,
some shorter, faster supply chains.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.6" class="koboSpan">More local
sourcing, the use of improved IT and of expedited logistics services are
encouraged. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.7" class="koboSpan">The
liner shipping industry faces prospects of a diminishing role, at least
in percentage terms, in international trade if the threat of congestion
were to remain. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.8"
class="koboSpan">The competitive advantages accruing to lines offering
short reliable transit times would increase.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.9" class="koboSpan">These are lines
on short routes, with fast ships and with related services that ensure
fast and reliable door-to-door service.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.56.10" class="koboSpan">Whether the
heightened value of short transit times would be sufficient to create a
market to support new fast ships in ocean services remains to be
seen.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">In pricing their
services, lines face heightened competitive conditions.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.57.2" class="koboSpan">The competition
for market share is increased by the traffic allocation strategies of
shippers, the legislative weakening of conferences and the rapid
increase in capacity resulting from the new generations of larger ships.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.57.3" class="koboSpan">The competitive
mix has also been affected by the entrance into international logistics,
including the services using liner shipping, of the integrated carriers
such as United Parcel Service (UPS) and FedEx.
