</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.57.4" class="koboSpan">Also, shippers
have available to them a widening range of manufacturing locations and
logistics strategies that place limits on the rates chargeable by lines
on particular routes.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">These changed
conditions create opportunities for the lines that respond well.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.58.2" class="koboSpan">Notably, the
strategies of lines to ensure faster, more reliable services are
resulting in greater attention to the coordination of operations along
the logistics chain and to on-going shifts in the span of activities in
which the shipping lines are engaged.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.58.3" class="koboSpan">Striving to
provide enhanced customer service is taking lines into additional
service areas and redefining relationships in international logistics
service. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.58.4" class="koboSpan">Before
examining the position of shipping companies in other services, it is
appropriate to examine developments in the logistics services
sector.</span>

### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">2.3 Changes in the logistics industry</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">It is customary for
firms with small volumes of international traffic destined for or
originating in a foreign country to use a freight forwarder.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">Freight
forwarders have long been specialists in arranging the transportation,
storage and handling of goods along with associated documentation
activities between and within
countries.</span><sup><a href="#Ch015.xhtml_fn0585" id="Ch015.xhtml_bck_fn0585"><span
id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan"> They manage the activities through their own offices
and through those of partners. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.62.2"
class="koboSpan">They may act as agents in arranging transportation or
act as a non-vessel owning common carrier (NVOCC) co-loading freight
onto a shipping line’s vessel and issuing their own bill of lading.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.62.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
DHL provides this service as Danmar Lines.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.62.4" class="koboSpan">In the trade of
countries with highly specialised logistics and transportation
conditions, even large firms with substantial volumes of trade into the
country have traditionally sought the assistance of such
specialists.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">The increased demand
for logistics services in the last 20 years has arisen with the growth
of global supply chains and the greater use of outsourcing for logistics
services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_463"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan">The result has been the creation of a multi-faceted,
large and complex logistics services industry.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.2" class="koboSpan">It has evolved
from various bases the most important of which has been the traditional
freight forwarding firms, the largest of which commenced from European
roots and had a wide international presence for most of the twentieth
century. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.3" class="koboSpan">They
were present in most continents but had varied intensities and relied on
partners in some countries. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.4"
class="koboSpan">In the last two decades they have increased the number
of countries in which they have a direct presence and have increased the
intensity of their presence in most countries.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.5" class="koboSpan">They have
generally done this by acquisitions and mergers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.6" class="koboSpan">In 2008, the
Swiss-based Kuehne & Nagel had an invoiced turnover of US\$20.3 billion
(CHF21.6 at CHF1 is US\$.94) of which US\$9.4 billion was for sea
freight services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.7"
class="koboSpan">In 2008, Panalpina also Swiss-based, had revenue from
its forwarding services of US\$10.0 billion (CHF10.6 at CHF1 is
US\$.94). </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.8" class="koboSpan">The
other leading European forwarders Danzas and Schenker are now owned by
Deutsche Post and Deutsche Bahn respectively.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.9" class="koboSpan">Deutsche Post
acquired Danzas in 1998 and branded its forwarding and logistics
services as the Danzas Group but following the acquisition of DHL (and
Exel) in 2005, it branded the services as DHL Global Forwarding and DHL
Freight. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.10" class="koboSpan">In
2008, Deutsche Post World Net reported revenue from forwarding, freight
and supply chain services as US\$41 billion (€27.9 billion at €1 is
US\$1.47). </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.11"
class="koboSpan">Express services had revenue of US\$20.0 billion.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.12" class="koboSpan">Deutsche Bahn
acquired Schenker in 2002 (and Bax Global in 2005) and conducts its
global business under DB Schenker Logistics.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.64.13" class="koboSpan">In 2008, DB
Schenker Logistics had revenue of US\$21.6 billion (€14.7 billion at €1
is US\$1.47).</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">The logistics services
industry has also experienced growth from firms with previously more
specialised businesses. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.2"
class="koboSpan">They include domestic transportation and warehousing
companies, courier and parcel services and liner shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">Particularly in
North America, changes occurred in transportation and logistics services
in response to the opportunities and challenges associated with the
growth of companies, the deregulation of the transportation industry and
the heightened service demands of evolving supply chain management
practices. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.4"
class="koboSpan">Contract logistics suppliers have developed to take
advantage of the interests of some large companies to out-source
logistics activities. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.5"
class="koboSpan">The best examples of these new third party logistics
providers in the US are Schneider Logistics and Ryder Logistics, which
expanded into logistics from trucking operations, and C.H.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.6" class="koboSpan">Robinson that
had a produce warehousing base. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.7"
class="koboSpan">These companies have subsequently expanded into
international logistics and supply chain services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.8" class="koboSpan">However, while
the firms are substantial in total, as public companies Ryder System and
C.H. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.9" class="koboSpan">Robinson
Worldwide reported revenues of US\$6.2 billion and US\$8.6 billion
respectively, their international revenues are still modest.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.65.10" class="koboSpan">This is
identifiable for Ryder in 2008 as US\$800 million, which is one half of
the company’s Supply Chain Solutions revenue.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">Companies in the
express and parcel businesses have also added logistics and freight
services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">UPS
expanded into international logistics services rapidly since it acquired
Menlo Worldwide Forwarding in 2004 and incorporated it into a newly
formed UPS Supply Chain Solutions.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">In 2008, the
revenue from Supply Chain Solutions and Freight was US\$8.9 billion and
from the international package business was US\$11.3 billion.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.66.4" class="koboSpan">(Revenue from
domestic packages was US\$31.3 billion.) FedEx has also expanded its
portfolio of services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.66.5"
class="koboSpan">In 2000, FedEx acquired Tower Group International, a
leader in the business of international logistics and trade information
technology and used this as the core of its new FedEx Trade Networks.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.66.6" class="koboSpan">In 2008, FedEx
Trade Networks initiated its first ocean-ground distribution service
with a service from Asia to the
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_464"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">US West Coast. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.67.2"
class="koboSpan">(In 2008, the total value of FedEx international
business was US\$8.5 billion compared with US\$27 billion of domestic
revenue.)</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, shipping
lines have made a significant entry into logistics services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">Responding to
the interests of shippers to deal with fewer suppliers and to outsource
logistics activities, most liner companies had introduced some logistics
services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.3"
class="koboSpan">However, the lines providing the most substantial
logistics service remain those that were the entry leaders between 1970
and 1980 serving the interests of importers of manufactured goods from
Asia. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.4" class="koboSpan">Importers
of Asian goods felt the need for better assistance in managing the flow
of imports. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.5" class="koboSpan">The
value of imports from Asia was increasing and the shipping lines were
interested in extending their range of services to customers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.6" class="koboSpan">The result was
the development of consolidation services, most notably initially by
Sea-Land (1970, known as Buyers), Maersk (1977, known as Mercantile),
and American President Lines (1980, known as American Consolidation
Services \[ACS\]). </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.7"
class="koboSpan">The services differed in some important respects from
the balanced directional services offered by freight forwarders.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.8" class="koboSpan">They were
focused on the needs of importers from Asia for monitoring the movement
of goods to consolidation points, managing the consolidation of goods
and shipping according to the specifications of the buyers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.9" class="koboSpan">The companies
were aided in the development of these services by existing familiarity
with the buyers’ needs through their shipping services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.68.10" class="koboSpan">They were able
to offer consolidation services with high visibility by utilizing their
existing links with the shipping lines’ documentation processes.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">Subsequently, these
and other shipping lines entered into logistics services with optimism
for a greater rate of growth of logistics than liner shipping; however,
they have remained a modest part of the companies’ business.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">The development
of these businesses is reviewed later.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">For all of the
logistics services companies, growth has also been marked by a shift of
suppliers’ strategies from being asset driven to being knowledge driven.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.70.2" class="koboSpan">An essential
component of the knowledge base is built around ICT.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.70.3" class="koboSpan">Traditional
freight forwarders have generally lagged behind new logistics service
companies in the use of ICT technologies.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.70.4" class="koboSpan">However,
increasingly, all logistics companies are introducing web-based
capabilities so that shippers can perform activities on line, including
arranging shipments and accessing information about the status of their
shipments. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.70.5" class="koboSpan">In
addition to the benefits for shippers of being able to track their
shipments, the resulting database becomes an integral tool for them to
plan, budget, forecast, negotiate, and manage their businesses.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.70.6" class="koboSpan">The
capabilities are being provided through proprietary systems and through
shared portals. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.70.7"
class="koboSpan">The trade literature is replete with logistics
companies adding to their ICT capabilities.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">Utilising their
information-based systems and specialised knowledge, the logistics
service companies have assumed greater supply chain and logistics chain
design and management responsibilities characteristic of 3PL
services.</span>

## <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.72.2" class="koboSpan">The Horizontal and Vertical Restructuring of Lines</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping lines have
faced pressures in the changing market place to expand their services
geographically and to widen the range of services offered.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">The response of
lines has differed depending on their views of market opportunities,
their resource base in terms of their financial resources, the initial
geographical extent of their services, the
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_465"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">range and level of supporting services, especially in
information technology, and the depth and breadth of their human
resources.</span>

### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 The horizontal restructuring of liner shipping</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">As large shippers have
followed supply chain strategies involving the use of fewer suppliers,
they have placed heightened value on the extent of the network of
services offered by liner companies.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.76.2" class="koboSpan">This is the
primary reason given by American President Line (APL) in 1995 for the
introduction of its first service from Asia to Europe through a
slot-charter agreement. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">The new service was a significant shift in APL’s policy
as up to that time it had a Pacific-only service strategy.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.76.4" class="koboSpan">The shift of
major lines to global networks is a major reason for the increased
concentration in liner shipping on a global basis.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.76.5" class="koboSpan">However, on a
route basis, the actual markets for shipping services, there has not
been an increased concentration although the 2008–2009 recession has led
to more vessel sharing agreements between lines.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">The strategies of
lines in extending the network of their services have been covered
extensively in the literature and feature prominently elsewhere in this
book. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">The
addition of routes by lines has been dominantly by slot charter,
alliance and merger or acquisition rather than the extension of own
services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.77.3" class="koboSpan">These
methods limit the need for new investments while extending route
networks and avoid reductions in the density of traffic in relation to
infrastructure costs by route, an important consideration in network
industries.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">There has been
speculation that the growth of global carriers will lead to the
development of global contracting for services by major shippers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">However, it
does not appear that global contracts are common even though shippers
have a preference for dealing with fewer carriers and, therefore, with
carriers with large networks. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.78.3"
class="koboSpan">Contracts still appear to be related mainly to traffic
volumes and service conditions by route.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.78.4" class="koboSpan">This is not to
say that in negotiations, traffic volumes and conditions across routes
are irrelevant. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.78.5"
class="koboSpan">Simply, there is no evidence so far that the more
global orientation of logistics is having a major effect on shipping
beyond encouraging the geographical expansion of companies’ services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.78.6" class="koboSpan">It is possible
that the legal end of liner conferences in European trades on 18
October, 2008 may lead to greater interest in multi-route contracts, but
given the prior existence of confidential contracts, the influence is
not likely to be strong. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.78.7"
class="koboSpan">Also, the interest in many global companies in 2009 to
increase responsiveness in their business by shifting to regional rather
than global responsibilities is consistent with route rather than global
negotiations. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.78.8"
class="koboSpan">The effects of logistics on the vertical structure of
the industry are more prominent.</span>

### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 The vertical restructuring of liner shipping</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">The vertical structure
of liner shipping has been affected by developments in logistics in a
number of ways. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.80.2"
class="koboSpan">The interests of shippers in dealing with fewer
suppliers have influenced lines to extend the vertical reach of their
services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.80.3" class="koboSpan">The
interests of shippers in faster and more reliable services have not only
affected the design of shipping services but also the relationship among
the services necessary to deliver value to shippers, for example, by
door-to-door services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.80.4"
class="koboSpan">The interests of shippers in outsourcing logistics
services have created an opportunity for shipping lines (and others) to
expand their third-party logistics services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.80.5" class="koboSpan">The expansion
of lines into services beyond shipping has
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_466"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">lead to greater vertical integration in the industry
but the organisational relationships vary with the nature of activities
and the interests of shippers in those activities.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.81.2" class="koboSpan">The added
services common in shipping are divided into three.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.81.3" class="koboSpan">They are
terminal operations, intermodal services and logistics services.</span>

#### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">3.2.1 Involvement in terminal management</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">Container terminals
are providing mainly intermediate services in international logistics.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">They are
designed to ensure the fast and efficient transfer of containers at hub
terminals in shipping networks and at throughput terminals for transfer
to inland carriers. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.83.3"
class="koboSpan">On-dock cargo-handling services, such as container
stuffing and de-stuffing, that might be requested by shippers have
become an insignificant part of the modern terminal business.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.83.4" class="koboSpan">The terminals
view their main customers as the shipping lines as the contracts with
them are the single largest determinant of their business volume.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.83.5" class="koboSpan">However, in the
long run, the success of terminals is dependent not only on how
efficiently they serve the ships but also the efficiency of the closely
related on-dock operations and the connections with inland carriers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.83.6" class="koboSpan">Efficient
terminal operation is measured by the speed and reliability with which
containers can be moved through terminals at a competitive cost in order
to meet the logistics needs of shippers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.83.7" class="koboSpan">Terminals must
have levels of capacity and performance compatible with the
same-day-of-the-week services of shipping lines.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.83.8" class="koboSpan">Increasingly,
they need to be able to tailor their operations to serve the
differentiated needs of shippers for expedited movement inland,
including boxes moving in time-defined services.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">Traditionally, the
port authority or a stevedoring company local to the port or region
managed port terminals. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.84.2"
class="koboSpan">However, starting with the introduction of
containerisation and the focus on customer service by Malcolm McLean of
Sea-Land Services in the US in the 1970s, the interest of large lines in
dedicated terminals has increased.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.84.3" class="koboSpan">For companies
with a sufficient volume of traffic, dedicated terminals were seen to
provide better opportunities to coordinate the operating philosophy and
day-to-day operations of vessels, terminals and inland transportation.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.84.4" class="koboSpan">Sea-Land, for
example, required containers to be placed on chassis on terminals and
not grounded. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.84.5"
class="koboSpan">Dedicated terminals are intended to serve the vessels
of a parent company. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.84.6"
class="koboSpan">However, when surplus capacity exists (berth time slots
and on-dock capacity) other lines may be served.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">Dedicated terminals
became common first in the US, in part because of the philosophy of
Sea-Land. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.85.2"
class="koboSpan">Elsewhere, concerns of governments and public port
authorities about the effects of dedicated terminals on competition led
to policies that inhibited dedicated terminals.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.85.3" class="koboSpan">In the 1990s,
the shortage of capital available to port authorities, the general
increase in privatisation and greater interest in intermodal
developments, resulted in a change in attitudes so that dedicated
terminals are now commonplace. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.85.4"
class="koboSpan">Given the importance of a close operating philosophy
and of operating practices between a line and its terminal, it is not
surprising that lines with dedicated terminals often began by managing
those terminals as units integrated with the shipping line.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.85.5" class="koboSpan">Only
occasionally did some lines contract with specialised terminal
management companies for the management of their terminals leased
long-term to them by port authorities.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">The rapid growth of
container shipping and the concurrent need for more capital investment
in ports created new opportunities in terminal management.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.86.2" class="koboSpan">In part, the
need was met by shipping lines entering into the terminal management
business, initially to serve primarily their own needs.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.86.3" class="koboSpan">Companies such
as Sea-Land, APL and Maersk continued for a number of years to manage
these terminals within the framework of
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_467"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan">their shipping lines.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">However, some
lines, as they developed their expertise, soon sought advantage for
these terminal enterprises as successful profit centres by expanding
into the terminal operating business serving others.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.87.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
P&O Steam Navigation Co., which had a 50% interest in P&O Nedlloyd,
established P&O Ports. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.87.4"
class="koboSpan">Orient Overseas International Ltd (OOIL), which owns
Orient Overseas Container Line (OOCL) managed four ports through a
Terminal Investment unit (the terminals were in Vancouver, New Jersey,
New York and Venice) although it retained two container terminals
operated as a part of and for OOCL.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.87.5" class="koboSpan">These were in
Kaohsiung and Long Beach.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">Subsequently, other
shipping companies have increased the separation of their lines from
terminal management. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.2"
class="koboSpan">In 2001, A.P. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.3"
class="koboSpan">Moller made its Maersk Ports, which was the terminal
operating company for the dedicated terminals of Maersk Sealand (Maersk
acquired Sea-Land in 1999) a stand alone unit known as APM Terminals
(Economics Intelligence Unit, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.4" class="koboSpan">The objective
of APM Terminals was “to strive for excellence in terminal management
while actively seeking new opportunities in port and terminal
development” (Economics Intelligence Unit, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.5" class="koboSpan">A.P.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.6" class="koboSpan">Moller saw its
terminal management business as having a scale warranting a stand alone
status and it anticipated that its substantial business with Maersk
Sealand (then 90% of its throughput) would not jeopardise its position
with other lines. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.7"
class="koboSpan">APM Terminals subsequent growth and the growth of
traffic of other carriers to 38% in 2008 attests to the validity of the
A.P. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.8" class="koboSpan">Moller
position. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.88.9" class="koboSpan">In
2008, APM Terminals was the fourth largest container terminal operator
in the world with 34 million TEUs handled.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">More recently, other
shipping lines have separated off their terminal businesses.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.89.2" class="koboSpan">In 2006, OOIL
announced the sale of its four container terminals to Ontario Teachers’
Pension Plan Board (The Standard, 2006).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.89.3" class="koboSpan">It saw the
US\$2.35 billion as yielding benefits greater than those of ownership.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.89.4" class="koboSpan">In 2008,
Neptune Orient Lines established three separate business units, APL (the
container line), APL Logistics and APL Terminals to facilitate Terminals
expanding its business in new locations (Container Management, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.89.5" class="koboSpan">The
implications of these changed relationships are considered later.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">The greatest change in
terminal management has been the growth of terminal management companies
as these firms have responded to the need for more capital investment in
ports to serve the growth in port businesses.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">Some companies,
such as Seattle-based SSA Marine, formerly Stevedoring Services of
America, provide terminal management services to a variety of types of
terminals, although container terminals are important to the company.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.90.3" class="koboSpan">However, the
dominant global companies in the industry focus on container terminal
management as the container business has been the leading growth sector
in ports.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">The leading container
terminal management companies today are Hutchison Port Holdings of
Hutchison Whampoa, PSA International (PSA) and DP World which handled
67.6 million, 63.2 million and 46.8 million TEUs respectively in 2008.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">DP World’s
sudden emergence as a global player after the founding of Dubai Ports
International only in 1999 is largely the result of acquisitions, CSX
World Terminals in 2005 and P&O Ports in 2006.</span>

#### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">3.2.2 Involvement in intermodal services</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">Traditionally, the
business of shipping lines was the movement of cargo on a port-to-port
basis. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">This may
still be true of smaller lines competing on a low-cost strategy and is
necessary for most or all lines in regions in which intermodal movements
are
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_468"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">impractical. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.94.2"
class="koboSpan">However, in Europe and in North America all the major
lines now offer door-to-door service.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.94.3" class="koboSpan">The
door-to-door services are designed to make available to shippers
reliable fast service through a single supplier.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping lines have
largely provided inland transport, so called carrier haulage, (the
alternative is ‘merchant haulage’ whether arranged by a shipper or
freight forwarder) through the purchase of inland transport.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">It has been
done mainly through a combination of long-term contracts and short-term
purchases under the responsibility of a group within the shipping
business, such as Maersk Intermodal at Maersk.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.95.3" class="koboSpan">Some lines own
some trucking capacity. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.95.4"
class="koboSpan">The incidence of carrier haulage varies from region to
region depending on the length of the inland movement, the
characteristics of the inland transport industry and the role of freight
forwarders in the trade.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping lines were
leaders in the development of rail intermodal services in North America
and are now playing leading roles in Europe and China because they have
been in a better position than freight forwarders to commit for the
volume of traffic necessary to make dedicated rail service viable under
long-term contracts. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
class="koboSpan">The need for direct ownership of rail services is
greater in Europe than elsewhere because of the domination of that
industry by state-owned passenger-oriented railways.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.96.3" class="koboSpan">However, under
the current deregulated environment in Europe, there are more
opportunities for services such as the Maersk-owned European Rail
Shuttle (ERS), started by other shipping lines in 1994, to play key
roles in intermodal services.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">The extension of
shipping lines into intermodal services was consistent with the
logistics needs of shippers and facilitated by the transaction economies
enjoyed by the lines and the effectiveness for coordinating operations.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.97.2" class="koboSpan">Shippers remain
free to select the port-to-port or the door-to-door service.</span>

#### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">3.2.3 Involvement in logistics services</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">Unlike intermodal
services which are managed within the shipping business, the conduct of
logistics services is largely done in independent business units,
although these are frequently branded to carry the group name.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
Mercantile and Buyers were joined as Maersk Logistics and ACS became APL
Logistics. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.99.3"
class="koboSpan">Other shipping companies added such units, for example
Cosco Logistics and NYK Logistics, but not all lines have adopted this
as a global initiative. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.99.4"
class="koboSpan">For example, Evergreen which had formerly focused its
strategy on excellence in meeting shippers’ requirements through their
shipping and door-to-door service capabilities, announced, in June 2002,
that it would invest in forwarding and logistics in Asia and South
America. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.99.5" class="koboSpan">In
2007, it established Evergreen Logistics Corp offering a full range of
logistics services in China, North America and Europe.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">The early development
of logistics services by lines was in locations in which the lines had
particular knowledge. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">For P&O, Nedlloyd and Maersk, the early services were
developed to serve mainly European shippers, for APL and Sea-Land to
serve the needs of US shippers. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.100.3"
class="koboSpan">Subsequently, however, the lines saw value-added
services in logistics as offering faster growth and better profitability
than shipping. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.100.4"
class="koboSpan">The developments at APL, P&O Nedlloyd and Maersk
Sealand reflect the past and current interests of these lines in
logistics. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.100.5"
class="koboSpan">There has been a great change in expectations in less
than ten years.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">Following its
acquisition of APL in 1997, NOL reorganised its logistics services into
APL Logistics (APLL) to advance its strategy of rapid growth in the
logistics area. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.101.2"
class="koboSpan">APLL was then the fastest-growing business unit in the
NOL Group. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.101.3" class="koboSpan">Its
growth
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_469"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">in 2001 was 72% reflecting the acquisition of GATX
Logistics, the second largest warehouse-based contract logistics company
in the US. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">The
acquisition enabled APLL to serve customers more effectively through the
primary (importing) and secondary (national) distribution phases of the
supply chain. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.102.3"
class="koboSpan">Flemming Jacobs, the President of NOL stated that he
wanted “the logistics business to challenge the Liner business as a
major breadwinner of the Group”.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.102.4" class="koboSpan">In 2001, liner
revenues were US\$3.6 billion, logistics revenues were US\$723 millions.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.102.5" class="koboSpan">The Annual
report for 2008 shows APL revenue as US\$7.9 billion and APL Logistics
revenue as US\$1.3 billion, so that the percentage of logistics to
shipping revenue has declined from 20.1 to 16.5%.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">With the acquisition
of Sea-Land, A. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.103.2"
class="koboSpan">P. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.103.3"
class="koboSpan">Moller also re-branded its logistics services, naming
it Maersk Logistics (ML) but it left the management independent of the
shipping line. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.103.4"
class="koboSpan">ML’s mission was to be an independent organisation
operating worldwide through locally incorporated companies.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.103.5" class="koboSpan">It is engaged
in satisfying customers’ expectations in respect of competitive,
international export and import management services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.103.6" class="koboSpan">It is largely
a non-asset-owning company managing its quality through the careful
selection of subcontractors. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.103.7"
class="koboSpan">It has offices in 93 countries.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">The A.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">P.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.104.3" class="koboSpan">Moller Group
has been less open than NOL about the role expected of ML within the
Group. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.104.4"
class="koboSpan">However, Soren Brandt, the head of ML, noted, “the
logistics activity could grow to outperform those of the liner, but it
will take a while” (Le Lloyd, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.104.5" class="koboSpan">He also
characterised the shipping and logistics businesses “as distinct
businesses.” </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.104.6"
class="koboSpan">ML made a number of acquisitions during 2001 of which
the largest was the US-based Distribution Services Limited (DSL) which
had offices in 60 countries and 1,500 employees, compared with ML’s
3,500 employees. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.104.7"
class="koboSpan">Wal-Mart was one of DSL’s major clients (Maersk
Logistics, 2001).</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">In 2005, Maersk
acquired the freight forwarding business Damco as a part of the
acquisition of P&O Nedlloyd. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.105.2"
class="koboSpan">In 2007, Maersk Logistics’ air freight and landside
services and its DSL Star Express was renamed “Damco”.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.105.3" class="koboSpan">In its 5 June
2009 News Release, Maersk announced that it will merge its supply chain
management activities branded as Maersk Logistics and its freight
forwarding activities branded as Damco, under the single brand name
“Damco”. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.105.4" class="koboSpan">Thus
Maersk has returned to the strategy of a separate branding for its
shipping and logistics-related businesses.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">The experience of the
now defunct P&O Steam Navigation Co.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">(P&O), the
senior company that held the 50% interest in P&O Nedlloyd, with
logistics management is still instructive.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">Most of the
logistics services of P&O were in different businesses from P&O Nedlloyd
but one was integral to the shipping business.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.4" class="koboSpan">When P&O
Nedlloyd was created by the merger, it brought together the previously
separately identified Global Logistics and some logistics services that
had evolved as ancillary to shipping activities.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.5" class="koboSpan">The new group
was named Value Added Services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.6"
class="koboSpan">It was intended to work with P&O Nedlloyd customers in
providing advanced logistics or supply chain management services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.7" class="koboSpan">Intermodal
transport arrangements were not the responsibility of VAS; they were
managed within shipping services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.8" class="koboSpan">P&O Nedlloyd
was attempting to bridge the gaps of different personnel skills and
backgrounds among its own employees in shipping and VAS.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.9" class="koboSpan">It had one
sales force, which it hoped would develop effective contact levels with
clients to deal with shipping and logistics interests.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.106.10" class="koboSpan">It expected
to identify effectively those clients for whom an integrated approach of
a line with its logistics service was practical and attractive.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">P&O did not follow
this model only. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.107.2"
class="koboSpan">It had three other logistics service groups that
operated quite separately from the shipping services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.107.3" class="koboSpan">Damco, a
separate but
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_470"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan">wholly-owned subsidiary of P&O Nedlloyd, engaged in
freight forwarding with its own offices in nine countries in NW Europe
and the Far East and with partnerships with local forwarding agents in a
further 40 countries. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.108.2"
class="koboSpan">P&O also owned P&O Trans European, a European-based
logistics service company, and Cold Logistics, which specialised in
serving the cold-product sector globally.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.108.3" class="koboSpan">The Chairman
of P&O in his message to shareholders in the 1999 Annual Report notes
that the company’s logistics services are “high growth, high return
businesses” and that “the ongoing P&O would focus on its high return
logistics activities.”</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">With the exception of
VAS, the logistics businesses of these companies were organised as
corporate units quite separate from shipping.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">A major reason
for this was the expectation of shippers that logistics service
providers (LSPs) act independently of interests in carriers when
choosing modes of transport and carriers to meet shippers’ logistics
needs. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.109.3" class="koboSpan">Thus,
even though logistics units may be branded with the name of the shipping
corporation, their executives pointed to the independence of those units
in selecting carriers.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">There were also
operating conditions relevant to the level of integration.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">Executives of
VAS recognised that the skills and outlooks of managers in consignor and
consignee firms generally differed between those responsible for the
management of transportation services and those responsible for the
management of supply chains. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.110.3"
class="koboSpan">VAS hoped that the differences would lessen and an
integrated approach would become possible.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.110.4" class="koboSpan">However, in
June 2002, P&O Nedlloyd announced the reorganisation of VAS into P&O
Nedlloyd Logistics. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.110.5"
class="koboSpan">The experiment was over.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">In spite of the
organisation of logistics units as separate structures, the actual level
and ways of sharing resources and information between the business units
remains uncertain. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.111.2"
class="koboSpan">The utilisation of common information systems provides
economies. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.111.3"
class="koboSpan">However, it is in the sharing of market intelligence
that uncertainty about relationships exists.</span>

## <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.112.2" class="koboSpan">Assessment of the Organisational Structure</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">Examination of the
attributes of the relationships of shipping with each of the three
services described above provides insights into the probable future of
the organisational structures. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.113.2"
class="koboSpan">The structure of each of the services is considered in
turn.</span>

### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 The organisation structure for terminal management</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">A line may prefer a
dedicated terminal so that it can ensure harmonisation of operating
practices through its network of operations.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.115.2" class="koboSpan">This was the
original reason that Sea-Land operated with dedicated terminals.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.115.3" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
Maersk’s interest in a dedicated terminal in Rotterdam in 2000 is
believed to have been based on its preference for operating practices
that allow for the flexibility in throughput rates it expects of its
terminals. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.115.4"
class="koboSpan">Also, the development of well-integrated ICT can be
facilitated through dedicated terminals.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.115.5" class="koboSpan">Thus, terminal
management by a line can be efficient when a line has a sufficient
volume of traffic to achieve an economic utilisation of the terminal
capacity and the line has a network of routes and terminals to achieve
economies of scale and proficiency in terminal management.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.115.6" class="koboSpan">Alternatively,
a line may contract a terminal management company to operate a terminal
on its behalf.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore, it can be
argued that dedicated terminals operated as a component of the shipping
line can be consistent with efficiency and coordination between the
shipping
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_471"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan">and terminal operations.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">Benefits can
be achieved without raising conflicts with the immediate interests of
shippers as terminals provide intermediate services in the process of
moving containers between inland and ocean transport.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.117.3" class="koboSpan">Shippers
retain the choice of arrangements for the movement of goods to and from
terminals.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">Concerns that
dedicated terminals may reduce competition between shipping services
have diminished as overall trade has grown and competition among lines
and routings has increased. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.118.2"
class="koboSpan">Lines and shippers have effective choices as long as
one or two of the major terminal management companies do not gain too
much control in a port range. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.118.3"
class="koboSpan">The protection of competition is not about dedicated
terminals but about the number of terminals controlled by one or two
terminal companies in a port range.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">While dedicated
terminals remain common, recent experience, for example APL and Mearsk,
has been for the management of lines and terminals to be treated as
separate businesses. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.119.2"
class="koboSpan">This allows the terminal management to focus more
effectively on commercial opportunities in its business.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.119.3" class="koboSpan">Further, the
evolution of terminal management has been associated with increased
sophistication and in many ways more standardised basic approaches as
terminals strive to increase throughputs through space-restricted
terminals. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.119.4" class="koboSpan">The
result is that the benefits for a line of operating its own terminals in
close association with its line may be less now than formerly.</span>

### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 The organisation structure for intermodal services</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">The case for the
close involvement of a shipping line in intermodal services is
comparable to that for terminals, except for two factors.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.121.2" class="koboSpan">First, the
diversity of traffic flows and modes would make it difficult for a
single agent to invest in, contract for and arrange all inland moves.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.121.3" class="koboSpan">The business
is heterogeneous so that control of all inland movements by lines is
impractical. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.121.4"
class="koboSpan">Second, the diversity of shipper interests in the
nature of inland transport arrangements means that the right of choice
is important for shippers to ensure that the right mix of service,
control and cost are preserved. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.121.5"
class="koboSpan">Whether the efficient coordination of the inland
transportation into the supply chain processes is achieved best by use
of carrier or merchant haulage (a “traditional” freight forwarding
function) is best left to the choice of shippers.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">However, shipping
lines can have an advantage over shippers and freight forwarders in
arranging intermodal transport services when the ability to commit
volumes of traffic is important to the viability of a service.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">This has been
the case with the introduction of dedicated trains and certain barge
services where reliable volume commitments are important.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.122.3" class="koboSpan">These are
situations in which there are economies of scale.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">The arrangement of
intermodal services by shipping lines has been a way for them to provide
door-to-door pricing and to provide a single responsibility along
logistics chains with good visibility.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.123.2" class="koboSpan">It has
provided a competitive service to the freight forwarders offering
door-to-door services as NVOCCs.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.123.3" class="koboSpan">However, the
needs of shippers have changed over time with the evolution of global
supply chain management. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.123.4"
class="koboSpan">The result has been some new responses from the lines
to coordinate shipping and inland transport services.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">The recession of 2001
resulted in surplus liner capacity and pressure on freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">It came at a
time when there was concern that container shipping service had become
so commoditised, so similar among lines, that competition was based on
price. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.124.3" class="koboSpan">In
March 2002, C.C. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.124.4"
class="koboSpan">Tung, the chief executive office of OOCL, expressed
concern about competition among “commoditised” shipping services as
contributing to the reduction of rates.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.124.5" class="koboSpan">To avoid
“over-commoditization” he urged “offering value-added products”
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_472"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan">(American Shipper, 2002).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">Earlier in
2001, the president of NOL, Flemming Jacobs, said that “Shippers and
ocean carriers are ‘confused’ when they focus on narrow yearly
negotiations on freight rates, instead of looking for opportunities to
increase overall supply chain efficiencies” (American Shipper, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.125.3" class="koboSpan">He went on “I
am going to give a wake-up call to those who still get their kicks from
yearly, or even more frequent, fights over freight rates with their
ocean carriers – those who just cannot wait for the 1st of May to come
around and who derive the greatest satisfaction from succeeding in
squeezing another \$50 from the carriers, even though in the process
they miss tons of opportunities in the total supply chain.”</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">The subsequent
expansion of global supply chains gave rise to the congestion problems
of 2004–2005. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.126.2"
class="koboSpan">The pressures on shipping capacity were severely
aggravated by congestion inland from ports.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.126.3" class="koboSpan">Traffic was
backed up so that terminals became congested.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.126.4" class="koboSpan">Shippers
responded subsequently by adopting new strategies to reduce the risks of
service failures. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.126.5"
class="koboSpan">They included extending the peak by shipping earlier,
using a greater number of shipping routes and negotiating new provisions
in confidential contracts with lines.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">One of the responses
of lines has been to consider services publicised with guaranteed
delivery times, an approach made more relevant in the international
market by the presence of the international package and freight services
and their logistics services such as UPS Supply Chain Solutions and
FedEx Trade Networks. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.127.2"
class="koboSpan">However, the provision of a truly guaranteed service
requires priority treatment for freight at port terminals, for vessel
space and for intermodal connections.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.127.3" class="koboSpan">In 2006, APL
Logistics was the first line to offer a port-to-door time guaranteed
less-than-container (LCL) service from China into the USA, with Con-way
Freight performing the inland carriage in the USA.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.127.4" class="koboSpan">The ocean
carrier is APL (Shippingline.biz, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.127.5" class="koboSpan">Japan, South
Korea, Singapore and Taiwan were added as origins in 2007 and Mexico was
added as a destination in 2009. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.127.6"
class="koboSpan">In 2008, a full-container guaranteed service was
introduced from China to the USA (3PL wire, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.127.7" class="koboSpan">The services
require not only new segmented operating practise in terminals and for
container handling on and off vessels but, also, new types of agreements
with specific intermodal carriers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.127.8" class="koboSpan">In 2009,
Hanjin and MOL have introduced time-guaranteed services on routes from
Asia to the US West Coast with distribution in the USA being handled by
Old Dominion Freight Line and the railway company BNSF,
respectively.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">The time-guaranteed
services are the latest evidence of lines and their associated
businesses working together to design and operate services that can
provide more reliable services to shippers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.128.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
examples also show that the design and operation of a well-coordinated
service does not require common ownership.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">Concurrently, other
lines have increased their attention to service reliability without the
introduction of service guarantees.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">Whether the
costs of differentiation turn out to be worthwhile and appropriate for
more lines depends on the size of the market segment for the premium
service. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">A
study by Kouvelis and Li (2009) identifies that there is a market niche
but its size and profitability remains to be determined.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.129.4" class="koboSpan">Whether this
form of service differentiation becomes a major strategy of lines in the
future, as suggested in a report by IBM Institute for Business Value
(2005), remains to be seen.</span>

### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 The organisation structure for logistics services</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">The organisation
structure appropriate to the relationships of logistics services with
shipping lines involves more issues than the relationships considered so
far for terminals
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_473"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan">and intermodal services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">The range and
scale of logistics functions affect the potential for economies from
integrated management and the interests of shippers in dealing with
integrated or separate service providers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.132.3" class="koboSpan">The
appropriate market structure is one that reflects the potential for
economies of scale and scope in integrated management and the interests
of shippers in their management of logistics and shipping service
purchases.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">Small shippers have
long used freight forwarders because of the rate and service benefits
that forwarders can provide through the consolidated volume they
control. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">New
LSPs can offer similar services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">For small
shippers, then, that do not have the volume of traffic to negotiate
effectively with shipping lines, the relationship of the LSP with the
shipping line is not important. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.133.4"
class="koboSpan">They have the ability to choose among the different
types of service offerings.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">Large shippers are in
a different position. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.134.2"
class="koboSpan">They have become more interested in outsourcing more
aspects of logistics to LSPs. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.134.3"
class="koboSpan">The LSPs may be relatively new to the logistics
business, as are some of the new “independents”, or they may be linked
to transportation companies or they may have a long history in freight
forwarding. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.134.4"
class="koboSpan">Large shippers do have volumes of traffic that enable
them to negotiate contract rates with lines so that the choice of
negotiating separate logistics and shipping services is relevant to
them. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.134.5"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, it is appropriate to ask do large shippers
negotiate rates and traffic allocations with shipping lines or do they
use LSPs offering integrated logistics and transportation services at
integrated rates?</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">It appears, based on
discussions with a few shippers, carriers and writers on the liner
shipping business that large shippers prefer to retain responsibility
for the negotiation of liner rates and the allocation of traffic among
lines. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.135.2"
class="koboSpan">Although there are undoubtedly exceptions to this, they
appear to be very infrequent and their incidence has been little
affected by the trade uncertainties of recent years.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.135.3" class="koboSpan">The reason for
shippers retaining responsibility for negotiating rates with lines can
be accounted for by four factors.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.135.4" class="koboSpan">They are: the
quality of the logistics chain; the value transportation services
negotiated; the nature of the negotiations; and tradition.</span>

#### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.1 The quality of the logistics chain</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">The value of the
quality of service required in a logistics chain is important to the
structure of the chain. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.137.2"
class="koboSpan">Chains in which time-sensitivity is high may require
“managed delivery” under tightly prescribed conditions.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.137.3" class="koboSpan">The efficiency
of delivering time-sensitive products may be improved by placing the
transport and inventory management with a single management and with a
single price for the services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.137.4"
class="koboSpan">Examples are: the just-in-time delivery of automobile
parts to an assembly plant involving both trucking and parts management;
and the international delivery and inventory management of computer
components by a courier company.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.137.5" class="koboSpan">In these
cases, the design of separate functions into an integrated service is
the business equivalent of the creation of a mixture in chemistry.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.137.6" class="koboSpan">The
characteristics of the mixture can be varied through different
proportions to serve particular purposes but the mixture is more
valuable than the component parts separately.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">The liner shipping
function by its nature is not as tightly bound to other logistics
activities as trucking or air transport in the examples above.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.138.2" class="koboSpan">The length and
uncertainty of time involved in the movement of goods by sea prevents
such tight coordination of transport and logistics operations.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.138.3" class="koboSpan">A result is
that a liner service between ports or extending inland through
intermodal services may be as readily provided by one line as another.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.138.4" class="koboSpan">Indeed, in
this sense, the service is commoditised although this is not to deny
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_474"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">the existence of important differences in service
attributes among lines. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.139.2"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, shippers are unlikely to bundle the
design and pricing of logistics and shipping services together in the
way that is done for more time-sensitive services.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">The recent marketing
of the LCL and, more recently, CL guaranteed fast service by three lines
and associated companies offers differentiated premium intermodal
transportation services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.140.2"
class="koboSpan">However, the services do not involve the service
providers assuming responsibility for logistics decisions of when and
how much to ship.</span>

#### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.2 The value of transportation services</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">Confidential
independent contracts between shippers and lines became the norm for
large shippers subsequent to the US Ocean Shipping Reform Act, 1998.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.142.2" class="koboSpan">The
elimination of conferences from European trades in October 2008 and
their expected demise elsewhere boost the importance of shipper
negotiation. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.142.3"
class="koboSpan">Shippers consider the negotiation of liner contracts as
important to them because of their financial value.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.142.4" class="koboSpan">Negotiations
are also often complex.</span>

#### <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.3 The nature of negotiations</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">The negotiation of
rate and service conditions by a shipper is usually the responsibility
of a specialised management group.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.144.2" class="koboSpan">Such an
internal organisation structure tends to preserve the negotiation role
with shippers, but it appears to do so for good reason and not just
resistance to change.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">Large shippers
negotiate on the basis of their traffic volume on single as well as on
multiple routes although volume is only a powerful argument when the
shipper has choices of other carriers and routes.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.145.2" class="koboSpan">Shippers
negotiate, therefore, on the basis of a range of competitive and
logistical alternatives actually or potentially available to them.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.145.3" class="koboSpan">For example, a
new plant or a new sourcing or marketing alternative that may shift
traffic from one region to another and from one carrier to another or
diminish the amount of ocean shipping needed in total can be arguments
for improved rate or service conditions.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.145.4" class="koboSpan">These are not
arguments that can be effectively executed by LSPs.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.145.5" class="koboSpan">However,
subsequent to the conclusion of shipper-carrier contracts, the
administration of the logistics activities, cargo tracking from the time
of purchase order, maintaining cargo allocations among lines and
monitoring freight charges are readily and commonly undertaken by LSPs
under contract to shippers.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore, although
new dimensions of service have become important in confidential rate
contracts between lines and shippers, the negotiation of shipping rates
and services by shippers has been conducted separately from the
negotiation of logistics services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.146.2" class="koboSpan">The
separability and substitutability of shipping services, the importance
attached to the negotiations by shippers and the advantages that
shippers have over LSPs in the negotiating process indicate that this
structure is likely to persist.</span>

## <span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.147.2" class="koboSpan">Overview of Responses of Lines to Supply Chain Management</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">The relationships
discussed in this chapter are evolving as lines respond to the
challenges and opportunities associated with the growth of trade and
greater emphasis on SCM.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_475"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">Greater horizontal integration in the industry is one
of the major developments in liner shipping, discussed in some detail
elsewhere in this book. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.149.2"
class="koboSpan">This chapter deals with the addition of added value
services by lines or their parent companies.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">The advantages of
integrating terminal management closely with shipping services gave rise
to the entry of shipping lines into terminal management.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.150.2" class="koboSpan">They were
initially generally managed by a unit closely related to the line or may
be managed by a contracted terminal operating company.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.150.3" class="koboSpan">However,
subsequently, the organisation of APM Terminals and APL Terminals as
profit centres separate from the lines and the sale of terminals by OOIL
suggest a weaker case today for integrated ownership and operations than
was previously the case. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.150.4"
class="koboSpan">The stronger opportunities to pursue terminal
management as a separate business and the need and opportunities for
close coordination between lines and terminals irrespective of ownership
have weakened the case for lines and terminals to be under the same
management.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">The ownership of
terminals by lines is not detrimental to the public interest.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.151.2" class="koboSpan">Terminal
operations are one of the intermediate services needed to deliver goods
to shippers. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.151.3"
class="koboSpan">There is no direct conflict for shippers in closer
relationship of terminal management with the lines.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.151.4" class="koboSpan">Shippers and
the public do have an interest in making sure that the terminal
management business continues to operate in a competitive
environment.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">The development of
intermodal transport capability is one of the inherent advantages
introduced with containerisation.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.152.2" class="koboSpan">The advantages
of lines in their ability to commit volumes of traffic to warrant
specialised inland rail and water services has been important to the
success of intermodal services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.152.3"
class="koboSpan">The carrier haulage arranged by the lines is provided
largely through contracts although lines participate in the ownership of
some trucking and, in Europe, of rail services.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.152.4" class="koboSpan">It is
important that shippers have available the option of port-to-port
service so that they or their agents can arrange merchant haulage.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.152.5" class="koboSpan">The congestion
experience in 2004–2005 has made all parties aware of the critical
nature of the port-inland connection and the capacity of inland routes.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.152.6" class="koboSpan">Shippers have
spread their shipping peak, diversified routes and made some changes to
their supply patterns. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.152.7"
class="koboSpan">Shipping lines have learned to pay more attention to
coordination with their inland carriers.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">Development of
logistics services by corporations with shipping lines is an important
aspect of the vertical integration in shipping.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.153.2" class="koboSpan">Some shipping
lines commenced their consolidation services during the early days of
containerisation and these have expanded through internal growth and
acquisitions to be substantial LSPs.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.153.3" class="koboSpan">They are
operated mainly as stand alone business units.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.153.4" class="koboSpan">They are
important units to the parent corporations but have grown less rapidly
than the companies hoped during the last decade.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.153.5" class="koboSpan">They remain
small relative to the LSPs that have expanded from freight forwarder
origins. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.153.6" class="koboSpan">The
existence of the lines’ LSPs is somewhat controversial with this latter
group. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.153.7" class="koboSpan">The
freight forwarders see the lines as competing directly against
them.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">The lines’ LSPs have
enjoyed an advantage in the integration of their ICT capability with
that of their related line, but this advantage appears to be diminishing
with the general development of ICT capabilities.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.154.2" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, the line-related LSPs have been at a disadvantage in that some
shippers are concerned about a possible bias to the related shipping
line. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.154.3" class="koboSpan">Large
shippers have preferred to negotiate liner rates and traffic volumes
quite separately from logistics services, no matter who the LSP.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.154.4" class="koboSpan">The position
of large shippers appears rational in the light of the separability of
the shipping service from logistics services and the substitutability
among shipping lines. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.154.5"
class="koboSpan">Further, large shippers are likely to regard the
negotiation of rates and traffic allocations as of a size
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_page_476"></span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan">and character to be of strategic importance.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">They are
unlikely to see the interests of LSPs sufficiently aligned with their
own and they have better and sometimes confidential grounds for the
negotiation of rate and service conditions.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.155.3" class="koboSpan">It is likely,
then, that the lines’ logistics services will remain in quite separate
entities for most lines.</span>

<span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">The recent
development of defined delivery dates as a guaranteed service is a
significant initiative to add service differentiation to lines’
services. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.156.2" class="koboSpan">It
remains to be seen whether the size of the market and the rates
supported will cover the added costs of the processes required.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.156.3" class="koboSpan">However, the
services go to the core of a major interest of shippers; greater service
reliability. </span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.156.4"
class="koboSpan">This type of service is unlikely to change the
structure of the managerial relationship of lines with the terminals,
inland carriers or logistics providers.
</span><span id="Ch015.xhtml_kobo.156.5" class="koboSpan">However,
improved coordination will be paramount.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml"></span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_book-columns">

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_480"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_481"></span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 16</span>\
<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Using Economic Measures for Global Control of Air Pollution from Ships</span>](#Preface1.xhtml_bck_ht0373)
===========================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Shuo</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Ma</span></span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0589" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0589"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">It is claimed that
maritime transport is environmentally friendly due to the fact that the
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan"> emission to transport one tonne of cargo for one
kilometre is 15 grams for a 8,000 dwt vessel; 50 grams for a heavy
truck, and 540 grams for a Boeing 747
freighter.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0590" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0590"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan"> However there is no guarantee that this “green” image
will always be associated with shipping since great efforts have been
made in recent years to reduce the emission levels of other modes of
transport, with higher standards continuously being introduced, while no
corresponding improvements have been evident in the maritime transport
sector. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">It is
estimated that should the current development trends continue shipping
will become a major source of air pollution.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.11.3" class="koboSpan">For example, it
has been reported that before 2020, international shipping would
overtake all land-based transport to be the biggest emitter of both NOx
and SOx in Europe (Friedrich, Heinen and Kamakaté, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.11.4" class="koboSpan">It is clear
that specific and bold actions have to be taken urgently if the shipping
sector is to massively reduce air pollution levels.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.11.5" class="koboSpan">Given the
growth perspective of seaborne trade, the environmental challenges faced
by the international shipping community are enormous.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">To address the air
pollution problems caused by the shipping industry, traditional
approaches are insufficient. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.12.2"
class="koboSpan">As far as international shipping is concerned, the
International Maritime Organisation (IMO) is the main regulatory body.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">Here the
control method is to set up technical standards then leave the
enforcement to the IMO Member States.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.12.4" class="koboSpan">This approach
is often referred to as the “command-and-control” method which has the
advantage of being clear, flexible and enforceable.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.12.5" class="koboSpan">However, it may
be argued that such approaches lack efficiency because by using uniform
standards the differences in pollution control costs between polluters
are ignored. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.12.6"
class="koboSpan">Economic approaches, which are also called market-based
instruments, take these costs into consideration by giving economic
incentives to those polluters whose control costs are low,
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_482"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">and consequently encouraging the employment of new and
more advanced control technologies.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.13.2" class="koboSpan">Market-based
instruments have been successfully used in a number of non-maritime
situations. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.13.3" class="koboSpan">It
is therefore time for the maritime community, within the framework of
the IMO, to embrace these economic approaches and use them as
supplementary tools in reducing emissions from ships and achieving
overall environmental objectives.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">At the IMO, the
market-based instrument is a relatively new concept which has not been
fully understood or appreciated. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.14.2"
class="koboSpan">This chapter has three objectives: first, to explain
why economic approaches can lead to a better and more cost efficient
emission control; second, to analyse the two major market-based
instruments and their application to the reduction of ship-originated
emissions; and third, to suggest an integrated approach using both
standards and market-based instruments for the control of emissions from
ships. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.14.3" class="koboSpan">The
chapter is divided into six sections.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.14.4" class="koboSpan">After the
introduction, Section 2 presents the theoretical framework and analyses
the features of the economic control method; Section 3 discusses the
reasons that economic approaches have not been used in shipping related
environmental regulations; Section 4 looks into the necessity of
introducing market-based instruments in maritime environmental
regulations; Section 5 concentrates on the application of market-based
instruments in shipping; and finally, Section 6 presents the
conclusion.</span>

## <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">For Environmental Protection, Public Intervention is Necessary</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">One of the
cornerstones of the market economy is the clearly defined
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan">property
rights</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">,
which are exclusive, transferable and protected.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">In the absence
of such property rights, markets will fail.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.3" class="koboSpan">This actually
is the case of environmental goods.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.4" class="koboSpan">These goods
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.5"
class="koboSpan">environment benefits or damages) have the
