characteristics of public goods. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.6"
class="koboSpan">For instance, there is no individual person who can be
identified as the exclusive victim of air pollution incurred in a
harbour. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.7"
class="koboSpan">Contrary to exclusive property rights, which imply
private and individual ownership, public goods are characterised as
non-exclusive in consumption. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.8"
class="koboSpan">This means that the damage caused to one person does
not increase or reduce the amount of damage to another person.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.9" class="koboSpan">Expressed in
another economic concept, environmental products have a zero marginal
cost. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.18.10" class="koboSpan">Such a
weakness or absence of property rights may result in an inefficient
allocation of resources and a failure to achieve environmental
objectives, as there is a lack of any incentive for a rational person to
make an investment since s/he cannot own, and transfer, the full
benefits.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Marine environmental
products, which are the same as any environmental product, create an
external cost or externality. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">Because of this, public intervention is desired to
internalise such a cost. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.19.3"
class="koboSpan">A ship, for example, emits exhaust air into the
atmosphere during operations either on the high sea or close to the
coast. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.19.4" class="koboSpan">Such
emission travels and may harm the health of a population far away.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.19.5" class="koboSpan">Obviously the
ship owner and the sufferers do not have any contractual relationship
between them and the environmental product, or the emission, is not
priced and stays outside the market.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.19.6" class="koboSpan">Often it is
practically impossible for the sufferer to identify the exact polluter
who has caused the damage. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.19.7"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, the production cost incurred to the
producer, who uses this to determine the production level in order to
maximise profit, is incomplete and in the case of negative externality
it is at a lower level than it actually should be.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.19.8" class="koboSpan">Such a</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0266" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00284.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: The effect of externality in a competitive market" /></span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_483"></span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0156"
id="Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0156"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan"> The effect of externality in a competitive
market</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">distorted cost curve
leads to the ship owners to produce more than they should, resulting in
badly allocated resources.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">This situation is
illustrated in </span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0156"
id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0156"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan"> where the demand curve for the port service, as
represented by D, is also the curve for marginal revenue in the case of
a competitive market. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.26.2"
class="koboSpan">MC</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan">P</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the marginal cost for the shipping company and MC
is the marginal social cost which includes the environmental cost
associated with the shipping operation.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">In this case
MC</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan">S</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan"> is always higher than
MC</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan">P</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> since the externality is negative and the society
bears both the costs of production and the environment-related costs
resulting from the production. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.32.2"
class="koboSpan">However, with unpriced environmental costs, the company
considers only its direct marginal cost and it will maximise its surplus
by keeping the transport production at Q.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.32.3" class="koboSpan">Such a
production level will incur a marginal production cost at P and a
marginal social cost at P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">, creating a net externality cost
(P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan"> – P). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.36.2"
class="koboSpan">In the above case such external costs are therefore
paid by the victims of the pollution, their families, insurance and the
social security system whenever applicable.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.36.3" class="koboSpan">The figure
indicates further that if such externality is internalised, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.36.4" class="koboSpan">the shipping
company is made to cover the social cost
P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan">, then the producer will reduce the production to
arrive at new demand–supply equilibrium.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.38.2" class="koboSpan">The production
is therefore reduced to Q</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">S</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan">, at which point the company has to raise its price,
which is based on the marginal social cost curve, to
P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan">S</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.42.2"
class="koboSpan">Also, at this reduces the production level, the
external cost diminishes and the total social cost decreases too, to
P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">S</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">Since the market fails
to reflect an important part of the production cost in the final price
of transactions, the social cost is unfairly paid for by society rather
than by those who benefit from the transaction.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">To correct
this, government intervention is required for the purpose of
internalising the external costs.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Economic instruments are better than regulatory instruments</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">As far as government
intervention is concerned, there are generally two approaches.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">The first is to
use economic instruments such as emission tax or emission trading</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0267" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00285.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: The effect of command and control method" /></span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_484"></span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0157"
id="Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0157"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan"> The effect of command and control method</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">schemes.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">The second is
to use rules and regulations in the form of compulsory emission
standards which are often referred to as the “command-and-control” (CAC)
method. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.51.3" class="koboSpan">This
approach consists of the promulgation of laws, rules and regulations
with the specification of objectives, standards, technologies and
operational procedures that polluters must comply with.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.51.4" class="koboSpan">In the broad
context of such laws and regulations, specific rules and standards are
normally established aiming at agreed objectives.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.51.5" class="koboSpan">From both the
theoretical and practical viewpoints, each of the regulatory and
economic approaches has advantages and disadvantages.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">Using the
“command-and-control” method, pollution could be controlled to its
optimal level through a “bargaining” process.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.52.2" class="koboSpan">This is because
the optimal pollution level is achieved when the marginal benefit (MB)
(or marginal control cost – MCC) and marginal external cost (MEC) are
identical. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.52.3"
class="koboSpan">While the MB or MCC can be measured, the calculation of
the level of MEC in a precise manner is difficult.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.52.4" class="koboSpan">The method
commonly used for the measurement is called “willingness to pay” (Ma,
2002) where the equilibrium of the two costs is normally achieved by a
process of “competition”. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.52.5"
class="koboSpan">This means that under the pressure of the public
opinion, which can be represented by, say, two opposing interest groups,
such as pro-business versus pro-environment groups, the emission
standard would then be negotiated and moved, mostly by the government or
similar public authorities, towards the optimal level of
pollution.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">This phenomenon can be
seen in </span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0157"
id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0157"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan"> above. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.55.2"
class="koboSpan">If the initial standard is set at
P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">0</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan"> which is stricter than the optimal level for the
society at P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">, such a policy would generate strong opposition from
the producers who would request for the standard to be revised.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">Then a
re-evaluation of the pollution damage and pollution control costs would
reveal that the initial standard is too stringent and as a consequence
an adjustment is likely to be undertaken in such a way that more
pollution would be allowed. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.59.3"
class="koboSpan">By the same token, if the emission standard is too
relaxed at P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">, which is below the optimal level of pollution, public
opinion would lean towards the advocates of the environment which would
lead to a strengthening of the rules with the amount of pollution being
permitted at a lower level.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Such a pollution
standard setting mechanism can also be seen in the establishment of
maritime legislation at, for example, the IMO.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.62.2" class="koboSpan">At any given
time and for a particular item of maritime regulation, optimal standards
are sought through consultation,
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_485"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">negotiation, debate and discussion; a “competitive
process” amongst various interest groups which are most often countries
or groups of countries. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.63.2"
class="koboSpan">As an outcome of such policy making, or
standard-setting process, the optimal pollution level, which is also the
optimal regulation level, is realised.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">An important
implication of this analysis is that the bigger the differences between
the interest groups, the harder the process will be and the longer time
it will take to reach a compromise.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.63.4" class="koboSpan">It is also true
that the bigger the divergence, the lower the average satisfactory level
of all the stakeholders, due to the fact that the “optimal” standards
please neither business-minded nor environment-minded people.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">The
“command-and-control” method has several advantages, which have made it
appealing and become the principal way of pollution control of most
governments. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.64.2"
class="koboSpan">Firstly, it is straightforward and with often an
explicit target and clearly defined technical or numerical norms;
Secondly, when a substance is known to be extremely harmful, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.64.3" class="koboSpan">a particular
type of paint used on ships, it can effectively limit or eliminate the
substance from the market;
Thirdly</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan"> the producers may like this method partly because the
industry input is often called for when the standard is set and partly
because it may be perceived as being a fair treatment to all producers;
Fourthly, this approach is quite attractive to both the
environmentalists and the politicians because emission standards, which
may well be in the form of strong statements, have an symbolic value to
demonstrate the activeness of a decision maker in response to the
expectations of specific interest groups or the general public (Stavins,
1998). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">The
regulatory instruments or the “command-and-control” approach have a
number of shortcomings too. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.66.3"
class="koboSpan">One of the most important weaknesses is that when the
technological level of different producers is not the same, which in
most cases is the reality, a single uniform emission standard will prove
to be ineffective, as shown in </span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0158"
id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0158"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan"> below.</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0268" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00286.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: The ineffectiveness of the regulatory method when firms have different MCCs" /></span>

<a href="#Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0158"
id="Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0158"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan"> The ineffectiveness of the regulatory method when
firms have different MCCs</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_486"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">In </span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0158)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">, two ships are operating in a market and they each use
a different pollution control technology, with ship 1 using a better
technology and thus having a lower marginal pollution control cost
(MCC-1) than ship 2 (MCC-2). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.74.2"
class="koboSpan">Supposing an environment mandate is fixed to control
the total amount of emission up to 200 units and consequently, the
public authority sets a uniform emission standard of 100 units for each
of the two ships, the pollution control cost for ship 1 would be
represented by area A and that for ship 2 would be represented by area
A + B. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.74.3" class="koboSpan">From the
figure, it can be clearly seen that to control the level of emission to
100 units, ship 1 spends much less than ship 2 (Y – X).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.74.4" class="koboSpan">The total
pollution control cost would have been much lower if ship 1 had
controlled more than 100 units while ship 2 had been allowed to control
less, correspondingly, than 100 units.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.74.5" class="koboSpan">Obviously, it
is when the marginal control cost is the same for both ships that the
lowest total control cost would be achieved.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.74.6" class="koboSpan">When single
emission standards are applied, no distinction is made between the ships
in terms of the type of technology they use.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.74.7" class="koboSpan">So, by the
uniform emission standard the most cost-effective pollution control can
only be achieved if all the ships in question are using identical
emission processing technology, therefore having the same pollution
control costs. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.74.8"
class="koboSpan">The reality is that in maritime transport, as in most
other sectors, such a condition does not exist.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">Another important
shortcoming of regulatory instruments is that the very principle of
determining the emission standard level may well become a
counterproductive factor to discourage shipping companies to invest in
new technology. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.75.2"
class="koboSpan">We can use </span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0159"
id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0159"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan"> below to illustrate this point.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">As explained
above, the optimal pollution level at which an emission standard is
established by the public authority is generally achieved through a
competitive bargaining process and such a standard is stabilised and
generally accepted when it is close or at the intersection of the
marginal control cost (MCC) and the marginal external cost (MEC).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.77.3" class="koboSpan">Such a
principle however implies that when costs change, either the MCC or MEC
or both, the emission standard ought to be re-established against the
point of the new equilibrium. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.77.4"
class="koboSpan">This is, in fact, where the problem arises.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.77.5" class="koboSpan">Assuming that
without regulation, a shipping company would not have taken any
pollution processing measures and would have emitted all waste at point
P,</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0269" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00287.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: The effect of the regulatory instrument on the use of new technology" /></span>

<a href="#Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0159"
id="Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0159"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4:</span></span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan"> The effect of the regulatory instrument on the use of
new technology</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_487"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">whereas, with a proper regulation, the initial emission
standard was set at P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">At this point, the ship’s pollution control cost is
A+B. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.83.3" class="koboSpan">By
regulation, the ship cannot emit more than
P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">, but theoretically, it can improve its profitability
by reducing the control cost if new technology is introduced.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.85.2" class="koboSpan">For the ship
owner to invest in this nonetheless, s/he has to be convinced that the
cost savings from the use of the new technology will be big enough to
recover the investment. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.85.3"
class="koboSpan">Assuming the use of the new technology would enable the
ship owner to shift the marginal control cost from MCC to
MCC</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan">, and given that the emission standard is always at
P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">, the new control cost would be B, the area below the
MCC</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
class="koboSpan"> curve, and the net cost saving would be area A.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
ship owner knows very well that such an investment would lead to a
reduction of the marginal control cost to
MCC</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan"> and consequently provide the regulatory authorities
and advocates of the environment with an argument to revise the emission
standard by making it more stringent.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">In such a case,
to satisfy the principle of equilibrium of MCC and MEC, the emission
standard would be set at P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the cost savings for the ship owner from the use
of the new technology would only be A–D.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">From the above
analysis, we can see an important implication that the bigger the
technological innovation is, the larger the reduction in the pollution
control cost will be. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
class="koboSpan">Given the increasing public awareness and global
concern about the environment, the marginal external cost curve (MEC)
would unlikely to be higher in the future.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.96.3" class="koboSpan">So a reduction
in the control cost would drive the balance of the two costs to the
left, which means the likelihood of more demanding regulations.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.96.4" class="koboSpan">With regard to
the use of new ship technology, a break-even point exists beyond which
the extra cost represented by area D will be bigger than the cost
savings represented by area A. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.96.5"
class="koboSpan">This in itself constitutes a disincentive for ship
owners to adopt new technology. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.96.6"
class="koboSpan">In addition, there are often high financial and
technical risks associated with the application of many major maritime
technological innovations. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.96.7"
class="koboSpan">As a result, a ship owner might rather refuse, delay or
hide the use of a new
technology.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0591" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0591"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 The main features of economic instruments</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">In contrast to the
above, economic instruments for pollution control have a number of
advantages over the “command-and-control” or regulatory approach.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">By properly
employing a market solution, the public authority can effectively
achieve the objective of pollution control with minimum abatement costs.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.99.3" class="koboSpan">As indicated
earlier, economic instruments usually come in the form of emission
charges (or pollution levy or tax) or tradable emission permits where,
for example, shipping companies receive an incentive for pollution
abatement on a sustainable basis.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.99.4" class="koboSpan">As a result,
government intervention is minimal, and, most important of all,
producers are encouraged to adopt new and better technologies of
pollution abatement.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">What is an emission
charge? </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">It is
a kind of levy expressed in per unit money terms on pollutants, for
example USD xx/tonne of CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.102.2"
class="koboSpan">It is generally imposed by a public authority on
producers for the effluent generated from the production.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.102.3" class="koboSpan">The tax
actually represents a message that “pollution is not free”.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.102.4" class="koboSpan">We can see,
with the help of </span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0160"
id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0160"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan">, how an emission charge would encourage a shipowner to
invest in a better method of pollution control and in the use of new
technology. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.104.2"
class="koboSpan">Without a pollution tax, the shipowner has no incentive
to control pollution and the emission level would be at point P.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.104.3" class="koboSpan">With an
emission charge
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"> imposed and given the marginal emission control cost
being MCC, it is in the ship owner’s interest to control the emission to
P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan"> as it</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0270" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00288.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 5: The effect of emission charges on the use of new technology" /></span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_488"></span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0160"
id="Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0160"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5:</span></span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan"> The effect of emission charges on the use of new
technology</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">would cost less to
control the emission than to pay the tax.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.112.2" class="koboSpan">For the ship,
keeping the emission level at
P</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan">, the total emission control cost would be the area
represented by A + B and the total emission charge payment would be C +
D + E. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.114.2"
class="koboSpan">Assuming there is new technology available, its use
will enable the ship to reduce its marginal control cost from MCC to
MMC</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.116.2"
class="koboSpan">Should such a technology be employed, the total control
cost would be the area B + D and the tax payment would be E.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.116.3" class="koboSpan">So the net
cost savings would be A + C with A as control cost savings and C as tax
cost savings. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.116.4"
class="koboSpan">Note that in the same situation the total cost savings
would only be area A if the regulatory instrument with uniform emission
standard is applied. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.116.5"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, area C represents an extra incentive for the
shipowner to invest in new technology.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">Other advantages of
emission charge, apart from the positive impact on the use of new
technology, are the following: it provides more opportunities to be a
fair as the chances for special interest groups to influence standards
is limited. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">It
requires less government intervention than the regulatory approach.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.117.3" class="koboSpan">It rewards
environmentally efficient ships and penalises the inefficient ones.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.117.4" class="koboSpan">It generates
an income, which can be used to support the administration of the
system. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.117.5" class="koboSpan">The
emission charge as a pollution control instrument is not perfect.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.117.6" class="koboSpan">Its major
weaknesses are: first of all it is difficult and costly to determine the
right charge level, to monitor the pollution and to exercise policy
enforcement; Secondly, as a tax, it represents a financial burden on
producers. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.117.7" class="koboSpan">It
may therefore create an unfairness between producers if the tax is not
levied universally; Thirdly, with market fluctuation, in the short-term,
when the market is high, producers, short of sufficient control
capability, may prefer to pollute more even by paying higher emission
charges.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">The idea of tradable
emission permits finds its origin in the Coase theorem on property
rights (Coase, 1960). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.118.2"
class="koboSpan">When first proposed in the 1960s, it was considered
as</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0271" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00289.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Two producers in the “emission permit trading” market" /></span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_489"></span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0161"
id="Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0161"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6:</span></span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan"> Two producers in the “emission permit trading”
market</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">an improvement to the
emission standard instrument whereby the public authority, instead of
simply decides on pollution standards, defines the total amount of
allowable emission which corresponds to the total amount of tolerable
pollution (Dale, 2002) and leaves the market to decide on who can
pollute how much. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.122.2"
class="koboSpan">The tradable emission permit is in essence designed to
create a market for pollution rights.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.122.3" class="koboSpan">What is
specific with the emission trading instrument is that the public
authority also allocates the initial pollution rights or permits among
polluters and allows them to trade such permits freely.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.122.4" class="koboSpan">For tradable
emission permits instruments to function, the following conditions have
to be satisfied.</span>

- <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">a polluter, a ship
  for example, has a legal right, in the form of permits, to
  pollute;</span>
- <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">such rights are
  clearly defined; any excess of permitted amount is subject to
  penalty;</span>
- <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">public authorities
  define the total amount of permits and distribute or sell initial
  permits to polluters;</span>
- <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">pollution permits
  are freely tradable in the market place.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">Given the above
conditions, an emission permit trading system can achieve the
environmental objectives with cost efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.127.2" class="koboSpan">This is
illustrated in </span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0161"
id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0161"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan"> where, for the sake of simplicity, we assume that two
ships are independently operating in the market.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">Without any
environmental regulation, each ship would discharge 200 tonnes of
sulphur dioxide per year into the air from the operation.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">The public
authority, after a consideration of all the relevant aspects and
information decides to cut the SOx emission level by half and thus
issues a total of 200 emission permits representing 200 tonnes of
sulphur dioxide per year. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.129.4"
class="koboSpan">The permits are equally distributed to the two ships,
which means that each ship is allowed to emit 100 tonnes of SOx per year
into
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_490"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">the atmosphere.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">Supposing that
the two ships are employing different technologies for emission control,
Ship 1 which is using a more efficient technology, has a marginal
control cost represented by curve MCC-1 or \$35 per tonne at the
one-hundredth tonne of SOx emission level.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.130.3" class="koboSpan">Whilst for
Ship 2, which is using a less efficient pollution control technology,
the marginal control cost, represented by MCC-2, is \$80 per tonne at
the one-hundredth tonne of emission level.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.130.4" class="koboSpan">Since the
emission permits are transferable, the two ships would engage in
mutually beneficial negotiations of permit trading.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.130.5" class="koboSpan">For Ship 1, it
is in its best interest to control more pollution and at the same time
sell some of the permits to Ship 2 as long as the extra control cost is
less than the income for the transfer.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.130.6" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
Ship 2 would also find it beneficial to control less pollution and at
the same time buy the corresponding emission permits from Ship 1, so
long as the control cost savings is more than the price paid for the
extra permits. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.130.7"
class="koboSpan">From </span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0161)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan">, we can see clearly that this is exactly the case.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">The two ships
would continue their negotiations and transactions until the marginal
control cost curves of the two ships are the same, the point at which no
more benefits can be drawn from the trading.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.132.3" class="koboSpan">This point of
equilibrium corresponds to the price of the permit at \$50 per tonne.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.132.4" class="koboSpan">Ship 1 has a
total benefit from selling permits equivalent to area A and Ship 2 has a
total benefit saving in control cost equivalent to area B.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.132.5" class="koboSpan">From the above
analysis we can conclude that, by using tradable emission permit
instrument, while the total emission level remains the same at 200
tonnes, both ships are better off and so is the society since the total
pollution control cost is reduced.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.132.6" class="koboSpan">The positive
impact of this tradable pollution permit on the use of new technology is
similar to the pollution tax as shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
5</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0160)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">Other important
implications of emission trading can be derived from the above
discussions.</span>

1.  <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">Under the
    condition of freely tradable permits the initial distribution of
    pollution permits, which is often considered to be a critical and
    difficult activity of the public authority, has no effect on how the
    permits are finally allocated among polluters through the market
    mechanism. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.136.2"
    class="koboSpan">Obviously the fair allocation of initial permits is
    an important issue.</span>
2.  <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">The example in
    </span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
    6</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0161)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
    class="koboSpan"> is a simple case of only two ships.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.139.2" class="koboSpan">However,
    the tradable pollution permit instrument works even better in a
    bigger market with larger number of parties involved in the
    transaction of emission permits.</span>
3.  <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">By free trading,
    the best allocation of environmental resources is achieved, which
    means that efficient technology is rewarded by being utilised to the
    maximum while inefficient technology is discouraged through minimal
    use.</span>
4.  <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">Thanks to the
    free emission trading market, environmental products have a price;
    for example in </span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
    class="koboSpan">Figure
    6</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0161)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
    class="koboSpan">, the equilibrium price is \$50 per permit.</span>
5.  <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">The amount of
    transactions is positively correlated with the differences of
    marginal pollution control cost, or the technology level, among the
    ships: the bigger the divergence of technological levels among
    ships, the more the trading will be and vice versa.</span>
6.  <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">The permit price
    level is negatively correlated with the average marginal control
    cost or the average level of technology: the higher the average
    level of technology, the lower the permit price, and vice
    versa.</span>
7.  <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">There is no limit
    to newcomers, even when the maximum emission level has been attained
    in a market. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.146.2"
    class="koboSpan">The emission permit trading policy encourages new
    and more efficient ships to enter the market by purchasing the
    emission needed.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_491"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">From the analysis of pollution tax and emission permit
trading, as illustrated in </span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures
4</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0159)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">5</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0160)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">, we can see clearly that the two approaches have the
same effect with regard to cost efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.151.2" class="koboSpan">Using either
of these approaches, the total control costs can be minimised and the
positive impact on incentives to use new technology is also similar.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.151.3" class="koboSpan">The ultimate
choice by the authority between the two methods depends on the following
aspects. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.151.4"
class="koboSpan">First, the non-economic factors, such as political
acceptability, are very important influential elements, effluent tax
being often rejected because of the political sensitivity.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.151.5" class="koboSpan">Secondly,
aspects concerned with implementation costs; this includes the
transaction cost, for example in the case of emission permit trading, or
control cost. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.151.6"
class="koboSpan">Thirdly, are the case-specific factors.</span>

## <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.152.2" class="koboSpan">For the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, Economic Instruments have not been Used</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">Given the nature of
the sector, the environmental regulation of maritime transport has a
unique character that it is more regulated at the international level
rather than at national levels. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.153.2"
class="koboSpan">In 1958, the International Maritime Organisation (IMO),
which is a specialised agency of the United Nations, was created</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">“to provide machinery
for cooperation among Governments in the field of governmental
regulation and practices relating to technical matters of all kinds
affecting shipping engaged in international trade; to encourage and
facilitate the general adoption of the highest practicable standards in
matters concerning maritime safety, efficiency of navigation and
prevention and control of marine pollution from ships”(UN, 1948).</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">Since then, the IMO
has produced many international treaties, conventions and agreements.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">The current
number of IMO conventions totals 29, seven of which are in the area of
marine environment protection; six being in force and one, the
convention adopted in 2004 on ballast water management, not yet in
force. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.155.3" class="koboSpan">These
conventions are summarised in
</span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fig0272" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0272"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan"> Among the seven IMO environmental conventions, MARPOL
73/78 is the most important covering a wide range of aspects of
ship-originated pollution. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.158.2"
class="koboSpan">This convention addresses different aspects of
pollution from ships through its six annexes which have been amended
several times according to the need.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.158.3" class="koboSpan">These Annexes
have entered into force on various dates with the latest, Annex VI on
air pollution from ships, entering into force in 2005.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Accidental versus operational pollution from ships</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">There are many
similarities between maritime safety and marine environment protection
regulations. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.160.2"
class="koboSpan">This is because when an incident or accident occurs, it
very often presents a threat to both the humans on board the ship and to
the surrounding environment. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.160.3"
class="koboSpan">However, there is a remarkable difference between
maritime safety and environmental protection; while maritime safety
related regulations exclusively deal with
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan">accidental</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan"> cases, environmental regulations deal with both
accidental and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan">operational</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan"> cases. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.164.2"
class="koboSpan">If maritime safety and environmental products can be
measured by their occurrence and consequences, in other words by the
frequency and severity of the safety and/or pollution events, then for
all maritime safety and part of marine environmental products, the
outcomes are</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0272" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_492"></span>[](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0272)

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00290.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0272)

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">uncertain.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.166.2" class="koboSpan">So these
products are accidental such as, for example, a ship grounding causing
casualties and oil spills. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.166.3"
class="koboSpan">For some environmental products, both occurrences and
consequences are fairly predictable.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.166.4" class="koboSpan">For example,
to legally discharge waste oil into the ocean or emit harmful exhausts
from the operating engine into the atmosphere.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.166.5" class="koboSpan">Such
discharges are allowed and are deliberately undertaken and are referred
to as operational.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">Obviously, because of
the differences in the nature of maritime safety and marine
environmental products, the corresponding regulations should have
different characteristics as well.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">For accidental
cases, the political objective might be a total
elimination,</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0592" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0592"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the statistical objective for the IMO regulations
is normally what is called ALARP or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">As Low As Reasonably
Practicable</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.171.2"
class="koboSpan">For operational cases, the objectives are to identify
the optimal</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0273" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_493"></span>[](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0273)

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00291.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0273)

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">pollution conditions
and levels and to make sure that these conditions and levels are
properly met. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.173.2"
class="koboSpan">Referring to the discussions of the earlier section,
this means to find out the marginal environmental damage cost curve and
the marginal pollution control cost curve.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.173.3" class="koboSpan">The type of
measures to take in order to implement the regulations is different too.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.173.4" class="koboSpan">For accidental
cases, risk management principles should be followed and techniques
should be employed. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.173.5"
class="koboSpan">The IMO conventions such as OPRC and INTERVENTION or
double hull requirements for tanker ships in MARPOL Annex I are examples
of this type of measures. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.173.6"
class="koboSpan">With regard to operational environmental cases, waste
management principles and techniques should be utilised.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.173.7" class="koboSpan">This may
include, for example, setting up the conditions and limits for the
discharge of waste, such as oil or sewage into the sea.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">To conclude, we can
say that the distinction of maritime safety and environmental
regulations between accidental and operational categories, as shown in
</span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fig0273" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0273"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan">, is very important in understanding the objectives of
the regulations and the appropriate measures to implement.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">Given the above
distinction, a discussion of regulation instruments can be done based on
the basic requirements of the IMO marine pollution prevention
conventions. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.177.2"
class="koboSpan">These conventions, in the form of regulations, can be
broadly divided into three
categories.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0593" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0593"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup>

1.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
    class="koboSpan">Pollution
    standards:</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
    class="koboSpan"> These concern the conditions and levels of
    pollution from ships. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.180.2"
    class="koboSpan">Some pollution is totally forbidden, such as
    TBT-based contents in paint.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.180.3" class="koboSpan">Some
    pollution is allowed to take place but with conditions, such as not
    discharging noxious substances within 12 miles of the nearest shore,
    or air pollution according to the NOx Code.</span>
2.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
    class="koboSpan">Technical
    norms:</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
    class="koboSpan"> The availability and technical standards of
    equipment may be required. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.182.2"
    class="koboSpan">Most technical norms are imposed on ships such as
    double-hull tankers, or segregated ballast tanks.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.182.3"
    class="koboSpan">Shore-based equipment may also be required, such as
    reception facilities.</span>
3.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
    class="koboSpan">Procedural
    requirements:</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
    class="koboSpan"> These are standards of operational processes; for
    example, keeping a bunkering book or a ballast management record on
    board, the packing, marking, documentation, stowage and notification
    of harmful substances on board.</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0274" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_494"></span>[](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0274)

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00292.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0274)

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">Since the sub ject of
this chapter concerns the use of economic instruments for ship pollution
control, the scope of the discussion should therefore be limited to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan">operational
</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan">environmental products only.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.188.2" class="koboSpan">This is
because one of the pre-conditions, as discussed in the previous section,
is that pollution has to be legal and
voluntary.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0594" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0594"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan"> This means that a ship should have the legal right to
pollute, which is the case of operational pollution, which is mostly
addressed by the MARPOL Convention.</span>

<a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fig0274" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0274"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan"> summarises the MARPOL Convention with an outline of
the basic requirements of each of the six Annexes.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.192.2" class="koboSpan">Each of these
regulatory instruments can then be grouped into one of the three
categories of pollution standards, technical norms or procedural
requirements, as discussed above.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.192.3" class="koboSpan">All these
methods are regulatory instruments coming under the sphere of the
“command-and-control” approach.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_495"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Why are "command-and-control" instruments favoured at the IMO?</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">So far, the IMO has
never used an economic approach or market-based instrument in its
environmental regulations. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.194.2"
class="koboSpan">As discussed above, the “command-and-control”
instruments have been a favourable choice for most public authorities
around the world in their environmental policies, and it is only
recently that economic approaches have become an option.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">At the IMO,
there are good reasons and powerful arguments in favour of the
“command-and-control” approach since a multinational and international
maritime regulatory body, using a regulatory or “command-and-control”
approach rather than economic method is always considered to be
politically more acceptable. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.194.4"
class="koboSpan">Such a situation can be examined from the angles of
three groups of people: (1) the maritime industry or the polluters; (2)
the governments or the regulators and (3) public opinion.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">The shipping
industry, such as the shipping companies, shipbuilders, marine engine
makers, classification societies, marine insurers, etc.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.195.2" class="koboSpan">can be
considered as the recipients of marine environmental regulations.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.195.3" class="koboSpan">For them,
“command-and-control” instruments are often
preferred.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0595" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0595"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.196.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan"> This is partly because they are relatively simple and
less resource demanding than, for instance, an economic solution like
pollution tax or tradable permits.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.197.2" class="koboSpan">This is partly
also because pollution standards are almost always made with substantial
inputs, in one way or another, directly or indirectly, from the existing
industry and large companies. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.197.3"
class="koboSpan">At the IMO, many countries’ delegates include
representatives of the leading maritime firms of the country, or clos e
consultation and other similar efforts are made so that the leading
industry’s opinions are sufficiently represented and their interests
adequately reflected in the country’s position
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">vis-à-vis</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan"> a particular piece of international maritime
regulation. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.199.2"
class="koboSpan">The industry’s influence on the regulation setting
tends to push the regulation in the direction so as to give advantages
for existing companies and constitute some sorts of barriers to
newcomers. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.199.3" class="koboSpan">If
an economic instrument is used, only the total amount of pollution is
decided by the regulator; the choices of control technology as well as
who is allowed to generate how much pollution being totally left to the
market to decide. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.199.4"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, the lobbying efforts, the influence and
special relationship would be much undermined.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">With regard to the
government side, the IMO has 170 Member States and territories.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.2" class="koboSpan">These are the
makers of international maritime regulations and conventions.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.3" class="koboSpan">When it comes
to marine environmental regulations, the governments have also a
preference for “command-and-control” instruments, due mainly to three
reasons. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.4"
class="koboSpan">First, most governments have a tendency to avoid all
sorts of risks; agreeing to a new type of tax on, for example, marine
bunkers, might be seen as a risky move in the context of the internal
politics of a country. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.5"
class="koboSpan">It is also because the effects of economic instruments
are not always directly presented; as they are more difficult to see,
they are seemingly less certain than that of the standards.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.6" class="koboSpan">For example, a
bunker tax should encourage operators to control pollution and eliminate
inefficient ships from the market, thus improving the environmental
performance as a whole. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.7"
class="koboSpan">However, the effects of economic driven pollution
control measures are only seen in the level of final consumption
aggregates, and ship inefficiency may be caused by numerous factors.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.8" class="koboSpan">It may appear
to be uncertain as to how much pollution has been reduced and whether or
not the most polluting ships have been driven out of the market by the
tax. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.9" class="koboSpan">On the
other hand, the effects of pollution standards are more certain; such
instruments therefore being less risky.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.10" class="koboSpan">Secondly, at
the IMO, a UN agency, decisions are made by consensus and resolutions
are formulated based on the votes of the member states.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.200.11" class="koboSpan">It is normal
that, in case a choice has
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_496"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan">to be made, “equality” is generally given much more
weight than “efficiency”. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.2"
class="koboSpan">Since the efficiency gap between the shipping
industries of the various countries can be quite large, economic
instruments, which by definition “discriminate” ship operators based on
cost efficiency, are generally seen as less “fair” than pollution
standards which are applicable equally to all.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.3" class="koboSpan">Pollution
permit trading is also seen by some as an instrument favouring a few
strong shipping countries at the expense of other countries in which the
shipping industry is relatively small and weak.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.4" class="koboSpan">Thirdly, most
governments are responsive to voters and public opinion.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.5" class="koboSpan">Given the
increasing public concern about climate change, global warming and the
general deterioration of the environment, many governments are choosing
an active environment policy as a top priority on their political
agenda. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.6" class="koboSpan">They
need strong statements, concrete objectives and visible targets to
demonstrate a strong commitment and active engagement.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.7" class="koboSpan">This is
particularly true when a serious marine environmental disaster occurs.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.8" class="koboSpan">For example,
shortly following the Erika oil spill, some European governments were
under tremendous pressure from public opinion to take bold actions and
concrete measures to prevent future accidents.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.201.9" class="koboSpan">Such an urgent
need for tangible results is then brought to the IMO and often leads to
more stringent pollution prevention standards.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">For the general
public, “command-and-control” methods in the form of pollution standards
are also favorable solutions. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.202.2"
class="koboSpan">Firstly, the idea of using economic methods to
internalise environmental externality, which happened in the first place
due to the failure of the economic system, is difficult to sell.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.202.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore
using a regulatory method to mend market failure seems to be a natural
choice. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.202.4"
class="koboSpan">Secondly, public opinion is generally hostile to taxes.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.202.5" class="koboSpan">We saw in the
later discussion that when a bunker tax was first proposed at an IMO
meeting, it was seen as an international taxation and met with strong
and immediate objections from a number of
countries.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0596" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0596"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan"> The “command-and-control” instruments have a function
to help disguise pollution control costs as compared to a market
approach by which these costs are directly placed on the surface for
someone to pay for. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.204.2"
class="koboSpan">Thirdly, the IMO has to make sure that its regulations
are generally understandable not only to the member states, but also to
the world maritime community as a whole and to the general public at
large. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.204.3" class="koboSpan">The
“command-and-control” instruments are straightforward, explicit and
unambiguous with clearly stated targets and specific requirements, which
are easy to explain. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.204.4"
class="koboSpan">Take for example, the obligation of the Member States
to provide reception facilities at ports, or 3.5% sulphur content of the
fuel from 1 January 2012. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.204.5"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, for the general public, the
objectives and the expected outcomes of pollution tax or tradable
emission permits are more difficult to grasp.</span>

## <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.205.2" class="koboSpan">A New Case for a Different Approach — Air Emission from Ships</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">We have seen the main
reasons, as discussed above, for only “command-and-control” instruments
to have been used at IMO for its international regulations regarding the
prevention of pollution from ships.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">It is
important to note that to use economic instruments, a number of specific
conditions, particularly the following two, have to be fulfilled: (1)
economic instruments are only for the control of operational pollution,
not accidental pollution; and (2) there must be different ways of
pollution control available, which means that the control technologies
not only should be different, they should also be dynamic or progressing
with new technologies being continuously introduced.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_497"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan">Between regulation-based and market-based approaches,
there are two most important aspects to observe: on the one hand, the
two approaches are entirely in common, on the other, the two are
fundamentally different. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.207.2"
class="koboSpan">The common point they share is that for both
approaches, the optimal pollution control level is the same and is based
on the equilibrium of the marginal pollution damage cost and the
marginal pollution control cost.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.207.3" class="koboSpan">So both
approaches face the same challenge, which is to identify the exact
levels of the two cost elements.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.207.4" class="koboSpan">The
fundamental difference between the two approaches is that regarding
pollution damage costs, regulatory instruments do not care about who
spends how much, while economic instruments do focus on individual
pollution control costs; another difference is that regarding the
pollution damage costs where regulatory instruments concentrate on
individual pollution levels, while economic instruments do not mind who
pollutes how much. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.207.5"
class="koboSpan">Take marine pollution from ships as an example: as long
as the total amount of pollution is within the requested level, the IMO,
using pollution standards, focuses on the uniform pollution level of
each individual ship and never pays attention to the differences in the
control costs between ships. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.207.6"
class="koboSpan">However, should a market-based approach be used by the
IMO, such as a pollution tax or permit trading, the market would
function so that an equal amount of pollution control cost exists for
each ship, never minding the differences in pollution levels between the
ships. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.207.7" class="koboSpan">These
two aspects are illustrated in </span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_cap_lbl0161)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Air pollution from ships has become a major global concern</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">It was relatively
recently that air pollution from ships started to draw the public’s
attention when certain well publicised investigations revealed the
growing gap between the air pollution control efforts of land-based
transport and maritime transport.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.211.2" class="koboSpan">Previously,
since ships sail mostly in international waters, operational pollution
from ships in the form of air emissions, was not considered to be such a
serious problem as air pollution from land-based transport which more
directly and immediately affects a populations’s health.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.211.3" class="koboSpan">Over the
years, land-based transport has introduced various control measures,
with increasingly stricter standards, whilst little has happened within
shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">Air pollution
emissions from ships include components emitted to the atmosphere as
exhausts due to fossil fuel consumption.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.212.2" class="koboSpan">These
components are carbon dioxide
(CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan">), nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulphur dioxide (SOx),
particulate matters (PM) and some other polluting substances.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.214.2" class="koboSpan">Such emissions
also indirectly influence the concentration of greenhouse gases and
cause climate change. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.214.3"
class="koboSpan">In order to determine the appropriate control level and
methods, it is important to have an idea of the inventory of ship
generated emissions.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">A number of studies
have been undertaken recently to quantify present and future air
emissions from ships, often in the context of global air pollution or
emission situations of other modes of transport.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.215.2" class="koboSpan">Many of these
studies concentrate on the estimates of the amount of greenhouse gas
emissions from ships and their environmental impact (Davies
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2000), (Corbett
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2003), (Endersen, 2003), (Eyring, Kohler, Aardenne
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005), (Eyring, Kohler, Lauer
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005) or the impact on economic costs (Gallagher and
Taylor, 2003). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.223.2"
class="koboSpan">Some recent studies provide up-dated information on the
inventory of greenhouse gases and air emissions from ships (Eyring
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007), (Lauer
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007), (Dalsoren
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2009). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.229.2"
class="koboSpan">Other investigations have been carried out about the
impact of ship emission on local and regional environment (Hammingh
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007), (Cofala
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007), for example, one estimate suggests that in
Europe,
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_498"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">ship-originated SOx and NOx will overtake that from
land in 2018 (Friedrich
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007), while another study says that shipping
contributes 33% of all air pollution in Hong Kong (Lloyd’s List, 23
March 2007, p. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.236.2"
class="koboSpan">1).</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">Further studies have
investigated the special impact of SOx, NOx and PM emissions from
shipping (Swedish NGO Secretariat on Acid Rain
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.239.2"
class="koboSpan">One study discussed the potential growth of the
maritime trade and the necessity to massively reduce the SOx content of
fuel to 0.5% and the NOx emission level by 60% to maintain the emissions
from global shipping at the level of 2002 (Corbett, Wang
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.241.2"
class="koboSpan">However, other research argued that the additional
costs, particularly the additional consumption and subsequent negative
environmental impact for producing higher quality of fuel at the
refineries, for example with 0.5% sulphur content, would be so important
that it could largely offset or totally reduce the emissions intended
(Leister and Tallett, 2007). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.241.3"
class="koboSpan">With regard to PM, Colbett
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2007) studied their increased ambient concentrations
due to ships’ emissions and the impact on human health and premature
mortality. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.243.2" class="koboSpan">It
was found that shipping-related PM emissions are responsible for about
60,000 deaths annually and this could increase by 40% by 2012 if no
radical actions are implemented to massively reduce emissions (Corbett,
Vinebrake </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007).</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">All these studies
have used similar research methodology by deriving the emission level
from fuel consumption estimates based on information of internationally
registered ships. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.246.2"
class="koboSpan">To date, the most comprehensive study of the inventory
of GHG emissions from ships is the “Second IMO GHG Study 2009” (IMO,
2009e). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.246.3" class="koboSpan">This
study shows that “shipping is estimated to have emitted 1,046 million
tonnes of CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan"> in 2007, which corresponds to 3.3% of the global
emissions during 2007. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.248.2"
class="koboSpan">International shipping is estimated to have emitted 870
million tonnes, or about 2.7% of the global emissions of
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan"> in 2007”. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.250.2"
class="koboSpan">The report also says that “by 2050, in the absence of
policies, ship emissions may grow by 150% to 250% compared to the
emissions in 2007 as a result of the growth in shipping”.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.251.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Problems with regulatory methods in marine pollution regulations</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">When using the
“command-and-control” method, the regulators often have to decide,
directly or indirectly, on the types of pollution prevention
technologies. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.252.2"
class="koboSpan">This has attracted a lot of criticism as to whether the
regulators and bureaucrats have the adequate knowledge to select the
most appropriate techniques for pollution control.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.252.3" class="koboSpan">Even if a
decision is made by so-called experts, there is always a limitation to
personal knowledge in finding the most suitable solution to the problems
which exist in a diversified background.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.252.4" class="koboSpan">At the IMO,
such situations are frequently seen; for example, the rule required for
a particular oil pollution prevention technical standard to be adopted
regardless of the environment in which a ship is trading.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.252.5" class="koboSpan">The “double
hull” requirement for tankers is believed to have a much limited effect
for the intended purpose (Brown and Savage, 1996).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.252.6" class="koboSpan">The choice of
a suitable pollution control instrument depends on many
location-specific factors, in the areas of, for instance, natural
conditions and social-economic environments.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.252.7" class="koboSpan">Given the
enormous variety of situations among IMO Member States, many technical
standards selected under the “command-and-control” approach are often
found to be incompatible or unsuitable to local conditions.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.252.8" class="koboSpan">As countries
are reluctant to ratify an inappropriate rule, extensive delays are
routinely experienced at the IMO for many important environmental
regulations to enter into
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_499"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan">force. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.253.2"
class="koboSpan">Recognising such deficiencies,
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan">goal-based</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan">” standards were introduced at the IMO for a general
applications in its
regulations.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0597" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0597"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">Another major
deficiency of the “command-and-control” instrument is that with this
method it is difficult to cope with the development dynamism of
pollution control technologies. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.257.2"
class="koboSpan">Choosing a specific technology at a particular point in
time will always come with the risk of technological obsolescence.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.257.3" class="koboSpan">New or
improved technologies may emerge at any time and when and how to start
using them is often a highly complex question which has rarely a uniform
answer. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.257.4" class="koboSpan">Given
the fact that the establishment of IMO regulations is characterised by
extensive delays in the process and a divergence of national interests,
along with the pursuit of the principle of consensus meaning compromises
have to be accepted and the best choices have to be sacrificed, the
chances are that by the time a convention has finally entered into
force, the pollution control technology required may have already become
long out-dated.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">The
“command-and-control” methods focus on environmental costs but ignore
the control costs. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.258.2"
class="koboSpan">It looks “fair” to the polluters as all sources of
pollution have to comply with the uniform emission standards, but it is
socially “unfair” and ineffective because the cheapest means of control
are not aimed at. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.258.3"
class="koboSpan">Today, under increasing economic pressure, it has
become a general understanding that both pollution damage cost and
pollution control cost have to be minimised so that the marine
environment is better protected, shipping development is more
sustainable and the use of new technology is more effectively promoted.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.258.4" class="koboSpan">It is now a
matter of urgency that the international maritime community agrees on
the principles and an action plan with a clear emission reduction
objective and timetable by using both regulatory and market
instruments.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0598" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0598"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan"> Should multi-national bodies such as the IMO fail to
