live up to the environmental challenge and the measures put in place do
not deliver the expected outcome, it is highly likely that regional
solutions will take the lead and the prevention of air pollution from
ships will be undertaken in a fragmented fashion (Torvanger
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007).</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">Air pollution from
ships is operational pollution, therefore the location, time and
quantity of emissions are predicable and controllable.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.2" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
the basic conditions of using economic pollution control instruments are
available. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.3"
class="koboSpan">When making marine environmental regulations two types
of decisions have to be made by the public authority, whether
“command-and-control” or “market-based” instruments are to be used.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.4" class="koboSpan">The first
decision concerns the pollution control level, or the goal.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.5" class="koboSpan">For either
“regulatory” or “economic” approaches, a goal has to be determined,
although, it can be explicit or implicit.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.6" class="koboSpan">In the case of
accidental pollution, the goal may be a reduced risk level, while for
operational pollution, explicit objectives are often given.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.7" class="koboSpan">The second
type of decision concerns how to achieve the goal, or the means to
employ. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.8" class="koboSpan">Here
the two approaches, regulatory and economic, are different.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.9" class="koboSpan">While in the
case of the former, the means of pollution control are specified by the
authority, in the case of the latter, the question of “how to control”
is left to the market. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.10"
class="koboSpan">It is obvious that when there are alternative control
technologies available, using market-based instruments would lead to
cost efficiency. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.263.11"
class="koboSpan">This is the case for the prevention of air pollution
from ships.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.264.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 The availability of different air pollution control technologies for ships</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">The analysis of the
previous section implies that availability of the assumed advantage of
market-based instruments for pollution control over regulatory
instruments depends
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_500"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">on the divergence of the marginal pollution control
costs incurred by different polluters.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.266.2" class="koboSpan">This means
that if all polluters have the same marginal control costs represented
by a single marginal cost curve, the two instruments, economic and
regulatory, would lead to the same results and efficiency.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">As far as the
prevention of pollution from ships is concerned, the differences in
pollution control cost come, to a large extent, from the different
control technologies used by various ships.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
control cost difference can broadly be represented and reflected by
technology differences. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.3"
class="koboSpan">At the IMO’s MEPC meeting in 2005, a number of European
countries presented a proposal for the revision of the air pollution
Annex of the MARPOL Convention (IMO, 2005a).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.4" class="koboSpan">The proposal
outlined the major technologies available for the control of air
pollution from ships. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.5"
class="koboSpan">According to this document, there are mainly three
types of technologies available to control the level of NOx emissions,
namely, water in combustion; catalytic absorbers; and selective
catalytic reduction. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.6"
class="koboSpan">The first method involves injecting water into the
combustion process, with 0.3 to 0.4 water fuel ratios, to reduce the
maximum combustion temperature, thus decreasing the NOx formation up to
30 to 40%. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.7" class="koboSpan">It
is claimed that such a method would only insignificantly increase fuel
consumption. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.8"
class="koboSpan">The second method uses a catalyst to absorb NOx during
the operation of diesel engines, which can reduce NOx emissions by an
additional 90%. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.9"
class="koboSpan">The third method, “selective catalytic reduction”, is
also catalyst based and uses ammonia to reduce NOx from the exhaust.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.267.10" class="koboSpan">This method
can also reduce NOx emissions by over 90%.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.268.1" class="koboSpan">With regard to SOx
emissions from ships, the most effective and approved means of control
is to reduce the sulphur content of the fuel.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.268.2" class="koboSpan">Another method
which is already being used in land-based SOx emission sources is also
allowed under Regulation 14 of Annex VI and is under experimentation on
ships. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.268.3" class="koboSpan">This
method involves the use of an exhaust gas scrubber where the exhaust is
mixed with sea water which can absorb about 80% of the SOx in the
exhaust.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">The primary
technology for reducing particulate matters from diesel engines involves
a diesel particulate filter (DPF).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.269.2" class="koboSpan">By using the
DPF, the soot portion of particulate matters are captured in a filter
media then burned. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.269.3"
class="koboSpan">The use of this technology can reduce PM up to 99%.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.269.4" class="koboSpan">However, it is
reported that the efficiency of DPF is considerably affected by the
sulphur content of fuel, since sulphur degrades catalyst oxidation
efficiency and forms sulphate particulate matters.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.270.1" class="koboSpan">The different
technologies available to control emissions from ships result in large
cost differences. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.270.2"
class="koboSpan">For instance, it is reported that the difference in
cost between different measures taken for reducing emissions of SOx from
ships is more than eight times ranging from 0.3 to 2.5 €/kg and for
reducing emissions of NOx from ships is as much as 60 times ranking from
0.1 to 6 €/kg (Swedish NGO Secretariat on Acid Rain
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.272.2"
class="koboSpan">It is believed that such enormous divergences in
control costs are due to the fact that in shipping, air pollution
control is still at an early stage compared to other sectors, therefore,
a whole range of control measures is available, whereas in the
land-based sectors, the most cost-effective technologies have already
been employed. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.272.3"
class="koboSpan">According to a recent estimate (IMO, 2009d), by using
various technologies in ship design, for example with new design
concepts, better hull and superstructure, better power and propulsion
systems, renewable energy, low carbon fuel, exhaust gas reduction
technology, etc, 10– 50% of
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.274.1"
class="koboSpan"> reduction could be realised.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.274.2" class="koboSpan">This, combined
with another 10–50% emission reduction through the operational
improvement of ships, which is potentially possible, could reduce the
total CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan"> from ships by as much as 20–75% in
2050.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0599" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0599"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_501"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan">Summarising the above, we conclude that there are
numerous control technologies for limiting the air pollution from ships
with different cost structures and varying effectiveness.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.278.2" class="koboSpan">It is
therefore up to the ship owners to choose and use a particular
technology. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.278.3" class="koboSpan">It
is believed that in the future new control technologies may well be
developed continuously as more investment is made into pollution
prevention research. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.278.4"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, it is possible that a market-based
instrument can be used. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.278.5"
class="koboSpan">Recent research shows that by using economic
approaches, shipping companies that have met all the emission
requirements can realise substantial savings from pollution control
costs (Wang, Corbett and Winebrake, 2007).</span>

## <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.279.2" class="koboSpan">Economic Instruments for the Control of Air Pollution from Ships</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">Since entering into
force in May 2005, the MARPOL Convention Annex VI on air pollution from
ships has provoked many discussions and debates at IMO, in particular
concerning the use of “unconventional” economic instruments to achieve
its intended
objectives.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0600" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0600"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan"> Of course, such discussions and debates have been
going on in the broad context of global environmental development such
as the Kyoto Protocol, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
(UNFCCC) and the general public concern about climate change caused by
the activities of human beings.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan">Using economic
instruments to deal with environmental problems is a proven solution and
an internationally recommended approach.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.283.2" class="koboSpan">Emission
permit trading, for example, is one of the three key mechanisms of the
Kyoto Protocol, and an accepted practice with a positive record in a
number of countries. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.283.3"
class="koboSpan">The first practical example of nationwide emission
trading scheme was in the United States under the 1990 Clean Air Act.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.283.4" class="koboSpan">It was a
large-scale and long-term environmental programme relying on tradable
emission permits with emission of sulphur dioxide as its target and acid
rain as its major
precursor.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0601" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0601"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan"> Because of the nature of most air pollution, which is
operational, market-based approaches have been mostly applied in this
area. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.285.2" class="koboSpan">However,
the applications are largely found in land-based pollution sources
including transportation activities and they are mostly on a national or
regional basis rather than global basis.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.285.3" class="koboSpan">In the Kyoto
protocol it is stated that the “parties included in Annex I (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.285.4" class="koboSpan">industrialised
countries) shall pursue limitation or reduction of emissions of
greenhouse gases not controlled by the Montreal Protocol from aviation
and marine bunker fuels, working through the International Civil
Aviation Organisation and the International Maritime Organisation,
respectively”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0602" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0602"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan"> Emissions from international shipping are excluded in
the UN Climate Change Convention, and the IMO is expected to coordinate
joint efforts to address GHG emission issues.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.287.2" class="koboSpan">To date
market-based instruments have not been applied to the prevention of air
pollution from international shipping.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Fundamental issues and concerns about using market-based instruments</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">At the IMO since the
entering into force of Annex VI of the MARPOL Convention, there have
been seven Maritime Environment Protection Committee meetings, with the
most recent one (59th session) being held in July 2009.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.289.2" class="koboSpan">At each of the
MEPC session, market-based instruments have been on the discussion
agenda, although the
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_502"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">discussions were at a low level at the beginning.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.290.2" class="koboSpan">At the MEPC53
in July 2005 for example, there no submission was received regarding
market-based instruments, but at the 59th session in July 2009, there
were more than 10 submissions from delegations on the
subject.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0603" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0603"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.291.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan"> As this was close to the COP15 in Copenhagen in
December 2009, there has been a growing interest and intensified efforts
have been made. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.292.2"
class="koboSpan">In June 2008 the first Intersessional Meeting of the
Working Group on Green House Gas Emissions from Ships was held in Oslo,
Norway. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.292.3" class="koboSpan">As an
item on the agenda, the air pollution reduction mechanism was debated.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.292.4" class="koboSpan">During the
same time period since 2005, a number of other studies or proposals have
also been published in Europe and North America, some of which have been
referred to at various IMO meetings.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.292.5" class="koboSpan">At the IMO,
the first and fundamental issue under discussion and debate is whether
market-based instruments should or should not be used.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">One of the early
studies in the subject area was commissioned by the European Commission
in 2000 (BMT, 2000) and in this study, economic approaches such as
incentives in the form of rebate or a levy based on ships’ SOx emission
levels at ports were recommended for wider use.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.293.2" class="koboSpan">In the latest
release of the Second IMO GHG Study 2009, the following statement was
made “The report finds that market-based instruments are cost-effective
policy instruments with a high environmental effectiveness.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.293.3" class="koboSpan">These
instruments capture the largest amount of emissions under the scope,
allow both technical and operational measures in the shipping sector to
be used, and can offset emissions in other sectors.”
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.293.4" class="koboSpan">(IMO, 2009d).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.293.5" class="koboSpan">Despite a
general recognition and, seemingly, an acceptance in principle of
market-based instruments, various concerns and reservations have been
expressed at IMO on both the substance and the practicality
aspects.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.294.1" class="koboSpan">At the IMO First
Intersessional Working Group Meeting on GHG Emissions from Ships in June
2008, the members were divided on the issue of introducing market-based
instruments. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.294.2"
class="koboSpan">Regarding, for example, the suggested introduction of a
pollution tax on marine bunkers, the major reservations have been in the
following areas: an international levy on bunker would represent a tax
on international trade; it is not clear whether the IMO has the mandate
to create such a tax and the IMO does not have the possibility to
implement it; such a tax on all ships may not be compatible with the
requirements of the UNFCCC; the tax may benefit a few countries at the
expense of some other countries,
etc.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0604" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0604"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan"> As for all global environmental negotiations, the
discussions at IMO turn often into a politically sensitive debate.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.296.2" class="koboSpan">The dilemma
confronted by the marine environmental regulator is that on the one hand
air pollution from ships is a truly global problem and only global
solutions which are non-discriminatory and applicable to all ships are
meaningful; on the other, due to the huge gap in the development level
between countries, affordability and fairness are critical issues which
can not be avoided or ignored. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.296.3"
class="koboSpan">To solve this dilemma, a principle of
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">common but differentiated
responsibilities</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan">” was adopted by several UN bodies, particularly in the
area of the reduction of
GHG.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0605" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0605"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.300.1" class="koboSpan">One of the critical
issues that divides the IMO membership is whether or not market-based
instruments should be applicable to all ships, regardless of their
flags.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0606" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0606"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.301.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan"> On the surface, this looks to be an irrelevant
question, since all IMO Regulations, whether on the marine environment
or not, have been non-flag-discriminatory.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.302.2" class="koboSpan">Not only has
non-flag-discrimination been a matter of principle for international
maritime regulations, known as
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan">no more favourable
treatment</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">” principle, it is practically impossible to do
otherwise, given the very nature of the global shipping industry today.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.304.2" class="koboSpan">The
nationality
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_503"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan">of a ship involved in international trade cannot be
defined easily in a straightforward and definite manner.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.305.2" class="koboSpan">Legally every
ship has a nationality symbolised by the flag of the State the ship
flies. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.305.3"
class="koboSpan">However, changing the flag from one State to another is
simple, easy and inexpensive, and is common practice within the
international shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.305.4" class="koboSpan">As a matter of
fact, as of January 2008, 67% of the world total fleet in DWT was under
foreign flags, or open registry flags (UNCTAD, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.305.5" class="koboSpan">If the flag of
a ship is not used for a differentiated regulation, the so-called
“effective or genuine control” of a ship might be another way to
identify the State a ship should belong to.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.305.6" class="koboSpan">However, there
again, it is never a clear-cut business, since on the one hand, merger,
acquisition and stock market listing have made modern shipping an
increasingly globalised business with a multinational ownership
structure that is often very complex and changing all the time.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.305.7" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, the location of the headquarters or the principle management of
shipping companies has also become today quite mobile across borders.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.305.8" class="koboSpan">Should a new
regulation be applied with a flag differentiation or with “effective
control”, it is highly possible that deliberate changes of nationality
of ships, or location of management, or even the nationality of ship
owners, would occur to the extent that serious distortion would result
and the intended objectives of the regulations would fail.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.306.1" class="koboSpan">Because of the
above-mentioned features of international shipping, flag-differentiation
does not look to be an option for international maritime regulations,
unlike some environmental regulations implemented in other sectors,
including those under the framework of the Kyoto Protocol, which have
differentiated applications between industrialised and developing
countries. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.306.2" class="koboSpan">The
IMO regulations have been so far generally considered as purely
technical standards and requirements.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.306.3" class="koboSpan">Such a
technical characteristic has made maritime safety and environmental
regulations less politically sensitive.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.306.4" class="koboSpan">Since
market-based instruments have been brought to the table, the economic
implications have become more direct, as to continue with ship
operations, one will have to buy emission permits or pay bunker taxes.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.306.5" class="koboSpan">Obviously, a
higher environmental standard always means more abatement costs for all
ships concerned; either such a standard is implemented through
regulation-based instruments or market-based instruments.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.306.6" class="koboSpan">Actually the
difference is, as explained in earlier sections, the total abatement
costs of all ships would be lower if market-based instruments were to be
chosen.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.307.1" class="koboSpan">The reaction from the
shipping industry to the introduction of market-based instruments for
air pollution is rather mixed. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.307.2"
class="koboSpan">While many, for example the Scandinavian shipping
companies, have been in support, others have expressed reservations.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.307.3" class="koboSpan">The main
concerns are related to the complexity regarding the implementation of
market-based instruments. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.307.4"
class="koboSpan">For example, high-transaction costs are expected to be
associated with an emission permit trading scheme.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.307.5" class="koboSpan">Unnecessary
and cumbersome procedures may undermine the efficiency and productivity
of shipping operations. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.307.6"
class="koboSpan">Some industry leaders believe that a standard
regulation would still be the most effective and appropriate way to
control air pollution from
ships,</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0607" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0607"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan"> while others think that there are better, simpler and
more effective ways to achieve the intended objectives than tax or
emission permit
trading.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0608" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0608"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">5.2 Pollution tax or emission trading or both?</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">As discussed in the
preceding section, pollution tax and emission trading should have the
same cost effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.312.2"
class="koboSpan">Since marginal pollution control costs increase when
more stringent emission control standards are applied, the marginal
control cost is thus
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_504"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.313.1"
class="koboSpan">represented by a negative sloping curve to the amount
of pollution. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.313.2"
class="koboSpan">The main differences between the two instruments are
that pollution tax is
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan">price
based</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">”
while emission trading is
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.316.1"
class="koboSpan">quantity
based</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">”.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.317.2" class="koboSpan">In the case of
the former, the price or tax is fixed based on the marginal
environmental cost and the marginal control costs and then the quantity
of emission is left to adjust to the price.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.317.3" class="koboSpan">In the case of
the latter, the total amount of emission is fixed, based also on both
the marginal environmental and the marginal control costs, and the
prices of the permits, which correspond to the total amount of emission,
are allowed to change to market forces.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.317.4" class="koboSpan">Due to the
above basic characteristics of the two approaches, the choice between
them should be made on a case-by-case basis.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.317.5" class="koboSpan">There is also
the possibility of using a hybrid solution, that is a combination of
both pollution tax and emission
trading.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0609" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0609"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">There have been
proposals for numerous principles or criteria for international
regulations on the control of air pollution from ships.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.319.2" class="koboSpan">At the 57th
session of the IMO’s MEPC, the following nine-point principles were
suggested (IMO,
2008b)</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0610" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0610"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.320.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan"> for any future IMO regulations in this regard: such a
regulation should be:</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">“(1) effective in
contributing to the reduction of total global greenhouse gas emissions;
(2) binding and equally applicable to all flag States in order to avoid
evasion; (3) cost-effective; (4) able to limit – or at least –
effectively minimise competitive distortion; (5) based on sustainable
environmental development without penalizing global trade and growth;
(6) based on a goal-based approach and not prescribe specific methods;
(7) supportive of promoting and facilitating technical innovation and
R&D in the entire shipping sector; (8) accommodating to leading
technologies in the field of energy efficiency; and C (9) practical,
transparent, fraud free and easy to administer.”</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.323.1" class="koboSpan">The above principles
are general criteria proposed for any solution to be considered.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.323.2" class="koboSpan">Most of those
principles have already been discussed in previous sections when
analysing market-based instruments with standard-based instruments.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.323.3" class="koboSpan">As far as the
choice between the two market-based instruments is concerned, there are
essentially two major and important practical conditions or criteria to
be considered: the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
class="koboSpan">acceptability
</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.325.1" class="koboSpan">and
the</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan">
implementability</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.327.2"
class="koboSpan">Each of these two criteria can be further divided into
three sub-criteria. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.327.3"
class="koboSpan">With regard to the acceptability of an instrument, the
political, economic and technical aspects should be examined.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.327.4" class="koboSpan">With regard to
the implementability of an instrument, the aspects of simplicity, cost
and time delay should be looked into.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.327.5" class="koboSpan">These are now
examined as follows.</span>

1.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.328.1"
    class="koboSpan">Political
    acceptability:</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
    class="koboSpan"> This means whether the philosophy or the concept
    of an instrument is politically acceptable.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.329.2" class="koboSpan">At the
    IMO, when two market-based instruments were discussed in 2008, some
    States expressed a strong reservation against the introduction of a
    levy on fuel which they regarded to be an international tax imposed
    on shipping rather than a means to reduce pollution (IMO, 2008d).
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.329.3" class="koboSpan">A solution
    might be to have a specific plan on how to use the funds collected.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.329.4" class="koboSpan">For
    example, if the majority of the fund could be used for research and
    development projects on new environmental technologies and/or for
    assistant projects in favour of the countries lacking financial
    means for implementing pollution control from ships and/or for
    acquisition of CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
    class="koboSpan">2 </span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
    class="koboSpan">allowances.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0611" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0611"><span
    id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.332.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.333.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Concerns were also expressed that a tradable
    permit scheme would lead to unfair competition by disfavouring less
    developed countries
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_505"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.334.1"
    class="koboSpan">whose vessels were generally less-efficient.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.334.2" class="koboSpan">They
    further argued that a flag-differentiated method should be adopted.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.334.3" class="koboSpan">As
    discussed above, the impracticability of the flag-differentiated
    rule for international shipping makes it unacceptable.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.334.4" class="koboSpan">Generally
    speaking, a pollution tax has a lower acceptability.</span>
2.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.335.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Economic acceptability:
    </span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
    class="koboSpan">This means the financial burden would fall on the
    shipping industry if such market-based instruments were implemented.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.336.2" class="koboSpan">Depending
    on the actual level of fuel tax, the extra cost to the shipping
    industry may be high. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.336.3"
    class="koboSpan">For example, if USD30 per tonne of fuel is charged,
    it would be a 6% increase when the bunker is priced at USD500/tonne.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.336.4" class="koboSpan">The cost
    for the tradable permit option may be relatively low since, as an
    option, initial distribution of emission permits can be free of
    charge. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.336.5"
    class="koboSpan">When it comes to the trading of permits, less
    efficient vessels would have to incur higher costs to buy emission
    allowance from more efficient vessels.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.336.6" class="koboSpan">The
    possibility of modal shifting from maritime to other modes of
    transport is not big due to the large cost competitive edge of
    shipping. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.336.7"
    class="koboSpan">However, the fluctuation of the maritime freight
    market may have an important impact.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.336.8" class="koboSpan">In the
    case of a high freight market, while a fuel tax would most probably
    stable in the short and medium terms, the trading prices of emission
    permits might be traded at a high price.</span>
3.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.337.1"
    class="koboSpan">Technical
    acceptability:</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
    class="koboSpan"> This means whether the required technology
    advancement would be acceptable or technically possible.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.338.2" class="koboSpan">For
    example, now some ambitious goals are expected from international
    shipping to reduce the climate impact below the 2005 level by 2020
    and below the 1990 level by 2050.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.338.3" class="koboSpan">Should
    international seaborne trade be allowed to grow in the future, such
    objectives would require a reduction of emission levels by too big a
    margin which is not achievable with the predictable technological
    improvement of today in the areas of ship design and operation (IMO,
    2009h). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.338.4"
    class="koboSpan">Another aspect of difficulty to consider is the
    lack of an all-sector global emission trading scheme.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.338.5" class="koboSpan">If such a
    system is to be established for international shipping, it would be
    a single sector scheme at global level.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.338.6" class="koboSpan">However,
    it is generally believed that an open emission trading system (all
    sectors inclusive) is much more effective in pollution reduction
    than a closed (single sector) system.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.338.7" class="koboSpan">In view of
    the above, pollution tax has a higher acceptability over emission
    trading.</span>
4.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.339.1"
    class="koboSpan">Simplicity of implementation:
    </span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.340.1"
    class="koboSpan">Both options would need a special legal framework
    to be established at the IMO.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.340.2" class="koboSpan">As for
    emission trading, the level of simplicity depends on whether the
    initial distribution of allowance is made through auction or by free
    allocation since while free allocation is believed to compromise
    efficiency, auctioning has normally higher transaction costs.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.340.3" class="koboSpan">The
    trading itself requires a specific market mechanism and monitoring
    capability. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.340.4"
    class="koboSpan">In the absence of a global cross-sector emission
    trading scheme, a trading mechanism for international shipping alone
    has to be set up and maintained.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.340.5" class="koboSpan">As for the
    tax option, a levy on marine bunker can be executed by direct
    contribution of ships when taking the bunker (IMO, 2009g).
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.340.6" class="koboSpan">The aspect
    of effectiveness of the implementation should also be considered.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.340.7" class="koboSpan">Some
    recent studies and experiences in other sectors have shown that it
    is more likely to achieve a fair, generally applicable and thus
    effective emission control by introducing a pollution tax rather
    than through a cap-and-trade
    system.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0612" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0612"><span
    id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.341.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup>
5.  <span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_506"></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
    class="koboSpan">Cost of implementation:
    </span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.343.1"
    class="koboSpan">Although both options incur transaction costs, as
    far as international shipping is concerned a cap-and-trade system
    would be more expensive to operate than an emission tax system.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.343.2" class="koboSpan">With
    regard to taxation, the expected cost for the tax collected, which
    is directly based on the quantity of bunker taken, is predictable
    and straightforward (IMO, 2009g).
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.343.3" class="koboSpan">As for the
    cap-and-trade option, the transaction cost should include market and
    handling expenses. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.343.4"
    class="koboSpan">The initial distribution of emission permits as
    well as the trading of pollution permits would also involve some
    costs. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.343.5"
    class="koboSpan">These should include: search costs, negotiation
    costs, contact costs, even insurance costs and probably emission
    trading brokers might need to be involved.</span>
6.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.344.1"
    class="koboSpan">Time-delay of implementation:
    </span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">An
    existing scheme of similar nature would provide an important
    precedent and thus a good basis for the successful implementation of
    a market-based instrument in emission control from ships.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.345.2" class="koboSpan">With
    regard to emission trading, there are regional examples such as the
    EU Green House Emission Trading Scheme (EU ETS) which started in
    2005.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0613" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0613"><span
    id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
    class="koboSpan"> However, there has been no experience of a truly
    global scheme, so if this was to be established for international
    shipping, it will have to start from scratch and would most probably
    be a time-consuming process.
    </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.347.2" class="koboSpan">With
    regard to a levy on fuel, the IMO’s International Oil Pollution
    Compensation (IOPC) Fund is often cited as an example, or a valuable
    and well-functioning model, for a possible new fund on shipping
    related
    GHG.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0614" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0614"><span
    id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.349.1" class="koboSpan">Based on the above
analysis,
</span><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fig0275" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0275"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.350.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.351.1"
class="koboSpan"> below is proposed.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.351.2" class="koboSpan">In the table,
both the criteria of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan">acceptability</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan">implementability
</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.355.1" class="koboSpan">are
divided into three levels: high, medium and low.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.355.2" class="koboSpan">Three points
are allocated for high acceptability and high implementability cases;
two points are allocated for medium acceptability and medium
implementability cases; one point is allocated for low acceptability and
low implementability cases. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.355.3"
class="koboSpan">In addition, a weighting factor is introduced.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.355.4" class="koboSpan">Given the
equal importance of acceptability and implementability for a successful
introduction of market-based instruments, the same weight factors are
given to the two criteria. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.355.5"
class="koboSpan">However, within each criterion, different weighting is
allocated to the three aspects for each of acceptability and
implementability.</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0275" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00293.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fig0275)

</div>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_507"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.357.1"
class="koboSpan">We believe that at IMO the political acceptability is
slightly more important than the economic and technical acceptability,
therefore 20% is allocated to political acceptability, and 15% each to
economic and technical acceptability.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.357.2" class="koboSpan">As for the
three aspects of implementability, we consider that the cost implication
of a scheme is somewhat more important than the aspects of simplicity or
time delays, therefore 20% is allocated to the costs of implementation
and 15% each to the aspects of simplicity and time-delays.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.358.1" class="koboSpan">To summarise, we
conclude that emission trading is better on
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan">acceptability</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan"> than pollution tax, mainly due to the political
preference of trading over a tax solution and the perceived lower costs
of emission trading to the industry, given that all or most emission
permits may be allocated free of charge to shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.360.2" class="koboSpan">However, when
it comes to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan">implementability</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan">, the overall score for pollution tax is much higher
than that for emission trading. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.362.2"
class="koboSpan">The main reasons are that there is no appropriate truly
global cap-and-trade system available, the current systems under the
Kyoto Protocol or regional, such as the EU ETS, or national schemes are
not entirely effective, and the transaction costs of such a scheme for
international shipping are expected to be high.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.362.3" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, regarding the emission levy option, the IMO’s International Oil
Pollution Compensation (IOPC) Fund, which is a well-functioning system,
provides a good precedent for the proposed IMO International GHG Fund
under which an emission-reduction-aimed marine bunker levy scheme would
be introduced. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.362.4"
class="koboSpan">Despite various differences between the existing IOPC
Fund and the suggested GHG Fund, there are sufficient commonalities
which may enhance the likelihood of a successful pollution tax option
being introduced.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.363.1" class="koboSpan">5.3 Amount of emission to reduce: level of tax or cap for emission trading</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.364.1" class="koboSpan">One of the important
aspects regarding the amount of emission for reduction is whether the
standard should be a relative ratio or an absolute number.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.364.2" class="koboSpan">This is
because the production, which is the source of pollution, is not static;
it normally grows with time. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.364.3"
class="koboSpan">Obviously, a relative standard can be more easily
achievable, but if shipping activities, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.364.4" class="koboSpan">the pollution
base, increases quickly, as it has been and will most probably continue
to do, the environmental objectives may fail.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.364.5" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, an absolute standard guarantees the achievement of the
environmental goal, but this is often technically very challenging and
can undermine economic development.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">One compromising
approach is to use a relative standard but with a progressively more
stringent requirement based on the prediction of future technology.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.365.2" class="koboSpan">The IMO has so
far been using this method for its regulations regarding the prevention
of air pollution from ships. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.365.3"
class="koboSpan">As part of MARPOL VI, the 2008 IMO SOx Standards and
NOx Technical Code as shown in Table 5 is an example.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.365.4" class="koboSpan">The
requirements for SOx and NOx emissions are many times more stringent for
future ships.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.366.1" class="koboSpan">The relative
standards, even with progressively tougher requirements, still carry
much uncertainty with regard to both the environmental impact as well as
future technology. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.366.2"
class="koboSpan">So the general trend, as demonstrated by the Kyoto
Protocol, is to use absolute standards.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.366.3" class="koboSpan">Since both tax
and cap are marginal cost based, the critical issue becomes the
measurement of the marginal environmental costs and marginal control
cost. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.366.4" class="koboSpan">However,
as discussed above, it is difficult to calculate the marginal
environmental damage costs of emissions from ships.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.366.5" class="koboSpan">Alternatively,
the global objective CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan"> emission level can be used as a benchmark for
calculating the tax rate and cap for trading.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.368.2" class="koboSpan">Such an
objective</span>

<div id="Ch016.xhtml_fig0276" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_508"></span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.369.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00294.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.370.1"
class="koboSpan">Table 6:</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.371.1"
class="koboSpan"> IMO SOx Standards and NOx Technical Code 2008</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.372.1"
class="koboSpan">CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.373.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.374.1"
class="koboSpan"> emission level is the one that is necessary to limit
global warming to within
2o</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.375.1"
class="koboSpan">C</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.376.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.376.2"
class="koboSpan">Big differences exist between estimates of how much the
reduction of GHG emission is needed, with amounts varying from 20% by
2020 of the baseline value in 2020 (IMO, 2009i) to 50% by 2050 relative
to 1990 levels (Meinshausen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.377.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.378.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2009).</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.379.1" class="koboSpan">At the IMO, shipping
specific emission standards for market-based instruments have been
proposed. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.379.2" class="koboSpan">For
example, based on a dedicated study, a suggestion was made on bunker
fuel tax which is within the range US\$15–US\$45 per tonne of bunker
fuel based on different conditions and aiming at different objectives
(IMO, 2009g). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.379.3"
class="koboSpan">Also as a result of another special research on the
emission permit trading scheme, a total
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.380.1" class="koboSpan">2
</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.381.1" class="koboSpan">emission
cap of </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.382.1"
class="koboSpan">740 million
tonnes</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.383.1" class="koboSpan">
in 2020 was proposed (IMO, 2009i).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.383.2" class="koboSpan">These tax or
cap standard proposals, which have been made within the IMO framework as
results of extensive discussions and investigations, are considered at
the IMO as both challenging and realistic.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.383.3" class="koboSpan">However, they
are not necessarily perceived as sufficient or bold enough by many
people outside shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.384.1" class="koboSpan">Given the seriousness
of the current environmental challenge and the growing general concerns
and consciousness of global climate change, high expectations from the
maritime transport industry and a sort of “shipping-has-to-change”
attitude are being formed. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.384.2"
class="koboSpan">As a consequence, some very ambitious emission
reduction objectives are also suggested for the shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.384.3" class="koboSpan">The European
Commission requested that an agreement should be reached in 2009 to
reduce the climate impact of maritime transport below 2005 levels by
2020, and significantly below 1990 levels by 2050 (EC, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_509"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.385.1"
class="koboSpan">A proposal put forward to the IMO by a group of NGOs
urged the shipping industry to reduce GHG emissions from ships to at
least 40% below the 1990 levels by 2020 and at least 80% below the 1990
levels by 2050 (IMO, 2009f). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.385.2"
class="koboSpan">Let us take a brief look to see if such objectives are
achievable or not. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.385.3"
class="koboSpan">Based on the Second IMO GHG Study 2009 (IMO, 2009e), in
1990, the total amount of
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.386.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.387.1"
class="koboSpan"> emissions from international shipping was 468 million
tonnes. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.387.2" class="koboSpan">With
regard to the CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.389.1"
class="koboSpan"> emissions from international shipping in 2050, there
are several scenarios with different patterns of economic, demographic
growth and efficiency of transport.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.389.2" class="koboSpan">If we take a
rounded balanced scenario at the base level, the estimated
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.390.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan"> emission by international shipping would be around
3,400 million tonnes in 2050. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.391.2"
class="koboSpan">To bring such “business as usual” 2050
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.392.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan"> emission to the 1990 levels already means a reduction
by as much as 86%, or by 97% to reach 80% below the 1990 levels.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.393.2" class="koboSpan">This is
certainly much higher than the most optimistic estimate of 75% of
possible CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.394.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.395.1"
class="koboSpan"> reduction based on the combined improvement measures
taken in ship design and operation.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.395.2" class="koboSpan">So if the real
objective is for international shipping originated
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.396.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.397.1"
class="koboSpan"> emissions in 2050 to
be</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.398.1"
class="koboSpan">
significantly</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.399.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.400.1"
class="koboSpan">80% </span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.401.1"
class="koboSpan">below the 1990 levels, then the answer will have to be
either a complete and revolutionary change of the energy pattern for
most ships or, alternatively, a huge sacrifice in the form of a
substantial reduction of international seaborne trade.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.401.2" class="koboSpan">The first
alternative is, obviously, a relatively remote possibility, while the
second alternative is not seen as a valid
option.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0615" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0615"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.402.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan"> Certainly, shipping is not alone; many other sectors
are facing similar challenges.</span>

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.404.1" class="koboSpan">5.4 Limitations of market-based instruments</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.405.1" class="koboSpan">As discussed at the
beginning of this chapter, “command-and-control” methods have the
advantages of simplicity, effectiveness and political attractiveness,
though with a lower cost efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.405.2" class="koboSpan">Yet
market-based instruments have also some major disadvantages which may
undermine the effectiveness of pollution control.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.405.3" class="koboSpan">In a way, all
the strengths of the “command-and-control” methods could be considered
as the weaknesses of the “market-based” methods, yet the most important
limitations of both cap-and-trade and emission tax instruments are
related to the effectiveness of application and to the fluctuation of
the market.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.406.1" class="koboSpan">With regard to the
first concern, which is the effectiveness of application, unlike a
technical standard, which can be clearly defined and relatively easily
monitored, for a cap-and-trade scheme it is hard to impose a strict,
general application. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.406.2"
class="koboSpan">Yet, without a same-to-all application, the system will
not succeed. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.406.3"
class="koboSpan">The Kyoto Protocol offers exemptions to developing
countries, and the EU ETS does not include some new member States and
many “special” sectors are also outside the scheme.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.406.4" class="koboSpan">With regard to
international shipping, it is generally envisaged that not all countries
would join when a shipping emission trading system is established
(Torvanger </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.407.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.408.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007).</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.409.1" class="koboSpan">The pollution tax
solution has not been a favourable option since taxation normally relies
on a country’s fiscal regime, which can only be effectively implemented
at the national level. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.409.2"
class="koboSpan">Air pollution, however, is an international problem
without borders, and would require international taxation that could be
very difficult to implement. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.409.3"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, international shipping might just be a
rare exception in this regard. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.409.4"
class="koboSpan">All ships, the emission from which should be taxed, are
operating in international waters.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.409.5" class="koboSpan">As a matter of
fact, a strong argument expressed at the IMO is that a pollution tax
addressing emissions from ships should be paid by all ships
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan">regardless
</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.411.1" class="koboSpan">of
their nationality.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_510"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.412.1"
class="koboSpan">With regard to the second concern, which is the effect
of market fluctuation, the situation for emission trading is different
from the situation of emission tax.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.412.2" class="koboSpan">There are two
problems with emission trading systems.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.412.3" class="koboSpan">The first
concerns price fluctuation. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.412.4"
class="koboSpan">It has been reported that the EU ETS which started in
2005, has seen recently that the carbon price dropped to about €10 per
tonne from €30 per tonne in the middle of 2008 (PriceWaterHouseCoopers,
2009). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.412.5" class="koboSpan">This is
believed to be much below the marginal control cost of even a low
efficient polluter. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.412.6"
class="koboSpan">With this low price, the incentive for pollution
control is much reduced. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.412.7"
class="koboSpan">The fact that carbon prices fluctuate so much is not
good for encouraging long-term investment in new control technologies.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.412.8" class="koboSpan">Another
problem with fluctuating carbon prices is that it invites speculators to
buy and sell large amounts of permits and therefore there is a
possibility of market manipulation.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.413.1" class="koboSpan">The problem of market
fluctuation for pollution tax is different.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.413.2" class="koboSpan">In
international shipping, the freight markets develop in cycles, where the
level of freight can fluctuate during a short period of time,
particularly in dry bulk markets which can be highly volatile.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.413.3" class="koboSpan">A pollution
tax, which is defined as a fixed amount to each tonne of bunker taken
has to be relatively stable. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.413.4"
class="koboSpan">It therefore would represent a variable percentage of
the ship’s marginal benefit. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.413.5"
class="koboSpan">When the market is high, a shipowner would not hesitate
to pollute more even if this involved paying more tax.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.413.6" class="koboSpan">So in the
short run, with a booming freight market the amount of pollution may
well pass the expected level. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.413.7"
class="koboSpan">During the shipping market boom of 2003–mid-2008, the
scraping of old ships was delayed and all ships were sailing at full
speed, even when the oil price was as high as US\$140 per barrel.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.413.8" class="koboSpan">To solve such
kinds of problems, a system with variable tax levels should be
introduced.</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.414.1" class="koboSpan">Given the
shortcomings of market-based instruments, an integrated approach should
be considered. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.414.2"
class="koboSpan">There are two levels of integration.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.414.3" class="koboSpan">If only
market-based methods are to be used, a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.415.1"
class="koboSpan">hybrid </span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.416.1"
class="koboSpan">system could produce better outcomes than using either
emission trading or emission tax alone.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.416.2" class="koboSpan">This is
because a combined system could prevent trading price fluctuation by
setting the emission tax as the floor, which becomes the minimum amount
a ship has to pay. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.416.3"
class="koboSpan">At the same time, some monitoring and an operational
mechanism can be established by selling additional permits at a ceiling
price when the prices of emission permits reach the ceiling.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.416.4" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, a </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.417.1"
class="koboSpan">hybrid</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.418.1"
class="koboSpan"> system could overcome the difficulties of containing
the level of pollution when the market is high by introducing a “cap”,
the maximum amount of emission allowed.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.418.2" class="koboSpan">Another level
of integration is to combine traditional regulatory and relatively new
economic approaches, or in other words, applying pollution standards
supplemented by market-based
instruments.</span><sup><a href="#Ch016.xhtml_fn0616" id="Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0616"><span
id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.419.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.420.1"
class="koboSpan"> In a complex sector such as international shipping, an
integrated policy could enhance the overall effectiveness of pollution
control and thus have a better chance of meeting ambitious environmental
objectives.</span>

## <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.421.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.421.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.422.1" class="koboSpan">So far, efforts to
reduce marine pollution from international shipping within the framework
of the IMO have exclusively employed the so-called “command-and-control”
approach which means setting up pollution standards and regulations that
are to be complied with. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.422.2"
class="koboSpan">However, today pressure is mounting to include
international shipping into the global climate change programme.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.422.3" class="koboSpan">The stakes are
high and objectives ambitious. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.422.4"
class="koboSpan">Traditional methods are unable to adequately deliver
the desired results due to
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_511"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.1"
class="koboSpan">their lack of efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.2" class="koboSpan">The biggest
deficiency of the “command-and-control” approach is that it cannot find
an optimal way to control pollution since such a policy takes only the
pollution damage cost into account, and not the control cost.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.3" class="koboSpan">Market-based
instruments such as pollution tax or emission permit trading can solve
efficiency problems by enabling shipping companies to use the most
appropriate control methods, providing incentives to those with lower
control costs and consequently encouraging the employment of more
advanced control technologies. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.4"
class="koboSpan">Since 2005, discussions have been on-going at IMO’s
MEPC concerning the introduction of market-based instruments for the
prevention of GHG emissions from international shipping.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.5" class="koboSpan">Much progress
has been made in spite of some serious difficulties and reservations,
mainly regarding whether or not all States should assume the same
responsibility, but given the nature of international shipping, it is
inconceivable to have a differentiated policy based on ships’ flags.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.6" class="koboSpan">For the time
being international shipping still has the reputation of being the most
environment friendly mode of transport.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.7" class="koboSpan">However, as
land-based transport modes are continuously making significant
improvements to their environmental performances, shipping may well lose
its reputation if the current situation is not rectified.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.8" class="koboSpan">Setting up
realistic but high environmental standards and exploring all the
potentials of market-based instruments will ensure the healthy growth of
international shipping along a sustainable path.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.9" class="koboSpan">While emission
tax and emission trading are two approaches with the same theoretical
efficiency, the emission tax option prevails as a more suitable
market-based instrument to use due to its higher implementability, while
a combination of the two instruments would most probably produce even
better outcomes. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.423.10"
class="koboSpan">Finally, the international maritime community should
continue to work within the framework of the International Maritime
Organisation where market-based instruments should be used as
supplementary methods to the technical and operational standards in
order to achieve the agreed environmental objectives.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.424.1"
class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0589)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.425.1"
class="koboSpan"> World Maritime University, Malmö, Sweden.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.425.2" class="koboSpan">Email:
</span><span class="italic">[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.426.1"
class="koboSpan">shuo.ma@wmu.sc</span>](mailto:shuo.ma@wmu.sc)</span>

<div class="footnote" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

### <span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.427.1" class="koboSpan">Endnotes</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.428.1"
class="koboSpan">1.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0590)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.429.1"
class="koboSpan"> The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), which
represents the shipping industry, released this information in July 2009
(ICS, 23 July 2009), four months prior to the UNFCCC Copenhagen meeting
to be held in December 2009, on which a new global agreement on climate
change might be concluded. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.429.2"
class="koboSpan">The ICS emphasised that the shipping industry will take
its due responsibilities and make all necessary efforts for the global
fight against climate change.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.430.1"
class="koboSpan">2.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0591)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.431.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is reported that lacking motivation, and/or
incentives, the shipping industry seemed uninterested in some of the
latest and more advanced pollution control technologies.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.431.2" class="koboSpan">As remarked by
the ship engine manufacturer Wärtsilä’s President of Finnish operations,
Juha Kytölä, “a lot of the technologies have been available for years,
and have been proven to work in land-based power plants for which
tougher emission rules, but lack of demand from the owners” (Eason, 15
July 2008).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.432.1"
class="koboSpan">3.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0592)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.433.1"
class="koboSpan"> Sweden promotes a “vision zero” policy with an
objective of zero road accident fatality.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.433.2" class="koboSpan">“The Vision
Zero policy”, as explained by Mr Claes Tingvall, the Traffic Safety
Director of the Swedish Road Administration, “is not a figure; it is a
shift in philosophy. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.433.3"
class="koboSpan">Normal traffic policy is a balancing act between
mobility benefits and safety problems.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.433.4" class="koboSpan">The Vision
Zero policy refuses to use human life and health as part of that
balancing act; they are non negotiable.”</span>

<span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_512"></span>[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.434.1"
class="koboSpan">4.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0593)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.435.1"
class="koboSpan"> A recent Norwegian report (Torvanger
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.436.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.437.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007) suggested to divide the standards into two
parts: design emission standards and operational emission standards.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.437.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the operational emission standards are with an associated fee which
should be paid by the polluter in case the emission exceeds the limit.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.437.3" class="koboSpan">Procedural
standards were not specifically considered.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.438.1"
class="koboSpan">5.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0594)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.439.1"
class="koboSpan"> To use economic methods for environmental pollution
control, the market mechanism is to be utilised based on economic
choices. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.439.2" class="koboSpan">For
this reason, the pollution has to be of a voluntarily and intentionally
committed nature (Hussen, 2004).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.440.1"
class="koboSpan">6.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0595)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.441.1"
class="koboSpan"> When a proposal on ship emission control was made that
the IMO should concentrate on the environmental outcome required, and
encourage different ways of achieving the agreed emission reduction
goals, the Hong Kong Shipowners’ Association rejected it and argued that
“regulation was the only way to ensure the industry used distillate
fuels with a global sulphur content cap of 1%”
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.442.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s
List</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.443.1" class="koboSpan">,
2007).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.444.1"
class="koboSpan">7.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0596)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.445.1"
class="koboSpan"> At the meeting of an IMO Working Group on GHG Emission
from Ships held in June 2008 in Oslo, Norway, hot discussions took place
on the proposal of a global levy on marine bunker fuel.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.445.2" class="koboSpan">Delegates from
some major shipping nations expressed strong objection to the proposal
(IMO, 2008d).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.446.1"
class="koboSpan">8.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0597)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.447.1"
class="koboSpan"> At the 80th session of the IMO’s MSC in May 2005, a
five-tier system of “goal-based standards” was agreed and it was also
agreed that the principles of IMO Goal-based Standards were “broad,
over-arching safety, environmental and/or security standards that ships
are required to meeting during their lifecycle; the required level to be
achieved by the requirements applied by class societies and other
recognised organisations, administrations and IMO; clear demonstrable,
verifiable, long standing, implementable and achievable, irrespective of
ship design and technology; and specific enough in order not to be open
to differing interpretations” (IMO, 2005c).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.448.1"
class="koboSpan">9.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0598)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.449.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the preparation for the 15th UNFCCC meeting in
December 2009 in Copenhagen, pressures have increased.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.449.2" class="koboSpan">Strong voices
are heard from the EC (European Commission, 2009) as well as from some
NGOs (IMO, 2009b). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.449.3"
class="koboSpan">The objective is to either have maritime transport
included in the forthcoming global emission control package after 2012,
or for international shipping to come up with a GHG reduction plan
within the framework of the IMO which should be in line with the global
package.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.450.1"
class="koboSpan">10.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0599)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.451.1"
class="koboSpan"> At IMO’s MEPC 59th Session, 13–17 July 2009, it was
agreed that a package of interim and voluntary technical and operational
measures were to be used on trial purposes to reduce greenhouse gases
(GHGs) from international shipping (IMO, 2009a).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.451.2" class="koboSpan">These measures
include: (a) interim guidelines on the method of calculation, and
voluntary verification, of the Energy Efficiency Design Index for new
ships, which is intended to stimulate innovation and technical
development of all the elements influencing the energy efficiency of a
ship from its design phase; (b) guidance on the development of a Ship
Energy Efficiency Management Plan, for new and existing ships, which
incorporates best practices for the fuel efficient operation of ships;
as well as guidelines for voluntary use of the Ship Energy Efficiency
Operational Indicator for new and existing ships, which enables
operators to measure the fuel efficiency of a ship.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.452.1"
class="koboSpan">11.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0600)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.453.1"
class="koboSpan"> Shortly after MARPOL Annex VI entered into force, at
the 54th session of IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee in
December 2005, the United
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_513"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.454.1"
class="koboSpan">Kingdom made a proposal on “the potential of emissions
trading to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from ships” (IMO, 2005b).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.454.2" class="koboSpan">The document
introduced the concept of emission trading, the benefits of it and the
possibilities as well as challenges of applying carbon dioxide emission
trading for shipping. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.454.3"
class="koboSpan">This was the start, at the IMO, of discussions on the
possible use of economic instruments in marine environmental
regulations.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.455.1"
class="koboSpan">12.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0601)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.456.1"
class="koboSpan"> Although a theory well accepted, the use of economic
instruments to deal with environment protection had not been attempted
until 1990. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.456.2"
class="koboSpan">Under Title IV of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments
(1990 CAAA Public Law 101-549), a tradable
SO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.457.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.458.1"
class="koboSpan"> emission permit system was created in the USA.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.458.2" class="koboSpan">Such a program
has been 2 implemented in two phases, 1995–1999 and 2000–2009
respectively (Joskow and Schmalensee, 2000).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.459.1"
class="koboSpan">13.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0602)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.460.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 in Kyoto, Japan
and entered into force on February 2005.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.460.2" class="koboSpan">It requires
industrialised countries to reduce their collective GHG emissions by
5.2% compared to the year 1990.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.461.1"
class="koboSpan">Emission
trading</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.462.1" class="koboSpan">
is one of the Protocol’s “flexible mechanisms” to allow the parties to
meet their GHG emission targets.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.463.1"
class="koboSpan">14.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0603)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.464.1"
class="koboSpan"> At the MEPC 54th session in March 2006, the
submissions by the UK (MEPC54/4/2) and Norway (MEPC/4/7) were the first
proposals to use a market-based instrument.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.464.2" class="koboSpan">At the MEPC
55th session in October 2006, 1 submission was received; at the 56th
session in July 2007, two submissions were received (EC and Norway); at
the 57th session, in March 2008, five submissions were received (Sweden
x 2, Denmark, x 2, Norway), in the 58th session in October 2008, four
submissions were received (IMarEst, Denmark, France/Germany/Norway, WWF)
and in the 59th session 11 submissions were received (Denmark, Norway,
France/Germany/Norway x 2, Japan x 3, OCIMF x 2, CLIA, ICS).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.465.1"
class="koboSpan">15.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0604)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.466.1"
class="koboSpan"> At the Intersessional Meeting of the GHG Working Group
held in May 2008 in Oslo, Norway, the delegates were divided into the
industrialised countries and the developing countries, particularly the
so-called “emerging economies”, respectively (IMO, 2008d).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.466.2" class="koboSpan">On the one
hand, Denmark, Norway and most other European countries, except Greece,
all supported the use of market-based instruments, either in the form of
a tax on bunkers or emission trading schemes.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.466.3" class="koboSpan">Such an
opinion was also supported by Japan, the USA and Australia.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.466.4" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, countries like Saudi Arabia, India, China, Brazil, South Africa
were against the introduction of market-based instruments.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.466.5" class="koboSpan">One of the
arguments was that under the Kyoto Protocol, only Annex 1 (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.466.6"
class="koboSpan">industrialised) countries were requested to commit on
pollution reductions. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.466.7"
class="koboSpan">An across the board type of solution, either a bunker
tax or emission trading, would violate such a UNFCCC principle.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.467.1"
class="koboSpan">16.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0605)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.468.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is generally accepted that despite their common
responsibilities, important differences exist between the stated
responsibilities of developed and developing countries.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.468.2" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.469.1"
class="koboSpan">Rio Declaration
</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.470.1" class="koboSpan">states:
“In view of the different contributions to global environmental
degradation, States have common but differentiated responsibilities.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.470.2" class="koboSpan">The developed
countries acknowledge the responsibility that they bear in the
international pursuit of sustainable development in view of the
pressures their societies place on the global environment and of the
technologies and financial resources they command.”
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.470.3" class="koboSpan">Similar
language exists in the UN
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.471.1"
class="koboSpan">Framework Convention on Climate
Change</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.472.1" class="koboSpan">
that parties should act to protect the climate system “on the basis of
equality and in accordance with their common but differentiated
responsibilities and
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_514"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.473.1"
class="koboSpan">respective capabilities.”
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.473.2" class="koboSpan">In recent
