interpretations of WTO law, there is movement towards an obligation to
consider the particular economic, social and environmental situation of
developing countries when adopting environmental measures.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.473.3" class="koboSpan">The WTO
dispute settlement panel in the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.474.1"
class="koboSpan">Shrimp </span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.475.1"
class="koboSpan">case expressly mentions the principle of “common but
differentiated responsibilities” in its conclusions.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.476.1"
class="koboSpan">17.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0606)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.477.1"
class="koboSpan"> At the 58th session of the IMO MEPC meeting in August
2008, some delegates argued that the Kyoto Protocol requests the
countries listed in Annex I (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.477.2" class="koboSpan">industrialised
countries) to the UNFCCC to work through IMO to pursue the limitation or
reduction of GHG emissions from marine bunker fuels and the principle of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.478.1"
class="koboSpan">common but differentiated
responsibilities</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.479.1"
class="koboSpan">, which is the fundamental principle accepted by the
UNFCCC in fighting climate change globally, should also be the guiding
principle of IMO’s efforts in addressing GHG emissions from
international shipping (IMO, 2008a).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.480.1"
class="koboSpan">18.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0607)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.481.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is reported in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.482.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s
List</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.483.1" class="koboSpan">
(2007) that “the Hong Kong Shipowners’ Association largely rejected the
Chamber’s (ICS) holistic approach and said regulation was the only way
to ensure the industry used distillate fuels with a global sulphur
content cap of 1%.” </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.483.2"
class="koboSpan">The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) was
advocating that the IMO should set up a cap and let the industry choose
the most appropriate way of controlling pollution.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.484.1"
class="koboSpan">19.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0608)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.485.1"
class="koboSpan"> It was reported that some shipping industry leaders in
such shipping capitals as Hong Kong, Oslo and Piraeus expressed concerns
about emission trade or bunker tax.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.485.2" class="koboSpan">They thought
that using a low sulphur fuel would be a much better solution to achieve
the goal (</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.486.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s
List</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.487.1" class="koboSpan">,
17 June 2008;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.488.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s
List</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.489.1" class="koboSpan">,
25 June 2008). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.489.2"
class="koboSpan">Some concerns were also expressed on whether
market-based instruments would be a hindrance to world trade
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.490.1"
class="koboSpan">Lloyd’s
List</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.491.1" class="koboSpan">,
28 November 2007).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.492.1"
class="koboSpan">20.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0609)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.493.1"
class="koboSpan"> At the IMO GHG Working Group meeting held in Oslo
2008, the Norwegian Government made a Hybrid system proposal (IMO,
2008c) as one of the market-based instrument options for the reduction
of ship-originated emissions. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.493.2"
class="koboSpan">The basic principle of a Hybrid system is to restrict
the price fluctuations of the emission permits by setting up a floor
which might be equivalent to the emission tax and a ceiling at which
additional permits would be issued.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.493.3" class="koboSpan">It is also
important that this “band” of allowed prices should increase over time
with economic growth to achieve the required carbon emission objectives
(PriceWaterHouseCoopers, 2009).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.494.1"
class="koboSpan">21.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0610)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.495.1"
class="koboSpan"> Although the 11-point principles were accepted at MEPC
57, reservations were expressed by some member countries.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.495.2" class="koboSpan">The
disagreement was on the second point which reads “binding and equally
applicable to all flag States in order to avoid evasion”.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.495.3" class="koboSpan">It was
considered that such a provision was in conflict with the Kyoto Protocol
notion of “</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.496.1"
class="koboSpan">common but differentiated responsibilities and
respective capabilities</span></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.497.1"
class="koboSpan">”.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.498.1"
class="koboSpan">22.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0611)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.499.1"
class="koboSpan"> Between 1990 and 2007, world seaborne trade increased
from 4,008 million tonnes to 8,022 million tonnes or 100% in 17 years
(UNCTAD, 1991–2008). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.499.2"
class="koboSpan">Unless a completely new energy source has been found
and economically adopted in the shipping industry, by 2050, the growth
of seaborne trade predicted would be much higher than the most
optimistic expected fuel efficiency improvement by 75% of the current
level by then. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.499.3"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, shipping would most probably have to buy
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.500.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.501.1"
class="koboSpan"> allowances from other sectors in the future.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.502.1"
class="koboSpan">23.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0612)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.503.1"
class="koboSpan"> Many believe that both the Kyoto Protocol and the
European Emission Trading Scheme have not effectively achieved their
intended objectives. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.503.2"
class="koboSpan">Some leading experts in the area demonstrated recently
that under the Kyoto Protocol, and
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_page_515"></span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.504.1"
class="koboSpan">using the cap-and-trade method, even countries that
accepted the toughest emission reduction targets, such as Japan, have
seen their emissions actually increase (Hansen, 2009); and emissions
under the ETS have actually increased by 10% (Shapiro, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.504.2" class="koboSpan">One of the
reasons is claimed to be the lack of fair and general applications: the
systems are flawed due to their openness to make all sorts of
exemptions. </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.504.3" class="koboSpan">In
international shipping, it is highly unlikely that all shipping nations
would join the cap-and-trade scheme.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.504.4" class="koboSpan">If so,
unfairness would occur and objectives would not be achieved.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.505.1"
class="koboSpan">24.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0613)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.506.1"
class="koboSpan"> The EU ETS, started in 2005, is the largest
multinational and multi-sector emission trading scheme in the world.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.506.2" class="koboSpan">A suggestion
(Kågeson, 2007) was made to include international shipping into the EU
ETS, despite the fact that the EU ETS is only a regional scheme.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.507.1"
class="koboSpan">25.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0614)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.508.1"
class="koboSpan"> The IOPC Fund is an intergovernmental compensation
scheme for pollution damage for oil spills from tankers.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.508.2" class="koboSpan">It is
suggested that a GHG Fund could be established based on the IOPC Fund.
</span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.508.3" class="koboSpan">However, there
are differences in a number of areas between the two schemes with regard
to the application, administration and management of the funds (IMO,
2009c). </span><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.508.4" class="koboSpan">On a
national level, Norway introduced a pollution tax from 2007 on NOx
emissions, where domestic shipping is included in the system.</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.509.1"
class="koboSpan">26.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0615)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.510.1"
class="koboSpan"> Referring to the EC request for shipping originated
CO</span><sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.511.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.512.1"
class="koboSpan"> to be significantly below the 1990 levels, Japan
expressed its reservations and called this “not imaginable” (IMO,
2009h).</span>

[<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.513.1"
class="koboSpan">27.</span>](#Ch016.xhtml_bck_fn0616)<span id="Ch016.xhtml_kobo.514.1"
class="koboSpan"> In a recent study of the European Commission (CE
Delft, 2006), an integrated solution was suggested in the form of three
policy options to reduce the climate impact of shipping which are: (1)
to include shipping into the EU ETS, which means a market-based
instrument; (2) to use a sort of “green tariff” at ports, which offers
an incentive to shipping companies based on their environmental
performances; and (3) to impose emission standards on ships calling at
European ports.</span>

</div>
