<span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_519"></span>[<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 17</span>\
<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Vessel Safety and Accident Analysis</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0393)
========================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Wayne</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">K.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Talley</span></span><a href="#Ch017.xhtml_fn0617" id="Ch017.xhtml_bck_fn0617"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">Vessel safety consists
of the safety of a vessel and the safety in the operation of a vessel.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">The safety of a
vessel is concerned with whether a vessel adheres to construction,
design or technical standards and therefore is seaworthy.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.8.3" class="koboSpan">Since safety in
the operation of a vessel is difficult to observe, input and outcome
proxies for vessel operation safety are often used.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.8.4" class="koboSpan">Input proxies
represent actions by shipping lines, ports and government to decrease
the probability of unsafe vessel operation; outcome proxies represent
unsafe outcomes of vessel operation.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.8.5" class="koboSpan">Vessel
maintenance and operator training expenditures are examples of input
proxies; ship accidents and fatalities and injuries from these accidents
are examples of outcome proxies. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.8.6"
class="koboSpan">Since little is known of the extent to which safety
inputs translate into vessel operation safety, outcome rather than input
proxies are often used as proxies for vessel operation safety.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">A vessel accident is an
unintended happening and may or may not result in damage to the vessel
and injuries to individuals on board.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.9.2" class="koboSpan">The probability
of a vessel sustaining damage in an accident is the product of two
probabilities: (1) the probability of involvement in an accident (event
probability), and (2) the probability of vessel damage given that an
accident has occurred (damage conditional probability).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.9.3" class="koboSpan">Similarly, the
probability of an injury in a vessel accident is the product of the
event probability and the probability of an injury given that an
accident has occurred (injury conditional probability).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.9.4" class="koboSpan">The severity of
an accident may vary from: no vessel damage to the loss of the vessel,
no injuries to fatalities, and no cargo damage to loss of cargo.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.9.5" class="koboSpan">A vessel may
remain seaworthy following an accident or may be non-seaworthy.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">The remainder of the
chapter is structured as follows: Section 2 presents a discussion of
vessel safety concerns. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.10.2"
class="koboSpan">Causes of vessel accidents and related injuries are
presented in Section 3 and vessel accident costs are discussed in
Section 4. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.10.3"
class="koboSpan">Determinants of vessel accident property damage costs,
injuries and injury severity, and seaworthiness are discussed in
Sections 5, 6 and 7, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.10.4" class="koboSpan">Statistics for
world accident vessel losses are presented in Section 8.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.10.5" class="koboSpan">A summary of
the above discussion is found in Section 9.</span>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_520"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">Vessel Safety Concerns</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">Prior to World War I
the need for uniform international vessel safety rules and their
enforcement became evident. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.12.2"
class="koboSpan">Since vessels involved in international commerce must
fly the flags of their countries of registry and obey laws of this
registry, the flag states (or countries) were asked to adopt and enforce
internationally agreed upon rules.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">The
multilateral enforcement of multilateral vessel safety rules worked well
until “flags of convenience” (FOCs) or open registries were adopted,
i.e. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.12.4" class="koboSpan">the
registration of vessels in countries other than those of its citizen
owners (Goss, 1994). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.12.5"
class="koboSpan">Prior to the 1950s, FOCs were insignificant in number.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.12.6" class="koboSpan">Today, over
one-half of the world’s shipping fleet is registered with open registers
– raising concern for enforcement of international safety rules, given
that some FOCs confine their interests to collecting registration dues,
having no interest in adopting or enforcing rules, and can not be
compelled to do so as sovereign powers.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.12.7" class="koboSpan">The major
open-registry flag countries include Panama, Liberia, Cyprus and the
Bahamas.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">What determines
whether a vessel will fly a foreign flag (FOC) or a national flag (the
flag of the country of its citizen owner)?
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.13.2" class="koboSpan">An
investigation into the determinants of vessel flag (for vessels that
trade internationally) is found in a study by Hoffmann, Sanchez and
Talley (2005). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.13.3"
class="koboSpan">The likelihood that the operator of a vessel will
choose a foreign flag decreases with vessel age and if the vessel was
built in the vessel operator’s country, but increases with the size of
the vessel, if the vessel is a container vessel, if the vessel
operator’s country is a developed country, and if the vessel is classed
by a member of the International Association of Classification Societies
(IACS).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">The ineffective FOC
enforcement of international vessel safety rules has been addressed by
some countries establishing port state control (PSC) systems, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">systems that
unilaterally enforce such rules (Payoyo, 1994).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.14.3" class="koboSpan">In 1982 12
European countries signed the Paris PSC Memorandum of Understanding,
arranging to inspect safety and other certificates carried by vessels of
all flags (including each other’s) visiting their ports, and to insist,
by detention if necessary, on deficiencies being rectified.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.14.4" class="koboSpan">The
International Maritime Organization (IMO) defines PSC as “the inspection
of foreign ships in national ports to verify that the condition of the
ship and its equipment comply with the requirements of international
regulations and that the ship is manned and operated in compliance with
these rules” (IMO, 2009). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.14.5"
class="koboSpan">In 1995 member countries inspected 8,834 vessels, of
which almost half had deficiencies; vessels were detained in port when
deficiencies were regarded as so serious that the vessel or those on
board were in danger, or where the marine environment could be
threatened (Porter, 1996).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">During the years 2002
to 2006, member countries of the Indian MoU for PSC undertook 26,515 PSC
vessel inspections,
</span><sup><a href="#Ch017.xhtml_fn0618" id="Ch017.xhtml_bck_fn0618"><span
id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan"> 7.7% of the vessels involved in these inspections were
detained. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.17.2"
class="koboSpan">Determinants of the probability that a vessel would be
detained based upon these data are found in a study by Cariou, Mejia and
Wolff (2008). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.17.3" class="koboSpan">A
strong positive relationship exists between this probability and the
vessel’s age at the time of the inspection.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.17.4" class="koboSpan">Also, the
inspecting authorities in Iran, India and Australia have a higher
probability of vessel detentions than inspecting authorities of other
member countries. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.17.5"
class="koboSpan">Further, general cargo/multi-purpose and chemical cargo
vessels are more likely to be detained.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">In addition to FOCs,
doubts also exist about the vessel safety enforcement performance of
classification societies. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.18.2"
class="koboSpan">Classification societies which are generally privately
owned inspect vessels to ensure that they are seaworthy, meet
national-flag requirements
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_521"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">and conform to international safety standards.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">Classification
societies also produce vessel specification rules and supervise the
construction and design of vessels to insure that these rules are
followed. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.19.3" class="koboSpan">There
are more than 50 classification societies worldwide with some having
been in existence for more than 200 years.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.19.4" class="koboSpan">The five
largest classification societies (based upon the number of vessels that
they classify) are the Bureau Veritas (France), Det Norske Veritas
(Norway), American Bureau of Shipping, Lloyd’s Register of Shipping and
Nippon Kaiji Kyokei.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">Both existing and new
vessels are classified. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.20.2"
class="koboSpan">Although vessels are not required to be classified,
vessel insurers must be confident that vessels are seaworthy and thereby
will insure only vessels that have been classified.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.20.3" class="koboSpan">Further,
charterers of vessels require that vessels be classed and owners of
non-classified vessels cannot obtain the necessary trading certificates
required by ports of call (Talley, 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">Since classification
societies have no legal authority, they compete for vessel-owner
clients. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.2"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, an insoluble conflict of interest arises
between themselves and vessel owners, since the latter hire
classification societies to class vessels.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.3" class="koboSpan">In a
competitive environment for vessel-owner clients and when vessel owners
themselves are facing stiff competition, societies are under pressure to
reduce their safety demands, possibly classing non-seaworthy vessels.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.4" class="koboSpan">By the end of
the 1970s, the UK P&I Club, responding to the concern that
classification societies could no longer provide an accurate evaluation
of vessel quality, established its own vessel appraisal system.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.5" class="koboSpan">Protection and
indemnity (P&I) clubs are vessel owners’ organisations that provide
liability insurance for the same vessel owners.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.6" class="koboSpan">The criticisms
of classification societies include: (1) extreme variations recorded in
the quality of services provided; (2) difficulty in obtaining vessel
inspection reports given the contractual links between societies and
vessel owner clients; (3) unwarranted extensions of the classification
of older vessels; and (4) safety rules that do not consider the
operational aspects of safety on board (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.7" class="koboSpan">crew quality
and operating standards (Boisson, 1994).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.8" class="koboSpan">The major
classification societies responded to their critics by establishing the
International Association of Classification Societies (IACS), having the
objectives of promoting the highest standards in vessel safety and
preventing marine pollution. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.21.9"
class="koboSpan">IACS members are bound to satisfy Quality System
Certification Scheme (QSCS) standards.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">Shrinking crew sizes
are also a safety concern, since fewer crew members may be available for
watch duties and on-board maintenance chores.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">Opponents of
smaller crew sizes (e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.3"
class="koboSpan">labour organisations) argue that safety has
deteriorated with smaller crews, (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.4" class="koboSpan">from increased
fatigue from longer working hours, poor vessel maintenance practices and
less time for on-the-job training).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.5" class="koboSpan">They further
note that crew fatigue was cited as a major contributing factor to the
Exxon Valdez oil spill in Alaska.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.6" class="koboSpan">Proponents
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.7" class="koboSpan">vessel
operators) argue that smaller crews are more safety conscious and are
better trained to operate automated systems.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.8" class="koboSpan">One study
(National Research Council, 1990) that investigated the issue concludes
that available information shows no link between crew size and
commercial vessel safety. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.22.9"
class="koboSpan">However, if crew sizes continue to shrink, they may
fall below safety threshold levels; if so, vessel operation safety will
deteriorate.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">The construction and
maintenance of vessels are also vessel safety concerns.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">New vessels are
often constructed with lightweight high-tensile steel, which is thinner
than plain steel and thus more likely to crack and suffer dangerous
stresses. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.23.3" class="koboSpan">In a
competitive environment, vessel operators are under pressure to decrease
the time that their vessels are in port.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.23.4" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
the maintenance of vessels in port is expected to decline as vessel time
in port declines.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_522"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan">Nearly 80% of vessel accidents are caused by human
error – a human action or omission identifiable as the immediate cause
of the event from which the liability arises, including blame worthy
behavior from simple mistakes in arithmetic, judgment, and deliberate
risk taking (Goss, 1994). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.24.2"
class="koboSpan">In the past, the focus of vessel safety regulation has
been the vessel rather than human actions aboard the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.24.3" class="koboSpan">However, this
focus has shifted: The International Safety Management Code for vessels
became mandatory in 1998, requiring shipping lines to document their
vessel management procedures for detecting and eliminating unsafe human
behavior. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.24.4" class="koboSpan">“This
code is at the heart of the industry’s plan to switch toward regulating
human factors instead of physical ones” (Abrams, 1996, p.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.24.5" class="koboSpan">8B).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.24.6" class="koboSpan">The code was
motivated by the fact that vessel accident insurance claims are often
attributed to human error and it is less expensive to change human
behavior than it is to redesign vessels for safety.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">Older vessels are also
a safety concern, especially older dry-bulk vessels.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.25.2" class="koboSpan">The overloading
and the use of 30-tonne buckets, pneumatic hammers, and bulldozers to
unload dry-bulk cargoes weakened the structures of older dry-bulk
vessels. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.25.3"
class="koboSpan">Inspections of older coal vessels, for example, reveal
that corrosion of side shells is common; moisture in coal vaporises and
re-condenses against side shells.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.25.4" class="koboSpan">The
availability of experienced crew to man and repairmen to maintain and
repair older vessels is also a safety concern.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">Safety concerns for
ferry vessels include insufficient fire protection and their
instability. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.26.2"
class="koboSpan">Roll-on roll-off ferries have giant holes that allow
for the loading (roll-on) and the unloading (roll-off) of automobiles
and other cargoes and preclude vertical watertight bulkheads that are
standard features on most vessels.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.26.3" class="koboSpan">If water gets
in and causes a pronounced list, the vessel will capsize and sink.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.26.4" class="koboSpan">If loading
doors are breached, ferry vessels can sink without warning –
approximately 60% of ro-ro ferries involved in accidents sink within 10
minutes (Talley, 2002). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.26.5"
class="koboSpan">In September 1994 lock design flaws and a slow response
by the crew were instrumental in the deaths of 852 people from the
sinking of the Estonia ferry during a Baltic Sea storm.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.26.6" class="koboSpan">It was Europe’s
worst maritime passenger disaster since World War II.</span>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">Vessel Accident and Injury Causes</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">The US Coast Guard
classifies the causes of vessel accidents into human, environmental and
vessel causes. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.28.2"
class="koboSpan">Human causes include stress, fatigue, carelessness,
operator error, calculated risk, improper loading, lack of training,
error in judgment, lack of knowledge, physical impairment, improper
cargo stowage, inadequate supervision, improper mooring/towing, design
criteria exceeded, psychological impairment, intoxication, failed to
yield right of way, improper safety precautions, failed to keep proper
lookout, and failed to proceed at safe speed.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">Environmental
causes include debris, shoaling, lightning, adverse weather, submerged
object, channel not maintained, unmarked channel hazard, hazardous
bridge/dock/pier, and adverse current/sea conditions.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.28.4" class="koboSpan">Vessel causes
include corrosion, cargo shift, dragging anchor, stress fracture,
brittle fracture, fouled propeller, improper welding, steering failure,
propulsion failure, static electricity, temperature stress, inadequate
controls/displays/lighting, inadequate horsepower, inadequate
lubrication, and auxiliary power failure.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">A vessel accident
seldom has a single unambiguous cause.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.29.2" class="koboSpan">Causes are
often a sequence of causes (or events).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.29.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
adverse weather, the initial (environmental) cause of an accident, may
in turn contribute to operator error, a secondary (human) cause of
accident. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.29.4"
class="koboSpan">However, if a single accident cause is to be selected,
the suggestions
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_523"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">include either the initial cause or the last cause
(beyond the initial cause) in the sequence of causes at which the
accident could have been prevented (Oster and Zorn, 1989).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">The market environment
in which shipping lines operate can also affect vessel safety.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.31.2" class="koboSpan">The
profit-safety argument (Loeb, Talley and Zlatoper, 1994) states that
there is a positive relationship between profitability and safety in the
shipping line industry. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.31.3"
class="koboSpan">That is to say, adverse financial conditions in the
industry are expected to lead to an increase in vessel accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.31.4" class="koboSpan">The
profit–safety argument opposes market forces for promoting vessel safety
and therefore favors regulation and more stringent public-sector
enforcement for such promotion.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">An underlying argument
of the profit–safety argument is that a positive relationship exists
between shipping line profits and safety expenditures (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">vessel
maintenance) and these expenditures, in turn, have a positive influence
on vessel safety – i.e. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.3"
class="koboSpan">a decrease in profits will lead to a decrease in safety
expenditures which, in turn, will reduce vessel safety, thereby
resulting in an increase in vessel accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.4" class="koboSpan">An
investigation of this linkage for the airline industry is found in
Talley (1993). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.5"
class="koboSpan">A highly statistically significant positive
relationship was found between airline operating margins, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.6" class="koboSpan">one minus
operating costs/operating revenue, and relative maintenance expenditures
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.7" class="koboSpan">the ratio
of maintenance expenditures to total operating costs) – thus implying
that a decrease in profits will result in a decrease in maintenance
expenditures. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.8"
class="koboSpan">However, a significant statistical relationship was not
found between relative maintenance expenditures and aircraft accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.9" class="koboSpan">Thus, the
profit–safety argument is only supported in part.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.10" class="koboSpan">A libewral
interpretation of these results is that lower profits lower the safety
margin (e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.32.11"
class="koboSpan">maintenance expenditures) of airlines but the lower
safety margin may not lead to more aircraft accidents.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">Market forces may also
promote vessel safety. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.33.2"
class="koboSpan">The market-response argument (Loeb, Talley and
Zlatoper, 1994) states that shipping lines anticipating a deteriorating
financial condition following a vessel accident will take safety
precautions in a market environment.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.33.3" class="koboSpan">Shipping lines
that are near bankruptcy might choose to reduce safety expenditures,
thereby reducing costs and avoiding bankruptcy, but increasing the risk
of vessel accidents. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.33.4"
class="koboSpan">If vessel accidents increase as a consequence, the
goodwill, however, of these lines will erode and their value to
potential acquirers is likely to be lower.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.33.5" class="koboSpan">The
market-response argument thus favors less regulation and public-sector
enforcement for promoting vessel safety.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">A test of the
market-response argument for the airline industry is found in Mitchell
and Maloney (1989). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.2"
class="koboSpan">Specifically, Mitchell and Maloney (1989, p.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.3" class="koboSpan">329) address
the following question: “Are consumers reluctant to fly with airlines
that have poor safety records or do they treat crashes merely as random
events that bear no reflection on the quality of the airline?”
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.4" class="koboSpan">If the former
is true, the goodwill (or the value of the brand name) of the airline
will decline, having an adverse effect on the performance of the
airline’s stock; if the latter is true, a crash will not affect the
performance of the stock. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.5"
class="koboSpan">The authors investigated the abnormal stock market
performance of airlines immediately following a crash.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.6" class="koboSpan">Two groups of
crashes were considered – those caused by pilot error and those in which
the airline was judged not to be at fault.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.7" class="koboSpan">Fifty-six such
crashes between 1964 and 1987 were examined.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.8" class="koboSpan">For crashes
caused by pilot error, the airline experienced statistically significant
negative stock returns; for crashes for which the airline was not at
fault, there was no stock market reaction.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.9" class="koboSpan">Mitchell and
Maloney (1989, p. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.34.10"
class="koboSpan">355) conclude: “since our results suggest the market is
quite efficient at punishing airlines for at-fault crashes, the need for
increased airline safety regulation is not apparent.”</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_524"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">Alcohol consumption and intoxication of a vessel’s crew
may not only cause the vessel to have an accident, resulting in crew
injuries and deaths, but may also result in crew injuries and deaths
without a vessel accident occurring.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">For passenger
vessels, passenger intoxication can have similar results.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.35.3" class="koboSpan">It is well
known that alcohol affects human performance.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.35.4" class="koboSpan">Specifically,
alcohol affects human balance, increases risk-taking behavior, increases
choice reaction time (the time a person needs to decide which of two
responses is correct), has a detrimental effect on hand-eye
coordination, and reduces one’s ability to make precise positioning
movements of limbs (US Department of Transportation, 1988).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.35.5" class="koboSpan">Since alcohol
affects balance, intoxicated crewmen and passengers are more likely to
fall overboard than when sober. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.35.6"
class="koboSpan">Further, given that water compounds the effects of
alcohol on human performance, intoxicated crewmen and passengers are
thus less likely to recover from falling overboard than when
sober.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">When crew or
passengers fall overboard, water may interact with alcohol and compound
alcohol’s effects on human performance.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.36.2" class="koboSpan">Specifically,
alcohol can magnify the effects of caloric labyrinthitis – becoming
disoriented, nauseous, or both, when water different from normal body
temperature enters one’s ears. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.36.3"
class="koboSpan">An intoxicated person whose head is immersed may become
so disoriented as to swim down to death instead of up to safety.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.36.4" class="koboSpan">Cold water can
affect muscle control (peripheral hypothermia) and thus compound
alcohol’s effects on physical coordination, further impairing a
swimmer’s abilities. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.36.5"
class="koboSpan">Also, cold water may further impair an intoxicated
swimmer’s air supply. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.36.6"
class="koboSpan">The combination of inhalation (or gasp) response when
suddenly placed in cold water and alcohol induced hyperventilation can
result in aspiration of water and rapid drowning.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">Safety regulation
itself may cause a vessel accident – i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.37.2" class="koboSpan">safety
regulation may affect the allocation of resources by increasing the
frequency of safety diminishing behavior (the safety offsetting behavior
hypothesis). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.37.3"
class="koboSpan">For example, the government regulation that automobiles
must contain air bags may result in the drivers of such automobiles to
be willing to undertake unsafe driving practices (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.37.4" class="koboSpan">driving
aggressively), thereby resulting in automobile accidents (Peterson,
Hoffer and Millner, 1995). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.37.5"
class="koboSpan">Alternatively, as is often expected, safety regulation
may have a safety compensating behavior effect – i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.37.6" class="koboSpan">safety
regulation will affect the allocation of resources by increasing the
frequency of safety enhancing behavior.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.37.7" class="koboSpan">For example, in
a study by McCarthy and Talley (1999) analysing recreational motorboat
boating accidents, increases in boating safety training of boat
operators increases the probability of the operators wearing safety
floatation devices while
boating.</span><sup><a href="#Ch017.xhtml_fn0619" id="Ch017.xhtml_bck_fn0619"><span
id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">Vessel Accident Costs</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">When a vessel incurs
an accident, not only may the vessel be damaged, but also its cargo and
near-by properties (e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.40.2"
class="koboSpan">waterfront facilities and pier structures).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.40.3" class="koboSpan">Also, society
may incur environmental costs (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.40.4" class="koboSpan">from oil
spills) and cargo shippers and/or receivers may incur logistics costs
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.40.5" class="koboSpan">an
increase in inventory costs from the delay in the delivery of
shipments). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.40.6"
class="koboSpan">Vessel and near by property damage costs are the costs
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.40.7" class="koboSpan">material
and labour) of restoring damaged vessels and near by property to their
service conditions that existed prior to a vessel accident.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">A vessel accident may
also result in the responsible party incurring liability and legal
costs. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.41.2" class="koboSpan">In March
1989 the tanker vessel, the Exxon Valdez, ran aground in Alaska,
spilling nearly 11 million gallons of oil into Prince William Sound.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.41.3" class="koboSpan">This spill was
the
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_525"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan">largest vessel oil spill ever in US waters.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.42.2" class="koboSpan">The
oil-polluted waters led to major losses in fisheries and wages to
fisherman and business firms. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.42.3"
class="koboSpan">The responsible party, Exxon, has expended \$2.2
billion for cleanup, \$1 billion to settle state and federal lawsuits,
and \$300 million for lost wages to 11,000 fisherman and business firms.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.42.4" class="koboSpan">In 1994 an
Alaskan jury awarded an additional \$5.3 billion in punitive and
compensatory damages to those negatively affected by the Exxon Valdez
oil spill. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.42.5"
class="koboSpan">Exxon appealed, but its appeal was rejected by an
Alaskan appeals court in March 2000.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">Vessel insurance rates
are likely to increase for vessels involved in accidents as well as for
those parties that are responsible for the accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.43.2" class="koboSpan">There are two
major types of commercial vessel insurance: protection and indemnity
insurance which protects vessel owners if their vessels incur
liabilities (e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.43.3"
class="koboSpan">personal injury claims by seamen) and hull insurance
which protects vessel owners if their vessels are damaged or lost.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.43.4" class="koboSpan">Hull insurers
are critical of classification societies that inspect and class vessels
to be seaworthy but are subsequently found to be non-seaworthy,
resulting in higher than expected hull insurance claims.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.43.5" class="koboSpan">As a
consequence, hull insurers now routinely order their own vessel
inspections which are then used with those of classification societies
to determine hull insurance rates for particular vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">Do hull insurance
rates reflect the accident vessel damage cost differentials among types
of vessels? </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.44.2" class="koboSpan">If
not, the rate payments by owners of one type of vessel may be
cross-subsidising the rate payments by owners of other types of vessels.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.44.3"
class="koboSpan">Cross-subsidisation among insurance payees occurs when
rate payments in excess of insurance claims by one group of payees are
used to cover rate payment deficits (where rate payments are less than
insurance claims) of another group.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.44.4" class="koboSpan">For example,
are container and bulk vessel hull insurance rates such that the payees
of the former cross-subsidise the payees of the latter?</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">Other related vessel
accident costs include the revenues that are foregone (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">opportunity
costs) by the vessel owner of a vessel involved in an accident (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.45.3" class="koboSpan">revenues
foregone for the vessel itself if it is not operational and for other
vessels of the vessel owner if they are perceived to be unsafe).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.45.4" class="koboSpan">The approach
typically adopted in the literature for investigating reduced-demand
accident-related costs borne by both carriers and vessel/vehicle
manufacturers is to investigate the reaction of the stock market (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.45.5" class="koboSpan">to investigate
the decline in the stock market value of carriers and vessel/vehicle
manufacturers following an accident).</span>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.46.2" class="koboSpan">Determinants of Vessel Accident Property Damage Costs</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">Hypothesised
determinants of the vessel damage cost to a vessel involved in an
accident (VESSEL-DAM) include the type of accident (TA), cause of
accident (CA), operating conditions (OC), and vessel characteristics
(VC), i.e.:</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0277" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00295.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">A vessel’s type of
accident includes allision, collision, material/equipment failure,
explosion, fire, flooding, grounding, capsize and sinking.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">An allision
accident occurs when a vessel strikes a stationary object (not another
vessel) on the water surface. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.49.3"
class="koboSpan">A collision accident occurs when a vessel strikes or
was struck by another vessel on the water
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_526"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">surface. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.2"
class="koboSpan">A grounding accident occurs when the vessel is in
contact with the sea bottom or a bottom obstacle.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">The accident
may also be a single (involving only one vessel) or a multi-vessel
(involving two or more vessels) accident.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.4" class="koboSpan">A collision,
capsise or sinking accident is expected to result in greater vessel
damage severity than a grounding accident.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.5" class="koboSpan">Greater vessel
damage is also expected for explosion and fire accidents, especially if
the vessel’s cargo (e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.6"
class="koboSpan">oil) could contribute to the explosion and/or fire.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.7" class="koboSpan">The
relationships between VESSEL-DAM and the remaining types of accidents
are unclear. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.8"
class="koboSpan">The cause of an accident, as discussed previously, may
be a human, an environmental, or a vessel cause.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.50.9" class="koboSpan">It is unclear,
however, which cause will result in greater vessel damage.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Operating conditions
describe the environment in which a vessel was operating at the time of
an accident, e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.51.2"
class="koboSpan">the type of waterway where the accident occurred,
weather/visibility characteristics, and phase of vessel operation.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.51.3" class="koboSpan">The type of
waterway includes an inland (river, harbor, lake, or a bay), a coastal,
or an ocean waterway. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.51.4"
class="koboSpan">For collisions and groundings, it is likely that vessel
damage severity will be less in inland than in coastal and ocean
waterways, since vessels often travel at lower speeds in the
former.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">Weather/visibility
characteristics include: fog, precipitation, wind speed, and whether the
accident occurred at nighttime versus daytime.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.52.2" class="koboSpan">Although
adverse weather and visibility conditions are likely to increase the
risk of a vessel accident, their impact on vessel damage severity is
unclear.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">The phase of vessel
operation includes whether the vessel was underway, docked/moored, or
adrift at the time of the accident.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">For collisions,
the expected relationship between VESSEL-DAM and underway is positive –
as speed increases, greater the force of impact and greater should be
the vessel damage severity of an accident.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.53.3" class="koboSpan">The
relationship involving explosion, fire, material/equipment failure, and
grounding accidents is unclear.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Vessel characteristics
include a vessel’s age and size and vessel safety regulation and
enforcement. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.54.2"
class="koboSpan">The expected relationship between VESSEL-DAM and vessel
age is positive, since vessel structural failure is expected to increase
with age. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.54.3" class="koboSpan">The
relationship for vessel size is unclear.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.54.4" class="koboSpan">On the one
hand, larger vessels may sustain less damage in collisions and
groundings, but on the other hand, may sustain greater damage in
explosion, fire and material/equipment failure accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.54.5" class="koboSpan">Greater the
number of safety regulations for a vessel and greater the enforcement of
these regulations (e.g. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.54.6"
class="koboSpan">from vessel inspections), less will be VESSEL-DAM,
especially from material/equipment failure accidents.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">Hypothesised
determinants of the damage cost to the cargo of a vessel involved in an
accident (CARGO-DAM) include type of accident (TA), cause of accident
(CA), operating conditions (OC), vessel characteristics (VC), and vessel
damage cost (VESSEL-DAM), i.e.:</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0278" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00296.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">The expected signs of
the relationships for the TA, CA, and OC variables with respect to
CARGO-DAM are the same as in equation (1).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.57.2" class="koboSpan">Regarding the
vessel characteristic, vessel size, larger vessels are generally more
seaworthy, less susceptible to hazardous weather and waterway conditions
and thus should incur less accident cargo damage costs than smaller
vessels. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.57.3" class="koboSpan">Since
a damaged vessel does not necessarily result in cargo damage, a
non-negative relationship is expected between VESSEL-DAM and
CARGO-DAM.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_527"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan">Hypothesised determinants of the damage cost to other
property (other than vessel and cargo) of a vessel involved in an
accident (OTHER-DAM) include type of accident (TA), cause of accident
(CA), operating conditions (OC), vessel characteristics (VC), vessel
damage cost (VESSEL-DAM), and cargo damage cost (CARGO-DAM),
i.e.:</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0279" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00297.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">The expected signs of
the relationships for the TA, CA, and OC variables with respect to
OTHER-DAM are the same as in equation (1).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">The
relationship between OTHER-DAM and the vessel characteristic, vessel
size, is unclear. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.60.3"
class="koboSpan">On the one hand, larger the size of the vessel, greater
the expected damage from an accident on surrounding property.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.60.4" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, greater water depths required of larger vessels will restrict the
accessibility of these vessels to surrounding property.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.60.5" class="koboSpan">A non-negative
relationship is expected with respect to OTHER-DAM from VESSEL-DAM and
CARGO-DAM, i.e. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.60.6"
class="koboSpan">a vessel and its cargo may be damaged in an accident
without causing damage to other property.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">Support for (or lack
thereof) for the above hypothesised determinants of vessel, cargo, and
other-property damage costs of bulk barge, tank barge, and tanker
accidents are found in studies by Talley (2001, 2000, 1999a).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">Specifically,
these studies estimate the above three-equation model using detailed
data of individual bulk barge, tank barge, and tanker accidents that
were investigated by the US Coast Guard.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.61.3" class="koboSpan">The barge (bulk
and tank) accidents are US flag barge accidents that occurred in US
inland waterways. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.61.4"
class="koboSpan">The tanker accidents are non-US flag tanker accidents
that occurred in US waters and US flag tanker accidents that occurred in
both US and non-U.S. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.61.5"
class="koboSpan">waterways. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.61.6"
class="koboSpan">All three studies utilised accident data for the years
1981–1991. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.61.7" class="koboSpan">The
costs are measured in real costs (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.61.8" class="koboSpan">damage costs
were adjusted for inflation).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Statistically
significant estimation results for the three-equation model for bulk
barge accidents (Talley, 2001) suggest that: (1) vessel damage cost is
less, but other-property damage cost is greater, when a bulk barge is
involved in a multi-vessel accident; (2) vessel damage cost increases,
but other-property damage cost decreases, with vessel age for explosion,
fire, groundings, and material/equipment failures; and (3) vessel damage
cost increases, but cargo and other-property damage costs decrease with
barge size. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.62.2"
class="koboSpan">Further, vessel damage cost is greater for collision,
explosion, fire, and material/equipment failure accidents than for
groundings and greater when the accident occurs in rivers, harbours, and
lakes than in bays. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.62.3"
class="koboSpan">Both vessel and cargo damage costs are greater when the
accident occurs at night. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.62.4"
class="koboSpan">Cargo damage cost is greater when the barge is docked
or moored than when underway.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">Collision and
multi-vessel accidents increase the vessel damage cost and
other-property damage cost of bulk barge accidents by \$21,874 and
\$148,260, respectively. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.63.2"
class="koboSpan">Vessel (other-property) damage cost increases
(decreases) by \$499 (\$1,432) per year of barge age for explosion, fire
and grounding accidents. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.63.3"
class="koboSpan">Vessel damage cost is \$25,137 greater if the accident
occurs in a harbour than in a bay.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.63.4" class="koboSpan">The accident
cargo damage cost is \$1,230 greater when the barge is docked or moored
than when underway. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.63.5"
class="koboSpan">A dollar of vessel damage cost increases other-property
damage cost by \$1.38, while a dollar of cargo damage cost increases
this cost by \$6.90.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">Statistically
significant estimation results for the three-equation model for tank
barge accidents (Talley, 2000) suggest that: (1) oil spillage and vessel
damage costs are less but other-property damage cost is greater when a
tank barge is involved in a
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_528"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">multi-vessel accident; (2) oil spillage is less but
vessel damage is greater for precipitation weather; (3) other-property
damage cost decreases but vessel damage cost increases with vessel size;
(4) vessel damage and other-property damage costs are greater for
collision, explosion, fire and material/equipment failure accidents than
for groundings; (5) oil spillage is greater for collision and
material/equipment failure accidents than for explosion, fire and
grounding accidents; (6) vessel damage and other-property damage costs
are greater if the initial cause of the accident is a human rather than
an environmental or vessel cause; and (7) oil spillage is greater if the
accident occurs in a river, as opposed to other inland waterways, and
increases with tank barge age.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">Among types of tank
barge accidents, a collision results in the largest increase in vessel
damage cost (\$27,983) as well as the largest increase in oil spillage
cost (\$863), whereas explosion and fire accidents result in the largest
increase in other-property damage cost (\$125,950).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">Further, a
dollar of oil spillage results in greater other-property damage cost
than a dollar of vessel damage cost (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">\$9.13 in
other-property damage cost for the former and \$0.51 for the
latter).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">Statistically
significant estimation results for the three-equation model for tanker
accidents (Talley, 1999a) suggest that: (1) vessel damage (oil spillage)
cost is greater (less) for collision, explosion, fire and
material/equipment failure accidents than for groundings; (2) vessel
damage cost is less in inland waterways and if the tanker is underway,
but greater if a vessel cause and if precipitation weather exist; (3)
oil spillage cost is less for a US flag tanker, but increases with
accident vessel damage; and (4) other-property damage cost is positively
related to vessel damage and oil spillage costs of the accident.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Among types of tanker
accidents, explosions and fires result in the largest unit (vessel gross
ton) increase in vessel damage cost (\$117), but the smallest unit
increase in oil cargo spillage cost (\$1.22).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">Alternatively,
grounding accidents incur the smallest unit increase in vessel damage
cost, but the largest unit increase in oil cargo spillage cost,
reflecting the difficulty of controlling oil cargo spillage subsequent
to such accidents. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.68.3"
class="koboSpan">A dollar of oil spillage results in greater
other-property damage cost than a dollar of vessel damage cost (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.68.4" class="koboSpan">\$1.55 in
other-property damage cost for the former and \$0.06 for the
latter).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">Although oil spills
from tanker accidents receive the most attention in the media, most
vessel oil spills are not the result of vessel accidents but vessel-oil
transfer activities (i.e. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.69.2"
class="koboSpan">in the movement of oil cargo and/or fuel oil to and
from vessels). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.69.3"
class="koboSpan">Examples of such activities include the loading and
unloading of oil cargoes, fueling, bilge pumping, cleaning tanks and
ballasting. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.69.4" class="koboSpan">In
a study by Talley
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2004) the vessel-oil-spill differences for vessel-oil
transfers versus vessel-accident oil spills that were investigated by
the US Coast Guard for the years 1991–1995 are analysed.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">The types of
vessels utilised in the analysis include the oil cargo vessels – tankers
and tank barges – and the non-oil-cargo vessels – freight ships, freight
barges, passenger vessels, tug boats, fishing boats and recreational
boats. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">The
parameters of in-water and out-of-water transfer/vessel-accident
accident oil spill equations were estimated.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.71.4" class="koboSpan">The estimation
results suggest that transfer (vessel-accident) in-water oil spills are
larger by 79 (4,217), 35 (9,585) and 37 (981) gallons for a tanker, a
tank barge and a tug boat than for other non-oil-cargo vessels,
respectively. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.71.5"
class="koboSpan">For out-of-water vessel oil spillage, a transfer spill
is larger than a vessel-accident spill by
120.</span><sup><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span></sup><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan"> gallons, all else held constant, and tank barges incur
larger out-of-water oil spills than other types of vessels.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">A study by
Talley </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2005), utilising the same raw data but analysing only
transfer oil spills, found that in-water vessel-oil
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_529"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan">transfer spillage per vessel gross ton is greater for
passenger, fishing, recreational and older vessels and greater in high
winds, but less in cold temperatures.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">Talley
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2008a, 2008b) have investigated determinants of the
vessel damage costs of cruise and ferry vessel accidents, utilising
information collected by the US Coast Guard in the investigation of
individual vessel accidents for the years 1991–2001.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.79.2" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately,
the damage cost related to vessel accidents in these data are not
separated by vessel, cargo and other-property damage costs of individual
vessel accidents, but rather are summed to obtain the total damage cost.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.79.3" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
Talley </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2008a, 2008b) investigate, utilising these data,
determinants of vessel accident’s real total damage cost per vessel
gross tonne. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.81.2"
class="koboSpan">The hypothesised determinants are the same as those
found in equation (1).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">The estimation results
for cruise vessel accidents obtained by Talley
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2008b) suggest that the real total damage cost per
vessel gross tonne for these accidents is greater for allision,
collision, equipment failure, explosion, fire, flooding and grounding
cruise vessel accidents than for other types of accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.84.2" class="koboSpan">Also, the unit
damage cost is greater when the cruise vessel accident is caused by a
human factor as opposed to environmental and vessel causes.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">The estimation results
for ferry vessel accidents obtained by Talley
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2008a) suggest that the real total damage cost per
vessel gross ton for these accidents is greater for allision, collision
and fire ferry vessel accidents than for other types of accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">Also, the unit
damage cost is greater for moored, docked and underway ferry vessel
accidents than for other phases of vessel operation.</span>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.88.2" class="koboSpan">Determinants of Vessel Accident Injuries and Injury Severity</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">Hypothesised
determinants of the number of individuals injured (fatal and non-fatal)
in a vessel accident (NUMINJ) include the number of individuals on board
the vessel (IOBD) and the accident damage to the vessel (VESSEL-DAM),
i.e.:</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0280" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00298.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">A positive
relationship is expected between IOBD and NUMINJ, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">as the number
of individuals on board a vessel increases, greater the likelihood that
one of these individuals will be injured when the vessel incurs an
accident. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.91.3"
class="koboSpan">Accident vessel damage should have a non-negative
effect on NUMINJ, given that a damaged vessel does not necessarily
result in injuries. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.91.4"
class="koboSpan">IOBD, in turn, may be expressed as a function of vessel
characteristics (VC) such as vessel size and age, i.e.:</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0281" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00299.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">Vessel size should
have a non-negative effect on IOBD, since a larger-sized vessel does not
necessarily have a larger number of individuals on board.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">A positive
relationship is expected between IOBD and vessel age, since older
vessels tend to be more crew labor intensive than newer ones.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.93.3" class="koboSpan">Substituting
equation (5) for IOBD and equation (1) for VESSEL-DAM and rewriting, the
reduced form equation for NUMINJ becomes:</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0282" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00300.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_530"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan">Separate estimates of equation (6) for fatal and
non-fatal crew injuries in vessel accidents are found in a study by
Talley (1999b). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.95.2"
class="koboSpan">Detailed 1981–1991 data of individual container,
tanker, and bulk vessel accidents that were investigated by the US Coast
Guard were used in the estimations.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.95.3" class="koboSpan">The vessel
accidents are non-US FLAG vessel accidents that occurred in US waters
and US flag vessel accidents that occurred in both US and non-US
waterways.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">The estimation results
for fatal injuries suggest that the number of fatal crew injuries are
greater: (1) for tanker than for container or bulk vessels; (2) if the
accident cause is human rather than an environmental or a vessel cause;
(3) for explosion and fire than for collision, material/equipment
failure or grounding accidents; and (4) for multi- than for
single-vessel accidents. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
class="koboSpan">The estimation results for non-fatal injuries suggest
that the number of non-fatal crew injuries are greater: (1) if the
accident cause is human as opposed to an environmental or a vessel
cause; (2) for explosion, fire and material/equipment failure than for
collision or grounding accidents; and (3) for multi- than for
single-vessel accidents.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">The results provide
strong evidence of a positive relationship between crew injuries and
human causes of vessel accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.97.2" class="koboSpan">Further, they
predict that vessel human-action regulations will reduce (if they are
effective in reducing human causes of ship accidents) the number of both
fatal and non-fatal crew injuries.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.97.3" class="koboSpan">Further,
policies that reduce explosion, fire and multiple-ship accidents are
likely to be efficacious in reducing crew injuries.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">Separate estimates of
equation (6) for fatal and non-fatal crew and passenger injuries in
ferry vessel accidents are found in a study by Talley (2002).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">Detailed
1981–1991 data of individual ferry vessel accidents that were
investigated by the US Coast Guard were used in the estimations.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.98.3" class="koboSpan">Estimation
results indicate that the average number of fatal injuries is 3.35%
higher for explosion and fire than for collision, material/equipment
failure or grounding accidents and 3.31% higher for multi-vessel than
for single-vessel accidents. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.98.4"
class="koboSpan">The average number of non-fatal injuries is 3.60% and
4.46% higher for collisions, explosion and fire than for
material/equipment failure or grounding accidents and 3.38% higher for
multi-vessel than for single-vessel accidents.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.98.5" class="koboSpan">Unlike the
fatal injury results, non-fatal injuries are higher when the weather is
foggy and fewer at night and the older the ferry vessel.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">Among types of ferry
accidents, explosions and fires result in the greatest number of fatal
and non-fatal injuries: Every 100 explosion/fire accidents are expected
to result in 6.1 fatal injuries, while each explosion/fire accident is
expected to result in approximately one non-fatal injury.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">The results
suggest that policies that reduce explosion/fire accidents are likely to
be efficacious in reducing both fatal and nonfatal ferry
injuries.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Talley
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2008a, 2008b) have investigated determinants of the
injury severity of ferry and cruise vessel accidents, utilising
information collected by the US Coast Guard in the investigation of
individual vessel accidents for the time period 1991–2001.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.102.2"
class="koboSpan">Vessel-accident injury severity (INJSEV) is
hypothesised to be a function of VC, TA, CA, OC and DISTRICT,
i.e.:</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0283" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00301.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">Where, DISTRICT is
the US Coast Guard District in which the vessel accident occurred.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">INJSEV takes
on a value of: 0 if no vessel-accident injuries occur, 1 if
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_531"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan">non-fatal vessel-accident injuries occur, and 2 if
fatal vessel-accident injuries occur in a given vessel accident.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">The injury severity
estimation results for ferry vessel accidents (Talley
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2008a) suggest that injury severity is greater when
the ferry vessel accident is caused by a human factor as opposed to
vessel and environmental factors.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">Also, injury
severity is less in Coast guard Districts 5 (the Mid-Atlantic coast) and
13 (the Pacific Northwest coast) than in other Coast Guard Districts and
less in an ocean waterway than in other waterways.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">The injury severity
estimation results for cruise vessel accidents (Talley
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2008b) suggest that injury severity is greater for
ocean cruise than for inland waterway and harbour/dinner cruise vessel
accidents and greater when the cruise vessel accident is caused by a
human factor as opposed to vessel and environmental factors.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.111.2" class="koboSpan">The results
also suggest that cruise vessel accident injury severity is greater in
Coast Guard Districts 2 (the Midwest) and 8 (the Gulf Coast).</span>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.112.2" class="koboSpan">Determinants of Vessel Accident Seaworthiness</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">An alternative
approach to investigating determinants of the damage to a vessel
involved in an accident is to investigate determinants of its
seaworthiness following an accident.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.113.2" class="koboSpan">Vessel
seaworthiness is the ability of a vessel to adhere to intended operation
requirements. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.113.3"
class="koboSpan">The literature also refers to vessel seaworthiness as
the trustworthiness of a vessel (see Boisson, 1994, p.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.113.4" class="koboSpan">368).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.113.5" class="koboSpan">In a study by
Talley (1999c) hypothesised determinants of the seaworthiness of a
vessel following an accident (SEAWORTHY) include the type of accident
(TA), cause of accident (CA), operating conditions (OC), vessel
characteristics (VC), and type of vessel (TV), i.e.:</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0284" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00302.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">Type of vessel
includes container, tanker, and bulk vessels.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.115.2" class="koboSpan">Detailed
1981–1991 data of individual container, tanker, and bulk vessel
accidents that were investigated by the US Coast Guard were used in the
estimation of equation (8). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.115.3"
class="koboSpan">Vessel accidents are non-US FLAG vessel accidents that
occurred in US waters and US flag vessel accidents that occurred in both
US and non-US waterways. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.115.4"
class="koboSpan">In the data the seaworthiness of a vessel following an
accident was described as seaworthiness not affected, vessel is not a
total loss but seaworthiness is negatively affected, or the vessel is a
total loss. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.115.5"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, in the estimation of equation (8),
SEAWORTHY was measured by an ordinal scale, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.115.6" class="koboSpan">equals to 2 if
seaworthiness is not affected, equals to 1 if vessel is not a total loss
but seaworthiness is negatively affected, and equals to 0 if vessel is a
total loss.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Statistically
significant estimation results suggest that the seaworthiness of a
vessel involved in an accident: (1) increases with vessel size; (2) is
greater if the vessel is manned by a licensed operator; (3) is less for
a tanker than a container or bulk vessel; (4) is less for collision,
fire/explosion and material/equipment failure accidents than for
groundings; (5) is less if the weather is foggy; (6) decreases with wind
speed; (7) is less when the vessel is underway but greater if the
accident occurs in a harbour than in open waterways; and (8) is less if
the vessel is involved in a multi-vessel accident.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">The probability that
a vessel will be a total lost from an accident decreases by .0053 if
manned by a licensed operator. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.117.2"
class="koboSpan">For an accident where seaworthiness is negatively
affected but the vessel is not a total loss, the probability declines by
.0841. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.117.3" class="koboSpan">If a
vessel is involved in fire/explosion and material/equipment failure
accidents, the probability that the vessel
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_532"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan">will be a total loss increases by .0231 and .0206,
respectively; the probability that the vessel’s seaworthiness is
negatively affected but the vessel is not a total loss increases by
.3680 and .3278, respectively. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.118.2"
class="koboSpan">The results suggest that policies that reduce
fire/explosion and material/equipment failure accidents and increase the
manning of ships by licensed operators are likely to be efficacious in
improving vessel accident seaworthiness.</span>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">8. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.119.2" class="koboSpan">Accident Vessel Losses</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">Statistics for world
vessel accidents for which vessels were lost are generally accurate;
vessel accident statistics for which vessels are not lost are less
accurate – the non-reporting of the latter is more difficult to detect.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.120.2" class="koboSpan">For vessels 20
gross tons and larger, the statistics in
</span><a href="#Ch017.xhtml_fig0285" id="Ch017.xhtml_bck_fig0285"><span
id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan"> reveal that the number of world vessels involved in
accidents that were lost was the highest in 2003, declined in 2004 and
2005, increased in 2006 and 2007, and then declined in 2008.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">In
</span><a href="#Ch017.xhtml_fig0286" id="Ch017.xhtml_bck_fig0286"><span
id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan"> the statistics for world tanker vessel accidents for
which tanker vessels were lost reveal that the highest number of tanker
vessel losses, 22 losses, occurred in 2001.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">Thereafter,
the losses ranged between 15 and 7 losses per year.</span>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0285" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00303.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch017.xhtml_bck_fig0285)

</div>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0286" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00304.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch017.xhtml_bck_fig0286)

</div>

<div id="Ch017.xhtml_fig0287" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_533"></span>[](#Ch017.xhtml_bck_fig0287)

[<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00305.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch017.xhtml_bck_fig0287)

</div>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">In
</span><a href="#Ch017.xhtml_fig0287" id="Ch017.xhtml_bck_fig0287"><span
id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan"> the statistics for world dry-bulk vessel accidents for
which dry-bulk vessels were lost reveal that the highest number of
dry-bulk vessel losses, 21 losses, occurred in 2000.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.131.2" class="koboSpan">Thereafter,
the losses ranged between 14 and six losses per year.</span>

## <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">9. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">Summary</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">Vessel safety
consists of the safety of a vessel and the safety in the operation of a
vessel. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">The
safety of a vessel is concerned with whether a vessel adheres to
construction, design or technical standards and therefore is seaworthy.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">Outcome rather
than input proxies are often used as proxies for vessel operation
safety. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.133.4" class="koboSpan">Vessel
safety concerns include ineffective enforcement of international vessel
safety rules by FOCs and classification societies, shrinking crew sizes,
the decline in vessel maintenance in a competitive shipping environment,
the use of lightweight high-tensile steel in vessel construction, the
aging of the world’s fleet of dry-bulk vessels, and insufficient fire
protection for and the instability of ferry vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">Causes of vessel
accidents have been classified into human, environmental, and vessel
causes. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.134.2"
class="koboSpan">However, a vessel accident seldom has a single
unambiguous cause. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.134.3"
class="koboSpan">Often there is a sequence of causes.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.134.4" class="koboSpan">The market
environment in which shipping lines operate can also affect vessel
safety. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.134.5"
class="koboSpan">Adverse financial conditions for the shipping industry
may lead to an increase in vessel accidents (the profit-safety
argument). </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.134.6"
class="koboSpan">Alternatively, shipping lines anticipating a
deteriorating financial condition following a vessel accident may take
safety precautions in a market environment (the market-response
argument).</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">The costs of a vessel
accident may include damage costs to the vessel, its cargo, and near by
properties as well as environmental and logistics costs.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">The
responsible party may also incur liability and legal costs.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.135.3" class="koboSpan">Hypothesised
determinants of the damage costs, number of injuries, and vessel
seaworthiness of vessel accidents include the type of accident (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.135.4" class="koboSpan">a collision
and a grounding), cause of accident (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.135.5" class="koboSpan">human and
environmental), operating conditions (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.135.6"
class="koboSpan">weather/visibility characteristics and phase of vessel
operation), and vessel characteristics (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.135.7" class="koboSpan">age and size).
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.135.8" class="koboSpan">For bulk and
tank barges, statistically significant results from estimated vessel
accident damage cost equations suggest that vessel damage costs: (1) are
less but other-property damage costs
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_page_534"></span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan">are greater when a barge is involved in a multi-vessel
accident and (2) increase, but other-property damage costs decrease with
barge size. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.136.2"
class="koboSpan">For tankers, the vessel damage (oil spillage) cost is
greater (less) for collision, fire/explosion and material/equipment
failure accidents than for groundings.</span>

<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">For container,
tanker, and bulk vessel accidents, the number of fatal and non-fatal
crew injuries is greater if the accident cause is human rather than
environmental or vessel related and for multi- than for single-vessel
accidents. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.137.2" class="koboSpan">For
ferry vessel accidents, a fire/explosion results in the greatest number
of fatal and non-fatal injuries.
</span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.137.3" class="koboSpan">For container,
tanker, and bulk vessel accidents, the seaworthiness of the vessel is
greater for larger-sized vessels and if the vessel is manned by a
licensed operator.</span>

[<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch017.xhtml_bck_fn0617)<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">Executive Director, Maritime Institute, Old Dominion
University, Virginia, USA. </span><span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.139.2"
class="koboSpan">Email:
</span><span class="italic">[<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan">wktalley@odu.edu</span>](mailto:wktalley@odu.edu)</span>

<div class="footnote" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

### <span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">Endnotes</span>

[<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan">1.</span>](#Ch017.xhtml_bck_fn0618)<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan"> The 2007 members of the Indian MoU include: Australia,
Bangladesh, Djibouti, Eritrea, India, Iran, Kenya, Maldives, Mauritius,
Mozambique, Myanmar, Oman, Seychelles, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Sudan,
Tanzania, and Yemen.</span>

[<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">2.</span>](#Ch017.xhtml_bck_fn0619)<span id="Ch017.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan"> A study by McCarthy and Talley (2001) that analyses
the same raw data of recreational motorboat boating accidents also found
that greater the boating safety training of boat operators the less will
be the injury severity of the operator and the passengers onboard a
recreational motorboat that is involved in an accident.</span>
