<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping Policy and Globalisation; Jurisdictions, Governance and Failure</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0406)
=============================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Michael</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Roe</span></span><a href="#Ch018.xhtml_fn0620" id="Ch018.xhtml_bck_fn0620"><span
id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.5.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">The shipping industry
is characterised by a number of very specific features which make it
unlike almost any other. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.7.2"
class="koboSpan">In particular it is inherently mobile – both physically
in that ships can be moved with relative ease to a very large number of
world locations – and in terms of capital, which involves no physical
movement of assets necessarily, but a transfer of ownership,
registration or other features to wherever makes most financial sense.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.7.3" class="koboSpan">These two
features are intrin sically linked in that the capital mobility of
shipping is enhanced by the physical mobility of the assets which
subsequently makes any sort of compulsory national, state association
very difficult.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">These two features of
mobility are also fundamentally important when it comes to the issue of
policy, and in this chapter we shall be examining the derivation of
shipping policy and in particular the relationship between shipping
policies at different levels of jurisdiction of origin and imposition –
international, supra national, national, regional and local (Roe, 2007c,
2009c). </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">The
issues of mobility outlined above are the major feature of shipping
which drives policy at all levels, although not to the exclusion of a
large range of other factors which needs to be assessed.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter will also
place shipping policy in the context of the growth of glob alisation and
its close relations, foreign direct investment and strategic alliances
discussed in the recent works of Frankel (1999), Ryoo and Thanopoulou
(1999), Thanopoulou
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.11.2"
class="koboSpan">(1999), Peters (2001), Randay (2001), Sletmo (2001),
Slack, Comtois and McCalla (2002) and Selkou and Roe (2004) –
developments which the shipping industry has experienced often before
any other and which are characteristic of the complexities that surround
governance policy relationships in the industry.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.11.3" class="koboSpan">These issues
have been further developed by Roe in a series of publications (2008a,
2008b, 2009a, 2009b, 2009c).</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter is
structured into seven sections. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.12.2"
class="koboSpan">The second section outlines the develop ment of
research into shipping policy and examines the range of different
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_540"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">studies that have taken place across the world and the
common themes that have emerged.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">The third section
provides a model of the major themes that underlie shipping policy today
and which are foremost in determining the detailed policy initiatives
that have emerged in the late twentieth and early twenty-first
centuries. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">It
also incorporates the development of a new model of shipping policy that
attempts to represent the more important influences that drive and
direct policy-making at each level.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">Using this new model,
the fourth section introduces the concepts of spatial policy levels –
international, supra-national, national, regional and local – and
provides examples of activities at each jurisdiction.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Here the
specific problems associated with deriving effective and inter-linked
policies for the shipping industry become apparent.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">Policy can never
emerge in any sector without interest groups – government, industry,
employers and employees, pressure groups etc – and shipping is no
exception. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.16.2"
class="koboSpan">Section five looks at the role of interest groups using
the model provided by Aspinwall (1995) and other work by Lu (1999) and
how these affect the interrelationships between the spatial levels of
jurisdiction that exist.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">Section six follows
the work of Ledger and Roe (1993) and examines the contextual factors
that affect the industry in the derivation of policies; this further
illustrates the problems of linking policies in shipping between the
jurisdictional levels outlined in section three.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">The final section
incorporates the role of globalisation and its impact upon shipping
industry policies. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.18.2"
class="koboSpan">In particular it focuses upon the problems of
reconciling the linkages between the jurisdictions of policy that exist
and an industry that works outside of many of the constraints that these
policy jurisdictions assume. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.18.3"
class="koboSpan">The chapter ends with a summary of the issues and
conclusions including an assessment of future policy issues.</span>

## <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping Policy - A Spatial Perspective</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping policy is an
area of research that has attracted interest over many years focusing on
issues from subsidies to safety, the environment to employment, from
taxation to inter-modalism and more.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">The key theme
of this chapter is the problems inherent in linking together the
different spatial levels of policy-making across the variety of
jurisdictions that exist. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.20.3"
class="koboSpan">The discussion deliberately focuses upon the
international, supranational and national levels as attempting to
include regional and local issues would prove to be too specific and
complex.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">The literature noted
here is not exhaustive but indicative of some of the trends in spatial
shipping policy and jurisdictional concerns that exist.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.21.2" class="koboSpan">The
international jurisdiction for policy-making has been well documented
and important works include those by Gold (1981) and Li and Cheng (2007)
on the international maritime sector in general, Schrier
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1985) on liberalisation in shipping, Benham (1994) on
UNCTAD’s role in the shipping sector, Moyer (1977) and his analysis of
shipping subsidies, Frankel’s works (1989, 1992) on shipping, logistics
and ports, Yannopoulos (1989) on shipping policy in general,
Ademuni-Odeke’s (1984) work on protectionism and shipping, Li and
Wonham’s (2001) discussion of the specific policy issues relating to
safety, and the earlier seminal work by Goss (1982).</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Examples of work at
the supra-national level can be found in the extensive literature
concerning the European Union including the seminal works by
Bredima-Savopoulou
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_541"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">and Tzoannos (1990), Wang (1993), Hart
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1993), Peeters
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.29.2"
class="koboSpan">(1995), Aspinwall (1995), Urrutia (2006) and Tongzon
(2007) and the journal articles by Van Der Linden (2001), Paixao and
Marlow (2001) and Marlow and Mitroussi (2008).
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.29.3" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the over-arching supra-national issues and their conflict with national
priorities are discussed in Brooks (2000) in terms of liner shipping
policies and the relationship between the USA, Canada and the EU.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.29.4" class="koboSpan">There is also a
large number of other publications which dwell on the specifics of
policy at the EU level and the complexities of imposing such policies on
nation state members who may or may not be willing to co-operate.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.29.5" class="koboSpan">Aspinwall’s
work here is especially significant and will be referred to later in
some depth.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">In Eastern Europe, the
work by Ledger and Roe (1995) and Roe (1998, 2007a, 2007b) dominates the
discussion of shipping policy issues in a framework where there is no
overriding authority (unlike in the European Union) but where regional
commonalities are sufficient to suggest that a supra-national
consideration of policies and policy implementation is appropriate.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">The authors
stress the difficulties of intro ducing common-themed policies for the
distressed shipping industries of Poland, Romania, Bulgaria Ukraine,
Russia, Latvia and Lithuania in the light of common approaches to EU
accession and the need to meet a set of widely applied rules and
requirements is clearly apparent.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.30.3" class="koboSpan">This is
particularly the case where national demands (and even regional and
local ones within a country) conflict with the more over-riding needs
and demands of the newly adopted supra-national authority.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">Other pseudo
supra-national policy work is typified by that of Hawkins and Gray
(1999, 2000), Sun and Zhang (2000) and Hawkins (2001) for the
Asia-Pacific region which again lacks a supra-national authority to give
it coherence and even less so than Eastern Europe, suffers from the
absence of an over-riding driving force of potential EU membership which
acts to compel national policies to work with each other and at
different levels. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.31.2"
class="koboSpan">Similar work in the Caribbean is provided by Wilmsmeier
and Hoffmann (2008).</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">At a national
policy-making level the published work is extensive and only a few
sources can be noted here. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.32.2"
class="koboSpan">In terms of UK policy much has been produced following
the introduction of a tonnage tax system in 2001 – an issue itself that
raises conflicting views with respect to the requirements of the EU,
relations with neighbouring countries and the international (for e.g.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.32.3" class="koboSpan">through the
effect on flags of convenience) and regional (for e.g.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.32.4" class="koboSpan">employment)
implications. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.32.5"
class="koboSpan">Particularly significant publications include
Brownrigg, Dawe and Mann (2001), Selkou and Roe (2002) and broader
policy discussions can also be found in Colvin and Marks (1984), Gardner
(1999), and Gardner, Naim and Obando-Rojas (2001).</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">Discussion concerning
policies and policy-making in other countries is extensive.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
Poland receives attention from Walenciak, Constantinou, and Roe (2001)
and Wrona and Roe (2002), Taiwan from Lu (1999), the USA from Whitehurst
(1983)</span><sup><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">3</span></sup><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">, Iran from Mirmiran (1994), the USA from Sletmo and
Williams (1981), Nigeria from Omosun and Nasiru (1987), Japan from Goto
(1984) and Managi (2007), Turkey from Yercan (1999), Yercan and Roe
(1999) and Barla
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2001), China from Flynn (1999), and Sun and Zhang
(1999), and Korea from Kokuryo (1985), Lee (1996, 1999) and Song,
Cullinane and Roe (2001). </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.37.2"
class="koboSpan">There are many other discussions focusing upon other
countries of the world emphasising the significance of the national
level of policy-making that exists in shipping and its importance in
relationship to other jurisdictional levels.</span>

## <span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_542"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.38.2" class="koboSpan">The Factors that Drive Shipping Policy</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">Hoyle and Knowles
(1998) provide a basis for analysing the generic factors that underlie
the emergence of transport policy at the end of the twentieth century.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">These factors
can be used as a basis for understanding the development of shipping
policy worldwide. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.39.3"
class="koboSpan">From there we can go on to look at the development of
shipping policy under different jurisdictions before analysing the
problems manifest in linking these policy levels together and in
achieving a meaningful and efficient governance framework.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">The work of Hoyle and
Knowles was directed essentially at understanding transport activity
from a spatial perspective and for this reason is particularly suited to
our discussion, although they were not considering policy making,
governance and policy applications, nor the shipping sector
specifically. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.40.2"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, the structure they employed is useful
consisting of five main factors that can be applied to the maritime
sector:</span>

1.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Historical
    perspective.</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
    class="koboSpan"> The shipping sector is partly at least, directed
    by its past, either immediate or more distant.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.42.2" class="koboSpan">Thus
    traditional trade routes, port locations and maritime seats of power
    are all established features of the market place.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.42.3" class="koboSpan">Shipping
    policy tends to emerge from, or be associated with, the established
    network of trade patterns, centres of activity and centres of power.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.42.4" class="koboSpan">Any policy
    development – regardless of where it emanates from – has to take
    this into account as well as any changes to the world maritime scene
    such as the emergence of new routes, ports or maritime powers.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.42.5" class="koboSpan">Services
    associated with exploitation of North Sea oil, the development of
    the Port of Fos/Marseille and the rise of China in world shipping
    are all recent examples.</span>
2.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Nodes, networks and systems.
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">The
    shipping sector is essentially a combination of nodes (ports),
    networks (trading routes) and systems (the organisation and
    infrastructure that connects the other two items together –
    including communications, financial agreements, a legal framework,
    shipbrokers, freight for warders etc.).
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.44.2" class="koboSpan">Both
    governance and policy making ultimately is about all these elements
    and the environment it creates for them.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.44.3" class="koboSpan">This might
    be to encourage activity in a certain location, trade or at a
    certain time (e.g. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.44.4"
    class="koboSpan">favourable tax regimes in EU Member States for
    shipping), or to control unwanted activity (e.g.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.44.5"
    class="koboSpan">sub-standard environmental or safety practices).
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.44.6"
    class="koboSpan">Policy-makers have to understand the series of
    inter-linkages that exist if the policies they create are to be
    specific, meaningful and to achieve what they are aimed to do.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.44.7" class="koboSpan">A suitable
    governance framework makes these linkages possible.</span>
3.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Modal choice, intermodalism and flexibility.
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
    class="koboSpan">Shipping works in a highly competitive environment,
    not just within the industry itself but also in competition with
    other modes. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.46.2"
    class="koboSpan">In Europe, short sea shipping faces intense
    competition from trucking across the whole continent, whilst even
    international rail services are increasingly competitive, as
    developments in East European infrastructure continue and new
    investments such as the Channel Tunnel and the Oresund link have
    become fully operational. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.46.3"
    class="koboSpan">Policy-makers need to have a full view of the
    choices available to shippers.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.46.4" class="koboSpan">In
    addition, the concept of intermodalism continues to expand with the
    support of the EU, so that shipping is now commonly seen as one link
    within a complex intermodal chain – including trucks and trailers on
    ferries, rail ferry operations, containerised services and the
    multitude of specialist facilities needed to ensure an adequate
    inter-linkage.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_543"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
    class="koboSpan">Policy making in shipping has much to do here to
    ensure that developments are co-ordinated and that the shipping
    industry plays its full role.</span>
4.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Deregulation and privatization.
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">Both
    deregulation (the reduction or removal of state control and
    influence) and privatisation (the partial or complete transfer of
    ownership from the state to the private sector) have been major
    trends worldwide in many economic sectors for some years now.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping is
    no exception. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.49.3"
    class="koboSpan">The substantial developments in Eastern Europe have
    resulted in many examples of both trends, but elsewhere the
    privatisation of ports, state shipping companies and ancillary
    activities coupled with the attempts by the EU to reduce state
    interference through relaxing cabotage rules and reducing state
    subsidies have been apparent also.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.49.4" class="koboSpan">Shipping
    policies have reflected these trends since the 1980s and will
    continue to do so although par adoxically, the need for tighter
    safety and environmental controls and the desire to see reduced
    state interference has raised government involvement at all
    jurisdictions in policing the industry’s activities.</span>
5.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
    class="koboSpan">
    Holism.</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.51.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Shipping policies have to recognise that shipping
    is part of a much wider activity that is closely linked with a
    multitude of other economic, social, political and technological
    developments which both influence the ship ping environment and are
    influenced by it. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.51.2"
    class="koboSpan">Thus shipping policy-makers have to understand that
    any changes, for example, in financial policy in the EU will have
    substantial impact upon the shipping investment climate and may
    necessitate further action incorporated into shipping policy
    measures. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.51.3"
    class="koboSpan">Shipping is an holistic activity that cannot be
    separated out from the complexity of the real world but this makes
    policy making both difficult and at times, very slow.</span>

## <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.52.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping Policy — Spatial Levels of Origin and Implementation</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">Policy in the shipping
sector both emerges and is applied to the industry at different spatial
levels. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">These
are indicated in </span><a href="#Ch018.xhtml_cap_lbl0162"
id="Ch018.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0162"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan"> which attempts to summarise the shipping policy
framework and the factors which influence the policies that emerge and
the players involved in its development.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">They can be
divided into five levels – in many ways a convenience as in real life
there remains overlap between them – but at the same time there are
clear distinguishing features of each which are significant for policy
derivation and implementation. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.55.3"
class="koboSpan">These different spatial policy levels (or
jurisdictions) and the problems of co-ordinating and making consistent
their policy initiatives is the central theme of this chapter and has
been identified in earlier work by Cafruny (1987, 1991), and Aspinwall
(1995). </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.55.4" class="koboSpan">The
following discussion focuses on the relationships between these levels
and the difficulties this sometimes presents.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">At the highest
jurisdiction there are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan">international policies
</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">derived
by international organisations which should, at least in theory, provide
an over-arching structure for the policies derived at lower levels.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.58.2" class="koboSpan">In the shipping
sector, the most prominent international policy-making institutions
include the United Nations International Maritime Organisation (IMO),
responsible amongst others for policies towards safety, security and the
environment in shipping generally, and the Organisation for Economic
Co-operation and Development (OECD), which is made up of the developed
countries of the world and which is active particularly in shipbuilding
policy and issues relating to
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_544"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">efficiency worldwide.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">In each case,
there is no compulsory legal requirement for nation-states to abide by
their policies and no direct powers of law-making rest with these
organisations, but at the same time, membership by individual (and
powerful) nations is extensive and requires that the policies and
recommendations are followed. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.59.3"
class="koboSpan">Hence in terms of influence they are some of the most
significant organisations.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">The policy framework
set out at the international level provides the general agenda for that
at the next –
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">supra-national –
</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">which is
typified by that of the European Union (EU) which generates policies
that are applied to all Member States and in the case of the EU, is
backed up by laws that are normally superior to national (Member State)
laws where there may be conflict (Brooks and Button, 1992; Kiriazidis
and Tzanidakis, 1995; Paixao and Marlow, 2001; Urrutia, 2006; Marlow and
Mitroussi, 2008).</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">Alternative
supra-national regimes include the North America Free Trade Association
(NAFTA) with a series of maritime related policies but no law making
powers, and in historical terms, the Council for Mutual Economic
Assistance (CMEA) which represented the countries of the Former Soviet
bloc but which again had no legislative powers (although considerable
persuasive ones) (Chrzanowski, Krzyzanowski and Luks, 1979; Ledger and
Roe, 1996).</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">Taking the EU as an
example, the policies which emanate from the deliberations of the
Commission (DGVII), Council of Transport Ministers and the Parliament
are normally designed to inter-act with international policies of (for
example) the IMO, so that recent EU legislation on double-hulled tankers
and other environmental and safety measures have avoided any conflict
between jurisdictions. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.64.2"
class="koboSpan">This may not necessarily be the case where the
interests of the EU conflict with those of the wider global or national
(Member State) framework and it is clear that divergences of
policy-making from interjurisdictional consistency will produce tensions
that are hard to reconcile. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.64.3"
class="koboSpan">The agreement of policy over implementation of the UNC
TAD 40/40/20 rule for liner shipping by the EU in 1979 reflected these
tensions as the EU’s commitment to free trade and liberalisation was
tested by UNCTAD’s demands for market interference on behalf of
developing countries. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.64.4"
class="koboSpan">An agreement was reached but the problems of achieving
consistency of policies across spatial boundaries where the agendas were
fundamentally different were apparent.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.64.5" class="koboSpan">Very recently,
problems continue in relationships between the EU (supranational) and
the IMO (international) over representation and policy-making reflecting
greater governance inadequacies that exist.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">This discussion of
supra-national policy-making also needs to refer to the problems of
compatibility with national policies, particularly with reference to the
EU and the difficulties experienced in reconciling EU policies on (for
example) state aids and cabotage with the desires and agendas that exist
in individual member states. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.65.2"
class="koboSpan">Aspinwall</span><sup><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan">8</span></sup><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan"> referred to the prolonged discussion that took place
before Greece agreed to the opening up of cabotage markets within the EU
to all ships of the EU, an agreement that eventually contained
safeguards for socially vulnerable markets and extended delays in
implementation to give the industry time to adapt.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.67.2" class="koboSpan">A good example
of this was the application of cabotage rules to the Greek Island trades
where intense seasonality of demand could lead to some islands losing
services altogether in winter as European shipowners from countries
other than Greece creamed off summer profits.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.67.3" class="koboSpan">These
concessions diluted the ambitions of the EU to open all shipping markets
to all ships and operators that were both safe and environmentally
friendly and reflected a divergence in policy ambitions between
supra-national and national interests.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.67.4" class="koboSpan">The provision
of shipping state aids have presented similar difficulties and the EU
Commission has compromised on its leading</span>

<div id="Ch018.xhtml_fig0288" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00306.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: The context for shipping policy-making" /></span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_545"></span><a href="#Ch018.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0162"
id="Ch018.xhtml_cap_lbl0162"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">The context for shipping policy-making</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">principle of free
markets and liberalisation so that some state aid remains in place at a
national level, albeit controlled in amount and characteristics.</span>

[<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch018.xhtml_cap_lbl0162)<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan"> also notes the existence of two more levels of
policy-making in the shipping sector upon which we shall not dwell here
but which also play a part in the conflict between jurisdictions –
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan">regional and local.
</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">These
two spatial levels, typified by regional governments (such as Devon
County Council in the UK) and city governments (such as Plymouth in the
UK) once again should derive policies that are compatible with the
levels above them at national, supra-national and international level as
not doing so
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_546"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">leads to problems of implementation.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">Thus a regional
authority within the EU might find problems in keeping to EU policies
limiting state aid to shipping when the local, dominant ship operator
needs regional support to remain financially solvent.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.77.3" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
local city ports need to match their policies with the regions where
they are located but at times political differences can interfere with
this process.</span>

## <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">Interest Groups and Stakeholders</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">The discussion above
has focused upon the role of the state at each spatial level in the
formation of shipping policy and has emphasised how important but also
how difficult it is for these different levels to work together and to
ensure that policy created at one level is co-ordinated with that at
each of the others to generate meaningful and consistent
initiatives.</span>

[<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch018.xhtml_cap_lbl0162)<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan"> also includes examples of interest groups or
stakeholders that have a significant role to play in the creation and
dissemination of shipping policy.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.81.2" class="koboSpan">These interest
groups are those parts of the shipping industry with an active position
in the sector and who are both the generators and those most affected by
the policies that are created; examples of them have been noted above.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.81.3" class="koboSpan">Thus at the
international level, the IMO, Greenpeace and major charities are
significant interest groups which both create and absorb international
shipping policy measures. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.81.4"
class="koboSpan">At the supra-national level, an organisations such as
the European Community Shipowners Association, based in Brussels
Belgium, and representing shipowners throughout the EU is a significant
interest group that places pressure upon EU and national policy-makers
to take account of their views. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.81.5"
class="koboSpan">At a national level, the UK Chamber of Shipping plays a
similar role in relation to the UK government, but also in discussion
with other interest groups (e.g. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.81.6"
class="koboSpan">the European Shippers Council or the UK seafarers
labour union). </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.81.7"
class="koboSpan">Similar relationships exist at local and regional level
for port authorities, environmetal pressure groups, local truck haulier
associations etc. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.81.8"
class="koboSpan">each of which has a voice feeding into the
policy-making process.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">These voices act
across jurisdictions – thus the UK Chamber of Shipping might input
policy initiatives directly to DGVII of the EU – and not just to their
respective spatial policy-makers (in this case the UK government
ministry responsible for shipping – the Department for Local Government,
Transport and the Regions) or those directly above or below.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">The situation
thus gets increasingly complicated as consistency and compatibility
vertically up and down policy-making bodies at state level now has also
to function horizontally with interest groups and also diagonally with
groups at different levels. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.82.3"
class="koboSpan">There is also a very large number of interest groups
for each policy level and issue, each inter-relating with each other to
a lesser or greater extent either in opposition or collaboration.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.82.4" class="koboSpan">To add to the
complexity, attitude can also vary with the issue concerned.</span>

## <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">The Contexts</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">The final piece of the
complex puzzle which makes up the shipping policy and governance model
is provided by the contexts within which all these policy initiatives
and relationships must operate and which in turn affect their
development, potential
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_547"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">and success (or otherwise).
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.85.2" class="koboSpan">A number of
these can be identified following the work of Ledger and Roe (1996).
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.85.3" class="koboSpan">They
include:</span>

1.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Economic:
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
    class="koboSpan">refers to the impact of economic factors upon the
    derivation and characteristics of shipping policy for any particular
    regime (international, supra-national etc.).
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">Thus it
    might well include the impact of the introduction of the Euro across
    EU states, the general depressed condition of the world economy in
    2008–2009, the specific implications of the state of the scrap
    market upon the shipping industry and the development of free
    markets in Eastern Europe. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.87.3"
    class="koboSpan">It is a significant but wide ranging context that
    is difficult to define and understand its full and detailed
    implications but which is fundamental to shipping policy at all
    jurisdictions.</span>

2.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
    class="koboSpan">Legal:
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
    class="koboSpan">refers to the legal framework within which the
    shipping sector has to operate.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.2" class="koboSpan">This will
    include national laws and regulations as well as those of a supra or
    international nature – thus shipping operators based within
    countries within the EU or operating to and from EU ports are
    required to meet not only the legislation relevant in their home
    state but also the multitude of EU regulations and directives that
    are imposed upon the sector. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.3"
    class="koboSpan">These include, for example, the large number of
    pieces of legislation referring to safety in the ferry industry,
    bulk carrier safety, competition rules for liner shipping and rules
    for cabotage operations. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.4"
    class="koboSpan">The competition rules for liner shipping are a good
    example of where different legal regimes apply to the same
    industrial sector dependent upon the spatial level that is
    considered. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.5"
    class="koboSpan">There are domestic laws in, for example, the United
    Kingdom, that control numerous shipping activities and impacts
    relating to the local environment (local government pollution
    controls), port safety (port regulations), seafarer employment
    (income tax and social security rules) and taxation (UK tonnage
    tax). </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.6" class="koboSpan">The
    US legal regime will also become relevant for liner shipping
    companies active in US trades as it regulates various aspects of
    liner competition. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.7"
    class="koboSpan">However, at the supra-national EU level there are
    further regulations that apply to competition between liner
    operators, agreements through consortia and conferences and the
    penalties that can be applied by the European Commission (including
    the once infamous 4054–4058/86 Regulations which included 4056/86.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.8" class="koboSpan">This
    provided for the existence of liner conferences despite their clear
    violation of the Treaty of Rome.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.9" class="koboSpan">By 2009
    this had finally been removed but its existence for over 20 years
    was a persistent anomaly). </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.89.10"
    class="koboSpan">Meanwhile at an international level, the industry
    is subject to the rules and recommendations of the IMO in terms of
    ship safety, seafarer training and environmental protection.</span>

    <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">The legal
    framework is constantly changing at each level as a response to a
    myriad of social, political and economic pressures and it is within
    this context that some of the more important failures of
    co-ordination between jurisdictions are evident.</span>

3.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
    class="koboSpan">Managerial:
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
    class="koboSpan">refers to the relationship of the internal
    structure of shipping companies with the policy framework that is
    imposed. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.92.2"
    class="koboSpan">Thus the size and complexity of shipping
    organisations and the changing range of functions that shipping
    companies have incorporated has an impact in terms of policy-making
    and its implementation. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.92.3"
    class="koboSpan">The latter point is particularly important as
    shipping companies increasingly integrate vertically, absorbing
    logistical
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_548"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
    class="koboSpan">functions traditionally carried out by separate
    organisations but now incorporated within one company structure.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">Thus
    Maersk’s interests in the full range of logistics from shipping to
    trucking and agency work to air transport has implications for
    policy-makers and vice versa in that it is no longer shipping policy
    which is solely important but a range of policies from competition
    to industrial, transport to regional development.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.93.3" class="koboSpan">This
    increase in the range of functions undertaken by traditional
    shipping companies adds to the complexities and has also increased
    pressure on the industry to conform to a wider range of policy
    initiatives. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.93.4"
    class="koboSpan">The problems faced by the TACA operators in liner
    shipping on the North Atlantic in the 1990s is evidence of this in
    that they fell foul of competition policies of the EU in the area of
    inland trucking (being accused of being anti-competitive for whole
    transport journeys and not just shipping links as permitted under
    Regulation 4056/86 of the EU) rather than any specific shipping
    offence. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.93.5" class="koboSpan">It
    is only whilst the economic and logistical benefits of vertical
    integration for shipping companies remain greater than the potential
    complexity that comes with it (and the risks of falling foul of
    legislation) that this trend will continue.</span>

    <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">A further example
    of complexity that changes within the managerial context can bring
    includes conflict within the liner industry again on the North
    Atlantic between the regimes of the EU and the FMC in the USA with
    their differing views on the permissible nature of liner conferences
    and also the option of including inland transport within overall
    conference legislation.</span>

4.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
    class="koboSpan">Organisational:
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
    class="koboSpan">refers in particular to the structure and
    characteristics of the shipping industry as a whole rather than
    company internal activities and two important trends here stand out
    in relation to policy-making at all levels – privatisation and
    globalisation. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
    class="koboSpan">Following the demise of the Soviet empire (and with
    it the role of state-owned shipping companies) and combined with the
    trend of a general divestment of state companies around the world in
    all sectors, the shipping sector as a whole has seen a considerable
    move towards private ownership.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.96.3" class="koboSpan">Thus the
    significance of state control has lessened as governments become
    distanced from company decisions, finance and operations.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.96.4" class="koboSpan">At the same
    time there has been a consequential increase in supra-national and
    international policy-making in the sector to control the external
    effects of the industry as it finds itself released from public
    sector obligations. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.96.5"
    class="koboSpan">This is evidenced in the increased activity in
    shipping policy-making of the EU, the FMC and the IMO in terms of
    safety, environment and competition with the objective of protecting
    public interests in areas where the market has no interest and there
    is no natural market mechanism to ensure that high levels of safety,
    low levels of environmental pollution and healthy competition
    between players in the shipping market are maintained.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.96.6" class="koboSpan">One problem
    that emerges here between spatial policy-making levels is that
    commonly it may be advantageous for competition policy (for example)
    to be neglected at a national level as this may ensure a strong
    international presence for a domestic fleet (for example through
    subsidy in many forms), whilst it is being strictly enforced at a
    supra-national level – for example at the EU level where subsidies
    are strictly controlled.</span>

    <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">In terms of
    globalisation, this has changed the characteristics of the shipping
    industry, which although has always operated at an international
    level, until recently was much more constrained by nationally The
    shipping industry
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_549"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
    class="koboSpan">is inherently global and able to take advantage of
    flexibility and mobility in its use of labour, finance and services
    almost at will. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.98.2"
    class="koboSpan">The result is a series of problems for
    policy-makers as the industry migrates from one national (flag)
    regime to another, trading off concessions between national
    regulators. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.98.3"
    class="koboSpan">Thus, the UK shipping company P&O was a major bulk,
    ferry and liner operator worldwide for many years but more recently
    has found it necessary to enter global strategic alliances and to
    merge its liner operations with Nedlloyd of the Netherlands.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.98.4"
    class="koboSpan">Policy-making in the shipping sector is directly
    affected by such moves particularly at the national level as
    national policies in the UK and the Netherlands may conflict (for
    example in terms of subsidy) causing at best, confusion with in the
    sector. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.98.5" class="koboSpan">In
    addition the increased impact of flags of convenience and
    international registers confuses the picture further as nationally
    based companies have to work more and more within an international
    framework whilst international and national policies towards
    training, labour and employment for example, may clearly conflict
    with the requirements of the international regime.</span>

5.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
    class="koboSpan">
    Political:</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
    class="koboSpan"> refers to the political context from which all
    shipping policies emerge. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
    class="koboSpan">It is never the case that a single economic,
    technical or legal framework stimulates and controls shipping policy
    formulation. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.3"
    class="koboSpan">In fact, the political acceptability of any
    particular policy is commonly the most significant context of all.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.4" class="koboSpan">Sizeable
    political changes (for example those that occurred in Eastern Europe
    from 1989–1992; the Arab-Israeli conflicts; or the effects of the
    World Trade Center incident in 2001) are often of less significance
    than the political relationships between players within and adjacent
    to the industry. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.5"
    class="koboSpan">A fine example, described in some detail by
    Aspinwall, refers to the political relationship between the European
    Commission (the executive body of the EU) and the Council of
    Ministers (the main legislature of the EU) concerning the
    introduction of Regulation 4056/86.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.6" class="koboSpan">This
    regulation effectively permitted the existence of liner conferences
    for shipping operators working into and out of EU ports, something
    that under the competition rules within the Treaty of Rome should be
    illegal. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.7"
    class="koboSpan">The Commission’s view was clearly that this should
    not be permitted but they were ignored by the Council in 1986 who,
    under pressure from the shipping industry and acting in a political
    rather than a legal or economic context, legislated to secure their
    existence. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.8"
    class="koboSpan">In this example an internal political conflict
    resulted in policy that conflicts with all other industrial sectors
    within the EU (none other has such an exemption from competition
    law) and which has presented a series of difficulties in
    co-ordinating different policy level initiatives since then.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.9" class="koboSpan">Other
    political pressures which have been significant at EU level in
    overtly affecting policy-making include the concessions granted to
    Greece over the delay in imposing cabotage laws and the continued
    existence of subsidies for shipping operations against all
    principles that the EU tries normally to uphold.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.100.10" class="koboSpan">Such
    political concessions do nothing to create a consistent and
    meaningful policy framework for the sector as a whole evidenced in
    the continuing friction between the European Shippers Council and
    the European Shipowners Association over shipping conferences and
    consortia and the maintenance of higher freight rates that the
    former believe is a consequence.</span>

6.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
    class="koboSpan">Social</span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
    class="koboSpan">: refers to a multitude of complex relationships
    between the shipping industry and the society in which it operates.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">These
    issues include the significance of maritime employment and policies
    which promote or reduce
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_550"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
    class="koboSpan">it – a major strand within policy-making at local,
    regional, national and supranational levels in particular.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.103.2" class="koboSpan">Much
    recent debate has focused within the EU upon the introduction of new
    tax regimes by nation states for shipping, partly at least aimed at
    encouraging or sustaining employment levels.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.103.3" class="koboSpan">In
    addition there have been widespread policy initiatives concentrating
    upon seafarer training, conditions of service and the environment
    all with strong social implications.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.103.4" class="koboSpan">Certainly
    at all levels, the social implications of a particular policy have
    to be noted by politicians when they choose policy initiatives as
    the relationship between the two is close and the impact can be
    sizeable.</span>

7.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Spatial:
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
    class="koboSpan">refers to the fact that shipping policy is not only
    derived at a variety of spatial jurisdictions as we have seen –
    international, supra-national, national, regional and local – but is
    also affected by a variety of spatial issues.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.105.2" class="koboSpan">These
    might include issues relating to peripherality and cohesion – a
    major theme within the EU – whereby the disadvantage felt by
    peripherally located regions and states (for example the accession
    countries of Eastern Europe; or the economically poor area of
    southern Italy) can be reduced through policies to promote good
    transport links including those by ship and through ports.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.105.3" class="koboSpan">By
    improving these links, the friction caused by a peripheral location
    can be reduced. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.105.4"
    class="koboSpan">Other spatial influences include promotion of short
    sea shipping in Europe to reduce dependence upon
    pollution-generating road transport and various regional policies to
    improve the lives of island based communities.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.105.5" class="koboSpan">The latter
    is evidenced in the EU through the cabotage Regulations which even
    after the liberalisation of these trades, allow countries to protect
    some domestic routes for social reasons.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.105.6" class="koboSpan">A
    multitude of other spatially related issues are important to
    shipping - including regional policies to develop economically
    backward areas and the consequent industrial and commercial impacts,
    the effects of the emergence of new countries including those of
    Russia, Yemen, Bosnia, Croatia, the Ukraine, and the Baltic States
    of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia and their relatively important
    shipping fleets and/or port facilities and the construction of new
    port facilities including for example those for oil export in the
    Baltic which recently has seen new developments in Russia, Latvia
    and Lithuania all affecting the required geographical focus of
    policy measures to promote or protect various shipping related
    activities or impacts.</span>

8.  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
    class="koboSpan"> Technical:
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
    class="koboSpan">refers to the changes in technical facilities and
    methods which have direct and indirect effects upon the shipping
    industry. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.107.2"
    class="koboSpan">Policies have to take account of these changes and
    this includes a multitude of new safety and environmental
    regulations at international, supra-national and national level to
    accommodate the growth in ship size both in terms of container and
    bulk vessels. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.107.3"
    class="koboSpan">Changes in ferry design and the need for improved
    technical and safety rules have stimulated further regulation
    especially within the EU and following the
    </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
    class="koboSpan">Herald of Free Enterprise
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">and
    </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
    class="koboSpan">Estonia
    </span></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
    class="koboSpan">disasters. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.111.2"
    class="koboSpan">New port facilities and changes in modal choice
    also have their effect and the continued growth in road transport
    and the construction of new pipeline facilities have implications
    for policy-makers in the shipping sector.
    </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.111.3" class="koboSpan">The EU’s
    continued promotion of intermodalism also has impacted technically
    upon the shipping policy sector.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">These eight major
contexts provide the external framework within which all shipping policy
– at whatever level – has to be placed; policy-making which ignores
their influence
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_551"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">has no chance of success.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.113.2" class="koboSpan">The relative
influence of each context will be dependent upon the spatial level and
the issue involved as well as a host of other inter-connected issues but
undoubtedly in the very large majority of cases, each context has a
significant role to play. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.113.3"
class="koboSpan">Some are ever-present and always central – particularly
political issues, but also the relevant legal framework and the economic
relationships that exist between shipping and its broader
setting.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">In addition, shipping
policy cannot ignore the wider context in which it has to be introduced
and implemented. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.2"
class="koboSpan">Thus shipping policy at all levels has to accept that
there are other policies – including industrial, financial,
environmental, competition, infrastructure, energy and so on – with
which it must co-ordinate and be aware of.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.3" class="koboSpan">Failure to do
so again results in conflict between policy-makers and other players
within the shipping sector and therefore ineffective policy-making.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,
shipping policy makers have to recognise the role of other transport
modes and the fact that policies for one mode may conflict with that for
another (for example, promotion of road transport through road building
and subsidised taxation for trucks has an inevitable impact upon the
short sea shipping industry). </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.5"
class="koboSpan">Clearly and ideally, the separate modal policies would
be integrated into one whole, but this is often made difficult as there
remains competition between modal interests and structurally these
policies commonly emanate from different government ministries.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.6" class="koboSpan">Meanwhile the
full range of stakeholders and interest groups need to be accounted for
as players in the policy-making game.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.7" class="koboSpan">Finally,
shipping policy if it is to be effective, has to be aware of its
inheritance in terms of industry structure, ownership, tradition and
importance. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.8"
class="koboSpan">These in turn will affect its role and potential in
terms of policy. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.114.9"
class="koboSpan">All these issues manifest themselves through the
governance framework that is in place for shipping policy-making.</span>

## <span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.115.2" class="koboSpan">Summary and Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">This discussion of
shipping policy has focused in particular upon two features – the
complexity of the influences that determine both its character and
success, and the significance of ensuring that there is compatibility
across all spatial levels if policies are to be effective.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.116.2" class="koboSpan">There is
nothing more likely to inhibit the success of shipping policy
initiatives than to have conflicting policy ambitions at say, national
and supra-national levels – something for example that has characterised
the industry in conflicts between Greece and the EU over cabotage
trades, and also between the USA’s FMC and the EU over liner conferences
and their operations on the North Atlantic.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">This consistency
across levels has to be maintained in the context of policies emerging
in other areas as well (for example the environment and economy) or else
conflict will again emerge which will effectively prevent the
achievement of the objectives that the policies are aimed at.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">There are many
examples of countries promoting both short sea shipping through tax
concessions as well as trucking, both operating within the same markets
in competition with each other. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.117.3"
class="koboSpan">These conflicts of interest that occur regularly within
the shipping policy arena have been made more significant and more
difficult to resolve with the increased globalisation of markets and the
impact that this has had upon the already highly internationalised
shipping industry and its increasing moves towards international joint
ventures and strategic alliances.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.117.4" class="koboSpan">In effect, it
is now only at an international level that shipping policy can ever be
truly effective. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.117.5"
class="koboSpan">Thus the EU may have ambitions to open up markets and
insist upon high environmental and safety
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_page_552"></span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan">standards for shipping but is prevented from achieving
these ideals and implementing appropriate policies because to do so
would destroy EU shipping fleets within a global context – a consequence
that would be politically and socially unacceptable.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">Thus the EU
compromises upon issues such as flags of convenience (which in many ways
it should welcome as a consequence of a free market) by allowing member
states to subsidise their own fleets through low taxation regimes
compared with other industries – thus breaking their own Treaty of Rome
competition principles. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.118.3"
class="koboSpan">The very international and mobile nature of shipping
makes this inevitable. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.118.4"
class="koboSpan">Similar compromises can be seen in terms of liner
shipping, cabotage and manning rules.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.118.5" class="koboSpan">Meanwhile,
Port State Control offers an interesting example of where the EU has
achieved much of what it wishes to promote within an international frame
work but at supra-national level: – by enforcing high standards upon
ships of all nationalities entering EU ports, safety and environmental
standards across the EU are maintained even where the ships concerned
are operated under a legal regime outside of the EU.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.118.6" class="koboSpan">Of course this
has little impact upon vessels that never enter EU ports.</span>

<span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">At the international
level (for example the IMO) it would in theory be possible to achieve
agreement across all nations for rules that then could be universally
applied at all spatial levels, right down to local.
</span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.119.2" class="koboSpan">As the
analysis in this chapter suggests, due to the complex and often
conflicting relationships between the different players in shipping and
the various spatial levels of shipping policy, such agreements are
difficult (if not impossible) to achieve and conflicts between policies
imposed at differing levels remain and will do so whilst nations, ship
operators, local interests and others see benefits in imposing their own
policy initiatives. </span><span id="Ch018.xhtml_kobo.119.3"
class="koboSpan">The globalisation of a complex and highly mobile
industry characterised by excessive international interests and heavily
entwined with other sectors – as shipping is – makes policy-making a
frustrating and difficult business but one which perhaps more than any
other, reflects the complete pattern of commercial interests that exist
throughout different areas of the world.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Joon</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Soo</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Jon</span></span><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fn0621" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fn0621"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">The health of the
global economy is the most important factor governing the international
shipbuilding industry but national economic policies play a crucial role
in determining the extent to which a country’s shipbuilding industries
develop and thrive or, alternatively, decline and possibly disappear.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">Together,
national and international factors can be referred to as the macro
economic environment. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.8.3"
class="koboSpan">If the economic climate is unfavourable then industrial
organisations, including shipbuilders, will face painful problems and
may even have to close their production facilities.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">While the macro
economic environment sets the conditions that will either allow a
shipbuilding industry to thrive, or not, the choices made, decisions
taken, by each individual shipbuilding business are crucial to its
survival and prosperity. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.9.2"
class="koboSpan">Good decisions at the enterprise level can partially
offset an unfavourable macro structural environment.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">Government policies in
promoting shipbuilding industry are largely implemented through various
types of financial assistance such as direct financial aid and or by
guaranteeing loans.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the main
objective of this chapter is to review the historic development of
successful shipbuilding countries and provide informative cases for
reference in the face of changing national and global circumstances.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">The structure
of this chapter is as follows. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.11.3"
class="koboSpan">The next section focuses on the impact of Government
intervention on the shipbuilding industry.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.11.4" class="koboSpan">Section 3
considers the global shift in the shipbuilding industry and structural
changes in this market. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.11.5"
class="koboSpan">Section 4 examines the role of government in developing
or supporting the shipbuilding industry.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.11.6" class="koboSpan">Section 5
explores the impact of recent changes in economic environment on the
leading shipbuilding countries such as Japan, South Korea and China.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.11.7" class="koboSpan">The final
section presents the summary and conclusions.</span>

## <span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_558"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">The Impact of Government Intervention on the Shipbuilding Industry</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Shipbuilding enterprise</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">Shipbuilding
enterprises can be categorised as falling into two distinct groups:
those that engage purely in shipbuilding and those that are diversified
enterprises where shipbuilding is only one of a portfolio of interests
that may have very little in common.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">In addition
there is also an important distinction to be made between shipbuilders
that are private firms and those that are state corporations.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">There are strengths
and drawbacks associated with being either an independent shipbuilding
enterprise or the shipbuilding arm of a conglomerate.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Not
surprisingly both structures are frequently found within a national
shipbuilding industry. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.15.3"
class="koboSpan">Shipbuilders belonging to diversified corporations have
the advantage of being able to rely on corporate resources for expansion
and support which are independent of the state of the shipbuilding
market. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.15.4"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, in periods of shipping recession, the
shipbuilding member of the group can call upon reserves acquired in
other market areas to overcome short-term cash flow difficulties.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.15.5" class="koboSpan">Moreover, this
shipbuilder may be able to use group resources to modernise its
production facilities at a time when independent shipbuilding firms are
being obliged to cut back their overheads and capacity.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.15.6" class="koboSpan">This enables
the shipbuilding member of the group to boost its competitive position
compared to other shipbuilders. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.15.7"
class="koboSpan">The flexibility inherent in the within-group transfer
of resources to the benefit of shipbuilding operations has been
important to the success of Japanese and South Korean
shipbuilders.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">Access to well
organised and funded marketing, and research and development, can be
another advantage of being part of a conglomerate.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">But there is
one more, less easily quantifiable, but very important, advantage to
being in a big group. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.16.3"
class="koboSpan">Conglomerates have political clout.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.16.4" class="koboSpan">These
diversified, large companies command respect and influence in
industrial, financial and political circles.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.16.5" class="koboSpan">This can mean
easier access to capital markets and more sympathetic treatment by
politicians, than could be expected by a dedicated shipbuilding company.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.16.6" class="koboSpan">These factors
add up to substantial competitive advantage for conglomerate
members.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">There is, though, a
downside to being part of a conglomerate.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">Although a
shipbuilding subsidiary should theoretically benefit from the resources
its parent group devotes to R&D and marketing, the bureaucracy
surrounding those functions in a large conglomerate may in practice
offset any gains.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately, a
hierarchical, overly-bureaucratic form of organisation can easily lead
to inflexible decision making and rivalry between the managements of
member organisations. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.18.2"
class="koboSpan">This can lead to individuals vying for power within the
hierarchy of corporate head-office rather than working for the good of
the shipbuilding enterprise.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Enterprises solely
focused on shipbuilding can, on the other hand, be much more flexible
and resilient. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">As Todd notes:</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">“They \[dedicated
shipbuilders\] tend to be more loosely organized and more flexible and
responsive to changing circumstances in consequence.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">The independent
shipbuilding firm may continue in shipbuilding operations because it
simply has no choice – other than closure – whereas the shipbuilding
subsidiary may find itself steadily undermined because its corporate
parent feels that greater profits can be made by switching assets
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_559"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">out of shipbuilding into a more lucrative field.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.21.2" class="koboSpan">No matter how
dedicated the shipbuilding managements of the subsidiary, their
subservience to the greater corporate interest takes precedence over
their sectoral interests and conceivably, group shipbuilding operations
may be phased out not because they are lacking in viability but owing to
their low profitability relative to other group interests.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.21.3" class="koboSpan">It is fair to
say that unless the independent shipbuilder can grow to such a position
that resources become little or no object, the chances of survival
cannot be
assured.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fn0622" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fn0622"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">2.2. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">Impact of government intervention</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">The state is not
necessarily, or even usually, a disinterested observer of the
shipbuilding scene. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.24.2"
class="koboSpan">Governments often intervene in their shipbuilding
industries. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.24.3"
class="koboSpan">Intervention can range from macro economic management
to direct intervention at enterprise level.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter looks at
two ways governments can intervene to shape the development of a
national shipbuilding industry. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.25.2"
class="koboSpan">One way open to the state is to order the building of
warships. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.25.3"
class="koboSpan">Through its allocation of naval contracts, the state
often appears to be supporting shipbuilding as a kind of implicit
regional policy. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.25.4"
class="koboSpan">Awarding warship orders to particular yards can be a
way of protecting employment. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.25.5"
class="koboSpan">The balance between ordering motivated by such social
factors and objective assessment of national defence needs, seems to
vary over time.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">The other way is
formulating policies to promote the shipbuilding industry in direct and
indirect ways. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.26.2"
class="koboSpan">Government’s role in developing the shipbuilding
industry has mainly focused on the financial assistance in various
forms.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">Governments act as
credit guarantors for the construction of ships at their domestic
shipyards and often cooperate with shipyards in devising new forms of
financial inducement to shipowners to place orders.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">These can take
the form of disguised subsidies to directors.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.27.3" class="koboSpan">Also a
government-sponsored shipbuilding programme with favourable financing
(in terms of interest rate and repayment period) provides a great
impetus to the development of the domestic shipbuilding industry.</span>

## <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">The Global Shift of the Shipbuilding Industry</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Structural change in world shipbuilding</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">In the early 1990s
South Korean shipbuilders embarked on an ambitious expansion strategy,
despite warnings from the rest of the global shipbuilding industry that
the move threatened price stability by creating a large excess of
capacity compared to supply. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.30.2"
class="koboSpan">The expansion of the South Korean capacity included new
building docks at Hyundai Heavy Industry, modifications at Samsung
allowing the building of VLCCs and similarly sized vessels and the
construction of the large, modern VLCC capable Halla yard at
Mokpo.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">Japanese shipbuilders
responded by booking large numbers of orders at comparatively lower
prices. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.31.2" class="koboSpan">The
price competitiveness of the Japanese shipbuilding industry then
deteriorated due to a sharp rise in the yen which rose at one time to as
high a level as ¥95 per US dollar.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.31.3" class="koboSpan">This
strengthening of the yen led Japanese yards to buy foreign materials and
equipment where possible. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.31.4"
class="koboSpan">Meanwhile the world orderbook increased, mainly due to
demand for large-size bulkers and containerships.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_560"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan">Trends of world economy, good or bad, generally begin
to produce their effect on shipping with a time lag of around one year,
and on shipbuilding one year later than shipping.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">3.1.1. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">Japan</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">The profitability of
the Japanese shipbuilding industry is greatly dependent on exchange rate
with the US dollar. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.34.2"
class="koboSpan">Because ship prices are usually denominated in US
dollars the sharp appreciation of the yen meant that prices realised by
the Japanese yards effectively fell dramatically.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">In 1994, the yen rose
further to a daunting level of ¥95 per US dollar.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">Although it
then returned to ¥100, these successive surges in the yen caused the
shipbuilding industry to become less and less price competitive.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.35.3" class="koboSpan">However, since
the late 1990s the weakening Japanese Yen has once again strengthened
the price-competitiveness of Japanese shipbuilders.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">3.1.2 South Korea</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">The OECD shipbuilding
working party group considered South Korea’s capacity expansion for the
first time at a meeting held in January 1995.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.37.2" class="koboSpan">A
representative of the South Korean government said that the government
had no legal basis to impose any restraint on expansion by private firms
because a matter of this sort was entirely left to the independent
judgment of each private enterprise.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.37.3" class="koboSpan">While the
expansion was happening the gap that had existed between Japan and South
Korea in the areas of non-price competitiveness, such as technological
skills and quality where Japan claimed to lead, was closing.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">South Korea succeeded
in achieving a level of quality comparable to that of Japan, at least as
far as the hull structure is concerned.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.38.2" class="koboSpan">This was
achieved as result of the large amount of experience gained throughout
the 1980s, building diverse types of ships and marine structures.
