</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.38.3" class="koboSpan">But South Korea
still lags behind Japan in such areas as marine engines and ship-related
equipment.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">3.1.3 Western Europe</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">Germany has finally
stabilised its economy following the economically difficult,
reunification. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.40.2"
class="koboSpan">The country’s shipbuilding industry, which had been not
been particularly dynamic in the 1980s gradually revived throughout the
1990s with an expanding order book.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">Orders were at a
healthy level during most of the decade, with the national industry
especially strong in the container ship and passenger vessel sectors.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.41.2" class="koboSpan">By the
beginning of the 2000s, however, Germany was facing major problems.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.41.3" class="koboSpan">In 2001
deliveries amounted to 55 ships, totalling just over 1m gt.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.41.4" class="koboSpan">But very few
orders were taken during that year with government-related contracts
playing an important part in the survival of many yards.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.41.5" class="koboSpan">A number of
yards also started to look more at conversions and refurbishments to
compensate for a lack of newbuilding orders.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Germany had become
vulnerable because of its specialistion.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.42.2" class="koboSpan">Korean
shipbuilders were increasingly able to beat German owners on price for
container ship orders while the sharp downturn in the cruise industry,
exacerbated by the 11 September terror attacks, hit passenger ship
builders like Meyer Werft very hard.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_561"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">Denmark is another important EU shipbuilding country.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.43.2" class="koboSpan">Odense Shipyard
is by far the country’s largest, and is particularly well known for its
high productivity attained through sophisticated computerisation and
robotics. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.43.3" class="koboSpan">A
large portion of its order book comes from A P Moller, one of the
biggest ship owners in Europe.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">3.1.4 Other countries</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">China has ranked as
the third largest shipbuilding country, after Japan and South Korea,
since 1992. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">In
1995, China constructed the New Dalian dockyard, with one building
capable of building 250,000 dwt ships.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">Poland built VLCCs
back in the 1970s but not in recent years.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.46.2" class="koboSpan">Since the
demise of communism, its yards have been successful in attracting
newbuilding orders from Greece and Western Europe.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.46.3" class="koboSpan">Although
existing shipbuilding facilities are old, domestic supplies of marine
equipment, including main and auxiliary engines makes the Polish
shipbuilding industry largely self-sufficient.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.46.4" class="koboSpan">This insulates
them from currency fluctuations and allows them to book orders at lower
prices. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.46.5" class="koboSpan">An
upward trend in the volume of ship construction has become apparent
since 1992 as a means to earn foreign currency reserves through ship
exports.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">Brazil is another
country with shipbuilding potential.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">However its
shipbuilding programme has suffered from economic turmoil and a shortage
of funds. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.47.3"
class="koboSpan">Although Brazil has technological skills comparable
with the international standards for building large-size vessels,
including DH (double hull) tankers, the real problem lies in its price
competitiveness. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.47.4"
class="koboSpan">In an attempt to rectify this Brazil is promoting the
rationalisation of its yards. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.47.5"
class="koboSpan">In 1995 the merger of ISIBRAS(Ishikawajima do Brasil)
Yard and Verolme was the largest ever in Brazil.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">Structural changes are
emerging on a global scale in the shipbuilding industry over the second
half of the 1990s and 2000s, while at the same time being affected by
structural changes in the shipping industry.</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Demand and ship cycles</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">Ship costs are
strongly affected by the costs of procuring materials and labour in the
shipyards. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.50.2"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, shipyard expenses and production costs in
general are very sensitive to technological change – a supply factor.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">Technological
change, however, has implications, which extend from supply to demand
factors.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Great store was put on
the effects of innovation on the competitiveness of industrial
organizations.</span><sup><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fn0623" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fn0623"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan"> According to this theory, shipbuilders fall into the
technological leader category and attract a growing market share as a
result of their progressive practices.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">Those
categorised as technological laggards, though, are compelled to react to
innovation to retain a share of the market.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Obviously,
technological change is having a dramatic impact on demand from both
perspectives: the lead firms taking away demand from the laggards and
they, in turn, being forced to find compensatory demand largely with
government help.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">It is important to
stress, however, that the level of aggregate merchant ship demand is set
independently from the actions of either shipbuilders as a whole, or
governments intervening to protect national shipbuilding industries.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">Aggregate
demand is, in fact, the outcome of conditions affecting world
trade.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_562"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">The actions of individual shipbuilding enterprises and
individual governments may partially regulate the demand for a small
component of world shipbuilding, but they will not greatly affect
overall demand conditions. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.56.2"
class="koboSpan">In other words, aggregate demand for shipping is very
largely an exogenous factor; something outside of the control of the
industry or government institutions.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">The approach adopted
here is one which sets shipping as the derived demand outcome of world
trade conditions. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.57.2"
class="koboSpan">It assumes that, derived broadly, it conforms to two
categories: a “traditional” ship cycle manifested through the effects of
trade on the production of “typical” ships; and a “modern” ship cycle in
which trade effects are expressed in varying ways depending on the type
of specialised ship.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">Warship production, of
course, is influenced by different factors.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.58.2" class="koboSpan">These vessels
not only have their own supply requirements which can be quite different
from those pertaining to merchant ships, but they also respond to a
peculiar form of derived demand that is very different from the ship
cycles affecting merchant ships.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">Governments intervene
in the market for two main reasons order; to bolster the demand for
ships and thereby provide support for an otherwise ailing domestic
shipbuilding industry. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.59.2"
class="koboSpan">Governments can also intervene in regional economies,
which are suffering from depressed conditions in order to bolster
regional development and ameliorate the consequences of locally
concentrated unemployment. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.59.3"
class="koboSpan">Ideally, the two objectives complement each other.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.59.4" class="koboSpan">Ailing
shipbuilders receive a boost from government aid, and depressed
communities receive a form of employment stabilisation through
government support for the job-creation organisations.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">Governments are most
able to affect demand by ordering warships.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">Policies using
warship procurement as a means of intervention have different effects on
shipbuilding than those aimed at stimulating merchant ship demand.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.60.3" class="koboSpan">This is because
demand for commercial vessels is linked to the international trade cycle
and is dependent upon the actions of a multitude of mainly private
shipping firms. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.60.4"
class="koboSpan">When it comes to warship building, however, national
governments are able to control demand, subject to limits on the overall
defence budget. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.60.5"
class="koboSpan">Wherever possible, governments support their national
shipbuilding industries by placing orders with local yards.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">Warship producers are
however highly vulnerable to government whims.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">Overall
economic factors also impact on warship building by putting pressure on
the national and defence budgets.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.61.3" class="koboSpan">In practice
warship production is, in its own way, as cyclically unstable as
commercial shipbuilding. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.61.4"
class="koboSpan">Warship producers can attempt to secure export orders,
but in general they are highly dependent on a single, very powerful
customer – their government.</span>

## <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">4 The Role of Government and Its Policies to Promote the Shipbuilding Industry</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 State subsidies, naval shipbuilding</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.1 State subsidies</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">Shipbuilding subsidies
have long been, and remain highly controversial.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">Ship prices are
frequently distorted by the effects of state subsidy.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">One commentary
points to the incompatibility of the “heavy over-tonnaging of virtually
all types of ships” on the one hand,
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_563"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan">and the continual scramble to garner newbuilding orders
on the other. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.66.2"
class="koboSpan">The motivation for the imbalance between supply and
demand is simple and stems from the belief held by all states that their
shipbuilders are too important to be allowed to fail.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
“there is great temptation to support ship production beyond ‘normal’
commercial limits. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.66.4"
class="koboSpan">Whatever form it takes, the end-result is a financial
subsidy borne by the
stat”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fn0624" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fn0624"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">In actual fact not all
states believe that shipbuilders “are too important to be allowed to
fail”. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">Since
the late seventies, for example, the UK has generally allowed the
decline of its shipbuilding industry to run its course although it did
pay subsidies to yards, up to the limit allowed by EU rules.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">The conventional
subsidy afforded by OECD countries was a credit scheme where 80% of the
ship price is funded through a loan repayable over a seven- to
eight-year period at a fixed interest rate of 7 or 8% per year.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">However, some
states juggled the terms to secure a more competitive position for their
shipbuilders. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.69.3"
class="koboSpan">This was usually accomplished by either the provision
of further subsidies, however described, or through a reduction of the
interest rate on the loans advanced.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">It is abundantly clear
that non-OECD countries offer better concessions in as much as their
repayment periods are extended beyond the norm, but, even OECD members
manipulate the loan terms to serve their own ends.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.70.2" class="koboSpan">Japan, for
example marginally extended the loan period to 8.5 years in the case of
a bulker ordered for US principals.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">The extent and
availability of financial concessions of this kind are ultimately
determined by overall economic conditions.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">In other words,
there is a tendency to subsidise during periods of downturn in ship
cycles and, correspondingly, a tendency to reduce subsidies when
conditions signal an upturn.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">This generalisation is
discernable from the sample of loan schemes applied to bulker
newbuildings since 1975. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.72.2"
class="koboSpan">In that year, financial concessions offered by Japanese
shipbuilders were relatively modest, covering as little as 50% of ship
costs. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.72.3" class="koboSpan">Such
schemes were permissible at that time because of the massive order
backlogs held by Japan, notwithstanding the disruption caused to the
industry as a result of the 1973 oil price rises.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">By the end of the
decade, however, there had been a significant change: loans were being
extended to cover up to 90% of ship prices in a variety of countries
including Japan. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.73.2"
class="koboSpan">The change was, of course, in response to heightened
competition for increasingly scarce orders.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">The level of subsidy
declined to the standard of 80% over eight years in the early 1980s by
virtue of international agreements among OPEC members on the allowable
loan scheme. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.74.2"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, this was considerably higher than the
mid-1970s level and reflected the desperation of many nations to secure
newbuilding orders at virtually any price.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">This behaviour harms
shipping, encouraging owners to buy vessels when they would probably
hold back if prices were at levels reflecting the true cost of
production. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">It
does, however, clearly demonstrate the serious commitment of governments
to support their shipbuilding industries.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">Government naval
procurement programmes are often designed to serve as countercyclical
measures for shipyard employment stabilisation.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.76.2" class="koboSpan">It is argued
that downturns in merchant shipbuilding demand can be countered by
building warships. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">Without naval orders, the decline in merchant
shipbuilding experienced by US shipbuilders would have put most of them
out of business. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.76.4"
class="koboSpan">There are, however, problems with using warship
building in this way. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.76.5"
class="koboSpan">Naval contracts can end up crowding out commercial
orders. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.76.6" class="koboSpan">Thus,
the use of warship orders as a counter-cyclical measure can only be
effective if
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_564"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">such orders are timed to truly use slack resources and
not divert resources from other production.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">In practice,
the timing of defence contracts has rarely been truly countercyclical
and may have done more harm than good.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.77.3" class="koboSpan">Moreover, not
all yards can build warships or naval auxiliaries efficiently, limiting
the scope of warship construction as a regional development tool.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.2 Naval shipbuilding</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">Since the World War
II, the USA has been the example of a nation whose shipbuilding has been
heavily dependent on defence contracts.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.79.2" class="koboSpan">At the present
time, something in the order of 75% of new ship construction in the USA
is destined for the US Navy.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">The residual merchant
shipbuilding industry is locked into high cost practices associated with
naval construction. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.80.2"
class="koboSpan">According to one official pronouncement, it is owing to
generally higher construction costs that the US shipbuilding industry
has not, on balance, been an export industry since the days of the
clipper ships. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.80.3"
class="koboSpan">As a consequence, merchant shipbuilding as well as
naval newbuilding is tied to domestic markets: markets which, in turn,
rely on an inordinate amount of government
regulation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fn0625" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fn0625"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan"> So while US shipbuilding is influenced by the global
shipbuilding market, to some extent, domestic circumstances peculiar to
US shipbuilding are much more important.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">The USA has
established a complex framework of federal policy, statute, and
regulation with respect to naval shipbuilding, subsidised commercial
shipbuilding, and cabotage, including the well-known Jones Act.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.82.3" class="koboSpan">Indeed, some
observers suggest that without subsidies amounting to up to 35% of
construction costs, mercantile newbuilding would have been abandoned in
the USA.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">By its nature, naval
shipbuilding is performance-oriented rather than cost-conscious.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">Navies worry
about design details and the fulfilment of target specifications.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.83.3" class="koboSpan">Ship owners
worry about the price of newbuildings, so builders of merchant shipyards
are preoccupied with cost efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.83.4" class="koboSpan">Consequently
shipyards that choose to specialise in warship work largely remove
themselves from the discipline of the market.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.83.5" class="koboSpan">These shipyards
may become entirely dependent on a government to the extent of the state
being the sole arbiter of demand – a monopolist in fact.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.83.6" class="koboSpan">In general
governments encourage technical competence in warship suppliers
irrespective of production efficiencies.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">Warship production
when not strictly required to meet defence needs is also justified on
strategic grounds. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.84.2"
class="koboSpan">It is argued that defence production capacity must be
maintained in a state of readiness for any national emergency.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.84.3" class="koboSpan">Governments are
also seen as being obliged to purchase products from defence suppliers
because the latter have committed so much of their resources to the
development of these highly specialised products that are tailored to
specific government requirements.</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Shipbuilding and national economic development</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">Economic planners and
politicians in Newly Industrialised Countries (NICS) have often seen
shipbuilding as having an important role in the modernisation process
and in national development. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.86.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipbuilding can appear to be an attractive development
tool for three reasons. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.86.3"
class="koboSpan">First, it is a medium technology industry, which suits
the factor–cost advantages of NICs.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.86.4" class="koboSpan">Thus,
technology does not act as a barrier to entry while the labour intensive
nature of shipbuilding favours countries with large, cheap labour
forces. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.86.5"
class="koboSpan">Secondly, the market is an international one and thus
shipbuilding can be a net earner of foreign exchange.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.86.6" class="koboSpan">Customers for
ships come from all parts of the world.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_565"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan">The existence of flag-of-convenience fleets adds to the
emphasis on price competitiveness in the market and allows shipowners to
circumvent market protection imposed by national governments.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">A newly
emergent producer, capitalising on low-factor costs, can offer
competitively priced ships, which rapidly find customers in such an open
market. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.87.3"
class="koboSpan">Finally, shipbuilding has strong links with other
industries. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.87.4" class="koboSpan">It
should, therefore, serve to foster other nascent industries in the
NICs.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">Not surprisingly,
shipbuilding has been singled out by a number of countries in recent
years as deserving of special treatment.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.88.2" class="koboSpan">At one extreme,
the state has taken the combined role of planner and shipbuilder.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.88.3" class="koboSpan">This was the
case with command economies such as China, Poland, and Yugoslavia and
the interventionist economy of India.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.88.4" class="koboSpan">At the other
extreme, the state has encouraged the industry in the name of national
development but left the practice of shipbuilding to private enterprise
– as is attested by Brazil and South Korea.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.88.5" class="koboSpan">In between are
NICs, such as Spain, which encourage both private and public enterprise
in shipbuilding. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.88.6"
class="koboSpan">The case of South Korea is highlighted here – as
perhaps the most successful of the NICs engaged in shipbuilding.</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 South Korea</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">The Korean
shipbuilding industry in the 1950s had to rely primarily on imported
materials, so the cost of building ships domestically exceeded
international ship prices. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.2"
class="koboSpan">This imposed a heavy burden on cash-strapped Korean
shipping companies, and demand for locally built ships declined.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.3" class="koboSpan">The government
legislated the Shipbuilding Encouragement Act on 11 March, 1958 in an
effort to stimulate development of shipbuilding industry as well as to
support the shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.4"
class="koboSpan">About this time, the shipbuilding industry’s sphere of
influence shifted dramatically. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.5"
class="koboSpan">As labour accounts for between 20% and 30% of the total
cost of building a ship, shipbuilding activities declined in the UK and
West Germany, where labour was becoming scarce and expensive.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.6" class="koboSpan">Meanwhile,
Japan had emerged as the world’s foremost shipbuilding nation as early
as 1956, and that country’s share of the world market continued to
increase, eventually reaching almost 50%.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.7" class="koboSpan">Korea also had
a large pool of highly skilled, low-cost labour.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.8" class="koboSpan">The government
realised the importance of shipbuilding, but it also understood that
private sector companies, which lacked capital, could not be expected to
build expensive, large-scale shipyards.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.9" class="koboSpan">Thus, the
government put forth a battery of industry development policies and
established state-run shipbuilding companies.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.10" class="koboSpan">Korea
Shipbuilding & Engineering Corp was founded in January 1950.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.90.11" class="koboSpan">Capital for
the project came from government US dollar reserves as well as the
Agency for International Development (AID).</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">During the 1960s, the
Korean government launched two successive five-year plans which rapidly
expanded the scale of the national economy.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">Fishing
companies of all kinds cropped up, causing domestic demand for ships to
soar.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">However, as Korea was
in the early stages of economic development, the overall industrial
structure was still weak, so the initial focus was put on light
manufacturing. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.92.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipbuilding and the rest of the heavy industrial
sector did not see significant progress.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.92.3" class="koboSpan">The Korean
government launched its Second Five-year Plan (1967–1971).
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.92.4" class="koboSpan">In 1967, the
government enacted the Shipbuilding Industry Promotion Act and
designated the period as a time to modernise facilities and raise
technology levels in order to improve national competitiveness.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.92.5" class="koboSpan">At the same
time, a foundation was to be laid for Korea to generate her own ship
demand as well as to gradually move towards ship exportation.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.92.6" class="koboSpan">At the same
time, world demand trends pointed to ships of ever-increasing size.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.92.7" class="koboSpan">However, the
government’s
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_566"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan">shipbuilding promotion policy was aimed mainly at
expanding the tonnage of small ships for Korean end-users.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">The policy did
help expand total industry output volume, but little was done to develop
large-sized ships or shipyards. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.93.3"
class="koboSpan">Demand for ships that could not be built domestically
was satisfied through imports, and the domestic shipbuilders only
supplied 20% of the total new ships bought by Korean shipping
companies.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">The Long-term
Shipbuilding Industry Promotion Plan was announced in March 1973, to
promote Korea to be a full-fledged ship exporting nation in the 1980s.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">Major
developments in the Korean shipbuilding industry during the 1970s
include the government’s establishment of the Planned Shipbuilding
Program (PSP) in 1976, which was initiated under a stated goal of
“Korean shipyards building Korean ships to carry Korean cargo”.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.3" class="koboSpan">Under the aegis
of this programme, government-financed projects were provided to Korean
shipbuilders, with the end-users being selected by the government.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.4" class="koboSpan">The program was
institutionalised with basis in Korean law in 1978.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.5" class="koboSpan">In addition,
Korea adopted an export credit system in 1972, a move that would have
greatly helped domestic shipbuilders to secure new orders.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.6" class="koboSpan">That is between
80 and 90% of the ships built in Korea from 1973 on were for export, and
the number of ships purchased by deferred payment increased with each
passing year. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.7"
class="koboSpan">However, Korean shipyards, which were just becoming
established in the world shipbuilding market, were not able to enjoy the
same interest rates or repayment periods as the world’s leading
shipyards could. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.8"
class="koboSpan">In the 1970s, the world shipbuilding market was
changing rapidly. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.9"
class="koboSpan">Soaring world seaborne trade volumes were spurring
demand for new ships, and shipowners were interested in buying ships of
ever bigger tonnage, in order to lower both the costs of building new
ships and transporting cargo. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.10"
class="koboSpan">In the mid-1960s, the largest ships being built were
100,000 deadweight tonnes; the average size was between 30,000 and
50,000 deadweight tons. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.11"
class="koboSpan">However, in the early 1970s 200,000 dwt vessels were
the norm, and the world’s shipyards were scrambling to expand
facilities. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.12"
class="koboSpan">Another big reason for the trend towards larger ships
was the rapid increase in the international movement of oil.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.13" class="koboSpan">In the 1960s,
oil tankers made up only 21.5% of all ocean-going merchant ships, but by
the end of the decade, 75% of the new ship orders were for oil tankers.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.94.14" class="koboSpan">The huge
increase was brought about by the closure of the Suez Canal, which
forced ships to travel much longer distances.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">To cope with this
change, the Korean government encouraged private sector companies to
look for an overseas joint venture partner who would transfer the
technology, and to find buyers for the ships it was to build.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">With government
encouragement, Hyundai which was the leading pioneer in the Korean
shipbuilding industry, approached A&P Appledore and Scott Lithgow in the
UK and, in September 1971, a contract was made for sales and technical
support. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.95.3"
class="koboSpan">Further technical support arrangements were concluded
with Kwasaki Heavy Industries in 1972 and at the same time an order of
two 230,000 dwt VLCC (Very Large Crude Carrier) was given to Hyundai by
the same company. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.95.4"
class="koboSpan">As part of the deal, Kwasaki provided design drawings
and trained Hyundai employees.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">From the mid-1970s,
the principal aspects of the government’s policy for advancing the heavy
industries: In order to globalise and modernise heavy industrial
facilities, the government would provide concentrated support for areas
that saved resources, were technology intensive and involved a high
degree of local assembly. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
class="koboSpan">Korean shipyards continued to increase their output
from the early 1970s, but major growth increases began during the fourth
five-year plan (1977–1981). </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.96.3"
class="koboSpan">During the period, the Korean merchant fleets lacked
the tonnage needed to handle the rapidly growing volume of goods being
transported to and from Korea. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.96.4"
class="koboSpan">To bolster their fleets, however, Korean shipping
companies were mainly buying used ships rather than commissioning the
idle
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_567"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">domestic shipyards to build new ones.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.97.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
steps were urgently needed to help the two industries develop
together.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">However, a major
problem remained: Where would project financing come from?
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">Government
provided state-run banks guarantee for those commercial loans secured by
private sector companies, from foreign financial institutes.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">On the other hand, the
government instituted the Planned Shipbuilding Program in 1976.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">For
pre-selected end-users, financial support would be provided for the
purchase of domestically-made ships.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.3" class="koboSpan">To help
domestic shipyards improve their productivity and design capabilities,
it was stipulated that a ship build under PSP have standardised hull
forms. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.4" class="koboSpan">At the
same time, the programme would provide each shipyard with a stable
supply of work. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.5"
class="koboSpan">The goal was for Korean-owned ships to end up carrying
a greater percentage of Korean-made goods and thereby help to improve
the international balance of payments.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.6" class="koboSpan">With the
establishment of the Export-Import Bank in 1975, Korea also began
offering an export financing programme for the shipowners to build their
ships at the Korean shipyards. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.7"
class="koboSpan">According to the Korea Shipbuilders’ Association,
Korean shipbuilding output was just 34 ships, totalling 12,000 gross
tonnes in 1973. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.8"
class="koboSpan">Five years later, that annual figure had surged to 208
ships, totalling 769,000 gross tonnes.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.99.9" class="koboSpan">Korean
shipbuilding began to take off in response to growing domestic demand,
and it continued to develop in step with the growth of other
export-driven Korean industries.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">The two Oil Shocks of
the </span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan">‘</span></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">1970s slowed world economy and the shipping volumes
were further cut. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.102.2"
class="koboSpan">Faced with the stagnant shipbuilding market, the Korean
shipbuilding industry began looking for ways to change form a business
based on quantitative growth to one that was more quality oriented.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.102.3" class="koboSpan">A cost-cutting
campaign and Total Quality Control programme were vigorously pursued.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.102.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the Korean shipbuilding industry geared up for greater diversification
into such non-shipbuilding sectors as off shore and engineering,
industrial plants, engines and machinery, robotics and heavy
equipment.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">It is a typical
phenomenon nowadays that international trade volumes do not increase
with the low economic growth rates and rising protectionism.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.103.2" class="koboSpan">To make things
worse, as the Korean shipyards had captured one quarter of the world
shipbuilding market and, thus, trade pressure on Korea from the US and
EC steadily intensified. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.103.3"
class="koboSpan">In March 1989, the EC nations (now EU) demanded that
ship prices be monitored and that market shares be adjusted.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.103.4" class="koboSpan">Then in June
of that year, the Shipbuilder Council of America claimed that government
subsidies and tax breaks granted to shipbuilders in Japan, Korea,
Germany and Norway, constituted unfair trade practice.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.103.5" class="koboSpan">The council
then filed a complaint against those four countries based on the Super
301 provisions of the US Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.103.6" class="koboSpan">Negotiations
dragged on for several years. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.103.7"
class="koboSpan">No more government intervention is the clear policy of
the Korean government at a moment.</span>

## <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">Structural Changes in Major Shipbuilding Countries</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Japan</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">The Japanese
shipbuilding industry continually increased its output until the late
1980s. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">Japan’s
dominant position as the top shipbuilding country has been threatened by
the emergence of South Korea. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.106.3"
class="koboSpan">This development led to significant changes in the
structure of Japanese shipbuilding, with both its capacity and workforce
size cut back considerably.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_568"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan">According to Lloyd’s statistics covering ships of 100GT
and above, volume of new completions in Japan reached a peak of about
16,991 million GT in 1975, and about 7,206 million GT in the 1990s.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.107.2" class="koboSpan">In and after
1988, the volume of new completions kept increasing year after year,
reaching about 9,263 million GT in 1995, and it went up to about 20,686
GT in 2000. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.107.3"
class="koboSpan">According to the Ministry of Transport (MOT)
shipbuilding statistics covering steel ships of 20GT and above, a
substantially similar tendency can be observed.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">A review of the ratio
of domestic ships to export ships in terms of the number of ships built
discloses the fact that the domestic
ship</span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan">’</span></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan">s share accounted for 70–80% throughout the past 30
years. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">In
terms of GT basis, however, export
ships</span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">’</span></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan"> share is greater than domestic
ships</span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">’</span></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan"> share because export ships are generally larger in
size than domestic ships. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.114.2"
class="koboSpan">This ratio of export ships to domestic ships has
undergone a significant change due to the multinationalisation of ships,
either owned or controlled, following the globalisation of Japanese
shipping firms.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">Export ships share
increased to 80–90% in the 1990s, and it will rise more in the
twenty-first century. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.115.2"
class="koboSpan">This structural change is featured by a decrease in the
tonnage of domestic ships due to a drastic decline in the volume of the
government-sponsored “planned shipbuilding programme”.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Such decline is
attributable to the changes occurred in the pattern of investments in
ships as a result of the multinationalisation of ships.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.116.2" class="koboSpan">The pattern of
ownership has changed from domestic owners to foreign ownership in areas
or countries of open registry (flag of convenience).
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.116.3" class="koboSpan">For this
reason, among export ships, there are a number of foreign-registry
ships, which are substantially owned by Japanese shipping firms.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">5.1.1 Changes in the composition of major shipbuilders</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">Japanese major
shipbuilders have implemented many restructuring measures, including
conversion of shipyards into offshore and construction facilities.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">As a result
the total capacity of major shipbuilders has declined.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">These changes also
affected medium-sized shipbuilders because the large ship builders have
each been associated with a number of medium-sized yards.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.119.2" class="koboSpan">Some of
Japan’s medium- and small-sized shipbuilders have increased newbuilding
output greatly over the past 30 years.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">A review of the
Japan’s shipbuilding industry shows that, since the second half of the
1980s when there were drastic cutbacks of shipbuilding capacity and
personnel, the volume of newbuilding output has varied from company to
company according to differences in their capacity, and differing
management strategies, while market shares of newbuilding output, too,
varied depending upon the measures taken by respective companies.</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">5.2 South Korea</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">East Asia’s financial
and currency crises had devastating effects on South Korea, causing
drastic structural changes in its economy and industry during the period
from the summer of 1997 to middle of 2000.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">Specifically,
the sharp decline in the value of South Korea’s currency, the WON, had a
severe effect on industries relying on imported commodities whose WON
price had soared. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.122.3"
class="koboSpan">The low value of the won did have some positive effects
and improved the price competitiveness of its exports.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.122.4" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless
the negative</span>

<div id="Ch019.xhtml_fig0289" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_569"></span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00307.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">effects of the
currency’s fall greatly outweighed the positive ones.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">South Korea’s
entire economy was forced into a critical situation and there was a
desperate attempt to obtain massive amounts of financial assistance from
such institutions as IMF.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">Because of this
situation, South Korea’s shipbuilding industry faces a number of tough
challenges, such as rationalisation (seen as essential to boosting
competitiveness), the rising cost of production, the need to cut out
inefficient facilities and to trim the industry’s large workforce.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">A “special
retirement programme” is underway and the industry has been compelled to
carry out drastic structural reforms.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.125.3" class="koboSpan">Meanwhile, the
need to face up to the overcapacity issue will not go away.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">5.2.1 Changes in volume of orders received</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">In 1991, according to
</span><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fig0290" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0290"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan">, South Korea’s volume of newbuilding orders stood at
about 5,433,970 GT in total. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.129.2"
class="koboSpan">In 1993 expansion of capacity by Halla Engineering and
Hanjin Shipbuilding pushed Korea to the top position in world
shipbuilding, overtaking Japan. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.129.3"
class="koboSpan">However, the economic crisis that hit South Korea in
1997 forced Korean shipbuilders to seek the improvement of productivity
that has resulted from drastic restructuring, which, together with
relative weakening of the won against the yen, has allowed South Korea
to maintain its competitiveness.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">5.2.2 Volume of new completions</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">South Korea’s share
of the world total of new completions has grown to such a level that it
will affect the distribution structure of the world output among
shipbuilding countries. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.131.2"
class="koboSpan">According to the Korean Shipbuilders’ Association’s
statistics covering merchant ships of GT, South Korea’s volume of new
completions increased from 4,429,952 GT in 1991 to 8,212,848 GT in 1999
(see
</span><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fig0291" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0291"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.133.2"
class="koboSpan">Completions peaked in 2000 at more than 9 million
GT.</span>

<div id="Ch019.xhtml_fig0290" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_570"></span>[](#Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0290)

[<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00308.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0290)

</div>

<div id="Ch019.xhtml_fig0291" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_571"></span>[](#Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0291)

[<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00309.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0291)

</div>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_572"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan">A predominant characteristic of South Korea’s volume of
new completions is that the share of ocean going vessels for export is
overwhelmingly greater than that of domestic vessels.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.136.2" class="koboSpan">This is
because the tonnage of the fleet owned by the South Korean shipping
industry is still small in world terms.</span>

### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">5.3 China</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">The two-digit growth
rate of economy experienced by China since the early 1990s has grabbed
the world’s attention. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.138.2"
class="koboSpan">Growth has been so strong that the Chinese government
has had to put a brake on its overheated economy.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">5.3.1 Changes in China's economy</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">In the first half of
the 1990s, China further promoted the policy of opening up its economy
to the outside world in accordance with its Eighth Five-Year Plan
(1990–1995). </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.140.2"
class="koboSpan">As a result, its economy grew at the high average
annual rate of 12.6% between 1992 and 1994.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">The growth of
industrial production centreing on the steel and heavy machinery
industries led to an increase in the production of capital goods and
durable consumer goods which are necessary to meet the domestic demand.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">And, in the
economic zones along the southeastern coast around Guangdong and Hong
Kong, the production of consumer goods, such as household electrical
appliances, textile and foodstuffs as the light industrial products has
dramatically increased. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.141.3"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, the mass movement of farmers from the country
side to these coastal regions as an ample source of low wage labour
force has significantly contributed to the boosting of China’s export
industry, thereby allowing it to shift from the exporter of primary
goods to that of secondary and finished
products.</span><sup><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fn0629" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fn0629"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, China’s
economy, supported by expanded domestic markets embracing about 1.3
billion population, has structurally changed to assume a more important
role in the export and import trades with not only Japan and Southeast
Asian countries, but also western countries, including the US, thereby
considerably affecting the development of the world economy.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">With a huge consumer
market supported by enormous domestic demand, China has tremendous
potential for growth. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.144.2"
class="koboSpan">So there has been a consistent inflow of foreign
capital into China from western as well as Asian countries, including
Japan and Korea, aimed at increasing export and import trades.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.144.3" class="koboSpan">In the medium
to long term, this is likely to continue.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">5.3.2 Changes in shipbuilding industry of China</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">It was in 1977 that
Lloyd’s commenced listing China’s tonnage data in its statistics
covering merchant ships of 100 GT and above.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.146.2" class="koboSpan">The volume of
newbuilding orders received by Chinese yards has kept increasing since
the second half of the 1980s. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.146.3"
class="koboSpan">According to Lloyd’s Register, orders totalled 777,000
GT in 1994 and reached 3,011, 000 GT in 1999.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.146.4" class="koboSpan">Chinese yards
then accounted for 10.4% of the total world orders.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">China publishes the
volume of tonnage built in terms of “composite tonne” which is
essentially the mixed unit of deadweight tonne for cargo ships,
including non-self-propelling steel ship and displacement tonne for
others. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.147.2"
class="koboSpan">According to these statistics, volume of tonnage newly
built started from almost 1,079,000 GT in 1994 (see
</span><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fig0292" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0292"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<div id="Ch019.xhtml_fig0292" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_573"></span>[](#Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0292)

[<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00310.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch019.xhtml_bck_fig0292)

</div>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">The volume of
completions in 1999 reached almost 1,556,000 GT, accounting for 5.6% of
the world total.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">5.3.3 The role of china state shipbuilding corporation (CSSC)</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">China State
Shipbuilding Corporation is essentially the core of China’s shipbuilding
industry and it exercises control over large- and medium-sized shipyards
capable of building ocean-going vessels and warships, as well as
large-size marine structures. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.153.2"
class="koboSpan">Small-size shipyards, engaged in the building medium
and small-size steel vessels to be used for inland waterways and for
coastal trading, are under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of
Communications or regional autonomous bodies.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">CSSC is one of the
state-owned mammoth enterprises belonging to the Ministry of
Machine-Building Industry. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.154.2"
class="koboSpan">With its headquarters located in Beijing, CSSC
exercises general control over major shipyards throughout China through
nine regional shipbuilding corporations located in Shanghai, Dalian,
Tianjin, Guagzhou, etc. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.154.3"
class="koboSpan">CSSC has control over the Merchant Ship Design &
Research Institutes which are located in regional centres such as
Shanghai and Wuhan.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">As for ship design,
basic plans are mainly drawn up in Beijing, while detailed plans are
worked out by these regional institutes.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">Depending upon
the type of ships ordered, however, there are cases where basic plans
are drawn up by regional institutes.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">In the early 1990s, a
new modernised large yard was constructed within the Dalian Shipyard.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.156.2" class="koboSpan">This new yard,
together with the old one and factories for the production of ship
related products, formed the “Dalian Group”.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.156.3" class="koboSpan">This is a sure
indication that the manner of the central control by CSSC has become
flexible enough to allow certain autonomy to part of the regional
institutes.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">The case of Guangzhou
Shipbuilding Industry Corporation is a typical example of this
flexibility. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.157.2"
class="koboSpan">Its corporate name changed to “Guangzhou Shipyard
International” with its stocks listed on the stock exchanges in Shanghai
and Hong kong. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.157.3"
class="koboSpan">Although this shipyard is still under the jurisdiction
of CSSC, it is essentially the advent of an independent shipyard as a
stock company with the same form of business organisation as those
commonly seen in the capitalist economy.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_574"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">China Shipbuilding Trading Corporation (CSTC) became
independent of the CSSC in 1987.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.158.2" class="koboSpan">Since then it
has promoted ship exports through collaboration with CSSC.</span>

#### <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">5.3.4 Change of global shipbuilding leader</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">The global
shipbuilding leader has changed dramatically in the last century.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.160.2" class="koboSpan">In the
nineteenth Century, the US was the dominant position in the shipbuilding
industries. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.160.3"
class="koboSpan">Afterwards, Great Britain became the strongest maritime
conqueror and monopolised a lions share of the world shipbuilding
capacity until World War II. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.160.4"
class="koboSpan">After World War II, it was Western Europe that played
the leading role in producing massive new building vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">From the 1990s,
Europe’s competitiveness deteriorated.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.161.2" class="koboSpan">This was due
to the surge in labour costs and taxation.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.161.3" class="koboSpan">Consequently
there was the rapid decrease of their flag tonnages Meanwhile, a large
portion of European vessels flagged out to the Flag of Convenience.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.161.4" class="koboSpan">Subsequently
emerging shipbuilding countries such as Japan and Korea took over
leadership. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.161.5"
class="koboSpan">Japan enjoyed the dominant position in the world
shipbuilding industries and was well armed with competitive edges such
as price and technology.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">However, as time
passed Korea took over Japan’s dominant position in the shipbuilding
Industries. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.162.2"
class="koboSpan">Korea, home to seven of the top 10 global shipbuilders,
has steamed ahead with innovative processes, strengthening reliability
among clients due to best quality, on-time delivery at competitive
prices. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.162.3" class="koboSpan">Korea
has the highest dock turnover rate in the world.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.162.4" class="koboSpan">This rate is a
reliable way of measuring shipyard’s technical capacity and production
efficiency. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.162.5"
class="koboSpan">Korean shipbuilders use ground instead of dry docks for
shipbuilding, which is an innovative method for shipbuilding and
production capacity can be further expanded to meet unexpected surge of
shipbuilding demand. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.162.6"
class="koboSpan">Korea built 40% of new tonnages in the world in
2008.</span>

## <span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.163.2" class="koboSpan">Summary and Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">Shipbuilding
enterprises come in two distinct groups: those which engage purely in
shipbuilding and those which are diversified enterprises where
shipbuilding is only one of a portfolio of interests that may have very
little in common.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">Shipbuilders
belonging to diversified corporations have the advantage of being able
to rely on corporate resources for expansion.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
in periods of shipping recession, the shipbuilding member of the group
can call upon reserves acquired in other market areas to overcome
short-term cash flow difficulties and to modernise its production
facilities and to avail itself of research and development initiatives
sponsored by the group as well. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.165.3"
class="koboSpan">The flexibility inherent in within-group transfer of
resources to the benefit of shipbuilding operations has been important
to the success of Japanese and South Korean shipbuilders.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.165.4" class="koboSpan">Also as a
member of a large group called
“chaebol”</span><sup><a href="#Ch019.xhtml_fn0630" id="Ch019.xhtml_bck_fn0630"><span
id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan"> this type of shipbuilder commands respect in
industrial, financial and political circles.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">This respect
may be manifested through easier access to capital markets and more
sympathetic treatment of the enterprise by policymakers.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">The state actively
seeks to regulate the activity levels of whatever portion of the
industry falls within its jurisdiction.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">In this way
the government can shape the shipbuilding industry.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_575"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan">Aggregate shipbuilding demand is the outcome of
conditions affecting world trade.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.169.2" class="koboSpan">The actions of
individual shipbuilding enterprises and individual governments may
partially regulate the demand for a small component of world
shipbuilding, but they will not greatly affect overall demand
conditions. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.169.3" class="koboSpan">In
other words, aggregate demand for shipping is very largely an exogenous
factor; something outside the control of the industry or government
institutions.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">The health of a
country’s shipbuilding industry has ramifications for the role of
governments on the one hand, and the prosperity of communities and
regions within countries on the other.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.170.2" class="koboSpan">In the first
instance, governments can intervene in the market in order to bolster
demand for ships and thereby provide support for an otherwise ailing
domestic shipbuilding industry. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.170.3"
class="koboSpan">In the second instance, governments can intervene in
regional economies which are suffering from depressed conditions to
bolster regional development and ameliorate the consequences of locally
concentrated unemployment.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">Ship prices are
frequently distorted by the effects of state subsidy.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.171.2" class="koboSpan">The motivation
for the imbalance between supply and demand is simple and stems from the
belief held by most states that their shipbuilders are too important to
be allowed to fail. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.171.3"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, “there is great temptation to support
ship production beyond ‘normal’ commercial limits”.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.171.4" class="koboSpan">Whatever form
it takes, the end result is a financial subsidy borne by the state.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.171.5" class="koboSpan">The extent and
availability of financial concessions of this kind are ultimately
dependent on the conditions prevailing in the economic
environment.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">Government support
for shipbuilding is not confined to loan schemes for newbuildings.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.172.2" class="koboSpan">It can be
manifested through direct forms of demand management.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.172.3" class="koboSpan">One of the
means often resorted to by governments is the formulation of naval
programmes such that they serve as counter-cyclical measures for
shipyard employment stabilisation.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">Shipbuilding has been
perceived as a key player in modernisation of society and the furthering
of national development which follows from industrialisation.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.173.2" class="koboSpan">Shipbuilding
is an enticing tool of development, it is a medium technology industry
which appears to suit the factor-cost advantages of NICs.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.173.3" class="koboSpan">Also
shipbuilding has strong links with other industries.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.173.4" class="koboSpan">It should,
therefore, serve to foster other nascent industries in the NICs.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">The Japanese
shipbuilding industry has had to adapt to an ever-changing environment.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.174.2" class="koboSpan">Japan’s
competitive edge was reduced as South Korea emerged as a major
shipbuilding country. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.174.3"
class="koboSpan">Worth noting as the measures that brought about
significant changes in the structure and constitution of the Japanese
shipbuilding industry were its drastic cutbacks of shipbuilding capacity
and mass dismissal of employees through a Special Retirement
Programme.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">East Asia’s financial
and economic crises had devastating effects for South Korea, causing
far-reaching structural changes in its economy and industry since the
summer of 1997. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.175.2"
class="koboSpan">Following the decline of its economy, South Korea’s
shipbuilding industry has faced a number of major challenges, such as
rationalisation to enhance competitiveness, the rising cost of
production, cutbacks in capacity and employees, and drastic structural
reforms. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.175.3" class="koboSpan">At
the same time South Korea is under pressure to find ways to deal with
overcapacity; an issue which is certain to remain controversial in the
twenty-first century.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">China’s economy,
supported by expanded domestic markets supporting about 1.3 billion
people, has changed structurally with exports and imports becoming more
important. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.176.2" class="koboSpan">The
volume of newbuilding orders received by Chinese yards has been kept
increasing since the second half of the 1980s.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.176.3" class="koboSpan">According to
Lloyd’s Register, orders
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_page_576"></span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan">totalled 777,000 GT in 1994 and reached 3,011,000 GT in
1999. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.177.2" class="koboSpan">Chinese
yards then accounted for 10.4% of the total world orders.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.177.3" class="koboSpan">China will
certainly continue with its ambitious shipbuilding expansion
plans.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">The shipbuilding
industry is simply a player in the commercial market, so any form of
subsidy distorts the price and damages free market mechanisms.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.178.2" class="koboSpan">Government
subsidy to shipyards merely undermines the strength of the commercial
market for new merchant ships. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.178.3"
class="koboSpan">This has resulted in a situation where the taxpayers of
many countries pay substantial sums to support uneconomic national
shipbuilding industries.</span>

<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">Artificially low
newbuilding prices represent a loss to all in the shipbuilding and
shipping markets. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.179.2"
class="koboSpan">In order to improve productivity, it is essential to
utilise automated machinery and tools and sophisticated automated
systems effectively. </span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.179.3"
class="koboSpan">Technological competence is equally important.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.179.4" class="koboSpan">It serves as
the basis for the development of design and engineering capabilities.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.179.5" class="koboSpan">This
technological competence coupled with efficient management know-how will
determine ultimate productivity.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.179.6" class="koboSpan">How to achieve
the superior productivity will determine the future of a country’s
shipbuilding industry.</span>

[<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch019.xhtml_bck_fn0621)<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan">Sogang University, Seoul, Korea.
</span><span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">Email:
</span><span class="italic">[<span id="Ch019.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">Jonsoo@ccs.sogang.ac.kr</span>](mailto:Jonsoo@ccs.sogang.ac.kr)</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_578"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_579"></span>[<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 20</span>\
<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">The Impact of Choice of Flag on Ship Management</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0447)
==================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Kyriaki</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Mitroussi</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">Peter</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Marlow</span></span><a href="#Ch020.xhtml_fn0633" id="Ch020.xhtml_bck_fn0633"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.9.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">Ship registration,
primarily a requirement under international law, evolved especially
after the second half of the twentieth century into an important and at
times quite complex commercial decision for ship owners.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">This change of
nature of ship registration from a legal condition to a business choice,
largely effected by the absence of universally binding provisions to
determine the “genuine link” between the flag state and the ship and by
successful and quick industry response to market pressures and
opportunities, has had a number of consequences at company, industry,
national and international level.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.10.3" class="koboSpan">Ship owners
were presented with an array of flag types and actual flags in which
freely to register their vessels; the industry found a means to improve
its competitiveness but also ended up with increased and serious safety
concerns; some nations came up with a way to earn revenue and gain some
political significance, while others were confronted with a national
threat along these same lines; at an international level, new sources of
supply of labour were developed with transfer of expertise and dynamics
changed. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.10.4" class="koboSpan">The
major issue has of course been the proliferation of the open registers
regime designed and established to provide mainly a cost reduction
service to ship operators in relation to the option of traditional
national flags. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.10.5"
class="koboSpan">Today the top 35 maritime countries account for 95.35%
of the world deadweight tonnage and 67% of this is under a foreign flag,
a figure which drops to 53.7% when the number of vessels is considered
(UNCTAD, 2008).</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">Although other types
of ship registration have sprung up, like the second or international
registers, the main dichotomy has been between flags of convenience and
traditional national flags and the choice between the two has
constituted a topical subject for research.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">Various myths
and realities have been widely explored.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.11.3" class="koboSpan">In the course
of research and with the passing of time some have been verified, others
have failed to point to safe conclusions and yet for others new scope of
thought has been triggered. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.11.4"
class="koboSpan">For example, the significant reductions in crew costs
advocated by open registers can
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_580"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan">be said to be an everyday reality felt by ship owners
around the world and manifested clearly in relevant research stipulating
that crew cost differences between selected EU flags and lower-cost open
registry vessels, for instance, range from +22% to +333% (Anon, 1995).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">Open registers
have conventionally been associated with poorer safety performance than
traditional flags and some research results have provided support to
this assumption (Li and Wonham, 1999; Alderton and Winchester, 2002).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">Yet, today some
of the most important open registries, like Liberia, Malta, Cyprus, and
the Bahamas are on the White List of the Paris MOU together with
important traditional flags like Greece, USA and the UK, while the most
important open registry, Panama, with 22.6% of the world tonnage
registered in it is on the former’s Black List (Paris, MOU 2007; UNCTAD,
2008). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.12.4" class="koboSpan">The
unprecedented growth of open registries has alarmed traditional maritime
nations which have seen their own flags retrenching with direct and
indirect economic, political and national repercussions.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.12.5" class="koboSpan">A study by
Peeters </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1994), however, exhibited another dimension to the
problem concluding that 70% of the value added by the Dutch shipping
industry actually came from onshore activities related to shipping, a
finding which was reflected in the new shipping policy introduced in
1996 in the Netherlands. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.14.2"
class="koboSpan">Overall, the examination of the two types of flags has
centred on their costs and benefits, their standing in the shipping
industry and, in a wider social context, selection criteria, fiscal
implications and safety issues.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">The two types of flags
have been seen to offer two distinct alternatives to ship operators,
each with its own advantages and disadvantages and with its own
commercial and operational requirements.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">It is within
these realms that the view is taken that flag choice has a bearing also
on various management issues in shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.3" class="koboSpan">The argument
put forward is that opting for a specific type of flag is in fact a
strategic business decision with broader consequences for ship
management. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.4" class="koboSpan">The
aim of this chapter is to address the issue of choice of flag in the
context of ship management with the object of assessing its expected
impact on management principles and practices.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.5" class="koboSpan">For the purpose
of the analysis the traditional, clear-cut distinction between national
flags and flags of convenience has been chosen to form the framework of
reference. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.6"
class="koboSpan">Their noted features and/or requirements are considered
in respect of the way they can affect management decisions and the
adoption of management approaches.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.7" class="koboSpan">The discussion
is based on the case where the flag choice decision is made by the same
entity that is both responsible for and also essentially carrying out
the management of the vessels. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.8"
class="koboSpan">In other words, the analysis relates to the paradigm of
the ship owner who is at the same time the ship operator - even if this
is concealed by the corporate veil.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.9" class="koboSpan">It does not
seek to address the situation where third party ship managers are used
and where an association between flag choice and management practice
might be differentiated (or not) because of a number of reasons inherent
in the characteristics of the service they provide.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.15.10" class="koboSpan">The subject
matter is treated on a theoretical basis developing a rationale founded
on critical analysis and appreciating that the influence between the
choice of flag and management functions can potentially be twofold and
may come from either direction.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">Initially, this
chapter will set the context of the analysis by looking into the
existing literature on ship registration reviewing the different
characteristics, conditions, benefits and constraints of the range of
ship flags available to ship owners.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">The authors
will then make a case that the choice of flag is a management decision
by examining different management dimensions which are related to it.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">Analytic
discussion of the effects of flag preference on managerial aspects will
follow; the analysis will focus particularly on the practical impact
which the choice between an open register and a national flag
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_581"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan">is expected to have on management issues relating
mainly to strategic management and human resource management.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">Lastly, an
evaluation of the current standing of open and national registries will
be presented together with a critical assessment of its effect on
contemporary ship management.</span>

## <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">Literature Review and Background</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Since its first
significant appearance in the 1950s, flagging out – the change of a
vessel’s registry from a national flag to a flag of convenience or open
registry – has been a topic of interest in the international shipping
industry. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">This
now widespread phenomenon has attracted a great deal of attention for a
variety of reasons. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.19.3"
class="koboSpan">First, open registry fleets have expanded at a faster
rate than any other fleet in the world.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.19.4" class="koboSpan">Secondly, it
has been felt that the expansion of the open registry has limited the
growth of the fleets of other countries and has caused the decline of
the fleets of the traditional maritime countries with all the related
consequences for their maritime clusters, the balance of payments, and
the supply of skilled labour.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">According to Boczek
(1962) a FoC can be defined as: “the flag of any country allowing the
registration of foreign-owned and foreign controlled vessels under
conditions which, for whatever reasons, are convenient and opportune for
the persons who are registering the vessels”.
