</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">However, this
definition still does not allow the clear identification of an open
registry flag. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.20.3"
class="koboSpan">Even the Rochdale Report (1970) did not give a precise
definition of flags of convenience but instead suggested a list of
criteria which should lead to the classification of these.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.20.4" class="koboSpan">It defined the
FoCs in terms of six common characteristics:</span>

- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">the country of
  registry allows ownership and/or control of its merchant vessels by
  non nationals;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">access to the
  registry is easy and transfer from the registry at the owner's option
  is not restricted;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">taxes on the income
  from the ships are not levied locally or are low.
  </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">A
  registration fee and an annual fee, based on tonnage are normally the
  only charge made;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">the country of
  registry is a small power with no national requirement under any
  foreseeable circumstances for all the shipping registered, but
  receipts from very small charges on large tonnage may produce a
  substantial effect on its national income and balance of
  payments;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">manning of ships by
  non-nationals is freely permitted; and</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">the country of
  registry has neither the power nor the administrative machinery
  effectively to impose any government or international regulations, nor
  has the country the wish or the power to control the companies
  themselves.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">The Report continues
that although one or more of the above features may be found in the
policies of many maritime countries, it is only when
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan">all</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan"> of these features exist that a country is
characterised as being an open register.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">Metaxas and Doganis
(1976) identified as a FoC: “the national flags of those states with
whom ship owners register their vessels in order to avoid the fiscal
obligations and the conditions and the terms of employment of factors of
production, that would have been applicable if their ships were
registered in their own countries.”
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">While
Bergstrand (1983) adopted the following definition: “A flag of
convenience is a flag of a state
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_582"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan">whose government sees registration not as a procedure
necessary in order to impose sovereignty and hence control over its
shipping but as a service which can be sold to foreign ship owners
wishing to escape the fiscal or other consequences of registration under
their own flags.”</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">The United Nations
Convention on the Conditions for Registration of Ships (1986), for the
first time defined the principles to be followed when granting
nationality to a ship. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.32.2"
class="koboSpan">The existence of a genuine link between a vessel and
its country of registry must be verified on the basis of the following
characteristics:</span>

- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">the merchant fleet
  contributes to the national economy of the country;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">revenues and
  expenditure of shipping, as well as the purchases and sales of
  vessels, are treated in the national balance of payments
  accounts;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">the employment of
  nationals on vessels;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">the beneficial
  ownership of the vessel.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter will
adopt a definition of “open register” which reflects the matters that
most concern the ship owners, such as: costs, accessibility of the
register and standards enforced by the state of registry.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.37.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore, an
open registry should be identified as a flag which allows:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">Lower crewing
    costs/manning requirements, since registration under a flag of
    convenience generally means: </span>
    - <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">unrestricted
      choice of crew in the international market;</span>
    - <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">not being
      subject to onerous national wage scales; and</span>
    - <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">more relaxed
      manning rules.</span>
2.  <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Lower operating
    costs generated by "lighter" maintenance programmes and less
    stringent enforcement of safety standards imposed by the
    register.</span>
3.  <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">Less regulatory
    control and avoidance of bureaucracy.</span>
4.  <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">The probable
    avoidance of corporate tax.</span>
5.  <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">Anonymity.</span>
6.  <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">Easy
    accessibility/exit to/from the registry.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">Nowadays, even though
traditional maritime countries continue to dominate the ownership of
world shipping, the extent of flagging out to Open Registries is such
that they account for a greater proportion of the total world fleet than
the traditional maritime countries themselves.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">The share of
world deadweight tonnage registered in the major Open Registries has
risen from about 4% in 1950 to over 54% in 2008 (UNCTAD, Review of
Maritime Transport 2008). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.47.3"
class="koboSpan">There exists no clear definition of “open and
international registries” but UNCTAD has created such a group by
including the 10 largest fleets with more than 90% of foreign-controlled
tonnage. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.47.4" class="koboSpan">These
fleets are Panama, Liberia, Bahamas, the Marshall Islands, Malta,
Cyprus, the Isle of Man, Antigua and Barbuda, Bermuda, and Saint Vincent
and the Grenadines.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">The motivation for
transferring a ship from one registry to another is no different in
principle from the motivation behind any other strategic decision on the
part of a profit-maximising firm.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.48.2" class="koboSpan">The basic
principles of the theory of the firm can be applied to the economics of
this behaviour. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.48.3"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies are assumed to be profit maximisers
which strive to reach their objective by seeking the production input
combination which allows them to minimise costs.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.48.4" class="koboSpan">However, their
choice of factors of production is constrained by their operating
environment. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.48.5"
class="koboSpan">Institutional factors and the characteristics of
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_583"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">the market in which they operate condition their
ability to make independent decisions.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">The selection
of factors, their quantities, their costs and quality appear to be
regulated in most of the so-called developed countries.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">However, the existence
of open registries creates a sort of dualism in the international
maritime transport sector splitting the industry into two segments
distinguished by operating characteristics peculiar to the two different
scenarios and by lower break-even points.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.50.2" class="koboSpan">The ship owner
like any other entrepreneur must chose the optimum amount of inputs to
obtain the desired service output and strives to have the freedom to do
so. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">Flagging
out is primarily caused by the desire to minimise costs under a
relatively lower cost regime but, as we shall see, the decision to flag
out might have an impact on several ship management functions.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Flag selection is a
high-level decision usually made, on a vessel-by-vessel basis, at the
time of vessel acquisition and is generally based on experience.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">Different
companies perceive different factors as being important to their
decision on flag (Bergantino and Marlow, 1998).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.51.3" class="koboSpan">A flag might be
chosen for political reasons, to ensure a supply of skilled labour, for
public relations reasons, for historical reasons, because of directives
from financial institutions, or for reasons related to the trade routes
of the vessel or to its characteristics.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.51.4" class="koboSpan">In the
Bergantino and Marlow study companies which had chosen not to use the
national flag gave crew costs as the most common reason for their
decision. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.51.5" class="koboSpan">Other
factors which had influenced them were: to escape bureaucratic control,
high costs of compliance with standards of the national flag, the
unavailability of skilled labour (the need to ensure a supply of same),
and fiscal reasons.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">In particular,
operating
costs</span><sup><a href="#Ch020.xhtml_fn0634" id="Ch020.xhtml_bck_fn0634"><span
id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan"> are identified as the ones where significant savings
would be achieved by registering the ship in an Open Register.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">It is in the
manning costs area where flagging out policies allow varying degrees of
freedom to be obtained from the constraints of Union agreements and
national manning regulations. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.54.3"
class="koboSpan">Hence, according to the vast majority of
authors,</span><sup><a href="#Ch020.xhtml_fn0635" id="Ch020.xhtml_bck_fn0635"><span
id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan"> shipowners, shipowners’ associations and trade union
representatives, the main reason for flagging out is to reduce manning
costs. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">It has
been stated by many authors that the adoption of an open registry flag
can lead to savings in the following categories of crew-related
costs:</span>

- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">direct and indirect
  wages;</span><sup><a href="#Ch020.xhtml_fn0636" id="Ch020.xhtml_bck_fn0636"><span
  id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">stores;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">maintenance.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">The authors share the
belief that crew costs can be considered as the main financial reason
behind the ship owner’s decision to flag out.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">The cost of
manning a ship can be considered the easiest variable to influence when
compared to other ship costs which appear to be mostly fixed
internationally, especially in the short run.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.61.3" class="koboSpan">Stores costs
are not as relevant as the other two categories and, furthermore, the
adoption of an open register flag does not necessarily imply a decrease
in this category of cost. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.61.4"
class="koboSpan">As for the maintenance costs it is argued that while
some crews can carry out certain tasks within the vessel, thereby
eliminating the use of shore labour, others cannot and the lack of such
maintenance and the subsequent neglect may lead to major damage claims
and therefore higher insurance costs.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.61.5" class="koboSpan">Operating
efficiency could, therefore, depend on the quality of the crew.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Manning costs have two
components which are considered of equal importance: the direct and the
indirect wage. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.62.2"
class="koboSpan">The basic wage depends on the standard of living in the
country of origin of the seaman, on the current exchange rate of the
seaman’s currency
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_584"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">against the US dollar, and on international regulation
and ITF policies framed to avoid the exploitation of the FoC crews.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.63.2" class="koboSpan">Indirect wage
costs are those which do not represent immediate payment to the employed
and are set independently by single national governments with regard to
national seafarers (i.e. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.63.3"
class="koboSpan">national insurance payment, leave entitlement,
pensions, training, employment taxes, medical expenses, and so on).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.63.4" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
indirect wage is the element of the manning costs where different
national policies could have a strong impact on the ship owners’
decisions regarding flag.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">By adopting a flag of
convenience the ship owner gains the ability to offer contracts with
gross salaries, transferring the responsibility for pension provision,
social security costs and coverage of medical expenses to the employee.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.64.2" class="koboSpan">At the same
time employment conditions such as lengths of duty and leave could be
re-negotiated on an individual basis.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.64.3" class="koboSpan">The governments
of most of the traditional maritime countries have modified their
policies to move them closer to the situation created by the legislation
of the Open Registry countries. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.64.4"
class="koboSpan">This has led to the introduction of second or
international registers but these will not feature as the focus of this
chapter.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">A group of factors
that might influence the shipowner’s decision, but which have been
partly ignored by the existing literature, are the characteristics of
the shipping companies and of the ships.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">It is observed
that only some companies of the same nationality decide to flag out, and
that the decision to flag out might concern either all or only part of
the fleet of the same shipping company.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">In the next
section flag choice as a management decision will be discussed.</span>

## <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">Flag Choice as a Management Decision</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">However
straightforward the attribution of nationality to a ship may initially
sound, the reality described in the previous section clearly shows the
variety of alternatives ship owners have at their disposal and the
diversity of parameters that have to be taken into account.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.67.2" class="koboSpan">It is this
absence of externally imposed legal conditions, this aspect of informed
and educated choice between alternatives that, first of all, makes the
preference for a specific type of registry a management decision.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.67.3" class="koboSpan">Previous
research (Bergantino and Marlow, 1998) showed that ship owners are
driven in their choice of flag by certain criteria many of which can be
seen to be related to management issues, such as marketing
considerations or the decision to reduce input costs, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.67.4" class="koboSpan">crew costs.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.67.5" class="koboSpan">However there
seems to be another direction in this relationship; the dimensions along
which flags differentiate touch upon management issues and therefore
flag choice can have an effect on management practices, too.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.67.6" class="koboSpan">In fact, the
direction of such associations can become quite blurred, especially
given that the choice of flag tends to be based on different sets of
criteria for individual ship owners and individual ships (Bergantino and
Marlow, 1998). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.67.7"
class="koboSpan">Within these realms the focus here will be on
identifying general management areas which are expected to be influenced
by ship owners’ choice of registry for their vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Firstly, the choice of
a ship’s flag is very likely to affect
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan">the location of the management
company</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">
itself. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.70.2"
class="koboSpan">Traditionally, the nationality of a vessel has been
connected with the nationality of its owner but well-known developments
in the international shipping scene have brought about the evolution of
the ship registration system and the plethora of registration schemes,
procedures and requirements. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.70.3"
class="koboSpan">Although, as already pointed out, there is no
international legal instrument that lays down universally accepted
registration provisions, the United Nations Convention on the Conditions
for the Registration
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_585"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">of Ships, 1986 – which is not in force and possibly
never will be – provides some useful guidance.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">Articles 7–10
(UN 1986) call for participation by nationals of the flag state in the
ownership, manning and management of the ships; either the ownership or
manning criterion has to be satisfied but the management criterion is to
be satisfied in all cases. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.3"
class="koboSpan">Many nations appear to have indeed taken up – part of –
its content at their discretion and to various degrees and today a
number of registries require some form of commercial presence in the
country. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.4" class="koboSpan">In
some cases, such as Liberia, the requirement for a Liberian shipowning
company can be easily satisfied by setting it up there only on paper and
so it is not thought to have any significant impact on management.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.5" class="koboSpan">In other cases,
like the Dutch registry, ships must be managed in that same country, a
condition with important management implications.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.6" class="koboSpan">Such
implications relate to the general legal framework of company operation
prevalent in the country but also to the wider cultural characteristics
which should be taken into account.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.7" class="koboSpan">On the
assumption that local management companies will be staffed mostly by
indigenous expertise, management action should take into account the
special features of its human resource as conditioned by cultural
differences. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.8"
class="koboSpan">Hofstede’s work (1980), on how national cultures can be
explained by four key factors, namely, individualism, power distance,
uncertainty avoidance and masculinity, has been most influential in this
respect. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.9" class="koboSpan">It has
shown how nationality affects human behaviour and consequently how it
also constrains management practice.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.10" class="koboSpan">For example,
he has found that countries which score highly in power distance and
uncertainty avoidance are likely to produce forms of organisation that
rely heavily on hierarchy and clear orders from superiors, but those
which score low in power distance and high in uncertainty avoidance will
produce organisations that rely on rules and procedures (Hofstede,
1991). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.11" class="koboSpan">If to
the above, the effect of the company’s macro environment is added, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.71.12" class="koboSpan">the general
national economic situation, the existence of infrastructure and
telecommunications etc, the expected impact of management location on
management practice becomes even more evident.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">Clearly, the legal
framework that the different registries offer touches upon a number of
dimensions in relation to management.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">Company
laws</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan">financial
laws</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">
relating to, for instance, the company’s organisation, the disclosure of
ownership of shares, or the auditing of the accounts, will obviously be
expected to have a bearing on management functions.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.76.2" class="koboSpan">Open registries
are generally believed to encompass more flexible and owner-friendly
commercial environments but many shipowning nations, such as Greece and
the UK, have also attended to the provision of an attractive commercial
context for ship operation. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">A specific trend between registries may perhaps be
difficult to observe but although such items may be rather
flag-specific, they nevertheless have important implications for ship
management.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">The way that open
registries and traditional ones have dealt with
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan">tax liabilities
</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">has
conventionally been one of the most fundamental differences between the
two. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.79.2" class="koboSpan">Open
registries have led the way with the early introduction of advantageous
taxation schemes for both ship’s tax and company tax.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.79.3" class="koboSpan">Although indeed
a significant parameter in ship owners’ choice of flag (Gardner
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1984), differing tax systems may be thought to affect
management practice to a small and mostly indirect extent.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.81.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
they may necessitate or not the existence of a separate sub-department
in the accounts department or require expertise in the form of outside
experts or outsourcing. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.81.3"
class="koboSpan">Indirectly they will influence the company’s balance
sheets, its cash flow and perhaps ultimately and long-term the
investment capability/options of the company.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.81.4" class="koboSpan">But, unless
seen from this perspective, diverse tax schemes cannot be seen to have a
considerable
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_586"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">impact on management practice.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">In terms of
ship’s tax, one more exception may apply; when the tax system, such as a
tonnage tax system, is tied to a training obligation, as in the case of
the UK and other nations, then, more obvious implications are developed
for the human resource management exercised by the company.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">The issue of flag has
mainly been related to cost differences.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">In other words
the main differentiating factor between traditional flags and open
registries is cost, translated into total crew costs, tax and high costs
of compliance with safety standards of national flags.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.83.3" class="koboSpan">Tax does not
really have a dramatic effect on management practices.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.83.4" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
the degree of preoccupation with cost as a formative parameter of
strategy and the repercussions for crew employment choices that occur
with the preference for a flag are the two issues with the most impact
on management decisions and these will be explored in some detail in the
following two sections.</span>

## <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.84.2" class="koboSpan">The Impact of Choice of Flag on Strategic Decisions</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">The choice of flag
also affects a number of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan">strategic decisions at corporate
level</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">In the first
place, the flag a vessel flies may influence the actual
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan">market
sectors</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">
in which a company engages. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.89.2"
class="koboSpan">Decisions about the fields and industries in which a
corporation’s Strategic Business Units (SBUs) will pursue commercial
activities are among the most significant decisions corporate executives
and top management are expected to make for the success and the
viability of every firm. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.89.3"
class="koboSpan">Consider the example of countries, Norway for instance,
which offer exclusive employment of vessels flying the national flag in
certain protected trades, such as coasting, or when there is a
preference for the national fleet for government cargoes, like the case
of the USA. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.89.4"
class="koboSpan">Clearly, the flying of a foreign flag automatically
prevents the company from involvement in specific market segments.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.89.5" class="koboSpan">Along the same
lines, a firm using reputable and highly recognised flags for its
vessels may have built up a respectable and dependable profile and may
thus enjoy further business opportunities for involvement in higher risk
trades, such as the tanker industry, which it could otherwise perhaps
not be provided with. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.89.6"
class="koboSpan">Hand in hand with these strategic choices come also
management decisions about the firm’s assets or features of the firm’s
fleet especially in terms of ship types and ship sizes, and so the
latter can also be seen to potentially be affected by the ship owners’
flag choice. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.89.7" class="koboSpan">In
connection with the above, ship management can also be influenced by the
choice of flag
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">at</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
class="koboSpan">an operational
level</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">Preference for
certain </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan">trade
routes</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">
may be effected by a need, for example, to avoid highly regulated
geographic regions, such as the USA especially after the introduction of
OPA 90, or the EU, or certain countries or strict Port State Control
areas if ships are flying a PSC-targeted flag.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">Interestingly, and
perhaps unexpectedly, flag choice can be seen to have an impact on yet
more strategic management issues.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">The formulation
of a corporate strategy can potentially be affected by a specific flag
choice when, for instance, flags give attractive incentives for building
new ships. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.95.3"
class="koboSpan">Fleet expansion is of course a management decision
primarily driven by market conditions, good freight rates, strong cash
flows, and optimistic expectations.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.95.4" class="koboSpan">But more often
than not, history in shipping has shown that ship owners in their
decision to invest in new ships are also influenced by favourable
building incentives, coming either from the yard or the government, to
such an extent that this behaviour has been thought to bring ultimately
negative results for the freight market (Strandenes, 2002).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.95.5" class="koboSpan">In other words,
although a rational assumption here, the impact
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_587"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
class="koboSpan">of appealing newbuilding support schemes as part of a
flag’s regime on a ship owners’ decision to adopt a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">growth
strategy</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">
is in fact a noted reality. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.98.2"
class="koboSpan">Growth and fleet expansion can be achieved also through
the acquisition of second hand ships.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.98.3" class="koboSpan">In this case,
too, the flag’s effect on the decision to expand can be considerable,
especially in situations when the flag provides ship owners with access
to loans at better rates of interest within the realms of its industry
support plan. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.98.4"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, the choice of flag does not only
have a bearing on whether top management takes up a growth corporate
strategy or not but also on the ways in which growth is to take place.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.98.5" class="koboSpan">A
straightforward example relates to the manner in which registries deal
with the issue of dual registration.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.98.6" class="koboSpan">If a flag does
not allow dual registration, this affects also the fleet expansion
policy as ship owners are restricted with regard to bareboat chartering
options under this registry system.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.98.7" class="koboSpan">On top of that,
management decisions on
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
class="koboSpan">fleet replacement
policy</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">
can at times be impacted by the choice of flag.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">This is so
since many registries, both traditional and open registers, have a
maximum ship’s age restriction which means that if ship owners, for a
number of reasons, wish their ships to fly this flag, they must adjust
their replacement policy accordingly.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">Associations between
the choice of flag and the formulation of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">business-level strategies
</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">can
also be considered. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.2"
class="koboSpan">According to Porter (1980), there are three generic
strategies that companies can pursue: a differentiation strategy; a cost
leadership strategy; and a focus strategy.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.3" class="koboSpan">The
differentiation strategy seeks to distinguish the company’s products or
services from those of the competitors’ in the industry along some
dimensions that are valued by clients.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.4" class="koboSpan">Such
dimensions may relate to the quality of the product/service, the
development of distinctive product features, etc, and receive higher
than average prices. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.5"
class="koboSpan">With the cost leadership strategy the company attempts
to gain competitive advantage by reducing production costs and selling
its product/service at lower prices than competitors.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.6" class="koboSpan">The company
will still offer comparable quality at these low prices and make a
profit. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.7" class="koboSpan">With
the focus strategy the company concentrates on a particular market
segment, a group of customers or geographical location, and adopts
either a differentiation focus or a cost leadership focus.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.8" class="koboSpan">Bearing in
mind that the use of open registries has been instigated particularly by
the drive for cost-cutting, it can reasonably be assumed that companies
opting for them would follow a cost leadership competitive strategy.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.103.9" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, ship owners who are willing to take on the additional costs of a
national flag and invest further in the image of a traditional, quality
operator would, in effect, opt for a differentiation strategy for their
business ventures.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">The strategic
decision of the top management concerning the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan">employment of third party ship
managers</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"> does not appear to be directly affected by the choice
of flag. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.106.2"
class="koboSpan">Relevant research indicated that flagging out was
ranked low down in importance by ship owners as a potential reason for
turning to third party ship managers (Mitroussi, 2004).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">Other
assumptions of indirect associations between flag choice and the use of
third party ship management can be attempted but seem to be less able to
hold up in a critical rationale, especially when additional dimensions
are considered. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.106.4"
class="koboSpan">For example, it has been shown, that when ship owners
do not use third party ship management it is very much because they want
to keep close overall control over vessels, both in terms of cost as
well as maintenance levels (Mitroussi, 2004).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.106.5" class="koboSpan">National
flags, on the other hand, are known to administer and therefore require,
on the part of their operators, close control in order to keep safety
standards high. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.106.6"
class="koboSpan">On these grounds a logical assumption would be that the
choice of national flag might deter the loss of absolute control and
therefore the use of third party ship management.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.106.7" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
market requirements, with charterers often
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_588"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan">preferring to do business with a recognised ship
manager rather than a small operator, especially in trades of high risk,
like the tanker sector, point to the idea that third party ship
management and control of safety standards might be on the same side of
the road. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.107.2" class="koboSpan">With
ship owners generally retaining the decision on the choice of flag even
when third party ship managers are used (Mitroussi, 2004), it seems that
although overall the choice of flag can influence ship management
practice, it does not have an impact on its outsourcing.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">Last but not least,
management is concerned with
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan">dealing with the external environment
</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan"> of a
company too, and even more so today, given the upsurge of the concept of
corporate social responsibility, with its various stakeholders.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">Although
shipping is indeed a truly international business, choice of flag by
definition has an effect on this aspect of management as it dictates the
micro external environment of a shipping company through the legal
framework it provides, such as the national shipping bodies, government
agencies, bureaucratic control and other aspects.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.110.3" class="koboSpan">In the case of
traditional flags usually some important work should be expected on the
part of the management of the company to achieve and enhance
relationship building with unions, flag officials, other contacts and
other shipping related associations.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.110.4" class="koboSpan">This can be
both time-consuming and require specific managerial, social and even
negotiation skills but it also allows room for lobbying, and gives
opportunities for recognition within the community and for making the
company’s voice heard. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.110.5"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, such aspects of management are
usually not required – certainly not to a significant extent – when the
ship operation concerns vessels registered in flags of convenience,
which are generally accepted to encompass lax governmental controls and
a minimum shipping infrastructure.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.110.6" class="koboSpan">Quite clearly,
the choice of flag touches upon management issues in this respect,
too.</span>

## <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.111.2" class="koboSpan">The Impact of Choice of Flag on Human Resource Management</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">Open registries and
the process of changing the flag – the flagging out – have been
particularly associated with the issue of ship manning.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.112.2" class="koboSpan">Applying
Vernon’s dynamic model of location of production (1966), flagging out is
regarded as analogous to the establishment of overseas subsidiaries by
large production firms and is considered to be the third wave of
maritime transport (Sletmo, 1989).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.112.3" class="koboSpan">Flagging out
is seen as part of the shipping industry’s effort to develop least cost
systems of ship operation by taking advantage of low cost labour.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.112.4" class="koboSpan">By definition,
therefore, the choice of flag has an axiomatic direct impact on the
human resource management of a shipping company.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.112.5" class="koboSpan">This impact,
although primarily related to crews, extends to the overall management
practice in a company, not least because crew management is an essential
part of it, but also due to the inevitable relationships developed
between onboard and shore-based human resource management.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">"Human resource
management involves all management decisions and practices that directly
affect or influence the people, or human resources, who work for the
organisation" (Torrington
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2002). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.115.2"
class="koboSpan">The term has in recent years been more and more used in
the place of the term ‘personnel management’ in order to signify a shift
in its importance and in its orientation.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.115.3" class="koboSpan">Torrington
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2008) talk about the changing nature of the
management of people underlining that personnel management is
preoccupied with managing the supply of people to the business, but
human resource management
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_589"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan">with managing the demand for human resources to meet
the operational needs of the business.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">In essence,
emphasis on a more strategic approach to people management is given, as
human resource management must integrate the firm’s goals with the
correct approach to managing its human capital (Baron and Kreps, 1999).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.118.3" class="koboSpan">Effective
human resource management has been positively associated with higher
employee productivity and better financial results (Delaney and Huselid,
1996; Huselid
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan">., 1997). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.120.2"
class="koboSpan">The role of human capital and its management in
sustaining competitive advantage has been stressed in the general
management literature (Pfeffer, 1995) but also more recently in
shipping-related literature. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.120.3"
class="koboSpan">Lorange (2005), examining contemporary evolutionary
forces in relation to shipping company strategies, talks of company
cases in which “the assets are the human capital” and underlines “a
strong emphasis on being ‘a people make the difference’ business,
without owning any ‘steel’ at all.”</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">Human resource
management is of particular significance in shipping, which although
traditionally capital intensive, particularly relies on its people for
successful and profitable ship operation.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.121.2" class="koboSpan">This is so,
not just due to their innate characteristics as service-sector
organisations, but particularly due to the unique idiosyncrasies of the
shipping business itself (Mitroussi and Chang, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.121.3" class="koboSpan">The special
features of shipping with regard to its people mainly relate to the
distinction between shore-based and ship-based personnel in the
companies, the inherent complexity of ship operation which places
capital intensive assets in the hands of very few (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.121.4" class="koboSpan">15 to 20)
people, the multinational aspect and immensely high turnover of the crew
and the social aspect of the staff’s time on board.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">The scope of human
resource management activities is quite broad and could perhaps best be
described as the effort to attract effective employees, develop them to
their potential and maintain them over the long term (Fisher, 1989).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">These main
areas include a number of activities ranging from human resource
planning, recruitment and selection, to training, development and
appraisal and yet further to managing employee relations and services,
such as welfare. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.122.3"
class="koboSpan">The focus in this chapter is primarily on the first two
areas, as these are thought to be more directly affected by the choice
of flag.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">One of the most
important aspects of people management in shipping is its
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">international
dimension.</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan"> International human resource management is a term
which has only recently appeared in shore industries and has emerged as
a consequence mostly of the establishment and expansion of overseas
subsidiaries and of course the development of globalised firms.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">Research
suggests that the majority of companies in shore industries have yet to
deal with and align their human resource policies and practices with
globalisation needs (Wellins and Rioux, 2000).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.125.3" class="koboSpan">International
manning is certainly not a new matter for the shipping business, given
its inherently international character; however, as already pointed out,
the burst of foreign recruitment on board vessels took place with the
third wave of shipping – the flagging out process.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.125.4" class="koboSpan">In other
words, if it is assumed that national flags have traditionally required
a full – or an overwhelming majority – of national crew complement, then
it can safely be deduced that international human resource management
should be expected to be more of a concern for companies opting for
flagging out. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.125.5"
class="koboSpan">This clearly indicates a considerable impact of the
choice of flag on human resource management of companies, as it points
to differences in human resource approaches and procedures for companies
registering their vessels in different flags.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.125.6" class="koboSpan">Ship managers
involved in dealing with a diverse pool of seafarers coming from around
the world are faced with a number of challenges.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.125.7" class="koboSpan">Cultural and
national differences have to be coordinated and accommodated; policies
and practices
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_590"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan">may have to be adjusted to take into account
differences in cultures and social norms; effective communication needs
to be maintained in different languages and for different backgrounds
and frames of reference. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.126.2"
class="koboSpan">As such, the special concerns of ship operators
managing a nationally diverse workforce encompass a number of aspects,
such as the organisation culture and the education programmes, and
primarily should concentrate on building human resource systems which
are bias-free in many respects (Cox and Blake, 1991).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.126.3" class="koboSpan">Special
attention must be paid to the significant issue of successful
communication not just from the office to the ship but also most
importantly among the crew onboard the vessel, not only because these
people will be the direct and first handlers of an emergency situation,
but also for the good social and working relations and the efficient
execution of duties onboard. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.126.4"
class="koboSpan">As language and cultural barriers are bound to be
present in the communication of multi-national crews, the proper mix of
crew nationalities and knowledge of such potential barriers play a vital
role in effective ship management.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.126.5" class="koboSpan">For example,
research has shown that people of different nationalities pay differing
degrees of attention to the social context – nonverbal clues, social
status, etc – when they communicate verbally (Kennedy and Everest,
1991). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.126.6" class="koboSpan">The
Chinese, for example, come from a high-context culture and tend to
derive meaning from context, whereas Scandinavians come from a
low-context culture and derive meaning primarily from words.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.126.7" class="koboSpan">The
implications for effective communication within these realms are quite
self-evident as well as the implications for the human resource
management of shipping companies involved with the manning of
multinational crews.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">Appropriate planning
is the starting point for successful human resource management.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">Human resource
planning</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the process for identifying an organisation’s
current and future requirements, developing plans to meet these
requirements and monitoring their effectiveness (Beardwell and Claydon,
2007). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">It is
an integral part of broader company planning as it is connected with the
organisation’s future development and objectives.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">Its main
stages encompass an assessment of current staffing needs, forecasting
the future personnel needs, formulating a staffing strategy and finally
evaluating and updating the whole process (Kreitner, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.4" class="koboSpan">Clearly, every
shipping company should engage in human resource planning, but
circumstances in the shipping business make this a rather challenging
task regardless of the flag the ships fly.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.5" class="koboSpan">Items related
to the phase of analysing existing needs constitute in fact and, to a
great extent, a requirement for shipping companies under international
law (i.e. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.6"
class="koboSpan">under the International Ship Management (ISM) Code).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.7" class="koboSpan">The reference
is for the process of job analysis which is made up of two parts: the
job description – the duties of a job, and the job specification – the
skills and qualifications needed for the job.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.8" class="koboSpan">Given the
widespread adoption and implementation of the SOLAS Convention important
differences with regard to this aspect of human resource planning should
not be expected to be observed, at least not in relation to staff
positions related to the safe management of the vessels.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.129.9" class="koboSpan">Difficulties
in the human resource planning arise for all shipping companies in
respect of the forecast of future supply and demand of labour.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">Relevant issues which
cause complications in human resource planning and are common for all
shipping companies, regardless of the flags they use for their vessels,
include the unpredictable fluctuations of the freight rate market and
the increased flexibility to trade in and out of market sectors
primarily through the sale and purchase (S&P) market activities.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">Of great
importance for the forecasting of projected staff needs is the ability
to predict revenues and demand for the service.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.130.3" class="koboSpan">Such
predictions, however, are notoriously hard to attain in the shipping
business, where forecasting tools generally
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_591"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan">fail to reflect and encompass the complexity and
volatility of macro and micro realities.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.131.2" class="koboSpan">The S&P market
offers shipping companies increased flexibility to trade in and out of
varied market sectors within short periods of time and often even at
short notice, which can cause further difficulties in the forecast of
demand of future labour needs. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.131.3"
class="koboSpan">Forecasting the supply of labour entails basically two
tasks: assessing the internal supply – the number and type of employees
expected to remain in the firm – and the external sources generally
available in the labour market. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.131.4"
class="koboSpan">Given the discussion above about the international
character of the human resource process in shipping, the difficulties
and complications of trying to anticipate availability of external
sources of labour are quite obvious.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.131.5" class="koboSpan">Within these
realms, the companies which use foreign flags are subject to greater
complexities in their human resource planning process, but also greater
opportunities as the human resource supply area for their ships becomes
effectively the whole world. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.131.6"
class="koboSpan">Another difference between firms using open registries
and those flying the national flag relates to the estimation of the
likely supply of internal candidates to satisfy future staffing needs.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.131.7" class="koboSpan">Traditionally,
shipping offices have been manned by ex-seafarers; this is still the
case today, especially in respect of certain office posts, such as the
marine superintendent, for which ex-shipmanship can be a requirement
(for a detailed account of such posts see Pettit
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan"> 2005). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies using national flags tend to have an
established pool of seafarers who regularly go on their ships.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">In order for
companies to retain the acquired expertise and be able to install more
easily commitment and corporate culture, companies often tend to keep
seafarers on their payroll, even for periods of time when they are not
serving onboard the company’s vessels.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.4" class="koboSpan">This creates a
source of internal supply of qualified employees for projected openings
in the company’s office. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.5"
class="koboSpan">Shipowners taking advantage of open registries cannot
easily build up this pool of dedicated skilled labour which can
potentially be used at the office due to the high turnover and the
practicalities of employing staff of different nationalities.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.6" class="koboSpan">Along the same
lines, companies using open registries while at the same time relying
for their recruitments on an “as needed” basis cannot plan succession
schemes for onboard posts either, that is, relating to officers
advancing from lower ranks to becoming masters or chief engineers.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.7" class="koboSpan">Exceptions of
companies who customarily use open registries but have developed strong
ties with foreign crew supply areas – for example, through the
establishment of representative crew offices locally, or supporting
marine schools there – do exist.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.8" class="koboSpan">However, it is
on these conditions of considerable investment on the part of shipping
companies in the crew supply areas that the existence of crew succession
schemes can be more readily associated with open registers and only
really with regard to onboard posts, leaving succession from the ship to
the office to still be a major concern.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.133.9" class="koboSpan">Given this
limited potential application of succession plans as well as the fact
that such investment in crew supply areas is usually related to a
critical company size, not necessarily satisfied by the majority of deep
sea tramp operators, some differences can be considered between shipping
companies flying the national flag and those using open registries in
the application of the human resource planning process.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">The next stage for an
organisation, after assessing its future human resource needs, is
recruitment and selection. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.134.2"
class="koboSpan">This stage is concerned with attracting and choosing
suitable people to meet the company’s human resource requirements.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.134.3" class="koboSpan">The importance
of effective
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">recruitment</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan"> is quite straightforward as both the quality as well
as the number of the candidates is crucial for the selection of
ultimately the most suitable employees.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.136.2" class="koboSpan">There are a
number of recruitment methods ranging from internal searches to
advertising in the press and on the internet, formal and informal
contacts, such as employee
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_592"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">referrals or simple “walk-ins”, education liaison and
recruitment agencies. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.137.2"
class="koboSpan">The choice of a national or foreign flag can have a
bearing on the recruitment techniques adopted by shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.137.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
companies with ships registered on the national registry and employing
nationals onboard their vessels can take advantage of informal contacts,
such as word of mouth and speculative applications or even use their own
shore or sea staff to recommend candidates for job openings.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.137.4" class="koboSpan">Traditional
ship owners in maritime nations, like Greece, for instance, are famous
for historically building their business relying on a pool of expertise
which would come from their own village or island and with whom they
shared a common background, culture, aspiration and therefore stronger
ties. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.137.5" class="koboSpan">This is
important as managers should consider not just the technical competence
but also the sociability of candidates, the degree to which they can fit
well into the cultural and social context of the company.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.137.6" class="koboSpan">This subtle
aspect of human resource recruitment is generally lost when the search
is only for the least expensive crew complement.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.137.7" class="koboSpan">In addition,
ship owners using the national registry may utilise the method of
college recruiting, especially as national flags often require the
training of cadets onboard registered vessels, as in the case of the
Greek flag.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">One very important
issue for consideration as an option for the recruitment process in a
shipping company is the extent of use of and reliance on crew agencies
for the manning of its vessels, in other words, the option and degree of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">outsourcing</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.2"
class="koboSpan">Outsourcing is increasingly being used on a global
scale for different management functions and human resource is one of
them, with the jobs outsourced mainly being administrative ones, like
payroll or recruitment. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.3"
class="koboSpan">In fact, research shows that human resource is one of
the most commonly outsourced business activities today (Lawler, 2004).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.4" class="koboSpan">Crew agencies
have been used in shipping to a great extent and for many decades not
least at national level, too, but once again the growth of open
registers has brought about an increased reliance on crew agencies.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.5" class="koboSpan">Expanding on
the aforementioned argument about the impact of flag choice on the
internationalisation of the human resource process, the choice of flag
is expected to have an effect also on the degree of HR outsourcing in a
shipping company. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.6"
class="koboSpan">Ship owners who choose open registries to take
advantage of lower crew costs by employing seafarers from third
countries, should obviously be expected to make considerably more use –
both in terms of general crew as well as officers – of outsourcing to
crew agencies as a means of access to distant labour supply areas.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.7" class="koboSpan">Management is
thus further affected by the potential advantages and disadvantages of
outsourcing. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.8"
class="koboSpan">In respect of advantages, ship managers opting for some
HR outsourcing are presented with: greater flexibility – an especially
good thing when a company’s needs can fluctuate quickly with the buying
in or selling of vessels; access to expertise that could be hard to find
otherwise; greater variety and mix of nationalities; reduced costs,
which can relate not only to lower crew wages but to the absence of any
need for keeping staff on standby and also to the lack of investment in
training. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.9"
class="koboSpan">However, disadvantages have also been noted.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.10" class="koboSpan">For instance,
recent research revealed that UK companies are reluctant to use
outsourcing due to fears of loss of control, loss of personal touch and
doubts about the quality and commitment of the relevant staff (Hammond,
2002). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.11"
class="koboSpan">Especially at the recruitment process the use of crew
agencies in shipping may mean that poor candidates can bypass the
initial screening process and enter the company’s pool with damaging
consequences for the business. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.140.12"
class="koboSpan">Additional potential disadvantages include loss of
skill and knowledge, reduction in the quality of service, loss of
employee morale, short term disruption and discontinuity and damage to
long-term competitiveness (Cooke
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_593"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">With regard to the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">selection
process</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">, shipowners are also presented with a variety of
techniques. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.145.2"
class="koboSpan">The choice of flag is thought to have some effect on
this dimension of the human resource management, too.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.145.3" class="koboSpan">Shipping
companies, who make use of international crew agencies for the manning
of the vessels they have under foreign flags, in reality give up
completely the activities connected with the recruitment stage and some
– if not all – of the activities connected with the selection phase.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.145.4" class="koboSpan">The first step
in the process of selection is ordinarily the review of application
forms followed by interviews, personality/psychometric/ability tests,
work simulations, or participation in assessment centres and medical
examinations including drug and alcohol tests.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.145.5" class="koboSpan">The degree to
which such activities are carried out by the agencies rather than the
shipping company itself varies but it should be expected that shipping
companies using open registries will exhibit a less “hands on” approach
in respect of many of them. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.145.6"
class="koboSpan">This is in line with the principle of cost-cutting
through outsourcing HR activities and it is not rare that newly
recruited, especially lower ranked, crew members never actually set foot
in the company’s office premises.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.145.7" class="koboSpan">The shrinkage
of direct selection costs, which comes with the shrinkage of the human
resource selection activities in which a shipping company gets involved
should, however, be weighed against the costs of selection failure, as
poor recruitment and selection can have obvious detrimental effects for
ship operation.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">Along the same lines
the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">training and
development</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan"> as well as performance appraisal of the human resource
management in shipping companies can be influenced by their choice of
flag. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.2" class="koboSpan">Training
refers to teaching employees how to do their present jobs, while
development focuses on building the knowledge and skills of employees
for future responsibilities and challenges.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.3" class="koboSpan">Given the
vital role of staff as a crucial and expensive resource, their
contribution to effective and efficient organisational performance and
the contemporary movement towards more flexible organisational
structures and employee empowerment, training and development clearly
constitute a critical HRM function.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.4" class="koboSpan">The main
difference that should be expected to be observed between companies
using open registries and others using national flags is the degree of
investment in training and development especially for their seafarers.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.5" class="koboSpan">Such an
investment will relate to the allocation of resources, planning, time,
money, equipment and should be considered to be less for shipping firms
registering their vessels in open registries and far more for those
using national registries. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.6"
class="koboSpan">The argument here continues from the reasoning
discussed above in connection with the earlier stages of human resource
management and concerns the extent to which HR functions are outsourced.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.7" class="koboSpan">Companies
relying extensively on crew agencies to take advantage of low-cost
distant supply areas cannot easily adopt a systematic approach to the
management of training. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.8"
class="koboSpan">Such a systematic approach entails several steps, from
an assessment of training needs to an embedding of commitment and
involvement of staff and from a clearly defined policy to a carefully
planned training, review and evaluation programme (Mullins, 1991).
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.9" class="koboSpan">A shipping
company which mans its vessels on an ad hoc, “as needed” basis from
crewing agencies around the world and with a high turnover will find it
quite difficult, for example, to engage in any objective assessment of
training needs. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.10"
class="koboSpan">This requires analysis at three distinct levels, the
organisation, the task and the person, and at high turnovers and with
minimum knowledge of the employees the chain of the assessment is broken
at the third tier of the analysis.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.11" class="koboSpan">In the same
way, the review and evaluation of training programmes can hardly be
effectively carried out when seafarers do not stay with the same company
for more than six to eight months.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.12" class="koboSpan">The choice of
flag may also affect the types of training that companies may adopt.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.148.13" class="koboSpan">To begin
with, since companies using open
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_594"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">registers may not usually invest in any long-term
employment relationship with their seafarers, they should be expected to
be less concerned with employee development, such as varied work
experiences or formal education.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.149.2" class="koboSpan">They should
also be less concerned with sea staff career development or management.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.149.3" class="koboSpan">Their training
programmes may be more oriented towards induction programmes, on-the-job
training or simply the training required by national/international
regulations, like the ISM or the ISPS Code.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.149.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,
they would not be expected to adopt apprenticeship training, as open
registries do not require any form of cadet training obligation on the
part of their vessels, unlike some of the tonnage tax regimes adopted by
traditional flags.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">The choice of flag is
also considered to have an impact on the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">performance appraisal
</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan">function of the human resource management again due to
the diverse crew employment conditions connected with different flag
types. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.2"
class="koboSpan">Performance appraisal is a review and assessment of the
behaviour and performance of staff and its systematic nature involves a
scheme of regular and continuous judgement and feedback.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.3" class="koboSpan">It is this
systematic approach to appraisal and its various implications for
several other managerial functions and decisions that give rise to
differentiations in respect of this HRM function between companies using
open and national registries. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.4"
class="koboSpan">First of all, the appraisal system should be designed
in accordance with organisational objectives and to fit its
organisational culture and policies, while supervisors should undergo
relevant training to avoid the costs of poorly administered appraisals.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.5" class="koboSpan">However, due
to the quick pace with which shipping companies using open registries
may change officers onboard their vessels, masters cannot receive
appropriate appraisal training nor can they readily align their
appraisal practice with the goals and culture of the company.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.6" class="koboSpan">Also, the
system needs to be evaluated regularly based on feedback from
supervisors, but again the frequent change of crew members onboard
foreign flagged vessels does not provide the conditions for effective
monitoring of the system and reliable, systematic feedback from the
appraisers, the masters/officers.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.7" class="koboSpan">In addition, a
successful performance appraisal scheme means that results are fed into
other HRM activities, for example, for validation of selection
techniques, for assessment of the impact of training programmes, for
forecasts of staffing needs or as a basis of a review of financial
rewards, promotions, etc. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.8"
class="koboSpan">It also means that employees are provided with
appropriate feedback to reflect on and improve their individual
performance, to identify training/development needs and plan career
progression. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.152.9"
class="koboSpan">The usually limited time of crew members onboard ships
flying flags of convenience and the ad hoc basis of their employment put
severe restrictions on the actual and successful application of
performance feedback procedures, while they also have an effect on the
frequency with which appraisals can be carried out.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">All of the above have
an impact on the organisation and structure of the office-based staff
too. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.153.2" class="koboSpan">The more
human resource activities are outsourced, the less the responsibilities
and activities of the office in respect of them and hence the smaller
the relevant department in the office and vice-versa.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.153.3" class="koboSpan">The operation
of the office of a shipping company is also affected in other ways, like
in respect of the succession planning, mentioned earlier or the
effective communication with the vessel, coordination of duties, the
provision of quality service, the attraction of business and other
indirect ways. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.153.4"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, with regard to the shore staff of
shipping companies, it must be underlined that some of the HRM functions
discussed above, such as the training and development or the performance
appraisal, are not considered to be directly influenced by the choice of
flag. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.153.5" class="koboSpan">Shipping
companies, for example, can make considerable investments in training
and development of shore staff and take advantage of the wide range of
training
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_595"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan">programmes for their office personnel without being
restricted by their choice of flag.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.154.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
given that ship owners may choose different flag regimes for different
vessels of the same fleet – research has suggested that the decision to
flag out is taken on a ship-basis and not a fleet-basis (Bergantino and
Marlow, 1998) – it is possible that many of the issues discussed above
cancel each other out when the overall management approach of a shipping
company is considered.</span>

## <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">Flag Regimes in Convergence</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">The basis for this
comparison of the management approach has been the traditionally
clear-cut distinction between open registers and national flags.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.156.2" class="koboSpan">Contemporary
developments, however, in the international ship registration regime
have brought the features of national flags and open registries much
closer. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.156.3" class="koboSpan">For
example, the overwhelming majority of the ocean-going fleet is suspected
to be under some form of tonnage tax system, while nationality
restrictions for crew complements become more and more lax for
traditional flags. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.156.4"
class="koboSpan">The ways in which flag regimes have recently come
towards some convergence as well as the potential impact of these
developments on expected management approaches by shipping companies in
the light of our discussion, will now be examined.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">A growing awareness
of the importance of the shipping industry to the international and
national economies and an increased interest in supporting it have
resulted in measures being taken by governments to foster the
competitiveness of their national shipping industries.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Within this
context and in order to encourage ships not to flag out, the European
Union has attempted to secure a level playing field for the shipping
industry by introducing a relevant regulatory framework.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.157.3" class="koboSpan">The 2004 State
Aid Guidelines are in force currently and for a time period of seven
years, that is until 2011 (Commission of the European Communities,
2004). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.157.4" class="koboSpan">The
2004 Guidelines regard shipping tonnage tax as a State Aid, a fiscal
incentive which can be endorsed to safeguard quality employment and
facilitate the development of community shipping in the global market;
they make provisions for reduced rates of contributions for social
security and reduced rates of income tax for Community seafarers on
board ships registered in a Member State; they propose,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia,</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">
other state aid initiatives, which include the reimbursement of
repatriation costs of Community seafarers, tax free reserves for capital
gains, specific investment aids, some forms of training initiatives, and
financial aid to cover up to 30% of operating costs for a new service
that will enable road transport cargoes to be diverted to sea.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">Indeed most of the
traditional shipping nations in the EU have taken advantage of the aid
measures allowed since the 1997 guidelines by introducing, for example,
tonnage tax systems and/or schemes to reduce crew costs.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.160.2" class="koboSpan">Tonnage tax
entered into force in the Netherlands and Norway in 1996, Germany in
1999, the UK in 2000, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Belgium and
France in 2002, and Italy in 2005.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.160.3" class="koboSpan">The current
system of tonnage tax in Greece has existed since 1975.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.160.4" class="koboSpan">At an
international level, too, the trend to come up with ways to support the
industry through fiscal and financial incentives is also evident.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.160.5" class="koboSpan">For instance,
Singapore operates the Approved Shipping Logistics Enterprise Scheme
which offers a 10% concessionary tax rate for a five-year period
(recently changed to ten years, 15/02/07); while the Hong Kong Shipping
Register introduced a range of schemes to attract quality tonnage, among
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_596"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan">them a six month annual tonnage charge reduction scheme
every two years provided their ships have not been detained (Grinter,
2007).</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">A re-examination of
the definitions of open register existent in the literature (section 2),
suggests that the older the definition provided, the more outdated it
appears, given the current status of affairs generally in the political
and economic environment and in the international shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.162.2" class="koboSpan">Traditional
flags have admittedly been adjusting their registration procedures to
make them more attractive, more “convenient” and “opportune” for ship
owners:</span>

- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">foreign-owned or
  foreign controlled vessels can be allowed to register in traditional
  flags, e.g the Norwegian Ordinary Ship Register (NOR) accepts EU
  citizens or companies as equivalent to Norwegian citizens or companies
