  to be registered as owners of vessels flying its flag;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">access to and
  transfer from national flags is made easy while the cost of
  registration fees has been brought down, e.g.
  </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.164.2" class="koboSpan">in the UK
  flag registration costs are amongst the lowest available in national
  flags while there are no annual renewal fees;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">taxes on the income
  of ships are not levied, a tonnage tax system is used instead, e.g.
  </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">Greece has
  the longest history in applying a tonnage tax regime that goes back to
  1939 (Moraitis, 2003), while the current taxation system applying to
  the shipping sector was introduced by Law 27 in 1975;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">fiscal obligations
  can be circumvented usually through the avoidance of corporate tax,
  e.g. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.166.2" class="koboSpan">as is
  the case with the UK and Dutch flag;</span>
- <span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">the manning of
  ships by non nationals is permitted to a smaller or a larger extent,
  e.g. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.167.2"
  class="koboSpan">recently a softening of Greek flag manning
  requirements with regard to the complement of Greek nationals has
  meant that, with the exception of masters, who must remain Greek,
  shipowners are free to choose whether the Greek contingent (minimum
  4-6) consists of officers, lower ranks or a combination of the
  two.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">In the light of these
changes to traditional registers, how can our discussion in the previous
sections be affected? </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.168.2"
class="koboSpan">If the basis of the theoretical rationale we have
developed, (i.e. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.168.3"
class="koboSpan">the clear-cut distinction between open registers and
traditional flags), is no longer so clear-cut, does this affect, and if
so to what extent, the assumptions made about the impact of choice of
flag on ship management?</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">The fundamental
distinction between national flags and the flags of convenience has been
the absence of a “genuine link” on the part of the latter.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.169.2" class="koboSpan">This can take
the form of a number of attributes and, if the UN relevant instrument on
Conditions for Registration of Ships is followed, such attributes can
relate mainly to the ownership, the manning and the management criteria
as well as the contribution to the national economy and its inclusion in
the national balance of payments accounts.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.169.3" class="koboSpan">With regard
then to the actual convergence between flag regimes, the real question
is not how close traditional flags have become to the attractive
features of open registers but whether, to what extent, and along which
dimensions such changes have altered the basic characteristic of
national flags, i.e. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.169.4"
class="koboSpan">the genuine link, and so the essence of the nature of
national flags.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">A detailed reasoning
of the potential impact of such developments on ship management choices,
in the lines of the discussion in the previous sections, will not of
course be attempted at this point, as this would be a valuable exercise
in its own right. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.170.2"
class="koboSpan">Rather
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_597"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">some basic, underlying principles will be addressed and
reviewed in relation to the issue of the recent convergence of
traditional and open registers.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">The adoption of
measures on the part of national flags which relate to the reduction of
bureaucracy in registration procedures or the decrease in
registration/annual fees is straightforwardly an aspect which should not
have an effect on the management behaviour of shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.172.2" class="koboSpan">The much
discussed and widely applied tonnage tax scheme, although indeed an
important aspect of convergence between the two main flag regimes and
with direct consequences to national economies, should not be expected
to affect management practice to any significant extent, as argued
earlier in this chapter.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">Of much greater
significance for both the determination of the existence/absence of the
genuine link with ships, as well as the management practice is the
degree to which national flags nowadays allow for the registration of
ships owned by non-nationals. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.2"
class="koboSpan">On the one hand the need to enhance competitiveness
and, on the other, the political reality of regional unions of sovereign
states, like the EU, has meant that traditional flags previously not
open to other nationalities, would have to accept foreign shipowners in
their register. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.3"
class="koboSpan">This development should be expected to affect at a
first level the cultural identity of the flag itself and then, as a
result of that, to potentially have some impact on a number of elements
of ship management for individual shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.4" class="koboSpan">Historically,
traditional flags have been associated with the maritime nation of their
countries, its reputation with regard to ship operation, the way it is
thought to conduct business, its know-how and expertise.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.5" class="koboSpan">They have
built up a certain image – positive, negative, peculiar, indifferent –
based on this. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.6"
class="koboSpan">With the participation of foreigners in their registers
such identity and consequently image will slowly be infused with
elements from the shipping experience and standing of other nations.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.7" class="koboSpan">Initially
ships, controlled by foreign interests, entering a newly
opened-to-foreigners traditional flag, should be expected to be drawn to
it because they also share some common principles in respect of the
business of ship operation. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.8"
class="koboSpan">Inevitably, there will be a two-way influence between
the two entities affecting the status of the flag itself.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.9" class="koboSpan">The degree to
which the traditional flag will sustain its attitude towards the
shipping business will largely depend on its desire to treat
registration as a procedure necessary to impose sovereignty and hence
control over its shipping. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.10"
class="koboSpan">In this way, recognising that national flags have the
expertise, the infrastructure, the procedures and tools and assuming
still also the will, to impose sovereignty then the relaxation of
ownership requirements, although bringing them closer to the known
attributes of flags of convenience, should not be expected to alter
significantly the management choices of the companies who prefer them.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.11" class="koboSpan">However, if a
national flag’s previous reputation for quality and high safety
standards is lost, then this may affect some of the strategic decisions
– as discussed in section 4 – of companies registered in it.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.173.12" class="koboSpan">In respect of
the legal framework of company’s laws and other laws inherently relevant
to every nation, a specific trend between registries may be difficult to
observe and such items should be rather flag-specific than flag
regime-specific.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">The genuine link
between registers and their vessels can also be demonstrated by the
management criterion, the fact, that is, that nationals must have some
presence in the actual management of the vessels.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.174.2" class="koboSpan">Many
traditional flags appear still to adhere to this requirement, despite
their opening up to other nationalities or the adoption of favourable
tax and registration systems. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.174.3"
class="koboSpan">This issue is of course related to the actual control
of and accountability and liability for ship operation but it is also
very much connected with the protection of the national maritime cluster
and national economy. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.174.4"
class="koboSpan">In recent years the realisation has been that actually
70% of the value added by the
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_598"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">shipping industry comes from on-shore activities
related to shipping (Peeters
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan">., 1994). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.177.2"
class="koboSpan">It seems, therefore, that maritime nations wishing to
keep the primary source of the industry’s contribution to their economy
and balance of payments – the valued added, the employment generation,
the investment generation, the preservation and enhancement of expertise
– are willing to “sacrifice” potential corporate tax income to protect
the management dimension of their shipping business.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.177.3" class="koboSpan">Examples of
traditional flags which have resorted to the adoption of tonnage tax but
have sheltered their shore-based shipping activity by including the
management requirement in their registration include the UK and Dutch
flag. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.177.4" class="koboSpan">Others,
like Greece, have for many years provided a favourable tax regime for
ship management companies established in the country in order to attract
more onshore business activity in
it.</span><sup><a href="#Ch020.xhtml_fn0637" id="Ch020.xhtml_bck_fn0637"><span
id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan"> Since the location of ship management has important
consequences for management practice, as also discussed in section 3,
the decision of traditional flags to retain management functions
nationally essentially distances the former from what open registers
stand for.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">National flags
generally go down the path of using open registers as a benchmark in
order to increase the competitiveness of their own national shipping
industry and extended maritime cluster rather than because they wish to
provide a service which can be sold to foreign ship owners wishing to
escape the fiscal or other consequences of registration under their own
flags. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.180.2" class="koboSpan">It is
in this distinctive philosophy that a main difference between
traditional and open flags is still to be observed.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.180.3" class="koboSpan">Shipping is
generally thought to be considered by traditional flags as an important
industry for their nation, one in which governments should invest and to
which private investment should be attracted.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.180.4" class="koboSpan">This creates
the environment and further encourages the development of shipping
related organisations, trade and shipowning associations, seafarers’ and
workers’ unions and other bodies, all of which should be seen to ensure
the sustainability of national shipping through promoting quality,
safety, training, expertise, fair working conditions and an appealing
commercial environment for conducting the business.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">The relaxation of
national manning requirements should also be viewed within these
parameters, although this development should be expected to have
significant repercussions for the adoption of ship management practices
by shipping firms. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.181.2"
class="koboSpan">It is in this regard that it can be said not only that
the two registry regimes are coming very close in disposition, but also
that this alters to a significant extent the assumptions made with
regard to the impact of the flag choice on human resource management
(section 5). </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.181.3"
class="koboSpan">The rationale about the human resource management
choices of shipping companies was built basically around the principle
that its international dimensions (outsourcing, the ‘as needed’ strategy
and high turnovers) were issues primarily connected with the use of
flags of convenience. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.181.4"
class="koboSpan">Given the new development of traditional flags now
adopting a more laissez-faire approach to the nationality of seafarers
onboard their ships, such issues and their consequences could no longer
be regarded as more relevant for companies choosing open registers.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.181.5" class="koboSpan">The difference
between shipping companies with regard to their people and their human
resource management should then be expected to stem more from the degree
of investment made by them in this key management dimension rather than
be implied by their flag choice.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.181.6" class="koboSpan">The
requirement for the training of nationals which is built into some
traditional flags is expected to bring some differences in management
practices, for instance, in relation to recruitment process.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.181.7" class="koboSpan">Overall, the
preoccupation with cost cutting in order to enhance the competitiveness
of flags is most vividly exhibited in the softening of national manning
requirements, and changes should be expected in the way the business
will be conducted.</span>

## <span id="Ch020.xhtml_page_599"></span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.182.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter has been
concerned with the impact of the choice of flag on ship management.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.183.2" class="koboSpan">The basis of
the analysis was the conventional distinction between open registers and
traditional, national flags. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.183.3"
class="koboSpan">The subject is treated in a theoretical context and the
examination reveals a number of management dimensions in a shipping
company which can be thought to be influenced by the choice of flag.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.183.4" class="koboSpan">General
management aspects such as the decision on the actual location of the
ship management company can be affected, but most importantly it is the
strategic management decisions and the human resource management process
that are considered to be particularly influenced by the company’s flag
choice. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.183.5" class="koboSpan">With
regard to strategic management, both corporate strategies and
business-level strategies of a shipping firm can be affected as, for
example, the use of open registers corresponds to a cost leadership
competitive strategy, while the use of national registers corresponds to
the differentiation strategy. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.183.6"
class="koboSpan">Human resource planning, the recruitment and selection
process, as well as the training and development and performance
appraisal programmes are regarded as management functions on which the
choice of flag can have a bearing.</span>

<span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">As stated earlier,
the basis for comparison of the management approach has been the
traditionally clear-cut distinction between open registers and national
flags. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.184.2"
class="koboSpan">Contemporary developments, however, in the
international ship registration regime have brought the features of
national flags and open registries much closer.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.184.3" class="koboSpan">The
overwhelming majority of the ocean-going fleet is suspected to be under
some form of tonnage tax system, while nationality restrictions for crew
complements become more and more lax for traditional flags, as in the
case of the Greek flag. </span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.184.4"
class="koboSpan">In the light of such developments a re-evaluation of
the different management approaches expected by shipping companies using
diverse ship registration regimes would be another valuable exercise.
</span><span id="Ch020.xhtml_kobo.184.5" class="koboSpan">This chapter
did not attempt to tackle all the issues in an holistic manner and other
considerations, such as cultural diversity and associated crew
management practices, could usefully be included in future.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_602"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_603"></span>[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 21</span>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Fleet Operations Optimisation and Fleet Deployment — An Update</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0457)
===================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Anastassios</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">N.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Perakis</span></span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0638" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0638"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">Optimising the
operation (i.e. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.8.2"
class="koboSpan">minimising operating costs, if revenues are fixed) of a
single merchant ship is not difficult to do and can be achieved by a few
simple calculations, which can point out the minimum of the operating
cost curve as a function of the speed, for example.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.8.3" class="koboSpan">Texts such as
Stopford</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0639" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0639"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan"> can provide useful info on the above.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">Optimising an
entire fleet of generally different ships, however, is definitely not as
simple, and requires certain levels of computer, probability,
optimisation and other mathematical skills, as we will see in the
following.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">Deployment of merchant
shipping fleets covers a wide range of problems, concerned with fleet
operations, scheduling, routing, and fleet design.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">Many use some
kind of economic criterion such as profitability, income or costs on
which to base decisions. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.11.3"
class="koboSpan">(Benford,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0640" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0640"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">
Marbury,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0641" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0641"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan"> Fischer and
Rosenwein,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0642" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0642"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Perakis
</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0643" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0643"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">Others use non-economic criteria such as utilisation or
service; these are more common in fleet deployment models used in the
liner
trades.</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0644" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0644"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan"> Reviews of various fleet deployment models and
problems are given
in.Ronen,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0645" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0645"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">
Ronen,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0646" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0646"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Perakis.</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0647" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0647"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">An aspect of fleet
deployment not covered extensively in the literature until the early
1980s was “slow-steaming” analysis and optimisation.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">“Slow steaming”
is the practice of operating a ship or fleet of ships at a speed less
than design or maximum (sustained) operating speed, in order to take
advantage of improved fuel economy and reduced operating costs, but,
most importantly, to reduce fleet overcapacity (if done by a large
number of ship owner).</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">Managers of merchant
ship fleets, especially bulk carriers and tankers, frequently find
themselves with excess transport capacity, and hence must decide which
ships to use (and at what speeds) and which to keep idle (or perhaps
make available to another fleet by sale or charter).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">Moreover, if
fuel prices become relatively high, excess transport capacity offers the
potentially profitable strategy of slow steaming some or all of their
ships. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">Such a
strategy not only substantially reduces the operating costs of the
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_604"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan">fleet, but furthermore reduces the supply of
tonne-miles of the existing total bulker fleet, thereby improving the
depressed freight rates. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.29.2"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, a sharp drop in fuel prices could
make it advisable to “fast-steam” ships built during the expensive fuel
era, although this would be limited by their design speed and associated
operating margin.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">The remainder of this
chapter is organised as follows: Section 1 discusses the correct
solution of a simple fleet deployment problem, which has been earlier
suboptimally solved in the literature.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">It is shown
that its correct solution can save over 15% of the annual fleet
operating costs, or \$7.93 million per year, for the same 10-ship fleet
of the previously published example.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.30.3" class="koboSpan">In Section 2,
more realistic, single-origin, single-destination, and even
multi-origin, multi-destination fleet deployment problems for (liquid or
dry) bulk shipping are formulated and solved, using both nonlinear and a
series of linear programmes. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.30.4"
class="koboSpan">In Section 3, fleet deployment problems for Liner
Shipping Fleets are solved, and specific examples are given from the
fleet of a major liner company. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.30.5"
class="koboSpan">Section 4 provides a summary and conclusions, as well
as recent developments in this area.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.30.6" class="koboSpan">An alphabetical
list of references is given at the end of this chapter.</span>

## <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.31.2" class="koboSpan">A Simple fleet Deployment Problem</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">The ships of a fleet
could be assumed to belong to N different groups, each consisting of
n(i) sister ships, i = 1, …, N, of equal cargo carrying capacity, speed
and fuel consumption (or in general, operating costs).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">Design speed,
cargo capacity and operating costs will in general be different among
different ship groups. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.32.3"
class="koboSpan">This is both an efficient and general model, since the
case of no two ships in a fleet being identical is obviously covered by
setting n(i) = 1, i = 1, …, N. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.32.4"
class="koboSpan">The mission of a fleet is assumed, for our purposes, to
be the movement of one commodity between two given ports.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">A simple (but
realistic) bulker fleet deployment problem was defined in Benford (see
endnote 2).Some of the assumptions inherent in the solution approach,
such as no-cost lay-up of unneeded vessels, a contract to move a given
quantity of a given commodity between one origin and one destination
port, availability of more than enough ships (tonnage) suited to the
trade, etc., were not unrealistic.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
method proposed for its solution did not give the optimal answer,
primarily because of an artificial constraint that all vessels must be
operated at a speed resulting in the same unit cost of operation per ton
of cargo delivered, imposed for ease of solution, but not a natural
constraint of the problem.
</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fig0293" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0293"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan"> below presents the approach adopted in Benford (see
endnote 2) and its results.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">In Perokis (see
endnote 5), the problem was correctly solved analytically, without the
above equal unit cost constraint, using Lagrange multipliers.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.36.2" class="koboSpan">The results
(see
</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fig0294" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0294"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan">) showed an improvement of at least 15% over those of
</span>[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch021.xhtml_fig0293)<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan">, thus verifying once more that ‘constraints impair
performance.’ </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.40.2"
class="koboSpan">More realistic and complicated versions of the problem
solved in that paper were subsequently formulated and solved.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">Comparing
</span>[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Tables
1</span>](#Ch021.xhtml_fig0293)<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span>[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span>](#Ch021.xhtml_fig0294)<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">, we see an annual cost reduction of \$7.93 million, or
over 15%. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">This
represents a considerable improvement.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.45.3" class="koboSpan">The difference
in costs could be even greater if lay-up charges are levied against
ships I and J in the solution presented in
</span>[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch021.xhtml_fig0293)<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.47.2"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, this difference could possibly be
reduced if ships I and J could be chartered or sold to a third party at
a particular price.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">Perhaps it is now
appropriate to clarify that in the above problem, the annual demanded
transport capacity is assumed to be a given output (constant).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.48.2" class="koboSpan">This is the
case for vessels operating under relatively long-term charters, which
normally specify, among other</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0293" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_605"></span>[](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0293)

[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00311.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0293)

</div>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0294" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00312.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0294)

</div>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">things, the freight
rate and the amount of cargo to be carried annually.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">In a normal
market environment, long-term charters are the overwhelming majority of
fixtures, whereas vessels operating in the spot market constitute less
than 10% of the available capacity.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">The conclusion from
the above is that, in contrast to past practices where significant
effort has been directed toward the optimisation of the design and
operation of individual ships, an owner of a fleet of ships (usually
non-uniform in terms of age, size and operating speed) should operate
each ship in a manner generally quite different from that dictated by
single-ship optimisation. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.52.2"
class="koboSpan">Adoption of the results of this and subsequent research
should result in significant cost savings in the operations of several
shipping companies.</span>

## <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">More Realistic Bulk Shipping Fleet Deployment Models</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Perakis and
Papadakis,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0648" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0648"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0649" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0649"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Papadakis and
Perakis,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0650" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0650"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan"> presented far more realistic and complicated fleet
deployment problems and their “optimal” solutions.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">The problem of
single-origin, single-destination fleet deployment was first studied.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.60.3" class="koboSpan">A computer
programme was developed to solve the problem and to help the fleet
operator to make slow steaming policy decisions.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.60.4" class="koboSpan">A detailed
discussion of the problem solution and a sensitivity analysis are
presented in Perakis and Papadakis (see endnote 10).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.60.5" class="koboSpan">Sensitivity
analysis provides the user with an understanding of the influence on the
total fleet operating cost of its various components.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.60.6" class="koboSpan">For small to
moderate changes of one or more cost components, the user can get an
extremely accurate estimate of his new total
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_606"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">operating cost without having to re-run the computer
programme. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">Some
interesting conclusions were made on the basis of the sensitivity
results.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">The fleet deployment
problem with time-varying cost components was also formulated and
solved. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.62.2" class="koboSpan">A
computer programme was developed to implement the solution of this
problem (Perakis, Papadakis and
Pogoulates).</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0651" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0651"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan"> The relevant algorithms are briefly described there as
well. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.64.2" class="koboSpan">The
problem of fleet deployment when the cost coefficients are random
variables with known probability density functions was formulated in
detail (see endnote 11), where analytical expressions for the basic
probabilistic quantities were presented.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.64.3" class="koboSpan">A shorter
description of the above is included in this presentation.</span>

### <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Objective function and constraints</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">A fleet, consisting of
a given number of ships, is available to move a fixed amount of cargo
between two ports, over a given period of time, for a fixed price.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">Each vessel in
the fleet is assumed to have known operating cost characteristics.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">The problem
objective is to determine each vessel’s full load and ballast speeds
such that the total fleet operating cost is minimised
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">and</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan"> all contracted cargo is transported.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">A first constraint
imposes upper and lower bounds on the vessel full load and ballast
speeds. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">These
speed constraints are necessary to ensure a feasible solution to the
problem; which is, that each speed is less than or equal to its maximum
and greater than or equal to its minimum operating limits.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.69.3" class="koboSpan">In practice,
the minimum speed is non-zero and is determined by the lower end of the
normal operating region of the vessel’s main engine.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.69.4" class="koboSpan">The minimum
speed should also be adequate for purposes of ship safety in
maneuverability and control. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.69.5"
class="koboSpan">The equality constraint must be satisfied to insure all
contracted cargo is transported.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">This formulation is
based on the following assumptions, some of which use state-of-the-art
empirical formulae taken from published articles, cited in the list of
refs of the detailed papers and reports of ours (see endnote
10)</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0652" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0652"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">A vessel carries a
    full load of cargo from load port to unload port.</span>

2.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">When the vessel is
    operating in restricted waters, it has a known and constant
    restricted speed which is usually the maximum allowable speed in the
    region in question, hence requiring a known, fixed power and fuel
    rate.</span>

3.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">The number of days
    a vessel spends in port per round trip is known and constant.</span>

4.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">The charges
    incurred at the load port and unload port per round trip are known
    and constant.</span>

5.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">The amount of fuel
    burned per day in the load port and unload port is known and
    constant.</span>

6.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">The annual costs
    of manning, stores, supplies, equipment, capital, administration,
    maintenance and repair, and make ready for sail are known and
    constant.</span>

7.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">The power of
    vessel i (in HP) may be expressed by:</span>

    <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
    class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00313.jpg"
    data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
    class="koboSpan"> for the full load and by:</span>

    <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
    class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00314.jpg"
    data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

    <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">for the ballast
    condition, where X</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
    class="koboSpan"> and Y</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
    class="koboSpan"> are the full load and ballast speeds of ship i
    respectively and the rest are appropriate constants.</span>

8.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">The all-purpose
    fuel rate for a fully loaded vessel i may be expressed by:</span>

    <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
    class="koboSpan">(R</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
    class="koboSpan">f</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
    class="koboSpan">)</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
    class="koboSpan"> = g</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
    class="koboSpan">·p</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
    class="koboSpan">2</span></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
    class="koboSpan"> + s</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
    class="koboSpan">·p</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
    class="koboSpan"> + d</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
    class="koboSpan"> for the full load and by</span>

    <span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_607"></span>

    <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
    class="koboSpan">(R</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
    class="koboSpan">f</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
    class="koboSpan">)</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
    class="koboSpan">bi</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
    class="koboSpan"> = g</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
    class="koboSpan">bi</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
    class="koboSpan"> · p</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
    class="koboSpan">bi</span></sub><sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
    class="koboSpan">2</span></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
    class="koboSpan"> + s</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
    class="koboSpan">bi</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
    class="koboSpan"> · p</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
    class="koboSpan">bi</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
    class="koboSpan"> + d</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
    class="koboSpan">bi</span></sub>

    <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">for the ballast
    condition where p</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
    class="koboSpan"> and p</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
    class="koboSpan">bi</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
    class="koboSpan"> are the normalised (percent)
    p</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
    class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
    class="koboSpan"> and p</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
    class="koboSpan">bi</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
    class="koboSpan"> respectively, and the rest are appropriate
    constants.</span>

9.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">The
    </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
    class="koboSpan">total</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
    class="koboSpan"> annual cost of laying up vessel i is known for all
    i = 1, …, z.</span>

10. <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">The number of
    days per year vessel i is out of service for maintenance and repair
    is known and constant.</span>

11. <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">This problem
    formulation and solution is for a single stage, “one-shot”
    decision.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">In the literature,
the number of tonnes carried per year is assumed to be a linear function
of a ship’s full load and ballast speeds.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.134.2" class="koboSpan">In our
research, we have shown that this assumption can be quite unrealistic.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.134.3" class="koboSpan">This function
is quite nonlinear in nature. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.134.4"
class="koboSpan">A derivation of this function may be found in Perakis
and Papadakis (see endnote 10).</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">Operating costs,
developed in detail in Perakis and Papadakis (see endnote
14)</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0653" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0653"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">, are considered to fit into one of two categories,
those that do not vary with ship speed, or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan">daily running
costs</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">,
and those that vary with ship speed, or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan">voyage
costs</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">Typical plots
for the total
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan">not</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan"> per tonne) operating costs per year for a particular
ship, for various ballast speeds, are given in Perakis and Papadakis
(see endnote 10).</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">A typical plot of
F(X</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">, Y</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan">) is also shown in Perakis and Papadakis (see endnote
10), as a function of the full load and ballast speeds.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.148.2" class="koboSpan">It is seen
that F is a smooth convex curve or surface with a single minimum.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.148.3" class="koboSpan">There is also
a finite speed range in which F is not very different from its minimum
value, a property which allows approximate solutions to the problem
using very different speeds for individual ships to produce total fleet
costs very close to one another and to the optimum cost itself.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.148.4" class="koboSpan">For
X</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan"> and/or Y</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan"> going towards either 0 or 8, F approaches infinity.
</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_cap_lbl0163"
id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0163"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 1</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_cap_lbl0164"
id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0164"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan"> are for the same ship and for constant route
data.</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0295" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00315.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Typical plot of cargo carried per year as a function of ship speeds" /></span>

<a href="#Ch021.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0163"
id="Ch021.xhtml_cap_lbl0163"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan"> Typical plot of cargo carried per year as a function
of ship speeds</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0296" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00316.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Typical plot for the total operating cost per year as a function of ship full load and ballast speeds" /></span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_608"></span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0164"
id="Ch021.xhtml_cap_lbl0164"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan"> Typical plot for the total operating cost per year as
a function of ship full load and ballast speeds</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">Introducing the
linear inequality constraints on the speeds complicates the problem
solution considerably. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.163.2"
class="koboSpan">In the first part of this research, an External Penalty
Technique (EPT) has been combined with the Nelder and Mead Simplex
Search Technique to solve our optimisation problem.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.163.3" class="koboSpan">The purpose of
a penalty function method is to transform a constrained problem into an
unconstrained problem which can be solved using the coupled
unconstrained technique.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">A computer programme
has been written to solve this problem using the techniques and the
formulation mentioned above. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.164.2"
class="koboSpan">The solution returned consists of the ship speeds, for
those vessels specified for analysis, that will minimise the total
mission operating costs and fulfil the cargo transport
obligation.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">For the lay-up
option, it is shown in the technical report that for even moderate
numbers of ships in a fleet, it is rather too time-consuming to use an
exhaustive enumeration scheme. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.165.2"
class="koboSpan">Instead, a dynamic programming-like sequential
optimisation approach is developed, significantly reducing the
computational burden. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.165.3"
class="koboSpan">If Z is the number of ships in the fleet, the maximum
number of fleets we will have to examine using this approach is
M</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">max</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan"> = Z(Z + 1)/2 – 1.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan">actual</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan"> number of fleets which we will have to consider will
be significantly smaller than
M</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">max</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">, due to the elimination of several fleets as
infeasible and much smaller than the upper limit of total possible
cases. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.171.2" class="koboSpan">The
above scheme has been implemented and referred to in the following as
the operating cost without re-running the programme.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.171.3" class="koboSpan">This property
holds for a given fleet and not in cases when
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_609"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">one or more ships are laid-up or chartered to a third
party (on top of the changes in the cost components).</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">The fleet deployment
problem with time-varying cost components was also studied.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.173.2" class="koboSpan">A time horizon
in this formulation is any interval within which cost components are
constant but at least one of them is different than its value in another
interval. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.173.3" class="koboSpan">In
other words, our cost components are given ‘staircase’ functions of
time. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.173.4" class="koboSpan">In the
case of rapidly changing costs, resulting in rather short intervals
where these costs are constant, the problem of non-integer number of
round trips per interval could be crucial.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.173.5" class="koboSpan">A heuristic
approach was developed to find the nearest integer solution
corresponding to the non-‘integer’ solution generally provided by the
SIMPLEX algorithm.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">Further details may
be found in Perakis and Papadakis (see endnotes 10, 11, 15), and the
associated user’s documentation, Perakis, Papadakis and Pogoulatos (see
endnote 13), where a more extensive multi-page flow-chart is
presented.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">The fleet deployment
problem for the case when some of the cost components are random
variables with known probability density functions was finally
considered (Perakis and Papadakis (see endnote 11)).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.175.2" class="koboSpan">We note that
the minimum of the possible mean values of the total annual operating
costs, C</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan">min</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the variance of
C</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan">min</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan"> can be found relatively “easily”.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.179.2" class="koboSpan">However, this
approach has not yet been implemented on a computer and probably will
not prove very useful: The inputs to the problem (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.179.3" class="koboSpan">the
user-supplied probability density functions) can have any particular
theoretical or experimental form, thus discouraging the development of
any general computer code for this problem.</span>

### <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 The multi-origin, multi-destination fleet deployment problem</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">The problem of
minimum-cost operation of a fleet of ships which has to carry a specific
amount of cargo from several origin ports to several destination ports
during a specified time interval was next examined.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">During the
season any vessel can be loaded in any source port (S) and unloaded at
any destination port (D) provided that these ports belong to a subset I
or J (respectively) of the total set of ports, such that draft and other
constraints for the corresponding vessel are satisfied.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.181.3" class="koboSpan">Under this
assumption for each vessel the number of possible routes (number of
possible sequences of S–D ports) is quite large.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.181.4" class="koboSpan">The full load
and ballast characteristics of each ship on each route are assumed to be
known.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">This nonlinear
optimisation problem consists of a nonlinear objective function and a
set of five linear and two integer constraints.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.182.2" class="koboSpan">The objective
function to be minimised is the total fleet operating cost during the
time interval (shipping season) in question.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.182.3" class="koboSpan">The following
constraints have to be satisfied:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">for each vessel,
    the total time spent in loading, travelling from origins to
    destinations, unloading and travelling from destinations to origins
    plus the lay-up time has to be equal to the total amount of time
    available for each ship in the shipping season,</span>
2.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">the total amount
    shipped to a particular destination j must be equal to the amount of
    cargo to be delivered to j during the shipping season (in
    tonnes),</span>
3.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">the total amount
    of cargo loaded from a particular source i must be less or equal to
    the cargo available at i,</span>
4.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">for each ship,
    the number of trips to destination j must be equal to the number of
    trips out of j,</span>
5.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_610"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
    class="koboSpan">same as (d) for all source ports;</span>
6.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">the full-load and
    ballast operating speeds have to be between given upper and lower
    limits,</span>
7.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">the numbers of
    full load and ballast trips for each vessel, origin and destination
    combination must all be non-negative integers.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">The constraints
presented above are linear except constraints (a) and (g).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.190.2" class="koboSpan">The maximum
number of unknown variables (if all source and destinations ports are
accessible by any ship of the given fleet) is (4·I·J+1)·Z.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.190.3" class="koboSpan">The number of
the associated constraints is 2Z+(1+J) (Z+1)+4·I·J·Z.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.190.4" class="koboSpan">For a case
with I=4, J=6 and Z=10 we have 970 variables and 1,090 constraints.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.190.5" class="koboSpan">Using today’s
personal computers, it is clear that we cannot use any classical
nonlinear optimisation technique, since the expected computation time
would be too long.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">In the case of the
multi-origin, multi-destination fleet deployment problem, it was seen
that the linear programming approaches to the literature do not take
into account significant nonlinearities of the relevant cost functions
and may lead to very suboptimal decisions.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.191.2" class="koboSpan">The iterative
procedure we developed uses a linear programming software in an
algorithmic scheme that takes into account these nonlinearities and
produces accurate results. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.191.3"
class="koboSpan">This approach is ideally suited for a personal computer
due to the reasonable running times of the LP software for almost any
practical situation. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.191.4"
class="koboSpan">A second, nonlinear approach to solve the multi-origin,
multi-destination problem was also implemented, using the available
MINOS nonlinear optimisation package.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">In \[endnote 12\],
the fleet deployment problem for a fleet of vessels operating between a
set of </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan">several loading and unloading
ports</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">
under certain time and cargo constraints was examined.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.194.2" class="koboSpan">Full load and
ballast voyage costs were treated as nonlinear functions of the ship
full load and ballast speeds, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">An
optimisation model, appropriate for bulk carrier fleets, minimising the
total operating cost, was formulated.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.194.4" class="koboSpan">The existence
of a coupling between the optimal speed selection and the optimal vessel
allocation on the available routes was demonstrated, and conditions
leading to the decoupling of these problems were established.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.194.5" class="koboSpan">Considerations
referring to the structure of the optimal solution resulted in a
substantial reduction of the dimensionality of the problem.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.194.6" class="koboSpan">We found that
in cases of low-to-moderate fleet utilisation, linear programming may be
applied to derive the optimal solution, while in cases of higher fleet
utilisation, use of nonlinear optimization may become necessary.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.194.7" class="koboSpan">The potential
benefits of our approach were demonstrated by several examples.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, we would
like to note that the algorithms and the computer codes, developed for
both the one-origin one-destination and for the multi-origin,
multi-destination fleet deployment problem can be easily used to find
not only the optimal fleet deployment policy within the given time
horizon, but also to help the fleet operator to make decisions in case
unexpected events like strikes or accidents occur.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.195.2" class="koboSpan">In such a case
the programs can be re-run for the remaining time interval and an
optimal decision can still be obtained.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.195.3" class="koboSpan">Other plans,
such as renewing or improving a part of the fleet and selling or
chartering decisions may also be evaluated.</span>

## <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.196.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.196.2" class="koboSpan">Fleet Deployment Models for Liner Shipping</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">In Perakis and
Jaramillo,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0654" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0654"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan"> we have reviewed the relevant work on liner shipping
deployment and described current industry practices.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.199.2" class="koboSpan">Our objectives
and assumptions were then presented.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.199.3" class="koboSpan">A model for
the optimisation of the deployment of a liner fleet composed of both
owned and chartered vessels was formulated.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.199.4" class="koboSpan">The
determination
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_611"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan">of the operating costs of the ships in every one of the
routes in which the company operates was carried out by a means of a
realistic model, providing the coefficients representing voyage cost and
time required for the input of the linear program presented in Jaramillo
and
Perakis.</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0655" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0655"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan"> A method for determining the best speeds and service
frequencies was also presented; the fixing of those two groups of
variables was required to linearize the deployment problem as formulated
there. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.202.2" class="koboSpan">The
overall optimisation method was described in detail, and a real-life
case study was presented, based on the co-author’s company (FMG, Flota
Mercante Grancolombiana) operations, (Jaramillo and Perakis (see endnote
17)).</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">In Powell and
Perakis,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0656" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0656"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> we extended and improved on the above.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.205.2" class="koboSpan">An Integer
Programming (IP) model was developed to minimise the operating and
lay-up costs for a fleet of liner ships operating on various routes.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.205.3" class="koboSpan">The IP model
determines the optimal deployment of the existing fleet, given route,
service, charter, and compatibility constraints.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.205.4" class="koboSpan">Two case
studies were carried out, with the same as above extensive actual data
provided by FMG. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.205.5"
class="koboSpan">The optimal deployment was determined for their
existing ship and service frequency requirements.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">The inputs to the
optimisation model (presented in Powell and Perakis (see endnote 18) are
based on the existing cost estimation model provided in Perakis and
Jaramillo (see endnote 16), including ship daily running costs, voyage
costs, costs at sea, costs at port, daily lay-up costs.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">The optimisation
model in Perakis and Jaramillo (see endnote 16) is given as:</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0297" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00317.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan">C</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan"> = operating cost per voyage for a type k ship on route
r</span>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">X</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan"> = number of voyages per year of a type k ship on route
r</span>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan">e</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan"> = lay-up cost for a type k ship</span>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan">Y</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan"> = number of lay-up days per year for a type k
ship</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">In Perakis and
Jaramillo (see endnote 16) and Jaramillo and Perakis (see endnote 17), a
Linear Programming (LP) approach was used to solve this optimisation
problem. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.222.2" class="koboSpan">Using
an LP formulation required the rounding of the number of ships allocated
to each route. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.222.3"
class="koboSpan">The rounding led to some variations in targeted service
frequencies and to sub-optimal results.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.222.4" class="koboSpan">An Integer
Programming formulation is used in Powell and Perakis (see endnote 18),
to eliminate any rounding errors in the previous LP solution.</span>

### <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Integer programming problem formulation</span>

#### <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.1 Decision variables</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan">N</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan"> = the number of a type k ship operating on route
r</span>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan">Y</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan"> = the number of lay-up days per year of a type k
ship</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">for k = 1 to K and r
= 1 to R; K is the number of ship types and R is the number of
routes.</span>

#### <span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_612"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.2 Objective function</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">The objective
function in the model minimises the sum of the operating costs and the
lay-up costs. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.233.2"
class="koboSpan">The objective function in terms of the decision
variables is:</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0298" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00318.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">C′</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan">kr </span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">= C</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan"> X</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">, are the operating costs of a type k ship operating on
route r</span>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan">e</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan"> = daily lay-up cost for a type k ship</span>

#### <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.3 Constraints</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan">Ship
availability</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.248.2"
class="koboSpan">The maximum number of ships of type k operating cannot
be greater than the maximum number of ships of type k available.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.248.3"
class="koboSpan">Therefore:</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0299" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00319.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan">N</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></sub><sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan">max</span></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan"> = maximum number of type k ships available</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan">Service
frequency</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.256.2"
class="koboSpan">Service frequency is the driving force in liner
shipping. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.256.3" class="koboSpan">With
all rates being set by conferences, the main product differentiation is
on service. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.256.4" class="koboSpan">To
ensure that minimum service frequencies are met, the following
constraint is included:</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0300" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00320.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan">t′</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan"> = yearly voyages of a type k ship on route r
and:</span>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan">t′</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan"> = t</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">/T</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></sub>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan"> = shipping season for a type k ship</span>\
<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan">M</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan">r</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan"> = number of voyages required per year in route
r</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">By finding the
highest load level for any given leg of route r and comparing this with
given ship capacity, we find the minimum required number of voyages per
year for a specific route.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan">Ship/route
incompatibility</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.276.2"
class="koboSpan">Some ships may be unable to operate on a given route
due to cargo constraints, government regulations, and/or environmental
constraints. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.276.3"
class="koboSpan">It is necessary to eliminate these ships from the
model. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.276.4"
class="koboSpan">Therefore:</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan">N</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.279.1"
class="koboSpan"> = 0, for given (k,r) pairs</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.280.1"
class="koboSpan">Lay-up
Time</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.281.2" class="koboSpan">The lay-up
time in our models is equal to the time a ship is not operating during
the year. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.281.3" class="koboSpan">This
includes dry-docking and repair time:</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0301" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00321.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan">Non-negativity</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.284.2"
class="koboSpan">The decision variables
N</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan"> must be non-negative.</span>

#### <span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_613"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.4 Software application</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">The software package
used to run the above example was “A Mathematical Programming Language”
(AMPL)
(Holmes,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0657" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0657"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Fourer, Gay and
Kerninham.</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0658" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0658"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.291.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">) and OSL, a mathematical programme solver.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.292.2" class="koboSpan">See Powell and
Perakis (see endnote 18) for more details.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.292.3" class="koboSpan">The output
file from AMPL gives the following information:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">optimal value of
    objective function;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.294.1" class="koboSpan">value of
    objective function with LP relaxation;</span>
3.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">number of
    iterations to find solution; and</span>
4.  <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">values of
    variables at the optimal solution.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.297.1" class="koboSpan">The values of the
N</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan">kr</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan"> variables will show how many type k ships should be
allocated to each route r. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.299.2"
class="koboSpan">The Y</span><sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></sub><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan"> variable will indicate the number of days for which
type k ships must be laid-up.</span>

#### <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.302.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.5 Optimisation examples</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.303.1" class="koboSpan">The following two
examples are for the fleet deployment for FMG.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.303.2" class="koboSpan">The fleet
consists of six types of owned ships and five types of chartered ships
(one long-term charter and four short-term charters).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.303.3" class="koboSpan">The data used
to calculate the coefficients for the optimisation model is taken from
Jaramillo and Perakis (see endnote 17).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.303.4" class="koboSpan">The cost and
time coefficients used are transformed from per voyage units to per ship
values.</span>

<span class="bold"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">Example
1:</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.305.1" class="koboSpan"> The
first example optimises the FMG fleet deployment for their current
shipping conditions. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.305.2"
class="koboSpan">This example uses FMG’s existing service frequencies
and the number of ships available of each type.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.305.3" class="koboSpan">The current
allocation is shown in
</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fig0302" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0302"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.306.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0302" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00322.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0302)

</div>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_614"></span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan">Example 1
results:</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan"> The IP optimal allocation is given in
</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fig0303" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0303"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.312.2"
class="koboSpan">The minimum objective function yields a total operating
cost of \$91,831,000. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.312.3"
class="koboSpan">This is compared with \$93,148,000 for the current
allocation. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.312.4"
class="koboSpan">This corresponds to a reduction in total operating
costs of 1.4% (a savings of \$1,317,000 per year).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.312.5" class="koboSpan">Analysing the
resulting allocation shows that all owned ships (k = 1 to 6) and the
long-term charter (k = 7) are in use for the entire shipping season.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.312.6" class="koboSpan">This is due to
the high lay-up costs associated with these ship types.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">None of ship type 9
are allocated. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.313.2"
class="koboSpan">This ship type has the highest operating cost of any of
the short-term charters.</span>

<span class="bold"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan">Example
2:</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">
Example 2 uses the frequency constraints of the LP model presented in
Jaramillo and Perakis (see endnote 17).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.315.2" class="koboSpan">The resultant
allocation of the LP model is contained in
</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fig0304" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0304"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.317.1"
class="koboSpan">.This example compares the results and highlights the
advantages of the IP model versus the results of the LP model.</span>

<span class="bold"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.318.1"
class="koboSpan">Example 2
results:</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.319.1"
class="koboSpan"> The IP optimal allocation of ships is given in
</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fig0305" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0305"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.320.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.321.2"
class="koboSpan">The minimum objective function gives a total operating
cost of \$99,400,000</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">The resulting
allocation of the IP optimisation model maintains all of the target
frequencies. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.322.2"
class="koboSpan">Routes 1, 3, and 5 exactly meet the target frequencies
while on routes 2, 4, 6, and 7 the frequency is improved.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.322.3" class="koboSpan">The
improvement ranges from 1.3 days to 3.3 days.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.323.1" class="koboSpan">For the LP comparison
example presented, the optimal objective function of the IP model is
\$99,400,000. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.323.2"
class="koboSpan">Although the cost produced by the LP model is
substantially</span>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0303" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00323.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0303)

</div>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0304" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_615"></span>[](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0304)

[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00324.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0304)

</div>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0305" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00325.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0305)

</div>

<div id="Ch021.xhtml_fig0306" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
