<span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_616"></span>[](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0306)

[<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00326.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0306)

</div>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">smaller, it is
important to note that the service frequencies are compromised in the
1991 LP solution, which leads to sub-optimal allocation.
</span><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fig0306" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fig0306"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.329.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the comparison between service frequencies of
the IP optimisation model and the LP model.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.331.1" class="koboSpan">Since service is a
priority in liner shipping, it is necessary to meet the target
frequencies. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.331.2"
class="koboSpan">The IP optimisation model ensures that all target
frequencies are met. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.331.3"
class="koboSpan">The LP model violates the target frequency for routes
1, 2 and 4. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.331.4"
class="koboSpan">This is an average increase in service time of 1.3 days
or 9.1%.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.332.1" class="koboSpan">Using Integer
Programming to solve integer problems always produces the optimal
solution for the given constraints.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.332.2" class="koboSpan">No
manipulation of results is necessary.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.332.3" class="koboSpan">Using Linear
Programming to solve IPs requires manipulation of the results to make
the decision variables integer numbers.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.332.4" class="koboSpan">This leads to
sub-optimal solutions and constraints being violated.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">Substantial savings
may be achieved by applying our IP optimisation model for the fleet
deployment of a liner shipping company.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.333.2" class="koboSpan">The first
example in Powell and Perakis (see endnote 18) compares our IP model
against the existing fleet deployment of a liner shipping
company.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.334.1" class="koboSpan">This example shows a
reduction in operating costs of 1.5%.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.334.2" class="koboSpan">The second
example compares our IP model with the LP model contained in Perakis and
Jaramillo (see endnote 16). </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.334.3"
class="koboSpan">The results of the IP model are optimal and meet all
service frequency constraints. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.334.4"
class="koboSpan">The LP model violates the service constraints in three
routes by an average of 9.1%.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">The solution
indicates that all owned and long-term charter ship types should be
operated for their entire shipping season, due to the high lay-up cost
associated with these ship types.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.335.2" class="koboSpan">Short-term
charters should only be used if the owned ships and long-term charters
cannot meet the cargo and service frequency constraints.</span>

## <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.336.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.336.2" class="koboSpan">Fleet Deployment and Operations Optimisation: An Update</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">Recent years have
been quite turbulent for the ocean shipping industry, especially
considering prices and freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.337.2" class="koboSpan">The huge
swings in the price of oil in the space of only a few months, from the
all-time high of \$147 per barrel in summer 2008 to its collapse a few
months later, with the help of the world economic crisis, and the
possibility
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_617"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan">of higher fuel prices in the future, when the world
economy recovers, and especially when China and other high-growth
emerging economies expand their demand for raw materials, and especially
fuel, has made the original fleet deployment idea, (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.338.2" class="koboSpan">the
determination of the optimal speeds of each individual ship in a fleet
for a specific mission) reappear back on centre stage.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.338.3" class="koboSpan">Interestingly,
none of the recent fleet optimisation references are in this classic
“fleet deployment” form. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.338.4"
class="koboSpan">Regardless, it may be worthwhile to look at some of
them and their main results:</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">Christiansen and
Fagerholt,</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0671" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0671"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.340.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan"> investigate the robustness of ship schedules using
time windows. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.341.2"
class="koboSpan">A main objective is to minimise the idle time of ships
in port. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.341.3" class="koboSpan">It
has to be ensured that ships arrive at times which are well before port
closure, if any (e.g. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.341.4"
class="koboSpan">Friday night). </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.341.5"
class="koboSpan">Such arrivals are considered to be “risky” and will be
considered using penalties. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.341.6"
class="koboSpan">Depending on the size of the penalty cost, the optimal
solution will prefer arrival times at less risky (and hence more robust)
times.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.342.1" class="koboSpan">Agrawal and
Ergun</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0672" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0672"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.344.1"
class="koboSpan"> combine the problems of ship scheduling and
containerised cargo routing to identify the most profitable routes.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.344.2" class="koboSpan">The paper
develops a model that maximises profit from satisfying a set of demand
patterns between sets of origin and destination ports on given days of
the week. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.344.3" class="koboSpan">An
important consideration of this model is the capturing of the weekly
frequency requirement for liner services.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.344.4" class="koboSpan">A
mixed-integer program is formulated and three solution approaches are
provided: a Greedy heuristic algorithm, column generation and Benders
decomposition. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.344.5"
class="koboSpan">The solutions are confirmed with application on a set
of real data as observed by OOCL and APL in 2005.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">Andersen
e</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.346.1"
class="koboSpan">t
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0673" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0673"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.347.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.348.1"
class="koboSpan"> present an optimisation model for the tactical design
of scheduled service transportation system networks (in general) and
focus on the importance of neighbouring systems in a multimodal
transportation system. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.348.2"
class="koboSpan">The main challenge that the paper addresses is how two
different transportation modes can be coordinated to minimize fleet
costs and throughput time. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.348.3"
class="koboSpan">The resulting model minimises cost and waiting time at
nodes subject to cover, count, vehicle balance and node balance
constraints such that the demands at the final destination nodes are
satisfied. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.348.4"
class="koboSpan">Finally, real data are applied to verify the
model.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.349.1" class="koboSpan">Christiansen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0674" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0674"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.351.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan"> give a summary of the developments in ship routing and
scheduling within the decade (approximately) before its publication.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.352.2" class="koboSpan">The reviewed
papers are divided in categories: Strategic ship planning (optimal
fleets, maritime supply, chain); Tactical/operational ship scheduling
(optimal assignment of cargoes to ships and ships to schedules); Liner
network design and fleet deployment and a group including all other
references such as Navy applications.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.353.1" class="koboSpan">In Bronmo
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0675" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0675"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.355.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan"> a ship scheduling model is initially formulated, which
requires an input of available combinations of ships and routes–these
are then considered through binary variables in an integer LP.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.356.2" class="koboSpan">A number of
initial solutions are generated by a constructive heuristic and then
improved by a local search. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.356.3"
class="koboSpan">Finally a computational study is demonstrated to verify
the solution methodology.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">Fagerholt presents
TurboRouter, a decision support system for ship fleet scheduling which
is based on interaction with the user rather than analytical methods for
optimisation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0676" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0676"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.358.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.359.1" class="koboSpan">Gunnarson
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0677" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0677"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.361.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan"> aim to generate a simultaneous model for terminal
location and the ship routing problem, in intermodal transportation.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.362.2" class="koboSpan">Using the case
of a pulp supplier, they formulate a mixed integer linear programming
model minimising total distribution cost, subject to a significant
number of network flow constraints, production capabilities and
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_618"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan">demand from various customers.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.363.2" class="koboSpan">They also
attempt to provide a solution methodology, as their set of columns is
very large. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.363.3" class="koboSpan">A
heuristic method, similar to column generation, is used.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.363.4" class="koboSpan">Fremont, gives
a practical (without any operations research applications) approach to
the advantages and disadvantages of the hub-and-spoke network contrasted
to the direct port-to-port network.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.363.5" class="koboSpan">The paper uses
extensively the example of Maersk’s geographical coverage through the
hub-and-spoke
network.</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0679" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0679"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.364.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">Bronmo
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.,</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0680" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0680"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.367.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan"> present a Danzig-Wolfe procedure for ship scheduling
with flexible cargo sizes. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.368.2"
class="koboSpan">This is a problem similar to the pickup and delivery
problem with time windows, but the cargo sizes are defined by intervals
instead of by fixed values. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.368.3"
class="koboSpan">The authors found it computationally hard to find exact
solutions to the subproblems, hence their method cannot guarantee
finding the optimum over all solutions.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.368.4" class="koboSpan">To be able to
show how good the solutions are, the authors generated bounds on
differences between the true optimal objectives and the objectives in
their solutions.</span>

## <span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.369.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.369.2" class="koboSpan">Summary and Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.370.1" class="koboSpan">The optimisation of
the operations of a fleet of ships is mathematically far more
complicated than the optimisation of the operations of a single ship.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.370.2" class="koboSpan">However,
trying to optimise the various full load and ballast speeds of each
different ship in the fleet can be even more complicated than that, and
necessitate the use of nonlinear programming algorithms and software, as
opposed to the largely linear-integer algorithms in cases when the
speeds are fixed and not optimised (slow-steaming).</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.371.1" class="koboSpan">Due to the very
different degree of competition in the bulker and liner markets, and
also due to the very dissimilar constraints on their respective
operations, optimal fleet deployment is quite different for each one.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.371.2" class="koboSpan">Over the past
several years, we have provided “exact” and “approximate” algorithms for
realistic, single or multi-origin and destination problems for bulker
fleet deployment, including optimal slow-steaming lay-up decisions,
under conditions of certainty or uncertainty for the various cost
components. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.371.3" class="koboSpan">We
then also solved problems in optimal strategic planning and ship-route
allocation for a major liner company, presenting independent models for
fixing both the service frequencies in the different routes and the
speeds of the ships, using at first linear and integer programming.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.371.4" class="koboSpan">Several
insights from a review and comparative study of the above were presented
here, starting from the proper problem definition (constraints
artificially imposed have resulted in 15% higher costs in early
literature on this problem) and ending with the benefits of optimal
integer solutions to the liner fleet deployment problems we
studied.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.372.1" class="koboSpan">Length limitations
prohibit us from discussing our extensive work in other areas of fleet
optimisation, such as the operational, day-to-day decisions for a major
oil company fleet, which we modelled and solved in Bremer and Peraklis
(see endnote 21) and Perakis and Bremer (see endnote 22), or go into
more details on the research modelling and results we did discuss in
this paper. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.372.2"
class="koboSpan">Our work with Bremer was an example of an operational
(as opposed to long-term or strategic) optimisation.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.373.1" class="koboSpan">We will also not
discuss the mathematical details of some recent work of ours (Cho and
Perakis (see endnote 23)) where we were able to re-formulate a
complicated bulk cargo ship scheduling problem formulation Ronen (see
endnote 24), from a nonlinear-integer to an equally accurate
integer-linear problem, with far fewer variables, using a generalisation
of the “capacitated facility location problem”, a classic result
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_619"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.374.1"
class="koboSpan">of optimisation theory.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.374.2" class="koboSpan">That problem
was referring to a single loading port, several unloading ports, and
fixed speeds (no slow-steaming allowed).</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.375.1" class="koboSpan">A major shortcoming
of the classic ship scheduling problem, addressing uncertainty, received
more attention after 2002. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.375.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipping networks are prone to a very volatile
behaviour. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.375.3"
class="koboSpan">Uncertainty can be considered into two categories:
internal and external in regards to the marine transportation network.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.375.4" class="koboSpan">Internal
uncertainty refers to schedule deviation that can occur due to ship
operation (within the transportation network), (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.375.5" class="koboSpan">bad weather
conditions, mechanical faults, speed variation, etc).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.375.6" class="koboSpan">External
uncertainty refers to schedule deviation which occur due to
network-related issues, such as the effect of market volatility and
inventory variation through supply and demand at origin and destination
ports.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.1" class="koboSpan">In an attempt to
attack internal uncertainty, Christiansen and Fagenholt (see endnote
33), introduced the concept of time windows, a technique which has been
used in the airline industry. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.2"
class="koboSpan">The concept of a time window in general is that
departures and arrivals are not considered as a single point in time,
but as a time window. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.3"
class="koboSpan">In the airline industry this provided with an advantage
of allocating flights more efficiently within the network.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.4" class="koboSpan">In maritime
operations, time windows account for deviation in arrival times and
hence slight delays or early arrivals should not affect the network.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.5" class="koboSpan">In this way
robustness is introduced in the model.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.6" class="koboSpan">Time windows
also simplify the model as they reduce the number of available time
slots. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.7"
class="koboSpan">However, a challenge with this technique is to define
the “size” of a time window. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.8"
class="koboSpan">Too small time windows may not reflect the ship’s
actual ability to follow the schedule, and the advantage of a time
window will be cancelled out. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.376.9"
class="koboSpan">Too large time windows might generate a more realistic
but inefficient model as the ship will always be on time, but the
terminal’s capacity will be inefficiently used.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.377.1" class="koboSpan">To address the
internal uncertainties, Christiansen and Fagenholt (see endnote 33) use
time windows to attack the issue of risky arrivals.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.377.2" class="koboSpan">In cases where
ports have restricted operating hours (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.377.3" class="koboSpan">no operation
overnight or during weekends), available operating hours can be modelled
as time windows. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.377.4"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the concept of risky arrivals is
introduced, which imply arrivals that are close to weekends and could
cause the ship to stay idle for several days.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.377.5" class="koboSpan">On the basis
of how risky an arrival is, each time window is associated with a
penalty. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.377.6" class="koboSpan">Risky
arrivals in the network will probably not be eliminated, but will be
penalised and therefore reduced.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.377.7" class="koboSpan">However, it
has to be noted that this methodology does not address uncertainty to a
sufficient extent. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.377.8"
class="koboSpan">It does not directly tackle the issue of delay
propagation in a ship’s schedule, but instead it tries to ensure that
delays will not be extended due to the port’s operating
timetable.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.378.1" class="koboSpan">External
uncertainties have received considerably more attention than internal
throughout the literature since 2002, due to the fact that they are
usually better defined. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.378.2"
class="koboSpan">An important uncertainty is in the supply and demand on
origin and destination ports respectively.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.378.3" class="koboSpan">It is often
the case that the vessel has arrived at its loading port, but has to
wait for the cargo to pile up. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.378.4"
class="koboSpan">Christiansen addressed this problem by considering a
combination of the ship scheduling problem and the inventory management
problem. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.378.5" class="koboSpan">The
objective of the model is to identify the sequence of port calls for
each ship with minimum cost while ensuring that inventories at ports are
never full or empty (so that ships can always proceed).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.378.6" class="koboSpan">This is
achieved by introducing “alarm levels” on the inventories, defined as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.379.1"
class="koboSpan">soft inventory
constraints</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.380.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.380.2"
class="koboSpan">These include an upper and a lower bound which are
tighter than the actual limits of the inventory.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.380.3" class="koboSpan">In the case
where a ship’s arrival would cause the inventory to shift beyond its
alarm level, a penalty cost will be introduced.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.380.4" class="koboSpan">In this way a
schedule including such a port call
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_620"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.381.1"
class="koboSpan">will be avoided.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.381.2" class="koboSpan">The benefits
of this model not only involve the ships, but also the ports as well,
since it ensures that they always have sufficient inventories.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.381.3" class="koboSpan">From a ship
scheduling point of view the results from this paper have a considerable
effect on robustness by reducing the possibility of port-related delays,
which nowadays is the most common source of delays.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.382.1" class="koboSpan">Hwang
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.384.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 40) deal with external uncertainty.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.384.2" class="koboSpan">Market
fluctuations are the most important source of uncertainty in the
maritime industry. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.384.3"
class="koboSpan">Unlike other scheduling models, Hwang considered profit
variability in the objective function of the problem, by analysing the
profit from assigning a cargo to a schedule.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.384.4" class="koboSpan">The paper
assumes that charter rates are linearly related to a single spot rate
and therefore a single market random variable can be used to account for
freight rate volatility. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.384.5"
class="koboSpan">However, this is not entirely correct, as rates in
different shipping sectors may not have such a strong correlation.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.384.6" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
unlike other models, the shipper had the option of chartering ships in
and out of his fleet through time or voyage charters.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.384.7" class="koboSpan">Assuming that
an operator aims for more sustainable profits, the model developed
reduces profit variability at the smallest possible cost.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.384.8" class="koboSpan">The paper
makes an important contribution, as there is very little research
considering market volatility, which is a driving factor in
shipping</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.385.1" class="koboSpan">For a detailed
exposition of liner shipping economics, the textbook by Janson and the
late D. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.385.2" class="koboSpan">S.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.385.3" class="koboSpan">Schneerson
(see endnote 25), is highly recommended.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.385.4" class="koboSpan">In the recent
liner logistics research, Rana and Vickson (see endnotes 26, 27)
presented nonlinear programming models, aiming to maximise total profit
by finding an optimal sequence of ports of call for each ship.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.385.5" class="koboSpan">For solution
methods, they used Lagrangean
relaxation</span><sup><a href="#Ch021.xhtml_fn0665" id="Ch021.xhtml_bck_fn0665"><span
id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.386.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.387.1"
class="koboSpan"> and decomposition methods.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.387.2" class="koboSpan">Their first
paper develops only a one-ship model, while their second is rather
complicated by its non-linearities in both objective function and
constraints. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.387.3"
class="koboSpan">The model of Perakis and Jaramillo (see endnote 16) and
its subsequent more accurate integer solution Powell and Perakis (see
endnote 18) is easier to use for a realistic situation, but does not
take into account the cargo demand forecasts that arise between pairs of
ports in the model.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.388.1" class="koboSpan">We have addressed
that in Cho and Perakis (see endnote 28), where we have suggested two
optimisation models. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.388.2"
class="koboSpan">The first is a linear programming model of profit
maximisation, providing an optimal routeing mix for each ship available
and optimal service frequencies for each candidate route.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.388.3" class="koboSpan">The second is
a mixed integer programming model with binary variables, providing not
only optimal routeing mixes and service frequencies, but also best
capital investment alternatives to expand fleet capacity, and is a cost
minimisation model. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.388.4"
class="koboSpan">In both models, we have suggested and used the concept
of “flow-route incidence matrix”, and discuss its usefulness for similar
route-ing and scheduling problems (see endnote 28).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.388.5" class="koboSpan">The most
important merit of using the flow-route incidence matrix is that it
links various cargo demands to route utilisation in a simple, systematic
way. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.388.6" class="koboSpan">These
models can help improve existing network of routes or service
frequencies, and their solution can be easily implemented with standard
linear or integer programming packages.</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.389.1" class="koboSpan">Other examples of
complicated operational models we have studied in detail are Ship
Weather Routing problems, but since we are restricting this chapter to
fleet, not individual ship, optimisation, we will not discuss them here.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.389.2" class="koboSpan">The models
described in this chapter are all strategic.
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.389.3" class="koboSpan">However, at
the request of the reviewer of this book chapter, we cite a few key
recent references in that area (see endnotes 29–31).</span>

<span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.390.1" class="koboSpan">The results of our
research in Fleet Deployment have been cited in graduate courses at
Michigan, MIT, and elsewhere in the US, but also in universities around
the world,
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_page_621"></span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan">such as in the recent textbook used at the Maritime
Studies Dept. </span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.391.2"
class="koboSpan">in Dalian, China (see endnote 32).
</span><span id="Ch021.xhtml_kobo.391.3" class="koboSpan">Further
dissemination of these results in this chapter will hopefully result in
more students and practitioners being exposed to the significant
benefits of proper optimisation and the pitfalls, and their heavy price
in higher fleet operating costs, of suboptimal policies.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Measuring Business Peformance in Shipping</span>](#Preface1.xhtml_bck_ht0474)

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Photis</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">M.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Panayides</span></span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fn0681" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fn0681"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">,

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan">Gong</span></span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fn0682" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fn0682"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a>

class="koboSpan">and
</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">Neophytos</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">Lambertides</span></span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fn0683" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fn0683"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">‡</span></a>

## <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">The success or failure
of any business depends to a large extent on valid and reliable
assessment of performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.17.2"
class="koboSpan">Despite the importance of performance measurement,
there is a relative gap in the context of the shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.17.3" class="koboSpan">The gap is
reflected in the absence of a consistent and coherent stream of research
and literature that deal with the issue of how shipping companies
measure their performance and what techniques, methods and measures are
actually available to improve the process and outcomes of performance
measurement. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.17.4"
class="koboSpan">For instance, performance may be related to economic or
financial performance and measured using accounting ratios or other
financial measures. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.17.5"
class="koboSpan">Performance may also be related to efficiency and the
effective utilisation of inputs into a production process, which in this
case, includes not only the provision of transportation services but
also the process of managing the transportation business and the
performance of the business entity.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.17.6" class="koboSpan">A key issue in
the context of the shipping industry is to develop a stream of research
that would deal with the different approaches to performance measurement
and their application to the major sectors of the shipping industry viz.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.17.7" class="koboSpan">dry bulk,
tanker and container shipping. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.17.8"
class="koboSpan">A stream of research dealing with the measurement of
business performance in shipping would also provide useful managerial
implications, not least because it will enable managers to assess the
performance of their companies and operations and therefore provide a
basis for further improvement.</span>

## <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">Approaches to Performance Measurement: A Literature Review</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Performance
measurement of organisations has received extensive attention in the
literature, since firm performance is the bottom line of a business.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">Performance
reflects
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_626"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan">the outcome of the implementation of any strategic task
and whether such outcome is deemed to be successful or
disastrous.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">One of the most widely
used operational measures for evaluating firm performance is market
share, which also serves as a surrogate measure of firm profitability
(Tanriverdi and Lee, 2008). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.21.2"
class="koboSpan">Studies that have focused on sectors characterised by
network externalities, customer switching costs, and lock-in have used
market share as a performance measure.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.21.3" class="koboSpan">A firm’s market
share is measured as the sum over all product markets of the
sales-weighted shares of each market (Tanriverdi and Lee, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.21.4" class="koboSpan">Other studies,
however, have used subjective means to capture market share and proved
that subjective measures are as good as the objective ones.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.21.5" class="koboSpan">Jain and Bhatia
(2007), adopting the method of previous studies, have used a "structured
non-disguised" questionnaire which requires respondents to state their
perceptions on their firm’s market share on a five-point Likert
scale.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">Nonetheless, most
studies in the literature have consistently used accounting-based ratios
or measures to assess firm performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">Such measures
include Return on Assets (ROA) (Hawawini, Subramanian and Verdin, 2003;
Short, </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007; O’Sullivan and Abela, 2007; Morgan, Vorhies and
Mason, 2009), Return on Investment (ROI) (Hult, Ketchen and Slater,
2005; Nadkarni and Narayanan, 2007), Return on Capital (ROC) (Capon
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1988), Return on Sales (ROS) (Makino, Isobe and Chan,
2004; Boone and Hendricks, 2009), Return on Equity (ROE) (Luo, Aric and
Tse, 2007; Hult, Ketchen and Slater, 2005), Return on Capital Employed
(ROCE) (Rajagopalan, 1997), and Return on Invested Capital (ROIC)
(Christensen and Montgomery, 1981).</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">Accounting-based
measures have been criticised by researchers as being unsuitable for
assessing firm performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.27.2"
class="koboSpan">They are historic in nature and do not focus on the
firm’s future performance or potential.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.27.3" class="koboSpan">What is more,
the differences in accounting policies and in methods of consolidating
accounts and the possibility of distortions due to depreciation
policies, inventory valuation, and specific treatment of income and
expenditure items make their sole use to evaluate firm performance
problematic (Chakravarthy, 1986).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.27.4" class="koboSpan">Hawawini
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2003) point out that one important aspect of firm
performance is the creation of value for the firm’s shareholders, in
terms of earning returns greater than the cost of capital.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.29.2" class="koboSpan">However,
accounting-based measures do not take into consideration the cost of
capital or the replacement value of assets and are thus inadequate to
measure the value the firm offers to its shareholders.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.29.3" class="koboSpan">On top of this,
Chakravarthy (1986) suggests that a firm should provide value not only
to its shareholders but also to the other stakeholders of the firm, such
as customers, employees, and the community, in terms of product or
service quality, ability to keep and develop talented people, and
responsibility towards the community.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.29.4" class="koboSpan">Clearly,
accounting-based measures do not reflect the value the firm is producing
for its stakeholders.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">Other studies (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">Morgan and
Rego, 2009), in an attempt to overcome the disadvantages previously
mentioned, have assessed firm performance by using Net Operating Cash
Flow (defined as “EBIT + Depreciation – Taxes”) and Cash Flow
Variability (defined as “the coefficient of variation of the net
operating cash flows”). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.30.3"
class="koboSpan">The first reflects current shareholder value and is
less dependent on the accounting practices of the firm, while the latter
takes into consideration the risk level and captures the stability of a
firm’s cash flows.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">Hawawini
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2003) measure the economic performance of a firm,
instead of the accounting performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">Measures of
economic performance are based on the concept of residual income, and
take into account capital costs, risk, and the time value
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_627"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">of money. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.34.2"
class="koboSpan">Unlike traditional accounting measures, they do reflect
shareholder value and are not affected by accounting policies.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.34.3" class="koboSpan">As measures of
performance, Hawawini
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2003) use Economic Profit (EP) per dollar of Capital
Employed (CE) and Total Market Value (TMV) per dollar of Capital
Employed (CE), where capital employed is the sum of equity capital and
debt capital. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.36.2"
class="koboSpan">The two measures are defined as follows:</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0307" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00327.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">ROIC = Return on
Invested Capital;</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">WACC = Weighted
Average Cost of Capital;</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">NOPAT = Net Operating
Profit after Taxes;</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">If ROIC is greater
than WACC, economic profit per dollar of capital employed is positive
and the firm creates value.</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0308" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00328.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">Where:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">TMV = Sum of the
firm’s market capitalisation (market value of equity) and the market
value of its debt;</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">If TMV is greater than
CE, the firm is deemed to have increased the value of capital invested
in the firm and created value.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">Many other studies
(Griffith, 2004; Bacidore,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1997; Ryan and Trahan, 2007) use economic
profit-related performance measures, such as Economic Value Added (EVA),
Refined Economic Value Added (REVA), Shareholder Value Added (SVA) or
Cash Flow Return on Investment (CFROI).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.49.2" class="koboSpan">One of the most
important economic performance measures is Economic Value Added (EVA),
which was developed by Stern Stewart & Co.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.49.3" class="koboSpan">EVA is defined
as “NOPAT – Cost of Capital\* Amount of Capital” and it attempts to
relate the firm’s accounting data to its stock price.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.49.4" class="koboSpan">Value-based
performance systems are deemed significant in the performance
measurement literature, as they drive value creation (Hawawini
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.51.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2003).</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">Another important
market-based measure, which is widely used to assess firm performance,
is Tobin’s Q (Short
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007; Chari, Devaraj and David, 2008; Uotila
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2009). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.56.2"
class="koboSpan">Tobin’s Q is defined as “the sum of the market value of
equity, the book value of debt, and deferred taxes divided by the book
value of total assets minus intangible assets” (Thomas and Waring,
1999). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.56.3" class="koboSpan">Tobin’s
Q compares a firm’s market value with the replacement value of its
assets; it reflects the investors’ views on how the firm will generate
value. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.56.4" class="koboSpan">A value
of Tobin’s Q greater than 1 implies that the investors assess that the
firm will generate greater value from its asset stock than if the assets
were deployed outside the firm (McGahan, 1999).</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">Heiens, Leach and
McGrath (2007) use market adjusted holding-period returns (HPR) to
assess firm performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.57.2"
class="koboSpan">The market adjusted HPR is defined as “the compounded
market holding period return minus the compounded stock holding period
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_628"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan">return”. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.58.2"
class="koboSpan">Other studies (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.58.3" class="koboSpan">Brammer and
Millington, 2009) use risk-adjusted HPR as a performance measure, since
it takes into consideration the risk of share ownership.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.58.4" class="koboSpan">This is defined
as:</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0309" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00329.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">P</span><sub><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">= The market price of the firm's share at time
t</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan">P</span><sub><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">t-1</span></sub><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan">= The market rice of the firm's share at time
t-1</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">DIV</span><sub><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"> = The dividend paid by the firm at time t</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">RISKFREE</span><sub><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">= The rate of return for a government bond at time
t</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, many
researchers are of the view that there is no single accounting or
financial measure that can adequately capture all aspects of firm
performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.73.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, instead of relying on only one measure to
determine firm performance, a multi-factor model should be used.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.73.3" class="koboSpan">Altman’s Z is
one such multi-factor performance-measurement model.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.73.4" class="koboSpan">Altman’s Z, an
established measure of credit default risk, has received increasing
consideration in the literature of performance measurement (Short
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007; Craighead, Hult and Ketchen, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">Bankruptcy is
considered by more and more managers as a strategic alternative (Short
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007); thus a measure which incorporates this
tendency is significant when appraising firm performance in order that
the prospects for firm survival are captured (Altman
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1981).</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">Altman’s Z is
calculated as follows:</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0310" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00330.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">a = working
capital</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">b = retained
earnings</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">c = operating
income</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">d = sales</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">e = total
assets</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">f = net worth</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">g = total debt</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">According to
Chakravarthy (1986), Altman’s Z can be a valuable index of the firm’s
well-being, since by measuring the distance from bankruptcy, the Z
factor can be a surrogate measure of strategic performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">However,
Altman’s Z is flawed in the sense that a well-managed firm does not
devote all of its resources only in the avoidance of bankruptcy.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.90.3" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the
calculation of the Z factor is mostly an empirical result rather than
the result of theory.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_629"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
class="koboSpan">Hence, an alternative multi-factor measure has been
proposed by Chakravarthy (1986). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.91.2"
class="koboSpan">Chakravarthy (1986) deals with the term “firm
excellence” and asserts that strategic management is the process through
which managers ensure the long-term adaptation of the firm to its
environment. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.91.3" class="koboSpan">In
this way, the useful measures of performance are those that help assess
the quality of the firm’s adaptation to its changing environment.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.91.4" class="koboSpan">A firm needs to
be evaluated on the basis of how well it serves all of its stakeholders
(not just its stockholders) and of how well it manages the net surplus
of its slack resources. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.91.5"
class="koboSpan">The slack resources will improve the firm’s ability to
adapt to uncertain or unknown future events.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.91.6" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
firm should be able to transform itself and adjust to the changing
environment around it. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.91.7"
class="koboSpan">Chakravarthy (1986) selects eight slack variables to
represent the ability of firm transformation: Cash Flow to Investment
ratio, Sales by Total Assets, R&D by Sales ratio, Market to Book Value,
Sales per Employee, Debt by Equity ratio, Working Capital by Sales
ratio, and Dividend Payout ratio.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">Despite the widespread
use of the various financial measures mentioned above, there has been
increased use of non-financial measures to evaluate firm performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">Proponents of
such measures insist that non-financial measures are better predictors
of long-term performance than financial measures and help management
focus on the long-term effects of their actions (Banker, Potter and
Srinivasan, 2000). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.92.3"
class="koboSpan">One of the most important non-financial measures used
is customer satisfaction (Ittner and Larcker, 1998; Banker
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2000; Jain and Bhatia, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">Other measures
include productivity (Koka and Prescott, 2008), product quality (Wisner,
2003), and manufacturing-related measures, such as cycle time, lead
time, setup times or inventory turnover (Perera
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1997; Dehning
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007).</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">One of the most
important performance measurement systems in the literature is the
Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan and Norton, 1992; Hult
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2008). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.101.2"
class="koboSpan">Kaplan and Norton (1992) assert that no single
performance measure can incorporate all the critical areas of a
business; thus, they developed four sets of perspectives that the firm
should focus on to evaluate its performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.101.3" class="koboSpan">These
perspectives are: customer performance, financial performance, internal
process performance, and innovation and learning performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.101.4" class="koboSpan">The measures
which will be included in each category will depend on the firm, its
goals, and the type of business it is into, but could include lead time,
on-time delivery, growth, profitability, cycle time, productivity or
ability to launch new products. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.101.5"
class="koboSpan">The Balanced Scorecard’s effectiveness lies in the fact
that it reduces information overload, as it limits the number of
measures used and that it ensures the optimisation of the whole system,
instead of the subsystem.
</span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fig0311" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0311"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents a summary of some key papers in the firm
performance measurement literature together with the performance
dimensions and indicators used.</span>

## <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">Performance Measurement of Shipping Companies</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">To determine the
extent to which the performance of the maritime industry has been
subjected to systematic examination, a key word search in the electronic
databases of the major shipping/transport journals was undertaken.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.105.2" class="koboSpan">The journals
targeted include Maritime Policy and Management (MPM), Transportation
Research (Part A and Part E), Journal of Transport Economics and Policy
(JTEP), Transport Policy (TP), Transport Reviews (TR), and Maritime
Economics and Logistics (MEL, formerly</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_630"></span>[](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0311)

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00331.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0311)

</div>

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00332.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00333.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
