class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00334.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">known as the
International Journal of Maritime Economics).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">The majority
of the papers identified examine productivity/efficiency issues related
to ports or container terminals.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.110.3" class="koboSpan">As there are
already some good reviews on port/terminal productivity (see, for
example, Cullinane, 2002; Panayides
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2009), we focus here on the performance of shipping
companies. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.112.2"
class="koboSpan">Less than a dozen papers have examined this important
issue. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.112.3" class="koboSpan">We make
reference to studies outside of shipping firms where appropriate.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">The existing studies
on the performance of shipping companies may be divided into three main
types: the first branch of the literature focuses on firms’ financial
performance or operational performance/efficiency, the second on the
stock market performance (i.e. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.113.2"
class="koboSpan">risk and return) of the listed firms, and the third on
other aspects of performance (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.113.3" class="koboSpan">third-party
rated performance or self-evaluation of performance).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.113.4" class="koboSpan">The
sub-sections below first review the main research findings of the
relevant studies,
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_634"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan">organised in chronological order.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.114.2" class="koboSpan">This is
followed by an evaluation/critique of the research designs and key
results of the said studies. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.114.3"
class="koboSpan">Future research directions and opportunities are then
discussed.</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Studies of the financial/operating performance of shipping companies</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Randoy, Down and
Jenssen (2003) examine the effect of corporate governance mechanisms on
the financial performance of 32 publicly traded maritime firms from
Norway and Sweden during the period 1996–1998.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.116.2" class="koboSpan">Using Return
on Assets (ROA), Return on Equity (ROE) and Return on Sales (ROS) as the
measure of firm performance, they find (through regression analysis)
that maritime firms with a founding family CEO have better financial
performance than maritime firms with a non-founding family CEO; a high
level of board independence enhances profitability in maritime firms;
but there is no significant relation between the level of board
ownership and firm profitability in maritime firms, although board
ownership control is significant in a control sample of manufacturing
firms. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.116.3" class="koboSpan">The
authors focus on cross-sectional analysis and provide minimal evidence
on the extent to which the sample maritime companies perform, either in
absolute terms or relative to a chosen benchmark.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.116.4" class="koboSpan">The same
criticism applies more or less to the other studies reviewed in this
sub-section.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">Lam, Yap and
Cullinane (2007) investigate the structure, conduct and performance of
major liner shipping routes during the period 1998–2002.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">They measure
performance using financial performance indicators such as turnover,
operating profit and net profit calculated on a per-TEU basis.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.3" class="koboSpan">The results
indicate that different companies experienced varying degrees of success
or failure in financial performance during the period under examination,
but there is no conclusive evidence of any relationship (based on
correlation coefficients) between either structure or conduct and
performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.4"
class="koboSpan">The authors note that while industry structure and the
conduct of shipping lines can affect performance, the direction of
causality may be reversed. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.5"
class="koboSpan">For instance, shipping lines that are able to reap
significant benefits from the adoption of a particular form of conduct
might be persuaded to repeat that strategy, whereas those shipping lines
whose conduct failed to generate sufficient returns will be motivated to
seek alternative strategies. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.6"
class="koboSpan">Similarly, healthy financial gains will enable shipping
lines to invest in greater capacity and alter the structure of the
market, while poor financial performance can lead to mergers and
acquisitions or even exit from the industry altogether (pp.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.7" class="koboSpan">372–373).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.8" class="koboSpan">In conclusion,
Lam, Yap and Cullinane (2007) interpret their results as providing
further validation of the assertion that the structure (high levels of
concentration) and conduct (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.117.9" class="koboSpan">inter-firm
collaboration) of shipping lines are the outcomes (as opposed to causes)
of low cost strategies for survival in a beleaguered shipping
sector.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">Lambertides and Louca
(2008) examine the relation between ownership structure and operating
performance of listed European maritime firms during the period
2002–2004. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.118.2"
class="koboSpan">They adopt multiple measures of operating performance,
including cash flow from operations on assets/sales, operating return on
assets/sales, capital expenditures on assets, and asset turnover.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.118.3" class="koboSpan">Judging by
these measures, the sample companies seem to be profitable in each of
the years under examination, with the average (median) cash flow from
operations on assets ranging from 7.3% (8.0%) to 9.4% (10.9%), whereas
the average (median) operating return on sales ranges from 1.9% (4.6%)
to 8.0% (8.9%). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.118.4"
class="koboSpan">There is also a steady improvement in maritime
operating performance
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_635"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan">through time. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.119.2"
class="koboSpan">By regressing operating performance measures on
ownership structure and control variables, Lambertides and Louca (2008)
find that firms with more foreign shareholders and greater participation
from investment companies have higher operating performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.119.3" class="koboSpan">These and
other results lead them to conclude that certain types of ownership
structure can result in better investor protection and hence better
operating performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.119.4"
class="koboSpan">They caution, however, against inferring causality from
these results, as both ownership structure and operating performance
might be associated with a third, omitted factor (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.119.5" class="koboSpan">management
quality).</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Studies of the stock market performance of shipping companies</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">One stream of the
literature deals with the risk-return characteristics and behaviour of
shipping company stocks and factors associated with stock market
performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.121.2"
class="koboSpan">Grammenos and Marcoulis (1996a) analyse the
determinants of the cross-section of expected stock returns of 19
shipping companies listed in the US, Norway, Stockholm and London.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.121.3" class="koboSpan">Among the
factors examined (company stock market beta, dividend yield, financial
leverage and average age of the company’s fleet), they find that the
industry-specific factor (average age of the fleet) and financial
leverage are significant in explaining shipping stocks’ returns, whereas
the stock market beta and the dividend yield are far less
significant.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">Grammenos and
Arkoulis (2002) present evidence, for the first time, about the
relations between global macroeconomic sources of risk and shipping
stock returns for 36 internationally listed shipping companies during
the period 1989–1998. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.122.2"
class="koboSpan">The return on the world equity market portfolio and
innovations in the following global macro variables are employed in the
analysis: (a) industrial production; (b) inflation; (c) oil prices; (d)
fluctuations in exchange rates against the US dollar; and (e) laid up
tonnage. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.122.3"
class="koboSpan">Several significant relationships are established
between the returns of international shipping stocks and global risk
factors. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.122.4"
class="koboSpan">Specifically, oil prices and laid up tonnage are found
to be negatively related to shipping stocks, whereas the exchange rate
variable displays a positive relationship.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.122.5" class="koboSpan">In addition,
it is found that, in general, the macroeconomic factors exhibit a
consistent pattern in the way in which they are linked to the shipping
industry, across countries. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.122.6"
class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and Marcoulis (2001, 2005) provide evidence
that microeconomic and company-specific factors as well as the market
factor are the driving force behind shipping companies’ stock
returns.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">Grammenos and
Arkoulis (2001) examine the long-run performance (for the initial 24
months subsequent to public listing) of 27 shipping initial public
offerings (IPOs) issued in the stock exchanges of seven different
countries during the period 1987–1995.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.123.2" class="koboSpan">By measuring
aftermarket performance respectively against the local stock market
indices and against the Morgan Stanley Capital Market (MSCI) index for
the shipping equity market, they find that the shipping IPOs
underperform the local stock market indices by as much as 36.79% by the
end of the second anniversary of public listing, but there is no
evidence of underperformance relative to the MSCI shipping index.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.123.3" class="koboSpan">They further
find that the two-year holding period returns of the sample firms are
positively related to the initial level of gearing and negatively
related to the fleet age of the companies at the time of the offering.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.123.4" class="koboSpan">In an earlier
study, Grammenos and Marcoulis (1996b) find relatively small but
statistically significant underpricing for 31 shipping IPOs worldwide
during the period 1983–1995. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.123.5"
class="koboSpan">In contrast, Cullinane and Gong (2002) find substantial
underpricing for 50 transportation IPOs in stock exchanges in Hong Kong
(with an average underpricing of approximately 44%) and the Chinese
mainland
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_636"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">(with an average underpricing of approximately 126%)
during the period 1972–1998. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.124.2"
class="koboSpan">The 23 shipping IPOs on average experienced as much as
126% underpricing, which is statistically higher than that for toll
roads, freight forwarders and airlines.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.124.3" class="koboSpan">They attribute
the higher level of underpricing for shipping IPOs to the fact that,
relative to other types of transport companies which are typically
guaranteed regular incomes through their status as monopolies or
franchises, the (usually freight-related) shipping companies are
associated with a higher level of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan">ex ante</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan"> uncertainty and thus they need to offer investors a
higher level of initial day returns in order to compensate investors for
the higher risk involved. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.126.2"
class="koboSpan">With the benefit of hindsight (and based on the results
in other related research), it is possible that the investors might have
simply overpaid for the IPOs, and that the more speculative investors in
the emerging Chinese stock market are just more likely to do so than
investors in the more mature stock markets.</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Other studies of performance of shipping companies</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">Panayides (2003)
examines the relationship between competitive strategy and performance
in the context of ship management companies.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.128.2" class="koboSpan">Recognising
performance as a multi-dimensional construct, he measures performance
using seven items of self-reported measures constructed from
questionnaires that contain instruments found to be valid and reliable
by previous research as well as pre-tested with managers and academics.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.128.3" class="koboSpan">The study
finds that companies that apply competitive strategies are more likely
to be high performers. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.128.4"
class="koboSpan">The strongest influences on performance seem to be
achieving economies of scale, differentiation (in particular through a
wider range of services offered), and market-focus and competitor
analysis. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.128.5" class="koboSpan">It
is suggested that high performers are more likely to pursue a
combination of the generic strategies rather than pursuing one of the
generic strategies in isolation.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">Jenssen and Randoy
(2006) investigate how innovation contributes to company performance in
Norwegian shipping. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.129.2"
class="koboSpan">They hypothesise that organisational and
inter-organisational variables influence innovation and innovation in
turn influences performance in the shipping firms.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">Performance is
said to be measured by financial results, market position and bargaining
power, although it is not clear from the paper how these are actually
computed and why they are considered appropriate.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.129.4" class="koboSpan">Using
regression analysis based on the results of a survey of 46 Norwegian
shipping companies (divided into highly differentiated companies and low
differentiated companies) and two measures of innovation
(product-process innovation, PPI, and market innovation, MI), they find
that PPI is positively associated with performance for the whole sample
and for highly differentiated firms, but not for low differentiated
firms. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.129.5" class="koboSpan">No
statistically significant relationship is found between MI and
performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.129.6"
class="koboSpan">Thus, the effect of innovation on performance seems to
depend on the companies’ degree of differentiation and the type of
innovation. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.129.7"
class="koboSpan">The authors suggest that future studies should use more
objective information, such as accounting and financial market data, in
order to gain more knowledge of the effect of innovation on
performance.</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Evaluation and a critique</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">The key objectives of
most of the existing studies on the performance of shipping companies
have been to investigate the relations between performance and specific
aspects of corporate strategy (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.131.2" class="koboSpan">inter-firm
collaboration, innovation, mergers and
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_637"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan">acquisitions) or governance (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">ownership
structure and control). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.132.3"
class="koboSpan">Few studies take it as their primary objective the
determination of objective shipping company performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.132.4" class="koboSpan">It is also
difficult to compare the results from the various studies because of the
different research designs and the inconsistent definition and
measurement of the variables used.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.132.5" class="koboSpan">Such
comparability issues are further complicated by the fact that the sample
firms usually come from, and sometimes are spread thinly over different
countries, which often adopt different accounting standards and
financial reporting practices. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.132.6"
class="koboSpan">It is not clear from the existing studies how well
shipping companies have performed, either in absolute terms or against a
chosen benchmark. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.132.7"
class="koboSpan">It is also not clear what factors, if any, are
associated with differential performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.132.8" class="koboSpan">The inference
problem is further made difficult because of potential omitted variable
bias, endogeneity bias, and/or other forms of model
misspecification.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">It is obvious that
the ability to draw any reliable inference with respect to shipping
companies’ performance hinges critically on a proper definition and
measurement of performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.133.2"
class="koboSpan">As is well-known and as previously noted, performance
is a multi-dimensional concept (Walker and Ruekert, 1987; Chakravarthy,
1986) and proves to be rather elusive if not also controversial (Eccles,
1991). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">The
literature review above suggests a number of possible measures of firm
performance, including financial indicators (those based on financial
ratios, cash flows, stock market risk-return indicators), operating
performance/efficiency indicators (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.133.4" class="koboSpan">labour
productivity, sales growth, asset turnover, “efficiency scores” based on
multiple inputs–outputs), and other performance indicators (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.133.5" class="koboSpan">innovation,
market share, customer satisfaction, social responsibility
“scores”).</span><sup><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fn0684" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fn0684"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan"> In order to enhance the reliability of the results and
strengthen any inference based on the results, it is important to adopt
multiple measures of performance and assess the robustness of the
results using different indicators of performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately,
however, when multiple criteria are adopted in performance
measurement/evaluation, one inevitably has to decide how best to
aggregate such criteria into a single easy-to-use “score”, or to decide
on a suitable “weighting
scheme”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fn0685" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fn0685"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan"> Naturally, certain performance indicators may be more
relevant to a given research objective than others, and thus should
receive more emphasis over the others.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.137.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
if the research objective is to examine the effect of corporate strategy
and practice on shareholder value, it seems appropriate to place
emphasis on measures of financial performance rather than operating
performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.137.3"
class="koboSpan">In reality, these measures are closely related rather
than diametrically opposed because high operational
performance/efficiency should eventually lead to high financial
performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.137.4"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, in any single research study the results
using different performance measures may be different, and it will be
useful to report the findings even when the data do not speak in the
same voice. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.137.5"
class="koboSpan">The reader can then weigh the various pieces of
empirical evidence before coming to a conclusion about shipping
companies’ performance.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">With respect to
studies that focus on the stock market performance of shipping
companies, an often-raised concern is their generally small sample size
(although in many cases the whole population of firms were examined),
the lack of a sufficiently rigorous research design, and tangential
contribution to the wider finance literature as a result of the industry
focus. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.138.2"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, these studies contribute to our knowledge
about the risk-return characteristics of the industry and the factors
driving shipping stock performance, and in some cases they do offer a
unique setting in which to test specific research hypotheses.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.138.3" class="koboSpan">This may be
considered an area of strength and is made possible by the researcher’s
in-depth knowledge of the industry itself and hence the
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_638"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">ability to structure empirical tests and/or to include
a concrete set of variables, something that may be difficult to do in
large sample studies typical in finance research.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.139.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
Cullinane and Gong (2002) utilise sector affiliation (water transport
versus other modes of transport, freight transport versus passenger
transport) to proxy for the level of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan">ex ante</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan"> uncertainty and are able to confirm the relationship
between this variable and the level of IPO underpricing.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">Such concrete
measures of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan">ex ante</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan"> uncertainty are difficult to find in the general
finance literature.</span>

## <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.144.2" class="koboSpan">Empirical Analysis: Measuring Performance Across Key Shipping Sectors</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">It is obvious from
the above discussion that it is important to illustrate how business
performance in shipping may be measured and also to gauge the possible
differences in the results when using different performance measures.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.145.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore, in
this section we present an empirical analysis of the performance of a
sample of publicly quoted shipping companies spanning the three key
shipping sectors, viz. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.145.3"
class="koboSpan">dry bulk, tanker and container shipping.</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 The performance measures</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">On the basis of the
discussion in the preceding sections, it is deemed appropriate to assess
performance using a number of key performance measures.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.147.2" class="koboSpan">The chosen
measures consist of competition performance measures, financial
performance measures, market-based performance measures and an
assessment of relative efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.147.3" class="koboSpan">The measures
are summarised in
</span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fig0315" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0315"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">This study provides
extensive findings on the relative productivity-efficiency and market
efficiency of maritime firms. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.150.2"
class="koboSpan">The relative productivity efficiency model incorporates
inputs and outputs related to operating performance consistent with the
prior financial accounting literature (Tsai
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2006; Barth
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1998; Collins
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1999).</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">As recognised by
Graham and Dodd (1962), fundamental analysis is a long-term oriented
exercise, where the management factor plays an essential role.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Well-managed
firms are more likely to keep generating a steady stream of revenues in
the future as well. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.157.3"
class="koboSpan">In general, firms aim at (a) maximising revenues given
their available resources; and/or (b) minimising cost given their output
production. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.157.4" class="koboSpan">To
determine these inputs and outputs we use information from the balance
sheet, income and cash flow statement.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.157.5" class="koboSpan">Specifically,
the first model (model 1) uses the following inputs and outputs:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">INPUTS:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">Total assets</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">Capex (capital
expenditure)</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">Employee (number of
employees)</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">OUTPUT:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">Revenue (Total
sales)</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan"> EBITDA</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan"> EBIT</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0315" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_639"></span>[](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0315)

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00335.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0315)

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">Following Tsai
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2006), the DEA methodology is employed to capture the
entirety of performance with respect to a set of output variables of
revenue, EBITDA, and operating profit (EBIT) with input variables of
total assets, capex, and employee numbers.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.169.2" class="koboSpan">Labour is
measured as the total number of employees (Karlaftis, 2004).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.169.3" class="koboSpan">The DEA
input-oriented models are chosen for the present study because cost
minimisation or reduction is used in this methodology (Tsai
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">et. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.170.2"
class="koboSpan">al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2006). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.171.2"
class="koboSpan">It is now popular to rely on non-GAAP financial
measures such as EBITDA and EBITDA margin (%) to assess the operating
performance of a company against that of its counterparts.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">This study sheds
light on the degree of relative market efficiency among maritime firms
as well. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.172.2"
class="koboSpan">Consistent with the efficient market hypothesis,
earnings, cash flows and book value shall contain significant
information for the valuation of market equity.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.172.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
second model (model 2) helps in identifying relative
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan">market</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan"> efficiency. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.174.2"
class="koboSpan">Following Barth
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1999), we assume that firm value is a function of
earnings, cash flow from operations and book value of equity:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">INPUTS:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">Earnings
(EBIT)</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan"> Cash flow from
operations</span>\
<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">Book value of
equity</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">OUTPUT:</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">Market Value (firms’
market price \* number of shares outstanding)</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_640"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">Barth
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1999) base their analysis on the valuation framework
in Ohlson (1999), in which the value relevance of an earnings component
depends on its ability to predict future abnormal earnings incremental
to abnormal earnings and the persistence of the component.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.185.2" class="koboSpan">Consistent
with their expectations they show that accruals and cash flows provide
explanatory power for equity market value incremental to equity book
value and abnormal earnings. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.185.3"
class="koboSpan">Our study is consistent with the Barth
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1999) valuation model.</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Sample</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">Our sample consists
of 18 major (leading) international maritime firms.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.189.2" class="koboSpan">The data on
inputs and outputs were collected from Datastream in 2007.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.189.3" class="koboSpan">Datastream
provides firm accounts and market information and places great emphasis
on accuracy, quality and consistency.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.189.4" class="koboSpan">Since our
study deals with markets which have different accounting systems, using
Datastream helps to mitigate the problem of inconsistency.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.189.5" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
to avoid exchange rate variation we denominated all figures to US
dollars.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">The sample firms are
shown in
</span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fig0316" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0316"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Empirical results: financial indicators</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">The results from the
analysis of the financial and market indicators are shown in
</span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fig0317" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0317"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.196.2"
class="koboSpan">We provide summary statistics for the performance
measures in
</span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fig0318" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0318"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">The results show that
the sample shipping firms have an average of 7% return on assets (ROA),
a ratio which indicates how profitable a company is relative to its
total assets. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.199.2"
class="koboSpan">The tanker and the dry bulk firms seem to out-perform
the container shipping firms in terms of ROA, with a ROA of 8% vs 4% for
the container shipping firms.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">A similar pattern is
observed for the return on investments (ROI) ratio.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.200.2" class="koboSpan">The average
ROI for all shipping firms is 10%.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.200.3" class="koboSpan">Again, the
tanker and dry bulk sectors exhibit a higher ROI than the container
sector.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">These findings are
mainly driven by the fact that container firms are generally much bigger
than tanker and dry bulk firms (see TA and ME in
</span>[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">Table
5</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_fig0318)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.203.2"
class="koboSpan">However, it must be stressed that any conclusions on
the basis of single financial ratio analysis need to be corroborated
with further evidence from using other indicators and should only be
considered as tentative in nature.</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0316" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00336.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0316)

</div>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0317" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_641"></span>[](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0317)

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00337.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0317)

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">As far as the Tobin’s
Q statistic is concerned, the shipping industry has an average value of
1.4, which indicates that the market value of the shipping sector is
greater than the value of the firms’ recorded assets.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">This suggests
that the market value reflects some unmeasured or unrecorded assets of
the shipping firms (i.e. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.3"
class="koboSpan">growth opportunities).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.4" class="koboSpan">Although all
three sectors have greater-than-unity Tobin’s Q, it seems that the dry
bulk firms have a slightly higher Tobin’s Q (1.5) than the tanker and
the container shipping firms (1.3).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.5" class="koboSpan">This may
suggest that dry bulk firms have more growth opportunities than other
shipping firms, presumably due to their greater flexibility to expand
their operations. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.6"
class="koboSpan">The results seem to be logical bearing in mind the
flexibility that characterises dry bulk shipping operations compared to
tanker and container ships. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.7"
class="koboSpan">In particular, dry bulk shipping may have higher growth
prospects because ships can be deployed more readily in areas and routes
that command higher freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.8" class="koboSpan">In contrast,
container ships by definition are deployed on fixed schedules
irrespective of the prevailing freight rates, whereas tankers need to
operate on specific routes to cater for oil demand and supply.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.206.9" class="koboSpan">Investors may
feel that the flexibility of dry bulk shipping firms provides them with
more growth opportunities, and these are accordingly reflected in a
higher market value.</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0318" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_642"></span>[](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0318)

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00338.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0318)

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_643"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan">The high growth prospects of the dry bulk sector are
confirmed by the growth rate in sales as well.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">Although the
average growth rate of the shipping sector is 26%, the dry bulk sector
exhibits a very high growth rate of 55%, which is almost five times
higher than the corresponding growth rate of the tanker and the
container sectors, which is 8% and 13%, respectively.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, the tanker
and the dry bulk firms seem to out-perform the container shipping firms
in terms of EBITDA margin, which measures a company’s power to generate
returns on shareholders’ investments.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.209.2" class="koboSpan">The tanker and
dry bulk sectors exhibit an average EBITDA margin of 53% and 64%,
respectively, whereas for the container sector it is 13%.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.209.3" class="koboSpan">These results
are in contrast to the DEA analysis of relative efficiency that is
carried out in the following section.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">A conclusion that
emerges from this analysis is the relative high pricing of dry bulk
shipping firms. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.210.2"
class="koboSpan">This could be due to one of two things: a) either dry
bulk shipping firms have more growth opportunities than other firms and
investors price these opportunities (correctly); or b) dry bulk shipping
firms are overpriced by investors (hence this becomes an issue of
mispricing). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.210.3"
class="koboSpan">Bearing in mind that only six firms from each sector
are used, these findings cannot be over-emphasised but instead should
only be interpreted as suggestive.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.210.4" class="koboSpan">One avenue for
future research is to first confirm these findings using all firms in
the dry bulk sector. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.210.5"
class="koboSpan">Asset pricing tests may then be conducted to explore
the growth-based explanation for the dry bulk sector relative to the
other sectors.</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 Empirical results: relative efficiency indicators</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">The data envelopment
analysis (DEA) approach ranks the performance of each stock relative to
the efficient frontier, indicating the (maximal output) production given
the optimal (minimal input) cost.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.212.2" class="koboSpan">For each
stock, we determine its location relative to the frontier.</span>

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">Table
5</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_fig0318)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan"> reports summary statistics for all inputs and outputs
used in our analysis (models 1 and 2).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.214.2" class="koboSpan">All variables
are expressed in thousand dollars (except the number of employees).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.214.3" class="koboSpan">The broad
range of values for market capitalisation (MV, TA), profitability (EBIT,
Revenue), and capital expenditure (Capex) indicates that the sample
consists of firms operating on different economic scales.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.214.4" class="koboSpan">For example,
the minimum EBIT of the sample is \$46.7K, whereas the maximum is
\$7,348.9K. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.214.5" class="koboSpan">In
particular, the summary statistics show that the sample includes both
small and large maritime companies.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.214.6" class="koboSpan">The smallest
firm in the sample has 408K total assets and 48 employees, whereas the
largest firm has 59,242K total assets and 108,530 employees.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">The results also
reveal a significant difference between the sizes of the three shipping
specialties. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.215.2"
class="koboSpan">Dry bulk shipping firms are small relative to the
tanker and container firms as far as the total assets, market value and
the number of employees are concerned.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.215.3" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, container shipping firms are by far the largest group.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.215.4" class="koboSpan">The average
total assets, market value and number of employees of the container
shipping firms are 17,144K, 10,920K, and 27,273, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.215.5" class="koboSpan">These figures
are almost four times higher than those of the tanker firms and more
than ten times higher than those of the dry bulk shipping firms.</span>

<a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fig0319" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0319"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the Spearman correlation coefficients of the
performance inputs and outputs. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.217.2"
class="koboSpan">Consistent with prior studies, market value and revenue
exhibit a high correlation with aggregate financial variables such as
EBIT, book value of equity, cash flow</span>

class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00339.jpg"

</div>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00340.jpg"

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">and total assets
(Barth </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1998; Collins
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1999). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.224.2"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, all input and output variables have a
positive and significant correlation between them.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.224.3" class="koboSpan">This is a
necessary and basic assumption of the DEA approach known as
“isotonicity”. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.224.4"
class="koboSpan">It guarantees that the increasing of an input will not
cause the decreasing output of another item.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.224.5" class="koboSpan">This result
corroborates the selection of our models.</span>

<a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fig0320" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0320"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows results on relative
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan">productivity</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan"> efficiency using model 1.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.228.2" class="koboSpan">The average
productivity efficiency of the maritime firms is 79.01%.
</span>[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">Table
7</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_fig0320)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that six maritime firms exhibit 100%
productivity efficiency using model 1.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.230.2" class="koboSpan">Two firms have
less than</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0321" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00341.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1. Productivity efficiency plot (EBITDA)" /></span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_646"></span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0165"
id="Ch022.xhtml_cap_lbl0165"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1.</span></span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan"> Productivity efficiency plot (EBITDA)</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.234.1" class="koboSpan">This figure describes
the DEA efficiency ratings using model 1 for relative productivity
efficiency. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.234.2" class="koboSpan">Y
axis is % efficiency score and X axis is EBITDA.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">50% productivity
efficiency. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.235.2"
class="koboSpan">The six 100% productivity efficient firms (of our
sample) are TBS International, Excel Maritime Carriers, Evergreen
marine, Frontline, Neptune Orient Lines, and Mitsui OSK Lines.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.235.3" class="koboSpan">Eagle Bulk
Shipping is the firm with the worst productivity efficiency rate
relative to its competitors (</span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_cap_lbl0165"
id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0165"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">Table
7</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_fig0320)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan"> also shows the EBITDA margins (%) of each firm.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.239.2" class="koboSpan">A higher
EBITDA margin means that a company has free cash flows to make
investments and generate returns on shareholders’ investments.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.239.3" class="koboSpan">Our sample
firms exhibit a mean of 43.74% EBITDA margin.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.239.4" class="koboSpan">This low level
of financial performance is in sharp contrast with our findings on
productivity efficiency using the DEA approach.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.239.5" class="koboSpan">Only the
EBITDA margin of Dryships (93.73%) is consistent with its high DEA
productivity efficiency score (87.08%).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.239.6" class="koboSpan">It is worth
noting that Eagle Bulk Shipping has a high EBITDA margin (63.04%)
relative to its corresponding low DEA efficiency score.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">As far as the average
efficiency scores of the three shipping sectors are concerned,
</span>[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">Table
7</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_fig0320)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that the container firms are more productivity
efficient than the tanker and the dry bulk shipping firms.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.242.2" class="koboSpan">The container
shipping firms have a mean efficiency score of 86.4%, whereas the
tankers and the dry bulk shipping firms have a mean of 74.8% and 73.5%,
respectively. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.242.3"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, the average EBITDA margin of these
groups shows the opposite results.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.242.4" class="koboSpan">Particularly,
the container shipping firms have a very low EBITDA margin (14.5%)
relative to the tankers and the dry bulk shipping firms, which have an
average EBITDA margin of 74.8% and 73.5%, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.242.5" class="koboSpan">These
differences between the two measures of performance are consistent with
the argument that it is not proper to draw conclusions based on only two
financial variables. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.242.6"
class="koboSpan">The advantage of the DEA approach is the ability to
consider various input and output variables simultaneously.</span>

<a href="#Ch022.xhtml_fig0322" id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0322"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.243.1" class="koboSpan">Table 8</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows market efficiency rates using model 2.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.244.2" class="koboSpan">Model 2
calculates market efficiency rates by maximising the market
capitalisation (output) given the corresponding</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0322" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_647"></span>[](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0322)

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00342.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fig0322)

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">earnings, cash flow
and book value of equity (inputs), the three primary summary measures of
the income and cash flow statements and balance sheet.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.246.2" class="koboSpan">Moreover,
</span>[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">Table
8</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_fig0322)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan"> provides the percentage market value improvement
required by each firm in order to achieve 100% relative market
efficiency. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.248.2"
class="koboSpan">This is the optimal market value (given the
corresponding earnings, cash flow and book value of equity) that would
set (shift) the firm on the efficient frontier.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">According to
</span>[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">Table
8</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_fig0322)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan">, the maritime firms exhibit an average market
efficiency of 77.05% (</span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_cap_lbl0166"
id="Ch022.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0166"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.253.2"
class="koboSpan">Five (5) of the maritime firms are 100% efficient,
whereas only one (1) firm exhibits less than 50% market efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.253.3" class="koboSpan">The firms with
the highest relative market efficiency score (100%) are Eagle Bulk
Shipping, Dryships, Frontline, Nippon Yusen KK, and Mitsui OSK Lines.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.253.4" class="koboSpan">A.P.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.253.5" class="koboSpan">Moller-Maersk
is the firm with the</span>

<div id="Ch022.xhtml_fig0323" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00343.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2. Market efficiency plot (ME)" /></span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_648"></span><a href="#Ch022.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0166"
id="Ch022.xhtml_cap_lbl0166"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2.</span></span></a><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan"> Market efficiency plot (ME)</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">This figure describes
the DEA efficiency ratings using model 2 for relative market efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.257.2" class="koboSpan">Y axis is %
efficiency score and X axis is market value of equity (ME).</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">smallest market
efficiency score (39.7%). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.258.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, two firms (Frontline and Mitsui) are
consistently rated as productivity and market efficient; as far as the
DEA efficiency scores are concerned (Mitsui OSK has a very low EBITDA
margin). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.258.3" class="koboSpan">It is
noted that although Eagle Bulk Shipping is not productivity efficient,
it is 100% market efficient. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.258.4"
class="koboSpan">Conversely, A.P.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.258.5" class="koboSpan">Moller–Maersk
is 94.7% productivity efficient, but it is not market efficient.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">In terms of the
market efficiency of the three shipping sectors,
</span>[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">Table
8</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_fig0322)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that the container shipping firms are more
market efficient (84.72%) than the dry bulk shipping firms (77.96%), and
the dry bulk sector is more market efficient than the tanker firms
(68.46%). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.261.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, container firms seem to be both productivity
and market efficient. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.261.3"
class="koboSpan">Although tanker and dry bulk shipping firms exhibit
similar productivity efficiency, dry bulk firms appear more market
efficient than tanker firms, though the difference is relatively
small.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">In summary,
conclusions on the productivity and market efficiency of the maritime
firms seem to depend on the specific performance measure used.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.262.2" class="koboSpan">It seems that
the container shipping sector is the most robust sector, being both
productivity and market efficient, whereas the tanker and dry bulk
sectors exhibit mixed evidence.</span>

## <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.263.2" class="koboSpan">Discussion and Implications</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.264.1" class="koboSpan">The discussions above
suggest several avenues for future research.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.264.2" class="koboSpan">First, there
is a need to more systematically and rigorously evaluate the performance
of shipping companies using multiple measures of operating and financial
performance as well as in the use of inputs and outputs for relative
efficiency measurement.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">Performance should be
measured both in absolute terms and relative to a chosen benchmark, such
as the industry average (in the case of using accounting ratios or
operating efficiency measures) or risk-adjusted metrics (as in stock
performance evaluation). </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.265.2"
class="koboSpan">Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) and Stochastic Frontier
Analysis have been extensively used in studies of container terminal or
port/airport performance but there
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_page_649"></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">is room to apply these and other performance
measurement methods (e.g. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.266.2"
class="koboSpan">Balanced Scorecard) to shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.266.3" class="koboSpan">One advantage
of these performance measurement methods (especially when the right
inputs and outputs are used) is that they may overcome difficulties in
making international comparisons which may result from
inconsistencies/differences in accounting and taxation rules in
different countries (Schefczyk, 1993).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.266.4" class="koboSpan">By capturing
the multi-dimensional nature of business performance, they may also
mitigate inference problems arising from the use of only a small number
of performance measures (variables).</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">In this chapter for
instance we used data envelopment analysis (DEA) to estimate the
so-called “efficient frontier” of international maritime firms in the
dry bulk, tanker and container sectors in order to analyse deviations
from such frontier corresponding to loss of efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.267.2" class="koboSpan">Consistent
with Barth, Beaver and Landsman (1998), we build on the seminal work of
Ohlson (1995) and Feltham and Ohlson (1995) concerning accounting-based
valuation models. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.267.3"
class="koboSpan">The use of this approach is innovative in the shipping
industry context.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.268.1" class="koboSpan">The second future
research opportunity is to investigate the possible determinants of
differential performance levels among shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.268.2" class="koboSpan">Both
within-country studies and cross-countries studies can be undertaken.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.268.3" class="koboSpan">Taken
together, these studies have the potential to shed light on
institutional, firm-specific as well as market-specific factors that are
associated with differential performance.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.268.4" class="koboSpan">Knowledge of
such factors is important for making informed decisions in resource
deployment and allocation. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.268.5"
class="koboSpan">In this regard, the finance, economics and management
literature offers much useful guidance on the possible factors that
determine firm performance. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.268.6"
class="koboSpan">A comprehensive review of this literature, supplemented
by implications for the shipping industry, is currently lacking but is
warranted. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.268.7"
class="koboSpan">This chapter makes an initial attempt at this important
task.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">On the managerial and
policy front, it will be useful to conduct more research on the
long-term performance of shipping companies conditional on the adoption
of a certain corporate strategy or change in industry policy.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.269.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
it will be of interest to know how shipping companies’ risk or cost of
capital is affected by regulatory changes such as implementation of the
International Safety Management (ISM) Code or the Tanker Management and
Self Assessment approach (TMSA).
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.269.3" class="koboSpan">It is also of
interest to assess the change (if any) in the competitive positioning of
a shipping company subsequent to the formation of alliances,
privatisation or restructuring. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.269.4"
class="koboSpan">There are only a limited number of studies that look
into these interesting topics, and the majority of the existing studies
tend to focus on short-term (as opposed to long-term) stock market
reactions. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.269.5"
class="koboSpan">Gong (2009) reviews some of the related studies in the
transport industry and presents a detailed discussion of the event study
methodology that is well suited for this type of research.</span>

<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.270.1" class="koboSpan">Given the distinct
possibility that different performance measures (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.270.2" class="koboSpan">financial,
operating, and market-based measures) may lead to different conclusions
on business performance, it is important to conduct a robustness check
by applying multiple performance measures before drawing any concrete
conclusion. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.270.3"
class="koboSpan">Only after such thorough analyses can reliable
conclusions be drawn on the profitability and performance of the
shipping industry as a whole, or of specific companies that have adopted
specific strategies. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.270.4"
class="koboSpan">Well-supported evidence of this type, which is
currently missing, will be useful to all of (existing as well as
prospective) investors in shipping, industry analysts, corporate
managers, and policy makers alike.</span>

### <span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">Endnotes</span>

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan">1.</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fn0684)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the shipping market context, Lagoudis, Lalwani and
Naim (2006) use 24 factors in 4 categories (quality, service, cost and
cycle time) to measure the performance (in terms of creating value) of
ocean transportation companies. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.284.2"
class="koboSpan">They find that the companies surveyed place the
strongest emphasis on quality but the least emphasis on time as a value
contributor. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.284.3"
class="koboSpan">Also see Chou and Liang (2001) for the use of multiple
criteria in assessing shipping company performance.</span>

[<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan">2.</span>](#Ch022.xhtml_bck_fn0685)<span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan"> Jensen (2001) argues for a single corporate objective
function, i.e. </span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.286.2"
class="koboSpan">maximising a firm’s long-term total market value, in
contrast with the view of traditional stakeholder theory which argues
for taking into account the interests of all stakeholders in a firm
including not only financial claimants but also employees, customers,
communities and even the environment.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.286.3" class="koboSpan">He proposes a
variant of value maximisation, known as Enlightened Value Maximization,
and argues it is identical to enlightened stakeholder theory (and
Balanced Scorecard, the managerial equivalent of stakeholder
theory).</span>

</div>

</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.568.2" class="koboSpan">and Amit, R.
</span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.568.3" class="koboSpan">(2008): “The
fit between product market strategy and business model: Implications for
firm performance”,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.569.1"
class="koboSpan">Strategic Management
Journal</span></span><span id="Ch022.xhtml_kobo.570.1"
class="koboSpan">, 29(1), 1–26.</span>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<span id="part9.xhtml"></span>

<div id="part9.xhtml_book-columns">

<div id="part9.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="part9.xhtml_page_656"></span><span id="part9.xhtml_page_657"></span>[<span id="part9.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Part Nine</span>\
<span id="part9.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping Investment, Finance and Strategy</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0491)

</div>
