<span id="Ch023.xhtml"></span>

<div id="Ch023.xhtml_book-columns">

<div id="Ch023.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_658"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_659"></span>[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 23</span>\
<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Investing in Twenty-First Century Shipping: An Essay on Perennial Constraints, Risks and </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.3.1" class="koboSpan">Great Expectations</span></span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0492)
====================================================================================================================================================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Helen</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Thanopoulou</span></span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0686" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0686"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.7.3" class="koboSpan">Investing In Ships Revisited</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">The extraordinary
twists and turns of the world economy since the start of the
twenty-first century could not be more revealing or instructive of the
inner workings of shipping investment.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping
economics exist as a separate branch of economics for two reasons: the
one is the cyclicality of the shipping markets; the other is the
idiosyncratic nature of shipping investment.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.8.3" class="koboSpan">The two are
inextricably linked: Investing in ships could be classified as an
astute, a brave or an irrational decision depending on the state and the
prospects of the shipping markets which rarely – if ever – fulfil the
promises they seem to give. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.8.4"
class="koboSpan">Yet the first decade of the current century unfolded as
if this latter element of uncertainty had been removed as investors
proceeded euphorically into taking the world fleet well over the one
billion dwt
mark.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0687" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0687"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan"> However, by the end of 2008 any doubts whether the
“endemic tendency to over-invest”, as astutely described by the late
B.N. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.10.2"
class="koboSpan">Metaxas,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0688" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0688"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan"> stills holds in shipping had dissolved as freight rate
lows - not seen since the dry-bulk crisis of the 1980s – succeeded the
records the market had kept breaking since 2003.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">Late 2008
developments were not, however, the result of investors’
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">great
expectations.</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan"> As the first decade of the new century is drawing to a
close pending massive future deliveries have yet to hit the market in
order to be measured against future demand which remains an unknown
quantity, literally. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.14.2"
class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, the prospect of supply developments
coinciding with an eventually protracted world trade recession have
revived investors’ worst basic fears while painfully inviting a return
to well-known basics of shipping economics.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">Less than a year from
September 2008 – and about a quarter of a century later from the early
1980s – a familiar picture has formed: dearth of orders, death of
shipyards, creation of equity funds to target distress sales of
second-hand vessels as companies winding-down leave wound-up creditors
with few options than to foreclose.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Looking at this
last cycle of shipping investment there are few better expressions to
describe the
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_660"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan">way events have been unfolding than
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan">Plus ça change plus c’est la même
chose</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.18.1"
class="koboSpan">”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0689" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0689"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan"> Despite main mechanisms and results remaining the
same, the picture in shipping investment has changed also: firstly in
the way physical and paper assets intertwine in what can be considered
anymore as commonly managed shipping-based portfolios; second, in the
way changes in the transactional setting in shipping resulted in
aggravating risks or even adding new to the “standard” one of market
cyclicality. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.20.2"
class="koboSpan">All types of risk were highlighted most powerfully in
the light of the manifestation of the “credit crunch” as a full-blown
“credit crash” in late 2008, upsetting markets along with theoretical
dogmas considered until then not only academically definitive but also
final.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0690" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0690"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter focuses
on traditional investment in physical shipping assets.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">The main text
begins with familiarising the reader with the idiosyncrasies of shipping
investment in the second section.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.22.3" class="koboSpan">Section 3
analyses the operational constraints that bulk and liner companies face
when deciding to invest in either new or second hand-vessels.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.22.4" class="koboSpan">Section 4
discusses the difficult balancing act of weighing anticipated vessel
endurance, cost differences and delivery lags in the investment
decision; section 5 focuses on asset play on the basis of the experience
from the last major shipping crisis with references to the period before
and after the September 2008 financial crisis.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.22.5" class="koboSpan">The penultimate
section 6 of the chapter reviews the setting for shipping investment in
the twenty-first century while the summary in section 7 concludes by
pointing to research themes that this decade’s developments bring to the
fore.</span>

## <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">Market Cyclicality and Investment in Commercial Vessels</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Market cycles are
common in competitive markets; fully competitive markets are, however,
rather uncommon in the modern economy.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">As discussed
earlier in this volume, while price fluctuations of fixed assets can be
assessed in other markets, there is little comparison with the
volatility asset prices in shipping have
shown.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0691" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0691"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan"> The parallel effect of recessional factors on the
shipping, shipbuilding and – usually – scrapping
markets</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0692" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0692"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan"> create an absolute impasse for investors who often
found themselves with very substantial amounts of tied-up capital and
practically little or no alternative use for assets often valued at no
more than an insignificant fraction of their acquisition price.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">Equally, as
developments related to cancellations following the 2008 financial
crisis reminded, precipitated adjustments of previous investment
decisions are achievable, often at a price that cash-poor market
conditions may justify as entirely necessary, but can hardly qualify as
totally ideal.</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Investing in the different shipping segments</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">While volatility of
asset prices can vary between individual shipping
markets,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0693" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0693"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> due to differences in the market structure of
traditional and specialised bulk shipping
markets,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0694" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0694"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan"> it remains a common feature of all bulk shipping
segments which make-up the majority of the world tonnage.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.34.2" class="koboSpan">Liner shipping
is not exempt from asset price volatility either; while liner shipping
idiosyncrasies may dictate a different approach with regard to
investment, recent policy and market developments have increased risk
for investors in container vessels as well.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">As far as the bulk
markets are concerned, volatility of both the freight markets and of
asset prices should be considered as the key factors which should – or
at least
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_661"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">common sense would require so – weigh heavily on all
decisions regarding investment in merchant vessels.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.36.2" class="koboSpan">In practice, an
ex post analysis of investment decisions reveals that despite volumes of
literature and a series of investment disasters there is still little
practical understanding of the nature of the bulk shipping markets and
of their idiosyncrasies. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.36.3"
class="koboSpan">In this sense, the repetitive nature of shipping
over-investment remains a conundrum especially when considering industry
returns,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0695" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0695"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan"> pointing to either
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">lack </span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan">of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan">investment memory
</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">or
simply to the competitive nature of most shipping markets, or to a
combination of both. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.42.2"
class="koboSpan">The history of world shipping is fraught with examples
of crises that can be blamed on excessive ordering more than they can be
blamed on any other
factor.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0696" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0696"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan"> When the competitive behaviour of investors is taken
into account in the context of the competitive nature of most of the
industry, the textbook ignorance of individual investors regarding the
impact of their own investment decisions is put in context.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.44.2" class="koboSpan">What is,
however, definitely intriguing is that patterns of over-ordering can be
easily traced in this century even in markets where “speculative”
investment (i.e. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.44.3"
class="koboSpan">investment with no guaranteed demand) was previously
unknown. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.44.4" class="koboSpan">This
has been the case of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG)
carriers,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0697" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0697"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan"> since around the millennium, as the segment was
evolving from a
“hybrid”</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0698" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0698"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">quasi-market</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan"> to its current –
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">more or
less</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">
competitive than other shipping
markets</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0699" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0699"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan"> – structure. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.53.2"
class="koboSpan">Regardless, however, of how different in nature the
different bulk shipping segments can be, the inherent risks investors
face are more or less common; they only differ in terms of the
particular weight they can potentially hold in each individual market.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.53.3" class="koboSpan">Although the
risks discussed below apply mostly to bulk shipping, it should be noted
that the liner sector – shielded to a degree from excessively violent
fluctuations until lately – remained exposed throughout its modern
existence to the potential risks of large sunk costs and of
technological obsolescence. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.53.4"
class="koboSpan">In one of these synchronicities that abound in
shipping, the manifestation of the financial crisis coincided with the
end of the exemption of shipping conferences from European competition
regulation; this was about a decade after US trades had seen the power
of conferences weakened through the practical
implications</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0700" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0700"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan"> of OSRA 1998. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.55.2"
class="koboSpan">Both regulatory changes increased the exposure of liner
shipping to trade volatility; shortly after September 2008, the latter
led to rate levels associated usually with bulk segments, smoothing in
its wake differences between bulk and liner shipping investment
risks.</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Different markets – common risks</span>

#### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">2.2.1 Uncertainty taken to the extreme</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">The first and foremost
risk investors face when committing their money to bulk shipping comes
from market volatility. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.58.2"
class="koboSpan">Most markets tend to present fluctuations more in terms
of volume of sales than in terms of price levels.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.58.3" class="koboSpan">Bulk fleets
which constitute the bulk of the world’s
tonnage</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0701" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0701"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan"> as well, are as a rule affected by both vessel
unemployment and rapidly declining prices at times of ever-returning
shipping recessions which can appear with or without any – mostly
unheeded by investors – warning. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.60.2"
class="koboSpan">Liner owners have been finding increasingly that their
predicament is not dissimilar. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.60.3"
class="koboSpan">The quick reversal of shipping market conditions in the
second half of 2008 has been in itself a “crash” course in what S.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.60.4" class="koboSpan">Kaplan and B.J.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.60.5" class="koboSpan">Garrick defined
in 1981 as the “set of triplets” related to
risk:</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0702" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0702"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan"> the specific
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">scenario”
</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">was in
the minds of very few at the time the bulk of – bulk and liner – orders
had been placed; it was considered of low
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">likelihood”
</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">in the
context of ever-growing confidence in infallible markets, but eventually
the sheer force
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_662"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">of the painfully felt
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan">consequence”
</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">finally
showed the range of magnitude that should have been attributed to the
risk taken. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.69.2"
class="koboSpan">While common investment appraisal techniques had
traditionally not served shipping, even more modern approaches could
well prove of limited use in investment planning in such extraordinary
circumstances.</span>

#### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">2.2.2 Problematic fitting of common investment appraisal techniques</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">The risk of reduced
sales or asset inactivity can be deemed common for shipping and all
other markets. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.71.2"
class="koboSpan">However, the prospect of freight levels continuously
fluctuating not only adds to the real risk of investment, it also
renders attempts for calculating this risk accurately rather
ineffective. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.71.3"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, most common investment appraisal techniques
require some degree of assumed stability of prices or a predictable path
of price changes and a reasonable chance of assets being fully employed
when the investment starts yielding.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.71.4" class="koboSpan">In the case of
bulk ships, common investment appraisal techniques can prove highly
misleading and their role should be limited to that of a guide about
what the investment would cost and what would be the expected
return.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0703" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0703"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan"> More sophisticated approaches need to take into
account long-term factors which are not always visible to outsiders to
the industry. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.73.2"
class="koboSpan">Unless investors and lenders alike are well versed in
shipping market volatility incorporating it into any effort to appraise
returns,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0704" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0704"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan"> only chance can reconcile predictions to
results.</span>

#### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">2.2.3 Large sunk costs</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">High volatility of
freight rates and asset price volatility combine to create the perfect
nightmare for the potential investor especially when resale values and
alternative uses of the vessel themselves are considered.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">As already
underlined, the scrap market usually shifts in parallel with the markets
for shipping services and the markets for ships; this has been most
evident over the crisis of the 1970s and the 1980s.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.77.3" class="koboSpan">That results in
a barrier to exit which is difficult to surmount by a resale of the
vessel for storage or other
uses.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0705" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0705"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is perhaps better that too many investors go ahead
with their plans ignoring the worst-case scenario or shipping would have
become a market suffering from chronic under-investment: taking into
account how few alternative uses and potential resale opportunities
there are in a crisis should normally make the bravest of investors fret
when considering the potential market depreciation of their assets.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.79.2" class="koboSpan">While there are
few sunk costs of another nature for bulk shipping companies, liner
companies face an additional sunk cost as they tend to invest heavily in
offices, agency networks and, eventually, terminals as well.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.79.3" class="koboSpan">The relative
stability of liner shipping business compared to the degree of
volatility of bulk shipping markets and the nature of liner competition
in the past moderated the exposure to sunk costs by limiting not their
potential magnitude in absolute terms but the likelihood of the related
scenario. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.79.4"
class="koboSpan">However, adverse trade developments following the
recent downturn, coupled by the impressive growth of the container fleet
and the termination of the EU conference exemption, have changed the
picture so drastically as to allow what has been recorded as
“zero”</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0706" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0706"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan"> rates to be observed in main routes.</span>

#### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">2.2.4 Technological obsolescence</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">Ships not only become
obsolete by wear and tear; they can also become obsolete through the
introduction of a new type of vessel which would be deemed superior in
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_663"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">terms of quality of service or indeed in terms of cost
for providing shipping services. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.84.2"
class="koboSpan">The product life cycle, as introduced by Dean many
decades
ago,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0707" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0707"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan"> finds application both in terms of types of tonnage as
well as in terms of type of
service.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0708" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0708"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan"> Although rarely taken into
account</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0709" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0709"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">, technological obsolescence can reverse estimates of
investment returns and shorten the economic life of a vessel
dramatically. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.90.2"
class="koboSpan">Developments in recent years in both specialised bulk
shipping markets, such as reefers, and in liner shipping, which had
provided in the 1960s the prominent example of the replacement of
conventional general cargo ships by cellular ones, require that the
impact of what could be termed broadly technological obsolescence –
incorporating the aspect of size – and ensuing commercial obsolescence
are taken into account. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.90.3"
class="koboSpan">In bulk shipping, the fading-out of an entire segment
of specialised bulk
tonnage</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0710" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0710"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan"> proved inevitable as technology and economies of scale
combined to allow the cost-competitive carriage of cargo under
controlled temperatures in suitable containers by liner operators.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">In the liner
sector, unless smaller markets develop at a pace sufficient to absorb
lower-capacity vessels removed from the main routes as carriers take
advantage of economies of scale (or ironically unless trade declines to
take vessel-capacity requirements to past levels), previous container
vessel generations are extremely
vulnerable</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0711" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0711"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan"> as new larger ones add to competitors’ fleets.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">These examples
from both liner and bulk shipping show a degree of commonality in terms
of the risks investors are faced with in both markets; however, it is
not necessarily so in terms of constraints under which investment
decisions are taken in bulk and liner shipping although in the latter
case the distinction between investor-operator and investor in tonnage
alone becomes critical.</span>

## <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">Operational Constraints of Bulk and Liner Acquisitions</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Examining investment
attitudes automatically leads to discussing the particular constraints
operating companies face when proceeding to vessel acquisitions.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.96.2" class="koboSpan">The question of
company motives for investing seems
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">prima
facie</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">
naive; a blanket statement on profit maximisation would seem to provide
the rule. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.98.2"
class="koboSpan">However, as business
goals</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0712" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0712"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan"> can deviate from this axiom so can investment motives.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">In the case of
shipping this will be largely dependant on the nature of the shipping
company. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.100.3"
class="koboSpan">Although a small minority today, state enterprises had
been a force to be reckoned
with</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0713" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0713"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"> in the not too distant past and for some, at the time,
the potential source of threats to free competition in shipping which
has yet to materialise. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.102.2"
class="koboSpan">State companies, however, are likely to have different
motives than the typical shipping company of private ownership when
considering investment. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.102.3"
class="koboSpan">By the same token, the profit maximisation rule is
unlikely to apply to integrated shipping divisions of non-shipping
companies; the most known example of companies of the latter type
historically is that of shipping divisions or
subsidiaries</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0714" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0714"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan"> of large oil
companies.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0715" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0715"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the case of state companies the motive for an
investment decision might be the balance of payments, national security,
including securing supply chains, or eventually that of national
prestige;</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0716" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0716"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan"> all result equally in particular constraints under
which investment decisions have to be taken.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">If investment
would for instance be decided to align to the growth of national trades,
new investment could be a multiple of what competitive advantage and
ship values would dictate, assuming that cash-flow and capital
availability do not come into play in the case of state companies.
</span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0167"
id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0167"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan"> summarises the different positions of each main type
of shipping</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_664"></span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0167"
id="Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0167"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan"> Investment/divestment constraints in
shipping</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0717" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0717"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup>

<div id="Ch023.xhtml_tbl0004" class="table"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

| <span class="bold"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">Company type</span></span> | <span class="bold"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">Constraints</span></span> |
|:---|:---|
| <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Bulk</span> | <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">insignifi cant in most cases</span> |
| <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">Liner</span> | <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">frequency constraints, cooperation constraints, route constraints</span> |
| <span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">Non-commercial:</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan"> state-owned or integrated</span> | <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">�share� of own transport as defi ned/desired by parent company or state policy</span> |

</div>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">company
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">vis-á-vis</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan"> the potential special constraints under which they
consider new investment in tonnage in addition to habitual business ones
associated with investment decisions.</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Investing in bulk shipping: no holds barred</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">The most significant
differences in terms of investment constraints exist between liner and
bulk shipping companies (assuming both are under private ownership).
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.127.2" class="koboSpan">Bulk shipping
companies, unlike liner companies, are usually exempt of limitations
when programming investment or divestment in ships and hence determining
company size. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.127.3"
class="koboSpan">In most cases a bulk shipping company will invest (or
divest) in whatever type or size of bulk vessel it considers profitable
on the basis of the state and the prospects of the freight and ship
markets. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.127.4" class="koboSpan">A
bulk shipping company mainly active in the dry bulk sector may invest in
tanker vessels also or even completely shift from the dry to the liquid
bulk market if the prospects of the tanker market look more promising or
vice-versa.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0718" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0718"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan"> By the same token, a bulk company can choose to
diversify by investing into more than one bulk shipping segment
including specialised shipping markets.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">Investment/
divestment flexibility may be affected mainly due to governance or
regulation issues pertaining to specific company structures such as
listed companies. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.129.3"
class="koboSpan">However, when it comes to the specialised bulk shipping
segments absolute investment freedom might in reality prove a little
more relative: specialised vessel types, such as Liquefied Petroleum Gas
carriers (LPGs), Liquefied Natural Gas carriers (LNGs) or chemical
carriers, still require a significant degree of know-how and experience
to consider entry into these markets as automatic or barrier free.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.129.4" class="koboSpan">The role of
bulk shipping
pools</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0719" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0719"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan"> in the specialised shipping markets and of other
companies open to manage outside tonnage alongside their own or
eventually act as managers
only,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0720" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0720"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan"> has nevertheless preserved the right of shipowners to
enter with minimum investment even in specialised shipping segments;
shipping pools had been found, however, to be a constraint for owners
when it comes to divestment affecting asset-play
opportunities.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0721" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0721"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Investing in liner tonnage: operational and cooperation constraints</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">Liner shipping
companies are without doubt under more constraints when considering
their investment policy not only by comparison to bulk shipping
companies but also
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_665"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">by comparison to a large number of industries.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.137.2" class="koboSpan">These
constraints relate not only to the specific characteristics of the
routes these companies serve, but also to the cooperation agreements
liner companies usually have; very few, usually among the top two or
three largest, have historically survived successfully without resorting
to what has been described as strategic or operational alliances of
various
forms.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0722" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0722"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan"> Pools and consortia – the latter evolving over the
last 15 years into global alliances – have dominated the supply of liner
shipping
services;</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0723" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0723"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan"> these forms of cooperation between container carriers
allowed to combine capacity to serve trade routes which became
increasingly demanding in terms of capacity and frequency.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">Operational
cooperation normally requires that operational capacity adjustments –
and hence investment decisions – are planned from a common perspective
otherwise under-utilisation of capacity and problems in network
planning, or equipment incompatibity lurk.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">It is possible
that a combination of these constraints together with the eagerness of
outside
investors</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0724" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0724"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan"> to invest in the container market has led to an –
increasing over recent years – part of tonnage being drawn from the
container charter
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0725" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0725"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan"> The nature of the liner business itself, which is the
provision of regular advertised and – increasingly over the
globalisation era – frequent sailings of containerships, precludes
drastic capacity reductions or service withdrawals through massive
asset-play motivated divestment due to loss of
goodwill,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0726" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0726"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan"> cyclical downturns notwithstanding.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.147.2" class="koboSpan">In this regard
the combination of co-operation agreements together with the existence
of a pool of container tonnage available in the container charter market
has added to the flexibility of liner shipping companies which would
otherwise remain much more restricted than their bulk counterparts in
terms of freedom in investment and divestment decisions.</span>

## <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.148.2" class="koboSpan">Newbuilding Vs Second-Hand Vessels: Balancing Delivery Lags With Vessel Endurance</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">Both bulk and liner
companies, are faced with a number of alternative choices when they
decide to proceed with new investment.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.149.2" class="koboSpan">Although often
a fraction of such levels, deep-sea going vessel values, especially of
newbuildings, have been on average in the order of tens of millions of
dollars in the past decades. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.149.3"
class="koboSpan">The globalisation of the shipbuilding industry and the
expansion of capacity have resulted in multiplying choices for placing
orders but equally in dividing prices by a factor analogous to the
observed successive waves of shipbuilding capacity coming into the
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0727" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0727"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">Despite, however, the
relatively easy access to shipping investment through the enlargement of
the circle of shipbuilding competitors, aggressive
competition</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0728" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0728"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan"> and abundant finance in the post-war period, the role
of fixed cost remains critical for shipping competitiveness.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.153.2" class="koboSpan">In this
regard, the choice between investing in a newbuilding or in a
second-hand vessel must take into account
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan">market prospects for both the freight and –
</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">the
closely
related</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan"> – ship
markets</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">current price
levels</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">
as well as </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">price
differences</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan"> between new and old tonnage.</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Know thy market: New-orders vs second-hand acquisitions</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">Acquiring vessels is
perhaps the major pillar of company strategy in an industry environment
that is characterised by cyclicality of both income and asset values
especially when the exit barriers already discussed are taken into
account. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.163.2" class="koboSpan">The
realisation by
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_666"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan">many firms of the importance of investment decisions in
this context is perhaps at the origin of the popularity of second-hand
acquisitions of vessels. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.164.2"
class="koboSpan">Otherwise, taking into account the existence of
abundant finance and – for most of the post-war period – of attractive
prices, grants or of a combination of all of the above, it would seem
surprising that second-hand vessels would be an investment option at
all. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.164.3" class="koboSpan">Investing
in secondhand tonnage implies not only a shorter economic life of the
vessel but also assuming the risk of hidden defaults that can eventually
still remain undetectable despite strict checks before the purchase of
the vessel.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">The reasons for the
popularity of second-hand acquisitions are in essence two-fold: (a) when
investing in a second-hand ship the shipping company faces a much lower
capital
cost</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0729" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0729"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan"> compared to the alternative of a newbuilding; and (b)
the waiting time for the actual delivery of the ship is minimal compared
to the “normal” 1.5 to two years in the case of new orders.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">Normality is,
however, the exception in a competitive market entirely open and
extremely vulnerable to the influence of a multitude of exogenous
factors. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.167.3" class="koboSpan">The
quick reversal of market conditions due to the oil shock of 1973 is in
that sense a classic example which shows how investment in newbuildings
can prove riskier than investment in second-hand vessels.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.167.4" class="koboSpan">During the
first half of the 1970s the expected delivery lag for orders placed at
the time was often much longer than the 18–24 month usual
range.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0730" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0730"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan"> As the case of the 1970s proved, lags can be
catastrophic if vessels are to be delivered so late that they cannot
catch even a glimpse of the short booms which characterise
shipping;</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0731" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0731"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan"> investors placing orders in the final years of the
latest peak were painfully reminded so.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.171.2" class="koboSpan">Delays
guarantee that delivery will come after – or sometimes long after – the
relatively brief period of prosperity has degenerated into a lengthy
recession if not into a full-blown depression as the case was for many
segments in the crisis of the 1970s and the 1980s.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">In view of these
remarks, it could seem that opting for readily available second-hand
vessels while freight rates are still climbing is more effective.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.172.2" class="koboSpan">At least the
market seems to share such a view as price differentials between
new-buildings and second-hand vessels tend to narrow – or even reverse –
as shipbuilding availability
tightens;</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0732" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0732"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan"> the repeat of this phenomenon in the twenty-first
century has a long history in modern shipping as data for the first
post-World War II years
suggest.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0733" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0733"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">47</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan"> Yet, as the most important disadvantage of a
second-hand acquisition is the – normally – much shorter economic life
of the ship, narrowing price differentials between new and second-hand
tonnage during market booms are a strong indication that shipping
investors obey to laws particular to this industry and often to this
industry alone: while the short duration of shipping booms is perhaps
the only certainty one can have about bulk shipping markets, even
cash-tight companies risk their liquidity betting on excessively priced
second-hand vessels at the peak of the market.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.176.2" class="koboSpan">The multitude
of arrests and foreclosures at the downturn of markets serve as ex-post
evidence that rationality of expectations or just plain
rationality</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0734" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0734"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">48</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan"> has found its way into the academic books but not in
investment behaviour in shipping.</span>

## <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.179.2" class="koboSpan">Investment Strategies, Risk and Asset Play: a Twenty-First Century Perspective</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">The frequent and very
ample fluctuations of second-hand ship prices which follow in general
the fluctuations in the freight rates – albeit not necessarily so in the
very short-run – create
the</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan"> opportunity</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">(not the
certainty)</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan"> of large profits from speculation
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_667"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">on ships, a strategy/activity called
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan">asset play.
</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">Asset
play has indeed compensated for lacklustre margin profits in shipping.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.186.2" class="koboSpan">It has,
however, overshadowed the advantages of astutely timed investment in
ships without – necessarily – the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan">ex-ante</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan"> intention to further sell them but simply the
acquisition of additional tonnage or fleet renewal at low(er) prices.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.188.2" class="koboSpan">While
investment strategies are associated often with asset play, if not with
asset play alone, there is scope for a company to formulate a general
strategy of acquisitions regardless of whether the intention is to use
ships for trade or trade them
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan">per se</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan"> as sheer commodities.</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Limiting risk: a shipping averse investment strategy</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">Risk aversion and
shipping investment are not necessarily antonyms but they would hardly
be classified as synonyms
either.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0735" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0735"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">49</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan"> However, had most market participants been following a
strategy with a view to avoiding risk entirely, supply of shipping
services would have been considerably
tighter</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0736" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0736"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">50</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan"> as the only real guarantee from cash-flow pressures
and company vulnerability in cyclical markets would be to finance
purchases entirely by equity. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.196.2"
class="koboSpan">Although not necessarily a net profit maximisation
strategy, as traditional loan finance may be more advantageous
especially at times of high inflation, it is definitely the most
conservative approach. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.196.3"
class="koboSpan">The use of some debt finance need not necessarily put
companies at bankruptcy risk as long as their cash-flow situation is
healthy and projections and decisions are balanced and guided
respectively by the knowledge of market cyclicality.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.196.4" class="koboSpan">Excesses in
all directions – including
expectations</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0737" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0737"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">51</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan"> – seem, however, to characterise all aspects of
shipping investment increasing risk but also creating market
opportunities as prices falter.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">Acquisition prices do
not have to be ridiculously low to allow for a competitive fixed-cost,
although this has been recorded in the past as well.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.199.2" class="koboSpan">To be
competitive in terms of capital cost companies have essentially to
acquire vessels at significantly lower prices than the prices
competitors had to pay for their own tonnage often just by waiting or
speeding up investment decisions by only a few months.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.199.3" class="koboSpan">The investment
strategy of a firm becomes thus a relative one and a continuous effort
to take advantage of significant asset price shifts over time periods
which may represent only a tiny fraction of the entire life expectancy
of the vessel. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.199.4"
class="koboSpan">As operating costs for similar vessels are easily
adjustable – variations which cannot be effectively hedged stemming
essentially from manning costs – market survival and success can easily
be shown to depend to a very large extent on fixed cost (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.199.5" class="koboSpan">essentially
capital cost in bulk shipping and hence on investment
strategies).</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">5.2 Fixed cost and investment strategy: still the essence of competitiveness</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping
competitiveness is a complex issue related to market structures.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.201.2" class="koboSpan">However, in
both liner and bulk shipping markets capital cost is, as a rule, the
single most important element of total cost, while investment strategies
can make or break companies as the impact of investment related paid-out
costs determines the resilience of companies in times of
crises.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0738" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0738"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">52</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan"> Fixed cost influences company competitiveness through
(a) differences in acquisition prices of either new buildings or
second-hand vessels; (b) differences in the way capital is raised; and
(c) differences in the terms of finance of vessel
acquisitions.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0739" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0739"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">53</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> Minimising fixed cost provides a significant advance
on competitors in
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_668"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan">the main bulk markets where cost leadership is still
the main viable option, without taking into account the idiosyncrasies
of some very specialised shipping segments or those of liner shipping
where quality of service and product differentiation may have a role to
play in company strategy.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping has always
been perceived as capital intensive and automation and the downsizing of
manning requirements have contributed little in changing this; on the
contrary, the labour to capital ratio seems to have declined in the
post-war
period.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0740" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0740"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">54</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan"> However, past progress towards automation combined
with quality concerns have removed the focus from the prospect of the
ever-more automated ship. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.209.2"
class="koboSpan">Hence, as there are few margins for minimising the cost
of main inputs such as bunkers or
stores,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0741" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0741"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">55</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan"> the efforts for achieving an overall low cost cannot
but concentrate on what constitutes on average half of the total cost of
shipping
services</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0742" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0742"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">56</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan"> (i.e. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.213.2"
class="koboSpan">capital cost).</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">Minimising
acquisition costs should not be mistaken as pointing necessarily to the
purchase of second-hand tonnage.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.214.2"
class="koboSpan">As</span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0168"
id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0168"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan"> Figures 1</span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0169"
id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0169"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan"> show there can occasionally be</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.227.1"

</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">various
dates.</span>

Clarkson Research,

class="koboSpan">World Shipyard
Monitor</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">, and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">Shipping Intelligence
Weekly</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">,
various dates.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_669"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">significant differences in new vessel prices over
relatively short periods of time which can be translated into the
difference between a low, but positive, profit margin and a limited, yet
definitely negative, loss if the total cost is considered.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">Tankers ordered at
the very high 1992 price levels for example
(cf.</span>[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan"> Figure
1</span>](#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0168)<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">) reached the market in the morose tanker markets of
the mid-1990s, while orders placed at the low prices of 1998 took
advantage of the millennium boom in tankers.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.241.2" class="koboSpan">As many
twenty-first century shipping investors in bulk carriers found out
ex-post and at their expense, for instance, a shorter than 12-month
delay would have resulted in millions saved between 2007 and 2008 (cf.
</span>[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0169)<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan">); in the latter case of course a timely cancellation
might had proved a few months later the only corrective action for
cash-poor companies.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan">Timing </span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan">of all types of shipping investment decisions is indeed
of essence; while investors’ expectations may well prove quite elastic
in the sense of Zannetos,
</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0743" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0743"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">57</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan"> budgets may not.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">Distress sales
– which are the ones to give rise to substantial asset play
opportunities along the evolution of the shipping cycle as analytically
discussed by
Stopford</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0744" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0744"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">58</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan"> – can be considered as a function of a number of
variables such as – or similar to – the ones discussed by Grammenos,
Nomikos and Papapostolou for high-yield bond
defaults.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0745" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0745"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">59</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the context of sales, the larger the variance in
liquidity positions of individual investors as defined mainly by
outstanding acquisition costs to be paid out, gearing levels and cash
reserves, which depend in turn mainly on actual vs predicted
rates/revenue differentials, the larger the potential asset-play gains
for the liquid ones.</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">5.3 Asset play: still “the bulk” of bulk shipping profits?</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">Asset play is often
put forward as the only justification for investors having kept
investing in markets with such low and precarious
profitability.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0746" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0746"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan">60</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan"> The expectation of profits</span>

<div id="Ch023.xhtml_fig0327" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00347.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch023.xhtml_bck_fig0327)

</div>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_670"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan">as high as the ones in
</span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fig0327" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fig0327"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan"> had constituted an evidently strong enough incentive
for betting on a future market reversal.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.259.2" class="koboSpan">Indeed, before
the “</span>[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan">dot.com</span>](http://dot.com)<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan">” bubble at the turn of the century there were few
legal possibilities for such rates of return especially when trading
non-innovative assets.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">Exceptional returns
from asset play (or the achievement of a significantly lower fixed cost
in relation to competitors) have been based on investing against the
tide or what has been called “anticyclical investment
strategy”</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0747" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0747"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">61</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan"> especially during major
crises</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0748" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0748"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">62</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan"> both
before</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0749" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0749"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">63</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan"> and after World War
II,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0750" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0750"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">64</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan"> as was the case in the early 1980s.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.270.2" class="koboSpan">Even less
turbulent markets provide opportunities to minimise fixed-cost or
achieve substantial capital gains: price differences for a 10-year-old
Panamax between their lowest 1994 levels and the autumn of 1995 highs
could be of the order of 25% easily providing for a total cost
differential of over 10% and allowing non-negligible asset-play profits.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.270.3" class="koboSpan">Shipping
companies </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan">with the necessary
liquidity</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan"> – possibly as a result of similar successful moves in
the past or as a result of refraining from investment during market
booms – or </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan">able to secure funds under terms that enable them to
wait for the revival of the markets,
</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">have
often exercised
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan">anticyclical investment
strategies</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.276.2"
class="koboSpan">In a sense, successful investment strategies are
self-sustained as astute moves in the past allow the build-up of
sufficient cash reserves to be invested in when the next opportunity
arises; conversely, unsuccessful asset players, along with all types of
shipping investors overextending during booms, carry the disadvantage of
both reduced liquidity and ability to raise credit at times of crises.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.276.3" class="koboSpan">Banks have
been traditionally reluctant not only to lend in such cases but some
refuse to even get involved in shipping when the market is depressed,
thus narrowing the circle of potential sources for raising capital.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.276.4" class="koboSpan">Banks tend to
return to the shipping business along with profits and
prosperity,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0751" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0751"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">65</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan"> but by then, the real opportunities for large profits
through the Sale and Purchase of vessels have lapsed; the experience of
late 2008 has hardly helped in inducing any changes in this regard.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.278.2" class="koboSpan">Stock markets
are equally rather unlikely candidates for providing the necessary funds
for such investment in periods of crises and of high uncertainty so,
unless astute entrepreneurs manage to convince investors to contribute
equity
capital,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0752" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0752"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">66</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.280.1"
class="koboSpan"> asset play remains largely a self-financed and indeed
historically self-sustained activity.</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">5.4 Asset play: risks and attitudes</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">Such bold Sale and
Purchase (S&P) strategies as described in the previous sub-section and
illustrated by </span>[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch023.xhtml_fig0327)<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan"> are of a high risk as there is no time pattern for
defining the point at which the market situation will turn, thus
providing opportunities for materialising S&P profits.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.284.2" class="koboSpan">“Intuition”,
often provided as a basis for such moves in S&P, is a rather poor basis
for decisions of this type. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.284.3"
class="koboSpan">The level of ship prices compared to the level of scrap
prices</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0753" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0753"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.285.1" class="koboSpan">67</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan"> seems a “safer” market signal for triggering purchases
provided, of course, there is sufficient liquidity.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.286.2" class="koboSpan">Still, there
are no guarantees about the relative success of such a move as the time
horizon of the – always much awaited – revival of the markets remains
uncertain under the influence of a multitude of factors often exogenous
to the shipping markets.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">The term asset play
is also used by researchers to describe activities related to buying and
selling of newbuilding contracts or even of newbuilding options; returns
from such activities seem to have been quite impressive in the past with
purchase and sale of such contracts taking place within relatively short
periods of
time.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0754" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0754"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">68</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan"> The market path which can generate profits following
the placement of a contract is one of a weak market
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_671"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">reversing or of an accelerated freight rate hike
generating expectations and additional demand for prompt deliveries,
both scenarios resulting in significantly higher newbuilding prices.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.290.2" class="koboSpan">Due to the
necessary lags between orders and vessel delivery, this type of asset
play could </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan">eventually</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan"> prove less risky if the order has been placed in poor
markets: if the market has hit low levels the reversal is likely to
occur some time in the mid-term future when the order should normally
have been transformed into a delivery or an imminent one.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.292.2" class="koboSpan">Conversely,
distress sales of tonnage on order by financially frustrated owners or
yards during recessions may be targeted by liquid buyers – with the
caveats discussed above – especially if their strategy is one of tonnage
renewal at lower prices more than an asset-play one.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">However, whatever
form asset play activity takes, the most significant danger associated
with it is the absence of any guarantees on the time or path for market
reversals; as the 1980s proved, market lows can be one more trough
further down into a deepening depression.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.293.2" class="koboSpan">Liquidity and
equity finance prove in this way the only guarantees, regardless of
whether the vessel is intended for further operation or for further
trading as an asset, while patience and flexibility emerge as the major
attributes of the ideal asset-player player whether this would be an
individual investor or a fund; in both cases, eventual lay-up costs
until the market reverses have to be taken into account in the
investment decision.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.294.1" class="koboSpan">Although speculation
on ships bought during periods of low vessel prices is an extremely
risky investment move, it should be reminded that the risk when
investing – in either new buildings or second-hand tonnage – in a
booming market can definitely be – and usually proves –
higher;</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0755" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0755"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.295.1" class="koboSpan">69</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan"> such timing requires that freight rates are further
sustained for a lengthy period of time at high levels.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.296.2" class="koboSpan">The far right
column of </span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0170"
id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0170"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows clearly the investment spike which – with
hindsight – a number of recent investors in new tonnage would have liked
to have avoided especially if they had been financing deals through
banks (many of the latter having experienced in the meantime similar
difficulties to their clientele’s) or through any type of debt
non-convertible to equity. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.298.2"
class="koboSpan">The absence of any time path for market
turns</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0756" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0756"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">70</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the short duration in principle of shipping booms
often condemn a large proportion of vessels acquired in similar
periods</span>

<div id="Ch023.xhtml_fig0328" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00348.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Freight rate development and new contracting 2002–2007 in Panamax bulk carriers" /></span>

<a href="#Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0170"
id="Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0170"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.302.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan"> Freight rate development and new contracting 2002–2007
in Panamax bulk carriers</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">Note:</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan"> On the basis of an index 2002=100 of HRds/ARA coal
freight rates in \$ per tonne and yearly new contracting.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.305.2" class="koboSpan">Calculated
from data in Clarkson Research,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan">World Shipyard
Monitor</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan">, December 2008 and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan">Shipping Review and
Outlook</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan">, Spring 2008.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_672"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan">to a chronic financial underperformance or even to an
early death through emergency scrapping under the pressure of cash-flow
problems. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.310.2"
class="koboSpan">Despite the extraordinary relative length of the 2003
to 2008 euphoric phase, recent developments reminded that the risk of
moving into a booming market is perhaps the only obvious one and should
be much better assessed as a move of this type requires long periods of
prosperity. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.310.3"
class="koboSpan">Through the market’s own “endemic tendency to
over-invest” or through an exogenous shock (or any unfortunate
combination) prosperity is bound to be cut short in shipping.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.310.4" class="koboSpan">The Reksten
case in the early
1970s</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0757" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0757"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">71</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan"> constitutes a typical example in this regard; the
recent downturn has yet to provide its full range of victims for
exemplary ones to emerge.</span>

### <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">5.5 Asset play: a “ game” with winners and losers</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">The review of S&P
activity over the period of the crisis of the 1970s and the 1980s in
shipping has proved that there are significant differences in investment
attitudes. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.314.2"
class="koboSpan">This dilutes efforts to make blanket assumptions on the
nature of investors’ expectations.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.314.3" class="koboSpan">Research in
the previous
decade</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0758" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0758"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">72</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.316.1"
class="koboSpan"> has pointed out that there had been marked differences
in both investment attitudes and in exposure to asset play between
leading traditional shipping communities during the last major crisis
but also among members of the same shipowning community.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.316.2" class="koboSpan">Although
associated with the increased resilience of many Greek companies, the
econometric investigation of the observed anticyclical investment
pattern – within limitations due to the nature of the available data –
resulted in showing that although there was a trend among this shipping
community to invest against the tide, the trend was not uniform and
definitely not a national exclusivity either.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.316.3" class="koboSpan">Some of the
most astute moves in the S&P market such as the purchases of VLCCs at
below their scrap price were made by Norwegian
owners</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0759" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0759"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">73</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.318.1"
class="koboSpan"> pointing that although investment behaviour can be
cultivated, propagated or exemplified within a shipping community,
talent in shipping investment knows no boundaries and is not a
geographically defined exclusive privilege.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.318.2" class="koboSpan">Most
attitudes, including varying investment patterns, are dictated by
objective constraints. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.318.3"
class="koboSpan">Norwegian owners traditionally invested in new
buildings while Greek owners, had built a reputation in the past for
successfully managing older fleets.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.318.4" class="koboSpan">At a time when
depression settled fast in the markets following the first oil shock in
1973, the former found themselves with young – and expensively acquired
– vessels with high demands in cash flow for their repayment.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.318.5" class="koboSpan">As fleet age
data indicate or rather
reveal,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0760" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0760"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">74</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan"> Greek owners could afford to be more resilient as
their older tonnage was by comparison far less burdened with fixed-cost
obligations since it was either bought second-hand or had been largely
depreciated already, or both.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.321.1" class="koboSpan">However, as the face
of shipping has undergone major changes in the past few years, so has
the age structure of major fleets especially as tankers went into a
phase of “compulsory
renewal”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0761" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0761"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">75</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan"> Similarly, the latest boom seems to have been
unprecedented in uprooting in its wake successful investment strategies
which had apparently survived at least well into the third year of the
last boom among close-knit communities of shipping
investors.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0762" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0762"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.324.1" class="koboSpan">76</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan"> However, while the change in fleet fundamentals may
have diluted discernable investment patterns, it has not diminished the
importance of investment timing.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.325.2" class="koboSpan">On the
contrary, as average tonnage age for most main competitors declined –
and with the extension of the economic life of vessels not being a
viable option
anymore,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0763" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0763"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.326.1" class="koboSpan">77</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan"> at least for tankers – the fate of national fleets and
individual companies may depend henceforth (even more than in the past)
on small differences in investment timing.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_673"></span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0171"
id="Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0171"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan"> Indicative potential differences in acquisition costs
in dollars of max. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.329.2"
class="koboSpan">five year-old vessels Mid 2008–Early 2009</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

| <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.336.1" class="koboSpan">PANAMAX BC</span> | <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">58 million</span> | <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.338.1" class="koboSpan">�68%</span> |
