<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">In second-hand
transactions, differences of the order of tens of millions of dollars
(or even impressively
more)</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0764" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0764"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.344.1" class="koboSpan">78</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.345.1"
class="koboSpan"> for vessels of similar type, size and age over just a
few months continue to point to the all-important potential fixed-cost
differences and the analogous importance of the timing of investment in
all types of physical shipping assets.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.345.2" class="koboSpan">While the more
limited acceleration of orders before 2007, (cf.
</span>[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0170)<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan"> supra.), seemed to have had relatively staved off the
“endemic tendency to over-invest”, developments since then only
confirmed it; otherwise, the level of price differentials in
</span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0171"
id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0171"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.348.1"
class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.349.1"
class="koboSpan"> would not be justified.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.349.2" class="koboSpan">Assessing how
new investment soared well into the boom period and how it subsequently
shrank a few months later to a single digit share of 2008
levels</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0765" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0765"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.350.1" class="koboSpan">79</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.351.1"
class="koboSpan"> pessimists would despair in repetition.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.351.2" class="koboSpan">Optimists
would continue to monitor transactions, be these of new or second-hand
vessels, and especially distress sales with a view to including them one
day into examples of successful anticyclical investment;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan">or not.</span></span>

## <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.353.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.353.2" class="koboSpan">Investing in an Environment of Increased Uncertainty</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.354.1" class="koboSpan">Despite the survival
of main mechanisms related to market and investment/divestment
cyclicality, world shipping is not what it used to be anymore.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.354.2" class="koboSpan">Changes
involve commercial, regulatory and technical aspects, often intertwined
in pairs; these have hardly removed uncertainty; on the contrary.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.354.3" class="koboSpan">In a number of
markets, the product cycle of tonnage categories and designs has
accelerated, increasing the risk of future technological obsolescence.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.354.4" class="koboSpan">This was
brought about either through competition increasing from
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.355.1"
class="koboSpan">outside </span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan">the segment – such as in the case of the successful
container threat to bulk reefer shipping – or from within, as in the
case of the now fully fledged and less “esoteric" nowadays LNG market
where on-board liquefaction of the boil-off gas and, more importantly,
regasification of the cargo, as in LNG RVs, are making inroads.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">Potential regulatory
changes are now a factor to be discounted in every investment decision
be that at varying rates, while the related focus on quality is
increasing. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.357.2"
class="koboSpan">Although attention has shifted away from ship
registration, as flags of convenience have become now the most
significant part of the world
fleet,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0766" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0766"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.358.1" class="koboSpan">80</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan"> other elements of competitiveness related to quality,
such as the length of exploitation of vessels, have come to the fore.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.359.2" class="koboSpan">In today’s
shipping, the age of tonnage has become significant even for dry bulk
carrier charterers, exceptions due to the “prompt ship” effect in
extreme markets
notwithstanding.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0767" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0767"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.360.1" class="koboSpan">81</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan"> The age issue is directly related to investment
strategies and especially asset play.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.361.2" class="koboSpan">Successful
asset play requires a total length of the economic life of the vessel
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_674"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan">which should not only cover this of the shipping cycle
but also allow to the ultimate buyer the chance, or at least the hope,
for a further profitable exploitation of an asset acquired – by
definition– at high prices. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.362.2"
class="koboSpan">Investing in older vessels is now practically
constrained by regulatory requirements as in the case of tankers; older
tonnage has been equally subject to enhanced surveys and to structural
modifications.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0768" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0768"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.363.1" class="koboSpan">82</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan"> Although, the scope for minimising fixed-cost or even
for asset-play has not disappeared, the continuing decline of the
average age of the world fleet and new tonnage specifications coupled by
the precipitated – since the
millennium,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0769" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0769"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">83</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan"> – banning of older designs in tankers have by
definition limited asset-play possibilities to a smaller range of
tonnage age. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.366.2"
class="koboSpan">Past experience prevents assigning a probability of the
direction of future regulatory developments and their impact on
investment as the ones in this century have extended from changes in the
operations management of ships – as those brought about shortly after
2001 by the ISPS 2002 – to the acceleration of the single-hull tankers’
withdrawal. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.366.3"
class="koboSpan">Regulatory goalposts impacting on trading opportunities
have kept moving adding to the uncertainty of investment in a
–</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan"> par
excellence</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan"> – volatile
environment.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0770" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0770"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.369.1" class="koboSpan">84</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.370.1" class="koboSpan">While shipping
investment is regarded now, especially for larger investors, as the act
of managing a portfolio of real and paper assets, (cf.
</span><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0172"
id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0172"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.371.1"
class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.372.1"
class="koboSpan">), risk can be managed eventually better, but it cannot
be eliminated. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.372.2"
class="koboSpan">Whereas the only risk-free position is at the very left
corner point of the lower left quadrant – the latter significantly
denoted by zero (0) – including low exposures to either the paper or
physical shipping markets of
atypical/diversified</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0771" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0771"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.373.1" class="koboSpan">85</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.374.1"
class="koboSpan"> investors from outside the segment, there is no
intended suggestion or compulsory assumption that risk increases as
investors move clockwise into quadrants I to III in terms of commitment
in physical and paper shipping markets.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.374.2" class="koboSpan">However, these
two categories of shipping-related investment do not necessarily create
perfect
hedges</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0772" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0772"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.375.1" class="koboSpan">86</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.376.1"
class="koboSpan"> unless intentionally and skilfully designed for.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.376.2" class="koboSpan">Equally, the
risk tolerance of typical shipping players will tend to insert some
element of speculation into Quadrant
II.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0773" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0773"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.377.1" class="koboSpan">87</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.378.1"
class="koboSpan"> Offsetting returns from financial instruments
notwithstanding, short to medium term strategies for investors in
Quadrants I and II in an environment of</span>

<div id="Ch023.xhtml_fig0327a" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<a href="#Ch023.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0172"
id="Ch023.xhtml_cap_lbl0172"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.379.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00347a.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span></a>

</div>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_675"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.380.1"
class="koboSpan">less than full fleet employment, remain focused on
improving operating costs. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.380.2"
class="koboSpan">Lack of employment is, however, among the usual “risks
of the trade”; some others which have emerged or re-emerged in this
decade, are
not.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0774" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0774"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.381.1" class="koboSpan">88</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.382.1" class="koboSpan">Following the market
collapse in September 2008, complex chains of sub-chartering activities,
previously fuelled by spiralling rates and ever-growing
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan">great expectations
</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.384.1" class="koboSpan">for
future gains equally collapsed. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.384.2"
class="koboSpan">In chain-like sub-letting activities, failures of a
middle or initial link can unleash domino effects.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.384.3" class="koboSpan">This was one
more uncertainty added to phenomena whose extent had been hitherto
marginal for post-war shipping business:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.385.1" class="koboSpan">the significant
    disruption of “shipping as usual” in the first months of the
    financial crisis due to the letters of credit
    problem,</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0775" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0775"><span
    id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.386.1" class="koboSpan">89</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.387.1"
    class="koboSpan"> threatening supply chains;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.388.1" class="koboSpan">the equally
    significant collapse of trust to chartering counterparties as some
    of the latter were collapsing themselves.
    </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.388.2" class="koboSpan">The
    extraordinary circumstances rallied to increase charter default
    risks which research by Adland and Jia had already found to be
    dependent on the state of the freight
    market;</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0776" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0776"><span
    id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.389.1" class="koboSpan">90</span></a></sup>
3.  <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.390.1" class="koboSpan">the significant
    number of successful (and unsuccessful) piracy attacks.
    </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.390.2" class="koboSpan">Although
    piracy is an insurable risk, unlike the investment one, the stress
    on the company’s operations management – often over a prolonged
    period – is comparable to dealing with a major accident; diversion
    from financial management in turbulent times creates risks in
    itself.</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.391.1" class="koboSpan">As the resurgence of
such an old phenomenon as piracy reminded even to the most optimistic
investor, shipping is a most idiosyncratic industry, capable of leaping
back and forth “in
time”</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0777" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0777"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.392.1" class="koboSpan">91</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan"> and market phase as easily as it traverses
meridians.</span>

## <span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.394.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.394.2" class="koboSpan">Summary and Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.395.1" class="koboSpan">Investment strategies
have been a core factor, if not the most critical one, for succeeding in
shipping, especially in the volatile bulk shipping markets.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.395.2" class="koboSpan">Market
cyclicality increases the risks for investors.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.395.3" class="koboSpan">The
competitive nature, however, of most of bulk shipping means that there
are few constraints in terms of investment and divestment.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.395.4" class="koboSpan">While the
fundamental characteristics of shipping investment in terms of risks and
attitudes in general have survived, uncertainty has further increased
due to often interrelated changes in technical, commercial and
regulatory aspects; this is not only in the bulk segments.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.395.5" class="koboSpan">Increasingly,
volatility concerns investors in liner tonnage more than in the past;
this is both through new, more competitive liner market regulation but
also through the increased number of outside investors targeting
employment opportunities of container tonnage by carriers.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.395.6" class="koboSpan">Asset play,
which is an extremely risky investment strategy but with potentially
high payoffs, remains as an investment opportunity across shipping in
volatile markets but with added caveats: these include sudden changes in
specification requirements through regulation and potentially
accelerating technological obsolescence; the latter is further supported
by increased competition in liner and specialist segments.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.395.7" class="koboSpan">Recent
experiences might prove enlightening in terms of research into triggers
of distress sales and of the – eventually varying through market phases
– attitudes and expectations of investors whose investment learning
curves remain to be assessed. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.395.8"
class="koboSpan">The largely underused, in shipping, tool of surveying
expectations</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0778" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0778"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.396.1" class="koboSpan">92</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.397.1"
class="koboSpan"> can serve equally in that direction as experts have
suggested in the past in the context of
macroeconomics</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0779" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0779"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.398.1" class="koboSpan">93</span></a></sup><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.399.1"
class="koboSpan"> from where researchers have often drawn hypotheses for
testing in the, nevertheless still idiosyncratic, shipping
markets.</span><sup><a href="#Ch023.xhtml_fn0780" id="Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0780"><span
id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.400.1" class="koboSpan">94</span></a></sup>

2008</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.410.1" class="koboSpan">,

[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.451.1"
class="koboSpan">12.</span>](#Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0698)<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.452.1"
class="koboSpan"> The term is used here to denote the embryonic state
and lack until recently of main market properties.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.452.2" class="koboSpan">It should not
be considered as the simple application of a most common term in
transaction cost economics (TCE).
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.452.3" class="koboSpan">However,
short-term spot market transactions and vertical integration are
considered as two extremes,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.453.1"
class="koboSpan">cf.</span></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.454.1"
class="koboSpan"> Boerner, C. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.454.2"
class="koboSpan">and Macher, J., “Transaction Cost Economics: An
assessment
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_page_677"></span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.455.1"
class="koboSpan">of Empirical Research in the Social Sciences”, accessed
as HMTL June 2002. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.455.2"
class="koboSpan">“Hybrids” include joint ventures such as the ones
existing in the LNG industry between plant and shipping partners and
thus the use of the term could be accommodated even in the strict TCE
terminology sense. </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.455.3"
class="koboSpan">However, long-term contracting would describe better a
large part of the market.</span>

[<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.527.1"
class="koboSpan">28.</span>](#Ch023.xhtml_bck_fn0714)<span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.528.1"
class="koboSpan"> There is really no essential difference between fleets
directly integrated in shipping divisions of oil companies and those
belonging to controlled subsidiaries.
</span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.528.2" class="koboSpan">In both case

company). </span><span id="Ch023.xhtml_kobo.528.4" class="koboSpan">More
sophisticated structures created in recent years through alliances and
joint ventures should not be confused with regard to the centre of
investment decisions.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_683"></span>[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 24</span>\
<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Valuing Maritime Investments with Real Options: The Right Course to Chart</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0516)
==============================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Helen</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Bendall</span></span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0781" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0781"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">Real option analysis
(ROA), an extension of discounted cash flow (DCF), has at its core the
calculation of shareholder value and thus is a very powerful metric to
value maritime investments. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.7.2"
class="koboSpan">The basic principles underlying real options are
intuitively appealing and readily understood by management, having been
used for millennia. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.7.3"
class="koboSpan">The first recorded real options deal being that of the
philosopher and mathematician, Thales of Miletus (circa 624BC–536 BC)
who made a fortune by taking an option on renting olive presses in
Miletus and Chios in Asia Minor at a set price and the crop turned out
to be
bountiful.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0782" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0782"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan"> Their intuitive appeal led Copeland and Antikarov
(2001), to predict that by the end of the first decade of the second
millennium AD that real option analysis, ROA, would become the standard
valuation metric. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.9.2"
class="koboSpan">It is indeed true that most mainstream academic finance
texts now include real option analysis as a tool for investment
evaluation but perhaps we are still a little distance off from the
analysis achieving “standard” investment evaluation status.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.9.3" class="koboSpan">Others (Triantis
and Borison, 2001 amongst many) suggest that it is the process and
discipline of framing an investment decision in real options terms that
provides the greatest benefit. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.9.4"
class="koboSpan">If used as a conceptual tool, it allows management to
characterise rather than calculate and communicate the strategic value
of an investment project. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.9.5"
class="koboSpan">Real options helps managers formulate their strategic
options (Amram and Kulatilaka, 2000) enabling investment strategy to be
crafted as a series of options that are continually being exercised to
achieve both short and long term returns on investment (Yeo and Qui,
2003). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.9.6" class="koboSpan">The real
option method enables decision-makers to leverage uncertainty and limit
downside risk. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.9.7"
class="koboSpan">In this current period of heightened business
uncertainty ROA offers managers a very useful and an appropriate
approach to evaluate investments and formulate strategy.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">A discussion of the
key issues of valuing investment in an uncertain world follows in
Section 2 with real options analysis, ROA, offered as an alternate
paradigm as it allows
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_684"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan">managers the ability to alter/adapt the project in
light of new information. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.11.2"
class="koboSpan">Various applications of real options in the maritime
industry are used to illustrate the scope and applicability of an option
approach. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.11.3" class="koboSpan">Real
options are embedded in most projects but there has been a certain
hesitation by management to forego their traditional DCF “comfort zone”.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.11.4" class="koboSpan">This is
somewhat surprising as ROA should not be viewed as a revolutionary
approach but evolutionary as it extends traditional DCF analysis.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.11.5" class="koboSpan">Section 3
reviews the reasons for this view and outlines and discusses several ROA
methodologies. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.11.6"
class="koboSpan">Section 4 demonstrates ROA by illustrating the power of
the technique in specific maritime case studies involving new
technology. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.11.7"
class="koboSpan">Section 5 concludes the chapter.</span>

## <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">Valuing Investments</span>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Limitations of traditional DCF</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">Conventional DCF
analysis for project evaluation is taught extensively in business
schools and is used by a majority of
firms.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0783" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0783"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan"> It appears that many academics and executives, by
implementing investment decisions based solely on traditional capital
budgeting techniques or by focusing on narrowly defined problems may
have failed to take into account uncertainty and the flexibility to
alter or adapt projects once begun.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">Often there is
a lack of understanding as to how to include strategic issues in an
analysis. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">This
is not to say that mangers have not recognised that the failure to do so
can lead to costly errors, but the difficulty of such planning leads
many to ignore the potential costs and hope that serious problems do not
arise (Teisberg, 1995). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.16.4"
class="koboSpan">Managers must be able to include uncertain future
outcomes and potential strategic responses in a prospective analysis of
a capital investment project.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">Because of its
inflexibility and the failure to take into account strategic or
competitive issues, DCF criteria may undervalue investment
opportunities, leading to lack of investment and loss of competitive
position. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.17.2"
class="koboSpan">Dissatisfaction with traditional DCF led some to
propose that the problem was simply a misuse or misapplication of the
underlying theory (Hodder and Riggs, 1985) or move strongly that DCF was
an inappropriate valuation method.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.17.3" class="koboSpan">Hertz (1964).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.17.4" class="koboSpan">Magee (1964)
suggested instead the use of simulation and decision trees, or Decision
Tree Analysis (DTA) as a means to capture the value of future operating
flexibility associated with many projects.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.17.5" class="koboSpan">Other academics
and company executives wanting to refine DCF have turned their attention
to technical questions related to the selection of the risk-adjusted
process without considering adequately the appropriateness of DCF for
valuation of particular projects which have strategic implications.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.17.6" class="koboSpan">The traditional
DCF approach cannot fully accommodate the interdependencies between
current and uncertain or contingent future decisions which make the
risk-adjusted discount rate non-deterministic.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">Traditional DCF is
based on value maximisation under
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">passive</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan"> or static conditions and on implicit assumptions
concerning a predetermined operating strategy in which the project would
be initiated immediately and operate continuously at base case until the
end of a pre-specified useful life.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">Ansoff (1965)
and Myers (1987) point out that traditional capital budgeting techniques
are unable to forecast the value of projects not yet in hand and that
they are difficult to use in situations involving multiple objectives or
substantial project interdependencies e.g.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.20.3" class="koboSpan">synergies or
other unique qualitative attributes (Lai and Trigeorgis, 1995).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.20.4" class="koboSpan">The standard
NPV although perfectly suitable for projects that once undertaken
require no further decisions or actions by the firm,
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_685"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">is of little assistance in the valuation of projects
which offer managerial flexibility in dealing with future contingencies.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.21.2" class="koboSpan">In summary, DCF
may be appropriate when applied to narrowly defined problems but is
inadequate when uncertainty and strategic considerations are paramount
(Pinches, 1982, Myers, 1987 amongst many).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.21.3" class="koboSpan">These
observations point to the existence of an extra parameter which managers
implicitly or explicitly factor into their investment decisions.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">Well before the
development of Real Options Analysis, ROA, managers and strategists
intuitively adjusted their investment strategies to include other
factors such as future growth considerations, realising that traditional
DCF criteria undervalued many investment opportunities.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">Kester (1984)
developed Myers’ (1977) concept of thinking of discretionary investment
opportunities as “growth options”.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.22.3" class="koboSpan">These embody
both strategic and competitive elements.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.22.4" class="koboSpan">For example,
shipping lines may enter a new market or trade not so much because the
immediate investment generates a positive NPV, indeed it may be the
opposite, but in order to keep a competitor out of the trade or to put
the line in an advantageous position for valuable follow up
opportunities. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.22.5"
class="koboSpan">An investment such as this is an example of a
multistage decision that involves “real” options.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.22.6" class="koboSpan">The decision to
enter the trade has the ability to create future assets (cash flow) as a
by-product of the initial investment decision.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.22.7" class="koboSpan">The shipping
line, by undertaking the initial investment, has the option in future to
expand the number of ships in the trade, or exit the trade depending on
market circumstances in the future.</span>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Real options</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Real options capture
the value of managerial flexibility to adapt decisions in response to
unexpected market developments, giving the manager the right to defer,
to expand, to contract or abandon the project once more information
becomes available. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.24.2"
class="koboSpan">Companies create shareholder value by identifying,
managing and exercising real options associated with their investment.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.24.3" class="koboSpan">The concept is
similar to financial
options.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0784" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0784"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan"> An option gives the right but not the obligation to
undertake an action i.e. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.26.2"
class="koboSpan">a business decision, at a predetermined cost (the
exercise price), for a predetermined period of time (the life of the
option). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.26.3" class="koboSpan">A
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan">call</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan"> option is the right to buy the underlying asset at the
predetermined (exercise) price. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.28.2"
class="koboSpan">As there is no obligation on the part of the holder of
the option to exercise the call, the option can lapse.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">However if the
option is exercised then the profit on the option is the difference
between the value of the underlying asset and its exercise price.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.28.4" class="koboSpan">A
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan">put</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan"> option is the right to sell the underlying asset to
receive the exercise price and thus is the opposite of a call.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">A
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan">European</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> option can only be exercised on its maturity date
where as an </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan">American</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan"> option can be exercised at any time during its life
and thus is more applicable to investment in real assets.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.34.2" class="koboSpan">An option is
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">in the
money</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">,
i.e. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.36.2" class="koboSpan">profitable
to exercise if the price of the underlying asset is above the exercise
price with a call option and below the exercise price with a put option.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.36.3" class="koboSpan">If not
profitable to exercise it is
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">out of the
money</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">Although examples of
real options have been recorded throughout history, the first to coin
the term “real options” was Myers (1977), who applied financial option
pricing theory to the valuation of a non-financial or “real” investment
in a multi-stage manufacturing plant expansion.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">Other academic
papers followed but it was not until the last 10 years that interest in
ROA began to attract considerable attention from corporates as a
potentially important tool for valuation and strategy (Borison, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.39.3" class="koboSpan">ROA has been
adopted by a number of organisations in the transport, energy, infocom
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_686"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan">and mining industries as well as large consumer and
industrial companies, particularly those engaged in R&D and involving a
multi-stage production process (Triantis and Borison, 2001).</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">Real options are often
classified by their flexibility. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.41.2"
class="koboSpan">If management wants to scale up production then
management needs to value an option to expand.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.41.3" class="koboSpan">They would need
to value an American call which gives them the right but not the
obligation to add additional capacity to their current project by
further investment at a later date.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.41.4" class="koboSpan">In contrast to
scale down an operation or to close an operation are examples of
American put options where management has the right to sell, but not the
obligation, should the operating environment worsen.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.41.5" class="koboSpan">An option to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan">contract </span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">allows management to sell a fraction of the operation
while an option to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">abandon</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan"> at a fixed price leads to closure for a predetermined
salvage value. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.45.2"
class="koboSpan">Being allowed to defer the decision to invest is an
option to </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">defer</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan"> while
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">switching</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan"> options are portfolios of American puts and calls
which allow the flexibility to switch inputs or outputs.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">Compound </span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.51.1"
class="koboSpan">options are options on options and point to the need
for sequential investment decisions while
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan">rainbow</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan"> options reflect multiple sources of
uncertainty.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0785" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0785"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">2.3 A taxonomy of maritime real options</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0786" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0786"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">2.3.1 Option to expand</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">Perhaps one of the
easiest real options to identify is the option to accelerate the rate or
expand the scale of operation by investing an additional outlay.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.2" class="koboSpan">Once
established in a trade, for example a shipping line can increase the
number of vessels in a trade, should market conditions warrant.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.3" class="koboSpan">This ability to
make a discretionary investment is similar to an American call option on
the increased scale of the project and with the exercise price, the
additional outlay. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.4"
class="koboSpan">The project then can be seen as the base scale project,
or static NPV, plus a call option on the future investment, which is the
value of flexibility. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.5"
class="koboSpan">The option becomes profitable to exercise, if future
demand turns out to be higher than expected.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.6" class="koboSpan">A major source
of value from infrastructure investments arises from the ability to
enhance the upside of a project during good market conditions by making
follow-on investments (Myers, 1977).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.7" class="koboSpan">Ports with
surplus land can build extra terminals and terminal operators can
increase the number of gantry cranes on a berth.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.8" class="koboSpan">This option,
which will be exercised only if future market developments turn out
favourably, can make seemingly unprofitable investments (based on static
NPV base-case) worth undertaking.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.9" class="koboSpan">Infrastructure
investments consist of both tangible and intangible core assets on which
individual operating flexibility options are based.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.10" class="koboSpan">Flexible
computer-based manufacturing systems, such as CAD-CAM manufacturing in
the ship building industry, are evidential.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.58.11" class="koboSpan">Investment in
training has intangible option benefits for ship and port operators if
for example the management has a multi-skilled workforce to
utilise.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">2.3.2 Growth options, strategic options, competitive options</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">Growth options are
similar to expansion options but with more emphasis on strategic or
competitive positioning. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.60.2"
class="koboSpan">They set the path for future opportunities.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.60.3" class="koboSpan">Growth options
are possible because of the firm’s ownership of intangible assets such
as patents, proprietary technologies, ownership of valuable resources,
managerial capital, reputation or brand name, scale and market power
which allow companies to grow through future
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_687"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">profitable investments and to more effectively respond
to unexpected adversity or opportunities in a changing technological
competitive or general business environment (Trigeorgis, 2000).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">The ownership
of growth options enhances management’s flexibility for future action
and gives the firm a sustainable competitive advantage.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Technological
superiority and know-how permit further sequential (or parallel)
developments ensuring competitive edge is maintained.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.62.2" class="koboSpan">In this way
growth options such as in this example are called complex or compound
options as growth comes from exercising a series of options (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.62.3" class="koboSpan">an option on an
option). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.62.4" class="koboSpan">For
the shipbuilding and related industries, R&D investment is essential in
a competitive environment with rapid technological developments.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.62.5" class="koboSpan">Australian
shipbuilders became world leaders in aluminium welding techniques and
design of high-speed craft which ensured that they remained ahead of
other competitors by continual design development.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.62.6" class="koboSpan">Thus the
development of first generation product can create a proprietary growth
option acting as a springboard for developing in the future lower cost
and improved design or indeed new applications.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.62.7" class="koboSpan">Investment in
Information Technology (IT) can be viewed at a growth option as it
provides a link in the chain to interrelated projects and growth
opportunities.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">Similarly development
of a new market/trade with an initial negative NPV can open up or
generate opportunities in other markets at a later stage or can pre-empt
the entrance of a competitor. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.63.2"
class="koboSpan">This investment may be viewed as a strategic
investment. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.63.3"
class="koboSpan">Strategic acquisitions such as purchase of a terminal
by a shipping company gives the shipping line control over competitor
access and timing to the facilities conferring on the company a
competitive edge via the proprietorial real option.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">Once investment
opportunities are properly seen as collections or a portfolio of real
options, strategic planning can be more readily viewed as involving the
explicit recognition, creation and management of current and future
investment opportunities (Lai and Trigeorgis, 1995).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.64.2" class="koboSpan">Examples taken
from Bendall and Stent (2005, 2007a) are used below in Section 4 to
demonstrate how real options can be used to value complex maritime
investment applications involving both mutually exclusive and
non-mutually exclusive investment strategies.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">2.3.3 Option to contact, option to abandon</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">Investors may also
have embedded options to contract or abandon if a project fails to
achieve the required rate of return envisaged, due to less favourable
market conditions. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.66.2"
class="koboSpan">If market conditions are weaker than originally
anticipated management can operate below capacity or even reduce the
scale of operations and thus save part of planned investment outlays as
well as reducing operating costs.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">This
flexibility to lessen the loss is analogous to a put option on part of
the base scale project with the exercise price being equal to the
potential cost savings. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.66.4"
class="koboSpan">The option to contract is particularly valuable in the
case of entering into a new market (trade) or in choosing among
technologies with different construction to maintenance cost mix.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.66.5" class="koboSpan">To illustrate
this point, management may chose initially a lower cost asset with
higher maintenance expenditures in order to acquire the flexibility to
contract operations by cutting down on maintenance if market conditions
worsen.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">If the project suffers
severe losses through a systemic market decline or for some other reason
such that the firm can no longer sustain its fixed costs then the
project should be shut down. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.67.2"
class="koboSpan">The more general purpose the capital asset (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.67.3" class="koboSpan">lower asset
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_688"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan">specificity, the higher will be the value of the
abandonment option). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.68.2"
class="koboSpan">For example a container ship or bulk ship would be
considered to have low asset specificity while a gas carrier would have
high asset specificity. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.68.3"
class="koboSpan">This real option is equivalent in this case to an
American put option. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.68.4"
class="koboSpan">The underlying asset is the current value of the vessel
where the salvage value is the exercise price.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">In contrast
infrastructure companies’ abandonment options may be less valuable than
that of shipping lines because of the sunk cost nature of the assets.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">This means that
their exercise price is low. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.69.3"
class="koboSpan">Once constructed a port or terminal cannot be moved to
another location or may not be profitably used for another purpose,
although port land can be turned over to recreational use.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.69.4" class="koboSpan">With low
exercise prices, the options and the business that own them would be
worth less than they would otherwise.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">2.3.4 Option to switch (output or input), location options</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">Product or input
flexibility is a valuable option for management.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">With an option
to switch, management can change the output mix (product flexibility) if
prices or demand change or alternately, the same output can be produced
using different types of inputs (input flexibility).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">For instance,
Kulatilaka (1993) found that the value of the flexibility provided by an
industrial dual-fired steam boiler that can switch between alternative
energy inputs (natural gas and oil), as relative prices fluctuate, far
exceeded the incremental cost of a single-fuel alternative.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.71.4" class="koboSpan">In fact,
because of the existence of the switch option, the firm should be
willing to pay a positive premium for flexible technology over a rigid
alternative that confers no or less choice.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">In the maritime
industry there are many examples where management has opted for
technology which allowed flexibility in output (product switch option)
or choice of inputs (input switch option).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.72.2" class="koboSpan">In the 1970s a
cement carrier was introduced into service on the Australian coast which
could switch between diesel and compressed natural gas.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.72.3" class="koboSpan">In a greener
world, the ability to use renewable resources to power vessels has been
welcomed. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.72.4" class="koboSpan">The
Solar Sailor can switch between wind, solar and diesel-electric power
sources or can use a combination of all three, depending on weather
conditions. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.72.5" class="koboSpan">New
vessel designs are incorporating sail features allowing operators the
option to save fuel by supplementing wind power Many ports/terminals opt
for more expensive technology which allows flexibility in output (output
switch) e.g. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.72.6"
class="koboSpan">cranes with flexibility to service both panamax and
post-panamax vessels. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.72.7"
class="koboSpan">These investments may appear expensive at the time of
purchase but the true valuation has included a (product or input) switch
option.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">Closely linked to
switch options are location options.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">Multinational
manufacturing firms are sensitive to changes in exchange rates and
switch production inputs to choose, ex-post, the lowest input mix (input
switch option) (Kogut and Kulatilka, 1994).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.73.3" class="koboSpan">Companies, such
as Nike have moved production sites from one country to another to
reduce costs and maximise profits as exchange rates, labour costs and
investment incentives change. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.73.4"
class="koboSpan">Shipping is a service industry sensitive to exchange
rates and exchange rates may affect export competitiveness.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.73.5" class="koboSpan">The changing
pattern of trade changes the demand for shipping services.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.73.6" class="koboSpan">However vessels
can be re-routed or positioned in a new trade.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.73.7" class="koboSpan">Ships, in
contrast to other capital intensive investments, usually have low asset
specificity (Bendall and Manger, 1991) and can be switched (output
switch) easily to a new trade. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.73.8"
class="koboSpan">A vessel owner has thus acquired a valuable switch
option which is nested in the initial cost of the ship.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_689"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">2.3.5 Option to defer or waiting to invest or timing options</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">An option to defer is
an example of an American call option with its exercise price the money
to be invested at a later date. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.2"
class="koboSpan">It can be found in most projects where one has the
right to delay the start of the project.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.3" class="koboSpan">If a
shipbuilder holds a patent for new technology, the builder can delay
marketing the new design until market conditions prove more favourable
or has sold existing vessels with older technology currently under
construction. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.4" class="koboSpan">A
deferral option is often at the heart of real option flexibility value
because it can be linked to other options.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.5" class="koboSpan">Being able to
postpone a business decision to expand, to contract, to change inputs or
outputs, to abandon etc until more information is available is extremely
valuable to management. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.6"
class="koboSpan">A project with a negative NPV may become profitable if
it can be deferred over a certain time period.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.7" class="koboSpan">If a ship
operator acquires a controlling interest in a port/terminal in a
different trade he can chose if and when his ships will use the
facilities, safe in the knowledge that he will take priority at the
berth over competitors in the future and thus the opportunity to enter
and control that trade. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.8"
class="koboSpan">If the firm chooses to invest “now” rather than invest
“later” the NPV must be raised to offset the loss of the timing option
(Dixit and Pindyck, 1994). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.75.9"
class="koboSpan">This is in contrast to the expansion or growth
opportunities where the option to expand makes up any shortfall in the
static NPV.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">A lease enables
management to defer investment. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.76.2"
class="koboSpan">If the fast ship/ferry operator had been able to obtain
a time charter (an operating lease) or an option to buy (or an option on
a financial lease) from the shipbuilder and was able to defer a
commitment to purchase until there was more certainty regarding oil
prices, or other market conditions then the ferry/ship operator would
have acquired a valuable real option (to defer).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.76.3" class="koboSpan">Similarly a
terminal may lease equipment before committing to buy, awaiting the
necessary growth in throughput to make the investment profitable.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">Time charters with
purchase options, T/C-POPs, investment strategies offer the owner of the
(call) option valuable flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">They are
options to defer the decision to buy, but can be combined with a number
of embedded options. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.77.3"
class="koboSpan">In a European style T/C-POP the charter is given the
opportunity to purchase the vessel at the end of the charter period at a
pre-determined price while in an American T/C-POP the owner can opt to
purchase the vessel at any time up before the expiry
date.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0787" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0787"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan"> The value comes from the flexibility to choose if and
when to buy the vessel (exercise the option) as uncertainty unfolds.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.79.2" class="koboSpan">T/C-Pops can be
structured to give the holder a number of strategy choices.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.79.3" class="koboSpan">The T/C-POP
holder may purchase of the vessel (exercising an expansion option) if
buying is more advantageous to the ship operator than opting to
continuing chartering or take on a new T/C-POP (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.79.4" class="koboSpan">deferring for
another period) or indeed to abandon the trade altogether (an
abandonment option).</span>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">2.4 The grantor of the real option</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">To encourage
investment in infrastructure projects governments often grant real
options to compensate for the sunk nature of the investment.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.81.2" class="koboSpan">This can be in
the form of a revenue guarantee or clauses guaranteeing buy-backs at
given prices. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.81.3"
class="koboSpan">Shipbuilders may offer as a safety net or security to
new investors/financial institutions an option to buy-back the vessel
should the profitability of the venture fail.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.81.4" class="koboSpan">The buy-back is
pre-set generally on a sliding scale at rates commensurate with
depreciation and the time value of money.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.81.5" class="koboSpan">This is a great
deal for the shipowner as the holder of the real option posses
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_690"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">a valuable asset, but as grantor of the option the
shipbuilder is bearing the risk as he takes on a contingent liability
until the option lapses. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.82.2"
class="koboSpan">Bendall and Stent (2007b) demonstrated how to value
such “sweeteners” from the shipbuilder’s point of view.</span>

## <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">Valuing Real Options</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">“Whether advocated in
its strong form as a core valuation tool or its more moderate forms as a
ranking tool, a heuristic or a metaphor, the appeal of real options lies
in its promise of structuring decision making under uncertainty” (Adner,
2007).</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">While the argument
that the advantage of ROA lies in its framing and structuring of the
investment decision in real option terms has great allure, Damodaram
(2005) advocates the importance of the strong form.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.85.2" class="koboSpan">He argues that
if used only in a qualitative way that there is danger that the approach
could be used to justify poor investments.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.85.3" class="koboSpan">Managers who
argue for taking on a project with poor returns or pay a premium for
acquisitions on the basis of embedded real options should be required to
value these real options and demonstrate that in fact the economic
benefits do indeed exceed the costs.</span>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Real options analysis</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">As described in
Section 2, the conceptional principles are similar to that of financial
market options. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.87.2"
class="koboSpan">The opportunity to put an additional ship in the trade
is similar to an American call option and is the right but not the
obligation to acquire a claim to the cash flow value.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.87.3" class="koboSpan">Similarly the
right, but not the obligation, to reduce the scale of operation, say
moving from two ships to one in a trade or exiting the trade altogether,
is an example of a put option. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.87.4"
class="koboSpan">ROA thus can correctly value managerial flexibility by
explicitly considering appropriate action at future dates on which
information about the project’s profitability is revealed.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.87.5" class="koboSpan">The project’s
true valuation may look more attractive when the value of this
flexibility is
incorporated.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0788" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0788"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan"> This means that a project may have a static NPV that
is negative and therefore would be rejected using traditional NPV rules
but may be accepted if the value of flexibility is added.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">Value of project with
flexibility = Value of project without flexibility + Value of
flexibility</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">Thus the value of the
project is equal to the traditional static NPV or base case plus a value
for active management. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.91.2"
class="koboSpan">An option’s approach views capital investment as an on
going process requiring active managerial involvement and ROA provides
the means to value this flexibility at the ouset.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">The quantitative
origins of real options’ pricing derives from the financial markets with
the seminal work of Black and Scholes (1973) and Merton (1973) in
pricing financial options. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.92.2"
class="koboSpan">The model was perceived to be complex and off-putting
to many practitioners (Trigeorgis, 2000).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.92.3" class="koboSpan">Cox, Ross and
Rubinstein’s (1979) binomial approach presented a more simplified
methodology by evaluating financial options in discrete time.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">Although the Black
Scholes’ model is mathematically challenging and the assumptions
necessary too restrictive for pricing of real options, the principles
are useful
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_691"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">in developing an understanding of real option
valuation. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">The
basic variables in their “closed form” financial option pricing model
are the value of the underlying asset; the exercise price; the time to
expiration of the option; the volatility (standard deviation) of the
underlying risky asset and the risk free rate of interest over the life
of the option.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">In the case of a real
option the underlying risky asset is the value of the investment or
project. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">If the
value of the project rises, so too would the value of the option.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.3" class="koboSpan">The exercise
price is the amount needed to exercise the option i.e.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.4" class="koboSpan">the additional
investment costs in a multistage project.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.5" class="koboSpan">Note that in
the case of a call options, as the value of the exercise price
increases, the value of the option decreases but increases the value of
the option in the case of a put. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.6"
class="koboSpan">As the time to expiration (maturity of the option)
increases so too does the value of the option.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.7" class="koboSpan">This makes
intuitive sense in situations where there is a great deal of
uncertainty. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.8"
class="koboSpan">Obviously the longer the time there is to delay the
investment decision the more information is likely to become available.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.9" class="koboSpan">The value of
the option is therefore sensitive to the degree of uncertainty or
riskiness (volatility) of the underlying asset.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.10" class="koboSpan">Again this
makes sense if we understand that the payoff of the call option depends
on the value of the underlying asset exceeding its exercise price.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.11" class="koboSpan">This is more
likely to occur if volatility increases.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.95.12" class="koboSpan">Lastly the
value of the option increases if the risk free rate rises as it
increases the time value of money advantage in deferring the investment
cost until more information is known.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Cox and Ross (1976)
recognised that an option could be replicated (to create a “synthetic”
option) from an equivalent portfolio of traded securities.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.96.2" class="koboSpan">The replicating
portfolio approach is based on the Law of One Price which simply states
that to prevent arbitrage (riskless) profits, two assets with the same
payoffs (“twin
security”</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0789" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0789"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan"> or “twin
asset”</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0790" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0790"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan">) in every state of nature are perfect substitutes
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">perfectly correlated) with the underlying risky asset
and therefore have the same price (value).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">The
risk-neutral probability approach is mathematically equivalent.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.100.4" class="koboSpan">A hedge
portfolio is created, composed of one share in the underlying risky
asset and a short position in
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">” shares of the option being priced.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">The hedge
ratio </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan"> is riskless as loss on the underlying asset is offset
by the gain on the option (and vice versa) – hence risk free.</span>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Risk neutral valuation example</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">The example, although
simple, illustrates ROA valuation principles.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">It
demonstrates how static NPV can underestimate the value of the project
simply by not taking into account the embedded real option.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">Assume that a firm is
considering an initial investment costing \$12 million.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.107.2" class="koboSpan">The value of
the project in one year’s time is dependent on the (currently unknown)
demand for the product or service.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.107.3" class="koboSpan">If demand
turns out to be high, the project will be worth \$15 million; if demand
turns out to be low, the project’s value including the original
investment would be only \$10
million.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0791" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0791"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan"> These high and low outcomes are equally likely, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">each occurs
with a 50% probability (a 50–50 chance).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.109.3" class="koboSpan">The present
value, PV, was determined by multiplying the value of the high and low
outcomes by the respective probability and discounting by the risk
adjusted discount rate of 12%. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.109.4"
class="koboSpan">See </span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0173"
id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0173"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.111.2"
class="koboSpan">The risk free rate is 5%.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.111.3" class="koboSpan">The parameters
are summarised in
</span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fig0330" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fig0330"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">If the standard NPV
analysis is applied by discounting the expected cash flows by the risk
adjusted discount rate the base project’s present value is
\$11,161,000.</span>

<div id="Ch024.xhtml_fig0329" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00349.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Project’s present value" /></span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_692"></span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0173"
id="Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0173"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan"> Project’s present value</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch024.xhtml_fig0330" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00350.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fig0330)

</div>

<div id="Ch024.xhtml_fig0331" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00351.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">NPV = Present Value −
Initial investment</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">= \$11.161m −
\$12m</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">= – \$839,000 →
negative. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">Do
not invest.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">The NPV of –
\$839,000 is obtained by subtracting the initial capital cost of \$12
million. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.123.2" class="koboSpan">In
the absence of managerial flexibility (real options), the DCF analysis
rule leads to a rejection of the project as acceptance would destroy
value in the firm. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.123.3"
class="koboSpan">This decision ignores the ability of management to
alter the investment in response to new information.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.123.4" class="koboSpan">Traditional
NPV is unable to capture the value of any embedded real option.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.123.5" class="koboSpan">Should demand
conditions be more favourable than expected one year later, management
would like the flexibility to expand (an expansion option).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.123.6" class="koboSpan">The
traditional NPV analysis deals with this by implicitly assuming that
management commits to a particular course of action (expand or not
expand) at the time the project is launched, regardless of the
conditions that subsequently prevail.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.123.7" class="koboSpan">This severely
underestimates the value of the investment by ignoring the ability of
management to respond to new information.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.123.8" class="koboSpan">ROA allows
management to incorporate this flexibity into the investment
valuation.</span>

<div id="Ch024.xhtml_fig0332" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00352.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: ROA project value" /></span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_693"></span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0174"
id="Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0174"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan"> ROA project value</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">Having determined the
base case NPV, the event (decision) tree is utilised to calculate the
additional payoffs under both demand states should an additional
investment be made in the next period.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.127.2" class="koboSpan">From
</span>[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_fig0330)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan">, an additional investment of \$1million would increase
the scale of operation by 20%. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.129.2"
class="koboSpan">In high state demand the project’s pay-off lifts to
\$18million (\$15m\*1.20), a net gain of \$2 million.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">However if low
demand occurred the payoff would rise by the 20% to \$12 million
(\$10m\*1.20), a net gain of \$1million.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.129.4" class="koboSpan">See
</span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0174"
id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0174"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">The next step in the
ROA analyis is to identify a portfolio that exactly mimics high and low
demand state-contingent payoffs.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">The ability to
construct a “synthetic claim” or an equivalent replicating portfolio
enables a solution for the present value to be independent of the actual
probabilites, in this case (0.5) or the investor’s risk attitudes (risk
adjusted discount rate = 12%). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.132.3"
class="koboSpan">In effect mangement can replicate the pay-off by
contructing a portfolio using
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan"> units of the base case NPV and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">b </span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan">units of the riskless bond (equivalent to financing the
purchase by borrowing at the riskfree rate of 5%).</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore the
replicating portfolio’s pay-off equals</span>

<div id="Ch024.xhtml_tbl0007" class="table"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

|  |  |
|:---|:---|
| <span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">\*</span></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">15 + </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">b</span></span><sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">\*</span></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">1.05</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">in the high-demand state and</span> |
| <span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">m</span></span><sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">\*</span></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">10 + </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">b</span></span><sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">\*</span></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">1.05</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">in the low-demand state.</span> |

</div>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">If this portfolio is
to replicate the option,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan">b</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan"> must satisfy the two equations</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">15
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan"> + 1.05
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">b</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan"> = \$2million</span>\
<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan"> 10
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan"> + 1.05
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">b</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan"> = \$1million</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">The first equation
says that the portfolio has the same payoff as the expansion option in
the high-demand state; the second equation says that it has the same
payoff as the expansion option in the low-demand state.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">Solving the
two linear equations with two unknown variable
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">b</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">) gives
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan"> = 0.2000 and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan">b</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan"> = − \$952,380.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.175.2" class="koboSpan">That is,
owning a portfolio consisting of 0.2 units of the base case project and
riskless borrowing of \$952,380 is equivalent to holding the option to
expand.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_694"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan">The ROA approach states that, since both have the same
future payoffs, the present value of the expansion option is the same as
the present value of the portfolio.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.176.2" class="koboSpan">Thus the ROA
option value = (0.2\*\$11,161,000) − \$952,380 = \$1,279,820 and a
project value of \$440,820 (−839,000 + \$1,279,820), found by adding the
real option value to the base case
NPV.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0792" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0792"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan"> As the value of the NPV is positive the project should
be accepted. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.178.2"
class="koboSpan">The base case NPV (value of the project without
flexibility) undervalued the project by not including in the valuation
the value of flexibility created by the expansion option.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">Value of project with
flexibility = Value of project without flexibility + Value of
flexibility</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">The example used
assumes that there are only two points in time and only two possible
future states, and ignores various real-world complications.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.180.2" class="koboSpan">The tree only
considers an expansion
option.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0793" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0793"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan"> However the valuation principle can be extended to
more complex and realistic situations.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.182.2" class="koboSpan">Although the
analysis becomes more complicated, it relies on the same fundamental
method; the principle that assets with the same future payoffs must have
the same present value.</span>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 ROA methodologies: which one to use?</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">Despite the extensive
literature</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0794" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0794"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan"> and practitioner interest in real options, Copeland
and Antikarov’s prediction that ROA would be the accepted metric for
investment valuation by 2010 seems unlikely at this stage, although in
recent years software making it easier for practitioner is more freely
available. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.186.2" class="koboSpan">NPV
took at least 25 years to gain the status it now enjoys as the principal
tool for investment evaluation. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.186.3"
class="koboSpan">A real option approach is appealing for high risk
projects and for industries such as the maritime industry operating with
a highly uncertain market environment as it allows managers to structure
decision making and incorporate the value of flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.186.4" class="koboSpan">Although some
applications are relatively simple and straightforward and suitable for
commercially available generic real option software, many real world
applications involve sequential projects (compound options) and/or
multiple uncertainties (rainbow options) requiring more complex
modelling, thus perhaps inhibiting a more general acceptance.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">To be more widely
accepted as an investment decision tool, managers should appreciate that
ROA is not a replacement for DCF analysis.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.187.2" class="koboSpan">It extends NPV
by being able to incorporate and value a firm’s ability to adapt to
changing information at the outset.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.187.3" class="koboSpan">While some
firms put more emphasis on using real options for strategic management
formulation rather than modelling in a quantitative way, firms such as
Boeing</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0795" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0795"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
