class="koboSpan"> have become committed to ROA and now apply an option’s
approach to most of their investment and strategic decision making
(Matthews and Datar, 2007). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.189.2"
class="koboSpan">However other firms appear hesitant and, although
managers may understand the basic concepts do not yet have the
confidence to use or use as a standalone technique.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.189.3" class="koboSpan">There are a
number of possible reasons for this.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.189.4" class="koboSpan">Some concern
stems from not fully understanding when and in what circumstances it is
more appropriate to use a real option framework.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.189.5" class="koboSpan">Not all
investment decisions contain an embedded real option or, if present, can
be simply accommodated into the standard NPV valuation.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.189.6" class="koboSpan">The NPV value
may be so convincing in some analyses that although also containing
embedded real options, further identifying and valuing the real option
component has little point.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">Real options really
come into their own in the “grey area” where NPV is close to zero.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.190.2" class="koboSpan">It is at this
point where uncertainty is greatest and management needs to make tough
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_695"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">decisions. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.191.2"
class="koboSpan">Having the means to quantify flexibility is extremely
helpful. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.191.3"
class="koboSpan">Copeland and Antikarov (2001) argue that if the NPV is
very negative then no amount of optionality is likely to rescue the
project. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.191.4"
class="koboSpan">Similarly when the NPV is high, additional options have
a low probability of being exercised.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.191.5" class="koboSpan">Adner and
Levinthal (2004) caution that an option approach may be misleading in
some instances by providing examples where an option framework is
unsuitable for some strategy applications involving sequential decisions
and abandonment, particularly where resolution of technical and market
uncertainty is largely unconstrained.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.191.6" class="koboSpan">They argue
strongly that knowing the boundaries of ROA only serves to make ROA a
more powerful and precise valuation tool.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">Perhaps the strongest
factor limiting wider application in practice may be the variety of
methodologies that have been proposed under ROA, causing concern that if
the “</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan">wrong</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan">” method should be applied then perhaps an incorrect
investment decision could result.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.194.2" class="koboSpan">This
apprehension too is understandable.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">However all
ROA approaches have at their core the calculation of value.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.194.4" class="koboSpan">Reviewing the
literature and applications it appears that it may be simply a case of
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan">if the cap
fits</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.196.1" class="koboSpan">”
i.e. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.196.2" class="koboSpan">the
appropriate real option methodology depends on the specific problem, the
market, the nature of the uncertainty, the type of the option being
valued and to a certain extent the disciplinary background strengths of
the researcher.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">ROA methodologies
encompass both finance and operations research/management science
disciplines. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.197.2"
class="koboSpan">In some circumstances the data are freely available in
the market and the appropriate methodology would be similar to financial
market option models. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.197.3"
class="koboSpan">However for some projects market data are not available
and may need to be replaced by subjective inputs and calculated by
drawing on other decision making techniques.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.197.4" class="koboSpan">The following
illustrate different approaches applicable for different data
sets.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.1 Using market data and replicating portfolio approach</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">If the investment can
be effectively hedged through a traded tracking portfolio, the data used
to value the investment can be taken from a traded portfolio or twin
security i.e. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.199.2"
class="koboSpan">market data, and the option value calculated is thus
the no-arbitrage value of the investment.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.199.3" class="koboSpan">The assumption
is that markets are complete with respect to all corporate investments
and can be tracked with a traded portfolio.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.199.4" class="koboSpan">Thus, the cash
flows from the project are replicated by a self-financing portfolio of
riskless securities and futures contracts (Brennan and Schwatz,
1985).</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0796" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0796"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan"> The twin security has the same risk characteristics
and thus can be viewed as being, if not perfectly correlated, closely
correlated with the project under consideration.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.201.2" class="koboSpan">As more
shipping companies become listed then shipping stocks or indices could
be used as the replicating portfolio to evaluate an investment in
shipping. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.201.3"
class="koboSpan">Having identified the replicating portfolio or twin
security and calculated price and volatility factors, the investment
then is “sized” in relation to the twin security.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.201.4" class="koboSpan">The traded
replicating portfolio from the financial market assumes that asset price
movements follow geometric Brownian motion, GBM, so standard financial
tools such as Black Scholes may be appropriately applied.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.2 Subjective assessment approach</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">For staged or
sequential investments, Luerhram (1997) and Howell
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2001) follow a similar approach of no-arbitrage
replicating portfolios but because of inadequate or non-availability of
market data, use subjective assessments.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.205.2" class="koboSpan">The authors
argue that if the
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_696"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan">option to be valued is a compound option, early stages
(investments) may or may not provide a direct cash flow but simply
provide the right to further investments.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">As the risks
of the option can be hedged away with a replicating portfolio and
uncertainty is assumed to follow geometric Brownian motion then standard
financial option pricing tools may be still used.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.206.3" class="koboSpan">The difference
in this approach to that above is that subjective assessments need to be
made, as opposed to data from traded markets, for value calculations.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.206.4" class="koboSpan">As it is no
longer possible to “size” the investment relative to an equivalent
traded investment, DCF may then be used to determine the value of the
underlying asset.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.3 Dynamic programming and DTA</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">In some cases, the
assumptions underlying the standard financial market option approach may
be too restrictive so real options analysis, based on a financial option
approach, is thus inappropriate.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">Where market
data are not available i.e. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.208.3"
class="koboSpan">markets are not complete and it is not possible to find
an asset which is perfectly correlated, Dixit and Pindyck,
(1994)</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0797" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0797"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Amram and Kulatilaka, (2000) apply management
science techniques such as dynamic programming and decision analysis to
value real options. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.210.2"
class="koboSpan">In place of standard option pricing, a decision tree
representing alternative strategies is constructed with probabilities
and values assigned to the company specific risk based on subjective
assessment. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.210.3" class="koboSpan">A
spreadsheet is used at each tree endpoint to calculate the
NPV,</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0798" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0798"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan"> with an appropriate WACC.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.212.2" class="koboSpan">The tree is
then rolled back to determine the optimum strategy.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.4 Public v private risk approach</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">Smith and Nau (1995)
and Smith and McCardle (1998) analyses also recognised that for many
investment decisions the assumption that markets are complete is
inappropriate. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.214.2"
class="koboSpan">They point out that markets are generally only
partially complete. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.214.3"
class="koboSpan">They were the first to separate the two types of risk,
public (market) and private (company specific risks) and incorporate
both into the decision-making process.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.214.4" class="koboSpan">For example,
in the case of a LNG ship investment the risk associated with the
international gas prices could be classed as a public risk (market risk)
and freight demand for a particular shipping company as a private risk
(company-specific risk). </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.214.5"
class="koboSpan">The valuation method of each differs depending on the
type of risk. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.214.6"
class="koboSpan">Rather than forcing real option valuation into an
either/or approach (standard financial option pricing versus decision
analysis), they incorporated both into their methodology.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.214.7" class="koboSpan">Traditional
option pricing methods should be used where risks can be hedged by
trading securities and that proportion of the asset driven by private
risks, by assigned probabilities in a decision analysis framework.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.214.8" class="koboSpan">A risk
adjusted decision tree would then be built based on investment
alternatives and tree branches representing public risks resolved by
identifying the replicating portfolio and applying standard finance
no-arbitrage option techniques such as Black Scholes or binomial lattice
(Leunberger, 1998), and private risks branches using subjective
probabilities, before folding back in the usual way.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.5 The MAD approach</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">The Market Asset
Disclaimer (MAD) approach does not rely at all on the existence of a
traded replicating portfolio. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.216.2"
class="koboSpan">Copeland and Antikarov (2001) point out the
difficulties of finding a market based “twin asset,” or “twin security”
that is perfectly
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_697"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">correlated with the underlying asset.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.217.2" class="koboSpan">Instead of
searching for a perfectly correlated asset in the market, or even a
close substitute, they propose that the present value of the project
itself be used as the value of the underlying asset.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.217.3" class="koboSpan">“What is
better correlated with the project than the project itself?”
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.217.4" class="koboSpan">The present
value of the project without flexibility becomes the best unbiased
estimate of the market value of the project, were it a traded asset.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.217.5" class="koboSpan">The MAD real
option approach built on previous studies by Kasanen and Trigeorgis
(1993), Trigeorgis (1999), Brealey and Myers (2000) amongst others.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.217.6" class="koboSpan">The underlying
asset is itself not traded. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.217.7"
class="koboSpan">The initial NPV is an estimate of the value of the
future behaviour that the asset would have if it was traded.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.217.8" class="koboSpan">The authors
point out that the real options are still able to be valued even though
not traded, because the process of capital budgeting determines the
value of the project’s cash flows in the
market.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0799" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0799"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.218.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">By using the MAD
approach we are no longer restricted to resolving projects in complete
markets. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.219.2"
class="koboSpan">Private versus public risk is dealt with directly with
the NPV calculation. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.219.3"
class="koboSpan">Samuelson’s proof that properly anticipated prices
fluctuate randomly ensures that even an irregular stochastic pattern of
future cash flows will follow a random walk through time with constant
volatility. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.219.4" class="koboSpan">A
binomial lattice can thus be used.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.219.5" class="koboSpan">Monte Carlo
simulation generates a distribution which is used to build a
risk-neutral binomial lattice and option value.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.219.6" class="koboSpan">There is now
no need to assume a specific discount rate or weighted average cost of
capital, WACC. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.219.7"
class="koboSpan">The underlying asset value is determined using a
spreadsheet. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.219.8"
class="koboSpan">The MAD approach is intuitively appealing for
practitioners as it extends NPV analysis and has a much wider
application to a number of real options investment valuation
problems.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.6 Probabilistic v possibilistic distribution approaches</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">Two recent real
option valuation methods also appear promising and arousing a lot of
interest. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.221.2" class="koboSpan">DM
and Fuzzy ROV may be solved using commercially available software and
require minimum modelling. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.221.3"
class="koboSpan">Thus they appear intuitively appealing to practitioners
with minimum modelling skills. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.221.4"
class="koboSpan">It can be used for strategy discussion before the
analytical valuation calculation, providing an opportunity for direct
input by managers in the firm at the formulation of the model stage.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.221.5" class="koboSpan">As with MAD,
information available from traditional project analysis using NPV also
forms the basis of Mathews and Datar (2004, 2007) and Matthews and
Salmon, (2007) DM methodology. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.221.6"
class="koboSpan">The DM option approach was initially developed to
evaluate staged projects for new product developments at Boeing
involving R&D (compound options) and thus would be applicable to similar
maritime applications, particularly in shipbuilding and marine
engineering fields. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.221.7"
class="koboSpan">Because of the uncertainty regarding operating profit
forecast each year, to value the option Monte Carlo simulation is used
to generate a probability distribution of project’s
value,</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0800" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0800"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan"> rather than a single expected value in other ROA
methodologies. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.223.2"
class="koboSpan">In this method a variety of discount rates can be
applied to reflect the risk of different aspects of the project’s cash
flow. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.223.3" class="koboSpan">For
example, projected profit cash flows could be discounted by an
appropriate risk adjusted discount rate while the discretionary
investment level (the exercise price of the call option on the new
venture), by the risk free rate.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.223.4" class="koboSpan">The risk free
rate here is appropriate as the risk is
low.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0801" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0801"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan"> Only positive outcomes are selected for the next stage
as the project would be terminated if a loss is forecast.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.225.2" class="koboSpan">Net profit,
equal to the difference between operating profit and exercise price, of
the positive outcomes is used to build a further payoff distribution.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.225.3" class="koboSpan">The real
option value is the weighted mean or average value of this positive
probability distribution.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_698"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">Their approach, the authors argue, simplifies and helps
manage complex strategic investment problems and is algebraically
equivalent to the Black Scholes when the same constraints are
used.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0802" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0802"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan"> It uses the language and framework of standard DCF.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.228.2" class="koboSpan">Because it can
be modelled on a spreadsheet using off-the-shelf simulation software to
incorporate uncertainty and timing decisions, the authors argue that is
easily more understood by management and so not only provides a
valuation method that is transparent, but can give structure to early
scenario based strategic discussion at all levels in the company
providing further modelling refinement from input of experts.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">Collan (2008)
proposes using fuzzy numbers to calculate the value of a compound real
option. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.229.2" class="koboSpan">Here,
the treatment of risk is different from the DM approach.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.229.3" class="koboSpan">Uncertainty
means that it may be difficult, or managers may not have the confidence,
to give absolutely correct (crisp) values.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.229.4" class="koboSpan">Fuzzy
sets</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0803" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0803"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan"> allow for graduation or qualitative estimates.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.231.2" class="koboSpan">In place of a
probabilistic distribution of the DM approach, the fuzzy pay-off method
uses a possibilistic distribution based on triangular or trapezoidal
fuzzy
numbers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0804" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0804"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan"> Simulation is not a necessary step and can be solved
using spreadsheet software. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.233.2"
class="koboSpan">Although the fuzzy set approach is a late addition to
the stable of real option methodologies, it is as yet to be tested
empirically and/or taken up by corporates.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.233.3" class="koboSpan">However, one
advantage of this method over other methods the author states, is that
it will be perceived as more realistic by management as it allows direct
input of non-crisp subjective values.</span>

#### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.234.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.7 So which course should maritime companies chart?</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">Although each method
has merit when applied to a specific set of variables or application,
the Market Asset Disclosure, MAD, approach has been shown to be far less
restrictive. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.235.2"
class="koboSpan">Instead of having to separate public from private risks
or search for a perfectly correlated asset in the market, the present
value of the project itself can be used as the best unbiased estimate of
the project were it to be traded, and thus can be applied to a wider set
of real option valuation problems.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.235.3" class="koboSpan">The approach
is intuitively appealing as it is not a “black box”.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.235.4" class="koboSpan">It does not
rely on using a correct weighted cost of capital, WACC.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.235.5" class="koboSpan">It extends NPV
analysis, a valuation technique well understood by management, by
valuing at the outset management’s flexibility to alter a project when
more information becomes available and uncertainty resolved.</span>

## <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.236.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.236.2" class="koboSpan">Valuing Complex Maritime Investment Decisions</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">Companies operating
in a changing and turbulent market environment must be flexible.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.237.2" class="koboSpan">The maritime
industry is no exception and operates in an environment characterised by
many volatile and uncertain factors.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.237.3" class="koboSpan">It is an
industry whose cash flows are exposed to daily changes in international
financial markets, to multi-currency risk, to multi-country sovereign
risk, to pirates, to movements in oil prices, to other competitors and,
above all, the trade cycle. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.237.4"
class="koboSpan">So the decision to proceed with the acquisition of new
ship technology or a new portainer crane can be regarded as a large
scale capital evaluation problem within the context of a great number of
volatile parameters. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.237.5"
class="koboSpan">Optimisation of the firm’s value is dependent on
correct investment choices by management.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.237.6" class="koboSpan">Management
thus needs sound and reliable tools to minimise the risk of poor
investment decisions.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_699"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">The following maritime examples of ROA are based on the
MAD approach and illustrate the advantage of a ROA approach over
traditional static NPV. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.238.2"
class="koboSpan">In each case, the value of flexibility, the real
option, is calculated and added to the present value of the original
strategy to derive the present value of the flexible strategy.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.238.3" class="koboSpan">The examples
chosen</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0805" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0805"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan"> demonstrate how to value alternate strategies in the
face of high uncertainty and how to correctly choose from a portfolio of
investment strategies which are not mutually exclusive.</span>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Maritime Example 1</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">The first maritime
example is that of an investment in a high speed hub and spoke feeder
service based on Singapore to Penang and
Klang.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0806" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0806"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.243.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan"> Three alternate investment strategies were proposed
involving the employment of one or two ships with port visits to each or
both.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">Demand and base
freight rates were modelled as triangular probability distributions and
a simulation
performed</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0807" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0807"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan"> to calculate the NPV of the three strategies.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">See
</span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fig0333" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fig0333"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.249.2"
class="koboSpan">A period of one year elapses (the time to build the
ship) between the decision to commit to a particular strategy and
commencement of the cash flow. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.249.3"
class="koboSpan">Consequently the present values of the cash flows need
to be discounted a further year at the cost of capital at 10% and the
cost of the vessel at the risk free rate of 5% to obtain the NPVs.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.249.4" class="koboSpan">These values
became the base case (static) NPV for the ROA.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">The flexible
strategys are summarised in </span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0175"
id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0175"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.252.2"
class="koboSpan">An option on the maximum of three risky assets (the
three strategys), is determined like a financial option using
no-arbitrage and added to the value to the base NPV case to obtain a
value for a flexible NPV.</span>

class="koboSpan">1</span><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.285.1" class="koboSpan">T</span></span></sub></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan">Change to strategy 3</span></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">Strategies 1 to 3 are
risky assets. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.287.2"
class="koboSpan">The flexible strategy is to proceed with original
Strategy 1 (NPV = −\$1.63m) with an option to change to original
strategies 2 or 3 as uncertainty is resolved.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.287.3" class="koboSpan">If the
combined value of the NPV of strategy 1 plus the option value exceeds
the NPV of strategy 3 (NPV = \$4.27m) then the flexible strategy is
preferred. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.287.4" class="koboSpan">The
option is an American style since the decision to exercise is not
restricted to a single fixed point in time.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.287.5" class="koboSpan">An efficient
multinomial lattice algorithm with risk neutral probabilities developed
by Kamad and Ritchken (1991) was used to calculate the option value by
valuing each path of the multinomial tree and then folding back,
checking for early exercise at decision points.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">The formula used at
the end of each path (time denoted by
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">) is</span>

<div id="Ch024.xhtml_fig0335" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00355.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.292.1" class="koboSpan">where
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan">M</span><sub><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan">iT
</span></sub></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan">is, for each original strategy
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan">i </span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">= 1,2,3, the market value generated along the path, and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan">max</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the function which assigns the maximum value of the
three arguments. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.299.2"
class="koboSpan">If the end of a path is reached then there has not been
earlier exercise and strategy 1 is still in operation.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.299.3" class="koboSpan">The formula
assigns the extra value that would result by making the best decision at
this time and is summarised in </span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0176"
id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0176"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.302.1" class="koboSpan">Since the value of
the second strategy is subject to the one-year time to build the second
ship, its value is discounted one year and the discounted cost of the
second ship,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan">S</span><sub><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></sub></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan">, as calculated above deducted.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan">r</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the risk-free rate.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.307.2" class="koboSpan">Folding back
from the end of the tree to the single starting node is performed in the
usual manner using the risk-neutral probabilities and the risk-free rate
of interest. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.307.3"
class="koboSpan">At a decision step, every six-months folding back, the
option value is the maximum of the folded-back value (wait) and the
early exercise value calculated as in Equation 1 with
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan"> now denoting the particular point in time.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">Value of project with
flexibility = Value of project without flexibility + Value of
flexibility</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">The value of the
option to expand the service (value of flexibility) was calculated to be
\$13.43 million. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.311.2"
class="koboSpan">To allow for the time elapse between the decision and
delivery of the vessel, the value of the real option also needs to be
discounted an extra year (to \$12.21m) and added to the NPV of Strategy
1 (−\$1.63m), the inflexible NPV.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.311.3" class="koboSpan">As the value
of the flexible strategy at \$10.57m exceeds the value of original
Strategy 3 of \$4.27m, then the flexible strategy is preferred.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.311.4" class="koboSpan">The flexible
strategy in this case was revealed to be more valuable than the three
inflexible strategies.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">These results
demonstrate that rather than purchasing one ship and servicing Klang as
indicated by traditional NPV analysis in Bendall and Stent (2001), ROA
has shown that a better strategy would be that as set out in
</span>[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0175)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.314.2"
class="koboSpan">The ship would initially be
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_701"></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan">used to service both ports, Klang and Penang.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.315.2" class="koboSpan">As uncertainty
is resolved either a second ship should be ordered to expand the
frequency of service being offered to each port (expansion option) or
the service to Penang should be abandoned (abandonment option) and the
one ship used to provide a more frequent service to Klang only.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.315.3" class="koboSpan">To determine
which branch to follow, the shipowner would need to re-work the exercise
at regular intervals. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.315.4"
class="koboSpan">The recalculation ensures that parameters and
stochastic variables can be updated in the light of actual
experience.</span>

### <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Maritime Example 2</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.317.1" class="koboSpan">Possessing options
expands the company’s opportunity set and attributes value to
management’s ability to react to changing circumstances.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.317.2" class="koboSpan">The more
options, the more valuable is the investment.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.317.3" class="koboSpan">In this second
example ROA is used to value more than one embedded real option, a
European put associated with a replacement investment and an option on
the maximum of two operating strategies; trading if buoyant demand, or
chartering out the vessel, should the trade prove not to be economically
viable.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">The case involved a
decision to invest in a new fifth vessel by an established shipping line
in the Trans-Tasman trade. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.318.2"
class="koboSpan">Because of the long lead time from the time of placing
an order to the vessel entering the trade the shipping line was faced
with a number of uncertainties regarding future operating conditions
such as demand, freight rates, risk of entry of competitors etc.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.318.3" class="koboSpan">Traditional
inflexible DCF analysis indicated that the project should not go ahead
as an NPV of −
\$1.346m</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0808" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0808"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan"> was negative and would thus be rejected.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.320.2" class="koboSpan">The present
value is of course an average of the simulated scenario cash flows.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.320.3" class="koboSpan">As an
alternate, a second strategy was proposed to buy the ship but then
charter it out which yielded a small positive NPV of \$0.515m.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.320.4" class="koboSpan">Here cash
flows from chartering,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan">c</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
class="koboSpan">, were discounted by the cost of capital,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan">k</span></span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
class="koboSpan">, to yield the present
value,</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan"> Q</span></span><sub><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan">0</span></sub><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan">, of
\$2.88m</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0809" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0809"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan"> using the following formula.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.329.2" class="koboSpan">The initial
discounting term
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan">1/(1+k)</span></span><sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
class="koboSpan">1.25</span></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.332.1"
class="koboSpan"> covered the 15 months required to build the
ship.</span>

<div id="Ch024.xhtml_fig0336" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.333.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00356.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.334.1" class="koboSpan">However in both these
traditional static NPV strategies some scenarios being averaged could
favour a decision to build or charter out, though others will not.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.334.2" class="koboSpan">With a static
analysis management does not have the flexibility to adapt to particular
scenarios as they unfold and thus ROA is a more appropriate methodology
to value the flexibility to respond as more information becomes
available.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">Three flexible
strategies were investigated. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.335.2"
class="koboSpan">The first combined the two static strategies by
building a ship initially for the trade but with an option to charter
out if the trade turns out not viable to support a fifth vessel with the
better of the two strategies selected after gaining more information.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.335.3" class="koboSpan">It was
modelled as an American style call.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.335.4" class="koboSpan">The second
flexible strategy was modelled as a European put on the fifth ship and
allowed the shipowner to use the ship as a replacement for the oldest in
the fleet, scheduled in four years time, if the trade was unable to
support a fifth ship. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.335.5"
class="koboSpan">The strike price is the savings in costs from delaying
the replacement of the fourth ship which would now not occur for a
further 11
years.</span><sup><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_fn0810" id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0810"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.336.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.337.1"
class="koboSpan"> The decision to exercise the put would occur in 2.75
years after allowing for time to build the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.337.2" class="koboSpan">However the
two flexible strategies are not mutually</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_702"></span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0177"
id="Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0177"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.338.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4:</span></span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.339.1"
class="koboSpan"> Valuation of three flexible strategies</span>

<div id="Ch024.xhtml_tbl0009" class="table"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

| <span class="bold"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.340.1" class="koboSpan">Strategy</span></span> | <span class="bold"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.341.1" class="koboSpan">NPV \$m</span></span> | <span class="bold"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.342.1" class="koboSpan">Option value \$m</span></span> | <span class="bold"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">ROA \$m</span></span> |
|:---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.344.1" class="koboSpan">Flexible strategy 1</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">-1.346</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">2.608</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.347.1" class="koboSpan">1.262</span> |
| <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">Flexible strategy 2</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.349.1" class="koboSpan">-1.346</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.350.1" class="koboSpan">1.888</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.351.1" class="koboSpan">0.542</span> |
| <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.352.1" class="koboSpan">Flexible strategy 3</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.353.1" class="koboSpan">-1.346</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.354.1" class="koboSpan">2.661</span> | <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.355.1" class="koboSpan">1.315</span> |

</div>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.356.1" class="koboSpan">exclusive and can be
combined to form the third flexible strategy to allow the shipowner the
flexibility to build a ship for trade, charter out or retire oldest
vessel.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">The flexible
strategies were valued. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.357.2"
class="koboSpan">The value of the flexible strategy, ROA, was found by
adding the value of the option to the static NPV valuation and are set
out in </span><a href="#Ch024.xhtml_cap_lbl0177"
id="Ch024.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0177"><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.360.1" class="koboSpan">In each case the
valuing the flexibility, ROA, increased the value of the strategy
compared to the static NPV, by the value of the real option.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.360.2" class="koboSpan">The more
alternate strategies present the more value will be added.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.360.3" class="koboSpan">With strategy
three, the combined case, the value was greater than either flexible
strategy one or two alone. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.360.4"
class="koboSpan">However the component values are not cumulative.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.360.5" class="koboSpan">In the study,
a sensitivity analysis showed that the more correlated are the
underlying projects (the strategies), the less net value will be added.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.360.6" class="koboSpan">A sensitivity
analysis also showed that the greater the volatility of the underlying
base project, the greater the value of the embedded real options and
thus the ROA.</span>

## <span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.361.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.361.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.362.1" class="koboSpan">Real options are
persuasive and valuable and are an essential tool to value investments
under uncertainty for decision makers in highly capital intensive
industries, such as the maritime industry.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.362.2" class="koboSpan">The standard
capital budgeting techniqes cannot capture the value of management
flexibility to respond to changes in market conditions, forcing mangers
to rely heavily on qualitative “strategic” judgment (managerial
experience) when valuing investment opportunities.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.362.3" class="koboSpan">Even without a
calculated financial value of the option ROA can be used as a powerful
conceptual tool to discuss future investment projects within the firm.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.362.4" class="koboSpan">The approach
can highlight and define concepts (underlying asset value, exercise
price, maturity etc), particularly of staged investments, in place of
vague concepts of flexibility. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.362.5"
class="koboSpan">However care must be taken to avoid poor investments if
only a qualitative approach is used.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.362.6" class="koboSpan">A ROA
quantitative approach will not only identify and value the embedded real
options but can demonstrate if the benefits of flexibility outweigh the
costs.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.363.1" class="koboSpan">The chapter described
a number of maritime real otion applications before outlining various
real option approaches. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.363.2"
class="koboSpan">ROA draws on both finance and operations
research/management science disciplines and in most cases the
appropriate methodolgy will depend on the actual application and the
data available. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.363.3"
class="koboSpan">The MAD approach was seen to be theoretically sound and
most applicable for the maritime applications chosen to illustrate ROA
in practice. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.363.4"
class="koboSpan">The ROA examples selected demonstrated that traditional
NPV analysis fails to capture managerial flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.363.5" class="koboSpan">If an ROA
approach valuing flexibility is not undertaken then project value may be
underestimated and if rejected on that basis, lead to under-investment
and opportunity loss. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.363.6"
class="koboSpan">Thus ROA should become a standard tool for investment
decision making and an appropriate course to chart for the maritime
industry.</span>

class="koboSpan">\*</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0781)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.365.1"

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.384.1"

</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.385.2" class="koboSpan">In this case

</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.385.3" class="koboSpan">For example a

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.388.1"

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.390.1"
class="koboSpan">10.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0791)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan"> The values of the project’s payoffs in year 1 are
assumed for illustration purposes.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.392.1"
class="koboSpan">11.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0792)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan"> The risk neutral probability approach yielded the same
project value of \$1.28million. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.393.2"
class="koboSpan">The PV of the hedge portfolio is multiplied by the
risk-free rate and set equal to the payout for the high (up) and low
(down) demand state. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.393.3"
class="koboSpan">The PV of the option is calculated using risk neutral
probabilities, (pu = 0.3438, pd= 0.6563).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.393.4" class="koboSpan">Note these
risk-neutral probabilities are not the same as the objective
probabilities in Table 1. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.393.5"
class="koboSpan">The Present Value of the option is equal to the
expected payoffs multiplied by (risk neutral) probabilities to adjust
them for their risk.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.394.1"
class="koboSpan">12.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0793)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.395.1"
class="koboSpan"> An option to abandon or an option to switch may be
appropriate but are abstracted from this example.</span>

<span id="Ch024.xhtml_page_704"></span>[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.396.1"
class="koboSpan">13.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0794)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.397.1"
class="koboSpan"> Real options are now widely found in corporate finance
literature, academic journals, financial texts and financial press
(Graham and Harvey, 2001, Phillippe, 2005).</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.398.1"
class="koboSpan">14.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0795)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.399.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Datar Matthews, DM method for solving real options
has been patented by the Boeing company (US patent 6862579).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.399.2" class="koboSpan">See
below.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.400.1"
class="koboSpan">15.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0796)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.401.1"
class="koboSpan"> See for example Amram and Kulatilaka (1999).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.401.2" class="koboSpan">Building on
the work of Brennan and Schwatz (1985) they evaluate a new mill using
listed textile mill shares as the replicating portfolio.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.402.1"
class="koboSpan">16.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0797)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan"> Dixit and Pindyck (1994) refer to real option pricing
as contingent claims analysis and applied their approach to a shipping
example. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.403.2"
class="koboSpan">Freight rates they argue are stochastic and follow a
GBM with no drift. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.403.3"
class="koboSpan">Their real options approach demonstrated if/when
tankers should be mothballed or scrapped (abandonment option) when
facing market condition uncertainty.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.403.4" class="koboSpan">Their
entry–exit-scrapping model is further developed in Sodal (2001).
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.403.5" class="koboSpan">He points out
the problems of assuming Dixit and Pindyck’s GBM and suggests that mean
reversion of freight rates is more likely.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.403.6" class="koboSpan">Sodal (2003)
uses a similar real options methodology to ascertain the appropriateness
of investment in fuel cell technology vessels (switching
options).</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan">17.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0798)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.405.1"
class="koboSpan"> Assuming a log-normal distribution.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.406.1"
class="koboSpan">18.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0799)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.407.1"
class="koboSpan"> The certainty equivalent (risk neutral) value of a
real option is likewise an estimate of the option’s market value if it
were traded (Brealey and Myers, 2000).</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.408.1"
class="koboSpan">19.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0800)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.409.1"
class="koboSpan"> Datar Matthews (2007) use Monte Carlo software to
create a triangular distribution for each year of the operating profit
forecast. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.409.2" class="koboSpan">The
authors point out that other distributions can be applied.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan">20.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0801)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.411.1"
class="koboSpan"> Risk is low as management controls the funds.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.411.2" class="koboSpan">The new
project would only be launched if there a good prospects for a
successful outcome. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.411.3"
class="koboSpan">Datar and Matthews (2007) used Boeing’s corporate bond
rate which was close to the risk-free rate as it was easier for
management to understand. </span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.411.4"
class="koboSpan">The degree of risk aversion reflected in the option
value is a function of the differential of the discount rates used.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.411.5" class="koboSpan">A risk-neutral
valuation would exist if the discount rates used were the same.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.412.1"
class="koboSpan">21.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0802)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.413.1"
class="koboSpan"> Black Scholes would only be an appropriate benchmark
only if the distribution is log-normal.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.413.2" class="koboSpan">However the DM
methodology has been found to be reliable using the Binomial process for
in-the-money calls and for out-of-the money calls with longer maturities
Datar and Matthews (2004).</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.414.1"
class="koboSpan">22.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0803)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.415.1"
class="koboSpan"> Zadeh (1965) developed the algebra for fuzzy sets.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.415.2" class="koboSpan">For fuzzy
logic applied to ROA see Carlsson and Fuller (2003), (Colan, Carlsson
and Majlender (2003), Carlsson and Majlender (2005).</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.416.1"
class="koboSpan">23.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0804)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.417.1"
class="koboSpan"> Scenario analysis can be used to generate the fuzzy
NPV or fuzzy numbers from the outset.
</span><span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.417.2" class="koboSpan">Collan
(2008).</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.418.1"
class="koboSpan">24.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0805)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.419.1"
class="koboSpan"> Examples are taken from Bendall and Stent (2005) and
Bendall and Stent (2007a).</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.420.1"
class="koboSpan">25.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0806)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.421.1"
class="koboSpan"> The hub and spoke strategies were based on an earlier
study (Bendall and Stent, 2001) where an optimising model determined the
most profitable routes to maximise returns.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.422.1"
class="koboSpan">26.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0807)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.423.1"
class="koboSpan"> The simulation over 15 years was based on 15,000
iterations.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.424.1"
class="koboSpan">27.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0808)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.425.1"
class="koboSpan"> For parameters and full analysis see Bendall and Stent
(2007a).</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.426.1"
class="koboSpan">28.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0809)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.427.1"
class="koboSpan"> This value was arrived at by using a seven-year daily
charter rate supplied by industry, less daily operational costs and a
further allowance for off-hire and overhaul.</span>

[<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.428.1"
class="koboSpan">29.</span>](#Ch024.xhtml_bck_fn0810)<span id="Ch024.xhtml_kobo.429.1"
class="koboSpan"> Economic ship life was assumed to be 15 years.</span>

</div>
