<div id="Ch025.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_709"></span>[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 25</span>\
<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Business Risk Measurement and Management in the Cargo Carrying Sector of the Shipping Industry — An Update</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0545)
===============================================================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Manolis</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">G.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Kavussanos</span></span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0811" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0811"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">Risk management in an
industry which is riddled with cyclicalities in its rates and prices and
which has made and destroyed millionaires over the years is extremely
important. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">The
issue has been discussed in
Gray,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0812" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0812"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0813" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0813"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan"> comparing traditional methods of hedging, as he calls
the choice of contract during ship
operation,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0814" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0814"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan"> with the “new” instruments that appeared in the market
at the time. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.14.2"
class="koboSpan">The latter were the futures contracts, which were
launched by the Baltic Exchange in London and the International Futures
Exchange in Bermuda, trading BIFFEX (Baltic International Freight
Futures Exchange) and INTEX contracts for the dry bulk and tanker
sectors, respectively.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">In the meantime a
number of developments have occurred, including the restructuring,
renaming and the eventual abandonment of the Baltic Freight Index (BFI)
in 2002 – the underlying commodity upon which BIFFEX contracts have been
trading. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">The
development of Over the Counter (OTC) Freight Forward Agreements (FFA)
since 1992, the introduction of clearing of these OTC contracts and the
appearance of options and swaps can be added to these developments, all
of which have major implications for the way risk is managed in the
industry today. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.15.3"
class="koboSpan">A comprehensive description of these developments is
provided in Kavussanos and
Visvikis.</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0815" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0815"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0816" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0816"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">At the same time
research has been published which has established formally a number of
relationships not fully worked out previously empirically, and has
uncovered new results on a number of important issues in the topic of
risk measurement and management in the shipping industry.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
Kavussanos,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0817" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0817"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0821" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0821"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan"> measures for the first time the (time varying)
volatility of ship prices and freight rates by sector and type of
contract, thus allowing for a formal comparison of risk levels between
sectors and freight contracts at each point in time.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">The later work
by Kavussanos and
Nomikos</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0822" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0822"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0826" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0826"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan"> on the now-abandoned BIFFEX, of Kavussanos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0827" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0827"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0828" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0828"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Kavussanos and Visvikiss (see endnotes
4–5)</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0829" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0829"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0830" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0830"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan"> on FFAs and of Kavussanos and
Dimitrakopoulos</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0831" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0831"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan"> on Value at Risk
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_710"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">(VaR) and extreme value methods has looked at
significant issues underlying the freight derivative instruments and
their use for risk management purposes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">This chapter
aims to provide a review of the issues in order to help the reader see
where we currently stand.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">Broadly speaking, the
owner of the assets, ships, is faced with a number of commercial
decisions. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.40.2" class="koboSpan">They
include decisions on:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">Whether to enter
    the shipping industry by buying or leasing ships?</span>
2.  <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">What kind of ships
    to purchase?</span>
3.  <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">When to buy the
    ships and when to sell them?</span>
4.  <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">How to finance the
    purchase of the assets – debt, equity, shareholding, etc.</span>
5.  <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">Once owning the
    vessels, where to operate them and what kind of contract to seek for
    them?</span>
6.  <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">Whether to use
    financial instruments, such as futures and forward contracts, to
    manage the risk in such markets as the freight, bunker, foreign
    exchange and interest rate market?</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">These are all real
decisions that the shipowner is faced with in everyday decision making.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">They all amount
to viewing ships as investments – as assets in portfolios, which
generate a stream of cash flows by operating the ships and a possible
capital gain if selling the assets at prices higher than they are bought
for. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.47.3" class="koboSpan">Given that
commercial investments have risks attached, one can immediately see that
the above issues are highly relevant for decision making.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.47.4" class="koboSpan">See Kavussanos
and Visvikis (see endnote 4) for a detailed discussion of these.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">The issues raised
become more evident when examining the shipowner’s balance sheet, in
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fig0337" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0337"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.50.2"
class="koboSpan">The shipowner’s cash flow problem is outlined in the
table, where:</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Cash Flow = Operating
Revenue – Operating Costs (Fixed) – Voyage Costs (Variable) – Capital
Costs (Fixed or Variable) + Capital Gain</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0337" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00357.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0337)

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_711"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan">Fluctuations in revenue or costs can cause fluctuations
in operating earnings. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.2"
class="koboSpan">This may be due to changes in revenue, which is
affected by changes in demand for freight services and by changes in
freight rates, or because of changes in voyage or operating costs (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.3" class="koboSpan">changes in
bunker prices, wage rates, exchange rates, etc).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.4" class="koboSpan">Operating costs
include manning, repairs and maintenance, stores and lubes, insurance,
administration, and are thought to be relatively constant, rising in
line with inflation. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.5"
class="koboSpan">In contrast to time charter markets, operations in the
spot market involve voyage cost payments by the shipowner.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.6" class="koboSpan">Thus, apart
from fluctuations in the freight market, owners are exposed to
fluctuations in voyage costs, the main part of which are bunker prices.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.7" class="koboSpan">This is one of
the reasons why spot markets are deemed riskier than time charter
markets. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.8" class="koboSpan">The
others relate to the nature of the relationship of spot and time charter
rates, which leads us to expect that spot rates trade at a premium to
time charters to compensate for the higher risk involved when operating
the ships spot. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.9"
class="koboSpan">The relationship is that, say, one-year time charter
rates must be the sum of a series of expected (monthly) spot rates plus
a risk premium. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.53.10"
class="koboSpan">This is discussed fully in Kavussanos and
Alizadeh.</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0832" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0832"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">The volatility in
freight rates, examined later in the chapter, and in Kavussanos (see
endnotes 6–10), could be a source of risk.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">From the above
table though it is apparent that voyage costs – in particular bunker
prices – are the source of a certain volatility apparent when operating
in the spot market, which does not affect the owner when operating in
the time charter market. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.55.3"
class="koboSpan">Alizadeh, Kavussanos and
Menachof</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0833" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0833"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan"> examine ways of mitigating bunker price risks through
derivatives trading. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.57.2"
class="koboSpan">They are discussed later in the chapter.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.57.3" class="koboSpan">Gray (see
endnote 1) and Kavussanos and Visvikis (see endnote 4) discuss how
selection of contract type can reduce freight risks, and Kavussanos (see
endnotes 6–10) examines the same and other issues at the empirical
level. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.57.4" class="koboSpan">The use
of freight futures contracts (BIFFEX) for freight risk management has
been examined in the past by
Cullinane,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0834" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0834"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">
Haralambides</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0835" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0835"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0836" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0836"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Kavussanos and Nomikos (see endnotes 11–15).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.63.2" class="koboSpan">Finally, with
the decline of interest in BIFFEX, Freight Forward Agreements (FFAs) and
other financial instruments have provided the alternative for freight
risk management. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.63.3"
class="koboSpan">The issue is examined in Kavussanos and Visvikis (see
endnotes 4,18) and in Kavussanos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnotes 16,17).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">These are
discussed later in the chapter.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">The other source of
risk for the owner apparent in the table is the interest rate risk.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">This relates to
the capital charges, associated with debt finance.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">They fluctuate
with interest rates. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.66.4"
class="koboSpan">The higher the debt-equity ratio in the financing of a
ship, the greater the financial leverage, and the more the residual cash
flow is at risk. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.66.5"
class="koboSpan">Thus, financial leverage compounds the risks created by
operating leverage.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">A further source of
risk comes from the fluctuation in the value of the asset – the ship.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.67.2" class="koboSpan">Often, owners
are involved in asset play, see
Stopford</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0837" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0837"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.69.2"
class="koboSpan">They see ships as assets whose prices fluctuate, and
offer the possibility of a capital gain or loss.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.69.3" class="koboSpan">This is shown
in the last part of</span>[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan"> Table
1</span>](#Ch025.xhtml_fig0337)<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.71.2"
class="koboSpan">Fluctuations in ship prices then influence the risk
level involved in the investment.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">A major part of
this chapter is concerned with this issue, which has been analysed in
papers such as Kavussanos (see endnotes 6–10).</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">Credit risk, or
counterparty risk, is yet another source of risk that shipowners face
and it refers to the possibility that the counterparty in a private
contract does not fulfil its obligations.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.72.2" class="koboSpan">This risk is
more prevalent under bad market conditions and when the other party is
losing money from the agreement. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.72.3"
class="koboSpan">Such risk is prevalent, amongst others, in freight
(voyage or time charter) contracts, in FFAs in bond issues, in interest
swaps, etc.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_712"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">In all the above, one has to add exchange rate risk,
which is present in such an international industry.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">It affects the
owner’s cash flow through a number of routes, including freight rates,
voyage expenses, purchasing of the asset, etc.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.73.3" class="koboSpan">Interest rate
and exchange rate risks fall outside the scope of this chapter.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.73.4" class="koboSpan">Sophisticated
derivative instruments exist in the finance profession, which enable
interested parties to deal with these risks – see Kavussanos and
Visvikis (see endnote 4) for a description.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.74.2" class="koboSpan">Risk/Return Trade-Offs in Shipping</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">In making commercial
decisions the owner has in mind that greater rewards are usually
achieved by undertaking higher risks.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">Usually such
risks are measured by the volatility of the variable a decision has to
be made for. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.75.3"
class="koboSpan">For example, because freight rates fluctuate widely,
say from month to month, taking a position in the market in a particular
month can produce substantial gains or losses depending on what happens
in subsequent months. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.75.4"
class="koboSpan">Fluctuations in freight rates around their average
values over a period of time may be used typically as measures of
freight risk; technically, by their variance or by its square root, the
standard deviation. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.75.5"
class="koboSpan">High (low) standard deviations reflect high (low)
volatility in rates and of the risks
involved.</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0838" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0838"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">Considering shipowners
as asset holders, who wish to maximise return and minimise risk on their
portfolio of shipping assets. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.77.2"
class="koboSpan">Can they do anything to mitigate the risk involved in
their shipping investments and in operations resulting from freight rate
fluctuations? </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.77.3"
class="koboSpan">Say the shipowner is a specialist in the tanker sector.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.77.4" class="koboSpan">He is faced
with two important decisions which can affect the risk/return position
of his portfolio; (1) what size ships to invest-on?
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.77.5" class="koboSpan">and (2) For a
given investment, whether to operate the vessels in the spot or in the
period (time charter) market? </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.77.6"
class="koboSpan">The issue of what size ships to invest-on, if
approached from the pure asset-play point of view, may be answered by
considering the risk-return profiles of different size vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">Vessel size
considerations are important as the markets for each size are distinct
in terms of the rewards and risks they carry, and so is positioning in
the spot or time-charter market. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.78.2"
class="koboSpan">From a different point of view,
Glen</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0839" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0839"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan"> has shown that the industry is divided into
sub-markets. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.80.2"
class="koboSpan">Kavussanos (see endnotes 6–10), shows that these
markets are distinct in terms of their risk return profiles.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.80.3" class="koboSpan">As a result,
investments in different size vessels can be thought of as having the
same portfolio diversifying effects as different stocks included in an
investor’s portfolio. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.80.4"
class="koboSpan">To see that consider the possible disaggregation of the
cargo carrying shipping industry discussed next.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.81.2" class="koboSpan">Market Segmentation of the Shipping Industry</span>

### <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 General cargo and bulk cargo movements</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">parcel size
distribution</span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan"> (PSD) of each commodity determines the shipping
consignment of the cargo, see Stopford (see endnote 26).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.85.2" class="koboSpan">Some
commodities are typically moved in larger sizes than others.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.85.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
iron ore and grain consignments are much larger than phosphate rock or
bauxite and alumna. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.85.4"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the consignment size or PSD of each
commodity changes over time and may be different on different routes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.85.5" class="koboSpan">The PSD depends
on: (1) Commodity demand and shipping supply economics (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.85.6" class="koboSpan">low value goods
move in large consignments); (2) Transport distances
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_713"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan">(consignment is directly proportional to distance) and
transport system restrictions (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.86.2" class="koboSpan">limited draft
in ports, regulations); (3) Vessel availability.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.86.3" class="koboSpan">Consignments of
over 2,000–3,000 tonnes can fill a whole ship (or hold) rather than part
of a ship, and are typically transported in bulk.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.86.4" class="koboSpan">Smaller
consignments, which fill only part of the ship (or hold), move as
general cargo.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">Bulk cargoes refer
mainly to raw materials and are transported on a one -ship, one-cargo
basis. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">They are
further sub-divided into liquid cargo and dry cargo.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.3" class="koboSpan">Liquid cargo
includes crude oil, oil products, chemicals (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.4" class="koboSpan">caustic soda),
vegetable oils and wine. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.5"
class="koboSpan">Dry Cargo is broadly divided in three categories: (a)
Majors (i.e. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.6"
class="koboSpan">iron ore, coal, grain, bauxite and phosphates), (b)
Minors (i.e. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.7"
class="koboSpan">steel, steel products, cement, sugar, gypsum, non
ferrous metal ores, salt, sulphur, forest products, wood chips and
chemicals; (c)Specialist bulk cargoes requiring specific handling or
storage requirements such as heavy lift, cars, timber and refrigerated
cargo. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.8" class="koboSpan">The
ships involved in bulk cargo transportation are tankers, bulk carriers,
combined carriers (they carry either dry or liquid bulk) and specialist
bulk vessels. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.9"
class="koboSpan">Bulk cargoes constitute two thirds of seaborne trade
movements, and are carried mainly by tramp ships, which constitute three
quarters of the world’s merchant fleet.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.10" class="koboSpan">These are
vessels which move around the world seeking employment in any
place/route of the globe. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.87.11"
class="koboSpan">Bulk ships usually carry one cargo in one ship at rates
negotiated individually for the service provided.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">General cargo, is also
dry cargo, but is not transported in bulk.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.88.2" class="koboSpan">A large part of
general cargo is transported in containers, multipurpose and other
specialised ships (Ro-Ro, car carriers, etc.).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.88.3" class="koboSpan">General cargo
(one third of seaborne trade) is transported in either tramp ships or
liners; the latter provide a regular, scheduled service, transporting
small cargo consignments at fixed tariff levels between areas of the
world.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">The economics of each
type of transport service are different.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.89.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
oligopolistic conditions prevail in liner markets, while conditions of
perfect competition guide tramp markets.</span>

### <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Bulk-cargo segmentation</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">For analysis, dry and
liquid bulk cargoes may be further subdivided according to the PSD
functions of the products carried.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.2" class="koboSpan">The PSD
function depends on the maximum size delivery an industry is able or
willing to accept at any one time.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.3" class="koboSpan">In some
industries stockpiles are around 10–15K tonnes, so a delivery of 50K
tonnes is too large. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.4"
class="koboSpan">Physical limitations on ship size draw a line between
groups. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.5" class="koboSpan">For
instance, Suezmax, Panamax, etc. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.6"
class="koboSpan">This is because size determines the type of trade the
ship will be involved in, in terms of type of cargo and route; this is a
result of the different PSD’s of commodities and the port and seaway
restrictions for certain size ships.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.7" class="koboSpan">Design features
are important. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.8"
class="koboSpan">For example, cargo handling gear (cranes), pumping
capacity and segregation of cargo tanks in tankers; certain ports in
developing countries cannot be used (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.9" class="koboSpan">ships which do
not have cargo handling gear). </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.91.10"
class="koboSpan">Also, coating of tanks and ballast spaces are
distinguishing factors.
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fig0338" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0338"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">Tables 2</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fig0339" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0339"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan"> present the submarkets that are distinguished for dry
and liquid bulk.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Very Large Ore
Carriers (VROC) vessels (200,000+ dead-weight tonnes (dwt)) transport
only iron ore from Brazil to West Europe (Rotterdam).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.96.2" class="koboSpan">They are VLCCs
converted into dry-bulk carriers.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.96.3" class="koboSpan">Capesize
vessels (100,000–199,999dwt) transport iron ore mainly from South
America and Australia and coal from North America and Australia.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.96.4" class="koboSpan">Panamax vessels
(around 60,000–99,999dwt) are used primarily to carry grains and</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0338" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_714"></span>[](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0338)

[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00358.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0338)

</div>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0339" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00359.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0339)

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">coal from North
America and Australia. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.99.2"
class="koboSpan">Handy vessels (around 10,000–59,999dwt) transport
grains, mainly from North America, Argentina and Australia, and minor
bulk products – such as sugar, fertilisers, steel and scrap, forest
products, non-ferrous metals and salt – virtually from all over the
world. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.99.3" class="koboSpan">Over
time, in the category of Handy vessels, Handysize (10,000–33,999dwt)
vessels have gradually become Handymax (34,000–53,999dwt), while
Supramax (54,000–59,999dwt) vessels have appeared over the last years,
as a consequence of vessel sizes becoming larger to satisfy the demand
for larger PSDs for dry bulk commodities.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Smaller vessels such
as Handy and Handymax in the dry bulk sector are, in general, geared so
that they can load and unload cargo in ports without sophisticated
handling facilities. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">They can avail of more ports compared to larger
vessels. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">As
ports</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0340" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_715"></span>[](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0340)

[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.101.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00360.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0340)

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">of the world have
been developed the new generation of Handymax and Supramax vessels are
carrying more and more of the trade the Handys carry.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">The same is
also true in the liquid bulk sector; the very large vessels trade in
only four-fifths of routes as the draught restrictions in ports and the
storage facilities required ashore are very large to accommodate them
and their cargoes. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.102.3"
class="koboSpan">The smaller vessels are more flexible in terms of the
routes and trades they are involved in.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.102.4" class="koboSpan">See Kavussanos
and Visvikis (see endnote 4) for more details.</span>

### <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 General (dry) cargo segmentation</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">When general dry
cargo is not moved by dry-bulk ships it is transported by liners.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">The following
distinctions are common. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.104.3"
class="koboSpan">Container ships, Ro-Ro, Multi Purpose MPP (Single-deck,
multi-deck, Semi-containers), Barge Carrying vessels (BCV).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.104.4" class="koboSpan">Other
specialised vessels include Refrigerated (Reefers), Car-carriers, Cement
carriers, Heavy lift, Ore carriers, Vehicle carriers, LPG tankers, etc.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.104.5" class="koboSpan">Within the
liner trades there is a move towards containerisation at the expense of
non-unitised cargo which used to be transported in MPP ships.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.104.6" class="koboSpan">Containerships
themselves have sub-markets according to size.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.104.7" class="koboSpan">These are
shown in
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fig0340" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0340"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">Just as with
dry-bulk, each of these sub-markets has its own economic
characteristics, and the risks and rewards involved for the shipowner
and the charterers are different.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">Comparison of Volatilities of Second Hand Ship Prices</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">Since smaller vessels
can approach more ports (due to their smaller size and the existence of
cargo handling gear on board) and can switch between different
trades/routes they are more flexible for employment.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">As a
consequence, they are less risky than the larger vessels.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.109.3" class="koboSpan">This is
established in the market by the volatilities of both their prices and
of their freight rates being lower than those of the larger vessels.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.109.4" class="koboSpan">This was first
shown formally in Kavussanos (see endnotes 6–10), who compares freight
rate and ship price volatilities between different vessel sizes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.109.5" class="koboSpan">This is
discussed next.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">Having obtained data
for freight rates and second-hand Handysize, Panamax and Capesize vessel
prices, monthly returns and volatilities are calculated.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">These
volatilities are compared between vessel sizes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.110.3" class="koboSpan">Investments in
vessels with higher volatilities are</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_716"></span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0178"
id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0178"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan"> F-statistics for equality of unconditional variances
in dry bulk ship prices</span>

compared to those with lower ones.
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0178"

class="koboSpan">Tables 5</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0179"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0179"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan"> show the results for the dry bulk and the tanker
sectors, respectively.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">Broadly speaking, for
asset players who choose to have ships in their portfolio of assets they
can reduce risk by investing in smaller vessels, compared to larger
ones. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.2"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, the results make sense as explained earlier.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.3" class="koboSpan">The smaller
vessels are more flexible as assets.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.4" class="koboSpan">They have a
lower risk of unemployment in adverse market conditions, as they can be
switched more easily between routes and trades to secure employment.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.5" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the cargo sizes that larger vessels carry makes them less useful for
charterers requiring transportation of smaller quantities.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.6" class="koboSpan">This makes the
demand for these vessels less flexible, and vessels cannot switch
between sea-lanes and charterers as easily as their smaller
counterparts. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.7"
class="koboSpan">For instance, if anything happens (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.8" class="koboSpan">a political or
economic change) in one of the routes the VLCC’s operate in this will
have a significant impact in rates in the market, which is translated
into high volatility in rates. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.157.9"
class="koboSpan">As a consequence, the income stream from operations of
smaller vessels, and their prices, as present values of the expected
future income, are subject to less fluctuations in comparison to the
larger vessels.</span>

### <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Dynamically adjusting volatilities</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">The studies by
Kavussanos, (see endnotes 6, 7) mentioned above, have gone a step
further in the analysis of ship price volatilities.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.159.2" class="koboSpan">They
introduce, for the first time in shipping, the class of Generalised
Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) models of
Engle</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0840" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0840"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Bolerslev,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0841" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0841"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan"> to estimate time varying volatilities of ship prices.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.163.2" class="koboSpan">Thus, price
volatilities are explained in terms of their past values, values of
squared shocks to long-run equilibrium in each market, and allow for the
possibly of introducing a set of exogenous factors.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.163.3" class="koboSpan">The general
form of the augmented GARCH-X(p,q) model of Bollerslev (see endnote 30)
can be represented by the following equations:</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0341" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_717"></span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00361.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0342" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00362.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">where,
μ</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">t-1</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the specification of the conditional mean, that is,
of the change in the log of ship prices,
Δ1nP</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">, ε</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan"> is a white noise error term with the usual classical
properties and a time-varying variance
h</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan">, which may include a set of exogenous factors,
Z</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan">, and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan">LL is </span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan">the corresponding log-likelihood function after
omitting the irrelevant constant.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.178.2" class="koboSpan">The parameters
of interest are those included in
μ</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan">t-1</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">, say
φ</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan">(L), </span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">and the GARCH parameters
α</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">0</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">,α</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">,β</span><sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan">j</span></sub><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan"> and δ and can be estimated by maximum likelihood
methods.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">The estimated time
varying volatilities allow the measurement and comparison of
volatilities at each point in time, rather than relying on the averages
over the period examined in </span>[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan">Tables
5</span>](#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0178)<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan"> and</span>[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan">
6</span>](#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0179)<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.193.2"
class="koboSpan">Considering average volatilities(standard deviations)
of ship prices (or freight rates) over a period of time as indicators of
risk levels provides a partial picture of the risk/return situation.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.193.3" class="koboSpan">This is
because uncertainty in prices, is not constant over time.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.193.4" class="koboSpan">The patterns
and relative levels of volatilities, at each point in time (market
situation) can now be measured, and compared between different ship
sizes. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.193.5" class="koboSpan">Such
estimates of time varying variances are also deemed important in the
financial literature, as they may be used in the construction of dynamic
portfolios of assets. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.193.6"
class="koboSpan">These time varying volatilities of ship prices for the
tanker and dry bulk sub-sectors are shown in
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0180"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0180"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 1</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0181"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0181"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan">, respectively.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">This method of
analysing volatilities and examining them graphically has allowed
further inferences for the dry bulk sector, such as that: Volatilities,
and thus risks, vary over time and across sizes; in particular,
volatilities are high during and just after periods of large imbalances
and shocks to the industry. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.198.2"
class="koboSpan">These include the period of the oil crisis of the early
1980s, the recovery period of 1986–1989 and the Gulf crisis of the early
1990s. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.198.3" class="koboSpan">Panamax
volatilities are driven by old “news”, while new shocks</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0343" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00363.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Vessel price volatilites in segments of the tanker sector" /></span>

<a href="#Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0180"
id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0180"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan"> Vessel price volatilites in segments of the tanker
sector</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0344" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00364.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Vessel price volatilities in segments of the duty bulk sector" /></span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_718"></span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0181"
id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0181"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan"> Vessel price volatilities in segments of the duty bulk
sector</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">are more important in
the Handy and Capesize markets. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.205.2"
class="koboSpan">Also, conditional volatilities of Handysize and Panamax
vessel prices are positively related to interest rates and Capesize
volatilities to time-charter rates.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">The three markets
tend to respond together to external shocks, and yet quite differently,
implying market segregation between different size ships.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">(i.e.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.206.3" class="koboSpan">there are some
common driving forces of volatilities in different size markets, and yet
there are idiosyncratic factors to each market that make each size-ship
volatility move in its own way).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.206.4" class="koboSpan">These
idiosyncratic factors relate to the type of trade each size ship is
engaged in. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.206.5"
class="koboSpan">Thus, volatility for Handysize and Capesize vessels has
several hikes, while that for Panamax is smoother.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.206.6" class="koboSpan">This differing
nature of volatil ities over ship sizes is manifested in the GARCH
alpha(news) coefficients being higher than the beta (persistence)
coefficients for Capesize and Handysize vessels, while the opposite is
true for
Panamax.</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0842" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0842"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">Regarding volatility
levels, Capesize volatility generally lies above the volatilities of the
other two sizes, except for two–three years in the mid-1980s.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">Similarly, the
Panamax volatility is, in general, at a level above Handysize, which,
however, is exceeded at times by the hikes in the Handy
volatility.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">Similar results are
reached by considering the time varying volatilities for the tanker
sector. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.209.2" class="koboSpan">In
addition, volatilities in the tanker sector and thus risks levels seem
to be positively related to oil prices.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.209.3" class="koboSpan">The downward
trends in volatilities observed in the dry bulk and tanker industry
sub-sectors seem to indicate that risks in the shipping industry have
decreased over time. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.209.4"
class="koboSpan">It should also be mentioned that the availability of
time varying volatility estimates for vessel prices, as with other
assets in the financial literature, may be used as inputs in pricing
derivative instruments such as options prices, etc.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.210.2" class="koboSpan">Comparison of Volatilities of Spot and Time Charter Rates</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">Theoretically, ship
prices are the present value of the expected stream of cash flows
(profits) from their operation. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.211.2"
class="koboSpan">The relationship has been investigated formally
in</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0345" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_719"></span>[](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0345)

[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00365.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0345)

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and
Alizadeh.</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0843" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0843"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan"> As a result of this theoretical relationship,
comparison of freight rate volatilities by vessel size should reveal a
similar relationship to that uncovered by examining the second hand
prices. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.215.2" class="koboSpan">This
is indeed the case; Kavussanos (see endnotes 6, 9) shows that
volatilities of spot rates and of time charter rates are smaller for
smaller size vessels, compared to those of larger ones.
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fig0345" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0345"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan"> compares these volatilities in the tanker
sector.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.218.1" class="koboSpan">In both the spot and
time charter markets the VLCC sector exhibits the highest volatility
compared to smaller sizes over the period examined.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.218.2" class="koboSpan">The Handymax
volatilities are the lowest in both markets compared to other sizes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.218.3" class="koboSpan">The Aframax
and the Suezmax sectors show significantly larger volatilities in
comparison to the Handymax sector and smaller ones compared to the VLCC
in both the spot and the time-charter markets.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.218.4" class="koboSpan">However, the
volatilities between the Aframax and Suezmax sectors are not
statistically different between them.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.218.5" class="koboSpan">Overall,
within the dry bulk and tanker sectors, risk levels, as expressed by
freight rate volatilities, are different between vessel sizes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.218.6" class="koboSpan">Coupled with
the different levels of return each vessel size yields, different size
vessels can be viewed as distinct asset classes in a portfolio of ships.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.218.7" class="koboSpan">This has
implications for investors.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">The above findings
then, of the possible diversification effects that may be achieved by
holding different size ships in a portfolio of assets have not been
discussed in the literature previously.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.219.2" class="koboSpan">The studies by
Kavussanos (see endnotes 4,7–11), have provided a formal justification
of pursuing such strategies. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.219.3"
class="koboSpan">In addition, these studies have also investigated, for
the first time, empirically some well-known propositions regarding the
possibility of operational risk reduction by choice of contract.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.219.4" class="koboSpan">Gray (see
endnote 1) discusses the gradual risk reduction effects that are
achieved by shipowners selecting to employ their vessels in markets such
as voyage charter(spot), trip time charter, period time charter and in
contracts of
affreightment,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0844" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0844"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan"> consecutively.</span>

<a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fig0346" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0346"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">Table 8</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan"> compares, statistically, pair-wise volatilities
between the spot and the time-charter market for each size ship in the
tanker sector. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.223.2"
class="koboSpan">In all vessel sizes, but the Aframax, the spot rates
are significantly more volatile compared to time-charters.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.223.3" class="koboSpan">In the Aframax
size there is no significant difference between spot and time-charter
volatilities. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.223.4"
class="koboSpan">Once again the evidence seems to be consistent with
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan">a priori</span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan"> expectations, in that the spot rates are much more
exposed to the day-to-day market conditions in determining rates
compared to time-charter rates. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.225.2"
class="koboSpan">The latter, being theoretically the discounted stream
of</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0346" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_720"></span>[](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0346)

[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00366.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0346)

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">12-months expected
spot rates, are smoother, and this is reflected in the smaller
volatilities in comparison to the one-month spot rates, see Kavussanos
and Alizadeh (see endnote 33) for an empirical formulation of this
relationship.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">It seems that the
risk involved in operating tankers in the spot markets is greater than
in the time-charter markets and this seems to hold irrespective of
size.</span>

### <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Comparison of time varying freight volatilities over vessel sizes</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">Risks in the spot and
time-charter tanker markets are a combination of industry-market risk
and “idiosyncratic” risk (e.g. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.230.2"
class="koboSpan">relating to individual vessel size).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.230.3" class="koboSpan">As long as one
is faced with more than one option over choices, then idiosyncratic risk
may be diversified. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.230.4"
class="koboSpan">The shipowner, for instance, may choose to use the spot
instead of the time-charter market, or may decide to invest in
alternative size ships. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.230.5"
class="koboSpan">Decisions about this process take place on a continual
basis. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.230.6" class="koboSpan">This is
not possible by considering the averages of volatilities over a 10–15
year period. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.230.7"
class="koboSpan">Monthly estimates of these volatilities though,
resolves the problem. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.230.8"
class="koboSpan">The results in Kavussanos (see endnotes 6–10) enable
this.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">Consider first how
the industry has been affected across markets by examining time-varying
risks in the spot and time charter tanker and dry bulk sectors, as
observed in </span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0182"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0182"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 3</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0185"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0185"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.235.2"
class="koboSpan">A tendency for volatility clustering is observed.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.235.3" class="koboSpan">Volatility is
high during and just after periods of large shocks and imbalances in the
industry; such as during the 1980–1981 oil crises and the decline in
demand for shipping services as the world economy slowed down following
the second oil shock; the supply of oil restrictions imposed by the OPEC
production ceiling in 1982–1983, the targeting of ships in the Gulf in
1984, the sharp decline in oil prices in 1986 and the 1990–1991 period
of the Gulf-war are particularly visible.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.236.1" class="koboSpan">The above incidents
affected all markets and are manifested in patterns of risk, which are
specific to vessel sizes. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.236.2"
class="koboSpan">In tanker markets for instance, the VLCC sector seems
to have the highest volatility and fluctuations are a lot sharper than
in any of the other sizes. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.236.3"
class="koboSpan">The sector involves vessels trading in four routes, all
lifting oil from the Gulf, which were severely disrupted in periods of
crises. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.236.4" class="koboSpan">The
Handymax volatility is the lowest in both the spot and time charter
markets reflecting the steady trades this type of ship is involved in.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.236.5" class="koboSpan">The Suezmax
and Aframax volatilities fluctuate between those of the Handymax and the
VLCC. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.236.6" class="koboSpan">In the
spot market, the levels of volatilities are interchanged with neither
being significantly above the other.</span>

<a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0184"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0184"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 5</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span>[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span>](#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0185)<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan"> compare time varying volatilities of spot and of time
charter freight rates between Handysize, Panamax and Capesize vessels in
the dry bulk sector. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.240.2"
class="koboSpan">Once more, risk, as manifested by volatility estimates,
is in general higher in larger vessels.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.240.3" class="koboSpan">The reasons
for the lower volatility levels in Handysize vessels as compared to the
other</span>

alt="Figure 3: Time charter volatilities by vessel size" /></span>

id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.242.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.243.1"

</div>

alt="Figure 4: Spot freight rate volatilities by vessel size" /></span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0183"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
4:</span></span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan"> Spot freight rate volatilities by vessel size</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">sizes and of Panamax
in comparison to Capesize have been explained before.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">Smaller ships
serve many more different trades than larger ones, with less draft
restrictions on certain ports because of size, and are not therefore
subject to so many ups and downs in the market.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.247.3" class="koboSpan">On the
contrary, larger size vessels may be thought of as operating in narrower
markets, serving only a few major commodities and being restricted to
approaching specific ports only.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.247.4" class="koboSpan">This has its
toll on volatility levels.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">Overall, it may be
said that the shipping markets tend to respond together to external
shocks, and yet quite differently implying market segregation between
different size ships. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.248.2"
class="koboSpan">That is, there are some common driving forces of
volatilities in different size vessels, and yet there are idiosyncratic
factors to each market that make each size-ship</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

alt="Figure 5: Spot freight rate volatilities by vessel size; dry-bulk sector" /></span>

id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"> Spot freight rate volatilities by vessel size;
dry-bulk sector</span>

</div>

dry-bulk sector</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">volatility move at
its own level and in its own way.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.255.2" class="koboSpan">These
idiosyncratic factors relate to the type and number of routes each size
ship is engaged in.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">The results suggest
that operational risks in the larger sub-sectors of the tanker and dry
bulk sectors of the shipping industry may be mitigated by holding
smaller vessels. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.256.2"
class="koboSpan">Hence, risk averse investors in shipping can diversify
risks in their portfolios by heavier weighting towards smaller size
vessels.</span>
