### <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">5.2 Comparison of time varying freight volatilities over type of contract, spot vs time-charter</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.264.1" class="koboSpan">With respect to the
choice between spot and time-charter markets, volatilities are compared
in </span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0186"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0186"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 7</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0189"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0189"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan">10</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">, between time-charter and spot freight rates for each
size vessel in the tanker sector.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.268.2" class="koboSpan">See Kavussanos
(see endnote 10) for full details of this exercise.
</span>[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">Figures
7</span>](#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0186)<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0188"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0188"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan">9</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan"> reveal that the volatility of spot-freight rates in
the Handymax and</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0353" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00373.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 9: Spot vs time-charter volatilities: Suezmax sector" /></span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_724"></span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0188"
id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0188"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 9:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan"> Spot vs time-charter volatilities: Suezmax
sector</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0354" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00374.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 10: Spot vs time-charter volatilities: VLCC sector" /></span>

<a href="#Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0189"
id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0189"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
10:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">
Spot vs time-charter volatilities: VLCC sector</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0355" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.279.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00375.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 11: Handysize sector: Spot vs time charter rate volatilities (SD’s)" /></span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_725"></span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0190"
id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0190"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
11:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">
Handysize sector: Spot vs time charter rate volatilities (SD’s)</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">Suezmax sectors are
clearly above the corresponding time charter rates over the whole
period. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.282.2" class="koboSpan">The
results are not so neat for the Aframax and VLCC
markets.</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0187"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0187"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan"> Figure 8</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that before 1987, the Aframax time charter
volatility was mostly at a higher level than the spot one, with the
reverse occurring once the market recovered.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.284.2" class="koboSpan">The
fluctuations in the volatility of time charter rates in the early period
are sharp and in wider bands as compared to the post-1987 period,
forcing the average in </span>[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
8</span>](#Ch025.xhtml_fig0346)<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan"> to be, though insignificantly so, above the spot rate.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.286.2" class="koboSpan">The story is
similar in the VLCC sector. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.286.3"
class="koboSpan">The downward trend in time charter risk, lying
constantly below the spot rate level of risk from 1988 onwards, is
particularly noticeable.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos (see
endnote 6) compares aggregated (over vessel sizes) spot with
time-charter volatilities for the dry-bulk sector.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.287.2" class="koboSpan">The results
there are somewhat in line with the findings in the Aframax and VLCC
sectors discussed above. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.287.3"
class="koboSpan">That is, when the market is low, time-charters are more
volatile than spot rates, probably because time-charter rates reflect
expectations of future events, which makes them more sensitive to
changing perceptions of the future market.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.287.4" class="koboSpan">When the
market is at the bottom and there is a feeling for a market upturn,
charterers rush to fix vessels on time charter.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.287.5" class="koboSpan">This results
in time-charter rates moving more steeply upwards than spot rates.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.287.6" class="koboSpan">The opposite
happens when the market is at its peak, where charterers fix in the spot
market and the lack of demand for time charters results in an abrupt
drop in their values.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">As the data used in
this last comparison of spot-with time-charter rates on the dry bulk
sector were at the aggregate level, and did not refer to time charter
rates of individual vessels, it was felt that more information could be
obtained if the results were refined by vessel size.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.288.2" class="koboSpan">Thus, time
varying volatilities of spot and of time charter rates in dry bulk have
been estimated and presented for the first time in this chapter for each
vessel size using GARCH models. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.288.3"
class="koboSpan">Their plots are shown
in</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0190"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0190"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan"> Figures 11</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0192"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0192"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan">13</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.292.2"
class="koboSpan">Spot volatilities seem to be above the one-year time
charter ones for each vessel size.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.292.3" class="koboSpan">This takes us
back to the traditional belief that spot rates are more volatile and
hence riskier than time charters.</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0356" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00376.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 12: Panamax sector: Spot vs time charter rate volatilities (SD’s)" /></span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_726"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0191"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
12:</span></span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan"> Panamax sector: Spot vs time charter rate volatilities
(SD’s)</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0357" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00377.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 13: Capesize sector: Spot vs time charter rate volatilities (SDs)" /></span>

<a href="#Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0192"
id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0192"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.297.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
13:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">
Capesize sector: Spot vs time charter rate volatilities (SDs)</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">The result is
justified in Kavussanos and Alizadeh (see endnote 21), and identify four
types of risk which the owner is faced with when employing the vessel in
the spot as opposed to the time-charter market.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.299.2" class="koboSpan">In a time
charter the vessel is fixed, say, over a year.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.299.3" class="koboSpan">Expenses are
being paid by the charterer, making income from operations quite
predictable. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.299.4"
class="koboSpan">The alternative to the one-year time charter would be,
say, 12-monthly spot fixtures, with expenses on the owner’s side.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.299.5" class="koboSpan">The owner
would thus be faced with the risk of not finding employment every month
on the vessel; even if employment is secured, the risk of having to
relocate the vessel to a nearby port, thereby increasing
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_727"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan">his costs; the risk of the freight market decreasing by
the time the next voyage contract is secured, thereby decreasing his
revenues; bunker prices may move adversely for him, thereby increasing
his costs. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.300.2" class="koboSpan">Of
course, seasonal factors may also be contributing to such risks.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.300.3" class="koboSpan">See for
example, Kavussanos and
Alizadeh</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0845" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0845"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.301.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0846" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0846"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.303.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan"> for their measurement and comparison in the dry bulk
and tanker sectors under different market conditions.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.304.2" class="koboSpan">Moreover, it
can be argued that, administratively, a time charter contract is simpler
to implement over the course of 12 months, in comparison to a series of
voyage contracts, and is hence a cheaper option for the shipping
company. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.304.3"
class="koboSpan">Finally, it is well known that a long period time
charter contract on a ship is viewed favourably by banks seeking
collateral to finance the vessel, thereby making it a “safer” option for
the shipping company in comparison to a series of voyage
contracts.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.305.1" class="koboSpan">On balance, one could
say that policy implications for risk averse shipowners with a choice of
employing ships between the spot and time charter markets, point to
preferring the lower risk time charter market over the spot market, in
general. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.305.2"
class="koboSpan">However, in prolonged “bad” periods for the industry,
time charter risk in some sectors, such as in the Aframax and VLCC
sectors, may rise above the corresponding spot market risk.</span>

### <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.306.1" class="koboSpan">5.3 Correlation coefficients amongst shipping and other asset classes</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.307.1" class="koboSpan">To reinforce the case
made above about different size vessels being distinct asset classes,
which if included in the same portfolio can have significant
diversification effects, correlation coefficients amongst segments of
shipping markets and some other potential investments – such as shares
and commodities – are considered next.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.307.2" class="koboSpan">In finance
portfolio theory it is well known that pairs of assets with low or
negative correlation coefficients of returns provide substantial risk
reductions, if combined in the same portfolio of investments.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.307.3" class="koboSpan">In that
spirit,
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fig0358" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0358"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">Table 9</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan"> displays correlation coefficients of daily logarithmic
returns of freight rates in dry bulk Capesize, Panamax and Supramax
sectors, and tanker dirty and clean sectors of shipping, as well as
share price (S&P500) and commodity prices (wheat, corn and Brent crude
oil) to represent alternative classes of investments that the
international investor – the shipowner – might consider to include in
his portfolio of assets.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">Consider first the
three correlation coefficients between the three subsectors of the dry
bulk shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.310.2"
class="koboSpan">Their values range from a low of 0.384 to a high of
0.517. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.310.3" class="koboSpan">Given
their relatively low values, around 50% and lower, there is scope for
diversification between subsectors of dry bulk shipping by investing in
different size ships. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.310.4"
class="koboSpan">The correlation coefficients between freight rates in
the dry bulk and the tanker subsectors are even lower and very close to
zero, the reason being that the drybulk and tanker shipping cycles,
particularly in the short run are distinct.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.310.5" class="koboSpan">The S&P500,
wheat and corn can provide good alternative investment assets for
shipowners, for diversification purposes, as seen by the very low –
almost zero – correlation coefficients that they display with freight
rates. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.310.6" class="koboSpan">As
expected, Brent crude oil prices has some positive but low correlations
with the dirty and clean tanker freight indices, again making a case of
a potential diversifying asset.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">The contribution of
the analysis so far, is to point to real possibilities of risk reduction
by choice of sub-sector within the dry bulk and tanker sectors of the
shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.311.2"
class="koboSpan">In addition, the use of GARCH models to estimate
time-varying volatilities points to a strategy of dynamic revisions of
assets to include in a portfolio of vessels.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.311.3" class="koboSpan">No empirical
analysis has yet been carried in the literature for the container
sector, but one</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0358" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_728"></span>[](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0358)

[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00378.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch025.xhtml_bck_fig0358)

</div>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">would expect similar
conclusions regarding volatilities in rates of different vessel sizes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.313.2" class="koboSpan">Once the
investments (ships) have been acquired, shipowners have to make similar
decisions on how to maximise their return from operations, subject to
the operational business risks that they face.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.313.3" class="koboSpan">The second
contribution of the analysis so far is to point to the possibility of
using period contracts as ways of reducing risks in a portfolio of
“long” positions on tonnage. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.313.4"
class="koboSpan">Caution needs to be exercised though, say in a dynamic
portfolio setting, to ensure that the relationship holds true in adverse
market conditions, as time charter volatility may rise above the spot
one.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">The strategies that
the above possibilities point to are useful, but may prove to be
expensive, non-existent or inflexible, if not planned properly.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.314.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
it costs to buy and sell ships and to go in or out of freight contracts.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.314.3" class="koboSpan">This reduces
their flexibility. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.314.4"
class="koboSpan">Long-term charters may be hard for owners to find when
the market is in decline. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.314.5"
class="koboSpan">The opposite is true when the market is improving.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.314.6" class="koboSpan">In addition,
when the conditions turn too much against one of the parties (owner or
charterer) it may be that they decide to abandon the agreement.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.314.7" class="koboSpan">The
introduction of derivatives contracts, such as freight futures, in 1985,
and of Over the Counter (OTC) freight-forward contracts, options and
swaps, since 1992 has helped to alleviate these problems with respect to
operational risk management. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.314.8"
class="koboSpan">They have made operational risk management cheaper,
more flexible and readily available to parties exposed to adverse
movements in freight rates.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.315.2" class="koboSpan">The use of Derivatives for Operational Risk Management in Shipping</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">Many other industries
have used derivative contracts to manage risks.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.316.2" class="koboSpan">To see for
instance how futures/forward contracts work, consider a “party” which is
“long” in a
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_729"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.317.1"
class="koboSpan">“commodity”. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.317.2"
class="koboSpan">For the shipowner this would be the freight service,
for the charterer it would be the cargo he wants to transport.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.317.3" class="koboSpan">If freight
rates are expected to decrease by the time the owner secures the next
contract with a charterer, he may want to avoid taking the risk of
reducing his revenue. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.317.4"
class="koboSpan">Apart from the traditional methods of managing this
risk, discussed earlier, such as entering a time charter contract, he
may decide to use, amongst others, freight futures, forwards, options or
swap contracts to hedge these risks.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">For these to
function, a market price of the underlying physical commodity is needed.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.318.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
if a “party” is long in coffee, a spot market price for coffee is needed
– which is available in the market – and based on that, futures
contracts could be issued, say one month ahead.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.318.3" class="koboSpan">The party that
owns coffee and expects its price to be lower next month will sell
futures contracts to buy them back in a month’s time at the lower price
prevailing in the market(provided his expectations materialise).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.318.4" class="koboSpan">He will thus,
make a profit from the selling and buying of the futures contracts at
different periods, which will offset the loss which will occur in the
physical market because of the reduction in the price of the
commodity.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.319.1" class="koboSpan">In a forward
agreement, the two parties (owner of coffee and potential buyer of
coffee) will come “directly” together.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.319.2" class="koboSpan">They will
agree on a forward price for coffee and the producer will deliver that
quantity at the agreed price. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.319.3"
class="koboSpan">This is a practice which has been used as a hedging
mechanism for years in a number of industries.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.319.4" class="koboSpan">Gray (see
endnote 2) claims that the problem with this is inflexibility and
unreliability; if either party wanted to change any part of the contract
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.319.5" class="koboSpan">quantity
delivered or price), they will not be able to do so without
renegotiating the whole contract.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.319.6" class="koboSpan">If there is a
futures market operating for the commodity both parties are flexible in
terms of being allowed to change the details of the original contract.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.319.7" class="koboSpan">Thus, delivery
date, quantity, price and other characteristics may be altered at
will.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.320.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.320.2" class="koboSpan">The Baltic Freight Index</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.321.1" class="koboSpan">The shipping industry
did not have an underlying “commodity”, which could be used to trade
futures contracts. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.321.2"
class="koboSpan">In 1985 the Baltic Freight Index (BFI) produced by the
Baltic Exchange in London and the International Futures Exchange in
Bermuda was established. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.321.3"
class="koboSpan">The latter was abandoned early.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.321.4" class="koboSpan">Until 2002 the
BFI was used as the underlying “commodity” for futures BIFFEX (Baltic
International Freight Futures Exchange) contracts trading for the dry
bulk sector of shipping. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.321.5"
class="koboSpan">Unlike physical goods, such as coffee, which could be
delivered physically at the expiry of the futures contract, the trade of
freight services amounted to delivering the cash value of the commodity.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.321.6" class="koboSpan">This cash
settlement procedure has enabled the introduction of BIFFEX contracts,
based on the BFI (Gray (see endnotes 1, 2)).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.321.7" class="koboSpan">The underlying
asset, which is delivered at the settlement date, is the cash value of a
freight rate index, the BFI. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.321.8"
class="koboSpan">This makes the whole process a paper transaction with
no ship or cargoes being involved.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">The BFI–previously
called the BDI (Baltic Dry Index) – is a weighted average index of dry
cargo freight rates (see e.g. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.322.2"
class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and Visvikis) (see endnote 4).The index is
revised every year from a panel of brokers appointed by the Baltic
exchange, namely the panellists.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.322.3" class="koboSpan">The revisions
are such so as to take into account the changing conditions in the
industry and keep the index up to date.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.322.4" class="koboSpan">For instance,
separate indices have been introduced for the Capesize, Panamax and
Handy sectors in recognition of the
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_730"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan">distinctiveness of the sectors, while the weightings of
the constituent routes of each of these indices (and of the BDI) have
changed over time, to reflect the relative importance of seaborne trades
in these routes.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.324.1" class="koboSpan">8. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.324.2" class="koboSpan">The Price Discovery Role of Freight Derivative Contracts</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.325.1" class="koboSpan">In the theory of
futures and forward markets it is claimed that there are two main
economic benefits that these markets provide to market agents.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.325.2" class="koboSpan">These are
price discovery (of future spot prices) and risk management through
hedging (see e.g. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.325.3"
class="koboSpan">Garbade and
Silber</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0847" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0847"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.326.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.327.2"
class="koboSpan">Price discovery is the process of revealing information
about current and expected spot prices through the futures or forward
markets.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and
Nomikos (see endnote 11), using BIFFEX contracts of one and two months
to maturity show that these contracts are unbiased predictors of the
spot price, (i.e. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.328.2"
class="koboSpan">of the BFI). </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.328.3"
class="koboSpan">The evidence on the three-months contract is marginal.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.328.4" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 16) show that FFA prices one and two
months prior to maturity are unbiased predictors of the realised spot
prices in routes 1, 1A, 2 and 2A.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.330.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
efficiency of the FFA prices three months prior to maturity provide
mixed evidence, with routes 2 and 2A being unbiased estimators, while
routes 1 and 1A being seemingly biased estimators of the realised spot
prices. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.330.3" class="koboSpan">Thus,
it seems that “unbiasedness” depends on the market and type of contract
under investigation.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.331.1" class="koboSpan">The evidence
uncovered by these studies is important for market agents in that they
can rely on the free information provided by the futures/forward markets
as to the level the spot market will be, say two months ahead.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.331.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
through the FFA contracts, market agents can get an indication of the
expected level of freight rates in the future.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.331.3" class="koboSpan">Moreover,
Kavussanos and Nomikos (see endnote 11) show that, BIFFEX prices provide
more accurate forecasts of the realised spot prices than forecasts
generated from forecasting models, such as the random walk, ARIMA and
the Holt-Winters exponential smoothing models.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.332.1" class="koboSpan">In addition to
providing a mechanism for market agents to form expectations regarding
spot prices that will prevail in the future, trading in futures/forward
markets also provides information regarding current spot prices.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.332.2" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and
Nomikos (see endnote 15) show that futures prices tend to discover new
information more rapidly than spot prices.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.332.3" class="koboSpan">Subperiod
results, corresponding to revisions in the composition of the underlying
index, show that the price discovery role of futures prices has
strengthened as a result of the more homogeneous composition of the
index in recent years. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.332.4"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, futures prices, when formulated as a VECM,
are found to produce more accurate forecasts of spot prices than VAR,
ARIMA and random-walk models, over several steps ahead.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and
Visvikis (see endnote 19) investigate the lead-lag relationships between
forward and spot markets, both in terms of returns and volatility.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.333.2" class="koboSpan">Causality
tests and impulse response analysis indicate that there is a
bi-directional causal relationship between spot and futures returns in
all routes. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.333.3"
class="koboSpan">The latter imply that FFA prices can be equally
important as a source of information as spot prices are.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.333.4" class="koboSpan">A closer
examination of the results suggests that causality from FFA to spot
returns runs stronger than the other way in all routes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.333.5" class="koboSpan">These results
are in line with those for futures contracts presented in Kavussanos and
Nomikos (see endnote 11).</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.334.1" class="koboSpan">Volatility spillovers
between the spot and FFA markets are also investigated in the Kavussanos
and Visvikis study (see endnote 19).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.334.2" class="koboSpan">Results from a
bivariate
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_731"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.335.1"
class="koboSpan">VECM-GARCH-X model, indicate that the FFA volatility
spills over to the spot market volatility in route 1.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.335.2" class="koboSpan">In route 1A
the results indicate no volatility spillover in either market.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.335.3" class="koboSpan">In routes 2
and 2A there is a bi-directional relationship, as each market transmits
volatility to the other.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.336.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, FFA prices seem
to contain useful information about subsequent spot prices, beyond that
already embedded in the current spot price, and therefore can be used as
price discovery vehicles. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.336.2"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the FFA contracts in routes 1, 2, and 2A
contribute in the volatility of the relevant spot rate, and therefore,
further support the notion of price discovery.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.336.3" class="koboSpan">In the absence
of futures contracts, following the de-listing of BIFFEX in April 2002,
FFAs seem to do an equally important job as vehicles of price discovery
of spot prices.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">Even if market agents
are not aware of the valuable information that FFA contracts incorporate
for them as a source of information regarding the likely developments of
the spot market, they would be keen to know how successful the use of
these contracts are in mitigating their risks in freight markets.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.337.2" class="koboSpan">This is
important as it relates to direct monetary benefits from the use of the
contracts. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.337.3" class="koboSpan">If
these are perceived important and the service offered by the existence
of FFA contracts is used enough by the industry it will survive to serve
the players in the industry.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.338.1" class="koboSpan">9. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.338.2" class="koboSpan">The Hedging Effectiveness of Freight Derivative Contracts</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">Risk management
refers to hedgers using futures contracts to control their spot price
risk. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.339.2" class="koboSpan">The
issue of the effectiveness of BIFFEX contracts in hedging freight risk
has been investigated in Thuong and
Vischer,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0848" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0848"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.340.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan"> in Haralambides (see endnotes 24, 25), and in
Kavussanos and Nomikos (see endnotes 12–14).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.341.2" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.343.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 17) and Kavussanos and Visvikis (see
endnote 19) investigate the risk management function of the FFA markets.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.343.2" class="koboSpan">As explained
earlier, hedging involves taking a position in the futures market that
is opposite to the position that one already has in the spot market.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.343.3" class="koboSpan">The shipowner
is “long” on tonnage and sells BIFFEX/FFA contracts to protect him
against a decline in freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.343.4" class="koboSpan">The charterer
is ‘short’ on tonnage, thus buying BIFFEX/FFA contracts to protect him
against a rise in freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.343.5" class="koboSpan">Of course, for
a trade to occur the views of these two “parties” to the trade must be
opposite. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.343.6"
class="koboSpan">Futures/forward markets simply transfer risks from one
willing party to another.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.344.1" class="koboSpan">In hedging, the
“party” interested in mitigating risks has to determine a hedge ratio,
which will make the hedge as “effective” as possible (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.344.2" class="koboSpan">he has to
decide on the number of futures/forward contracts to buy or sell for
each unit of spot commodity on which he bears price risk).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.344.3"
class="koboSpan">Johnson,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0849" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0849"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.346.1"
class="koboSpan">
Stein,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0850" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0850"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.347.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.348.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Ederington,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0851" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0851"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.349.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan"> apply the principles of portfolio theory to solve the
problem. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.350.2" class="koboSpan">They
show that the hedge ratio, which minimises the spot market risk equals
the covariance between spot and futures/forward price changes over the
variance of futures/forward price changes.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.351.1" class="koboSpan">The effectiveness of
the hedge is determined by the degree of variance reduction it achieves
in the hedged portfolio. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.351.2"
class="koboSpan">Alternatively, effectiveness is determined by the
proportion of risk in the spot market that is eliminated through the
futures/forward position (hedging).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.351.3" class="koboSpan">Alternative
strategies in calculating hedge ratios involve a naïve one-to-one hedge,
under which for each \$ exposition in the spot market a \$ position is
opened in the futures market. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.351.4"
class="koboSpan">This may be sub-optimal.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.351.5" class="koboSpan">Other
strategies involve using constant or time varying optimal hedge ratios.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.351.6" class="koboSpan">The latter
would be justified if the
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_732"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan">distributions of the covariance and/or the variance
entering the calculation of the optimal hedge ratio are time varying.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.352.2" class="koboSpan">In this case,
at each point in time, a different hedge ratio would be appropriate.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.352.3" class="koboSpan">To make this
point evident, </span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0194"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0194"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 15</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan"> plots the estimated constant and time varying hedge
ratios for spot and FFA contracts for route 1 of the BDI.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.354.2" class="koboSpan">It is obvious
that using the constant hedge ratio, instead of the time varying one, in
observation 30 on the graph would have provided estimates, which are way
off the most efficient hedge.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.355.1" class="koboSpan">The “technology” to
calculate time varying hedge ratios for BIFFEX contracts has been
introduced by Kavussanos and Nomikos (see endnotes 12–14) to individual
routes of the BFI and in FFA contracts by Kavussanos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.357.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 17) and Kavussanos and Visvikis (see
endnote 19). </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.357.2"
class="koboSpan">These time varying hedge ratios, have been calculated
by extracting time varying variances and covariances of spot and futures
prices from the estimation of multivariate GARCH models, with a VECM
specification of the mean of the variables.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.357.3" class="koboSpan">Alternative
hedging strategies are evaluated by comparing the portfolio variance
reduction from the use of a particular hedge ratio (strategy) to a
benchmark portfolio – that of the unhedged position.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.357.4" class="koboSpan">The larger the
reduction in the unhedged variance, the higher the degree of hedging
effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.357.5"
class="koboSpan">Whether time varying or constant ratios for BIFFEX or
FFA contracts are appropriate for each individual route cannot be
determined </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan">a priori</span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.359.2"
class="koboSpan">It is a matter of empirical evidence.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.1" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and
Nomikos (see endnotes 12–14) examined the issue of hedging effectiveness
for BIFFEX contracts. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.2"
class="koboSpan">Two cases are distinguished: in-sample and the more
pragmatic out-of-sample hedge ratios.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.3" class="koboSpan">In the former
case time-varying hedge ratios are superior in routes 1, 1A, 3A, 7 and
10. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.4"
class="koboSpan">Out-of-sample results indicate that time-varying hedge
ratios perform better in routes 1, 1A, 3A and 8.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.5" class="koboSpan">In route 3,
the constant hedge ratio seems superior.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.6" class="koboSpan">The naive
hedge is the worst hedging strategy in all in sample results.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.7" class="koboSpan">For out of
sample, in routes 7 and 10, hedging increases the portfolio variance
compared to the unhedged position, suggesting that market participants
should leave their positions unhedged.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.8" class="koboSpan">Also the naive
hedge in route 9 seems superior.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.9" class="koboSpan">Overall, the
average variance reduction for the Panamax routes is higher than that
for the capesize routes across all the estimated models.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.10" class="koboSpan">This is not
surprising as the Panamax routes represent 70% of the total BFI
composition. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.11"
class="koboSpan">Ultimately, the user of the futures contracts is
interested in the variance reduction that may be achieved with the best
method of hedging available. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.12"
class="koboSpan">The above study shows that the highest variance
reduction possible is in route 1A (23.25%) and the lowest is in route 7
(–14.86%). </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.13" class="koboSpan">It
seems then that for all routes a large proportion of the variability of
the unhedged portfolio is not eliminated.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.360.14" class="koboSpan">It explains
the decreasing interest in the use of BIFFEX by market participants,
which lead to its eventual abandonment.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.361.1" class="koboSpan">During its history,
the composition of the BFI has been restructured several times (see
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0193"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0193"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 14</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan">) to make it more representative of the industry, and
to improve the hedging performance of BIFFEX contracts.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.363.2" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and
Nomikos (see endnotes 11,15) show that the restructuring of the BFI has
helped improve the price discovery function of the futures market.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.363.3" class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and
Nomikos (see endnote 13) also investigate whether the other function of
futures markets, that of hedging performance, has changed as a result of
changes in the composition of the BFI.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.363.4" class="koboSpan">There seems to
be no evidence of statistical change in the hedging performance of
BIFFEX on any route, following the inclusion of time-charter routes in
the BFI. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.363.5"
class="koboSpan">However, performance improves in route 1 following the
exclusion of the handysize routes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.363.6" class="koboSpan">The exclusion
of the capesize routes from the index, in November 1999, making the
index more homogeneous increases the</span>

<div id="Ch025.xhtml_fig0359" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

alt="Figure 16: Yearly Volumes of the BIFFEX Contract (May 1985–June 1999)" /></span>

<a href="#Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0195"
id="Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0195"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.375.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
16:</span></span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.376.1" class="koboSpan">
Yearly Volumes of the BIFFEX Contract (May 1985–June 1999)</span>

class="koboSpan">: LIFFE, 1999</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_734"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.379.1"
class="koboSpan">in-sample hedging effectiveness for every route (except
route 1) in comparison to the pre-November 1999 period.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.379.2" class="koboSpan">This improved
variance reduction is as high as 23.03% in route 3A, with an overall
average improvement (over routes) of 14.36%.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.379.3" class="koboSpan">For the BPI
then the highest hedging effectiveness achieved through the use of
BIFFEX was in route 3A, reaching a figure of 39.95%.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.380.1" class="koboSpan">It seems that the
increased homogeneity of the index has had a positive impact on hedging
effectiveness, despite leaving the variance reduction achieved well
below that evidenced in other markets in the literature.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.380.2" class="koboSpan">At the time of
writing, Kavussanos and Nomikos (see endnote 13) argued that: “the
magnitude of the observed increases in hedging effectiveness is still
small, and may not be sufficient to induce market agents in actively
using the market for hedging purposes.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.380.3" class="koboSpan">This also
seems to be in line with the trading preferences of participants in the
shipping markets who are now increasingly using over-the-counter (OTC)
forward contracts which are cash settled against the underlying shipping
routes of the BPI. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.380.4"
class="koboSpan">Because these contracts are traded against specific
routes, rather than a general index, they also avoid the problem of
basis risk, which is evidenced in the BIFFEX market.”</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.381.1" class="koboSpan">Unfortunately trading
volumes, seen in </span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0195"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0195"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.382.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 16</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan">, have not turned around sufficiently to justify the
BIFFEX contract’s existence for LIFFE.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.383.2" class="koboSpan">Over the
period September 1992 to October 1997 the average daily trading volume
has been 210 contracts per day, the equivalent of the average freight
cost of transporting 220,000 tons of grain from the US Gulf to Rotterdam
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.383.3" class="koboSpan">four
voyages in Route 1 of the BFI). </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.383.4"
class="koboSpan">This had become minimal for the later years of the
history of BIFFEX. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.383.5"
class="koboSpan">As a consequence, LIFFE stopped trading BIFFEX in April
2002.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.384.1" class="koboSpan">Currently, in order
to hedge freight rate risk, one has to turn to OTC financial products.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.384.2" class="koboSpan">Their
performance is examined in a series of seminal papers by Kavussanos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.385.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.386.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnotes 16,17) and Kavussanos and Visvikis (see
endnotes 18,19). </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.386.2"
class="koboSpan">Kavussanos and Visvikis (see endnote 18) investigate
the risk-management function in the FFA markets.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.386.3" class="koboSpan">In sample, the
time-varying hedge ratios perform better, in increasing hedging
effectiveness, in capsize route C4 (59.96%) and in the panamax PTC
(62.69%), capesize CTC (64.02%) and supramax STC (42.18%) time-charter
baskets. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.386.4" class="koboSpan">In
contrast, in route P2A, the simple conventional model (63.96%)
outperforms other specifications.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.386.5" class="koboSpan">Out-of-sample,
specifically, for the period March to October 2008 investigated in
routes P2A and C4, and in the PTC, CTC and STC time-charter baskets for
June to October 2008, results show that-in routes P2A (76.59%) and C4
(85.69%) and in the CTC basket (65.73%), naïve (one-to-one) hedge ratios
produce the highest variance reductions.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.386.6" class="koboSpan">In contrast,
in the STC basket, the constant hedge ratio produced by the VECM model
provides the greatest variance reduction (52.17%).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.386.7" class="koboSpan">In the PTC
basket, the time-varying VECM-GARCH-X model seems to outperform the
alternative hedging strategies (75.76%).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.386.8" class="koboSpan">The hedging
performance results in this paper, with the greatest variance reduction
of 86%, compares favourably with results, achieved through the use of
futures contracts, in other markets – (57.06% for the Canadian Interest
rate futures (Gagnon and
Lypny</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0852" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0852"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.387.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan">), 69.61% and 85.69% for the corn and soybean futures
(Bera </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.389.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0853" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0853"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.390.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan">) and 97.91% and 77.47% for the SP500 and the Canadian
Stock Index futures contract, respectively (Park and
Switzer</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0854" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0854"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.392.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.394.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, Kavussanos
and Dimitrakopoulos (see endnote 20), consider appropriate Value at Risk
(VaR) and extreme value methods of determining the maximum loss that may
be sustained from long positions on freight, and which can drive
decisions on whether to hedge freight exposures through the use of
freight derivatives – see also Kavussanos and Visvikis (see endnote
4).</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_735"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.395.1" class="koboSpan">10. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.395.2" class="koboSpan">Forward Freight Agreements (FFAS)</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.396.1" class="koboSpan">As mentioned earlier,
FFAs are principal-to-principal contracts, between a seller and a buyer
to settle a freight or hire rate, for a specified quantity of cargo or
type of vessel, for usually one, or a combination of the major trade
routes of the dry-bulk and tanker industries.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.396.2" class="koboSpan">Settlement is
made on the difference between the contracted price and the average
price for the route selected in an index over the last seven working
days. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.396.3" class="koboSpan">The
indices published by the Baltic exchange on routes of the tanker and dry
bulk industry are used as the “underlying commodity” on which to base
the FFAs.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.397.1" class="koboSpan">In OTC derivative
agreements there is credit risk involved.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.397.2" class="koboSpan">For the
agreement to go ahead, the parties have to approve each other–i.e.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.397.3" class="koboSpan">each party
accepts the credit risk from the other party.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.397.4" class="koboSpan">Over the past
years, clearing houses, such as those of the London Clearing House (LCH
Clearnet) in 2005, the Norwegian Options and Futures Clearing House
(NOS) in 2002 and Singapore Asia Clear in 2006, have provided the
facility of clearing FFAs for a fee, if one counterparty was not
prepared to accept the credit risk of the other counterparty in an FFA
agreement – see Kavussanos and Visvikis (see endnote 4) for full details
of this issue.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.398.1" class="koboSpan">Institutions, which
facilitate FFA markets are major shipbrokers, investment banks, and
other financial intermediates in the fund management industry.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.398.2" class="koboSpan">The
International Maritime Exchange (IMAREX) has also been established in
Oslo and since 2002 trades and clears (through the NOS) FFAs, in what
resembles futures contracts on freight.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.398.3" class="koboSpan">The New York
Merchantile Exchange (NYMEX) made a similar move and has provided
futures contracts for the tanker industry since 2005.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.399.1" class="koboSpan">The primary advantage
of an OTC market is that the terms and conditions are tailored to the
specific needs of the two parties.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.399.2" class="koboSpan">It is a
private market in which the general public does not know that the
transaction was done. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.399.3"
class="koboSpan">It is considered to be flexible in the sense that the
“parties” can introduce their own contract specifications to cover their
specific needs, saves money by not normally requiring initial,
maintenance, and variation margins (common in the futures organised
exchanges), and allows the market to quickly respond to changing needs
and circumstances by developing new variations of old contracts.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.400.1" class="koboSpan">In the dry-bulk
sector, FFAs are available to match the Capesize, Panamax, Supramax and
Handymax routes. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.400.2"
class="koboSpan">For those wishing to hedge long-term freight risk,
time-charter based FFAs, typically “baskets” of routes of the indices
are tradeable with settlement based on the difference between the
contract price and the daily average of the spot “basket”.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.400.3" class="koboSpan">It is
customary to divide the period into monthly settlements to establish
cash-flow. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.400.4"
class="koboSpan">These routes are regularly reviewed to ensure their
relevance to the underlying physical market.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.400.5" class="koboSpan">The
combination of time-charter routes can create the equivalent of a period
time-charter trade (Clarkson
Securities</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0855" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0855"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.401.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.402.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0196"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0196"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 17</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the tremendous growth in FFA contracts, which,
according to Clarkson’s, have grown to an estimated 17,000 contracts in
2007. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.404.2" class="koboSpan">In value
terms, they have surpassed the value of the physical trading of freight.
</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0197"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0197"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.405.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 18</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.406.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_cap_lbl0200"
id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0200"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.407.1"
class="koboSpan">21</span></a><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.408.1"
class="koboSpan"> present the near-month FFA prices against the spot
prices (underlying asset) in Panamax routes 1 (US
Gulf/Antwerp-Rotterdam-Amsterdam), 1A (Transatlantic round to
Skaw-Gibraltar range), 2 (US Gulf/Japan) and 2A (Skaw
Passero–Gibraltar/Taiwan–Japan), respectively.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.408.2" class="koboSpan">In every route
the FFA and spot prices move closely together.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.408.3" class="koboSpan">This is
verified by the values of the correlation coefficients of logarithmic
differences of FFA prices with spot prices in routes 1, 1A, 2 and 2A.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.408.4" class="koboSpan">They are,
respectively, 0.965, 0.972, 0.986, and 0.985.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.426.1" class="koboSpan">11. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.426.2" class="koboSpan">The Effect of FFA Trading on Spot Price Volatility</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.427.1" class="koboSpan">It is often claimed
that the advent of futures or forward prices can have an adverse impact
on spot price volatility. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.427.2"
class="koboSpan">Kavussanos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.428.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.429.1"
class="koboSpan">(see endnote 17) investigate the issue in the FFA
market. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.429.2" class="koboSpan">The
results suggest that the onset of FFA trading has had (i) a stabilising
impact on the spot price volatility in routes 1 and 2; (ii) an impact on
the asymmetry of volatility (market dynamics) in routes 2 and 2A; and
(iii) substantially improved the quality and speed of information flow
in routes 1, 1A and 2. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.429.3"
class="koboSpan">Overall, the results indicate that the introduction of
FFA contracts has not had a detrimental effect on the underlying spot
market. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.429.4" class="koboSpan">On the
contrary, it appears that there has been an improvement in the way that
news is transmitted into prices following the onset of FFA trading.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.429.5" class="koboSpan">By attracting
more, and possibly better informed, participants into the market, FFA
trading has assisted in the incorporation of information into spot
prices more quickly. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.429.6"
class="koboSpan">Thus, even those market agents that do not directly use
the FFA market have benefited from the introduction of FFA
trading.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_738"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.430.1" class="koboSpan">12. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.430.2" class="koboSpan">Stabilising Voyage Costs: Hedging Bunker Price Risk</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.431.1" class="koboSpan">Returning to the cash
flow position of shipowners, as mentioned in section 1 and shown
schematically in </span>[<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.432.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch025.xhtml_fig0337)<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.433.1"
class="koboSpan">, the major and most volatile part of their voyage
costs comes from bunker price fluctuations (amounting to 50% of voyage
costs, according to Stopford (see endnote 26)).
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.433.2" class="koboSpan">Yet, with the
exception of some financial
institutions,</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0856" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0856"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.434.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.435.1"
class="koboSpan"> offering tailor-made OTC derivatives products such as
forwards, swaps and options, there were no tradable futures contract for
the bunker
fuel</span><sup><a href="#Ch025.xhtml_fn0857" id="Ch025.xhtml_bck_fn0857"><span
id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.436.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.437.1"
class="koboSpan"> until a few years ago.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.437.2" class="koboSpan">In the absence
of bunker futures contracts, hedging against bunker price fluctuations
using other similar futures contracts, such as energy futures, involves
a cross-hedge. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.437.3"
class="koboSpan">In order to offer market participants the possibility
to eliminate credit risk involved in OTC bunker fuel contracts, in 2006
SGX AsiaClear introduced clearing of bunker forward contracts, with cash
settlement against a monthly average of the Platts daily quotations.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.437.4" class="koboSpan">Since December
2005, IMAREX introduced bunker fuel futures contracts for the most
popular bunker fuel grades, and for contract durations up to two
calendar years ahead. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.437.5"
class="koboSpan">The settlement prices used are those of Platts and
Bunkerworld and the settlement period is the average of the
month.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.438.1" class="koboSpan">Although marine
bunkers are bought and sold in almost every port in the world, the world
bunker market can be broadly divided into three major regional markets
in which the bulk of physical bunkering activities takes place.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.438.2" class="koboSpan">These are:
Singapore, Rotterdam and Houston.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.438.3" class="koboSpan">Singapore has
long flourished as a transhipment centre due to its strategic
geographical location. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.438.4"
class="koboSpan">The Singapore bunker market is by far the largest
marine fuels market in the world, and is duly considered to be a prime
benchmark for the industry. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.438.5"
class="koboSpan">Singapore’s turnover in marine fuel oil in 2000 was
18.7 million tonnes. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.438.6"
class="koboSpan">In Europe, the Amsterdam–Rotterdam–Antwerp (ARA) region
sells as much as 16 million tonnes of bunker fuel annually.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.438.7" class="koboSpan">The heart of
the ARA region is Rotterdam, which sells about 8 to 9 million tonnes of
bunker oil and lubes annually, helped by a hub of oil refining and
storage facilities sited in its Europort complex, which handles around
100 million tonnes of crude annually.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.438.8" class="koboSpan">Bunkering on
the US Gulf coast is dominated by Houston, recording an annual sales
volume of 3 million tonnes in 2000.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.439.1" class="koboSpan">Before the
introduction of bunker futures contracts, Alizadeh, Kavussanos, and
Menachof (see endnote 22), explored the possibility of using a number of
traded petroleum futures contracts as instruments for risk reduction in
relation to this major operating expense for the shipowner.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.439.2" class="koboSpan">They examined
the effectiveness of hedging marine bunker price fluctuations in
Rotterdam, Singapore and Houston using different crude oil and petroleum
future contracts traded at the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) and
the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) – now Intercontinetal
exchange – in London.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.440.1" class="koboSpan">Using both constant
and dynamic hedge ratios, it is found that in and out-of-sample hedging
effectiveness is different across regional bunker markets.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.440.2" class="koboSpan">The most
effective futures instruments for out-of-sample hedging of spot bunker
prices in Rotterdam and Singapore are the IPE crude oil futures, while
for Houston it is the gas oil futures.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.440.3" class="koboSpan">However, they
achieve only up to 43% variance reduction when using IPE crude oil to
hedge bunker prices in Rotterdam.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.440.4" class="koboSpan">Hedging
effectiveness varies from one bunker market to the other.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.440.5" class="koboSpan">For agents
determined to use futures contracts to hedge bunker price risk, policy
action points to using IPE crude oil contracts to hedge bunker price
fluctuations when loading in Rotterdam, NYMEX gas oil contracts when
loading in Singapore, and IPE gas oil futures contracts when using
Houston for refuelling vessels. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.440.6"
class="koboSpan">The maximum hedging effectiveness are 43%, 15.9% and
14% in each case. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.440.7"
class="koboSpan">This compares unfavourably with other futures
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_page_739"></span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.441.1"
class="koboSpan">contracts. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.441.2"
class="koboSpan">However, as discussed earlier, the availability of
bunker fuel futures contracts at IMAREX, and the existence of an active
OTC bunker fuels market in association with the market clearing of these
products serves the market in a much better way – see Kavussanos and
Visvikis (see endnote 4) for further discussion of these issues.</span>

## <span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.442.1" class="koboSpan">13. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.442.2" class="koboSpan">Summary—Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.443.1" class="koboSpan">Shipowners are faced
with substantial business risks in the international environment that
they operate. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.443.2"
class="koboSpan">Risks emanate from fluctuations in freight rates,
bunker prices, the price of the investment ship, interest rates,
exchange rates, etc. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.443.3"
class="koboSpan">This chapter has put forward a framework for
identifying and measuring these risks, and has proposed solutions on how
to handle the question of risk management.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.443.4" class="koboSpan">In the
process, a review of the literature and some new ideas about how risks
can be managed in the shipping industry have been put together.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.443.5" class="koboSpan">At the same
time the chapter provides the state of the art of where we stand now
technically in calculating instruments that can be used to hedge risks,
such as the calculation of time varying hedge ratios.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.443.6" class="koboSpan">It offers a
review of where we stand research-wise in the area, and can provide a
stepping-stone for further research and innovations in the area.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.443.7" class="koboSpan">Naturally, a
lot of the details underlying the research have not been reproduced
here, due to lack of space. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.443.8"
class="koboSpan">However, these details can be found in the original
papers, referenced here.</span>

<span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.444.1" class="koboSpan">The ideas put forward
in this chapter include: The sectoral disaggregation of the dry bulk,
tanker and container sector of the cargo carrying shipping industry,
based on distinct risk-return characteristics.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.444.2" class="koboSpan">As a
consequence, it is suggested that shipowners can mitigate risks by
holding portfolios of assets–ships– of different size; The possible risk
diversification effects in ship operation by switching between contracts
of different duration; The use of freight derivatives, such as futures
and forward contracts to manage freight rate risks; The economic
functions of price discovery and risk management of these financial
instruments are discussed critically.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.444.3" class="koboSpan">The review
looks back at BIFFEX and their role in serving the industry as hedging
instruments for freight rates. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.444.4"
class="koboSpan">It compares their performance with other financial
instruments and finds it somewhat lacking.
</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.444.5" class="koboSpan">In a way, it
identifies why the industry has turned gradually to OTC products and
explains the withdrawal of freight futures contracts after 17 years of
existence. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.444.6"
class="koboSpan">Naturally it is impossible to cover all aspects
involved in one chapter. </span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.444.7"
class="koboSpan">The book by Kavussanos and Visvikis (see endnote 4)
aims to close this gap and provide interested readers with all the
relevant information in the area of risk analysis and management in
shipping, particularly on the use of derivative instruments.</span>

</span><span id="Ch025.xhtml_kobo.612.4" class="koboSpan">This proved
