<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_744"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_745"></span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 26</span>\
<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Managing Freight Rate Risk Using Freight Derivatives: An Overview of the Empirical Evidence</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0569)
================================================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Nikos</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">K.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Nomikos</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">and
</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Amir</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">H.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan">Alizadeh</span></span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0858" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0858"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">Over the last decade,
the tramp shipping markets have undergone a fundamental transformation.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">This period is
characterised by very high volatility in the level of freight rates as
well as the emergence, and corresponding growth in the derivatives
market for freight. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.12.3"
class="koboSpan">Traditionally, this was a market that was used by
players in the physical freight market, such as shipowners, operators
and trading houses, to hedge their risks although this is now changing
rapidly with the increasing participation of investment banks, hedge
funds and other traders that may not be involved in the underlying
physical market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.12.4"
class="koboSpan">This has resulted in the commoditisation of the freight
market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.12.5"
class="koboSpan">Nowadays, freight rates can be bought and sold like any
other commodity, despite the fact that freight rates essentially
represent the cost of providing the service of seaborne transportation
and, hence, are not classified as a tangible commodity.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">Overall, this has
created a shipping environment where market participants are more aware
of the risks they face and also try to explore avenues to hedge or
manage those risks. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.13.2"
class="koboSpan">For a ship-operator, the most important source of risk
is freight rate risk. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.13.3"
class="koboSpan">Freight rate risk refers to the variability in the
earnings of a shipping company due to changes in freight rates and the
importance of this risk factor stems from the fact that volatility in
the freight market has a direct impact on the profitability of a
shipping company. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.13.4"
class="koboSpan">The focus of this chapter therefore is to introduce and
analyse the derivative instruments that are used in the market to
control freight rate risk. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.13.5"
class="koboSpan">In particular we focus on managing freight rate risk
using forward and option contracts.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.13.6" class="koboSpan">We describe the
structure and functioning of the Forward Freight Agreement (FFA) market,
the trading practices, documentation and types of contract used in the
trades, applications and uses of FFAs for risk management as well as how
to deal with issues such as basis risk.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_746"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">We also discuss freight options and their use in risk
management and speculation. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.14.2"
class="koboSpan">First, we consider the properties of freight options
and present the profit patterns from buying or selling call and put
options; we also discuss the practicalities of trading freight options
and then examine risk management applications of freight options using
caps, floors and collars. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.14.3"
class="koboSpan">Finally, we also discuss the topic of options pricing
and the different approaches that are currently used in the
market.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">It should be stressed
that the emphasis on freight rate risk management in this chapter is on
the tramp sector of the industry.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Risk management
techniques are markedly different across the liner and tramp shipping
sector due to the unique characteristics of each one of those sectors.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.15.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
while freight rates in tramp shipping are determined through the
interaction of supply and demand for shipping services in a nearly
perfect market, freight rates in the liner sectors are determined
through “conferences” and “alliances” which are reviewed only
periodically (see
Stopford</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0859" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0859"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
McConville</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0860" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0860"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">As a result, liner rates are less volatile compared to
rates in tramp shipping and therefore the approach toward risk
management used by liner operators is markedly
different.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0861" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0861"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">The structure of this
chapter is as follows. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.21.2"
class="koboSpan">In the next section we present a historical overview of
the freight derivatives market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.21.3"
class="koboSpan">In section 3 we discuss the FFA market, the
practicalities of using FFAs for risk management and how to deal with
the issue of basis risk. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.21.4"
class="koboSpan">Section 4 presents the freight options market, how to
use options for risk management and how to price freight options.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.21.5" class="koboSpan">Finally,
section 5 concludes this chapter.</span>

## <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">Historical Overview of the Freight Derivatives Market</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">The benefits of
providing a futures market in freight rates had been recognised by
shipping market practitioners as early as the 1960s
(Gray</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0862" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0862"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.25.2"
class="koboSpan">However, such a market was eventually established only
in 1985. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.25.3" class="koboSpan">The
reason is that the underlying asset of the market – the service of
seaborne transportation – is not a physical asset which can be delivered
at the expiry of the futures contract; by its very definition, a futures
contract is an agreement to deliver a specified quantity and grade of an
identified asset, at a certain time in the future.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.25.4" class="koboSpan">This obstacle
was overcome with the introduction of the cash settlement procedure for
stock index futures contracts in 1982; when the underlying asset is not
suitable for actual physical delivery then an alternative is to deliver
the cash value of the asset at that time.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">This innovation led to
the development of the first exchange traded freight futures contract.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.26.2" class="koboSpan">Trading on the
Baltic International Freight Futures Exchange (BIFFEX) contract
commenced on 1 May 1985. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.26.3"
class="koboSpan">The contract was traded at the London Commodity
Exchange, which is now part of Euronext.LIFFE Exchange in London; the
underlying asset of the contract was the Baltic Freight Index (BFI), a
freight index that initially consisted of 13 voyage routes covering a
variety of cargoes ranging from 14,000 metric tons (mt) of fertiliser up
to 120,000 mt of coal. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.26.4"
class="koboSpan">It quickly won worldwide acceptance as the most
reliable general indicator of movements in the dry cargo freight market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.26.5" class="koboSpan">Over the years,
the constituent routes of that original index have been refined to meet
the ever increasing and changing needs of the freight derivative
markets. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.26.6"
class="koboSpan">Trip-charter routes were added to the index and
gradually, handysize and capesize routes were excluded from the index.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.26.7" class="koboSpan">As a result, in
November 1999, the Baltic Panamax Index (BPI) superseded the BFI as the
underlying asset of the BIFFEX
contract.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0863" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0863"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_747"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan">The asset which was delivered at the settlement date of
the futures contract was the cash equivalent of the general level of the
freight market at that time as represented by the level of the BFI.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">The settlement
price was computed as the average value of the index over the last seven
trading days of each contract month and the monetary value of the
settlement price was \$10 per index point.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">The
introduction of the BIFFEX contract gave, for the first time, the
opportunity to shipping market agents to control their freight rate risk
in the physical market, through hedging.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.28.4" class="koboSpan">This was an
entirely “paper” financial transaction and no real ships or cargoes were
involved. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.28.5"
class="koboSpan">Additionally, through the price-discovery function,
futures prices could also help reveal information about expected spot
prices and, hence, provide valuable signals to market agents regarding
the likely future direction of freight rates in the markets; this was
shown empirically by
Nomikos</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0864" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0864"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Kavussanos and
Nomikos.</span><sup>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fn0864)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0866" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0866"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan"> Although the BIFFEX contract was quite innovative at
its time, it quickly became apparent that the heterogeneous composition
of the underlying index, affected dramatically the performance of hedges
in the market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.34.2"
class="koboSpan">This was due to the fact that futures prices did not
capture accurately the fluctuations on the individual routes that
comprised the BFI but, rather, followed the movements of the BFI itself.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.34.3" class="koboSpan">Effectively
therefore, hedging on BIFFEX was like a cross-hedge.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">Unlike other futures
markets, in which futures contracts are used as a hedge against price
fluctuations in the underlying asset, in the BIFFEX market futures
contracts are employed as a cross-hedge against freight rate
fluctuations on the individual shipping routes which constitute the BFI.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">As such, there
is the risk that fluctuations on these routes may not be accurately
tracked by the futures prices, thus, reducing the effectiveness of the
contract as a hedging instrument.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.35.3" class="koboSpan">Cross-hedging
freight rate risk using an index-based futures contract is only
successful when the freight rate and the futures price move together.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.35.4" class="koboSpan">However, when a
large number of underlying routes constitute an index, then the
relationship between these routes and the index will not be very strong.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.35.5" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
BIFFEX market participants, who use the contract to hedge their freight
rate risk on specific shipping routes, have small gains in terms of risk
reduction. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.35.6" class="koboSpan">In a
series of studies, Nomikos</span><sup>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fn0864)</sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Nomikos and
Kavussanos</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0868" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0868"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0869" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0869"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan"> have shown that the hedging effectiveness of the
BIFFEX contract varies from 19.2 to 4% across the different shipping
routes which constitute the underlying index.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.41.2" class="koboSpan">This is well
below the risk reduction evidenced in other commodity and financial
markets which ranges from 70–99%.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">The poor hedging
performance of the contract is also thought to be the primary reason for
the low trading activity evidenced in the market.
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0201"
id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0201"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents the volume of trade for the BIFFEX contract,
for the period from 1994–2002. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.44.2"
class="koboSpan">Over the period from February 1996 to June 2000, the
average daily trading volume in the market was only 146 contracts.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.44.3" class="koboSpan">The daily
monetary value of these contracts roughly corresponds to the average
freight cost of transporting 108,000 tonnes of Grain from the US Gulf to
Japan; market sources estimate that this level of futures trading
activity corresponds to only 10% of the total physical activity in the
dry-bulk shipping market, during the same period.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.44.4" class="koboSpan">As a result of
the lack of trading interest in the market, the BIFFEX contract was
eventually de-listed in April 2002.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">The reduction in the
trading activity of the BIFFEX contract after the mid-1990s was also due
to the development of an over-the counter forward market for shipping
freight called Forward Freight Agreements (FFA), which are cash-settled
against an underlying shipping route.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">Because of the
fact that these contracts are traded against specific routes, rather
than a general index, they also eliminate the problem of basis
risk,</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0367" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00387.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: BIFFEX trading volume (1994–2002)" /></span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_748"></span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0201"
id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0201"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan"> BIFFEX trading volume (1994–2002)</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">Euronext.LIFFE. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.50.2"
class="koboSpan">Each contract trades the expected value of the BFI.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">The value of
each contract is \$10 per index point.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">evidenced in the
BIFFEX market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.51.2"
class="koboSpan">The mechanics of the FFA contracts are described in the
next section.</span>

## <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.52.2" class="koboSpan">Forward Freight Agreements</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">From the early 1990s a
new market for trading the forward value of freight emerged, primarily
as a response to the needs of market players who were aware of the
deficiencies of the BIFFEX contract as a hedging instrument and wanted a
hedging tool which would provide a more precise match to their exposure
in the physical market and, hence, a more accurate hedging mechanism.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">A Forward
Freight Agreement (FFA) is an agreement between two counterparties to
settle a freight rate or hire rate, for a specified quantity of cargo or
type of vessel, for one of the major shipping routes in the dry-bulk or
the tanker markets at a certain date in the future.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.53.3" class="koboSpan">The underlying
asset of the FFA contracts can be any of the routes or basket of routes
which constitute the indices produced by the Baltic Exchange, or by
other reputable providers of underlying market information, such as
Platts.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Currently, the Baltic
Exchange produces a wide range of shipping indices covering different
vessel sizes and different cargo types, such as the Baltic Panamax Index
(BPI), which reflects freight rates for Panamax vessels of 74,000 metric
tonnes (mt) dead-weight (dwt); the Baltic Capesize Index (BCI) – for
capesize vessels of 172,000 mt dwt; the Baltic Supramax Index (BSI) –
for Supramax size vessels of 52,000 mt dwt; and the Baltic Handysize
Index (BHI) – for Handysize vessels of 28,000 mt dwt.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
there are indices covering the movement of tanker cargoes: The Baltic
Clean
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_749"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan">tanker Index (BCTI) and Baltic Dirty Tanker Index
(BDTI). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">The
current composition of the BPI is presented in
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0368" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0368"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.57.2"
class="koboSpan">We can see that the index consists of four trip-charter
routes; Route P1A_03 is the trans-Atlantic route for a voyage across the
Atlantic; the charterer takes delivery of the vessel in the continent in
the range between Cape Skaw (in North Continent) and Gibraltar; the
vessel will go across the Atlantic to either US Gulf, East Coast South
America or East Coast North America for transportation of cargoes back
to the Continent, where the vessel will be re-delivered.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.57.3" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
Route P2A_03 is the trip out to the Far East.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.57.4" class="koboSpan">The vessel is
delivered in the Continent to perform a voyage to the Far East for
redelivery in the region between Taiwan and Japan.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.57.5" class="koboSpan">Route P3A_03 is
the Trans-Pacific panamax route where the vessel is delivered in the
range between Japan and South Korea for a voyage to load cargo in
Australia or North Pacific and then redeliver the vessel to the same
region. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.57.6"
class="koboSpan">Finally, route P4_03 is the return leg of Route P2A_03
where the panamax vessel is delivered in the Far East for a voyage to
the continent via the West Coast of US.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.57.7" class="koboSpan">All these
trip-charter routes are estimated on the basis that the trip is
performed by a standard “Baltic Panamax” vessel, the particulars of
which are presented in </span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fig0368)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0870" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0870"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">FFAs are settled in
cash on the difference between the contract price and an appropriate
settlement price. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.61.2"
class="koboSpan">The settlement rate is usually calculated as the
average of the underlying route over the settlement month, although
there are some exceptions to that general
rule.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0871" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0871"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan"> The calculation of an average settlement rate is used
in order to ensure</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0368" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00388.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0368)

</div>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0369" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00389.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Spot, 1st, 2nd and 3rd quarter FFA rates for BPI 4TC" /></span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_750"></span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0202"
id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0202"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan"> Spot, 1st, 2nd and 3rd quarter FFA rates for BPI
4TC</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Baltic Exchange</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">that settlement rates
are not susceptible to large moves due to very high volatility or market
manipulation on any specific trading day.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.70.2" class="koboSpan">Although trades
are possible for every route published in the market, there seems to be
a tendency for trades to concentrate on certain routes only.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.70.3" class="koboSpan">For instance,
in the Panamax market the majority of the trades are on the BPI four TC
average, which is the equally weighted average of the four TC routes of
the BPI.</span>

<a href="#Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0202"
id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0202"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">Figures 2</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan"> and </span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0203"
id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0203"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">3</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan"> present the spot and FFA rates for the first three
quarters for the average of the four trip-charter routes of BPI and BCI,
respectively. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.74.2"
class="koboSpan">The graphs cover the period from March 2005 to January
2010. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.74.3" class="koboSpan">We can
note that there is a strong degree of co-movement between the spot and
FFA rates. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.74.4" class="koboSpan">The
strength of the relationship is also evident during the collapse of the
market in the fourth quarter of 2008 when freight rates for Capesize
vessels dropped from a peak of 240,000 US\$/day in July to a rate of
less than 5,000 US\$/day in November.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.74.5" class="koboSpan">We can see that
during that period FFA rates followed the spot market very closely.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.74.6" class="koboSpan">Finally, we can
also note that as we move from the spot to the forward rates, the
forward rates appear to be less volatile than the spot rates, which is
indicative of a volatility term structure pattern in the forward
rates.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">The FFA market has
evidenced considerable growth over the period from 2005 to 2008 as a
result of the surge in freight rates, particularly in the dry sector,
which also resulted in an increase in the use of freight derivatives for
risk management purposes. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.75.2"
class="koboSpan">Market volatility has also generated trading interest
from players outside of the shipping markets; therefore, over the recent
years we evidenced an influx of new participants in this market such as
investment banks and hedge funds.
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0204"
id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0204"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents the volume of trades in the FFA market for
the period 1997 to 2009; these figures are</span>

id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.80.1"

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">estimates provided by
the London-based FFA broker Freight Investor Services (FIS) (until 2007)
and the Baltic Exchange (from 2007 onwards) and reflect the estimated
number of lots which have been traded in the dry market; the market
convention is to measure the volume of trades in terms of lots where one
lot either represents 1,000 mt of cargo carried or one-day of
trip-charter hire. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">From 2005 to 2008, the average annual growth in the FFA
market was 10%. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.83.3"
class="koboSpan">However, the sudden drop in freight rates during the
fourth quarter of 2008 resulted in a corresponding reduction in the
activity in the paper market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.83.4"
class="koboSpan">As a result, trading volume in the fourth quarter of
2008 was less than 15% of the total for the year; trading volume in 2009
also remained in low levels and was at half the level of trading in
2008, although the second half of the year saw an increase in trading
interest, compared to the first half.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">Since July 2007,
information on the volume of trade has also been reported by the Baltic
Exchange. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.84.2" class="koboSpan">This
information is provided to the Baltic Exchange on a weekly basis by
major international FFA brokers, Clearing Houses and Exchanges, and is
then aggregated and reported to the market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.84.3" class="koboSpan">In the dry
sector, trading volume, defined as lots traded, is estimated for the
Capesize, Panamax, Supramax and Handysize markets, and the trades are
also classified as to whether they are cleared or not; as in the
previous case, a dry lot is defined as either one trip-charter day or
1,000 tonnes of voyage-based ocean transportation.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.84.4" class="koboSpan">In each case a
single transaction, although having a buyer and a seller, is counted
only as one lot. </span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0205"
id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0205"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents the volume traded by contract type for
2009.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">We can see that of the
total volume, about 45% of the trades are on the Capesize market, 39% on
Panamax, 10% on Supramax vessels and the remaining 6% in the</span>

</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">Reported
figures are market estimates provided by major FFA brokers and

hire.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_753"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan">Handysize sector.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">This pattern
in the distribution of FFA trades amongst the different size vessels is
not in line with the distribution of the world total fleet where
currently 40% of the world trade is conducted by Handysize and Supramax
vessels, 40% through Panamaxes and only 20% through Capesizes.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">The low volume
in the Supramax and Handysize FFA sectors may be attributed to the fact
that, for the smaller sizes, the underlying shipping market is more
fragmented, with smaller trades not represented by the Baltic Indices,
as opposed to the panamax and capesize sectors.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.100.4" class="koboSpan">Finally, it is
also interesting to note that currently more than 90% of the contracts
are cleared via one of the clearing houses.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.100.5" class="koboSpan">This increased
considerably compared to 2008 and 2007, when the percentage of cleared
contracts was only 40%, and reflects the tighter credit conditions that
prevailed in the market in 2009.</span>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 How are forward freight agreements traded?</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">Forward Freight
Agreements can be traded either over the-counter (OTC) or through an
organised exchange such as the International Maritime Exchange (IMAREX),
as shown in </span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0206"
id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0206"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.104.2"
class="koboSpan">Trading in the OTC market, takes place though
specialist FFA brokers via “traditional” telephone based broking.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.104.3" class="koboSpan">Trades can be
either on the basis of a principal to principal contract between the two
counterparties, using one of the standard contract forms that are used
in the market, such as FFABA 2007 or ISDA Master Agreement, or,
alternatively, trades may be cleared through one of the clearing houses
that provide services to the freight market, such as the London Clearing
House (LCH.Clearnet), the Singapore Exchange (SGX) AsiaClear Service,
the Norwegian Futures and Options Clearing House (NOS) or the New York
Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.104.4"
class="koboSpan">In addition, FFAs can also be traded through a “hybrid”
exchange, the most popular of which is the International Maritime
Exchange
(IMAREX);</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0872" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0872"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"> IMAREX provide a trading screen where standardised
contracts are traded, which are then</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00393.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Trading structure of the FFA market" /></span>

<a href="#Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0206"
id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0206"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6:</span></span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan"> Trading structure of the FFA market</span>

id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_754"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">cleared straight through NOS.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.113.2" class="koboSpan">A more
detailed discussion of these trading options is presented in Alizadeh
and
Nomikos.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0873" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0873"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Hedging using forward freight agreements</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Market agents are
confronted with risks that arise from the ordinary conduct of their
businesses. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.116.2"
class="koboSpan">Derivative markets provide a way in which these risks
may be transferred to other individuals who are willing to bear them,
through hedging. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.116.3"
class="koboSpan">Hedges are either short or long.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.116.4" class="koboSpan">A
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan">short</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan">selling</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan"> hedge involves selling FFAs as a protection against an
unexpected decline in freight rates; for instance, shipowners or ship
operators who want to protect their freight income can sell FFAs – since
when freight rates fall, the reduction in the freight income will be
compensated through a gain in the forward position.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.120.2" class="koboSpan">A
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan">long</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan">buying</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan"> hedge, on the other hand, involves buying futures as a
protection against a price increase.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">For instance
charterers can buy FFAs; this enables them to protect their forward
freight requirements, in case the physical market rises, thus forcing
them to pay higher freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.124.3" class="koboSpan">FFAs were
initially traded for risk management purposes by charterers and
shipowners although, currently, they are also used for the purpose of
speculating on the future direction of the freight markets.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.124.4" class="koboSpan">The following
example illustrates the use of FFAs for hedging purposes.</span>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Trip-charter hedge</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">This is an example
where we consider the use of BPI FFA contracts to hedge panamax earnings
for a period of six months. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.126.2"
class="koboSpan">An owner operates a 65,000 mt dwt panamax vessel built
in 1997. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.126.3"
class="koboSpan">Currently, on 10 October 2005, the vessel is under a
six-month time-charter for 22,000 \$/day which will expire in three
months, around the middle of January.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.126.4" class="koboSpan">Under the
terms of the charter the vessel will be re-delivered to her owner at
around 10–15 January 2006 in the Far East.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.126.5" class="koboSpan">The owner is
worried about the possibility that the market may soften when the vessel
will be open in the market and he, thus, decides to hedge the vessel’s
earnings for the first six months of 2006.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.126.6" class="koboSpan">Since he wants
to hedge against the volatility in the Panamax sector, the most
appropriate strategy is to sell the four TC average of the BPI for Q1
and Q2 2006. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.126.7"
class="koboSpan">Freight Investor Services (FIS) quote FFA rates of
21,750 \$/day and 20,750 \$/day for Q1 and Q2 2006, respectively, as
shown in
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0374" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0374"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.128.2"
class="koboSpan">Effectively each one of those contracts is a strip of
three monthly</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0374" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00394.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0374)

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_755"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">FFA, covering the respective quarter, at the given
rate. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">He thus
sells Q1 2006 at 21,750 \$/day and Q2 2006 at 20,750 \$/day which he
holds until he can find suitable employment for his vessel.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.130.3" class="koboSpan">By selling the
FFAs for January and February, the owner locks in a charter rate of
21,750 \$/day for each day in January and February, which implies
monthly earnings of \$674,250 (=21,750 \$/day\* 31) for January and
\$609,000 (=21,750 \$/day \* 28) for February.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">In order to
illustrate how this hedging strategy can be implemented, we are going to
consider two different variations regarding the owner’s choices in the
physical market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.131.2"
class="koboSpan">In the first case, the owner will be operating the
vessel in the spot market and as he fixes a voyage he will be gradually
unwinding some of his FFA positions; in the second case, the owner will
fix his vessel on a period time-charter basis for the first six months
of 2006 so that he will have to unwind his entire FFA portfolio at once.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.131.3" class="koboSpan">Consider each
case next.</span>

#### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.1 First case — Shipowner operates his vessel in the spot market</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">In the first case,
the owner decides to operate the vessel in the spot market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">He feels that
the Pacific basin presents the most attractive employment opportunities,
so he will be fixing the vessel for consecutive Trans-Pacific round
voyages (i.e. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.133.3"
class="koboSpan">route 3A of the BPI in
</span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fig0368)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">) for the next six months.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">The first
voyage is fixed at around the end of December 2005 for delivery to take
place in the middle of January; the vessel will be chartered for a
Trans-Pacific round voyage (route BPI 3A) for an estimated voyage
duration of 47 days at around 16,500 \$/day.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.135.3" class="koboSpan">In this case,
the vessel is fixed approximately 15 days before the date it is actually
delivered to the charterer, which corresponds to the laycan for that
route.</span><sup>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan">16</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fn0874)</sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">The owner has now
secured employment for his vessel from the middle of January until the
end of February (47 days) and, as a result, he no longer requires the
hedging position for January and February.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.137.2" class="koboSpan">He thus
unwinds the January 2006 and February 2006 contracts at a rate of 16,014
\$/day and 16,276 \$/day,
respectively.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0875" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0875"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan"> The outcome of this strategy is presented
in</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0375" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0375"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan"> Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.141.2"
class="koboSpan">The hedging position is closed as soon as the owner has
secured the next voyage for the vessel, at around the end of December
2005, and the FFA contracts for January and February are thus settled at
16,014 \$/day and 16,276 \$/day, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">For instance,
for the January contract, this results in a profit of 5,736 \$/day
(=21,750 – 16,014) or a total profit of \$177,816 (5,736 \* 31) for the
entire month of January. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.141.4"
class="koboSpan">The vessel is then delivered to the charterer for the
TransPacific round voyage at 16,500 \$/day for a voyage duration of 47
days resulting in trip earnings of \$775,500, as shown in Panel B of
</span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">Table
3</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fig0375)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0876" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0876"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">The vessel will be
delivered back to her owner in early March, so the owner needs to make
provisions for fixing her next voyage.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.145.2" class="koboSpan">Around the
middle of February the vessel is fixed for another Trans-Pacific round
voyage of 47 days for 18,500 \$/day, for delivery in early March.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.145.3" class="koboSpan">Again, as soon
as the owner has secured employment for his vessel for the next 47 days,
he has to unwind his FFA positions for March and April.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.145.4" class="koboSpan">He thus
settles his short March and April FFA contracts at a rate of \$18,550
\$/day and at 16,925 \$/day, respectively, as shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">Table
3</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fig0375)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.147.2"
class="koboSpan">Notice as well that by closing the April contract when
he fixes the second voyage, the owner no longer has cover against
freight rate changes for the second part of April.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.147.3" class="koboSpan">This can be
important because the vessel will be open again after 18 April so the
owner will be exposed to freight rate volatility for the period 18–30
April. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.147.4" class="koboSpan">One way
round this, could be for the owner to close the</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0375" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_756"></span>[](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0375)

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00395.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0375)

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_757"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">April contract later, when he fixes his third voyage;
this of course would result in an uncovered or speculative short FFA
position for the first part of April.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.149.2" class="koboSpan">Alternatively,
the owner could settle half of his April contract (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.149.3" class="koboSpan">15 days) when
he fixes his second voyage and the remaining 15 days when he fixes his
third voyage; this would provide a more accurate hedge but such a
strategy could be hindered by the fact that liquidity in trading half
months in the market is more limited.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">Overall, by fixing
his vessel spot, the owner would realise earnings of \$3,078,000 for the
first six months of 2006. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.150.2"
class="koboSpan">Combining this with the total payoff from the FFA
contracts, which is \$638,915, results in a total income from the
physical and the paper market of \$3,716,915.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.150.3" class="koboSpan">Notice that
the owner was aiming to lock in a total income of \$3,845,750 for the
first six months of 2006, when he entered the hedge back in October
2005. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.150.4" class="koboSpan">There is
therefore a discrepancy of 3.4% between the expected and the actual
freight income, which is the hedging error from implementing this
strategy.</span>

#### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.2 Second case — Shipowner charters his vessel for a period time charter of six months</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">In this case, the
owner secures a period time-charter contract for the first six months of
2006. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.152.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, around the end of December 2005 he fixes his
vessel for a six-month time charter, with a duration of 183 days, for
15,500 \$/day. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.152.3"
class="koboSpan">At the same time, he offsets his FFA position by buying
Q1 and Q2 06 contracts at a rate of 16,250 \$/day and 15,500 \$/day,
respectively.
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0376" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0376"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents the outcome of this strategy.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.154.2" class="koboSpan">We can see
that the six-month period time-charter provides earnings of \$2,836,500;
combined with the profit from the FFA position, this results in overall
earnings of \$3,809,250, which suggests a hedging error of 0.95%
compared to the expected locked-in value.</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0376" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00396.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0376)

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_758"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan">Overall, we can note that the hedging strategy worked
reasonably well with a relatively small hedging error.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.156.2" class="koboSpan">The magnitude
of the hedging error and, hence, the effectiveness of a hedging
strategy, depends on a number of factors, some of which include:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">Timing mismatch
    between paper and physical
    contracts</span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
    class="koboSpan">: </span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
    class="koboSpan">paper contracts are settled at the end of each
    month, whereas fixtures in the physical market can be concluded any
    time in that period. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.159.2"
    class="koboSpan">Depending on the volatility of the underlying
    market this mismatch can have an important effect on the performance
    of the hedge; Alizadeh and Nomikos (see endnote 15) report this
    error to be as high as 17% for route 3A of the BPI.</span>
2.  <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">Basis risk: basis
    risk arises due to the fact that the route underlying the FFA is
    different from the exposure that we have in the market.
    </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.160.2" class="koboSpan">For
    instance, in the example presented here, we use BPI 4TC FFAs to
    hedge exposure on route P3A.
    </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.160.3" class="koboSpan">Although
    one could use FFA on this route, the performance of the hedge could
    be affected by liquidity costs since FFAs on this route are less
    liquid than on the 4TC routes, particularly for longer maturities;
    basis risk is discussed more extensively in the next section.</span>
3.  <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">Size mismatch:
    size mismatch could also cause basis risk when the vessel whose
    earnings we want to hedge is different from the reference vessel
    used in the calculation of the underlying rates.
    </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.161.2" class="koboSpan">For
    instance, in this example we operate a eight-year old 65,000 mt dwt
    Panamax vessel, whereas the Baltic assessments are calculated on the
    basis of a 74,000 mt dwt “Baltic” Panamax type vessel, with a
    maximum age of seven years.</span>
4.  <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">Relocation or non
    earning-day mismatch: this could arise if, for instance, the vessel
    is off-hire for some days during the six-month period; in this case
    there is a mismatch because the earnings period we hedge is actually
    different from the period over which we receive earnings from the
    operation of the vessel.</span>
5.  <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">Liquidity Risk:
    finally, another type of risk that participants face in the market
    is liquidity risk. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.163.2"
    class="koboSpan">If liquidity in the market is low then,
    establishing a hedging position or unwinding a hedge will occur at a
    premium due to the nonavailability of counterparties to trade in the
    market at the specified rate.
    </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.163.3" class="koboSpan">This can
    particularly be the case if one trades on routes where there is
    little trading interest, and also in cases when one trades at the
    far end of the forward curve where liquidity in general tends to be
    low.</span>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Basis risk in the FFA market</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">Basis risk refers to
the mismatch between the specification of the FFA contract and the
exposure of the hedger in the physical market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">Basis is
defined as the difference between the spot and the forward or futures
price for a commodity, at any point in time.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.165.3" class="koboSpan">For instance
the basis for the BPI 4TC contract is the difference between the BPI 4TC
spot Baltic Assessment and the BPI 4TC forward contract for a specific
maturity; therefore, for each specific maturity we can have a different
basis. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.165.4" class="koboSpan">Basis
risk refers to the uncertainty about the level of the basis when a hedge
is lifted and usually arises when the route we want to hedge is not
exactly the same as the route underlying the futures contract or when we
are uncertain as to the exact date on which a vessel is to be fixed, and
we may have to close an FFA position before its expiry.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.165.5" class="koboSpan">In the latter
case,
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_759"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">the effectiveness of the hedge is somewhat reduced,
because there is uncertainty about the level of the basis when the hedge
is
lifted.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0877" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0877"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">Basis risk also
arises when there is a mismatch between the FFA contract and the
exposure in the physical market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">For instance
this could arise when we use supramax FFAs to hedge exposure in the
handysize sector; when using Panamax FFAs – which are based on a 74,000
mt dwt Panamax vessel – to hedge freight income on a 65,000 mt dwt
Panamax vessel; or even using a basket of trip-charter routes, such as
BPI 4TC, to hedge exposure on a specific panamax route, say route BPI
3A. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.168.3" class="koboSpan">In all
these cases market participants could achieve better hedging results if
they were to use the FFA which most closely matches their exposure in
the market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.168.4"
class="koboSpan">However, this may not always be possible: for instance,
when liquidity in the FFA market is low, as is the case for instance
with the handysize FFAs; when the underlying physical route does not
have a corresponding FFA market, as is the case particularly in the
handysize market where the underlying physical base is highly fragmented
and FFAs are available only for six representative trip-charter routes;
finally, when the specification of the vessel we want to hedge is
different from the representative “Baltic” type vessel used in the
calculation of the indices. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.168.5"
class="koboSpan">In all the above cases, there is a mismatch between the
exposure of the hedger in the physical market and the forward contract
that is used for hedging; and, as a result, the hedger will be exposed
to a degree of basis risk.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">In order to ensure
that basis risk is minimised, there are two parameters which need to be
considered. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.169.2"
class="koboSpan">First, hedgers need to select an FFA route that has
strong correlation with their exposure in the physical market and then
use that FFA route to hedge their physical risk.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.169.3" class="koboSpan">The higher the
correlation between the physical market and the FFA contract the lower
the variability of the hedged cash flows and hence the more effective
the hedge. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.169.4"
class="koboSpan">Secondly, in order to implement the hedge effectively,
the hedger also needs to calculate the ratio of the quantity or size of
the FFAs to buy or sell to the size of the exposure in the physical
market – which is known as the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">hedge
ratio</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.171.2" class="koboSpan">In the hedging
example we presented in the previous section, we implicitly used a hedge
ratio of one; in other words, in order to hedge 1,000 mt of physical
cargo we use 1,000 mt of FFAs, which is known as a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">one-to-one</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan">naïve</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan"> hedge ratio
(Ederington</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0878" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0878"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.177.2"
class="koboSpan">However, when the correlation between the FFA and the
physical rate is imperfect, or when the level of the average freight
rate is different between the physical and the FFA market, this ratio
will have to be modified accordingly to take into account these
differences. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.177.3"
class="koboSpan">For instance, consider
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0207"
id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0207"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan"> which presents the Baltic Handysize (BHSI) and
Supramax (BSI) TC averages, as well as their ratio (measured on the
right hand side axis). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.179.2"
class="koboSpan">It is evident that there is a strong degree of
co-movement between the two series, the correlation in levels between
the two series being 98.5%. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.179.3"
class="koboSpan">We can also note that the average BHSI/ BSI ratio is
70%; in other words, on overage, if the BSI increases by 1,000 \$/day,
it is expected that the BHSI will increase by 700 \$/day.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.179.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,
this ratio has been relatively constant during the period of
investigation with a range of 10%, a maximum value of 77% and a minimum
value of 67%.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">Given that liquidity
in the Handymax FFA market is relatively low, participants in the
handysize market can use the much more liquid Supramax FFA market to
hedge their exposure. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.180.2"
class="koboSpan">In doing so they are exposed to basis risk and, since
the average level of freight rates are different in the two markets as
we can see in </span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
7</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0207)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">, the use of an appropriate hedge ratio is required for
this strategy to be effective. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.182.2"
class="koboSpan">From the analysis presented here it seems that an
appropriate hedge ratio is about 0.7 which suggests</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0377" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00397.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7: Baltic Handysize (BHSI) and Supramax (BSI) indices and their ratio" /></span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_760"></span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0207"
id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0207"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 7:</span></span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan"> Baltic Handysize (BHSI) and Supramax (BSI) indices and
their ratio</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan"> Baltic Exchange</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">hedging the monthly
BHSI exposure using 70% of a monthly BSI contract; this is equivalent to
buying 0.70 \* 30 = 21 days of the BSI
contract.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0879" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0879"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">To illustrate how
effective this strategy is, consider the case of Handysize operator in
early September 2006, who wants to secure his freight income for the
last quarter of 2006 (Q4 2006) and the first quarter of 2007 (Q1 07).
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.190.2" class="koboSpan">In order to
hedge his earnings from operating in the charter market for that period
he sells </span><span class="bold"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">0.7</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan"> BSI 5TC FFAs for Q4 06 and Q1 07 at 30,500 and 26,000
\$/day, respectively – which were the market rates at the time; in other
words he sells 30 \* 0.7 = 21 days of BSI 5TC contracts per month for
each month of Q4 06 and Q1 07. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.192.2"
class="koboSpan">This way he locks in a freight income of 21,350 \$/ day
(=30,500 \* 0.7) and 18,200 \$/day (=26,000 \* 0.7) for Q4 06 and Q1 07,
respectively.
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0378" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0378"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents the outcome of this hedge.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.194.2" class="koboSpan">The first two
columns present the settlement rates, calculated as the monthly averages
of the BHI and BHSI spot rates for each maturity month.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">The following
two columns present the Profit or Loss from the FFA position.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.194.4" class="koboSpan">For instance,
the owner sold the BSI 5TC October contract at 30,500 \$/day and the
settlement rate is 29,018 \$/day resulting therefore in a profit of
1,482 \$/ day per contract or a total profit of 31,112 (=1,482 \* 21)
for the entire 21-day position. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.194.5"
class="koboSpan">Therefore for the entire monthly hedge, this translates
into an equivalent value of 1,037 \$/day (=31,112/30) for the Handysize
hedge. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.194.6"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, the total income from the operation in
the physical market plus the income from the FFA position is 22,185 \$/
day (=21,148 + 1,037); since the locked value was 21,350 \$/day, the
deviation of the hedged position from the locked value is 3.84%
(=22,185/21,350 −
1).</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0880" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0880"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan"> If we repeat this process for the remaining
maturities, we can see that overall the deviation from the locked value
remains at low levels and the maximum deviation in any given month is
only 7.07%.</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0378" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_761"></span>[](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0378)

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00398.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0378)

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">Overall, this
strategy seems to have been quite effective which is due to the fact
that the correlation between the two routes is quite strong and the
strength of this relationship does not change over the examination
period; this is also evident by the fact that the ratio between the two
routes remains almost constant at a level of 70% which is perhaps the
most important factor in guaranteeing the success of this
strategy.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">For other routes it
could be the case that correlations are less favourable, in which case
the hedge ratios will need to be modified accordingly and alternative
techniques for their estimation will have to be used, such as the
Minimum Variance Hedge Ratio (MVHR).
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.199.2" class="koboSpan">This is
estimated as the ratio of the covariance between spot and FFA price
changes (returns) over the unconditional variance of FFA price returns,
as follows:</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0379" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00399.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">The MVHR is the hedge
ratio that minimises the risk of a given position in the physical market
(see endnote 20). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.201.2"
class="koboSpan">Applications of this methodology in the freight futures
(BIFFEX) market by Nomikos (see endnote 6) and Kavussanos and Nomikos
(see endnotes 10,11) have shown that hedgers can achieve greater risk
reduction by using the MVHR compared to a hedge ratio of 1.0.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.201.3" class="koboSpan">An extension
of that approach is to estimate time-varying hedge ratios (TVHR).
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.201.4" class="koboSpan">This procedure
involves re-estimating the MVHR at frequent intervals, and re-adjusting
the position in the forward market accordingly, as shown by Kroner and
Sultan</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0881" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0881"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan"> and applied in the freight futures market by
Kavussanos and Nomikos (see endnotes 10, 11) using Multivariate GARCH
models. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.203.2" class="koboSpan">The
motivation behind this process is the fact that the variance and
covariance between spot and FFA
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_762"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan">prices are time-varying and, consequently, the hedge
ratios estimated through equation (1) should also be time-varying.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">Although
theoretically the use of TVHR may improve the hedging results even
further, in practice its implementation in the market presents some
difficulties most notably the fact that it requires market participants
to be able to buy or sell FFAs in smaller quantities than full cargoes.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.204.3" class="koboSpan">Also, since
this strategy requires frequent rebalancing of the FFA position, the
level of transaction costs should be considered which may consequently
reduce the effectiveness of this strategy.</span>

## <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.205.2" class="koboSpan">Options on Freight Rates</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">As we have seen in
the previous section, the use of FFA as a trading and speculative
instrument has been increasing on a constant basis since their
introduction in the early 1990s.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">As the market
grows and becomes more mature, market participants also look at ways of
exploring the usefulness of other derivatives instruments, most notably
options. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.206.3"
class="koboSpan">Although FFAs provide reasonable hedging effectiveness
and enable participants to lock in a given freight rate over a period of
time, they lack the flexibility that would enable their users to
maintain the hedge, if the market moves against them, and to be able to
participate in the market when market conditions are favourable.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.206.4" class="koboSpan">Option
contracts, on the other hand, offer this flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.206.5" class="koboSpan">Freight
options are traded as OTC instruments, in the same fashion as FFAs, and
over the recent years they have become more popular with shipping market
practitioners. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.206.6"
class="koboSpan">Shipping freight options were first introduced in 1990
when trading options on BIFFEX started.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.206.7" class="koboSpan">Like the
BIFFEX contracts itself, however, trading on these options never
picked-up and eventually, they were de-listed in April 2002.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.206.8" class="koboSpan">Therefore, in
this section, we discuss freight options, their use in risk management
as well as the techniques that are used for their pricing.</span>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 A primer on freight options</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">There are two types
of option contracts: call options and put options.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">A
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan">call</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan"> option is a contract, which gives its holder (or
buyer) the right, but not the obligation, to buy an underlying asset
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.210.2" class="koboSpan">freight
rate) from the seller (or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan">writer</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan">) of the call option at a certain price, known as the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">strike
price</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">
or </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan">exercise
price</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">
and, at a certain point in time, known as the expiration date or the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">maturity</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.218.2"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan">put</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan"> option gives its holder the right, but not the
obligation, to sell an underlying asset to the writer of the put option
at a certain strike price and at the expiration date.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.220.2" class="koboSpan">In order to
have such a right, the buyer of the option pays a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">premium</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan"> to the writer of the option.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.222.2" class="koboSpan">The premium is
also known as the option price. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.222.3"
class="koboSpan">Option contracts are also classified according to the
date on which they can be exercised: a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">European</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan"> option can only be exercised at the maturity of the
option; an </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan">American</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan"> option can be exercised at any time during the life of
the option, including the maturity.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.226.2" class="koboSpan">Options give
their holders the flexibility of buying or selling an underlying asset
at a certain pre-specified price during – or at a certain – period.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.226.3" class="koboSpan">This is
important as the holder is under no obligation to settle the contract,
in contrast to futures, forward and swap contracts; whereas the writer
is obliged to transact if the holder decides to do so.</span>

<a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0380" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0380"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents the option premia (in Worldscale points – WS)
for call and put options written on route TD3 of the BDTI (260,000 mt of
Crude oil from Persian Gulf to Japan) from Imarex, across three
different maturities and three different strike</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0380" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_763"></span>[](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0380)

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00400.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0380)

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">prices.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.230.2" class="koboSpan">Consider, for
instance, the September 2005 Call option with a strike price of 80 WS.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.230.3" class="koboSpan">The buyer of
this option has the right, but not the obligation, to buy (settle) the
freight rate for TD3, at the end of September 2005, as the difference
between the strike price and the average of TD3 in September.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.230.4" class="koboSpan">For instance,
if the average TD3 rate in September is 90 WS, the buyer of the option
will exercise the option and receive 10 WS points per contract.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.230.5" class="koboSpan">If, on the
other hand, the market goes down and the average freight rate is, say,
70 WS points, the option holder will let the option expire worthless,
forfeits the premium, and will fix in the spot market at a reduced rate
of 70 WS. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.230.6"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, the holder of a call option essentially has
the same positive payoff as a long FFA contract on TD3 but without the
downside if the spot rate goes below the strike price.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.230.7" class="koboSpan">The payoff of
the call option can, thus, be described mathematically as:</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0381" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00401.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">Where
S</span><sub><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">ave</span></sub><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the average spot freight rate and X is the strike
price. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.234.2" class="koboSpan">These
options which are settled using the average freight rate over the
settlement month, instead of the freight rate on the last day of the
month, are called Average Price or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">Asian</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan"> options.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">In order to buy the
contract, the option buyer has to pay the option premium of 8.9 WS
points per ton of cargo to be hedged, upfront on 23/08/2005; assuming a
flat rate for TD3 of 12.15 \$/mt, the total premium is: \$281,151(=
12.15 \* 8.9/100 \* 260,000). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.237.2"
class="koboSpan">The payoff of the strategy is shown in
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0382" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0382"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 8</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan">, Panel (a). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.239.2"
class="koboSpan">We can see that if the freight</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0382" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00402.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0382)

</div>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0383" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00403.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 8: Long call and put option payoffs" /></span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0208"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
8:</span></span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan"> Long call and put option payoffs</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_764"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan">rate at expiry is less than 80 WS points, the option
expires worthless and the call option buyer loses the premium.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.244.2" class="koboSpan">If the average
freight rate in September is more than 80, then the option is exercised
and for every WS point increase of the freight rates in the market, the
call option buyer makes a corresponding WS point profit in the payoff,
as shown by the 45° degree line on the payoff diagram; the option is
settled in cash and the option buyer thus receives the difference, in
cash, between the exercise price and the settlement price multiplied by
the WS flat rate and the contract
size.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0882" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0882"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan"> Finally, for the option buyer to recover the cost of
buying the option, the underlying market (TD3 rates) must rise above
88.9 WS points, which is the strike price plus the cost of the option
premium, i.e. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.246.2"
class="koboSpan">the break-even rate for the option.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">Consider next the
September 2005 put option with a strike price of 80 WS.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.247.2" class="koboSpan">The buyer of
this option has the right but not the obligation, to “sell” or short TD3
freight rate at the end of September 2005.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.247.3" class="koboSpan">For instance,
if the average TD3 rate in September is 70 WS, the buyer of the put will
exercise the option and receive 10 WS points per contract.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.247.4" class="koboSpan">If, on the
other hand, the freight rate increases to 90 WS points, then the option
holder will let the option expire worthless in the market, as shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
8</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fig0382)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan">, panel (b). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.249.2"
class="koboSpan">The payoff of the put option can thus be described
mathematically as:</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0384" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00404.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.251.1" class="koboSpan">Similarly, we can
construct the payoff profiles for a short call or short put option
contract. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.251.2"
class="koboSpan">There are two parties for every option contract; the
buyer (or long), and the writer (or short).
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.251.3" class="koboSpan">This also
implies that the buyer’s and seller’s payoffs from entering into an
option agreement are reversed. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.251.4"
class="koboSpan">In this case, the payoff of the short call is – min (0,
S</span><sub><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan">ave</span></sub><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.253.1"
class="koboSpan"> – X) and is shown
in</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0385" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0385"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan"> Figure 9</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan">, panel (a). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.255.2"
class="koboSpan">We can see that if the call option is not exercised,
the option seller keeps the option premium which is also the maximum
profit he can make by selling the option.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.255.3" class="koboSpan">However, if
the option is exercised, then the seller of the option is obliged to
transact at the price specified by the contract and this potentially may
lead to very large losses. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.255.4"
class="koboSpan">This, therefore, implies that the position of an option
seller can be very risky due to potentially large and unbounded losses.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.255.5" class="koboSpan">This is also
the reason why traditionally in the OTC market, there tends to be a
larger number of option buyers than sellers.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.255.6" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the very risky profile of a short option position also means that
traders need to somehow hedge their
exposure.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0883" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0883"><span
