id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan"> Finally, </span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
9</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fig0385)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan"> panel (b) presents that payoff profile of a short put
option.</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0385" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00405.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0385)

</div>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0386" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00406.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 9: Short call and put option payoffs" /></span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0209"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
9:</span></span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan"> Short call and put option payoffs</span>

</div>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_765"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.264.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Practicalities of trading options in the freight market</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">Freight options are
traded in a similar way that the underlying FFAs are transacted and with
similar maturities. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.265.2"
class="koboSpan">Buyers and sellers of options agree on a strike price,
and then negotiate a premium. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.265.3"
class="koboSpan">The premium is quoted in \$/day for trip-charter
routes, in \$/tonne for voyage routes and in WS points for tanker
routes. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.265.4" class="koboSpan">Option
contracts are executed between two counterparties through a broker,
either as an OTC contract, or cleared through a clearing house (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.265.5" class="koboSpan">NOS, or
LCH.Clearnet). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.265.6"
class="koboSpan">In addition, freight options on certain routes are also
available for trading through the IMAREX screen.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.1" class="koboSpan">For options traded in
the OTC market, the option premium is payable by the option buyer within
five business days after the confirmation of the trade.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.2" class="koboSpan">At the
settlement of the option, which is the last day of the maturity month,
if the option expires ITM then, the option seller will have to pay the
settlement sum to the option buyer within five business days following
the settlement date. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.3"
class="koboSpan">The broker in an OTC option trade will receive
commission which is agreed in advance with the principals, and is
typically 5% of the option premium.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.4" class="koboSpan">The contract
documentation choices for freight options are similar to those available
for the FFA market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.5"
class="koboSpan">There is a separate FFABA contract for trading freight
options, known as the FFABA 2007 Freight Option Agreement.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.6" class="koboSpan">The contract
is similar to the FFABA 2007 FFA contract, with some additional clauses
which are specific to freight options trading.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.7" class="koboSpan">Options may
also be cleared through a clearing house (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.8" class="koboSpan">LCH.Clearnet
or NOS). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.9" class="koboSpan">For
the option buyer, the maximum loss is the amount of premium paid which,
as discussed earlier, will have to be paid within five business days
after the option agreement. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.10"
class="koboSpan">Since this is the maximum loss for a buyer, he is not
required to maintain a margin and his position will not be marked to
market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.266.11" class="koboSpan">The
option seller, on the other hand, will have to deposit in his clearing
account the amount of premium that he receives and then the short option
position will be marked-to-market accordingly.</span>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Risk management strategies using options</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.268.1" class="koboSpan">Due to their
flexibility and asymmetric risk profile, options are very effective
hedging instruments since they enable hedgers to be covered on the
downside, and participate in the market, on the upside.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.268.2" class="koboSpan">Hedging
positions can be established by entering into long call or put option
contracts. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.268.3" class="koboSpan">For
instance, a shipowner who wants to protect his freight income against a
decline in freight rates will be buying put options; in this case if
freight rates decrease then the put option will expire in-the-money and
will compensate the owner for the decline in freight rates and loss of
earnings in the physical market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.268.4" class="koboSpan">Similarly, a
charterer who wants protection against an increase in the cost of
transportation will be buying call options.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.268.5" class="koboSpan">The profile of
these positions is shown in
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0387" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0387"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 10</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan">, panels (a) and (b), respectively.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">Consider for instance
the shipowner’s hedge. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.271.2"
class="koboSpan">The shipowner is long on freight so his risk is that
freight rates in the market may fall.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.271.3" class="koboSpan">Assuming that
he does not want his freight income for September to fall far below 80
WS, he buys a September TD3 put with a strike price of 80, paying 7.8 WS
premium. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.271.4" class="koboSpan">If he
combines the long freight with the long put position, the payoff will be
similar to a long call as shown in panel (a).
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.271.5" class="koboSpan">This
essentially means that if the freight rate in the market is below the
strike price of 80 WS points in September, the option will be exercised
and, as a result, the owner’s income will remain at 80 WS points less
the premium of 7.8 WS. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.271.6"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, in this case the</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0387" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_766"></span>[](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0387)

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00407.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0387)

</div>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0388" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00408.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 10: Hedging positions using long calls and puts" /></span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0210"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.274.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
10:</span></span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan"> Hedging positions using long calls and puts</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">owner has created a
floor at 72.8 WS. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.276.2"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, if freight rates in the market
increase above the level of the strike price the put option will expire
out-of-the-money and the owner will be able to take advantage of the
higher freight rates in the market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.276.3" class="koboSpan">In any case,
his effective freight rate will be reduced by the level of the option
premium, of 7.8 WS points, that he paid in order to buy the put.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.276.4" class="koboSpan">This strategy
is also called a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan">protective
put</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.279.1" class="koboSpan">Similarly, a
charterer who is short physical freight can hedge his freight exposure
using a long call position. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.279.2"
class="koboSpan">Combination of the charterer’s short freight with the
long call position results in a payoff that looks like a put option as
shown in </span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.280.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
10</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fig0387)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.281.1"
class="koboSpan">, Panel (b). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.281.2"
class="koboSpan">In this case, the maximum freight cost will be the
strike price plus the cost of the option premium; if the option expires
OTM then the charterer will take advantage of the lower rates in the
market. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.281.3" class="koboSpan">This
strategy is also called a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan">covered
call.</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan">
We can see therefore, that in both cases the long call or put positions
are very similar to an insurance policy.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.283.2" class="koboSpan">The hedger
pays the insurance premium upfront; if the option expires ITM, the
insurance policy will indemnify the hedger.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.283.3" class="koboSpan">If, on the
other hand, the market moves in favour of the hedger the option is not
exercised and expires worthless.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.283.4" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
maximum loss is limited to the insurance premium; in this case, the
hedger can take advantage of the more favourable conditions in the spot
market.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">In the previous
examples we considered the long call and long put positions.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.284.2" class="koboSpan">It is also
interesting to examine the positions that the sellers of these options
would have. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.284.3"
class="koboSpan">These are shown in
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0389" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0389"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.285.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 11</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.286.2"
class="koboSpan">Consider for instance Panel (a); an individual who
sells a call option will be exposed to unbounded losses if the
underlying market rises. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.286.3"
class="koboSpan">He therefore, has to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan">cover </span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.288.1"
class="koboSpan">this potentially risky position by owning the
underlying asset; hence the name
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan">writing covered
call.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0884" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0884"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.290.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the case of freight, this essentially means that
the seller of the call should have a long position in the underlying
freight route, either by holding tonnage or by having a long FFA, to
cover the potential exercise of the option.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.291.2" class="koboSpan">“Covered”
therefore means that the call seller owns the underlying asset which he
can deliver, if the call is exercised, without incurring any further
cost – apart from an opportunity cost in delivering it for less than the
market price. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.291.3"
class="koboSpan">Similarly, a short put position can be protected using
a short freight position; i.e. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.291.4"
class="koboSpan">by selling FFA; this strategy is known as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">writing protective
put</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.294.1" class="koboSpan">The above strategies
can also be used to enhance the return of a given position.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.294.2" class="koboSpan">Generally,
call options sellers would prefer to sell OTM calls.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.294.3" class="koboSpan">A call being
OTM means</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0389" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_767"></span>[](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0389)

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00409.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0389)

</div>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0390" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00410.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 11: Writing covered and protective positions" /></span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0211"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
11:</span></span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan"> Writing covered and protective positions</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">that the price of the
underlying asset must rise before the call is exercised against the
seller; thus, the seller of an OTM call receives the premium, which is
his maximum profit, along with some potential for profit from the
underlying. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.299.2"
class="koboSpan">For instance, consider again the case presented in
</span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.300.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
11</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_fig0389)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan">, Panel (a). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.301.2"
class="koboSpan">Assume that a trader has bought an FFA contract at say,
80 WS points. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.301.3"
class="koboSpan">He also has a subjective, maximum return that he would
like to make on this position; this would depend on his risk-return
profile and on his expected return on the market and, of course, is
subjective and varies from trader to trader.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.301.4" class="koboSpan">In this
example, we assume that the trader is happy to sell the FFA at say 100
WS points and thus realise a “maximum” desired gain of 20 WS points.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.301.5" class="koboSpan">He can then
sell an OTM call option with a strike price of 100 WS points.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.301.6" class="koboSpan">In doing so he
receives the option premium which enhances the return on his investment.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.301.7" class="koboSpan">If the market
rises above 100 WS points, then the call option will be exercised and
his profit will be capped to 20 WS points plus the option premium he
received upfront. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.301.8"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, in following this strategy, the investor has
“enhanced” the yield of his investment; however, it should be noted that
what is being enhanced is not the objective risk return characteristics
but, instead, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">subjective
</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan">expected returns of the investor.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.303.2" class="koboSpan">These
strategies are also called
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">yield
enhancement</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan">call
overwriting</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategies and are frequently used by investors,
particularly in stagnant markets, to enhance the yield on their
investment. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.307.2"
class="koboSpan">(see also Hull
</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0885" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0885"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Neftci</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0886" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0886"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

#### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.1 Hedging example using options</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">Consider the
following hedging example illustrating the use of Options on FFAs.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.313.2" class="koboSpan">It is late
August 2005 and an oil trading company has sold a VLCC cargo of crude
oil (2 million barrels or approximately 260,000mt) to receivers in the
Far East, for shipment in November.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.313.3" class="koboSpan">Shipment will
take place in late November and under the sale agreement, the seller of
the cargo will be responsible for paying the transportation costs; the
cargo will be shipped from Persian Gulf to the Far East.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.313.4" class="koboSpan">The trading
house is therefore worried over its exposure to freight risk since an
appreciation in freight rates over the coming months will increase the
transportation costs.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">In an effort to
control the freight rate costs, the charterer considers the use of
freight derivatives. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.314.2"
class="koboSpan">He could use FFA to “lock” in a certain freight cost,
however, he is concerned that such an approach is inflexible and does
not enable him to take advantage of a potential fall in freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.314.3" class="koboSpan">For that he
decides to buy an October 2005 call option for route TD3 of the BDTI
(260,000 tons crude from the Gulf to Japan); the choice of
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_768"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan">the October contract is due to the fact that the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.316.1"
class="koboSpan">laycan</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.317.1"
class="koboSpan"> for the route is 30–40 days ahead of the index, so the
settlement in October reflects cargo liftings at the end of November.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.317.2" class="koboSpan">His broker
advises him that there is a counterparty willing to “write” him an
October 2005 call option with a strike price of 90 WS at a premium of
7.8 WS points. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.317.3"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, the total premium that the trader will pay
to the seller of the call is 7.8/100 \* 260,000 \* 12.15 = \$ 246,402.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.317.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the owner will have to pay a brokers commission which is 5% of the total
option premium paid, (i.e. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.317.5"
class="koboSpan">\$12,320).</span>

<a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0391" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0391"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.318.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.319.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents the outcome of this hedge under two different
scenarios. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.319.2" class="koboSpan">In
the first case, the average freight rate in October is below the strike
price; in this case, the option expires OTM and is not exercised so the
trader takes advantage of the lower freight rates in the market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.319.3" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, if the freight market increases to say, 110 WS points, the option
expires ITM and the total freight cost is then capped to 90 WS points
plus the cost of the option premium (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.319.4" class="koboSpan">97.8 WS points
or a total of \$3,089,502) irrespective of how far above the strike
price, the level of freight rates in the market is.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.320.1" class="koboSpan">Therefore, options
are a flexible hedging instrument since they enable the charterer to
lock in a specific rate when freight rates increase, and to fix his
vessels at the prevailing spot rate when freight rates decrease.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.320.2" class="koboSpan">More
specifically, if the spot rate is greater than the strike price at the
expiration of the call option, then the option is exercised</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0391" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00411.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0391)

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_769"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
class="koboSpan">and, as a result, the effective freight rate for the
company is the strike price plus the option premium.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.322.2" class="koboSpan">Similarly, if
the spot rate is lower than the strike price, the option expires
worthless, and the effective freight rate is the current spot rate in
the market plus the option premium.</span>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.323.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 Hedging using collar</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.324.1" class="koboSpan">Although options
provide an effective form of hedging, the fact that the hedger has to
pay the option premium upfront may sometimes be a factor that decides
against the use of the options as a hedging tool.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.324.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
in the previous example, the charterer would have to pay an upfront
premium of \$246,402. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.324.3"
class="koboSpan">One way of reducing this cost would be for the
charterer to “sacrifice” some of his upside potential when the market
goes down in return for protection against possible freight rate up
turns. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.324.4" class="koboSpan">That
would, therefore, involve the charterer selling an OTM put option with a
low strike price, say at 70 WS, on the same underlying and with the same
maturity as the call option. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.324.5"
class="koboSpan">Selling a put provides income which the charterer can
use to offset the cost of the call.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.324.6" class="koboSpan">This strategy
is known as a collar strategy. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.324.7"
class="koboSpan">The most popular type of a collar is a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan">zero cost
collar,</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.326.1" class="koboSpan">
where the cost of the call is offset fully by the premium received from
the short put so that the overall cost of the hedge is zero.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.326.2" class="koboSpan">By following
this strategy, the charterer has a maximum freight cost of 90 WS points.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.326.3" class="koboSpan">If the market
falls below the strike price of the put, then the put will be exercised
against him and his total cost will be “floored” to the put strike price
of 70 WS points. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.326.4"
class="koboSpan">Thus, the charterer has financed the downside insurance
protection provided by the long call, by selling part of the upside
potential of the freight market, with a short put.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.326.5" class="koboSpan">Similarly, an
owner could construct a collar by buying a put and selling an OTM, high
strike price
call.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0887" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0887"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.327.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">4.5 Constructing a zero-cost collar in the dry-bulk market</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.329.1" class="koboSpan">In mid-June 2007, a
Panamax owner is concerned about the volatility in the freight market
and wants to secure his freight income for 2008.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.329.2" class="koboSpan">There are a
number of hedging choices available: first, the shipowner could sell a
Calendar 2008 FFA contract for the BPI 4TC average, currently quoted at
36,500 \$/day; however, he is uncertain about the direction of the
market and, hence, does not want to lock in a forward rate, in case the
market rises further than that. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.329.3"
class="koboSpan">The second option would be to buy one Calendar 08 BPI
4TC put option. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.329.4"
class="koboSpan">Currently there is a quote for a Cal-08 put with a
strike price of 33,500 \$/day for a premium of 3,000 \$/day.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.329.5" class="koboSpan">This is
essentially a strip of 12 monthly options for each of the 12 months in
2008. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.329.6" class="koboSpan">Each
option will be settled separately at the end of each month and the
settlement rate will be calculated as the average of the month for BPI
4TC; the total payoff for each month will therefore be:
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan">max(33,500
S</span><sub><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
class="koboSpan">ave</span></sub><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.332.1"
class="koboSpan">, 0)\*number of days in the
month</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">,
where </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.334.1"
class="koboSpan">S</span><sub><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.335.1"
class="koboSpan">ave</span></sub></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the average freight rate over the settlement month.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.336.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
if the average freight rate in January is 30,000 \$/day the payoff of
the option would be \$108,500 (= 3,500 \$/day \* 31).
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.336.3" class="koboSpan">Although such
a hedge would effectively guarantee the owner a minimum income of 33,500
\$/day – minus the option premium – for 2008, he is also conscious of
the fact that this is a rather expensive hedge since, in order to buy
the options, he would have to pay an up-front premium of \$1,098,000 (=
3,000\$/day \* 366 days). </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.336.4"
class="koboSpan">The third hedging option would</span>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0392" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_770"></span>[](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0392)

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.337.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00412.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0392)

</div>

<div id="Ch026.xhtml_fig0393" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00413.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 12: Owner’s zero cost collar" /></span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_cap_lbl0212"><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.339.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
12:</span></span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.340.1"
class="koboSpan"> Owner’s zero cost collar</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.341.1" class="koboSpan">thus be for the owner
to “sacrifice” some of his upside potential by selling an OTM call
option at a higher strike price.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.341.2" class="koboSpan">The broker has
identified a counterparty for this trade, who is willing to sell to the
owner the Cal-08 4TC put with 33,500 \$/day strike, and buy from the
owner the Cal-08 4TC call at a strike of 41,000 \$/day.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.341.3" class="koboSpan">Since the
premia from the long put and short call positions exactly match, this
strategy would effectively be a zero cost strategy.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.342.1" class="koboSpan">The outcome from this
strategy is shown in
</span><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fig0392" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fig0392"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 12</span></a><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.344.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.344.2"
class="koboSpan">Panel (a) presents the payoff from the combined options
and physical positions for any given maturity and panel (b) shows the
owner’s possible net freight income from the collar hedge; we can see
therefore, that the income is guaranteed to be between 33,500 and 41,000
\$/day for every month of 2008. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.344.3"
class="koboSpan">This strategy guarantees that the shipowner’s income
will not fall below \$33,500 \$/day but, at the same time, the income is
also capped at 41,000 \$/day. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.344.4"
class="koboSpan">If, on the other hand, the owner had opted for the FFA
hedge, then his income would have been 36,500 \$/day.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.344.5" class="koboSpan">Thus, the
collar strategy provides more flexibility and also allows the owner to
take advantage of any potential upside in the market whilst, at the same
time, he is protected on the downside.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.344.6" class="koboSpan">We can also
note that there is a link between the collar strategy and the FFA hedge.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.344.7" class="koboSpan">In fact, if
the strike prices for the call and the put are identical then the collar
hedge is identical to an FFA hedge and the strikes in that case should
be equal to the FFA rate; this argument follows directly from the
put-call parity which links the prices of calls and puts that are
written on the same asset and have the same maturity.</span>

### <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">4.6 Pricing freight options</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">As discussed, freight
options are becoming increasingly popular with practitioners and are
used both for risk management and speculation purposes.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.346.2" class="koboSpan">From the point
of view of traders in the market and particularly for option sellers, an
important consideration is how to determine the fair option premium to
charge when selling a freight option.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.346.3" class="koboSpan">This should
reflect, among other things, the risks option sellers face in the market
and should provide a fair level of compensation for those risks.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.346.4" class="koboSpan">The premium
should be fair
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_771"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan">because if it is too high then the option will be
overpriced; on the other hand, if the premium is too low then the
premium will not provide an adequate level of compensation for the risks
the seller is facing.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">Pricing freight
options, presents a number of challenges for researchers.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.348.2" class="koboSpan">First, the
underlying asset of the option, which is the freight rate produced by
the Baltic Exchange, is not a tradable asset since freight rates reflect
the cost of providing the service of seaborne transportation which, by
its own nature, cannot be stored or carried forward in time.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.348.3" class="koboSpan">As a result,
arbitrage between the underlying spot freight market and options across
time and space is limited. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.348.4"
class="koboSpan">Although the spot Baltic rates are not tradable assets,
the FFAs on these routes are regularly traded contracts which can be
used in a replicating strategy, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.348.5" class="koboSpan">when delta
hedging a short option position.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.348.6" class="koboSpan">Therefore the
information contained in the FFA rates should be used when pricing
derivatives on freight and, hence, the pricing model used for freight
options should be based on the Black 76 model for pricing options on
futures.</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0888" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0888"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.349.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.350.1" class="koboSpan">Second, freight
options are settled as Average Price Asian Options.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.350.2" class="koboSpan">Asian options
are options whose final payoff is based on the average level of the
underlying asset price over a period of time.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.350.3" class="koboSpan">As is the case
with the FFAs, the calculation of an average settlement rate is used in
order to ensure that settlement rates are not susceptible to large moves
due to very high volatility or market manipulation on any specific
trading day. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.350.4"
class="koboSpan">For instance, an attempt to manipulate the underlying
price, just before settlement, will have little impact on the settlement
price if this is calculated as the average of the month and consists of
21 individual data points. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.350.5"
class="koboSpan">This also explains why Asian options are quite popular
in either thinly traded markets, or in markets where there is very high
volatility, such as the market for freight.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.350.6" class="koboSpan">In addition,
since the volatility of the average price is less than the volatility of
the underlying, the premium for an Asian option will generally be lower
than the premium for an otherwise identical European option.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.351.1" class="koboSpan">Pricing Asian options
is more complicated than pricing “plain vanilla” European options.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.351.2" class="koboSpan">The main
reason for this is that, when the asset is assumed to be lognormally
distributed as is the assumption in the Black 76 (see endnote 30) option
pricing model, the arithmetic average of a set of lognormal
distributions does not have analytically tractable properties.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.351.3" class="koboSpan">In this case,
the distribution is approximately lognormal and this leads to a number
of analytical approximations for the valuation of these options such as
the Turnbull and
Wakeman,</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0889" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0889"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.352.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan">
Levy</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0890" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0890"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.354.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.355.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Haug
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0891" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0891"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Curran</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0892" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0892"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.359.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan"> approximations, as well as the valuation model of
Koekebakker
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><sup><a href="#Ch026.xhtml_fn0893" id="Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0893"><span
id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.363.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan"> for the valuation of average price freight options;
Alizadeh and Nomikos (see endnote 15) find that the option premia
generated from these models are very similar and approximate well the
option premia generated using Monte Carlo simulation.</span>

## <span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.365.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.365.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.366.1" class="koboSpan">The role of risk
management in shipping operations has become increasingly important in
recent years. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.366.2"
class="koboSpan">This is because the shipping industry has become an
integral part of the world economy in connecting sources of supply and
demand for raw materials and manufactured goods around the globe.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.366.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
fluctuations and uncertainty in the global economy, whether short term
or long term, are expected to affect the profitability and hence the
long-term survival of shipowners and ship operators.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.366.4" class="koboSpan">The aim of
this chapter was to review and discuss the risk management tools and
instruments available to market practitioners to control freight rate
risk.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_772"></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan">In this chapter, we discussed the practicalities of
trading FFA as well as how FFA can be used to risk manage a variety of
exposures in the underlying freight market.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.367.2" class="koboSpan">We also
analysed the issues that hedgers need to be aware of in setting-up their
hedging strategies. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.367.3"
class="koboSpan">Since their introduction in the early 1990s trading
volume in the FFA market has increased constantly on a year by year
basis. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.367.4" class="koboSpan">The
continuous growth in the market and the influx of new traders, such as
investment banks, trading houses, hedge funds etc., also led to the
development of more sophisticated trading strategies using FFA – such as
spread and arbitrage trades – as well as to the increasing use of
freight options for hedging and speculative purposes.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.368.1" class="koboSpan">The major advantage
of freight options is that they enable market participants to be hedged
if the market moves against them, but also to take advantage of
favourable conditions if the market moves in their favour.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.368.2" class="koboSpan">Freight
options are becoming more and more popular with market practitioners and
are increasingly used for both risk management and speculation purposes.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.368.3" class="koboSpan">In this
chapter we considered the profit patterns from buying or selling call
and put options, the practicalities of trading freight options as well
as risk management applications.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.368.4" class="koboSpan">Perhaps the
major issue in the freight options market today is the issue of
determining the fair premium to pay for a freight options and we briefly
discussed the different approaches that are currently used in the
market.</span>

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.424.1"
class="koboSpan">13.</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0871)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.425.1"
class="koboSpan"> In general, for FFA on the average of the Trip-Charter
(TC) routes of the BCI, BPI, BHSI and BSI – which represent the majority
of the trades – the settlement rate is calculated as the average of the
month; on the other hand, the settlement rate for FFAs on individual
routes from the BCI or BPI is calculated as the average of the route
over the last seven trading days of a month.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.425.2" class="koboSpan">This is
because FFAs on individual routes are typically used to hedge specific
voyages so averaging over a shorter period of time and, therefore,
having better correlation with the underlying physical route during
settlement, is preferred. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.425.3"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, market participants use basket
routes, such as the average of the four TC routes of BCI or BPI, to
hedge their average monthly earnings; in this case, calculating the
settlement rate as the monthly average is preferred, since it provides a
better fit to the requirements of the traders in the physical market and
more closely matches the monthly earnings of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.425.4" class="koboSpan">Finally,
tanker FFAs are also settled as the average of the month.</span>

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.426.1"
class="koboSpan">14.</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0872)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.427.1"
class="koboSpan"> IMAREX operates as an exchange, in the sense that it
provides a regulated market place to trade standardised contracts,
principals can trade in the market either directly or through an IMAREX
broker, and all trades are guaranteed through a clearing house.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.427.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
market is not open to brokers outside IMAREX.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.427.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore, FFA
brokers cannot use the IMAREX system to post prices or to facilitate
trades for their clients. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.427.4"
class="koboSpan">In that sense therefore, IMAREX operates a “hybrid” or
“almost-exchange” market system since the market is not open to all
market participants, in particular non-IMAREX based competitive FFA
brokers.</span>

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.428.1"
class="koboSpan">15.</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0873)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.429.1"
class="koboSpan"> Alizadeh A. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.429.2"
class="koboSpan">and Nomikos, N.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.429.3" class="koboSpan">(2009):
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.430.1"
class="koboSpan">Shipping Derivatives and Risk Management
</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.431.1"
class="koboSpan">(London, Palgrave Macmillan).</span>

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.432.1"
class="koboSpan">16.</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0874)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.433.1"
class="koboSpan"> In general there are two dates which reflect the
delivery period to the charterer; these are known as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.434.1"
class="koboSpan">laycan</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.435.1"
class="koboSpan"> which is sort for laydays cancelling.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.435.2" class="koboSpan">For instance
in the example presented here the laycan period could be laydays 13
January cancelling 16 January. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.435.3"
class="koboSpan">This means that the charterer is not obliged to accept
delivery of the vessel until after the first of these dates (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.435.4" class="koboSpan">13 January)
and has the option to cancel the charter agreement altogether if the
vessel arrives after the end of the second of the dates.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.435.5" class="koboSpan">All the Baltic
Panamax indices have a laycan period of 15–20 days ahead of the index
which effectively means that today’s spot rate reflects a delivery
period which is at least 15 days forward.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.435.6" class="koboSpan">For hedging
purposes, this means that if one wants to hedge a voyage that will
commence, say, in the middle of September, the appropriate contract
maturity to use for hedging is that of August.</span>

<span id="Ch026.xhtml_page_774"></span>[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.436.1"
class="koboSpan">17.</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0875)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.437.1"
class="koboSpan"> These rates are the BPI 4TC FFA assessment rates,
reported by the Baltic Exchange, at the time the hedge is lifted.</span>

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.438.1"
class="koboSpan">18.</span>](#Ch026.xhtml_bck_fn0876)<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.439.1"
class="koboSpan"> In the example presented here we ignore broker’s
commission on both the physical and FFA markets.</span>

risk</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.443.1" class="koboSpan"> to

</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.443.2" class="koboSpan">and Wolyniec,

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.444.1"

Management</span></span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.445.1"
class="koboSpan"> (New Jersey, Wiley Finance).
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.445.2" class="koboSpan">It should be
noted that when the specification of the FFA contract matches exactly
the underlying position and an FFA position is carried until the expiry
of the contract then there is no basis risk since – due to the
convergence of spot and forward prices – the basis of the contract at
maturity will be equal to zero.</span>

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.448.1"

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.450.1"

the fact that most of the BSI contracts are traded for a full calendar
month and liquidity for buying part of the month is limited.
</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.451.2" class="koboSpan">However, a
handysize operator can still use this strategy to hedge, for instance

contracts, which roughly corresponds to a 70% ratio.</span>

[<span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.452.1"

rounding. </span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.453.2" class="koboSpan">In

</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.453.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore,

</span><span id="Ch026.xhtml_kobo.453.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,

class="koboSpan">Finally, for simplicity we also assume that each month

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_776"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_777"></span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 27</span>\
<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Revisiting Credit Risk, Analysis and Policy in Bank Shipping Finance</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0589)
=========================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Costas</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Th.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Grammenos</span></span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0894" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0894"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">There are three main
groups of sources of shipping finance: Equity finance, which includes
retained earnings and equity offerings, either public or
private;</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0896" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0896"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan"> mezzanine finance, which encompasses hybrids, such as
warrants and convertibles, subordinated debt and preference
shares;</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0897" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0897"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan"> and debt finance, which contains bank loans, export
finance, tax leases, private placements (traditional and 144A) and
public debt
issues.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0898" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0898"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter
concentrates on bank finance – which is still the largest source of
capital in the shipping industry – with particular reference to
commercial bank loans. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.14.2"
class="koboSpan">Bank shipping loans are granted to borrowers by a
number of different financial institutions, such as: export–import
banks; development banks; banks specialising in shipping; and commercial
banks. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.14.3" class="koboSpan">These
institutions deal primarily with the major risk – the credit risk (or
default risk) – which is the uncertainty over the repayment of the
granted loan and payment of its interest, in full, on the promised
date.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping departments
of a sizeable number of commercial banks, or banks specialising in
shipping, have seen their profitability fluctuate substantially over the
years. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.15.2"
class="koboSpan">Increased profits strengthened the presence of
commercial banks committed to shipping, and attracted newcomers.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.15.3" class="koboSpan">The early
1970s, the late 1980s, part of the 1990s and the second half of the
current decade are good examples of high bank shipping profitability
stemming from booming shipping markets.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.15.4" class="koboSpan">However, heavy
losses over periods of shipping recession or depression have also been
realised and have led a number of banks to abandon the finance of
shipping. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.15.5" class="koboSpan">Here,
the mid-1980s is a representative example to abandon ship
financing.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0899" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0899"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">Loan losses may
significantly reduce the return on equity (ROE) of a bank and,
therefore, destroy value for the bank, or loan profits may increase the
ROE and, consequently, create value for the bank.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">The rest of this
chapter is organised as follows. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.18.2"
class="koboSpan">Section 2 focuses on credit risk, while Section 3
discusses key issues of credit risk analysis.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.18.3" class="koboSpan">Section 4 deals
with collateral securities, including mortgage, assignment of revenue,
assignment of insurance
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_778"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">and guarantees. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">Covenants are covered in Section 5, while Section 6
presents a further discussion of credit analysis and issues, such as
pricing of the loan, syndication and capital adequacy rules.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.19.3" class="koboSpan">The focus of
Section 7 is loan monitoring; while Section 8 covers shipping credit
policy. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.19.4" class="koboSpan">In
Section 9, the conclusions are presented.</span>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">Credit Risk</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">The lending function
of the bank deals with credit risk, and has four
parts:</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0900" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0900"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan"> the first is the origination of the loan which
includes initiation of the loan, analysis, documentation, due diligence
and approval; the second is the funding, during which external and/or
internal funds are used for the draw-down of the loan; the third is the
follow-up part when principal and interest rate payments are made; and
the fourth is the monitoring part, which is carried out in parallel with
the “follow up” of the loan, through collecting, processing, and
analysing data and information regarding the borrower.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">The objective
of the lending function is to create value for the bank, through
granting sound loans; and sound loans are the ones which are paid
off.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">The main risk in bank
shipping finance is the credit – or default –
risk.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0901" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0901"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan"> This is primarily due to the volatility of the
vessel’s income, which is the main source of the loan repayment; and the
consequent fluctuations in the vessel’s market value which is, in most
cases, the main security for the loan.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">The financial
institutions provide loans of varying forms to shipping companies, the
core being the term loan under which the bank lends a certain amount to
the shipping company for vessel acquisition over a specific period
(above one year), to be repaid normally from the income generated by the
vessel(s) to be financed and, possibly, by its/their residual value.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">The loan is
tailor-made to suit the needs of the borrower and the lender, in the
particular
circumstances.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0902" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0902"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan"> Thus, equal or unequal instalments can be arranged and
a moratorium for one or two years can be granted, whereby only interest
payments are made for a certain period of time, to allow for poor
shipping market conditions. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.29.2"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, a balloon payment can be approved for a
loan – that is to say, a large amount of the loan, which reflects the
residual value of the vessel (between 25 to 30% of the vessel’s current
market value), should be paid with the last instalment.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.29.3" class="koboSpan">In reality, the
balloon payment is usually refinanced for one year or longer – provided
the borrower has met his commitment and depending upon the amount of the
balloon, the value of the vessel and the freight income of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.29.4" class="koboSpan">In this way,
the loan repayment period can be stretched further without the bank
committing itself to doing so from the beginning, because the repayment
period of the loan would be longer and this would increase further the
uncertainty.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">The interest rate
normally fluctuates and is based on LIBOR (London Interbank Offered
Rate), plus a margin (spread), which represents a significant part of
the gross income of the bank from the loan.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">While the
margin is fixed in advance, the LIBOR is renewed periodically, such as
every three or six months, in the eurodollar interbank market, should
the currency denomination be in
dollars.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0903" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0903"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"> Such fluctuating interest rates, if un-hedged, prevent
the shipping company and the bank from calculating, with certainty, the
future interest payments. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.32.2"
class="koboSpan">In comparison with a fixed interest rate for the entire
loan repayment period – a rather infrequent feature in bank shipping
loans nowadays – the fluctuating interest rate allows the bank to pass
on the interest rate risk to the borrower, whose cost rises with
increasing LIBOR or decreases with falling
LIBOR.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0904" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0904"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_779"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">During the parts of the lending function the two
cooperating parties, the bank and the borrower, may have different goals
and division of labour. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.34.2"
class="koboSpan">The bank wants its loan to be paid off and increase its
profitability. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.34.3"
class="koboSpan">The borrower wants to make its project a success.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.34.4" class="koboSpan">For this
relationship to be sound, the accuracy and quality of risk analysis of
the project is critical. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.34.5"
class="koboSpan">The agency
theory</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0905" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0905"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan"> deals with the two problems that may appear between
the banker (as a principal) and the borrower (as its agent) in a
relationship that the principal delegates work to the agent.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.36.2" class="koboSpan">The problems
emerge due to asymmetry of information which may exist between the
banker and the borrower regarding the project to be financed or already
financed. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.36.3"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, the borrower (as an insider) may have more
accurate information than the banker in areas such as the financial
accounts and the condition of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.36.4" class="koboSpan">These problems
are adverse selection and moral hazard.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.36.5" class="koboSpan">Adverse
selection refers to uncertainty regarding the viability of the project;
while moral hazard refers to the reliability of the borrower.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">A characteristic
example of adverse selection is the shipping loan portfolio of a
relatively small financial institution, at the end of the 1970s, which
consisted almost exclusively of loans extended for the purchases of
over-aged vessels, while charging high interest rates.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.37.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
many of the owners were small with only two or three vessels.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.37.3" class="koboSpan">When the
shipping market conditions deteriorated, from 1982 onwards, the freight
income decreased dramatically and was not enough to cover the vessels’
running expenses, let alone the loan repayment.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.37.4" class="koboSpan">At the same
time, the vessel market values had declined to their scrap value, while
the vessels had been purchased, at the end of the 1970s, at quite high
prices. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.37.5" class="koboSpan">This
particular institution suffered great financial losses from its shipping
loans.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">Regarding moral
hazard: Examples include when a borrower deceives the banker, or change
his/her behaviour; false items in the running expenses of vessels; false
statements regarding overall net worth; liquidity of the shipping group;
or transfer of income from mortgaged vessels to other companies; this
may be permissible in some circumstances, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.38.2" class="koboSpan">where a
corporate guarantee is provided.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">The financial
institutions, in order to increase their value and also deal effectively
with the agency problems, incur certain costs – the agency costs.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">These are
related to – among others – the collection, processing and analysis of
data for the loans granted and to be granted.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.39.3" class="koboSpan">However, one
has to keep in mind the very special role of the financial institutions,
as intermediaries between savers and users of funds.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.39.4" class="koboSpan">In this
capacity, and due to the limited ability of the savers to obtain and
analyse information regarding initial and continuing creditworthiness of
the end fund users (borrowers), the financial institutions undertake
this role on their behalf. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.39.5"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, the financial institutions have a greater
incentive to collect and process this information, due to the large
number of savers who appoint them as their “delegated
monitors”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0906" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0906"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan"> In so doing, the financial institutions are also
protecting the wealth of their shareholders, who are expecting to see it
increase. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.41.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, the lending function should guard the
interests of depositors and shareholders, and increase the value of the
bank.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">The question that
arises now, is, how does a the shipping banker dealing with the credit
risk?</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0907" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0907"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">There is an array of
tools at the banker’s disposal, to minimise credit risk: credit risk
analysis; collateral securities; covenants in the loan agreement and the
mortgage; monitoring of the granted loans; and shipping credit policy.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.44.2" class="koboSpan">These issues
will be discussed in the following sections.</span>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_780"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">Credit Risk Analysis</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">Grammenos</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0908" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0908"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0909" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0909"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan"> introduced the five “Cs” of Credit in Bank Shipping
Finance as a sound credit risk analysis method of assessing the
probability of the repayment of the loan proposals for acquisition of
secondhand vessels and newbuildings, based on five key words that start
with “C”: Character, Capacity, Capital, Conditions, Collateral.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.50.2" class="koboSpan">“Company” was
added at a later date for reasons of clearer presentation.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">This credit
analysis method has been adopted by a large number of financial
institutions. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.50.4"
class="koboSpan">Bearing in mind that the interest margin and fees are
fixed and, therefore, the upside return of the loan is fixed and the
downside risk is substantial, since the loan capital and interest may
not be paid as promised, the credit risk analysis of the loan has to
assess the probability of their payments in full.
</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fig0394" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0394"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan"> summarises the main elements of the credit risk
analysis that a loan officer has to carry out.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Character/capacity</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">The first column of
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0394)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan"> concentrates on the head of the shipping company and
the management team. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.56.2"
class="koboSpan">Their expertise accumulated over years, their
resourcefulness during the lower parts of the shipping cycle, and their
integrity, are areas of investigation.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.56.3" class="koboSpan">The head of the
shipping company and his/her team will specify the mission and goals of
the company and the strategic plan for their materialisation.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.56.4" class="koboSpan">They are
responsible for designing and applying the strategies to achieve the
goals.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">The head and team are
assessed for their managerial quality as a team and their performance
versus plan on strategies over a long period, for instance, over the
last two or three cycles or last
generation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0910" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0910"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan"> In particular, investment and finance, chartering,
insurance, technical, cost management, risk management, creditors, and
human resources strategies, are looked at for their overall return to
the equity; and whether they managed to decrease costs, increase
revenues and profits and create efficiencies.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">The head’s and
team’s “modus operandi”, in comparison with their peers in the same
sector, may be useful.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Capital</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">The second column
refers to Capital. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.61.2"
class="koboSpan">When a shipowner has a relatively large shareholding
stake it shows confidence in the company; while the financial structure
shows the way the company has been financed.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.61.3" class="koboSpan">Shipping is a
capital-intensive industry, requiring substantial funds primarily, for
contracting placement of newbuilding orders; and, secondarily, the
purchase of secondhand vessels. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.61.4"
class="koboSpan">All elements in this column are important, but the
gearing ratio, the hull (market value) to debt ratio, the net worth and
the cash flow, are of paramount importance.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.61.5" class="koboSpan">A high gearing
ratio (debt to total assets) is a double-edged sword: in a flourishing
shipping market it may cause the profits and return to equity to soar,
in a declining market it may endanger the existence of the company
itself.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0911" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0911"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan"> Retained cash flow over net debt is calculated after
dividend payments and includes the capital component of operating
expenses. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.63.2" class="koboSpan">The
higher this measure, the more indicative it is of the ability of the
business to generate cash, the availability of cash debt payments or its
ability to undertake capital investments.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">Interest
coverage shows how many times operating profit or Earnings before
Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, Amortisation (EBITDA) covers the
interest.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0912" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0912"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan"> Hull-to-debt
ratio</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0913" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0913"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan"> is important, not only in a declining or rising
shipping market, but also when the time charter, or contract of
affreightment ends. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.67.2"
class="koboSpan">It shows the relationship between the loan and market
value of the vessel. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.67.3"
class="koboSpan">(See further on this ratio in Section 4.1.)</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0394" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_781"></span>[](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0394)

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00414.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0394)

</div>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0395" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_782"></span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00415.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_783"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">As long as the bank knows that the real economic net
worth – the difference between the market value of assets and the market
value of liabilities, as opposed to book value – is positive, then it
also knows that the loan is relatively secure.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.70.2" class="koboSpan">Cash flow is
the main source for the loan repayment, while the cash cushion – the
existence of accumulated cash from operating profits and/or sale of
vessel(s) – is important to cover temporarily interest payments and
capital instalments, should the freight market
decline.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0914" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0914"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan"> In a falling shipping market, other sources of finance
– e.g. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.72.2" class="koboSpan">capital
markets – and strong banking relationships may be necessary, hence, an
analysis of the different ways that a shipping company is financing its
projects and its relationships with different banks is essential.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.72.3" class="koboSpan">Finally, widely
accepted accounting methods such as the Generally Accepted Accounting
Principles (GAAP) give the comfort of an international accounting
measure, but are not always used by shipping companies; while
consolidated audited accounts, despite the fact that they give an
overall view of a shipping group, are not always provided by the
shipping companies.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Company</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">The third column
refers initially to the ownership structure of the company.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.74.2" class="koboSpan">Very often
one-vessel
companies</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0915" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0915"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan"> registered in an open registry country, such as
Panama, Liberia, Cyprus, Malta, are established and their vessels may be
managed by a management company controlled by the shipowner/manager, or
owned by a holding company. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.76.2"
class="koboSpan">In the first case, the banker deals with an entity
where there is no – or limited – recourse to the management company and
the loan is paid by the income and secured by the mortgaged vessel, or
some other form of security; while, in the second, he/she deals with a
coherent group structure (corporate) that owns a fleet and the repayment
of the loan may be only based on the cash flow of the company.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">The column then
scrutinises sources of income and expenditure.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">It shows the
chartering strategy of the company and the stability – or the
vulnerability – of its income. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.77.3"
class="koboSpan">A company with time charters, or contracts of
affreightment, has more secured income in comparison with a company that
operates its vessels in the spot market, the income of which fluctuates.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.77.4" class="koboSpan">Bankers and
investors are comfortable with the former case, nervous with the latter
one. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.77.5" class="koboSpan">The
chartering strategy also reveals the marketing ability of the company;
the quality and efficiency of its services; the financial strengths and
weaknesses of its charterers; the effective utilisation of the vessels
in two, or all, legs of a voyage.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">This column also
investigates the managerial effectiveness regarding operating and voyage
costs. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">The
competitiveness of the company depends not only on its ability to
produce income but also how it operates within a competitive budget of
costs. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.78.3" class="koboSpan">However,
a record of detentions may indicate costs being cut too much, or
insufficient maintenance expenditure.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.78.4" class="koboSpan">The capital
costs are included in this column and, when they are the costs of debt
financing, income stability is of paramount
importance.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0916" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0916"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan"> The last part of this column looks into the market(s),
where the company operates, its market share, and the company’s
operating position against its competitors.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Conditions</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">The fourth column
refers to the examination of the competitive and changing international
economic, financial and political environment, within which the company
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_784"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan">makes decisions and operates.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">The conditions
in financial markets; interest rates; the decisions of governments of
exporting or importing countries; overall political conditions;
developments in the world economy; world industrial production;
international and seaborne trade, and the conditions in commodity
markets, are issues of utmost importance for shipping markets and
companies, since demand for shipping services is a derived one.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.83.3" class="koboSpan">As
Metaxas</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0917" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0917"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan"> argues: “Vessels carry cargoes and goods that are
imports and exports of various countries, the direction and volatility
of which have a direct impact on the demand for shipping.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.85.2" class="koboSpan">Indeed, trade
cycles in advanced economies and their resultant international trade
cycles affect the magnitude of demand for tramp shipping services and,
for this reason, their freight rate movements tend – to a certain degree
– to coincide with those of international trade.”
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.85.3" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
structural changes in the above markets, and national economies, may
have a more profound and lasting impact on the company’s business than
cyclical ones. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.85.4"
class="koboSpan">Examples of these structural changes could be shifts of
industrial production from one country to another, which may have an
effect on the pattern of shipping trade flows and on the type and size
of vessels that are employed or the technological changes that affect
the vessel’s efficiency, size and number of crew.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.85.5" class="koboSpan">Scenario
analysis of demand and supply of shipping market(s) where the company
operates, with sensitivity analysis, is required for the discussion of
their current and future conditions.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.85.6" class="koboSpan">Volatility in
freight rates and vessel market values, that is to say the market risk,
is the major parameter for the creation of the loan’s credit risk that
the financial institution faces.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping companies
operate within a shipping investment cycle, the four stages of which
(recovery, boom, recession, depression) are linked with the resultant
freight rate as it is established by the demand for – and supply of –
vessels.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0918" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0918"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan"> When freight rates are high and profits increase, an
over-investment in newbuildings is noticed, which may increase the level
of supply of vessels and result in an imbalance between supply and
demand. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.88.2" class="koboSpan">In a
period of expansion of supply, even a check to the rate of growth of
demand will be sufficient to trigger off a downward trend in freight
rates. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.88.3" class="koboSpan">During
recession and depression, speculative ordering may take place, often due
to subsidised shipbuilding. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.88.4"
class="koboSpan">This lowers the barriers to entry for shipping
companies into newbuilding markets and may also prolong the low freight
rates. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.88.5" class="koboSpan">On the
other hand, purchase of a vessel, or placing a newbuilding order during
this period of low market values, is excellent timing, since this
shipowner may compete with vessels bought or ordered during a boom
period at high
prices.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0919" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0919"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan"> Furthermore, the sale of this vessel during a
following prosperity phase is very profitable.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">However, for
the banker who undertakes credit risk analysis, stable cash flow is
required for the repayment of the loan, not the asset play.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.90.3" class="koboSpan">In addition,
owners may take advantage of low asset costs during a depression but
will often be reluctant to mitigate revenue to volatility by fixing a
long-term timecharter at the prevailing low rates.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.90.4" class="koboSpan">It is important
for the lending banker to figure out the stage of the shipping cycle,
during which it provides finance.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.90.5" class="koboSpan">Financing
over-valued secondhand vessels and newbuildings during a boom period,
may result in problematic loans in a period of recession and depression
(the comment in endnote 16 is very relevant).</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">Within the regulatory
framework, the International Maritime Organization (the IMO) safeguards
the international standards, safety and marine pollution of the shipping
industry; flag states, where vessels are registered, impose the
regulations of the IMO when they have ratified them; port authorities
inspect vessels when they call in; the classification societies
supervise the construction, safety and seaworthiness of
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_785"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan">the vessels during their life; the insurance companies
and Protection and Indemnity Clubs deal with the insurance aspects of
the vessels; and the major oil companies undertake their own detailed
inspections of the tankers that they are going to employ.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">All these are
major parameters for the developments in the shipping regulatory
environment which, as time passes, becomes tighter.
