</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.92.3" class="koboSpan">As such, new
investments and their overall cost, sale and purchase market, vessels’
operating expenses, and their revenue, may be seriously affected by the
official and corporate regulatory environment.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.92.4" class="koboSpan">These demand
the attention of the banker.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">3.5 Collateral</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">The last column
concentrates on the company’s fleet.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">Its composition
is important. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.94.3"
class="koboSpan">Fleet specialisation may develop expertise, operational
efficiency and better marketing. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.94.4"
class="koboSpan">However, such a fleet may be vulnerable to market
recession. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.94.5" class="koboSpan">The
diversified one, which may offer higher income security, normally
requires a larger fleet in operation.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.94.6" class="koboSpan">The fleet’s
condition and the company’s maintenance and repair policy must be taken
into account, as often the vessels are the mortgaged assets which
produce the (often assigned to the bank) income that repays the loan(s)
and they have to be operated safely within the required standards</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">Apart from the vessel
and the mortgage on it, other forms of securities also strengthen the
position of the banks: the assignment of income to the bank by which the
capital instalments and the interest are paid; assignment of insurance
in the case of a casualty or other specific circumstances; corporate
guarantees of the holding or management company and personal guarantees
of director(s) of the management company, which may cover the bank
should the company default in its payment of the loan and/or payment of
interest. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">All
forms of security are discussed in Section 4.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">3.6 Analysis of cash flow</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">Having analysed the
specific areas of the six “Cs” of credit, the bank has to make a cash
flow calculation to ascertain whether the total receipts will cover the
total costs of the vessel(s) to be financed, allowing for a balance
(cash cushion) sufficient to cover unexpected negative financial
developments. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.97.2"
class="koboSpan">The resulting breakeven estimates must be analysed to
determine how lucky the vessel is going to need to be in the future spot
market to cover its costs. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.97.3"
class="koboSpan">This cash flow
estimate</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0920" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0920"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.99.1"
class="koboSpan"> should be prepared for the proposed acquisition of
vessel(s); also, for the group’s fleet with – and without – the proposed
acquisitions.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Assessing the
stability of the fixed revenue of this statement, and its quality in
terms of charterers, requires understanding the legal documents of time
charters and contracts of affreightments; and assessing the
creditworthiness of
charterers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0921" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0921"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"> While quality of future revenue, based on assumptions,
requires an emphasis on the overall creditworthiness of the borrower as
revealed through the six “Cs” of credit analysis; and the use of
appropriate securities and documentation which is, naturally, the job
for the bank’s lawyers. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.102.2"
class="koboSpan">Now, the attention turns to securities and covenants,
and credit
analysis.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0922" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0922"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_786"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.104.2" class="koboSpan">Collateral Securities</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0923" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0923"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">In granting a
shipping loan, the bank has three possible areas from which to recoup
its funds. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">The
first or “intended” way out is from cash flow generated by the financed
acquisition, second, from the mortgage on the financed vessel (“direct”
security) and third, from additional securities (“indirect” security).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">It must be
stressed that a bank, by taking securities, does so in the expectation
that a problem loan will not develop and that sufficient cash flow will
be generated by the project to service the outstanding debt without it
being required to enforce its rights on the securities of the loan.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.106.4" class="koboSpan">The decision
to be taken by the financial institution, on the appropriate security or
securities, depends upon the individual case of the loan and shipping
company to be financed. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.106.5"
class="koboSpan">Among the securities are the mortgage, assignment of
revenue, assignment of insurance, mortgagee interest insurance,
assignment of requisition compensation, guarantees, comfort letters,
cash collateral security, share security and the assignment of
shipbuilding contract and refund guarantee.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.106.6" class="koboSpan">A short
analysis follows.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Mortgage</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">A mortgage duly
registered in the country whose flag the vessel flies, and carrying
conditional ownership of the acquired vessel that becomes void when the
debt is repaid, is the normal method of providing bank security for
vessel acquisitions. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.108.2"
class="koboSpan">Note that the type of mortgage will depend on the
legislation applicable in the vessel’s country of registry.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">Statutory mortgages
originated in the UK and adapted in jurisdictions modelled on the UK
legal system, protect the mortgagee’s rights by law.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">UK
legislation</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0924" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0924"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan"> gives every registered lender or security trustee for
group of lenders of a UK ship “the power absolutely to dispose of the
ship or share in respect of which he is registered, and to give
effectual receipts for the purchase money”.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.111.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
under UK common law, the mortgagee has the right to take possession of
the mortgaged vessel whenever the owner is in default of payment of the
principal or interest secured by the mortgage, or creates an event of
default under the loan agreement, or when the owner acts in a way which
impairs the security of the loan.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.111.3" class="koboSpan">A preferred
mortgage ensures the mortgagee’s right by express provision in the
mortgage agreement. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.111.4"
class="koboSpan">It is usually detailed and flexible, while the
statutory mortgage only stipulates general
conditions.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0925" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0925"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">The convenience of a
mortgage lies in the fact that the shipowner can run the business as a
going concern, at the same time giving the mortgagee the following basic
rights</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0926" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0926"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan"> to: take possession of the vessel and operate it or
proceed to a jurisdiction for arrest; arrest the vessel; sell the vessel
at auction or privately; appoint a receiver to handle the affairs of the
vessel; and to assume absolute title of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.115.2" class="koboSpan">All these
measures aim at protecting the bank and represent an agreement between
the borrower and the lender with respect to vessel maintenance,
insurance and operation.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">One of the major
problems encountered in the area of mortgages is in establishing the
vessel’s market value, which represents the value of the bank’s
security. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.116.2" class="koboSpan">The
market value can be regarded as the average price at which a willing
seller could be expected to make an acceptable offer, at arm’s length,
to a willing purchaser on the open market, and is different from a
vessel’s fixed insurance
value</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0927" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0927"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan"> or the depreciating book
value.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0928" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0928"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_787"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan">In order to protect against adverse fluctuations in
vessel values, banks have attached great importance to the hull-to-debt
ratio (particularly when financing single companies):</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0396" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00416.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">where,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan">HDR = Hull-to-Debt Ratio</span></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">MV = Current Market Value of the Vessel</span></span>\
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan">D</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan"> =
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan">Outstanding amount of the loan (debt)</span></span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">The hull-to-debt
ratio represents the surplus of the market value of the vessel over the
outstanding amount of the loan. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.128.2"
class="koboSpan">If this ratio falls below a predetermined level –
normally between 120–135%, the bank may require additional security from
the borrower. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.128.3"
class="koboSpan">As vessel prices can fall substantially in depressed
markets, the availability of additional security may cause serious
problems and friction between them.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.128.4" class="koboSpan">This has
happened in the early 1980s and, recently, in 2009–2010.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.128.5" class="koboSpan">However, many
banks accept the realities of depressed shipping markets and remain
satisfied as long as loan instalments and interest are paid, so they
temporarily freeze the ratio.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">Vessels can also be
subject to additional second, third, etc.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">mortgages.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">A second
mortgage is defined as existing when a first mortgage already exists on
a vessel. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.129.4"
class="koboSpan">These mortgages lie behind preferred mortgages in
creditor ranking and are usually offered as additional security,
provided consent of the first mortgagee has been given.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Assignment of revenue</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">General assignment of
revenue allows present and future revenue from the vessel(s) to be paid
directly to the shipowner until an event of default occurs, and reflects
the degree of confidence by the lender as to the likelihood of the debt
service; while there is another format, the retention account where
every month, the owner will transfer a pro-rata proportion of the next
amount of interest and instalment from the earnings account to a blocked
and pledged retention account with the bank; thus the mortgagee,
accumulates the necessary monthly freight revenue to meet the next
interest and principal payments.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">Under the strict
format of specific or legal assignment of revenue, all the specific
rights of the borrower arising from a charterparty are assigned to the
bank provided the charterer’s consent has been given.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
all charterparty payments are made directly to the bank, which will
normally allow the shipowner to withdraw the necessary funds ensuring
that the vessel remains operative to service the debt.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">The effectiveness of
the revenue assignment securities will be directly dependent upon the
reliability of the revenue streams, which will in turn be determined by
the relevant charterparties. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.133.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, the quality, integrity, and financial
condition of the charterer in terms of honouring obligations, and the
quality of the charterparty itself in terms of drafting and inflation
escalation or market adjustment clauses, are particularly important.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.133.3" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
sub-standard charterparty performance by the owner is often subject to
deductions from freight and, as a result, may cause a reduction or
cancellation in the level of assigned revenue.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_788"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Assignment of insurance</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">Insurance coverage is
required as an additional security should the vessel be damaged, lost,
or subject to a claim from third parties.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">Insurance
protection in shipping finance primarily involves the assignment of all
insurance payments due to the borrower, to be paid either directly to
the bank or requiring the bank’s express consent before being paid to
the borrower, subject to an agreed major claim threshold.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.135.3" class="koboSpan">Different
types of insurance protection are: hull and machinery insurance which
protects the bank by ensuring compensation if the vessel is lost or
damaged, as does war and strikes cover; the loss of hire or earnings
insurance which protects against interruption in cash flow; and other
insurance protection important for the bank to ensure cash flow and debt
service, include protection and
indemnity,</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0929" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0929"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan"> which covers third-party risks, such as collision
liability, loss of life, cargo liability; and freight, demurrage and
defence insurance, which provides the shipowner with legal advice and
assistance, and covers expenses in pursuing claims and resisting
disputes of a more operational nature.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 Mortgagee's interest insurance</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">Mortgagee’s interest
insurance is an additional insurance which protects the bank in the
event of a policy becoming void if certain warranties are broken, (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.139.2" class="koboSpan">it covers the
interest of the mortgagee in the case of a disputed claim by the
underwriters on the grounds of fraud).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.139.3" class="koboSpan">The
mortgagee’s interest claim will usually be withheld, pending the
conclusion of litigation. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.139.4"
class="koboSpan">Since this can take some considerable time, and the
outstanding loan plus the accruing interest are set at a default rate,
the final interest claim may not cover in full the amount due.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.139.5" class="koboSpan">A solution to
this problem is the simultaneous payments of mortgagee’s interest during
litigation, subject to return if underwriters are subsequently forced to
pay. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.139.6"
class="koboSpan">Alternatively, an escrow interest-bearing account can
receive the mortgagee’s interest claim and be subject to release, should
the underwriters be compelled to pay.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">4.5 Assignment of requisition compensation</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">This security
consists of the borrower assigning to the bank, any compensatory
payments in the event of vessel requisitioning, either in terms of
absolute title, or for hire purposes during times of war, hostilities or
nationalisation.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">4.6 Guarantees</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">A guarantee is an
undertaking, given to the bank by the guarantor, to be answerable for
the loan and interest granted by the bank to a shipping company, upon
the loan becoming defaulted. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.143.2"
class="koboSpan">In accepting guarantees, the bank should also
investigate the legal authority of the guarantor to give guarantees.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.143.3" class="koboSpan">Guarantees are
normally personal or corporate.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">Under a personal
guarantee agreement, the guarantor is liable – on demand – for the
discharge of all liabilities to the bank up to the stated amount or
proportion, in the event of default on the part of the borrower.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.144.2" class="koboSpan">The personal
guarantee is based on the guarantor’s personal assets which may
sometimes be registered in the names of other family members or
“offshore” companies. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.144.3"
class="koboSpan">Legal recourse, when necessary, against the
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_789"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">borrower and the guarantor, who is usually the owner or
major shareholder of the shipping company, is often questionable and
difficult. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.145.2"
class="koboSpan">Thus, personal guarantees are now often recognised by
the banking sector as being an indication of good faith or moral
commitment on behalf of the owner, rather than a cast iron legal
security. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.145.3" class="koboSpan">They
are currently out of favour, but they may well return for the
family-owned entities.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">Corporate guarantees
are usually given by the group holding company in conventional
structures, or by related management shipping companies in single vessel
structures. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.146.2"
class="koboSpan">These guarantees are becoming very important in the
latter case, when the security is only the mortgage and the assignment
of income. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.146.3"
class="koboSpan">Should a payment default develop, the bank has recourse
to the guarantor.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">4.7 Comfort letters</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">Comfort letters are a
form of intermediate, less strict, guarantees usually containing
assurances and intent.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">4.8 Cash collateral security</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">Cash securities
usually comprise a special cash collateral account, blocked by the bank,
which may be established on an initial lump sum or monthly payment
basis. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.150.2" class="koboSpan">The
reason for their existence is that the bank lowers its loan exposure and
also holds cash, which can be used for the payment of interest and
repayment of loan instalments should the shipping company be unable to
cover them in a falling freight market, during which the vessel may face
temporary employment problems. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.150.3"
class="koboSpan">Cash collateral accounts are normally interest-bearing,
subject to negotiation.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">4.9 Share security</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">The share security,
which is normally taken in addition to the mortgage, consists of the
vessel-owning company depositing shares of the borrowing shipping
company that he/she controls, with the bank, for a specific period or up
to the final amortisation of the loan.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.152.2" class="koboSpan">This enables
the lending bank, when a shipping company is in default for the loan
repayment, to assume ownership of the vessel-owning company as opposed
to the vessel itself, resulting in the bank becoming the new owner as
opposed to a mortgagee, thus benefiting from any rights and assets of
the company (e.g. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.152.3"
class="koboSpan">charter parties, positive hedging arrangements, cash
balances and other receivables such as insurance claims.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.152.4" class="koboSpan">Banks have a
mixed view of share pledges. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.152.5"
class="koboSpan">Some prefer the pledge as it gives them quick control
of the company, but others do not as it comes with potential pollution
liability and existing creditors.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.153.1" class="koboSpan">A share pledge
normally applies where the shares are in bearer form, So the title
passes – on delivery of the shares – to the bank; while, a share charge
applies to shares of registered form, and delivery will need to be
accompanied by executed undated transfer forms.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">4.10 Assignment of the shipbuilding contract and refund guarantee</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">Banks finance the
construction of the vessels and grant loans to shipping companies for
this purpose. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.155.2"
class="koboSpan">The loan is granted in stages, from the signing of the
shipbuilding contract
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_790"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan">to the delivery of the vessel – a period that may last
for over two years. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.156.2"
class="koboSpan">The number and the amount of instalments to be paid by
the shipping company to the shipyard varies in time and countries.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.156.3" class="koboSpan">Five
instalments, each one 20% of the purchase price is a scheme often used
nowadays by shipyards and shipowners.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.156.4" class="koboSpan">Under this
scheme, the bank may grant 60–80% of the instalments with the remaining
20–40% paid by the borrowing shipping company.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.156.5" class="koboSpan">Since during
the construction period of the vessel (gestation period) the lending
bank does not have any security for the loan granted, the shipbuilding
contract is assigned by the borrowing shipping company – alongside all
its beneficial interests, benefits, right and title in, to and under the
shipbuilding contract – to the bank.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">The assignment
becomes very useful to the bank in case the borrowing company defaults
in the payment of the instalment(s) to the shipyard, and abandons the
transaction due to, for instance, the deterioration of the shipping
market. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Then
the bank may be able to successfully re-negotiate with the shipyard and
lower the price of the vessel; to replace the original shipping company
which placed the construction order with another willing to purchase the
vessel under construction and continue the completion of the
transaction. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.157.3"
class="koboSpan">Needless to say, the initiator of the construction
order loses the money already paid in instalments and accepts its
replacement by another company.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">The refund guarantee
is a security which is given by a financial institution to a shipping
company that has placed a newbuilding order to a shipyard and guarantees
the return of all sums paid in instalments by the shipping company to
the shipyard during the construction period if the vessel will not be
constructed due to the inability of the shipyard to complete the order.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.158.2" class="koboSpan">In this case,
the refund guarantee is assigned by the shipping company to the lending
bank which becomes entitled to enforce its rights stemming from the
guarantee.</span>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.159.2" class="koboSpan">Covenants</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">Covenants are
contractual obligations of the borrower to the lender, that are included
in the loan agreement and those referring to the vessel in the mortgage,
and refer to certain actions that the borrower should or should not
undertake. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.160.2"
class="koboSpan">They, therefore, fall into one of two groups:
affirmative or negative. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.160.3"
class="koboSpan">In a non-shipping study, where financial differences
between small and large firms are discussed, Walker and
Petty</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0930" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0930"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan"> referred to four areas that are always covered by
covenants in the loan agreements: liquidity, profitability, financial
leverage, and dividend policy. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.162.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipping is no exception.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">According to Apilado
and
Millington,</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0931" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0931"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan"> covenants impose contractual limits on the action of
the borrower and serve to reduce risk exposure.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">The prime
objective behind the covenants is the protection of the assets’ value of
the borrower. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.165.3"
class="koboSpan">Thus, the financial institution wants to maintain the
market value of the assets at a higher rate than the market value of the
liabilities. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.165.4"
class="koboSpan">In such a case, when a positive net worth exists, the
shipping company has a value for the borrower and serves as security for
the lender. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.165.5"
class="koboSpan">The problems are created when the market value of the
assets (vessels and other assets) decreases and, when abstracting the
liabilities from the assets, the net worth becomes negative.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.165.6" class="koboSpan">This is the
reason that the hull-to-debt ratio covenant is imposed and regular
valuation of the market value of the vessels, by reputable firms of
independent shipbrokers, has to take place.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.165.7" class="koboSpan">In addition,
further debt is not allowed without prior written consent of the bank
and the vessel has to be well maintained and operated by the
borrower.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">Other covenants
address: liquidity, such as the maintenance of minimum current account
balances – this covenant may apply to the vessels that are financed by
the
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_791"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">bank and the accounts with the bank, or those held by
other financial institutions; profitability, an example would include a
ratio of EBITDA to net interest expense (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">not less than
2.5 to 1.0); and dividend policy, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.167.3" class="koboSpan">the
distribution of dividends by the management to shareholders, which is
not allowed without – again – the prior written consent of the
bank.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">Through these
covenants, the bank oversees the liquidity and controls the cash flow of
the company or the group, and watches over their further investment
activities. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.168.2"
class="koboSpan">Examples may include: the borrower will procure the
prompt payment of operating expenses (including repairs, special
surveys, maintenance and operating costs); the bank may, from time to
time, and at the borrowers expense, require the borrower to obtain
independent valuations of the vessel(s).</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">There is a wide
variety of other covenants imposed by the loan agreement or the mortgage
which is, of course, to be expected as protective measures in the
lender’s interest. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.169.2"
class="koboSpan">This is because shipping companies operate in a very
complex international business – and legal – environment and may be
incorporated in one country; vessel(s) may fly the flag of another
country (where the mortgage on the vessel will be registered); sail in
various parts of the globe, often under dangerous conditions; the
finance may take place by a bank in a different country and the loan
agreement may be governed by the law of another country; and the crew
may be nationals of other countries.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.169.3" class="koboSpan">Many of these
diametrically different conditions and factors, which may have an effect
on the repayment of the loan, should be dealt with within the covenants
section.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">The bank’s objective
in using covenants is to maintain a positive net worth of the borrowing
company, to create compliance incentives for the borrower, and to
establish the legal background for loan monitoring.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.170.2" class="koboSpan">Failure of the
borrower to comply with covenants is an event of default, which may
accelerate the repayment of the loan or allow the lender to enforce its
rights. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.170.3"
class="koboSpan">According to
Myers</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0932" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0932"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan"> borrowers accept the added costs of restrictive
covenants as part of the price of acquiring funds needed for their
business operations. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.172.2"
class="koboSpan">However, shipping banks, when imposing covenants,
should maintain a balance between their need to secure the shipping
company’s net worth and its operating flexibility and investment
expansion. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.172.3"
class="koboSpan">High restrictions may prevent a company’s growth,
whereas an approach that is too relaxed may occasionally lead to moral
hazard.</span>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.173.2" class="koboSpan">Further Discussion on Credit Analysis</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">Having looked at the
securities and covenants, we can further discuss some aspects of credit
analysis.
</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fig0397" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0397"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the statistical analysis and results of a
study</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0933" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0933"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan"> on the effect of the six “Cs” of credit, on individual
companies. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.178.2" class="koboSpan">The
study was based on a questionnaire, as well as on long and detailed
personal discussions with the senior shipping finance staff of 14
international commercial banks in London, Piraeus, Hong Kong and
Rotterdam.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">From the bank finance
viewpoint, shipping companies fall into two broad groups: corporate
shipping companies and project shipping or single-vessel companies.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.179.2" class="koboSpan">In the first
group, the company owns, leases, charters and operates its vessels and
has a strong balance sheet, particularly with respect to liquidity and
gearing. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.179.3" class="koboSpan">The
paid-in capital, together with retained earnings, should provide a
buffer against market price fluctuations.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.179.4" class="koboSpan">Additionally,
cash flow should be relatively stable and cover debt service</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0397" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_792"></span>[](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0397)

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00417.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0397)

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">(interest payments
and contracted amortisations) by a fair margin.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">Collateral
securities depend on the financial standing of the shipowner as well as
the repayment period. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.181.3"
class="koboSpan">Exposure of up to one year may on occasions be
unsecured. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.181.4"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, unsecured lending can be provided up to
seven years to very low risk classes by a few banks
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_793"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">or, alternatively, secured financing up to a level of
60–70% of the market value of the vessel.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">A “shipping project”,
or single-vessel company, is an activity which can be considered
separately from the activities of the sponsor (owner) of the project.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.183.2" class="koboSpan">In this case,
the repayment of the loan is based on the cash flow of the venture, with
security cover primarily on the assets of the venture, and with no (or
limited) recourse to the sponsor.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.183.3" class="koboSpan">All such
exposures are covered by collateral.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.183.4" class="koboSpan">In this case,
the loan does not normally exceed 70% of market value at any time.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.183.5" class="koboSpan">Exceptions to
this rule may be considered if, for example, a favourable time charter
with a satisfactory charterer is in place.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.183.6" class="koboSpan">Loans are also
considered with a tenor of up to 10 or 12 years, for newbuildings, to
accommodate structures which are typically up to two years’ pre-delivery
and maximum 10 years’ post delivery.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.183.7" class="koboSpan">This applies
to both “corporate” and project loans.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">In
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0397)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">, two of the financial institutions put an emphasis on
corporate financing or “near corporate financing” in the sense that the
single shipping company proposals for financing are assessed as part of
one larger group – above 15 vessels – and the qualitative analysis
treats both the credit risk of an individual project and that of the
overall group. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.186.2"
class="koboSpan">The other 12 financial institutions have both kinds of
clients: large groups and smaller shipping companies, who own between
four and 10 vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">According to
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0397)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan">, character, managerial capacity and creditworthiness,
collateral and cash flow, account for 32% of individual factors; while
collateral and cash flow account for 13%.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.189.2" class="koboSpan">It seems,
indeed, that these banks focus – or, at least, want to focus – on name
lending, where managerial capacity, expertise, past investment and loan
record, resourcefulness and tenacity, during a recession and depression
period, are highly appreciated by them.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">In 2010 discussions
were held with 10 banks out of the original 14 institutions in
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0397)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.192.2"
class="koboSpan">There have been some interesting developments.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.192.3" class="koboSpan">First of all,
eight of the banks, in addition to financing single-vessel companies,
are now involved to a greater or lesser extent with financing shipping
companies which have a corporate structure or near corporate structure
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.192.4" class="koboSpan">a large
group which owns single-vessel companies).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.192.5" class="koboSpan">This is
partially due to the influx of public companies listed at the various
stock exchanges, and in particular the New York Stock Exchange, where
\$US15 billion was raised through IPOs and secondary issues between 2004
and 2009. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.192.6" class="koboSpan">A
few of these companies have also raised funds in the US high yield bond
market.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">During the last 10
years the size of these shipping companies has also increased.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.193.2" class="koboSpan">This is mainly
due to increased profitability, the purchase of newbuilding and/or
secondhand vessels and mergers and acquisitions.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.193.3" class="koboSpan">Thus, banks
have become accustomed to dealing with public shipping companies;
private corporate entities; near corporate shipping companies which
manage a large number of single-vessel companies; and smaller entities
which operate single-vessel companies.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.193.4" class="koboSpan">As a result,
the banks assess shipping loans on a corporate basis, on a single-vessel
basis and on a combination of the two; with the six “Cs” of credit
analysis covering all three cases.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0397)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan"> currently applies mainly to the single-vessel approach
or the nearly corporate structure company.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.195.2" class="koboSpan">However, for
the corporate case it seems that the weights for factors 1 and 2 remain
almost the same; on the other hand, the weights of factors 20, 21 and 22
– namely financial statements, company size, and company structure –
have increased to approximately 5% for each component.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.195.3" class="koboSpan">At the same
time, the weights for factors 15, 16, and 17 – chartering policy, world
economy conditions, and reputation of charterers – have been raised to
5% per item. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.195.4"
class="koboSpan">This is due to the relatively weak and
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_794"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">uncertain market conditions.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.196.2" class="koboSpan">The same
applies for the specific sector conditions factor (Factor No 9).</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, changes in
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0397)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan"> are indeed a manifestation of the dynamic nature of
credit analysis which follows the cyclical developments of the shipping
markets. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.199.2"
class="koboSpan">Generally speaking,
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">Table
2</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0397)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan"> remains in most of its parts strong.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">The six “Cs” of
credit is an analysis which investigates the past and makes inquiries
for – and projection to – the future.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.202.2" class="koboSpan">It requires
meetings with principals of the company and key staff, analysis of
financial statements and legal chartering contracts.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.202.3" class="koboSpan">It also
necessitates the existence of a web of contacts for obtaining
information about the shipping company, such as other banks that have
provided finance for its vessels, its trade creditors and shipbrokers.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.202.4" class="koboSpan">In essence,
the loan officer and his/her independent credit committee have to be in
a position to assess the parameters of a qualitative model which, in a
brief summary form, includes: the management’s expertise and integrity;
the debt, equity and net worth; the cash flow; the mortgaged vessels and
the guarantees for the loan; and the external economic and financial
environment, where the company operates.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.202.5" class="koboSpan">This model
provides a deep knowledge of the borrower’s company and its loans.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.202.6" class="koboSpan">The assessment
should provide the probability of loan repayment or default.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">Over the last two
decades, a number of banks have rated the shipping companies, shipping
groups, and the loans offered, in a similar way the rating
agencies</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0934" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0934"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> rate the bond and other debt issues.
</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fig0398" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0398"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the rating scale of Standard and Poor’s and
Moody’s.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0935" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0935"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan"> The financial institutions undertake their credit risk
analysis (based on the six “Cs” of credit), and they then feed with
financial information – mainly ratios – their own rating model, in order
to produce the rating of the project – and/or the company – to be
financed. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.209.2" class="koboSpan">The
rating indicates the default probability.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.209.3" class="koboSpan">A large number
of smaller financial institutions do not use
models,</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0936" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0936"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan"> but do use ratings provided by methodologies developed
by rating agencies (such as Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s) based on the
experience of both the rating agency and the lending bank.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.211.2" class="koboSpan">This has
become a widespread practice in banking industries after the imposition
of the new capital agency rules in 2008.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.211.3" class="koboSpan">(See Section
6.3.)</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0398" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00418.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0398)

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_795"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">The credit decision to grant the loan is, thus, based
on the six “Cs” of Credit Risk Analysis and on the rating of the
company. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.213.2" class="koboSpan">Other
factors which impinge on decisions, such as pricing and capital
availability, are discussed below.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.213.3" class="koboSpan">The shipping
industry, due to the volatility of freight rates has a BB, Ba rating,
which places it into the “somewhat speculative” group of
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">Table
3</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0398)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.215.2"
class="koboSpan">There are certainly companies which belong to AA, Aa;
and companies and loans whose rating is CCC, Caa as well.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.215.3" class="koboSpan">It is for the
financial institution to target the desirable group of clients and to
attract them. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.215.4"
class="koboSpan">Should a loan, in any way, have a low rating, the
provision of appropriate securities may be required.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.215.5" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the pricing will reflect the rating, which is the topic of the next
section.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">6.1 Pricing of the loan</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.217.1" class="koboSpan">The process of
assessing the probability of credit risk, or default, is also linked
with the pricing of shipping loans.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.217.2" class="koboSpan">In general,
shipping companies, which are closer to risk-free business, should
compensate the banks with lower returns on shipping loans, while the
ones with an increased probability of default should reimburse the banks
with a higher return. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.217.3"
class="koboSpan">The difference between the risk-free loan and the risky
one is the default risk premium, the compensation of the bank for the
additional risk involved.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.218.1" class="koboSpan">A pricing model for
shipping loans may contain four components: the marginal cost of funding
the loan, which is normally the LIBOR; the bank’s administrative and
overhead cost structure to initiate, analyse and monitor the shipping
loan; the default risk premium of the shipping loan to be granted; and a
profit margin that includes an acceptable return to shareholders.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.218.2" class="koboSpan">The bank, when
charging the interest rate on a shipping loan, uses LIBOR (or the cost
of the customer deposits that will be converted into loans) which is the
first component, as a basis, and adds a spread (margin) which contains
all the other three components.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">In addition to
spread, the financial institution charges fees for the provision of the
loan. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.2" class="koboSpan">Two
usual forms of fees are “facility fee” and “commitment fee”.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.3" class="koboSpan">The facility
fee is normally a flat fee, rewarding the bank for administering the
proposal and granting the loan. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.4"
class="koboSpan">Commitment fee is the percentage fee paid from the time
the Loan Agreement is executed until it is drawn.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.5" class="koboSpan">It usually
lasts for a period between six months and a year.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.6" class="koboSpan">Finally, the
borrower may be asked to maintain a compensating deposit balance in the
current account of the shipping company, kept with the bank.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.7" class="koboSpan">This requires
that a minimum balance of the account will be maintained by the
borrower, either on an average annual basis or an absolute flat amount
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.8" class="koboSpan">the
minimum balance of the account will never be below \$1m).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.9" class="koboSpan">Since such
accounts are interest-free, or may command a lower interest rate, the
effective cost of the loan increases.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.219.10" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
the bank controls – or follows closely – the borrower’s liquidity; thus,
also the profitability of the bank.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">When a financial
institution is setting spread, fees, and compensating balances, the hard
competition in the banking market for creditworthy and desirable
customers is taken into account.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.220.2" class="koboSpan">The more
competition that exists, the greater the probability that the bank will
head for a leaner profit. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.220.3"
class="koboSpan">In a competitive international banking environment,
funding, administrative costs and default risk are determined by the
bank’s internal decisions, while the profit margin is also influenced by
external competition</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">Bank Shipping Finance
is, for many banks, primarily relationship banking, which refers to the
provision to an existing borrower of an array of banking products – such
as: cash management; derivatives; foreign exchange dealings; letters of
credit; letters
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_796"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan">of guarantee; and advisory services.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.222.2" class="koboSpan">Here, the
financial institution increases the fee income from the borrower and
strengthens their relationship and mutual loyalty.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">Financial
institutions measure the overall profitability of the borrower and, for
this reason, the following relationship can be
established.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0937" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0937"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0399" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00419.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.226.1" class="koboSpan">The numerator of this
formula includes all sources of income in a particular year, such as the
expected interest rate, loan fees, commission from foreign exchange
transactions, cash management, letters of credit less all the costs that
are incurred in the same period, for the provision of the services.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.226.2" class="koboSpan">These costs
include – among others – salaries, utilities, rent, expenses for the
initiation, analysis and monitoring of the loan, interest on this
borrower’s deposits, and costs of funds to lend to this borrower.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.226.3" class="koboSpan">The
denominator includes the average loan amount of the year in question
minus this borrower’s average amount of deposits after subtracting the
reserves that may be required by the monetary authorities.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.226.4" class="koboSpan">However, in
the eurodollar market, deposit reserves are not required.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.226.5" class="koboSpan">Should the
rate of return be positive, the loan proposal may proceed from the
profitability viewpoint, since the required income exceeds the expenses.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.226.6" class="koboSpan">In case the
rate of return is negative, the income and cost items should be
reconsidered.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">Grammenos
(1995)</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0938" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0938"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan"> investigates the profitability of the shipping
departments of four international banks from 1988–1995.
</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fig0400" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0400"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the major components which are: interest and
fees from loans; commission from foreign exchange dealings and
remittances; collection of cheques and deposits; letters of credit and
guarantee. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.231.2" class="koboSpan">It
is evident that there is an increasing trend for non-interest
activities, the volume of which – and therefore the profits –
increase.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">In a survey
Grammenos</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0939" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0939"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">44</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan"> discusses, again, the profitability concept from
1998–2001 as he revisits the same departments, where he identifies two
fundamental changes. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.234.2"
class="koboSpan">The first is the very intense focus on the overall
return to the departments, through relationship banking.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.234.3" class="koboSpan">This is
evidenced by their target return imposed by the head offices</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0400" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00420.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0400)

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_797"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">and the detailed sourcing of the earnings and the
costs. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.236.2" class="koboSpan">The
second is the appearance of new sources, such as derivatives and
advisory services, and the intensification of banking efforts for cash
management of the shipping companies by large sophisticated banks.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.236.3" class="koboSpan">Thus, as is
evident from the first column of
</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fig0401" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0401"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">Table 5</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">, the main source of their income remains the loan
(loan interest and fees), ranging from 45–60% of their total return from
loan and services, while the borrower-related fee services account for
42–60%. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.238.2" class="koboSpan">These
two fundamental changes are in line with the need for a rise in the
banks capital base rate, which, through increased profitability, enables
them to expand. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.238.3"
class="koboSpan">It is partly a consequence of capital adequacy, a topic
which is discussed in Section 6.3 of this chapter.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">In 2010 the same four
banks were revisited (after the credit crunch in 2008–2010).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.239.2" class="koboSpan">This followed
the creation of toxic assets, initially from the USA and then
internationally, and led governments to give a helping hand to some
banks (which faced a solvency crisis) by recapitalisation through
partial nationalisation; central banks to provide cheaper credit to
financial institutions; banks to face serious difficulties with the
granting of shipping loans due to lack of liquidity in the interbank
market, which resulted in higher cost of funds for the banks and,
consequently, for shipowners; and shipowners to cancel, postpone or
convert their newbuilding orders into other vessels.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">As a result, the
income from loan interest has increased due to rising spreads (see
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">Table
5</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0401)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan"> below).</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.243.1" class="koboSpan">Fees from syndication
have decreased due to the fact that, in accordance with the accounting
regulations, they have to be split equally over the repayment period of
the loan. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.243.2" class="koboSpan">The
income of cash management has decreased due to strong competition in the
market. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.243.3"
class="koboSpan">However, profitability continues to be one of the three
major goals of senior and junior management (the other two are sound
business and competitiveness) as a means to strengthen much-needed
banking capital; expand the banking business; and attain an acceptable
return for shareholders.</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0401" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00421.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0401)

</div>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_798"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">6.2 Syndication</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">Syndication is a
common method nowadays for bank shipping finance, when a loan is made by
two or more financial institutions, on similar terms and conditions,
using common documentation and administered by a common
agent.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0940" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0940"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan"> It can involve over 60 participating banks where the
lead banks do the structuring and pricing and receive higher fees than
participants. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.248.2"
class="koboSpan">In shipping, it is mostly the smaller form, four to
eight banks, all of them have shipping expertise and portfolio, all
members are equal, all contribute to structuring and all receive same
fees; this is known as “club syndication”.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">In the loan interest
item of </span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">Table
5</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0401)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan">, interest is included from both bilateral and
syndicated loans - but it has not been possible to specify the exact
percentage of each, since the ratio of bilateral to syndicated loans is
quite diverse, reflecting the bank’s loan syndication policy.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">The reasons for
syndication lies in a number of factors, the most important of which
are: the need for large amounts to be financed; the spreading of risk;
the increased banking return (only for the bank (s) underwriting the
syndication nor for the participating banks) which includes
spread</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0941" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0941"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan"> and additional fees charged to the borrowers; and the
opportunity for banks to gain experience, international reputation and
opportunities which they might not have otherwise, to participate in the
financing of leading shipping companies, who are the target clients for
syndication. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.254.2"
class="koboSpan">The main negative elements are a disagreement with a
decided course of action; a slower decision-making process in comparison
with bilateral financing, which involves only one bank; and ancillary
business which is spread too thinly or a bank may only be lending cheap
dollars and have no additional justification for the transaction.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">Fees from syndication
include the arrangement fee for the arranger, which is normally the
leading bank of the syndication; the participation fee, which is given
to each participating bank in accordance with its paid on amount; the
commitment fee, which is based on the undrawn amount of the loan until
its full drawdown; and finally, the annual agency fee, which is the
amount of remuneration of the agent/bank which monitors and administers
the loan and handles all payments of the borrower to the
syndicate.</span>

### <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">6.3 Capital adequacy rules</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">Traces of the
emphasis on profitability can be partly found in the Capital Adequacy
Rules imposed, on 1 January 1993, by the Basel Accord on International
Convergence on Capital (Basel I).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.257.2" class="koboSpan">It was the
first time that the capital of the bank – and therefore its solvency –
had been linked with the varying degree of credit risk of the bank’s
groups of assets (e.g. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.257.3"
class="koboSpan">cash, bonds, residential mortgages, commercial loans)
on and off its balance sheets. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.257.4"
class="koboSpan">Each asset group was given a different weight of risk
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.257.5" class="koboSpan">cash 0%,
municipal bonds 20%, loan mortgagees for residential properties 50% and
commercial loans 100%) and the total capital of the bank – core capital
and supplementing capital, or tiers I and II – should be a minimum, or
higher, of 8% of the risk-adjusted total assets.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.257.6" class="koboSpan">This produces
the Risk Asset Ratio, the formula of which is as follows:</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0402" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00422.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_799"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan">According to the 1993 Basel regulations, shipping (and
all other commercial) loans had the same risk weight (100%), despite the
fact that different companies and loans represent different degrees of
risk (i.e. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.259.2"
class="koboSpan">AAA, A, B- or CCC).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.259.3" class="koboSpan">However, it
was later argued that a 100% weight may induce bankers to concentrate on
more risky loans to boost their return on assets and increase their
capital base, consequently creating value for the banks and at the same
time increasing their risk exposure.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.259.4" class="koboSpan">This may
result an escalation of their loan losses which could subsequently
destroy value for the bank.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">The new rules of the
Basel Committee for Capital Adequacy Rules (Basel II) were introduced in
January 2008. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.260.2"
class="koboSpan">Two principal options are used for the measurement of
credit risk: the standardised approach (SA) and the internal
rating-based approach (IRB). </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.260.3"
class="koboSpan">Both apply to corporate exposures and include many
shipping transactions. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.260.4"
class="koboSpan">The SA introduced the use of credit risk ratings,
similar to Moody’s and Standard and Poor’s, while it draws on external
credit assessments for determining the risk weights.
</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fig0403" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0403"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.261.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that a wider range of weight groups has been
introduced. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.262.2"
class="koboSpan">Most of the shipping companies operating in a risky
environment fall into the groups of 100 or 150% with a corresponding 8
or 12% capital adequacy requirement.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">The IRB approach, on
the other hand, has two variables: foundation and advance.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.263.2" class="koboSpan">Under
foundation, the banks assess the risk of default of the borrower, but
estimates of additional risk factors are derived through the application
of standardised supervisory rules.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.263.3" class="koboSpan">To follow the
foundation approach, a financial institution has to demonstrate that it
has an appropriate internal rating system, risk management process and
ability to estimate the risk components.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.264.1" class="koboSpan">The advance IRB
approach is for institutions that are currently using a well-developed
risk management system to assess both their credit risk profile and
their capital adequacy. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.264.2"
class="koboSpan">As such, a central measurable concept is the
probability of default (PD) of a borrower.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.264.3" class="koboSpan">This is in
association with the magnitude of likely loss on the exposure, the loss
given default (LGD), and with the amount the bank was exposed to the
borrower at the time of default, the exposure of default (EOD).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.264.4" class="koboSpan">Finally the
maturity of the exposure (M) is taken into account.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.264.5" class="koboSpan">The PD, LGD
and M are estimated and used as inputs to calculate corresponding risk
weights. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.264.6" class="koboSpan">The
risk weights are multiplied by EOD and the resultant amounts are added
across the portfolio of the bank.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.264.7" class="koboSpan">Thus, the
required capital adequacy of the bank can be calculated.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.264.8" class="koboSpan">Needless to
say, models are in use for this calculation.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">In October 2001,
“Object Finance” was included among other areas of finance in a Working
Paper published by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) on
“Internal Ratings-Based Approach to Specialised Lending Exposures”.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.265.2" class="koboSpan">Object finance
deals with providing finance for equipment – such as ships, aircraft,
trains; it is the method used in bank shipping finance for pledged
vessel(s), which generate cash flow, assigned to the</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0403" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00423.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0403)

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_800"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan">bank. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.267.2"
class="koboSpan">In this case, the concepts LGD, PD and M, in order to
be quantified, and Capital Adequacy to be determined, an object rating,
a client rating and an integrated rating, are required.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.267.3" class="koboSpan">The object
rating takes into account the characteristics of the vessel(s) to be
financed, the financing terms and the shipping market risks.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.267.4" class="koboSpan">The client
rating considers parameters, such as, the borrower’s management
capacity, track record, and financial data (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.267.5" class="koboSpan">information
contained in the six “Cs” of credit analysis).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.267.6" class="koboSpan">Finally, an
integrated rating will be created, which combines both object and client
rating.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.268.1" class="koboSpan">IRB and object
finance differ in that the first deals with corporate exposures and the
second with specialised lending exposures.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.268.2" class="koboSpan">However, not
all transactions will fit neatly into one group.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.268.3" class="koboSpan">The object
finance method takes into account the collateral securities of the loan,
while IRB does not.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">A consequence of the
2008 Capital Adequacy Rules is that smaller shipping companies may be at
a disadvantage, since the capital adequacy requirements may be higher
for them than the current 8%, due to, for instance, a higher percentage
of financing – over 60% – or the lack of sufficient secured income; or
lack of transparency due to the bank being provided with annual
non-consolidated (and often unaudited) accounts from the shipping
company. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.269.2" class="koboSpan">This
would result in an increase in the adequate capital of the bank, the
cost of which would be passed on to the customer.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.269.3" class="koboSpan">In addition,
these companies, being smaller, show a lower overall profitability in
their banking transactions for their lending banks.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.269.4" class="koboSpan">As a result,
they may not be included on the list of desirable clients of these
financial institutions. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.269.5"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, a number of banks have three customer tiers
(I, II and III) based on the credit risk rating, the resulting capital
adequacy requirement and overall profitability from relationship
banking.</span>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.270.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.270.2" class="koboSpan">Loan Monitoring</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">Loan monitoring is
essentially the periodic evaluation of the shipping loan portfolio, by
the shipping department, through the qualitative model of credit risk
analysis (referred to above) and the six “Cs”.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.271.2" class="koboSpan">This may
happen, for instance, twice a year or whenever there are developments in
the loans that require the attention of the bank.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.271.3" class="koboSpan">The prime
objective is for the loan officer to ensure:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.272.1" class="koboSpan">the borrower’s
    compliance with the covenants and also that his/her management
    capacity and integrity remain at the required levels;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.273.1" class="koboSpan">the net worth is
    sufficient for the loan’s overall security and/or the target hull to
    debt ratio remains as required;</span>
3.  <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">vessel(s)
    continue to be employed efficiently;</span>
4.  <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.275.1" class="koboSpan">cash flow is
    satisfactory for the payments of capital instalments and interest;
    and</span>
5.  <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">the financial
    conditions of the personal or corporate guarantors have not
    deteriorated.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">All these factors are
scrutinised at the time of the periodic review of the loan and under
future probable, economic, financial, and shipping conditions.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">Management
restructuring, splits and death, may have a negative implication for the
operation and financial condition of a shipping company.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.278.2" class="koboSpan">While changes
in an owner’s character and integrity in a period of depression may be
an exceptional event, moral hazard expects a demanding monitoring
requirement, particularly in a depressed shipping
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_801"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.279.1"
class="koboSpan">market. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.279.2"
class="koboSpan">Debt repayment and cash flow of financed vessel(s),
vessel(s) financed by other banks, and overall group fleet, should be
analysed for the purpose of identifying over-borrowing and adverse
revenue and cost developments, which may squeeze the cash flow available
for the debt service.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">Market movements are
the main cause of a decrease in freight rate revenue, although likely
reasons also include an aggressive chartering policy, (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.280.2" class="koboSpan">vessels are
chartered in the spot market where income is higher for a short period)
in comparison with the time charter market; unsatisfactory vessel
performance in contrast to what is expected in accordance with the
charterparties; default on the part of charterer; vessel inactivity from
factors such as arrest, repair and blacklist.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.280.3" class="koboSpan">Costs may
increase due to factors such as running cost escalation (mainly crew,
technical and insurance), and adverse interest and currency
movements.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.1" class="koboSpan">The bank will
normally monitor overall conditions in the world economy and
international trade, related industry or commodities, and the shipping
market, which may have implications for the repayment of its loan(s).
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.2" class="koboSpan">These include:
changes in economic policies (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.3" class="koboSpan">as
anti-inflationary economic policies in the early 1980s); political
events (e.g. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.4"
class="koboSpan">the nationalisation of the Libyan oil assets in 1971
and the Iranian political unrest in 1979); new legislation the Oil
Pollution Act of 1990 that was decided unilaterally by the USA, or the
International Safety Management Code of the International Maritime
Organisation); and vessel blacklisting.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.5" class="koboSpan">In addition,
scenario analysis for the cash flow and repayment of the loan under
different economic conditions and assumptions is part of the job.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.6" class="koboSpan">The
unpredictable fluctuations of income and asset value levels mean that a
constant review of a vessel’s market value and the practical
effectiveness of collateral securities is an essential part of the
monitoring process. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.7"
class="koboSpan">In terms of mortgages and vessel value, the main
reasons for a decrease in value are current and expected or unexpected
market conditions – although vessel condition, technology and new
legislation are also relevant. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.8"
class="koboSpan">A decrease in vessel value may result in the
hull-to-debt ratio falling below permitted levels.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.9" class="koboSpan">This indicates
an increase in the probability of default, as the real economic worth of
the company decreases. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.281.10"
class="koboSpan">Finally, falling freight rates and vessel market values
– which may affect payments of loan instalments and securities of the
loan, dry up compensating balances and postpone payments for trade
creditors – are usually strong indicators of future problematic
loans.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">Once or twice a year,
and whenever extraordinary conditions demand, a review of the shipping
loan portfolio takes place as part of the monitoring process.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.282.2" class="koboSpan">Should loans
be identified as having weaknesses regarding their repayment, they would
be adversely classified according to the probability of loan
loss.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0942" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0942"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan">47</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan"> This normally happens in a bad market.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.284.2" class="koboSpan">In this case,
the bank may take immediate steps to minimise the loan loss
effect.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0943" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0943"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.285.1" class="koboSpan">48</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan"> However, this discussion is beyond the scope of this
analysis.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">Additional issues of
importance for monitoring are the amount of a vessel(s) revenue assigned
to the bank and the validity of insurance security in respect of paying
premiums and complying with policy clauses.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.287.2" class="koboSpan">Liquidity
problems may also arise from trade creditors.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.287.3" class="koboSpan">A sharp rise
in the amount owed to trade creditors (they should not normally be in
excess of 90 days) may indicate a difficulty in meeting short-term
obligations. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.287.4" class="koboSpan">A
bank being paid promptly may prove to be of limited use if the crew or
creditors – such as suppliers – have serious outstanding debts.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.287.5" class="koboSpan">This could
lead to arrests, disputes and non-performance of the vessel, which would
affect liquidity and, in turn, the bank’s loan.</span>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_802"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">8. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.288.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping Credit Policy</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">A shipping credit
policy is a package of general and specific guidelines that refer to
important factors for providing bank shipping loans, allocating
responsibilities and creating a mechanism of control.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.289.2" class="koboSpan">It creates an
internal shipping framework for the bank, within which loans are
initiated, analysed, approved, granted and monitored and is a means of
comparing the actual and projected performance.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.289.3" class="koboSpan">This may
differ from bank to bank. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.289.4"
class="koboSpan">For example, large commercial banks may have a credit
