manual for controls and responsibilities and procedures for all
departments, then specific guidelines for shipping setting only credit
boundaries for the portfolio; a financial institution that concentrates
on shipping and transport may have a more detailed shipping credit
policy.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.290.1" class="koboSpan">The skeleton outline
in
</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fig0404" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0404"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.291.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan"> covers the fundamental areas of the content of a
credit policy chart. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.292.2"
class="koboSpan">The overall exposure of the bank to the shipping
industry depends upon the decision for diversification or
specialisation. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.292.3"
class="koboSpan">The rule of thumb of portfolio theory is
diversification. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.292.4"
class="koboSpan">The extent of the bank’s involvement in shipping
finance, percentage-wise, versus other sectors, such as manufacturing,
agriculture, energy, aviation and real estate, depends upon a number of
factors, among which are the bank’s size; its geographical position
(small local bank or international bank operating in large business
capitals); its shipping expertise; the strength of its shipping
department and credit committee; the fact that the bank may be more
energy focused and therefore the shipping department more tanker
oriented; the bank’s loan loss experience, the shipping loan(s)’
perceived risk and its/their profitability compared to other sectors,
and the shipping sector’s overall security cover in comparison with that
of other banks. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.292.5"
class="koboSpan">Large international or regional commercial banks may
have an exposure to shipping between 1 and 5%, although a higher
exposure (such as 10%) is not totally unthinkable.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">A financial
institution may decide to allocate lending funds to different
geographical locations and/or shipping markets and/or shipping companies
to diversify its shipping portfolio.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.293.2" class="koboSpan">Geographical
diversification involves traditional or newer shipping centres, such as
London, New York, Piraeus, Oslo, Hamburg, Rotterdam, Nicosia, Istanbul,
Tokyo, Hong Kong, Singapore, Seoul and Shanghai.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.293.3" class="koboSpan">Market
diversification includes financing companies which operate different
types of vessels, for instance, wet/dry, container, cruise, passenger
and car. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.293.4" class="koboSpan">These
factors, individually or in combination, may affect the overall risk
profile and the bank’s exposure to such risk, in particular
during</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0404" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00424.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0404)

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_803"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan">a falling shipping market when income decreases and
payment of the loan capital and interest may become problematic.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">A shipping credit
policy may detail all types of shipping loans that the bank is to grant,
the maximum percentage of the market value of the vessel(s) to be
financed, in conjunction with the securities offered or the maximum
amount to be lent to a low-risk shipping company, on the basis of a
stable and sufficient cash flow.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.296.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
the spread, maturity, amortisation schedules, interest rates and
currencies may be discussed. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.296.3"
class="koboSpan">The array of securities, their usefulness and
limitations, in conjunction with properly documenting the loan, are part
of the credit policy. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.296.4"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, banks have been shocked to realise that poorly
drafted loan agreements and mortgages, or lack of proper communication
with insurance underwriters, have restrained or delayed them from
enforcing their rights, as lenders, on the borrower’s assets and other
collateral.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.297.1" class="koboSpan">In a credit policy
document, the bank should clarify whether shipping loans will be
financed on a syndicated or an individual basis.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.297.2" class="koboSpan">Syndication
strengthens the collective financial power of the bank and increases its
profitability through syndication fees.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.297.3" class="koboSpan">Individual
financing by a bank, in combination with relationship banking offered
services, strengthens profitability and loyalty.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">Administrative
aspects of loans, such as the maximum amount that can be granted by loan
officers, or at a higher level, and the type of decision-making
structure (centralised or decentralised), can be seen in a credit policy
document. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.298.2" class="koboSpan">In
the 1970s and 1980s, many European and Japanese banks were more
“bureaucratic”, while American banks followed the speedy
decentralisation approach. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.298.3"
class="koboSpan">In recent years there has been a distinct improvement
in the decision-making process for bank loans, which recognises the need
for a rapid reaction in the dynamic vessel sale and purchase market; the
new banking generation seems to be more oriented (and receptive) to
banking competition and, at the same time, is prepared to cooperate
through syndication. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.298.4"
class="koboSpan">Finally, the role of the credit committee and its
composition should also be explained in a credit policy document, as a
body which discusses, modifies, approves or turns down, credit proposals
of the shipping department.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.299.1" class="koboSpan">A powerful example of
the usefulness of credit policy is given in
</span><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fig0405" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0405"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.300.1" class="koboSpan">Table 8</span></a><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.301.2"
class="koboSpan">This shows the results of a survey on the shipping
credit policy of 10 international commercial banks and how it progressed
between 1979 and
1994.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0944" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0944"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.302.1" class="koboSpan">49</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan"> In 1979, the results of the study indicated that three
of the banks had quite clear (as detailed as in
</span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.304.1" class="koboSpan">Table
7</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_fig0404)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan">) shipping credit policies, while six had a vague
policy and one did not have an established</span>

<div id="Ch027.xhtml_fig0405" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00425.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fig0405)

</div>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_804"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan">shipping policy; in 1984, the two with a clear credit
policy suffered small to moderate loan losses; the banks with a vague
credit policy, and the third with a clear credit policy, suffered
moderate to substantial loan losses; while the losses of the bank
without credit policy were
devastating.</span><sup><a href="#Ch027.xhtml_fn0945" id="Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0945"><span
id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.308.1" class="koboSpan">50</span></a></sup><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan"> In 1994 the credit policy of the same banks were
reexamined. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.309.2"
class="koboSpan">The results reveal that nine of these 10 banks had
formulated a clear shipping credit policy, while the remaining bank,
which did not have a credit policy in 1979, was no longer in
business.</span>

## <span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">9. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.310.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.311.1" class="koboSpan">In this chapter,
minimising credit risk in bank shipping finance, for the acquisition of
vessels, has been discussed within the framework of the lending
function. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.311.2"
class="koboSpan">During this process, banks may be challenged by
information asymmetry, adverse selection and moral hazard.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">Bank Credit Policy
provides the framework within which credit risk analysis – as manifested
by the six “Cs” of credit – of shipping loan proposals takes place.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.312.2" class="koboSpan">Both bank
credit policy and credit risk analysis are the backbone of credit risk
control. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.312.3" class="koboSpan">Banks
also have other means – not cast iron, of course – to strengthen the
soundness of shipping loans: securities, covenants and
monitoring.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.313.1" class="koboSpan">Credit risk, or
credit default, may be measured by rating the loan and the shipping
company. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.313.2"
class="koboSpan">Rating is also linked to the default risk premium and
thus, to pricing. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.313.3"
class="koboSpan">Shipping loans are a substantial part of bank shipping
revenue, which is based on a wider web of services offered to shipping
companies – the relationship banking.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.313.4" class="koboSpan">As such it may
increase the gross profits of banks, and may strengthen their capital
base, a necessary path for increasing their value and a contributor to
sound banking expansion. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.313.5"
class="koboSpan">Capital soundness is a requirement of the Capital
Adequacy Rules; in 2008 new regulations were introduced across the
banking spectrum, on the use of rating and advanced statistical
techniques.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">In 1977 (see endnote
13) and in 1979 (see endnote 14) Grammenos stated that the market and
credit risk in bank shipping finance can be minimised by the use of two
basic tools.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.315.1" class="koboSpan">“…the formulation of
sound credit policy by the bank officials, after careful consideration
of relevant factors; and accurate and prudent credit analysis of each
shipping project proposed for finance.”</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">These still remain
the basic tools.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan">5.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0900)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan"> Altman, E. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.364.2"
class="koboSpan">I. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.364.3"
class="koboSpan">(1980), “Commercial Bank Lending: Process, Credit
Scoring and Costs of Errors in Lending”,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.365.1"
class="koboSpan">The Journal of Financial and Quantitative
Analysis</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan">, Proceedings Issue, Volume XV, No.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.366.2" class="koboSpan">4.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.366.3" class="koboSpan">In this paper,
Altman refers to the following four steps of the lending function: (i)
application for a loan; (ii) credit evolution; (iii) loan review; and
(iv) repayment performance.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan">6.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0901)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan"> A financial institution that lends funds to shipping
companies for acquisitions of secondhand vessels or placements of
newbuilding orders may face additional
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_806"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.369.1"
class="koboSpan">risks – such as interest rate risk, where the
probability of a change in interest rates may adversely affect the
bank’s profit margin (this happens when a financial institution converts
a deposit into a loan and does not match the deposit’s period of its
customer, or the deposit’s period that obtains from the Interbank Market
with the period of the loan); liquidity risk which is the probability of
the bank not having sufficient cash and proper borrowing capacity (cash
destruction) to match deposit withdrawals, resulting in its paying
higher interest rates on borrowed funds; or solvency risk which is the
probability of a financial institution withdrawing from the market due
to inadequate funds (capital destruction) to meet losses from bank loans
or deterioration in the market value of the asset portfolio.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.369.2" class="koboSpan">Cash
destruction leads to liquidity crisis; while capital destruction leads
to solvency crisis.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.370.1"

class="koboSpan">Th. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.371.3"
class="koboSpan">(1979),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.372.1"
class="koboSpan">Bank Finance for Ship
Purchase</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.373.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.374.1"
class="koboSpan">Occasional Papers in
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.375.1"
class="koboSpan">, University of Wales Press, Ch.2.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.376.1"
class="koboSpan">8.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0903)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.377.1"
class="koboSpan"> The shipping industry uses mainly the eurodollar
market, which is the largest unregulated market for deposits in dollars
placed outside the United States; and for euroloans which are dollar
denominated loans granted by banks outside the United States.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan">12.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0907)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan"> This chapter discusses the management of credit risk
by using physical instruments (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.404.2" class="koboSpan">collateral
securities); however, in corporate finance they quantify such a risk and
often use very expensive credit derivatives.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.404.3" class="koboSpan">These
derivatives have been mainly – and not widely – used, during the last
decade, by major financial institutions for large shipping loans of
higher perceived credit risk. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.404.4"
class="koboSpan">For more details on credit derivatives, see for example
Hull, J. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.404.5"
class="koboSpan">(2008),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.405.1"
class="koboSpan">Options Futures and other
Derivatives</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.406.1"
class="koboSpan">, Prentice Hall International; and for a discussion on
the use of credit derivatives by banks to secure the risk associated
with loans, see Duffee, G. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.406.2"
class="koboSpan">R. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.406.3"
class="koboSpan">and Zhou, C. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.406.4"
class="koboSpan">(2001), “Credit Derivatives in Banking: Useful Tools
for Managing Risk”,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.407.1"
class="koboSpan">Journal of Monetary
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.408.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2001, Vol. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.408.2"
class="koboSpan">48, No. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.408.3"
class="koboSpan">1, 25–55; and Minton
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.409.1"
class="koboSpan">et al. </span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan">(2009), “How Much Do Banks Use Credit Derivatives to
Hedge Loans?”,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.411.1"
class="koboSpan">Journal of Financial
Reserves</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.412.1"
class="koboSpan">, Vol. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.412.2"
class="koboSpan">35, 1–31.</span>

<span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_807"></span>[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.413.1"
class="koboSpan">13.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0908)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.414.1"
class="koboSpan"> Grammenos, C. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.414.2"
class="koboSpan">Th. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.414.3"
class="koboSpan">(1977), “The Need for Credit Policy and Analysis in
Bank Shipping Finance”, Paper presented at Institute of European
Finance, Bangor.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.415.1"
class="koboSpan">14.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0909)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.416.1"
class="koboSpan"> Grammenos, C. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.416.2"
class="koboSpan">Th. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.416.3"
class="koboSpan">(1979),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.417.1"
class="koboSpan">Bank Finance for Ship
Purchase</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.418.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.419.1"
class="koboSpan">Occasional Papers in
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.420.1"
class="koboSpan">, University of Wales Press.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.420.2" class="koboSpan">In this book,
the author processed and analysed over 350 confidential files of loans
granted by five international banks, and one regional, to shipping
companies mainly for second-hand purchases, but also for newbuildings.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.420.3" class="koboSpan">Principles for
granting sound loans were established through the introduction of credit
analysis (the so called five C’s of Credit Analysis) and credit
policy.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.421.1"
class="koboSpan">15.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0910)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.422.1"
class="koboSpan"> See Section 3.4.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.423.1"
class="koboSpan">16.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0911)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.424.1"
class="koboSpan"> Grammenos, C. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.424.2"
class="koboSpan">Th. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.424.3"
class="koboSpan">(1994), Nautical Institute Annual Lecture, Royal
Society of Arts, London. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.424.4"
class="koboSpan">In this presentation, the author referred to 100
problematic loans as they stood in 1984.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.424.5" class="koboSpan">The loans were
granted between August 1979 and end 1980 to medium-size shipping
companies, by international medium- to large-size banks.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.424.6" class="koboSpan">The striking
common elements of all of them are that loans were provided when freight
rates and market values of the vessels were high; the financing of the
market value of the vessels was between 75 and 85%; and these vessels
had to compete in a recessed or depressed shipping market from 1983–1986
with other vessels bought at much lower prices.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.425.1"
class="koboSpan">17.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0912)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.426.1"
class="koboSpan"> Pre-Tax Funds flow and Interest Coverage = Net Income
(Loss) from continuing operations + Gross Interest Expense – Interest
Capitalised + Income Tax Expense + Depreciation + Amortization ÷ Gross
Interest Expense.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.427.1"
class="koboSpan">18.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0913)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.428.1"
class="koboSpan"> The market value of the vessel over the outstanding
debt that the company incurs for the vessel’s purchase.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.428.2" class="koboSpan">See for
further explanation, section 4.1.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.429.1"
class="koboSpan">19.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0914)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.430.1"
class="koboSpan"> Two ratios related to cash flow and cash cushion,
employed at a great extent by Moody’s in their rating methodology of
shipping high yield bonds, are the free cash flow (FCF) to debt and the
cash reserves. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.430.2"
class="koboSpan">The FCF-to-debt ratio reflects the cash flow after
capital expenditure, and focuses on the assessment of debt repayment
capacity. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.430.3" class="koboSpan">A
company with a negative FCF-to-debt ratio is considered more vulnerable
to liquidity shocks than a company with a positive ratio.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.430.4" class="koboSpan">Cash reserves,
measured as cash and cash equivalents to total assets, is a snapshot
measure of immediate cash availability (Moody’s, 2010.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.430.5" class="koboSpan">Shipping
Rating Methodology: Global Shipping Industry).</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.431.1"
class="koboSpan">20.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0915)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.432.1"
class="koboSpan"> An important reason for the establishment of such
companies is the “sister ship” principle, which is found in many
jurisidictions, according to which a claim
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.433.1"
class="koboSpan">in rem</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.434.1"
class="koboSpan">, that is to say a claim in object, can be transferred
to any other vessel, which belongs to the same beneficial owner.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.434.2" class="koboSpan">The creation
of different shipping companies of limited liability, each one of which
owns one vessel and all of these still controlled by the same owner,
over-rides the “sister ship” principle.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.434.3" class="koboSpan">Claims which
arise against a particular vessel of this fleet, for example, by a bank
or trade creditors, cannot be transferred to any other vessel of the
fleet.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.435.1"
class="koboSpan">21.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0916)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.436.1"
class="koboSpan"> Capital costs are affected by the capital structure of
the company. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.436.2"
class="koboSpan">The cost of banking loans is still the lowest, in
comparison with bond and high yield issues, while the cost of equity is
the highest. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.436.3"
class="koboSpan">The overall cost of capital including debt, preferred
stock and common equity, the weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
decreases initially with marginal increases in debt until the point that
the company reaches
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_808"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.437.1"
class="koboSpan">its optimal capital structure.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.437.2" class="koboSpan">Beyond this
point, an increase in debt may result in increase of WACC.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.437.3" class="koboSpan">For more
information on the WACC concept and estimation see Myers and Brealey
(2005), Principles of Corporate Finance, McGraw-Hill/Irwin, Chapter 17
and Ferro (2009), “The Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) for Firm
Valuation Calculations”, International Research Journal of Finance and
Economics, Issue 26, 148–150.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.438.1"
class="koboSpan">22.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0917)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.439.1"
class="koboSpan"> Metaxas, B. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.439.2"
class="koboSpan">N. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.439.3"
class="koboSpan">(1971),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.440.1"
class="koboSpan">The Economics of Tramp
Shipping</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.441.1"
class="koboSpan">, The Athlone Press, chapter 7.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.441.2" class="koboSpan">In this
quotation, Metaxas refers to “tramp shipping services”, since his book
is on tramp shipping. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.441.3"
class="koboSpan">However, his quotation applies to liner as well.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.442.1"
class="koboSpan">23.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0918)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.443.1"
class="koboSpan"> For an analysis of fluctuations in shipping and
shipping cycles, see Metaxas, B.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.443.2" class="koboSpan">N.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.443.3" class="koboSpan">(1971),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.444.1"
class="koboSpan">The Economics of Tramp
Shipping</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.445.1"
class="koboSpan">, The Athlone Press, chapter 3; Stopford, M.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.445.2" class="koboSpan">(1997),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.446.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.447.1"
class="koboSpan">, Routledge, chapter 2; Grammenos, C.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.447.2" class="koboSpan">Th.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.447.3" class="koboSpan">(1979),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.448.1"
class="koboSpan">Bank Finance for Ship
Purchase</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.449.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.450.1"
class="koboSpan">Occasional Papers in
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.451.1"
class="koboSpan">, University of Wales Press, chapter 2.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.451.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
see Chapter 9 of this volume for a detailed analysis of shipping market
cycles.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.452.1"
class="koboSpan">24.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0919)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.453.1"
class="koboSpan"> For a more detailed discussion on different types of
shipping investment, including speculative asset play in relation to
shipping cycles, see Chapter 23 of this volume.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.454.1"
class="koboSpan">25.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0920)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.455.1"
class="koboSpan"> The cash flow calculation for vessel(s) to be financed
will be based on total cash receipts minus total operating and capital
costs covering the period over which the loan will be repaid with a view
to estimate the breakeven freight rate of the vessel(s) and the overall
fleet and undertake a risk evaluation for the bank.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.455.2" class="koboSpan">Cash receipts
include operating gross revenue, which could be fixed should there be
contract of affreightment or time charter; while assumed revenue, should
the vessel operate in the spot market, may be based on past (average
over the last 10 years), prevailing, and expected, conditions in the
vessel(s)’ market. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.455.3"
class="koboSpan">Operating expenses should be comparable to expenses of
similar vessels; while projected ones should be escalated to take into
account the rate of inflation. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.455.4"
class="koboSpan">Debt service should be projected in accordance with
actual loan repayment with assumed interest rates, should the interest
be fluctuating. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.455.5"
class="koboSpan">These items should be part of a scenario analysis
(positive and negative), where sensitivity analysis is used.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.456.1"
class="koboSpan">26.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0921)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.457.1"
class="koboSpan"> In a depression phase of the shipping cycle, the
charterers may be hit by the market as well.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.457.2" class="koboSpan">Thirty of the
100 problematic loans referred to in 16 of this chapter became
problematic due to the financial troubles of the charterers of the
vessels.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.458.1"
class="koboSpan">27.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0922)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.459.1"
class="koboSpan"> See section 6 of this chapter.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.460.1"
class="koboSpan">28.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0923)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.461.1"
class="koboSpan"> This section draws on Grammenos, C.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.461.2" class="koboSpan">Th.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.461.3" class="koboSpan">(1979),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.462.1"
class="koboSpan">Bank Finance for Ship
Purchase</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.463.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.464.1"
class="koboSpan">Occasional Papers in
Economics</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.465.1"
class="koboSpan">, University of Wales Press, chapter 2, and Grammenos,
C. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.465.2" class="koboSpan">Th.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.465.3" class="koboSpan">and Xilas, E.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.465.4" class="koboSpan">M.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.465.5" class="koboSpan">(1988),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.466.1"
class="koboSpan">Shipping Investment and
Finance</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.467.1"
class="koboSpan">, V ol. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.467.2"
class="koboSpan">II, unpublished notes for MSc Students in Shipping,

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.468.1"
class="koboSpan">29.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0924)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.469.1"
class="koboSpan"> UK Merchant Shipping Act 1894.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.470.1"
class="koboSpan">30.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0925)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.471.1"
class="koboSpan"> The Statutory Mortgage is normally accompanied by
further terms and conditions in a separate agreement that acts as back
up.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.472.1"
class="koboSpan">31.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0926)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.473.1"
class="koboSpan"> However, holders of maritime liens have a priority
over the claims of a mortgagee. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.473.2"
class="koboSpan">Maritime lien is a claim against a vessel, which can be
made effective by the seizure of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.473.3" class="koboSpan">It is a right
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.474.1"
class="koboSpan">in rem</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.475.1"
class="koboSpan">, that is to say, it is attached to the vessel even
after change of ownership. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.475.2"
class="koboSpan">Among maritime liens are: salvage, seamen’s and
master’s wages, master’s disbursements, damages caused by the
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_page_809"></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.476.1"
class="koboSpan">vessel (e.g. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.476.2"
class="koboSpan">in collision). </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.476.3"
class="koboSpan">Possessory lien is the right of a holder of such claim,
to retain possession of the vessel for any incurred expenses until the
debt is paid. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.476.4"
class="koboSpan">A typical example in this context is the ship repairer
or shipyard. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.476.5"
class="koboSpan">The possessory lien will be lost as soon as the
claimant ceases possession of the vessel.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.476.6" class="koboSpan">Some rights of
possessory liens may be created by statute (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.476.7" class="koboSpan">unpaid port
and canal dues). </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.476.8"
class="koboSpan">The importance for the lender is that the holder of
maritime, possessory and statutory liens will have – depending upon the
jurisdiction – a priority over its claims.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.477.1"
class="koboSpan">32.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0927)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.478.1"
class="koboSpan"> The value for which a vessel is insured.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.479.1"
class="koboSpan">33.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0928)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.480.1"
class="koboSpan"> The value of a vessel in terms of historical cost
minus accumulated depreciation.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.481.1"
class="koboSpan">34.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0929)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.482.1"
class="koboSpan"> Protection and Indemnity falls outside the scope of
ordinary marine insurance. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.482.2"
class="koboSpan">It is structured through membership of Protection and
Indemnity Associations (often referred to as P & I Clubs), which are
formed and run by shipowners.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.483.1"
class="koboSpan">35.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0930)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.484.1"
class="koboSpan"> Walker, E. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.484.2"
class="koboSpan">W. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.484.3"
class="koboSpan">and Petty, J. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.484.4"
class="koboSpan">W. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.484.5"
class="koboSpan">(1978), “Financial Differences Between Large and Small
Firms” </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.485.1"
class="koboSpan">Financial
Management</span></span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.486.1"
class="koboSpan">, Winter, 61–68.</span>

[<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.487.1"
class="koboSpan">36.</span>](#Ch027.xhtml_bck_fn0931)<span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.488.1"
class="koboSpan"> Apilado, V. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.488.2"
class="koboSpan">P. </span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.488.3"
class="koboSpan">and Millington, J.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.488.4" class="koboSpan">K.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.488.5" class="koboSpan">(1992),
“Restrictive Loan Covenants and Risk Adjustment in Small Business
Lending”, </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.489.1"
class="koboSpan">Journal of Small Business

</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.520.3" class="koboSpan">Three

</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.520.4" class="koboSpan">They are:

the bank; “Substandard” loans which have some deficiencies that may be

statements) and appear to carry lower risk of borrower default.
</span><span id="Ch027.xhtml_kobo.520.6" class="koboSpan">All other
loans are considered to be sound.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping Finance and International Capital Markets</span>](#Preface1.xhtml_bck_ht0619)

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Theodore</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">C.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Syriopoulos</span></span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fn0946" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fn0946"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fn0947" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fn0947"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a>

## <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter discusses
key issues in modern shipping finance and explores the growing role of
global capital markets in fund-raising for investment projects of
shipping firms. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.9.2"
class="koboSpan">We critically assess the attractiveness and efficiency
of international equity and bond markets in particular, as important
ship financing mechanisms that offer funding opportunities distinctive
from traditional bank lending.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">The structure of the
chapter is as follows. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.10.2"
class="koboSpan">Section 2 discusses the financial decisions in shipping
and the implications of the capital structure mix for the financial
performance of the firm. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.10.3"
class="koboSpan">The major phases in modern ship finance are summarised
and the dynamic role of global capital markets in shipping finance is
assessed. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.10.4"
class="koboSpan">Section 3 examines in details the function of equity
markets as a financing mechanism, discusses the pricing of equity
issues, analyses the risk return and volatility profile of shipping
stocks and concludes with a brief presentation of alternative hybrid
financing instruments. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.10.5"
class="koboSpan">Section 4 covers the role and functions of bond markets
with a focus on shipping bond credit rating and probability of default.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.10.6" class="koboSpan">Section 5
contributes a note on the important issue of efficient corporate
governance mechanisms, emphasising on implications for shipping firms.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.10.7" class="koboSpan">Section 6
concludes.</span>

## <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">Financial Decisions in Shipping</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Strategic finance dynamics</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">An important shift has
been seen recently in shipping finance instruments.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.13.2" class="koboSpan">International
capital markets, predominantly equity and bond markets, have gradually
gained a growing share in fund-raising for shipping firms (Syriopoulos,
2007). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.13.3" class="koboSpan">The
capital intensity and
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_812"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan">magnitude of shipping investments requires capital
availability at reasonable cost, but also careful project selection,
based on a solid capital budgeting framework (Cullinane and Panayides,
2000). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">In a
highly dynamic and volatile business environment, modern shipping
finance becomes highly sophisticated, innovative and complex.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping is a cyclical
industry with idiosyncratic characteristics, highly leveraged assets,
active second hand market and an estimated average ROA at 10% (Veraros,
2008). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Market
timing is critical to shipping investment decisions that bear high
levels of risk and uncertainty. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.15.3"
class="koboSpan">The behavioural pattern of shipping business is related
to a number of factors, including, predominantly, the derived nature of
shipping demand being sensitive to economic growth and trade,
cyclicality in freight rates and vessel prices, demand and supply
imbalances and fragmented business structure.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.15.4" class="koboSpan">The issue of
optimal capital structure mix and the appropriate funding method is
critical for an industry that is capital intensive and its operation
employs real assets (vessels) of high commercial value.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">Strategic decision
making in shipping firms gradually shifts from simple profit
maximisation to corporate value enhancement.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">To attain this,
shipping firms require a selection of investment plans that bear growth
potential and produce positive returns higher than the respective cost
of capital employed. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.16.3"
class="koboSpan">Intensified competition and tighten margins in the
shipping markets have led companies to constantly pursue managerial
efficiency, operational flexibility, and robust financial liquidity.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.16.4" class="koboSpan">A shipping
company can attain business growth by following either an internal or
external course of development. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.16.5"
class="koboSpan">Subject to freight market conditions, shipping firms
can expand their fleet by building new assets or purchasing second hand
vessels. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.16.6" class="koboSpan">On the
other hand, mergers, acquisitions and strategic alliances can be an
alternative external growth path.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.16.7" class="koboSpan">In any case,
these corporate growth strategies, combined with replacement
requirements of ageing fleets, require substantial capital funding and
careful financial planning.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">As shipping companies
adjust to a dynamic and rapidly changing environment so do the financial
methods and instruments available to funding their investments.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">Convenient,
cheap and timely access to capital financing is a prerequisite for a
flexible capital structure mix, competitiveness, undisturbed operation
and sustainable growth, particularly for shipping business.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.3" class="koboSpan">Two broad
approaches in fund raising can be distinguished: (1) self-sustained or
internal funding, by own (shareholder) equity finance; and (2) external
funding, by debt finance (borrowing).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.4" class="koboSpan">Increases in
own equity are based on corporate profitability and robust retained
earnings sufficient to finance prospective investment projects.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.5" class="koboSpan">This source of
funding is directly affected by the dividend policy of the firm that
defines profit share distribution to shareholders, albeit at the expense
of potential reinvestment decisions.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.6" class="koboSpan">As to external
financing, shipping firms can alternatively turn towards international
capital markets in order to raise investment funding.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.7" class="koboSpan">Debt financing
may come from bank lending of wide variety and sophistication (bank
mortgages, leasing, mezzanine finance, securitisation).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.8" class="koboSpan">In fact, this
has been the prevailing and dominant source of ship funding over the
years. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.9"
class="koboSpan">Alternatively, shipping firms can turn into
international debt markets to issue corporate bond securities or
commercial paper. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.17.10"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, global equity markets can enhance own
equity funding by issues of Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) or Seasoned
Equity Offerings (SEOs).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">The role of capital
markets is critical for the promotion of shipping business growth and
the creation of corporate value, since capital markets perform the
following fundamental functions. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.18.2"
class="koboSpan">As ‘primary’ markets, capital markets act as
intermediaries to provide the funds required to financing new investment
projects and sustain business
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_813"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">growth. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">Fresh funds are channelled to firms in need through the
issuance of securities. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.19.3"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, as ‘secondary’ markets, capital markets
provide an efficient mechanism for valuation and trading of outstanding
equity and bond securities. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.19.4"
class="koboSpan">Growth potentials then of the underlying shipping firm
(issuer) are reflected on the price movements of the issued securities,
signalling investors’ perception of the firm’s value creation
prospects.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">Despite the marginal
participation of international capital markets in ship finance for a
number of years, some revitalisation is seen in public equity and bond
issues more recently, on top of dominant bank lending.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
recent global financial crisis, escalated since mid-2008, may affect
shipping firms’ priorities as to their sources of capital funding.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.20.3" class="koboSpan">This is related
to the fact that this unprecedented crisis and the induced economic
recessionary phase directly involve the international banking system as
a cause of the problem rather than simply as a victim of it.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.20.4" class="koboSpan">Combined with
pressures imposed by a much more demanding disciplinary framework, such
as the Basel II Accord and governmental supervisory constraints, bank
lending is expected to become more careful, selective, conservative
(relative to commercial risks undertaken) and, ultimately,
scarce.</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Capital structure and financial performance</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">A company can obtain
long-term financing in the form of equity (issuing shares), debt
(borrowing), retained profits or some combination.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">There is a
fundamental distinction between equity and debt as sources of capital:
equity refers to firm’s own funding by its shareholders and shares
correspond to ownership rights. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.22.3"
class="koboSpan">Debt, on the other hand, implies a core liability the
firm has to meet over a plausible time horizon.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.22.4" class="koboSpan">A fundamental
financial decision then relates to which of the two major fund raising
approaches or mix should the firm prefer to finance its investment
projects. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.22.5" class="koboSpan">The
relative proportion of debt, equity and other outstanding securities
constitutes the firm’s capital structure.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">When corporations
raise new funds from outside investors, they must choose which type of
security to issue. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.23.2"
class="koboSpan">The most common choice is financing through equity
alone or through a combination of debt and equity.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.23.3" class="koboSpan">Whatever the
firm’s choice, this affects the weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
and has critical implications for the firm’s ROE and risk.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.23.4" class="koboSpan">The firm can
attain growth and enhance corporate value only in case it undertakes
investment projects that produce returns higher than their cost of
capital funding. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.23.5"
class="koboSpan">An incorrect financing decision may result in many
forms of higher direct or indirect costs, such as higher cost of
capital, lower stock price and lost growth opportunities, increased
probability of bankruptcy, higher agency cost and possible wealth
transfers from one group of investors to another.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">The seminal
Modigliani-Miller (MM) theorem on the ‘capital structure irrelevance
principle’ has been the cornerstone of the firm’s capital structure
decisions in perfect markets (Modigliani and Miller, 1958).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">According to
the MM theorem, in an efficient market that follows a certain price
process (random walk), in the absence of taxes, bankruptcy costs and
asymmetric information, the value of a firm is unaffected by how that
firm is financed. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.24.3"
class="koboSpan">It does not matter if the firm’s capital is raised by
issuing stock or selling debt or what the firm’s dividend policy is.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.24.4" class="koboSpan">In other words,
the market value of a firm is determined by its earning power and the
risk of its underlying assets and is independent of the way it chooses
to finance its investments or distribute dividends (Pagano, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.24.5" class="koboSpan">However, as a
firm’s debt increases, critics of the MM theorem argue, the increased
risk of bankruptcy is ignored, though it can be substantial.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.24.6" class="koboSpan">Bankruptcy
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_814"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">costs have two components: (1) the probability of
financial distress; and, (2) the costs that would be incurred given that
financial distress occurs. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.2"
class="koboSpan">This relates to the ‘trade-off theory of leverage’ in
which firms trade off the benefits of debt financing (favourable
corporate tax treatment) against higher interest rates and bankruptcy
costs. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.3" class="koboSpan">In
practice, managers often have better information than outside investors,
implying asymmetric (and not symmetric) information effects.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.4" class="koboSpan">Financing
decisions then indicate some signalling to market participants about the
firm’s prospects, according to the ‘signalling theory’.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.5" class="koboSpan">For instance,
the announcement of a stock offering is generally taken as a signal that
the firm’s prospects, as seen by its management, are not bright.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.6" class="koboSpan">A firm with
positive prospects would try to avoid selling stock and seek to raise
new capital by other sources instead; a debt offering is then taken as a
positive signal. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.7"
class="koboSpan">Issuing stock emits a negative signal, potentially
depressing the stock price (even if the firm’s prospects are positive),
so the firm should maintain a ‘reserve borrowing capacity’ to finance
exceptional investment opportunities.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.8" class="koboSpan">This in turn
implies that firms should, in normal times, use more equity and less
debt than is suggested by the trade-off theory of leverage.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.9" class="koboSpan">However, the
presence of flotation costs and asymmetric information may cause a firm
to raise capital according to a ‘pecking order’.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.10" class="koboSpan">In this case,
a firm first raises capital internally by reinvesting its net income and
selling its short-term marketable securities.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.11" class="koboSpan">When that
supply of funds has been exhausted, the firm will issue debt and perhaps
preferred stock. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.25.12"
class="koboSpan">The firm will only issue common stock as a last
resort.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">To conclude, the
optimal capital structure for the firm is that which maximises corporate
market value (the firm’s stock price).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.26.2" class="koboSpan">This generally
calls for a debt ratio that is lower than the one that maximises
expected earnings per share (EPS).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.26.3" class="koboSpan">As a brief
illustration,
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0406" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0406"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan"> summarises the capital structure and financial
performance of a diversified sample of shipping firms listed in the US
equity markets (NYSE, NASDAQ), as they are depicted by the debt-equity
ratio, Return on Equity (ROE) and Return on Assets (ROA).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">An anticipated,
though striking, finding points to the extremely high debt/equity ratios
for most of the shipping firms in the sample, albeit at diverging
levels. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">This
holds irrespective of the corresponding market segment and supports the
view that shipping finance is heavily dependent on debt funding over
time.</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">2.3 Major phases in modern shipping finance</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">During the last 30
years, international shipping markets have been moving through a
volatile sequence of upward and downward swings but culminated in an
extraordinary eight-year boom from 2001 to 2008.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">Over this
period, daily earnings soared persistently from US \$24,000 to US
\$50,000. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.30.3" class="koboSpan">Then,
the global financial crisis and economic recession hit the world economy
as well as the shipping markets. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.30.4"
class="koboSpan">Freight earnings crashed down to a daily bottom of US
\$5,000 in (handymax) dry bulk markets before gradually adjust to US
\$8,500 by mid-2009, with many vessels though still earning less than
operating costs. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.30.5"
class="koboSpan">At the same time, the bulker fleet grew by a robust
10.8% rate and the balance in fundamentals worsened (Stopford, 2009,
2010). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.30.6"
class="koboSpan">Diverging shipping demand and supply imbalances were
already apparent in the 2007 figures; there were three times as many
orders as deliveries (270 mln dwt vs 80 mln dwt).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.30.7" class="koboSpan">Based on
end-2009 estimates the market value of a consolidated order book was
standing at around US \$300 bn, a figure which raises scepticism as to
the recovery horizon of the shipping business.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.30.8" class="koboSpan">This gloomy
international environment has captured shipping companies into unfolding
capital investment programmes, abrupt earnings decline and excess
tonnage</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_815"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0406)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00426.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0406)

</div>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0407" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_816"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0407)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00427.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0407)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">capacity, with an
ailing global banking system under restructuring (Clarkson Research
Services, 2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.33.2"
class="koboSpan">This in turn raises market concerns about the critical
adjustments required in shipping firms’ capital funding decisions and
the most appropriate financing instruments for the time being.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">The methods,
instruments and characteristics of ship finance are seen to change over
time, adjusting accordingly to the prevailing economic, market and
sectoral conditions. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.34.2"
class="koboSpan">Five major phases in modern ship finance can be
distinguished during 1950–2000, according to Stopford (2002); we expand
this framework to add a recent, sixth, ship finance phase (see
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0407" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0407"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.36.2"
class="koboSpan">These phases have been closely associated with shifts
in shipping market fundamentals, predominantly international trade and
fleet growth.</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0408" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00428.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Major sources of ship finance" /></span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_817"></span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0213"
id="Ch028.xhtml_cap_lbl0213"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan"> Major sources of ship finance</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan"> Lloyd’s Shipping Economist (2005)</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, according
to Lloyd’s estimates, the contribution of major capital funding sources
to shipping is seen to diverge substantially over time (Matthews, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.42.2" class="koboSpan">‘Debt
financing’, predominantly bank loans, continues accounting for the
largest share of shipping finance.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.42.3" class="koboSpan">Over the last
decade, the annual volume of syndicated debt gradually five-folded, from
US \$2 bn to over US \$10 bn. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.42.4"
class="koboSpan">A broad source of funding, termed ‘other’, corresponds
to more than one-third of the pie and incorporates diversified financing
instruments, such as bilateral loans, shipyard credit, governmental
contributions and internal equity finance.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.42.5" class="koboSpan">International
capital markets are seen to gradually gain an active role in shipping
finance. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.42.6" class="koboSpan">The
respective shares of global equity markets (IPOs) and debt markets (bond
issues) are estimated at 2–3% each.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.42.7" class="koboSpan">The K/S
partnerships in Norway and particularly the KG companies in Germany are
also considered critical financing vehicles in shipping business.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.42.8" class="koboSpan">The remaining
capital share is associated with a variety of funding sources
(see</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_cap_lbl0213"
id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0213"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan"> Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">2.4 The dynamic role of capital markets in shipping</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">Following a period of
fast and robust growth rates, shipping markets collapsed in the fourth
quarter of 2008. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.46.2"
class="koboSpan">Freight earnings evaporated abruptly, as the global
financial crisis escalated. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.46.3"
class="koboSpan">In an environment of severe adjustments in the banking
sector, liquidity constraints and overcapacity conditions, shipping
market players have been wondering what their next steps should be.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.46.4" class="koboSpan">Fundamental
questions, as to whether to expand business operations, consolidate with
a competitor or proceed to asset liquidation and exit the market, remain
unanswered. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.46.5"
class="koboSpan">These strategic decisions are examined against a
consolidated order book of an estimated contract value exceeding \$300
bn (end-2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.46.6"
class="koboSpan">This, nevertheless, remains an attractive capital pie
for financiers, shipyards and brokers (Clarkson Research Services,
2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.46.7" class="koboSpan">In this
setting of recessionary conditions, banking
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_818"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan">restructuring and freight market swings, a key question
remains where all this funding will come from.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">A convenient
and timely response to the question of capital fund raising has critical
implications for shipping firms’ capital structure, cost of capital,
cash flow liquidity, profitability and performance (ROA, ROE) and
ultimately shareholder value. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.47.3"
class="koboSpan">As has been invariably the case in past shipping market
history, financial crises also imply entrepreneurial opportunities for
prudent shipowners.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">The shipping business
consists of approximately 30,000 companies and is one of the most
finance-intensive industries. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.48.2"
class="koboSpan">Financing requirements per annum have been roughly
estimated at US \$80 bn for funding only new buildings (Goulielmos and
Psifia, 2006). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.48.3"
class="koboSpan">Traditional bank lending dominates ship finance over
time, although some decline in its share has been recorded more recently
at around 65%, in favour of alternative forms of financing (Petropoulos,
2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.48.4" class="koboSpan">Shipping
finance techniques and instruments become more innovative and synthetic.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.48.5" class="koboSpan">An increasing
number of shipping companies is seen to gradually switch towards
international capital markets, to finance their ambitious investment
projects by equity funding (stock markets) or debt issuing (bonds
markets). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.48.6"
class="koboSpan">Traditional and modern ship finance instruments can be
distinguished into three broad classes: (1) equity finance: public
funding (IPOs); seasoned equity offerings (SEOs); retained earnings
(operations and sales), private equity funding; (2) debt finance: bank
lending (wide variety and sophistication), corporate bond issues,
specialised financial institutions, shipyard finance, private debt
finance; (3) alternative finance: lease, mezzanine finance,
securitisation, hybrid finance (Syriopoulos, 2007).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">The year 2005 was
declared ‘the year of the shipping IPOs’, as 12 new shipping firms
raised more than US \$4 bn in US equity market IPOs, most of them of
Greek shipownership. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.49.2"
class="koboSpan">In fact, from 2005–2007, Greek shipping companies alone
raised total funds of about US \$1.5 bn in the US markets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.49.3" class="koboSpan">The renaissance
of shipping IPO market was confirmed by a tenfold increase in the funds
raised by the industry, according to Lloyd’s estimates.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.49.4" class="koboSpan">As market
timing proved to be right, fund raising was further supported by freight
rates sky-rocketed at record levels and international investors’
appetite for ‘fashionable’ shipping stocks.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.49.5" class="koboSpan">Investors,
after all, remain in constant search of attractive investment
opportunities and alternative style investments (Bernstein, 1995).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.49.6" class="koboSpan">This trend
underlines an important shift not only in shipping finance decisions and
the capital structure of the firm but in the corporate governance front
as well. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.49.7"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies, previously private, family owned
and managed, introverted, with no disclosure constraints were now being
transformed into publicly listed, extrovert, multi-shareholder entities
with ownership dilution and extensive disclosure responsibilities
(Syriopoulos and Theotokas, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.49.8" class="koboSpan">These issues
have considerable implications for the growth prospects of shipping
firms as well as for the risk-return profile of the listed shipping
stocks and can directly affect shareholder value and investors’ asset
allocation decisions.</span>

## <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.50.2" class="koboSpan">Equity Markets and Shipping IPOs</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Shipping firms discover equity markets</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">Despite the fact that
bank lending continues dominating shipping finance, a gradual shift in
shipping firms’ funding attitudes has been apparent more recently in
favour of international equity markets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.52.2" class="koboSpan">This shift has
been associated with the interactive impact of critical factors,
including internationalisation and integration of global capital
markets;
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_819"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan">deficiencies and consolidation of major banking
players; emphasis on capital adequacy and ‘solvency ratios’ by banks,
shipping firms and investors; liquidity constraints and erosion of firm
capital reserves; substantial funding requirements to replace ageing
fleets; structural and cultural adjustment of shipping firms, partly
induced by capital market requirements and investors’ expectations;
extrovert market approach and promotion of wider multi-shareholdership;
market visibility and prestige towards institutional and private
investors; emphasis on the concepts of corporate governance, social
responsibility and business ethics.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Expanding on these
issues, major advantages for shipping firms going public include: (i)
access to capital markets that are not readily available to private
companies; (ii) liquidity, at potentially higher valuations, if the
company’s fundamental are compelling enough to attract new investors;
(iii) stock options as a means to attract and retain key personnel; (iv)
opportunities for companies to utilise their stock to acquire other
companies. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.54.2"
class="koboSpan">However, the long-term attractiveness of international
equity markets for shipping companies will only be sustained in case
freight and equity market performance remains robust and corporate
profitability is less volatile.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">Until 2004, equity
markets had played only a marginal role in shipping finance, despite
their prime role as an investment funding mechanism.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">From an
investor’s point of view, historically, shipping stocks were not a
particularly attractive choice for fund allocation but had a rather
‘negative’ reputation. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.55.3"
class="koboSpan">This adverse attitude can partly be related to a series
of shipping defaults in the 1990s, including, bank loans, high yield
bonds and corporate bankruptcies.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.55.4" class="koboSpan">Other reasons
include close family ownership ties, reluctance of shipowners to dilute
company control, non-disclosure of sensitive company information and the
unattractiveness of shipping stocks due to volatile earnings
(Syriopoulos, 2007). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.55.5"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies only recently have discovered the
virtues of public listing on international stock exchanges.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.55.6" class="koboSpan">The shipping
IPO wave, during 2000–2007, has tackled investors’ appetite, as the
latter also discover the attractiveness of exchange traded shipping
firms. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.55.7" class="koboSpan">This
trend has been supported by booming freight rates and strong balance
sheets in an environment of bullish stock markets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.55.8" class="koboSpan">Steady growth
rates in the US economy and high growth rates in the Chinese economy,
particularly during 2003–2007, led the shipping sector into a unique
growth super-cycle during 2002–2008, generating strong earnings and cash
flows.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping IPOs are
distinct from those of ordinary industrial or service companies.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">The market
value of a shipping company is often closely associated with the
underlying value of the physical assets (vessels).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.56.3" class="koboSpan">In this
respect, shipping IPOs bear similarities with the respective IPOs of
closed-end funds and property firms.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.56.4" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
due to extensive information flows in international vessel sales and
purchase markets, shipping IPOs tend to exhibit lower information
asymmetry. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.56.5" class="koboSpan">Due
to the cyclical nature of shipping business, shipping firms tend to
prefer listing on the equity markets whenever shipping market prospects
appear to be robust.</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Leading equity markets in shipping IPOs</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">In the 1980s, the
universe of publicly listed shipping stocks was small and London was the
principal equity market for shipping stocks.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.58.2" class="koboSpan">Apart from
London, shipping stocks were also listed in the New York stock market.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.58.3" class="koboSpan">In the 1990s,
Oslo took the top position in Europe as the leading stock exchange for
shipping IPOs. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.58.4"
class="koboSpan">Due to market shifts, London has gradually lost its
leading role in shipping IPOs, partly due to companies
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_820"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">going private or to mergers and acquisitions, such as
the P&O acquisition by DP Ports World (Erdogan, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">In general,
European equity markets have experienced declining trends in shipping
market value from more than 1% in the early 1990s to 0.6% of total
market value recently (Matthews, 2006).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.59.3" class="koboSpan">In the US
equity markets, a series of de-mergers and spin-offs of shipping
businesses led to the restructuring of the shipping sector.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.59.4" class="koboSpan">Shipping firms
and investors have more recently switched towards a number of upcoming
Asian stock markets that now attract shipping IPOs, including Hong Kong,
Singapore, Bangkok and Taiwan.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">The transportation
sector, on aggregate, lags behind in global equity market values.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">The market
capitalisation of global transportation companies increased
substantially during the last 30 years.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.3" class="koboSpan">It reached a
high of US \$700 bn corresponding to a share of total market
capitalisation of above 4% (end of 1980s), before declining to below 2%
(2006). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.4" class="koboSpan">As a
comparison, the oil and gas sector and the financial sector account for
nearly 20% and 15% of global stock market capitalisation, respectively
(Matthews, 2006). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.5"
class="koboSpan">Against an estimated 8–9% of GDP in OECD countries, the
low market share in capitalisation indicates that transportation remains
persistently neglected in international stock markets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.6" class="koboSpan">The shipping
sector, in particular, has also seen a marginal capitalisation share at
about 0.4% of global equity market value; liner shipping covers the
largest share (Matthews, 2006). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.7"
class="koboSpan">Despite the recent IPO activity, this figure reflects
low shipping market participation, taking into account that the shipping
sector is estimated at about 2% of world GDP.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.8" class="koboSpan">Only a limited
number of about 30 shipping firms have been estimated to bear a market
value of above US \$1 bn, with A.P.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.60.9" class="koboSpan">Moller-Maersk
Group, a Danish shipping conglomerate, the only firm accounting for
about 20% (around US \$30 bn) of total shipping stock market value
globally (Syriopoulos, 2007).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">More recently, the US
stock markets (NYSE, NASDAQ) have seen some revitalised IPO activity,
attracting jointly the largest number of shipping IPO issues and
regaining their leading role as preferred equity markets to IPO
launches. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">Oslo
follows at a distance now, leaving London Stock Exchange behind (Merikas
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">., 2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.63.2"
class="koboSpan">Strong advantages of the US capital markets include
fund-raising depth, reputable position in the investment community,
improved share liquidity, reliable pricing, high corporate prestige and
exposure to an international investor base.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">According to
Clarkson’s data, there were about 170 shipping companies listed
worldwide by 2006, corresponding to an estimated market value of US
\$210 bln, although pure shipping firms are only about half that number
(Matthews, 2006). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.63.4"
class="koboSpan">During the recent intensive IPO cycle (mid-2004 to
end-2005), total shipping IPO value and secondary listings were
estimated in excess of US \$4 bln, whereas in the first half of 2006
alone, international shipping IPOs amounted to a value of more than US
\$100 bln (Matthews, 2006).</span>

<a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0409" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0409"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents a summary of major shipping IPO issues per
country and per stock market, during 1984–2007.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">Over this time
span, the US equity markets (NYSE, NASDAQ) confirm their leading
position, as they have seen the largest IPO number (55 issues).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">The Oslo Stock
Exchange enjoys persistently high levels of shipping IPO activity and
follows with 15 IPOs but the London Stock Exchange (LSE) ranks lower (6
IPOs). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.65.4" class="koboSpan">Of these
sample IPOs, only 38 firms were listed before 2000; most of these IPOs
have come into equity markets after 2000, supporting the shift of
shipping firms towards global equity markets, as discussed
earlier.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">Taking into account
the leading role of the US markets and the upcoming Asian markets,
European stock markets may see further declines in shipping market
value.</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0409" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_821"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0409)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00429.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0409)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Major reasons that
explain the limited presence of the shipping sector in the European
markets include the highly fragmented industry structure, the
concentrated ownership (as founding families remain major shareholders),
the large number of relatively small private companies, the decision of
some public shipping companies to go private and the limited number of
IPOs in Europe compared with the US.</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Key issues in shipping IPOs</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.1 Models of IPO pricing</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">A company can be
listed and traded on a Stock Exchange by issuing new shares.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">Whenever this
share offering to investors takes place for the first time, it is known
as an Initial Public Offering (IPO).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">The company
‘goes public’ and its shares can then be freely traded in the open
equity market. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.71.4"
class="koboSpan">The IPO price is the price at which the new
shareholders buy the shares at issue.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.71.5" class="koboSpan">The initial
return of an IPO relates to the difference between the equilibrium price
following the issue and the IPO price.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.71.6" class="koboSpan">The IPO price
is jointly decided by the underwriter and the listing firm at the end of
the IPO procedure, according to financial analysts’ valuations and the
demand expressed for
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_822"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">the shares. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.72.2"
class="koboSpan">The definitive offer price is generally lower than the
first equilibrium price; this is well known under the term of ‘IPO
underpricing’ (Ljungovist, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.72.3" class="koboSpan">The IPO
motives, pricing, initial market appraisal and long-run performance have
been the focus of a large theoretical and empirical financial
literature.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">Alternative
theoretical approaches, such as the information asymmetry and signalling
models or the life cycle and market-timing models, have been proposed to
explain these issues (Ritter and Welch, 2002; Drobetz
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005; Derrien and Kecskes, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">The primary
motive as to ‘why do firms go public’ relates to their decision to raise
equity capital and to create a public market in which the founders and
other shareholders can convert part of the corporate value they possess
into cash at a future date. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.75.3"
class="koboSpan">In addition, being the first in an industry to go
public sometimes confers a first-mover advantage, whereas IPOs allow
more ownership dispersion with relevant advantages and disadvantages.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.75.4" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, by
going public, entrepreneurs help facilitate the acquisition of their
company for a higher value than what they would earn from an outright
sale (Brau </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2002). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.77.2"
class="koboSpan">Market timing is also important to IPO decisions.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.77.3" class="koboSpan">An IPO may be
delayed, if a bear market phase can potentially result to a low firm
value; whereas a bull market may offer more favourable pricing
conditions (Lucas and McDonald, 1990).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.77.4" class="koboSpan">It has been
also argued that larger companies and companies in industries with high
market-to-book ratios are more likely to go public and companies going
public seem to have reduced their costs of credit.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.77.5" class="koboSpan">IPO activity is
affected by investor sentiment and follows high investment and growth,
not vice versa (Pagano
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
