class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1998; Lowry, 2003).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.79.2" class="koboSpan">To recap, the
evidence of large variation in the number of IPOs suggests that market
conditions are the most important factor in the decision to go public.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.79.3" class="koboSpan">The other
important factor seems to be the life cycle stage of the firm.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">A large body of
empirical studies documents a systematic price increase from the offer
IPO price to the first-day closing price (‘IPO underpricing puzzle’).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.2" class="koboSpan">Ritter and
Welch (2002), for instance, study a sample of 6,249 IPOs from 1980–2001
and estimate an average ‘first day’ return of 18.8%.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.3" class="koboSpan">Approximately
70% of the IPOs end the first trading day at a closing price greater
than the offer price. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.4"
class="koboSpan">This pattern of underpriced IPOs is seen to apply in
different firms, sectors, markets and countries.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.5" class="koboSpan">A possible
justification of the IPO ‘undepricing puzzle’ relates to reasons of
asymmetric information between market participants, as IPO issuers are
expected to be more informed than investors.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.6" class="koboSpan">Better quality
issuers deliberately sell their shares at a lower price than the market
believes they are worth, which deters lower quality issuers from
following. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.7"
class="koboSpan">These issuers can recoup their initial value sacrifice
post-IPO, either in future issuing activity, favourable market responses
to future dividend announcements or analyst coverage.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.8" class="koboSpan">In line with a
body of signalling models, firms demonstrate that they are high quality
by throwing money away; one way to do this is to leave money on the
table in the IPO. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.80.9"
class="koboSpan">Empirical evidence indicated that the relationship
between IPO price and underpricing may be U-shaped, whereas in contrast,
post-IPO turnover may display an inverted U-shaped relation to IPO price
(Fernando </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2004). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.82.2"
class="koboSpan">However, the conclusions produced on these issues
remain rather mixed. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.82.3"
class="koboSpan">Compared with the rich financial literature on a
country level, the body of studies on individual sectors, especially
shipping, remains thin.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">The long-run stock
price underperformance in the years after the IPO offering is another
key topic of interest in IPO research (‘IPO long-run underperformance
puzzle’). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">Measuring long-run performance can focus either on
absolute (raw) performance, or relative performance (abnormal returns vs
market benchmark). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.83.3"
class="koboSpan">Empirical evidence
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_823"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">indicates that IPOs underperform in the long run.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.84.2" class="koboSpan">A number of
IPOs in the US, for instance, were seen to underperform significantly
relative to non-issuing firms for three to five years after the listing
date (Ritter, 1991; Loughran and Ritter, 1995).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.84.3" class="koboSpan">According to
other estimates (Ritter and Welch, 2002), an investor who buys shares at
the first-day closing price and holds them for an investment horizon of
three years, would attaint IPO returns of 22.6%.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.84.4" class="koboSpan">However,
compared to a market benchmark (CRSP value-weighted market index), the
average IPO price underperforms by 23.4%.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.84.5" class="koboSpan">IPO long-run
performance remains a controversial issue, sensitive to the empirical
approach employed and directly dependent on the preferential theoretical
stance of market efficiency or behavioural finance framework.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.84.6" class="koboSpan">Many studies
have contributed international evidence on the long-term IPO
underperformance consistent with what has been found for the US market,
including Australia (Lee
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1996); Japan (Cai and Wei, 1997); Sweden (Brounen and
Eichholtz, 2002); Germany (Jaskiewicz
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005); United Kingdom (Goergen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2006); France and Greece (Chahine, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">In a
pan-European study, evidence of long-run underperformance has been
documented for a sample of 15 countries, indicating long-term abnormal
returns in Europe to be negative (Gajewski and Gresse, 2006).</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.2 Shipping IPO pricing</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">Capital markets can
play a key role in promoting shipping business growth and value
creation. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">They
may act as an intermediary mechanism to provide funds required to
finance new investment projects and sustain business growth.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.92.3" class="koboSpan">Fresh funds can
be channelled to shipping firms in need through the issuance of new
securities by an IPO process. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.92.4"
class="koboSpan">As secondary markets, capital markets provide an
efficient mechanism for trading outstanding securities.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.92.5" class="koboSpan">Following IPO
market listing and trading, a shipping company has the privilege to
regularly return to stock market investors and request additional
funding through seasoned equity offerings (SEOs).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">Major factors that
contribute to corporate value creation, as reflected on the firm’s stock
price upward behaviour, include,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">:
robust fundamentals; efficient and well reputed management; high cash
flows/earnings; realistic market valuations; M&A corporate stories; and
growth potential. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.95.2"
class="koboSpan">The positive behaviour of shipping stocks can be
further enhanced by upward freight markets, bullish stock market trends
and rich cash liquidity conditions.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.95.3" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
private and institutional investors have remained sceptical for years
about shipping firms’ stocks. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.95.4"
class="koboSpan">This investors’ attitude has been adversely affected by
‘inward’ family organisation, structure and management; ship-owners’
reluctance to expand shareholder base; non-disclosure of critical
corporate actions; low or no dividend yield; non-appealing risk-return
trade-off; highly volatile freight markets, resulting to abnormal
corporate earnings and highly risky investments.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">A critical question
relates to the motives driving shipping firms’ shift towards listing on
international equity markets. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
class="koboSpan">In the past, the strict requirements of transparency
and disclosure that listed companies should meet was a constraint for
many shipping firms, especially at volatile market times and earnings
fluctuations. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.96.3"
class="koboSpan">However, this is seen to gradually change.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.96.4" class="koboSpan">Equity markets
appear now to be an attractive choice for firms with stable income flows
and growth potential. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.96.5"
class="koboSpan">With interest rates remaining at low levels, banking
finance may still appear to be a cheap funding alternative.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.96.6" class="koboSpan">However, a
number of shipping companies have decided to go public recently and
raise funds quickly
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_824"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">(despite significant public listing costs), to take
advantage of the robust freight markets and investors’ positive
sentiment towards shipping stocks.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.97.2" class="koboSpan">Still, a number
of shipping firms have experienced substantial market value losses,
since freight markers moved downwards amidst conditions of global
financial crisis and economic recession.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">These developments are
anticipated to have an adverse impact on cautious investors’
expectations, probably making it more difficult for shipping firms to
raise financing from the equity markets in the near future.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">Good quality
shipping IPOs can be successful, though there have been cases in the
recent past that it was not always easy to sell shipping shares to
investors. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.98.3"
class="koboSpan">Despite the fact that investors’ sentiment may not
remain as positive as it was earlier, fair IPO pricing, backed by robust
earnings cash flow streams and stable freight markets, can conclude to
successful shipping IPOs. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.98.4"
class="koboSpan">A critical advantage of shipping firms’ listings is
related to the fact that shipping is a real asset-backed business and
certain risk levels can still be acceptable with some confidence by
investors. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.98.5" class="koboSpan">The
most risky bet appears to be on whether institutional and private
investors will continue to consider shipping stocks as an attractive
alternative ‘style’ investment class, hence, facilitating shipping
firms’ funding (Syriopoulos and Roumpis, 2009).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">The pricing of IPO
equity issues remains a central issue for shipping firms interested in
raising equity funding in global stock markets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">Since the
majority of shipping IPOs refers to bulk shipping offerings, the issuer
will set an IPO price at or near market-adjusted net asset value (NAV)
per share. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.99.3" class="koboSpan">This
is reasonable in cases where company earnings and cash flows fully
support NAV (Stokes, 1997). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.99.4"
class="koboSpan">In practice, however, ship prices in the second-hand
market do not necessarily reflect operating cash flow and earnings
generated by the ships. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.99.5"
class="koboSpan">More frequently, ship prices represent a very high
multiple of operating cash flow, whereas in certain bulk shipping
segments operating earnings were negative for a number of years.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Equity financing can
be an attractive source of capital for shipping companies, taking into
account the relatively lower implied cost of capital against other
sources of funding. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">This is related to the fact that shipping companies
traditionally pay low or no dividend to investors and investors accept
this practice, since, due to the capital intensive nature of shipping
business, retained earnings are channelled to fleet replacement and
expansion. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">On
the other hand, investors’ target of expected return on equity is set at
high levels. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.100.4"
class="koboSpan">Assuming that a shipping company can borrow at a spread
over Libor (+1% to 2%), this can result to borrowing costs on senior
debt of, say, 7%. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.100.5"
class="koboSpan">Subordinate debt might cost 10–12% per annum, on a
10–year maturity. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.100.6"
class="koboSpan">Investors, however, will typically seek a return on
equity of 15–20% per annum, given the volatile freight markets and their
risk exposure (Stokes, 1997). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.100.7"
class="koboSpan">Taking into account that many shipping companies are
rated below investment grade, this implies that they must attain return
on equity well above average stock market returns to prevent their share
price from declining.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">The key role of
equity markets in shipping business has been surprisingly neglected in
past empirical research. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.101.2"
class="koboSpan">A pioneer exception is Grammenos and Marcoulis (1996),
who study shipping IPOs in a cross-country framework.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.101.3" class="koboSpan">A sample of 31
IPO cases is examined in seven different countries (US, Norway, Sweden,
Greece, Luxembourg, Hong Kong and Singapore), over 1983–1995.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.101.4" class="koboSpan">Shipping
companies with prime business on vessel operations are mainly considered
and critical factors associated with shipping IPOs are investigated.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.101.5" class="koboSpan">As these
companies grow bigger over time, they reorganise their structures and
meet their capital needs in the stock markets more frequently.</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0410" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_825"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0410)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00430.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0410)

</div>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0411" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00431.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0411)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">The following
important factors are evaluated as to their impact on shipping IPO stock
market performance: gross proceeds of the IPO issue; size of the
company; proportion of equity offered; gearing level; age of the
company; and, age of the fleet. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.104.2"
class="koboSpan">Gearing is argued to be the single most statistically
significant factor in explaining IPO stock market performance.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.104.3" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
the average initial day return of the sample shipping IPOs is found to
be consistent with past empirical evidence.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.104.4" class="koboSpan">Shipping IPO
underpricing of small magnitude is concluded at about 5.32% on average.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.104.5" class="koboSpan">IPO costs are
estimated at 8% of the amount raised with a high fixed cost component in
average direct costs; the highest direct costs are seen in the US stock
markets and the lowest in Norway.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.104.6" class="koboSpan">The purpose of
the issue, the number of offers, the average proceeds, the average
company size and the cross-country listings of these IPOs are summarised
in
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0410" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0410"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Tables 4</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0411" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0411"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.108.2"
class="koboSpan">Vessel acquisitions receive by far the highest part of
IPO funding and asset play strategies follow at a distance.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping companies
with high pre-IPO gearing levels are seen to experience more
underpricing of their share issues than the companies with low pre-IPO
gearing levels. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.109.2"
class="koboSpan">In the context of reorganisation strategy, shipping
companies may have to lower their gearing level to minimise potential
stock market underpricing. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.109.3"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, shipping companies that offer more equity
to the public exhibit higher underpricing than those offering less
equity. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.109.4" class="koboSpan">This
is related to information signalling to market participants,
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_826"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan">implying a kind of ‘private’ valuation by shipowners
for the amount of equity retained.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">Risk averse
shipowners would improve expected utility by holding a diversified
portfolio and not only a large stake in their own firm.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.110.3" class="koboSpan">Since this
argument does not seem to apply to the case of companies offering
limited equity, it may signal that these shipowners are based on an
implicit ‘fair’ firm value. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.110.4"
class="koboSpan">In this case, shipowners of high value companies would
prefer to forego diversification benefits but avoid selling undervalued
stocks. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.110.5" class="koboSpan">As
investors realise shipowners’ positioning, they would be keen to invest
on shipping stocks of companies where owners are retaining larger
holdings.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">The topic of IPO
underpricing and long-term performance in global shipping issues has
been the subject of a recent study (Merikas
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2009), the key points of which we now summarise.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.113.2" class="koboSpan">The study
investigates the short- and long-term price performance of 143 global
shipping IPOs, listed during 1984–2007, in major stock exchanges.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.113.3" class="koboSpan">It also tests
whether relevant theories can adequately explain shipping IPO behaviour
in the aftermarket. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.113.4"
class="koboSpan">The study calculates estimates of ‘Buy-and-Hold
Abnormal Returns’ (BHARs) of the IPOs for six months and up to 36 months
after listing on the stock market and ‘Cumulative Average Returns’
(CARs) on a three-year basis to better test the stability and the
Fama-French 3-Factor model. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.113.5"
class="koboSpan">The empirical findings indicate that shipping IPO
underpricing stands at an average adjusted first day return of 17.7%.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.113.6" class="koboSpan">This
underpricing is positively related to the age of the firm, the
reputation of the stock exchange the IPO is listed on and the market
conditions prevailing at the time the firm went public, whereas it is
negatively related to the reputation of the underwriters.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.113.7" class="koboSpan">In the long
run, shipping IPOs are seen to underperform after a five-month holding
period. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.113.8" class="koboSpan">As to
the long-run shipping IPO performance, when BHARs is taken as a
benchmark, the empirical findings indicate that investors, who buy
immediately after listing and hold shares for three years, will make a
loss of –9.91%, –4.40% and –15.72%, after the first, second and third
year of listing, respectively.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">The study
incorporates several variables to explain cross-sectional variations of
shipping IPO underpricing. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.114.2"
class="koboSpan">First, the history of the firm prior to going public is
anticipated to exert a negative impact on IPO underpricing, since a
short history before the IPO increases the risk to investors so that a
larger underpricing is required.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.114.3" class="koboSpan">Secondly, the
regulated market and the respective segment in which the shipping IPO is
listed, since firms that are listed in the parallel market segment
(small capitalisation – high growth) will have their shares underpriced
in order to attract a large number of shareholders.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.114.4" class="koboSpan">Thirdly, the
reputation of the underwriter is a ‘quality’, lower risk, signal to the
market and a banking syndicate or an established investment bank can
attain a more efficient penetration to new shareholders.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.114.5" class="koboSpan">Empirical
evidence indicates that underwriters proceed to stock price
stabilisation during a short period of time after the IPO to avoid any
issue failure (Rock, 1986). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.114.6"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the mean long-term underperformance of
firms introduced by more prestigious underwriters is found to be weaker
(Ruud, 1993). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.114.7"
class="koboSpan">Fourthly, the IPO size is argued to affect the post-IPO
stock price reaction (Carter
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1998; Stehle
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2000). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.118.2"
class="koboSpan">To gain a better insight on that, the sample was
divided into four size categories.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.118.3" class="koboSpan">Fifthly,
market conditions are also considered to be important for IPO price
reaction. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.118.4"
class="koboSpan">Empirical evidence indicates that the number of IPOs
tends to increase in bullish markets because the placement of stocks is
easier, the risk of failure for an IPO is lower and securities are
priced higher, which softens the cost of initial underpricing (Helwege
and Liang, 1999; Lowry, 2003). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.118.5"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, IPOs taking place in hot market conditions
(robust investor interest for IPOs) are expected to yield larger returns
in the first few trading days than IPOs made in a cold market.</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0412" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_827"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0412)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00432.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0412)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">Subsequently, IPO
prices in a hot market reverse as a result of adjustments in investors’
perception that excessive optimism may have been attributed to the new
IPO issues (overvaluation) under hot market conditions.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.120.2" class="koboSpan">The average
number of shipping IPOs per year in the sample under study indicates
only two shipping IPOs per year over 1984–1987; around three shipping
IPOs per year over 1988–1997; and, on average, 11 shipping IPOs per year
over 1998–2007, rendering this decade a hot shipping IPO market
globally. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.120.3"
class="koboSpan">Finally, the reputation of the stock exchange where the
IPOs are listed is considered to be an important factor in explaining
IPO underpricing. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.120.4"
class="koboSpan">For that, shipping IPOs are classified into two major
groups: (a) IPO listings on the main global stock markets (NYSE, NASDAQ
and LSE), to reflect strict listing requirement implications; and (b)
IPO listings on other stock exchanges.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.120.5" class="koboSpan">A summary of
the empirical findings is presented in
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0412" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0412"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">Table 6</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">Long-term performance
estimates of shipping IPOs are produced by calculating returns over a
three-year investment horizon. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.123.2"
class="koboSpan">According to the ‘buy-and-hold’ trading strategy
employed, each IPO is bought at the end of the first day of trading and
is sold at the end of the first, second and third year of trading.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.123.3" class="koboSpan">The same
amount of invested funds is allocated on every IPO (equally-weighted
long-term returns).
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0413" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0413"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan"> reports the average BHARs of the global shipping IPO
sample listed during 1984–2007 and summarises adjusted returns based on
the listing price of the new issues.</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">3.3.3 Shipping stock returns, risk and volatility</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">The cyclical and
highly volatile behaviour of shipping business and corporate earnings
has been an issue of great concern for shipowners, bankers, charterers
and investors and has raised an adverse sentiment against asset
allocation to shipping stocks (Syriopoulos and Roumpis,
2009)</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.129.1"
class="koboSpan">The various forms of risks in shipping business can be
broadly grouped into the following major classes: business risk;
liquidity risk; default risk; financial risk; credit risk; market risk;
political risk; and, technical and physical risk (Syriopoulos,
2007).</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0413" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_828"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0413)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00433.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0413)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">Empirical work on
shipping market behaviour remains limited in number and scope.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.131.2" class="koboSpan">More recently,
few empirical studies have investigated the relationship between
shipping business and stock markets from different perspectives.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.131.3" class="koboSpan">These include,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">,
the performance of shipping stocks in the international equity markets;
the identification of key risk-return characteristics in shipping
stocks; and, the dynamic management of shipping equity portfolios.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">Other studies
investigate certain aspects of shipping volatility patterns; validity of
the efficient market hypothesis; and, risk-return comparisons with
complementary or substitute transportation sectors (Kavussanos, 1997,
2003; Kavussanos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2003; Gong, 2003; Tvedt, 2003; Mulligan and Lombardo,
2004; Chen and Wang, 2004; Syriopoulos and Roumpis, 2006; Syriopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2006; Andriosopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.139.2"
class="koboSpan">These studies follow a market or even a
route-disaggregated approach to investigate volatility behaviour in dry
bulk, tanker and container market segments.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.139.3" class="koboSpan">The empirical
findings indicate that shipowners can diversify business risks by
holding portfolios of ships of different size; switching between
contracts of different duration; and, hedging with forward freight
contracts; vessels of small and medium size were found to show
relatively lower volatility compared with larger size vessels.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.139.4" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
the impact of trading volume (activity) on vessel price changes is
assessed, since trading volume can contribute useful information to a
market where real assets are traded.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">The macroeconomic
environment can exert a significant impact on shipping stock returns,
according to Grammenos and Arkoulis (2002), who study a sample of 36
shipping companies, listed in 10 stock exchanges worldwide, during
1989:12–1998:3. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.140.2"
class="koboSpan">The model employs returns on a world equity market
portfolio as the dependent variable in the following pre-specified set
of global macroeconomic variables: (a) industrial production; (b)
inflation; (c) oil prices; (d) exchange rate fluctuations against the US
dollar; and (e) laid up tonnage.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.140.3" class="koboSpan">Empirical
evidence indicates several significant relationships between returns of
international shipping stocks and global risk factors.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.140.4" class="koboSpan">Oil prices and
laid up tonnage are found to be negatively related to shipping stocks,
whereas the exchange rate variable to display a positive relationship.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.140.5" class="koboSpan">These
macroeconomic factors are seen to exhibit consistent interrelationship
patterns in the way they are linked to the shipping industry
worldwide.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">The dynamic asset
allocation and active management of shipping stock portfolios has been
the core objective in Syriopoulos and Roumpis (2009).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">Alternative
dynamic</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0414" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00434.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Shipping markets vs equity markets" /></span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_829"></span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0214"
id="Ch028.xhtml_cap_lbl0214"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan"> Shipping markets vs equity markets</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">volatility models
investigate the risk and return characteristics of a carefully selected
portfolio of shipping stocks, in order to gain some insight on potential
asset allocation opportunities. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.145.2"
class="koboSpan">As private and institutional investors are in search of
alternative style investments, the assessment of stock volatility is a
critical issue for efficient asset allocation, dynamic portfolio
management and firm valuation. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.145.3"
class="koboSpan">Shipping stock portfolio returns are compared against
representative stock market indices, since a key issue to portfolio
investors remains whether shipping stock picking can potentially lead to
superior stock returns relative to the market portfolio.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.145.4" class="koboSpan">Shipping stock
selection may then be considered as an investment style that can add
value to other styles such as value, growth, technology or emerging
markets. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.145.5"
class="koboSpan">According to the empirical findings, shipping stock
returns exhibit a highly volatile profile, in accordance with the
respective (tanker and dry bulk) earnings volatility.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.145.6" class="koboSpan">Sectoral and
company fundamentals may affect shipping stock volatility that is found
to be sensitive to asymmetric shocks.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.145.7" class="koboSpan">The results
indicate superior portfolio returns for shipping stock portfolios
relative to market benchmarks, albeit associated with higher risk levels
(</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_cap_lbl0214"
id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0214"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">As the shipping
industry is exceptionally capital intensive, volatile and highly risky,
alternative risk management approaches have been proposed to control for
shipping risk (Kavoussanos and Visvikis, 2006; Alizadeh and Nomikos,
2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.148.2" class="koboSpan">To
hedge against underlying risks, predominantly freight rate volatility,
shipping market participants have gradually turned their attention into
specialized derivatives products, particularly freight forward
agreements (FFAs) and freight
options</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">The freight derivatives market has grown rapidly in
recent years and traded volumes have more than quadrupled since 2000
(Syriopoulos, 2007).</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">3.4 Alternative hybrid finance instruments</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">A number of
innovative alternative methods have been employed more recently in ship
finance, to take advantage of the benefits equity markets offer.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.152.2" class="koboSpan">We briefly
discuss these shipping finance methods that have been well received by
the capital markets. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.152.3"
class="koboSpan">These
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_830"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">are: (a) merger with a Specified Purpose Acquisition
Company (SPAC); (b) the combination of reverse merging into a publicly
traded corporation and funding through a Private Investment in a Public
Equity (PIPE); (c) private equity funding; (d) mezzanine finance; and,
(e) ‘At-The-Market’ (ATM) offerings.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.153.2" class="koboSpan">These
financing options of accessing capital and going public are good
examples of the creativity of the shipping business community when
presented with funding challenges.</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">3.4.1 SPACs — PIPEs</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">A recent approach to
financing a shipping firm is merging with a Specified Purpose
Acquisition Company (SPAC). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.155.2"
class="koboSpan">A SPAC is a newly formed industry-specific publicly
traded buyout/venture capital fund.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.155.3" class="koboSpan">The purpose of
the SPAC is to acquire an operating business in a specified industry, in
this case shipping. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.155.4"
class="koboSpan">The SPAC is managed by highly experienced management
teams and advisors who are recognised leaders in their field.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.155.5" class="koboSpan">Performance
results have been mixed for those SPACs that have announced or have
completed deals.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">An alternative method
is the combination of reverse merging into a publicly traded corporation
and funding through a PIPE. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.156.2"
class="koboSpan">In essence, a reverse merger is a transaction in which
a private company becomes public through a combination with an existing
public company, with the private company ending up in control of the
combined entity. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.156.3"
class="koboSpan">More often than not, the public entity in a reverse
merger is a ‘shell’ company, with neither operating business nor assets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.156.4" class="koboSpan">Potential
advantages of a reverse merger include: (i) ability to complete the
transaction without engaging an underwriter, thus reducing overall
costs; (ii) avoidance of IPO process rigors, including long road shows;
(iii) less vulnerable than an IPO to the vicissitudes of the public
markets and risk of being unsuccessful; and, (iv) the ability to
complete the transaction in a shorter time, provided the private company
has audited financial statements and other required information
available at the time of the transaction.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">In the past, reverse
merging into a public vehicle often resulted into a company only
achieving one thing: increasing its legal and accounting expenses.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Today,
however, with the advent of PIPE financing, this has changed for many
well-represented companies. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.157.3"
class="koboSpan">The turbulent public markets of the last years have
resulted to increased interest by private investors in PIPE
transactions. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.157.4"
class="koboSpan">PIPE investors purchase securities directly from a
publicly traded company in a private placement transaction, typically at
a discount to the market price of the company’s common stock.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.157.5" class="koboSpan">This private
sale of securities is often not pre-registered with the SEC; as a result
these securities are ‘restricted’ and cannot be immediately resold by
the investors into the public markets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.157.6" class="koboSpan">Accordingly,
the company will agree as part of the PIPE deal to promptly register the
securities with the SEC. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.157.7"
class="koboSpan">Thus, the PIPE transaction can offer the company the
speed and predictability of a private placement, while providing
investors with a nearly-liquid security at a discount from the current
trading price.</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">3.4.2 Private equity funding</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">Private equity
funding activity has been recently seen in shipping finance.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.159.2" class="koboSpan">Private equity
funding is equity capital that is not quoted on a public exchange and
can be considered to have a complementary, yet independent, financing
function to equity markets. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.159.3"
class="koboSpan">Private equity consists of funding by private investors
and funds that make investments
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_831"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">directly into private companies or conduct buyouts of
public companies that result in a delisting of public equity.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">Capital for private
equity is raised from retail and institutional investors and can be used
to fund new technologies, expand working capital within an owned
company, make acquisitions or strengthen the balance sheet.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.161.2" class="koboSpan">The large part
of private equity originates from institutional investors and accredited
investors who can commit large sums of funding for long periods of time.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.161.3" class="koboSpan">Private equity
investments often demand long holding periods to allow for a turnaround
of a distressed company or a liquidity event such as an IPO or sale to a
public company. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.161.4"
class="koboSpan">The size of the private equity market has grown
steadily since the 1970s. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.161.5"
class="koboSpan">Private equity firms will sometimes pool funds together
to take very large public companies private.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.161.6" class="koboSpan">Many private
equity firms conduct what are known as leveraged buyouts (LBOs), where
large amounts of debt are issued to fund a large purchase.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.161.7" class="koboSpan">Private equity
firms will then try to improve the financial results and prospects of
the company in the hope of reselling the company to another firm or
cashing out via an IPO.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">Private equity firms
are seen to exhibit growing interest in shipping companies, as they are
searching for new industries to invest and are backed by strong capital
liquidity. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.162.2" class="koboSpan">In
contrast to other sectors, the penetration of private equity funding in
shipping remains at modest levels in the US, although it is anticipated
to have potential for further increase.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.162.3" class="koboSpan">Since shipping
business is an international activity, private equity firms seek to have
a regionally dispersed presence worldwide.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.162.4" class="koboSpan">Private equity
firms offer advisory and arranger services in diversified and innovative
shipping finance structures, including US finance, UK tax leases and KG
finance. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.162.5" class="koboSpan">A
core objective for private equity firms remains whether their financial
support to shipping companies results to enhancing the firm’s corporate
value. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.162.6" class="koboSpan">Part of
the increasing attention paid to private equity finance is supported by
the fact that investors are better informed and more diligent on fund
investing relative to IPO investors.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.162.7" class="koboSpan">As investors’
interest in listed shipping stocks is seen to slowdown and shipping
companies become more experienced in the use of capital markets, private
equity funds can take advantage of new financing opportunities.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">In spite of the high
risk element seen in shipping investment returns, private equity funds
have already financed a number of shipping companies, including,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">,
Quintana, Eagle Bulk, US Shipping and Horizon (Syriopoulos, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.165.2" class="koboSpan">Still, a
growing number of private equity funds are active in raising capital to
shipping finance. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.165.3"
class="koboSpan">AMA Capital Partners, for instance, has raised funding
at US \$100 mn to finance marine and rail transportation projects.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.165.4" class="koboSpan">Earlier
funding (2000), at US \$45 mn, raised jointly with fund partners NIB
Capital and GATX, was used to acquire ships and succeeded in attaining a
net IRR above 20% for its shareholders (Matthews, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.165.5" class="koboSpan">A number of US
private equity firms (such as Carlyle, Wexford Capital, Castle Harlan,
Stockwell Fund, Blackstone Group, and Sterling Investment Partners) have
been involved in shipping finance.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.165.6" class="koboSpan">Navigation
Finance Corporation (NFC), for instance, a joint venture between DVB
Bank and Northern Navigation, entered into a US \$181 mn sale-and
lease-back deal with Singapore based offshore vessel operator Ezra
Holdings (McGroarty, 2006).</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">3.4.3 Mezzanine finance</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">Mezzanine finance is
a hybrid of equity and debt financing.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.167.2" class="koboSpan">It is
typically used to finance the expansion of existing companies and has
been also employed in shipping business
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_832"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.168.1"
class="koboSpan">as an alternative vehicle of finance (Harwood, 2006).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">Mezzanine
finance is basically debt capital that gives the lender the rights to
convert to an ownership or equity interest in the company, if the loan
is not paid back in time and in full.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.168.3" class="koboSpan">It is
generally subordinated to debt provided by senior lenders, such as banks
and venture capital companies. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.168.4"
class="koboSpan">Since mezzanine finance is usually provided to the
borrower in short time with limited due diligence on the part of the
lender and limited or no collateral on the part of the borrower, this
type of financing is aggressively priced with the lender targeting a
return at an estimated range of 20–30%.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">Mezzanine financing
is advantageous because it is treated like equity on a company’s balance
sheet and that may make it easier for the firm to obtain standard bank
lending. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.169.2" class="koboSpan">To
attract mezzanine financing, a company usually must demonstrate a track
record in the industry with an established reputation and product, a
history of profitability and a viable investment plan for the business
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.169.3"
class="koboSpan">expansions, acquisitions, IPO).</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">3.4.4 ATM offerings</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">An at-the-market
(ATMs) offering refers to securities offered on a continuous or delayed
basis in the future, at a price that is not fixed at the time of
registration. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.171.2"
class="koboSpan">This is one of the latest techniques in financial
engineering to raise capital in bad markets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.171.3" class="koboSpan">They are also
known as ‘dribble programmes’ or ‘controlled equity offerings’ and allow
the issuer to ‘dribble out’ a share offering, when market or price
conditions are more favourable. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.171.4"
class="koboSpan">This is in contrast to a conventional secondary
offering that takes place all at once.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.171.5" class="koboSpan">Hence, the
issuer gains flexibility to set a floor below which will not sell and
can seek best prices over time; or, the issuer can stop selling ATM
shares. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.171.6" class="koboSpan">Apart
from banks, other corporations that have found ATM offerings preferable
recently include Delta Airlines, Carnival Corporation, UAL Corporation
and the Ford Motor Company.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">Ailing publicly
listed shipping companies are also seen to employ this technique to
raise capital and recapitalise their impaired balance sheets (Majarian,
2010). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.2" class="koboSpan">When a
shipping company is interested in selling a large trance of shares in
unfavourable equity market conditions, it will be extremely difficult to
attract investors’ attention. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.3"
class="koboSpan">Under these circumstances, institutional investors
would make a placement only in case they can acquire a percentage of
shares at a substantially discounted price.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.4" class="koboSpan">However, these
offerings, when used to pay down debt and recapitalise, are highly
dilutive. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.5" class="koboSpan">The
firm’s longer-term prospects and the prospects of the freight markets
are important for investors’ allocation decisions.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.6" class="koboSpan">Because the
trading process is blind, investors do not really know whether they are
buying existing shares or new shares being marketed by an underwriter.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.7" class="koboSpan">With no
pressure to complete an issue within a tight time-framework, companies
can proceed at their own pace and, ideally, have some control over what
price the shares are sold at over weeks or months.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.8" class="koboSpan">At a
recessionary market phase, many publicly listed companies (especially in
the dry bulk sector) are under pressure to pay down debt in conformance
to their debt/asset coverage covenants.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.9" class="koboSpan">Whether an ATM
offering targets additional funding to repay debt is an important issue
for investors to evaluate. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.172.10"
class="koboSpan">According to market experts, increased trading volumes
seen at times in a number of listed shipping companies may have been
boosted by ATM share offerings rather than primary trading activity
(Majarian, 2010).</span>

## <span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_833"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.173.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping Bonds and Yield Risks</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 The shipping bond market</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">A major alternative
source of capital to fund shipping investments is debt finance,
especially by issuing bond securities.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.175.2" class="koboSpan">This is a
funding choice distinctive from equity finance, bears certain merits but
is also associated with risks. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.175.3"
class="koboSpan">Traditionally, financing shipping projects with bond
issues has not been a prime choice for shipowners, as low interest rates
have supported banking finance; furthermore, shipping IPOs have
attracted substantial funding in the international capital markets
recently. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.175.4" class="koboSpan">This
section overviews the high yield bond market for shipping companies, as
this capital market segment has also experienced some revitalised
activity.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">One important
distinction of bond markets refers to that of primary and secondary bond
markets. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.176.2" class="koboSpan">The
primary bond market is the market where a new bond issue is initially
offered to investors for the first time.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.176.3" class="koboSpan">The secondary
market, refers to the market where a bond issue, following its initial
offering (in the primary market), is already traded, driven by demand
and supply forces. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.176.4"
class="koboSpan">However, as liquidity in shipping bond issues has
proven to be historically low in the secondary market and trading in a
large sum has been difficult, shipping companies rely predominantly on
the primary market. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.176.5"
class="koboSpan">According to their credit rating grade – that signals
lower or higher default risk – bonds can be broadly rated as of
‘investment grade’ or ‘high yield’ bonds (HYB).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.176.6" class="koboSpan">Due to their
highly risky profile, many shipping bonds have been graded as ‘high
yield’ bonds (speculative bonds).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">Past empirical
research on shipping debt and high yield bonds remains surprisingly
thin. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.177.2" class="koboSpan">A
pioneer exception is Grammenos and Arkoulis (2003), who examine
significant determinants affecting primary pricing of new shipping high
yield bond offerings in the US, during 1993–1998.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.177.3" class="koboSpan">Based on the
empirical framework of Fridson and Garman (1998), the study investigates
the impact of key factors on shipping high yield bond spreads, such as
credit rating, callability, term (years to maturity), float (issue
amount), default rate, security, gearing, fleet age, market conditions
(laid-up tonnage), and, 144a status.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.177.4" class="koboSpan">Primary
pricing refers to the determination of spread of the new high yield bond
offerings. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.177.5" class="koboSpan">The
spread is defined as the difference between the yield to maturity on a
coupon-paying corporate bond and the yield to maturity on a
coupon-paying government bond of the same maturity.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">In a background of
low interest rates over the past years, HYB markets have played a
peripheral only role in shipping finance until recently, when this
capital market segment attracted anew the interest of shipping companies
and international investors. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.178.2"
class="koboSpan">The first high yield bond in shipping was issued in
1992 by Sea Containers, targeting an amount of US \$125 mn in
subordinated debentures. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.178.3"
class="koboSpan">During 1992–2005, more than 60 shipping issues have
taken place in the US HYB market alone
(</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0415" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0415"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">Table 8</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.180.2"
class="koboSpan">Total funding in this speculative grade bond segment
have come up to US \$10.1 bn with an average coupon of 9.73% and an
average term to maturity of 9.5 years (Grammenos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2008). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.182.2"
class="koboSpan">The years 1993 (9 issues), 1997 (9 issues), 1998 (17
issues), 2003 (10 issues) and 2004 (5 issues) have shown intensive
activity in shipping bonds. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.182.3"
class="koboSpan">This translates into a total of 50 shipping high yield
bonds and corresponds to 82% of the overall issues during 1992–2005.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.182.4" class="koboSpan">During
2003–2005 alone, 16 new shipping bond issues have come into play,
pointing to a robustly revitalised interest of shipping firms in bond
market financing. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.182.5"
class="koboSpan">Major reasons that led to this exceptional activity in
the revitalised HYB market in shipping include the relatively modest
interest rate levels (1993);</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0415" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_834"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0415)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00435.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0415)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">replacement needs of
ageing fleets, backed with high gearing (1998); and a particularly
positive performance of shipping and bond markets (2003–2005).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">However,
international investors remain sceptical towards shipping firms’ bond
issues in the HYB market, due to a range of concerns.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.185.2" class="koboSpan">Cyclicality,
volatility and high leverage may jeopardise shipping companies’ expected
cash flows, especially in economic recessions.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.185.3" class="koboSpan">These
conditions can further result to deterioration of corporate credit
quality and increase the probability of default of shipping bonds.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.185.4" class="koboSpan">Financial
crises and economic shocks exert a critical adverse impact on the
shipping markets, as did, particularly, the Asian financial crisis and
the Russian economic upheaval, during 1997–1998.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.185.5" class="koboSpan">The
deterioration in global terms of trade affects mostly the shipping firms
that are exposed to high gearing and operate mainly in the spot market,
resulting to problematic servicing of high debt.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">The adverse
reputation of shipping bonds has worsened further by a series of
defaults and bankruptcies seen in the sector during the 1990s.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.186.2" class="koboSpan">In the past,
depressed market conditions hit shipping markets and led to dramatic
declines in freight rates and vessel prices in most market segments.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.186.3" class="koboSpan">As a
consequence, several shipping companies proceeded to default on their
high yield bond issues. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.186.4"
class="koboSpan">In 1999, for instance, ten shipping firms defaulted on
their high yield debt issues. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.186.5"
class="koboSpan">This negative performance overshot shipping bond
default rates up at 38% against a corresponding figure of 1.28%
for</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0416" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_835"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0416)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00436.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0416)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">overall public debt
default rates (Grammenos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.190.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2008). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.190.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipping industry issuers have been estimated to
represent less than 0.5% of the overall public debt by issuer
outstanding ( January 2000). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.190.3"
class="koboSpan">However, total shipping industry defaults reached
nearly 9% of all defaults by issuer in 1999.</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.191.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Shipping bond credit rating</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">4.2.1 Bond rating grades</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">Credit rating is a
critical issue in fund raising through bond issues and we now discuss
this topic briefly. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.193.2"
class="koboSpan">Since the early 1900s, bonds have been assigned quality
ratings that reflect their probability of going into default.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.193.3" class="koboSpan">The major US
rating agencies are Moody’s Investors Services (Moody’s), Standard &
Poor’s Corporation (S&P), Fitch Investors Service (Fitch) and Duff &
Phelps.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">Bonds are rated
either as of ‘investment’ or ‘non-investment’ grade (termed ‘high yield’
or ‘junk’ bonds). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.194.2"
class="koboSpan">This distinction is based on the credit ratings these
bonds receive from the rating agencies.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.194.3" class="koboSpan">Bonds rated in
the range of Aaa/AAA (Moody’s/S&P’s) to Baa/BBB (Moody’s/S&P’s) are
considered as ‘investment grade’.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.194.4" class="koboSpan">Any bonds
rated B (Moody’s/S&P’s) or below are included in the ‘high yield’ class
(</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0416" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0416"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">Table 9</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.196.2"
class="koboSpan">Adjustments</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0417" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_836"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0417)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00437.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0417)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">can be made within a
rating category by adding a + or – (Moody’s) or 1, 2 and 3 (S&P’s) to
indicate a higher or lower issue in its class.</span>

#### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">4.2.2 Key factors to bond credit rating</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">Bond ratings are
based on a number of both qualitative and quantitative factors, the most
important of which are now briefly discussed: financial ratios
(including debt ratio and EBIDTA coverage ratio); mortgage provisions
(bond security by collateral); subordination provisions (bond
subordination to other debt); guarantee provisions (guaranteed by third
party); sinking fund (to ensure systematic repayment); maturity (longer
maturity–higher risk profile); stability (in sales and earnings);
regulation (regulated or not issuer and implications); antitrust
(actions pending against issuer); overseas operations (overseas
percentage of operations and earnings); environmental factors (heavy
expenditures for pollution control); product liabilities (product
safety); pension liabilities (unfunded pension exposures); labour unrest
(labour tensions and problems); accounting policies (conservative
approaches).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">A strong correlation
is apparent between high bond ratings and sound financial performance
(predominantly relating to liquidity, operational profitability, debt
exposure and debt servicing capability;
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0417" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0417"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">Table 10</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.203.2"
class="koboSpan">Plausibly, companies with lower debt ratios, higher
cash flow to debt, higher returns on capital, higher EBITDA interest
coverage ratios and EBIT interest coverage ratios typically gain higher
bond ratings. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.203.3"
class="koboSpan">In general, credit rating agencies take into account
sovereign/macroeconomic issues, industry outlook, management quality,
operating position, financial position, company structure, and, issue
structure.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">Market participants
pay particular attention to bond ratings as a key factor that affects
rate spreads and bond value. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.204.2"
class="koboSpan">Since bond rating indicates competitive credit risk of
any two investments within the group of rated instruments, rating also
can support forecasts of probability of default.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.204.3" class="koboSpan">It is
considered as an indicator of investors’ protection in case a bond
issuer faces adverse long-term economic conditions.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.204.4" class="koboSpan">To evaluate
shipping bonds, credit rating takes into account a number of specific
issues, including</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0418" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_837"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0418)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00438.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0418)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">the impact of
cyclicality and volatility on shipping markets; the uncertainty about
the future direction of freight rates; the shipping business allocation
into spot or chartered markets; the ability of the issuing shipping
companies to attain sustainable future cash flows; and the issuer’s
vulnerability to economic cycles and implications for interest and
principal payment (Standard and Poor’s, 2009).</span>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Spread determinants in shipping bonds</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">Bond ratings are
important both to firms and to investors.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">Most bonds are
purchased by institutional investors rather than individuals; many
institutions are restricted to investment-grade securities.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.208.3" class="koboSpan">If a firm’s
bonds fall below BBB, it will be rather difficult to sell new bonds
because many potential investors will not proceed to buy them.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.208.4" class="koboSpan">Furthermore, a
number of bonds incorporate covenants stipulating that the coupon rate
on the bond is to automatically increase, in case the rating falls below
a specified level. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.208.5"
class="koboSpan">In addition, because a bond rating is an indicator of
its default risk, the rating has a direct, measurable influence on the
bond’s yield. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.208.6"
class="koboSpan">Changes in a firm’s bond rating affect the default risk
premium on its debt, the ability of the firm to borrow long-term capital
and the firm’s cost of capital.</span>

<a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0418" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0418"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">Table 11</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicates that yields increase monotonically as
ratings become lower. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.210.2"
class="koboSpan">In other words, investors demand higher required rates
of return as a bond’s risk increases.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.210.3" class="koboSpan">It is
interesting that the AAA spread is only marginally (0.44%) above a
Treasury-bond (T-bond), indicating that the two bonds are very similar
except with respect to default risk and liquidity.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.210.4" class="koboSpan">Because AAA
bonds often have good liquidity, this spread is an estimate of the
default risk premium for AAA bonds.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.210.5" class="koboSpan">The spread
between a bond and a T-bond of a similar maturity is often used as an
approximation of the default risk for the bond.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.210.6" class="koboSpan">Based on that,
it would be reasonable to estimate the default risk premium for a BBB
bond at about 1.44%. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.210.7"
class="koboSpan">The analysis of bond spreads could also take place
between
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_838"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan">any two corporate bonds.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.211.2" class="koboSpan">It can be seen
that spreads increase dramatically for junk bonds which reflects their
risk and the fact that institutional investors are not allowed to hold
junk bonds in many cases. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.211.3"
class="koboSpan">Apart from rating, spreads also vary with respect to
maturity; longer maturity bonds are expected to have higher spread
reflecting a higher risk profile.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.211.4" class="koboSpan">For instance,
a five-year AAA bond may have only a spread of, say, 0.37% while a
10-year AAA bond of 0.44% (Ehrhardt and Brigham, 2009).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">In this framework,
Grammenos and Arkoulis (2003) conclude that rating is a prime factor in
pricing high yield shipping bonds and plays a key role in setting bond
spreads. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.2"
class="koboSpan">Significant correlation has been detected between bond
rating and high yield bond spreads.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.3" class="koboSpan">Lower rated
issues are associated with higher default probabilities.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.4" class="koboSpan">Hence, one
would anticipate a positive relationship between rating and the spreads
on new shipping high yield bond issues.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.5" class="koboSpan">Callability of
a shipping bond implies that the issue has a call option embedded and
the issuer retains the right to retire (call back) the bond at specified
prices before maturity. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.6"
class="koboSpan">This option is of value in case of lower interest rate
expectations, since the issuer may have the opportunity to refinance
debt with a lower interest rate instrument, thus improving company debt
terms. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.7"
class="koboSpan">However, investors are exposed to reinvestment risk;
hence, they would target higher returns for that.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.8" class="koboSpan">Primary
pricing may be affected by the maturity term of a bond and a negative
relationship between maturity and spread is anticipated.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.9" class="koboSpan">The float
(issue amount) of a shipping bond indicates the liquidity of the issue.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.10" class="koboSpan">Larger bond
issues are expected to have lower risk premiums than smaller bond issues
traded in thinner markets. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.212.11"
class="koboSpan">Hence, an inverse relationship is anticipated between
float and spread (smaller issues – larger spreads).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">The default rate is a
measure of credit risk in the high yield bond market.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.213.2" class="koboSpan">It reflects
relative likelihood that there may be a difference between what
investors were promised and what they actually receive by the bond
issuer. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.213.3" class="koboSpan">That
is, a default implies any missed or delayed disbursement of interest or
principal. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.213.4" class="koboSpan">It
includes, furthermore, ‘forced exchange’, in case a bond issuer has
offered a new instrument containing a diminished financial obligation,
such as preferred or common stock or debt with a lower coupon or par
amount (Fabozzi, 2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.213.5"
class="koboSpan">Since higher default rates are associated with higher
risk premium and investors demand a higher spread for compensation, a
positive relationship between default rate and spreads would be
plausible. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.213.6" class="koboSpan">The
spread is also affected by subordination (in terms of debt claims
priority) and is related to whether debt is secured (collateralised by
assets) or unsecured; unsecured bond issues are expected to carry wider
spreads.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">Gearing has critical
financial implications for shipping companies and is affected by high
swings in freight rates and vessel prices.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.2" class="koboSpan">In periods of
market growth, cash flow capacity may suffice to cover investment needs;
however, in recession periods, external financing may be necessary.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.3" class="koboSpan">Shipping bonds
issued by highly geared companies are associated with wider spreads.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.4" class="koboSpan">The fleet age
can also be an important factor, since it affects vessel value.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.5" class="koboSpan">New vessels
are usually more expensive and companies with younger fleet are seen to
perform better in the capital markets.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.6" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless,
in strongly upward markets and tight demand conditions, vessels can earn
similar freight rates regardless of their age factor.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.7" class="koboSpan">High-yield
bonds issued by companies with an older fleet (higher running costs) are
associated with wider spread (higher risk).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.8" class="koboSpan">Finally, since
larger laid-up tonnage reflects weakening demand interest and
deteriorating industry conditions, the larger this factor the wider the
associated high-yield bond spreads.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.214.9" class="koboSpan">Of the
previous factors discussed, rating predominantly but also gearing and
laid-up tonnage appear to be statistically significant in explaining
shipping high-yield bond spreads (Grammenos and Arkoulis, 2003).</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0419" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00439.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Default distribution prior to ‘D’: 1981–2008" /></span>

id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan"> Default distribution prior to ‘D’: 1981–2008</span>

</div>
