class="koboSpan">Source</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan">: Standard & Poor’s (long-term averages)</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0420" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00440.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0420)

</div>

### <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 Probability of default in shipping bonds</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">Based on Standard &
Poor’s aggregate bond data, over 1981–2008, the (long-term average)
default distribution of bond issues for ratings above ‘D’ indicates that
the lower the rating grade of the bond, the higher the default
vulnerability (probability). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.222.2"
class="koboSpan">Whereas, for instance, bonds rated ‘A’ exhibited a
marginal default rate (0.10%), more than half (58.2%) of the bonds rated
‘CCC/C’ proceeded to default (</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_cap_lbl0215"
id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0215"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">Within the high yield
(speculative) grade category, the lower the original rating on an
issuer, the shorter the time to default over the long term.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.225.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
for the entire pool of defaulters (1981–2008), the average times to
default for issuers that were originally rated in the ‘BB’ and ‘B’
categories were 6.0 years and 4.6 years (from initial rating),
respectively; whereas, issuers in the ‘CCC’ rating category or lower had
an average time to default of 2.7 years.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.225.3" class="koboSpan">These
empirical conclusions are further validated in
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0420" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0420"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.226.1" class="koboSpan">Table</span></a>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0421" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_840"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0421)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00441.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0421)

</div>

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan">12</span>](#Ch028.xhtml_fig0420)<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan">, where data on fastest cumulative defaulters among
global corporates from original rating, during 1981–2008, are summarised
in percentages of total defaults per rating category and time
frame.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">The evaluation of
industry risk is an important prerequisite for the evaluation of
respective corporate issuers, since it provides a robust understanding
of the company’s external business and operating environment (growth
prospects, competition, risks, challenges).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.230.2" class="koboSpan">Although the
characteristics significant to credit risk across industries are broadly
similar, the impact of these factors can vary substantially between
industries. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.230.3" class="koboSpan">As
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0421" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0421"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">Table 13</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan"> highlights, a common set of industry
characteristics/metrics can be applied to identifying the relative
credit impact of key industry factors across some major industries in
the US (Standard and Poor’s, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.232.2" class="koboSpan">The nature and
impact of key characteristics can vary markedly between countries for a
given industry. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.232.3"
class="koboSpan">Utilities, telecoms and retail tend to be more affected
by national characteristics. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.232.4"
class="koboSpan">By contrast, shipping, oil and gas, chemicals and
technology sectors are more global in nature.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.232.5" class="koboSpan">Factors with a
high level of impact on credit risk are cyclicality, degree of
competition, capital intensity, technological risk,
regulation/deregulation, and energy cost sensitivity.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">As to the industry
profile of bond defaults, some variation is seen by sector (Standard and
Poor’s, 2009). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.233.2"
class="koboSpan">Of the 1,668 defaults recorded globally over the
long-term, six sectors display an average time to default that is lower
than the overall average of 5.7 years.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.233.3" class="koboSpan">These sectors
are energy and natural resources, financial institutions, high
technology, leisure time/media, real estate and telecommunications.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.233.4" class="koboSpan">If the median
time to default is considered, then transportation should also be
included in this group (</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_cap_lbl0216"
id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0216"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.235.2"
class="koboSpan">The variation in industry stems partly from
differentiation in the rating mix across sectors, since some sectors
have a much higher representation of speculative-grade ratings than
others (e.g., leisure/media vs financial institutions or
insurance).</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0422" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00442.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: Share of speculative-grade rating to total by industry" /></span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_841"></span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0216"
id="Ch028.xhtml_cap_lbl0216"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4:</span></span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan"> Share of speculative-grade rating to total by
industry</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan"> Standard & Poor’s (2009)</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">As to the shipping
sector, two recent complementary studies focus on a sample of shipping
high yield bonds to identify factors that affect yield premia dynamics
(Grammenos </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2007); and, to assess the risk profile of these
shipping bonds and estimate their probability of default (Grammenos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2008). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.245.2"
class="koboSpan">The former study employs a sample of 40 seasoned high
yield bonds offered by 32 shipping companies between April 1998 and
December 2002 and investigates the impact of a set of microeconomic,
macroeconomic and industry-related factors.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.245.3" class="koboSpan">Despite market
perception about yield changes of corporate bonds, key determinants of
credit spread changes have not been clearly identified (Collin-Dufresne
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2001). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.247.2"
class="koboSpan">Empirical evidence indicates that the dynamics of
credit premia of seasoned shipping high yield bonds can be explained by
credit rating; term-to-maturity; changes in earnings in the shipping
market, as well as in the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds; and the yield
on the Merrill Lynch single-B index.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.247.3" class="koboSpan">The second
study focuses on an updated sample of 50 shipping high yield bonds,
issued during 1992–2004 and employs a binary logit model to predict the
probability of default. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.247.4"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, the explanatory power of critical factors
in best predicting the probability of default for shipping bonds at the
time of issuance is also statistically tested.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">Of the total 50
shipping bond issues in the sample under study, 13 issues were defaulted
as of the end of 2004 and the remaining 37 issues were still trading in
the market or had expired. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.248.2"
class="koboSpan">The respective credit ratings and the categorisation in
defaulted and non-defaulted issues of this bond sample are summarised in
</span><a href="#Ch028.xhtml_fig0423" id="Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0423"><span
id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">Table 14</span></a><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.250.2"
class="koboSpan">Most of the new shipping high-yield bonds were assigned
a credit rating falling into the BB level (68% of the sample); few
issues were rated at the B level (30%) and one issue at the C level
(2%). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.250.3" class="koboSpan">Of this
sample, 8.82% of the BB rated bonds defaulted compared to 53.3%</span>

<div id="Ch028.xhtml_fig0423" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_842"></span>[](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0423)

[<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00443.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch028.xhtml_bck_fig0423)

</div>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">of the B rated bonds.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.252.2" class="koboSpan">This outcome
implies that investors that prefer higher rated shipping bonds in a
shipping bond portfolio stand on average a lower probability of default.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.252.3" class="koboSpan">This, however,
is not necessarily the case on an individual bond basis.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">A number of important
financial, industry and issue specific variables are considered,
including issue amount raised to total assets (issue factors); current
assets to current liabilities (current ratio); cash to freight revenue
(liquidity indicators) and pre-issue gearing as a debt indicator
(financial factors); and, laid-up tonnage to total fleet (industry
factors). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.253.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies with low liquidity (current ratio),
high gearing levels and operating in the spot market are anticipated to
have difficulties in meeting short-term obligations to their
bondholders. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.253.3"
class="koboSpan">The lower the liquidity indicators of a shipping
company, the higher the probability of default for its high yield bonds,
particularly in adverse shipping market conditions.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan">The gearing level is
a most important factor for the probability of default.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.254.2" class="koboSpan">Pre-issue
gearing is calculated as the ratio of long-term debt over long-term debt
plus shareholder equity. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.254.3"
class="koboSpan">A higher exposure to debt indicates higher
vulnerability of the shipping company during recession phases and higher
risk for bondholders due to higher probability of default.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.254.4" class="koboSpan">These negative
conditions have jeopardised the viability of several shipping companies
in previous years, whereas a number of high yield bond issues have
defaulted, as in 1998–1999. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.254.5"
class="koboSpan">A substantially large amount raised in the high yield
bond issue over the company’s total assets indicates a higher risk
exposure for bondholders; hence, a higher probability of default.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.254.6" class="koboSpan">High laid up
tonnage over total fleet indicates weak demand and depressed market
conditions, which in turn increases the probability of default for
shipping bonds.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">To conclude, despite
some overcapacity conditions and demand–supply imbalances in the
shipping markets recently, the shipping industry is anticipated to face
considerable capital requirements over the coming years, as a result of
ageing fleets, loan rescheduling and intensified trade flows (Leggate,
2000), whenever the global financial
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_843"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan">crisis will be over.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.256.2" class="koboSpan">This growth in
demand will be in contrast to a potential contraction in the number of
banks willing to support the industry and a general tightening of credit
facilities. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.256.3" class="koboSpan">As
a result, shipping companies will have to reconsider accessing the
capital markets for equity and debt.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.256.4" class="koboSpan">The
difficulties experienced particularly in the bond markets have led to an
early dismissal of this relatively new form of ship finance.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.256.5" class="koboSpan">Debt finance
with bond issues remains largely dependent on the perception
institutional investors bear of the shipping industry.</span>

## <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.257.2" class="koboSpan">Corporate Governance in Shipping</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">The issue of
efficient corporate governance is a critical topic directly related to
the firm’s financial decisions and capital structure and has attracted
increasing theoretical and empirical attention recently (Syriopoulos,
2007). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.258.2" class="koboSpan">This
section explores briefly the topic of corporate governance and shipping
firm performance.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">Corporate governance,
according to the OECD (2004), is the system by which business
corporations are directed and controlled.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.259.2" class="koboSpan">In other
words, corporate governance specifies the distribution of rights and
responsibilities among different participants in the corporation, such
as the Board of Directors (BoD), managers, shareholders and other
stakeholders, and spells out the rules and procedures for making
decisions on corporate affairs. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.259.3"
class="koboSpan">The following main pillars can be distinguished:
ownership structure and influence of major stakeholders; shareholder
rights; transparency, disclosure and audit; and, board effectiveness.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.259.4" class="koboSpan">A variety of
internal and external corporate mechanisms contributes to an efficient
corporate governance model (Jensen and Meckling, 1976; Shleifer and
Vishny, 1997; Mallin, 2007). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.259.5"
class="koboSpan">These mechanisms include,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.261.1" class="koboSpan">,
managers’ monitoring by BoDs, independent BoD members, ownership
structure and dispersion, committee formation, managerial remuneration
(stock options) and transparent market disclosure processes (internal
level); as well as, the market for corporate control (takeovers),
external stakeholders’ monitoring, shareholder minority rights or active
institutional investor shareholder clauses (external level).</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">The shift seen in
funding sources towards global capital markets and international
investors brings about fundamental shifts in the corporate governance
model of the shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.262.2" class="koboSpan">This shift has
been partly imposed by the institutional framework of the host capital
markets, particularly the US. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.262.3"
class="koboSpan">A fundamental prerequisite for shipping firms going
public refers to compliance with a core set of corporate governance
practices. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.262.4" class="koboSpan">A
number of reasons justify the empirical interest in corporate governance
of shipping firms. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.262.5"
class="koboSpan">For a start, in a highly risky, capital-intensive
industry, the business operation takes place on a global scale.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.262.6" class="koboSpan">The property
of the shipping firms constitutes super-national subjects, whereas human
resources can emanate from all over the world (Randoy, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.262.7" class="koboSpan">Shipping firms
have been argued to gain comparative advantages from the combination of
‘local’ characteristics (internal environment) and ‘international’
characteristics (external environment) of corporate governance (Randoy
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2003). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.264.2"
class="koboSpan">Moreover, the earlier traditional private, family-owned
and managed shipping firms are now transformed into publicly listed,
multi-shareholder entities. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.264.3"
class="koboSpan">On top of that, a gradual separation of ownership and
management is seen to prevail in shipping firms’ top management level.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.264.4" class="koboSpan">Empirical
research in these issues remains, surprisingly, limited.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">In this background, a
recent empirical study investigates corporate governance implications
for the financial performance of shipping firms (Syriopoulos and
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_844"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">Tsatsaronis, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.266.2" class="koboSpan">Based on a
carefully selected sample of Greek shipping companies listed in US
equity markets, the study assesses the implications for and evaluates
the impact on corporate value of the following: (1) managerial
executives (CEOs) directly related to the founding family (founding
family CEO); (2) the level of independence of the Board of Directors
(BoD independence); and, (3) the Board of Directors’ ownership stake in
firm’s equity (BoD ownership concentration).
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.266.3" class="koboSpan">To sum up the
main empirical findings, founding family CEOs are found to exert a
positive impact on shipping firms’ financial performance (measured by
ROE or ROA ratios). </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.266.4"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, a positive impact is confirmed between
equity ownership of BoD members and the firm’s financial performance.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.266.5" class="koboSpan">Despite the
perception that the participation of independent members in BoDs is a
good corporate governance practice, this is not confirmed for the sample
shipping firms. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.266.6"
class="koboSpan">It should be noted though, that shipping firms have
traditionally experienced strong growth rates based on the advantages of
a family-type management and ownership model.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.266.7" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, listing on global stock exchanges has encouraged shipping firms to
now follow more extrovert managerial strategies and modernise their
corporate governance principles, including top management duality and
separation of ownership from management.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.266.8" class="koboSpan">Empirical
evidence supports that sound corporate governance mechanisms can
mitigate the ‘agency conflict problem’ (divergence of managers’ vs
shareholders’ interests) and can have a positive impact on corporate
value (Panayides and Gong, 2002; Randoy
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2003; Syriopoulos and Theotokas, 2007).</span>

## <span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.269.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.270.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter has
discussed key issues on shipping finance and global capital markets and
has assessed the attractiveness and efficiency of equity and bond
markets as important financing mechanisms for shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.270.2" class="koboSpan">Alternative
financing vehicles, such as SPACS, PIPEs, private equity, mezzanine
finance and ATM offerings have been also briefly presented.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">The contribution of
capital markets to shipping finance has evolved in a background of
recent super-cycle trends in the freight markets and robust performance
of international equity markets, before the global financial crisis
affects both markets dramatically.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.271.2" class="koboSpan">The
extraordinary growth rates seen in the shipping markets over the last
years resulted to unprecedented corporate profits and robust liquidity
reserves for shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.271.3" class="koboSpan">Based on this
booming environment, many shipping firms pursued an intensive fleet
expansion strategy, albeit at high vessel values, building tense
overcapacity conditions and creating serious demand-supply imbalances.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.271.4" class="koboSpan">In any case,
this business growth was predominantly funded by external sources of
financing and led many shipping firms conclude this period at alarming
levels of leverage.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.272.1" class="koboSpan">The recent shipping
IPO wave in global equity markets indicates that an increasing number of
shipping firms appear to discover the virtues of equity finance.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.272.2" class="koboSpan">Key factors
for successful shipping IPOs include attractive valuation, efficient
management, robust organic growth prospects, modern corporate governance
and successful investment plans.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.272.3" class="koboSpan">Focusing on
shipping firm valuation, the following parameters are critical: cash
flows, net asset value, revenue and operational earnings, total book
value and enterprise value. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.272.4"
class="koboSpan">Empirical evidence supports that the well documented
puzzle of IPO underpricing and long-run underperformance also applies in
the case of newly listed shipping firms.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.272.5" class="koboSpan">Global bond
markets offer alternative fund raising opportunities to shipping
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_page_845"></span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan">firms that have exhibited a revitalised interest with a
number of bond issues traded over the last decade.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.273.2" class="koboSpan">Despite their
high yield profile, the majority of the shipping bond issues have
performed decently and credit default rates have remained low.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.273.3" class="koboSpan">Overall, the
financing decisions of the shipping firm have important implications for
its risk, profitability, growth and value creation.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.273.4" class="koboSpan">The choice
between alternative capital funding sources, equity or debt finance, and
the resulting capital structure mix is a complex issue and cannot be
uniformly decided a priori for each shipping firm.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.273.5" class="koboSpan">It is guided
by the optimal mix that enhances ultimately the firm’s corporate value.
</span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.273.6" class="koboSpan">As the number
of shipping companies going public increases, interesting management
issues come high in priority, especially, the implementation of
efficient corporate governance systems, including the active role of
BoDs, the application of duality between BoD Chairman and CEO,
information transparency and dissemination or shareholder rights
protection.</span>

<span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">To conclude, for
companies interested in expanding their fleets, international capital
markets and relevant financing instruments present interesting
opportunities to fund raising. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.274.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies realise they should apply more
outward-looking business strategies and take advantage of international
capital mobility, following a more tailor-made use of global capital
markets. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.274.3"
class="koboSpan">Although the recent shipping IPO wave may not be
repeated soon, further activity is anticipated in international capital
markets by shipping firms. </span><span id="Ch028.xhtml_kobo.274.4"
class="koboSpan">At the same time, shipping finance appears to have
reached a stage where innovative financing methods are combined with
traditional approaches to create new, sophisticated instruments.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_850"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_851"></span>[<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 29</span>\
<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Framing a Canvas for Shipping Strategy</span>](#Preface1.xhtml_bck_ht0648)
==================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Kurt</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">J.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Vermeulen</span></span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_fn0948" id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_fn0948"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">A voluminous body of
research and literature has been produced in the domain of strategy for
non-shipping companies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.8.2"
class="koboSpan">Yet, the shipping industry which transports more than
90% in volume of those companies’ physical output has been allotted an
altogether humble share of strategy researchers’ time.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.8.3" class="koboSpan">It is only in
the 1970s and 1980s that we see strategy literature coming to the fore,
perhaps not coincidentally in periods when shipping experiences its
periodical crises. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.8.4"
class="koboSpan">Recently, strategy for ocean shipping companies has
enjoyed somewhat more of an interest from various angles including
economic historiography, organisational behaviour, operational research,
game theory, behavioural economics and quantitative finance.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.8.5" class="koboSpan">In the public’s
mind, shipping is readily associated with some of its charismatic
denizens past and present like Aristoteles Onassis, Stavros Niarchos,
Erling Naess, John Fredriksen and Chang Yung-fa.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.8.6" class="koboSpan">This is
testimony to the entrepreneurial nature of the shipping industry, and
entrepreneurs tend by nature, and out of business necessity, to take a
holistic view. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.8.7"
class="koboSpan">It is this wider, more holistic, approach which
deserves more attention in future research.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.8.8" class="koboSpan">Prior to
engaging in such a review, it is necessary to assess where shipping
strategy stands in the literature to date and how holistic in nature
this strategy analysis has been.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">Section 2 sets out the
approach this author adopted in finding and selecting the literature to
review and analyse. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.9.2"
class="koboSpan">Out of this analysis came a distinct three pronged
approach consisting of: (i) a review and analysis of the strategy
literature “proper”; (ii) the development of a conceptual framework for
literature classification taking into account the holistic and
entrepreneurial nature of a shipping entrepreneur’s perspective; and
(iii) a review and analysis of the literature with reference to the
proposed conceptual framework. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.9.3"
class="koboSpan">The section proceeds in outlining the proposed
conceptual framework. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.9.4"
class="koboSpan">Section 3 adopts this approach and makes a start with a
review and analysis of the strategy literature “proper”.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.9.5" class="koboSpan">It, firstly,
gives a brief overview of key authors who have influenced the theory of
strategy applied to shipping and, then, focuses in particular on Michael
Porter’s work whose strategy theory and concept of sustainable
competitive advantage
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_852"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan">have come to dominate the field of shipping strategy.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">Section 4
discusses the strategy literature pertaining to shipping specifically.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.10.3" class="koboSpan">Section 5 draws
some conclusions from this analysis, whilst Section 6 will complete the
review by outlining broader areas for future research.</span>

## <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.11.2" class="koboSpan">Data and Methodology</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">With a view to gather
the largest possible body of literature on the subject matter, we
performed an English language only database search on EBSCO Business
Source and EconLit covering their full historical extent.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">The search
string terms encompassed simply shipping, maritime and strategy
keywords. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">This
generated some 120,000 headlines which were summarily reviewed.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.12.4" class="koboSpan">Some 800
articles, all shipping specific, published between 1965 and March 2010
were retained for further screening.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.12.5" class="koboSpan">Of those, we
retained for incorporation in this review nearly 100 articles published
in peer reviewed academic journals.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.12.6" class="koboSpan">The remainder
of articles is in use for the suggested future research.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.12.7" class="koboSpan">Further, our
literature review also encompasses material taken from various
monographs or edited collective volumes.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.12.8" class="koboSpan">The author does
not profess this and subsequent reviews to be exhaustive, but does
believe it to be sufficiently encompassing to get a good understanding
of the state of research in the ocean shipping strategy domain.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">Having reviewed this
literature, we found a very broad range of topics being addressed from a
topical or discipline perspective, yet whose relevance to strategy does
not seem to be explored further. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.2"
class="koboSpan">Many journal contributions from a maritime economics
perspective explore in a robust manner issues such as the value of time
and flexibility, yet find little echo in the strategy literature with
respect to the impact of the need for, and value of, flexibility.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.3" class="koboSpan">Or, still,
corporate finance instruments such as the use of financial derivatives
may be explored in great detail with respect to hedging efficiency yet
find their relevance for paper based shipping activities, asset
portfolio composition and risk management policies quasi ignored from a
shipping strategy perspective. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.4"
class="koboSpan">This author thinks this may be partly due to the
specialist nature many of the social scientists have been led to adopt
over time. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.5" class="koboSpan">Gone
seem the times when Stanley Sturmey (1962) would report on the state of
British shipping and review the whole field of maritime economics in the
process, or Moreby (1975) would review the role of the human element in
shipping and place such in a technoeconomic context whilst having also
regard for relevant findings in the fields of psychology and
organisational behaviour. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.6"
class="koboSpan">But, have those times really gone?
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.7" class="koboSpan">Stopford’s
(2009) authoritative work has grown from a maritime economics textbook
(Stopford, 1988) into a veritable compendium of the economic history of
the shipping industry and research pertaining to it.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.8" class="koboSpan">Wijnolst and
Wergeland (2009) are in the process of doing the same in the field of
shipping technology and innovation by bringing together various strands
of research ranging from strategy to ship design to innovation theory.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.13.9" class="koboSpan">These are signs
that the call for a return of “Renaissance Man” is being echoed in the
field of maritime economics in particular and the study of shipping in
general.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">This author’s attempt
to contribute to this recent development is to seek to place the
substantial extant body of literature in a more holistic framework
reflecting the reality that shipping strategy pertains not just to the
group level strategic objectives, but also to its implementation in
specific market segments or its implementation through various
operational and managerial functions.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">As such, it is
proposed to classify the literature</span>

<div id="Ch029.xhtml_fig0424" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00444.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1" /></span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_853"></span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0217"
id="Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0217"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></span></a>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.18.1"
class="koboSpan">Author</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">by means of a
three-dimensional grid representing a holistic entrepreneurial approach
(see </span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0217"
id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0217"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.20.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan"> above). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.21.2"
class="koboSpan">It has as advantage that we cover not only the pure
strategy literature, but also the non-strategy literature whose findings
are of relevance to strategy or the very application of it.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">first
dimension</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.1"
class="koboSpan"> represents the key financial statements of any
business enterprise; a balance sheet, profit and loss statement (P&L)
and a cash flow statement. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.2"
class="koboSpan">In this manner, any aspect of the strategy literature
should be related back to any of the business attributes affecting a
company’s financial performance, but also vice versa.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.3" class="koboSpan">That is, one
assesses the implications for strategy of the literature pertaining to
topical non-strategy matters. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.4"
class="koboSpan">Those financial statements can also be subdivided into
their component business attributes.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.5" class="koboSpan">The subdivision
this author proposes is for conceptual purposes and not necessarily
compliant with accounting rules, such as IFRS.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.6" class="koboSpan">For examples we
and the management science literature may treat a management team as a
company’s intangible asset albeit this would not meet IFRS
classification requirements. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.7"
class="koboSpan">The balance sheet encompasses assets, liabilities and
Ordinary Shareholders’ Funds (OSF).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.8" class="koboSpan">Assets in the
shipping business would comprise tangible assets (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.9" class="koboSpan">vessels,
offices, handling terminals) and intangible assets (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.10" class="koboSpan">brand name,
know how, customer list, the team of key employees, software, patents,
trademarks, design rights, database rights, trade secrets, rights under
concession agreements and rights to berthing slots or container slots).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.24.11" class="koboSpan">The
liabilities consist of debt whilst the OSF encompasses equity, reserves
and minority interests.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_854"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">The P&L components used in our proposed classification
are not those commonly found in the eponymous financial statement, but
three of the five key models constituting jointly a business model
(Mullins and Komisar, 2009). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.2"
class="koboSpan">They are the revenue model, the gross margin model and
the operating model. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.3"
class="koboSpan">The two other models are the working capital model and
the investment model, both of which fall under the cash flow component
of this dimension of our classification.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.4" class="koboSpan">The revenue
model pertains to questions such as: whom to sell to, what to sell, why
does the customer buy this, when do they buy it, what services to
provide as part of the sale and at what price?
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.5" class="koboSpan">The gross
margin model addresses the cost of sales such as brokerage fees payable
to ship brokers, costs of goods sold (COGS) encompassing bunkers and
labour, port fees, survey fees and, crucially, the choice of margin mix
(time charter/COA/FFA vs. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.6"
class="koboSpan">spot market, portfolio composition).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.7" class="koboSpan">The operating
model (OPEX) addresses sales, general and administrative expenses
(S,G&A) including ship management fees, freight rates payable, hedging
costs and, importantly, those costs associated with the provision of
non-standard specific services requested by the customer.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.8" class="koboSpan">Finally, the
working capital model addresses the working capital components that
influence timing of cash flows such as inventory (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.9" class="koboSpan">capacity),
debtors (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.10"
class="koboSpan">freight receivable) and creditors (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.25.11" class="koboSpan">supplier
invoices owed) whilst the investment model addresses capital expenditure
(CAPEX) on either new assets or Research and Development (R&D).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan">second
dimension</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan"> of our proposed classification grid is composed of the
shipping market as a whole, and could be considered as part of future
research to be expanded to include specific shipping market segments,
respectively bulk (dry bulk, liquid bulk, break bulk and neo-bulk),
liner/container and specialty (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">chemicals).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">A
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan">third, and final,
dimension</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan"> of our proposed grid consists in effect of the various
disciplines or technical areas whose practitioners have made
contributions that are pertinent to strategic planning in the ocean
shipping industry including in no particular order, law (competition
law, antitrust law), organisational behaviour, behavioural economics,
marketing, economic geography, scenario planning, governance, business
intelligence, competitive intelligence, corporate social responsibility,
information technology, operational research, logistics/supply chain
management, quality assurance/total quality management and economic
historiography and, of course, strategy.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">It is this
variety of disciplines whose contributions are to be reflected in future
research, which will most aptly illustrate the holistic nature of
strategy.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">In this contribution,
we will now focus on the literature of strategy proper pertaining to the
ocean shipping industry in general (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.31.2" class="koboSpan">to the
exclusion of a review of strategy literature specific to a single
shipping market segment).</span>

## <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">About Strategy Proper and Shipping</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 What is strategy?</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">It is only fitting
that we start our review with the literature pertaining to strategy
proper. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.34.2"
class="koboSpan">Strategic choices made by shipping companies will
address the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">Where</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">How</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan"> to compete and, therefore, consist of corporate
strategy and business strategy (Grant, 2008).
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">Corporate
strategy</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">
addresses the markets within which a shipping firm decides to compete
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.40.2" class="koboSpan">dry bulk,
chemicals, CPP, oil) and will address decisions on vertical integration,
diversification, horizontal integration, new ventures, divestments and
allocation of
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_855"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan">resources between the different businesses.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.41.2" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan">business
strategy</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">aka</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">competitive strategy,
</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">addresses how the shipping firm will establish a
competitive advantage over its rivals.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.46.2" class="koboSpan">Finally,
strategy gets implemented on the functional level or business line
level. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.46.3" class="koboSpan">Strategy
can fulfil a variety of functions in the firm, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.46.4" class="koboSpan">communication
across organisational units, decision support, facilitating
organisational learning and, most importantly, set targets.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.46.5" class="koboSpan">Strategy is not
a product, but a continuous process making use of strategy tools (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.46.6" class="koboSpan">industry
analysis) in researching, devising, implementing strategy and
controlling its execution.</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 The evolution of the theory of strategy</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">Before proceeding with
a review of shipping strategy literature, it is perhaps appropriate to
outline the evolution of the theory of strategy, as summarised by Michel
Godet (Godet, 2007). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.48.2"
class="koboSpan">Godet considers Henri Fayol (Fayol, 1916) as one of the
founding fathers of
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">planning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">”. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.50.2"
class="koboSpan">Fayol summarises management as anticipation,
organisation, command, coordination and control.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">His
contribution was to translate management into 14 principles including
but not limited to, the division of labour, unity of command, the
subordination of specific interest to the general interest,
centralisation and decentralisation, unity of direction, remuneration,
stable work force, initiative, solidarity with personnel, equity and
order. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.50.4" class="koboSpan">It is
notable that several of these ideas are only now coming back to the
fore.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">Contrary to Fayol’s
ideas and the then prevailing Fordism, Mary Parker Follett (1924)
pioneered the behaviourist approach to management built on
decentralisation, the role of the group as an integrating entity for
individuals, competency-based authority and control through trust and
communication. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.51.2"
class="koboSpan">The Interbellum was characterised by the separation of
strategic from tactical plans and the diffusion of statistical and
financial techniques, a by-product of war time logistics planning by
means of operational research. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.51.3"
class="koboSpan">Note, in this respect, the genesis of modern day
econometrics by Tjalling Koopmans, and its pioneering application to
tanker freight rate forecasting and tanker shipping cycle analysis
(Koopmans, 1939). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.51.4"
class="koboSpan">DuPont de Nemours and General Motors, then under the
chairmanship of Alfred P. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.51.5"
class="koboSpan">Sloan, started applying those new principles to their
respective organisations, which were characterised by divisional
objectives setting. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.51.6"
class="koboSpan">A Sloan contemporary contributed to the reorganisation
of GM and subsequently wrote the
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan">Concept of the
Corporation</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan">” (Drucker, 1946) about the newly formed
multi-divisional company.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Drucker (1955) then
went on to posit the five fundamental activities of a manager: setting
objectives, structuring the firm and organising personnel, motivating,
communicating, setting performance targets, supervising and developing
staff. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">The
1950s and 1960s feature the nascent discipline of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan">long-range
planning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">
which adds a long term planning component to the annual budgeting cycle.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">This rapidly
became </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan">corporate
planning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">
as the needs for corporate wide growth targets and diversification
policies were acknowledged. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.58.2"
class="koboSpan">Chandler (1962) observed the organisational setup
changed only through trial and error in reaction to environmental
changes. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.58.3" class="koboSpan">Ansoff
(1965) argued for a proactive approach through reorganisation of the
corporation based on the anticipation of environmental change.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.58.4" class="koboSpan">The feelings of
insecurity engendered by the recession of 1973 reinforced the need for
corporate planning, now
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">strategic
planning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan">, taking into account the possible futures.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">Ansoff (1979)
argued against the redundant character of planning based on
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">a priori</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan"> objectives and advocated
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">strategic
management</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan"> (i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.64.2"
class="koboSpan">the capability to react and adapt
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_856"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan">to environmental change).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">Porter (1998b)
developed approaches to competitive analyses of firms and industries
around the concept of sustainable competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">Barney (1991)
reoriented the concept of sustainable competitive advantage towards the
unique internal resources of the firm, thus, creating a resource-based
theory of the firm (Conner, 1991).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.65.4" class="koboSpan">The concepts
posited by Porter, and more recently Barney, are the ones that have come
to dominate the shipping strategy literature.</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 The market structure and features of ocean shipping</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">Strategy is a function
of the market features in which the subject company is active.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.67.2" class="koboSpan">The demand for
shipping services, as a transport function, is a derived demand
correlated to the general economic development.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.67.3" class="koboSpan">Developments in
shipping, such as technological innovation, and associated freight rate
declines based on resultant economies of scale, cannot by themselves
lead to enlargement of the demand for shipping services.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.67.4" class="koboSpan">Jacks and
Pendakur’s (2008) analysis of the 1870–1913 globalisation movement
showed income growth and convergence were the drivers of world economy
globalisation, and not the maritime transport revolutions of steamships,
metal hulls and propellers. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.67.5"
class="koboSpan">Maritime innovation and its corollaries are the result
of a “demand” for economic growth.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">The market structure
of shipping is, firstly, characterised by serving mainly industrial
consumers with an ocean going merchant fleet comprising 26,280 vessels
owned by 4,795 companies (Stopford, 2004).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">In other words,
the average shipowner has five vessels and is, thus, unlikely to be able
to exercise influence over the market.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">The market’s main
transactional currency was the US Dollar, albeit anecdotal evidence
suggests this may be under review after the 2007/2008 credit crunch led
to a severe decline in the dollar value.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">Vessels are
high capital investment assets and have an economic lifetime of over 20
years. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.69.3" class="koboSpan">Earnings
are highly volatile as the demand for shipping services is a derived
demand linked to the world business cycle.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">Bulk markets are very
competitive, which competitiveness is aided by homogenous cargo, many
market participants (both ship operators and shippers), low barriers to
entry besides capital investment and adequate information flows ensuring
market transparency. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.2"
class="koboSpan">Specialist shipping markets have fewer customers and
fewer market participants and competition is focussed on service and
specialisation. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.3"
class="koboSpan">There can be substitution between some vessels
operating in specialised market segments and those operating in the bulk
segments (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.4"
class="koboSpan">combined vessels).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.5" class="koboSpan">Liner shipping
serves both volume shippers directly (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.6" class="koboSpan">full truck load
with truck meaning a TEU container) as well as lessthan-truckload
\[LTL\] shippers through freight forwarders or Non Vessel Operating
Common Carriers \[NVOCCs\]. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.7"
class="koboSpan">Stopford (2004) considers liner competition mostly from
a price perspective. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.8"
class="koboSpan">Finally, in all market segments, shipping operators
engage in various forms of collaboration including shipping pools with a
view to improve service frequency, asset utilisation and transport
efficiency. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.70.9"
class="koboSpan">Fearnley Consultants (Fearnleys, 2007) estimated
approximately 40 pools were in operation as of 2007, whereby the pool
operator operates in nearly all cases independently from the pool
members.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">Further, there is an
established view that going long, by entering into longer term
chartering arrangements (COAs, FFAs, Time Charters) is a risk averse
strategy whilst going short, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">trading spot,
is more risky (Lorange and Norman, 1973).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">The recent
shipping boom has shown, though, that going long may have its own risks,
such as charter default risk. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.71.4"
class="koboSpan">Charter default risk is, finally, one risk aspect of
the shipping business in addition to business risk, liquidity risk,
default risk, financial risk, non-charter
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_857"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan">credit/counterparty risk, market risk, political risk,
technical risk and physical risk (Kavussanos and Visvikis, 2006).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.72.2" class="koboSpan">Any strategic
plan should address how all such risks will be managed and compensated
for through an appropriate return.</span>

## <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">Strategy Literature Pertaining to Shipping Overall</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">This section reviews
the strategy literature in relation to the ocean shipping industry as a
whole (i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.74.2"
class="koboSpan">addressing shipping as a single market, rather than
specific shipping market segments).</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 The drivers of formal strategies and strategy processes</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.1 Internal drivers</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">Throughout countries,
shipowners have operated for many years in a “club system” whereby the
long-time practice of shipping, sometimes across many family
generations, engendered trust between rival ship owners enabling
cooperation. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.77.2"
class="koboSpan">This is not new in itself, as shown by the history of
Greek or Spanish shipping in late nineteenth century (Valdaliso, 2000;
Theotokas and Harlaftis, 2009). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.77.3"
class="koboSpan">The use of conferences and shared ownership and
promotion of an idiosyncratic business culture would further the
build-up of such confidence between parties even if they had never
worked together before – the club membership vouchsafed for a common set
of values (Miller, 2003). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.77.4"
class="koboSpan">An increase in demand for maritime transport and
technology-led operational improvements led to a heavy rise in capital
requirements which were, initially, met by
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan">horizontal
integration</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan"> on the back of established social networks built
around </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan">trust</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">loyalty</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">This club approach minimised transaction costs.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.83.3" class="koboSpan">It is only
during a later stage shipowners sought
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">vertical
integration</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan"> albeit with risk mitigation through transactions
involving only other shipping related activities such as shipbroking and
stevedoring, as Valdaliso (2000) illustrates with the evolution of
Spanish shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">However, we can
surmise that the club approach was no longer sufficient as the changing
economic environment for shipping led to an increasing capital intensity
of shipping and a concurrent rise in the concentration of tonnage
supply. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.86.2" class="koboSpan">Whilst
this concentration might to “a considerable extent” be indigenous,
citing liner consortia as an example (Metaxas, 1978), its resulting
requirement was for massive capital injections which were unlikely to
have been met from within the “club”.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.86.3" class="koboSpan">The time had
come for seeking funds externally and plan for a business with more risk
factors than before. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.86.4"
class="koboSpan">This did not imply that shipping lost its human touch,
as business development would remain for a long time dependent on the
social networks built through the eponymous “business trip” (Miller,
2003).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">The increasing
internationalisation of shipping with respect to capital raising and
market participants, the rise of offshore flag of convenience registries
and shipping joint ventures between developing countries and the
developed world also implied that shipowners were now exposed to a far
wider range of risk factors whose assessment required a more structured
approach (Metaxas, 1978; Frankel, 1982b).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">The increasing
vessel sizes and technological complexity also led to more complex
management (Frankel, 1982a).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">Greek shipping,
though, resisted the implications of those trends for a long time under
influence of its fragmented ownership, familial character and
idiosyncratic business philosophy (Theotokas and Harlaftis, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.88.2" class="koboSpan">For Greek
shipowners, shipping was
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_858"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">not so much a cash flow generating business as a
lifestyle, an “arena”. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.89.2"
class="koboSpan">Professional managers were only hired in those
businesses which had various non-shipping activities or had reached such
a scale as to require non-familial assistance.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.89.3" class="koboSpan">In Greece, the
outsourcing of ship management to third parties can be a reflection of
disagreements among family members and the need to see those resolved by
having independent third parties brought in (Mitroussi, 2004).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.89.4" class="koboSpan">It is those
parties, in turn, who will insist on a strategic plan meeting with their
approval.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">A final consideration
pertaining to the internationalisation of shipping is the oft quoted
life cycle theory of industries by Vernon (1966).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.2" class="koboSpan">The starting
point of all industrial innovation is that pioneering business ideas are
first executed in those markets where the entrepreneur, for it is the
entrepreneur who pioneers, is privy to the most effective communication
between the potential market (demand) and the potential supplier
(supply). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.3" class="koboSpan">It is
not the factor inputs and their cost which are important in an Early
Stage market, for price elasticity is low, but the market feedback
allowing for proper product specification and externalities.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.4" class="koboSpan">The product is
unstandardised so that the producer can change inputs at leisure, and as
a result production is not cost but specification driven based on
effective market feedback. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.5"
class="koboSpan">The Maturing Product exhibits a certain degree of
standardisation to allow for production economies of scale (reduced
labour cost, increasing capital cost), albeit some differentiation is
retained as a competitive advantage with which to avoid price
competition. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.6"
class="koboSpan">The market has by now accepted a set of general
standards and probability of demand is being complemented by increasing
certainty of cost estimates and increasing price elasticity.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.7" class="koboSpan">Exports and
production relocation are considered where labour cost advantages in
target markets are lower than domestic labour and freight costs combined
or, more importantly, where a strategic threat to future exports
emerges. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.8" class="koboSpan">The
Standardised Product is now highly standardised and has well established
export markets whilst retaining further export potential.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.9" class="koboSpan">The price
elasticity is very high and production processes are now “set” so as to
allow for high capital investment in machinery allowing for maximum
economies of scale (low labour input, high capital input).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.10" class="koboSpan">Competition is
now fought on the basis of innovation induced by direct market feedback
(information). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.11"
class="koboSpan">Imports into the market are characterised by high
labour input and vertical integration into “external economies” (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.12" class="koboSpan">capital inputs
which are not readily available in the exporters’ markets and thus need
to be secured). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.90.13"
class="koboSpan">Thus, the original export market will by now invest in
low risk self-contained production processes for standardised products
with little inventory risk.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">The life cycle theory
has been applied by some authors to shipping (Sletmo, 1989; Tenold,
2009; Thanopoulou, 1995). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.91.2"
class="koboSpan">It has the merit to provide a simple canvas on which to
draw a shipping strategy and suggests in essence that any industry will
have to continuously reinvent itself as a pioneer if it does not wish to
be superseded by competitors emanating from erstwhile export markets.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.91.3" class="koboSpan">This emphasises
the need for any shipowner to possess at all times a clear strategic
plan as to how to continue to innovate on the basis of ever more skilled
labour inputs and differentiated service offerings so as not to wither
away as a mature industry.</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">4.1.2 External drivers</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">The need for external
funds, (i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.93.2"
class="koboSpan">funds from outside the traditional shipping community)
required a vetting of the corporate strategy and shipping marketing
approaches by third party financiers (Goss, 1987; Grammenos, 1979;
Syriopoulos, 2007; Grammenos
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_859"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">and Choi, 1999).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">This is
especially so as the capital requirements are several magnitudes of the
annual cash flow their investment may generate.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.94.3" class="koboSpan">It is ironic,
then, that the availability of finance is also held responsible for the
homogenisation of strategy in that easy credit has pushed investors to
fund more and more “niche” operators turning the niche market into a
“commoditised” shipping market (Lorange, 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">Regardless, it is one
thing to have a strategy and quite another to successfully communicate
such to third parties. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.95.2"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies have many difficulties in accessing
the bond markets on competitive terms as a consequence of failing to
obtain favourable ratings from the rating agencies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.95.3" class="koboSpan">The latter is
in turn being attributed to shipping companies’ failure in getting
rating analysts sufficiently comfortable with the esoteric specificities
of the shipping industry (Leggate, 2000).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.95.4" class="koboSpan">Thus, the
strategy process should also address the ability of the shipping company
to adequately communicate its adopted strategy to third parties with a
view to obtain,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">, a
lower cost of funding and better access to external funding.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">In addition, shipping
has become an increasingly regulated industry with its objectives coming
under scrutiny of regulatory authorities.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">The increasing
public involvement in service industries and the increase in complexity
of shipping require shipping companies to frequently revisit their
stated objectives (Frankel, 1982b).</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Setting a strategic objective for shipping companies</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Whilst some companies
operate with their strategy emerging as they go along, others set a
strategic objective and set out to achieve this through the strategy
process. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">The
wording of such an objective is critical as it needs to embody the
current and future activities of the shipping company.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">Flexible
objectives are, thus, argued for (Rich, 1978b).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.100.4" class="koboSpan">For example,
state as objective the “provision of transport” rather than the
provision of mere “ocean shipping”.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.100.5" class="koboSpan">Frankel
(1982a) considers too little attention is being paid to formulating
objectives and, if any, to setting criteria of the shipping enterprise.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.100.6" class="koboSpan">Criteria such
as profit maximisation, utilisation maximisation, market share
maximisation can be internally conflicting and need proper drafting to
facilitate planning implementation.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.100.7" class="koboSpan">To obtain
flexibility, an effective feedback process needs to be devised so as to
ensure the periodic or even continuous assessment, and if required,
restatement of the strategic objectives of the shipping company
(Frankel, 1982b).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">To be motivational
and permit a long-term perspective, the objectives should also target
growth (Rich, 1978b). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.101.2"
class="koboSpan">Whilst objectives should be internally consistent (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.101.3" class="koboSpan">not in
conflict with one another) they should also be consistent with existing
resource commitments, fit the company’s capabilities and requirements,
such as prior or traditional commitments (Frankel, 1982b).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.101.4" class="koboSpan">Also, prior to
formulating its objective(s), the organisation should have assessed its
strengths and weaknesses by means of a review of past and present
performance and failures (Langley Jr, 1983).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.101.5" class="koboSpan">Langley also
suggests a mission statement as a prerequisite to formulating strategic
objectives. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.101.6"
class="koboSpan">Note the absence in the shipping strategy literature of
the concept of shipping companies having to articulate a
“vision”.</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">4.3 Process and organisational features of strategy development</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">The earlier
literature (Rich, 1978a; Frankel, 1982b) on shipping strategy analysed
the corporate planning process in selected shipping companies and placed
their strategies</span>

<div id="Ch029.xhtml_fig0425" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00445.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2" /></span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_860"></span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0218"
id="Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0218"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></span></a>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan">Adapted from Frankel (1982b)</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">in the context of the
frameworks developed by strategy authors, such as Drucker and
Ansoff.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">A graphical overview
of a strategy process is shown in
</span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0218"
id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0218"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan"> above.</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.1 Planning approaches</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">Two planning
approaches are distinguished; a
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan">top down</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.115.1"
class="koboSpan">” or hierarchical approach and the decentralised
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan">bottom-up</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan">” approach. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.117.2"
class="koboSpan">This establishes also the link between planning and
organisational structure, the latter being a tool to enable the former.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.117.3" class="koboSpan">Frankel
(1982a) distinguishes between two poles of organisation, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan">traditional</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"> centralised hierarchical structure and the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
class="koboSpan">organismic</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan"> decentralised structure.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.121.2" class="koboSpan">The former is
a hierarchy of command, control and communication paired to top level
concentration of information. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.121.3"
class="koboSpan">The latter is a network with distributed knowledge and
those centres of knowledge become, on a topical basis, centres of
control. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.121.4" class="koboSpan">A
shipping company will use the former if dealing with a known slowly
changing environment, and the latter when operating in changing
conditions. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.121.5" class="koboSpan">In
reality, acknowledges Frankel, a shipping company will opt for a mix of
both management systems and approaches which can result in adoption of a
matrix structure.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">Notwithstanding,
Frankel (1982b) is decisively in favour of the top down approach and
argues the responsibility for planning lies with the elected Board of
Directors regardless of the organisational setup (Frankel, 1982a).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.122.2" class="koboSpan">Note that
Frankel uses terms such as policy and planning, with the former
seemingly referring to strategic planning
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_861"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan">and the latter more to competitive planning and
functional planning
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">infra</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.125.2"
class="koboSpan">An alternative view of those respective approaches is
to label them as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan">portfolio</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan"> approach (topdown) and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">deal
view</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">
(bottom-up), as Lorange (2001) does.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">Put another
way, the top down approach can address the shipping company’s activities
from a portfolio level, whereas the bottom-up approach addresses the
vessels (</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">aka</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan"> bottoms). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.131.2"
class="koboSpan">Note in this respect that both Lorange (2001) and
Stopford (2004) consider every single vessel as a business unit in its
own right.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">Hawkins and Gray
(2000) developed a taxonomy of non-shipping specific strategies tailored
for application to different organisational levels (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">the
traditional distinction between
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan">corporate
planning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan"> (at group level),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan">competitive</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.136.1"
class="koboSpan"> or business
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">planning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan"> (at business unit level) and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">functional
planning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan"> (at business line level)).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.140.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
predominance of smaller shipping companies with a fleet size not
exceeding five vessels suggests a flat organisation with single level
planning activities, if at all. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.140.3"
class="koboSpan">The planning process participants’ hierarchical
position may also provide some indications in this respect.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.140.4"
class="koboSpan">Notwithstanding, planning at various organisational
levels may occur within the minority of bigger shipping groups (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.140.5" class="koboSpan">liner shipping
conglomerates).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">In arguing for a
top-down approach, Frankel reflects the established planning practice of
Greek shipping where CEO involvement extends to setting aims and
objectives, choosing alternatives, controlling and evaluating the
company’s operations (Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.143.2"
class="koboSpan">Involvement of the CEO has a signalling function with
respect to the importance of the process (Frankel, 1982b).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.143.3" class="koboSpan">The advantage
of the top down approach is that it may also address venturing into new
business areas which a bottom-up approach is less likely to contemplate
due to a self-preservation instinct among divisional heads.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.143.4" class="koboSpan">This is in
contrast to Rich (1978b) who argues hierarchical top-down planning
processes are assessed as more risk averse, as reflected in the
incremental nature of their strategy initiatives, whereas bottom-up
approaches tend to be more entrepreneurial and risk-friendly.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.143.5" class="koboSpan">Lorange (2001)
argues a balance should be struck between both approaches by adopting a
complementary process.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">The risk friendliness
