of the shipping company in choosing a strategy is argued by Rich (1978b)
to be linked to the prevailing planning approach.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.144.2" class="koboSpan">The
organisational structure is reactive to environmental changes and the
strategic objectives are consequently affected by the interplay between
ownership and management control.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.144.3" class="koboSpan">The
hierarchical approach will typically be driven by a central planning
staff (Rich, 1978a). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.144.4"
class="koboSpan">The observed lack of participation of lower- and
middle-management levels, as opposed to the key role played by the CEO,
in Greek (Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005) and Asian-Pacific (Hawkins and Gray, 1999)
shipping companies’ planning processes confirms this approach.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.146.2" class="koboSpan">However,
planning approach should not be confused with the extent of
participation of staff at all hierarchical levels in the planning
process.</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.2 Planning process elements</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">A textbook strategy
process proper, an illustration of which was shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0218)<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan"> above, commences with an assessment of internal and
external factors with strategic influence.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.150.2" class="koboSpan">In the process
drawn by Frankel (1982b) this is termed factor identification.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.150.3" class="koboSpan">Various
methodologies exists which are non-shipping specific and, hence, need
not be elaborated on in this review.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.150.4"
class="koboSpan">Notwithstanding, it is appropriate to briefly mention
the relevance of competitive intelligence in this respect.</span>

##### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_862"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.151.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.2.1 Competitive intelligence</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">Aristoteles Onassis
was well known to carry around with him at all times a notebook in which
he duly noted anything or everything that was relevant to his business.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.152.2" class="koboSpan">Onassis
intuitively practiced a form of competitive intelligence (CI) gathering.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.152.3" class="koboSpan">In industries
other than shipping, this intuitive CI gathering has been formalised and
institutionalised and has become the preserve of competent
professionals. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.152.4"
class="koboSpan">In those organisations, competitive intelligence is a
systematic programme for gathering and analysing information about your
competitors’ activities and general business trends to further one’s own
company’s goal (Kahaner, 1997). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.152.5"
class="koboSpan">CI should not be confused with business intelligence
(BI), which pertains to internally generated and thus company specific
data devoid
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">per se</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan"> of relevance to the competitive environment.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.154.2" class="koboSpan">BI is,
however, useful in benchmarking exercises whereby the shipping company
can measure its strengths and weaknesses in operational and financial
performance against those of its competitors.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">To perform an
assessment of internal and external factors with strategic relevance to
the firm, CI gathering and analytical processes are the tools of the
trade. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">It is
notable that Asia-Pacific shipping companies’ strategy processes tend to
attribute more importance to informal discussions between experienced
executives exchanging, in effect, internalised CI rather than practising
formalised strategy development processes (Hawkins and Gray, 1999).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.155.3" class="koboSpan">By way of
illustration, Evergreen’s founder stated the management philosophy of
his company is,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">,
to stay well informed to ensure a company’s sustained competitiveness.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Evergreen’s
employees are the backbone of the company’s long-term survival,
suggesting in the process employees always need to keep their eyes and
ears open for CI (Chang, 1999). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.157.3"
class="koboSpan">It can be surmised the CI gathering and analysis
process is well formalised in Evergreen.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.157.4" class="koboSpan">Onassis and
Evergreen are therefore good illustrations of two of the three stages of
competitive development as described by West (2001).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.157.5" class="koboSpan">Onassis was
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.158.1"
class="koboSpan">competitor
aware</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">,
his data collection was informal in nature and based on a natural
curiosity albeit without a reported organisational setup or systems
backup for managing his CI. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.159.2"
class="koboSpan">Evergreen is probably
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">competitor
intelligent</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan"> with a formal data collection process, for application
in anticipating competitor moves and industry trends, managed by a CI
manager who enjoys the backup of dedicated IT-based CI systems.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.161.2" class="koboSpan">In between
these two states is the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan">competitor
sensitive</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan"> company, which combines both informal and formal
approaches to gather CI on competitors with a view to emulate them.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.163.2" class="koboSpan">This
responsibility often lies with the marketing management information
officer who uses for this purpose an existing marketing information
system. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.163.3" class="koboSpan">An
example of the latter approach was documented for erstwhile chemical
shipping company Panocean-Anco (Tomlinson, 1980).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">Shipping is generally
considered to be a secretive industry whilst the wide availability of
data sources is only a recent phenomenon.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.164.2" class="koboSpan">Yet, shipping
pioneered the gathering and use of competitive intelligence with the use
of “cartographers” like Ortelius and Mercator.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.164.3" class="koboSpan">Or, the East
India Company sending Hakluyt in 1602 to report in 500 volumes on
navigation, geography, resources, politics and economics (Moeller and
Brady, 2007). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.164.4"
class="koboSpan">Zannetos is reported in Ronen (1980) to have said that
the reason behind secrecy in shipping is the inability of those who
possess the data to use it for managerial decisions.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.164.5" class="koboSpan">Ronen puts
this comment in a context of a multitude of data sources (data
overload), lack of data selectivity (lack of information), lack of
comparisons and summaries (no topical analytical capabilities).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.164.6" class="koboSpan">This is a
frequent problem with competitive intelligence gathering, or rather
explaining the lack thereof. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.164.7"
class="koboSpan">Ronen’s (1981) case study
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_863"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">reports on a successful implementation of a commercial
intelligence system in shipping companies to gather competitive
intelligence which in turn can be used in a strategy setting process
including trade flow estimation, freight rate determination and
competitor analysis.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">There is, thus, some
evidence that shipping companies have moved on from Onassis’ CI practice
towards becoming more competitor sensitive.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.166.2" class="koboSpan">This is
particularly relevant as shipping strategies are often considered to be
imitative, as illustrated by Greek shipping (Theotokas and Harlaftis,
2009). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.166.3"
class="koboSpan">However, it is noteworthy that some organisations have
elevated CI gathering to formalised processes practiced by all employees
with a view to maximise the intelligence gathered.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.166.4" class="koboSpan">This is in
contrast to the documented practice (see below) of keeping strategy
confined to top management with little to no participation by middle
management and lower-level executives.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.166.5" class="koboSpan">This puts into
question to what extent the resulting strategies are reflective of the
evolving competitive environment as experienced first hand by those
latter executives.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">Once the internal and
external data have been gathered, they will need to be categorised and
structured in a framework after which suitable analytical methods can be
applied with a view to deduce intelligence relevant to strategy
development. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.167.2"
class="koboSpan">Such methods are generic to all industries and need not
be dwelled upon here, but comprise chronology lists, source listing,
event analysis, alternative scenarios, analysis of competing hypotheses,
opportunity analysis and linchpin analysis (Harkleroad and Sawka, 1996).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.167.3" class="koboSpan">There is a
distinct need for future research in the area of CI pertaining to
shipping with respect to a survey of existing literature, existing
practices, development of new practices, applications and their results
in terms of defining strategies and building sustainable competitive
advantages.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">Having highlighted
the relevance to strategy of gathering CI, we can now address some
shipping specific environmental factors that CI gathering should
encompass and their framing for analytical purposes.</span>

##### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.2.2 Environmental analysis</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">In practice, a survey
of Greek shipping companies’ planning processes indicates a bias towards
operating performance, financial projections and functional budgets.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.170.2" class="koboSpan">Environmental
analysis, e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.170.3"
class="koboSpan">PEST (Political, Economic, Social and Technology)
analysis, and SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats)
analysis are considered least important.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.170.4" class="koboSpan">Of those
external elements taken into account, regulatory issues, general
business climate and competitive climate score highest, followed closely
by technological factors, customer preferences and supplier trends
(Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.173.1" class="koboSpan">The observed bias of
those shipping companies in approaching planning as a finance-related
matter could limit the benefits those companies can obtain from the
planning process. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.173.2"
class="koboSpan">This is also suggested by a 2009 McKinsey survey of
non-shipping managers who admit to a focus of strategic planning on
financial objectives (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.173.3"
class="koboSpan">cash conservation), yet feel discomforted by the lack
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan">viz</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.175.2"
class="koboSpan">absence of an adequate balance between short-and
long-term perspectives in their planning process (Cheung
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2009). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.177.2"
class="koboSpan">It is noteworthy that Asia-Pacific managers also place
financial resources as the second most important constraint on the
strategy selection resulting from the strategic reflection process.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.177.3" class="koboSpan">However,
differences in their planning process exhaustiveness did vary by market
segment of the shipping company concerned, with liner companies doing
more environmental analysis than bulk shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.177.4" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
tanker companies
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_864"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan">seem to do more planning than dry bulk companies
(Hawkins and Gray, 2000). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.178.2"
class="koboSpan">The minority who do use specific analytical techniques
did so by using the SWOT model (Hawkins and Gray, 2000).</span>

##### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.2.3 Planning formality</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.180.1" class="koboSpan">The Asia-Pacific
shipowners have mostly no formalised strategic plans, but do have a high
intensity “discussion process” involving senior management (Hawkins and
Gray, 1999). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.180.2"
class="koboSpan">The content of this process is not detailed in the
authors’ articles. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.180.3"
class="koboSpan">Asia-Pacific managers seem to pursue strategic
objectives regardless of changes in the environment, and as such do not
attach much importance to the use of external information, preferring to
rely on personal knowledge, experience and intuition.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.180.4" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
a majority see no use for decision support tools such as scenario
analysis and simulations (Hawkins and Gray, 1999).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">Greek shipping
companies, again, do differ in their practice.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">Their planning
formality is mainly geared towards creating a climate supportive of
planning efforts and the development of a formal statement.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.181.3" class="koboSpan">The use of the
company’s plans for controlling managerial performance are considered
least important as is the acceptance of such plans by the persons who
are to attain the goals set out therein (Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.183.2"
class="koboSpan">This is quite an evolution, as Grammenos and Choi
(1999) found Greek shipping companies not to have any formal rules for
strategic decision making at all.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.183.3" class="koboSpan">As such,
planning in those shipping companies seems geared towards giving the
organisation a sense of direction rather than to develop a detailed
plan, (i.e forward looking). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.183.4"
class="koboSpan">The forward-looking nature is also reflected in the
perceived emphasis on development of internal capabilities as opposed to
backward looking failure analysis (Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.185.2"
class="koboSpan">Notwithstanding, it is noteworthy that in a historical
context Greek shipowners were also noted to have had an “emerging” asset
play strategy i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.185.3"
class="koboSpan">it became a strategy after it had been tried and tested
rather than adopted as a strategy by design (Theotokas and Harlaftis,
2009).</span>

##### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.2.4 Environmental factors</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">Harding (1969) and
Frankel and Marcus (1973) emphasise the inclusion of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.188.1"
class="koboSpan">technological
planning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan"> in ocean shipping-related planning to encompass
interaction with interfaces, feeder systems, competing and complementary
transport modes, the political social and physical environment, and the
“economic realities”.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">Pallis (2007)
strongly argues that the Greek paradigm of shipping has moved toward a
horizontal view of shipping (i.e.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">shipping as part of a
process</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan">) and thus emphasises the need for shipowners to
consider those downstream (intermediate and end customers) and upstream
(suppliers) trading partners in their strategy assessment.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">Cafruny (1985) and
Lorange (2009) posit any shipping strategy analysis should take into
account </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan">geopolitical
factors</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.195.1" class="koboSpan">
in light of history teaching us that any conflict over shipping reflects
a general crisis over the political economy.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.195.2" class="koboSpan">This is
pointedly illustrated by the changes in the political economy of Greece
as a result of the changes brought about by the periodic realignment of
the Greek shipping industry with the evolution of the world economy in
general and international trade in particular (Serafetinidis
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1981). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.197.2"
class="koboSpan">Similarly, the promotion of container shipping by the
USA can be seen as an element of its competitive maritime strategy
aiming to erode the prominence of
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_865"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">European liner shipping companies whilst the
encouragement of vertical integration by natural resource mining
companies into shipping aimed to achieve,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia,</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">
the same result in bulk shipping (Cafruny, 1985; Cafruny, 1987).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.201.1" class="koboSpan">With respect to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan">regulatory
matters</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan">, due attention should be paid to the shift from
national flag/port state regulation to polycentric and multi-level
governance which allows for input from a wider circle of stakeholders
(Roe, 2002, 2009). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.203.2"
class="koboSpan">This implies a wider circle of environmental factors
should be scanned for.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">With respect to the
general business climate, attention should be paid to the “triple bottom
line” (3BL) approach advocated by companies such as Wilhelmsen (Hargett
and Williams, 2009), which approach advocates
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan">Corporate Social
Responsibility</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan"> (CSR) in shipping companies’ activities.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">This is not
insignificant in light of the highly publicised, and potentially value
destroying, regular occurrences of oil pollution incidents involving the
shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.206.3"
class="koboSpan">As such, all factors pertaining to CSR will also have
to be part of an environmental scan and assessed for their impact on
possible strategies.</span>

##### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.207.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.2.5 Situation audit</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">Concurrently with the
environmental analysis, Frankel (1982b, 1982a) and Cerit (2002b) argue
for a concurrent situation audit to assess available resources,
resources already used, market share, services performed and financial
situation. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">The
combination of factor assessment and situation audit allow for
identification of appropriate strategic alternatives.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.208.3" class="koboSpan">The process
should also be run periodically and a feedback process linked to an
updating of a database which supports the strategy process.</span>

##### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.2.6 Planning control</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, planning
processes should have a control system so as to ascertain whether the
shipping company is achieving its strategic objectives.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.210.2" class="koboSpan">Where shipping
companies are active in the provision of logistics services, their
measurement and control will entail the building of appropriate
information systems for data gathering and reporting, the establishment
of “good performance” measures, variance analysis and corrective action
procedures (Mentzer and Firman, 1994).</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.3 Planning horizon</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2005) argue due consideration should be given to the
planning horizon. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.214.2"
class="koboSpan">The choice of an appropriate planning horizon should be
with reference to the product life cycle, technological change, lead
time, present value, organisation life cycle and the validity in time of
the planning premises. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.214.3"
class="koboSpan">Several of these factors, though, are interrelated.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.214.4" class="koboSpan">Indeed, the
rate of technological obsolescence can have a determining impact on the
economic life of a vessel. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.214.5"
class="koboSpan">Lorange advocates a dual horizon whereby market driving
strategies are developed with both longer term and shorter term market
driven outlooks, respectively visionary and revenue oriented (Lorange,
2001).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">In this author’s
opinion, though, one could argue the economic life time of the fleet of
the subject business of the planning exercise should be a determining
factor for strategic planning purposes.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.215.2" class="koboSpan">It should be
noted this life time is very market segment specific and can vary over
time within each segment. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.215.3"
class="koboSpan">One should avoid confusing the planning horizon for
strategic planning purposes with that for other strategy related
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_866"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan">planning processes, such as scenario planning, where
the forecast horizon is determined with reference to the objective of
the study (Van der Heijden, 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.217.1" class="koboSpan">The survey of Greek
shipping companies indicated that only 41% of companies have a planning
horizon in excess of five years.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.217.2" class="koboSpan">This suggests
the majority of planning processes are considerably shorter than the
economic life time of any vessel.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.217.3" class="koboSpan">Whilst this
might be suggestive of the regularity with which the process is run, it
could also suggest Greek shipping companies are mostly reactive to their
environment (Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.219.2"
class="koboSpan">The published survey data, however, did not indicate
the standard deviation of the average planning horizon and as such do
not indicate if some companies did have longer term planning horizons.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.219.3" class="koboSpan">Finally, this
author speculates as to whether the survey data may also not be
suggestive of the fact that Greek shipping companies feel unsure about
how to systematically analyse and interpret the external environment
and, thus, prefer to focus on less abstract financial and operational
data.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">In their survey of
Asia-Pacific shipowners, Hawkins and Gray noted a minority of companies
did have formalised strategic plans whose planning horizon did not
exceed five years (Hawkins and Gray, 1999).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.220.2" class="koboSpan">Both Greek and
Asia-Pacific shipping companies review their plans annually.</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">4.3.4 Planning process participants</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">Langley argues for
participation in the planning process by all those personnel levels
involved in the implementation of the resultant strategic plans (Langley
Jr, 1983). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.222.2"
class="koboSpan">Boyce (2003) has pointed to historical precedents where
British shipping industry networks facilitated structured information
flows by connecting senior management with middle management possessing
financial and technical expertise, not only on intra-firm or intra-group
basis, but also on an inter-firms basis.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.222.3" class="koboSpan">However, we
have seen above how the planning process in Greek shipping companies
seems confined to the CEO and senior management levels, to the exclusion
of middle and lower management staff.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.222.4" class="koboSpan">Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2005) suggest in their article, with further
literature references, that this may be reflective of the limited means
such shipping companies make available for planning processes.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">An alternative
explanation might be found in the peculiar business philosophy and
family character of Greek shipping companies (Theotokas and Harlaftis,
2009) which has resulted in even those few Greek shipping companies
which hired professional managers to retain the strategy making function
for the founding family. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.225.2"
class="koboSpan">Perhaps, the small size of such companies – again, a
result of the fragmentation of ownership characterising Greek shipping
in general and tramp shipping in particular – with an observed average
fleet size of five vessels precludes lower level staff from not
attending to daily operational matters.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.225.3" class="koboSpan">Koufopoulos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan"> refer to extant literature in asserting this exclusion
of lower and middle management may affect the extent, quality and speed
with which strategically relevant information from the external
environment is taken into account in the planning process.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">The situation is not
different in Asia-Pacific shipping where corporate strategy is also the
preserve of senior management. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.228.2"
class="koboSpan">The absence of formalised plans and informal nature of
strategy selection is facilitated by the informal nature of the strategy
genesis by way of “intense discussions” amongst senior managers (Hawkins
and Gray, 1999). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.228.3"
class="koboSpan">The same authors note strategy selection is more
decisive with those managers who
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_867"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan">are older (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.229.2" class="koboSpan">more
experienced albeit with less formal education than their younger
counterparts (Hawkins and Gray, 2000)).</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">4.4 Generic shipping strategies</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">Goss (1987)
prosaically summarised, in the midst of another shipping downturn, “how
money can be made” in shipping: (i) by buying vessels at a low and
selling them high, i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.231.2"
class="koboSpan">an
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan">asset
play</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">
strategy; (ii) to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">do things much better than
others</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">
involving areas such as ship design, operations and general cost saving
measures; or (iii) devising and adopting
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">technical
advances</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan"> with concurrent economic benefits to exploit and
sustain economies of scale and reduce turnaround times.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.237.2" class="koboSpan">Some 20 years
later, the same author expanded on this with (iv) a strategy of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">chartering tonnage
in</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan"> but
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan">not
owning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">
it; (v) </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">buying cheap
</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.243.1" class="koboSpan">second
hand vessels,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan">operate</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan"> them
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan">cheaply</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan"> to the point of abandonment with a view to maximise
cash flow (Goss, 2008).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">Lorange (2009) argues
this buy low/sell high asset play strategy may no longer hold after the
most recent shipping boom, which seemed to have changed the duration of
cyclical swings of freight rates.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.248.2" class="koboSpan">As a
consequence, Lorange argues an increasing importance for shipowners to
maintain cost efficient operations so as to be able to ride out
uncertain freight outlooks. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.248.3"
class="koboSpan">In this respect, Greek shipping companies should be
well positioned as Theotokas and Harlaftis (2009) consider such to be
following a cost leadership strategy, built on distinctive features of
the Greek entrepreneurial shipping culture: business philosophy,
organisational culture, advanced control and know how of ship operations
and the familial character of firms.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.248.4" class="koboSpan">This strategy
was as much by tradition and choice as by necessity given the post World
War II industry structure of multiple owners operating an old and small
fleet lacking in both specialisation and economies of scale.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.248.5" class="koboSpan">The familial
character extended to outsourcing of ship management, where practiced,
to “related” companies in a bid to extract the lowest possible cost.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.248.6" class="koboSpan">However, they
recognise a smaller group of Greek shipowners has combined cost
leadership with (i) innovation through e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.248.7" class="koboSpan">constant
upscaling of bulk vessels, development of combined carriers and
mini-bulk-carriers; or (ii) market development by offering in-house ship
management services to third parties.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">Having outlined some
of the generic strategies practiced in shipping, it is now appropriate
to start reviewing the literature classifying such strategies with
relevance to perceived industry shipping trends or features.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.249.2" class="koboSpan">An oft-used
tool in this respect is the 2×2 matrix pioneered by consultancy SRI Inc.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.249.3" class="koboSpan">Its most
well-known application is the product portfolio matrix,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan">aka</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"> the BCG matrix, developed by Henderson (2006) at
Boston Consulting Group and classifying products based on market share
and growth outlook. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.251.2"
class="koboSpan">The use of two classification dimensions allows for
reduction of strategies to the bare essential drivers.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.251.3" class="koboSpan">But this
simplicity is, perhaps, also its biggest weakness as strategy is
multidimensional and not always easily reduced to just two
dimensions.</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">4.4.1 A review of shipping-specific strategy matrices</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">The products/markets
matrix approach (Rich, 1978b) suggests four generic strategies for
shipping companies, as shown in
</span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0219"
id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0219"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan"> below. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.255.2"
class="koboSpan">A low
risk</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.256.1"
class="koboSpan"> market
penetration</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategy seeks to build on expansion in growth markets
so as to avoid retaliation from competitors (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.257.2" class="koboSpan">Townsend’s
Thoresen then scale expansion in the existing Channel ferry</span>

<div id="Ch029.xhtml_fig0426" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00446.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3" /></span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_868"></span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0219"
id="Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0219"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></span></a>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan">Rich (1978b) with attribution to SRI</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">market).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.262.2" class="koboSpan">This strategy,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan">aka</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">horizontal
integration</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">, also benefits from immediate effects as opposed to
longer term newbuilding programmes but comes with an acquisition premium
price tag. </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan">Market
development</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.267.1"
class="koboSpan"> aims to develop new markets for an existing service,
such as introducing existing vessels, or vessel types, on new routes
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.267.2" class="koboSpan">then
Bell Lines’ expansion of multimodal container transport from European to
African destinations). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.267.3"
class="koboSpan">This strategy aims for asset utilisation maximisation
and exhibits limited risk insofar the existing organisation can handle
this type of expansion.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">Product development
</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">
strategies aim to introduce new products on existing markets such as new
vessels on existing routes (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.269.2" class="koboSpan">P&O’s
introduction of container carriers on existing cargo liner routes,
Restis’s introduction of fast ferries on Greek-Italian routes).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.269.3" class="koboSpan">Rich notes
disapprovingly that those UK operators who did introduce containers
carriers did so with a view to obtain economies of scale, rather than
aim for diversification by providing customers with an altogether new
service offering and, thus, grow their market.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.270.1" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan">diversification</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan"> approach is the most risky insofar the right mix of
existing and new activities requires optimisation by means of
quantitative techniques such as sensitivity analysis, probabilistic
returns assessment and scenario driven “outcome matrices”.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.272.2" class="koboSpan">In support of
this strategy, Rich documents P&O’s acquisition of construction company
Bovis, Ocean Transport and Trading’s acquisition of inland transport and
distribution services – a case of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.273.1"
class="koboSpan">vertical
integration</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.274.1"
class="koboSpan"> – and London & Overseas Freighters (LOF) acquisition
of shipbuilders – a case of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.275.1"
class="koboSpan">diagonal integration
</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">– which
allowed both companies,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan">inter
alia,</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">
to smooth out shipping induced cash flow volatility.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.278.2" class="koboSpan">Diagonal
integration aims to link related activities which are not in a vertical
supply relationship and achieve economies of scope, system gains and
synergies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.278.3"
class="koboSpan">Diversification strategies are also motivated by
synergies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.278.4"
class="koboSpan">Synergies encompass (i) sales synergies where common
distribution channels are used (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.278.5" class="koboSpan">inland trucker
MacLean selling Sea-Land liner shipping services to existing customers,
or vice versa); (ii) operating synergies aiming for leveraging off the
fixed cost base through increased volume and asset utilisation (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.278.6" class="koboSpan">former Denholm
providing ship management services for third party ship
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_869"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.279.1"
class="koboSpan">owners); (iii) investment synergies aiming for joint
use of fixed assets (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.279.2"
class="koboSpan">former Silja Line using a passenger ferry for cruises);
(iv) financial synergies (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.279.3"
class="koboSpan">use of accrued tax loss credits and tax favourable
vessel depreciation policies by P&O after acquiring cash rich Bovis)
(Rich, 1978b, Casson, 1986); and (v) operating synergies (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.279.4" class="koboSpan">favourable
access to shipyard slots for repairs, newbuildings) (Kindleberger and
Johnson, 1985).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">Another oft quoted
matrix model was developed in 1989 by consultants McKinsey & Co.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.280.2" class="koboSpan">and the Centre
for International Economics and Shipping at the Norwegian School of
Economics and Business Administration with a view to advise the
Norwegian government on shipping policy options.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.280.3" class="koboSpan">Both Lorange
(2001) and Wijnolst and Wergeland (2009) describe this matrix (see
</span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0220"
id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0220"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.281.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan"> below) having one axis accounting for
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.283.1"
class="koboSpan">economies of
scale</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.284.1" class="koboSpan">
and another for
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan">differentiation</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.286.1"
class="koboSpan"> potential, thus allowing for four types of shipping
strategies.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan">Commodity
shipping</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.288.1"
class="koboSpan"> prevails in a fragmented industry with few economies
of scale, cost efficiency focus, homogenous service and a very liquid
sale and purchase market for vessels suitable for asset plays.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan">Specialty
shipping</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan"> seeks entry deterring local monopolies with limited
scale effects and some tailoring of the service offering to customers.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan">Contract
shipping</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan"> is a concentrated industry with significant scale
effects, a homogenous but world class quality focused service, close
customer contact and a liquid S&P market enabling a life-cycle costing
based asset renewal programme. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.292.2"
class="koboSpan">Finally,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan">industry
shipping</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan"> is equally concentrated, exhibits economies of scale,
has lifecycle costing based asset renewal programmes and offers
tailor-made services with specialised vessels for which the S&P market
is illiquid. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.294.2"
class="koboSpan">This matrix model seems a strategic operationalisation
of Vernon’s (1966) product life-cycle model, which sees an industry
develop from “new product” to “maturing product” and finally to
“commoditised" or “standardised product”.</span>

<div id="Ch029.xhtml_fig0427" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00447.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4" /></span>

<a href="#Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0220"
id="Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0220"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.296.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></span></a>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.297.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan">McKinsey & Co (1985) reproduced in Wijnolst and
Wergeland (2009)</span>

<div id="Ch029.xhtml_fig0428" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00448.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 5" /></span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_870"></span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0221"
id="Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0221"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.300.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></span></a>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan">Source: </span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">Lorange (2001)</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.303.1" class="koboSpan">Lorange (2001)
advocates for shipping the use of a growth opportunities/resource
mobilisation potential matrix (see
</span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0221"
id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0221"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan"> above), which offers four strategies mixing “brain”
(software or know how) and “brawn” (hardware or assets, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.305.2" class="koboSpan">vessels).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.305.3" class="koboSpan">He argues
shipping is erroneously seen as an overly mature industry where
competition is mainly price driven whereas Lorange posits shipping, in
line with other industries, is increasingly moving from an asset-driven
to a brain-driven approach. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.305.4"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan">pioneer</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategy is akin to that of product development.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.307.2" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan">rapid
expansion</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategy seems a variant thereof and aims for a first
mover advantage by rapidly introducing the new product commensurate with
the development of new marketing capabilities.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.309.2" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan">restructure
</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan">strategy is a defensive strategy which aims for
reducing costs so as to ride the cycle in a low growth environment.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.311.2" class="koboSpan">A variant of
the market penetration strategy is the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan">dominate</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.313.1"
class="koboSpan">-</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan">defend </span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategy which aims to strengthen execution skills
with a view to rapidly reduce a cost base whilst seeking scale in a
stagnant market with a view to crowd out existing competitors and deter
new entrants. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.315.2"
class="koboSpan">Alternatively, this type of asset play strategy could
also lead to an exit event if neither objective can be reached in a
timely fashion, i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.315.3"
class="koboSpan">well before the cyclical trough.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.315.4" class="koboSpan">Note that all
strategies can equally apply to business/vessel level and portfolio
level.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.316.1" class="koboSpan">Lorange (2005)
subsequently revised his strategy based on a conceptual model developed
to further internally generated growth of industrial corporations, which
model he co-developed with Bala Chakravarthy.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.316.2" class="koboSpan">In his adapted
model for shipping, the strategy matrix (see
</span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0222"
id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0222"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.317.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.318.1"
class="koboSpan"> below) has axes representing the know how resource of
the shipping firm vs market understanding.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.318.2" class="koboSpan">The four
resulting strategies are termed “leverage” or “commodity niche”,
“transform” or “speculation niche”, “protect/extend” or “commodity" and
“build” or “niche”. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.318.3"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.319.1"
class="koboSpan">commodity</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategy prevails in well understood</span>

<div id="Ch029.xhtml_fig0429" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00449.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6" /></span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_871"></span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0222"
id="Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0222"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.322.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></span></a>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
class="koboSpan"> Chakravarthy & Lorange (2004) reproduced in Lorange
(2005)</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.325.1" class="koboSpan">and well-established
market where actors have appropriate know how to compete against a wide
range of competitors. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.325.2"
class="koboSpan">A commodity strategy is, thus, aiming at cutting costs,
understanding the market better and marginally extending service ranges.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.325.3" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan">commodity
niche</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.327.1" class="koboSpan">
aims to repeat a success story in a new market, whilst the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.328.1"
class="koboSpan">niche </span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan">strategy aims to add new technologies to a strategy
already established through a commodity approach, and finally, a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan">speculation
niche</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.331.1" class="koboSpan">
aims to adopt new technologies whilst entering new markets
concurrently.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.332.1" class="koboSpan">In his latest work,
Lorange (2009) has fundamentally revised the strategic options for
shipping companies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.332.2"
class="koboSpan">Whereas his previous models were providing a
descriptive context to shipping industry developments, his latest model
adopts a more prescriptive approach (see
</span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_fig0430" id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_fig0430"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.333.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.334.1"
class="koboSpan"> below). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.334.2"
class="koboSpan">Fundamental to this review are the extraordinary market
circumstances shipping has experienced over the preceding decade, and
which were of such a scale and nature to have enlarged the market to an
extent permitting new market entrants and new business models to be
developed and experimented with.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.334.3" class="koboSpan">As a
consequence, Lorange considers the traditional shipping business model
with integrated vessel ownership, vessel operations and related shipping
services such as broking, otiose.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.334.4" class="koboSpan">Shipping
companies are moving to become “pure play” operators or diversified
conglomerates composed of “pure play” businesses.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan">steel
owning</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">
business has a national business culture infusing a top-down management
process focused on physical and financial resources and aiming for
ever-increasing efficiency. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.337.2"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan">steel
using</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">
business has a global culture guiding a people centric bottom-up
management process aiming for customer service improvements through
novel value creating processes. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.339.2"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.340.1"
class="koboSpan">steel
operating</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan"> business is, again, infused by national culture</span>

<div id="Ch029.xhtml_fig0430" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_872"></span>[](#Ch029.xhtml_bck_fig0430)

[<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00450.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch029.xhtml_bck_fig0430)

</div>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">in its top-down
management processes aiming for cost efficiency measures implemented by
cost-conscious staff. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.343.2"
class="koboSpan">Finally, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.344.1"
class="koboSpan">steel-related product
innovating</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.345.1"
class="koboSpan"> company has a global culture promoting novel and
creative ways to bring about innovations generated by the company’s
creative human resources.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">Hawkins and Gray
surveyed the corporate strategies applied by commercial shipowners in
the Asia-Pacific region and found five generic strategies: grow,
develop, stabilise, turnaround and harvest (see
</span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0223"
id="Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0223"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></a><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.348.1"
class="koboSpan"> below). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.348.2"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.349.1"
class="koboSpan">grow</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.351.1"
class="koboSpan">develop</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.352.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategies seem the equivalents of respectively Rich’s
market penetration and market development strategies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.352.2" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan">stabilisation</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.354.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.355.1"
class="koboSpan">turnaround</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategies seem similar to Lorange’s dominate/defend
approach whilst the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.357.1"
class="koboSpan">harvest</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan"> strategy is a sub-case of this (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.358.2" class="koboSpan">the divestment
of an ailing business) (Hawkins and Gray, 1999).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.358.3" class="koboSpan">It is
noteworthy that 65% of the shipowners surveyed owned ten or more
vessels, of which nearly 20% own more than 35 vessels.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.358.4" class="koboSpan">This size is
about nine times the world average fleet size per shipping company as
calculated by Stopford (2004). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.358.5"
class="koboSpan">The pecking order of strategies is pursuing growth, a
combination of several strategies, stabilisation and, finally,
develop/turnaround strategies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.358.6"
class="koboSpan">Only half of the shipowners would consider exiting the
market (harvest) if the going got rough.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.358.7" class="koboSpan">Regardless,
significant reservations were expressed in applying the grow and
develop/turnaround strategies in the sense that up to one-third of
shipowners would not fully follow such strategies or frequently modify
them by means of adopting a combination of strategies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.358.8" class="koboSpan">As a rule,
Asian-Pacific shipowners would not adapt their plans to environmental
changes unless the strategic objectives run counter to market conditions
in which case the anticipated strategy changes would not be
implemented.</span>

<div id="Ch029.xhtml_fig0431" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00451.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7" /></span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_873"></span><a href="#Ch029.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0223"
id="Ch029.xhtml_cap_lbl0223"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.360.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 7</span></span></a>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.361.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan"> Hawkins and Gray (1999)</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.363.1" class="koboSpan">4.4.2 Strategies specific to family controlled firms</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.364.1" class="koboSpan">Whilst the above
generic strategies have been applied to the shipping industry, we cannot
ignore the potential impact on strategy of the family controlled nature
of many shipping companies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.364.2"
class="koboSpan">We have not found any literature pertaining
specifically to the impact of this family controlled nature on the
strategy setting within shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.364.3" class="koboSpan">Zellweger
(2007), however, has posited in an analysis of the lower cost of equity
of family controlled firms how such cost of capital effects can provide
options with respect to generic investment strategies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.364.4" class="koboSpan">The author
indicates how such firms, which have a longer term horizon, are in
Europe disproportionately active in cyclical industries, and from there
to argue such firms can pursue either a “perseverance strategy” or an
“out-pacing strategy” which is not available to short-term oriented
firms. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.364.5" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.365.1"
class="koboSpan">perseverance
strategy</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan"> consist of investments in lower return projects albeit
with a risk profile equal to those projects of more short-term oriented
competitors. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.366.2"
class="koboSpan">The resulting cash flow when discounted at a lower cost
of capital for family firms results in a higher net present value.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.366.3" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan">outpacing
strategy</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan"> aims to invest in higher risk projects with a return
equal to those opted for by short-term oriented competitors.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.368.2" class="koboSpan">The associated
investment returns when compared to the lower cost of capital for family
firms imply an excess return similar to those of short-term oriented
firms.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.369.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, family
controlled firms can opt to participate in longer-term low-return
projects or tolerate a higher degree of risk on short-term projects than
their short-term oriented peers.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.369.2" class="koboSpan">Of course,
these conclusions would not apply to those family shipping firms which
have adopted a short-term investment horizon due to their investor
requirements (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.369.3"
class="koboSpan">listed family shipping firms or firms with publicly
traded securities).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_874"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.370.1"
class="koboSpan">In this respect, there would be merit to study how the
issue of traded financial securities by family shipping firms has
affected, if at all, their investment outlook.</span>

#### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.371.1" class="koboSpan">4.4.3 Factors predisposing to a choice of strategy</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.372.1" class="koboSpan">Having formulated
some generic strategies, it is appropriate to turn attention to some
more specific factors which may lead to preference of one or other
strategy. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.372.2" class="koboSpan">It
is suggested a diversification strategy will depend on whether a company
has a </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.373.1"
class="koboSpan">tramping or liner
background</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.374.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.374.2"
class="koboSpan">In this vein, liner companies are deemed to be lower
risk/lower return whilst tramping is higher risk/higher return and the
latter are thus less likely to diversify into lower yielding liner
businesses with restrictive market practices (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.374.3" class="koboSpan">conferences)
and require specific expertise. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.374.4"
class="koboSpan">Tramping companies are thus more likely to expand “on
the fringes” or outside of shipping (Rich, 1978b).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.374.5" class="koboSpan">This is
confirmed by the situation in the Greek shipping industry, which has
historically had a bias towards tramping in which market shipping
companies have to this day remained small whilst diversifying into real
estate and other activities so that no expertise was required from
“outside the family” (Theotokas and Harlaftis, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.374.6" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
Asia-Pacific companies conform to this pattern with tramping companies
expressing a preference for more aggressive strategies and risk, whilst
their liner counterparts play it safer (Hawkins and Gray, 1999).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.375.1" class="koboSpan">Casson (1986, 1989)
suggests vertical integration between cargo generators and shipping
companies is typically favoured when shipping services are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.376.1"
class="koboSpan">government regulated,
</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.377.1" class="koboSpan"> when a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.378.1"
class="koboSpan">natural monopoly
power</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.379.1" class="koboSpan">
exists on a shipping route leading to a lack of price discrimination,
when </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.380.1"
class="koboSpan">transfer pricing
opportunities</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.381.1"
class="koboSpan"> exist, when vertical integration can
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.382.1"
class="koboSpan">deter new entrants by raising rivals’ capital
investment requirements</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan">, when the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.384.1"
class="koboSpan">production
requirements</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.385.1"
class="koboSpan"> for a secure timely shipping service require such,
when there is a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.386.1"
class="koboSpan">requirement for a near-customised nature of the
shipping service</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.387.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan">technological
development</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.389.1"
class="koboSpan">, and the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.390.1"
class="koboSpan">need to ensure strict service
quality</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.391.1" class="koboSpan">
due to cargo perishability issues.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.391.2" class="koboSpan">The
specialised shipping market segment seems to exhibit various cases of
vertical integration (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.391.3"
class="koboSpan">car carriers, reefer vessels).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.391.4" class="koboSpan">Vertical
integration will be discouraged if there are differences in scale of
operations between cargo generators and vessels which would result in
capacity underutilisation, or the need to find cargo for the return leg.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.391.5" class="koboSpan">A detailed
overview of vertically integrated UK shipping companies in 1984 is given
by Casson, and he concludes therefrom that vertical integration is rare
in practice and predominantly occurs where shipping companies wish to
offer a comprehensive range of services of assured quality to their
customers. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.391.6" class="koboSpan">In
most other cases, alternative contractual arrangements can substitute
for vertical integration.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.392.1" class="koboSpan">Dutch shipbuilding up
to 1800, though, offers a historical antithesis in that the
concentration of the shipbuilding industry was the result of widespread
vertical integration with shipowners who were mostly also merchants
generating their own cargo and sourcing their own wood supplies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.392.2" class="koboSpan">The
concentration was beneficial for achieving
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan">economies of
scale</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.394.1" class="koboSpan">,
but adverse for
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.395.1"
class="koboSpan">technological
innovation</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.396.1"
class="koboSpan"> as production standardisation spread and shipwright
training declined (Unger, 1975).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.396.2" class="koboSpan">This process,
and the latter factor in particular, was to lose the then Dutch
shipbuilding industry its competitive advantage just like it would lose
Bergen’s vertically integrated specialist shipping and shipbuilding
firms their advantage in chemicals shipping and open hatch bulkers some
160 years later (Tenold, 2009). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.396.3"
class="koboSpan">Kindleberger and Johnson (1985) argue exactly the
opposite and find that integration into shipyards favours a more
risk-friendly attitude with respect to developing more innovative
vessels. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.396.4" class="koboSpan">This
view finds support with Chida
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_875"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.397.1"
class="koboSpan">and Davies (1990) who cite the example of National Bulk
Carrier’s acquisition of the Kure shipyard in Japan which furthered
significant innovations in Japanese shipbuilding technique.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.398.1" class="koboSpan">Heaver
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.399.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.400.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2000) confirm the recent trend in the maritime
industry to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.401.1"
class="koboSpan">seek greater control of the logistics
chain</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.402.1" class="koboSpan">,
and by doing so has encouraged the vertical integration between
stevedores, inland transport and shipping companies with a view for all
parties to avoid a ruinous price based competition built upon ever
greater scale
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan">cum</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan"> bargaining power.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.405.1"
class="koboSpan">Finance</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.406.1"
class="koboSpan"> may also be a driver of choice of strategy insofar
lack of finance will prevent acquisition of new tonnage and lead to
strategies favouring use of second hand tonnage in, at least, the short
term (Grammenos, 1979, Theotokas and Harlaftis, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.406.2" class="koboSpan">Similarly, the
choice of investment in newbuildings is also indicative of a long term
commitment by the shipowner and should, presumably, reflect a longer
term strategy (Theotokas and Harlaftis, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.406.3" class="koboSpan">This is,
however, not always the case as newbuildings could just be a technique
to hedge against short term cost exposure by acquiring more efficient
new vessels, obtain finance in those cases where risk averse fund
providers prefer not to invest in second-hand tonnage and where the
owner expects a shortage of tonnage in the short to medium term
providing for an asset play exit, in some cases even before the build of
the vessel is completed. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.406.4"
class="koboSpan">The sale of shipyard slots over the past boom decade is
an example thereof.</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.407.1" class="koboSpan">4.5 Competitive advantage in shipping strategy</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.408.1" class="koboSpan">At the core of many
strategy plans is the pursuit of Michael Porter’s concept of
“competitive advantage”, and more specifically
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.409.1"
class="koboSpan">sustainable competitive
advantage</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan">” (Porter, 1998b).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.410.2" class="koboSpan">This concept
can be described as the firm employing its distinctive competencies,
developed with the firm’s resources and capabilities, to reach a cost
advantage or differentiation advantage which leads to value creation.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.410.3" class="koboSpan">If this
advantage is of a nature to allow the firm to sustain a degree of
profitability in excess of the average of its industry, then the firm
can be considered to have a sustainable competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.410.4" class="koboSpan">Barney (1991)
argues a sustainable competitive advantage, whilst not everlasting,
cannot be rendered ineffective by actions of actual or potential future
competitors. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.410.5"
class="koboSpan">It is appropriate in light of the prominence given by
shipping strategy authors to Porter’s theories (Hawkins and Gray, 2000;
Wijnolst and Wergeland, 2009), we use his concepts in trying to identify
the competitive advantage concepts associated with shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.410.6" class="koboSpan">To do so, one
firstly needs to assess the features of a sustainable competitive
advantage.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.411.1" class="koboSpan">Grant sets out
various isolating mechanisms which can be used by companies to sustain
their competitive advantage, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.411.2" class="koboSpan">to prevent
competitive advantages from being challenged by competitors through
imitation or innovation (Grant, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.411.3" class="koboSpan">Those
mechanisms can be to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.412.1"
class="koboSpan">obscure</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.413.1"
class="koboSpan"> its superior performance,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.414.1"
class="koboSpan">deterrence</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.415.1"
class="koboSpan"> through limit pricing,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.416.1"
class="koboSpan">pre-emption</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.417.1"
class="koboSpan"> by exploiting as the first mover in a small market all
investment opportunities which could give rise to the same sustainable
competitive advantage,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.418.1"
class="koboSpan">complexity</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.419.1"
class="koboSpan"> of the elements of which the advantage is to be
composed disabling the establishment of a clear causal relation between
element and advantage, as well as to ensure the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.420.1"
class="koboSpan">resources
</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.421.1" class="koboSpan">and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.422.1"
class="koboSpan">capabilities</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.423.1"
class="koboSpan"> employed to ensure distinctive competencies are
immobile and difficult to replicate.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.423.2" class="koboSpan">We will now
use those criteria to review the literature with respect to sustainable
competitive advantage in shipping.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.423.3" class="koboSpan">Please note
this chapter reviews only
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_876"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.424.1"
class="koboSpan">the literature pertaining to the whole shipping market
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.424.2" class="koboSpan">not
specific to any of its constituent market segments).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.425.1" class="koboSpan">In identifying
possible sources of a competitive advantage, we can either consider
those advantages attributed as such to shipping companies as well as
those sustainable competitive advantages attributed to shipping-related
industries but of mutual benefit to shipping companies (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.425.2" class="koboSpan">a ship design
patent jointly owned by a shipyard and the shipping company based on
joint research and development).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.425.3" class="koboSpan">Due regard
should be had to the specific market structure as some markets, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.425.4" class="koboSpan">regulated
markets, can confer sustainable competitive advantage on different
criteria than unregulated markets.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.425.5" class="koboSpan">Indeed,
companies operating in regulated markets such as cabotage or the
carrying of government cargo are more likely to be restricted in their
entrepreneurial freedom and focused on satisfying regulatory authorities
(Mulligan and Lombardo, 2008).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.426.1" class="koboSpan">Sletmo and Hoste
(1994) have argued the applicability of Porter’s theory to shipping,
albeit from a national shipping policy point of view, implying
traditional maritime countries can further the survival of their
national fleet by seeking to pursue either an absolute cost advantage
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.426.2" class="koboSpan">creation
of international shipping registers) and/or differentiation through
value-added services (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.426.3"
class="koboSpan">furthering the integration of shipping with
logistics/inland transport through multimodal hubs and favourable
terminal operating conditions) and or seeking to operate in special
niches (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.426.4"
class="koboSpan">subsidising shipyards to build market segment specific
shipbuilding expertise such as cruise vessels or chemical carriers).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.426.5" class="koboSpan">This in turn
could encourage national carriers to explore those strategic options.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.426.6" class="koboSpan">These authors
quote Svendsen in suggesting survival in shipping is strongly dependent
on the existence of a “shipping milieu” or maritime cluster possessing
shipping knowledge, maritime intelligence and technical competencies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.426.7" class="koboSpan">Perhaps, it is
in the presence of the latter that we find a hint of a possible company
specific element of sustainable competitive advantage (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.426.8" class="koboSpan">the shipping
company being a constituent part of a maritime cluster).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.427.1" class="koboSpan">In this respect,
Grammenos and Choi (1999) suggest ethnic homogeneity as a factor uniting
the “club”, in particular the Greek shipping community.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.427.2" class="koboSpan">The club
structure permits a reduction in transaction costs due to common
cultural concepts and values which can also be policed by the club
members, which in turn can contribute toward establishing brand values
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.428.1"
class="koboSpan">vis-à-vis</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.429.1"
class="koboSpan"> third parties.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.429.2" class="koboSpan">The club also
establishes networks beyond its immediate members through which
information can be channelled to club members.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.429.3" class="koboSpan">However, to
what extent a homogeneic club makes for a sustainable competitive
advantage is an open question in an industry where globalisation has
brought a degree of internationalisation that stretches beyond the
geographic borders of the Greek diaspora and where the diversity of crew
nationalities aboard vessels proverbially rivals that of the United
Nations. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.429.4" class="koboSpan">Boyce
(2003) also pointed to the benefits of membership of a network, the
establishment of network routines and the resulting reduction in
transactional costs in addition to non-quantitative benefits such as
knowledge management, organisational learning and the furthering of
personalised business. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.429.5"
class="koboSpan">Veenstra and Bergantino (2000) analysed the flagging in
and flagging out under the Dutch flag, re-stating the definition of flag
with reference to any of the following links: beneficial ownership, ship
management and vessel flag. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.429.6"
class="koboSpan">They found that in the period 1994–1998 foreign vessels
were actually still migrating to the Dutch flag and deduced this was
related to the attractions offered by the Dutch maritime cluster to
“local” shipping companies.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.430.1" class="koboSpan">Further analysis on
the importance of the cluster, defined as a peer group of companies
