combining a set of competencies, was put forward by de Langen and Nijdam
(2003) who equally analysed the Dutch maritime cluster.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.430.2" class="koboSpan">Adopting a
Porterian approach
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_877"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.1"
class="koboSpan">(Porter, 1998a) to identifying industrial clusters,
they argue leader firms of the cluster exhibit mutual benefit to and
dependency on the competitiveness of the cluster member companies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.2" class="koboSpan">Key benefits
are the sharing of innovative technologies, sharing of environmental
intelligence, high quality of supplies and high degree of international
competitiveness. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.3"
class="koboSpan">These benefits are a result of the availability and
quality of input factors, the qualitative and quantitative nature of
local demand, the existence of an industrial network and the quality of
the components (i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.4"
class="koboSpan">individual firms) thereof, and, finally, the domestic
market structure, strategy oriented regulation and degree of competition
within the cluster. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.5"
class="koboSpan">It could, thus, be argued that the membership by a
shipping firm of a competitive “domestic” industrial cluster could
critically influence its ability to develop a sustainable competitive
advantage. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.6"
class="koboSpan">Midelfart Knarvik and Steen (2002) found that the
cluster can generate those positive externalities only if all firms are
at a similar level of development.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.7" class="koboSpan">They also
argue that the cluster externalities did lead to performance
improvements for Norwegian shipping companies and related maritime
services providers. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.8"
class="koboSpan">Wijnolst and Wergeland (2009) posit that membership of
a cluster makes it more likely that shipping companies can succeed in
integrating core competencies within and between firms and, thus, gain a
sustainable competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.9" class="koboSpan">Jenssen (2003)
argues that membership of a cluster furthers innovation which in turn
may lead to a sustainable competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.10" class="koboSpan">Tenold (2009)
illustrated how the existence of such a cluster in Bergen furthered the
emergence of competitive advantage in specialist shipping, albeit not a
lasting one. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.431.11"
class="koboSpan">The commoditisation of advanced technology through S&P
markets, in addition to competitors’ own technological advances, cannot
allow a cluster to sustain its competitive advantage unless the cluster
can maintain its ability to out-innovate.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.432.1" class="koboSpan">A cluster of an
altogether different kind is the one surveyed by Shang and Sun (2004),
i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.432.2" class="koboSpan">Taiwanese
manufacturing firms (not shipping) with extensive logistics competencies
such as positioning, integration, agility and measurement.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.432.3" class="koboSpan">The findings
were surprising in that the logistics competency cluster is not
associated with employees, sales and industry but with the ability to
leverage combinations of inimitable logistics competencies in producing
sustainable competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.432.4" class="koboSpan">This echoes
the competencies integration hypothesis put forward by Wijnolst and
Wergeland. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.432.5"
class="koboSpan">Shang and Sun argue conclusively logistics competencies
can be regarded as a strategic source for acquiring sustainable
competitive advantage, and quote a substantial body of extant literature
in support of their findings. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.432.6"
class="koboSpan">Durvasula
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.433.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.434.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2007) consider the ability to mix and match logistics
service attributes with the maximisation of customer satisfaction in
mind as critical to differentiation of the product offering.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.434.2" class="koboSpan">This may lead
to loyalty and sustainable competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.434.3" class="koboSpan">The nature of
this symbiotic relationship between shipper and shipping company, based
on quality of service and degree of customer satisfaction, is
highlighted by the finding that the choice of carrier represents a hedge
for shippers against their competition (Wagner and Frankel,
1999).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.435.1" class="koboSpan">The importance of
trust as an important ingredient of sustainable competitive advantage,
esp. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.435.2" class="koboSpan">in an era
of integration between logistics and shipping, has been highlighted
early on. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.435.3"
class="koboSpan">Neuschel (1987) argues that management’s ability to
create a climate of trust is key to instituting change and building the
carrier/shipper relationship. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.435.4"
class="koboSpan">Further success factors are the judicious use of
information technology, a low-cost approach and customer service
orientation or a “servant model of leadership”.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.435.5" class="koboSpan">Lagoudis and
Theotokas (2007) also expound the joint importance of cost and supply
chain concepts of quality, service, cost and time in a shipping context
by establishing those qualities as the
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_878"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.436.1"
class="koboSpan">hallmark of the competitive advantage of Greek
shipping. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.436.2" class="koboSpan">More
specifically, their survey reveals quality and time to be “qualifying”
criteria and cost and service “winning” criteria.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.436.3" class="koboSpan">They caveat
their conclusion with reference to differences in applications based on
company size, single- or multi-segment operations and dominant
philosophies with respect to supply chain strategies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.436.4" class="koboSpan">Research into
the nature and effects of supplier integration has since confirmed the
validity of this approach (Kirst and Hofmann, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.436.5" class="koboSpan">Kirst and
Hofmann formulate a caveat to deep integration between suppliers
(shipping companies) and customers (shippers) in respect of the
significant barriers to exit created by the commitment of substantial
resources to an idiosyncratic relationship and the associated loss of
flexibility due to a self-imposed reduced access to the market.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.436.6" class="koboSpan">The nature of
such a sustainable competitive advantage is thus inherently linked to
the successful balancing of both parties’ objectives as opposed to being
purely under the control of one party.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.1" class="koboSpan">Panayides and Gray
(1999) apply Porter’s theory to shipping, based on their interpretation
of Sletmo and Hoste (1994) and argue a ship manager’s competitive
advantage may consist of amongst others a relational competitive
advantage (i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.2"
class="koboSpan">an intangible asset formed out of the established
relationship between a ship manager and a shipowner).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.3" class="koboSpan">This asset is
made up of a bond of trust, significant client-specific investments and
service, investment of time in personal contacts and knowledge
management about the client and the avoidance of conflicts.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.4" class="koboSpan">The authors
did not indicate whether the financial performance of the ship managers
exhibiting these features did lead to financial outperformance of their
peers on a sustained basis. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.5"
class="koboSpan">Also, the features quoted in support do not seem to
meet the criteria to confer a sustainable competitive advantage as they
can be replicated, do not deter new entrants and are not built on
immobile distinctive competencies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.6" class="koboSpan">This author
considers ship management a professional service where the value of the
relationship lies with the skill and knowledge of the inherently mobile
ship manager. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.7"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, it seems doubtful that the established
relations between shipping companies and their ship managers could
constitute a sustainable competitive advantage to either party.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.8" class="koboSpan">The analysis
by Mitroussi (2004) also suggests that the true key motivators for
hiring and selecting a third-party ship manager are their perceived
expertise in certain market segments the shipping company wishes to move
into on short notice, and the price of the service package.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.9" class="koboSpan">These two
factors seem to this author neither unique to a specific ship manager
nor sustainable. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.10"
class="koboSpan">In addition, Mitroussi (2003) has noted the significant
concerns shipowners have about ship managers’ potential conflicts of
interests if they were put in a position of commercial management.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.437.11" class="koboSpan">These
concerns are, in the opinion of this author, unlikely to allow for a
very deep integration between shipping companies and their ship
managers, let alone turn this integration into a factor of sustainable
competitive advantage for either party.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.438.1" class="koboSpan">Pringle and Kroll
(1997), in their analysis of the Royal Navy’s win of the Battle of
Trafalgar, posit the implications for the Royal Navy’s strategy to date.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.438.2" class="koboSpan">Physical
resources and environmental analysis do not constitute a sustainable
competitive advantage as they can be duplicated or imitated.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.438.3" class="koboSpan">The key to
success lies in the foci on intangible resources (especially know how),
an enabling heritage (e.g. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.438.4"
class="koboSpan">trust among staff), a change embracing corporate
culture, the application of innovative strategies, the role of the CEO
in leading by example, investment in training and empowerment of staff
at all hierarchical levels. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.438.5"
class="koboSpan">There is no reason why these lessons should not be
applicable to today’s merchant shipping environment.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.438.6" class="koboSpan">In this
respect, it would seem that most of Greek and Asia-Pacific companies
have failed to develop this type of sustainable
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_879"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.439.1"
class="koboSpan">competitive advantage given the top-down focus, lack of
empowerment, inherent conservatism and focus on cost efficiency rather
than intangibles.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.440.1" class="koboSpan">The very concept of
sustainable competitive advantage implies the firm has already exploited
it to achieve sustained excess financial returns.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.440.2" class="koboSpan">However,
future exploitation on a sustainable basis requires, according to
Plomaritou (2008b, 2008a), the need for a proper effective marketing
policy based on the marketing mix of competitive advantages.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.440.3" class="koboSpan">The
constituent elements of a sustainable competitive advantage need to be
combined and marketed in a manner so as to underpin the sustainable
nature of the competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.440.4" class="koboSpan">Given the
intangible nature of transport services, the effective marketing thereof
could perhaps be considered as an enabling part of the sustainable
competitive advantage
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.441.1"
class="koboSpan">per se</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.442.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.442.2"
class="koboSpan">Cerit (2002a) points in this respect to the experience
of shipyards in strengthening their competitive position through more
developed marketing organisations and the resulting increased market
orientation. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.442.3"
class="koboSpan">This in turn might favourably affect performance,
although that performance link has not been proven to date for the
shipping industry. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.442.4"
class="koboSpan">The experience of other industries suggests, though,
that successful business strategy implementation is necessary to achieve
superior performance. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.442.5"
class="koboSpan">Marketing is instrumental in strategy implementation,
although its implementation is contingent on the specific strategy in
use (Olson </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.443.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.444.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.445.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, Zellweger
(2007) argues that the lower cost of equity, and thus the lower cost of
capital of long-term oriented family firms, can contribute towards
establishing a sustainable competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.445.2" class="koboSpan">In itself,
though, a lower cost of capital is no sustainable competitive advantage
as it can be easily replicated by any firm adopting a longer-term
investment horizon. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.445.3"
class="koboSpan">This is also intimated by the findings of Pointon and
El-Masry (2006) which suggest that dividend- and earnings-based
estimates of the cost of equity over periods of competitive advantage
are significantly different from those suggested by the traditionally
used Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.446.1" class="koboSpan">4.6 Strategy tools in shipping strategy</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.1" class="koboSpan">Datz (1971) wrote
that shipping company managers needed to base their intuitive decision
making on timely and accurate information generated by a “practical data
base” based on the World War II naval operations room concept.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.2" class="koboSpan">The database
referred to was in effect a simulation game.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.3" class="koboSpan">Various
strategy tools have since been developed and are applicable to all
industries. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.4"
class="koboSpan">They need not be analysed in this contribution.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.5" class="koboSpan">Tools
discussed in detail by Coyle (2004) comprise mind maps, impact wheels,
“why” diagrams and influence diagrams.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.6" class="koboSpan">The prime
purpose of these tools is to model out a complex strategic environment
exhibiting the broad variety of factors affecting strategy.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.7" class="koboSpan">The tools used
to perform competitive analysis, as opposed to strategic competitor
analysis, are the already documented matrices, tabular overviews,
diagrams, strengths/weaknesses analyses, opportunities/threats analyses,
PEST analysis, SWOT matching, potential/resources analysis,
price/service diagrams, “potential” analysis, life-cycle analysis,
market attractiveness/competitive strength portfolio analysis, customer
attractiveness/supplier position portfolio analysis, technology/resource
availability portfolio analysis, price/customer satisfaction portfolio
analysis, share of turnover/profitability portfolio analysis and
multi-dimensional web analysis (Kairies, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.8" class="koboSpan">A combination
of several of these techniques has also become popular with the creation
of the “balanced scorecard” by Kaplan and Norton (1996).
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.447.9" class="koboSpan">Finally,
Luehrmann (2004) also conceptualised strategy as a portfolio of real
options thereby establishing a direct link between strategy and
value.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_880"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.448.1"
class="koboSpan">Yet, the tools used by the shipping industry and
reported in the literature are quite different.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.448.2" class="koboSpan">Rich posits
that corporate planning relies heavily on operational war time research
techniques (Rich, 1978a) and this is probably reflected in the
quantitative
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.449.1"
class="koboSpan">viz.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.450.1"
class="koboSpan"> financial orientation of the strategy processes of the
time. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.450.2"
class="koboSpan">Theotokas and Harlaftis (2009) confirmed this
financial/operational orientation for Greek shipping companies and
Hawkins and Gray (1999) for Asia-Pacific ones.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.450.3" class="koboSpan">The financial
orientation is also exhibited in the application of real options
analysis to maritime investment strategies (Bendall and Stent, 2003,
2007), strategic decisions pertaining to market switching (Sødal
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.451.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.452.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2008), strategic/operational decisions pertaining to
scrapping and lay-up decisions (Dixit and Pindyck, 1994) and trading of
ships in the sale and purchase market (Sødal
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.453.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.454.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2009).</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.455.1" class="koboSpan">For Asia-Pacific
shipping companies, the survey by Hawkins and Gray (1999) suggested a
lack of exposure to strategic management theory and a resulting lack of
exposure to current developments in that discipline.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.455.2" class="koboSpan">In a later
work (Hawkins and Gray, 2000), these authors also refer to literature
highlighting the lack of credibility of traditional strategy tools with
Asia-Pacific shipowners due to their untested character in a shipping
context. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.455.3" class="koboSpan">This
observation echoes the findings of Saxena and Joshi (1992) with respect
to low level of usage of information technology (IT) by ship managers in
Hong Kong and attributable to lack of “user seductiveness”, lack of
tailoring to the rigours and specifics of the shipping environment in
addition to shipowners’ inherent conservatism.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.456.1" class="koboSpan">The lack of IT
adoption has certainly not prevented the development of decision support
tools. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.456.2"
class="koboSpan">Fagerholt
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.457.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.458.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2009) developed a “strategic planning” decision
support tool assisting with contract analysis and fleet size/mix issues
by means of optimisation and simulation, albeit this pertains more to
implementation of strategy than strategy planning.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.458.2" class="koboSpan">Similarly, an
automated Multi Criteria Decision Model (MCDM) has been developed which
can take into account a user-defined hierarchy of both qualitative and
quantitative data analysis to assist in performance assessment by means
of combining fuzzy set theory, Analytical Hierarchy Process and entropy
concepts (Chou and Liang, 2001).</span>

### <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.459.1" class="koboSpan">4.7 Organisational benefits of the strategy process</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.460.1" class="koboSpan">A textbook planning
process can generate many benefits for shipping companies besides the
planning output itself. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.460.2"
class="koboSpan">Firstly, assuming a wider participation level
encompassing all high to low management levels, would allow the company
to identify potential intrepreneurs in its ranks.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.460.3" class="koboSpan">This may in
time allow for avoidance of succession issues if the founding family is
no longer to be involved in the business.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.460.4" class="koboSpan">Further, the
process can identify cost efficient outsourcing opportunities which
bring new capabilities to bear on the performance of the company,
thereby building a network organisation.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.460.5" class="koboSpan">Finally,
participation in the process constitutes a learning process for both the
participants and the organisation in understanding the shipping market
and managing knowledge residing with the company’s senior and more
experienced managers (Lorange, 2001).</span>

## <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.461.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.461.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.462.1" class="koboSpan">In this chapter, we
suggested a holistic and entrepreneurial perspective in reviewing and
analysing the strategy literature pertaining to shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.462.2" class="koboSpan">It has as its
objective to relate the literature subject matter back to the relevant
financial statement
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_881"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.463.1"
class="koboSpan">items and business models and can take as input
contributions from a broad range of disciplines and technical areas
going well beyond the strategy literature proper.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.463.2" class="koboSpan">We then
outlined the strategy concepts that have come to influence the authors
of shipping strategy literature, in particular the theory developed by
Porter. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.463.3" class="koboSpan">After
this, we reviewed the extant body of strategy literature pertaining to
shipping in general.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.1" class="koboSpan">This contribution
aimed to answer two key questions.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.2" class="koboSpan">First, where
does shipping strategy stand in the literature?
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.3" class="koboSpan">Secondly, how
holistic in nature is the literature pertaining to shipping strategy?
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.4" class="koboSpan">As this
contribution was focused on the shipping market overall, we excluded
from our review an extant body of research pertaining to specific
shipping market segments, such as the strategy of container shipping
companies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.5"
class="koboSpan">Yet, we found a limited amount of literature discussing
the shipping strategy process, and some literature addressed generic
shipping company strategies identified through the use of 2x2 matrices.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.6" class="koboSpan">Relations were
identified between strategic orientation and organisational features, as
well as between strategy type and type of trading/market segment.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.7" class="koboSpan">We also
identified a limited number of internal and external factors furthering
the development of strategies by shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.8" class="koboSpan">The
contribution also lists the factors identified in the literature as
contributory towards the acquisition of a sustainable competitive
advantage, and notes in this respect the increasing importance of
brain-driven strategies as opposed to asset-driven strategies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.9" class="koboSpan">As such
brain-driven strategies are knowledge dependent, we observed such
knowledge resides in the middle-management levels.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.10" class="koboSpan">The
implication for strategy development is the need for such, and other
related management processes, to become decentralised or at least made
more accessible to personnel hitherto excluded from them.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.464.11" class="koboSpan">This is
especially relevant as these executives also have first hand experience
of market and competitive developments, which are highly relevant inputs
into the competitive intelligence gathering process.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.465.1" class="koboSpan">We noted in this
respect the scarce literature regarding competitive intelligence in a
shipping context and the relatively unsophisticated nature of CI
gathering and analysis by shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.465.2" class="koboSpan">This was
related back to the organisational features of shipping companies which
are typically small companies, locked into intent competition based
mainly around cost efficiency and with seemingly little time left for
strategising. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.465.3"
class="koboSpan">Strategy seems predominantly finance oriented, echoing
the importance of cost efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.465.4" class="koboSpan">We noted
differences in focus and approach between Greek and Asia-Pacific
shipping companies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.465.5"
class="koboSpan">This leads us to answer the second question in the
negative – there is very little evidence of a holistic approach to
shipping strategy.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.466.1" class="koboSpan">The latter conclusion
justifies in this author’s opinion a tentative future approach to
classify a wider body of literature with reference to implied strategic
relevance. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.466.2" class="koboSpan">A
classification structure was proposed to this effect which can be framed
by the observations above.</span>

## <span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.467.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.467.2" class="koboSpan">Areas for Future Research</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.468.1" class="koboSpan">By framing the
strategy process in shipping companies and proposing a literature
classification approach for a wide body of shipping literature, we have
made the first steps towards creating a canvas for drawing shipping
strategies. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.468.2"
class="koboSpan">This canvas should reflect the broad range of
approaches and issues pertinent to strategy making, establishing in the
process the link to the strategy framework.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.468.3" class="koboSpan">This canvas
can in due course serve to assess current strategic theories and,
perhaps, assist with original future research in this domain.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_page_882"></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.469.1"
class="koboSpan">The introduction to this chapter highlighted the
delineation of the application area of our analysis with respect to the
shipping market as a whole. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.469.2"
class="koboSpan">This leaves considerable scope for expansion of the
research into the more specific shipping market segments enumerated in
section 2 above (i.e. </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.469.3"
class="koboSpan">bulk shipping, specialist shipping and liner/container
shipping). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.469.4" class="koboSpan">The
colossal capital investment and trade flows associated with the latter,
and the concomitant degree of organisational institutionalisation, have
also led to an increased amount of attention from the academic research
community resulting in a substantial body of literature pertaining
mainly to strategy and operational research.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.469.5" class="koboSpan">This volume of
research dwarfs that pertaining to bulk shipping, traditionally the most
fragmented market exhibiting perfect competition features.</span>

<span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.470.1" class="koboSpan">By systematic review,
we aimed to address the oft-repeated accusation that transportation
strategy literature is no more than anecdotal evidence devoid of broader
structural theories (Gibson
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.471.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.472.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1993). </span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.472.2"
class="koboSpan">Theotokas and Harlaftis (2009) have made a start with a
more encompassing review of individual shipping companies’ history with
a view to distil common strategic and strategy related traits.
</span><span id="Ch029.xhtml_kobo.472.3" class="koboSpan">Finally, this
author also believes there is a need for review of the foreign language
literature which has made equally relevant contributions to the shipping
strategy domain.</span>

<div id="Ch030.xhtml_book-columns">

<div id="Ch030.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_890"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_891"></span>[<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 30</span>\
<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Port Management, Operation and Competition: A Focus on North Europe</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0683)
========================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Hilde</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Meersman</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">and
</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">Eddy</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Van de
Voorde</span></span><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0949" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0949"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.9.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">In the past decades,
the role of port management has changed quite fundamentally.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.10.2" class="koboSpan">It has
gradually evolved from being a supervisory and determining capacity to a
more subordinate function that often consists solely of providing the
required facilities for the various parties involved in port
operations.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">The port landscape has
also altered in many respects. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.11.2"
class="koboSpan">New technologies and strategic developments have led
almost automatically to greater port competition, both at port authority
level and at the level of companies operating within the various ports.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.11.3" class="koboSpan">All port
players, from authorities to terminal operators and agents, are looking
for ways to maximise profits, to maintain or increase market share, or
simply to survive. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.11.4"
class="koboSpan">These goals are not so easily achieved in an era of
internationalisation of production, consumption and trade.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">National and regional
authorities are also monitoring these developments closely.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">A strong and
efficiently run seaport can be an important asset for a country or
region in trying to improve its economic position.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.12.3" class="koboSpan">For one thing,
port activities generate value added and employment.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.12.4" class="koboSpan">Moreover, a
seaport can be an important point of attraction for a broad range of
industries.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">This in part explains
why European ports, especially in the Hamburg–Le Havre range, are
involved in such a fierce competitive struggle for attracting goods
flows, shipping lines, and infrastructure and industrial investment.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.13.2" class="koboSpan">Economic
resources are scarce, which explains the ferocity of the competitive
struggle in which port authorities in particular were engaged until just
a few years ago. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.13.3"
class="koboSpan">Watching from the sidelines were a number of other
“players”: consignors, goods-handlers, shipping companies, etc.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.13.4" class="koboSpan">This situation
has now changed.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">The supposed strategic
importance of seaports to the economy of a country (or region) has
prompted quite a few national and regional authorities to artificially
protect their seaport(s), among other things through partial or full
subsidising of port
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_892"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan">infrastructure and maritime access routes.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">This, in turn,
has led to mutual accusations of (attempts at) distortion of
competition. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.15.3"
class="koboSpan">This seems quite understandable in a context where
different ports within the same range have similar investment plans and
are competing for the same goods flows.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">The above demonstrates
quite clearly that there is a connection between port management and the
manner of competition. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.16.2"
class="koboSpan">Each port management is concerned primarily with its
own competitive position in the range to which it belongs.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">Decision making
is geared towards safeguarding or preferably improving this competitive
position. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.16.4"
class="koboSpan">Strategic moves by competing ports are monitored very
closely.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">In this contribution,
we shall discuss this issue in some greater detail.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">We shall deal
consecutively with evolutions in port management, the ever-changing port
environment and the need for an appropriate set of analytical tools.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.17.3" class="koboSpan">Finally, we
shall consider some recent findings in research into port
competition.</span>

## <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">Evolutions in Port Management</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">Port management used
to be almost exclusively in the hands of the port authorities.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">However, over
the years, and especially in the past decade, this situation has changed
quite profoundly. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.19.3"
class="koboSpan">The power of the port authority has clearly dwindled.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.19.4" class="koboSpan">It must now
undergo the might of the strong(er) port players, in particular the
shipping companies and terminal operators.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.19.5" class="koboSpan">Still, it is
interesting to consider how the theory and practice of port management
has changed, especially in terms of the objectives pursued and the tools
applied.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0950" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0950"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">The objectives of a
port authority are closely connected with what is considered to be the
economic purpose of a seaport. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.21.2"
class="koboSpan">In the past, these goals were restricted mainly to
increasing throughput, generating value added, creating local
employment, or maximising operating profits.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.21.3" class="koboSpan">However,
today’s reality is more complex and more dynamic than that, primarily
because of the specific nature of the “port product”.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">The port product is in
itself a chain of consecutive links, while the port as a whole is
likewise a link in the global logistics chain.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">In the course
of time, the relative importance of these various links has clearly
changed. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.22.3" class="koboSpan">This
was due to, among other things, significant technological developments
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.22.4"
class="koboSpan">increasing containerisation rate, larger vessels, more
speedy handling …) which have increased efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.22.5" class="koboSpan">In other words,
it no longer suffices to concentrate on one or just a few links in the
chain.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">However, to move
beyond such a fragmentary approach and take full advantage of possible
benefits of scale, clear insight is required into the generalised cost
structure of the constituting links and of the chain as a whole.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">It is important
to know how out-of-pocket costs and costs associated with loss, damage,
and delay have an impact on the choice of port.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Within a logistics
chain, the port cost usually constitutes only a fraction of the total
cost. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">Overall
demand for port services in a particular range will therefore be
inelastic, especially in the absence of alternatives.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.24.3" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, competition between goods handlers, ports and countries within the
same range is often fierce. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.24.4"
class="koboSpan">The possibilities for substituting one port for another
are often so great that the price elasticity for a specific port may be
quite considerable after all.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">In view of the
considerable number of players in any given port (authorities, port
management, consignors, shipping lines, trade unions …), each of whom
has different
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_893"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan">objectives, the nature of port activities is inevitably
heterogeneous. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.26.2"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, the goals of a port authority are
determined in part by the degree to which this authority is, directly or
indirectly, subjected to foreign influences, external control or
competition from other ports. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.26.3"
class="koboSpan">Not surprisingly, then, these goals may differ quite
considerably and indeed may change profoundly over the course of
time.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0951" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0951"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">It is also striking in
this respect that one often needs to search for a compromise between the
priorities of the various important market players.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.28.2" class="koboSpan">As the relative
strength of the different market players may change in the course of
time, so might the objectives of the port authority.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.28.3" class="koboSpan">We shall return
to this issue later on.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">At the same time,
evolutions in port managerial structures are also a direct consequence
of technological developments and changes in the socio-economic
environment. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.29.2"
class="koboSpan">The British port sector is a very good example in this
respect: it was nationalised after World War II and grouped in the
British Transport Docks Board (privatised as Associated British Ports in
1981) followed by a government decision in 1991 that the most important
ports could be privatised. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.29.3"
class="koboSpan">While the situation did not develop equally drastically
in continental Europe, there was clearly a trend towards more autonomy
for port authorities and a greater private stake in goods
handling.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">Far-reaching
mechanisation and sweeping technological changes have also resulted in a
sharp decline in the employment of dock workers and indeed in a thorough
reorganisation of the work itself.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">A typical
example of this trend is found in container transhipment.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.30.3" class="koboSpan">After all, the
capital-intensive nature of liner shipping demands that capacity
utilisation be maximised with a view to achieving an acceptable return
on investment. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.30.4"
class="koboSpan">Ports and terminal operators are thus forced to strive
constantly for a further improvement of efficiency and productivity of
labour. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.30.5" class="koboSpan">Under
this considerable pressure, an important part of port activity has
become capital intensive, with a very high level of investment in
infrastructure and cargo-handling
equipment.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0952" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0952"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">It follows from this
evolution that the role of government has changed.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">Much attention
has been paid in this respect to possible financial or other support
from government for port authorities and the consequences this may have
on the competitive balance between companies and ports.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">However, it is very
hard to make sensible comparisons between ports, as they usually operate
in different economic, legal, social and fiscal environments.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">Consequently,
there are until today considerable differences in the management of
European ports: the Anglo-Saxon tradition of independent port
authorities, the centralising Latin tradition in France, Spain and
Italy, or the municipal Hanseatic tradition in Germany, the Netherlands
and
Belgium.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0953" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0953"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">These different
traditions have resulted in two important, but diametrically opposed,
philosophies. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.35.2"
class="koboSpan">First, there is the continental approach whereby “the
port in the limited sense of the word is managed and operated by the
port authority, the maritime access routes and the connections with the
interior are more the responsibility of the central authorities, and the
cargo-handling and various other services are in private
hands”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0954" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0954"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"> Diametrically opposed to this continental tradition
stand the ports that are run as ‘total organisations’ (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.37.2" class="koboSpan">such British
ports as Felixstowe), whereby the maritime access, the port and
cargo-handling are the responsibility of a single organisation that
supervises all port operations.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, seaports possess
characteristics of public utilities on the one hand and of private
enterprises on the
other.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0955" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0955"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan"> Cargo-handling and related activities are commercial
operations that, under normal circumstances, do not need subsidising.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.40.2" class="koboSpan">By contrast,
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_894"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan">port infrastructure has many characteristics of public
good and is thus approached from a socio-economic perspective (cf.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.41.2" class="koboSpan">the application
of socio-economic cost–benefit analyses to determine whether or not an
investment is justified).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Is it imaginable that
we may evolve towards a port landscape in which government does not
fulfil a regulatory role? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.42.2"
class="koboSpan">For the time being, it would appear that the (national)
authorities had best remained an interested party, if only for strategic
and safety reasons, and to prevent that monopolies are abused by port
authorities, terminal operators or dock workers.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.42.3"
class="koboSpan">Goss</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0956" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0956"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan"> asserts in this respect that “the conclusion must be
that there are likely to be many instances of ‘market failure’ in
seaports, e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.44.2"
class="koboSpan">in the processes of planning, controlling externalities
and promoting competition if these were left wholy to the private
sector: but there are also many opportunities for ‘government failure’,
whether in port authorities or in other official bodies, including
government departments supervising the port authorities”.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">In a fiercely
competitive market such as the port business, the role of government may
however continue to be hotly debated.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.45.2" class="koboSpan">Indeed, it may
be the source of continual mutual accusations of distortion of
competition. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.45.3"
class="koboSpan">Can a European port policy resolve this issue?
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.45.4" class="koboSpan">Is Europe able
to take due account of existing differences between its
ports?</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0957" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0957"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">One of the most
important points of debate remains whether port infrastructure,
particularly maritime access routes to ports, has the nature of public
goods. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.47.2" class="koboSpan">These
are defined as goods that would, in all probability, not be produced in
a satisfactory manner and in sufficient amounts, if at all, by a
competitive industry. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.47.3"
class="koboSpan">It concerns goods for common or non-rivalrous
consumption, whereby it is impossible to exclude those who cannot
pay.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">Goss</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0958" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0958"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan"> was quite clear on this matter when he asserted that:
“non-rivalrous consumption occurs with all beacons, buoys and other
fixed or floating navigational aids because their cost will be exactly
the same no matter how many people are using them.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.50.2" class="koboSpan">The same is
true of dredged entrance channels up to the point where they are
congested. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.50.3" class="koboSpan">If
the opportunity cost of using any of these is zero, then imposing any
specific charge would have the effect of deterring the marginal user and
reducing economic welfare.”</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">The kind of port
infrastructure referred to has two important characteristics: the
indivisibility of the enormous investments involved and their great
longevity. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">No
private company is assured of a sufficient return over such long periods
of time. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.51.3" class="koboSpan">The
amount of infrastructure provided would therefore lie below the optimum
if such investments were left to the private sector.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.51.4" class="koboSpan">However, one
can wonder whether the discussion about the public goods nature of
maritime entrance is not outdated in an era of remote transhipment
centres with natural deep-water sites.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">It is apparent from
the foregoing that theory and practice of port management have evolved
quite dramatically. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.52.2"
class="koboSpan">The role of government, and particularly the issue of
government support, remains a point of considerable controversy.</span>

## <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.53.2" class="koboSpan">The Radically Changed Port Environment</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Until the 1990s,
players in the port business acted very much as independent entities.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">Shipping
companies competed for the same goods flows.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.54.3" class="koboSpan">Port
authorities presented themselves as mainports, both to each other and to
the market as a whole. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.54.4"
class="koboSpan">Fierce competition unfolded between goods handlers
operating within the same port. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.54.5"
class="koboSpan">The
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_895"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.55.1"
class="koboSpan">hinterland modes (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">rail, road,
inland navigation) were preoccupied with maximising their market
shares.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">Then a new trend
emerged, as competition was unfolding increasingly at the level of
logistics chains, in which port authorities, transhipment companies and
the hinterland modes are the most important links.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.56.2" class="koboSpan">Those players
who are able to contribute to the lowest generalised cost of the
transport chain are most likely to be included.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.56.3" class="koboSpan">This also means
that systematic mutual trade-offs are made between links in the
transport chain. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.56.4"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, it may still be the case that serving an
inland port (e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.56.5"
class="koboSpan">Antwerp and Hamburg) is more expensive per tonne
shipped, but that this higher cost is compensated for by cheaper
hinterland
transportation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0959" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0959"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.58.1" class="koboSpan">This new market
structure as such provides an incentive for establishing cooperation
agreements and strategic alliances.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.58.2" class="koboSpan">Theoretically,
the market players should after all benefit from gaining control of as
large as possible a share of the logistics chain, be it for competitive
purposes or for other reasons (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.58.3"
class="koboSpan">stability).</span>

<a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fig0432" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0432"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan"> provides an overview of the cooperation agreements
that exist within the maritime and port sectors.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">We shall
restrict ourselves to the main actors (shipping companies, port
authorities, terminal operators, hinterland transport modes).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">A detailed analysis of
</span>[<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch030.xhtml_fig0432)<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that shipping companies in particular have been
taking initiatives in this respect, forging forms of partnership with
each other as well as with other market players.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.63.2" class="koboSpan">The mutual
forms of cooperation are mostly cartels of various description, but
takeovers and mergers have also occurred.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">Through these
arrangements, the shipping companies hope to increase their degree of
control over the total logistics chain.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.63.4" class="koboSpan">By means of
price agreements, they also attempt to gain control over hinterland
transportation and, as the case may be, goods handling.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.63.5" class="koboSpan">Consider the
following examples.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">In 1992, the North
Atlantic route was marked by a considerable surplus loading capacity in
liner shipping. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.64.2"
class="koboSpan">This led to sharp losses for shipping companies, even
though there were conferences where two or more shipping companies
contributed vessels and shared loading space.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">The shipping
companies’ response came in 1992 in the shape of the Transatlantic
Agreement (TAA), which became operational in 1993.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">With this
cartel, the main shipping companies intended to acquire greater control
over the seriously loss making North Atlantic shipping market by jointly
determining rates, capacity supplied and the transport conditions.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">The
consequences were clear to see: over 80% of the market was controlled in
this manner, and, partly because of a shrinking capacity, rates
increased sharply (by between 30 and 50% in some years).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">Consignors responded
fiercely, as they suddenly found it much harder to obtain loading space
and were now unable to negotiate directly with shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.66.2" class="koboSpan">They demanded a
sufficient degree of competition, coupled with free supply and demand
and the possibility of negotiating with companies separately.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.66.3" class="koboSpan">As the Treaty
of Rome prohibits cartelisation, the TAA was outlawed because of its
manipulation of tariffs, the capacity policy pursued and the fact that
cartel agreements also applied to pre-carriage and on-carriage.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">It speaks for itself
that these kinds of cartel agreements were regarded suspiciously by
ports. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.67.2" class="koboSpan">The
possibility of higher prices may, after all, result in less maritime
transport (and thus in a decline in port throughput).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">A similar reasoning is
followed by ports in the case of mergers, as reorganisations and cost
saving often result in fewer, but larger and stronger port users.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">This is
illustrated</span>

<div id="Ch030.xhtml_fig0432" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_896"></span>[](#Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0432)

[<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00452.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0432)

</div>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_897"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">quite well by the merger in 1996 of the container
liners P&O and Nedlloyd into P&O Nedlloyd Container Line.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.70.2" class="koboSpan">After the
merger, the company had a fleet at his disposal of 112 vessels which it
either owned or chartered, for 540,000 TEU containers and a turnover of
USD 4 billion. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.70.3"
class="koboSpan">Also, the merger implied that the company would be the
same size as its main competitors (including Maersk, Evergreen,
Sealand). </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.70.4" class="koboSpan">This
was achieved through cost saving and scale increases.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.70.5" class="koboSpan">Not taking into
account the one-off restructuring costs, the annual cost saving was
estimated at approximately USD 200 million, which amounted to about 5%
of the total cost of container operations.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.70.6" class="koboSpan">In meantime P&O
Nedlloyd has been integrated into Maersk.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">Within the port
perimeter, the competitive struggle between terminal operators, for
example, has evolved in different directions.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">A first
possibility was that existing competition was retained, resulting in a
combination of low profit margins and large volumes.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">Another
possibility was an evolution towards a single operator, as clients were
growing increasingly large and handlers needed to increase the scale of
operations accordingly. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.71.4"
class="koboSpan">Scale increases among goods handlers is necessary in
order to be considered as a fully-fledged partner by shipping companies.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.71.5" class="koboSpan">This is
ultimately what happened in Antwerp in 2002, first with a merger between
the two largest stevedores, Hessenatie and Noordnatie, into
HesseNoordnatie, followed by a move in which 80% of the capital stock
was taken over by Port of Singapore Authority (PSA).
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.71.6" class="koboSpan">Thus, terminal
operating companies also became subject to attempts at
integration.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">The above examples
illustrate two important trends. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.72.2"
class="koboSpan">First, there is a clear trend towards increasing the
scale of operations by mergers, cartels and other cooperation
agreements. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.72.3" class="koboSpan">At
the same time, efforts are made to obtain greater control over larger
parts of the logistics chain. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.72.4"
class="koboSpan">Shipping companies in particular took the initiative in
this respect, but other market players soon followed suit.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">What is the intended
purpose of such forms of cooperation?
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.73.2" class="koboSpan">Is it connected
with the market structure (i.e. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.73.3"
class="koboSpan">is it aimed at realising economies of scale or
acquiring market power)? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.73.4"
class="koboSpan">Is it aimed at management efficiency?
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.73.5" class="koboSpan">Or do tax
considerations come into play?
</span><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fig0433" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0433"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan"> provides an overview of possible objectives and the
tools used by the various market players for achieving these goals, as
well as the possible consequences.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">In the case of mergers
between such companies as P&O and Nedlloyd, the most obvious motivation
is achieving economies of scale. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.76.2"
class="koboSpan">By merging, one intends to become an equally large
market player as the main competitors and, at the same time, one aims at
spreading the relatively high fixed costs over a more substantial
output. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">However, Cowling
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0962" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0962"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan"> already observed that economies of scale are often
only achieved “through an active programme of rationalisation and
investment by which the constituent of scale and scope were moulded into
a new entity”. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.79.2"
class="koboSpan">Be that as it may, if realising economies of scale and
scope is the reason for merging, it often takes a long time before this
objective is achieved.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">Another rational
objective besides the realisation of economies of scale may be the
acquisition of greater market power, perhaps even market dominance.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.80.2" class="koboSpan">By merging and
cooperating, players may intend to obtain control over a greater share
of industrial and commercial activities.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">A further objective
may be to increase efficiency. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.81.2"
class="koboSpan">In order to ascertain whether or not this is the case,
one would need to test whether the initiating party is more efficient
than the party that is approached and whether merging is a
profit-generating activity. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.81.3"
class="koboSpan">There may also be tax benefits to take into account, in
the sense that merging can, in the first instance, sometimes have the
effect of reducing the aggregate tax basis.</span>

<div id="Ch030.xhtml_fig0433" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_898"></span>[](#Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0433)

[<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00453.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0433)

</div>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_899"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan">Finally, merging may also be regarded as a tool for
achieving market entry, sometimes internationally, so that in a sense it
stimulates competition. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">On the other hand, competition may be reduced or even
replaced with a monopoly.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">Now that we have
identified a number of possible goals, the question arises: what are the
possible consequences? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.84.2"
class="koboSpan">Note that quite a few of the cooperation agreements
presented in </span>[<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch030.xhtml_fig0432)<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan"> have a direct impact on the internal functioning of
the seaports and on the competition between ports.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">Consider the example
of a collaboration leading to the establishment of dedicated terminals.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">Obviously,
other shipping companies will not be inclined to have cargo handled at
terminals that are operated by potential competitors.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.87.3" class="koboSpan">In other words,
such dedicated terminals may result in a diversion of freight traffic.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.87.4" class="koboSpan">So while a port
authority may have intended to improve its competitive position by
providing new transhipment infrastructure, the net result in terms of
throughput may in fact be negative.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.87.5" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the
port authority in question also runs the risk that future traffic
evolutions may become dependent upon the competitiveness and strategy of
a limited number of shipping companies that are tied to terminal
operators. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.87.6" class="koboSpan">The
success of a port, then, may eventually be determined by the
competitiveness of the shipping companies concerned.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">Vertical cooperation
agreements aimed at obtaining control over a larger share of the
logistics chain may also have an impact on port throughput.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.88.2" class="koboSpan">Productive
ports, with low terminal handling costs and/or good hinterland
connections, are at risk of being shunned as a port of call if they do
not fit into the strategy of the group controlling the logistics chain.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.88.3"
class="koboSpan">Cross-subsidising may also play a role in this
respect.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">In the past, there has
always been relatively strong internal competition between transhipment
companies in the Hamburg–Le Havre range.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.89.2" class="koboSpan">However,
vertical mergers of logistics firms or horizontal mergers of, for
example, terminal operating companies may destroy this historical
advantage. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.89.3"
class="koboSpan">After all, cooperation can have the effect of
suppressing competition. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.89.4"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, this argument has often been used to justify
government regulation. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.89.5"
class="koboSpan">Stead</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0963" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0963"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
class="koboSpan"> asserts in this respect that many studies “include the
assumption that not only is monopoly power itself socially undesirable
but so too are resources spent on competition to acquire or maintain a
dominant monopolistic position”.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">It would appear to be
advisable in the relatively short term to conduct theoretical and
empirical research on the possible consequences of cooperation
agreements. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.92.2"
class="koboSpan">Relevant research questions are:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">How do market
    players in the logistics chain (shipping companies, transhipment t
    companies…) operate within different market structures?
    </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.93.2" class="koboSpan">What is the
    relationship between company size and profitability on the one hand
    and the likely effects in terms of market concentration, market
    power and efficiency on the other?
    </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.93.3" class="koboSpan">To what
    extent does government influence industrial organisation?</span>
2.  <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">What is the
    strategic behaviour of the above-mentioned market players?
    </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">To what
    extent is greater efficiency related to a lower production unit cost
    coupled with returns to scale and greater market power through
    collusion on the part of certain companies in order to keep prices
    high?</span>
3.  <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">To what extent can
    other forms of alliances (e.g.
    </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.95.2" class="koboSpan">licensing
    and cross-licensing, subcontracting …) be established that imply
    less commitment, control and mutual dependency?</span>
4.  <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">What is the
    relationship between market control stemming from alliances and
    mergers on the one hand and pricing behaviour on the other?
    </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.96.2" class="koboSpan">The
    existence
    </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_900"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
    class="koboSpan">of an oligopoly or a high level of concentration
    with one dominant company can result in different types of pricing
    mechanism: price leadership, price discrimination, limit pricing,
    collusion, predatory pricing …</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">Until empirical
research proves otherwise, we may assume that the unique market
structure in the maritime and port business does not exist.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.98.2" class="koboSpan">Nonetheless,
certain developments are quite clear to see, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.98.3" class="koboSpan">the role of
government in the discernible trend towards acquiring greater control
over (a larger share of) the logistics chain.</span>

## <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">Management in a Growth Environment</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Until now world ports
operated in a growth environment.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.100.2" class="koboSpan">This also
holds for the principal ports in the Hamburg–Le Havre range.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">However,
growth presupposes adequate capacity and the absence of bottlenecks that
may cause congestion. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.100.4"
class="koboSpan">The accumulation of sufficient capacity in turn demands
correct decision making. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.100.5"
class="koboSpan">In the past, one could count on unbridled government
intervention, often resulting in excess capacity.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.100.6" class="koboSpan">This, however,
is no longer the case. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.100.7"
class="koboSpan">Today, ports bear responsibility for their own
investment decisions.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">From a long-term
perspective, ports will be inclined to make sure that the available
capacity does not present a limit to their growth potential.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.101.2" class="koboSpan">In order to be
able to ascertain whether or not this is the case, one needs a constant
supply of reliable forecasts of future goods
flows</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0964" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0964"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.103.2"
class="koboSpan">However, predictions used by port authorities often
consist merely in trend extrapolations of, among other things,
throughput within a range under the assumption of a constant market
share. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.103.3" class="koboSpan">If one
takes general traffic forecasts as a starting point, it is equally
important to acquire adequate insight into the factors determining this
market share. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.103.4"
class="koboSpan">Only on the basis of this knowledge can one arrive at
correct decisions about whether or not extension of capacity is called
for.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">Modelling of port
throughput, however, is complicated and, thus far, not always equally
transparent. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.104.2"
class="koboSpan">It requires a scientifically well-founded set of tools
that allows one to simulate the consequences of policy measures and
exogenous influences on the continuous struggle for goods flows and
related activities (port transhipment, warehousing,
distribution).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Although some general
trends in the evolution of the world economy and maritime trade can be
recognised, there remains a lot of uncertainty on a number of factors
such as the speed of globalisation, the trade policies of the major
economic blocks, the role of the emerging economies, the persistence of
trade imbalances, the evolution of oil prices, the role of the public
sector, etc. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.105.2"
class="koboSpan">These factors will have an impact on the magnitude and
direction of the trade flows of the different commodities.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.105.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore
forecasts of maritime traffic and port activity should incorporate in
one way or another the uncertainties the world economy is facing.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">One way to handle the
uncertainties when forecasting maritime traffic and port activity, is
the use of scenarios as is done for example by the Dutch government for
its long-term projections. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.106.2"
class="koboSpan">The forecasts are based on four scenarios with
plausible future developments for Europe and are described in detail in
de Mooij and
Tang.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0965" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0965"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan"> They bring together two groups of uncertainties the
European and the world economy might face.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">The first
concerns international cooperation: to what extent are nation states
willing and able to cooperate within international organisations like
the WTO and the European Union? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.108.3"
class="koboSpan">The second key uncertainty concerns national
institutions: to what extent will the mix of public and private
responsibilities change?</span>

<div id="Ch030.xhtml_fig0434" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_901"></span>[](#Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0434)

[<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00454.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0434)

</div>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">The scenarios are
quantified using WorldScan, a computable general-equilibrium model for
the world economy developed at CPB
(Lejour</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0966" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0966"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.112.1"
class="koboSpan">) to give among others the projections of world trade
and economic growth of
</span><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fig0434" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fig0434"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.114.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">Starting from the
trade flows, projections are made for freight flows to and from the
Netherlands for different transport modes and for port throughput.
</span><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_cap_lbl0224"
id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0224"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan"> gives for the four scenarios the Dutch port throughput
projections for 2020 and 2040 split into containers and other traffic.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">The average
annual growth over the period 2002–2020 of container throughput varies
between 3.5% and 6.9%. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.117.3"
class="koboSpan">For the period 2021–2040 it varies between 0.8% and
4.6%. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.117.4" class="koboSpan">In the
Regional Communities scenario total port throughput in 2040 is even
somewhat lower than in 2002. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.117.5"
class="koboSpan">In the case of Global Economies however, the throughput
in 2040 is projected to be nearly the threefold of the quantity of 2002.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.117.6" class="koboSpan">This clearly
illustrates the importance of considering a number of scenarios to
forecast maritime and port traffic.</span>

id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.120.1"
