<span class="italic"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan"> Besseling, Francke and Saitua
Nistal</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0968" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0968"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_902"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.124.1"
class="koboSpan">Both port management and companies located in ports
require a set of tools that can help them resolve part of the
uncertainty that exists in a rapidly changing environment.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">However, while
demand forecasts based on (economic) models can provide a useful
indication, they cannot explain reality in its entirety.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.124.3" class="koboSpan">Thus,
additional explanations need to be sought, e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.124.4" class="koboSpan">at the supply
side and in cost analysis. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.124.5"
class="koboSpan">This brings us back to such factors as available
capacity, capacity utilisation, and productivity.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.124.6" class="koboSpan">It is after
all quite clear that performance, yield and productivity of a port
cannot be determined on the basis of a single measure.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.124.7" class="koboSpan">On the one
hand, there is the complexity of port operations, while on the other
there are interactions between various relevant factors (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.124.8" class="koboSpan">vessel
configuration, shifts of workers, depth of quay walls, type of loading
and unloading equipment, etc).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">The above material
may constitute a useful framework for further exploration of this topic.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">When
considering potential traffic, for example, one needs to take into
account the strategic behaviour of the various market players involved,
including consignors of goods and transport firms.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.125.3" class="koboSpan">As regards the
competitive environment of ports, further attention should be paid to
the choice of hinterland mode. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.125.4"
class="koboSpan">With respect to further empirical research, a concerted
effort is required to develop more and qualitatively more adequate
databases.</span>

## <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.126.2" class="koboSpan">Surviving in a Competitive Environment</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">Throughout this
contribution, we have emphasised the importance of port competition and
competitiveness. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.127.2"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, most ports are engaged in a tough competitive
struggle, not only for tonnage and volume, but also for shipping lines
and investment in infrastructure and industry.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">This explains why
more and more attention is being paid in the European transport debate
to the issue of port competition.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.128.2" class="koboSpan">Distortion,
some would say “falsification”, of conditions of competition between and
within ports has become an important issue on the political agenda.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.128.3" class="koboSpan">The debate
revolves around, among other things, the granting of concessions within
ports (e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.128.4"
class="koboSpan">dedicated or other container terminals), traffic
diversion between ports (e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.128.5"
class="koboSpan">Antwerp v Rotterdam), (illicit) subsidising of
investments in port infrastructure (Rotterdam v Antwerp) and hinterland
connections (e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.128.6"
class="koboSpan">the rail connections known as “Betuwe Line” and the
“Iron Rhine”, Antwerp v Rotterdam).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">In terms of tonnage,
value added or employment, the European port picture is quite clear: a
strong concentration of activity in a limited number of ports in the
Hamburg–Le Havre range, less so in the Baltic range, and a rapidly
emerging Mediterranean range (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.129.2" class="koboSpan">considerable
investments in container capacity at Giao Tauro, Taranto and Cagliari).
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.129.3" class="koboSpan">This situation
is connected not only with structural aspects (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.129.4" class="koboSpan">geographical
location), but also with differences in terms of costs, productivity
(and speed) and technologies applied.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">In the literature,
one still often refers to Verhoeff’s definition of port
competition.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0969" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0969"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan"> He distinguishes between four levels of seaport
competition: competition between port undertakings; competition between
ports; competition between port clusters (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">a group of
ports in each other’s vicinity with common geographical
characteristics); competition between ranges (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.132.3" class="koboSpan">ports located
along the same coastline or with a largely identical hinterland).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">The factors
influencing competition may vary from level to level.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">The
competitive strength of individual undertakings within a port is
determined mainly by the factors of
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_903"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan">production (labour, capital, technology, and power).
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.134.2" class="koboSpan">Competition
between ports, port clusters and port ranges on the other hand is also
affected by regional factors, such as the geographical location, the
available infrastructure, the degree of industrialisation, government
policy, the standard of performance of the port (measured in terms of
proxy variables, such as the number and frequency of liner services, and
the cost of transhipment, storage and hinterland transportation).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">As we have already
pointed out, this traditional approach to port competition must now make
way for an approach based on competition between logistics chains, in
which seaports (and seaport undertakings) are merely links.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">As the most
important consideration is the overall cost of the transport chain, it
is inevitable that, besides throughput, the industrial and commercial
functions (including warehousing and distribution of goods) as well as
hinterland transportation will come to occupy an increasingly important
position.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">A port and the
undertakings established in it compete directly with a limited number of
other ports, usually within the same range.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.136.2" class="koboSpan">There are few
types of goods flows for which ports belonging to different ranges might
compete directly (e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.136.3"
class="koboSpan">in the fixing of shipping schedules and in determining
ports of call). </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.136.4"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, the crucial question in port competition
is what determines the choice of port?
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.136.5" class="koboSpan">In other
words, why is one port preferred to another?
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.136.6" class="koboSpan">Why are
certain undertakings located in that port chosen?
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.136.7" class="koboSpan">What are the
preferred hinterland transport modes and routes?</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">Port users think
predominantly in financial and economic terms.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.137.2"
class="koboSpan">Frankel</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0970" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0970"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.138.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan"> asserts in this respect that “they consider the net
revenue contribution of a port call which is usually defined as the
difference between the added revenue generated by the port call minus
the costs of making the port call”.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.139.2" class="koboSpan">Costs are
understood to include all possible items: vessel-related costs (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.139.3" class="koboSpan">the time
factor, taking into account possible delays), port-related costs (port
dues, pilotage …), cargo-handling costs, cargo-storage costs, feeder
costs.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, the objective
for management, be it of the port or of the undertakings concerned, is
clear to see: to minimise the cost of terminal handling and delay of
vessels. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.140.2" class="koboSpan">For
that matter, the principle of cost minimisation applies to all links in
the transport chain, in the sense that the ultimate goal must be to
arrive at the lowest possible cost for the chain as a whole.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">The port that
contributes to the cheapest logistics chain is, in theory at least, most
likely to be called at. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.141.2"
class="koboSpan">The ultimate decision process of the port user would
appear, then, to be a matter of common sense: does the port considered
offer advantages compared to other ports serving the same hinterland?
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">Does the port
offer sufficient advantages in order to be considered as an additional
port of call for an existing or yet-to-be-established liner or indeed
feeder service? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.141.4"
class="koboSpan">The decision process of the port user concerns the
transport chain, but he will also have to take due account of market
factors (e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.141.5"
class="koboSpan">potential customers, competition from other shipping
lines and consignors of goods …).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">It is important for a
port authority to know who that port user is, who makes the choice of
port and which factors influence this choice.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.142.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
term “port user” covers quite a heterogeneous group that includes
shipping companies, consignors of goods, owners of goods, goods
handlers, … It is a group whose members would appear to depend on one
another, but who are nevertheless often engaged in a fierce competitive
struggle. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.142.3"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, it is not always easy to determine who
ultimately makes the choice of port.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.142.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,
there is the question of which (cost) variables are most significant in
the decision process (cf. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.142.5"
class="koboSpan">the problem of factor assessment).
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.142.6" class="koboSpan">In this
respect, one needs to realise that the cost structure is determined by
both exogenous factors
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_904"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan">(e.g. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.143.2"
class="koboSpan">scale increases in world trade, or rapidly developing
cargo-handling equipment) and endogenous factors within the port’s
direct sphere of influence.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">Port competition has
been the subject of much interdisciplinary
research.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0971" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0971"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan"> After all, the competitive position of a port is
determined by strategic and legal factors besides purely economic
variables. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.146.2"
class="koboSpan">Research has shown that, in the case of the port of
Antwerp, political and legal considerations rather than purely economic
or geographical determinants are perceived as factors that may influence
the position of the port negatively.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.146.3" class="koboSpan">Indeed, if a
port has a fundamental weakness, this is often occasioned by a lack of
clarity in terms of administrative responsibility.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.146.4" class="koboSpan">This lack of
clarity may, for example, relate to who is the competent legislator
and/or executor of an infrastructure project, and who is responsible for
necessary amendments of existing
legislation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0972" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0972"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0973" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0973"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.149.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">A study by Huybrechts
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch030.xhtml_fn0974" id="Ch030.xhtml_bck_fn0974"><span
id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.152.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan"> has shown that there is also an urgent need for a
broader knowledge base with regard to the competitive environment in
which individual ports, port clusters or port ranges operate.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.153.2" class="koboSpan">Research to
this end should preferably be multidisciplinary in nature, grounded on a
sound theoretical basis, but taking an empirical approach.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.153.3" class="koboSpan">In order to
make such research possible, qualitatively more adequate databases are
an absolute necessity. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.153.4"
class="koboSpan">Sound scientific research into the maritime business
environment requires model-based simulations of various goods flows,
transported to and from different ports, in different batch sizes and at
various times. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.153.5"
class="koboSpan">The knowledge that is thus acquired may contribute to a
better understanding of, and more adequate response to, factors that
influence port competition and competitiveness.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.153.6" class="koboSpan">Or, as is
suggested by the title of this section, it may provide insight into the
question of how best to survive in a competitive environment.</span>

## <span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.154.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">In this contribution,
we have discussed the relationship between port management and
operations by that management on the one hand and port competition on
the other. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">All
are agreed that the port landscape has changed very rapidly, partly as a
consequence of ever-growing port competition at different levels.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">In most ports, port
management has found it hard (to continue) to keep up with the pace of
change. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.156.2"
class="koboSpan">Furthermore, an important aspect of the legitimacy of a
separate port management is being undermined, namely the previously
often heard argument of the strategic significance of seaports to the
economy of a country or region.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.157.1" class="koboSpan">There is clearly a
connection between port management and the manner in which players
compete within or between ports.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Each port
management is preoccupied with protecting and/or improving its
competitive position in a fierce struggle with any party that is
considered a potential threat. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.157.3"
class="koboSpan">The question arises what are the remaining tools and
degrees of freedom? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.157.4"
class="koboSpan">In the first instance, one can help prepare and outline
strategies in relation to additional port infrastructure.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.157.5" class="koboSpan">However,
financially and legally, one is still dependent upon government.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.157.6" class="koboSpan">Furthermore,
there is the aspect of granting concessions for dedicated or other
terminals. </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.157.7"
class="koboSpan">Here one encounters increasingly strong opponents, i.e.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.157.8" class="koboSpan">ever more
powerful shipping companies (and the alliances to which they may
belong).</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">The question is
therefore: what next? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.158.2"
class="koboSpan">Will the role of port management be restricted to
correctly enforcing regulation (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.158.3" class="koboSpan">with respect
to “Port State Control”)? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.158.4"
class="koboSpan">Or will port management be tempted to actively
participate as a market player, by acquiring a stake in terminal
operating companies? </span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.158.5"
class="koboSpan">If one does enter into the market, there is
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_page_905"></span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan">the danger that conflicts of interest may arise and
that the port community may, quite rightly, no longer consider the port
management as a neutral regulator.</span>

<span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">The present race for
new port infrastructure and additional capacity suggests that port
competition will become even greater in the near future.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.160.2" class="koboSpan">At the same
time, the role and indeed the raison d’être of port management would
appear to be becoming even more uncertain.
</span><span id="Ch030.xhtml_kobo.160.3" class="koboSpan">Clearly, then,
here lies largely unexplored territory for multidisciplinary research
with a solid scientific basis but with empirical implementation and
verification.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_907"></span>[<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 31</span>\
<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Revisiting the Productivity and Efficiency of Ports and Terminals: Methods and Applications</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0692)
================================================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Kevin</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Cullinane</span></span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0975" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0975"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">Over the past decade,
there has been a proliferation of research which investigates the
efficiency of ports and terminals.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Given the
increasing prominence of container shipping within the maritime sector
and the relative ease of analysis in situations where unit cargoes are
standardised, it is not surprising that the majority of this work has
been applied to the container port sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.7.3" class="koboSpan">It is also
justified by the fact that container ports form a vital link in the
supply chains of trading companies and nations worldwide.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.7.4" class="koboSpan">In terms of the
logistics cost which they account for within any given supply chain, the
level of a container port’s performance and/or relative efficiency will,
to a large extent, determine the competitiveness of a nation and can
ultimately have an influence upon industrial location decisions and the
benefits derived from the economic policies of national governments.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.7.5" class="koboSpan">Thus, although
productivity and/or efficiency analyses can provide a powerful
management tool for port operators, they can also constitute a most
important input to studies aimed at informing regional and national port
planning and operation.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">It is unfortunate,
therefore that, in everyday use, the terms “productivity” and
“efficiency” are used interchangeably.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">As a result, the
precise meanings of the two terms have become blurred and indistinct.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.8.3" class="koboSpan">In the ensuing
discussion of port and terminal productivity and efficiency, however, it
is important to distinguish between them.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan">Productivity</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan"> can very simply be defined as the ratio of outputs
over inputs. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.10.2"
class="koboSpan">This yields an absolute measure of performance that may
be applied to all factors of production (inputs) simultaneously (as well
as to all outputs) or to merely an individual factor of production.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.10.3" class="koboSpan">In this latter
case, the outcome of such a calculation is more correctly
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_908"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan">referred to as a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan">partial
productivity</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan"> measure. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.13.2"
class="koboSpan">As is shown in the review contained in section 2 of
this chapter, most historic analyses of port performance involved the
calculation of partial productivity measures across a range of ports
and/or terminals and the comparison of such calculated measures.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.13.3" class="koboSpan">Since the
publication of the first edition of this
handbook,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0976" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0976"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan"> however, there has been a veritable explosion in the
number of applications utilising the two main contemporary methods for
the measurement of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan">technical
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.18.1"
class="koboSpan">productive
efficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">These more rigorous, holistic and scientific
methodologies are introduced and described in detail in sections 4, 5
and 6 of this Chapter. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.19.3"
class="koboSpan">Sections 5 and 6 also contain reviews of the major
applications of each of these methods to the derivation of technical
efficiency measures in the container port and/or terminal sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.19.4" class="koboSpan">Prior to that,
in section 3 of this chapter, the theory underpinning the study of
economic efficiency is presented.</span>

## <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">Lessons Learned from Traditional Port Performance and Productivity Studies</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">The measurement of
port efficiency is complicated by the large variety of factors that
influence port
performance.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0977" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0977"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan"> The most obvious influences can be generalised as the
economic input factor endowments of land, labour and capital.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">Dowd and
Leschine</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0978" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0978"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan"> argue, in fact, that port and/or terminal productivity
measurement is a means of quantifying efficiency in the utilisation of
these three resources. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.25.2"
class="koboSpan">However, there are other influences that are not so
easily classified, nor indeed even capable of being quantified, for the
purpose of empirical investigation.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.25.3" class="koboSpan">A few examples
of these influences include: the level of technology that is utilised in
the operations of a port or terminal; the industrial relations
environment within the port or terminal (and, hence, the risk of
disruptions to the supply of labour); the extent of co-operation or
integration with shipping lines and, as analysed in Cullinane and
Song,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0979" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0979"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan"> the nature of the ownership of the port and the impact
that this may have on the way that the port is managed and/or
operated.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">Despite these
difficulties, attempts at estimating port or terminal productivity have
been legion. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.28.2"
class="koboSpan">This is particularly the case in container handling
where, as might be imputed from the plethora of studies that focus on
this sector, the need for high productivity or high efficiency levels is
probably greater than in port facilities that concentrate on serving
other forms of shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">Traditionally, the
performance of ports has been variously evaluated by calculating
cargo-handling productivity at berth
(e.g.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0980" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0980"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0982" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0982"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan">), by measuring a single factor productivity (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.33.2" class="koboSpan">labour as in
the case
of</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0983" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0983"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0985" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0985"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan">) or by comparing actual with optimum throughput for a
specific period of time
(e.g.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0986" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0986"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">Dowd and
Leschine</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0987" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0987"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.42.1"
class="koboSpan"> approached the issue specifically in relation to
container terminal productivity and highlight the fact that, probably
because of the standard nature of the cargo that is handled in such
facilities, there is an incessant demand in the industry for some form
of universal standards or benchmarks for container terminal
productivity. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.42.2"
class="koboSpan">For the better terminals, there are obvious marketing
advantages to be had from this. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.42.3"
class="koboSpan">One major stumbling block in seeking to achieve such a
standard is the lack of uniformity in productivity measurement across
the sector. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.42.4" class="koboSpan">By
way of exemplifying this, while some terminals will count rehandles and
hatchcover removals as “moves”, others do not.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_909"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">A second problem exists in that each participating
player has a different interest in port or terminal productivity.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.43.2" class="koboSpan">For the port or
terminal itself, the main goal may be to reduce the cost per unit of
cargo handled and, thereby, raise profitability.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.43.3" class="koboSpan">For the port
authority, the main goal may be to maximise the throughput per unit area
of land that it leases to the terminal operator, so as to maximise the
benefits derived from the investments it makes.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.43.4" class="koboSpan">For the
carrier, the goal may be to minimise the time that a ship spends in
port.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">In an effort to
provide a more rigorous and holistic evaluation of port performance,
several alternative methods have been suggested, such as the estimation
of a port cost
function,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0988" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0988"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan"> the estimation of a total factor productivity index of
a
port</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0989" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0989"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the establishment of a port performance and
efficiency model using multiple regression
analysis.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0990" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0990"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">Chang
</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0991" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0991"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan"> appears to have made one of the earliest efforts to
estimate a production function and the productivities of inputs within
the port sector. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.52.2"
class="koboSpan">This was done for the port of Mobile in the US.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.52.3" class="koboSpan">In attempting
to derive a port production function, the author focuses on general
cargo-handling volume as a measurement of port performance and assumes
that port operations follow the conventional Cobb-Douglas case as
expressed by:</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0436" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00456.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">where</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">Y = annual gross
earnings (in real terms)</span>\
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">K</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan"> = the real value of net assets in the port</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan">L</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan"> = the number of labourers per year and the average
number of employees per month each year</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan">e</span><sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">γ</span></sup></span><sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan">(</span></sup><span class="italic"><sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.63.1"
class="koboSpan">T/L</span></sup></span><sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.64.1"
class="koboSpan">)</span></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.65.1"
class="koboSpan"> a proxy for technological improvement in which
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan">T/L</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">) shows the tonnage per unit of labour.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">The author argues
that, for the estimation of a production function of this form, the
output of a port should be measured in terms of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan">either</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan"> total tonnage handled at the port
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.71.1"
class="koboSpan">or</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.72.1"
class="koboSpan"> its gross earnings.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">De Neufville and
Tsunokawa</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0992" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0992"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan"> undertook an analysis of the five major container
ports on the east coast of the US and derived an estimate of a container
port production possibility frontier on the basis of the panel data
collected. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">They
deduced that Hampton Roads and Baltimore were consistently operating
inefficiently during the period 1970–1978 and attributed this to poor
management as the root cause. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.75.3"
class="koboSpan">The findings highlight the importance of economies of
scale in port/terminal productivity and, as such, the authors conclude
that, because of the economic returns to be reaped, policy makers should
promote and place greater investment into large load centre ports,
rather than into the proliferation of smaller, more regionally focussed
port developments.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan">Suykens</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0993" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0993"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan"> points out that the measurement of productivity and
subsequent comparison between ports is extremely difficult.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">Quite often,
this is due simply to differences in the geophysical characteristics of
the ports to be compared. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.78.3"
class="koboSpan">For instance, there will be fundamental constraints on
the productivity of ports where locks are needed, or which are located
up river estuaries or in the middle of a port town as opposed to at a
greenfield location. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.78.4"
class="koboSpan">Difficulties also arise where the type of cargo handled
at the comparison
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_910"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
class="koboSpan">ports differ or when one port is primarily serving its
own hinterland and another is primarily a transhipment port.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.79.2" class="koboSpan">Under all these
scenarios, it would be fundamentally unfair and possibly misleading to
make productivity comparisons on a straightforward basis.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.79.3" class="koboSpan">It may be
argued, therefore, that in order to properly evaluate the performance of
a port, it is important and necessary to place it within a proper
perspective by drawing comparisons with other ports that operate in a
similar environment.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">Tongzon and
Ganesalingam</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0994" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0994"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan"> applied cluster analysis to compare the port
performance and efficiency of ASEAN ports with counterparts overseas.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">The rationale
for this analysis lay primarily with a purported requirement for such a
comparison to be conducted only amongst ports that are similar in terms
of their management or operational environment.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.82.3" class="koboSpan">The results
suggested that the ASEAN ports, especially Singapore, were more
technically efficient in terms of the utilisation of cranes, berths and
storage areas, but that they were generally less efficient in terms of
timeliness, labour and tug utilisation.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.82.4" class="koboSpan">In addition, it
was deduced that port charges in ASEAN ports were significantly higher
than those of their overseas counterparts falling within the same
cluster (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.82.5"
class="koboSpan">comparable ports).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.83.1"
class="koboSpan">Tongzon</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0995" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0995"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan"> elaborated upon this benchmarking concept by utilising
an approach based on principal components analysis for the
identification of suitable benchmark ports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.85.2"
class="koboSpan">Ashar</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0996" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0996"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan"> is critical of this approach.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">In particular,
the need for such an analysis to be conducted at the level of the
terminal is highlighted by reference to the fact that several of the
ports included in Tongzon’s sample were, in fact, landlord ports (as
defined
in</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0997" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0997"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">Sanchez
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0998" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0998"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan"> also apply principal components analysis to generate
different port efficiency measures based on data from a survey of Latin
American common user ports. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.93.2"
class="koboSpan">These efficiency estimates are then incorporated as one
of the explanatory variables in the estimation of a model of waterborne
transport costs. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.93.3"
class="koboSpan">Their analysis reveals that port efficiency, liner
shipping calls, distance and value of goods are all significant
determinants of waterborne transport costs and, therefore, impact
directly on a nation’s competitiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">Braeutigam, Daughety
and
Turnquist</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn0999" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn0999"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
class="koboSpan"> note that ports come in different sizes and face a
variety of traffic mix. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.96.2"
class="koboSpan">As such, they suggest, the use of cross-sectional
time-series, or even panel data, may fail to show basic differences
between ports; thus leading to a misjudgement as to each port’s
performance. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.96.3"
class="koboSpan">They attest, therefore, that it is crucial to estimate
econometrically the structure of production in ports at the level of the
single port or terminal, using appropriate data such as the panel data
for a terminal. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.96.4"
class="koboSpan">This view and suggested alternative approach also
receives support
elsewhere.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1000" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1000"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1002" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1002"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">In undertaking the
comparison of port productivities conducted within their study, Tongzon
and
Ganesalingham</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1003" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1003"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan"> compare ports on the basis of a basket of standard
port productivity measures such as: shipcalls per port employee, net
crane rate, ship rate, TEUs per crane, shipcalls per tug, TEUs per metre
of berth, berth occupancy rate, TEUs per hectare of terminal area, port
charges, pre-berthing time, berthing time and truck/rail turnaround
time. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.102.2" class="koboSpan">Since
the primary role of ports is to facilitate the movement of cargoes, the
authors recognise that it is vital to evaluate port performance in
relation to how efficient are their services from the perspective of the
port user: the shipowners, shippers (importers and exporters) and the
land transport owners. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.102.3"
class="koboSpan">It is obvious, therefore, that port performance
assessment cannot be based on a single measure.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.102.4" class="koboSpan">As is clear
from the list of productivity measures employed, whilst it does contain
certain operational productivity measures, it also recognises that this
is only meaningful to port users when it translates into lower costs to
them.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_911"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan">Frankel</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1004" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1004"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan"> is highly critical of the productivity measures that
are applied in ports when he suggests that most port performance
standards are narrowly defined operational measures that are useful only
for comparison with ports that have similar operations or against
proposed supplier standards. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.105.2"
class="koboSpan">He asserts that port user interest in port productivity
(and the service quality that it relates to) is much more wide-ranging
and it is vitally important that ports attempt to address this disparity
in outlook. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.105.3"
class="koboSpan">Port users, he asserts, are concerned with issues such
as the total time and cost of ship turnarounds and (increasingly) of
cargo throughput. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.105.4"
class="koboSpan">The realignment of what a port considers to be valid
performance measures is required because the commercial environment of
port operations is becoming increasingly competitive as hinterlands
overlap. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.105.5" class="koboSpan">In
such a context, port users have a real choice in the selection of the
ports that they want to use.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">The focus which
Frankel advocates, on the port users’ perspective of port efficiency, is
particularly interesting and important in that it shifts the need for,
and usefulness of, valid port and/or terminal productivity and
efficiency measures away from the fulfillment of an internally-oriented
managerial (cost minimisation) objective and towards an
externally-oriented marketing (revenue-maximisation) objective.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan">Chapon</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1005" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1005"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan"> specifically states that the overall cost of
cargo-handling in a port comprises two separate components: the cost
price of the actual handling and the cost price of immobilizing the
seagoing vessel for the period of its stay in port.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">In other
words, this second cost is, in economic terms, the opportunity cost
associated with the revenue lost or, in the terminology of logistics,
the cost of lost sales. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.109.3"
class="koboSpan">This second component has risen to even greater
prominence as ships have become increasingly expensive (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.109.4" class="koboSpan">exhibiting
high fixed to variable cost ratios), a feature that is particularly
relevant to the liner trades over recent years.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.109.5" class="koboSpan">Several
studies of productivity have adopted this perspective in undertaking
productivity measurement and
comparisons.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1006" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1006"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1007" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1007"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.113.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is fundamentally this perspective which has
prompted the plethora of OR-based analyses of ship–shore interactions
aimed at optimal crane deployment and/or loading/unloading operations, a
comprehensive review of which is provided by Stahlbock and
Voss.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1008" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1008"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">All this points to
the fact that productivity levels in ports have implications for the
real cost of loading and discharging a ship.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.115.2"
class="koboSpan">Suykens,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1009" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1009"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan"> however, points to the need for caution in making such
comparisons since the higher productivity in a port may be reflected in
the wages it pays and/or the depreciation charges it incurs as the
result of the investment in state-of-the-art equipment that has been
made. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">Both of
these influences on higher port productivity will be mirrored in the
port tariff that is charged. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.117.3"
class="koboSpan">Thus, there is a need for a balanced and joint view of
both port pricing and productivity.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.117.4" class="koboSpan">Other
commentators have pointed to the need to assess the range of prices
payable for different levels of port productivity within the context of
the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.118.1"
class="koboSpan">effectiveness</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan"> of service
provision.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1010" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1010"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.121.1"
class="koboSpan"> This, of course, has prompted empirical studies of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.122.1"
class="koboSpan">quality</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan"> of port performance as an adjunct to the many
analyses, using very varied methodologies, which focus on the
quantitative assessment of relative port
productivities.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1011" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1011"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">Ports have an
interaction with other parts of the logistical chain.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">Indeed, the
suggestion has been made that the real value of productivity
improvements in ports depends upon whether this results in an
improvement to the efficiency of the total logistical system or whether
it merely shifts a “bottleneck” from one part of the system to
another.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1012" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1012"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan"> This calls for the adoption of a still wider
perspective on the issue of port productivity and
efficiency.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1013" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1013"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">In relation to the
issue of technical efficiency rather than productivity measurement and
comparison, it can be deduced that by the very nature of investments in
cargo
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_912"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">handling technology and the expansion of space in
ports, additions to capacity have to be large compared to the existing
facilities. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">In
other words, when investments are made, they are made primarily on an
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.131.1"
class="koboSpan">ad hoc</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan"> basis and with a view to future expectations of
expanded demand. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.132.2"
class="koboSpan">In consequence, since available capacity cannot be
fully utilised in the years immediately following the time that such
investments in additional capacity come on stream, then technical
inefficiency is inevitable.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">In any analysis of a
single port’s time series of technical efficiency, therefore, the
situation must be defined by numerous inefficient observations being
bounded by a comparatively few observations that are deemed efficient.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.133.2" class="koboSpan">Because of
this characteristic (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.133.3"
class="koboSpan">that efficiency in operations cannot be assumed), De
Neufville and
Tsunokawa</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1014" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1014"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.134.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.135.1"
class="koboSpan"> point to the inadequacy of any approach that is based
on a least squares regression analysis to estimate the production
function for the industry. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.135.2"
class="koboSpan">This is because any such analysis has to be based on
the complementary assumptions that all observations are efficient but
that any deviation of an observation from the production function is due
to random effects. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.135.3"
class="koboSpan">Without explicitly acknowledging the fact, this
assertion points to the need for the adoption of contemporary approaches
to the measurement of efficiency.</span>

## <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.136.2" class="koboSpan">The Economic Concept of Efficiency</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">In simple terms, the
performance of an economic unit can be determined by calculating the
ratio of its outputs to its inputs; with larger values of this ratio
associated with better performance or higher productivity.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.137.2" class="koboSpan">Because
performance is a concept that is only meaningful when judged relatively,
there are many bases upon which it may be assessed.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.137.3" class="koboSpan">For instance,
a car manufacturer uses materials, labour and capital (inputs) to
produce cars (outputs). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.137.4"
class="koboSpan">Its performance in 2010 could be measured
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan">relative to
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">its
2009 performance or could be measured
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan">relative to
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">the
performance of another producer in 2009, or could be measured
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan">relative to
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">the
average performance of the car industry, and so on.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">Economic
efficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan"> relates specifically to a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">production possibility
frontier</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">; an economic concept which is useful in explaining two
distinctive concepts of
efficiency</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan">: productive (or technical)
efficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">allocative
efficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.151.2"
class="koboSpan">In economic theory, costs can exceed their minimum
feasible level for one of two reasons.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.151.3" class="koboSpan">One is that
inputs are being used in the wrong proportions, given their prices and
marginal productivity. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.151.4"
class="koboSpan">This phenomenon is known as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan">allocative
inefficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.153.2"
class="koboSpan">The other reason is that there is a failure to produce
the maximum amount of output from a set of given inputs.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.153.3" class="koboSpan">This is known
as </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.154.1"
class="koboSpan">productive (or technical)
inefficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.155.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.155.2"
class="koboSpan">Both sources of inefficiency can exist simultaneously
or in isolation. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.155.3"
class="koboSpan">As implied above, these sources of inefficiency can be
easily explained by using the concept of a production frontier.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">An economic unit
operating within an industry is considered
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">productively (technically) efficient
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">if it
operates </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan">on </span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">the frontier, whilst the unit is regarded as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan">productively inefficient
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan"> if it
operates </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.163.1"
class="koboSpan">beneath</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.164.1"
class="koboSpan"> the frontier. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.164.2"
class="koboSpan">When information on prices is available and a
behavioural assumption (such as profit maximisation or cost
minimisation) is properly established, we can then consider
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan">allocative
efficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.166.2"
class="koboSpan">This is present when a selected set of inputs (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.166.3" class="koboSpan">material,
labour and capital) produce a given quantity of output at minimum cost,
given the prevailing input prices.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.166.4" class="koboSpan">An economic
unit is judged
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.167.1"
class="koboSpan">allocatively inefficient
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">if
inputs are being used in the wrong proportions, given their prices and
marginal productivity.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_913"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.169.1"
class="koboSpan">Fundamentally, however, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
class="koboSpan">technical
efficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
class="koboSpan"> of an entity is a comparative measure of how well it
processes inputs to achieve its output(s), as compared to its maximum
potential for doing so – as represented by its production possibility
frontier, which is widely used to define the relationship between inputs
and outputs by depicting graphically the maximum output obtainable from
the given inputs consumed. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.171.2"
class="koboSpan">In so doing, the production frontier reflects the
current status of technology available to the industry.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.171.3" class="koboSpan">By
implication, therefore, the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">production possibility
frontier</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan"> of an entity may change over time due to changes in
the underlying technology deployed.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.174.1" class="koboSpan">In the container port
sector, an example might be the greater reach of contemporary gantry
cranes over their historic counterparts.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.174.2" class="koboSpan">Over the past
decade in particular, this innovation in technology has facilitated a
very significant improvement in partial productivity measures such as
container moves per hour. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.174.3"
class="koboSpan">Depending upon the relationship between the cost of
investing in such cranes and the reduction in operating cost per
container moved, it could also mean greater output for the same level of
input at all scales of production (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.174.4" class="koboSpan">this
represents an outward move in the production possibility frontier).
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.174.5" class="koboSpan">If it could be
established that this innovation has led directly to an improvement in
the overall (total factor) productivity of the port (even where this
compares favourably to that of other suitable benchmark ports), but that
the new cranes like the old ones were still being optimally employed at
full capacity, then a situation would exist where
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">technical
efficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.176.1"
class="koboSpan"> has remained the same (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.176.2" class="koboSpan">at a maximum),
but there has been an improvement in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.177.1"
class="koboSpan">productivity</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan"> (even comparatively).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.179.1" class="koboSpan">In a similar fashion,
the scale of output(s) or inputs can be altered to take advantage of
efficiencies due to scale. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.179.2"
class="koboSpan">This too may mean that an entity can remain at 100%
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">technical
efficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan"> (so that output is at the maximum possible level for a
given level of input) by moving along the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan">production possibility
frontier</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">, but that its (total factor) productivity can
simultaneously increase. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.183.2"
class="koboSpan">It may be inferred from this explanation that
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">technical efficiency
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">productivity</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.187.1"
class="koboSpan"> also have time-scale connotations, whereby the former
is much more of a long-term phenomenon, while the latter is a concept
that is grounded more firmly in the short-term (see Coelli, Prasada Rao
and
Battese</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1015" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1015"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan"> for a comprehensive treatment of productivity and the
different forms of efficiency).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">With respect to how
to measure the different sources of (in)efficiency, let us suppose that
the production frontier of an economic unit is as depicted in
</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0225"
id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0225"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan"> and can be denoted by Y =
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan">f </span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan">(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan">, x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.198.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan"> ), where two inputs
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.200.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.202.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> ) are used, in some combination, to produce one output
(Y). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.205.2" class="koboSpan">It is
also assumed that the function is characterised by constant returns to
scale. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.205.3" class="koboSpan">In this
case, the isoquants Y</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.206.1"
class="koboSpan">A</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Y</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan">B</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.209.1"
class="koboSpan"> indicate all possible combinations of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.210.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.212.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan"> that give rise to the same level of output.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">Assume that the
firm’s efficiency is observed at point A, rather than C.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.216.2" class="koboSpan">This position
is neither </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">allocatively</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan"> nor
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan">productively
efficient</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.220.2"
class="koboSpan">Its level of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">productive efficiency
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">is
defined as the ratio of OB/OA. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.222.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, productive inefficiency is defined as
1-(OB/OA) and can be interpreted as the proportion by which the cost of
producing the level of output could be reduced given the assumption that
the input ratio
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan">/</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan"> ) is held constant.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.228.2" class="koboSpan">Under the
assumption of constant returns to scale, productive inefficiency can
also be interpreted as the proportion by which output could be increased
by becoming 100% productively efficient.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.228.3" class="koboSpan">The level of
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan">allocative efficiency
</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">is
measured as OD/OB (or C</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.232.1"
class="koboSpan">/C</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.234.2"
class="koboSpan">Thus
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">allocative
inefficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan"> is defined as 1-(OD/OB) and measures the proportional
increase in costs due to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan">allocative
inefficiency</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">Consider position B
in </span>[<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.240.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0225)<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.241.2"
class="koboSpan">At this point, the firm is allocatively inefficient
since it can maintain output at Y but reduce total costs by changing the
input mix to that</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0437" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00457.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: A firm’s frontier production function" /></span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_914"></span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0225"
id="Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0225"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.243.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan"> A firm’s frontier production function</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">which exists at point
C. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.245.2" class="koboSpan">At point B,
however, the firm is productively efficient since it cannot increase
output with this input combination of
x</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan"> and x</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.249.1"
class="koboSpan"> and, given a suboptimal input mix (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.249.2" class="koboSpan">allocative
inefficiency), the firm has minimised the cost of producing this level
of output.</span>

## <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.250.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction to More Contemporary Methods of Efficiency Measurement</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.251.1" class="koboSpan">In the last decade of
the twentieth century, a family of methods for measuring efficiency were
proposed which revolve around utilising the economic concept of an
efficient frontier. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.251.2"
class="koboSpan">Under this concept, efficient decision-making units
(DMUs) are those that operate on either a (maximum) production frontier
or a (minimum) cost frontier. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.251.3"
class="koboSpan">In contrast, inefficient DMUs operate either below the
frontier when considering the production frontier, or above it in the
case of the cost frontier. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.251.4"
class="koboSpan">Relative to a DMU located on a production frontier, an
inefficient operator will produce less output for the same cost.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.251.5" class="koboSpan">Analogously,
relative to any DMU located on a cost frontier, an inefficient operator
will produce the same output but for greater cost.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">As suggested by
Bauer,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1016" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1016"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan"> there are several reasons why the use of frontier
models is becoming increasingly widespread:</span>

- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">the notion of a
  frontier is consistent with the underlying economic theory of
  optimising behaviour;</span>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">deviations from a
  frontier have a natural interpretation as a measure of the relative
  efficiency with which economic units pursue their technical or
  behavioural objectives; and</span>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_915"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
  class="koboSpan">information about the structure of the frontier and
  about the relative efficiency of DMUs has many policy
  applications.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">The literature on
frontier models was inaugurated in the seminal contribution of
Farrell,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1017" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1017"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">42</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.260.1"
class="koboSpan"> who provided a rigorous and comprehensive framework
for analysing economic efficiency in terms of realised deviations from
an idealised frontier isoquant. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.260.2"
class="koboSpan">The proliferation of attempts to measure economic
efficiency through the application of the frontier approach can be
attributed to an interest in the structure of efficient production
technology, an interest in the divergence between observed and ideal
operation and also to an interest in the concept of economic efficiency
itself.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.261.1" class="koboSpan">Within the family of
models and methods that are based on the frontier concept, a distinction
exists between those methods that revolve around a parametric approach
to deriving the specification of the frontier model and those that
utilise non-parametric methods. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.261.2"
class="koboSpan">Another distinction exists with respect to whether the
model employed is stochastic or deterministic in nature.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.261.3" class="koboSpan">With the
former, it is necessary to make assumptions about the stochastic
properties of the data, while with the latter it is not.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.261.4" class="koboSpan">The
nonparametric approach revolves around mathematical programming
techniques that are generically referred to as Data Envelopment Analysis
(DEA). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.261.5" class="koboSpan">The
parametric approach, on the other hand, employs econometric techniques
where efficiency is measured relative to a frontier production function
that may be statistically estimated on the basis of an assumed
distribution.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">Econometric
approaches have a strong policy orientation, especially in terms of
assessing alternative industrial organisations and in evaluating the
efficiency of government and other public agencies.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.262.2" class="koboSpan">Mathematical
programming approaches, on the other hand, have a much greater
managerial decision-making
orientation.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1018" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1018"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">43</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1020" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1020"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.265.1" class="koboSpan">45</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.266.1"
class="koboSpan"> Several
studies</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1021" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1021"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">46</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1023" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1023"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">48</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan"> have compared the performance of alternative methods
for measuring efficiency, focusing on the econometric method (in
particular, the stochastic frontier model) and the mathematical
programming method. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.270.2"
class="koboSpan">As measured by the correlation coefficients and rank
correlation coefficients between the true and estimated relative
efficiencies, the results show that when the functional form of the
econometric model is well specified, the stochastic frontier approach
generally produces better estimates of efficiency than the approaches
based on mathematical programming, especially when measuring
DMU-specific efficiency where panel data are available.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.270.3" class="koboSpan">In addition,
certain authors consider that the econometric approaches have a more
solid grounding in economic
theory.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1024" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1024"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">49</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1025" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1025"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.273.1" class="koboSpan">50</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.274.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.274.2" class="koboSpan">Data Envelopment Analysis</span>

### <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.275.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Method</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.276.1" class="koboSpan">Data Envelopment
Analysis (DEA) can be broadly defined as a non-parametric method for
measuring the relative efficiency of a DMU.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.276.2" class="koboSpan">The method
caters for multiple inputs to, and multiple outputs from, the DMU.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.276.3" class="koboSpan">It does this
by constructing a single “virtual” output that is mapped onto a single
“virtual” input, without reference to a pre-defined production
function.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.277.1" class="koboSpan">There has been a
phenomenal expansion of the theory underpinning DEA, the methodology
itself and applications of the methodology over the past few
decades.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1026" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1026"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.278.1" class="koboSpan">51</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.279.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1029" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1029"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">54</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.281.1"
class="koboSpan"> A significant stimulus to this corpus of literature
came with the publication of a seminal</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0438" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.282.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00458.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: DMU and homogeneous units" /></span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_916"></span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0226"
id="Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0226"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan"> DMU and homogeneous units</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.285.1" class="koboSpan">work on the topic by
Charnes, Cooper and Rhodes in
1978.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1030" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1030"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">55</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.287.1"
class="koboSpan"> This work espoused a model for solving the DEA linear
programming problem which has subsequently become widely known by the
acronym of the authors’ surnames; the CCR model.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.287.2" class="koboSpan">The
significance and influence of this paper is reflected in the fact that
by 1999, it had been cited over 700 times in other papers incorporating
applications of the DEA methodology or concerned with the theory or
methodology of DEA.
</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1031" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1031"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.288.1" class="koboSpan">56</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.289.1" class="koboSpan">In common with other
approaches based on the frontier approach, the fundamental idea in DEA
is that the efficiency of an individual
DMU</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1032" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1032"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.290.1" class="koboSpan">57</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan"> or
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">Unit of
Assessment</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1033" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1033"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.293.1" class="koboSpan">58</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan"> is compared relative to a bundle of homogeneous units.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.294.2" class="koboSpan">Implicit in
this idea is the assumption that each individual DMU exercises some sort
of corporate responsibility for controlling the process of production
