and making decisions at various levels of the organisation, including
daily operation, short-term tactics and long-term strategy.</span>

<a href="#Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0226"
id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0226"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates that DEA is used to measure the relative
efficiency of a DMU by comparing it with other homogeneous units that
transform the same group (types) of measurable positive inputs into the
same group (types) of measurable positive outputs.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.297.1" class="koboSpan">In the ports context,
for example, DEA may be applied to compare the relative efficiency of a
single container terminal to a set of other container terminals where
the common output may be defined in terms of an annual throughput
measured in TEU. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.297.2"
class="koboSpan">Similarly, in this case, the common inputs may be the
annual financial costs incurred in the provision of capital, land and
labour or, alternatively, physical proxies for these factor inputs such
as total length of berths, container stacking capacity, number of
cranes, number of employees, total land available etc.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.297.3" class="koboSpan">The input and
output data for </span>[<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.298.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0226)<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan"> can be expressed in terms of matrixes denoted by
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.300.1"
class="koboSpan">X</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">Y </span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan">as shown below, where the element
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.305.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.306.1"
class="koboSpan"> in the matrix
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan">X</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan"> refers to the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.309.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></span><sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.310.1"
class="koboSpan">th</span></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan"> input data item of DMU
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.312.1"
class="koboSpan">j</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.313.1"
class="koboSpan">, whereas the element
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.314.1"
class="koboSpan">y</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan">ij</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.316.1"
class="koboSpan"> represents the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.317.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></span><sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.318.1"
class="koboSpan">th</span></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.319.1"
class="koboSpan"> output data item of DMU
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan">j</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.321.2"
class="koboSpan">In
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
class="koboSpan">X</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan">, there are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan"> input variables
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_917"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan">and in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan">Y</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.328.1"
class="koboSpan">, there are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan"> output variables.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.330.2" class="koboSpan">In both input
and output matrices, there are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
class="koboSpan">s </span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.332.1"
class="koboSpan">DMUs considered.</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0439" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.333.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00459.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.334.1" class="koboSpan">The basic approach to
utilising DEA to measure the relative efficiencies of DMUs can be
explained by the following example.
</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fig0440" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fig0440"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan"> presents some basic production statistics for eight
hypothetical container terminals.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.336.2" class="koboSpan">The
“Throughput/stevedore” in </span>[<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.337.1"
class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch031.xhtml_fig0440)<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan"> can be interpreted as a standard productivity measure.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.338.2" class="koboSpan">In an
extremely simplistic sense that is useful for the purpose of
illustrating the basic approach to DEA, this productivity measure can be
employed to determine a simplistic and concise form of “relative
efficiency” by comparing all DMUs against the best in the sample.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">From
</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0227"
id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0227"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.340.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.341.1"
class="koboSpan"> it is clear that in terms of the particular
relationship between inputs and outputs that we are looking at here
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.341.2"
class="koboSpan">throughput/stevedore),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.342.1"
class="koboSpan">T2</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.343.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the most efficient container terminal compared with
the others (as represented by the other points on the graph).
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.343.2" class="koboSpan">The straight
line from the origin that passes through
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.344.1"
class="koboSpan">T2</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.345.1"
class="koboSpan"> can be termed an “efficient frontier” since all points
along it have the maximum observed productivity measurement of one for
throughput per stevedore. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.345.2"
class="koboSpan">All the other points are inefficient compared with
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.346.1"
class="koboSpan">T2</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan"> and are “enveloped” by the efficient frontier.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.347.2" class="koboSpan">Within the
context of DEA, the relative efficiencies of these other container
terminals, as shown in the bottom line of
</span>[<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.348.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch031.xhtml_fig0440)<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.349.1"
class="koboSpan">, are measured by comparing the productivity measure
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.349.2" class="koboSpan">in this
case throughput/stevedore) for each of these “inefficient” container
terminals with that of T2. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.349.3"
class="koboSpan">The term “Data Envelopment Analysis” stems from the
fact that the efficient frontier “envelops” the inefficient observations
and that they, in turn, are “enveloped” by the frontier.</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0440" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.350.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00460.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch031.xhtml_bck_fig0440)

</div>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0441" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.351.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00461.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Theoretical comparison of efficiencies of container terminals (CCR model)" /></span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_918"></span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0227"
id="Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0227"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.352.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.353.1"
class="koboSpan"> Theoretical comparison of efficiencies of container
terminals (CCR model)</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.354.1" class="koboSpan">It should be apparent
that the complexity of measuring true relative efficiency (or indeed of
even simply portraying the problem graphically) increases exponentially
as the number of total input and output variables increase.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.354.2" class="koboSpan">It is this
difficulty that the CCR model overcomes.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.354.3" class="koboSpan">This is
because it was specifically devised to address the measurement of
relative efficiencies of DMUs with multiple inputs and outputs.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.355.1" class="koboSpan">The CCR model can be
expressed as the following fractional programming problem
(1)–(4):</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0442" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.356.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00462.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.357.1" class="koboSpan">Subject to:</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0443" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.358.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00463.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0444" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.359.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00464.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0445" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.360.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00465.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.361.1" class="koboSpan">Given the data
matrices </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.362.1"
class="koboSpan">X</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.363.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.364.1"
class="koboSpan">Y</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.365.1"
class="koboSpan"> shown earlier, the CCR model measures the maximum
relative efficiency of each DMU by solving the fractional programming
problem in (1) where the input weights
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.366.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.367.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.368.1"
class="koboSpan">, v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.369.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.370.1"
class="koboSpan">, …
v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.371.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.372.1"
class="koboSpan"> and output weights
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.373.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.374.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.375.1"
class="koboSpan">, u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.376.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.377.1"
class="koboSpan">, …
u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.378.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.379.1"
class="koboSpan"> are variables to be obtained.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.380.1"
class="koboSpan">o</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.381.1"
class="koboSpan"> in (1) varies from 1 to
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.382.1"
class="koboSpan">s</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.383.1"
class="koboSpan"> in relation to the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.384.1"
class="koboSpan">s</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.385.1"
class="koboSpan"> optimisations that are required for all
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.386.1"
class="koboSpan">s</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.387.1"
class="koboSpan"> DMUs. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.387.2"
class="koboSpan">The constraint in (2) defines the fact that the ratio
of “virtual output”
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.388.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.389.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.390.1"
class="koboSpan"> y</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.391.1"
class="koboSpan">10</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.392.1"
class="koboSpan">
+</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.393.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.394.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.395.1"
class="koboSpan">y</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.396.1"
class="koboSpan">20</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.397.1"
class="koboSpan">
+</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.398.1"
class="koboSpan">…+u</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.399.1"
class="koboSpan">n</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.400.1"
class="koboSpan"> y</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.401.1"
class="koboSpan">no</span></sub>
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.402.1" class="koboSpan">) to “virtual
input” (</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.403.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.404.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.405.1"
class="koboSpan"> x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.406.1"
class="koboSpan">10</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.407.1"
class="koboSpan">
+</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.408.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.409.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.410.1"
class="koboSpan"> x</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.411.1"
class="koboSpan">20</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.412.1"
class="koboSpan">
+</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.413.1"
class="koboSpan">…</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.414.1"
class="koboSpan">+</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.415.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.416.1"
class="koboSpan">m</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.417.1"
class="koboSpan"> x</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.418.1"
class="koboSpan">mo</span></sub></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.419.1"
class="koboSpan">) cannot exceed unity for each DMU.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.419.2" class="koboSpan">This
Fractional Programming (FP) problem represented in equations (1)–(4) has
been proved to be equivalent to the following Linear Programming (LP)
formulation shown in equations
(5)–(9).</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1034" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1034"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.420.1" class="koboSpan">59</span></a></sup>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0446" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.421.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00466.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_919"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.422.1"
class="koboSpan">Subject to</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0447" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.423.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00467.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0448" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.424.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00468.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0449" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.425.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00469.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0450" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.426.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00470.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.427.1" class="koboSpan">It is important to
recognise and note that the computation of the DEA CCR model has been
greatly facilitated by the transformation from its original Fractional
Programming (FP) formulation into a Linear Programming (LP) form of the
model. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.427.2" class="koboSpan">This
transformation has contributed greatly to the rapid development of the
DEA technique and the proliferation of DEA applications.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.427.3" class="koboSpan">This has
occurred because the solution of LP problems has a long-established
history where numerous sophisticated computational methods have been
developed and where commercial software packages are widely available.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.427.4" class="koboSpan">As such,
calculating the complicated relative efficiencies of DMUs with multiple
inputs and outputs is then rendered a comparatively simple task.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.428.1" class="koboSpan">One assumption that
underpins the early DEA approaches, including the CCR model, is that the
sample under study exhibits constant returns to scale.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.428.2" class="koboSpan">There is a
voluminous body of evidence that suggests that this assumption is
particularly inappropriate to the ports sector where, it is quite
commonly asserted, economies of scale are quite
significant.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1035" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1035"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.429.1" class="koboSpan">60</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.430.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1037" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1037"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.431.1" class="koboSpan">62</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.432.1"
class="koboSpan"> To cater for such situations where variable returns to
scale may be more the norm, the CCR model has been modified so that
scale efficiencies, for example, may be separated out from the pure
productive (or technical) efficiency measure that the standard CCR model
yields.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.433.1" class="koboSpan">The main modified
forms of the CCR model that are utilised in practice are referred to as
the Additive model and the BCC model, the latter being named after its
creators.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1038" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1038"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.434.1" class="koboSpan">63</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.435.1"
class="koboSpan"> Accordingly, the efficient frontiers that are
estimated by these models are different from that of the CCR
model.</span>

<a href="#Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0228"
id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0228"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.436.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.437.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows a hypothetical efficient frontier for situations
when either the Additive or BCC models are applied to a sample of
container terminals (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.437.2"
class="koboSpan">there is an assumption that variable returns to scale
prevail). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.437.3" class="koboSpan">In
this illustrative example, the sample observations denoted by
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.438.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.439.1"
class="koboSpan">1</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.440.1"
class="koboSpan">, T</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.441.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.442.1"
class="koboSpan">, T</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.443.1"
class="koboSpan">6</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.444.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.445.1"
class="koboSpan">T</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.446.1"
class="koboSpan">8</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.447.1"
class="koboSpan"> lie on a non-linear efficient frontier and are all
defined as efficient since each observation cannot dominate any of the
others given the condition of variable returns to scale.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.447.2" class="koboSpan">The other
points that are ‘enveloped’ by (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.447.3" class="koboSpan">lying below)
these technically efficient points are deemed inefficient.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.448.1" class="koboSpan">The Additive and BCC
models are identical in terms of the efficient frontiers that they
estimate. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.448.2" class="koboSpan">The
main difference between them is the projection path to the efficient
frontier that is employed as the basis for estimating the levels of
relative (in)efficiency for those DMUs in the sample that are not
located on the efficient frontier.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.448.3" class="koboSpan">For instance,
in </span>[<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.449.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
4</span>](#Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0228)<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.450.1"
class="koboSpan">, for the BCC estimate of inefficiency, the inefficient
observation T3 can be projected either to
T3</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.451.1"
class="koboSpan">I</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.452.1"
class="koboSpan"> or T3</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.453.1"
class="koboSpan">O</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.454.1"
class="koboSpan"> depending upon whether an input or output orientation
is adopted. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.454.2"
class="koboSpan">For the Additive model, however, T3 will be projected
to T2 on the efficient frontier.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.454.3" class="koboSpan">This different
approach to projection determines the different relative efficiencies
for different inefficient DMUs. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.454.4"
class="koboSpan">This is because the level of (in)</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0451" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.455.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00471.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: A comparison of container terminal efficiency (BCC and additive models)" /></span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_920"></span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0228"
id="Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0228"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.456.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4:</span></span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.457.1"
class="koboSpan"> A comparison of container terminal efficiency (BCC and
additive models)</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.458.1" class="koboSpan">efficiency for
inefficient observations is derived from the distance it is located from
the efficient frontier; a measure that is, of course, dependent upon the
projection path that is utilised.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.459.1" class="koboSpan">Irrespective of which
model is selected for application, the main advantages of utilising a
DEA approach to efficiency estimation can be summarised as
follows:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.460.1" class="koboSpan">both multiple
    outputs and multiple inputs can be analysed simultaneously;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.461.1" class="koboSpan">more extraneous
    factors that have an impact on performance can be incorporated into
    the analysis (such as those relating to the commercial and
    competitive environment of the port operation, as well as other
    qualitative factors);</span>
3.  <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.462.1" class="koboSpan">the possibility
    of different combinations of outputs and inputs being equally
    efficient is recognised and taken into account;</span>
4.  <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.463.1" class="koboSpan">there is no
    necessity to pre-specify a functional form for the production
    function that links inputs to outputs, nor to give an
    </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.464.1"
    class="koboSpan">a
    priori</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.465.1"
    class="koboSpan"> relationship (by pre-specifying the relative
    weights) between the different factors that the analysis accounts
    for;</span>
5.  <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.466.1" class="koboSpan">rather than in
    comparison to some sample average or some exogenous standard,
    efficiency is measured relative to the highest level of performance
    within the sample under study; and</span>
6.  <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.467.1" class="koboSpan">specific
    sub-groups of those DMUs identified as efficient can be ring-fenced
    as benchmark references for the non-efficient DMUs.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.468.1" class="koboSpan">In the specific case
of port efficiency, the ability to handle more than one output is a
particularly appealing feature of the DEA technique, because a number of
different measures of port output exist that may be used in such an
analysis, with the selection depending upon what aspect of port
operation constitutes the main focus of the evaluation.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.468.2" class="koboSpan">Surprisingly,
however, this capability is rarely utilised in practice, with a clear
preference amongst empirical analyses for focusing solely on a single
output, most usually container throughput.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_921"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.469.1"
class="koboSpan">In addition to providing relative efficiency measures
and rankings for the DMUs under study, DEA also provides results on the
sources of input and output inefficiency, as well as identifying the
benchmark DMUs that are utilised for the efficiency comparison.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.469.2" class="koboSpan">This ability
to identify the sources of inefficiency could be useful to port and/or
terminal managers in inefficient ports so that the problem areas might
be addressed. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.469.3"
class="koboSpan">For port authorities too, they may provide a guide to
focusing efforts at improving port performance.</span>

### <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.470.1" class="koboSpan">5.2 Applications</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.471.1" class="koboSpan">Applications of the
DEA approach to efficiency estimation in the general transport industry
are now quite common and examples exist of applications to virtually all
modes. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.471.2" class="koboSpan">(This
section is based on Cullinane and Wang, (see endnote 76) but has been
supplemented by a review of more recent applications.) For example, a
comprehensive review of DEA applications and other frontier-based
approaches to the railway industry was conducted by Oum
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.472.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.473.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1039" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1039"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.474.1" class="koboSpan">64</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.475.1"
class="koboSpan"> Similarly, De Borger
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.476.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.477.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1040" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1040"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.478.1" class="koboSpan">65</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.479.1"
class="koboSpan"> carried out just such a review for attempts to measure
public transit performance. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.479.2"
class="koboSpan">It is with the air industry, however, that the greatest
proliferation of DEA applications may be
found.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1041" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1041"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.480.1" class="koboSpan">66</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.481.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1047" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1047"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.482.1" class="koboSpan">72</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.483.1"
class="koboSpan"> This is interesting because of the great similarity
that exists between the air and maritime industries, particularly the
analogous positions of ports and airports; a feature that would suggest
that there remains great scope for further applications of the DEA
approach to the port sector.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.484.1" class="koboSpan">In relation to the
applications of DEA to ports that have already been undertaken, it is
particularly interesting that there has been very little correspondence
between the studies as to the choice of input and output variables that
are considered. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.484.2"
class="koboSpan">As Thanassoulis points
out,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1048" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1048"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.485.1" class="koboSpan">73</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.486.1"
class="koboSpan"> this is significant because the identification of the
inputs and the outputs in the assessment of DMUs tends to be as
difficult as it is crucial. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.486.2"
class="koboSpan">In addition, Ashar
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.487.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.488.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1049" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1049"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.489.1" class="koboSpan">74</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.490.1"
class="koboSpan"> attribute a lack of transparency to the use of the DEA
technique as applied to the estimation of port and/or terminal
efficiency.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.491.1" class="koboSpan">Roll and
Hayuth</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1050" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1050"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.492.1" class="koboSpan">75</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.493.1"
class="koboSpan"> were the first commentators to explicitly advocate the
use of DEA for the estimation of efficiency in the port sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.493.2" class="koboSpan">By presenting
a hypothetical application of the methodology to a fictional set of
container terminal data, they reveal what potential the approach might
hold. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.493.3" class="koboSpan">They
point particularly to the applicability of the DEA approach to the
measurement of productive efficiency in the service sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.493.4" class="koboSpan">In addition,
they highlight the fact that while the DEA approach does not require a
pre-specified standard against which to benchmark the performance
measurements pertaining to an individual port or terminal, such
standards can be incorporated into the analysis should this be
desirable. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.493.5"
class="koboSpan">This latter characteristic is particularly important in
countering the argument that the weights estimated by DEA might be
either misleading or, indeed, fundamentally wrong as a result of the
possibility that they may be different from some prior knowledge or
widely-accepted views on the relative values of the inputs or
outputs.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1052" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1052"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.494.1" class="koboSpan">77</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.495.1" class="koboSpan">Martinez-Budria
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.496.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.497.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1053" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1053"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.498.1" class="koboSpan">78</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.499.1"
class="koboSpan"> use DEA to analyse the relative efficiency of the
Spanish Port Authorities over the period 1993–1997.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.499.2" class="koboSpan">The
methodology as they apply it involves the classification of the 26
different ports within their sample into three categories according to
their “complexity”. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.499.3"
class="koboSpan">This classification system would appear to be highly
correlated to the size and/or throughput of the ports considered in the
analysis. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.499.4" class="koboSpan">The
results of the analysis reveal that the three groupings followed three
distinct evolutionary paths in terms of relative efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.499.5" class="koboSpan">The most
“complex” ports (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.499.6"
class="koboSpan">roughly equating to those
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_922"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.500.1"
class="koboSpan">of largest size and throughput) display the highest
levels of efficiency in absolute terms and a high growth rate in
efficiency over time. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.500.2"
class="koboSpan">Ports in the medium level of ‘complexity’ category
displayed only low levels of efficiency growth over the sample period,
while ports of low ‘complexity’ actually yielded a negative trend in
relative efficiency levels during the period under study.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.500.3" class="koboSpan">This seems to
suggest that not only are there significant economies of scale to be
reaped in port operation, but also that this and other factors may be
contributing to a concentration of cargo throughput in larger ports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.500.4" class="koboSpan">It can also be
inferred that the diminishing role of the smaller ports has an adverse
impact upon their relative efficiency levels that, in turn, creates a
vicious circle of cargo diversion away from this group of ports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.500.5" class="koboSpan">By analysing
the value of the slack variables to emerge from solving the DEA Linear
Programming problem, this study found that the worst source of
inefficiencies were, in general, due to excess capacities.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.501.1"
class="koboSpan">Tongzon</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1054" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1054"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.502.1" class="koboSpan">79</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.503.1"
class="koboSpan"> uses both DEA-CCR and DEA-additive models to analyse
the efficiency of four Australian and 12 other international container
ports for 1996. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.503.2"
class="koboSpan">This cross-sectional efficiency analysis incorporates
two output and six input variables, the data for which was collected for
the year 1996. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.503.3"
class="koboSpan">The output variables are cargo throughput and ship
working rate, where the former is the total number of containers loaded
and unloaded in TEUs and the latter is a measure of the number of
containers moved per working hour.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.503.4" class="koboSpan">The input
variables considered in the analysis were the number of cranes, number
of container berths, number of tugs, terminal area, delay time (the
difference between total berth time plus time waiting to berth and the
time between the start and finish of ship working) and the number of
port authority employees (as a proxy for the labour factor
input).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.504.1" class="koboSpan">Without precise
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.505.1"
class="koboSpan">a priori</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.506.1"
class="koboSpan"> information or assumptions on the returns to scale of
the port production function, two sets of results – for the CCR and
Additive DEA models – are presented and discussed.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.506.2" class="koboSpan">A comparison
of the results reveals that the CCR model identifies slightly more
inefficient ports (six vs three) than the Additive model.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.506.3" class="koboSpan">As the author
points out, this is not a surprising result as the CCR model assumes
constant returns to scale, while the Additive model is based on the
assumption of returns to scale that are variable.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.506.4" class="koboSpan">In
consequence, the latter will require a larger number of ports to define
the non-linear efficiency frontier.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.507.1" class="koboSpan">The results of the
initial analysis seemed to suggest that the model was over-specified for
the sample size (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.507.2"
class="koboSpan">that the sample data were insufficient to estimate a
meaningful frontier). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.507.3"
class="koboSpan">Since it was impossible to increase the sample size for
the study, a solution was to reduce the number of output variables
considered down to just one; the number of TEUs handled.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.507.4" class="koboSpan">The results of
the DEA analysis using only one output identified Melbourne, Rotterdam,
Yokohama and Osaka as inefficient with both the Additive and CCR models.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.507.5" class="koboSpan">Felixstowe,
Sydney, Fremantle, Brisbane, Tilbury and La Spezia were identified as
efficient using the Additive model, but as inefficient under the
assumption of constant returns to scale that is implicit in the CCR
model.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.508.1" class="koboSpan">The four ports judged
to be inefficient with both DEA models have opposite characteristics in
terms of size and function. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.508.2"
class="koboSpan">The port of Melbourne is quite small relative to
Rotterdam. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.508.3" class="koboSpan">The
port of Rotterdam is a hub port, while the ports of Melbourne, Yokohama
and Osaka generate most of their cargo internally.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.508.4" class="koboSpan">The findings
imply, therefore, that the technical efficiency of this sample of ports
does not depend solely upon size or function.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.508.5" class="koboSpan">The ports of
Hong Kong, Singapore, Hamburg, Keelung, Zeebrugge and Tanjung Priok are
found to be efficient irrespective of the returns to scale assumption
and number of outputs employed in the analysis.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.508.6" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
this seems to indicate
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_923"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.509.1"
class="koboSpan">(at least for the sample under study) that port size or
function alone is not the primary determinant of port efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.509.2" class="koboSpan">The enormous
slack variable values deduced for the number of container berths, the
terminal area and labour inputs for the ports of Melbourne, Sydney and
Fremantle confirm the particular need, according to the author, for the
government of Australia to refocus its waterfront reform initiatives as
an essential step towards improving port efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.509.3" class="koboSpan">Clearly
plagued by a lack of available data and the small sample size (only 16
observations). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.509.4"
class="koboSpan">More efficient ports than inefficient ports are
naturally identified. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.509.5"
class="koboSpan">Realising this serious drawback, the author concludes
that further work should be done in collecting more observations to
enlarge the sample analysed.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.510.1" class="koboSpan">Valentine and
Gray</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1055" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1055"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.511.1" class="koboSpan">80</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.512.1"
class="koboSpan"> use the DEA-CCR model to analyse data relating to a
sample of 31 container ports from the top 100 container ports for the
year 1998. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.512.2"
class="koboSpan">This analysis yielded an efficiency measure for each of
the ports in the sample, which the authors then compared to the port’s
ownership and organisational structures.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.512.3" class="koboSpan">It is
suggested that the gap between the top three ports that are deemed to be
efficient (Hong Kong, Singapore and Santos) and Houston in fourth place
is quite considerable and that the reason for this may be that while the
top three concentrate on the handling of container traffic, the other
ports in the study seem to diversify substantially into the handling of
other types of cargo.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.513.1" class="koboSpan">The main objective of
the study is to compare the efficiency ratings that are derived from the
application of DEA to the categorisation of the sample ports into
different forms of ownership and organizational structures.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.513.2" class="koboSpan">To this end,
the study concludes that cluster analysis does make a viable tool for
identifying organisational structures and that the ports sector exhibits
three structural forms that seem to have a relationship to estimated
levels of efficiency. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.513.3"
class="koboSpan">The most efficient form of organisational structure (as
assigned to individual ports on the basis of the output from a cluster
analysis) is the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.514.1"
class="koboSpan">simple
structure</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.515.1"
class="koboSpan"> (as defined in
Mintzberg</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1056" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1056"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.516.1" class="koboSpan">81</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.517.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.517.2"
class="koboSpan">The authors suggest, therefore, that predictions can be
made about the performance of a port and its likely associated
efficiency rating by simply examining its organisational chart to
determine which of the Mintzberg categories is applicable.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.517.3" class="koboSpan">On the other
hand, the study finds that the ownership structure does not seem to have
any significant influence upon efficiency; a conclusion that contradicts
that of Cullinane and
Song</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1057" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1057"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.518.1" class="koboSpan">82</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.519.1"
class="koboSpan"> who utilise an alternative methodology to arrive at
their conclusion.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.520.1" class="koboSpan">No details of the
precise model form employed for the analysis are given.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.520.2" class="koboSpan">However,
because only three ports (Hong Kong, Singapore and Santos) were found to
be efficient, it is probably safe to assume that the linear CCR model
was utilised. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.520.3"
class="koboSpan">Since most studies of returns to scale in ports have
found that significant scale economies are present, perhaps the
utilisation of the BCC or Additive model for the analysis of this data
might provide an interesting extension of the research.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.521.1" class="koboSpan">For the period
1990–1999,
Itoh</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1058" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1058"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.522.1" class="koboSpan">83</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.523.1"
class="koboSpan"> conducted a DEA window analysis using panel data
relating to the eight international container ports in Japan.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.523.2" class="koboSpan">Tokyo was
found to be consistently efficient in terms of its infrastructure and
labour productivity over the whole period, while Nagoya performed well
during the early part of the period covered by the analysis.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.523.3" class="koboSpan">At the other
extreme, efficiency scores for Yokohama, Kobe and Osaka were found to be
low throughout the duration of the period under study.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.524.1"
class="koboSpan">Barros</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1059" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1059"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.525.1" class="koboSpan">84</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.526.1"
class="koboSpan"> applies DEA to the Portuguese port industry in 1999
and 2000. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.526.2" class="koboSpan">The
motivation for the analysis is to determine what relationship exists
between the governance structure that has been established for the
Portuguese port sector, the incentive
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_924"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.527.1"
class="koboSpan">regulation promulgated under this structure and the
ultimate impact on port efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.527.2" class="koboSpan">The author
concludes that extant incentive regulation has been successful in
promoting enhanced efficiency in the sector, but that this could be
improved upon by the implementation of recommendations aimed at
redefining the role of Portugal’s Maritime Port Agency, the regulatory
body responsible for port matters.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.528.1" class="koboSpan">This time using data
for 1990 and 2000,
Barros</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1060" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1060"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.529.1" class="koboSpan">85</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.530.1"
class="koboSpan"> again applies DEA to the Portuguese port industry to
derive estimates of efficiency that can then be utilised to determine
the source of any inefficiency that may be identified.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.530.2" class="koboSpan">One of the
results of the analysis is that while Portuguese ports have attained
high levels of technical efficiency over the period covered by the
analysis, the sector has generally not kept pace with technological
change. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.530.3" class="koboSpan">The
author concludes that the financial aids to investment that form part of
the EU’s Single Market Program have stimulated greater efficiency in the
port sector, particularly as the result of the greater competition that
is faced; a feature that is particularly relevant for Portuguese ports
located near the border with Spain.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.530.4" class="koboSpan">Through the
application of Tobit regression analysis, it is also found that
container ports are more efficient than their multi-cargo counterparts
(suggesting that there are diseconomies of scope in cargo handling),
that efficiency is positively related to market share and, finally, that
greater public sector involvement is negatively related to
efficiency.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.531.1" class="koboSpan">In yet another
extension of this work, Barros and
Athanassiou</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1061" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1061"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.532.1" class="koboSpan">86</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.533.1"
class="koboSpan"> apply DEA to the estimation of the relative efficiency
of a sample of Portuguese and Greek seaports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.533.2" class="koboSpan">The broad
purpose of this exercise was to facilitate benchmarking so that areas
for improvement to management practices and strategies could be
identified and, within the context of European ports policy,
improvements implemented within the seaport sectors of these two
countries. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.533.3" class="koboSpan">The
authors conclude that there are economic benefits from the
implementation of this form of benchmarking and go on to evaluate their
extent.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.534.1" class="koboSpan">Bonilla
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.535.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1062" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1062"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.536.1" class="koboSpan">87</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.537.1"
class="koboSpan"> apply a version of DEA that includes a statistical
tolerance for inaccuracies in input and output data to the investigation
of commodity traffic efficiency within the Spanish port system.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.537.2" class="koboSpan">Their sample
comprises 23 ports and annual data are collected for 1995–1998
inclusive. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.537.3" class="koboSpan">The
analysis is unusual in that the sample ports handle a range of
cargoes–solid bulk, liquid bulk and general break-bulk–rather than being
restricted to a single form of cargo (most usually containers).
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.537.4" class="koboSpan">Given a
calculated high level of correlation between prospective input
variables, a single input encapsulating infrastructure endowment is
incorporated into the analysis. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.537.5"
class="koboSpan">The most and least efficient Spanish ports are
identified and, using an “incidence analysis”, the authors conclude by
identifying which ports are most sensitive to variations in traffic
volumes among the different types of cargo handled.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.538.1" class="koboSpan">Given the
characteristics of the container port industry and the random effects
associated with a single measured value of production for each port or
terminal in a sample and the level of measured efficiency associated
with it, Cullinane
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.539.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1063" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1063"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.540.1" class="koboSpan">88</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.541.1"
class="koboSpan"> recognised that the analysis of cross-sectional data
will inevitably provide inferior estimates of efficiency than those
based on panel data. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.541.2"
class="koboSpan">In seeking to allow for this potential, they applied
alternative DEA approaches based respectively on cross-sectional and
panel data analysis. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.541.3"
class="koboSpan">The authors conclude that by so doing, the development
of the efficiency of each container port or terminal in a sample can be
tracked over time and that this provides interesting and potentially
useful insights for both policy formulations and management.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.542.1" class="koboSpan">Recognising the
limitations in assessing the efficiency of ports solely on the basis of
capital and labour inputs, Park and
De</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1064" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1064"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.543.1" class="koboSpan">89</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.544.1"
class="koboSpan"> develop what they refer to as a “Four-Stage
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_925"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.545.1"
class="koboSpan">DEA Method”. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.545.2"
class="koboSpan">This involves the disaggregation of the overall
efficiency model into its constituent components, so that better insight
can be gained into the real sources of efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.545.3" class="koboSpan">The model
comprises individual DEA components that determine the respective
efficiency related to productivity, profitability, marketability and
overall. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.545.4" class="koboSpan">In
applying their method to a sample of Korean ports, the authors conclude
that improving the marketability of Korean seaports should be the utmost
priority of port authorities.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.546.1" class="koboSpan">Turner
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.547.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1065" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1065"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.548.1" class="koboSpan">90</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.549.1"
class="koboSpan"> applied DEA to the determination of changes in
infrastructure productivity in North American ports over the period 1984
to 1997. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.549.2" class="koboSpan">They
then went on to use the productivity estimates as the dependent variable
within a Tobit regression model which sought to determine the causal
factors affecting the scores they derived.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.549.3" class="koboSpan">Perhaps most
significantly, the authors conclude that there are significant economies
of scale present within the North American sector, both at port and at
terminal level–a finding that concurs with the outcomes of most research
investigating economies of scale in the port sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.549.4" class="koboSpan">They also find
that access to the rail network is a pivotal determinant of container
port infrastructure productivity in North America, but that there is no
evidence to suggest that specific investment in on-dock rail facilities
is a productive use of the land-take involved.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.550.1" class="koboSpan">DEA was applied by
Estache </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.551.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1066" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1066"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.552.1" class="koboSpan">91</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.553.1"
class="koboSpan"> to measure the changes in, and sources of, efficiency
following the decentralisation of control over the Mexican port system
from central government to regional port authorities.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.553.2" class="koboSpan">Analysing data
from Mexico’s 11 main ports using data from between 1996 and 1999, the
findings suggest that total factor productivity rose by an average of
4.1% per annum over the period of analysis.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.553.3" class="koboSpan">Disaggregating
the results, in all but a single case, Mexican ports either maintained
or improved their pure technical efficiency during the sample period.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.553.4" class="koboSpan">The authors
propose the outcomes of this sort of analysis as a rationale for, and
justification of, policy decisions to deregulate.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.554.1" class="koboSpan">Cullinane
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.555.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1067" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1067"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.556.1" class="koboSpan">92</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.557.1"
class="koboSpan"> empirically examine the relationship between
privatisation and relative efficiency within the container port
industry. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.557.2" class="koboSpan">The
sampling frame comprises the world’s leading container ports ranked in
the top 30 in 2001, together with five other container ports from the
Chinese mainland. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.557.3"
class="koboSpan">DEA is applied in a variety of panel data
configurations to eight years of annual data from 1992 to 1999, yielding
a total of 240 observations. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.557.4"
class="koboSpan">The analysis concludes that there is no evidence to
support the hypothesis that greater private sector involvement in the
container port sector irrevocably leads to improved efficiency.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.558.1"
class="koboSpan">Barros</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1068" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1068"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.559.1" class="koboSpan">93</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.560.1"
class="koboSpan"> used DEA on a combination of financial and operational
variables to evaluate the performance of Italian ports using data from
2002 to 2003. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.560.2"
class="koboSpan">The author concludes that the sample under study
exhibited relatively high levels of efficiency and goes on to isolate
the influence on port efficiency of factors such as size, the degree of
containerisation of cargo and labour.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.561.1" class="koboSpan">Rios and Gastaud
Macada</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1069" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1069"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.562.1" class="koboSpan">94</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.563.1"
class="koboSpan"> apply a DEA-BCC model to derive estimates of relative
efficiency for 23 container terminals in the Mercosur region (15
Brazilian, 6 Argentinian and 2 Uruguayan) using data from 2002, 2003 and
2004. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.563.2" class="koboSpan">The
analysis incorporated five inputs (number of cranes, number of berths,
number of employees, terminal area, amount of yard equipment) and two
outputs (TEUs handled and average number of containers handled per
hour/ship). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.563.3"
class="koboSpan">The results suggested that 60% of the terminals under
study were efficient over the study period, with terminals in the ports
of Zarate, Rio Cubatão and Teconvi revealed as the benchmarks to which
inefficient terminals should aspire.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_926"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.564.1"
class="koboSpan">Using cross-sectional data for 2002, Cullinane and
Wang</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1070" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1070"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.565.1" class="koboSpan">95</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.566.1"
class="koboSpan"> apply DEA to the derivation of estimates of relative
efficiency for a sample comprising 69 of Europe’s container terminals
with annual throughput of over 10,000 TEUs.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.566.2" class="koboSpan">The sample was
distributed across 24 European countries.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.566.3" class="koboSpan">The main
finding is that significant inefficiency pervades the European container
handling industry, with the average efficiency of container terminals
under study amounting to 0.48 (assuming constant returns to scale) and
0.42 (assuming variable returns to scale).
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.566.4" class="koboSpan">Most of the
container terminals under study exhibit increasing returns to scale,
with large container terminals more likely to be associated with higher
efficiency scores. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.566.5"
class="koboSpan">A further conclusion was that there was significant
variation in the average efficiency of container terminals located in
different regions, with those in the British Isles found to be the most
efficient and Scandinavia and Eastern Europe the least efficient.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.566.6" class="koboSpan">These findings
were validated in a follow-up
study</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1071" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1071"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.567.1" class="koboSpan">96</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.568.1"
class="koboSpan"> that investigated the efficiency and scale properties
of 104 of Europe’s container terminals with annual throughput of over
10,000 TEUs in 2003, distributed across 29 European countries.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.568.2" class="koboSpan">Again, the
main finding was that significant inefficiency was present within most
of the terminals under study and that large scale production tends to be
associated with higher efficiency.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.569.1" class="koboSpan">As part of their
competitive strategies to extend their hinterlands, Spain’s regional
Port Authorities have invested heavily in port infrastructure with a
view to increasing the efficiency of the services offered.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.569.2" class="koboSpan">Garcia-Alonso
and
Martin-Bofarull</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1072" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1072"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.570.1" class="koboSpan">97</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.571.1"
class="koboSpan"> apply DEA with a focus on the ports of Bilbao and
Valencia; not only are they important Spanish ports, but their
investments in new infrastructure have also been significant.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.571.2" class="koboSpan">On the basis
of inter-port traffic redistribution from the land side before and after
the investments are made, the authors determine the extent to which
improvements in efficiency have occurred and to what extent any
efficiency gains translate into an enhanced ability to attract traffic.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.571.3" class="koboSpan">They conclude
that the differential effect on the two ports has been quite marked and
that the influence of port location on port efficiency and the capacity
to attract traffic is quite significant.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.572.1" class="koboSpan">Lin and
Tseng</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1073" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1073"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.573.1" class="koboSpan">98</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.574.1"
class="koboSpan"> apply five different DEA models to acquire a variety
of complementary information about the operational efficiency of major
container ports in the Asia-Pacific region and to identify trends in
port efficiency. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.574.2"
class="koboSpan">By applying efficiency value analysis, the root causes
of any empirically-determined inefficiency are established and an
analysis of slack variables is then conducted to reveal potential areas
of improvement for the set of inefficient ports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.574.3" class="koboSpan">Finally, the
returns to scale status of each of the ports in the sample is assessed
and a a sensitivity analysis is implemented to identify which input or
output variables have the greatest influence over efficiency
levels.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.575.1"
class="koboSpan">Liu</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1074" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1074"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.576.1" class="koboSpan">99</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.577.1"
class="koboSpan"> applies the DEA-CCR and DEA-BCC models, as well as a
three-stage DEA model, to evaluate the changes in efficiency that took
place between 1998 and 2001 in 10 ports in the Asia-Pacific region.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.577.2" class="koboSpan">The main
finding of this work was that different models led to different results.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.577.3" class="koboSpan">An attempt is
made to explain why this should be the case.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.577.4" class="koboSpan">Similarly,
Hung, Lu and
Wang</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1075" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1075"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.578.1" class="koboSpan">100</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.579.1"
class="koboSpan"> also derive DEA efficiency estimates for Asian
container ports, taking into account both scale efficiency targets and
the variability of the estimates.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.580.1" class="koboSpan">In Italy, Port
Authorities exercise some discretion over terminal concession fees.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.580.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
way these fees are charged in practice does not provide terminal
operators with the necessary incentives to boost throughput.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.580.3" class="koboSpan">In a
relatively novel application of the methodology and with a focus on the
port of Genoa, Ferrari and
Basta</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1076" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1076"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.581.1" class="koboSpan">101</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.582.1"
class="koboSpan"> utilise DEA efficiency estimates as the basis for
setting terminal concession fees under a price-cap rule.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_927"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.583.1"
class="koboSpan">Cheon</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1077" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1077"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.584.1" class="koboSpan">102</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.585.1"
class="koboSpan"> evaluates the relationship between the different types
of global terminal operators (GTOs) – defined as global stevedores,
global hybrids and global carriers – and the level of efficiency which
they exhibit. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.585.2"
class="koboSpan">The author applies a tiered DEA to determine both crane
and relative technical efficiency of the ports in the sample.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.585.3" class="koboSpan">The results
suggest that the involvement of “global stevedores” in a terminal
operation induces higher crane efficiency, but that this efficiency is
not effectively transformed into port-level technical efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.585.4" class="koboSpan">In contrast,
terminal operations run by “global carriers” in dedicated leased
terminals result in significantly lower levels of efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.585.5" class="koboSpan">The most
important implication of this work is that port authorities may be
motivated to increase levels of intra-port competition to address
efficiency concerns at a port level.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.586.1" class="koboSpan">One important
motivation for applying DEA to the issue of port and/or terminal
efficiency estimation is in order that inefficient DMUs in a sample can
benchmark themselves against their efficient counterparts.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.586.2" class="koboSpan">This aspect of
DEA studies is becoming increasingly popular.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.586.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
Sharma and
Yu</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1078" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1078"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.587.1" class="koboSpan">103</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.588.1"
class="koboSpan"> highlight the problem that the reference set of
efficient ports or terminals may be very diverse in terms of their size,
location, operating environment and operational practices.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.588.2" class="koboSpan">Based on the
fusing of data mining with DEA, they outline an approach for overcoming
this problem that prescribes a step-wise projection of inefficient units
onto the production frontier which takes into account maximum capacity
and similar input properties. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.588.3"
class="koboSpan">The same authors are similarly motivated to
operationalise the benchmarking role of
DEA</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1079" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1079"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.589.1" class="koboSpan">104</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.590.1"
class="koboSpan"> by identifying and prioritising target factors for
efficiency improvements and prescribing improvement paths for
inefficient units. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.590.2"
class="koboSpan">This involves the development of a decision-tree based
DEA model that differentiates between the performance of each
inefficient DMU and identifies DMU-specific, significant attributes that
are most pivotal for improving these different performance
levels.</span>

## <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.591.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.591.2" class="koboSpan">The Stochastic Frontier Model (SFM)</span>

### <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.592.1" class="koboSpan">6.1 Method</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.593.1" class="koboSpan">As has already been
stated and as in the case of DEA, the econometric approach to efficiency
measurement is also based on utilising the concept of an efficient
frontier. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.593.2" class="koboSpan">This
section represents a summary of the theoretical background to the
analysis undertaken in Song, Cullinane and Roe (see endnote 111).
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.593.3" class="koboSpan">The
econometric approach, however, involves the specification of a
parametric representation of technology.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.593.4" class="koboSpan">The early
parametric frontier
models</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1080" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1080"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.594.1" class="koboSpan">105</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.595.1"
class="koboSpan">–</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1081" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1081"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.596.1" class="koboSpan">106</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.597.1"
class="koboSpan"> are deterministic in the sense that all DMUs share a
common fixed and pre-determined class of frontier.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.597.2" class="koboSpan">This is
unreasonable and ignores the real possibility that the observed
performance of the DMU may be affected by exogenous (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.597.3" class="koboSpan">random shock)
as well as endogenous (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.597.4"
class="koboSpan">inefficiency) factors.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.597.5" class="koboSpan">The fact that
there is no allowance for the possible influence of statistical noise is
also widely regarded to be the most serious limitation of
DEA.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1082" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1082"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.598.1" class="koboSpan">107</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.599.1"
class="koboSpan"> To allocate all influential factors, whether
favourable or unfavourable and whether under or beyond the control of
the DMU (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.599.2"
class="koboSpan">either endogenous or exogenous), into a single
disturbance term and to refer to the mixture as inefficiency is clearly
a dubious and imprecise generalisation.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.600.1" class="koboSpan">As an alternative,
the now much more widely applied stochastic frontier model (SFM) is
motivated by the idea that deviations from the production frontier might
not be entirely under the control of the economic unit being
studied.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1083" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1083"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.601.1" class="koboSpan">108</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.602.1"
class="koboSpan"> Both Aigner
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.603.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1084" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1084"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.604.1" class="koboSpan">109</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.605.1"
class="koboSpan"> and Meeusen and van den
Broeck</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1085" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1085"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.606.1" class="koboSpan">110</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.607.1"
class="koboSpan"> independently constructed a more reasonable
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_928"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.608.1"
class="koboSpan">error structure than a purely one-sided one.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.608.2" class="koboSpan">They
considered a linear model for the frontier production function as
follows:</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.609.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00472.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.610.1" class="koboSpan">where</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.611.1"
class="koboSpan">Y</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.612.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.613.1"
class="koboSpan"> denotes the appropriate form of output for the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.614.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.615.1"
class="koboSpan">th DMU at time
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.616.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.617.1"
class="koboSpan">X</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.618.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.619.1"
class="koboSpan"> is a vector of inputs associated with the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.620.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.621.1"
class="koboSpan">th DMU at time
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.622.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.623.1"
