class="koboSpan">β</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.625.1"
class="koboSpan"> is a vector of input coefficients for the associated
independent variables in the production function.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.626.1" class="koboSpan">Their disturbance
term </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.627.1"
class="koboSpan">ε</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.628.1"
class="koboSpan"> consists of the following two parts:</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0453" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.629.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00473.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.630.1" class="koboSpan">The component
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.631.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.632.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.633.1"
class="koboSpan">,represents a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.634.1"
class="koboSpan">symmetric disturbance
term</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.635.1" class="koboSpan">
permitting random variation of the production function across economic
units due not only to the effects of measurement and specification
error, but also due to the effects of exogenous shock beyond the control
of the economic unit (e.g. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.635.2"
class="koboSpan">weather conditions, geography or machine performance).
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.635.3" class="koboSpan">The other
component</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.636.1"
class="koboSpan"> u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.637.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.638.1"
class="koboSpan"> (≥0) is a
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.639.1"
class="koboSpan">one-sided disturbance</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.640.1"
class="koboSpan">term </span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.641.1"
class="koboSpan">and represents ‘productive inefficiency’ relative to
the stochastic production function.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.641.2" class="koboSpan">The
nonnegative disturbance
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.642.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.643.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.644.1"
class="koboSpan"> reflects the fact that output lies on or below its
frontier. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.644.2" class="koboSpan">The
deviation of an observation from the deterministic kernel of the
stochastic production function (equation 10) arises from two sources:
(i) symmetric random variation of the deterministic kernel
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.645.1"
class="koboSpan">f</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.646.1"
class="koboSpan"> (X</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.647.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.648.1"
class="koboSpan">;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.649.1"
class="koboSpan">β</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.650.1"
class="koboSpan">) across observations that is captured by the component
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.651.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.652.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.653.1"
class="koboSpan">; and (ii) asymmetric variation (or productive
inefficiency) captured by the component
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.654.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.655.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.656.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.656.2"
class="koboSpan">The term
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.657.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.658.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.659.1"
class="koboSpan"> measures productive inefficiency in the sense that it
measures the short-fall fall of output
Y</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.660.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.661.1"
class="koboSpan"> from that implied by its maximum frontier given by
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.662.1"
class="koboSpan">f</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.663.1"
class="koboSpan">(X</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.664.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.665.1"
class="koboSpan">;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.666.1"
class="koboSpan">β</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.667.1"
class="koboSpan">)
exp(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.668.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.669.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.670.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.670.2"
class="koboSpan">The measure of a DMU’s efficiency should be defined,
therefore, by:</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0454" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.671.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00474.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.672.1" class="koboSpan">relative to the
stochastic frontier
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.673.1"
class="koboSpan">f </span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.674.1"
class="koboSpan">(X;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.675.1"
class="koboSpan">β</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.676.1"
class="koboSpan">)
exp(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.677.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.678.1"
class="koboSpan">).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.679.1" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, any
estimate of a DMU’s efficiency level is not consistent, as it contains
statistical noise as well as productive inefficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.679.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
stochastic frontier models suffer from two other difficulties.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.679.3" class="koboSpan">One is the
requirement of specific assumptions about the distributions underlying
productive inefficiency (e.g. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.679.4"
class="koboSpan">half-normal and exponential) and statistical noise
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.679.5" class="koboSpan">normal).
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.679.6" class="koboSpan">The other is
the required assumption that regressors (the input variables contained
in the vector
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.680.1"
class="koboSpan">X</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.681.1"
class="koboSpan">) and productive inefficiency are independent.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.681.2" class="koboSpan">This may well
be an unrealistic assumption since if a DMU knows its level of
inefficiency, then this should affect its input choices as it attempts
to address the problem. </span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0229"
id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0229"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.682.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 5</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.683.1"
class="koboSpan"> is a graphical representation of the basic idea that
underpins stochastic frontier model estimates of productive (technical)
efficiency.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.684.1" class="koboSpan">A further development
in the modelling of frontiers lies with the use of estimation techniques
that involve panel data. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.684.2"
class="koboSpan">Initially, the stochastic frontier model (10) was
developed for cross-sectional data.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.684.3" class="koboSpan">Hausman and
Taylor,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1087" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1087"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.685.1" class="koboSpan">112</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.686.1"
class="koboSpan">
Baltagi,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1088" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1088"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.687.1" class="koboSpan">113</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.688.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Blundell</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1089" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1089"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.689.1" class="koboSpan">114</span></a></sup>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0455" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.690.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00475.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 5: A conceptual representation of the Stochastic Frontier Model Approach to efficiency estimation" /></span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_929"></span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0229"
id="Ch031.xhtml_cap_lbl0229"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.691.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 5:</span></span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.692.1"
class="koboSpan"> A conceptual representation of the Stochastic Frontier
Model Approach to efficiency estimation</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.693.1" class="koboSpan">list a number of
attractive features of using panel data, one of which is that panel data
allows for the control of individual effects which may be correlated
with other variables included in the specification of an economic
relationship, thus making the analysis of relative efficiency on the
basis of single cross-sections extremely difficult.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.694.1" class="koboSpan">With respect to the
frontier model, consistent estimates of the productive efficiency of a
DMU can be obtained as the number of time periods tends to infinity.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.694.2" class="koboSpan">As a result,
strong distributional assumptions are not necessary.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.694.3" class="koboSpan">Moreover, the
parameters and the DMU’s level of efficiency can be estimated without
assuming that the input variables are uncorrelated with productive
inefficiency. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.694.4"
class="koboSpan">Therefore, as Schmidt and
Sickles</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1090" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1090"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.695.1" class="koboSpan">115</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.696.1"
class="koboSpan"> note, a variety of different estimates will be
considered, depending on what the analyst is willing to assume about the
distribution of productive inefficiency and its potential correlation
with the regressors.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.697.1" class="koboSpan">Initially, it was
claimed that productive efficiencies for individual DMUs could not be
estimated and predicted. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.697.2"
class="koboSpan">In an effort to explore this unresolved problem with
the previous models, along with attempting to reap the benefits of the
aforementioned advantages of panel data, Pitt and
Lee</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1091" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1091"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.698.1" class="koboSpan">116</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.699.1"
class="koboSpan"> were the first to develop techniques using panel data
to estimate the frontier production function.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.699.2" class="koboSpan">Jondrow
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.700.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.701.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1092" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1092"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.702.1" class="koboSpan">117</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.703.1"
class="koboSpan"> presented two estimators (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.703.2" class="koboSpan">for
half-normal and exponential cases) for the DMU-specific effect for an
individual DMU under the assumption that the parameters of the frontier
production function were known and cross-sectional data were available
for given sample DMUs. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.703.3"
class="koboSpan">Schmidt and
Sickles</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1093" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1093"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.704.1" class="koboSpan">118</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.705.1"
class="koboSpan"> suggested three different estimators for individual
DMU effects and productive efficiencies for panel data.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.706.1" class="koboSpan">A major breakthrough
in the area of panel data models was achieved by Battese and
Coelli,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1094" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1094"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.707.1" class="koboSpan">119</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.708.1"
class="koboSpan"> who presented a generalisation of the results of
Jondrow </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.709.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.710.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1095" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1095"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.711.1" class="koboSpan">120</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.712.1"
class="koboSpan"> on
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_930"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.713.1"
class="koboSpan">the assumption of a more general distribution for DMU
effects to be applied to the stochastic frontier model.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.713.2" class="koboSpan">Their model is
given by:</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0456" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.714.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00476.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.715.1" class="koboSpan">The main difference
between models (10) and (13) is the absence of the subscript
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.716.1"
class="koboSpan">t </span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.717.1"
class="koboSpan">associated with
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.718.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.719.1"
class="koboSpan"> in the latter.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.719.2" class="koboSpan">Thus,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.720.1"
class="koboSpan">u </span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.721.1"
class="koboSpan">captures DMU-specific time-invariant variables omitted
from the previous function. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.721.2"
class="koboSpan">The symmetric terms
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.722.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.723.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.724.1"
class="koboSpan"> are assumed to be identically and independently
normally distributed with mean zero and variance
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.725.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00477.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.726.1"

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.727.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.728.1"
class="koboSpan">it </span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.729.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00478.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.730.1"
class="koboSpan"> The one-sided terms
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.731.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.732.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.733.1"
class="koboSpan"> (≥0) are assumed to be identically and independently
distributed non-negative random variables which capture
a</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.734.1"
class="koboSpan"> DMU</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.735.1"
class="koboSpan"> effect but no
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.736.1"
class="koboSpan">time</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.737.1"
class="koboSpan">
effect.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1096" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1096"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.738.1" class="koboSpan">121</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.739.1"
class="koboSpan"> In addition, the error terms
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.740.1"
class="koboSpan">v</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.741.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.742.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.743.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.744.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.745.1"
class="koboSpan"> are assumed to be independently distributed of the
input variables as well as of one another.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.746.1" class="koboSpan">The most frequently
defined distribution for the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.747.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.748.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.749.1"
class="koboSpan"> is the half-normal (i.e.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.750.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.751.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.752.1"
class="koboSpan"> ~
\|</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.753.1"
class="koboSpan">N</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.754.1"
class="koboSpan">(0, </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.755.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00479.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.756.1"
class="koboSpan"> though other distributional assumptions for
the</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.757.1"
class="koboSpan"> u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.758.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.759.1"
class="koboSpan"> terms have been proposed by several researchers.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.759.2" class="koboSpan">For example,
the
exponential,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1097" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1097"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.760.1" class="koboSpan">122</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.761.1"
class="koboSpan"> the truncated
normal</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1098" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1098"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.762.1" class="koboSpan">123</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.763.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the
gamma.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1099" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1099"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.764.1" class="koboSpan">124</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.765.1" class="koboSpan">As far as the
productive efficiency of a DMU is concerned, Battese and
Coelli</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1100" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1100"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.766.1" class="koboSpan">125</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.767.1"
class="koboSpan"> define it as the ratio of the DMU’s mean production,
given its realised DMU-specific effect, to the corresponding mean
production with the DMU effect being equivalent to zero.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.767.2" class="koboSpan">The productive
efficiency of the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.768.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.769.1"
class="koboSpan">th DMU (PE</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.770.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.771.1"
class="koboSpan">) is defined, therefore, as:</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0457" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.772.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00480.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.773.1" class="koboSpan">where
Y</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.774.1"
class="koboSpan">it</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.775.1"
class="koboSpan"> \* represents the output of production for the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.776.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.777.1"
class="koboSpan">th DMU at time
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.778.1"
class="koboSpan">t</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.779.1"
class="koboSpan">, and the value of the
PE</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.780.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.781.1"
class="koboSpan"> lies between zero and one (0 ≤
PE</span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.782.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.783.1"
class="koboSpan"> ≤ 1).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.784.1" class="koboSpan">If a DMU’s productive
efficiency is calculated as 0.65, for example, then this implies that,
on average, the DMU realises 65% of the production possible for a fully
efficient DMU having comparable input values.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.784.2" class="koboSpan">From the
perspective of efficiency measurement, the definition contained in
equation (14) has a thread of connection with that of equation
(12).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.785.1" class="koboSpan">If the model (13) is
transformed to a logarithm of a production function, such as:</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0458" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.786.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00481.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.787.1" class="koboSpan">then the measure of
productive efficiency for the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.788.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.789.1"
class="koboSpan">th DMU is defined by:</span>

<div id="Ch031.xhtml_fig0459" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.790.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00482.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.791.1" class="koboSpan">The measure shown in
equation (16) does not depend on the level of the input variables for
the DMU, while the definition provided by equation (14) for calculating
the productive efficiency of a DMU clearly shows that its estimation
depends significantly on inferences concerning the distribution function
of the unobservable DMU effect
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.792.1"
class="koboSpan">u</span></span><sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.793.1"
class="koboSpan">i</span></sub><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.794.1"
class="koboSpan">, given the sample observations.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.795.1" class="koboSpan">This technique is
relevant to a case where productive efficiency is time-invariant.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.795.2"
class="koboSpan">Schmidt,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1101" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1101"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.796.1" class="koboSpan">126</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.797.1"
class="koboSpan"> however, states that unchanging inefficiency over time
is not a particularly
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_931"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.798.1"
class="koboSpan">attractive assumption; a criticism which is readily
admitted by Battese and Coelli. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.798.2"
class="koboSpan">With the assumption that productive efficiency does
vary over time, an alternative approach has been adopted by
econometricians such as Cornwell
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.799.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.800.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1102" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1102"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.801.1" class="koboSpan">127</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.802.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
Kumbhakar.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1103" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1103"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.803.1" class="koboSpan">128</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.804.1"
class="koboSpan"> None of these studies succeed, however, in completely
separating inefficiency from individual DMU
effects</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1104" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1104"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.805.1" class="koboSpan">129</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.806.1"
class="koboSpan"> and, in any case, the methods proposed thus far are
too complicated for empirical
application.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1105" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1105"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.807.1" class="koboSpan">130</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.808.1" class="koboSpan">6.2 Applications</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.809.1"
class="koboSpan">Liu</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1106" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1106"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.810.1" class="koboSpan">131</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.811.1"
class="koboSpan"> was the first to apply the stochastic frontier model
to a maritime context. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.811.2"
class="koboSpan">He set out to test the hypothesis that public sector
ports are inherently less efficient than those in the private-sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.811.3" class="koboSpan">A unique set
of panel data relating to the outputs and inputs of 28 commercially
important UK ports over the period 1983 to 1990 is collected for
analysis. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.811.4"
class="koboSpan">Ownership is hypothesised as a potential factor input
to the frontier production function and the effect of its presence on
inter-port efficiency differences is investigated by applying the
stochastic frontier model to derive the required efficiency
estimates.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.812.1" class="koboSpan">The results reveal
that the efficiency difference between ports in the public versus the
private sector is negligible and insignificant between trust and
municipal ports on the one hand (the public sector) and private ports on
the other. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.812.2"
class="koboSpan">Capital intensity is found to have little relationship
to efficiency and the impact of size is found to have a small, but
significant, impact. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.812.3"
class="koboSpan">Taken together with the scale elasticity that is
estimated as part of the analysis, this is not really supportive of the
expectation that substantial economies of scale exist within the sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.812.4" class="koboSpan">A peculiarity
of this analysis of the UK situation is that port location was
discovered to be a significant influence on efficiency, with ports on
the west coast of the UK (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.812.5"
class="koboSpan">on what many shipping commentators have described as
the “wrong” side of the country) being 11% less efficient, on average,
than the rest of the sample.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.813.1" class="koboSpan">Cullinane and
Song</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1107" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1107"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.814.1" class="koboSpan">132</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.815.1"
class="koboSpan"> were among the first to specifically address the
unique characteristics of the container port sector by providing a
framework for, and recommended approach to, the application of the
stochastic frontier model within this context.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.815.2" class="koboSpan">They
enumerated the required data for collection, the alternative possible
forms which this might take and the likely sources of data.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.815.3" class="koboSpan">Banos-Pino
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.816.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1108" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1108"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.817.1" class="koboSpan">133</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.818.1"
class="koboSpan"> were the first to implement a fully fledged
application of the stochastic frontier model to the container port
context. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.818.2" class="koboSpan">They
adopted a translog functional form to develop a cost frontier based on
panel data from 27 Spanish container ports over the period 1985–1997.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.818.3" class="koboSpan">The main
conclusion drawn was that Spanish container ports were generally
inefficient due to large levels of overcapitalisation during the period
of analysis.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.819.1" class="koboSpan">Notteboom
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.820.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1109" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1109"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.821.1" class="koboSpan">134</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.822.1"
class="koboSpan"> apply a Bayesian approach based on Monte-Carlo
approximation to the estimation of a stochastic frontier model aimed at
assessing the productive efficiency of a sample of 36 European container
terminals located in the Hamburg–Le Havre range and in the Western
Mediterranean. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.822.2"
class="koboSpan">The data analysed relates to 1994.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.822.3" class="koboSpan">The robustness
and validity of the estimated model is tested by comparing the results
with those of four benchmark terminals in Asia (Singapore, Kaohsiung and
Hong Kong’s MTL and HIT terminals).</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.823.1" class="koboSpan">This study found that
10 of the terminals, including all four Asian terminals, have efficiency
levels of about 80%, with the majority of ports in the Hamburg–Le Havre
range falling into the 75–80% efficiency category.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.823.2" class="koboSpan">The Belgian
container terminals were found to be some of the most efficient in the
sample, as were the Spanish terminals
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_932"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.824.1"
class="koboSpan">included in the analysis.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.824.2" class="koboSpan">Container
terminals in Italy were generally found to be the most inefficient.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.824.3" class="koboSpan">The results
also suggested that small terminals do tend to be less efficient than
large ones, although a more thorough secondary analysis revealed that
small terminals located in large ports are, in general, more efficient
than small terminals located in smaller ports.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.825.1" class="koboSpan">Several relationships
can be inferred from the results of this study.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.825.2" class="koboSpan">For instance,
situations where intra-port competition is formidable (with no single
terminal predominant) seem to have a positive effect upon average
terminal efficiency within the port.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.825.3" class="koboSpan">In addition,
hub ports tend to be more productively efficient than typical feeder
ports. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.825.4"
class="koboSpan">However, whether the terminal is publicly or privately
owned seems to have no bearing upon the level of efficiency derived.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.825.5" class="koboSpan">Finally,
terminals in the North of Europe were found to be generally more
efficient than those in the South of Europe.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.825.6" class="koboSpan">All of these
relationships were investigated, however, on an individual basis and no
insight was gained into the potential impact of joint effects.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.825.7" class="koboSpan">This would
appear to constitute, therefore, an interesting avenue for the extension
of this research.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.826.1" class="koboSpan">Coto-Millan
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.827.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1110" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1110"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.828.1" class="koboSpan">135</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.829.1"
class="koboSpan"> applied a stochastic frontier model to estimate the
economic efficiency of 27 Spanish ports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.829.2" class="koboSpan">Panel data for
the period 1985–1989 was collected and analysed using the Cobb-Douglas
and translog versions of the model.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.829.3" class="koboSpan">The study
finds that the translog version of the stochastic frontier model best
represents the level of technology within the industry.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.829.4" class="koboSpan">Quite
surprisingly, it appears
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.830.1"
class="koboSpan">prima
facie</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.831.1" class="koboSpan">
that large ports are found to be rather more economically inefficient
than their smaller counterparts, despite the fact that the analysis also
reveals the simultaneous existence of significant scale economies within
the sector. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.831.2"
class="koboSpan">Indeed, in order of efficiency, the top five positions
are occupied by the smallest ports, while the worst five in the
efficiency rankings are relatively the largest ports with the greatest
degree of autonomy. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.831.3"
class="koboSpan">A more detailed second-stage analysis of the findings,
however, reveals that it is not really size which explains the levels of
economic efficiency that have resulted from the analysis.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.831.4" class="koboSpan">Rather, it is
the degree of autonomy in management that is the critical determining
factor, with those ports that are highly autonomous being less efficient
than the rest. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.831.5"
class="koboSpan">Technical progress was ascertained to be insignificant
over the period covered by the analysis.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.832.1" class="koboSpan">The efficiency
effects of the port reforms that were implemented in Mexico in 1993 are
assessed by Estache
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.833.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1111" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1111"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.834.1" class="koboSpan">136</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.835.1"
class="koboSpan"> The authors estimate a stochastic production frontier
based on port data covering the period 1996–1999.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.835.2" class="koboSpan">The results
show that Mexico’s ports achieved, on average, a 2.8–3.3% average annual
efficiency gain since the reform programme was instigated.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.835.3" class="koboSpan">Port-specific
measures of efficiency over the whole period of analysis reveal
consistent levels of performance for individual ports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.835.4" class="koboSpan">The authors
point to a significant advantage of the adopted approach by suggesting
that the identification of individual port “leaders and laggards” would
not have emerged from a simple analysis of common partial productivity
indicators. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.835.5"
class="koboSpan">They conclude that derived measures of relative
efficiency of this sort can promote yardstick competition between port
infrastructure operators, particularly if the information could be built
into an explicit incentive-based regulatory regime.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.836.1" class="koboSpan">Cullinane, Song and
Gray</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1112" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1112"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.837.1" class="koboSpan">137</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.838.1"
class="koboSpan"> use the “port function matrix” due to
Baird</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1113" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1113"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.839.1" class="koboSpan">138</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.840.1"
class="koboSpan"> to analyse the administrative and ownership structures
of major container ports in Asia.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.840.2" class="koboSpan">The relative
efficiency of these ports is then assessed using the cross-sectional and
panel data versions of the stochastic frontier model.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.840.3" class="koboSpan">The estimated
efficiency measures are broadly similar for the two versions of the
model tested. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.840.4"
class="koboSpan">From the results of the analysis, it is concluded that
the size of a port or terminal is closely correlated with its efficiency
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_933"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.841.1"
class="koboSpan">and that some support exists for the claim that the
transformation of ownership from public to private sector improves
economic efficiency. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.841.2"
class="koboSpan">It is concluded that while this does provide some
justification for the many programmes in Asian ports that aim to attract
private capital into both existing and new facilities, it is also the
case that the level of market deregulation is an important intervening
variable that may also exert a positive influence on efficiency
levels.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.842.1" class="koboSpan">Cullinane and
Song</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1114" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1114"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.843.1" class="koboSpan">139</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.844.1"
class="koboSpan"> assess the success achieved by Korea’s port
privatisation policies in increasing the productive efficiency of its
container terminals. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.844.2"
class="koboSpan">The UK container terminal sector provides a useful
benchmark for comparison since privatisation and deregulation have
formed an integral part of UK port reforms for nearly 20 years and the
effect on efficiency, having had time to mature, is much easier to
gauge. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.844.3" class="koboSpan">The
stochastic frontier model is justified as the chosen methodology for
estimating productive efficiency levels and is applied to
cross-sectional data under a variety of distributional assumptions.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.844.4" class="koboSpan">A panel data
model is also estimated. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.844.5"
class="koboSpan">Results are consistent and suggest that: (1) the degree
of private sector involvement in sample container terminals is
positively related to productive efficiency; and (2) improved productive
efficiency has followed the implementation of privatisation and
deregulation policies within the Korean port sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.844.6" class="koboSpan">Even though
not categorical, these conclusions are important because the market for
container throughput is internationally competitive and if policies
which promote competition between Korean container terminals lead to
greater productive efficiency, this will inevitably make the sector as a
whole more competitive internationally.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.845.1" class="koboSpan">Tongzon and
Heng</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1115" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1115"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.846.1" class="koboSpan">140</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.847.1"
class="koboSpan"> use the SFM as the basis for quantifying the
relationship between port ownership structure and port efficiency to
determine whether port privatisation is a necessary prerequisite to
ports gaining a competitive advantage.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.847.2" class="koboSpan">The study is
based on a sample of selected container terminals around the world, The
results of the analysis are utilised in a supplementary principal
component analysis (PCA) and linear regression model to identify the
determinants of port competitiveness and to examine the influence they
exert. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.847.3" class="koboSpan">The
authors conclude that greater private sector participation in the port
industry can improve port efficiency, which will in turn enhance port
competitiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.848.1" class="koboSpan">Using the SFM to
estimate a cost frontier for the industry, the extent of technology
change and changes in technical efficiency within Portuguese ports
between 1990 and 2000 is analysed by
Barros.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1116" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1116"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.849.1" class="koboSpan">141</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.850.1"
class="koboSpan"> He assumed a translog function and employed a maximum
likelihood technique to estimate the model.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.850.2" class="koboSpan">The results
show that the average inefficiency score over the period analysed was
39.6%, signifying a high degree of wastage in the resources deployed.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.850.3" class="koboSpan">This is
despite the fact that technological change had contributed to a
significant reduction of costs over the period.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.851.1" class="koboSpan">Cullinane and
Song</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1117" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1117"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.852.1" class="koboSpan">142</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.853.1"
class="koboSpan"> estimate the relative technical efficiency of a sample
of European container ports using the cross-sectional version of the SFM
under the assumption that the functional form of the production frontier
is the log-linear Cobb-Douglas function.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.853.2" class="koboSpan">The estimated
efficiency measures are broadly similar for the three assumed error
distributions that were tested. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.853.3"
class="koboSpan">From the results of the analysis, it is concluded that
the size of a port or terminal is closely correlated with its
efficiency. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.853.4"
class="koboSpan">Ports in the United Kingdom were found to have the most
efficient infrastructure usage; a finding consistent with the shortage
of container handling capacity. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.853.5"
class="koboSpan">Scandinavian and Eastern European container terminals
yielded the lowest estimates of relative efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.853.6" class="koboSpan">Geographical
location (i.e. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.853.7"
class="koboSpan">the deviation distance from the mainline
intercontinental
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_934"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.854.1"
class="koboSpan">container trades) and below average size are proposed
as possible explanations for this result.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.855.1" class="koboSpan">Rodriguez-Alvarez
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.856.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1118" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1118"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.857.1" class="koboSpan">143</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.858.1"
class="koboSpan"> test the hypothesis that, having controlled for
changing levels of technology and prices, terminal inputs within the
port of Las Palmas in Spain are not optimally allocated in the sense
that costs are not minimised. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.858.2"
class="koboSpan">To achieve this aim, the authors estimate a system of
equations based on the SFM under the assumption of a translog input
distance function to calculate both technical and allocative efficiency
of cargo handling firms within the port.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.858.3" class="koboSpan">From a
methodological perspective, this work is highly innovative in that the
model applied allows for the unbiased estimation of allocative
inefficiency of input use in two ways: an error components approach and
a parametric approach. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.858.4"
class="koboSpan">The approach also deals simultaneously with both firm
and time varying technical and allocative efficiency of port
terminals.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.859.1" class="koboSpan">Gonzalez and
Trujillo</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1119" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1119"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.860.1" class="koboSpan">144</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.861.1"
class="koboSpan"> quantify the evolution of technical efficiency in port
infrastructure service provision in the major Spanish container ports
and analyses the extent to which port reforms that took place in the
1990s had an impact on the efficiency of the Spanish container ports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.861.2" class="koboSpan">They apply a
SFM based on a translog distance function with multiple outputs.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.861.3" class="koboSpan">The results
from the analysis reveal that Spanish port reforms resulted in
significant improvements in technological change, but that technical
efficiency changed little on average over the period of analysis.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.861.4" class="koboSpan">However, as a
result of these reforms, the results also showed a significant movement
of efficiency within ports over time.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.862.1" class="koboSpan">The relationship
between the size of a port, its level of efficiency and growth in
transhipment is investigated by Sohn and
Jung.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1120" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1120"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.863.1" class="koboSpan">145</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.864.1"
class="koboSpan"> This work tests the hypothesis that the higher the
share of transhipment traffic within a port’s traffic make-up, then the
higher will be the throughput level of the port, as long as the size
effect guarantees better “relative” container handling efficiency as
compared to direct competitors. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.864.2"
class="koboSpan">The SFM is applied to analyze overall changes in the
efficiency of major Asian container ports and to produce relative
efficiency indices for the sample ports.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.864.3" class="koboSpan">Panel data
analysis is then employed to investigate the relationship between
efficiency indices and container transhipment volumes.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.864.4" class="koboSpan">The results
suggest that larger Asian ports have higher levels of relative
efficiency in container handling and larger market shares in container
transhipment. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.864.5"
class="koboSpan">It is deduced that this size effect begins to become a
factor in this, once annual container throughput reaches 5 million
TEUs.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.865.1" class="koboSpan">In a very novel
application within the maritime field,
Odeck</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1121" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1121"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.866.1" class="koboSpan">146</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.867.1"
class="koboSpan"> uses data on 82 Norwegian ferries over the period
2003–2005 to estimate technical efficiency using the SFM and input
productivity using subsequently derived Malmquist indices.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.867.2" class="koboSpan">His results
point to great potential for efficiency improvements (in the range
19–20%) in the Norwegian ferry sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.867.3" class="koboSpan">It is also
found that while Norwegian ferries have a general tendency to improve
their technical efficiency over time, because of their age, there is
simultaneously a general failure to adopt new technologies.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.867.4" class="koboSpan">Since ferries
in Norway are considered as part of the nation’s road network, they are
subsidised by the government because they operate at a loss.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.867.5" class="koboSpan">It is
therefore important for government agencies to assess and understand the
potential for efficiency and productivity improvements.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.867.6" class="koboSpan">The results of
this analysis imply that any change in the subsidy system alone will not
be sufficient to ensure efficiency improvements and that incentives for
investments in new ferries are required.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.868.1" class="koboSpan">Yan
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.869.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1122" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1122"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.870.1" class="koboSpan">147</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.871.1"
class="koboSpan"> build an empirical SFM to assess production
efficiencies of container terminal operators from the world’s major
container ports in the years between 1997
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_935"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.872.1"
class="koboSpan">and 2004. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.872.2"
class="koboSpan">The empirical model measures efficiencies, efficiency
changes and time-persistence of efficiencies after controlling for
individual heterogeneity in technology and technical change.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.872.3" class="koboSpan">The results
point to a mean efficiency level in the range of 70–90%, with a marginal
improvement in the mean over the period of analysis.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.872.4" class="koboSpan">The number of
terminal operators working at maximum efficiency has increased, however,
since 1997. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.872.5"
class="koboSpan">Testing the robustness of the model, the authors find
that results can alter dramatically if individual heterogeneity and
technical change are not properly controlled for.</span>

## <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.873.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.873.2" class="koboSpan">Concluding Remarks</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.874.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter has
defined the fundamental nature of port productivity and efficiency and,
in so doing, has reinforced the difference between them.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.874.2" class="koboSpan">It has also
illustrated how practical and policy-relevant research into the
measurement of port and/or terminal productivity and efficiency has
developed over time. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.874.3"
class="koboSpan">In so doing, it is clear that the progression of
applications to the port sector has mirrored, and corresponded closely
with, the theoretical and empirical evolution of techniques for
productivity and efficiency assessment.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.875.1" class="koboSpan">In particular, over
the past five years or so, there has been a mushrooming of applications
to ports and terminals that utilise either DEA or stochastic frontier
models. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.875.2" class="koboSpan">So
much so, in fact, that this surfeit of port efficiency studies has
prompted two major reviews of the literature – that of Panayides
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.876.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1123" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1123"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.877.1" class="koboSpan">148</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.878.1"
class="koboSpan"> in relation to DEA specifically, and that of Gonzalez
and
Trujillo</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1124" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1124"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.879.1" class="koboSpan">149</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.880.1"
class="koboSpan"> who focus primarily on the methodological
characteristics of port efficiency research.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.880.2" class="koboSpan">However, it
should be emphasised that since both DEA and SFM approaches have their
own unique pros and cons, there can be no clear-cut “best” method for
deriving efficiency estimates for the sector.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.880.3" class="koboSpan">This is
evidenced in empirical works, such as those by Cullinane
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.881.1"
class="koboSpan">et
al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1125" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1125"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.882.1" class="koboSpan">150</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.883.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1126" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1126"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.884.1" class="koboSpan">151</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.885.1"
class="koboSpan"> which compare the outcomes from applying different
methods.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.886.1" class="koboSpan">There exists great
scope for the continued expansion and further development of port
efficiency studies:</span>

- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.887.1" class="koboSpan">Port efficiency
  studies have thus far been overwhelmingly concerned with the container
  sector. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.887.2" class="koboSpan">This
  is not without justification; not only does it provide the largest
  proportion of worldwide port revenue, it is also (arguably) the most
  straightforward sector to analyze (in terms of standard cargo forms,
  access to data etc). </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.887.3"
  class="koboSpan">However, ports often encompass the handling of other
  forms of cargo and other activities.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.887.4" class="koboSpan">Even though
  certain of the extant efficiency estimation methodologies do have the
  capability of catering for multiple outputs, it is not a feature that
  has very often been utilised in empirical work.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.887.5" class="koboSpan">As such,
  scope exists for adopting a more holistic approach to port efficiency
  estimation that really does account for multiple outputs.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.887.6" class="koboSpan">Such a
  development would sit well with the contemporary perspective of ports
  as the </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.888.1"
  class="koboSpan">foci</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.889.1"
  class="koboSpan"> for logistics
  activities</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1127" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1127"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.890.1" class="koboSpan">152</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.891.1"
  class="koboSpan">,
  </span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1128" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1128"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.892.1" class="koboSpan">153</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.893.1"
  class="koboSpan"> and with the theoretical framework for assessing
  port performance from a logistics and supply chain management
  perspective proposed by Bichou and
  Gray.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1129" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1129"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.894.1" class="koboSpan">154</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.895.1"
  class="koboSpan"> In this respect,
  Zhu</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1130" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1130"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.896.1" class="koboSpan">155</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.897.1"
  class="koboSpan"> presents a DEA-based supply chain model to measure
  both the overall efficiency of a supply chain and its individual
  components or members.</span>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_936"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.898.1"
  class="koboSpan">Even without diversifying into the efficiency
  analysis of port activities other than container handling, there
  remains scope for differentiating the outputs in relation merely to
  container throughput. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.898.2"
  class="koboSpan">Cochrane</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1131" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1131"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.899.1" class="koboSpan">156</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.900.1"
  class="koboSpan"> has demonstrated that exogenous market differences
  can have a significant effect on the throughput of terminals managed
  and operated at similar levels of efficiency and that, therefore,
  aggregate analyses of container terminal efficiency should
  disaggregate the output measure into separate components.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.900.2" class="koboSpan">The most
  obvious example where such disaggregation may be advantageous is
  between transhipment and gateway traffic.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.900.3" class="koboSpan">Such an
  approach has the distinct disadvantage, however, of requiring larger
  sample sizes and more comprehensive data sets, particularly if varying
  returns to scale are to be assessed.</span>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.901.1" class="koboSpan">The selection of
  input and output variables has been the subject of significant
  theoretical discussion and a number of potential approaches have been
  suggested, many of which have yet to be applied within the port
  context. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.901.2"
  class="koboSpan">Examples include: determining the most appropriate
  set of input variables based on the actual influence they may
  hypothetically exert over container handling efficiency; how to take
  account of
  context-dependent,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1132" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1132"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.902.1" class="koboSpan">157</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.903.1"
  class="koboSpan"> environmental,
  qualitative</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1133" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1133"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.904.1" class="koboSpan">158</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.905.1"
  class="koboSpan">,
  </span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1134" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1134"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.906.1" class="koboSpan">159</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.907.1"
  class="koboSpan"> and/or
  non-discretionary</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1135" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1135"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.908.1" class="koboSpan">160</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.909.1"
  class="koboSpan"> variables and; how to reduce the number of variables
  under consideration etc.</span>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.910.1" class="koboSpan">There are a number
  of issues in relation to the estimated weights that are attached to
  variables within efficiency analysis.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.910.2" class="koboSpan">Most of this
  research effort has been aimed at incorporating weight restrictions
  into the estimations, but some is more innovative.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.910.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
  cross-efficiency
  estimation</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1136" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1136"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.911.1" class="koboSpan">161</span></a><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.912.1"
  class="koboSpan">,
  </span><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1137" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1137"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.913.1" class="koboSpan">162</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.914.1"
  class="koboSpan"> aims at accounting for optimal peer multipliers to
  supplement the self-evaluation that is a fundamental characteristic of
  mainstream DEA. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.914.2"
  class="koboSpan">This approach has already found its way into the port
  efficiency literature in a recent application by Wu
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.915.1"
  class="koboSpan">et</span></span>
  <span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.916.1"
  class="koboSpan">al</span></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.917.1"
  class="koboSpan">.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1138" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1138"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.918.1" class="koboSpan">163</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.919.1"
  class="koboSpan"> where it is used to account for regional disparities
  in the nature of port locations and/or environments.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.919.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
  cross-efficiency approach has recently been extended by Liang
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.920.1"
  class="koboSpan">et
  al.</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1139" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1139"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.921.1" class="koboSpan">164</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.922.1"
  class="koboSpan"> to encompass a game-theoretic perspective where
  individual DMUs are viewed as players in a competitive game of
  efficiency maximisation. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.922.2"
  class="koboSpan">Such an approach would seem to fit well with the
  container port context, particularly in relation to shared hinterlands
  and transhipment traffic.</span>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.923.1" class="koboSpan">Having derived a
  set of efficiency scores for DMUs within a sample, researchers have
  been motivated to explain these scores in terms of a set of
  hypothesised causal factors. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.923.2"
  class="koboSpan">Early efforts at doing so within the port sector
  involved the application of the tobit regression
  model.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1140" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1140"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.924.1" class="koboSpan">165</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.925.1"
  class="koboSpan"> The application of bootstrapping techniques has been
  advocated by Simar and
  Wilson</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1141" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1141"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.926.1" class="koboSpan">166</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.927.1"
  class="koboSpan"> as a more analytically rigorous approach to this
  problem.</span>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.928.1" class="koboSpan">Despite a few
  applications to the container port sector that specifically address
  the issue of how to deal with time series
  data,</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1142" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1142"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.929.1" class="koboSpan">167</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.930.1"
  class="koboSpan"> there remains significant potential for the
  application of the DEA
  Windows</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1143" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1143"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.931.1" class="koboSpan">168</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.932.1"
  class="koboSpan"> and other alternative approaches.</span>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.933.1" class="koboSpan">Specifically in
  relation to DEA, an emergent family of models that can be applied
  within the port sector to cater for multiple outputs includes
  multistage/serial models (encompassing the previously referred to
  supply chain model), parallel models (where resources are shared as
  would be the case for the gateway/transhipment split of container
  throughput) or hierarchical/nested
  models.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1144" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1144"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.934.1" class="koboSpan">169</span></a></sup>
- <span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.935.1" class="koboSpan">Specifically in
  relation to SFM applications, there is always the potential to select
  alternative and more flexible functional forms as the specification of
  the
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_page_937"></span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.936.1"
  class="koboSpan">empirical model to be applied.
  </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.936.2" class="koboSpan">Gonzalez and
  Trujillo</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1145" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1145"><span
  id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.937.1" class="koboSpan">170</span></a></sup><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.938.1"
  class="koboSpan"> point to the potential of the translog distance
  function for port applications.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.939.1" class="koboSpan">Irrespective of how
exactly port efficiency research develops into the future, what is very
clear is the continued critical need for efficiency estimation and
partial productivity comparison.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.939.2" class="koboSpan">The continuous
monitoring of comparative measures of performance (in all relevant
forms) is pivotal to the successful management of port and terminal
operations. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.939.3"
class="koboSpan">The pressure for this comes from the relentless trend
towards ever-greater competition, both in the inter-port and intra-port
contexts. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.939.4"
class="koboSpan">Despite a tendency towards increasing concentration in
the worldwide container handling sector, competition regulation and the
trend towards the privatisation of state-owned assets will ensure that
this characteristic of the contemporary port industry is unlikely to be
curtailed in the short- to medium-term.</span>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.940.1" class="koboSpan">Where comprehensive
information on port productivity and efficiency is available, there are
also significant advantages accruing to the formulation of macroeconomic
policies. </span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.940.2" class="koboSpan">At
this point in time, the most relevant use to which such information is
put is deciding on national port planning issues, including the likely
effectiveness of port devolution
policies.</span><sup><a href="#Ch031.xhtml_fn1146" id="Ch031.xhtml_bck_fn1146"><span
id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.941.1" class="koboSpan">171</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.942.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, it is
important to bear in mind that port productivity and efficiency cannot
be assessed and judged in isolation.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.942.2" class="koboSpan">While such
measures do play a major role in the evaluation of service quality, it
is also the case that quality comes at a price.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.942.3" class="koboSpan">As such, port
charges need to be evaluated within the context of the quality of
service that is being offered by a port.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.942.4" class="koboSpan">Balancing the
price/efficiency trade-off has become a major consideration of both port
managers in their supply-side decisions and of shipping lines in their
procurement of container handling services.
</span><span id="Ch031.xhtml_kobo.942.5" class="koboSpan">Indeed, it is
this trade off that lies at the heart of the recent trend towards
incentive-based contracts for container handling services in
ports.</span>
