<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_947"></span>[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 32</span>\
<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">Organisational Change and Effectiveness in Seaports from a Systems Viewpoint</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0706)
=================================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Cimen</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Karatas</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Cetin</span></span><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_fn1147" id="Ch032.xhtml_bck_fn1147"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">and
</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">A.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.9.1"
class="koboSpan">Güldem</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan">Cerit</span></span><sup><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_fn1148" id="Ch032.xhtml_bck_fn1148"><span
id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.11.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a></sup>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.12.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">Ports are not only the
intersection points between land and sea transport systems, but they are
regarded as more complex, logistics and multimodal transport centres and
value added organisations. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.13.2"
class="koboSpan">Seaports are the main links in the supply chain systems
that add value to the port users and final customers.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.13.3" class="koboSpan">Ports play an
important role in the management and co-ordination of materials and
information flows, as the transport is an integral part of the entire
supply chain (Carbone and Martino, 2003).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">Ports play the
significant role in this system by providing effective functioning of
the whole system and creating value to the players of the supply chain.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.14.2" class="koboSpan">The instigation
of new logistics patterns of maritime and intermodal transportation
means that modern ports can now compete for far-reaching cargoes with
far-distant counterparts (Bichou and Gray, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.14.3" class="koboSpan">Therefore,
overall organisational effectiveness should be achieved in seaports for
maintaining the competitive positions in the port industry.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">While the seaports
have uncertainty and complexity in their environments their
effectiveness can be achieved by the flexibility of the ports against
the changing conditions, intensive communication between the parties in
the supply chain, quality and efficiency of the operations and in brief
the integrity of the whole system.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">However, these
measures of effectiveness are not the only ones.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.15.3" class="koboSpan">From the
earlier stages of organisational theory on effectiveness to present,
there is still an ambiguity about the definition and measurement
criteria of effectiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">In the port system,
there is a direct link between the change and effectiveness concepts.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">A port cannot
be effective without adapting to the changes in its environment.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">As a sub-system
of the supply chain, the seaports are affected from the changes in the
logistics and supply chain, transport industry and in a broader concept
the trade
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_948"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.17.1"
class="koboSpan">and manufacturing industry.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">The
fluctuations in these markets have direct and indirect effects on port
organisation and managements.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">Seaports are open
systems interacting with their turbulent environments and affecting
world trade with their maritime transport and technological
developments. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.18.2"
class="koboSpan">They are like living organisms being exposed to change
every day. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.18.3" class="koboSpan">As
Darwin claimed in “Origin of the Species”; “it is not the strongest
species that will survive, nor the most intelligent, but the one most
responsive to change”, the ability of responsiveness and flexibility to
the changing market and environmental conditions is a must for the
survival of seaport organisations.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.18.4" class="koboSpan">However,
survival is not enough in today’s competitive transport market.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.18.5" class="koboSpan">The important
point here is how to manage change to achieve organisational
effectiveness and sustain competitive advantage.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">When we look at the
organisation theories of change and effectiveness, the direct link can
easily be seen. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.19.2"
class="koboSpan">Main objective of organisations conducting change is to
achieve effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.19.3"
class="koboSpan">These two terms can be analysed from the systems
viewpoint which perfectly fits with the nature of the seaport
systems.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">In this study first of
all, the systems approach to management is widely explained containing
the theories developed and methods conducted.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">The meaning of
effectiveness and its differences between the terms efficiency and
performance are stated. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.20.3"
class="koboSpan">Then the meaning of and approaches to organisational
effectiveness are explained. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.20.4"
class="koboSpan">The main approaches to and measures of organisational
effectiveness are stated by a broad review of the management studies in
this field. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.20.5" class="koboSpan">The
systems approach, which emphasises both the subsystems (internal) in the
organisation and the interaction of the organisation with its
environment (external) is clarified and found applicable to determine
the main measures of effectiveness in seaports.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">Then, the
organisational change concept; the types, theories about change, and the
methods of change are defined. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.21.2"
class="koboSpan">The relationship between the organisational change and
effectiveness concepts are stated.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.21.3" class="koboSpan">The port
organisations as value-added systems, their relations and integrations
with the supply chain and the turbulence in their environments are
explained. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.21.4" class="koboSpan">The
importance of adaptability to the changing conditions is
clarified.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">As effectiveness
cannot be achieved without adapting to the changes in the environment, a
model concerning ports “as complex adaptive systems” has been developed
including the effects of changes in logistics and transport systems,
supply chain system and global production and trade system to the port
system.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, with
combining the change and effectiveness concepts in port management “an
organisational change and effectiveness model for ports” is developed.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">The four basic
steps in the model are respectively: external drivers for change as
determinants; port system model as the organisation system; methods of
change as the intervention strategy used in the change process; and
finally, the major port effectiveness measures.</span>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">Systems Theory in Management</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">All organisations
function:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">within the value
    patterns of cultural environment in which they are embedded;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">within the
    political structure or pattern of legal norms and statues that
    define their formal legitimacy and limit their activities;</span>
3.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_949"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
    class="koboSpan">within the economic environment of competitive
    markets and competitive sources of input such as labor force and
    materials;</span>
4.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.29.1" class="koboSpan">within the
    informational and technological environment;</span>
5.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">within the natural
    and physical environment of geography, natural resources and
    climate.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">In other words,
organisations exist and adapt to five environments – the cultural, the
political, the economic, the technological and the ecological (Katz and
Kahn, 1978). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.31.2"
class="koboSpan">Emery and Trist (1965) described the four general
dimensions of environment as stability/turbulence, uniformity/diversity,
clustered/random, scarcity/munificence.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.31.3" class="koboSpan">Systems Theory
paradigm is being used extensively in the investigation of relationships
between subsystems within organisations and in studying the
environmental interfaces (Kast and Rosenzweig, 1972).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">From a systems theory
perspective, an organisation is a social system which, in its
interaction with its environment, activates at least four systemic
processes:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">inputs of various
    types of resources;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">transformations of
    resources with the aid of social and/or technical mechanism;</span>
3.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">outputs which are
    transmitted to other systems; and</span>
4.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">feedback effects
    whether negative or positive (Evan, 1976).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">The term “systems
approach” is applied to</span>

1.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">the formulation of
    systems and subsystems;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">the relating of
    changes in any part of the system to total performance; and</span>
3.  <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">the use of a
    developing body of knowledge related to the functioning and
    measurement of various types of systems (Fox, 1974).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.41.1" class="koboSpan">According to Optner
(1968) a “system” is defined as some ongoing process of a set of
elements, each of which are functionally and operationally united in the
achievement of an objective. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.41.2"
class="koboSpan">Cleland and King (1975) defines a “system” as an
organised or complex whole, an assemblage or combination of things and
parts forming a complex and a unitary whole.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.41.3" class="koboSpan">According to
the systems theory, a “system” is an organised, unitary whole composed
of two or more independent parts, components or subsystems and
delineated by identifiable boundaries from its environmental
supra-system. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.41.4"
class="koboSpan">According to Kast and Rosenzweig (1979) an
organisation’s subsystem – an interdependent component with some
relationship in an organisation – is composed of goals and values,
technical, psychosocial, structural and managerial subsystems.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.41.5" class="koboSpan">The social
structure of the organisation is previously defined by Etzioni (1960)
as: “the organisations are the systems of coordinated activities of more
than one actor.”</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">The five basic
considerations about the definition of the systems are (Churchman,
1979):</span>

- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.43.1" class="koboSpan">the total system
  objectives and the performance measures of the whole system;</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">the system's
  environment;</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">the resources of the
  system;</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.46.1" class="koboSpan">the components of
  the system, their activities, goals and measures of performance;
  and</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.47.1" class="koboSpan">the management of
  the system.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_950"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">The system concept includes two different definitions
according to their interactions with the environment: the closed and
open systems. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.48.2"
class="koboSpan">The closed system has rigid, impenetrable boundaries,
whereas the open system has permeable boundaries between itself and a
broader supra-system. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.48.3"
class="koboSpan">The boundaries set the domain of the organisation’s
activities (Berrien, 1976).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">The derivation of the
general systems theory relevant to formal human work organisations has
the name open systems theory. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.49.2"
class="koboSpan">The central propositions of this theory are concerned
with system boundaries, differentiation and integration of the
subsystems that are parts of the focal system,
input–transformation–output processes, boundary transactions and system
maintenance processes (Seashore, 1983).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">Open systems theory
emphasises the close relationship between a structure and its supporting
environment. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.50.2"
class="koboSpan">The other major emphasis is on throughput: the
processing of production inputs to yield some outcome that is then used
by an outside group or system. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.50.3"
class="koboSpan">According to Katz and Kahn (1978) open systems have 10
main characteristics including importation of energy, the throughput,
the output, systems as cycles of events, negative entropy, information
input, negative feedback and the coding process, the steady state and
dynamic homeostasis, differentiation, integration and coordination and
equifinality. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.50.4"
class="koboSpan">As organisations are open systems, Jackson (2000)
proposes that the primary subsystems of an organisation are mainly: the
goal, technical, human and managerial subsystems.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">The interaction of the
organisation with its internal resources to the changing environment
refers that they are open systems which places a great deal of emphasis
on flexibility and external focus, and would stress flexibility and
readiness (as means) and growth, resource acquisition, and external
support (as ends) (Quinn and Rohrbaugh, 1983).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.51.2" class="koboSpan">Open systems
emphasises the distinctiveness of the organisation as an identifiable
social structure or entity, and it emphasises the interdependency
processes that relate the organisation to its environment (Yuchtman and
Seashore, 1967). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.51.3"
class="koboSpan">The “organisations-as-open systems” approach looks at
all the subsystems, their interrelationships, and the interactions
between the subsystems (and the organisation as a whole) and the
environment (Jackson, 2000).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">In the socio-technical
systems approach, the goals and values, as well as the technical,
structural, psycho-social and managerial subsystems are shown as the
integral parts of the overall organisation (Kast and Rosenzweig, 1972).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.52.2" class="koboSpan">Social
organisations are flagrantly open systems in that the input of energies
and the conversion of output into further energetic input consist of
transactions between the organisation and its environment.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.52.3" class="koboSpan">Every surviving
system must provide some output acceptable usually to a collateral or
supra-system (Berrien, 1976). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.52.4"
class="koboSpan">Two basic criteria for identifying social systems and
determining their functions are (1) tracing the pattern of energy
exchange or activity of people as it results in some output, and (2)
ascertaining how the output is translated into energy that reactivates
the pattern (Katz and Kahn, 1978).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">In a social system,
the organisational boundaries are not easily definable and are
determined primarily by the function and activities of the organisation
(Berrien, 1976). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.53.2"
class="koboSpan">A reason for the indefiniteness of the boundaries in a
social organisation is the rapidly changing conditions in its
environment and the continuous interaction between the environment and
organisation. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.53.3"
class="koboSpan">Organisations do not exist in a static world.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.53.4" class="koboSpan">The surrounding
environment is in a constant state of flux, and a rigid technical
system, even if protected by excellent support structures.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.53.5" class="koboSpan">Organisations
develop adaptive structures whose function is to gather advance
information about trends in the environment, carry
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_951"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan">out research on internal productive processes, and plan
for future developments (Katz and Kahn, 1978).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.54.2" class="koboSpan">These complex
adaptive systems are open systems in intimate interchange with an
environment characterised by a great deal of shifting variety and its
constraints (Buckley, 1968). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.54.3"
class="koboSpan">Morel and Ramanujam (1999) state that organisations are
routinely viewed as dynamic systems of adaptation and evolution, which
contain multiple parts that interact with one another and the
environment.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">Another approach to
measure the complex dynamics systems has been conceived and developed in
the late 1950s in Massachusetts Institute of Technology by Jay Forrester
and his team. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.55.2"
class="koboSpan">The advent of System Dynamics (SD) is generally
considered to be the publication of Forrester’s pioneering book,
“Industrial Dynamics” in 1961 (Santos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.,</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.57.1"
class="koboSpan"> 2002). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.57.2"
class="koboSpan">Sterman (2000) used system dynamics modelling for the
analysis of policy and strategy, with a focus on business and public
policy applications. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.57.3"
class="koboSpan">System Dynamics has its origins in control engineering
and management; the approach uses a perspective based on information
feedback and delays to understand the dynamic behaviour of complex
physical, biological, and social systems (Angerhofer and Angelides,
2000). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.57.4" class="koboSpan">It
focuses on the structure and behavior of systems composed of interacting
feedback loops. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.57.5"
class="koboSpan">The objective of this approach is to capture the
dynamic interaction of different system variables and to analyse their
impact on policy decisions over a long-term horizon (Sachan
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.,</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan"> 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">System Dynamics is
widely used in business and management fields and related to our study
is a method that portrays the process of organisational change.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.60.2" class="koboSpan">Many studies
have been published about the application of system dynamics methodology
to the process of change in organisations (Frechette and Spital, 1991;
Samuel and Jacobsen, 1997). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.60.3"
class="koboSpan">SD is also used in supply chain management (Angerhofer
and Angelides, 2000; Kumar and Yamaoka, 2007) and in maritime transport
concepts (Engelen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.61.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan">., 2006).</span>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.63.2" class="koboSpan">Organisational Effectiveness and Systems Approach</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">Organisations are
constructed to be the most effective and efficient social units.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.2" class="koboSpan">The actual
effectiveness of a specific organisation is determined by the degree to
which it realises its goals. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.3"
class="koboSpan">There is some further ambiguity between the terms
efficiency and effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.4"
class="koboSpan">Efficiency defines how well the processes of the
organisation perform (Jumara, 2005) and the efficiency of an
organisation is measured by the amount of resources used to produce a
unit of output (Etzioni, 1964). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.5"
class="koboSpan">Efficiency is an economic index of the ratio of
measured inputs to measured outputs (Cummings, 1983).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.6" class="koboSpan">Effectiveness
is a term related with the outputs and goals of an organisation; however
efficiency describes the optimal use of current resources (Hirsch,
1975). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.7" class="koboSpan">Katz and
Kahn (1966) linked effectiveness explicitly to an external referent, and
efficiency to internal activities more easily controlled by the
organisation and state that efficiency is a criterion of the internal
life of the organisation, especially the economic and technical aspects
(Katz and Kahn, 1978). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.8"
class="koboSpan">However, the effectiveness is the aggregation of
opportunities provided to the members of the unit (in the case of the
organisational level, it is the opportunities provided by organisational
membership to the individual). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.9"
class="koboSpan">For an organisation to be effective, a subsystem must
be concerned with showing that performance meets the standards that
external and internal constituencies (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.64.10" class="koboSpan">resource
suppliers and customers) monitor (Cummings, 1983).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">In some studies of
organisational effectiveness (Gibson
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1973; Webb, 1974), efficiency is used as a criterion
for the measurement of effectiveness of an organisation.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_952"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.68.1"
class="koboSpan">Cunningham (1977) defines efficiency from the
organisational and systems perspective and states that efficiency is an
indication of the organisation’s ability to use its resources in
responding to the most important subsystem needs.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.68.2" class="koboSpan">However,
Sproles (2001) states that effectiveness is the domain of the end user
who wishes to know if the system is able to meet a need (Sayareh,
2007).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">Barnard (1938)
reasoned that organisations are “co-operative systems.”
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">His definition
of organisational effectiveness is couched in terms of the process of
cooperation. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.69.3"
class="koboSpan">Organisational effectiveness is the accomplishment of
the recognised objectives of the cooperative action.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.69.4" class="koboSpan">However,
organisational efficiency is defined as follows: the efficiency of a
cooperative system is the resultant of the efficiencies of the
individuals furnishing the constituent efforts, that is, as viewed them
(Barnard, 1938). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.69.5"
class="koboSpan">Effectiveness and efficiency are achieved through the
interactions among people as managed by both the formal (studied by
traditional theory) and informal (studied by human relations theory)
structures of the enterprise (Jackson, 2000).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">In the management
discipline many researchers studied the relationship between the
organisational effectiveness and the environment of the organisations
(Etzioni, 1960; Yuchtman and Seashore, 1967; Osborne and Hunt, 1974;
Hirsch, 1975). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.70.2"
class="koboSpan">According to Yuchtman and Seashore (1967) most existing
definitions of organisational effectiveness have been formulated,
implicitly or explicitly, in terms of a relation between the
organisation and its environment.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.70.3" class="koboSpan">A study of
effectiveness has to include an analysis of the environmental conditions
and of the organisation’s orientation to them (Etzioni, 1960).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.70.4" class="koboSpan">Hirsch (1975);
Lawrence and Lorsch (1967) and Negandhi and Reimann (1973) are all
concerned with the interrelationships between organisational structure
and environment, which prompts them to measure organisational
effectiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">Katz and Kahn (1966)
proposed defining organisational effectiveness as “the maximisation of
return to the organisation by all means.”
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">Georgopoulos
and Tannenbaum (1957) concur with this statement and explicate that the
definition of organisational effectiveness must encompass two aspects:
the objectives of organisations (the ends); and the means through which
they sustain themselves and attain their objectives.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">Robbins (1990)
also states that organisational effectiveness must consider both means
(process) and ends (outcomes).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">Organisational
effectiveness may be typified as being mutable (composed of different
criteria at different life stages), comprehensive (including a
multiplicity of dimensions), divergent (relating to different
constituencies), transpositive (altering relevant criteria when
different levels of analysis are used), and complex (having
non-parsimonious relationships among dimensions) (Cameron, 1978).</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Approaches to organisational effectiveness</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">The widely studied and
practiced organisational effectiveness models include the goal
attainment approach (Etzioni, 1960), the systems resource approach
(Yuchtman and Seashore, 1967), the internal process approach (Bennis,
1966; Steers, 1977; Pfeffer, 1977; Nadler and Tushman, 1980), the human
relations approach (Argyris, 1964; Ahmed, 1999), the multiple/strategic
constituencies approach (Pfeffer and Salancik, 1978; Connolly
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.,</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.76.1"
class="koboSpan"> 1980; Jobson and Schneck, 1982; Keeley, 1984; Tsui,
1987; Zammuto, 1984; Ehreth, 1988), the competing values approach (Quinn
and Rohrbaugh, 1983; Shilbury and Moore, 2006) and the ineffectiveness
approach (Henri, 2004).</span>

- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_953"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
  class="koboSpan">The
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
  class="koboSpan">goal attainment
  approach</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.79.1"
  class="koboSpan"> views effectiveness in terms of internal
  organisational objectives and performance (Molnar and Rogers, 1976)
  and organisations as purposeful and coordinated agents (Georgopoulos
  and Tannenbaum, 1971). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.79.2"
  class="koboSpan">Keeley (1978) proposes two variants of the goal
  models: official and operative goal models.</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">The
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
  class="koboSpan">internal process
  approach</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
  class="koboSpan"> focuses on the internal functions of the
  organisation and stability and efficiency remain two of the criteria
  of such effectiveness (Heffron, 1989).</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">The
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
  class="koboSpan">human relations
  approach</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
  class="koboSpan"> focuses on the people and upholds the satisfaction
  of employees' needs as the most important end (Argyris, 1964).</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">The
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
  class="koboSpan">strategic constituencies
  approach</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
  class="koboSpan"> proposes that an effective organisation is one that
  satisfies the demands of those constituencies in its environment from
  whom it requires support for its continued existence (Robbins,
  1990).</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">The
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
  class="koboSpan">competing values
  approach</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
  class="koboSpan"> constitutes a synthesis and an extension of the
  other organisational effectiveness models (Pfeffer and Salancik, 1978;
  Quinn and Rohrbaugh, 1983).</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">The
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
  class="koboSpan">ineffectiveness
  approach's</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
  class="koboSpan"> basic assumption is that it is easier, more
  accurate, more consensual and more beneficial to identify problems and
  faults (ineffectiveness) than criteria of competencies (effectiveness)
  (Henri, 2004).</span>
- <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">The
  </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.96.1"
  class="koboSpan">system
  approach</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
  class="koboSpan"> views organisations as open systems, which work in
  close relationship with the environment (Yuchtman and Seashore, 1967;
  Molnar and Rogers, 1976; Ahmed, 1999).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">A review of
organisational effectiveness literature between the years 1949–2009
shows that there are many different approaches to the effectiveness
concept in organisations.
</span><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_fig0460" id="Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0460"><span
id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.100.1"
class="koboSpan"> encompasses 58 publications, composed of books, book
chapters and important articles in leading academic journals in business
and management fields. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">Many of the authors wrote in the early stages of the
organisational effectiveness concept and are the pioneer theorists in
this field (Etzioni, 1960; Yuchtman and Seashore, 1967; Pfeffer and
Salancik, 1978). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.100.3"
class="koboSpan">The approaches to the concept changed and developed
through the years. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.100.4"
class="koboSpan">Some alternative models which were generally the
enhanced versions of the main approaches mentioned above were developed
and applied to different types of organisations in recent years (Ridley
and Mendoza, 1993; Herman and Renz, 1998; Ahmed, 1999; Henri,
2004).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">The systems approach
to organisational effectiveness is a widely studied model as can be seen
from </span>[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch032.xhtml_fig0460)<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.103.2"
class="koboSpan">Seventeen (29%) of the authors used the principles of
this approach in explaining and measuring effectiveness.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.103.3" class="koboSpan">The
goal-attainment and multiple constituency approaches are both discussed
in 10 publications, where competing values approach is embraced by five
authors and internal process approach just by four.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Systems approach to organisational effectiveness</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">The concept of
organisational effectiveness is ordinarily used to refer to goal
attainment (Georgopoulos and Tannenbaum, 1957).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.105.2" class="koboSpan">But, according
to Etzioni (1960) the system model is theoretically more powerful and
avoids certain value judgments than the goal model of organisational
effectiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">According to Yuchtman
and Seashore (1967) an adequate conceptualisation of organisational
effectiveness cannot be formulated unless factors of
organisation–environment</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_954"></span>[](#Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0460)

[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.107.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00483.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0460)

</div>

<div id="Ch032.xhtml_fig0461" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_955"></span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.108.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00484.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_956"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.109.1"
class="koboSpan">relationships are incorporated into its framework.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.109.2" class="koboSpan">However, both
the goal and functional approaches cannot give an adequate consideration
to the conceptual problem of the relations between the organisation and
its environment.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">Gaertner and
Ramnarayan (1983) categorise organisational effectiveness approaches
according to two dimensions: focus of definition (process/structure or
outcome) and intended use concepts (general or organisation-specific).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">The systems
approach is located in the intersection of process/structure and general
concept. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.110.3" class="koboSpan">This
refers that systems approach is not only related with the outputs and
goals of the organisation, but also the process/structure and means
(resources) used in this process are the main concerns in this approach.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.110.4" class="koboSpan">This approach
takes the environment and the whole system into consideration, not just
the organisation itself.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">In the systems
approach of the organisational effectiveness the starting point is not
the goal itself, but a working model of a social unit which is capable
of achieving a goal (Etzioni, 1960) which focuses on behavior conceived
as continuous processes of exchange and competition over scarce and
valued resources rather than focusing on goals only (Yuchtman and
Seashore, 1967). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.111.2"
class="koboSpan">Unlike a goal, it is a model of a multi-functional
unit.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">Georgopoulos and
Tannenbaum (1957) define organisational effectiveness from the systems
perspective as: “Organisational effectiveness is the extent to which an
organisation as a social system, given certain resources and means,
fulfills its objectives without incapacitating its means and resources
and without placing undue strain upon its members.”</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">The systems resource
model defines the organisation as a network of interrelated subsystems.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.113.2" class="koboSpan">The outputs of
one subsystem may become the inputs of another subsystem; the
organisational system functions effectively to the degree that its
subsystems are in harmony and are coordinated to work together
(Cunningham, 1977). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.113.3"
class="koboSpan">Universally required resources are mainly, personnel,
physical facility, technology and money as a liquid resource (Yuchtman
and Seashore, 1967).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">In the systems
resource model, the interdependence between the organisation and its
environment takes the form of input–output transactions.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.114.2" class="koboSpan">Three phases
of the systems model are: the importation of resources, their use
(including allocation and processing) and their exportation in some
output form that aids further input (Yuchtman and Seashore,
1967).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">According to
Cunningham (1977) an organisation, in order to survive, must satisfy
some basic needs: (1) acquiring resources; (2) interpreting the real
properties of the external environment; (3) production of outputs; (4)
maintenance of internal activities; (5) coordination of relationships
between subsystems; (6) responding to feedback; (7) evaluating the
effect of its decision; and (8) accomplishing goals.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">However there are
some limitations of the systems approach to organisational
effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.116.2"
class="koboSpan">The three most important shortcomings of this approach
relate to the fact that measurements for all of a systems needs are
difficult to develop (Cunningham, 1977), the debate that whether means
really matter (Robbins, 1990) and are more expensive for the researcher
(Etzioni, 1960).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">The systems approach
looks at factors such as relations with the environment to assure
continued receipt of inputs and favourable acceptance of outputs,
flexibility of response to environmental changes, the efficiency with
which the organisation transforms inputs to outputs, the clarity of
internal communications, the level of conflict among groups and the
degree of employee job satisfaction (Robbins, 1990).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">General systems
theory with its biological orientation would appear to have an
evolutionary view of system effectiveness.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.118.2" class="koboSpan">The living
system which best adapts to its
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_957"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.119.1"
class="koboSpan">environment prospers and survives.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.119.2" class="koboSpan">But, this is
not the case in social organisations.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.119.3" class="koboSpan">According to
Kast and Rosenzweig (1972) the questions of organisational effectiveness
must be concerned with at least three levels of analysis: the level of
the environment, the level of the social organisation as a system, and
the level of the subsystems (human participants) within the organisation
Emery and Trist (1959) stress that the primary task of managing an
enterprise as a whole is to relate the total organisational system to
its environment, and not just internal regulation.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.119.4" class="koboSpan">The basic
organisations-as-systems prescription remains: if an organisation is not
functioning effectively, examine its subsystems to see that they are
meeting its needs to ensure it is well adjusted to its environment
(Jackson, 2000).</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">3.3 Measures of organisational effectiveness</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">Evaluating the
overall effectiveness of an organisation is one of the most difficult
problems in organisation theory.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.121.2" class="koboSpan">There is still
a lack of consensus as to measure what constitutes a useful and valid
set of effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.121.3"
class="koboSpan">According to Steers (1975) this is because
effectiveness is an abstract idea rather than a concrete phenomenon.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.121.4" class="koboSpan">Quinn and
Rohrbaugh (1983) concur with this idea and state that effectiveness is
not a concept but a construct. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.121.5"
class="koboSpan">Henri (2004) agrees and states that there is a serious
ambiguity and confusion surrounding the construct of
effectiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">Steers (1975) states
that researchers face many problems in the measurement of organisational
effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.122.2"
class="koboSpan">The ambiguity of the construct “effectiveness”, the
transitory nature of the many effectiveness criteria, the conflicts that
can emerge between these criteria, the difficulty to measure them and
the inapplicability of the same criteria to different situations and
organisations are the main problems in the measurement of organisational
effectiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">The criteria of an
effective organisation can be classified into two categories: (a)
tangible or inorganic criteria; and (b) intangible or organic criteria.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.123.2" class="koboSpan">The tangible
or inorganic criteria refer to the quantitative measures of an
organisation (Sahni, 2000) such as performances in finance, sales,
manufacturing, purchasing, and profits.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">It is possible to
identify two general types of models: (1)
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.125.1"
class="koboSpan">normative,</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan"> or prescriptive, models, which attempt to specify
those things an organisation must do to become effective; and (2)
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.127.1"
class="koboSpan">descriptive</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan"> models, which attempt to summarise the characteristics
found in successful organisations (Steers, 1975).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">A useful framework
for assessing organisational effectiveness suggests four main
categories: (1) achieving goals; (2) increasing resourcefulness; (3)
satisfying clients; and (4) improving internal processes (Cameron, 1980;
Bramley, 1986; Redshaw, 2000).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">Yuchtman and Seashore
(1967) specify the steps needed for the comparative assessment of
organisational effectiveness: (1) to provide a taxonomy of resources;
(2) to identify the different types of resources that are mutually
relevant for the organisations under study; and (3) to determine the
relative positions of the compared organisations on the basis of
information concerning the amount and kinds of resources that are
available for the organisation and its efficiency in using these
resources to get further resources.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">Georgopoulos and
Tannenbaum (1957) observed that the common practice of measuring
effectiveness by univariate measures, such as productivity or profit,
was inconsistent with the broad meaning attached to effectiveness in the
organisational literature (Keeley, 1978).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.131.2" class="koboSpan">Many
researchers have studied several possible criteria available in the
measurement of organisational effectiveness.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.131.3" class="koboSpan">A major
advantage of the multivariate</span>

<div id="Ch032.xhtml_fig0462" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_958"></span>[](#Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0462)

[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.132.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00485.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0462)

</div>

<div id="Ch032.xhtml_fig0463" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_959"></span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00486.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<div id="Ch032.xhtml_fig0464" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_960"></span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00487.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">models is their
comprehensive nature, subsuming several variables under one unifying
framework. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.135.2"
class="koboSpan">Unfortunately, this advantage can simultaneously
represent a major weakness where such criteria are in conflict with one
another (Steers, 1975).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">As an extension of
</span>[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch032.xhtml_fig0460)<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_fig0462" id="Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0462"><span
id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.1"
class="koboSpan"> lists the studies and the major organisational
effectiveness criteria used in these studies.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.2" class="koboSpan">The studies
cover the articles, book chapters and books in this field.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.3" class="koboSpan">By the review
of many theoretical and empirical publications on organisational
effectiveness concept, just 38 of them prominently state the
effectiveness measures that should be used or are used in their studies.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.4" class="koboSpan">A total of 107
effectiveness measures are derived from these studies.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.5" class="koboSpan">The
frequencies of occurrence of these criteria are measured.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.6" class="koboSpan">As a criterion
of effectiveness, adaptability has the maximum frequency with 11;
however flexibility which has a very close meaning with adaptability has
a frequency of 6. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.7"
class="koboSpan">Many studies use these measures interchangeably.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.8" class="koboSpan">Therefore, the
adaptability and flexibility concepts can be combined and used as a
single criterion. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.140.9"
class="koboSpan">According to the results, the other important measures
of effectiveness and their frequencies are productivity (10),
profitability (8), efficiency (8), employee satisfaction (7), support
(6), growth (6), planning (6), survival (5), integration (5), resource
acquisition (4), morale (4), organisational commitment (4), cohesion
(4), satisfaction (4), communication (4) and stability (4).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">The main
effectiveness criteria are the tangible measures such as productivity,
profitability and efficiency whose measurements are easier than the
intangible measures. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.141.2"
class="koboSpan">The intangible measures are related to the human
resources of the organisation like satisfaction, morale, commitment and
cohesion. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.141.3"
class="koboSpan">These are related to the internal processes of the
organisation where the tangible measures have an external focus and are
directly related to its goals. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.141.4"
class="koboSpan">When we look at the results, it is obvious that the
criteria used in systems approach to measure the organisational
effectiveness are adaptability/flexibility, support, growth and resource
acquisition (Quinn and Rohrbaugh, 1983) have high frequencies and are
widely used in the assessment of organisational effectiveness.</span>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_961"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.142.2" class="koboSpan">A Systems Model of Organisational Effectiveness at Ports</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">In port business
literature, there have been many studies relating to port performance
and efficiency (Monie, 1987; Tongzon, 1995; De Langen, 2001; Tongzon,
2001; De and Ghosh, 2003; Paixao and Marlow, 2003b; Bichou and Gray,
2004; Barros and Athanassiou, 2004; Lam 2005; Wang and Cullinane, 2006;
Wang </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.145.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2006; De Langen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.147.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2006; Owino
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2006; Panayides and Song, 2006; Beresford and Pettit,
2007; Brooks and Pallis, 2007; Wang
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.150.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.,</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan"> 2007). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.151.2"
class="koboSpan">De Langen
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan">et al</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.153.2"
class="koboSpan">(2006) lists the name and definitions of the major port
performance indicators in their study.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.153.3" class="koboSpan">However there
are only a few approaches considering the effectiveness of seaport
organisations (Sayareh and Lewarn, 2006; Sayareh, 2007).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">The difference
between the measures of effectiveness and performance is that a measure
of effectiveness is a standard against which we judge how well we
achieved what we intended or wanted to achieve; a measure of performance
is the measure of what was achieved (Sproles, 2000).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.154.2" class="koboSpan">It can be
referred that measures of effectiveness are representative of certain
properties of the solution and they are concerned with the outcomes
(external view) of a solution (Sproles, 2002).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">As mentioned above
there are not many studies about the effectiveness concept in port
management, however some studies use port success or port
competitiveness terms that can be used in place of the term
effectiveness.
</span><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_fig0465" id="Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0465"><span
id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.156.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan"> lists some port studies that mention the measures a
port should achieve to be successful or, in other words, effective.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.157.2" class="koboSpan">Within these
studies only Sayareh and Lewarn’s, 2006 study uses the term “port
effectiveness”.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">As discussed earlier,
multiple criteria should be used for assessing the organisational
effectiveness of seaports. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.158.2"
class="koboSpan">It is because of the complexity and dynamism in the
structure (sub-systems) and environment of the port systems.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.158.3" class="koboSpan">A system model
of organisatinoal effectiveness is a model of a multi-functional unit,
considering the inputs that are needed for the process/transformation
and the outputs that may become the inputs of another following
subsystem. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.158.4"
class="koboSpan">Where the seaports are the major parts of the supply
chain system and have a complex structure containing many different
interdependent units, the systems approach to organisational
effectiveness is used as the model (Karatas and Cerit, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.158.5" class="koboSpan">This approach
has three basic elements which are inputs or resources that are needed
for a process/subsystem, the process itself and the outputs or outcomes
of these processes.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.159.1" class="koboSpan">In the systems
approach to organisational effectiveness it is recognised that no
organisation can reach overall effectiveness if one or more subsystems
are performing inadequately. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.159.2"
class="koboSpan">Therefore the subsystems in a seaport organisation
should be identified to reach and assess the whole effectiveness of the
system.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.160.1" class="koboSpan">Since the seaports
are multi-functional and multi-faceted organisations with complex
structures, they encompass many functions in their systems.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.160.2" class="koboSpan">These
functions or subsystems can also be regarded as the processes or
transformations in the ports. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.160.3"
class="koboSpan">Every function needs certain inputs where some
subsystems have common inputs used to form outputs.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.160.4" class="koboSpan">The outputs of
each function and the coherence and harmony between these functions
directly affect the effectiveness of the port system.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.161.1" class="koboSpan">The systems model of
seaport effectiveness covers 11 port sub-systems which are mainly the
port engineering facilities (port infrastructure, superstructure,
equipment repair and maintenance); port operations (cargo handling,
pilotage and towage and</span>

<div id="Ch032.xhtml_fig0465" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_962"></span>[](#Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0465)

[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.162.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00488.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0465)

</div>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">services to ships);
logistical and industrial aspects (value-added services, distribution
parks, manufacturing facilities); social issues (port labour,
interaction with the city and nation); economic and financial issues
(economic impact to the region, creation of employment, arrangement of
port tariffs, profit, finance of investments, employee expenditures);
political and legal issues (customs, immigration); environmental issues
(marine pollution); safety and security issues; marketing issues
(customer relations); human resources (relations with employees,
motivation, training); and finally, organisational and managerial issues
(organisation structure, leadership, strategic planning).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">The effectiveness
measures that are also applicable to port organisations are categorised
as outputs under the port sub-systems according to the relevancy with
each sub-system. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.164.2"
class="koboSpan">The major effectiveness measures for each port process
are listed in
</span><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_fig0466" id="Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0466"><span
id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.165.1" class="koboSpan">Table 4</span></a><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.166.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">All these facets or
different interdependent units of the port system intersect at one
point, at the port management function which reflects the overall
effectiveness of the seaport organisation.</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
