class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00489.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch032.xhtml_bck_fig0466)

</div>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.169.2" class="koboSpan">Organisational Change Concept</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.170.1" class="koboSpan">Representative
descriptions of change vary with the level of analysis (Ford and Ford,
1994). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.170.2" class="koboSpan">At the
most general level, change is a phenomenon of time.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.170.3" class="koboSpan">It is the way
people talk about the event in which something appears to become, or
turn into, something else, where the something else is seen as a result
or outcome (Weick and Quinn, 1999).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.171.1" class="koboSpan">There is no single
accepted definition of organisational change.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.171.2" class="koboSpan">This is
perhaps not surprising given the wide diversity of change experienced by
organisations and individuals. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.171.3"
class="koboSpan">Porras and Silvers (1991) define organisational change
as the “process by which organisations move their present state to some
future state to increase effectiveness” (Jumara, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.171.4" class="koboSpan">From the
perspective of organisational development, change is a set of
behavioural science-based theories, values, strategies, and techniques
aimed at the planned change of the organisational work setting for the
purpose of enhancing individual development and improving organisational
performance, through the alteration of organisational members on-the-job
behaviour (Porras and Robertson, 1992).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.171.5" class="koboSpan">Hitt
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_964"></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.172.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1998) state that organisational change is closely
connected to the technology explosion phenomenon – particularly with
respect to information and telecommunication technologies, also to the
resulting globalisation of economic activities through free trade and
movement of products and capital and, to a lesser but accelerating
extent, of human resources (Prastacos
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.175.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2002).</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Theories of change</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">In the 1950s, social
psychologist Kurt Lewin developed a theory of social change.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.177.2" class="koboSpan">According to
his theory, successful change requires unfreezing the status quo, moving
to a new state and refreezing the change to make it permanent (Robbins,
1990). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.177.3" class="koboSpan">Some
researchers have put together more complete models of understanding
change, Hinings and Greenwood’s (1988) model of change dynamics,
Pettigrew’s (1985) process/content/context model, and Burnes (2004)
change management framework are all in this category (Bamford and
Daniel, 2005). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.177.4"
class="koboSpan">Kanter
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.178.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1992) claimed that change is both “ubiquitous and
multidirectional” and thus Lewin’s model does not come close to the
level of complexity needed to address the phenomenon of organisational
change (Hatch, 1997). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.179.2"
class="koboSpan">Kanter
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.181.1"
class="koboSpan"> (1992) defined organisations as a “bundle of
activities” and claim that change itself occurs at three levels of
analysis specified by organisation theory – environment
(macroevolutionary forces for change), organisation (microevolutionary
forces for change) and individual (political forces for change).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">In symbolic–
interpretive theory, the changes are more normative in nature and the
entire system is a political and socially constructed reality rather
than the economic and technological reality of the modernist perspective
(Hatch, 1997).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.182.1" class="koboSpan">Van de Ven and Poole
(1995) identify four process theories of organisational change and
development according to the unit and mode of change:
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.183.1"
class="koboSpan">life-cycle, evolutionary,
dialectical</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan">
and</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.185.1"
class="koboSpan"> teleological
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.186.1"
class="koboSpan">(Gebhart, 2004).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.186.2" class="koboSpan">According to
their meta-theoretical scheme; the life-cycle model depicts a prescribed
change within an entity, the teleological model contains a constructive
change within an entity. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.186.3"
class="koboSpan">However, in evolutionary model and dialectical models,
change takes place in multiple entities, but modes of change differ as
being prescribed and constructive respectively.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.186.4" class="koboSpan">Van de Ven and
Poole (2005) developed a typology of four approaches to study
organisational change. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.186.5"
class="koboSpan">They looked organisational change according to
ontological and epistemological aspects including two approaches:
variance and process approaches to organisational change.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">5.2 Types of change</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">From the literature
of organisational change and development there would appear to be two
main approaches to change: planned and emergent.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.188.2" class="koboSpan">Robbins (2000)
defines planned change as “the deliberate design and implementation of a
structural innovation, a new policy or goal, or a change in operating
philosophy, climate and style”. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.188.3"
class="koboSpan">The major difference between planned and emergent
change is that, in emergent change, the emphasis is on “bottom-up”
action rather than “top-down” control as is the case in planned change.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.188.4" class="koboSpan">Dawson (1994),
as a proponent of emergent rather than planned change, claims that
change must be linked to developments in markets, work organisation,
systems of management control and the shifting nature of organisational
boundaries and relationships (Bamford and Daniel, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.188.5" class="koboSpan">For the
proponents of emergent change, it is the uncertainty of the environment
that makes planned change inappropriate and
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_965"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.189.1"
class="koboSpan">emergent change more pertinent.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.189.2" class="koboSpan">This point is
emphasised by Strickland (1998), who draws on systems theory to
emphasise the way that organisations are separate from, but connected
to, their environment (Bamford and Daniel, 2005).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">Weick and Quinn
(1999) see change as a genre of organisational analysis and point out
two types of change:
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">episodic</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.192.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.193.1"
class="koboSpan">continuous</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.194.1"
class="koboSpan">.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan">Episodic
change</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.196.1" class="koboSpan">
is used to group together organisational changes that tend to be
infrequent, discontinuous, and intentional.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.196.2" class="koboSpan">However, in
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.197.1"
class="koboSpan">continuous
change</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">,
organisations are emergent and self-organising, and change is constant,
evolving, and cumulative. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.198.2"
class="koboSpan">Robbins (2000) discusses how change can be measured by
two categories:
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.199.1"
class="koboSpan">evolutionary
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan">revolutionary
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">change.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan">Evolutionary change
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">is
gradual, incremental and specifically focused.
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan">Revolutionary
change</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">
is sudden, drastic and organisation-wide (Jumara, 2005).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">Sherman
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2006) see the notion from open-systems theory and
define evolutionary change, long-run change, as change related with the
system’s driving forces as well as the relative adaptability of the
parts of that system.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">5.3 Sources of change</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">Organisational
changes have their sources either from outside the organisation or from
within. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.210.2"
class="koboSpan">According to Connor and Lake (1994), among external
sources are
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.211.1"
class="koboSpan">social
changes</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">
concerning beliefs, values, attitudes and opinions;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">political/legal
changes</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">
including the liberalisa tion, deregulation, regulation and laws;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.215.1"
class="koboSpan">changes in economic
conditions</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">technological
developments</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan"> directly affecting the macro and micro environment of
organisations. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.218.2"
class="koboSpan">Internal sources of changes, originating primarily from
inside organisations, are mainly professional associations, new
organisational goals and excess organisational resources (Connor and
Lake, 1994). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.218.3"
class="koboSpan">However, Hannan and Freeman (1977) state that internal
limitations are capital and personnel expenditures, constraints in
information processing, costs of upsetting the political equilibrium,
history and tradition. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.218.4"
class="koboSpan">External constraints are legal barriers, fiscal
limitations, and costs of securing legitimacy and political support from
external forces. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.218.5"
class="koboSpan">Robbins (1990) states that changes in strategy, size,
technology, environment, or power can be the probable sources of
structural change.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">5.4 Objects and methods of change</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">Objects of change can
be classified into four categories.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.220.2" class="koboSpan">These are
mainly, changes in individual task behaviours; organisational processes;
strategic direction of the organisation; and organisational culture
(Connor and Lake, 1994). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.220.3"
class="koboSpan">They refer the methods of change as
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan">technological”
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">which
are mostly related to the operations and processes of an organisation,
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">structural”
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">related
to the functions, roles and relationships in the organisation,
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan">managerial”
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan">covering administrative actions, and finally
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.227.1"
class="koboSpan">people”</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan"> which is directly related to the human resources of an
organisation.</span>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.229.2" class="koboSpan">Approaches to Change and Effectiveness</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">Morel and Ramanujam
(1999) state that organisations are routinely viewed as dynamic systems
of adaptation and evolution containing multiple parts which interact
with one another and the environment.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.230.2" class="koboSpan">The
interaction of the organisation with its internal resources to the
changing environment refers that they are open systems which places a
great deal of emphasis on flexibility and external focus, and would
stress flexibility and
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_966"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan">readiness (as means) and growth, resource acquisition,
and external support (as ends) (Quinn and Rohrbaugh, 1983).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">The primary
relationship between change and effectiveness comes from the definition
of the term “effectiveness”. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.232.2"
class="koboSpan">Effectiveness means efficiency plus adaptability, where
efficiency comprises achieving existing objectives with acceptable use
of resources. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.232.3"
class="koboSpan">The effective organisation is both efficient and able
to modify its goals as circumstances change (Carnall, 2003).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.232.4" class="koboSpan">Argyris (1964)
focuses on three core activities of an effective organisation: achieving
objectives, maintaining the internal system and adapting to the external
environment.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.233.1" class="koboSpan">The systems approach,
a dynamic model of change, covers both the organisational change and
effectiveness concepts in management.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.233.2" class="koboSpan">The systems
approach to organisational effectiveness, which is a model of
multi-functional unit, the interdependence between the organisation and
its environment takes the form of input–output transactions (Yuchtman
and Seashore, 1967). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.233.3"
class="koboSpan">This approach views the organisation as a unified
system composed of interrelated units and forming part of larger
external environment (Harvey and Brown, 1996).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.234.1" class="koboSpan">Harvey and Brown
(1996) state that an organisation can be viewed as a socio-technical
open system interacting with its environment consisting of five primary
components such as;
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">structural, technical, psychosocial(cultural), goals
and values </span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan">managerial
subsystems.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan"> Any change in the environment of the organisation has
a different effect on these subsystems and total systems effectiveness
can be only achieved by the interaction of these units.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.239.1" class="koboSpan">An organisation’s
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan">technologies, processes
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">and</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">
structures</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan"> must be well suited to each other and to the
organisation’s
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.244.1"
class="koboSpan">environment</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan"> to sustain organisational effectiveness and survival
(Huber and Glick, 1993). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.245.2"
class="koboSpan">According to Carnall (2003), effective or high
performing organisations emphasise the following nine characteristics:
concern for the future, concern to develop human resources, focus on
product/service being provided, orientation to the technologies in use,
concern for quality, excellence and competence, orientation to
customers, the community and shareholders, constant adaptation of reward
systems and corporate values, focus on the basis of “making and selling”
and finally, openness to new ideas.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.245.3" class="koboSpan">Harvey and
Brown (1996) state that the changing organisation of the twenty-first
century has five main characteristics:
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan">customer orientation, quality conscious, being
responsive to innovation and change, adding value to human
resources</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan">having more autonomous
units.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">
Prastacos </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.251.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2002) argue that to address the continuously
increasing challenges and to successfully manage change, organisations
needs to be
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan">innovative
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.254.1"
class="koboSpan">flexible.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.255.1"
class="koboSpan"> According to their model regarding the objectives for
managing change in the new competitive landscape; organisations should
change their strategies from duplicated mediocrity to virtual world,
from formal rigor to ad hoc support, from sequenced steps to produce to
systemic flows for value, from people as workforce to people as
competitive force. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.255.2"
class="koboSpan">When we look at the characteristics needed to achieve
effectiveness in organisations, we’ll see every variable of a “systems
model of organisational effectiveness at seaports” in Karatas and Cerit
(2008) as the main effectiveness measures for ports.</span>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">7. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.256.2" class="koboSpan">Change and Effectiveness in Seaport Systems</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">Port organisations
experience dynamism and turbulence in their environments because of the
effects of the driving forces like globalisation, technological advances
and changes
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_967"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.258.1"
class="koboSpan">in the expectations of the players in the supply
chains. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.258.2" class="koboSpan">Ansoff
and McDonnell (1990) and Rosen (1995) assess the level of environmental
turbulence with the two measures of “changeability” and
“predictability”, both of which have two elements, where complexity and
novelty are the elements of changeability, and rapidity of change and
visibility of the future are the two elements of predictability (Ferch
and Roe, 1998). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.258.3"
class="koboSpan">When we look at turbulence in the port environment, we
can see that there has been a rapid change in the maritime and related
industries such as ship building, the secondhand market, the freight
market, trade volumes and routes–these all have an effect on ports and
their environments.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.259.1" class="koboSpan">The unexpected
changes and complexity in the market are explained by Paixao and Marlow
(2003b) as: (1) the significance of ports to the international economic
environment; (2) the increasing levels of competition that ports have
been facing for the last couple of years; (3) the impossibility of
competing on costs alone but focusing on quality of service; (4) the
globalisation phenomenon; (5) the important organisational,
technological, and commercial evolution that is taking place in the
transport sector; and (6) the introduction of fast communication
systems.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">Due to the effect of
globalisation and higher demand for products and services, shipping
companies formed alliances and mergers and acquisitions to reduce the
transport costs by sharing costs and risks.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.260.2" class="koboSpan">These resulted
in increasing vessel sizes to benefit from economies of scale and
widening the operational areas to benefit from economies of scope.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.260.3" class="koboSpan">Global port
operators, having foreseen these events, are already repositioning their
container terminals through joint ventures, port terminals concessions,
or to meet this increase in vessel size (Paixo and Marlow, 2003a).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.260.4" class="koboSpan">The changes in
the network structure by the increase of vessel sizes forced the ports
to compete globally rather than regionally.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.260.5" class="koboSpan">The rapid
increase in the port competition have pressures on ports to improve the
quality of the traditional port services, implementing differentiation
strategy by providing more specialised, value-added services and
delivering door-to-door transport solutions.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.260.6" class="koboSpan">These forces
change the role of ports from being places providing loading and
discharging operations to intermodal terminals in the supply chain
systems that add value to the port users and final customers.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.260.7" class="koboSpan">The
integration of the supply chain actors and the introduction of seamless
transport systems using state of the art technology force ports to be
more flexible to respond the parties in the supply chain and adapt to
the changing conditions in the uncertain environment of port
business.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.261.1" class="koboSpan">As ports are the main
links in the supply chain adding value to the whole system, the
structural changes in the supply chain and logistics force ports to
adapt to the changing conditions in the turbulent environment of
transport industry. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.261.2"
class="koboSpan">Most shipping lines are expanding their scope to
include terminal operations and hinterland transportation to lower the
cost burden of door-to-door transport (Notteboom and Winkelmans, 2001).
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.261.3" class="koboSpan">These changes
in the transport industry have direct effects on port structure.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.261.4" class="koboSpan">Dedicated
terminals are an example for this situation.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.262.1" class="koboSpan">Both the horizontal
and vertical integration in the transport industry result in a
concentration of power of port customers and the increase of the
bargaining power of the customers over port managements.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.262.2" class="koboSpan">These
emphasise the importance of
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.263.1"
class="koboSpan">customer
satisfaction</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.264.1"
class="koboSpan">” in the port industry.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.264.2" class="koboSpan">In the new
competitive landscape, the port authorities have such roles to
effectively manage the port organisation to sustain the competitive
position in the changing environment of the port industry.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.264.3" class="koboSpan">These are:
concentrating on value added logistics; development of information and
communication systems to
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_968"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">enhance the integration of the supply chain actors; and
port networking by strategic cooperation with other ports (Notteboom and
Winkelmans, 2001).</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.266.1" class="koboSpan">Paixao and Marlow
(2003a) suggest that a new logistics approach, agility should be adopted
by port organisations to cope with the uncertainty and the complexity in
the port environment. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.266.2"
class="koboSpan">According to Notteboom and Winkelmans (2001) in the
port industry key elements in obtaining a competitive advantage are: (1)
flexibility to adapt quickly to changing opportunities; and (2) an
integral approach to logistics issues in transport chains.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.266.3" class="koboSpan">Robinson
(2006) suggests that there is a critical need to understand that
fundamental restructuring in port landside operations is a function of
two key issues – pervasive value migration in landside operations and
progressive strategy decay as ports struggle to redefine
themselves.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">UNCTAD (1992) and
then Beresford
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.1"
class="koboSpan"> (2004) classify the seaports according to the
evolutions of different aspects in the port organisations.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.2" class="koboSpan">The changes
faced in the type of main cargo, attitude and strategy of port
development, port activities, organisation structure, production
characteristics and the decisive factors in the port systems were
analysed on a timeline. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.3"
class="koboSpan">These practices vary significantly from generation to
generation. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.4"
class="koboSpan">While the first generation ports are labour intensive,
the second-generation ports seem to be more capital intensive and the
decisive factor in third-generation ports are technology and know how.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.5" class="koboSpan">Logistics
chain and value added aspects of port organisations become important in
third-generation ports. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.6"
class="koboSpan">However, according to Paixao and Marlow (2003b) the two
main characteristics of fourth generation ports are leanness and agility
which means more specialisation in services and flexibility to respond
to the changes in the port environment, respectively.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.7" class="koboSpan">Port
generations stated by UNCTAD (1992) prove the validity of “evolutionary
change” concept in the port industry.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.8" class="koboSpan">We define the
ports as open systems, having inputs, processes and outputs and
interacting with their internal resources to the changing environment.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.9" class="koboSpan">Open-system
theory of management, define the evolutionary change, long-run change,
as change related with the system’s driving forces as well as the
relative adaptability of the parts of that system.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.269.10" class="koboSpan">This means
that the adaptation of port organisational structure to the external
driving forces sourcing from the changing conditions in the environment
provide the effective functioning of the port systems, with its input,
sub-systems and outputs.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.270.1" class="koboSpan">As effectiveness
cannot be achieved without adapting to the changes in the environment, a
model concerning ports “as complex adaptive systems” has been developed.
</span><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_cap_lbl0230"
id="Ch032.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0230"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.271.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan"> depicts the port system with indefinite organisational
boundaries and the supra-systems of ports which are mainly logistics and
transport systems, supply chain system and global production and trade
system. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.272.2" class="koboSpan">The
interaction between the supra-systems and the effects on ports are shown
in the figure. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.272.3"
class="koboSpan">The changes and developments in each system directly or
indirectly affect the port organisation.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.272.4" class="koboSpan">Many numbers
of variables influence the complexity of the port environment and the
rapidity of change assesses how fast the environmental changes in
relation to the ports’ response time are.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.273.1" class="koboSpan">The major
shareholders in the port system and their places in the port system are
also given because they are the main parties affecting the performance
of the port organisation. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.273.2"
class="koboSpan">The shifts in their role have important effects on the
port system. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.273.3"
class="koboSpan">The structural changes – the vertical and horizontal
integration – of the shipping lines and other parties in the supply
chain increase the bargaining power of port customers and force ports to
be more competitive. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.273.4"
class="koboSpan">Evolving structure of liner shipping networks,
increasingly complex network structures have pressures on ports to
compete globally rather than locally.</span>

data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.274.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00490.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Ports as complex adaptive systems: an effectiveness model" /></span>

id="Ch032.xhtml_cap_lbl0230"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.275.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.276.1"
class="koboSpan"> Ports as complex adaptive systems: an effectiveness
model</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.277.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.278.1"
class="koboSpan"> Karatas, Cetin and Cerit (2009a)</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_970"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.279.1"
class="koboSpan">In the inner side of the port system, the internal
networks of port processes are shown.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.279.2" class="koboSpan">The inputs
that are needed approximately for all the subsystems are mainly port
labor/personnel, physical facility (port infrastructure,
superstructure), technology and money/capital.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.279.3" class="koboSpan">All port
processes that transform the inputs into outputs that are stated in
</span>[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.280.1" class="koboSpan">Table
4</span>](#Ch032.xhtml_fig0466)<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.281.1"
class="koboSpan"> are interrelated with the one another where the port
management is in the center of all the port sub-systems and coordinates
the port organisation. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.281.2"
class="koboSpan">Every port process has its own effectiveness measures
related with its function and domain.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.281.3" class="koboSpan">The effective
functioning and the integration of all sub-systems is a must for
achieving the organisational effectiveness in a port system.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.281.4" class="koboSpan">Therefore
every port sub-system should attain the objectives/effectiveness
measures that are stated in the figure.</span>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.282.1" class="koboSpan">8. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.282.2" class="koboSpan">An Organisational Change and Effectiveness Model for Seaports</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.283.1" class="koboSpan">It is a necessity for
ports as adaptive systems in new competitive landscape to adapt their
strategies, structures and processes to the changes in the turbulent
environment to achieve effectiveness and sustain competitive position in
the industry. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.283.2"
class="koboSpan">“Organisational change and effectiveness model for
seaports” is a model developed by Karatas Cetin and Cerit (2009b)
displaying the effectiveness of seaports by systems approach.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.283.3" class="koboSpan">Four stages
constituting the determinants of change, model of the organisation that
needs to change because of the pressures of external factors, the
methods of change to be used and finally the results or objectives of
the change process are depicted in
</span><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_cap_lbl0231"
id="Ch032.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0231"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.284.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.285.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.286.1" class="koboSpan">8.1 Determinants — External drivers of change</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.287.1" class="koboSpan">Paixao and Marlow
(2003a) state that ports having been surrounded by environmental
turbulence face many external drivers forcing them to change.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.287.2" class="koboSpan">In the model,
the external drivers for change are classified into two groups; macro-
and micro-external environmental factors.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.287.3" class="koboSpan">The
macro-external environmental factors covering
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.288.1"
class="koboSpan">international
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.289.1"
class="koboSpan">(globalisation effect, increase of the international
demand on goods and services, market liberalisation and privatisation);
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.290.1"
class="koboSpan">economical
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.291.1"
class="koboSpan">(economic welfare of the countries, the tendency to
minimise the costs),
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.292.1"
class="koboSpan">technological</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.293.1"
class="koboSpan"> (faster product innovation due to increased
speed-to-market demand, technological change and diffusion of
technological knowledge, advanced ICT systems);
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.294.1"
class="koboSpan">social-cultural</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.295.1"
class="koboSpan"> (changing societal concern) and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.296.1"
class="koboSpan">political-legal
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.297.1" class="koboSpan">(new
regulatory policies and/or government regulations, national and
international policies to promote sustainable transport, increased
safety and security levels) factors are the main remote determinants
affecting the trade markets, transport and logistics industries and the
port business industry in the scope of derived demand.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.298.1" class="koboSpan">However,
micro-external environmental factors including customers, competitors,
suppliers, distribution, substitute modes and community which are also
regarded as industry environment have more direct effects on ports.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.298.2" class="koboSpan">De Langen and
van der Lugt (2007) summarise the relevant changes in the port industry
in the recent years under three categories; trade and manufacturing,
transport and logistics. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.298.3"
class="koboSpan">The structural changes – the vertical and horizontal
integration – of the shipping lines and other parties in the supply
chain increase the bargaining power of port customers and force ports to
be more competitive. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.298.4"
class="koboSpan">Evolving structure of liner shipping networks,
increasingly complex network structures have pressures on ports to
compete globally rather than</span>

<div id="Ch032.xhtml_fig0468" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.299.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00491.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: An organisational change and effectiveness model for seaports" /></span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_971"></span><a href="#Ch032.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0231"
id="Ch032.xhtml_cap_lbl0231"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.300.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.301.1"
class="koboSpan"> An organisational change and effectiveness model for
seaports</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.302.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.303.1"
class="koboSpan"> Karatas, Cetin and Cerit (2009b)</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_972"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.304.1"
class="koboSpan">locally. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.304.2"
class="koboSpan">The changing structure of transport and logistics, the
increasing importance of logistics networks and outsourcing activities,
the value added logistics concept can be regarded as a distribution
factor forcing ports to adapt to the changing conditions.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.304.3" class="koboSpan">The forces
from local stakeholders to improve the safety and security standards of
the ports (Gilman, 2003) and from port community to change the structure
towards flexibility and transparency (Slack and Fremont, 2005) are the
other micro-external environmental drivers of change.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.304.4" class="koboSpan">These many
numbers of variables influence the complexity of the port environment
and the rapidity of change assesses how fast the environmental changes
in relation to the ports’ response time are.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.305.1" class="koboSpan">8.2 Model of the organisation — Port system model</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.306.1" class="koboSpan">The sub-systems or
processes in the port organisation are taken from the previous model
developed by Karatas and Cerit (2008) and named as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.307.1"
class="koboSpan">Port System Model
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.308.1"
class="koboSpan">covering engineering, operations, logistics/industrial,
social/environmental, economic/financial, political/legal, information
and communication technology, human resources, marketing, management and
organisation. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.308.2"
class="koboSpan">All these sub-systems are interrelated with each other
and in total form the port system.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.309.1" class="koboSpan">8.3 Intervention strategies — Methods of change</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.310.1" class="koboSpan">Connor and Lake
(1994) refer the methods of change as
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.311.1"
class="koboSpan">technological”
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.312.1" class="koboSpan">which
are mostly related with the operations and processes of an organisation,
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.313.1"
class="koboSpan">structural”
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.314.1" class="koboSpan">related
with the functions, roles and relationships in the organisation,
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.315.1"
class="koboSpan">managerial”
</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.316.1"
class="koboSpan">covering the administrative actions and finally
“</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.317.1"
class="koboSpan">people”</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.318.1"
class="koboSpan"> which is directly related with the human resources of
an organisation. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.318.2"
class="koboSpan">In the rapidly changing environment of port business,
in some cases the methods of change should be used together however in
other cases a small change in the technology or people factors may be
sufficient to initiate change. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.318.3"
class="koboSpan">The dimension and importance of the change is
determinative. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.318.4"
class="koboSpan">However, there should be a perfect fit between the
changes implemented in strategy, structure, people and processes.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.318.5" class="koboSpan">The
relationship between the external drivers of change and the methods of
change is also shown in </span>[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.319.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch032.xhtml_cap_lbl0231)<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.320.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.321.1"
class="koboSpan">Strategy/Managerial:</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.322.1"
class="koboSpan"> Strategy refers to the central action that
decision-makers in the firm implement to: (a) help the firm to achieve a
better fit with its environment; (b) match the firm resource base with
market opportunities; and (c) achieve a competitive advantage by
creating value for its customers (Sherman
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.323.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.324.1"
class="koboSpan">, 2006). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.324.2"
class="koboSpan">According to Baltazar and Brooks (2007) two dimensions
of strategy are particularly relevant to ports concerned with economic
performance: product and market scope and competitive emphasis.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.324.3" class="koboSpan">Baltazar and
Brooks (2007) state that in the port devolution process,
effectiveness-oriented configurations are characterised by high levels
of environmental uncertainty, a broad product–market scope or a
differentiation approach in delivering products and services.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.324.4" class="koboSpan">The important
measure for port performance is the fit between strategy, structure and
environment. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.324.5"
class="koboSpan">Customer orientation and satisfaction as one of the
most important effectiveness measures for ports should be situated in
the centre of the strategies of a port management.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.325.1"
class="koboSpan">Structure:</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.326.1"
class="koboSpan"> An organisation’s structure is a pattern of
relationships that govern the performance of organisational roles.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.326.2" class="koboSpan">The structural
method of change typically involves creating new roles, new work units
or new reporting relationships (Connor and
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_973"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.327.1"
class="koboSpan">Lake, 1994). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.327.2"
class="koboSpan">Effecting a change by structural means can involve any
of the following dimensions: complexity, formalisation, centralisation
and coordination. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.327.3"
class="koboSpan">An organisation's ability to respond, adapt, innovate
to change depends on the extent on to which it has built coordinating,
decentralised decision making, less formalised and highly differentiated
(complex) mechanisms into its system.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.328.1" class="koboSpan">The environmental
diversity, actual differentiation and actual integration levels factors
defined by Lorsch (1970), are high in the port industry.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.328.2" class="koboSpan">This means,
the integrative devices in the port organisation design should cover
teams, roles, departments, hierarchy, plan and procedures to achieve
effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.328.3"
class="koboSpan">The structural change through effectiveness in the port
organisations can be achieved by coordination and integration between
the horizontally and vertically differentiated systems, decentralised
decision making and low formalisation that covers general guidelines not
rules to guide people in the performance of their work.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.328.4" class="koboSpan">Lean,
flexible, non-bureaucratic and result oriented port organisations can
achieve effectiveness by providing collaboration with virtual
networks.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.329.1"
class="koboSpan">Process/Technology:</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.330.1"
class="koboSpan"> Processes must be seen as something that involve the
procedures, the tasks, the schedules, the mechanisms, the activities and
the routines by which port services are delivered to the customers
(Payne, 1993). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.330.2"
class="koboSpan">In other words, a process is an activity or a group of
activities that together are inputs to be processed and whose output is
the development of a value-added product which enriches the customer
(Berry </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.331.1"
class="koboSpan">et al.</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.332.1"
class="koboSpan">, 1999). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.332.2"
class="koboSpan">In the port processes that are explained before, first
need to adapt to the changes is innovation and integration of all the
processes. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.332.3" class="koboSpan">The
agility concept, the rapid response to the market is directly related
with the use of information and communication technologies in the port
operations and also through the supply chain.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.332.4" class="koboSpan">The usage of
state of the art technology accelerates the port operations, decrease
costs, provides time and space utilisation and integrates the port with
the final customer through networks.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.332.5" class="koboSpan">The efficiency
and productivity of port operations are the results of the use of proper
physical and information technologies at ports.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.332.6" class="koboSpan">Knowledge
management, the creation, storage, transfer and usage of corporate
knowledge, together with the use of information communication
technologies is an important part of the value streaming processes in
the port industry.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.333.1"
class="koboSpan">Human
Capital:</span></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.334.1"
class="koboSpan"> Port labour is one of the most important inputs for
the port processes. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.334.2"
class="koboSpan">Quality of port labour is a direct determinant for a
port’s success. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.334.3"
class="koboSpan">Port training and education programs, managerial
development methods, motivation, safe working conditions, personnel
policies and practices designed to help employees excel and develop
quality work life can be various methods of change in the human capital
for the port business. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.334.4"
class="koboSpan">The labour policy of a port should be “people as a
competitive force” rather than workforce.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.335.1" class="koboSpan">8.4 Objectives, results — effectiveness measures</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.336.1" class="koboSpan">Effectiveness
measures relate to how well the firm or agency uses its strategies,
structures, and task environment to meet its mission and stated goals
(Brooks and Pallis, 2008). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.336.2"
class="koboSpan">The effectiveness measures for ports are derived from
the results of the delphi study that can be found in Karatas Cetin and
Cerit (2009b). </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.336.3"
class="koboSpan">Eight of the 24 effectiveness measures are chosen from
the experts as the most important ones.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.336.4" class="koboSpan">The relation
between the port sub-systems and the effectiveness measures is shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.337.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
2</span>](#Ch032.xhtml_cap_lbl0231)<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.338.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

### <span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_974"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.339.1" class="koboSpan">8.5 Value</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.340.1" class="koboSpan">The final outcome of
the model is the value generated to the port customers, the community,
the stakeholders, the industry and the region/country.</span>

## <span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.341.1" class="koboSpan">9. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.341.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusion</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.342.1" class="koboSpan">Seaports, as the
interface points between land and sea and central links in the supply
chain can also be considered as value added organisations.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.342.2" class="koboSpan">They are the
most important subsystems of the whole supply chain traditionally acting
as an interface between land and sea transport systems, but also as
logistics and trade centers providing distribution facilities,
multimodal transport opportunities and industrial activities.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.342.3" class="koboSpan">Seaports are
now not just the places providing cargo handling operations but much
more than this.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.343.1" class="koboSpan">Seaports need to
identify the changes in the market before they occur, by capturing the
latest data about the market, intensity and direction of the cargo
demands and by tracking regulations, technological advancements and
needs of the port users. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.343.2"
class="koboSpan">They need to adapt to the unexpected changes in the
environment to maintain their competitiveness in the market.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.343.3" class="koboSpan">However,
efficiency and performance measurements alone cannot provide a
competitive position to the port organisations.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.343.4" class="koboSpan">There is a
broader term that should be assessed to generate value-added to the port
users and meet the rapidly changing expectations in the market “the
overall organisational effectiveness”.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.344.1" class="koboSpan">This study focuses on
two topical concepts in port business industry: change and
effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.344.2"
class="koboSpan">Change as its nature is a frequently studied subject in
port literature. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.344.3"
class="koboSpan">However, the relation between these two concepts has
not been searched in great detail before.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.344.4" class="koboSpan">The study
makes contributions on the literature on measures of effectiveness that
should be used to assess the ports’ organisational effectiveness.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.344.5" class="koboSpan">These set of
measures for the ports are primarily: productivity, efficiency, service
quality, innovation, adaptability/flexibility, information and
communication management, profitability, organisation’s worth, human
resource quality and customer satisfaction.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.344.6" class="koboSpan">These measures
can be regarded as the objectives that should be achieved or in a more
optimistic manner the outcomes of the port organisation.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.344.7" class="koboSpan">However, it is
sufficient to determine the basic effectiveness criteria but the way to
achieve this in a change process should also be explained.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.1" class="koboSpan">The organisational
change and effectiveness model shows the four stages in the change
process. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.2" class="koboSpan">First
of all, the determinants of change are needed to be determined because
the source of the change and the method of the change to be used are
directly related. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.3"
class="koboSpan">The external drivers of change for ports are stated in
the model. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.4"
class="koboSpan">Then the organisation should be analysed since every
organisation is unique in its nature.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.5" class="koboSpan">Here, the port
organisation is defined as an open system including different sub
systems as port operations, marketing, logistics, etc.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.6" class="koboSpan">where each of
the sub-system is interrelated with the other, forming the port system
model holistically. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.7"
class="koboSpan">The port system needs different method of change to
achieve effectiveness. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.8"
class="koboSpan">These methods are classified under four headings:
strategy, structure, process and human capital.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.9" class="koboSpan">Efficient
usage of these methods provides the effectiveness in the port
organisation. </span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.345.10"
class="koboSpan">The value generated as an outcome of the model reach
the customers, community, the region and the country.</span>

<span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.346.1" class="koboSpan">This model is an
initial stage of the studies that will continue in change and
effectiveness concepts in port business.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.346.2" class="koboSpan">Further
research should be conducted by broader ana lysis of the organisational
change concept in the ports of the real world.
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.346.3" class="koboSpan">The
</span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_page_975"></span><span id="Ch032.xhtml_kobo.347.1"
class="koboSpan">strategies used in managing change in different port
organisations should be analysed and compared, empirically.</span>
