<span id="Ch033.xhtml_page_985"></span>[<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 33</span>\
<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">The Economics of Motorways of the Sea: Re-Defining Maritime Transport Infrastructure</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0729)
=========================================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Alfred</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">J.</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">Baird</span></span><a href="#Ch033.xhtml_fn1149" id="Ch033.xhtml_bck_fn1149"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a>

## <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">When referring to
maritime transport infrastructure, very often the focus is on ports
(Haralambides, 2002; Verhoeven, 2009).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.8.2" class="koboSpan">Defining (or
rather re-defining) maritime transport infrastructure is an important
outcome of this chapter, in particular setting out how this relates
specifically to the ship or seaway.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">Ships and ports are
considered also in the context of modal shift; that is, transferring
freight from road to sea, or the so-called “Motorways of the Sea” (MoS).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.9.2" class="koboSpan">Reviewing MoS
policy and developments in the context of comparable road and rail
infrastructure allows for new insights about the reality of maritime
transport infrastructure.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">Whilst there is
universal acknowledgement that
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan">roadways</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan"> and
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">railways</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.14.1"
class="koboSpan"> are indeed transport infrastructure platforms, there
appears to be rather more uncertainty about what constitutes the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan">seaway </span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan">platform. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.16.2"
class="koboSpan">To argue that maritime transport infrastructure is
simply the port (i.e. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.16.3"
class="koboSpan">the node) seems inadequate when talking at the same
time about roadway and railway infrastructure platforms along a given
corridor which may be several hundred kilometres or more in
length.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter briefly
considers the general policy approach to developing MoS in Europe and
the influence this has had in helping to re-appraise our understanding
of maritime transport relative to land transport modes.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">This is
followed with an analysis of modal shift MoS examples, emphasising some
of the challenges faced, which tend to relate to market realities
determined by policy approaches and influenced by traditional
definitions of transport infrastructure.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.17.3" class="koboSpan">Thereafter the
discussion centres on developing, explaining and justifying the need to
re-define our understanding of the term
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.18.1"
class="koboSpan">maritime transport
infrastructure</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.19.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

## <span id="Ch033.xhtml_page_986"></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">Motorways of the Sea Policy</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">In Europe, governments
at EU and Member State levels are now working to facilitate MoS services
leading to large-scale modal shift.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.21.2" class="koboSpan">According to
the European Commission, the sea represents the only real solution to
tackle road freight traffic growth in Europe, hence the inclusion of MoS
projects in the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) (Commission of
the European Communities, 2004). </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.21.3"
class="koboSpan">Whilst such motives are indeed honourable, the
appreciation of what exactly constitutes seaway infrastructure still
requires careful consideration, more especially in view of economic
distortions resulting from ongoing public financing of land transport
infrastructure generally.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">The TEN-T of MoS is
intended to recreate the road and rail network on the water, by
concentrating flows of freight in viable, regular searoutes.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.22.2" class="koboSpan">TEN-T MoS
project sare expected to improve port facilities and infrastructure, as
well as electronic logistics management systems, safety and security and
administrative and customs procedures, as well as access routes for
year-round navigability. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.22.3"
class="koboSpan">The policy and funding emphasis, therefore, is largely
aimed at ports and transport access to ports.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">The EU Van Miert
High-Level Group, during its deliberations on extending Europe’s TEN-T
network, nevertheless decided that MoS were “Floating Infrastructure”
(Commission of the European Communities, 2004).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.23.2" class="koboSpan">This
corresponded with ideas put forward by GIE (2007), albeit the latter
went further by highlighting the need for public financing of the “boat
infrastructure” in the specific context of integrating waterborne
transport into the Trans-European Networks.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.23.3" class="koboSpan">Clearly there
is a recognition here that the ‘boat’ needs to be taken into
account.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Such views were
supported through the findings of the SUTRANET project funded by the EU
Interreg IIIB North Sea Programme (SUTRANET, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.24.2" class="koboSpan">Both GIE and
SUTRANET findings consider the role of the port as being that of
(merely) a transport node, and certainly not a seaway or MoS.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.24.3" class="koboSpan">In this regard,
defining a seaport as maritime transport infrastructure seems to be
totally insufficient.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">EU funding is aimed at
counteracting ongoing transport market distortions favouring land
transport modes, and Member States themselves are also requested to do
more in this area. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.25.2"
class="koboSpan">The various EU TEN-T MoS initiatives are intended to
facilitate new developments through current limited financial
intervention. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.25.3"
class="koboSpan">Some success is also occurring with the EU Marco Polo
Programme which aims to support MoS service start-ups, albeit over a
limited period of three–four years.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.25.4" class="koboSpan">However, the
bulk of investment in MoS projects is expected to be provided by private
transport operators.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">At the same time,
public funding of roadway and railway infrastructure is set to continue
at high levels for the foreseeable future, which will lead to ongoing
challenges for MoS start-ups. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.26.2"
class="koboSpan">The key question here is – why should there be limited
short-term support for maritime transport when large-scale public sector
funding for roadway and railway infrastructure continues?</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.27.1" class="koboSpan">EU Member States have
been requested to co-finance MoS initiatives themselves as well and
under the new EU TEN-T MoS policy this is now allowable.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.27.2" class="koboSpan">In addition to
international services between states, MoS services could also comprise
domestic/coastal routes within states.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.27.3" class="koboSpan">Where road
transport does not pay its full cost of using road infrastructure (as in
the UK) then the need for MoS support is found to be greater (UK Marine
Motorways Study, 2002).</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">In Italy, the EcoBonus
MoS incentive scheme is perhaps the most advanced modal shift initiative
so far within the EU. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.28.2"
class="koboSpan">This provides for state support of €240 million over
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_page_987"></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan">three years towards MoS services, with some 30 MoS
routes qualifying, and allowing for a 20–30% fare rebate to truckers to
help equalise costs with road transport.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.30.1" class="koboSpan">Another MoS scheme for
routes between France and Spain has been implemented rather differently.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">In this
instance a tender process was developed for an Atlantic Spain–France MoS
service, based on an agreement between both countries, and supervised by
the EC. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.30.3" class="koboSpan">In this
MoS scheme the ports have been selected by bidders themselves, not by
the state. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.30.4"
class="koboSpan">Subsidy is considered as start-up aid to support
operations (over three or five years) with the criteria of evaluation
for bids being:</span>

- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">30% for traffic
  shifted from road (min 100,000 lorries);</span>
- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">30% for the quality
  of the proposition;</span>
- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">35% the economic and
  financial performance; and</span>
- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">5%: for other
  factors.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">Clearly, the
development of MoS initiatives in Europe is still at an early stage.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.35.2" class="koboSpan">The EC and
Member States are also at a formative stage of really understanding what
MoS is, and how it fits into the wider transport policy context.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.35.3" class="koboSpan">Implementation
of different MoS funding schemes by individual Member States results in
non-standardisation and could lead to confusion amongst service
providers. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.35.4"
class="koboSpan">Conversely, those States not implementing any MoS
scheme at all may be unlikely to gain the modal shift benefits from the
start-up of MoS services.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">This implies that
there needs to be a better understanding of what is meant by the term
“maritime transport infrastructure”, or MoS, as well as a shift towards
some standardisation on attractive and easy to use/implement MoS funding
methods and incentives which take full account of subsidies applying to
alternative land transport modes.</span>

## <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.37.2" class="koboSpan">Modal Shift and Motorways of the Sea (Mos)</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">New MoS modal shift
transport services have developed in a number of countries over recent
years. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.38.2" class="koboSpan">Italy
has been at the forefront of European MoS developments over the last 15
years or so. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.38.3"
class="koboSpan">MoS in the modern sense arguably began when state-owned
Finmare introduced the innovative Viamare service in 1991.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.38.4" class="koboSpan">That service
employed five three-deck Ro-Ro ships each capable of carrying well over
100 trailers plus 50 drivers, to provide a daily link between two
dedicated out-of-town terminals at Voltri (Genoa) and Termini Imerese
(near Palermo). </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.38.5"
class="koboSpan">While the Viamare “Autostrade del Mare” experiment was
not without its difficulties (Baird, 1997), the initiative demonstrated
for the first time in Europe what could be achieved in terms of
road-to-sea modal shift on a large scale.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">Since then ship design
and efficiency has continued to improve and today the right ships are
available now to do the job of modal shift very effectively.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.39.2" class="koboSpan">Existing Ro-Ro
and Ro-Pax (i.e. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.39.3"
class="koboSpan">freight plus limited passenger capacity) vessels offer
fast speed (22 knots or more), coupled with high payload, and high
reliability (</span><a href="#Ch033.xhtml_cap_lbl0232"
id="Ch033.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0232"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.41.2"
class="koboSpan">Although ships of 2,000 lane metres (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.41.3" class="koboSpan">around 150
trailer capacity) have become something of a standard size for many MoS
services, far larger ships are now in service offering 4,000 lane
metres, and new ships of over 5,000 lane metres will be delivered by
2010.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Such vast ship sizes
means that seaway economies of scale are un-matched by other transport
modes. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.42.2" class="koboSpan">On the
roadway, a single trailer is the norm, while on rail, even where rail
systems can accept trailers on railcars (many railway systems are unable
to carry</span>

<div id="Ch033.xhtml_fig0469" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00492.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: ‘Standard’ type 2,300 lane metre/400 passenger 24-knot Ro-Pax" /></span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_page_988"></span><a href="#Ch033.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0232"
id="Ch033.xhtml_cap_lbl0232"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.44.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan"> ‘Standard’ type 2,300 lane metre/400 passenger 24-knot
Ro-Pax</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan"> courtesy of Norfolk Line</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.48.1" class="koboSpan">trailers due to
gauge/tunnel/width constraints), the maximum number of units carried
tends to be under 50.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.49.1" class="koboSpan">Other strengths of the
Ro-Ro/Ro-Pax MoS option include (SUTRANET, 2007):</span>

- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">the ability of
  vessels to carry temperature-controlled units and unaccompanied or
  accompanied vehicles, with drivers using the ferry trip as a statutory
  rest break;</span>
- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">reduced wear and
  tear of trucks and trailers, less vehicle maintenance costs, and lower
  insurance; and</span>
- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">lower fuel costs and
  avoidance of road tolls and weekend bans on truck movement by
  road.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">In this regard the
Ro-Ro or Ro-Pax ferry/MoS functions in a complementary fashion to the
long-distance trucking sector. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.53.2"
class="koboSpan">In cost terms, whilst size/scale benefits give the MoS
a basic unit cost-per-km advantage over road, other factors such as
ongoing state subsidy for roadways and railways, plus Ro-Ro terminal
handling charges (the latter not applicable in the case of road
transport), and local road haulage tend to limit the overall benefit of
MoS in terms of total costs. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.53.3"
class="koboSpan">Previous research suggests that the sea leg of MoS
services may actually represent less than half the total door-door cost
of a trailer movement by MoS (Baird, 2008).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.53.4" class="koboSpan">The other half
or more comprises terminal handling costs plus local road haulage costs
at the beginning and end of a trip.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.54.1" class="koboSpan">Nevertheless, a number
of MoS routes have been successfully developed over the last 10 years or
so, each achieving success in freight modal shift from road to sea
transport (see
</span><a href="#Ch033.xhtml_fig0470" id="Ch033.xhtml_bck_fig0470"><span
id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.56.2"
class="koboSpan">The examples presented in
</span>[<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">Table
1</span>](#Ch033.xhtml_fig0470)<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"> help illustrate the complex reality and challenges
surrounding development of new MoS services (or seaways).</span>

<div id="Ch033.xhtml_fig0470" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_page_989"></span>[](#Ch033.xhtml_bck_fig0470)

[<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00493.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch033.xhtml_bck_fig0470)

</div>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">For example, the 1990s
Balkans conflict coupled with poor road quality/access and problematic
border crossings initially helped the UN Ro-Ro and Superfast Ferries
services to develop. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.60.2"
class="koboSpan">Illustrating MoS complementarity with trucking, UN
Ro-Ro was itself established and owned by Turkish road transport
operators (Torbianelli, 2000).</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">In Italy, road tolls
and weekend bans on freight transport by road have played a major part
in helping to move freight from road to sea.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">Moreover, where
a sea route offers a distance advantage over an alternative roadway
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.61.3"
class="koboSpan">Genoa–Palermo, Genoa–Barcelona), this is also an
important factor favouring MoS.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">In all of these
examples the application of modern ship technology, and in particular
the use of modern, fast-conventional Ro-Ro/Ro-Pax ferries offering high
payloads and attractive transit times, has had a large part to play in
the success of MoS services competing against parallel roadways.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">However, in instances
where roads are still provided and maintained by the state more or less
free to truckers (i.e. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.63.2"
class="koboSpan">no road tolls), the alternative private sector provided
seaway is not so readily a viable proposition.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">Indeed,
although it can be demonstrated that Ro-Ro/Ro-Pax ferry MoS solutions
can work successfully in a number of different circumstances,
policymakers need to exert care when developing or facilitating
initiatives. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.63.4" class="koboSpan">In
the absence of a level playing field it remains difficult for the
private sector alone to take the risk of starting up a MoS
service.</span>

## <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.64.2" class="koboSpan">Redefining Maritime Transport Infrastructure</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">Researchers,
policymakers and commercial actors generally consider “maritime
transport infrastructure” to be the port (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.65.2" class="koboSpan">Haralambides,
2002; IMPRINT-NET, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_page_990"></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.66.1"
class="koboSpan">Thus the understood position across the three main
surface transport modes is that the principal surface transport
infrastructure includes:</span>

- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.67.1" class="koboSpan">road
  infrastructure;</span>
- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">rail infrastructure;
  and</span>
- <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.69.1" class="koboSpan">port (i.e.
  </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">maritime)
  infrastructure.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">On the European
Continent, at least, port infrastructure receives considerable public
sector investment, and ports there are treated more or less in the same
way from a public investment perspective as roads and railways (Baird,
2004).</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">However, ports are
also regarded as “nodal points along a transport chain” (UNCTAD, 1992).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">This implies
that ports themselves are not the transport chain; ports act as an
interface, or in other words, as points of transfer between transport
modes.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">Indeed, the paramount
good a port must provide to facilitate its wide range of services is not
sea, but </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan">land</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.74.1"
class="koboSpan"> (Haralambides, 2002).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.74.2" class="koboSpan">Although it is
correct to say that ports depend on sea transport, they are also highly
dependent on land transport, (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.74.3" class="koboSpan">road, rail,
pipeline, and in some cases inland waterways).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.74.4" class="koboSpan">The ship in
this sense is only one of many different transport vehicles that serve,
and are served by, a port.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">If roadway and railway
infrastructures, the latter extending hundreds if not thousands of
kilometres, both represent a transport platform between points, it is
evident that a port does not offer the same comparable good (or anything
close to it). </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.75.2" class="koboSpan">A
transport platform (or transport “way”) must consist of more than just a
port/node, which merely acts as a static interface between modes.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">It has been suggested
that EU ports will play an important role in the development of MoS
services (Psaraftis, 2005). </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.76.2"
class="koboSpan">Such a perspective further implies that MoS is more
than just simply ports. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.76.3"
class="koboSpan">If ports, being nodes, are not the “transport platform”
or “way”, then the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan">seaway</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.78.1"
class="koboSpan"> (or MoS) must represent the platform.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">And if the port
is not seaway or MoS infrastructure, then that raises another question,
namely – what is seaway/MoS infrastructure?</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">Whereas state entities
generally provide, finance, and maintain roadway and railway
infrastructure, and in many countries ports as well, this is not the
case with the seaway. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.79.2"
class="koboSpan">The port is evidently not the seaway, because it is a
transport node, so in that sense port infrastructure is not in any way
comparable to roadway and railway infrastructure, the latter offering a
transport platform over long distances.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">This is the point at
which any contention that maritime transport infrastructure consists
only of the port becomes particularly weak and unconvincing
(</span><a href="#Ch033.xhtml_cap_lbl0233"
id="Ch033.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0233"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.81.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.82.2"
class="koboSpan">Consequently, maritime transport infrastructure (the
seaway) has to be a good deal more than the port.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">Installation of any
transport infrastructure platform provides for territorial continuity
(GIE, 2007). </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">This implies that, once transport infrastructure is in
place, there is the capacity for unhindered movement of persons and
goods across the Earth’s surface.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.83.3" class="koboSpan">Once created,
road and rail infrastructure offers this potential.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.83.4" class="koboSpan">But the sea on
its own does not.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">For the sea there is
also a need to create a basic transport platform (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.84.2" class="koboSpan">a seaway
platform), that is comparable in a functional sense to roadway and
railway. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.84.3" class="koboSpan">As an
illustration, if a truck or a train was placed onto the sea, in its
natural state, neither would move anywhere other than where wind or tide
might take them (</span><a href="#Ch033.xhtml_cap_lbl0234"
id="Ch033.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0234"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.86.1"
class="koboSpan"> illustrates this and the need for a seaway platform).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.86.2" class="koboSpan">Therefore, in
the absence of a seaway platform (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.86.3" class="koboSpan">maritime
transport infrastructure) sea transport cannot occur (SUTRANET, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.86.4" class="koboSpan">In other words,
sea transport cannot function without a platform, which would</span>

<div id="Ch033.xhtml_fig0471" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00494.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Ports are nodes, not seaway transport infrastructure platforms comparable with roadway and railway platforms" /></span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_page_991"></span><a href="#Ch033.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0233"
id="Ch033.xhtml_cap_lbl0233"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.88.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan"> Ports are nodes, not seaway transport infrastructure
platforms comparable with roadway and railway platforms</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch033.xhtml_fig0472" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00495.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: The seaway transport platform (i.e. maritime transport infrastructure) is the deck of a ship, without which the “seaway” does not exist" /></span>

<a href="#Ch033.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0234"
id="Ch033.xhtml_cap_lbl0234"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan"> The seaway transport platform (i.e.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">maritime
transport infrastructure) is the deck of a ship, without which the
“seaway” does not exist</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan"> author</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">comprise, in effect,
maritime transport infrastructure, with the purpose of ensuring
territorial continuity.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">Transport
infrastructure comprises any kind of works and structures that
establishes the platform of a means of transport (GIE, 2007).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.96.2" class="koboSpan">In this regard
it can be argued that the seaway/MoS platform, if it is not the sea,
must therefore be the deck of a ship.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.96.3" class="koboSpan">This is already
in part recognised at EU level, reflecting the statement by the van
Miert EC High-Level Group on TEN-T that a boat/ship is a “floating
structure” (Commission of
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_page_992"></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.97.1"
class="koboSpan">the European Communities, 2002); however the full
policy implications of this
(</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.98.1"
class="koboSpan">vis-a-vis
</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan"> road
and rail) have not yet been thought through.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.99.2" class="koboSpan">In other words,
the boat has yet to be termed “maritime transport infrastructure” or
considered as such from a policy and funding perspective.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">The floating
structure (i.e. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">the ship) comprises both the infrastructure and the
platform of waterborne transport.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.3" class="koboSpan">This notion of
the boat as floating infrastructure has therefore now taken root.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.4" class="koboSpan">The need to
better support MoS services has raised calls (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.5" class="koboSpan">in France
(GIE, 2007)) for the financing of the “boat infrastructure” by public
authorities (i.e. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.6"
class="koboSpan">up to 30% of the ship value).
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.7" class="koboSpan">This estimate
more or less equates to the cost of a ships’ basic hull (or cargo
platform), leaving the costs of propulsion machinery, accommodation and
navigation/bridge systems etc. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.8"
class="koboSpan">for the market/operator to provide.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.100.9" class="koboSpan">This approach
would go some way to help equalise the effect of subsidies applying to
road and rail infrastructures, thereby levelling the playing field
between sea and land transport.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">Ports, and indeed
navigation aids (e.g. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.101.2"
class="koboSpan">port access channels, lights etc) may be considered as
auxiliary to waterborne transport infrastructure, which is composed
fundamentally of the floating infrastructure of boats/ships’.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.101.3" class="koboSpan">But ports are
not the (sea) transport infrastructure platform necessary to convey
goods over long distances, and cannot function in any way comparable to
parallel alternative road/rail platforms covering long distances.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">The ship, albeit
mobile, must therefore be acknowledged as what it is –
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan">maritime transport
infrastructure</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.104.2"
class="koboSpan">The ship might also be termed the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.105.1"
class="koboSpan">seaway
platform</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.106.2"
class="koboSpan">Irrespective of the terminology used, the ship, which
is maritime transport infrastructure, must be considered as comparable
to roadway and railway transport infrastructure in providing for
territorial continuity. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.106.3"
class="koboSpan">Transport policies need to be revised in order to
reflect this.</span>

## <span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.107.2" class="koboSpan">Conclusions</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">Despite policies
tending to favour land transport infrastructure, ongoing MoS
developments have helped signal the need for a new definition of
maritime transport infrastructure.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">This new
definition elevates the seaway in relation to the port, the latter being
simply a node.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">The theory explained
and presented here states that the maritime transport infrastructure
platform (i.e. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.109.2"
class="koboSpan">the
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.110.1"
class="koboSpan">seaway</span></span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.111.1"
class="koboSpan">) is the deck of a ship.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.111.2" class="koboSpan">The port is
not a seaway platform; the seaway platform and therefore directly
comparable transport infrastructure to roadway and railway
infrastructure is the ship. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.111.3"
class="koboSpan">It is the ship that provides for territorial continuity
(not the port).</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">MoS experience has
shown that more efficient Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ship technology in particular
has helped facilitate effective MoS solutions in an effort to overcome
road transport problems and associated externalities resulting from
increasing land transport usage.
</span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.112.2" class="koboSpan">However, it is
still the case that incentives are needed to further develop the seaway
in order to alleviate market distortions in favour of land transport and
facilitate change.</span>

<span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">EU and Member State
MoS/maritime transport policies will require appropriate adjustment to
more adequately reflect the new definition of maritime transport
infrastructure outlined here. </span><span id="Ch033.xhtml_kobo.113.2"
class="koboSpan">Respecting the new definition of maritime transport
infrastructure should enable policy-makers to develop and implement
policies and initiatives that ensure seaway transport infrastructure
receives appropriate consideration relative to other surface transport
modes.</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_book-inner">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_996"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_997"></span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 34</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">International Logistics Strategy and Modal Choice</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0738)
==================================================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Kunio</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Miyashita</span></span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1150" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1150"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.5.1" class="koboSpan">*</span></a>

## <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.6.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.6.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.7.1" class="koboSpan">The container shipping
mode of transportation has in large part cooperated with, but has also
competed against, the air transportation mode.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.7.2" class="koboSpan">The concepts of
both total distribution costs and the opportunity cost support a
division of labour by the two modes (air and sea) and explain the
existence of a competitive grey zone.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.7.3" class="koboSpan">However,
traditional theory is not sufficient to explain a recent trend towards
air-oriented cargo flows. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.7.4"
class="koboSpan">The modal choice problem is not in the sole domain of
the transport field, but has a new dynamic dimension, which involves
integration with both logistics strategy and the supply chain management
of shippers. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.7.5"
class="koboSpan">This chapter brings insight into the traditional
economic phenomenon of modal choice and its innovative research
frontiers related with the logistics
strategy.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1151" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1151"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.8.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">The interaction between
the shipping and air modes of transportation has been dominated by a
trend towards air-oriented
transport,</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1152" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1152"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.10.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan"> if observed from the point of view of the value of
trade volumes. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.11.2"
class="koboSpan">Needless to say, in terms of total volume as measured
by weight-tonne, sea shipments are responsible for more than 99% of
total international physical distribution.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.11.3" class="koboSpan">Hence, the
shipping industry plays a core status role in the international
transport industry. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.11.4"
class="koboSpan">However, in terms of value of the goods shipped, the
share of industrial goods transported by air has increased
significantly.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1153" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1153"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.12.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.13.1" class="koboSpan">Traditionally, the
principle of total cost based on the difference in the service quality
between the two modes of transportation has explained modal
choice.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1154" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1154"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.15.1"
class="koboSpan"> This view is important even today.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">However, a
point has been reached where it has become necessary for a new
analytical angle based on logistics theory to be combined with the
aforementioned traditional argument.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.15.3" class="koboSpan">In other words,
there is a need for a greater level of entrepreneurial spirit in the
shipping industry, especially in relation to container shipping and air
transportation, which supports the logistics activities of the shipper.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.15.4" class="koboSpan">In this
chapter, we discuss a hypothesis in which structural change in both
shipping
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_998"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.16.1"
class="koboSpan">and air transportation modes will be derived according
to the international logistics strategy of shippers.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">The core
problem of modal choice will be closely related to a shippers’ logistics
strategy, under which international direct investment, the product cycle
and the stability of international transactions will generate a rational
causal relationship with modal choice.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">In accordance
with a shipper’s logistics strategy, international physical distribution
markets will be composed of both sea and air-based logistics systems.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.16.4" class="koboSpan">Both of these
types of system will either compete or cooperate, so that the modal
choice problem of transport is gradually absorbed into the logistics
system.</span>

## <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.17.2" class="koboSpan">Competition and Cooperation of Container Shipping and Air Transportation</span>

### <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">2.1 Total distribution cost as the criterion of modal choice</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">The higher the value
of a good is, the faster the speed of the transport mode being selected
will be. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.19.2" class="koboSpan">This
is the reason why inventory costs will fluctuate in proportion to both
the price of goods and the transportation period.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.19.3" class="koboSpan">Hence, it is
preferable to transport high value goods by the speedier air-based mode
to reduce the transportation period (inventory period), if the saving
rate of the inventory cost is higher than the increased rate in the
transportation cost. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.19.4"
class="koboSpan">The sum of these two costs is referred to as the total
distribution cost. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.19.5"
class="koboSpan">In this case, the total distribution costs relating to
high value goods will be decreased if a high-speed mode is utilised.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.19.6" class="koboSpan">The
establishment of the concept of total distribution cost is very
important in terms of determining modal choice between container
shipping and air transportation. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.19.7"
class="koboSpan">It is the concept of distribution costs that has led to
the transport of high value goods by air since the 1960s.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">According to the
concept of total distribution costs, the value of a good is negatively
correlated with the transport period.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">As is commonly
known, if we select the transport period as the measure of the
horizontal axis and total distribution costs as the measure of the
vertical axis, a downward convex total distribution curve can be
generated. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.20.3" class="koboSpan">On
the contrary, if we select the value of the good instead of the
transport period as the measure of the horizontal axis, an upward convex
total distribution curve will be generated as shown in
</span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0235"
id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0235"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.21.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.22.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.23.1" class="koboSpan">In
</span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0235)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.25.1"
class="koboSpan">, the total distribution cost curve for container
shipping intersects with the cost curve for air transportation at the
value of the product
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.26.1"
class="koboSpan">e.</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan"> If the value of the product is greater (more
expensive) than
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.28.1"
class="koboSpan">e,</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan"> it will be advantageous to transport a particular
product by air, and vice versa. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.29.2"
class="koboSpan">Hence, it can be hypothesised that a division of labour
between the two modes can be confirmed at
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">e.</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.31.1"
class="koboSpan"> In addition, the higher the value of the product, the
higher the opportunity cost will be for products transported by
container shipping. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.31.2"
class="koboSpan">If a seasonal product, such as a currently fashionable
good, is transported by the sea mode, large scale, temporary opportunity
costs will be generated. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.31.3"
class="koboSpan">In this case, the opportunity cost will increase in a
greater proportion to the value of product as indicated by curve
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.32.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00496.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.33.1"
class="koboSpan"> If we add opportunity costs to the total distribution
cost of container shipping, a new interactive point (intersection)
indicating the total distribution costs of air transport can be realized
at/, which is located to the left of the existing point
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.34.1"
class="koboSpan">e.</span></span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0473" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.35.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00497.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Competitive grey zone between container shipping and air transportation" /></span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_999"></span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0235"
id="Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0235"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.36.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.37.1"
class="koboSpan"> Competitive grey zone between container shipping and
air transportation</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.38.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, it is possible
to discriminate between three kinds of value ranges for a particular
product:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.39.1" class="koboSpan">Shipment by
    container is the logical modal choice if the value range of a
    particular product is lower than
    </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.40.1"
    class="koboSpan">f</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
    class="koboSpan">;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">Air transportation
    is the logical modal choice if the value range of a particular
    product is greater than
    </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
    class="koboSpan">f</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
    class="koboSpan">; and</span>
3.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.45.1" class="koboSpan">A value range
    between </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
    class="koboSpan">e</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
    class="koboSpan"> and
    </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
    class="koboSpan">f</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
    class="koboSpan"> indicates a ‘grey zone’, where modal choice is
    extremely competitive.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.50.1" class="koboSpan">The relationship in
terms of modal choice between container shipping and air transportation
is in principle complementary but if it is considered from a total
distribution cost point of view, it will be competitive.</span>

### <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.51.1" class="koboSpan">2.2 Turning point in modal choice</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.52.1" class="koboSpan">Recent Japanese export
trade volume data in </span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0236"
id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0236"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.53.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows that between 1980 and 1992 existed a parallel
relationship between the export share of goods transported by container
shipping and the share of goods transported by air
transportation.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">The share of goods
shipped by air transportation increased steadily as new markets were
exploited, while container shipping continued to maintain its share of
the conventional liner shipping business.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.55.2" class="koboSpan">However, after
reaching a plateau in 1992, container shipping gradually began to lose
share relating to export transport.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.55.3" class="koboSpan">Since 1992,
modal share has fluctuated in a downward direction.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.55.4" class="koboSpan">In 1992,
container shipping was responsible for 52% of all export shipments.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.55.5" class="koboSpan">By 1998, this
share had decreased to 47%.</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0474" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.56.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00498.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: Development of trade by air in Japan: competitive and complementary relationship with container shipping" /></span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1000"></span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0236"
id="Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0236"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"> Development of trade by air in Japan: competitive and
complementary relationship with container shipping</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.59.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.60.1"
class="koboSpan"> Ministry of Finance Japan</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">On the contrary, in
1992, the modal share for air transportation was 18%.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.61.2" class="koboSpan">This had
increased to 29% by 1998.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.62.1" class="koboSpan">Thus, it appears that
1992 can be considered to be the turning point in share fluctuation
between the two modes in the case of exports from Japan.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.62.2" class="koboSpan">It should be
noted that it is the shipper who has changed the international physical
distribution strategy. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.62.3"
class="koboSpan">In addition, the modal choice problem has structurally
changed since 1992 in Japan. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.62.4"
class="koboSpan">Generally speaking, it is necessary to generate a
different model of modal choice for the period before 1990 as opposed to
model considered representative of the
1990s.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1155" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1155"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">2.3 Modal choice model prior to 1990</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">Before 1990, the
principle of total distribution costs dominated the modal choice
behaviour of shippers. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.65.2"
class="koboSpan">Following, the principal and complementary relationship
between two modes will be determined.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">As shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
1</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0235)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">, opportunity costs will generate a competitive grey
zone. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.67.2" class="koboSpan">In this
case, it can be hypothesised that while air transport service is not a
superior good, a container shipping service cannot be considered to be
an inferior good. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.67.3"
class="koboSpan">If this is indeed the case, the question of which type
of modal service will be preferred by shippers remains to be answered,
especially if the income (revenue, profit) of a shipper determines modal
choice.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">Accordingly, the modal
choice activity function will be noted as follows.</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0475" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00499.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.70.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">ETA = value of export
trade volumes by air transportation,</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">ETS = value of export
trade volumes by container shipping,</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0476" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1001"></span>[](#Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0476)

[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.73.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00500.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0476)

</div>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">TCA = total
distribution costs by air transport,</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.75.1" class="koboSpan">TCC = total
distribution costs by container shipping,</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">GDP = gross domestic
product of export country,</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.77.1" class="koboSpan">OPC = opportunity cost
of container shipping,</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">TAS = preference by
shippers for freighter, and </span>\
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">i
</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.80.1" class="koboSpan">=
specific time point.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">The data for the
variables ETA, ETS, GDP and TAS are readily available in each of the
countries under study. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.81.2"
class="koboSpan">An approximation of total distribution costs can be
determined hypothetically by calculating the reciprocal of freight share
as measured by
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.82.1"
class="koboSpan">commodity price/freight
rate</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.83.2" class="koboSpan">This type of
approximation is only available if the ratio of container freight rate
in container cargo price is constant or in other words its technological
progress is comparatively
stable</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1156" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1156"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.84.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a></sup><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.85.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">In equation (1), the
dependent variable (the ratio of trade volumes between air
transportation and container shipping) will fluctuate in a reverse
direction as compared to the ratio of the total distribution cost
between the two modes, if their respective transport services are both
substitutive and competitive. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.86.2"
class="koboSpan">In this case, the sign of the ratio representing total
distribution costs will be negative.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.86.3" class="koboSpan">However, if the
trade volume ratio fluctuates in the same direction as the total
distribution cost ratio, both transport modes will possess a
complementary relationship. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.86.4"
class="koboSpan">In this case, the sign of the total distribution cost
ratio will be positive as per our hypothesis.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.87.1" class="koboSpan">Next, we assume that
as the GDP of an export country increases, its trade volume ratio will
increase. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.87.2" class="koboSpan">Thus,
the sign of the GDP ratio will be positive.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.87.3" class="koboSpan">In this case,
an increase in the GDP of a particular country will lead to an increase
in air transport volumes, which represents the numerator in the trade
volume ratio. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.87.4"
class="koboSpan">Hence, air transportation service can be classified as
a superior good with container shipping service representing an inferior
good. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.87.5" class="koboSpan">On the
contrary if the sign of GDP ratio is negative, air transportation
service can be classified as neither a superior or inferior good.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1002"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan">In general, the opportunity cost of container shipping
will have a positive sign, because the total distribution cost of air
transportation will lead to cost advantages over container shipping.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.88.2" class="koboSpan">The preference
by shippers for freighter will likely increase the share of trade volume
flows by the air transportation mode, so it can be assumed that its sign
will be positive.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.89.1" class="koboSpan">For Japan, the signs
of the variables in equation (1) and the estimated results of the
equation are summarised in
</span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fig0476" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0476"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.90.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.91.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.91.2"
class="koboSpan">Equation (1) is specified in the logarithmic form and
is estimated by the least square method.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.92.1" class="koboSpan">The estimated results
with respect to the sign of the coefficient indicate a complementary
relationship between air transport and container shipping.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">The
coefficients of both the total distribution cost ratio of air transport
to container shipping and the GDP of the export country (Japan) are
statistically significant and demonstrate a complementary causality.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.92.3" class="koboSpan">At the same
time, the basic relationship is influenced by both the opportunity cost
of container shipping and the preference for the shipper to freighter,
which leads to the existence of a competitive zone, which we refer to as
a grey zone.</span>

### <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.93.1" class="koboSpan">2.4 Increases in substitution causality in the 1990s</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.94.1" class="koboSpan">Next, we expand the
estimated period to cover the years 1980–1996.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.94.2" class="koboSpan">In the 1990s,
in addition to the total distribution cost ratio of air transport to
container shipping, the function of the logistics network is also a
determinant factor. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.94.3"
class="koboSpan">Such network effects, as represented by foreign direct
investment, will absorb the traditional function of opportunity cost,
income and preference on a shipper’s modal choice behaviour.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.94.4" class="koboSpan">Direct
investment will determine the shipper’s international logistics strategy
to the extent that the existing simple modal choice mechanism will no
longer be appropriate due to the structural change in the network
effects. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.94.5" class="koboSpan">The
function is thus adjusted as follows:</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0477" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.95.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00501.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">DIU = direct Japanese
investment in the US</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">DIE = direct Japanese
investment in the EU and</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">DIS = direct Japanese
investment in Asia.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Equation (2) is
specified in the logarithmic form and is estimated by least square
method as in equation (1). </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.100.2"
class="koboSpan">The estimated results are detailed in
</span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fig0478" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0478"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">Table 2</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.102.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0478" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.103.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00502.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0478)

</div>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1003"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.104.1"
class="koboSpan">The estimated results of the total distribution cost
ratio as detailed in
</span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fig0480" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0480"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">Table 3</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.106.1"
class="koboSpan"> suggest a fundamental complementary relationship
between air transportation and shipping.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.106.2" class="koboSpan">However, the
effects of direct investment on modal choice vary considerably.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.106.3" class="koboSpan">The sign
representing the coefficient of direct investment in Asia is positive,
indicating that the shipper regards air transport as the superior good.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.106.4" class="koboSpan">In the Asian
region, the substitutive nature of air and sea services are clearly
indicated. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.106.5"
class="koboSpan">However, direct investment in the EU strongly indicates
the complementary nature of the services.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.106.6" class="koboSpan">Finally, the
coefficient representing direct investment in the US is not
statistically significant. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.106.7"
class="koboSpan">Thus, the network function as related to air
transportation and shipping services is neither complementary nor
substitutive. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.106.8"
class="koboSpan">In the Pacific region, the effect of service quality on
modal choice is neutral.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">It is important to
keep in mind that the estimation period of equation (2) includes data
for the 1980s. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.107.2"
class="koboSpan">During that period, the competitive zone was limited to
the aforementioned grey zone. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.107.3"
class="koboSpan">Hence, the estimated results of equation (2) do not
necessarily reflect the characteristics of a shipper’s logistics
strategy and its network operations.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.107.4" class="koboSpan">However, it is
possible to recognise a trend towards the utilisation of an air-based
logistics system in the global economy.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.107.5" class="koboSpan">In particular,
it is necessary to consider closely the economic circumstances behind
the investment behavioural patterns of the three regions.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.107.6" class="koboSpan">For example,
why is it possible to discriminate between modal choice behaviors in the
three regions? </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.107.7"
class="koboSpan">The answer is that the modal choice in a specific
region will be affected by a logistics strategy, which is based on the
competitive advantage of a specific product.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.107.8" class="koboSpan">In next
section, we try to access this problem.</span>

## <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.108.2" class="koboSpan">Logistics Strategy and Modal Choice</span>

### <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">3.1 Determinant factors supporting the shippers' behaviour</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">From the previous
section, it is clear that shippers of Japanese exports base modal choice
on the level of direct investment in a particular region.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.110.2" class="koboSpan">In this
section, we attempt to construct a more sophisticated modal choice
model, which represents export logistics systems.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">The basic
determinants of modal choice from the shippers’ point of view are the
following two factors which are based on the analysis in Section 2 and
logistics concepts in general:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">the total
    logistics cost ratio of air-based logistics systems to sea-based
    logistics systems to different destinations from Japan;</span>
2.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">the level of
    direct investment by shippers in different regions of the
    world.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">The total logistics
cost ratio is the main factor determining basic modal choice between an
air-based logistics system and a sea-based logistics system.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.114.2" class="koboSpan">Carriers such
as airlines and container lines act as logistics service providers
striving to realise an advantage in terms of reducing total logistics
costs. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.114.3" class="koboSpan">In the
current logistics era, forwarders also act as logistics service
providers.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">Certainly from an
historical point of view of the transport service provider, air
forwarders have maintained an advantage over air carrier in terms of the
network available for cargo booking.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.115.2" class="koboSpan">In contrast,
container-shipping carriers have dominated booking activity for cargo
flows over sea borne forwarders.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.115.3" class="koboSpan">At this stage
of development, it is possible to classify both the carrier and
forwarder as transportation service
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1004"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.116.1"
class="koboSpan">providers. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.116.2"
class="koboSpan">Based on their background, it is possible to find
different advantages in terms of booking power between the carrier and
the forwarder in different markets.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.117.1" class="koboSpan">In the transition
period, during which the transportation service provider gradually
developed into a logistics service provider, shippers have strived to
combine successively and cross-functionally value added logistics
services with their procurement (physical supply), production support
and sales marketing (physical distribution) activity.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">Based on the
Bowersox concept, a logistics system is composed of both a value-added
inventory flow as mentioned above and other required information
relating to market forecasts, order analysis, production planning, and
procurement
planning.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1157" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1157"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">During the process of
logistics development, the product cycle became shorter and shorter and
industrial shippers preferred “speedier” logistics systems.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.119.2" class="koboSpan">In addition,
there was a considerable increase in foreign investment in global
markets at the same time. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.119.3"
class="koboSpan">Currently, debates revolve around where the optimum
location for assembly and parts production is.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.119.4" class="koboSpan">It has become
necessary for parts production and assembly to be relocated in a timely
fashion, in response to cross-functional logistics system analysis.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.119.5" class="koboSpan">Courier
transport has been developing at a tremendously high growth rate with
companies such as FedEx and UPS being representative.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.119.6" class="koboSpan">These
companies have taken advantage of a preferential environment in which
information technology has been utilised to exploit a new frontier of
logistics system integration amongst different firms.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.119.7" class="koboSpan">Supply chain
management (SCM) responsive strategy has become a common component of
logistics
systems.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1158" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1158"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">8</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">Under a SCM strategy,
international express service companies are playing a leading role as an
integrated carrier. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.121.2"
class="koboSpan">FedEx utilises an SCM responsive strategy in terms of
its integration with Dell Computers, Hewlett Packard, Laura Ashley,
Rosh, and American
Express.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1159" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1159"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">9</span></a></sup><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.123.1"
class="koboSpan"> The integrated carrier plays the dual role of the
logistics system builder and the logistics operator.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.123.2" class="koboSpan">Enterprising
forwarders also commonly utilise this type of strategy.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.123.3" class="koboSpan">The role
played by the integrated carrier is referred to as third-party logistics
(3PL).</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1160" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1160"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">10</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">International express
services as well as enterprising air forwarder services have been
developing as part of the package of services provided by the logistics
system provider. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.125.2"
class="koboSpan">This has had the effect of increasing the preference
for the air mode. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.125.3"
class="koboSpan">If this is indeed the case, it’s becomes necessary to
select the following (c)–(d) as determinant factors of modal
choice.</span>

- <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.126.1" class="koboSpan">(c) International
  air express services.</span>
- <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">(d) Enterprising
  air forwarder services.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.128.1" class="koboSpan">These two factors
function in the incremental zone of modal choice.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.128.2" class="koboSpan">Needless to
say, there has been a trend towards the greater utilisation of SCM in
the development process of logistics.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.128.3" class="koboSpan">Under a SCM
strategy, partnership among SCM members is the key factor leading to
sustainability. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.128.4"
class="koboSpan">The international logistics industry should insist on
maintaining an equal partnership as a core member of a strategy
utilising SCM. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.128.5"
class="koboSpan">As a result, it is necessary to reflect on the level of
customer satisfaction amongst member shippers in an SCM responsive
logistics system. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.128.6"
class="koboSpan">Under SCM, it is necessary to achieve cooperation
amongst the final assembly company and the parts and accessory
manufacturing companies. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.128.7"
class="koboSpan">The main issue facing each member of SCM thus becomes
the product cycle of the industrial goods manufactured and traded in a
specific SCM system.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">The product cycle has
certainly been the most important factor not only during the period of
the transport service provider but also currently with the logistics
service
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1005"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.130.1"
class="koboSpan">provider. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.130.2"
class="koboSpan">The role of the product cycle becomes even more
important for the logistics system provider under SCM.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.130.3" class="koboSpan">Thus, it is
necessary to add this factor as a key environmental component of modal
choice in international logistics.</span>

- <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">(e) At each stage
  in the logistics system, the product cycle in each region (US, EU and
  Asia) is distinct from each other.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">There are basically
five factors determining modal choice for a shipper, which are
represented by the circles in </span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0237"
id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0237"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.133.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.134.2"
class="koboSpan">The circles with the dotted lines represent the
environment factors in tiers 1 and 2, which were detailed previously.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.134.3" class="koboSpan">The arrow
indicates a causal relationship between a basic logistics strategy (tier
1), the different types of providers (tier 2), five theoretical
determinant factors circled by solid line (tier 3), their practical
proxy variables in quadrangles (tier 4) and modal choice behaviour (tier
5).</span>

### <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">3.2 Modal choice behaviour under global logistics linkage</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">In tier 4 in
</span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.137.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0237)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan"> total logistics cost is dived into two components,
(i.e. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.138.2" class="koboSpan">space
transfer cost (transportation cost) and time transfer cost (inventory
cost). </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.138.3" class="koboSpan">Due to
the recent rapid changes in technology, it is not appropriate to
evaluate total logistics cost by the reciprocal of freight share as
measured by
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.139.1"
class="koboSpan">commodity price/freight
rate</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.140.2" class="koboSpan">In this
scheme, the effect of air integrator and forwarder services on
logistical modal choice can be grasped by the coefficient dummy variable
of time transfer cost since 1993, because 1992 was the turning point for
the existing shippers’ behaviour.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.141.1" class="koboSpan">The most important
structural change in the world economy will be the increasing trend of
global linkage among Asia, the EU and the US.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.141.2" class="koboSpan">In
</span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.142.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
3</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0237)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.143.1"
class="koboSpan"> the key factors to combine three kinds of district
economies with each other, will be the level of investment and the
product cycle. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.143.2"
class="koboSpan">First, the Asian economy can be regarded as the
operator of investment buffer in the global economy and has the long
reach to absorb the impact of direct investment in the EU and the US.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.143.3" class="koboSpan">The terms of
Japan’s trade with Asia by air will play a key role in the direct
investment behaviour in the global economy.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.143.4" class="koboSpan">Secondly, the
effect of innovational edge of product cycle on modal choice can be
observed in US trade, strictly in the terms of Japan’s trade with US by
air.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.144.1" class="koboSpan">Then the modal choice
function in Japan trade with US is built up in
</span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">Table
3</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_fig0480)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.146.1"
class="koboSpan">, where the rational sign conditions of five
independent variables are summarised.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.146.2" class="koboSpan">In the
logistics age it is especially important to avoid the increase in time
transfer costs, which tends to induce the trade by air.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.146.3" class="koboSpan">Originally air
trade has the advantage to decreasing inventory costs.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.146.4" class="koboSpan">It is the
reason why two kinds of variables concerned with time transfer cost are
positive. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.146.5" class="koboSpan">On
the contrary the change in the space transfer cost brings about the
normal demand behaviour, so that its sign will be negative.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.146.6" class="koboSpan">Product cycle
in US represented by the terms of Japan’s trade with US by air has a
positive sign, whereas the investment buffer function represented by the
terms of Japan’s trade with Asia by air has a negative sign.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.146.7" class="koboSpan">The latter two
variables function as the factors combining the Japan with Asia, the EU
and the US.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">The basic model of
global economic linkage is grasped by the modal choice behaviour of
Japanese shippers’ trade with the US.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.147.2" class="koboSpan">Then their
networks extend via the EU trade to Asia as shown in
</span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0238"
id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0238"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.148.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.149.2"
class="koboSpan">The time lag structure of trade transactions among
three districts is assumed to follow the specific lag type of the
Shiller model. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.149.3"
class="koboSpan">Certainly</span>

</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.168.2" class="koboSpan">Based on this

</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.183.2" class="koboSpan">The

dominated by shippers’ logistics strategies.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.183.3" class="koboSpan">Also in other

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.184.1" class="koboSpan">The product cycle
impact is different among three trades, where US trade has the lowest
elasticity despite its higher level of product cycle.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.184.2" class="koboSpan">The modal
choice impact tends to be gradually accumulated and growing as the main
trend of logistics strategy.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">Terms of air trade
with Asia is the proxy variable of the buffer function of global trade.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.185.2" class="koboSpan">The weaker the
trend of air-orientated behaviour, the stronger its buffer function to
compensate the decrease in global trade.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.185.3" class="koboSpan">The negative
sign of its elasticity represents the rational response of Asian
economy. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.185.4" class="koboSpan">Its
elasticity is largest in three trades to restore the inverse trend of
global economy.</span>

class="koboSpan">, we can depict, in

class="koboSpan">, the long-term ripple effect of Japanese shippers’
modal choice behaviour in exports to the US.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.192.2" class="koboSpan">In Asian trade
its effect tends to continue for seven years and in the EU for five

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1010"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
