## <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.197.2" class="koboSpan">Logistics Cycle and Modal Choice Perspective</span>

### <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Logistics cycle hypothesis based on product cycle and modal choice</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">As is well known,
product cycle theory as proposed by Raymond Vernon can explain the
relationship between investment behaviour and cargo flows between
specified
countries.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1161" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1161"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">11</span></a></sup><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan"> Vernon introduced three phases – innovation, maturity
and simple standardisation – which occur during the developing stages of
the product cycle. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.201.2"
class="koboSpan">Mark Casson then modified Vernon’s research slightly
and added a new original third stage referred to as standardised
differentiation, which falls between the maturity and simple
standardised
stages.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1162" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1162"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">12</span></a></sup><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.203.1"
class="koboSpan"> Thus, the Vernon–Casson model depicts the total
dynamics of the product cycle as follows.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.204.1" class="koboSpan">During the initial
stages of the life cycle, innovative products including parts and
accessories are manufactured solely in the country of origin and one
then exported to other industrial countries.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.204.2" class="koboSpan">Technical
advancements are directed towards reductions in labour costs.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.204.3" class="koboSpan">These
advancements tend to be repeated to keep pace with consumer demand.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.204.4" class="koboSpan">As information
exchanges between the production and sales arms increase, it becomes
more conducive to relocate the production centre closer to the market.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.204.5" class="koboSpan">However, it is
too early in the cycle to establish the know-how necessary to utilise
this technique. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.204.6"
class="koboSpan">Only a few industrial countries are able to continue
such innovative market research, production and marketing in their home
countries. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.204.7"
class="koboSpan">Direct investment is restricted to establishing and
expanding sales centres as foreign subsidiaries.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.204.8" class="koboSpan">As it is only
finished goods, which flow between the parent company and the foreign
subsidiary, a horizontal physical distribution flow is dominant among
industrial countries in the innovative stage.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.205.1" class="koboSpan">In the second stage,
the transfer of manufacturing technology to foreign subsidiaries located
in industrial countries is instigated by the introduction of a
technological manual used for manufacturing.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.205.2" class="koboSpan">In this
scenario, the promotion of import–oriented production is increased.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.205.3" class="koboSpan">Foreign
subsidiaries begin to produce and assemble almost all of the necessary
parts. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.205.4" class="koboSpan">The
parent company concentrates on producing the key components of the
product, in such a way that a vertical type of physical distribution
appears among industrial countries.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.205.5" class="koboSpan">On the
contrary, horizontal physical distribution is common between developed
and developing countries.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">The third stage of
the production cycle is referred to as standardised differentiation,
where a rational production method is introduced involving the division
of labour among foreign subsidiaries.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.206.2" class="koboSpan">Under the
concept of selection and concentration, each subsidiary is ordered to
produce specific components if an inherent comparative advantage exists.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.206.3" class="koboSpan">Such a
production system will promote both a refined division of labour as well
as lead to a reduction in production costs.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.206.4" class="koboSpan">New products
can be introduced by utilising different combinations of components even
though the components themselves are standardised.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.206.5" class="koboSpan">Such an
exchange system of components allows products to remain fresh and
maintain differentiation. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.206.6"
class="koboSpan">In this sense, the third stage of the product
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1011"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan">cycle determines whether or not the cycle will survive
over a period of time. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.207.2"
class="koboSpan">As a result, subsidiaries in developing countries and
economies are able to produce the general components necessary for
assembly, although even in this stage, a limited amount of the key
components necessary to produce a given good are manufactured by the
parent company. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.207.3"
class="koboSpan">The main flow of physical distribution is horizontal
with components moving from developing countries and economies to
industrialised countries.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.208.1" class="koboSpan">As we move towards
the end of the product cycle, goods become perfectly standardised and
gradually begin to lose market status.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.208.2" class="koboSpan">At this stage,
new innovative products will begin to appear in the market.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">According to product
cycle theory, it is possible to construct a modal choice hypothesis
pertaining to export shippers in an international logistics
system.</span>

1.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">During the first
    stage, export shippers prefer to utilise an air-based logistics
    system. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.210.2"
    class="koboSpan">This is due to the highly value-added nature of
    innovative products, which leads to high inventory costs over time.
    </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.210.3" class="koboSpan">In order
    to minimise total logistics costs, the share of this product shipped
    by air in terms of total product shipped will grow rapidly as
    opposed to a reduced share for a sea-based logistics system.</span>
2.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">Next comes the
    growing stage. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.211.2"
    class="koboSpan">At this stage the air-based logistics system is
    growing more and more, because the new entry of producers to the
    market increases. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.211.3"
    class="koboSpan">Based on this market competition, the price of
    product concerned is decreasing, so that the share of sea-based
    logistics system is increasing in comparison with the first
    stage.</span>
3.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">At the third
    stage, as the product’s life cycle begins to mature, a sea-based
    logistics system will be developed in parallel with an air based
    logistics system. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.212.2"
    class="koboSpan">The assembly line is relocated gradually to other
    developed industrial countries.
    </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.212.3" class="koboSpan">Exports of
    both components from the parent company and finished goods from the
    subsidiary lead to a trade off relationship between air-based and
    sea-based logistics systems.
    </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.212.4" class="koboSpan">At this
    point, the second stage reaches peak levels.</span>
4.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.213.1" class="koboSpan">During the fourth
    stage, the share of product moved by a sea-based logistics system
    increases to a greater level than the share of product moved by an
    air-based logistics system. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.213.2"
    class="koboSpan">Standardised differentiation promotes the
    utilisation of a sea-based logistics system for goods moving from
    emerging countries and economies to countries worldwide.
    </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.213.3" class="koboSpan">However,
    the share of the core components shipped from the parent country is
    decreasing.</span>
5.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.214.1" class="koboSpan">At some point, a
    simple standardised product loses market share due to the appearance
    of new innovative products. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.214.2"
    class="koboSpan">In this final stage, the volumes of goods shipped
    not only by air-based but also by sea based logistics systems will
    decrease simultaneously.</span>
6.  <span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">Finally, new
    innovation product of next generation appears.
    </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.215.2" class="koboSpan">This stage
    can be called the potential innovation.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.216.1" class="koboSpan">Based on the above
hypothesis, it is possible to construct
</span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0240"
id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0240"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.217.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 6</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan">, where the vertical axes represents the share of
product shipped by an air-based logistics system on a specific export
route from a specific country and the horizontal axes the share of the
same product shipped by a sea-based logistics system.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.218.2" class="koboSpan">A logistics
cycle with a circular line of the same orientation much like the hand of
watch is generated.</span>

### <span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1012"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.219.1" class="koboSpan">4.2 Estimated result of the logistics cycle in Japan export trade and some perspective on the business cycle</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.220.1" class="koboSpan">In order to
generalise this hypothesis, we formulate the share of product shipped by
an air-based and sea-based logistics system where:</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.221.1" class="koboSpan">S = share of products
shipped by a sea-based logistics system (%),</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.222.1" class="koboSpan">A = share of products
shipped by an air-based logistics system (%),</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.223.1" class="koboSpan">i = destination of
products shipped from the export country (e.g.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.223.2" class="koboSpan">1 = US, 2 =
EU, 3 = Asia), and</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.224.1" class="koboSpan">j = specific year
(e.g. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.224.2" class="koboSpan">j =
1998),</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.225.1" class="koboSpan">thus,</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0486" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.226.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00510.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">By observing the time
series path of both S</span><sub><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.228.1"
class="koboSpan">i,j</span></sub><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.229.1"
class="koboSpan"> and A</span><sub><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.230.1"
class="koboSpan">i,j</span></sub><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.231.1"
class="koboSpan">, it is possible to draw three theoretically generated
circular lines based on the three destinations of the goods exported
(i).</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">If we input data for
Japanese exports to the US, EU and Asia into the set of
S</span><sub><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">i,j</span></sub><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan"> and A</span><sub><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.235.1"
class="koboSpan">i,j</span></sub><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.236.1"
class="koboSpan">, it is possible in practice to trace a successive two
kind of full circle as shown in
</span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.237.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0240)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.238.1"
class="koboSpan">, which will suggest the modal choice of the logistics
systems in each destination between 1983–2004.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.238.2" class="koboSpan">It is clear
that a modal choice hypothesis based on the dynamic product cycle as
shown in </span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure
6</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0240)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan"> coincides with the current export logistics systems
utilised in Japan. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.240.2"
class="koboSpan">The main characteristic of such a system is the
increase in the share of volume being shipped by an air-based logistics
system. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.240.3" class="koboSpan">This
tends to cause the central point of the circle to shift in a northwest
direction as shown in </span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0241"
id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0241"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.241.1"
class="koboSpan">figure 7</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0487" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00511.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 6: Logistics cycle based on product cycle and modal choice for export trade in a specific destination: hypothetical case" /></span>

<a href="#Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0240"
id="Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0240"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 6:</span></span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.245.1"
class="koboSpan"> Logistics cycle based on product cycle and modal
choice for export trade in a specific destination: hypothetical
case</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.246.1"
class="koboSpan">Note</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.247.1"
class="koboSpan">: 1 = Innovative stage; 2 = Growing stage; 3 = Maturity
stage; 4 = Standardised differentiation stage; 5 = Simple
standardisation stage, 6 = Potential innovation stage.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1013"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.248.1"
class="koboSpan">The logistics cycle in
</span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">Figure
7</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0241)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.250.1"
class="koboSpan"> represents the long-term economic fluctuation in US
economy from the modal choice and product cycle concept.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.250.2" class="koboSpan">Also it is
effective to predict the current economic conditions.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.250.3" class="koboSpan">Why logistics
cycle has been linked with product cycle, depends on the time lag
between the air -based logistics system dominant period and the
sea-based one. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.250.4"
class="koboSpan">In other word, the current sea-based logistics system
is the cumulative result of past air-based logistics system.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.251.1" class="koboSpan">As already mentioned,
before 1992 the complementary relationship was dominant between sea
transportation and air transportation.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.251.2" class="koboSpan">Since 1993 the
air-based logistics system has been the leading strategy supporting the
international logistics. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.251.3"
class="koboSpan">So assuming the partial adjustment process of sea-based
logistics system before 1992 and the consecutive cumulative role of
air-based logistics system in the export trade to the US, EU and Asia
following the Shiller lag model, we have the Japanese shippers’ sea-
based logistics system function in equation (3).</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0488" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.252.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00512.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>

</div>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">where:</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan">SLS = Share of
sea-based logistics system,</span>\
<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">ALS = Share of
air-based logistics system,</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">DES = Dummy variable
representing the dominant effect of sea-based logistics
system(1980–1992=1.0, otherwise 0),</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.257.1" class="koboSpan">λ = Adjustment speed
of the share of sea-based log istics system (0\<λ\<1 or λ=1), and</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">δ = Cumulative
Shiller lag distribution on share of air-based logistics system
ALS.</span>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0489" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00513.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 7: Logistics cycle in the export trade to US (1980–2004)" /></span>

<a href="#Ch034.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0241"
id="Ch034.xhtml_cap_lbl0241"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 7:</span></span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.261.1"
class="koboSpan"> Logistics cycle in the export trade to US
(1980–2004)</span>

</div>

<div id="Ch034.xhtml_fig0490" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1014"></span>[](#Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0490)

[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.262.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00514.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0490)

</div>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.263.1" class="koboSpan">Equation (3) is
specified in the logarithmic form and is estimated by least square
method. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.263.2" class="koboSpan">The
estimated results are detailed in
</span><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fig0490" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fig0490"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.264.1" class="koboSpan">Table 7</span></a><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.265.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.266.1" class="koboSpan">For the period
1980–1993, the adjustment speed(λ) of the share of sea-based logistics
system shippers in US trade is 0.92673 (=1–0.07327).
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.266.2" class="koboSpan">In EU trade, λ
is 0.90616 and in Asian trade 0.89221.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.266.3" class="koboSpan">Shippers
prefer sea-based logistics system, succeed in the almost perfect
adjustment behaviour every year, which demonstrates the sea-based
logistics system to be dominant for 1980–1992.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.266.4" class="koboSpan">But after 1993
the sea-based logistics system tends to suffer only from the share of
air based logistics system.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.267.1" class="koboSpan">The air-based
logistics system continues to give the cumulative effect on the current
sea-based logistics system for total estimated period.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.267.2" class="koboSpan">It is the
air-based logistics system
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_page_1015"></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.268.1"
class="koboSpan">that can play continuously the role of logistics cycle
driver in Japan trade. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.268.2"
class="koboSpan">Based on the estimated result in
</span>[<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.269.1" class="koboSpan">Table
7</span>](#Ch034.xhtml_fig0490)<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.270.1"
class="koboSpan">, the logistics cycle in US trade has the eight years’
distributed lag, which represents the eight years’ periodicity.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.270.2" class="koboSpan">The so-called
Juglar cycle has the similar cycle operation of with 8–11 years’
periodicity based on the fluctuation of investment of
firms.</span><sup><a href="#Ch034.xhtml_fn1163" id="Ch034.xhtml_bck_fn1163"><span
id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.271.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a></sup><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.272.1"
class="koboSpan"> The periodicity of cycle in EU trade is five years and
in Asian trade six years, which are a little shorter than the Juglar
cycle but a longer than the Kitchin inventory cycle with an average of
40 months’ periodicity. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.272.2"
class="koboSpan">According to the existing statistical studies of cycle,
the logistics cycle in Japan export trade can be regarded to belonging
to the Juglar cycle. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.272.3"
class="koboSpan">It means the logistics cycle is generated by the
technological revolution, which accompanies the fixed investment of the
shipper’s firms.</span>

<span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.273.1" class="koboSpan">If we can analyse the
causality and the distributed lag structure between the logistics cycle
and the business cycle more precisely in the long-term, we will be able
to use it to predict the turning point of business cycle, because the
logistics index tends to be the leading indicator of the manufacturing
index. </span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.273.2" class="koboSpan">It is
necessary to gain insight into the national economy in a specific
country in order to understand the business cycle fluctuation from the
viewpoint of international logistics cycle.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.273.3" class="koboSpan">This will be
an important topic for further research.</span>

</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.336.1"
class="koboSpan">How to Survive the Recession and the
Recovery</span></span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.337.1"
class="koboSpan"> (London, Canada, Insomniac Press) pp.
</span><span id="Ch034.xhtml_kobo.337.2" class="koboSpan">36–41.</span>

</div>

</div>

</div>
