<span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1017"></span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.1.1" class="koboSpan">Chapter 35</span>\
<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.2.1" class="koboSpan">It in Logistics and Maritime Business</span>](#contents.xhtml_bck_ht0752)
==========================================================================================================================

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.3.1"
class="koboSpan">Ulla</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.4.1"
class="koboSpan">Tapaninen</span></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1164" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1164"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.5.1"
class="koboSpan">*</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.6.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.7.1"
class="koboSpan">Lauri</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.8.1"
class="koboSpan">Ojala</span></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1165" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1165"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.9.1" class="koboSpan">†</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.10.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.11.1"
class="koboSpan">and
</span></span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.12.1"
class="koboSpan">David</span></span>
<span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.13.1"
class="koboSpan">Menachof</span></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1166" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1166"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.14.1" class="koboSpan">‡</span></a>

## <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.15.1" class="koboSpan">1. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.15.2" class="koboSpan">Introduction</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.16.1" class="koboSpan">This chapter deals
with contemporary information technology (IT) solutions and applications
in logistics, and focuses on their usage in maritime business.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.16.2" class="koboSpan">The chapter
discusses some of the underlying reasons for the pervasive use of IT,
and exemplifies some existing solutions on various levels in shipping.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.16.3" class="koboSpan">More
specifically, the chapter is organised under the following
sections:</span>

1.  <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.17.1" class="koboSpan">intra-company
    systems, applications and uses of IT (operational systems in
    capacity allocation, tracking and tracing, ERP/ES-based on
    management level etc.)</span>
2.  <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.18.1" class="koboSpan">inter-company
    systems between business operators (exchange of operational data on
    cargo, shipments, payments etc.
    </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.18.2" class="koboSpan">on a
    system-to-system basis using EDI, XML, etc., and relying either on
    shared software or dedicated (proprietary) systems)</span>
3.  <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.19.1" class="koboSpan">company-public
    authority exchange of data (such as to/from trade and transport
    authorities – port agencies, customs, border/coast guard
    etc.)</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.20.1" class="koboSpan">The list is not
exclusive, for example various public sector systems, either within or
between public bodies are left outside the presentation.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.20.2" class="koboSpan">One should also
realise that these categories are simplified, and that many of the
systems will have overlap into the other sections, but are classified as
to their main section.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.21.1" class="koboSpan">The interesting
linkages of IT to Vessel Traffic Service or Management Systems
(VTS/VTMIS) and Automatic Identification Systems (AIS) of vessels
related to IMO’s International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea
(SOLAS) convention, to safety at sea, or regional (port) development are
beyond the scope of this
chapter.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1167" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1167"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.22.1" class="koboSpan">1</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.23.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1168" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1168"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.24.1" class="koboSpan">2</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.25.1" class="koboSpan">As far as various
sectors of maritime business are concerned, liner shipping is perhaps
most affected by IT
development.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1169" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1169"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.26.1" class="koboSpan">3</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.27.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1170" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1170"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.28.1" class="koboSpan">4</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.29.1"
class="koboSpan"> In liner shipping, the service offered has
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1018"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.30.1"
class="koboSpan">become a commodity, which is transacted in very high
quantities with relatively little negotiation between the parties.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.30.2" class="koboSpan">The increasing
logistics or supply chain management (SCM) needs of shippers also
underline the need of efficient information management along the whole
supply chain.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.31.1" class="koboSpan">In industrial
shipping, the number of transactions is typically much smaller than in
liner shipping, but the operations often require more negotiation
between the trading partners, or parties involved in transport
operations. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.31.2"
class="koboSpan">Industrial shipping solutions tend to be dedicated and
more long-term arrangements with multiple parties.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.32.1" class="koboSpan">The maritime business
includes a large number of operators both on the seaside and the
landside that are, or that could be, involved.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.32.2" class="koboSpan">This chapter
deals mainly with shipping companies within liner and industrial
shipping, and port communities. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.32.3"
class="koboSpan">For IT and information flows in (industrial) bulk
shipping, see, e.g. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.32.4"
class="koboSpan">Hull.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1171" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1171"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.33.1" class="koboSpan">5</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.34.1" class="koboSpan">Despite the pervasive
use of IT and its immense importance in shipping and maritime
operations, it has received surprisingly little research coverage in
both logistics and supply chain management
literature</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1172" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1172"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.35.1" class="koboSpan">6</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.36.1"
class="koboSpan">,</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1173" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1173"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.37.1" class="koboSpan">7</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.38.1"
class="koboSpan"> as well as in maritime economics literature.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.38.2" class="koboSpan">For example in
journals such as
</span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.39.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime Policy and Management
</span></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.40.1" class="koboSpan">(MPM)
and </span><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.41.1"
class="koboSpan">Maritime Economics and Logistics
</span></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.42.1" class="koboSpan">(MEL),
only a handful of papers during the past 7–8 years have touched upon the
issue, often from the point of view of a specific
problem.</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1174" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1174"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.43.1"
class="koboSpan">8</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.44.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1175" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1175"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.45.1"
class="koboSpan">9</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.46.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1176" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1176"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.47.1"
class="koboSpan">10</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.48.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1177" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1177"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.49.1"
class="koboSpan">11</span></span></a><span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.50.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1178" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1178"><span
class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.51.1"
class="koboSpan">12</span></span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.52.1"
class="koboSpan"> Perhaps because of the focus of the textbooks and the
legacy of their authors, the most recent maritime economics or shipping
textbooks do not address the IT issue as a separate section
either.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1179" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1179"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.53.1" class="koboSpan">13</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.54.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1180" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1180"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.55.1" class="koboSpan">14</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.56.1" class="koboSpan">As there seems to be
an apparent lack of coverage of the issue, this section attempts to
provide a short and updated overview of this
topic.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1181" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1181"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.57.1" class="koboSpan">15</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.58.1"
class="koboSpan"> The text tries to avoid excessive technical detail and
acronyms that are ubiquitous in this field.</span>

## <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.59.1" class="koboSpan">2. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.59.2" class="koboSpan">It in Logistics and Supply Chain Management</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.60.1" class="koboSpan">SCM enables the
coordinated management of material and information flows throughout the
chain from your sources to your
customers.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1182" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1182"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.61.1" class="koboSpan">16</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.62.1"
class="koboSpan"> The US-based Council of Supply Chain Management
Professionals (CSCMP) provides the following definition of SCM:</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.63.1" class="koboSpan">“Supply chain
management encompasses the planning and management of all activities
involved in sourcing and procurement, conversion, and all logistics
management activities. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.63.2"
class="koboSpan">Importantly, it also includes coordination and
collaboration with channel partners, which can be suppliers,
intermediaries, third party service providers, and customers.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.63.3" class="koboSpan">In essence,
supply chain management integrates supply and demand management within
and across
companies.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1183" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1183"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.64.1" class="koboSpan">17</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.65.1" class="koboSpan">The supply chain is
both a network and a system. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.65.2"
class="koboSpan">The network component involves the connections needed
in the flow of products and information.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.65.3" class="koboSpan">The systemic
properties are the interdependence of activities, organisations and
processes. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.65.4" class="koboSpan">As
one example, transportation transit times influence the amount of
inventory held within the system.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.65.5" class="koboSpan">Generally said,
actions in one part of the system affect other
parts.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1184" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1184"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.66.1" class="koboSpan">18</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.67.1"
class="koboSpan">Mentzer</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1185" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1185"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.68.1" class="koboSpan">19</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.69.1"
class="koboSpan"> defines a supply chain as a set of three or more
companies directly linked by one or more of the upstream and downstream
flows of products, services, finances and information.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.69.2" class="koboSpan">To be
supply-chain oriented means that the company consciously develops the
strategic system approach to enhance the processes and activities
involved
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1019"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.70.1"
class="koboSpan">in managing the various flows in a supply chain.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.70.2" class="koboSpan">Supply chain
management can envisage almost all of the company’s main functions, or
at least those functions like sales, marketing, R&D and forecasting can
be handled within a supply chain context.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.70.3" class="koboSpan">To sum it up,
SCM means a systemic coordination of the traditional business functions
within a particular company and across businesses within the
chain.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.1" class="koboSpan">Information is an
essential part of logistics and supply chains.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.2" class="koboSpan">The flow of
information consists of data that is needed to launch the flows of
material and capital and to steer them.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.3" class="koboSpan">Information can
be generated in three ways: current information, forecasts and
historical information. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.4"
class="koboSpan">Some logistics models are based on current information.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.5" class="koboSpan">As an example,
vehicle dispatching models need information about today’s orders,
vehicles available and driver status.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.6" class="koboSpan">Other models
are based on forecasts. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.7"
class="koboSpan">Historical data is then used to predict future demand,
available production capacity, and so on.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.8" class="koboSpan">Some models use
actual historical data to calibrate model accuracy.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.71.9" class="koboSpan">This means that
model outputs can be compared to what actually happened to ensure the
model is
valid.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1186" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1186"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.72.1" class="koboSpan">20</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.73.1" class="koboSpan">Enterprise resource
planning is one of the most essential functions in a modern
manufacturing company and it also has a very strong supply chain
implication. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.73.2"
class="koboSpan">The old MRP-originated model, nowadays running at the
core of the most sophisticated ERP systems: “What do I need, what do I
have, what do I need to get and when” is right at the backbone of the
integrated supply chain. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.73.3"
class="koboSpan">The requirements are taken from a customer or from
internal
forecasts.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1187" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1187"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.74.1" class="koboSpan">21</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.75.1"
class="koboSpan"> This has also had a profound effect on the way in
which major companies now operate their global manufacturing and supply
chains. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.75.2"
class="koboSpan">“Innovative supply chain management structures are
rapidly emerging. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.75.3"
class="koboSpan">These incorporate expanded access to ‘e-sources’ of
supply, which use web-based exchanges and hubs, interactive trading
mechanisms and advanced optimisation and matching algorithms to link
customers with suppliers for individual
transactions.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1188" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1188"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.76.1" class="koboSpan">22</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.77.1"
class="koboSpan"> Many industries have embarked on reengineering efforts
to improve the efficiency of their supply chains.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.77.2" class="koboSpan">The goal of
these programs is to better match supply with demand so as to reduce the
costs of inventory and stockouts, where potential savings are
substantial.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.78.1" class="koboSpan">One key initiative is
information sharing between partners in a supply chain.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.78.2" class="koboSpan">Sharing sales
information has been viewed as a major strategy to counter the so-called
“bull-whip effect”, which is essentially the phenomenon of demand
variability amplification along a supply chain.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.78.3" class="koboSpan">It can create
problems for suppliers, such as grossly inaccurate demand forecasts, low
capacity utilisation, excessive inventory, and poor customer
service.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1189" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1189"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.79.1" class="koboSpan">23</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.80.1"
class="koboSpan"> The result for many companies is an expanded role of
global sourcing of supply, and global reach in the search for customers.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.80.2" class="koboSpan">This, in turn,
signifies an increasingly important role for liner shipping companies in
making supply chains more efficient.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.80.3" class="koboSpan">It is this
visibility that today’s IT systems are able to provide.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.81.1" class="koboSpan">Trade and transport
operations invariably involve numerous partners both in the public and
the private sector, such as banking and insurance agents, in addition to
various logistics service providers.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.81.2" class="koboSpan">Likewise, the
trading partners (buyers and sellers or consignors and consignees)
evaluate the practicalities often on a case-by-case basis.</span>

## <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.82.1" class="koboSpan">3. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.82.2" class="koboSpan">Intra-Company Information Flows</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.83.1" class="koboSpan">It is not possible to
describe all the possible uses of IT for intra-company information
purposes, and many of these intra-company systems integrate with
intercompany systems. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.83.2"
class="koboSpan">What we will attempt to do is describe some of the
systems in place
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1020"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.84.1"
class="koboSpan">and highlight the key issues that are related to these
systems. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.84.2" class="koboSpan">It
should also be noted that the logistics functions must still take place
whether or not there is an IT solution available.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.84.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
before ERP programs, accounting data was still maintained, Bills of
Materials were still created, sales orders were still processed, but
much less efficiently than today.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.85.1" class="koboSpan">Enterprise Resource
Planning programmes are the foundation for many firms’ IT capabilities.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.85.2" class="koboSpan">Companies like
SAP, J.D. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.85.3"
class="koboSpan">Edwards, PeopleSoft, and Oracle are the major companies
in this multi-billion dollar industry.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.85.4" class="koboSpan">All ERP
providers are looking to extend the capabilities of their products by
adding additional functionality to their product.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.85.5" class="koboSpan">The three major
functional areas of ERP are: Manufacturing & Logistics, Finance &
Accounting, and Human Resources & Payroll (see
</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fig0491" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fig0491"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.86.1" class="koboSpan">Table 1</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.87.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.87.2"
class="koboSpan">Various environmental calculation systems have become a
significant part of present-day accounting systems, reporting e.g.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.87.3"
class="koboSpan">CO</span><sub><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.88.1"
class="koboSpan">2</span></sub><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.89.1"
class="koboSpan"> emissions, fuel consumption, amounts of waste and
waste water.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.90.1"
class="koboSpan">Jakovljevic</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1190" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1190"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.91.1" class="koboSpan">24</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.92.1"
class="koboSpan"> identifies some of the key reasons why ERP systems
have become so popular and are essential to the modern firm.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.92.2" class="koboSpan">These are
strategic, tactical and technical.</span>

<div id="Ch035.xhtml_fig0491" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.93.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00515.jpg"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" /></span>](#Ch035.xhtml_bck_fig0491)

</div>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1021"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.94.1"
class="koboSpan">Strategic reasons:</span>

- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.95.1" class="koboSpan">enable new business
  strategies;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.96.1" class="koboSpan">enable
  globalisation;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.97.1" class="koboSpan">enable growth
  strategies;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.98.1" class="koboSpan">extend supply/demand
  chain;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.99.1" class="koboSpan">increase customer
  responsiveness.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.100.1" class="koboSpan">Tactical
reasons:</span>

- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.101.1" class="koboSpan">reduce cost/improve
  productivity;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.102.1" class="koboSpan">increase
  flexibility;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.103.1" class="koboSpan">integrate business
  processes;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.104.1" class="koboSpan">integrate
  acquisitions;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.105.1" class="koboSpan">standardise
  business processes;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.106.1" class="koboSpan">improve specific
  business processes/performances.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.107.1" class="koboSpan">Technical
reasons:</span>

- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.108.1" class="koboSpan">standardise
  system/platform;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.109.1" class="koboSpan">improve quality and
  visibility of information;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.110.1" class="koboSpan">enhance technology
  infrastructure to handle the immense amount of data.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.111.1" class="koboSpan">Programmes that
“plug-in” to ERP systems are gaining in popularity, as enhanced
functionality not offered by the base ERP system is required to gain
competitive advantage.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.112.1" class="koboSpan">Customer Relationship
Management (CRM) software is designed to keep track of more than just
customer orders. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.112.2"
class="koboSpan">Delivery preferences, and past ordering profiles are
among some of the information captured by CRM systems.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.113.1" class="koboSpan">In addition to ERP,
Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) is a commonly used technique in
logistics companies. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.113.2"
class="koboSpan">EDI stands for standardised automated transmission of
data between two information systems.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.113.3" class="koboSpan">An example of
the use of EDI is transmission of different documents, such as orders,
invoices and customs documents. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.113.4"
class="koboSpan">With EDI, these are automatically transmitted from the
sender company’s IT system to the receiving company’s information
system. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.113.5" class="koboSpan">The
use of EDI is very reasonable when there are large flows of goods and
the company’s partners are established.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.113.6" class="koboSpan">The building
of EDI connections is expensive and there has to be quite a large number
of transactions for the system to pay itself back.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.113.7" class="koboSpan">These facts
make it unprofitable for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to
use EDI.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.114.1" class="koboSpan">The versatility of
standards can also be considered as a downside of EDI.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.114.2" class="koboSpan">It is possible
that a company is forced to use different kinds of EDI messages with
different customers because of the customers’ demands.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.114.3" class="koboSpan">Some logistics
companies have begun to use the open standard Extensible Markup Language
(XML) aside EDI. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.114.4"
class="koboSpan">XML is an extensible language, because the user can
define the mark-up elements. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.114.5"
class="koboSpan">The purpose of XML is to help information systems share
structured data, especially through the Internet, to encode documents,
and to serialise data. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.114.6"
class="koboSpan">The main difference between these two is that EDI is
designed to serve the needs of business, and is a process, whereas XML
is a
language.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1191" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1191"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.115.1" class="koboSpan">25</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.116.1" class="koboSpan">Because of the
extensive cost in implementing EDI or XML systems SMEs usually make
bookings to transportation companies using the company’s own web-based
booking systems. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.116.2"
class="koboSpan">The advantage of these systems is a reduction of errors
and a decrease in costs, but SMEs may have to book on multiple internet
platforms.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1022"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.117.1"
class="koboSpan">After a day of sales orders being generated and
shipments organised, companies that have their own delivery fleets must
send those vehicles out on the road to deliver to their customers.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.117.2" class="koboSpan">This is the
job of routing and scheduling software, provided by firms such as IBM
through ILOG, Radical, ALK Technologies and Paragon.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.117.3" class="koboSpan">Simple routing
and scheduling problems can be solved by Linear Programming (LP) but as
the number of constraints grows, the ability to obtain an optimal
solution decreases. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.117.4"
class="koboSpan">This is where the complex algorithms used by these
specialised programmes come into their own.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.118.1" class="koboSpan">In liner shipping
companies, where changes of shipping routes are very seldom done, the
allocation of vessels on routes is usually done by combining expert
knowledge and experience with spreadsheet systems.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.119.1" class="koboSpan">In routing problems,
the objective is generally to minimise cost subject to constraints such
as total travel time, road distance between deliveries, waiting time at
each stop, and driver work regulations.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.119.2" class="koboSpan">Costs are
assigned to each type of constraint, and the programme searches for a
feasible solution. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.119.3"
class="koboSpan">PCmiler (ALK associates) is just one version of this
type of software programme.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.120.1" class="koboSpan">Scheduling is a much
more complex task, as it must incorporate many more requirements.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.120.2" class="koboSpan">Routing
software generally doesn’t check to see if the total quantities you are
trying to ship exceed the capacity of the vehicle.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.120.3" class="koboSpan">Scheduling
looks at total capacities and also looks at additional constraints such
as delivery time windows.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.121.1" class="koboSpan">Many companies
working with just-in-time production facilities need strict delivery
times. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.121.2" class="koboSpan">They
cannot take delivery early or later than specified periods, and thus a
vehicle that could deliver to all the customers in terms of capacity
constraints might be unable to deliver those goods within the time
parameters set by the customers.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.121.3" class="koboSpan">The costs and
distance travelled using scheduling constraints is generally higher than
when routing only issues are required.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.122.1" class="koboSpan">ILOG Solver software
from IBM allows a user to integrate shipment data from their ERP system
by consolidating all the shipments for a given time period, then using
the available fleet information along with the information for all of
the shipments, to generate a set of shipping plans to assist in the
order of deliveries for each vehicle required to meet all of the
constraints. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.122.2"
class="koboSpan">If no feasible solution is found, the user is notified,
and will have to make management decisions as to which shipments will be
unable to be delivered within their time windows, or must attempt to
find additional vehicles that enable a feasible solution to be
found.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.123.1" class="koboSpan">Warehouse Management
Systems are another popular “plug-in” adding enhanced capabilities for
inventory control. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.123.2"
class="koboSpan">While ERP systems have some ability to keep inventory
storage location data, it is not nearly enough for complex warehouse
operations. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.123.3"
class="koboSpan">For example, more recent automated warehouses may have
Automated Storage and Retrieval Systems (AS/RS).These systems need to
know where the inventory is stored, which the ERP system can provide,
but the ability to schedule and run the automated forklifts requires
additional computing power, provided by WMS.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.123.4" class="koboSpan">Warehouses
today can have the most simple of functions – just keeping the inventory
dry but they have also become some of the most IT-intensive aspects of
the supply chain.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.124.1" class="koboSpan">Because they have
been around for so long, one may not think of a barcode as much of an IT
solution, but that little printed symbol can help a warehouse run
smoothly. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.124.2" class="koboSpan">At
Wal-Mart’s distribution centres, automated conveyor belts scan the
barcodes on packages, redirecting them to specific conveyor belts
assigned to each store’s destination.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.125.1" class="koboSpan">Radio Frequency
Identification (RFID) has come to the markets to “compete” with bar
code. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.125.2" class="koboSpan">Radio
identification systems that use short-range radio technique are a
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1023"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.126.1"
class="koboSpan">rapidly growing area of interest.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.126.2" class="koboSpan">The system
consists of (a) RFID tags that are identified by their unique serial
number or with some other certain data; and of (b) one or more RFID
readers. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.126.3" class="koboSpan">The
whole system is controlled by an RFID IT system and the company’s other
IT systems. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.126.4"
class="koboSpan">Many different radio technical solutions and different
frequency ranges can be used within RFID systems.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.126.5" class="koboSpan">RFID
technology does not provide real-time data but rather status
information. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.126.6"
class="koboSpan">The information is created every time the tag is read
and then the status of the delivery is updated.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.126.7" class="koboSpan">Despite the
promising outlook for RFID technology, a number of institutional,
organisational, financial and technological issues have so far prevented
it from becoming the “killer application” across international supply
chains.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1192" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1192"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.127.1" class="koboSpan">26</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.128.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1193" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1193"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.129.1" class="koboSpan">27</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.130.1" class="koboSpan">Many traditional
warehouses that use forklift trucks are being upgraded to use RFID
technology to save time and reduce errors.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.130.2" class="koboSpan">Picking and
storage information is sent directly to a screen on the forklift, giving
the driver instructions on where to go for their next movement.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.130.3" class="koboSpan">Once the
driver gets to the location, using a handheld scanner, he/she scans the
barcode for that location to verify he/she is in the right place, and
then picks or stores the correct quantity.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.130.4" class="koboSpan">Once
completed, he/she sends a signal that he/she is ready for the next
movement. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.130.5"
class="koboSpan">There is no need to come back to the office to collect
the next movement order. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.130.6"
class="koboSpan">The drivers can stay on their forklifts, and are more
productive than previously.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.131.1" class="koboSpan">In many operations,
firms do not have their own fleet to deliver the shipments, so they use
commercial carriers. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.131.2"
class="koboSpan">There are now systems that take information for each
shipment and, based on the weight/volume, destination, and time
constraints, calculate the best carrier to use, and print the specific
waybill required for that carrier, thus minimising shipment costs.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.131.3" class="koboSpan">For example, a
firm can choose a national logistics service provider, between a UPS, or
DHL to deliver the shipment. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.131.4"
class="koboSpan">Checking each tariff manually to find the lowest cost
would be extremely time consuming for high-volume businesses.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.132.1" class="koboSpan">The number of
business parties, logistics providers and officials taking part in a
trans-ocean transport for each individual shipment is very large.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.132.2" class="koboSpan">Thus, it is
very difficult to control the overall information flow along the route.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.132.3" class="koboSpan">In order to
stay competitive in the global logistics markets, practically all major
liner shipping operators now offer extensive door-to-door tracking and
tracing services (see e.g. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.132.4"
class="koboSpan">Heaver</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1194" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1194"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.133.1" class="koboSpan">28</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.134.1"
class="koboSpan"> and the websites of liner shipping operators such as
Maersk or APL).</span>

## <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.135.1" class="koboSpan">4. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.135.2" class="koboSpan">Inter-Company Information Flows</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.136.1" class="koboSpan">The information flows
in shipments requiring several modes of transport can be very
complicated. </span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_cap_lbl0242"
id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0242"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.137.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 1</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.138.1"
class="koboSpan"> shows the standard structure of a multimodal logistics
chain, where there are multiple data transfers within one cargo
shipment. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.138.2" class="koboSpan">The
interface is critical in relation to customs.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.138.3" class="koboSpan">Also, the
changes in carriers cause critical points of information
exchange.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.139.1" class="koboSpan">Combining physical
distribution with electronic information transfer and management,
Bowersox and
Closs</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1195" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1195"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.140.1" class="koboSpan">29</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.141.1"
class="koboSpan"> define three main drivers in the development of a
logistical system. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.141.2"
class="koboSpan">The first driver is the customer interface.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.141.3" class="koboSpan">Satisfied
customers require easy and rapidly available information regarding their
product locations, conditions and transport schedules.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.141.4" class="koboSpan">Secondly, good
information resources reduce warehousing needs and help to provide more
“on demand” services. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.141.5"
class="koboSpan">Thirdly, information resources add</span>

<div id="Ch035.xhtml_fig0492" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.142.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00516.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 1: Information transfer needs in a multimodal logistics chain30" /></span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1024"></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0242"
id="Ch035.xhtml_cap_lbl0242"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.143.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 1:</span></span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.144.1"
class="koboSpan"> Information transfer needs in a multimodal logistics
chain</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1196" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1196"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.145.1" class="koboSpan">30</span></a></sup>

</div>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.146.1" class="koboSpan">flexibility to the
process and help to adapt to new situations if unforeseen events take
place.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.147.1" class="koboSpan">There have been many
recent developments in inter-company information flows.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.147.2" class="koboSpan">Supply Chain
Event Management (SCEM) software works with companies’ ERP programmes by
defining responses to specified events.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.147.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
HighJump Software’s Event Advantage solution promotes proactive customer
service and reduces costs by alerting managers and trading partners to
supply chain events and exceptions via e-mail, pager, fax or phone.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.147.4" class="koboSpan">For example, a
delayed shipment could trigger such a response, allowing the customer to
take alternative action. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.147.5"
class="koboSpan">By creating better visibility in the supply chain, all
parties involved will have earlier notification and will be potentially
able to respond before things become critical.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.148.1" class="koboSpan">An illustrative
example of these initiatives is the Collaborative Planning, Forecasting,
and Replenishment (CPFR), which was launched in 1995.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.148.2" class="koboSpan">The process of
implementing CPFR involves sharing information to better provide for end
customer requirements. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.148.3"
class="koboSpan">As in any collaborative process, the key is the
commitment from the firms involved.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.148.4" class="koboSpan">Theoretically,
CPFR could take place without IT systems, but as the number of
Stock</span>

<div id="Ch035.xhtml_fig0493" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.149.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00517.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 2: The CPFR® model" /></span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1025"></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0243"
id="Ch035.xhtml_cap_lbl0243"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.150.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 2:</span></span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.151.1"
class="koboSpan"> The CPFR® model</span>

</div>

<span class="italic"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.152.1"
class="koboSpan">Source:
</span></span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.153.1"
class="koboSpan">www.vics.org/committees/cpfr/</span>](http://www.vics.org/committees/cpfr/)

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.154.1" class="koboSpan">CPFR® and the CPFR®
model are registered trademarks of VICS – the Voluntary Interindustry
Commerce Solutions association. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.154.2"
class="koboSpan">Used with the kind permission of VICS.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.155.1" class="koboSpan">Keeping Units (SKUs)
increases, the ability to track the information manually becomes less
manageable. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.155.2" class="koboSpan">In
general, CPFR involves three stages and is summarised in
</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_cap_lbl0243"
id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0243"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.156.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 2</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.157.1"
class="koboSpan">.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.1" class="koboSpan">The Planning Stage,
involves an initial front-end agreement regarding what information is
going to be shared, how it is to be shared, when, and other details.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.2" class="koboSpan">Then there is
a quarterly planning session which looks at the wider strategic issues
of the collaboration. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.3"
class="koboSpan">The Forecasting Stage involves several steps.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.4" class="koboSpan">In step one,
each firm will create a sales forecast for the upcoming period, and once
that has been done, the information is centralised.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.5" class="koboSpan">Step two
compares the forecasts and identifies any exceptions.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.6" class="koboSpan">The initial
agreement might state that if both forecasts differ by more than 20%,
this record is flagged as an exception.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.7" class="koboSpan">The third step
is for both parties to meet and resolve the exceptions.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.8" class="koboSpan">Typically, one
firm will host the database on their computer system and allow the other
remote access to their data, using the internet and the appropriate
security methods. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.9"
class="koboSpan">The Replenishment Stage follows the steps of the
Forecasting Stage, but looks at existing inventories along with the
forecasts to determine how much to supply for the upcoming period.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.158.10" class="koboSpan">Once this
stage is completed, the actual order is processed and submitted into
each firms’ ERP system.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1026"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.159.1"
class="koboSpan">The Process then continually repeats itself, with the
end goal of enhanced inventory management, resulting in better customer
satisfaction. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.159.2"
class="koboSpan">Another example of where intracompany information can
be exchanged is by firms using Vendor Managed Inventory (VMI).
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.159.3" class="koboSpan">“VMI has been
around for some time, but it is becoming increasingly accessible and
relevant now as data communications systems
improve.”</span><sup>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.160.1"
class="koboSpan">30</span>](#Ch035.xhtml_fn1196)</sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.161.1"
class="koboSpan"> EPOS (Electronic Point of Sales) data is automatically
transferred to the vendor, who will be responsible for replenishment of
the stock based on agreed service standards and inventory levels.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.161.2" class="koboSpan">“The control
of his customer delivery and visibility on customer needs, which VMI
gives to the vendor, enables him to plan production and supply more
reliably.”</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1197" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1197"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.162.1" class="koboSpan">31</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.163.1" class="koboSpan">Although there is
much that can be done electronically, the paperless supply chain is not
yet here. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.163.2" class="koboSpan">One
major issue that international logistics faces is documentary
requirements by government agencies worldwide.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.163.3" class="koboSpan">Likewise,
people still like the security of a physical document, even though
electronic PODs (Proof of Deliveries) are being used by major delivery
companies on a regular
basis.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1198" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1198"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.164.1" class="koboSpan">32</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.165.1"
class="koboSpan"> To be able to increase the efficiency of maritime
transportation, the European Union has introduced an e-Maritime policy
with the aim of promoting “coherent, transparent, efficient and
simplified solutions in support of cooperation, interoperability and
consistency between member States, sectors, business and systems
involved in the European Transport
System”.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1199" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1199"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.166.1" class="koboSpan">33</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.167.1" class="koboSpan">The e-Maritime
initiative can be divided to following areas:</span>

- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.168.1" class="koboSpan">Administration
  Domain Applications, including reporting using Single Windows and
  eCustoms</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.169.1" class="koboSpan">Improved Shipping
  Operations, including eNavigation, ship reporting, e.g.
  </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.169.2"
  class="koboSpan">CO</span><sub><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.170.1"
  class="koboSpan">2 </span></sub><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.171.1"
  class="koboSpan">operational index, and VTS-systems</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.172.1" class="koboSpan">Improved Port
  Operations; including Port Community systems, Integration of
  authorities, e.g. </span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.173.1"
  class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.174.1"
  class="koboSpan">, SafeSeaNet</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.175.1" class="koboSpan">Integration into
  logistic chains; including Short Sea Shipping and intermodalism</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.176.1" class="koboSpan">and eFreight</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.177.1" class="koboSpan">Promote seafaring
  profession and sea-shipping, including eHealth at sea and improving
  image of EU shipping.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.178.1" class="koboSpan">Although Business to
Business (B2B) procurement websites have come and gone, B2B procurement
will be, if it is not already, an important tool for many companies.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.178.2" class="koboSpan">B2B is not
new, and was the basis for the use of EDI.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.178.3" class="koboSpan">It was a
direct relationship between one company and its supplier.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.178.4" class="koboSpan">It was
expensive, but for large companies who could afford it, offered
competitive advantage over smaller competitors.</span>

<a href="#Ch035.xhtml_cap_lbl0244"
id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0244"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.179.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 3</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.180.1"
class="koboSpan"> identifies the general type of e-procurement concepts.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.180.2" class="koboSpan">On the
vertical scale, the nature of the transaction is measured, while the
horizontal looks at the infrastructure and access to the system.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.180.3" class="koboSpan">Looking at the
bottom right quadrant, with open access to the public, and a direct
relationship between buyer and seller, general e-commerce is transacted
here. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.180.4" class="koboSpan">As we
move to many buyers and sellers getting together, we move to the
e-marketplaces, with hubs designed to bring those parties together.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.180.5" class="koboSpan">Some are
private, while others are open to anyone.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.180.6" class="koboSpan">Conceptually,
they are appealing to the buyer, with more choice and enhanced price
competition. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.180.7"
class="koboSpan">However, for the seller, the proposition is less than
appealing at the moment. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.180.8"
class="koboSpan">Sellers have been staying away as price is the only
selling point, and things like reputation and quality are hard to factor
in at this point in time.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.181.1" class="koboSpan">B2B exchanges come in
several general models with vertical and horizontal hubs.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.181.2" class="koboSpan">Vertical hubs
are generally industry/commodity based, attempting to bring together
all</span>

<div id="Ch035.xhtml_fig0494" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.182.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00518.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 3: Types of business to business procurement models" /></span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1027"></span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0244"
id="Ch035.xhtml_cap_lbl0244"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.183.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 3:</span></span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.184.1"
class="koboSpan"> Types of business to business procurement
models</span>

</div>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.185.1" class="koboSpan">players in the steel
industry, for example. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.185.2"
class="koboSpan">Other vertical hubs exist in plastics, chemicals,
energy, telecoms, and even flowers.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.186.1" class="koboSpan">Horizontal hubs
attempt to look at specific functions, that are used across industries.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.186.2" class="koboSpan">Logistics hubs
fit into this area. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.186.3"
class="koboSpan">Transcore 3sixty Freight Match is a US-based firm that
attempts to match companies excess transport capacity with firms who are
looking for capacity. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.186.4"
class="koboSpan">According to Richard Hunt, past-president of the
Chartered Institute of Logistics and Transport International, more than
30% of road haulage vehicle miles are run either empty or under
capacity. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.186.5"
class="koboSpan">There is significant scope for improved efficiency.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.186.6" class="koboSpan">Although there
is significant consolidation taking place in the industry currently, as
firms figure out how to become profitable providing online procurement
services, it is evident that the desire for the services are needed.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.186.7" class="koboSpan">The keys to
success in this rapidly developing arena include integration with
participating firms’ back-end systems (ERP), value creation for all
parties, and the critical mass needed to bring the initial fixed costs
of these IT investments down to reasonable per transaction costs.</span>

### <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.187.1" class="koboSpan">4.1 Illustrative case: Port process</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1200" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1200"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.188.1" class="koboSpan">34</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.189.1" class="koboSpan">The transportation
process requires a large amount of information, in particular when the
transport mode is changed. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.189.2"
class="koboSpan">To illustrate the amount of data interaction in one
shipment in one position, we look closely at the process in a sea port.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.189.3" class="koboSpan">In sea ports,
the central operating partners are (a) a shipping company; (b) a
stevedoring company; (c) a land transport company; (d) port authorities;
(e) Customs; (f) a terminal/warehousing operator; and (g) a drayage
haulage. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.189.4"
class="koboSpan">Customs and port authorities control the sea transport,
they are in charge of safety and security and they take care of
collecting taxes and other duties.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.190.1" class="koboSpan">The representative of
the shipping company agrees with the shipper about the transportation.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.190.2" class="koboSpan">Based on this
agreement, the shipping company reserves a certain quota of the vessel
capacity. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.190.3" class="koboSpan">The
shipper starts the transportation by making a booking, usually by EDI or
a web-based booking platform. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.190.4"
class="koboSpan">The shipping company informs the stevedoring company
about the booking (usually on-line).
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.190.5" class="koboSpan">If there are
dangerous cargoes in
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1028"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.191.1"
class="koboSpan">question, the shipper must apply for permission to
carry them from the port authorities and present the necessary
information to all parties.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.192.1" class="koboSpan">The shipper organises
the land transport, and informs the loading port of the arrival of the
cargo. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.192.2" class="koboSpan">The
cargo and its details are presented to Customs, who gives permission to
load it on the vessel. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.192.3"
class="koboSpan">The information about the cargo that has arrived on
port is also given to the shipping company (usually on-line by combining
stevedoring and shipping company’s systems) who can control the booking
situation. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.192.4" class="koboSpan">The
shipping company decides which cargo is loaded on the vessel and gives
loading permission to the stevedore.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.193.1" class="koboSpan">The representative of
the vessel decides how the cargo is to be located in the cargo hold
using specialised software based on stability of the vessel, dangerous
cargo rules, etc. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.193.2"
class="koboSpan">This Cargo Plan is given to the stevedoring company
usually by on-line systems. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.193.3"
class="koboSpan">When the loading is finished, the stevedore informs the
shipping company and Customs about the cargo that was loaded.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.193.4" class="koboSpan">Based on this
list, the shipping company creates a manifest – a list of the cargo on
board and delivers it to Customs and port authorities.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.194.1" class="koboSpan">Before arrival at the
destination port, the representative of the vessel makes an announcement
to Customs and port authority (see case
</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.195.1"
class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.196.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.196.2"
class="koboSpan">The shipping company makes a special declaration of any
dangerous cargo. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.196.3"
class="koboSpan">Using this information, the port authority gives
permission to unload the dangerous cargo with special requirements.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.196.4" class="koboSpan">The
stevedoring company receives the Cargo Plan and is able to execute the
unloading process. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.196.5"
class="koboSpan">After unloading, the stevedoring company reports the
unloaded cargo and the manifest can be updated.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.197.1" class="koboSpan">The stevedoring
company is in charge of the cargo until the permission to deliver the
cargo to next partner is received from Customs, the shipping company and
the port authorities. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.197.2"
class="koboSpan">When the permission is received, the haulier arranges
the land transport and informs the stevedoring company which truck has
permission to take the cargo.</span>

## <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.198.1" class="koboSpan">5. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.198.2" class="koboSpan">Company-Public Authority Exchange of Data</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.199.1" class="koboSpan">Due to the events and
aftermath of September 11 2001, the growing pressure from external
regulatory sources has made it necessary for maritime industry players
to fully integrate the security element into both strategic plans and
operational procedures. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.199.2"
class="koboSpan">The 24-hour rule has the most profound effect on
maritime IT-systems. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.199.3"
class="koboSpan">Under this rule, detailed information of 14 data
elements (e.g. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.199.4"
class="koboSpan">number and quantity of packages, shippers names and
Addresses, vessel flag, name and number) on container cargo on board
vessels call at, or transiting via US ports must be submitted
electronically to US Customs authorities at least 24 hours prior to
departing from a foreign port.
</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1201" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1201"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.200.1" class="koboSpan">35</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.201.1"
class="koboSpan">,
</span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1202" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1202"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.202.1" class="koboSpan">36</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.203.1" class="koboSpan">Port community
systems (PCS) have been developed to assist the rapid flow of
information between all of the firms involved in moving goods in/out of
a port. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.203.2" class="koboSpan">Since
many of them were developed before clear standards were created, they
were generally independent from each other.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.203.3" class="koboSpan">For example,
Port of Charleston has the Orion system, Felixstowe has its own system,
and as illustrated below, and Finnish ports use the
</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.204.1"
class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.205.1"
class="koboSpan"> system. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.205.2"
class="koboSpan">(For review of port community systems, see Srour et al.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.205.3"
class="koboSpan">2007</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1203" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1203"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.206.1" class="koboSpan">37</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.207.1"
class="koboSpan">). </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.207.2"
class="koboSpan">The general concepts of PCSs are the same, although the
systems and interfaces may be different at each port.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.207.3" class="koboSpan">One of the
major benefits is the reduction in time needed to transmit information.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.207.4" class="koboSpan">For example, a
container vessel’s load plan may have been upwards of 60 pages, sent by
fax or telex. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.207.5"
class="koboSpan">Once received by the port, a computer operator would
enter the data into their system, with many chances for errors
occurring. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.207.6"
class="koboSpan">These systems
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1029"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.208.1"
class="koboSpan">eliminate that need for re-keying of data, maintaining
the accuracy and integrity of the
information.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1204" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1204"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.209.1" class="koboSpan">38</span></a></sup>

### <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.210.1" class="koboSpan">5.1 Illustrative case: A Finnish port community system: </span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.211.1" class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.212.1" class="koboSpan">The
</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.213.1"
class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.214.1"
class="koboSpan"> is a national port community system that offers a
single administrative desk for all the declarations required with
vessel’s arrival and departure to major ports and authorities in
Finland.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1205" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1205"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.215.1" class="koboSpan">39</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.216.1"
class="koboSpan"> It is used by shipping lines, ship agents, a number of
ports, the Customs, and Maritime Administration.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.216.2" class="koboSpan">It has over
1,000 users in Finland.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.217.1" class="koboSpan">The
</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.218.1"
class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.219.1"
class="koboSpan"> extranet application was implemented in year 2000 when
it replaced the previous application in use since 1994.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.219.2" class="koboSpan">The newest
version of </span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.220.1"
class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.221.1"
class="koboSpan"> was taken into test use in 2009.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.221.2" class="koboSpan">As shown at
the website of the Finnish Maritime Administration
(</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.222.1"
class="koboSpan">www.fma.fi</span>](http://www.fma.fi)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.223.1"
class="koboSpan">), the main users of
</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.224.1"
class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.225.1"
class="koboSpan"> are:</span>

- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.226.1" class="koboSpan">ship agents (see
  below);</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.227.1" class="koboSpan">customs (check the
  data);</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.228.1" class="koboSpan">port authorities
  (use the information in invoicing, statistics and dangerous cargo
  handling);</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.229.1" class="koboSpan">maritime
  authorities (for traffic follow-up and statistics);</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.230.1" class="koboSpan">coastguard (for
  traffic control);</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.231.1" class="koboSpan">haulage and
  stevedoring companies (for vessel time of arrivals).</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.232.1" class="koboSpan">The procedures for
vessels entering or leaving the port are in principle mirror images.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.232.2" class="koboSpan">For
illustration purposes, the procedure for vessels leaving the port are
highlighted below in </span><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_cap_lbl0245"
id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0245"><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.233.1"
class="koboSpan">Figure 4</span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.234.1"
class="koboSpan">. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.234.2"
class="koboSpan">When using the Web interface, the reporting principles
similar, but instead of EDIFACT messages, XML-based messages are
used.</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1206" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1206"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.235.1" class="koboSpan">40</span></a></sup>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.236.1" class="koboSpan">Before the vessel
arrives, information of the vessel and its voyage has to be transferred
to the Customs 24 hours before. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.236.2"
class="koboSpan">If this cannot be achieved, the exceptions must be
agreed with the Customs office of the port of call.</span>

<div id="Ch035.xhtml_fig0495" class="fig"
data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.237.1"
class="koboSpan"><img src="Images/fig00519.jpg" data-xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
alt="Figure 4: Information flows for arriving ships in Port@Net" /></span>

<a href="#Ch035.xhtml_bck_cap_lbl0245"
id="Ch035.xhtml_cap_lbl0245"><span class="italic"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.238.1" class="koboSpan">Figure 4:</span></span></a><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.239.1"
class="koboSpan"> Information flows for arriving ships in
</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.240.1"
class="koboSpan">Port@Net</span>](mailto:Port@Net)

</div>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.241.1" class="koboSpan">Adapted from
</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.242.1"
class="koboSpan">http://virtual.vtt.fi/virtual/proj6/fits/julkaisut/hanke8/IP_FITS_loppuraportti_020121.pdf</span>](http://virtual.vtt.fi/virtual/proj6/fits/julkaisut/hanke8/IP_FITS_loppuraportti_020121.pdf)

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_page_1030"></span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.243.1"
class="koboSpan">The procedure for the agent if giving cargo report on
manifest level is the following:</span>

- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.244.1" class="koboSpan">before the vessel's
  arrival the cargo report is transmitted using the CUSCAR
  message;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.245.1" class="koboSpan">several cargo
  reports can be sent per one advance notice (supplementary
  B/L's);</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.246.1" class="koboSpan">the cargo report(s)
  refer to the same Customs' arrival/departure reference number;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.247.1" class="koboSpan">cargo information
  can be updated or modified before the arrival of the vessel;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.248.1" class="koboSpan">after the vessel
  has arrived, the agent can send updated cargo reports BUT then the
  changed information has to be faxed to the local Customs
  office;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.249.1" class="koboSpan">the agent will fill
  in the information of the general Customs declaration, sign it, attach
  a copy of the manifest to it and deliver the papers to the Customs
  office;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.250.1" class="koboSpan">the Customs office
  accepts the general declaration and gives permission for
  discharging;</span>
- <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.251.1" class="koboSpan">the port operator
  unloads the cargo and delivers the list of discharged cargo to the
  Customs.</span>

## <span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.252.1" class="koboSpan">6. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.252.2" class="koboSpan">Epilogue</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.253.1" class="koboSpan">Despite the profound
change the development of IT has brought about in many fields, including
the maritime business, it could be argued that the age of digital
networks is only starting to take shape.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.253.2" class="koboSpan">One of the
developments that would profoundly change the international logistics
and shipping operations and business is the possibility to track, trace
and control individual parcels and shipments wirelessly, and virtually
in real time. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.253.3"
class="koboSpan">Many of the technological breakthroughs required for
that to happen have already been made, and their cost is likely to
approach the level of commercial exploitation fairly soon.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.253.4" class="koboSpan">This type of
technology could even change the nature of maritime business, or at
least the liner shipping part of it beyond recognition.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.254.1" class="koboSpan">Particularly, while
port are so important nodes for information where dozens of operators
are in contact with each other when handling a piece of cargo, there is
still very many improvements to be realised.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.254.2" class="koboSpan">It can be
assumed that the biggest improvements in future of maritime logistics
information handling will be seen in cargo track and trace operations
and streamlining the data exchange between various operators in
ports.</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.255.1" class="koboSpan">In the previous
edition of this book in 2002, we concluded our
</span>[<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.256.1" class="koboSpan">chapter
1</span>](#Ch01.xhtml_ht0058)<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.257.1"
class="koboSpan"> by quoting
Churchill:</span><sup><a href="#Ch035.xhtml_fn1207" id="Ch035.xhtml_bck_fn1207"><span
id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.258.1" class="koboSpan">41</span></a></sup><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.259.1"
class="koboSpan"> “This is not the end.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.259.2" class="koboSpan">It is not even
the beginning of the end. </span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.259.3"
class="koboSpan">But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.”</span>

<span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.260.1" class="koboSpan">During the years that
have passed since, much has happened in the usage and applications of IT
systems both in the business and public sector.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.260.2" class="koboSpan">Still, there
is a long way to reach the full potential of IT and mobile technologies
in maritime and logistics business and practice.
</span><span id="Ch035.xhtml_kobo.260.3" class="koboSpan">But one might
say that the end of the beginning is nigh.</span>
